en: The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll One.
Added by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇas Huìyán and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter One: The Introduction. The First Chapter: The Introduction.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Kuśinagara, in the birthplace of the Mallas, between the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Āciravatī River.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly of eight billion hundred thousand bhikṣus.
On the fifteenth day of the second month, as he approached his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha, through his spiritual power, uttered a great sound.
This voice pervaded all realms up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and in accordance with the various languages of beings, it universally proclaimed to all sentient beings:

"Today, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who has compassion for sentient beings, who protects and shelters sentient beings, who regards all beings equally as he does Rāhula, who acts as their refuge, and who is the shelter of the world—the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, is about to enter parinirvāṇa."
"If all sentient beings have any doubts, you may now ask them all; this shall be your final question.

At that time, during the early morning, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face. These lights were of diverse colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, and agate—and their radiance shone throughout this trichiliocosm Buddha-world;
even so it was in the ten directions as well.
Among them, all sentient beings of the six realms who encounter this light have their karmic defilements and afflictions entirely eliminated.
Upon seeing and hearing this, these beings are filled with great distress; simultaneously raising their voices, they wail and weep, crying out:
"Alas, Compassionate Father!"
"Alas! How bitter!
they cried, raising their hands to strike their heads, beating their breasts and wailing aloud; some among them trembled with their entire bodies, weeping and sobbing with choked voices.
At that time, the great earth, all the mountains, and the vast oceans all shook violently.
Then all sentient beings said to one another:
"Let us each restrain ourselves; do not be so deeply distressed."

Let us go together quickly to the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, and upon reaching the place where the Tathāgata is, let us prostrate ourselves at his feet in reverence and entreat him not to enter parinirvāṇa, but to remain in the world for an eon, or slightly less than an eon.
Holding each other’s hands, they spoke again:
“The world is empty; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and unwholesome karmas have increased and appeared in the world.”
"Virtuous ones, you must go now, go quickly! The Tathāgata will surely enter parinirvāṇa before long.
He spoke further, saying:
"The world is empty; the world is empty!"
From this day forward, we shall have no protector and no one to revere; we are impoverished and left destitute.
Having once more been separated from the Unsurpassed World-Honored One, to whom shall we turn when doubts arise?

At that time, there were immeasurable great disciples—Venerable Mahākātyāyana, Venerable Bakula, Venerable Upānanda, and other such great bhikṣus—who, upon encountering the Buddha’s light, had their bodies tremble and shake so violently that they could not support themselves; their minds became turbid and bewildered, and they let out loud cries, experiencing all manner of such sufferings and afflictions.

At that time, there were also eighty hundred thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats who had attained mastery of mind, fulfilled their tasks, abandoned all afflictions, and disciplined their faculties; who possessed great majesty like great dragon kings, had accomplished the wisdom of emptiness, and realized their own benefit; who were like a sandalwood grove surrounded by sandalwood trees, or like a lion king surrounded by lions; who had perfected such immeasurable merits and were all true sons of the Buddha—each departed from their permanent residences at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, and while using willow twigs for cleansing, they encountered the Buddha’s radiance and said to one another:
"Virtuous ones, you should quickly rinse and purify yourselves."

Having spoken these words, the hairs on his entire body stood on end, blood appeared all over his frame like *pāṭala* flowers, and with tears filling his eyes, he was overcome by great suffering and distress.

Desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, to manifest the Tathāgata’s secret teachings of skillful means, to ensure that the various methods of preaching the Dharma would not be interrupted, and for the sake of providing the causes and conditions for the subduing of all sentient beings, he quickly proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there were also the nun Kuṭilā, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā, the bhikṣuṇī Upānandā, and the bhikṣuṇī Sāgaramati, together with six billion bhikṣuṇīs—all of whom were also great arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had attained mastery over their minds, who had accomplished what was to be done, who were free from all afflictions, whose faculties were subdued like great dragons, who possessed great majestic power, and who had perfected the wisdom of emptiness—also at the hour of dawn when the sun first rose, felt their body hairs stand on end and blood appear all over their bodies like *palaśa* flowers; their eyes filled with tears as they wept, giving rise to great suffering and distress.

Furthermore, desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, to reveal the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings on skillful means, to ensure that various modes of Dharma exposition are never interrupted, and for the sake of providing the causal conditions for the discipline of all sentient beings, he quickly proceeded to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and with palms joined in reverence, withdrew to sit to one side.

Within the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, there were further bhikṣuṇīs who were all bodhisattvas, dragons among men, whose rank was that of the ten stages (bhūmi). They dwelt immovably therein, manifesting female bodies for the sake of transforming sentient beings; they constantly cultivated and accumulated the four immeasurable minds (apramāṇa-citta), attained the power of mastery, and were able to manifest as Buddhas.

At that time, there were also bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—dragons among men, who had attained the stages of the ten bhūmis, remained immovably established therein, and manifested their bodies through skillful means.
They were headed by such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as Sāgarabuddhi and Akṣayamati.

Their minds were entirely respectful toward the Mahāyāna, securely established in the Mahāyāna, deeply understanding the Mahāyāna, delighting in the Mahāyāna, and protecting the Mahāyāna; they were well able to accord with all the world and made this vow:
"Those who have not yet been delivered, we shall cause them to attain deliverance."

Having cultivated and maintained pure precepts throughout incalculable eons in past ages, he has skillfully upheld his conduct and brought understanding to those who were unenlightened; he has sustained the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it remains uninterrupted.
In future ages, he shall turn the wheel of Dharma, adorning himself with great adornments.
Having accomplished such immeasurable merit, he regards all sentient beings equally, as if looking upon an only son.

Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, he encountered the Buddha’s radiance; his hair stood on end, blood appeared all over his body like *pāṭala* flowers, and with tears filling his eyes, he was overcome by great anguish.

Furthermore, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, to reveal the Tathāgata’s secret teachings of skillful means, to ensure that various modes of preaching are never interrupted, and as a causal condition for the subduing of all sentient beings, he quickly proceeded to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, there were also as many upāsakas as the sands of two Ganges Rivers who had received and maintained the five precepts and were fully endowed with dignified deportment.
They were led by such foremost figures as the upāsaka King of Undefiled Majestic Virtue and the upāsaka Good Virtue.
They deeply delight in contemplating the various gates of antidotes, namely:

suffering and pleasure, permanence and impermanence, purity and impurity, self and non-self, reality and unreality, refuge and non-refuge, sentient beings and non-sentient beings, constancy and non-constancy, peace and non-peace, the conditioned and the unconditioned, cessation and non-cessation, nirvana and non-nirvana, and the superior and the non-superior.
They constantly delight in observing such gates of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*), and they also desire to hear the unsurpassed Mahāyāna;
having heard it as it is, they are able to explain it to others.
They uphold the pure precepts well and thirst for the Mahāyāna; having themselves attained fulfillment, they are further able to satisfy others who likewise thirst for it.
They are skillfully able to grasp unsurpassed wisdom, delighting in the Mahāyāna and protecting the Mahāyāna;
they are skillfully able to accord with all worlds, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated.

They shall continue the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it is never severed; in future ages they shall turn the wheel of Dharma, adorning themselves with great adornments, and their minds shall always deeply savor pure conduct of the precepts.
They were all able to accomplish such merits as these, giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings with impartiality and non-duality, as if looking upon each one as their only child.

Furthermore, at dawn when the sun first rose, in order to cremate the body of the Tathāgata, every person took ten thousand bundles of fragrant wood—such as sandalwood, aloeswood, gośīrṣa-candana, and celestial incense. The grain and joints of each piece of wood possessed the subtle radiance of the seven treasures, like various colorful paintings; by the power of the Buddha, they had these wondrous colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—which were delightful for all sentient beings to behold.

All the trees were anointed with various fragrances, such as saffron, aloeswood, and resinous incense; they were further adorned by being strewn with many flowers: blue lotuses (utpala), white lotuses (kumuda), red lotuses (padma), and white water lilies (puṇḍarīka).
Above the various fragrant trees hang five-colored banners, soft and exquisite, like celestial garments, kauseya silk, or kṣauma brocade.
These fragrant trees are carried upon precious chariots.
These precious chariots emitted various kinds of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—and their shafts and spokes were all inlaid with the seven treasures.
Each chariot was drawn by four horses, and each horse was as swift as the wind.
Before each chariot stood fifty-seven exquisite jeweled banners, covered above by nets of pure gold.
Each jeweled chariot also possessed fifty subtle and wonderful jeweled canopies.

Upon each chariot hung various flower garlands—blue lotuses (utpala), white lotuses (kumuda), red lotuses (padma), and white water lilies (puṇḍarīka)—the petals of which were made entirely of pure gold and their centers of diamond.
Within these flower pedestals, many black bees gather and swarm, enjoying themselves in pleasure and emitting wondrous sounds, namely:
impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Within these sounds, there was further explained the path originally practiced by Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, amidst various forms of song, dance, and instrumental music—such as the *kṣaṅgā*, flute, *vīṇā*, *śiṅkhā*, lute, drum, and trumpet—these words emerged from the musical tones:
"Alas! Alas! How bitter!"
"The world is empty.

Before each chariot, an upāsaka held aloft a table made of the four jewels; upon these tables were various flowers—utpala, kumuda, padma, and puṇḍarīka—as well as saffron and other incenses, all of which were most exquisite and supreme.

The upāsakas prepared various provisions for food for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, providing everything in full abundance; all were matured by means of sandalwood, aloeswood, fragrant fuel, and water of eight virtues.
The food was sweet and delicious, possessing six kinds of flavors:
first, bitter; second, sour; third, sweet; fourth, pungent; fifth, salty; and sixth, bland.
Furthermore, there were three qualities:
first, lightness and softness; second, purity and cleanliness; third, conformity with the Dharma.
Having prepared such various adornments, he proceeded to the twin śāla trees at the birthplace of the Malla.
Furthermore, he spread golden sand over the ground, covering the sand with garments of kālinga, kṣaumaka, and various silken fabrics, extending completely all around for twelve yojanas.

For the Buddha and the Sangha, he prepared lion thrones made of the seven precious jewels; these thrones were as high and large as Mount Sumeru, and upon each throne there was a jeweled canopy draped with various necklaces and pendants.
All the śāla trees were hung with various kinds of exquisite banners and canopies; various fine incenses were used to anoint the trees, and various named flowers were scattered among them.
Each of the upāsakas thought to themselves:
"If any sentient being lacks anything—whether food and drink, clothing, a head, eyes, or limbs—I shall provide them with whatever they require."

When making such an offering, one is free from desire, hatred, and the poisonous mind of defilement; without any further thoughts or aspirations seeking worldly blessings or pleasures, one’s resolve is set solely upon unsurpassed, pure bodhi.
These upāsakas had all already established themselves in the bodhisattva path, and they further thought:
"The Tathāgata, having now accepted our food, shall enter parinirvāṇa."
Having formed this thought, the hairs on his body all stood on end; blood appeared over his entire frame like *pāṭala* flowers, and with tears filling his eyes, he was overcome by great anguish.

Each person brought their own offerings, loading them onto precious chariots—incense wood, banners, streamers, jeweled canopies, and food and drink—and quickly proceeded to the Buddha’s abode. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, wishing to present their offerings to the Tathāgata, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times. Raising their voices, they wailed and wept, their grief moving heaven and earth; they beat their breasts and cried out, tears falling like rain.
They spoke to one another again, saying:
"Alas, O virtuous ones!
The world is empty; the world is empty!"
He then raised his entire body and threw himself before the Tathāgata, addressing the Buddha:
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
The World-Honored One, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept it.
Thus, although he requested three times, he was refused in every instance.
The upāsakas, failing to achieve their wish, remained silent with hearts filled by sorrow and distress, much like a compassionate father whose only son has suddenly fallen ill and passed away;
having performed the funeral rites and returned home, he is overcome with the utmost grief and affliction.
The upāsakas likewise wept with grief and distress; they arranged their various offerings in one place, withdrew to one side, and sat in silence.
At that time, there were also as many upāsikās as the sands of three Ganges Rivers, who upheld the five precepts and were perfect in their dignified conduct.
Their names were Upāsikā Jīvaśrī, Upāsikā Guṇamālā, Upāsikā Viśākhā, and others, with eighty-four thousand serving as their leaders.

She was fully capable of upholding and protecting the True Dharma; for the sake of delivering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, she manifested in a female body to censure the ways of the household life.
She contemplated her own body as being like four venomous snakes;
this body is constantly being devoured by immeasurable worms.
This body is foul and impure, a prison bound by craving and desire;
this body is loathsome, like a dead dog;
this body is unclean, with its nine orifices constantly discharging filth.

This body is like a city: blood, flesh, sinews, bones, and skin wrap its exterior; the hands and feet serve as watchtowers and battlements for repelling enemies; the eyes are the apertures; the head is the palace hall; and the king of the mind dwells within.

Such is this city of the body, abandoned by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, yet constantly relished and clung to by foolish ordinary people; within it dwell the rākṣasas of greed, lust, hatred, and delusion.
This body is not solid; it is like reeds, *eranda* trees, foam on the water, or the trunk of a plantain tree.
This body is impermanent, not abiding for even a single moment of thought, like a flash of lightning, a torrential flood, or a mirage.
It is also like drawing on water: as soon as one draws, it immediately merges back together.
This body is easily destroyed, like a great tree standing on a steep riverbank;
this body will not last long before it is devoured by foxes, wolves, owls, crows, vultures, eagles, ravens, magpies, and hungry dogs.
What wise person would take pleasure in this body?
One might as well attempt to contain the waters of the great ocean within the hoof-print of an ox; one cannot fully describe the impermanence, impurity, and foul stench of this body.

One might as well roll the great earth into pellets the size of jujube fruits, gradually reducing them to the size of mustard seeds and even down to minute atoms; one still could not fully describe the faults and afflictions of this body.
Therefore, one should abandon them as one would discard mucus or spittle.

For this reason, these upāsikās constantly cultivate their minds through the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they deeply delight in inquiring about and receiving the Mahāyāna sūtras, and having heard them, they are also able to expound them for others.
They uphold their original vows, reviling the female body as something deeply loathsome and inherently unstable.

Their minds constantly cultivate and accumulate such right contemplation, thereby destroying the boundless cycle of birth and death. They thirst for and yearn for the Mahāyāna—having themselves attained fulfillment, they are further able to satisfy others who likewise yearn for it—and they take profound delight in the Mahāyāna and protect the Mahāyāna.
Although she manifests in a female body, she is in truth a bodhisattva.
She is skillfully able to accord with all worlds, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated.

She continues the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it shall never be severed; in future ages, she shall turn the wheel of Dharma, adorning herself with great adornments, and firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts.
Having fully accomplished such merits, they gave rise to great compassion for all sentient beings with impartiality and non-duality, as if looking upon each as their only child.
Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, they said to one another:
"Today we ought to go to the space between the twin trees."

The offerings prepared by the upāsikās were twice as magnificent as those before; they carried them to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"We have now prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha; we only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our offering.
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not grant his permission.
The upāsikās, their wishes unfulfilled, sat to one side with hearts full of sorrow.

At that time, there were also men and women, elders and youths, wives and children, and retinues from the Licchavis of Vaiśālī—equal in number to the sands of four Ganges Rivers—as well as the kings of Jambudvīpa and their retinues. For the sake of seeking the Dharma, they had well-cultivated their moral conduct and were fully endowed with dignified deportment; they had subdued heterodox teachers and those who would destroy the True Dharma.
They constantly said to one another:

"We shall take these treasuries of gold and silver to ensure that the nectar-like, inexhaustible, and profound treasury of the True Dharma remains long in the world; may we always be able to study and practice it."
"If there be anyone who slanders the Buddha’s true Dharma, I shall cut out their tongue.
He further made this vow:
"If there be any who have left the household life and violate the prohibitions and precepts, I shall compel them to return to secular life and employ them as laborers."
If there are those who can deeply delight in protecting and upholding the True Dharma, I shall honor them as I would my own parents;
if there are members of the Sangha who can practice the True Dharma, I shall rejoice in their merit and cause them to attain power and influence.
They constantly desired to hear Mahāyāna sūtras, and having heard them, were also able to explain them extensively for others.
They had all fully accomplished such meritorious virtues.
Their names were as follows:
The Licchavi Vimalagarbha, the Licchavi Vimalapramāda, and the Licchavi Gaṅgānirghoṣavimalaguṇa, and others like them, said to one another:
"Gentlemen, you should now go quickly to where the Buddha is."

The various requisites for the offering they had prepared were fully complete; each Licchavi individually adorned eighty-four thousand great elephants, eighty-four thousand precious chariots drawn by four horses, and eighty-four thousand moon-bright jewels, as well as eighty-four thousand bundles of firewood made of celestial wood, sandalwood, and aloeswood—of each kind there were eighty-four thousand.
Before each elephant were jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies; the smallest of these canopies measured a full yojana in circumference and extent;
the shortest of the pennants was thirty-three yojanas long;
and the lowest of the jeweled banners was one hundred yojanas high.
Carrying such articles of offering as these, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We have now prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha; we only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our offering.
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not grant his permission.

The Licchavis and others, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress; through the Buddha’s supernormal power, they rose seven *tāla* trees above the ground and remained silently suspended in mid-air.

At that time, there were also ministers and elders as numerous as the sands of five Ganges Rivers—those who revered the Mahāyāna and who possessed the power to subdue any followers of heterodox schools who slandered the True Dharma, just as a shower of hail destroys grass and trees.
Their names were the Elder Sūryaprabha, the Elder Lokapāla, and the Elder Dharmapāla; these and others served as their leaders.

The offerings they prepared were five times greater than before; together they carried them to the space between the twin trees, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We have now prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha; we only pray that you will take pity on us and accept our offerings.
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept them.

The elders, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress; through the Buddha’s supernatural power, they rose seven *tāla* trees above the ground and remained silently suspended in mid-air.

At that time, there were also the King of Vaiśālī along with his harem, wives, and retinue; all the kings within Jambudvīpa—with the exception of Ajātaśatru—and the people of the cities, towns, and villages.
Their names were King Vimalacandra and others; each, having arrayed the fourfold army, desired to proceed to where the Buddha was.
Each of these kings had a retinue of one hundred and eighty million people.
These chariot troops were drawn by elephants and horses; the elephants had six tusks, and the horses were as swift as the wind.

The ornamental offerings were six times more magnificent than before; among the precious canopies, even the smallest measured eight yojanas in circumference and extent, while the shortest banners were sixteen yojanas long.
The base of the jeweled banner extends thirty-six yojanas.

These kings abide securely in the True Dharma, despise and loathe false teachings, revere and honor the Mahāyāna, and take profound delight in the Mahāyāna; they cherish all sentient beings equally, as if they were their only child.
The fragrance of the food and drink he carried wafted forth, filling four yojanas.

Furthermore, at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, he took these various kinds of exquisite and delicious delicacies and went to the twin trees; arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"We have prepared these offerings for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; we only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will accept our final offering.
Although the Tathāgata knew the proper time, he did not grant his permission.
These kings, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, there were also queens of seven Ganges-sands of kings, with the sole exception of King Ajātaśatru’s queen.
To deliver sentient beings, they manifest in female bodies; they constantly observe their physical conduct and cultivate their minds through the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Their names are Lady Wondrous of the Three Realms and Lady Loving Virtue, and others such as these, who were the consorts of various kings.
They all dwelt securely within the True Dharma, practicing the prohibitive precepts with perfect deportment, and regarding all sentient beings with compassion as if they were their only child.
They said to one another:
"We should now go quickly to the place where the World-Honored One resides."

The offerings provided by the queens of the various kings were seven times greater than before: incense, flowers, precious banners, silken streamers, pennants, canopies, and the most exquisite food and drink. Among them, the smallest of the precious canopies measured sixteen *yojanas* in circumference and breadth;
the shortest of the pennants was thirty-six *yojanas* long;
and the lowest of the precious banners was sixty-eight *yojanas* high.
The fragrant aroma of the food and drink spread everywhere, filling eight yojanas.
Carrying such articles of offering, they went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We have prepared these offerings for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; we only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will accept our final offering.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept.

At that time, the ladies of the court, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress; they tore out their hair, beat their breasts, and wailed loudly, like a compassionate mother who has recently lost her beloved child. They then withdrew to one side and sat in silence.
At that time, there were also goddesses as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers,
headed by the goddess Viśālanetrī,
who spoke these words:
“Sisters, observe closely, observe closely!
These various multitudes have prepared all manner of sublime and excellent offerings, desiring to present them to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus.”
"We, too, shall likewise prepare such exquisite offerings to worship the Tathāgata; once the Tathāgata has accepted them, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Sisters! It is extremely rare for Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, to appear in the world, and it is even more difficult to offer the final worship."
"If the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, the world will become empty.
These goddesses—delighting in the Mahāyāna and desiring to hear it, having heard it, they were also able to explain it extensively for others;
thirsting for the Mahāyāna, once they themselves were satisfied, they were further able to satisfy those who likewise thirsted for it.
He protects the Mahāyāna; should there be followers of other teachings who harbor malice toward the Mahāyāna, he has the power to crush them, just as hail destroys grass.

He upholds the practice of precepts and is fully endowed with dignified deportment; he is skillfully able to accord with all worldly ways, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated.
In future ages, they shall turn the wheel of Dharma, succeeding to the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it remains unbroken.

They shall study and practice the Mahāyāna, adorning themselves with great adornments, and achieve such immeasurable merit as to regard all sentient beings with equal compassion, as if looking upon an only child—likewise, at dawn when the sun first rises, each shall take various kinds of celestial wood incense and the like, which are twice as fragrant as all the incense-wood found in the human world; the fragrance of this wood is able to extinguish all manner of foul odors among humans.
There were white chariots with white canopies, each drawn by four white horses; upon every chariot was spread a white curtain, and from the four sides of these curtains hung various golden bells.
There were all kinds of fragrant flowers, jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies, as well as exquisite delicacies and various musical performances, while lion thrones were laid out.
The four legs of each seat were made of pure, deep-blue lapis lazuli; behind each seat there was a reclining couch made of the seven treasures, and before each seat there was further a golden table.
Furthermore, they fashioned lamp-stands out of the seven treasures, using various kinds of precious gems as lamps, while exquisite celestial flowers were strewn across the ground.
Having made these offerings, the heavenly maidens felt a sense of poignant grief; their tears flowed freely as they were overcome with great anguish.

Furthermore, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, to accomplish the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna, to reveal the Tathāgata’s secret teachings on skillful means, and to ensure that the various methods of preaching the Dharma would not be interrupted, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
Knowing the proper time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept it.
The goddesses, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress; they withdrew to one side and sat in silence.
At that time, there were also dragon kings as numerous as the sands of nine Ganges Rivers dwelling in the four directions,
with the Dragon King Vāsuki, the Dragon King Nanda, and the Dragon King Upananda serving as their leaders.

These dragon kings also, at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, prepared various offerings—twofold more than those of humans and devas—and brought them to the Buddha’s dwelling. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.”
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept.
These dragon kings, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, there were also spirits and divine kings as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, with King Vaiśravaṇa as their leader, who each said to one another:
"O virtuous ones!..."
"You should now go quickly to the Buddha's dwelling.

The offerings they prepared were twice as many as those of all the other nāgas; carrying them to the Buddha's dwelling, they prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not grant his request.
These kings of ghosts, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, there were also twenty Ganges-sands of garuḍa kings, with the Garuḍa King Vanquisher of Enemies as their leader.
There were also thirty Ganges-sands of gandharva kings, with the Gandharva King Narada as their leader.
Furthermore, there were kings of the kiṃnaras, as numerous as the sands of forty Ganges Rivers, with King Sudarśana as their leader.
Furthermore, there were kings of the mahoragas, as numerous as the sands of fifty Ganges Rivers, with King Mahāsudarśana as their leader.
Furthermore, there were sixty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* asuras, with King Śumbhali as their leader.
Furthermore, there were seventy *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* dhānava kings, with King Vimalanadi and King Bhadradatta as their leaders.

Furthermore, there were eighty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Rākṣasa kings, with King Bhīṣaṇa as their leader; they abandoned their evil intentions and ceased eating humans, giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward those they previously hated. Though their forms were once hideous, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they all became handsome and upright.
Furthermore, there were forest spirit kings as numerous as the sands of ninety Ganges Rivers, with King Delighting in Fragrance as their leader.
Furthermore, there were mantra-holding kings as numerous as the sands of a thousand Ganges Rivers, with Great Illusion Mantra-Holding King as their leader.
Furthermore, there were one hundred million *gaṅgā*-sands of *yakṣa* spirits who lust after physical form, with King Sudarśana as their leader.
Additionally, there were ten billion *gaṅgā*-sands of celestial maidens, with Lambā, Urvaśī, Tilottamā, and Viśvakā as their leaders.
Furthermore, there were as many kṣetrapāla kings as there are grains of sand in ten billion Ganges Rivers, with King Baiśe (Vaiśravaṇa) as their leader.
There were also as many sons of gods and celestial kings as there are grains of sand in ten trillion Ganges Rivers, including the Four Heavenly Kings and others.

Furthermore, there were wind deities of the four quarters, as numerous as the sands of ten trillion *Ganges* rivers, who blew upon the trees, scattering seasonal and out-of-season flowers among the twin *śāla* trees.
Additionally, there were cloud-and-rain deities, as numerous as the sands of ten trillion *Ganges* rivers, all of whom thought to themselves:

"When the Tathāgata enters *nirvāṇa* and his body is cremated, we shall pour down rain to extinguish the fire at the proper time and provide cool relief for those in the assembly who are distressed by the heat."

Furthermore, there were great fragrant elephant kings as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers—headed by the elephant king Rāhu, the golden elephant king, the sweet-flavored elephant king, the deep-blue elephant king, and the fragrance-desiring elephant king—who revered the Mahāyāna and delighted in the Mahāyāna. Knowing that the Buddha would soon enter parinirvāṇa, they each plucked countless and boundless exquisite lotus flowers and came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there were as many lion kings as there are sands in twenty Ganges Rivers, with the Lion’s Roar King as their leader; bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings, they brought various flowers and fruits to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there were kings of twenty *gaṅgā* rivers’ worth of flying birds—including wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, gandharva-birds, kāraṇḍava-birds, mynas, parrots, *kūṭarāja* birds, *vakhiga* birds, *kalaviṅka* birds, and *jīvajīvaka* birds—such as these various birds, carrying flowers and fruits, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Furthermore, there were water buffaloes, oxen, and sheep, as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers, who went to where the Buddha was and yielded milk of wondrous fragrance.
This milk flowed until it filled all the ditches and pits of the city of Kuśinagara, being fully endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.
Having accomplished these tasks, they withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there were as many ṛṣis from the four continents as there are grains of sand in twenty Ganges Rivers, with the Ṛṣi Kṣāntivādin at their head. Carrying various fragrant flowers and sweet fruits, they approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept our final offering.”
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not grant his request.
At that, the sages, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Among all the bee-kings in Jambudvīpa, the Bee-King Wondrous Sound was the foremost; carrying various kinds of flowers, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha once, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, all the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs in Jambudvīpa assembled, with the sole exception of the two groups led by the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda.

Furthermore, there were all the mountains within the intermediate spaces of immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds like the sands of the Ganges, as well as those in Jambudvīpa, with Sumeru, the King of Mountains, as their foremost.

That mountain was magnificent and adorned; its groves were lush and verdant, with branches and leaves so thick they shielded the sunlight. It was embellished everywhere with various exquisite flowers, and dragon springs and flowing streams were pure, fragrant, and pristine.
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, as well as seers, spell-casters, performers, musicians, and suchlike multitudes filled it completely.
These mountain deities also came to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there were incalculable numbers of deities of the four great oceans and various river deities, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges; they possessed great majestic virtue and were endowed with great supernormal powers, and the offerings they presented were twice as magnificent as those before.

The bodily radiance of the various devas and the light of their musical instruments and lamps completely eclipsed the sun and moon so that they no longer appeared. They scattered campaka flowers over the River Hiraṇyavatī and approached the Buddha’s dwelling, where they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the śāla grove of the city of Kuśinagara turned white, like white cranes.

In the midst of the void, there spontaneously appeared pavilions made of the seven treasures, with carvings, engravings, and ornate decorations clearly defined, surrounded by railings interspersed with various jewels.

Below the hall there were many flowing springs and bathing pools, filled with the most exquisite lotus flowers, just like the northern continent of Uttarakuru, or like the Nandana Garden of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
at that time, the various adornments within the Śāla grove were likewise exceedingly lovely and delightful.
All these devas, humans, asuras, and others beheld the signs of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa; they were all moved by grief, filled with sorrow and distress, and found no joy.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and Śakra Devānām Indra each said to one another:
"Observe how the gods, humans, and asuras are making grand offerings, desiring to offer their final tribute to the Tathāgata."
"We, too, shall make offerings in this same manner.
If I am the last to receive such offerings, then my perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) will be accomplished and fulfilled without difficulty."
At that time, the offerings presented by the Four Great Kings were twice as magnificent as before;
they brought *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *karkārava* flowers,
*mahākarkārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, and *saṃtānikā* flowers.
...mahāsaṃtānikā flowers, priyaṅgu flowers, mahāpriyaṅgu flowers, samantabhadra flowers, mahāsamantabhadra flowers,
kāla flowers, mahākāla flowers, gandhapura flowers, mahāgandhapura flowers,
nandana flowers, mahānandana flowers, kāmaruci flowers, and mahākāmaruci flowers.
...the *gandhamādana* flower, the *mahāgandhamādana* flower, the *samantagandha* flower, the *mahāsamantagandha* flower, the *divyakanakapatra* flower,
the nāga-flower, the *pārijātaka* tree flower, and the *kovidāra* tree flower; furthermore,
they brought various kinds of exquisite and delicious foods to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and paid their respects.
The radiance of all these devas and humans was able to eclipse the sun and moon so that they no longer appeared; with these offerings, they wished to make an offering to the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept them.
At that time, the various devas, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Then Śakra Devānām Indra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven prepared various offerings even more magnificent than before; the flowers they brought were likewise so, their fragrance being subtle and exquisite, most delightful. Carrying the Hall of Victory (Vaijayanta) along with all its smaller pavilions, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"We deeply delight in and cherish the Mahāyāna; we only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our food.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept it.
At that time, the Śakras of the various heavens did not achieve their wishes; with hearts filled with sorrow and distress, they withdrew to stand to one side.

This continued up to the sixth heaven, where the offerings prepared became increasingly superior to those before: the precious banners, streamers, and canopies—wherein the smallest precious canopy covered the four continents, the shortest streamer encircled the four seas, and the lowest banner reached as far as the Heaven of Sovereign Mastery—and when a gentle breeze blew upon the banners, it produced wondrous sounds. Carrying exquisite delicacies, they came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
Knowing the proper time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept it.
These devas, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.
From the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the rest of the Brahma assemblies, everyone gathered together.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King and the other Brahma assemblies emitted bodily radiance that pervaded the four continents; the light of the sun and moon among humans and devas in the desire realm no longer appeared at all.

Carrying various jeweled banners, silken streamers, pennants, and canopies—some of the shortest pennants hanging from the Brahma palaces down to the space between the śāla trees—they approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
“We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
Knowing the proper time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept it.
At that time, the Brahmās, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, together with an immeasurable retinue of great asuras, whose bodily radiance surpassed that of the Brahmā heavens, carrying various jeweled banners, silken streamers, pennants, and canopies—some of which were so small that they could cover a thousand worlds—and bringing exquisite, sweet delicacies, came to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept this final offering from us.”
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept [the offering].
The asuras, their wishes unfulfilled, were filled with grief and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, the King of the Desire Realm, together with his retinue, the celestial maidens, and an immeasurable, boundless, incalculable multitude, opened the gates of hell and provided clear, cool water, saying to them:

"Now you can do nothing at all; you should simply focus your minds on the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and establish this final offering of sympathetic joy, which shall bring you peace for a long night."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas completely removed the swords, blades, and immeasurable bitter poisons within the hells, and caused a torrential rain to fall to extinguish the blazing, raging fires.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he further conceived this thought:
"I shall cause all my kinsmen to abandon their swords, blades, bows, crossbows, armor, weapons, spears, lances, long hooks, golden mallets, battle-axes, war-discs, and nooses."

The offerings they carried were twice as magnificent as those presented by all the devas and humans; even the smallest of their parasols could cover a medium chiliocosm. Arriving at the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and addressed him, saying:
"We now delight in the Mahāyāna and shall protect the Mahāyāna."
“World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of making offerings, out of fear, for the sake of deceiving others, for the sake of wealth and profit, or by following others, receive this Mahāyāna—whether it be genuine or counterfeit—we shall at that time eliminate their fears for such persons and recite this mantra:

‘Ta ki | Ta-ta-ra ta ki | Lu-ha-le ma-ha lu-ha-le a-ra | Ca-ra | Ta-ra | Svāhā. This mantra is able to cause those who have lost their minds, those who are fearful, those who preach the Dharma, and those who do not sever the True Dharma—to subdue non-Buddhists, protect their own bodies, protect the True Dharma, and protect the Mahāyāna; therefore, we recite this mantra.”

If there are those who can uphold such a mantra, they will have no fear of wild elephants; even when they reach desolate wildernesses, empty marshes, or perilous places, they will give rise to no fear, nor will they suffer from water, fire, lions, tigers, wolves, bandits, or royal calamities.
"Bhagavān!
If there are those who can uphold such a mantra, they will be able to completely eliminate all such fears. Bhagavān!"
"Whoever upholds this mantra, we shall protect them as a tortoise hides its six limbs.
World-Honored One!
We do not speak these words now out of flattery."
"To those who uphold this mantra, I shall sincerely augment their power.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our final offering.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Māra Pāpīyas, saying:

"I do not accept your offerings of food and drink; I have already accepted the divine mantra you have spoken for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings and the fourfold assembly."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, he remained silent and did not accept.
Thus, although he requested three times, he was refused each time.
At that moment, Māra Pāpīyas, his wishes unfulfilled, felt sorrow and distress, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the offerings presented by the Great Lord Śiva (Maheśvara), together with his retinue, immeasurable and boundless multitudes of devas, and the assembly of gods, completely eclipsed all the offering implements of Brahmā, Śakra, the Four World-Protecting Kings, the eight classes of humans and non-humans, and others. The offerings prepared by Brahmā and Śakra appeared no more, like a mass of ink beside a conch shell. Even the smallest of the precious canopies was able to cover a trichiliocosm.
Carrying such articles of offering as these, they approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The humble offerings we present are like mosquitoes making an offering to me;
they are like someone casting a single handful of water into the great ocean,
or like lighting a small lamp to assist the hundred thousand suns.
In the months of spring and summer, when all flowers are in full bloom, one might take a single flower to add to the multitude;
or one might take a mustard seed to add to Mount Sumeru. But how could these possibly benefit the great ocean, the brilliance of the sun, the multitude of flowers, or Mount Sumeru?
World-Honored One!
The meager offerings I now present are likewise so.
Even if one were to fill a trichiliocosm with fragrant flowers, music, banners, and canopies to make offerings to the Tathāgata, it would still not be worth mentioning.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings, constantly undergoes various sufferings and afflictions within the evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
For this reason, World-Honored One!
"You should look upon us with compassion and accept our offerings.

At that time, to the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands, there was a buddha-field named Manojña-ruta-garbha. There, the Buddha was named Ākāśasama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, that Buddha addressed his foremost great disciple, saying:
"Good son, you should now go to the Sahā world in the western direction."
In that land there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
That Buddha will soon enter parinirvāṇa.
Son of good family!
You may take this fragrant food from our world—its fragrance is exquisite and it brings peace and security to those who eat it—and offer it to that Blessed One, the World-Honored One.
After the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he entered parinirvāṇa.
"Good sons!
You should all pay him homage and request that he resolve your doubts."

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantagātra, having received the Buddha’s instruction, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and together with an immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya multitude of great Bodhisattvas, set out from that land and arrived here in this Sahā world.
At that moment, the great earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

Within the assembly, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Great Kings, Māra Pāpīyān, Maheśvara, and the rest of the great multitude, seeing this earthquake, had the hair on their bodies stand on end; their throats and tongues became parched, and they were struck with such terror and trembling that they each wished to flee in all directions. They saw that their own bodies no longer possessed radiance, and all their majesty and virtue were extinguished without remainder.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, rose from his seat and addressed the great assembly:
"Virtuous sons! Do not be afraid; do not be afraid."

Why is this? To the east of here, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands, there is a world named Manojñābhigarjita. There, the Buddha is named Ākāśasama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
There is a bodhisattva there named Anantakāya, who, together with immeasurable bodhisattvas, intends to come here to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
It is by the power of that bodhisattva’s majestic virtue that the radiance of your body no longer appears at all.
"Therefore, you all should give rise to joy and harbor no fear.
At that time, the great assembly all saw that Buddha and his multitude from afar, as if looking at their own bodies in a clear mirror.
Then Mañjuśrī addressed the great assembly once more:
"What you now see of that Buddha and his great assembly is just as you see this Buddha;
by the Buddha's spiritual power, you shall likewise come to see the immeasurable Buddhas of the nine directions."
At that time, the great assembly said to one another: "Alas, alas!
The world is empty; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the entire great assembly clearly beheld the Bodhisattva Anantagātra and his retinue.
From each and every pore of that bodhisattva’s body, a great lotus flower was produced.

Each lotus flower contains seventy-eight thousand cities, equal in length and breadth to the city of Vaiśālī; their walls and moats are interspersed with the seven treasures, and rows of precious *tāla* trees stand in sevenfold succession.
The population was flourishing, living in peace, security, and abundance; the city walls were made of Jambūnada gold.

Each defensive wall was adorned with various groves of trees made of the seven treasures, their flowers and fruits lush and abundant, emitting subtle and wondrous sounds as they were stirred by gentle breezes.
The sound was harmonious and elegant, like celestial music; when the people within the city heard this sound, they immediately experienced supreme and wondrous bliss.
These moats were filled with exquisite water, pure, fragrant, and clean as genuine lapis lazuli.
Within these waters are boats made of the seven treasures; people board them to frolic, bathe, and enjoy one another’s company, their happiness being beyond measure.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable lotuses of various colors—utpala, kumuda, padma, and puṇḍarīka flowers—each of which was as large in length and breadth as a chariot wheel.
Upon the banks of those moats there are many groves and gardens; within each garden are five spring-pools.
Within these pools there are various flowers: blue lotuses (utpala), yellow lotuses (kumuda), red lotuses (padma), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka).
The flowers there are as large in length and breadth as chariot wheels; their fragrance is rich and pervasive, most delightful.
The water is pure and its softness is unsurpassed, where wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks sport and play.

In each of those gardens there are numerous palatial residences made of various jewels; each residence is four yojanas square in length and breadth. Their walls are composed of the four precious substances—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with windows of pure gold and railings surrounding them on all sides. The ground is made of *māṇikya* gems, strewn upon with golden sand.

Within this palace complex, there are many flowing springs and bathing pools made of the seven treasures; by the side of each pool, there are eighteen golden stairways, and the plantain trees are made of Jambūnada gold—just like the Nandana Garden of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
In each of these cities, there were eighty-four thousand kings; each king had immeasurable consorts and court ladies with whom he enjoyed himself, delighting in pleasure and happiness.
The rest of the people were likewise; each enjoyed themselves together at their respective dwellings.
Among them, sentient beings heard no other names, but heard only the sound of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.

Within each of these flowers, there was a lion throne; the four legs of each throne were made of deep blue lapis lazuli, and soft, white garments were spread upon the seats—garments so exquisite that they surpassed all things within the triple world.

Upon each seat sat a king, who taught and transformed sentient beings through the Mahāyāna Dharma; some sentient beings copied, upheld, read, recited, and practiced according to the teachings, thus disseminating the Mahāyāna sūtras.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Anantagātra had established these immeasurable sentient beings within his own body, he caused them to renounce worldly pleasures and spoke these words:
"Alas! Alas! How bitter it is!"
"The world is empty; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, having manifested such supernormal powers, took these various and immeasurable offerings as well as exquisite and delicious food and drink.
If anyone should hear the fragrance of this food, their afflictions and all impurities will be completely extinguished.
By the power of this bodhisattva’s supernormal faculties, the entire great assembly is able to behold such transformations.
The body of the Bodhisattva Anantagātra is infinitely large, its measure equal to empty space; except for the Buddhas, no one else is able to perceive the limits of this bodhisattva’s body.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra and his retinue prepared offerings even more magnificent than those before; they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We only pray that you will have compassion for us and accept our food.
The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, remained silent and did not accept it.
Thus he was invited three times, yet he did not accept on any occasion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra and his retinue withdrew to stand to one side.

Likewise, from the Buddha-worlds of the south, west, and north, there were immeasurable Bodhisattvas named Anantagātra, whose offerings were twice as magnificent as those before; they came to where the Buddha was and, in the same manner, withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the auspicious and blessed site of the twin śāla trees was thirty-two yojanas in length and breadth, filled with a great assembly such that there was no empty space between them.
At that time, the places where the Bodhisattvas of Boundless Body from the four directions and their retinues sat were like the tip of an awl, the point of a needle, or a mote of dust.

Great Bodhisattvas from as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are motes of dust all gathered together, as did the entire great assembly of Jambudvīpa—excepting only the two groups of Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda, and King Ajātaśatru along with his retinue—even down to venomous snakes whose gaze can kill, earthworms, dung beetles, vipers, scorpions, and those who commit the sixteen kinds of evil deeds—all came together.

The Dānavas, Asuras, and others all abandoned their evil thoughts and gave rise to hearts of compassion toward one another, regarding each other as fathers, mothers, elder sisters, or younger sisters;
the sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm likewise directed their minds toward one another with compassion, with the sole exception of the icchantikas.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the ground of this trichiliocosm became entirely soft and supple; it was free of mounds, ravines, soil, sand, pebbles, stones, thorns, and poisonous weeds, and was adorned with various jewels like the world of Sukhāvatī of the Buddha Amitāyus in the western quarter.

At that time, the great assembly all beheld the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, just as one sees one's own body in a clear mirror; their vision of the various Buddha-lands was likewise so.

At that time, five-colored light issued from the Tathāgata’s face; its radiance shone forth, overshadowing the entire great assembly so that the bodily radiance of all those present was no longer visible.
Having performed what was to be done, the light returned and entered through the Buddha’s mouth.

At that time, the devas, humans, and the entire assembly, including the asuras, seeing the Buddha’s radiance return and enter his mouth, were all seized with great terror, and the hair on their bodies stood on end.
He further spoke these words:

"The radiance of the Tathāgata has emerged and now returns; it cannot be without cause or condition. It must be that what was to be done throughout the ten directions has been accomplished, and this is surely the sign of his final nirvāṇa."
How bitter it is! How bitter it is!
How can the World-Honored One suddenly abandon the four immeasurable minds and no longer accept the offerings presented by devas and humans?
The sun of the Noble One’s wisdom has now forever extinguished; the unsurpassed Dharma-ship has sunk here.
Alas, how painful!
What great suffering for the world!

Raising his hands, he beat his breast, wailing and weeping in grief; his limbs trembled so violently that he could not support himself, and blood flowed from all the pores of his body, drenching the ground.
*The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
*The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
The *Cuntuo-pin* (Chapter on Cunda), the second, added by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
At that time, there was in the assembly an upāsaka who was the son of a craftsman from the city of Kuśinagara, named Cunda, together with fifteen of his peers.
In order to cause the world to obtain wholesome fruits, he set aside his dignified demeanor and rose from his seat.

Baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee upon the ground, he joined his palms toward the Buddha, his eyes brimming with tears of sorrowful emotion. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will compassionately accept our final offering, for the sake of delivering immeasurable sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth, we are without a master, without kin, without rescue, without protection, without refuge, and without a destination; impoverished and famished, we wish to seek our future sustenance from the Tathāgata.”
We only pray that you will compassionately accept our humble offering and then enter parinirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!
It is like a kṣatriya, or a brāhmaṇa, vaiśya, or śūdra, who, because of poverty, travels far to another country to labor in the fields.
One obtains well-trained oxen; the good field is level and even, free from all saline soil, weeds, and desolation, awaiting only the rain from heaven.
"Well-trained oxen" is a metaphor for the seven [faculties] of body and speech;
"the good field is level and even" is a metaphor for wisdom.
The removal of saline soil, weeds, and desolation is a metaphor for the removal of afflictions.
World-Honored One!
My body now possesses tamed oxen and fertile fields; having weeded out all impurities, I only long for the Tathāgata’s rain of ambrosial Dharma.
Those of the four castes who are poor are none other than ourselves, impoverished of the wealth and treasures of the unsurpassed Dharma.
We pray only that you will take pity on us, severing our poverty and suffering, and extending your salvation to immeasurable beings tormented by distress.
Although my current offering is meager, I hope it may suffice for the Tathāgata and his great assembly.
Now I am without a master, without kin, and without refuge; I pray that you will look upon me with compassion, as you do Rāhula.
At that time, the World-Honored One—the one possessed of all-encompassing wisdom and the unsurpassed tamer—addressed Cunda, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
I shall now eliminate poverty for you and let the unsurpassed rain of Dharma fall upon the field of your body, causing the sprouts of Dharma to grow.
If you now seek from me long life, physical beauty, strength, peace and happiness, and unimpeded eloquence, I shall bestow upon you constant life, beauty, strength, peace, and unimpeded eloquence.
For what reason?
Cunda! There are two kinds of giving food, yet their karmic rewards do not differ.
What are these two?
First, having received [the prediction], they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; second, having received [the prediction], they enter *nirvāṇa*.
"I now accept your final offering, so that you may fulfill the *dānapāramitā*.
At that time, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As for what the Buddha has said—that there is no difference between the karmic rewards of these two kinds of giving—this meaning is not so."

Why is this? Those who receive offerings first have not yet exhausted their afflictions and have not yet attained the realization of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); nor have they yet been able to cause sentient beings to fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

Those who receive offerings later have already exhausted their afflictions and have already attained the realization of all-knowledge; they are thus able to cause sentient beings everywhere to fully possess the perfection of giving.
Those who first receive the offerings are still sentient beings;
those who later receive the offerings are the God among Gods.
Those who first receive the offerings possess bodies that consume mixed food, bodies of affliction, final bodies, and impermanent bodies.
The recipient who later receives the gift possesses a body free from afflictions, a vajra-body, a dharma-body, an eternal body, and a boundless body.
How can it be said that the karmic rewards of these two types of giving are equal and without distinction?

The one who receives the gift first has not yet fulfilled the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, and possesses only the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), having not yet attained the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) up to the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*).
The one who receives the gift later has already attained fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, and is fully endowed with the Buddha-eye up to the wisdom-eye.
"How is it that you say the karmic rewards of these two types of giving are equal and without distinction?
World-Honored One!
When the first recipient receives the gift, having received it, they eat it; once it enters the stomach and is digested, they obtain life, physical form, strength, peace, and unimpeded eloquence."
"If the recipient of the gift later does not eat it or digest it, there will be no fruit from these five matters.
How then can you say that the retributive fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! The Tathāgata has, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, been without a body of food or a body of afflictions; he possesses no final body, but rather a constant body, a dharma-body, and a vajra-body.”
"Good son! Those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature are said to possess a body of afflictions and a body sustained by mixed food; this is the final body.
When the Bodhisattva has partaken of food at that time, he enters the Vajra-samādhi. Once this food is digested, he immediately sees the Buddha-nature and attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Therefore, I say that the retributive fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva destroyed the four māras; now, upon entering nirvāṇa, he likewise destroys the four māras.
Therefore, I say that the retributive fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction.

Although the Bodhisattva at that time did not extensively expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures, he had already mastered them beforehand; now, upon entering nirvana, he will extensively analyze and explain them for the sake of sentient beings.
Therefore, I say that the retributive fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction. "Good son!
The body of the Tathāgata has not received food or drink for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; yet, for the sake of the śrāvakas, he says: "
"Only after first receiving the milk-gruel offered by the two cowherd girls, Nanda and Nandabalā, did I subsequently attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"I truly do not eat.
It is now for the sake of this entire assembly that I accept your final offering; in truth, I do not eat.

At that time, when the great assembly heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had universally accepted Cunda’s final offering out of compassion for the great gathering, they leaped for joy and, with one voice, praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
How rare you are, Cunda!
The name by which you are now established is truly worthy of its meaning.”
As for the name Cunda, it means "one who understands the wondrous meaning.
Since you have now established such a great principle, the name is established according to its actual meaning; therefore, he is called Cunda.
In this present life, you have attained great fame and profit; your virtue and vows are fulfilled.
How extraordinary, Cunda!
Having been born among human beings, you have further obtained this unsurpassed benefit so difficult to attain.
Excellent, Cunda!
Just as the udumbara flower is rare in the world, so too is the appearance of a Buddha in the world exceedingly difficult;
to encounter a Buddha, give rise to faith, and hear the Dharma is even more difficult still.
To be able to provide this final offering when the Buddha was on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa is even more difficult than that.
Namo Cunda! Namo Cunda!
You have now fully perfected the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
You are like the full moon on the fifteenth night of autumn: pure and complete, free from all clouds and obscurations, and there is no sentient being who does not look up to you with reverence.
You are likewise so regarded by us as our object of veneration.
The Buddha has already accepted your final offering, thereby enabling you to fulfill the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Namo Cunda! Therefore it is said that you are like the full moon, whom all sentient beings gaze upon with reverence. Namo Cunda!
"Though you have received a human body, your mind is like the Buddha-mind.
You, Cunda, are now truly a son of the Buddha, just like Rāhula; there is no difference between you.
At that time, the great assembly spoke these verses:
"Though you have been born into the human realm, you have already transcended the sixth heaven.
I and all the assembly now prostrate ourselves and entreat you, O Most Victorious Honored One among men: you are about to enter parinirvāṇa."
You should have compassion for us; we only pray that you will quickly invite the Buddha to remain long in this world to benefit immeasurable multitudes,
and to proclaim the unsurpassed nectar-like Dharma praised by the wise.
"If you do not invite the Buddha, my life will not be preserved;
therefore, you ought to act on my behalf and respectfully entreat the Teacher of Men.
At that time, Cunda was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, like a person whose parents have suddenly died and are then restored to life.
Cunda’s joy was likewise so.
He rose again, prostrated before the Buddha, and spoke this verse:
“How wonderful! How marvelous!”
Having attained one's own benefit and successfully secured this human form, one eliminates greed, anger, and the like, forever departing from the three evil realms.
How joyful!
Having attained one's own benefit, One encounters a hoard of gold and jewels; Meeting the Tamer of Men, One fears no longer falling into the realm of animals.
The Buddha is like the udumbara flower; To encounter him and give rise to faith is difficult;
Having encountered him and planted roots of goodness, One shall forever extinguish the sufferings of the hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, they are able to diminish the ranks of the asuras.
To cast a mustard seed onto the point of a needle is easier than for a Buddha to appear in the world.
By means of my perfected generosity, I deliver beings from the cycle of birth and death among gods and humans.
The Buddha is unstained by worldly dharmas, like a lotus flower in the water;
having skillfully severed the seeds of the Peak of Existence, he has forever crossed the stream of birth and death.
It is difficult to be born as a human in this world, and it is likewise difficult to encounter the age of a Buddha.
Just as a blind turtle in the great ocean Meets the floating hole of a yoke,
May this food now offered by me Attain the unsurpassed fruition;
May all fetters of affliction Be shattered and rendered without solidity.
In this place, I now do not seek the state of gods or humans;
even if I were to obtain such states, my heart would find no joy therein.
Since the Tathāgata has accepted my offering, my happiness is immeasurable.
Just as the eranda flower, though born from sandalwood,
My body is like the eranda flower, yet the Tathāgata accepts my offering;
Like the emergence of sandalwood fragrance, for this reason I rejoice.
I have now attained manifest retribution in this most excellent and sublime state;
Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas have come together to make offerings to me.
All the worlds, Are filled with great suffering and distress,
Knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Now intends to enter nirvana.
They cry out these words in a loud voice:
"In this world there is no tamer.
One should not abandon sentient beings, but should regard them as one's only son.
When the Tathāgata is amidst the Saṃgha, he expounds the unsurpassed Dharma.
Like the precious Mount Sumeru, securely situated within the great ocean;
the Buddha’s wisdom can thoroughly sever the darkness of our ignorance,
just as when clouds arise in the sky, one attains refreshing coolness.
The Tathāgata is able to skillfully eliminate all afflictions,
just as when the sun rises, it dispels the clouds and its light shines everywhere.
These sentient beings, out of longing and devotion, increase their grief and lamentation.
All are adrift upon the waters of suffering within birth and death.
For this reason, World-Honored One,
you should increase the faith of sentient beings and remain long in the world in order to sever the suffering of birth and death.
The Buddha told Cunda:
"So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said."
"A Buddha's appearance in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower;
to encounter a Buddha and give rise to faith is likewise exceedingly difficult;
to be able to fulfill the perfection of dāna by offering food at the very moment the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa is even more difficult still."
"Cunda, do not now grieve so greatly;

you should instead rejoice and feel profound gratitude for having encountered this final opportunity to make offerings to the Tathāgata, thereby fulfilling the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
You should not request that the Buddha remain long in this world."
"You should now observe that the realms of all Buddhas are entirely impermanent;
the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise so.
He then spoke these verses for Cunda:
“In all the worlds, those who are born must all return to death;
though one’s lifespan may be immeasurable, it must inevitably come to an end.
Indeed, prosperity is followed by decline, and meeting is followed by parting.”
Vigorous youth does not endure for long; flourishing beauty is assailed by disease;
life is swallowed by death—no phenomenon remains eternally.
Though kings attain sovereign power and possess peerless might, [they too must pass away].
All things are subject to change and extinction;
so too is the span of life.
The wheel of manifold suffering is boundless, revolving without rest.
The three realms are all impermanent; All states of existence are entirely without joy.
The fundamental nature and characteristics of the Path Are all empty and non-existent.
Destructible phenomena undergo transmigration, Constantly accompanied by sorrow, affliction, and the like.
Terror, various evils, old age, sickness, death,
and decline— these are all boundless; easily destroyed and assailed by enemies,
they are entangled by afflictions, just like a silkworm within its cocoon.
What person of wisdom would ever take delight in this place?
This body is a collection of suffering;
it is entirely impure, a yoke, a fetter, a boil, and a wound—its very foundation is devoid of benefit.
Up to the bodies of the various devas, all are likewise thus.
All desires are impermanent; therefore, I do not cling to them.
Free from desire and with skillful reflection, I have realized the true Dharma.
Having utterly severed existence, today I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
I have crossed to the further shore of existence and transcended all suffering;
therefore, at this very moment, I experience only supreme and wondrous bliss.
At that time, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; it is truly as the Holy Teaching declares.”
"My present wisdom is so slight and shallow, like that of a mosquito; how could I possibly conceive of the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!"
I have now already [entrusted this] to the great nāga-elephants among bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have severed all fetters and outflows, such as Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince.
World-Honored One!
It is just as when a youth has only recently left the household life; although he has not yet received full ordination, he is nonetheless included within the ranks of the Saṃgha.
I am also like this: by virtue of the supernatural power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I have come to be numbered among such great Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, I now wish to cause the Tathāgata to dwell long in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
Just as a hungry person will never vomit up what they have eaten,
I only pray that the World-Honored One will likewise remain forever in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed Cunda, saying: "Cunda!
You should not now utter such words."
