"If you wish for the Tathāgata to abide forever in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa, it should be like that hungry person who neither vomits nor changes his state.

You should now contemplate the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); by practicing such contemplation, you will possess the *śūnyatā-samādhi*. If you seek the True Dharma, you should train yourself in this manner.
Cunda asked, "Mañjuśrī! As for the Tathāgata,
he is the most honored and most supreme among devas and humans."
In this way, could the Tathāgata be something that undergoes conditioned activity?
If he were one who undergoes conditioned activity, he would be a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
He would be like a bubble on water, quickly arising and quickly perishing, revolving and circulating like a chariot wheel.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise so.
I have heard that the lifespans of the various devas are extremely long;
why then, World-Honored One, is the lifespan of you, the God among Gods, even shorter, not exceeding a hundred years?

Just as a village headman possesses sovereign power and, by the force of that sovereignty, can command others, when this person’s merit is exhausted, he subsequently becomes poor and lowly; despised by others, he is made to serve at their beck and call.
Why is this? Because its power has been lost.
The World-Honored One is likewise, being identical to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
If one possesses conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one cannot be called the God among Gods.
Why is this? Because all conditioned phenomena are the dharmas of birth and death.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī,
do not regard the Tathāgata as being identical to conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī:
Do you speak thus out of knowledge or out of ignorance when you say,
"The Tathāgata is identical with all conditioned phenomena"?
If the Tathāgata were identical with all conditioned phenomena, then one could not say:
"Within the three realms, he is the God among Gods, the Sovereign Dharma King.
It is like a king who possesses a great strongman whose strength equals that of a thousand men, and whom no one else can subdue; therefore, this man is called "one who equals a thousand."
Thus, this wrestler was beloved by the king, who bestowed upon him special ranks and emoluments, and whose rewards and honors were granted naturally;

for this reason, he was called "one who equals a thousand. This man did not necessarily possess strength equal to a thousand, but because his various arts and skills could overcome a thousand, he was therefore called "one who equals a thousand."
The Tathāgata is likewise; having subdued the Māra of afflictions, the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of devas, and the Māra of death, he is therefore called the Honored One of the Three Realms.

Just as a single strongman can match a thousand others, by these causes and conditions he has fully accomplished and perfected all manner of immeasurable, true merits; thus he is titled the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Mañjuśrī! You should not now engage in conceptualization or discrimination by treating the Dharma of the Tathāgata as being the same as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
It is, for example, like a wealthy elder who fathers a son, and an physiognomist examines him and finds signs of a short lifespan.
Having heard this, the parents knew he was unfit to inherit the family lineage; they no longer held him in high regard and looked upon him as if he were mere grass.
Indeed, one who is short-lived is not respected or remembered by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others, whether male or female, young or old.

If the Tathāgata were the same as those who practice, he too would not be honored and revered by all the world’s humans, devas, and sentient beings; furthermore, there would be no one to receive the true Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, which is unchanging and non-different.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī,
you should not say:
"The Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
it is like a poor woman who has no home or protector, and moreover is oppressed by the suffering of illness, hunger, and thirst, wandering about to beg for alms."
Having stayed at another person's lodging with one son, the owner of the lodging drove them out.

Carrying the child in his arms, he wished to travel to another country; however, on the way, he encountered a violent wind and rain, and both cold and suffering assailed him. He was also bitten and stung by many mosquitoes, gadflies, bees, and venomous insects.
Crossing the Ganges while cradling her child, she did not let go even as the waters rushed swiftly past; thus, mother and child both perished together.
By virtue of the merit of such compassionate mindfulness, after her life ended, the woman was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
Mañjuśrī! If there are good men who wish to protect the True Dharma, they must not say:
"The Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena, or he is not identical to all conditioned phenomena."
One should only reproach oneself, thinking:
"I am now foolish and lack the eye of wisdom; the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is inconceivable.
For this reason, one should not proclaim it [to others]:
"If one possesses right view, they should say:
'The Tathāgata is definitively unconditioned.'"
Why is this? Because they are able to give rise to wholesome dharmas in sentient beings and because they give rise to compassion.
It is like that poor woman who, by the Ganges River, sacrificed her own life out of love for her child.
“Good son! A Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma should likewise act thus: rather than sacrificing his own body and life, he would never say, ‘The Tathāgata is identical with the conditioned.’”
One should say:
"The Tathāgata is identical with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Because it is taught that the Tathāgata is identical with the unconditioned, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just as that woman attained birth in the Brahma-heaven.
Why is this? It is because of the protection of the Dharma.
How does one protect the Dharma?
As it is said:
"The Tathāgata is identical to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). O noble son!
Such a person, though not seeking liberation, will find liberation arrive of its own accord; it is like that poor woman who did not seek Brahmā, yet Brahmā appeared to her spontaneously.
“Mañjuśrī! It is like a man traveling a long distance who, becoming utterly exhausted on the way, takes shelter in another’s house.
While he is sleeping, a great fire suddenly breaks out within that room.
Immediately he woke up in alarm and reflected to himself:
"I shall certainly die now; of this there is no doubt.
Out of a sense of shame and remorse, he wrapped his body in his robes and then passed away, being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

From this point forward, he will fulfill eighty cycles as the Great Brahmā King and be born for one hundred thousand lifetimes among humans as a Wheel-Turning King; such a person shall no longer be reborn in the three evil realms, but will instead be continuously reborn in places of peace and happiness.
For this reason, Mañjuśrī,
a son of good family who possesses a sense of shame and modesty should not view the Buddha as being identical to conditioned phenomena. Mañjuśrī!

While it may be said that the heterodox views of outsiders equate the Tathāgata with the conditioned, a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts should not conceive of the Tathāgata as being conditioned in such a manner.
If one says that the Tathāgata is conditioned, this is false speech; know that such a person, upon death, will enter hell as if returning to their own home.
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is truly an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); one should not further say that he is conditioned.
From this day forward, within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), you should abandon ignorance and seek right knowledge; you should know that the Tathāgata is precisely the unconditioned.”
If one can contemplate the Tathāgata in this manner, they shall fully attain the thirty-two marks and swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, praised Cunda, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Well done, son of good family!"
You have now created the causes and conditions for long life, being able to know that the Tathāgata is a dharma that is eternally abiding, a dharma that is unchanging, and an unconditioned dharma.
You have now skillfully concealed the conditioned marks of the Tathāgata.

Just as a person who has been burned covers their body with a garment out of a sense of shame and modesty, so too does one, through this wholesome mind, give birth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and further become a Brahmā King or a Cakravartin Universal Monarch; not falling into the evil realms, they constantly experience peace and happiness.

You, too, are like this: because you have skillfully concealed the conditioned marks of the Tathāgata, in a future age you will certainly attain the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, be endowed with the eighteen unique qualities, and possess an immeasurable lifespan. You shall no longer abide in birth and death, but constantly experience peace and bliss, and before long you will achieve the state of an Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Cunda! The Tathāgata will later explain this in detail himself. Both you and I shall likewise cover the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) aspects of the Tathāgata.

For the time being, let us set aside both the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); you should promptly offer food according to the occasion. Such an offering as this is the foremost among all offerings."

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās are exhausted from a long journey, one should provide them with whatever they require that is pure and appropriate for the occasion; giving thus swiftly is the very root-seed for fulfilling the dānapāramitā.

Cunda! If there is anyone who would offer a final gift to the Buddha and the Sangha—whether it be much or little, sufficient or insufficient—you should act quickly and take this opportunity, for the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa.
Cunda replied: "Mañjuśrī!
For what reason do you now covet this food, speaking of much or little, sufficient or insufficient, so as to prompt me to give it at this time?"
Mañjuśrī! When the Tathāgata practiced austerities for six years in the past, he was still able to sustain himself; how much more so today for a mere moment? Mañjuśrī!
"Do you truly believe that the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, partakes of this food?
However, I know for certain:
the body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, not a body sustained by food."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as Cunda has said.
Excellent, Cunda!"
"You have already accomplished subtle and wondrous great wisdom and have skillfully entered the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
Mañjuśrī said to Cunda,
"If you consider the Tathāgata to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then the body of the Tathāgata is itself long-lived."
"If one understands it in this way, the Buddha will be pleased.
Cunda replied, "The Tathāgata is not pleased with me alone; he is likewise pleased with all sentient beings."
Mañjuśrī said: “The Tathāgata is fully pleased with you, with us, and with all sentient beings.
Cunda replied:
"You should not say:
'The Tathāgata is pleased.
For that which is called 'pleasure' is, in fact, a perverted conception."
If there is inverted perception, that is birth and death;
where there is birth and death, there are conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī!
Do not say that the Tathāgata is conditioned.
If one were to say that the Tathāgata is conditioned, both I and you would be acting in delusion. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata has no thought of affectionate attachment.

As for such affectionate attachment, it is like a dairy cow that loves her calf; even when she is hungry or thirsty and goes out seeking water and grass, whether they are sufficient or not, she suddenly returns home.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no such thoughts; they regard all beings equally as they do Rāhula. Such a way of thinking is precisely the realm of the Buddhas' wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! It is like a king who, while driving a team of four noble horses, wishes to have a donkey-cart catch up with them; such a thing is impossible.
My relationship with you is likewise: it is impossible for you to exhaustively fathom the subtle, secret, profound, and deep mysteries of the Tathāgata.

Mañjuśrī! It is like the garuḍa, which soars into the void for immeasurable yojanas and looks down upon the great ocean, seeing all the watery creatures—fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, and the various species of dragons—as well as its own reflection. Just as one sees all forms in a clear mirror, ordinary people of little wisdom are unable to fathom what is thus seen.
"I and you, O virtuous one, are likewise unable to fathom the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī said to Cunda, "So it is, so it is;
it is just as you have said."
"I am not ignorant of this matter; I simply wished to test you regarding the affairs of the bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face, and those radiant beams shone upon Mañjuśrī’s body.
Having encountered this light, Mañjuśrī immediately understood its significance and promptly addressed Cunda:
"The Tathāgata has now manifested this auspicious sign; before long, he will surely enter into parinirvāṇa."
"You should now, at this very moment, present the final offering you have prepared to the Buddha and the great assembly.
Cunda, you should know that the Tathāgata’s emission of these various kinds of light is not without cause or condition."
Having heard this, Cunda was choked with grief and remained silent.
The Buddha said to Cunda:
“The time has now come for you to present your offerings to the Buddha and the great assembly; the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa.”
A second and a third time, he did likewise.
At that moment, having heard the Buddha’s words, Cunda raised his voice and wept, speaking with a sobbing throat:
"Alas! Alas! How bitter it is!"
"The world is empty.
He then addressed the great assembly again:
"We should now all together prostrate ourselves with our five limbs touching the ground and, with one voice, entreat the Buddha not to enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Cunda:

"Do not weep so bitterly as to disturb your own mind. You should contemplate this body as being like a plantain tree, a mirage in the heat, a bubble on water, a magical illusion, a city of the Gandharvas, a fragile earthen vessel, a flash of lightning; it is also like drawing lines upon water, a prisoner facing execution, a ripe fruit, a piece of meat; it is like a weaving shuttle that has run out of thread, or like a pestle moving up and down."
"One should contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being like food mixed with poison; the dharmas of the conditioned are full of many faults and afflictions.
Thereupon, Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the Tathāgata does not wish to remain long in this world, how could I not weep?"
Alas, alas! The world is empty and void.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and all sentient beings, remaining long in this world and not entering parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Cunda:
"You should not now speak such words as,
'Out of compassion for me, remain in the world for a long time.'"
"Out of compassion for you and for all beings, I therefore wish to enter nirvana today. Why is this?
Such is the nature of all Buddhas; it is likewise for all conditioned phenomena."
For this reason, the Buddhas have spoken this verse:
"Conditioned phenomena are by nature impermanent;
having arisen, they do not abide; nirvana is bliss."

“Cunda! You should now observe that all conditioned phenomena are mixed; all dharmas are without self, impermanent, and non-abiding. This body has many immeasurable faults and afflictions, just like a bubble on the water.”
"Therefore, you should not weep now.
At that time, Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying, "So it is, so it is;
it is truly as Your Reverence has taught."
Although I know that the Tathāgata’s manifestation of entering nirvāṇa is a skillful means, I cannot help but harbor grief and distress;
yet, upon further reflection, joy arises once more.
The Buddha praised Cunda:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are able to understand that the Tathāgata manifests a skillful means of parinirvāṇa identical to that of ordinary beings."
Cunda! You should now listen:
Just as the śarabha birds all gather together at Lake Anavatapta during the months of spring;
All Buddhas are likewise; they all arrive at this place. Cunda!

You should not now contemplate whether the Buddhas have long lives or short lives. All dharmas are like illusory appearances, and the Tathāgata, being within them, remains unstained by attachment through the power of skillful means.
Why is this? Such is the nature of all Buddhas, Cunda!
I now accept the offerings you have presented, desiring to enable you to cross over and be liberated from birth-and-death and all outflows (*āsrava*).
If any humans or devas offer their final veneration to me here, they shall all attain the fruit of immovability and forever experience peace and happiness.
Why is this? Because I am a field of merit for all sentient beings.
If you also wish to act as a field of merit for all sentient beings, prepare what you intend to give quickly; it is not fitting to delay long.
At that time, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to liberation, Cunda lowered his head, suppressed his tears, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
If I were capable of serving as a field of merit, I would be able to discern whether the Tathāgata is in nirvāṇa or not in nirvāṇa.
As for us now, along with all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, our wisdom is like that of mosquitoes or gnats; we truly cannot measure whether the Tathāgata is in nirvāṇa or not in nirvāṇa.

At that time, Cunda and his retinue were filled with grief and wept; they surrounded the Tathāgata, burning incense and scattering flowers, honoring him with all their hearts. They then took their leave of Mañjuśrī and departed from their seats to prepare the food and utensils.

Chapter Three: Lamentation. In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Chapter Three, "Lamentation": Not long after Cunda had departed, at that moment this earth shook in six ways, and even as far as the Brahma world, it was likewise so.
There are two kinds of earthquakes:
either an earthquake or a great earthquake.
A minor tremor is called an "earthquake."
That which is greatly shaken is called a great earth-quake;
that which has a small sound is called an earth-quake;
that which has a great sound is called a great earth-quake.
When only the earth shakes, it is called an "earthquake";
when the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas all shake, it is called a "great earthquake.
When there is movement in only one direction, it is called an "earthquake."
When it revolves and turns in all directions, it is called a "great earth movement.
A movement is termed an "earth movement";
when such a movement can cause the minds of sentient beings to tremble, it is termed a "great earth movement."
When a Bodhisattva first descends from Tuṣita Heaven to Jambudvīpa, it is called an earthquake of the great earth;
likewise, at his birth, his renunciation, his attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, his turning of the wheel of Dharma, and his parinirvāṇa, it is called an earthquake of the great earth.
"Today the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa; for this reason, this earth shakes so greatly.

When the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans heard these words, the hair on their bodies stood on end, and they wept piteously with one voice, speaking in verse:
"We prostrate to the Teacher, the Tamer of Men; We now entreat you, [do not pass away]."
Far removed from the Sage among Men, we shall forever lack protection.
Now that we see the Buddha enter nirvana, we are submerged in the ocean of suffering;
filled with longing and grief, we are like calves who have lost their mother.
Destitute and without protection, like a suffering patient who,
lacking a physician, follows his own whims and eats what he ought not to eat;
so too are sentient beings afflicted by the disease of the afflictions, constantly harmed by various views.
Far removed from the King of Physicians who is the Dharma, they consume the poison of false teachings.
Therefore, the World-Honored Buddha should not abandon us;
it would be like a land without a sovereign, where the people all suffer from famine.
We are just like this, having lost both our refuge and the flavor of the Dharma.
Now that we hear of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, our minds are bewildered and distracted,
like the great earth shaking, leaving us disoriented as to all directions.
The Great Sage has entered parinirvāṇa; the Buddha-sun has fallen to the earth.
The waters of the Dharma have all dried up; we shall surely die.
With the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, sentient beings suffer extreme anguish.
Just as the son of an elder, having recently lost his parents,
So it is when the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa; If he does not return,
we and all sentient beings Will be entirely without protection or refuge.
When the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, even all the animals are filled with grief and fear;
their hearts are scorched by suffering and affliction.
How could we, on this day, not be sorrowful and distressed?
The Tathāgata casts them aside, Just as one discards mucus or spittle.
Like the sun when it first rises, Its radiance is exceedingly brilliant;
It illuminates itself and, At the same time, destroys all darkness.
The light of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers can remove my suffering and distress;
standing amidst the great assembly, he is like Mount Sumeru.
“World-Honored One!”
It is like a king who begets sons of handsome appearance, whom he constantly cherishes in his heart.
He first teaches them the arts until they have mastered them all, and only then does he abandon them, entrusting them to the *caṇḍālas*.
World-Honored One!

We are today sons of the Dharma; having received the Buddha’s instruction, we have attained right view. We pray that you will not abandon us, for if you were to abandon us, we would be no different from [ordinary] princes.
I only pray that you will dwell for a long time and not enter nirvana.
World-Honored One!
It is like a person who has well studied various treatises, yet develops a sense of fear toward this very treatise.
The Tathāgata is likewise; though he has thoroughly realized all dharmas, he nevertheless gives rise to fear regarding those dharmas.
If the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for a long time, preaching the flavor of the ambrosia to satisfy all beings, then sentient beings would no longer fear falling into the hells.
“World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person newly learning a craft who was seized by officials and confined in a prison.
Someone asked him:”
"What have you received?
he asked. He replied, "I am now experiencing great sorrow and suffering."
"If one attains liberation, one then attains peace and happiness.

The World-Honored One is likewise; for our sake, he practiced various ascetic penances, yet we have not yet escaped the suffering and affliction of birth and death. How, then, could the Tathāgata enjoy peace and happiness?"
“World-Honored One!

It is like a king of physicians who is well-versed in prescriptions and medicines; he teaches his secret formulas exclusively to his own son, and does not teach them to other students who come from outside.”
The Tathāgata is likewise; he alone teaches the most profound and secret treasury exclusively to Mañjuśrī, while neglecting us and failing to show us his compassionate regard.
Regarding the Dharma, the Tathāgata should have no such secrecy or parsimony.

Just as that king of physicians teaches his own son exclusively and does not teach outsiders who come to study with him, the reason that physician cannot teach universally is that he harbors feelings of competition and thus keeps things secret and withheld.
"The mind of the Tathāgata is ultimately free from contention; for what reason, then, do you not grant us such instruction?
We only pray that you will dwell long in this world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!"

It is like an old man, a youth, or one suffering from illness who abandons a broad, level road to travel a perilous path; that perilous path is full of hardships, and they undergo all manner of suffering.
Furthermore, there was another person who, seeing him and feeling pity for him, immediately showed him a level and excellent path.
World-Honored One,
I am just like this.
That which is called "young" is a metaphor for one who has not yet developed the *dharmakāya*;
that which is called "old" is a metaphor for heavy afflictions (*kleśa*);
and that which is called "sick" is an analogy for one who has not yet escaped birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
What is called the "perilous path" is a metaphor for the twenty-five states of existence.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will show us and guide us along the nectar-like true path, remaining long in this world and not entering parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus, do not grieve, lament, or weep like ordinary worldlings, devas, and humans; you should instead apply yourselves with diligent vigor and bind your minds to right mindfulness."

At that time, the devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had said, ceased their weeping; they were like people who, having buried a beloved son after the funeral rites were completed, restrain themselves from crying.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"You all should open your minds; you ought not to grieve so greatly.
Such is the nature of all Buddhas' dharmas; therefore, you should remain silent."
Delighting in heedfulness, guarding the mind with right mindfulness,
and staying far removed from all that is unrighteous, one finds self-comfort and experiences joy.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!..."
If there be any doubts, you should now ask them all.

Whether it be regarding emptiness or non-emptiness, permanence or impermanence, suffering or non-suffering, reliance or non-reliance, departure or non-departure, refuge or non-refuge, constancy or non-constancy, annihilation or eternity, sentient beings or non-sentient beings, existence or non-existence, reality or unreality, truth or untruth, cessation or non-cessation, secrecy or non-secrecy, duality or non-duality—if you have any such doubts concerning these various dharmas, you should now inquire about them. I shall, in accordance with your needs, sever them for you; I shall first preach the Ambrosia for you, and only thereafter enter into Nirvana.
“O bhikṣus! It is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world; it is difficult to obtain a human body;
and it is likewise difficult to encounter a Buddha and give rise to faith.”
To be able to endure what is difficult to endure is also difficult;

to accomplish the prohibitive precepts, making them complete and without deficiency, and thereby attain the fruit of Arhatship—this matter is likewise as difficult as seeking golden sand or the Udumbara flower.
"O bhikṣus! Having escaped the eight difficulties, it is rare to obtain a human body; you who have encountered me must not let this opportunity pass in vain.
Through various ascetic practices in the past, I have now attained such unsurpassed skillful means."
For your sake, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have sacrificed my body, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain.
Therefore, you should not be negligent.
"O bhikṣus! How does one adorn the precious city of the True Dharma?
It is fully endowed with the various treasures of merit, with precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom serving as its walls and moats."
Now that you have encountered this precious city of the Buddha-dharma, you should not take these deceptive and false things.
It would be like a merchant leader who, having reached a city of genuine jewels, takes up shards and rubble and returns home.
"You are just like this: having encountered a precious city, you have taken up counterfeit goods.
You bhikṣus, do not give rise to contentment with an inferior mind; although you have now left the household life, you do not conceive a longing for this Mahāyāna."
"O bhikṣus, although your bodies are clothed in the dyed robes of the kāṣāya, your minds have not yet been imbued with the pure Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
O bhikṣus, although you wander for alms through many places, you have never before sought the food of the Mahāyāna Dharma."
"O bhikṣus, although you have shaved off your hair and beards, you have not yet eliminated the various fetters (saṃyojana) for the sake of the True Dharma. O bhikṣus!
I now truly instruct and exhort you."
I am now present, and the great assembly is in harmony; the Tathāgata’s dharmatā is true and unerring.
Therefore, you all should apply yourselves with diligence, collect your minds, and courageously crush all fetters and afflictions.
Once the sun of the wisdom of the Ten Powers has set, you shall be shrouded by ignorance.
O Bhikṣus! It is like the great earth, with its mountains and medicinal herbs, which exists for the use of sentient beings.
My Dharma is likewise: it gives rise to the exquisite and virtuous flavor of the nectar of Dharma, serving as the excellent medicine for the various diseases of affliction of sentient beings.
I shall now cause all sentient beings, as well as my sons—the fourfold assembly—to dwell entirely within the Secret Treasury;
I too shall likewise dwell therein and enter into nirvana.
What is called the "Secret Treasury"?
It is like the letter *i*: if the three dots are placed side by side, they do not form the letter *i*; if they are placed vertically, they likewise do not form it.
Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara does it form the letter *i*; if the three dots are separated, it cannot be formed either.

I am also like this: the dharma of liberation is not nirvāṇa; the body of the Tathāgata is not nirvāṇa; mahāprajñā is not nirvāṇa; nor is it nirvāṇa for these three dharmas to be distinct from one another.
"I now abide in these three dharmas and, for the sake of sentient beings, am said to enter nirvana, like the worldly letter 'I'.

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was certain to enter nirvana, they were all filled with grief; their body hair stood on end and their tears flowed profusely. Prostrating at the Buddha's feet and circumambulating him countless times, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Please speak quickly of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
World-Honored One!
It is like this: among all the tracks of living beings, the elephant's track is the foremost."
This perception of impermanence is likewise so; it is the foremost among all perceptions.

If there are those who diligently practice it, they will be able to eliminate all craving for the realm of desire, craving for the realms of form and formlessness, ignorance, conceit, and even the perception of impermanence itself.
World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata were to be separated from the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*), he would not now enter into parinirvāṇa;

yet if he were not separated from it, why do you say that by cultivating the perception of impermanence one becomes detached from craving for the three realms, as well as ignorance, pride, and the perception of impermanence itself?
“World-Honored One!
Just as a farmer, during the autumn months, deeply plows his fields to remove weeds, so too is this perception of impermanence:
it can eliminate all craving for the desire realm, craving for the form and formless realms, ignorance, pride, and even the perception of impermanence itself.”
World-Honored One!
It is as if, among all methods of plowing, plowing in autumn is supreme;
and as if, among all footprints, the footprint of an elephant is the most excellent.
"Among all perceptions, that of impermanence is supreme, World-Honored One! It is like a sovereign who,
knowing his life is about to end, grants a general amnesty to all prisoners and those in confinement throughout the realm, allowing them all to be set free before he passes away."
The Tathāgata should now likewise deliver all sentient beings who are bound and confined by ignorance and lack of wisdom, causing them all to attain liberation, and only thereafter enter parinirvāṇa.
"We have not yet attained deliverance; why does the Tathāgata wish to abandon us and enter parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
It is like a person possessed by a ghost who, upon meeting a skilled master of incantations, is cured through the power of those spells."

The Tathāgata is likewise: for the sake of all śrāvakas, he eliminates the demon of ignorance and causes them to dwell securely in dharmas such as the Mahāprajñā and liberation, just like the worldly letter *i*.
“World-Honored One!

It is like a fragrant elephant that has been bound by men; although there may be a skilled trainer, he cannot restrain it. The elephant suddenly snaps its tether and chain, departing at its own will.”
“I have not yet been thus liberated from the bonds of the fifty-seven afflictions; how can the Tathāgata wish to abandon me and enter parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!”
Just as a person suffering from malaria, upon meeting a skilled physician, finds their affliction removed;
so too am I, burdened by many ailments and sufferings, by wrong livelihood, and by the fever of passion.
Although they have encountered the Tathāgata, their illness has not yet been cured, nor have they attained unsurpassed peace, security, and eternal bliss.
Why, then, would the Tathāgata wish to abandon them and enter parinirvāṇa?
“World-Honored One!

It is like a drunken man who is unaware of himself; he does not recognize his kin or strangers, nor his mother, daughter, or sister. Confused and delirious with lustful disorder, his speech is unrestrained, and he lies amidst impurity.”
At that time, there was a skilled physician who gave him medicine and instructed him to take it.
Upon taking it, he immediately vomited; he then recollected his past and felt shame and remorse in his heart, deeply reproaching himself:
"Alcohol is unwholesome and the root of all evils; if one can eliminate and sever it, one will remain far removed from all transgressions."
“World-Honored One! I am also like this;

since time immemorial, I have transmigrated through birth and death, intoxicated by sensual passion and craving the five desires. I perceived those who were not my mother as my mother, those who were not my elder sister as my elder sister, and those who were not my daughter as my daughter; I even conceived the notion of a living being toward that which is not a living being. For this reason, I transmigrate and undergo the suffering of birth and death, just like that drunken man lying amidst impurity.”
"The Tathāgata shall now bestow upon me the medicine of the Dharma, so that I may vomit forth the foul wine of afflictions.
Yet I have not yet attained a mind of awakening; how can the Tathāgata wish to abandon me and enter into parinirvāṇa?"
“World-Honored One!
It is as if someone were to praise the plantain tree for its solidity; such a thing is impossible, World-Honored One.”

Sentient beings are likewise; if one were to praise the self, the person, the sentient being, the life-span, the nourisher, the knower and seer, the agent, or the experiencer as being real, such a thing is impossible.
"We cultivate the perception of non-self in this way.
World-Honored One!
It is like the dregs of fermented liquor, which have no further use."
This body is likewise thus: it is without self and without master.
World-Honored One!
It is like the seven-leaf flower, which has no fragrance.
This body is likewise thus: without self and without master.
We should, in this manner, constantly cultivate the perception of non-self in our minds, as the Buddha has said:
"All phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self; you, monks, should practice this.
Having practiced thus, you will eliminate the conceit of 'I am'; having abandoned the conceit of 'I am,' you shall enter nirvāṇa."
“World-Honored One!
For example, it is impossible for bird tracks to appear in the sky;
likewise, it is impossible for one who can cultivate the perception of non-self to possess various [wrong] views.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have skillfully cultivated the perception of non-self."
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We do not merely cultivate the perception of non-self; we also further cultivate other perceptions, namely, the perception of suffering, the perception of impermanence, and so forth.”
“World-Honored One!
It is like a person who is intoxicated; their mind is dazed and confused, and they perceive all mountains, rivers, cities, palaces, and the sun, moon, and stars as spinning around.”
World-Honored One!

If there are those who do not cultivate the perception of suffering, the perception of impermanence, or the perception of non-self, such persons are not called noble ones; they are full of negligence and wander through the cycle of birth and death.
“World-Honored One!
By these causes and conditions, we have skillfully cultivated such perceptions.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
As for the analogy of the intoxicated person you have just cited, you know only the words but have not yet grasped their meaning.
What is the meaning?
Just as that intoxicated man sees the sun and moon above and, though they do not actually revolve, gives rise to the perception that they are revolving;

so too it is with sentient beings: shrouded by various afflictions and ignorance, they give rise to perverted minds, conceiving of what is non-self as self, the impermanent as permanent, the impure as pure, and suffering as pleasure.

Because they are shrouded by afflictions, although they give rise to this perception, they do not comprehend its true meaning; it is like that intoxicated person who perceives motion where there is no motion.
"Self" (ātman) is the meaning of Buddha;
"permanence" (nitya) is the meaning of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya);
"bliss" (sukha) is the meaning of Nirvana.
"Purity" is the meaning of the Dharma. "O bhikṣus!
How can you say that those who possess the notion of a self are arrogant, conceited, and wander through birth and death?"
If you were to say,
"We also cultivate the perceptions of impermanence, suffering,
and non-self," these three types of cultivation would lack any real meaning.
I shall now explain the superior method for cultivating the three trainings.
To perceive suffering as pleasure and pleasure as suffering is a perverted dharma;
to perceive the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent is a perverted dharma.
To conceive of non-self as self, or to conceive of self as non-self, is a perverted dharma;
to conceive of the impure as pure, or to conceive of the pure as impure, is a perverted dharma.
There are these four kinds of inverted dharmas; such people do not know how to correctly cultivate the various dharmas. O bhikṣus!
You conceive the notion of pleasure within suffering, the notion of permanence within impermanence, the notion of self within non-self, and the notion of purity within impurity.
"In the world there are also permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
in the supramundane there are also permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
As for mundane phenomena, they have words but no meaning."
That which is supramundane possesses both words and meaning. Why is this?
Because worldly dharmas are characterized by the four inversions, one does not know the true meaning.
Why is this so? Because there are inversions of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), inversions of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and inversions of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
Due to these three inversions, people in the world perceive suffering within what is pleasant, the impermanent as permanent, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure; this is called inversion.
Because of their inversions, people in the world know the words but do not know the meaning.
What is meant by "meaning"?
That which is "selfless" is precisely birth and death.
The "I" is the Tathāgata.
The impermanent refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the permanent refers to the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
Suffering refers to all non-Buddhists;
bliss is precisely nirvana.
Impurity refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
"Purity" refers to all the true dharmas possessed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
this is called being non-erroneous.
Because it is non-erroneous, one knows both the words and their meanings.
"If you wish to distance yourself from the four inversions, you should know that permanence, bliss, self, and purity are thus.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught:
"One who is free from the four inversions attains the knowledge of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Since the Tathāgata is now forever free from the four inversions, he has already attained the knowledge of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

If you have already fully realized permanence, bliss, self, and purity, for what reason do you not remain for a kalpa or half a kalpa to instruct us and cause us to abandon the four inversions, but instead abandon us and desire to enter nirvana?
If the Tathāgata would deign to look upon me and grant me instruction, I shall receive it with the utmost sincerity, honor it upon my head, and practice it.
If the Tathāgata were to enter parinirvāṇa, how could I continue to dwell together with this poisonous body and cultivate the holy life?
"We, too, shall follow the Buddha, the World-Honored One, into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should not speak such words."
I now entrust all my unsurpassed, true Dharma to Mahākāśyapa.
This Kāśyapa shall serve as your great reliance.
Just as the Tathāgata serves as a place of reliance for all sentient beings,
so too shall Mahākāśyapa serve as a place of reliance for you all.
For example, when a great king who governs many territories goes on a tour of inspection, he entrusts all matters of state to his ministers.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he has entrusted all the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa.
"You should know this: the previously cultivated perceptions of impermanence and suffering are not the ultimate truth.
It is like those people who, during the springtime, were bathing and playing by boat in a great lake when they lost a lapis lazuli gem, which sank into the deep water."

At that time, all the people entered the water together to search for this treasure; they vied with one another to seize tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and pebbles, each thinking to themselves that they had found a lapis lazuli gem. They joyfully brought them out, only then realizing they were not genuine.
At that time, the precious gem was still within the water; by the power of the gem, the water became entirely clear and transparent.

At that time, there was a wise man among the crowd who, through the power of skillful means, entered the water calmly and slowly, and immediately obtained the pearl.

You monks should not, like those people who each took tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, or gravel for a precious jewel, practice the notions of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity as if they were ultimate truths.
You all should skillfully learn expedient means and constantly cultivate the perception of self,
the perception of permanence, the perception of bliss, and the perception of purity in every place.
Furthermore, you should know that the characteristics of the four dharmas previously practiced are entirely inverted.
Those who wish to cultivate the various perceptions that accord with reality should do so like that wise person skillfully extracting precious jewels— namely,
the perception of self, and the perceptions of permanence, bliss, and purity.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously stated:"
"All phenomena are without self; you should train yourselves in this!

being free from the notion of a self, you will be free from pride."
"One who is free from pride attains entry into Nirvāṇa.
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

You have now skillfully questioned me on this matter in order to sever your own doubts.

There was a physician who was by nature stubborn and dull-witted, yet the king did not discern this and bestowed upon him a generous salary.
In treating various ailments, he used exclusively milk as medicine, nor did he understand the underlying causes of the diseases.

This king could not distinguish whether this physician understood the quality of the milk—whether it was wholesome or unwholesome, beneficial or harmful.

Furthermore, there was a skilled physician who was proficient in the eight branches of medical science, adept at treating various ailments, and well-versed in all prescriptions and medicines; he arrived from a distant land.
At that time, the resident physician did not seek his counsel or instruction, but instead gave rise to arrogance and a mind of contempt.
At that time, the physician of clear insight immediately sought him out as a patron, requesting to take him as his teacher and inquiring after the secret and profound methods of medical treatment.
He said to the former physician, "I now request you, sir, to be my master; I only pray that you will expound and explain them for me."
The old physician replied,
"If you can now serve as my attendant for forty-eight years, only then shall I teach you the medical arts.
At that time, the wise physician immediately accepted his instruction.
"I shall do so; I shall do so. I will serve as a messenger according to my ability.
At that time, the former physician led the visiting physician together into the presence of the king.
At that time, the visiting physician immediately explained various medical prescriptions and other arts to the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know that one must skillfully distinguish these methods: such a method as this can be used to govern a kingdom, and such a method as this can be used to treat illness."

When the king heard these words, he finally realized that the former physician was deluded, ignorant, and lacking in wisdom; he immediately expelled him, ordering him to leave the kingdom’s borders, and thereafter redoubled his respect for the visiting physician.
At that time, the visiting physician thought to himself,
"Now is the very moment to instruct the king.
He then spoke to the king, saying:

If you truly love and cherish me, you should grant me one wish.
The king then replied:
"From this right arm and all other parts of my body, I shall grant you whatever you desire.
The visiting physician said,

What we now seek is that Your Majesty issue a proclamation throughout the entire kingdom:
"From this day forward, it shall no longer be permitted to take the medicinal milk prescribed by the former physician. Why is this?
This medicine is poisonous and harmful because it causes much injury and damage.
If anyone should intentionally take it, their head shall be severed.

Once this lactation-stopping medicine has been administered, there will never again be anyone who dies an untimely death; they shall always abide in peace and happiness, and for this reason, I seek this vow.
The king then replied,
"What you seek is hardly worth mentioning.
He immediately issued a proclamation throughout the entire kingdom:
"None of those who are ill shall be permitted to use milk as medicine; if anyone uses it as medicine, their head shall be cut off.
At that time, the visiting physician compounded various medicines—namely those with pungent, bitter, salty, sweet, and sour tastes—to treat the many illnesses, such that none failed to recover.
Not long thereafter, the king fell ill again and immediately summoned the physician, saying:

The physician, having diagnosed the king's condition, determined that a medicinal preparation of milk was required, and he promptly addressed the king, saying:

"The King now suffers from a fever; he ought to take milk.

If the milch cow does not eat wine dregs, slippery grass, or wheat bran; if her calf is well-trained; if the pasture is neither on high ground nor in low-lying wetlands; if she drinks clear water; if she is not made to run; if she is not kept in the same herd as bulls; and if her food and drink are moderate and her movement and rest are appropriate.
This milk can eliminate all diseases; it is therefore called the wondrous medicine of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Apart from this milk, everything else is termed poisonous and harmful.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King praised him, saying:

Excellent, excellent!"
"From this day forward, I have come to know the milk medicine for its virtues and vices, its excellence and its flaws.
He then immediately consumed it, and his illness was cured.

When the people of the country heard this, they all gave rise to resentment and said to one another:
"Great King! Are you now possessed by a ghost, or are you mad?"
"And yet he deceives us by making us drink milk again!
All the people, harboring resentment, gathered at the king's palace.
The king said:

At that time, the great king and all the people leaped for joy and, with redoubled reverence, made offerings to this physician.
All the sick took the milk medicine, and their illnesses were completely cured.

“O bhikṣus! For specific reasons, I also speak of a self.
This is like a skilled physician who knows well which milk is medicinal and which is not; it is not like the "self" imagined by ordinary people.
Regarding the "self" as conceived by foolish ordinary people, some say it is as large as a thumb, some say it is like a mustard seed, and others say it is like a minute particle.
The Tathāgata’s teaching on the self is not like this at all; therefore, he says that all phenomena are without self, yet in reality, they are not without self.
What is this self?
If there were a phenomenon that was real, true, permanent, sovereign, and a refuge, whose nature is unchanging—this is what is called the self.
Just as that great physician was well-versed in medicinal milk preparations, so too is the Tathāgata;
for the sake of sentient beings, he teaches that within all dharmas there truly exists a self.
You, the fourfold assembly, should practice this teaching in such a manner.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Two.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Three.

‘Whether it be ten years or twenty years, when the business is finished you shall return; upon your return, restore it to me.

World-Honored One!

It is, for example, like a man twenty-five years of age, in the prime of his vigor and handsome in appearance, who possesses abundant wealth and treasures—gold, silver, and lapis lazuli—and whose parents, wife, children, retinue, and kinsmen are all still living.

Because Bodhisattvas are well able to engage in such question and answer, this jewel of the Dharma will endure for a long time, increasing and flourishing for immeasurable thousands of lifetimes, benefiting and bringing peace to sentient beings, just as a strong man receives a deposit entrusted to him by another.
For this reason, it is only the great Bodhisattvas who are able to inquire.
Our wisdom is like that of mosquitoes or gnats; how could we possibly request the profound Dharma of the Tathāgata?
At that time, the śrāvakas remained silent.

My lifespan is immeasurable, and my eloquence in joyful exposition is inexhaustible; you should all inquire as you please regarding either the precepts or the refuges.
A second and a third time, it was likewise.

How does one, regarding this sutra, reach the ultimate further shore?
We pray that the Buddha will reveal its subtle mysteries and speak extensively for the sake of all sentient beings.

how is it that all bodhisattvas are able to perceive the nature that is difficult to see?

I now entreat the Tathāgata, for the sake of all bodhisattvas,

Within all dharmas, there exists entirely the nature of peace and bliss.

the Honored One among two-legged beings, and the wondrous medicine, will explain this to me in detail.
I now wish to inquire about the aggregates, yet I possess no wisdom.
"Even the bodhisattvas who are diligent in effort cannot know such profound realms as these of the Buddhas.

son of good family!

"Kāśyapa! Would that father and that teacher incur the sin of killing?"
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
"Out of affection and with the desire for their accomplishment, and without any ill intent, one who instructs them in this way will gain immeasurable merit.
'Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise; he regards those who destroy the Dharma as equal to his only son.'"

The Tathāgata now entrusts this unsurpassed True Dharma to the kings, ministers, prime ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. These kings and the fourfold assembly should exhort and encourage all those who study, so that they may attain superior morality, concentration, and wisdom.

If there are those who do not study these three categories of Dharma, who are indolent, violate the precepts, or disparage the True Dharma, the king, his ministers, and the fourfold assembly should sternly punish them.
"Good son! Would these kings and the fourfold assembly incur any offense? "No, they would not."
“World-Honored One!
‘Good son! Even these kings and the fourfold assembly have no fault, let alone the Tathāgata.’”
"Good son! The Tathāgata skillfully cultivates such equanimity that he regards all sentient beings as his only child.
Cultivation in this manner is called a bodhisattva cultivating a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, regarding them as his only child."
“Good son!
When a bodhisattva practices this karma in such a manner, they will attain long life and will also be able to skillfully know the events of their past lives.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:
‘If a bodhisattva cultivates a mind of equanimity and regards all sentient beings as being the same as his own children, he shall attain long life.’”
The Tathāgata should not speak such words. Why is this?
It is like a person who, while knowing the Dharma, can preach various teachings on filial piety, yet upon returning home, strikes and hurls tiles and stones at his parents.

Yet these parents are a fertile field of merit, bringing great benefit; they are difficult to encounter and difficult to meet, and thus should be properly honored with offerings. To instead cause them distress and harm is to know the Dharma while one’s words and actions contradict each other.

The words of the Tathāgata are likewise thus: a bodhisattva who cultivates an impartial mind toward sentient beings, regarding them as his own children, shall attain long life, possess knowledge of past lives, abide eternally in the world, and remain subject to no change.
Now, for what reason and by what causal conditions is the World-Honored One’s lifespan so extremely short, as if identical to that of ordinary humans?
Could it be that the Tathāgata harbors thoughts of resentment or aversion toward sentient beings?
“World-Honored One!
What evil karma did you commit in the past, and how many lives did you take, that you have obtained such a short lifespan, not even reaching a hundred years?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Good son! For what reason have you now uttered such coarse words before the Tathāgata?
The Tathāgata is long-lived, the most supreme and excellent among all lifespans; the eternal dharma he has attained is the foremost among all that is eternal.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the Tathāgata attains immeasurable longevity?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son! It is like the eight great rivers:"
First is named Gaṅgā; second, Yamunā; third, Sarayū; fourth, Aciravatī; fifth, Mahī; sixth, Sindhu; seventh, Vakṣu; eighth, Sītā.
Just as these eight great rivers and all the small streams flow entirely into the great ocean,

Kāśyapa, so too do all the great rivers of life among humans, devas, on earth, and in space flow entirely into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s life-span; therefore, the life-span of the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
it is like the Lake Anavatapta, from which the four great rivers flow;
so too is the Tathāgata, who brings forth all life."
Kāśyapa! Just as among all eternal phenomena, space is foremost;
so too is the Tathāgata, being the most supreme among all that is eternal.
Kāśyapa! Just as among all medicines, clarified butter (ghṛta) is foremost;
so too is the Tathāgata, for among all sentient beings, his lifespan is foremost.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the lifespan of the Tathāgata is such as this, he should remain for a full kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, constantly proclaiming the wondrous Dharma like the pouring down of great rain.”
“Kāśyapa! You should not now conceive the notion of extinction regarding the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa!”

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or even non-Buddhist practitioners who have attained the five supernatural powers and mastery, remaining for a kalpa or less than a kalpa, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down freely in mid-air, emitting fire from their left side and water from their right side, with smoke and flames issuing from their bodies like a mass of fire; [they all fall under my power].
If one wishes to remain in this life, one can attain it according to one's will, having mastery over the length or brevity of one's lifespan.

If even those with these five supernormal powers can thus exercise such sovereign spiritual power at will, how much more so the Tathāgata, who has attained mastery over all phenomena—could he not remain for half an eon, or one eon, or a hundred eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or even immeasurable eons?
For this reason, you should know that the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma and an unchanging dharma.

This body of the Tathāgata is a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), not a body sustained by various foods; it manifests as being like a poisonous tree in order to deliver sentient beings, and for this reason, he appears to relinquish it and enter nirvana.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Buddha is the eternal Dharma, the unchanging Dharma.
Within this ultimate truth, you should apply yourselves with diligent effort and cultivate it with a single-minded focus;
having cultivated it, you should explain it extensively for the sake of others.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is the distinction between the supramundane Dharma and mundane dharmas?"
As the Buddha has said:
"The Buddha is the eternal dharma, the unchanging dharma.
The world also says:
"Brahmā is eternal, and Maheśvara is eternal and unchanging;
the self is eternal, nature is eternal, and even atoms are eternal.
If it is said that the Tathāgata is an eternal dharma, for what reason does the Tathāgata not manifest eternally?
If they do not manifest constantly, what difference is there?
Why is this so? Because from the Brahmā realm down to the subtlest atom, even the primordial nature (*pradhāna*) does not manifest.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Suppose, for example, there is an elder who has many cows; though they are of various colors, they form a single herd. He entrusts them to a cowherd, instructing him to let them graze by water and grass, solely for the sake of the *mṛdvīkā* (cream-of-ghee), and not seeking milk or curd."
That cowherd, having milked them, would eat it himself.
When the elder passed away, all his cattle were plundered by a band of thieves.
Having obtained the cattle, the thieves had no women with them; they themselves milked and squeezed the cows, and having obtained the milk, they ate it.
At that time, the bandits said to one another:
"That great elder keeps this cow not for the sake of milk or curd, but solely for the sake of the clarified butter (ghṛta)."
"What means should we now employ to obtain it?
For *amṛta* (clarified butter) is called the foremost and most excellent flavor in the world.
We lack the vessel; even if we were to obtain the milk, we would have no place to store it."
They further said to one another, "Only a leather bag can contain it.
Although there was a place to hold it, they did not know how to churn it; even liquid butter (maṇḍa) was difficult to obtain, let alone fresh butter (navanīta).
At that time, the thieves added water to the *sarpis* (clarified butter) for the sake of the *sarpis*.
Because of the excess of water, the milk, the curd, and the *sarpis* were all lost together.
It is the same with ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*): although they possess wholesome dharmas, these are all merely remnants of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.

Why is this? After the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa, those who secretly steal the Tathāgata’s remaining wholesome dharmas—whether they be precepts, concentration, or wisdom—are like those bandits who plunder a herd of cattle.
Although ordinary persons may attain this morality, concentration, and wisdom, they lack skillful means and thus cannot achieve liberation.

For this reason, they are unable to obtain the eternal morality, eternal concentration, and eternal wisdom-liberation; they are like those bandits who, not knowing the skillful means, lost the clarified butter.
Furthermore, it is like a band of thieves who, for the sake of obtaining clarified butter (*sarpis*), add water to it.

Ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) are likewise: for the sake of liberation, they speak of a self (*ātman*), a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-span (*jīva*), a person (*pudgala*), Brahmā, Maheśvara, atoms (*paramāṇu*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as liberation (*vimukti*), and claim that the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is itself *nirvāṇa*. Yet in reality, they do not attain liberation or *nirvāṇa*, just as those thieves did not obtain the clarified butter.

These ordinary worldlings possess a small measure of pure conduct and provide for their parents; by these causes and conditions, they attain birth in the heavens and experience a small degree of peace and happiness, like that milk into which the bandits added water.

Yet these ordinary persons truly do not know that by practicing even a small amount of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and making offerings to one's parents, one may be reborn in the heavens; nor can they understand precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, or taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
Because they do not know, they speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; yet although they speak of them, they truly do not know them.
Therefore, it is only after the Tathāgata has appeared in the world that he expounds permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Just as when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, by the power of his merit, the bands of robbers retreat and disperse, and no oxen lose their lives.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King entrusts the oxen to a single herdsman who is highly skillful and resourceful."
Through the skillful means of the cowherd, one immediately obtains the *sarpis-manda* (the finest cream).
Because of this *sarpis-manda*, all sentient beings are free from affliction and suffering.

When the Holy Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, those ordinary persons who are unable to expound upon precepts, concentration, and wisdom are abandoned by him, like thieves who retreat and scatter.
At that time, the Tathāgata skillfully expounded both worldly dharmas and world-transcending dharmas.
For the sake of sentient beings, he caused the bodhisattvas to propagate these teachings according to the capacities of others.

Having themselves attained the *amṛta* (the supreme essence), the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas further enabled immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to universally obtain the unsurpassed flavor of the Dharma of ambrosia—namely, the Tathāgata’s permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*).
For this reason, son of good family, the Tathāgata is eternal and a phenomenon that does not change;
he is not like the Brahmā and other deities whom worldly, ordinary, and foolish people claim to be eternal phenomena.
This eternal Dharma is designated as the Tathāgata, and not any other dharma.
Kāśyapa, you should understand the body of the Tathāgata in this way.
“Kāśyapa! All sons and daughters of good family should constantly bind their minds to the cultivation of these two words: ‘The Buddha is eternally abiding.
Kāśyapa!”
If there are good sons or good daughters who cultivate these two words, you should know that such persons follow my practice and reach the place I have reached.
Good sons!
If there are those who cultivate these two characters as the mark of cessation, you should know that for such persons, the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
Good son!
"The meaning of nirvana is precisely the dharma-nature of all Buddhas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of the 'nature of the Buddha-dharma'?
World-Honored One!
I now wish to know the meaning of the nature of dharmas; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will explain it in detail."
Now, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is precisely the relinquishing of the body.
That which is the relinquishing of the body is called "non-existence.
If there is non-existence, how could the body persist?
If the body still exists, how can you say that the body possesses the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*)?
If the body possesses the nature of dharmas, how could it continue to exist?
How should I now understand this meaning?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: “Good son,
you should not now speak in such a manner.”
"It is said that 'this dharma-nature is extinguished.
Now, dharma-nature itself is without extinction.
Good son!"
For example, in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva), beings possess the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) yet lack the perception of form;
one should not ask, "How do these devas dwell, experiencing joy and pleasure?"
"What is the nature of their mental formations?
What is their seeing and hearing? "Good son!
The realm of the Tathāgata is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
O son of good family!
One should not say:
“The body of the Tathāgata is a phenomenon subject to extinction. Good son!
This extinction of the Tathāgata is the realm of the Buddha; it is not something that can be attained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
"Good son!
You should not now speculate as to where the Tathāgata dwells, where he moves, where he sees, or where he delights.
Good son!"
Such meanings as these are not within your knowledge, nor are the various inconceivable skillful means of the Buddhas' Dharma-body.
"Furthermore, good son!
One should cultivate the perception of permanence regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Regarding these three dharmas, there is no perception of difference, no perception of impermanence, and no perception of change.

If one cultivates divergent perceptions regarding these three dharmas, you should know that such persons have no basis for the pure Three Refuges; all their prohibitive precepts will be incomplete, and they shall ultimately be unable to realize the fruits of the enlightenment of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
If one can cultivate the perception of permanence regarding this inconceivable [reality], then there will be a place of refuge.
Good son! It is like how, because of a tree, there is a tree’s shadow.
The Tathāgata is likewise; because he possesses the nature of permanence, there is a refuge, and he is not impermanent.
If one were to say that the Tathāgata is impermanent, then the Tathāgata would not be the place of refuge for all devas and people of the world.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a tree in the darkness, yet no shadow.”
“Kāśyapa! You should not say:
‘There is a tree without a shadow.’”
"It is simply that it cannot be seen by the fleshly eye. Good son!
The Tathāgata is likewise; his nature is eternally abiding and immutable, yet those who lack the eye of wisdom cannot perceive him, just as one cannot see the shadow of a tree in the darkness."
It is just the same when ordinary people, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, say:
"The Tathāgata is a phenomenon that is impermanent."
If one were to say that the Tathāgata is distinct from the Dharma and the Saṅgha, then the three objects of refuge could not be established.
Just as your father and mother are each distinct from one another, they are therefore impermanent.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward, I shall enlighten my parents regarding the three things—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha—which are eternally abiding, and cause them, even unto the seventh generation, to uphold them all.”
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
I shall now train myself in the inconceivability of the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
having trained myself, I shall also extensively expound this meaning for others."
If there are those who cannot believe and accept this, you should know that such people have long cultivated the notion of impermanence; for these individuals, I shall act as frost and hail.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are now well able to protect and uphold the True Dharma; thus protecting the Dharma, you do not deceive others.”
"By virtue of the karmic conditions of the wholesome deed of not deceiving others, one attains long life and the ability to know past lives.
Chapter Five: The Diamond Body The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Five: The Diamond Body At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Kāśyapa: "Good son!
The body of the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding body, the indestructible body, the vajra-body; it is not a body sustained by various foods, but is indeed the Dharma-body.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for such bodies as the Buddha has described, I do not see them at all; I see only bodies that are impermanent, subject to destruction, like dust and earth, and composed of various impurities.”
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is now about to enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do not now say that the body of the Tathāgata is not firm, is subject to destruction, or is like the body of an ordinary person. Good son!

You should know now that the body of the Tathāgata is firm and difficult to destroy for immeasurable billions of kalpas; it is not a human or celestial body, nor a body of fear, nor a body sustained by various foods."
The body of the Tathāgata is no-body; this body is neither born nor extinguished, neither practiced nor cultivated, immeasurable and boundless, leaving no trace.
It is without cognition and without form, ultimately pure, and without movement.
It is without sensation and without volitional formations, neither abiding nor acting.
It is without flavor and without admixture; it is not conditioned, nor is it karma or its fruit;
it is neither practice nor cessation; it is not mind and not mental enumeration. It is inconceivable and eternally beyond deliberation.
It is without consciousness and detached from the mind, yet not detached from the mind. Its mind is equanimous: it is both non-existent and existent, yet non-existent.
Coming and going, yet also coming and going; neither broken nor destroyed, neither interrupted nor severed, neither arising nor ceasing;
neither a master nor a master, neither existent nor non-existent, neither conceptualization nor observation, neither syllable nor non-syllable, neither fixed nor unfixed, and invisible.
Clearly seeing that there is no place yet it is a place, no dwelling yet it is a dwelling, no darkness and no light,
no tranquility yet it is tranquil; this is non-existence, neither receiving nor giving, pure and stainless,
without contention and having severed contention, abiding in non-abiding, neither grasping nor...
It is neither dharma nor non-dharma, neither a field of merit nor a non-field of merit;
it is inexhaustible, not inexhaustible, and free from all exhaustion. It is emptiness, yet free from emptiness; though it does not abide permanently, it is not subject to momentary extinction.
It is without defilement, without words, and free from words; it is neither sound nor...
It is neither spoken nor practiced; it is beyond measure or calculation; it is neither one nor different;
it is neither form nor characteristic, yet adorned with all marks; it is neither courageous nor fearful; it is neither tranquil nor non-tranquil;
it is neither feverish nor non-feverish; it cannot be seen and possesses no perceptible appearance.
“The Tathāgata delivers all sentient beings because there is no delivering;
he liberates sentient beings because there is no liberating;
he awakens sentient beings because there is no awakening.”
He teaches the Dharma according to reality; because there is no duality, it is immeasurable and equal to the unequaled.
It is level as space, devoid of form or appearance, identical in its nature of non-arising, neither annihilated nor eternal.
The Tathāgata’s body has accomplished such immeasurable merits as these:

it constantly practices the One Vehicle, yet sentient beings perceive three; it is non-retrogressive and non-revolving, having severed all fetters; it neither battles nor contends; it is neither nature nor abiding in nature; it is neither joined nor dispersed; it is neither long nor short, neither round nor square; it is neither the aggregates, bases, and elements, nor yet the aggregates, bases, and elements; it is neither increasing nor diminishing, neither victorious nor defeated. Thus is the body of the Tathāgata perfected.

"There is no one who knows, yet no one who does not know; there is no one who sees, yet no one who does not see. It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither mundane nor non-mundane; neither created nor uncreated; neither dependent nor independent; neither the four great elements nor not the four great elements; neither caused nor uncaused; neither a sentient being nor not a sentient being; neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa. This is the Lion, the Great Lion. It is neither body nor not-body, and it is ineffable. With the exception of the single characteristic of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa), which cannot be calculated, at the time of parinirvāṇa, he does not enter parinirvāṇa. Thus are all the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and its immeasurable, subtle, and wondrous merits fully accomplished."
Kāśyapa! Only the Tathāgata knows this mark; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. "Kāśyapa!"
Such merits constitute the body of a Tathāgata; it is not a body nourished by various kinds of food.
Kāśyapa, since the merits of the true body of a Tathāgata are thus, how could it ever suffer from various ailments and pains, being fragile and unstable like a vessel of unbaked clay?
Kāśyapa! The reason the Tathāgata manifests the suffering of illness is because he wishes to discipline and subdue all sentient beings.
O son of good family!
You should now know that the body of the Tathāgata is a diamond body (*vajrakāya*).

From this day forward, you should always single-mindedly contemplate this meaning; do not think of it as a body sustained by food, and you should also explain to others that the body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Tathāgata has accomplished such meritorious virtues, how could his body be subject to the suffering of illness or the destruction of impermanence?”

From this day forward, I shall constantly contemplate that the body of the Tathāgata is eternal, the Dharma-body, and the body of bliss; furthermore, I shall expound upon it in this manner extensively for others.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is adamantine and indestructible, yet we do not yet know what its cause is.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“By virtue of the causes and conditions of being able to protect and uphold the True Dharma, one attains this adamantine body.
Kāśyapa! Through the causes and conditions of protecting the Dharma in the past, I have now attained this adamantine body, which is eternally abiding and indestructible.”
"Good son!

Those who protect and uphold the True Dharma, even if they have not received the five precepts nor cultivated dignified deportment, should carry swords, blades, bows, arrows, spears, and lances to guard and protect bhikṣus who maintain pure precepts."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bhikṣu who is free from protection and dwells alone in a secluded place, among tombs or at the foot of a tree, one should say that such a person is a true bhikṣu.”
"If there are those who travel followed and guarded by attendants, you should know that such people are merely shaven-headed householders.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do not speak such words, saying:"
“Shaven-headed householder!

If there is a bhikṣu who, wherever he goes, takes only what is sufficient for his own sustenance, recites and studies the sūtras, reflects upon them while practicing seated meditation, and when someone comes to ask about the Dharma, he explains it for them—namely, the merit of giving, observing the precepts, having few desires, and knowing contentment.”
Although he is able to preach the Dharma in such various ways, he is nevertheless unable to let out the lion’s roar, is not surrounded by lions, and cannot subdue those who are unrighteous and evil.
Thus, a bhikṣu who cannot benefit himself nor benefit sentient beings should be known as one who is indolent and lazy.
Although he may be able to uphold the precepts and guard pure conduct, it should be known that such a person is incapable of accomplishing anything.

"If there is a bhikṣu whose requisites for sustaining the body are also always abundant, who is further able to guard and uphold the precepts he has received, and who can roar the lion’s roar by extensively expounding the sublime Dharma—namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, and avadānas—and thus extensively explains these nine divisions of the scriptures to others."
For the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, he uttered these words:
“In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is ordained that bhikṣus must not keep slaves, oxen, sheep, or any other improper things; if there is a bhikṣu who keeps such impure items, he should be disciplined.”
