The Tathāgata previously stated in a different sūtra that there were bhikṣus who possessed such unrighteous items; a certain king governed them according to the law, driving them out and forcing them to return to lay life.

"If there should be a bhikṣu who can utter such a lion’s roar, and if those who have broken the precepts hear these words, they will all together become enraged and seek to harm this Dharma-preacher."
Even if this preacher of the Dharma should eventually pass away, he is nonetheless called one who upholds the precepts for the benefit of both self and others.
For these reasons, I authorize rulers, ministers, high officials, and all lay devotees (upāsakas) to protect those who preach the Dharma.
If there are those who wish to protect the True Dharma, they should train themselves in this way. Kāśyapa!
Those who thus break the precepts and do not protect the Dharma are called "shaven-headed householders."
One who does not uphold the precepts cannot obtain such a name. "Good son!

In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in this city of Kuśinagara, named Saṃtoṣavardhana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."

At that time, the world was vast, majestic, and pure; it was abundant, prosperous, peaceful, and secure. Its population was flourishing, free from hunger and thirst, like the various bodhisattvas in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, remained in the world for immeasurable time; having brought sentient beings to transformation, he subsequently entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
After the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, his bequeathed Dharma remained in the world for immeasurable billions of years.

Forty years later, before the Buddha-dharma had yet perished, there was a precept-observing bhikṣu named Jue-de (Jñānaśrī), who was surrounded by a great multitude of disciples and followers. He was able to roar the lion’s roar, proclaiming and extensively expounding the ninefold canon, and he established rules forbidding bhikṣus from keeping slaves, oxen, sheep, or any other improper things.
At that time, there were many precept-breaking bhikṣus who, upon hearing these words, all conceived evil intentions and seized swords and staves to threaten this Dharma-preacher.

At that moment, there was a king named Yǒudé (Possessing Virtue) who, having heard of these events, went immediately to where the preacher of the Dharma was for the sake of protecting the Dharma; he engaged in fierce combat with those wicked, precept-breaking bhikṣus, enabling the preacher of the Dharma to escape harm.
At that time, the king’s entire body was pierced by spears.
Then, Jue-de immediately praised the king, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You are now truly a protector of the True Dharma; in a future age, this body shall become an immeasurable vessel for the Dharma.
When the king heard this teaching, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately passed away to be reborn in the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya, becoming that Buddha’s foremost disciple.

The king, along with his retinue, the people, and his kinsmen—whether they were warriors or those who followed with joy—all attained non-retrogression from the bodhicitta and, at the end of their lives, were all reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha.
After his life comes to an end, the bhikṣu Jñānaguṇa will likewise attain rebirth in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha, becoming the second disciple among that Buddha’s assembly of śrāvakas.
"If there is a time when the True Dharma is about to perish, one should uphold and protect it in this manner.
Kāśyapa! At that time, the king was none other than myself."
The bhikṣu who preached the Dharma was Kāśyapa Buddha. Kāśyapa!
Those who protect the True Dharma obtain such immeasurable rewards as these.
“By these causes and conditions, I have today attained various marks with which to adorn myself, and have accomplished the Dharma-body and the indestructible body.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The eternal body of the Tathāgata is like an inscription carved in stone.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."
For these reasons, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās should diligently protect and uphold the True Dharma; the karmic fruit of protecting the Dharma is vast and immeasurable.
"Good son!
For this reason, lay followers who protect the Dharma (upāsakas) should take up swords and staves to guard such bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma.
If there are those who merely receive and maintain the five precepts, they cannot be called people of the Mahāyāna."
One who does not receive the five precepts, yet for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, is called a follower of the Mahāyāna.
One who protects the True Dharma should carry swords, blades, and weapons to serve and guard the Dharma Master.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If bhikṣus associate as companions with such upāsakas who carry swords and staves, do they still have a teacher?”
Is he without a teacher?
Is he one who upholds the precepts,
or is he one who violates them?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do not say that these people are those who have broken the precepts. Good son!
After my parinirvāṇa, in an age of turbidity and evil, the lands will be desolate and in chaos, with people plundering one another and the populace suffering from hunger.
At that time, many will resolve to leave the household life for the sake of escaping hunger; such persons are called "bald men."
When these shaven-headed ones see a pure bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, is endowed with dignified deportment, and protects the True Dharma, they drive him out, or even kill or harm him.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should those who uphold the precepts and protect the True Dharma travel through villages, towns, and cities to teach and transform others?”
“Good son! For this reason, I now permit those who uphold the precepts to rely upon laypeople who carry swords and staves as their companions.
If kings, ministers, elders, or upāsakas carry swords and staves for the sake of protecting the Dharma, I declare that such persons are called ‘upholders of the precepts.’”
"Even if one holds a sword or a staff, one should not take life.
If one can act in this way, one is called the foremost in upholding the precepts. Kāśyapa!"

Now, those who protect the Dharma are said to possess right view and are able to widely proclaim the Mahāyāna sūtras; they never hold royal parasols, oil flasks, grains, or various fruits and melons, nor do they draw near to kings, ministers, or elders for the sake of profit and sustenance.

One who is free from flattery and crookedness toward all donors, maintains perfect dignified conduct, and subdues those evil persons who violate the precepts—such a person is called a teacher who upholds the precepts and protects the Dharma.
He is able to serve as a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings, his mind vast and expansive like the great ocean.

"Kāśyapa, if there is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma to others for the sake of gain and offerings, the disciples and followers in his retinue will likewise emulate that teacher in their greedy pursuit of gain and offerings; in this way, such a person brings about the ruin of his own assembly."
“Kāśyapa, there are three kinds of assemblies:
first, the assembly of those who violate the precepts; second, the assembly of the ignorant; and third, the pure assembly.”
A monastic community that is corrupt through broken precepts is easily destroyed;
however, a pure monastic community that upholds the precepts cannot be destroyed by the causes and conditions of material gain.
What is meant by a monastic community that is corrupt through broken precepts?

If there is a bhikṣu who, although upholding the prohibitive precepts, for the sake of gain and offerings sits, rises, walks, or comes together with those who have broken the precepts, associating closely with them and sharing in their activities, this is called breaking the precepts and is also called being a "mixed" monk.
What is the deluded Saṃgha?

If there is a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya who has dull faculties, is dark-minded, obtuse, and bewildered, yet practices few desires and begs for alms; if on the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and at the time of the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), he instructs his own disciples to perform pure confession, but when seeing non-disciples who have frequently violated the prohibitions, he is unable to instruct them to perform pure confession, and instead proceeds to recite the precepts and hold the *pravāraṇā* together with them—this is called the deluded Saṃgha.
What is meant by the "pure Saṃgha"?

There is a community of bhikṣus whom hundreds of thousands of billions of māras cannot destroy. This assembly of bodhisattvas is pure by nature; they are able to harmonize the two aforementioned groups and cause them all to dwell securely within the pure assembly. Such individuals are called unsurpassed great masters who protect the Dharma and are skilled upholders of the Vinaya.

“Desiring to discipline and benefit sentient beings, he knows whether the characteristics of various precepts are light or heavy; that which is not the Vinaya he does not realize or know, while that which is the Vinaya he does indeed realize and know.”
What is meant by "taming sentient beings"?

It refers to when bodhisattvas, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, constantly enter villages without regard for the time or season; they may even stay together with widows or courtesans in their dwellings for many years.
If that which is improper for a śrāvaka to do is instead called "subduing and benefiting sentient beings," how is one to know what is grave?
It is when one sees that the Tathāgata has established a precept due to a specific incident, saying: "From this day forward, you must be careful not to transgress it again."

Just as the four grave prohibitions are things that those who have left the household life ought not to commit, yet one who intentionally commits them is neither a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya; this is what is called "grave."
What constitutes a light offense?
If one commits a light matter and, after being thus admonished three times, is able to relinquish it, this is called "light.
Regarding "not associating with those who do not testify to the Vinaya": if there are those who praise and advocate for the use of impure things, one should not dwell together with them.

Regarding those who should be certified in this Vinaya: they have studied the precepts well, do not associate with those who break them, and feel joy in their hearts upon seeing conduct that accords with the Vinaya.
Thus, they are able to understand what has been enacted in the Buddha-dharma and are skilled at explaining it; such a person is called a Vinaya Master.
It is the same for one who skillfully understands a single word or skillfully upholds the sūtras.
Thus it is, son of good family:
the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and inconceivable.
“The Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
It is so, it is so; it is truly as the holy teaching declares.
The Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and inconceivable;
the Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable.
"Therefore, know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, indestructible, and without change.
Having now learned this well, I shall also extensively proclaim this meaning for others.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
The body of the Tathāgata is the indestructible vajra-body; a bodhisattva should train well in this manner, with right view and right knowledge.”
If one can thus understand and perceive with clarity, this is precisely to see the Buddha’s vajra-body, the indestructible body, like seeing various forms and images within a mirror.

Chapter Six: On the Merit of Names. At that time, the Tathāgata again addressed Kāśyapa: "Good son! The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Six: On the Merit of Names. At that time, the Tathāgata again addressed Kāśyapa: "Good son!"
"You should now properly uphold the words, phrases, and all the merits of this sutra.
It is impossible for any son or daughter of good family who hears the name of this sutra to be reborn in the four miserable realms."
Why is this? Such a sūtra as this is that which has been practiced by immeasurable and boundless Buddhas; I shall now describe the merit thereby obtained.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this sutra be named?”
"How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This sutra is named 'Mahāparinirvāṇa'; its beginning is excellent, its middle is excellent, and its end is excellent."
The meaning is profound and the phrasing is excellent.
It is purely complete and perfect, containing the pure Brahma-conduct; it is a treasury of vajra-jewels, full and without deficiency.
Listen well and attentively, for I shall now speak.
Good son! That which is called "great" is termed "eternal.
It is like the eight great rivers, all of which flow back to the great ocean.

This sutra is likewise: having subdued all fetters, afflictions, and the nature of all Māras, it subsequently requires the relinquishing of body and life in Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is named "Great Parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! It is also like a physician who possesses a secret formula that encompasses all medical arts. Good son!”

The Tathāgata is likewise; all the various sublime dharmas and the secret, profound, and deep treasuries of teachings he has expounded all enter into this Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is named Great Parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! It is like a farmer who, when sowing seeds in the spring months, always harbors expectations; yet once the fruit is harvested, all those expectations come to rest. Good son!”

All sentient beings are likewise: while practicing and studying other sūtras, they constantly crave their flavors; yet if they hear this Mahāparinirvāṇa, their longing for all the flavors found in those other sūtras is forever severed.
This Great Nirvana enables sentient beings to cross over the various streams of existence.
"Good son! Just as among all footprints, the elephant's footprint is the foremost;
This sutra is likewise the foremost among all sutras and samādhis.
Good son! It is like plowing a field; autumn plowing is the most excellent.
This sutra is likewise the most excellent among all sutras.

Good son! Just as among all medicines, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is the foremost for effectively curing the feverish afflictions and the distracted minds of sentient beings; so it is with this sutra.
This Great Nirvana is the most supreme. "Good son!
It is like sweet ghee, which is endowed with eight flavors;
The Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise thus, being fully endowed with eight flavors.

What are these eight? First, permanence; second, constancy; third, peace; fourth, coolness; fifth, freedom from aging; sixth, freedom from death; seventh, freedom from defilement; eighth, bliss. These are the eight flavors.
It is endowed with eight flavors; therefore, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others dwell securely within this, they are further able to manifest parinirvāṇa in various places; therefore, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.

“Kāśyapa! If good sons and good daughters wish to attain parinirvāṇa through this Great Parinirvāṇa, they should all train in this way: that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, and so too are the Dharma and the Saṃgha.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
The merits of the Tathāgata are inconceivable."
The Dharma and the Sangha are likewise inconceivable;
this Great Nirvana is also inconceivable.
If there are those who cultivate and study this sutra, they will attain the gateway to the True Dharma and be able to act as a skilled physician.
If they have not yet studied, you should know that such persons are blind and lack the eye of wisdom, being shrouded by ignorance.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
The Sòng dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán and others supplemented this based on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Chapter Seven: The Four Marks (Catur-lakṣaṇa-varga), Part One.
The Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa:
“Good son! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva analytically reveals that the Great Parinirvāṇa has four aspects of meaning.
What are these four?
First, being correct oneself; second, correcting others; third, being able to answer according to questions; and fourth, skillfully understanding the meaning of causes and conditions.
"Kāśyapa!..."
What is meant by "correcting oneself"?
It is when the Buddha-Tathāgata perceives various causes and conditions and speaks accordingly.
For example, it is like a bhikṣu who, seeing a great mass of fire, speaks these words:
"I would rather embrace this blazing mass of fire than ever dare to slander the twelve divisions of the sutras and the secret treasury taught by the Tathāgata, saying:
'These sutras were spoken by Māra.'"
If one says, "The Tathāgata,
the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are impermanent," speaking in such a manner is to deceive oneself and also to deceive others.
"It would be better to cut out one's own tongue with a sharp blade than ever to say:
'The Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are impermanent.
Even if one hears others say this, one should not believe or accept it; rather, one should feel compassion for those who speak such words."
"The Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are inconceivable; one should uphold them as such. To regard one's own body as being like a mass of fire is called 'self-correction. Kāśyapa!"
What is meant by "correcting others"?

When the Buddha was preaching the Dharma, there was a woman nursing an infant who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and having something on her mind, she sat to one side after reflecting within herself.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the answer, asked intentionally:
"Out of affectionate concern, you gave the child much ghee to consume, without considering whether he could digest it or not.
Then the woman addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
You have skillfully known the thoughts within my mind. I only pray that the Tathāgata will instruct me as to how much [I should give].
World-Honored One!"
"Today at dawn, I gave my son much ghee; fearing he might not be able to digest it, I worry that his life may be cut short prematurely.
I pray only that the Tathāgata will explain this for me.
The Buddha said:
"What your child eats will be digested immediately, and his lifespan will be increased.
Upon hearing this, the woman’s heart leaped with great joy, and she spoke again:
"The Tathāgata speaks the truth; therefore, I am filled with gladness."

Thus, for the sake of subduing all sentient beings, the World-Honored One skillfully distinguishes and explains what is digested and what is not digested, and he also teaches that all phenomena are without self and impermanent.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, were to first teach that [the self] is permanent, those who have come to receive his transformation would say,
"This Dharma is the same as that of the non-Buddhists," and would immediately depart.
He spoke again to the woman:

"If your child grows up and is able to come and go on his own, then regarding whatever he eats—whether it be easily digested or difficult to digest—the butter you originally provided will no longer suffice."
"My śrāvaka disciples are also like this: just as your infant cannot digest this Dharma of permanence, for that reason I previously taught suffering and impermanence."
If my śrāvaka disciples have fully prepared their merit and are capable of practicing the Mahāyāna sūtras, I shall expound for them in this sutra the six flavors.
What are the six flavors?

It is said that suffering is the flavor of bitterness, impermanence is the flavor of saltiness, non-self is the flavor of pungency, pleasure is the flavor of sweetness, self is the flavor of acridity, and permanence is the flavor of blandness.

In that world there are three kinds of flavors, namely: impermanence, non-self, and suffering. Taking the afflictions as firewood and wisdom as fire, these causes and conditions produce the food of nirvana—namely, permanence, bliss, and self—which causes all disciples to relish it with delight.
He further addressed the woman:
"If you have business that requires you to go elsewhere, you should drive out the wicked sons from the house and entrust the entire treasure store to the good son."
The woman said to the Buddha, "It is truly as the Holy One has taught: a treasury of precious jewels should be shown to a good son, not to a wicked son.
"Sister! [the Buddha replied.]
I am also like this.

At the time of my parinirvāṇa, I shall not bestow the subtle, secret, and unsurpassed Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata upon the śrāvaka disciples, just as you did not show your treasure-store to your unworthy son;
rather, I must entrust it to the bodhisattvas, just as you entrusted your treasure-store to your worthy son.
Why is this? Because the śrāvaka disciples give rise to the notion of change, thinking that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has truly entered parinirvāṇa, whereas I have not truly entered parinirvāṇa.
Just as when you have traveled far and have not yet returned, your wicked son says that you are dead, though you are in fact not dead;
so too do the bodhisattvas declare:
"The Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging."
"Just as your good sons do not say that you have died,
for this reason, I entrust this unsurpassed secret treasury to the bodhisattvas. "Good son!
If there are sentient beings who say that the Buddha is eternally abiding and unchanging, you should know that in their household there is a Buddha; this is called correcting others.
"Kāśyapa!..."
What is meant by "being able to respond appropriately to questions"?
Suppose someone were to come and ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
"How should I act so that, without relinquishing wealth or property, I may be called a great donor and patron (mahādānapati)?"
The Buddha said:
"If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who have few desires and are content, who do not receive or keep impure things, one should give them slaves and servants;
to those who practice the pure life (brahmacarya), one should give women."
To those who abstain from wine and meat, he gives wine and meat;
to those who do not eat past midday, he gives food past midday;
to those who do not wear flowers or perfumes, he gives flowers and perfumes.
"Such a donor’s fame for giving spreads abroad and their reputation resounds throughout the world, yet they have never suffered even a hair’s breadth of personal expense.
This is what is called being able to answer according to the question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
One should not give meat to those who eat meat."
"Why is this? Because I see that those who do not eat meat possess great merit.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have now been able to well understand my intention; a Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma should act in this way.
Son of good family!”
From this day forward, I do not permit my śrāvaka disciples to eat meat.
When receiving offerings of food from donors with faith, you should regard such food as being like the flesh of your own child.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why does the Tathāgata not permit the eating of meat?”
“Good son! Those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Why did the Tathāgata previously allow bhikṣus to eat the three kinds of pure meat?
"Kāśyapa! These three kinds of pure meat were permitted as a gradual regulation according to circumstances."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions do you not permit the ten kinds of impurity, up to and including the nine kinds of purity?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This, too, was established gradually according to circumstances; you should know that this is precisely the meaning of the present prohibition against eating meat.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the Tathāgata praises fish and meat as fine foods? "Good son!
I do not say that things such as fish and meat are fine foods."
I declare that sugarcane, non-glutinous rice, rock honey, all grains and wheat, as well as dark stone honey, milk, curd, and clarified butter constitute excellent foods.
"Although it is said that one should keep various kinds of clothing, those things which should be kept must be of dyed colors; how much more so regarding the attachment to the taste of fish and meat?
Kāśyapa spoke again:

"If the Tathāgata were to prohibit the eating of meat, then those five kinds of flavors—milk, curd, whey, fresh butter, and clarified butter—as well as sesame oil, and furthermore, various garments such as *kauśeya* silk, shells, leather, and vessels of gold and silver—none of these items should also be accepted."
“Good son! You should not share the views of those Nirgranthas.
Each of the prohibitions established by the Tathāgata has its own underlying intention; because of these differing intentions, he permitted the eating of the three kinds of pure meat.”
Because of these various perceptions, ten kinds of meat are forbidden;
because of these various perceptions, all [meat] is forbidden, including that from animals that have died of natural causes. Kāśyapa!
"From this day forward, I decree that my disciples shall no longer eat any kind of meat. Kāśyapa!
For those who eat meat—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—all sentient beings, upon smelling the odor of their flesh, will give rise to terror."
For example, suppose there is a person who has drawn near to a lion; when others see him, they become terrified upon smelling the stench of the lion.
"Good son! It is like a person who eats garlic; because it is foul-smelling and loathsome, others who see him will smell the odor and depart."
If even those who see them from afar do not wish to look upon them, how much less would they approach them?

It is the same for all meat-eaters: when all sentient beings smell the odor of their flesh, they are utterly terrified and conceive the thought of impending death; whether they be of water, land, or air, all living creatures abandon them and flee, all saying, "This person is our enemy."

"For this reason, a bodhisattva does not habitually consume meat; rather, in order to deliver sentient beings, he manifests the act of eating meat. Although he appears to eat it, in reality, he does not."
"Good son!
Thus, a bodhisattva does not even consume pure food, much less eat meat. Good son!"
After my parinirvāṇa, when countless hundreds of years have passed, the noble ones of the four paths will all likewise enter parinirvāṇa.

After the extinction of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), during the period of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), there will be bhikṣus who merely possess the outward appearance of upholding the Vinaya and read the sūtras but little; they will be greedy for food and drink, nourishing their own bodies. Their clothing will be coarse, shabby, and ugly; their physical forms will be haggard and lacking in majestic virtue. They will keep and raise cattle and sheep, carry firewood and grass upon their backs, and their heads, beards, hair, and nails will all grow long and unkempt.
Though they wear the kashaya robe, they are like hunters; they observe closely and move slowly like a cat stalking a mouse, constantly proclaiming, "I have attained arhatship.

Afflicted by many illnesses and suffering, they lie amidst filth and excrement; appearing virtuous and good on the outside while harboring greed and envy within, they are like Brahmins who have taken a vow of silence.
In truth, they are not śramaṇas, yet they manifest the appearance of śramaṇas; their false views are rampant, and they slander the True Dharma.

Such persons destroy the precepts, right conduct, and dignified demeanor established by the Tathāgata, while claiming to teach the fruit of liberation. They abandon the impure dharmas and subvert the profound secret teachings, each according to their own whims, contrarily interpreting the sūtras and vinaya, and saying:
"The Tathāgata has permitted us all to eat meat."
Having originated this doctrine themselves, they claim it is the word of the Buddha and engage in mutual disputes, each calling themselves śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya.
"O son of good family!

At that time, there were also various śramaṇas who stored up raw grain, accepted fish and meat, prepared their own food with their own hands, and carried oil flasks, jeweled parasols, and leather sandals. They associated with kings, ministers, and elders; they practiced astrology and physiognomy, diligently pursued the way of medicine, kept male and female slaves, and amassed gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, crystal, pearls, coral, amber, jade, conch shells, and various kinds of fruits and gourds. They studied various arts and crafts—such as painting, masonry, calligraphy, teaching, and horticulture—as well as sorcery, incantations, illusions, the compounding of medicines, performing as actors and musicians, adorning the body with perfumes and flowers, and playing games such as *chūpú* and *wéiqí*, or studying various technical skills.
"If there be a bhikṣu who can remain free from such evil matters as these, I declare that person to be my true disciple.
At that time, Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

“Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās live depending on others. If, while begging for alms, they obtain food mixed with meat, how should they eat it so as to be in accordance with the pure Dharma?”
The Buddha said,
“Kāśyapa! You should wash it with water until it is separated from the meat, and only then eat it.”
If a food vessel has been defiled by meat, provided that it no longer retains the flavor [of meat], its use is permitted and incurs no offense.
However, if one observes that there is much meat within the food, one should not accept it.
One must not eat any meat that is visible; those who eat it incur transgression.

I now proclaim this regulation against eating meat; were I to explain it in detail, it would be inexhaustible. Since the time for *nirvāṇa* has arrived, I have spoken briefly. This is what is called being able to provide answers in accordance with questions.
“Kāśyapa! How does one skillfully understand the meaning of dependent origination?
Suppose the fourfold assembly were to come and ask me:”
“World-Honored One!

Regarding this meaning, why did the Tathāgata, upon his initial appearance in the world, not explain this profound and subtle Dharma-gate to King Prasenajit? Why is it that at times you speak of the profound and at times the shallow, and that what is called an offense at one time is called non-offense at another?”
"What is meant by 'falling' (pāta)?
What is meant by 'discipline' (vinaya)?
And what is the meaning of 'prātimokṣa'?"
The Buddha said:
"Prātimokṣa is called 'contentment,' the accomplishment of dignified deportment, and the state of possessing nothing; it is also called 'pure livelihood.'"
"Falling" refers to the four evil destinies.

Furthermore, "falling" means falling into the hells, even down to Avīci; its swiftness exceeds that of a torrential rain. Those who hear this should be struck with awe and fear, firmly upholding the prohibitions and precepts, not violating the rules of decorum, practicing contentment, and refusing to accept any impure things.
Furthermore, "falling" (pāta) refers to being nourished within the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts;
for these reasons, it is called "falling.
*Prātimokṣa* is the departure from unwholesome and evil actions of body, speech, and mind.

The Vinaya consists of the entry into the precepts and dignified deportment, as well as the profound sūtras and their excellent meanings; it prohibits the acceptance of all impure things and the conditions for such impurity, and likewise prohibits the four pārājika offenses, the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa, the two aniyata dharmas, the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika, the ninety-one pāyattika, the four pratideśanīya dharmas, the numerous śaikṣa dharmas, and the seven adhikaraṇa-śamatha dharmas.
"Furthermore, there may be someone who violates all the precepts.
What constitutes 'all'?
This refers to the four grave offenses (pārājika) up to the seven rules for settling disputes (adhikaraṇa-śamatha)."

Furthermore, there may be those who slander the true Dharma and the profound sutras, as well as icchantikas who have fully accomplished [their ends], for whom all marks have ceased and no causes or conditions exist; such people say of themselves:
"I am clever and of sharp intelligence," while concealing all their offenses, whether light or grave.
They conceal their various evils as a tortoise hides its six limbs; thus, these many transgressions remain unrepented throughout the long night.
Because they do not repent, they increase day and night.
These bhikṣus never disclose the various offenses they have committed, which causes their transgressions to further proliferate and spread.
"Therefore, having understood this matter, the Tathāgata has established the precepts gradually and not all at once.
At that time, a son of good family or a daughter of good family addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata has known such matters for a long time; why did he not establish the prohibitions beforehand?
Could it be that the World-Honored One intends to cause sentient beings to enter the Avīci Hell?
It is like many people wishing to go to another land who lose the correct path and follow a deviant one instead.
Because these people do not know their delusion, they all claim this is the Way; furthermore, they see no one to ask about right and wrong.
Sentient beings are thus deluded regarding the Buddha-dharma and do not perceive what is correct and true. The Tathāgata should first explain the Right Path to them and instruct the bhikṣus:
"This is a violation of the precepts; this is the upholding of the precepts. It shall be regulated in this manner."

Why is this? The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is the one of ultimate truth; he knows and perceives the true path. Only the Tathāgata, the God among Gods, is able to expound the superior merit of the ten wholesome actions and their essential meaning.
"Therefore, we request that you first establish the precepts.
The Buddha said, "Good sons!"
If one says,
"The Tathāgata is able to proclaim for sentient beings the superior merit of the ten wholesome actions," then the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as he does Rāhula.
How can one raise such an objection as:
"Does the World-Honored One perhaps wish to cause sentient beings to enter hell?
If I see even a single person possessing the causes and conditions for falling into the Avīci Hell, I will remain in this world for an eon, or slightly less than an eon, for that person's sake.
I possess great compassion for all sentient beings; for what reason would I deceive those whom I regard as my own children and cause them to enter hell? Good son!
It is like a person within a king’s realm who wears patched robes: only when he sees a hole in the cloth does he then mend it.
The Tathāgata is likewise; seeing that sentient beings possess the causes and conditions for entering the Avīci Hell, he immediately uses the goodness of the precepts to provide for them. Good son!

For example, a Wheel-Turning Sage King first teaches the ten wholesome dharmas to sentient beings; subsequently, as there are those who gradually begin to commit evil, the king suppresses such acts progressively according to the circumstances. Once all evils have been eliminated, he then personally practices the dharma of a sage-king.
Good son! I am also like this:

although I have something to say, I do not establish a precept beforehand; rather, it is only after bhikṣus gradually engage in unrighteous conduct that I subsequently establish a precept according to the specific matter.
Sentient beings who delight in the Dharma practice according to the teachings; it is through such assemblies that one is able to behold the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
Just as the wheel-treasure possessed by a Cakravartin King is inconceivable, so too is the Tathāgata inconceivable.
The two jewels of the Dharma and the Saṃgha are also inconceivable;
those who can expound the Dharma and those who hear the Dharma are all inconceivable.
This is called skillfully understanding the meaning of dependent origination.
“When a bodhisattva thus analytically explains these four kinds of characteristics, this is called the meaning of causes and conditions within the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, ‘correcting oneself’ refers to attaining this Great Parinirvāṇa.”
Regarding "correcting others," Kāśyapa, I have said to the bhikṣus:
"The Tathāgata exists eternally and is unchanging.
This is answering in accordance with the question. Kāśyapa!
Because of your question, I am able to extensively expound upon this profound and subtle meaning for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

Regarding the meaning of causes and conditions: śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not understand such a profound meaning; they have not heard that the three dots of the letter *i* constitute liberation and nirvāṇa, nor that the Mahāprajñāpāramitā constitutes the secret treasury.
I shall now expound and analyze this here to open the eye of wisdom for all śrāvakas.
Suppose someone were to say:
"How can these four matters be one?"
"Is it not false?
One should then counter-question:
"In this emptiness, what difference is there between these four things: non-existence, immobility, and non-obstruction?"
"Could this possibly be called false? "No,
World-Honored One."
"These various phrases all have but one meaning, namely, the meaning of emptiness.

"The same applies to self-correction, correcting others, being able to respond to questions, and understanding the meaning of dependent origination; they are likewise identical to Great Nirvāṇa, without any difference."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who speak thus:
'The Tathāgata is impermanent.'"
How should one know that this is impermanent?
As the Buddha has said:
"The extinction of all afflictions is called nirvāṇa."
"Just as when a fire is extinguished, nothing remains at all;
the extinction of all afflictions is likewise, and for this reason it is called nirvāṇa.
How then can the Tathāgata be an eternally abiding dharma, immutable and unchanging?"
As the Buddha has said:
"That which is free from all modes of existence (bhava) is called nirvāṇa.
Since there is no mode of existence within this nirvāṇa, how can the Tathāgata be a permanently abiding dharma, immutable and unchanging?
Just as when a garment is completely worn out, it is no longer called a "thing," so too with nirvāṇa:
because all afflictions have been extinguished, it is not called a "thing.
How then can the Tathāgata be a permanently abiding dharma, immutable and unchanging?
As the Buddha has said:
"The cessation of desire and tranquility is called nirvana.
It is like a person whose head is severed; once the head is gone, there is no longer a head.
Detachment from desire and the state of quiescence are likewise thus; because they are empty and devoid of anything existent, they are called *nirvāṇa*.
How then can the Tathāgata be an eternally abiding dharma, immutable and unchanging?
As the Buddha said:
"For example, like glowing iron beaten by a hammer, sparks fly out; once scattered, they are instantly extinguished, and their whereabouts can no longer be known."
"Having already crossed over the mire of sensual desire and all states of existence, he has attained the immovable state,
and it is not known where he has gone.
"In what way is the Tathāgata a permanently abiding dharma, unchanging and immutable?"
“Kāśyapa! If anyone raises such an objection, it is called a false objection. Kāśyapa!”
You should not entertain such a thought as that the nature of the Tathāgata is subject to extinction.
Kāśyapa, that which extinguishes afflictions is not called a "thing."
Why is this? Because it is eternally ultimate, it is therefore called "constant.
This phrase is quiescent, unsurpassed, having extinguished all marks without remainder.
This phrase is pure and white, eternally abiding and never regressing.
For this reason, nirvāṇa is called "eternally abiding";
the Tathāgata is likewise, eternally abiding and unchanging.
What is called "the falling of stars" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

That they scatter and are immediately extinguished, such that their location cannot be known, means that once the afflictions of the Tathāgatas have been extinguished, they no longer abide within the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma, free from change or alteration.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
that which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
"Therefore, the Tathāgata is revered and made offerings to;
because the Dharma is eternal, all Buddhas are likewise eternal.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the fire of afflictions were extinguished, the Tathāgata would also be extinguished; thus, the Tathāgata would have no permanent abode.
Just as when those flying sparks of iron, once their red glow has faded, one knows not where they have gone;
so too it is with the Tathāgata’s afflictions: when extinguished, they go nowhere."
Furthermore, just as that iron, once its heat and redness have ceased, no longer exists;
so it is with the Tathāgata: having ceased, he is impermanent. When the fire of the afflictions is extinguished, he enters nirvāṇa; one should know that the Tathāgata is thus impermanent.
“Good son! That which is called ‘iron’ refers to all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Although ordinary persons may extinguish their afflictions (*kleśa*), once they have been extinguished, they arise again; therefore, they are called impermanent.”
The Tathāgata is not like this; once extinguished, he does not arise again, and for this reason he is called "eternal.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"When the red color of iron has been extinguished, if it is placed back into the fire, the red color arises once more."
"If it were so for the Tathāgata, he would have to give rise to fetters again;
if fetters were to arise again, he would be impermanent.
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! You should not now speak such words as:
‘The Tathāgata is impermanent.’”
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is eternal.
O son of good family!
Just as when wood is burned, there remains ash after it has been extinguished;
so too, once the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been extinguished, there is *nirvāṇa*.
The analogies of the ruined garment, the severed head, and the broken jar are likewise. Such things each have their own names, called "ruined garment," "severed head," and "broken jar."
Kāśyapa! Just as iron that has grown cold can be made hot again, it is not so with the Tathāgata;
having severed the afflictions, he is ultimately cool, and the blazing fire of the afflictions shall never arise again.
Kāśyapa, you should know that immeasurable sentient beings are like that iron; with the blazing fire of my untainted wisdom, I burn away the fetters of affliction within those sentient beings.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“Excellent, excellent!
I now truly understand that the Tathāgata has taught that all Buddhas are eternal.”
The Buddha said: “Kāśyapa!
It is like a noble wheel-turning monarch who, while residing in his inner palace, sometimes goes out for recreation in his rear garden.”
"Although the King was not among the court ladies, one could still not say:
'The Holy King has passed away. Good son!"
The Tathāgata is likewise; although he does not manifest within the realm of Jambudvīpa and has entered into nirvana, he is not called impermanent.
Having emerged from immeasurable afflictions, the Tathāgata enters the place of nirvanic peace and bliss, wandering among the flowers of awakening and enjoying joy and happiness.
Kāśyapa asked again:
“As the Buddha has said:
‘I have long since crossed the great ocean of afflictions.’”
"If the Buddha has already crossed the ocean of afflictions, for what reason did he again take Yaśodharā as his wife and father Rāhula?
By this cause and condition, one should know that the Tathāgata has not yet crossed the great ocean of the various fetters of affliction."
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain its causes and conditions.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should not say this:"
"The Tathāgata has long since crossed the great ocean of afflictions; for what reason, then, did he again take Yaśodharā as his wife and father Rāhula?
By this cause and condition, one should know that the Tathāgata has not yet crossed the great ocean of the fetters of affliction."

"Good sons! This Great Nirvāṇa is able to establish the great purpose. You should now listen with a sincere mind and attentively; explain it extensively for others, and do not give rise to alarm or doubt."
If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who dwells in the Great Nirvāṇa, he can take this Mount Sumeru, King of Mountains—so high and vast—and cause it entirely to enter into a mustard seed.
Yet the sentient beings who depend upon Mount Sumeru will not feel any constraint; they will have no perception of coming or going, remaining exactly as they were before, without any difference.
Only those who were ready for deliverance saw this bodhisattva place Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed, and then restore it to its original location. "Good son!
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Nirvāṇa and are able to place a trichiliocosm within a mustard seed.
The sentient beings therein experience no sense of confinement or of coming and going; they remain exactly as they were before, without any difference.
Only those who were ready for deliverance saw this bodhisattva place this trichiliocosm within a mustard seed, and then restore it to its original location.

“Good son! Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Nirvāṇa and are able to take the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system and place it within a single pore, and even the original location remains exactly as it was.

“Good son! Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Nirvāṇa, who take up the worlds of the three thousandfold great thousand-fold universe of the ten directions and place them upon the point of a needle as if threading a jujube leaf, and then cast them into other Buddha-worlds in distant directions.”

Among them, all sentient beings do not perceive their coming and going, nor where they are; only those who are to be delivered can see them, and this is likewise true even regarding their original abodes.

“Good son! Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Nirvāṇa, who take up the various Buddha-worlds of the trichiliocosm throughout the ten directions and place them in their right palm like a potter’s wheel, and then cast them into other worlds as numerous as motes of dust.
Not a single sentient being has the perception of coming or going; only those who are to be delivered perceive it, and even their original locations are likewise so. "Good son!
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa, take up all the immeasurable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions and entirely contain them within their own bodies.

The sentient beings therein do not feel any oppression, nor do they have any perception of coming and going or of dwelling places; only those who are ready to be delivered can perceive this, and it is likewise even as far as their original locations.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Great Nirvāṇa and place the worlds of the ten directions within a single mote of dust.
The sentient beings therein experience no sense of confinement or of coming and going; only those who are ready to be delivered can perceive this, and it is likewise for their original locations.”
“Good son! When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the Great Nirvāṇa, he is able to manifest various and immeasurable supernatural transformations; therefore, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.”

These immeasurable supernatural transformations manifested by this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cannot be fathomed by any sentient being; how then can you now know that the Tathāgata indulged in sensual desire and fathered Rāhula?

“Good son! I have long dwelt in this Great Parinirvāṇa, manifesting various supernatural transformations and miraculous powers. Within this trichiliocosm of ten billion suns and moons and ten billion Jambudvīpas, I manifest these various displays in detail, as extensively explained in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Within this trichiliocosm, or specifically in Jambudvīpa, I manifest parinirvāṇa, yet I do not ultimately undergo final nirvāṇa.
Or, in Jambudvīpa, I enter my mother’s womb, causing her and my father to conceive the thought that I am their son; yet this body of mine is ultimately not born from the union of desire.

For immeasurable kalpas past, I have long been free from craving and desire; this present body of mine is the Dharma-body, which I manifest entering the womb only in accordance with worldly conventions.

"Good son! In this Jambudvīpa, within the Lumbinī Garden, he manifested birth from his mother Māyā; immediately upon being born, he was able to walk seven paces to the east and proclaimed these words:
'I am the most honored and supreme among humans, devas, and asuras.'"
When their fathers, mothers, humans, and devas saw this, they were filled with wonder and joy, giving rise to a sense of rarefied amazement.
These people thought it was an infant, yet my body has long since been free from such states for immeasurable eons.

Such a body is the Dharma-body; it is not established by means of flesh, blood, sinews, veins, bones, or marrow. It is manifested as an infant only in accordance with the ways of worldly sentient beings.
"Stepping seven paces to the south, he manifested his desire to serve as the supreme field of merit for immeasurable sentient beings;
stepping seven paces to the west, he manifested that his births were exhausted, that he had forever severed old age and death, and that this was his final body;
stepping seven paces to the north, he manifested that he had already transcended the cycle of birth and death within all realms of existence."
He took seven steps toward the east, demonstrating that he would act as a guide for all sentient beings.

He took seven steps toward the four intermediate directions, manifesting the severance of the various afflictions and the natures of the four Māras, thereby attaining the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Walking seven steps upward, he manifested that he is not defiled by impure things, being like empty space;
walking seven steps downward, he manifested the rain of Dharma to extinguish the fires of hell, causing those sentient beings to receive peaceful and secure bliss.
To those who violate the prohibitions and precepts, he manifests as frost and hail.
After seven days have passed since his birth in Jambudvīpa, he manifests the shaving of his hair; all people say, "I am but an infant, having only now had my hair shaved for the first time."
Among all humans, devas, Māra Pāpīyas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, there is none who is able to see the mark of my crown; how much less could anyone hold a blade to it to shave my hair?
It is impossible that anyone could come with a blade to my crown;
for immeasurable kalpas I have long since shaved off my beard and hair, yet I manifest this shaving of hair only to accord with the ways of the world.
“Once I was born, my parents took me into a celestial shrine and presented me to Maheśvara.
As soon as Maheśvara saw me, he joined his palms in reverence and stood to one side.”
For immeasurable kalpas, I have long since abandoned such practices as entering celestial shrines; I manifest them in this way only for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions.

"I manifested the piercing of my ears in Jambudvīpa; yet, in reality, there is no one among all sentient beings who can pierce my ears. I manifested this in accordance with the worldly ways of sentient beings."

Furthermore, I have adorned my ears with lion-shaped earrings made of various jewels; however, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have been free from such ornaments, and I manifest them now only to accord with the ways of the world.

"Although I demonstrated entering the schoolhouse to study the scriptures, I have already fully accomplished all perfections throughout immeasurable eons. Having surveyed all sentient beings within the three realms, I found none capable of being my teacher; yet, in order to conform to worldly conventions, I manifested entering the schoolhouse, and for this reason I am called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
My training in riding elephants, horsemanship, wrestling, and various other arts was likewise so.

Furthermore, within Jambudvīpa, I manifested as the crown prince; all sentient beings saw me as a prince, enjoying and delighting in the five desires. Yet, throughout immeasurable eons, I have already renounced such pleasures of the five desires; I manifested these appearances only because I wished to conform to worldly conventions.
"The physiognomist divined of me:
'If you do not leave the household life, you shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja) and rule over Jambudvīpa.
All sentient beings believe these words; however, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King to become a Dharma-Wheel King."

"In Jambudvīpa, having manifested detachment from female attendants and the pleasures of the five desires, and having seen old age, sickness, death, and a śramaṇa, he left the household life to practice the Way."
All sentient beings say:
"Prince Siddhārtha has only now first gone forth into homelessness.
However, I have already gone forth to study the Way throughout immeasurable kalpas; it is only to accord with worldly conventions that I manifest such a display.

"In Jambudvīpa, I manifested the renunciation of the household life, received full ordination, and through diligent cultivation of the Path, attained the fruit of a Stream-enterer, the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, and the fruit of Arhatship."
Everyone said,
"The fruit of Arhatship is easily attained and not difficult. Yet,
I have already realized the fruit of Arhatship throughout immeasurable kalpas.
“Desiring to deliver all sentient beings, I sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree with grass for my seat and subdued the hosts of Māras.

Although everyone says that I have only now begun to subdue the palaces of Māra at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, I have in fact already subdued them for immeasurable kalpas; I manifested this transformation only because I wished to subdue sentient beings who are stubborn and fierce.”

"I further manifest the passing of excrement and urine, as well as exhaling and inhaling breath; all people say that I truly have excrement, urine, exhalation, and inhalation. However, this body of mine, which is the fruition of karmic retribution, is free from such afflictions; it is only to conform to worldly conventions that I manifest these things."
"I further manifest receiving the offerings of the faithful; yet this body of mine is entirely free from hunger and thirst, and I display such things merely to accord with worldly conventions.

I further manifest falling asleep to appear identical to all sentient beings; yet I have, throughout immeasurable kalpas, been fully endowed with unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous wisdom, having long transcended the three realms of existence, and my deportment is majestic and dignified."

"When my head, eyes, belly, back, or entire body were afflicted with pain; when I was struck by wooden spears; when I washed my hands and feet, cleansed my face, rinsed my mouth, or purified myself with *śīrṣapuṣpa* twigs—everyone said that I engaged in such things. Yet this body of mine never had such matters at all; my hands and feet were pure like lotus flowers, and the breath from my mouth was as clean and fragrant as the scent of the *utpala*."
"All sentient beings say, 'I am a human being,' yet I am truly not a human being.
Furthermore, I manifest the wearing of rag-robes, washing, rinsing, and mending them; however, I have long since had no need for such clothing."

"All people say that Rāhula is my son, King Śuddhodana is my father, and Queen Māyā is my mother; yet, while dwelling in the world and enjoying all manner of pleasures, I abandoned such things to leave the home life and study the Way."
The multitude spoke again:
"This Prince Gautama, of a great clan, has distanced himself from worldly pleasures to seek the Dharma that transcends the world.
However, I have long since been free from worldly desire; such matters as these are entirely manifestations.
"All sentient beings say that this person has entered nirvana, yet I am truly not so. Good son!
Although I repeatedly manifest entry into nirvana here within Jambudvīpa, I do not, in truth, enter ultimate nirvana."

Yet all sentient beings say that the Tathāgata has truly entered extinction; however, the nature of the Tathāgata does not in fact perish eternally. Therefore, one should know that this is a permanently abiding dharma, an unchanging dharma.
“Good son! Great Nirvāṇa is the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

I further manifest my appearance in the world within Jambudvīpa, and sentient beings all say that I have only now attained Buddhahood; yet I have already accomplished what was to be done throughout immeasurable kalpas. Because I conform to worldly conventions, I again manifest my initial attainment of Buddhahood in Jambudvīpa.”

“Furthermore, I manifest in Jambudvīpa as one who does not uphold the precepts and commits the four grave offenses; all people see this and believe that I have truly committed them. Yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have strictly upheld the precepts without any lapse or deficiency.”
"Furthermore, I manifest as an icchantika in Jambudvīpa; all people see me as an icchantika, yet in reality, I am not an icchantika."
"How can an icchantika achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

Furthermore, I manifest in Jambudvīpa as one who breaks the harmony of the Saṅgha; sentient beings all say that I am the breaker of the Saṅgha, yet I observe that among humans and devas there is no one capable of breaking the harmony of the Saṅgha."
“Furthermore, I manifest myself in Jambudvīpa to protect and uphold the True Dharma; all people say that I am a protector of the Dharma and are filled with wonder and astonishment.
Such is the nature of all Buddhas; one should not be astonished or amazed.”

“Furthermore, I manifest as Māra Pāpīyas in Jambudvīpa, and all people say, ‘This is Pāpīyas. Yet for immeasurable kalpas, I have been free from the deeds of Māra; I am pure and unstained, like a lotus flower.”
“Furthermore, I manifest the attainment of Buddhahood in a female body within Jambudvīpa; when people see this, they all say:
‘How extraordinary! A woman can attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
The Tathāgata ultimately does not receive a female body; it is only for the sake of taming immeasurable sentient beings that he manifests a female form.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, he further displays various kinds of physical appearances.

“Furthermore, I manifest birth within the four realms of existence in Jambudvīpa; yet, I have long since severed all causes for the realms of existence. While others fall into the four realms due to the cause of karma, I am born therein for the sake of delivering sentient beings.”

"Furthermore, I manifest myself as the Brahmā King within Jambudvīpa, causing those who serve Brahmā to dwell securely in the True Dharma; yet I am not truly so, and all sentient beings nevertheless regard me as the true Brahmā.
My manifestation in the likeness of celestial beings throughout all the temples of the devas is likewise."
“Furthermore, I manifest entering the houses of courtesans in Jambudvīpa; yet, in truth, I have no thought of lustful desire, remaining pure and unstained like a lotus flower.”

For the sake of sentient beings who are greedy for sensual pleasures and attached to form, I proclaim the sublime Dharma at the crossroads; yet, in truth, I have no mind of lustful defilement, though the multitude says that I am guarding women.

“Furthermore, I manifested entry into the household of a maidservant in Jambudvīpa in order to attract and transform beings so that they might abide in the True Dharma; however, I truly possess no such evil karma as to have fallen into the state of a maidservant.”
“Furthermore, I manifest myself within Jambudvīpa as a teacher, instructing the ignorant and leading them to abide in the True Dharma.

Again, I manifest myself within Jambudvīpa at various drinking gatherings and places of gambling and chess, displaying all manner of victories, defeats, disputes, and litigation, desiring thereby to rescue and deliver those sentient beings.”
Yet, in truth, I have no such evil karma, though all sentient beings claim that I have committed such deeds.
Furthermore, I manifest dwelling for a long time in cemeteries, assuming the body of a great vulture to deliver various flying birds.
Yet all sentient beings think that I am truly a vulture body; however, I have long since been free from such karma, and I manifest this form only for the sake of delivering those birds and vultures.
"Furthermore, I manifest as a great elder within Jambudvīpa, desiring to establish immeasurable sentient beings in the True Dharma.
Moreover, I manifest as various kings, ministers, princes, and high officials, being the foremost among each of these groups, occupying the royal throne for the sake of upholding the True Dharma."

“Furthermore, I manifest the arising of an epidemic kalpa within Jambudvīpa, wherein many sentient beings are afflicted by disease; first I bestow medicine, and thereafter I preach the subtle and wondrous True Dharma for them, causing them to dwell securely in unsurpassed bodhi, while all people say that this is merely the arising of an epidemic kalpa.”

Furthermore, he manifests the arising of an eon of famine within Jambudvīpa; according to their needs, he provides them with food and drink, and thereafter preaches the subtle and wondrous True Dharma for them, causing them to dwell securely in unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, he manifests the arising of the kalpa of weapons within Jambudvīpa, and immediately preaches the Dharma for them so that they may be freed from enmity and harm, enabling them to abide securely in unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, he manifests [these teachings], preaching the perception of impermanence to those who conceive of permanence; preaching the perception of suffering to those who conceive of pleasure; preaching the perception of non-self to those who conceive of a self; and preaching the perception of impurity to those who conceive of purity.
If there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to the triple world, he immediately preaches the Dharma for them to cause them to leave that place.
