Just as the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is both form and non-form, I also declare it to be non-form.
If someone were to object:
"If the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is non-form, how can it abide, come, go, advance, or stop?"
Such meanings are the realm of the Buddhas, not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Liberation is likewise: it is both form and non-form, yet is described as non-form;
it is both perception and non-perception, yet is described as non-perception.
"Such meanings are the realm of all Buddhas; they are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that you will take pity on us and once again graciously explain in detail the meaning of the practice and liberation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Good son! True liberation is called being far removed from all fetters.
If one is truly liberated and free from all fetters, then there is neither birth nor conjunction.
For example, it is like parents uniting to produce a child;
true liberation is not like this.
Therefore, liberation is called "non-arising."
“Kāśyapa! Just as the nature of clarified butter is pure, so too is the Tathāgata;
he is not born from the union of father and mother, for his nature is pure.”
The reason he manifests having parents is because he wishes to transform and deliver all sentient beings.
True liberation is precisely the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata and liberation are non-dual and without distinction.
"For example, when various seeds are sown in the spring months, they sprout immediately upon encountering warmth and moisture;
true liberation is not like this.
Furthermore, liberation is called 'emptiness' (śūnyatā)."
Emptiness is liberation, and liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is emptiness; he is neither a creator nor a created thing.
Whatever is created—such as city walls, towers, or pavilions—is not the Tathāgata.
True liberation is not like this.
Therefore, liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
For example, a potter makes a vessel only to break it again;
liberation is not like this. True liberation is neither born nor extinguished.
Therefore, liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is likewise: he is neither born nor extinguished, neither ages nor dies, neither breaks nor disintegrates, and is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
"What is the meaning of 'entering Great Nirvana, being neither aging nor dying'?
Aging is defined as transformation and change, such as white hair and wrinkled faces;
death is the dissolution of the body and the end of life."
Such dharmas as these do not exist within liberation; because such things are absent, it is called liberation.
The Tathāgata likewise lacks the conditioned phenomena of white hair and wrinkled face; therefore, the Tathāgata does not undergo aging.
Because there is no aging, there is no death.
Furthermore, liberation is called being free from illness.
What is meant by "illness" refers to the four hundred and four diseases, as well as other external factors that invade and damage the body.
Because this [sickness] is absent therein, it is called liberation.
One who is free from illness is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Since the Tathāgata is without illness, the Dharma-body likewise has no illness.
In this way, being free from illness is itself the Tathāgata.
"Death" refers to the dissolution of the body and the end of life.
That place where there is no death is the Deathless (Amṛta).
This ambrosia is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Since the Tathāgata has accomplished such merit and virtue, how could one say that the Tathāgata is impermanent?
If one were to say that it is impermanent, such a thing is impossible.
How could this vajra-body be impermanent?
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not said to have reached the end of his life.
The Tathāgata is pure and free from defilement; the body of the Tathāgata is not sullied by the womb.
Just as the *puṇḍarīka* lotus is pure by its very nature, so too is the liberation of the Tathāgata.
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is pure and stainless.
Furthermore, liberation is the state where all the sores and ulcers of the outflows (*āsrava*) are forever eliminated without remainder;
the Tathāgata is likewise, possessing none of the sores and ulcers of any outflows whatsoever.
"Furthermore, liberation is free from strife.
For example, a hungry person who sees the food and drink of others gives rise to thoughts of greed and desire to seize it;
liberation is not like this."
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'tranquil stillness.
Ordinary people say:
'As for tranquil stillness, it refers to Maheśvara.'"
"Such words as these are false and illusory.
One who is truly tranquil is ultimately liberated, and ultimate liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called peace and security."
Just as a place with many bandits is not called peaceful, while a clear and level place is called peaceful, so too within this liberation there is no fear; therefore, it is called "peaceful."
Therefore, peace and security are true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata; and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation has no equal.
Those who have equals are like the kings of various nations who have neighboring kingdoms;
those in true liberation are not like this.
Those without equals are like the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings, for whom none can be their equal.
Liberation is likewise without equal;
that which is without equal is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata, the King who Turns the Wheel of Dharma.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has no equal; it is impossible for him to have an equal.
Furthermore, liberation is called freedom from sorrow.
Those who possess sorrow are like a king who gives rise to anxiety out of fear of a powerful neighbor;
for one who has attained liberation, such things do not exist.
It is like having destroyed an enemy, where there is no longer any cause for worry.
Liberation is also like this: it is free from sorrow and fear.
That which is free from sorrow and fear is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of both sorrow and joy.
For example, suppose a woman has an only son who has gone away on official business.
She suddenly receives the news of his death; hearing it, she is filled with grief and suffering. Later, she hears that he is alive, and she immediately feels joy.
In liberation, such things do not exist.
That which is without sorrow or joy is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is free from all dust and defilement.
For example, in the spring months, after the sun has set, winds may rise up dust and mist.
Within liberation, however, no such thing exists.
The absence of dust and mist is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
"Just as the bright jewel within the topknot of a noble wheel-turning monarch is free from all defilement, so too is the nature of liberation; it is likewise free from defilement.
That which is free from defilement is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata."
"Just as the nature of pure gold, when unmixed with sand and stone, is called a true treasure, and someone who obtains it conceives the thought that it is wealth;
so too is the nature of liberation, like that true treasure."
That true treasure is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
"For example, when an earthen jar is broken, it makes a harsh, rattling sound;
a diamond treasure-jar is not like this."
Furthermore, liberation is likewise without cracking or breaking.
The adamantine precious vase is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the body of the Tathāgata is indestructible.
"As for that sound of cracking, it is like the sound of sesame seeds bursting when placed in a great heat.
Now, liberation is not such a thing.

It is like a vessel made of genuine diamond-jewels, which produces no sound of cracking or breaking; even if immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people were to shoot at it together, none would be able to destroy it."
The absence of hoarse or broken sounds is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
It is like a poor man who, because he owes another goods, is bound by others with shackles and fetters, subjected to flogging and punishment, and made to endure various bitter sufferings.
In liberation, such things do not exist; there is no debt.
It is like a householder who possesses immeasurable billions of wealth and treasures, whose power is sovereign, and who owes nothing to others.
Liberation is likewise so: it possesses immeasurable wealth and treasures of the Dharma, with sovereign power and freedom from all debt.
To be free from debt is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'absence of oppression.
It is like encountering heat in spring, eating sweets in summer, or touching cold in winter;
within true liberation, there are no such disagreeable matters."
The absence of affliction is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, "absence of affliction" is like a person who has eaten their fill of fish and meat and then drinks milk; such a person will soon approach death.
Within true liberation, such things do not exist.
Just as a person who obtains excellent ambrosial medicine is cured of their ailment,
so too is it with true liberation.
The ambrosial medicine is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
"What is meant by being oppressed and not being oppressed?
For example, an ordinary person, conceited and self-exalting, thinks to himself:"
"Among all things, who could harm me?
Thinking thus, he immediately seizes snakes, tigers, and venomous insects.
It should be known that such a person will not complete their natural lifespan but will instead die an untimely death.
In true liberation, such things do not exist.
"Not being oppressed" is like the divine pearl possessed by a wheel-turning king (cakravartin), which can subdue ninety-six kinds of venomous insects, such as earthworms and dung beetles.
If anyone hears the fragrance of this divine pearl, all poisons will be eliminated.
True liberation is likewise so: it causes one to remain far removed from the twenty-five states of existence.
The extinguisher of poison is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, that which is unafflicted is like space;
liberation is likewise so.
That which is space is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, as for "oppression," it is like lighting various lamps near dry grass: when one is near them, they burn fiercely;
in true liberation, no such thing exists.
"Furthermore, 'not being oppressive' is like how the sun and moon do not oppress sentient beings;
liberation is likewise, for it does not oppress any sentient beings."
The absence of oppression is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the immovable dharma.
Just as there are distinctions between enemies and kin, such things do not exist within true liberation.
"Furthermore, that which is immovable is like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who has no other noble king as a close friend; if there were another such friend, it would be impossible.
Liberation is likewise: it has no further kin, and if it did have kin, it would also be impossible."
That king’s lack of kin is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is, moreover, the Dharma.
Furthermore, "immovability" is like a plain white garment that easily takes dye.
Liberation is not like that.
Furthermore, as with the *vārṣika* flower, it is impossible for it to have a foul odor or to be blue in color;
liberation is likewise, and it is impossible for it to have a foul odor or any [other] colors.
Therefore, liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "rare.
For example, it is not rare for a lotus flower to grow in water; however, that which grows within fire is truly rare, and anyone who sees it will give rise to joy.
True liberation is likewise so: those who behold it give rise to joy in their hearts.
That which is rare is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata, and that Tathāgata is the Dharmakāya.
"Furthermore, that which is rare is like an infant whose teeth have not yet emerged; they grow gradually until, after reaching maturity, they finally appear.
Liberation is not like this; it is neither arising nor non-arising."
"Furthermore, liberation is called emptiness and stillness; there is no such thing as indetermination.
As for 'indetermination,' it would be impossible for an icchantika to never change at all, or for one who has committed a grave transgression to fail to achieve the Buddha-way."
Why is this? If such a person attains pure faith in the Buddha’s true Dharma, at that moment they immediately extinguish the icchantika-nature;
if they further become an upāsaka, they likewise become capable of extinguishing the icchantika-nature.

One who has committed a grave transgression shall attain Buddhahood once this sin has been extinguished; therefore, it is impossible to say that one is definitively immovable and will not achieve the Way of the Buddha.
Within true liberation, there is absolutely no such matter of cessation or extinction.
Furthermore, that which is empty and quiescent falls within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As the nature of the dharma-realm is itself true liberation, true liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, if an icchantika were to completely extinguish [all roots of goodness], they could no longer be called an icchantika.
What, then, is meant by an icchantika?

An icchantika is one who has severed and destroyed all roots of goodness, whose mind does not take any wholesome dharmas as an object of focus, and who does not give rise to even a single thought of goodness.
In true liberation, none of these things exist at all.
Because these things do not exist, it is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called immeasurable.
For example, the quantity of a heap of grain can be known;
true liberation is not like this.
For example, the great ocean cannot be measured.
Liberation is also like this: it cannot be measured.
That which is immeasurable is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the "immeasurable dharma."
Just as a single sentient being has many karmic retributions, so too is liberation: it possesses immeasurable retributions.
That which is immeasurable retribution is true liberation; that which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'vast.
Just as the great ocean has no equal;
so too is liberation, for nothing can equal it."
That which has no equal is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "supreme.
It is like space, which is highest and beyond compare.
Liberation is also like this: it is supreme and beyond compare.
That which is supreme and beyond compare is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "that which nothing can surpass."
For example, wherever a lion dwells, none of the hundred beasts can pass him by;
liberation is likewise, such that none can surpass it.
That which cannot be surpassed is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'unsurpassed.
For example, just as the northern direction is the highest among all directions,
so too is liberation unsurpassed."
That which is unsurpassed is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the "supreme among the supreme.
For example, the north is the supreme among the directions relative to the east.
Liberation is also like this; there is nothing superior to it.
That which has nothing superior to it is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the eternal dharma.
For example, when the bodies of humans and devas perish at the end of their lives, this is called "constant," not "inconstant";
liberation is likewise, it is not inconstant.
That which is not inconstant is true liberation; that which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'solid and substantial.
Just as *khatvāṅga*, sandalwood, and aloeswood are solid and substantial by nature, so too is liberation; its nature is solid and substantial."
That which is solid in nature is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "non-empty.
For example, the substance of bamboo and reeds is hollow and porous; [liberation is not like this].
Liberation is not like that;
you should know that liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "uncorruptible."
For example, when a wall has not yet been plastered or treated, mosquitoes and gadflies will settle upon it and sport there.
However, if it is plastered, painted, and adorned with carvings, the insects will not remain once they smell the scent of the pigments.
Thus, non-abiding is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "boundless.
For example, a village always has boundaries; [but liberation does not].
Liberation is not like that.
Just as space has no boundaries, so too is liberation; it has no boundaries.
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "invisible," just as the tracks of a bird in the sky are difficult to see.
Thus, that which is difficult to see is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "profound. Why is this?
It is that which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot enter.
That which cannot be entered is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, "profound" refers to that which is revered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
For example, the merit of a filial child who supports and nourishes their parents is exceedingly profound.
This profound merit is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'invisible.
It is like a person who cannot see the crown of their own head;
liberation is likewise, such that it cannot be seen by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
That which cannot be seen is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "having no abode.
It is like space, which has no abode.
Liberation is also like this.
What is called a "house" is a metaphor for the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
One who has no house is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'ungraspable.
Just as the *āmalaka* fruit can be grasped and held by a person, liberation is not like that;
it cannot be grasped or held."
That which cannot be grasped or maintained is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "ungraspable.
It is, for example, like a magical illusion that cannot be grasped or held.
Liberation is likewise; it cannot be grasped or held.
That which cannot be grasped or held is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation has no physical body.
For example, suppose there were a person whose body was afflicted with leprosy, various carbuncles, madness, or emaciation;
in true liberation, such ailments do not exist.
The absence of such ailments is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'one flavor.
Just as milk has one flavor, so too does liberation; it possesses only this single flavor."
This single flavor is itself true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called purity;
it is like water free from silt, still and perfectly clear.
Liberation is likewise thus: it is still, tranquil, and pure.
This stillness, tranquility, and purity is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "the single flavor."
Just as rain falling from the sky is of one flavor and pure, this single-flavored purity is a metaphor for true liberation; true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "removal."
Just as the full moon is free from all clouds and obscurations, so too is liberation free from all clouds and obscurations.
That which is free from all clouds and obscurations is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called tranquility.
For example, when a person recovers from a feverish illness, their body attains tranquility;
liberation is likewise, for the body attains tranquility."
The attainment of tranquility by the body is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is equanimity.
It is like a wilderness field where venomous snakes, mice, and wolves all possess a murderous intent.
Liberation is not like this; it is devoid of the intent to kill.
That which is without the intent to kill is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, "equality" is like parents who maintain an impartial mind toward their children.
Liberation is also like this: its mind is equanimous.
That which is equanimous of mind is true liberation; that which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "the state of non-differentiation."
For example, suppose there is a person who dwells only in a most excellent and pure residence and has no other place to go;
liberation is likewise, having no other place.
That which has no other place is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called contentment.
For example, when a hungry person encounters delicious food, they eat it without satiety.
Liberation is not like this; it is like having eaten milk gruel, after which nothing more is required."
There is nothing further required; this is likened to true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "severance.
It is like a person who has been bound: by severing the bonds, they attain release.
Liberation is likewise so: it severs all fetters of doubt.
Such severance of doubt is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'reaching the other shore.
For example, a great river has both this shore and the other shore;
liberation is not like this, for although it has no 'this shore,' it does have an 'other shore.'"

That which possesses the further shore is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata. Furthermore, liberation is called silence. It is like the great ocean: when its waters overflow, there are many sounds; yet, when the tide recedes and the water subsides, all sounds vanish. In the same way, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is like the great ocean, and his various teachings are like the sounds within it. When he enters the samādhi of the extinction of all phenomena, all sounds cease. This cessation of all sounds is called liberation. Therefore, liberation is indeed silence. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of sound. Why? Because liberation is free from all conceptualization and discrimination. Just as the great ocean is free from all waves, so too is liberation free from all conceptualization and discrimination. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of sound. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of speech. Why? Because liberation transcends all words and names. Just as the great ocean has no sound of speech, so too does liberation have no sound of speech. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of speech. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of verbal expression. Why? Because liberation is beyond all paths of speech. Just as the great ocean has no path for speech, so too does liberation have no path for speech. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of verbal expression. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of discourse. Why? Because liberation is free from all discursive thought. Just as the great ocean has no discursive thought, so too does liberation have no discursive thought. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of discourse. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of clamor. Why? Because liberation is free from all noise and confusion. Just as the great ocean is free from all clamor, so too is liberation free from all clamor. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of clamor. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of contention. Why? Because liberation is free from all strife and conflict. Just as the great ocean is free from all contention, so too is liberation free from all contention. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of contention. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of dispute. Why? Because liberation is free from all arguments and disputes. Just as the great ocean is free from all dispute, so too is liberation free from all dispute. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of dispute. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of conflict. Why? Because liberation is free from all opposition and hostility. Just as the great ocean is free from all conflict, so too is liberation free from all conflict. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of conflict. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of strife. Why? Because liberation is free from all turbulence and agitation. Just as the great ocean is free from all strife, so too is liberation free from all strife. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of strife. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of rivalry. Why? Because liberation is free from all emulation and rivalry. Just as the great ocean is free from all rivalry, so too is liberation free from all rivalry. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of rivalry. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of competition. Why? Because liberation is free from all vying and competing. Just as the great ocean is free from all competition, so too is liberation free from all competition. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of competition. Just as the great ocean is free from all contest, so too is liberation free from all contest. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of contest. Just as the great ocean is free from all strife, so too is liberation free from all strife. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of strife. Just as the great ocean is free from all discord, so too is liberation free from all discord. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of discord. Just as the great ocean is free from all contention, so too is liberation free from all contention. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of contention. Just as the great ocean is free from all rivalry, so too is liberation free from all rivalry. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of rivalry. Just as the great ocean is free from all competition, so too is liberation free from all competition. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of competition. Just as the great ocean is free from all contest, so too is liberation free from all contest. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of contest. Just as the great ocean is free from all dispute, so too is liberation free from all dispute. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of dispute. Just as the great ocean is free from all contention, so too is liberation free from all contention. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of contention. Just as the great ocean is free from all strife, so too is liberation free from all strife. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of strife. Just as the great ocean is free from all strife, so too is liberation free from all strife. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of strife. Just as the great ocean is free from all discord, so too is liberation free from all discord. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of discord. Just as the great ocean is free from all contention, so too is liberation free from all contention. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of contention. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of rivalry. Why? Because liberation is free from all emulation and rivalry. Just as the great ocean is free from all rivalry, so too is liberation free from all rivalry. Therefore, liberation is indeed the absence of rivalry. Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of competition. Why?
Liberation is not like that; such liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "exquisite."
For example, when various medicines are mixed with harītakī, their taste becomes bitter;
liberation is not so, for its taste is like nectar (amṛta).
This "taste like nectar" is a metaphor for true liberation, and true liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation eliminates all afflictions.
It is like a skilled physician who compiles various medicines to effectively treat all manner of illnesses;
liberation is likewise able to eliminate afflictions."
One who eliminates afflictions is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "unconfined.
For example, a small house cannot accommodate many people; [whereas liberation is not so].
Liberation is not like that; it is capable of containing much.
To be capable of containing much is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the extinction of all cravings and is unmixed with sensual desire.
For example, a woman has many desires;
liberation is not so.
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he is free from the fetters of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth.
Furthermore, liberation is called the absence of craving.
There are two kinds of craving:
first, the craving of hungry ghosts; second, the craving for the Dharma.
One who has attained true liberation is free from the craving of hungry ghosts; yet, out of compassion for sentient beings, they possess the craving for the Dharma.
Such craving for the Dharma is itself true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is free from "I" and "mine."
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is cessation, being free from all craving for existence.
This liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is protection; it is able to rescue all those who are terrified.
This liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is the place of refuge;
if one takes refuge in such liberation, one seeks no other refuge.
For example, it is like a person who relies upon a king and seeks no other refuge;
although such reliance on a king may involve instability, reliance on one who has attained liberation is free from instability.
That which is immovable is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is called a dwelling place.
For example, if a person travels through a vast wilderness, there are dangers and difficulties;
liberation is not like this, for it is free from danger and difficulty.
That which is free from danger and difficulty is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is fearlessness.
Just as the lion king feels no fear toward any of the hundred beasts;
so too is liberation, for it feels no fear toward any of the hosts of Māra."
One who is without fear is truly liberated; one who is truly liberated is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is not narrow or constricted.
It is like a narrow path that cannot even accommodate two people walking abreast.
Liberation is not like that; such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is "not being constricted," which is like a person who, fearing a tiger, falls into a well.
Liberation is not like that. Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, there is "not being constricted," which is like one who, in the midst of a great ocean, abandons a ruined small boat and obtains a sturdy vessel; riding upon it across the sea, they reach a place of peace and security, and their mind attains happiness.
Liberation is likewise; the mind attains happiness.
One who attains happiness is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation uproots all causes and conditions.
For example, it is like obtaining curd from milk, ghee from curd, and clarified butter (sarpis) from ghee;
yet within true liberation, none of these causes exist.
That which is devoid of such causes is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation can subdue arrogance.
For example, a great king may look down upon a lesser king;
liberation is not like this.
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation subdues all forms of negligence;
those who are negligent possess much craving and desire.
Within true liberation, there is no such name.
That which is without such a name is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is able to eliminate ignorance.
Just as the finest ghee is called *ghṛta* only after all impurities have been removed;
so too is liberation: when the dregs of ignorance are removed, true illumination arises.
This true illumination is itself true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called tranquility, pure and singular without a second.
Just as a wild elephant in the wilderness is solitary and without a companion;
so too is liberation—solitary and without a second."
Being solitary and peerless is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "solid and real.
It is like bamboo, reeds, and hemp: while their stalks and trunks are hollow, their seeds are solid and real.
Except for the Buddha, the Tathāgata, all other beings among devas and humans are not solid or substantial.
One who has attained true liberation is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and the like; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called that which can fully awaken to and augment the self.
True liberation is also like this; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata."
"Furthermore, liberation is called the relinquishing of all modes of existence (*bhava*).
It is like a person who, having finished eating, vomits;
liberation is likewise, for it relinquishes all modes of existence."
To abandon all modes of existence is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "certainty.
For example, the fragrance of the *vārṣika* flower does not exist within its seven petals.
Liberation is also like this. Such liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the water element.
For example, among the great elements, the element of water is preeminent, for it can moisten all grasses, trees, and seeds;
liberation is likewise, for it can moisten all classes of sentient beings.
Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "entry.
Just as where there are gates, there is a path for entry;
Where there is the nature of gold, gold may be obtained.
Liberation is likewise; as with that gateway, those who cultivate non-self can enter therein.
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'good.
It is like a disciple who follows his teacher and is named 'good' for faithfully carrying out his instructions;
liberation is likewise."
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the supramundane dharma, for it transcends all dharmas most completely;
just as, among all flavors, clarified butter and milk are the most excellent.
Liberation is also like this. Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "immovable."
For example, just as the threshold of a door cannot be moved by the wind,
so it is with one who has attained true liberation.
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'without waves.
Just as the waters of that great ocean are subject to surging waves,
liberation is not so."
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is like a palace;
liberation is also thus.
You should know that liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called "utility.
It is like Jāmbūnada gold, which has many uses and for which no one can point out any fault or defect.
Liberation is likewise thus, being free from faults and evils.
To be free from faults and evils is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is the relinquishing of infantile conduct.
It is, for example, like an adult abandoning the behavior of a child;
liberation is likewise the relinquishing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
This relinquishing of the five aggregates is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called 'ultimate.
It is like one who has been bound gaining release from those bonds, bathing for purification, and then returning home;
liberation is likewise, being ultimately pure."
Ultimate purity is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the bliss of non-action;
the bliss of non-action arises from having cast off greed, hatred, and delusion.
It is like a person who, having mistakenly drunk a poisonous drug, takes an emetic to eliminate the poison.
Once vomiting has occurred, the poison is expelled and cured, and the body attains peace and well-being.
Liberation is also like this: having expelled the poison of all afflictions and fetters, the body attains peace and bliss, which is called the bliss of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-sukha*).
This bliss of non-action is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called the severance of the four kinds of poisonous snakes of affliction.
To sever these afflictions is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata."

"Furthermore, liberation is called being free from all modes of existence (*bhava*), the extinction of all suffering, and the attainment of all happiness; it is the eternal severance of greed, hatred, and delusion, and the uprooting of the very foundation of all afflictions."
That which uproots the source is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called the severing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and the giving birth of all untainted wholesome phenomena (*anāsravakuśaladharma*). It blocks all paths, namely: the notions of self, non-self, neither self nor non-self, and neither not-self. It severs only grasping and attachment, but does not sever the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*); this view of self is called the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
"Buddha-nature is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called 'not empty of emptiness.
'Empty of emptiness' refers to non-existence."

That which is "nothingness" refers to the liberation conceived by non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others; however, these Nirgranthas do not actually possess liberation, and therefore it is called "emptiness of emptiness."
True liberation is not like this; therefore, it is not "empty-of-emptiness.
That which is not "empty-of-emptiness" is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, liberation is called both empty and non-empty.

It is like jars for water, wine, milk, curd, ghee, or honey: even when they contain no water, wine, curd, ghee, or honey, they are still called 'water jars' and so forth; yet these jars cannot be said to be either empty or non-empty."
If one says it is empty, then there can be no form, fragrance, taste, or touch;
if one says it is not empty, yet there is likewise no reality such as water or wine.
Liberation is also like this: it cannot be said to be form or non-form, nor can it be said to be empty or non-empty.
If one says it is empty, then permanence, bliss, self, and purity could not exist;
if one says it is not empty, who would experience this permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
For this reason, it cannot be said that there is emptiness or non-emptiness.
"Emptiness" refers to the absence of the twenty-five states of existence, as well as all afflictions, all suffering, all marks, and all conditioned formations;
it is like a jar being called empty when it contains no curd.
"Non-empty" refers to true, wholesome form, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; it is immovable and unchanging.
It is like the color, fragrance, flavor, and touch of that vase; therefore, it is called "non-empty."
Therefore, liberation is likened to that jar.
That jar may be destroyed when it encounters conditions;
liberation is not so, for it cannot be destroyed.
That which is indestructible is true liberation; true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called the departure from craving.
For example, it is like a person whose heart is filled with craving and who yearns for Śakra-devendra, Mahābrahmā, or Maheśvara-devendra.
Liberation is not like that; once one has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is neither craving nor doubt.
To be without craving and without doubt is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
If one says that liberation possesses craving or doubt, such a thing is impossible.

Furthermore, liberation is the severing of all craving for existence, the severing of all marks, all fetters, all afflictions, all birth and death, all causes and conditions, and all karmic retributions.
Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is itself nirvāṇa.
"Because all sentient beings fear birth and death and the various afflictions, they take refuge in the Triple Gem."
For example, when a herd of deer is terrified of a hunter and manages to escape, each leap they take is likened to one refuge;
likewise, three leaps are likened to the three refuges. By means of these three leaps, they obtain peace and happiness.
Sentient beings are likewise; because they fear the four Māras, those evil hunters, they take refuge in the Triple Gem.
By taking refuge in the Triple Gem, they obtain peace and happiness;
those who obtain peace and happiness have attained true liberation.
True liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is nirvāṇa;
nirvāṇa is the inexhaustible.
That which is inexhaustible is the Buddha-nature;
the Buddha-nature is certainty;
and certainty is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If nirvāṇa, the buddha-nature, certainty, and the Tathāgata are one and the same meaning, why do you speak of there being three refuges?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son! All sentient beings, fearing birth and death, therefore seek the Three Refuges."
By virtue of the Three Refuges, one knows that the Buddha-nature is definitively Nirvana.
Good son! There are dharmas whose names are identical but whose meanings differ; there are also dharmas whose both names and meanings differ.

Regarding "the name is one while the meanings differ": the Buddha is permanent, the Dharma is permanent, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus is permanent; nirvāṇa and space are likewise all permanent. This is called "the name is one while the meanings differ."

Regarding those where both name and meaning differ: the Buddha is named "Awakened" (Buddha), the Dharma is named "Non-awakening," the Saṃgha is named "Harmony," Nirvāṇa is named "Liberation," and empty space is named "Non-virtuous" and also "Unobstructed. This is what is meant by both name and meaning being different.
"Good son! The three refuges are likewise thus; their names and meanings are distinct, so how could they be one?
For this reason, I told Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:..."
"Do not make offerings to me; you should make offerings to the Saṃgha.
If you make offerings to the Saṃgha, you will have fully fulfilled the offerings made to the Three Refuges.
Mahāprajāpatī then replied to me:
"If there is neither Buddha nor Dharma within the Sangha, how can you say that by making offerings to the Sangha, one fully accomplishes the offering to the Three Refuges?
I replied again:

"If you follow my words, you are making an offering to the Buddha; because it is for the sake of liberation, you are making an offering to the Dharma; and since the Sangha is the recipient, you are making an offering to the Sangha."
"Good son! For this reason, the three refuges cannot be considered as one. Good son!"
The Tathāgata may at times explain one as three, or explain three as one; such meanings are the domain of the Buddhas, not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Regarding what the Buddha has said—that ultimate peace and bliss is called nirvāṇa—what is the meaning of this?
For as for nirvāṇa, it involves the relinquishing of the body and the relinquishing of wisdom."
"If one abandons both body and mind, who would experience pleasure?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
For example, suppose there is a person who, having eaten, feels a sense of mental distress and goes outside wishing to vomit.
Once he has vomited, he returns again.
A companion asks him:
"Has your ailment finally been cured that you have come back again?
He replied, "It has been cured;
my body has attained peace and happiness."

The Tathāgata is likewise: having ultimately transcended the twenty-five states of existence, he has forever attained the state of nirvāṇa and peace, which is immovable and inexhaustible; having severed all sensations, it is called the bliss of non-sensation.
Thus, the absence of sensation is called eternal bliss.
It is impossible for the Tathāgata to possess the experience of pleasure;
therefore, ultimate bliss is precisely nirvāṇa.
"Nirvana is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Is this non-arising and non-ceasing what constitutes liberation?"
"So it is, so it is, son of good family!
That which is neither born nor extinguished is itself liberation; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"If that which is without birth or cessation is liberation, then the nature of empty space is also without birth or cessation; it should therefore be the Tathāgata."
"The nature of the Tathāgata is itself liberation.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."
"This is not so. "World-Honored One, why is it not so?"
“Good son! Suppose there were the kalaviṅka and the jīvajīvaka birds; their voices are pure and exquisite—could they possibly be the same as the cries of crows and magpies? “No, sir.”
“World-Honored One!
Compared to the *jīvajīvaka* and other such birds, the voices of crows and magpies cannot be compared to them by even a hundred thousand million times.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“The kalaviṅka and other such birds possess voices that are subtle and exquisite, and their bodies are likewise unlike [those of common birds].
How can the Tathāgata compare them to crows and magpies?
It is no different from comparing a mustard seed to Mount Sumeru.”
"The Buddha and empty space are likewise so: the voice of the kalaviṅka may be used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s voice, but it cannot be used as a metaphor for the cry of a crow or a magpie.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! You have now well understood that which is extremely profound and difficult to understand.
There are times when the Tathāgata, for the sake of certain causes and conditions, cites space as a metaphor for liberation; such liberation is itself the Tathāgata."
True liberation cannot be illustrated by any analogy among humans or devas, yet even this empty space is not truly an adequate metaphor for it.
Nevertheless, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, that which is not a metaphor—empty space—is used as a metaphor.
You should know that liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and the nature of the Tathāgata is itself liberation.
Liberation and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction.
“Good son! That which is beyond analogy is like an incomparable object that cannot be illustrated by comparison; however, because there are causes and conditions, it can be illustrated by analogy.
As it is said in the sutra:”
"The countenance is upright and handsome, like the full moon;
the white elephant is fresh and pure, like the Snowy Mountains.
Yet the full moon cannot be identical to the face, nor can the Snowy Mountains be the white elephant itself.
Good son! True liberation cannot be illustrated by metaphors; it is only for the sake of transforming sentient beings that metaphors are employed.
By means of these various analogies, one should know that the nature of all dharmas is likewise thus.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“In what way does the Tathāgata give two kinds of teachings?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is like a person who, grasping a sword, desires to harm the Tathāgata with a mind of hatred.
Yet the Tathāgata remains serene and pleasant, showing no sign of anger or resentment.”
"Would this person incur the destruction of the Tathāgata’s body and thereby commit a heinous crime? "No,
World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because the realm of the Tathāgata’s body is indestructible. For what reason?
Because there is no aggregate of a physical body, there is only the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Since the principle of the nature of phenomena is indestructible, how could such a person destroy the Buddha’s body?
It is solely due to their evil intention that they commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
"By these causes and conditions, one may lead through various parables to the knowledge of the true Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
That which I intended to say, you have now spoken.
Furthermore, good son!"
For example, suppose a wicked man wishes to harm his mother.
He stays in a wild field beneath a stack of grain, and his mother comes to bring him food.
Upon seeing her, he immediately conceives a murderous intent and steps forward to sharpen his knife.
When the mother realized this, she fled and hid within a thicket.
The man, holding a sword, circled around the edge of the thicket and hacked at it.
Having finished hacking, he felt joy, having conceived the thought that she was already dead.
Her mother then went out and returned home.
What do you think?
Has this person committed an ānantarya offense?
“World-Honored One!
It cannot be definitively stated. Why is this?
If one says there is a transgression, the mother’s body ought to have been destroyed;
if the body was not destroyed, how can one say there is?
If one says there is no transgression, yet having formed the thought of killing upon her birth, the mind harbored joy—how then can one say there is none?
"Although this person has not fully committed the heinous crimes, they are nonetheless guilty of them.
By means of these causes and conditions, one can lead through various parables to understand the true Dharma.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
For this reason, I have employed various skillful means and parables to illustrate liberation.”
Although there are immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* analogies, in reality they cannot truly serve as comparisons;
for while there may be certain causes and conditions that can be explained through metaphors, there are also certain causes and conditions for which no illustration can be drawn.
Therefore, liberation achieves such immeasurable merit.
For those who proceed toward nirvana, and for the Tathāgata who is nirvana itself, there likewise exists such immeasurable merit.
"Because it is fully accomplished through such immeasurable merits as these, it is called 'Great Nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have now for the first time realized that the destination reached by the Tathāgata is inexhaustible.
If his destination is inexhaustible, one should know that his lifespan must likewise be inexhaustible.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
you have now skillfully upheld the true Dharma.”
"If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to sever the afflictions and all fetters of bondage, they should protect and uphold the True Dharma in this manner.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Five;
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
The Sòng Dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán and others added the "Chapter on the Four Reliances" (Sìyīpǐn) based on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Four Reliances.
The Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa:

“Good son! Within this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, there are four kinds of persons who can protect the True Dharma, establish the True Dharma, and keep the True Dharma in mind; they are able to bring great benefit and compassion to the world, serving as a reliance for the world and bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas.”
What are the four?
There is one who appears in the world possessing the nature of afflictions; this is called the first.
Those who are *srotāpannas* and *sakṛdāgāmins*; these are called the second.
The Anāgāmin is called the third; the Arhat is called the fourth.
These four types of persons appear in the world, able to bring great benefit and compassion to the world, serving as a refuge for the world and bringing peace and happiness to gods and humans.
"What is meant by 'possessing the nature of afflictions'?
It refers to a person who is able to uphold the prohibitive precepts, is complete in dignified deportment, and establishes the True Dharma.

Having heard from the Buddha, they understand the meaning of the texts and, in turn, analyze and proclaim them for others, saying: 'Few desires are the Path; many desires are not the Path,' and so forth, extensively explaining the eight awakenings of a great man."
If there are those who have committed offenses, he instructs them to disclose them, repent, and thereby eliminate them.

He skillfully understands the secret dharmas practiced through the expedient means of Bodhisattvas; such a person is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), not one who has reached the eighth stage.
The eighth person is not called an ordinary being (pṛthagjana), but is named a bodhisattva, and is not named a buddha.
The second person is named a srotāpanna or a sakṛdāgāmin.

If one attains the true Dharma and upholds the true Dharma, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, one writes it down, receives and maintains it, recites it, and explains it to others just as it was heard.
If, having heard the Dharma, one does not copy it, receive it, uphold it, or explain it, but instead says:
"The Buddha permitted the keeping of slaves and impure things."
Such a thing is impossible.
This is called the second type of person.
Such a person, though not yet having attained the second or third stage of abiding, is said to be a bodhisattva who has already received the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
"The third person is called an Anāgāmin.
An Anāgāmin is one who slanders the true Dharma, or says:
'It is permitted to keep male and female slaves, servants, and impure things.'"

"It is impossible for one who upholds the scriptures and treatises of non-Buddhist paths, who is obstructed by adventitious afflictions, who is shrouded by various karmic afflictions, who conceals the true relics of the Tathāgata, who is afflicted by external diseases, or who is invaded by the four great poisonous snakes, to discourse upon the self."
If one speaks of non-self, that is possible;
if one speaks of worldly dharmas [as eternal], that is impossible.
If one speaks of the Mahāyāna continuing without interruption, that is possible.
It is impossible that the body one has received should harbor eighty thousand worms;
it is possible, however, that one who is forever free from sexual desire shall not emit impurity even in dreams.
It is also impossible that such a person would experience fear on the day of their death.
What is meant by the term *anāgāmin*?
Such a person does not return.

As explained above, they can never be defiled by any faults or afflictions; though they may still travel back and forth, they are called Bodhisattvas who have already received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and before long they will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is what is called the third type of person.
"The fourth person is named Arhat.
An Arhat has severed all afflictions, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, completed what was to be done, dwells in the tenth stage, and has attained sovereign wisdom."
According to the inclinations of beings, they are able to manifest all manner of forms and images;
just as they have adorned themselves, should they wish to attain the Buddha-way, they are able to achieve it.
Because they can accomplish such immeasurable merits, they are called Arhats.

"These are called the four persons who appear in the world to bring great benefit and compassion to the world; they are the refuge for the world, bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas. Among humans and devas, they are most honored and most supreme, just like the Tathāgata; they are called the victors among men and are the place of refuge."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I do not rely upon these four kinds of people.”
Why is this? As stated in the *Ghoṣila-sūtra*, the Buddha said to Ghoṣila:
"If gods, Māras, or Brahmās, desiring to cause destruction, were to manifest in the form of a Buddha, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."
His halo extends one fathom, his face is perfectly round like the full moon in its brilliance,
and the tuft of white hair between his brows surpasses jade or snow in purity.
As he approaches you with such adornments, you should examine him closely to ascertain whether he is real or false.
"Once one has recognized them, one should subdue them.
"World-Honored One!

If Māra and his like can even transform themselves into the form of a Buddha, how much more so could they not transform themselves into the four kinds of bodies, such as those of Arhats? Could they not sit or lie in mid-air, emit water from their left side and fire from their right side, or produce smoke and flames from their bodies like a mass of fire?"
For these reasons, no faith arises in my heart toward them; nor can I accept what they say, nor do I regard them with reverence as those upon whom I should rely.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If one harbors doubt regarding what I have taught, they should not accept it; how much more so in the case of such things as these?"
Therefore, one should skillfully discern what is wholesome and unwholesome, and what may or may not be done.
Having acted in this way, one will experience happiness for a long night.
“Good son! It is like a thieving dog that enters a person’s house at night.
If the servants of that household should perceive it, they ought immediately to drive it out and scold it:”
"Get out at once! If you do not leave, I shall take your life.
Upon hearing this, the thief dog immediately departed and did not return.
From now on, you all should likewise subdue Pāpīyān by speaking these words:
“Pāpīyān! You should not now assume such a form.
If you persist in doing so, I shall bind you with the fivefold fetters.”
Upon hearing this, Māra will immediately depart, just as that thieving dog never returns again.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha said to the householder Ghoṣila:
"If one can thus subdue Māra, one may also draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
Why, then, must the Tathāgata specify these four persons as places of reliance?
"What these four persons may say is not necessarily to be trusted.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."
What I have said is likewise so; it is not otherwise.
Good son!
I speak of "subduing Māra" for the sake of śrāvakas who possess only the fleshly eye, but I do not speak thus for those training in the Mahāyāna.
Although śrāvakas possess the divine eye, it is called the fleshly eye;
whereas those who study the Mahāyāna, though they possess only the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye. Why is this so?
This Mahāyāna sūtra is named the Buddha Vehicle; this Buddha Vehicle is the most supreme and the most excellent. "Good son!
It is like a person who is courageous, robust, and majestic, upon whom those who are timid and weak constantly come to rely."
Those brave and courageous men constantly instructed the timid ones, saying:
"You should hold the bow and grasp the arrow in this manner, and practice the arts of the spear, the long hook, and the lasso."
Furthermore, he spoke again:

"In battle, though it may be like treading upon blades, one should not give rise to thoughts of fear; rather, one should regard gods and humans as being light and weak, and should resolve within oneself to cultivate a spirit of valor and strength."

At times there may be someone who, lacking courage and valor, falsely assumes the appearance of a hero; he takes up bows, swords, and various weapons to adorn himself, and comes into the midst of the ranks, shouting loudly with an urgent voice.
You should likewise not give rise to anxiety or fear toward such people.
If those of this kind see you and do not feel terror, you should know that such people will soon fall apart and perish.
"Just as that thieving dog, O noble son, so too is the Tathāgata; he tells all the śrāvakas:
'You should not fear Māra Pāpīyān.'"
If Māra Pāpīyān should manifest in the form of a Buddha and come to where you are, you should apply yourself with diligence and firm your resolve so as to subdue him.
Then Māra will immediately become sorrowful and displeased, and will depart by the way he came.
“Good son! Just as that strong man does not learn from others, so too it is with those who study the Mahāyāna:
upon hearing various profound and esoteric sūtras, their hearts rejoice and they do not give rise to alarm or fear.”

Why is this? Because such persons who train in the Mahāyāna have already made offerings to, honored, and prostrated before immeasurable tens of billions of Buddhas of the past; therefore, even if immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of māras come to harass them, they will ultimately feel no alarm or fear regarding these matters.
“Good son! It is like a person who obtains the *agada* medicine; because of the power of this medicine, they have no fear of any venomous snakes or the like, and it can also eliminate all poisons.”
This Mahāyāna sūtra is also like this: just as by the power of that medicine one does not fear any of the evil poisons of Māras and is able to subdue them so that they do not arise again.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a dragon whose nature is extremely fierce and evil; when it wishes to harm a person, it may do so either by staring with its eyes or by hissing with its breath."
Therefore, all lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, and dogs give rise to fear.
Upon hearing its sound, seeing its form, or being touched by its body, none of these predatory beasts fail to lose their lives.

There are those who possess skillful mantras; by the power of these mantras, they are able to cause such evil venomous dragons, garuḍas, and others, as well as wicked elephants, lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, and wolves, to become gentle and docile, so that all may be ridden and controlled at will.
Just as these beasts are immediately tamed upon seeing that skillful incantation, so it is with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:
they all give rise to fear upon seeing Māra Pāpīyān, yet Māra Pāpīyān does not give rise to a heart of dread, continuing instead to perform his demonic deeds.

It is the same for those who study the Mahāyāna: seeing that the śrāvakas fear demonic activities and thus fail to give rise to faith and joy in this Mahāyāna, [the Bodhisattva] first employs skillful means to subdue all demons, making them entirely well-disciplined and fit to serve as a vehicle; he then extensively expounds various sublime dharmas for their sake.

When the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas see that Māra has been subdued, they give rise to no fear; rather, they develop faith and joy toward this unsurpassed true dharma of the Mahāyāna and speak these words:
"From this day forward, we shall not create obstacles within this true dharma."
"Furthermore, good son!
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas give rise to fear toward the various afflictions, whereas those who study the Mahāyāna have no fear at all; such is the power of practicing and studying the Mahāyāna."
For this reason, what was previously taught was intended to subdue the various māras for the sake of those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and not for the Mahāyāna.
This subtle and wondrous sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa cannot be extinguished or subdued; it is most marvelous and extraordinary.

If there are those who hear this and, having heard it, believe and accept it—being able to believe that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma—such persons are exceedingly rare, like the udumbara flower.

After my parinirvāṇa, if there are those who hear such a subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtra as this and give rise to a heart of faith and reverence, you should know that they shall not fall into the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas in future ages.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: "Good son!
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings who will slander and lack faith in this subtle and wondrous sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how long will it be before these sentient beings begin to slander this sutra?”
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, what kind of purely virtuous sentient beings will be able to rescue those who slander the Dharma?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Good son! After my parinirvāṇa, for forty years it shall be widely propagated throughout Jambudvīpa; thereafter, it shall eventually disappear into the earth.”
“Good son! It is like sugarcane, rice, rock honey, cream, curd, and clarified butter: wherever these are found, the people of that land all say, ‘This flavor is the foremost among all flavors.’”
Or again, there may be someone who eats only millet and the seeds of wild grasses, and that person also says:
"What I eat is the very best.
This is because such a person of meager merit is experiencing the retribution of their past karma.
If one is a person of merit, their ears shall never hear the names of millet or wild rice; what they consume consists solely of non-glutinous grain, sugarcane, rock honey, and clarified butter.
This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise: those of dull faculties and meager merit do not delight in hearing it, just as those of meager merit loathe polished rice and rock honey.
The followers of the two vehicles are likewise thus: they loathe and detest the unsurpassed *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Yet there may be sentient beings whose hearts delight in hearing and receiving this sūtra; having heard it, they rejoice and do not give rise to slander, like those fortunate people who eat fine non-glutinous rice.

“Good son! It is like a king who dwells in a remote mountain region, a place of peril and hardship. Although he possesses sugarcane, non-glutinous rice, and rock honey, because these are difficult to obtain, he greedily hoards them and does not dare to eat them, fearing they will run out; he eats only millet and wild grasses.
A certain king of another country heard of this and took pity on him; he immediately loaded carts with non-glutinous rice and sugarcane and sent them as a gift.
Having received them, the king distributed them throughout his entire kingdom for all to eat together.
Once the people had finished eating, they all felt great joy and spoke these words:
"It is because of that king that we have obtained this rare and exquisite flavor."
“Good son! These four kinds of people are likewise such generals of this unsurpassed Great Dharma.

Among these four, there may be one who sees bodhisattvas in other directions who, though studying such Mahāyāna sūtras—whether copying them themselves or having others copy them—do not extensively proclaim them to others for the sake of gain and offerings, for the sake of fame and praise, for the sake of understanding the Dharma, for the sake of relying [upon them], or for the sake of exchanging them for other sūtras.”
Therefore, take this subtle and wondrous sutra and deliver it to that region to give to those bodhisattvas, causing them to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta and to abide securely in enlightenment.

Once this bodhisattva has obtained this sutra, he immediately expounds it extensively for others, enabling immeasurable multitudes to receive the flavor of such a Mahāyāna Dharma; all of this is due to the power of this single bodhisattva, who causes them to hear all the sutras they have never heard before, just as those people obtain rare food by virtue of the king’s power.
"Furthermore, good son!
Wherever this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is circulated, you should know that the ground there is itself vajra, and the people therein are likewise like vajra."
If there are those who are able to hear such a sutra as this, they shall not regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all their vows shall be fully accomplished, just as I have proclaimed today.
"You monks, you should receive and uphold this well.
If there are sentient beings who are unable to hear such a sutra as this, you should know that these people are truly to be pitied."
"Why is this? Because such people are unable to receive and uphold the profound meaning of such Mahāyāna sūtras.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
During the forty years following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, this Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, shall be widely circulated and disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa.”
"After this has passed and they have sunk into the earth, how long will it be before they emerge again?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
"If my True Dharma remains for eighty years, during the first forty years, this sutra shall again rain down the great Dharma-rain upon Jambudvīpa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

When this sūtra exists during the time when the True Dharma is perishing, when the True Precepts are being destroyed, when unrighteousness increases, and when there are no sentient beings who act according to the Dharma—who will be able to hear and receive it, uphold it, read and recite it until they master it, honor and revere it, transcribe it, and explain it?

I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings, will analyze and explain this extensively, so that all bodhisattvas, having heard it, may receive and uphold it; and having upheld it, they shall immediately attain non-retrogression from their mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"
"You have now skillfully asked about such a meaning. 'Good son!

If there are sentient beings who, in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the River Śītā, have resolved their minds toward Bodhi, they will then be able to receive, uphold, and recite such a sūtra as this in this degenerate age, without giving rise to slander.'"

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, to refrain from slandering this Dharma and to cherish and delight in this scripture, yet they will not be able to analyze and explain it extensively for others.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who have awakened the bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as the sands of two Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma, but to correctly understand it, believe in it with joy, receive and uphold it, and recite it; yet they still will not be able to explain it extensively for others.”

"If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on *bodhicitta* in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in three Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil world, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and copy its scrolls; yet, even as they explain it to others, they will not yet understand its profound meaning."

"If there are sentient beings who have resolved their minds on bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in four Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and copy its scrolls, and to extensively explain for others even one-sixteenth part of its meaning; yet, even though they expound it, they will not do so in its entirety."

"If there are sentient beings who have resolved upon bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in five Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls, and extensively explain to others the meaning of eight out of sixteen parts.

"If there are sentient beings who have generated the bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in six Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil age, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls, and extensively explain for others the meaning of twelve out of the sixteen sections."

"If there are sentient beings who have generated the bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in seven Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil world, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls, and extensively explain for others fourteen-sixteenths of its meaning."

"If there are sentient beings who have generated the bodhicitta in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are sands in eight Ganges Rivers, they will then be able, amidst this evil world, not to slander this Dharma, but to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe its scrolls, and also to exhort others to transcribe them."
One is able to hear and receive it oneself, and further exhorts others to hear and receive it, read and recite it, master it, protect and uphold it;
out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, one makes offerings to this sutra and likewise exhorts others to make offerings to it;
the same applies to honoring, revering, reading and reciting, and prostrating before it.
Fully endowed with the capacity for understanding, they exhaustively realize its meaning and flavor—namely, that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, ultimately peaceful and blissful.
They extensively teach that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and skillfully know the entire Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata.
Having made offerings to such Buddhas as these, one establishes this unsurpassed True Dharma and upholds and protects it.

If there are those who have first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should know that such persons will, in future ages, certainly be able to establish this True Dharma and uphold and protect it.
Therefore, you should not now remain ignorant of those who will protect the Dharma in future ages.
Why is this? Because those who have resolved their minds [upon enlightenment] will certainly be able to uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma in the future.
“Good son! There are wicked bhikṣus who, upon hearing of my parinirvāṇa, do not feel sorrow, but instead think:
‘Today the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa; how joyful this is!’”
"While the Tathāgata was in the world, he obstructed our gains; now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, who will there be to obstruct or seize them from us?
If there is no one to obstruct or seize them, we shall regain our former gains and offerings."

"While the Tathāgata was in the world, the prohibitions and precepts were strict; now that he has entered nirvana, you should all cast aside the saṃghāṭī robes you have received. Originally intended as a formal ritual, they shall now be discarded and ruined, like wooden banners."
"Such persons as these slander and reject this Mahāyāna sūtra. Good son!
You should now remember and uphold it in this way."
If there are sentient beings who have accomplished and fulfilled immeasurable merit, they will be able to believe in this Mahāyāna sūtra, and having believed, they will receive and uphold it.

As for other sentient beings who delight in the Dharma, if one can extensively explain this sūtra for them, once those people have heard it, all the evil karma they have committed throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas of the past will be entirely extinguished.
"If there are those who do not believe in this sutra, they shall, in their present bodies, be afflicted by immeasurable suffering from illness and be frequently reviled and insulted by many people."
After their lives have ended, they will be despised by others; their countenances will be ugly and coarse, and their livelihoods will be difficult, never being sufficient.

Even if they obtain a small amount of food, it will be rough, harsh, and of poor quality; from birth to birth, they will always dwell in poverty and lowliness, within families that slander the True Dharma and hold false views.
If at the time of death, one encounters chaos and turmoil, the concurrent rise of weapons and warfare, the tyranny of a ruler, or the harassment and oppression of enemies and rivals;
or if, despite having virtuous friends, one does not meet them, and cannot obtain the necessities of life when seeking them.
Although he may obtain some slight benefit, he constantly suffers from hunger and thirst, and is regarded and recognized only by the common folk.
Kings and ministers do not deign to take him into account;
even if they hear what he proclaims, even if it be the truth, they ultimately neither believe nor accept it.
Such a person does not reach a good destination.
Just as a bird with broken wings cannot fly, so too is this person;
in future lives, they will be unable to attain a favorable rebirth among humans or devas.
