"If there should be another person who is able to believe in such Mahāyāna sūtras as these, although their original physical form may be coarse and ugly, by the merit of these sūtras they will immediately become handsome; their majestic appearance, complexion, and strength will increase day by day."
He is always joyfully beheld by humans and devas, who revere, love, and cherish him, never wishing to be parted from him.
When kings, ministers, and their kinsmen hear what he says, they all respond with reverence and faith.
If among my śrāvaka disciples there are those who wish to perform the foremost and most rare deed, they should widely proclaim such Mahāyāna sūtras as these for the sake of the world.
“Good son! It is like mist and dew; though they may seem to persist for a time, they do not last beyond sunrise.
Once the sun has risen, they vanish without a trace.”
Good son! All the evil karma of these sentient beings is likewise; the power of its persistence will not last beyond the moment they behold the sun of the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Once this sun has risen, it is able to completely eliminate all evil karma.
"Furthermore, good son, it is like a person who has left the household life and shaved his hair; although he wears the kāṣāya robe, he has not yet received the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera."
Suppose a householder comes to invite the assembly of monks; those who have not yet received the precepts join the great assembly in accepting the invitation.
Although they have not yet received the precepts, they are already reckoned as members of the Saṃgha.
"Good son!

If there are sentient beings who resolve their minds to begin studying this Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and likewise transcribe, uphold, read, and recite it, then even though they have not yet fully attained the rank of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they have already entered the number of those dwelling in the ten stages."

There may be sentient beings—whether they be disciples of the Buddha or not—who, whether out of greed and stinginess or for the sake of gain and offerings, hear and receive even a single verse of this sutra; having heard it, they do not slander it. You should know that such persons have already drawn near to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! For these reasons, I say that four kinds of persons are the refuge of the world. Good son!”
It is impossible that these four persons would claim that what was spoken by the Buddha was not spoken by the Buddha.
For this reason, I say that these four persons are the refuge of the world.
"Noble son!
You should make offerings to these four kinds of persons.
"World-Honored One!"
"How should I recognize such a person so as to make offerings to them?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there are those who establish and protect the True Dharma, one should request instruction from such persons and should offer them service even at the cost of one's own body and life."
"As I have stated in this Mahāyāna sūtra:
'If there is one who knows the Dharma, whether they be old or young, they should therefore be supported,
honored, and prostrated to, just as one serves the fire or the Brahmins.'"
Whosoever knows the Dharma, whether old or young, should therefore be supported,
honored, and prostrated to, just as the devas serve Śakra.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, one should indeed provide for one’s teachers and elders in this manner.”
I now have a doubt and pray that you will explain it in detail:
If there is an elder who upholds the prohibitive precepts and seeks out instruction on what he has not yet heard from those who are younger, should one pay him homage and respect?
If one were to pay homage [to such a person], it would not be called upholding the precepts.

Furthermore, if a youth who guards the prohibitions and precepts were to receive from an elderly person who has broken the precepts teachings he has not heard before, should he also pay homage to him?
If a renunciant receives instruction on what they have not yet heard from a layperson, should they again pay homage?
Indeed, a renunciant should not pay homage to those who live at home.

Nevertheless, within the Buddha-dharma, those who are young and junior should show reverence to the elders and seniors; for these seniors have previously received full ordination and have perfected their dignified deportment, and therefore they should be honored and respected.
As the Buddha said:
"Those who break the precepts are not tolerated within the Buddha-dharma, just as a fertile field contains much tares and weeds.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"There is one who knows the Dharma—whether old or young—who therefore should be honored as if serving Śakra.
What is the meaning of these two lines?
"Is it not that the Tathāgata has spoken falsely?
For as the Buddha said:
'Even a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts may commit transgressions.'"
For what reason did the Tathāgata speak thus?
The World-Honored One has also stated in other sūtras that one may listen to and undergo treatment for the breaking of precepts; the meaning of such statements remains unclear.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son! I have spoken these verses for the sake of future bodhisattvas who study the Mahāyāna, not for the sake of the śrāvaka disciples."
"Good son!
As I have previously said:

when the True Dharma has perished and the true precepts are being violated; when the breaking of precepts increases and unrighteousness flourishes; when all the sages have hidden themselves and do not appear; and when the impure practice of keeping slaves and servants prevails—at that time, one person from among these four types of people shall appear in the world, shave off their hair and beard, leave the household life, and cultivate the Way."

He saw that the various bhikṣus each accepted and kept slaves, servants, and impure things; they knew nothing of what was pure or impure, nor did they recognize what was in accordance with the Vinaya or contrary to it.
In order to subdue such bhikṣus, this person harmonizes with them while remaining untainted by their defilements.
Being well able to distinguish between his own sphere of conduct and the sphere of the Buddha’s conduct, he remains silent and does not expose others even when he sees them commit pārājika offenses.
Why is this? I have appeared in the world desiring to establish and protect the True Dharma; for this reason, I remain silent and do not reprimand or discipline them. Good son!
Such a person, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, is not said to have broken the precepts even if they commit an offense. "Good son!
It is like a king who has passed away from illness, leaving behind a crown prince who is too young to succeed him."

There was a caṇḍāla who possessed abundant wealth and treasures, whose riches were immeasurable and whose retinue was vast; he then used force to usurp the royal throne, taking advantage of the kingdom's weakness.
Not long after he had begun his rule, the people of the country, householders, brahmins, and others deserted him and fled, seeking refuge in distant foreign lands.
Even those who remained did not wish to so much as look upon this king with their eyes.
There were some elders, brahmins, and others who did not leave their native lands, just as various trees die where they were born.
King Caṇḍāla, knowing that many of his subjects had fled in rebellion, immediately dispatched more caṇḍālas to patrol and guard all the roads.
Again, for seven days, he beat the drums and issued a proclamation:
"To any brāhmaṇa who can serve as my consecration preceptor, I shall grant half the kingdom as a reward."
Although all the brahmins heard these words, none of them came;
each of them said, "How could there be one of the brahmin caste who would perform such an act?"
The Caṇḍāla king spoke again, saying:

"If not even a single person among the brāhmaṇas will become my teacher, I shall certainly compel all the brāhmaṇas to live, eat, and sleep together with the caṇḍālas, and to share their same occupations."
"If there be anyone capable of coming to consecrate my head with the royal aspersion, half the kingdom shall be granted as a fief; this word is not false.
Furthermore, the exquisite nectar of immortality obtained through incantations from the Heaven of the Thirty-three shall likewise be shared and consumed by us together."
“At that time, there was the son of a brahmin, in the prime of his youth, who practiced pure conduct, wore long hair as his characteristic mark, and was well-versed in incantations.”
He went to the king's presence and said,
"Great King! Whatever Your Majesty commands me to do, I am fully capable of performing."
At that time, the Great King felt great joy in his heart and accepted this youth as his consecration preceptor.
When the brahmins heard of this matter, they were all filled with indignation and rebuked the youth, saying:
"How can you, a brahmin, act as a preceptor for a candāla?"
At that time, the king immediately divided half of his kingdom with the youth, and they ruled the country together for a long period.
Then, the youth said to the king:
"I left my family life to become Your Majesty’s teacher and have taught you all the subtle and secret incantations; yet, Your Majesty still does not treat me as a relative."
Then the king replied,
"Why would I not be intimate with you now?
The youth answered:
"The immortal elixir possessed by the former kings has not yet been shared among us.
The King said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Great Master!
I truly did not know; if you require it, I pray that you take it.
At that time, having heard the king's words, the youth immediately took it home, invited the various ministers, and ate it together with them.
After the ministers had finished eating, they said together to the king:
"How wonderful! Our Great Master possesses such ambrosia, the medicine of immortality.
Once the king knew this, he spoke to his teacher, saying:
"How is it that the Great Master alone, together with his ministers, partakes of the ambrosia while we are not granted a share?
At that time, the youth immediately gave the king another medicine mixed with various poisons to consume.
Once the king had taken the medicine, after a short while its effects took hold; he fell to the ground in a state of delirium, unconscious like one who is dead.
At that time, the youth established his former crown prince back upon the throne as king, saying these words:

"The Lion Throne is such that, according to the Dharma, a *caṇḍāla* should not be allowed to ascend it. From ancient times until now, I have never heard of nor seen one of the *caṇḍāla* caste become a king."
"It is impossible for a *caṇḍāla* to govern a kingdom or rule over the people;
Your Majesty should now return to succeed the former king and rule the country with the True Dharma.
At that time, having thus managed the situation, the youth gave the antidote to the *caṇḍāla* to cause him to awaken.
Once he had awakened, they drove him out of the country.
At that time, although the youth had performed these deeds, he still did not lose his status as a Brahmin.
When the other householders, Brahmins, and others heard what he had done, they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
O virtuous one,
you have skillfully driven away the Caṇḍāla king.”

“Good son! After my parinirvāṇa, those bodhisattvas who protect and uphold the true Dharma shall likewise, through the power of skillful means, engage in the same activities as those monks who break the precepts, who are merely nominal, and who accept and store all manner of impure things.”

At that time, if a bodhisattva sees someone who, despite having committed many transgressions of the precepts, is able to discipline those evil bhikṣus who violate the prohibitions, he shall immediately go to that person’s place, pay respectful homage, provide the four types of offerings, and present all his scriptures and personal belongings to him.
If one does not possess them oneself, one must employ skillful means to seek and beg for them from various donors.
For this purpose, one should keep the eight kinds of impure items.
Why is this? It is because such a person acts to discipline wicked bhikṣus, just as that youth drove away the caṇḍālas.
At that time, although the bodhisattva may respectfully prostrate to such a person and accept or keep the eight kinds of impure things, he incurs no fault whatsoever.

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas, desiring to expel and discipline wicked bhikṣus, wish to enable the pure Saṃgha to dwell in peace and security, to cause the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras to be disseminated, and to benefit all devas and humans.

“Good son! For this reason, I have spoken these two verses within the sutras, so that all bodhisattvas may together praise those who protect the Dharma, just as those householders and brahmins praised the youth, saying:
‘Excellent, excellent!’”
"The Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma should indeed act in this way.

If there is anyone who sees a person protecting the Dharma engaging in the same activities as one who has broken the precepts and says that [the protector] is guilty of an offense, you should know that such a person will themselves suffer the calamity; the one who protects the Dharma is truly without fault.

“Good son! If there is a bhikṣu who, having violated the prohibitive precepts, conceals them and does not repent out of a mind of arrogance, you should know that such a person is truly one who has broken the precepts.”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts for the sake of protecting the Dharma, even if they commit an offense, it is not called a violation of the precepts.
Why is this? Because they are free from arrogance, and because they confess and repent.
“Good son!
For this reason, in the sutras I have spoken these verses with their meaning concealed:
‘If there is one who knows the Dharma, whether old or young, they should therefore be honored and supported.’”
They pay homage and prostrate, just as the fire-worshipping Brahmins and others do;
like those in the second heaven, they serve Śakra.
“For these reasons, I have not spoken this verse for the sake of those training as śrāvakas, but solely for the sake of bodhisattvas.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Are the precepts originally received by such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these still fully intact, even though they have become lax regarding the precepts?
The Buddha said,
"Good sons!..."
You should not speak in such a manner now. Why is this?
The precepts originally received are not lost as they were; should one commit an offense, one must immediately repent, and having repented, one becomes pure again.
“Good son! It is like an old embankment or dam that has been breached; if there is a hole, the water will leak through. Why is this?
Because it is not maintained by anyone.
If there were someone to maintain it, the water would not flow out.

It is the same with the Bodhisattva: although he may perform the *poṣadha*, receive the precepts, and engage in the communal affairs of the Saṃgha together with those who have broken the precepts, all his moral discipline is like a dam that has been breached and is leaking away.
Why is this? If there are no persons who maintain pure precepts, the Saṃgha will decline and become lax, and negligence will increase day by day;
if there are persons who maintain pure precepts, they will be able to remain complete and not lose their fundamental precepts.
“Good son! To be lax regarding the vehicle is what is called laxity; to be lax regarding the precepts is not called laxity.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not allow the mind to become indolent or arrogant toward this Great Vehicle, this is called upholding the precepts.”
"To protect the True Dharma, one bathes oneself with the water of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, although a bodhisattva may appear to violate the precepts, this is not called laxity.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Within the Saṃgha there are four kinds of persons, like the mango fruit, which is difficult to distinguish as raw or ripe; how can one recognize those who break the precepts and those who uphold them?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
By means of this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it can be easily understood.
How is it that through this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* it may be known?
It is like a farmer who plants rice and weeds out the tares and barnyard grass; when viewed with the physical eye, it is called a "pure field."
When they reach full maturity, the grass and grain are each distinct.
In this way, these eight matters can defile the Sangha; if one can eliminate them, then by observing with the physical eye, one will know it is pure.
Whether one maintains the precepts or violates them, when no evil is being committed, it is difficult to distinguish between them by means of the fleshly eye.
However, if evil becomes manifest, it is easy to know; it is like the ease with which one can distinguish between weeds and grain.

It is the same within the Sangha: if one can remain far removed from the eight kinds of impure, venomous snake-like dharmas, such a person is called a pure field of merit for the noble assembly and should be venerated by humans and devas.
The retribution of purity cannot be distinguished by the physical eye.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a *kālakā* forest where the trees are numerous; within this forest there is but one tree named *candana*.
These *kālakā* trees and *tinduka* trees have fruits that are so similar they cannot be distinguished.
When the fruits ripen, a woman gathers them all; yet of the *tinduka* fruits there is but one part, while of the *kālakā* fruits there are ten parts.
This woman did not recognize it; she brought it to the market and offered it for sale.
An ignorant child, likewise unable to distinguish it, purchased the kālakā fruit and ate it, whereupon his life came to an end.
When those wise people heard this matter, they immediately asked the woman:
"Sister! From where did you obtain these fruits?"
At that time, the woman pointed out the location.
The people then said:
"In such a place there are many, immeasurable *kālakā* trees, and there is only a single *tinduka* tree."
When the people realized this, they laughed and departed. "Good son!

It is the same with the eight impure things within the great assembly. Among them, many make use of these eight impure things; yet there is but one person who maintains pure precepts and does not accept these eight impure things. He clearly knows that the others are receiving and storing what is unlawful, yet he associates with them and does not abandon them, just like that single tinduka tree in the forest."
There may be upāsakas who, seeing that these people frequently engage in unrighteous conduct, do not show them respect or provide offerings.
If they wish to make offerings, they should first ask:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Are these eight matters permitted for one to receive and keep?
Are they authorized by the Buddha?
If it is said that the Buddha has authorized them, may such a person participate in the *poṣadha*, the *karmavācanā*, and the *pravāraṇā* together with the community?"
After this upāsaka had asked thus, the assembly all replied:
"The Tathāgata, out of compassion, has permitted the possession of all these eight things."
The upāsaka said:
"In the Jeta Grove Monastery, there are bhikṣus who say that the Buddha permitted the possession of gold and silver, while others say he did not permit it."

Regarding those who speak of "listening": one does not dwell together with such non-listeners, nor does one recite the precepts or perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony with them; furthermore, one does not even drink water from the same river as them, nor share any material gains or offerings with them at all.
"How can you say that the Buddha has permitted this?
Although the Buddha, the God among Gods, may have accepted it, you members of the Saṃgha must not keep it yourselves.
If there are those who accept it, you should not even perform the *Poṣadha*, the *Pravāraṇā*, the *Karmavācanā*, or any communal affairs of the Saṃgha together with them."

If they participate together in the recitation of the precepts, the *pravāraṇā*, the *karmavācanā*, or communal monastic affairs, they shall fall into hell immediately upon death, just as those people did who died after eating the kāla fruit.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a man selling medicine in a city who has a wondrous sweet medicine produced from the Snowy Mountains, yet he also sells many other miscellaneous medicines that are similar in their sweet taste."

At that time, there were many people who all wished to purchase [the medicine] but could not distinguish it; they went to the place where the medicine was being sold and asked, "Do you have the Snowy Mountain medicine?
The medicine seller immediately replied:
"There is. This person is deceitful; using other miscellaneous medicines, he says to the buyer:
"This is a sweet, excellent, and wonderful medicine from the Snowy Mountains."
At that time, because the buyer possessed only fleshly eyes, he was unable to distinguish it well; he immediately purchased it and took it home, whereupon he thought to himself:
"I have now obtained the sweet medicine of the Snowy Mountains."

"Kāśyapa! Within the community of śrāvakas, there may be those who are monks in name only, those who are monks in reality, and those who constitute a harmonious saṃgha—whether they uphold the precepts or violate them—one should equally offer them offerings, respect, and prostrations."

Because this upāsaka possesses only the fleshly eye, he is unable to distinguish—just as that person could not distinguish the sweet medicinal herbs of the Snowy Mountains—who among them maintains the precepts and who violates them, or who is a true monk and who is a false monk; only one with the divine eye can make such distinctions.
Kāśyapa! If a lay follower knows that a bhikṣu is one who has broken the precepts, he should not provide him with alms, nor should he pay him homage or offer him worship.
If he knows that such a person accepts and keeps the eight [forbidden] things, he likewise should not provide him with his necessities, nor should he pay him homage or offer him worship.
"If there are those within the Sangha who have broken the precepts, one should not pay them respect or prostrate before them merely because they wear the kashaya.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Excellent, excellent!
What the Tathāgata has spoken is true and not false; I shall receive it upon the crown of my head as if it were a vajra, a rare jewel, or a wondrous object.
As the Buddha has said:
"These bhikṣus should rely upon four dharmas.
What are these four?"

One should rely on the Dharma and not on the person; rely on the meaning and not on the words; rely on wisdom and not on consciousness; and rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and not on sūtras of interpretable meaning. These four principles should be realized and known; they are not for the four types of persons.
The Buddha said:
"Good son! That which accords with the Dharma is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Parinirvāṇa."
All Buddha-dharmas are the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and that which is the dharma-nature is the Tathāgata.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Furthermore, if there should be one who says:
"To say 'the Tathāgata is impermanent' is for such a person not to know and not to see the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If one does not know and see this nature of phenomena, one should not rely upon [such a teacher]."
As stated above, those four individuals who appear in the world to protect and uphold the Dharma should be realized and relied upon as a refuge.

Why is this? Because these persons skillfully understand the subtle, secret, and profound treasury of the Tathāgata; they are able to know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging. If one says:
"It is impossible that the Tathāgata is impermanent or subject to change.
These four persons are themselves called the Tathāgata."
Why is this? Because such a person is able to understand the Tathāgata’s esoteric speech and is able to expound it.

If there is someone who can thoroughly comprehend the Tathāgata’s profound and secret treasury and knows that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, yet such a person, for the sake of gain and support, says:
To say "The Tathāgata is impermanent" is impossible;
such a person may still be relied upon, how much more so those who do not rely on these four kinds of people?
To rely on the Dharma is to rely on the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); to rely on persons is to rely on the śrāvakas.
The nature of phenomena is the Tathāgata; the śrāvaka is that which is conditioned (saṃskṛta).
The Tathāgata is eternally abiding, whereas that which is conditioned is impermanent. Good son!
If there is a person who violates the precepts and, for the sake of gain and offerings, says:
"One who says, 'The Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to change,' is a person upon whom one should not rely.
Good son!"
This is called the definition.
Regarding "rely on the meaning, not on the words":
"meaning" refers to awakening and realization.
The meaning of awakening is called non-deficiency;
non-deficiency is called fulfillment;
the meaning of fulfillment is called the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding and unchanging nature.
The meaning of the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging nature is precisely the eternity of the Dharma;
the meaning of the eternity of the Dharma is precisely the eternity of the Saṃgha.
This is called relying on the meaning and not relying on the words.
What kind of speech should not be relied upon?

It refers to various treatises that employ flowery rhetoric, claiming they are like the immeasurable sutras spoken by the Buddha; being insatiably greedy for them, using craftiness and flattery, feigning intimacy, seeking profit through hints and signs, and managing affairs for laypeople as their servants.
Furthermore, he proclaimed:

"The Buddha permits bhikṣus to keep male and female slaves and impure things; gold, silver, precious gems, granaries of grain, and cattle, sheep, elephants, and horses for the purpose of trade and seeking profit."

"In times of famine, out of compassion for his sons, he further permitted the bhikṣus to store up old provisions, to eat food prepared by their own hands, and to consume food that had not been formally received.
Such words as these should not be relied upon.
"Relying on wisdom and not on consciousness:
that which is called wisdom is the Tathāgata.
If there are śrāvakas who cannot properly know the merits of the Tathāgata, such consciousness should not be relied upon."
If one knows that the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, such true wisdom is what should be relied upon.
If, however, one perceives the Tathāgata as the body of expedient means, saying:
"This is comprised of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and is nourished by food."
One should not rely upon them either.
Therefore, one should know that a teacher cannot be relied upon as a refuge.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who speaks thus, and their scriptures as well, one should not rely upon them.
"Relying on sūtras of definitive meaning and not relying on sūtras of interpretable meaning:

'interpretable' refers to the Śrāvaka vehicle. Upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s profound and secret treasury, they all give rise to doubt and wonder; they do not know that this treasury gives birth to the great ocean of wisdom. They are like infants who lack discernment—this is what is called 'interpretable meaning. "

"Definitive meaning (nītārtha) refers to the true wisdom of a bodhisattva; according to their own mind's unimpeded great wisdom, it is like a great person who knows all things—this is called definitive meaning."
"Furthermore, the Śrāvakayāna is called 'of provisional meaning' (neyārtha),
whereas the unsurpassed Mahāyāna is called 'of definitive meaning' (nītārtha).
If one says:"
To say, "The Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to change," is called a teaching of provisional meaning;
whereas if one says:
"The Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging"—
this is called the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
That which is spoken by the śrāvakas as something to be realized is called the non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
That which is spoken by the Bodhisattva and should be realized is called definitive meaning (nītārtha).
If it is said:
"The Tathāgata is sustained by food."
This is of provisional meaning; if it says:
"It is eternally abiding and unchanging."
This is called the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
If it is said:
"The Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa just as fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted," [this is the definitive meaning].
This is called the provisional meaning;
whereas if one says:
"The Tathāgata has entered the dharma-nature," [this is the definitive meaning].
This is called the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
One should not rely upon the vehicle of the Śrāvakas. Why is this?
The Tathāgata, desiring to deliver sentient beings, employs the power of skillful means to teach the Śrāvaka vehicle, just as an elder teaches his children the half-syllables. Good son!
The Śrāvaka-yāna is like the first plowing, from which no fruit has yet been obtained; thus it is called "of provisional meaning.
Therefore, one should not rely upon the Śrāvaka-yāna.
The Dharma of the Mahāyāna should be relied upon. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata, desiring to deliver sentient beings, taught the Mahāyāna through the power of skillful means; therefore, it should be relied upon, and this is called the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
"These four reliances should be realized and understood.
Furthermore, 'reliance on the meaning'—meaning (*artha*) is called straightforwardness;
straightforwardness is called illumination."
"Radiance" is named "not weak or inferior";
"not weak or inferior" is named "Tathāgata.
Furthermore, "radiance" is named "wisdom."
That which is upright and straightforward is called eternally abiding.
That which is eternal in the Tathāgata is called relying upon the Dharma.
The Dharma is called eternal; it is also called boundless, inconceivable, ungraspable, and unboundable, yet it can also be seen.
If there is one who says that [the Dharma] is invisible, such a person is not to be relied upon.
Therefore, rely on the Dharma and do not rely on the person.
Furthermore, if there is someone who proclaims impermanence with subtle and refined words, such speech is not to be relied upon.
Therefore, rely on the meaning and not on the words.
"Relying on wisdom" means that the Sangha is permanent, unconditioned, and immutable, and does not store the eight kinds of impure things.
Therefore, rely on wisdom and do not rely on consciousness.
If someone were to say:
"Consciousness acts; consciousness experiences."
There is no Saṃgha of harmony. Why is this?
That which is called "harmony" is, in fact, non-existent.
"Since it is non-existent, how can it be called permanent?
For this reason, this consciousness cannot be relied upon.

"Relying on the definitive meaning (nītārtha) means that 'definitive' refers to contentment; one never feigns dignified deportment, purity, arrogance, self-exaltation, or the pursuit of gain and offerings. Furthermore, one does not give rise to attachment toward the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata through skillful means according to what is appropriate—this is called the definitive meaning."
If there are those who can abide within such [teachings], it should be known that these persons have already attained abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
For this reason, it is said: "Rely on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and do not rely on those of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*)."
"Regarding the 'provisional meaning' (neyārtha), it is as stated in the sūtras:
'All things are ablaze; all things are impermanent; all things are suffering; all things are empty; all things are without self.'"
This is called the "provisional meaning" (neyārtha). Why?
Because by being unable to understand such meanings, it causes sentient beings to fall into the Avīci Hell.
Why is this? Because of grasping and attachment, one does not understand the meaning.
"All that is burned" refers to:
"The Tathāgata says that even nirvāṇa is burned.
If all things are impermanent, then nirvāṇa is also impermanent;
suffering, emptiness, and non-self are likewise so.
Therefore, these are called sutras of provisional meaning (neyārtha) and should not be relied upon. "Good son!
If someone should say:
"The Tathāgata has compassion for all sentient beings and well understands the appropriateness of the timing.
Because he knows the timing, he may speak of what is light as heavy, or speak of what is heavy as light."

The Tathāgata observes and knows that among his disciples, there are those who have donors providing all their necessities so that they lack for nothing; for such persons, the Buddha does not permit the keeping of slaves, gold, silver, wealth, treasures, or the buying, selling, and trading of impure things.

If my disciples have no donors to provide their necessities, and at a time when the world suffers from famine and food and drink are difficult to obtain, I permit my disciples—desiring to establish and uphold the True Dharma—to accept and possess slaves, gold, silver, vehicles, fields, houses, grain, and rice, and to sell or exchange these for what they require.
Although one may accept and keep such items as these, they must be given through pure dedication (*pariśuddha-dāna*) by a donor of firm faith.
These four dharmas are those upon which one should rely; furthermore, if there are Vinaya, Abhidharma, or Sūtras that do not contradict these four, those too should be relied upon.
If someone were to say:

"Whether it be the proper time or the improper time, whether one is able to protect the Dharma or unable to protect the Dharma, the Tathāgata permits all bhikṣus to accept and store such impure things."
Regarding such words, one should not rely upon them.
Even if there are corresponding explanations within the Vinaya, Abhidharma, or Sūtras, one should likewise not rely upon these three divisions [of the Tripiṭaka].
"I have taught these four reliances for the sake of sentient beings who possess only the fleshly eye, and never for those who possess the eye of wisdom.
Therefore, I now declare these four reliances: 'Dharma' refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena);
'Meaning' refers to the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging presence."
"The wise one" is one who knows that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
"one who understands the definitive meaning" is one who thoroughly comprehends all Mahāyāna sūtras.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Added by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇas Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter Nine: The Chapter on the Nature of Deviance. Chapter Nine: The Nature of Deviance.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the four kinds of persons mentioned above, should one rely upon them?”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is. Good son!"
You should rely upon what I have taught. Why is this?
Because there are four Māras.
"What are these four?
They are those who can receive and uphold other sutras and vinayas as taught by Māra.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught that there are four kinds of māras,
how should I distinguish between what is spoken by a māra and what is spoken by the Buddha?”
“There are sentient beings who follow the ways of Māra, and there are those who comply with the teachings of the Buddha; how, then, can such as these be known?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Seven hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this Māra Pāpīyān will gradually corrupt and disrupt my True Dharma.”

For example, just as a hunter might dress himself in the robes of the Dharma, so too does Māra Pāpīyān assume the forms of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā; he further conjures the body of a srotāpanna, and even conjures the bodies of arhats and the form-body (rūpakāya) of a Buddha.
The Māra King, using this tainted form to manifest as an untainted body, shall destroy my True Dharma.
When this Māra Pāpīyān destroys the True Dharma, he will speak these words:

"In the past, the Bodhisattva descended from the Tuṣita Heaven and came here to the palace of King Śuddhodana in Kapilavastu; relying upon his parents and through the union of their desire, he was born with this body."
If it is said:
"There is a person born among humans who is venerated by the great assembly of devas and humans in all the worlds," such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, it is said:
"In the past, through various acts of asceticism and giving—offering his head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, city, wife, and children—he has therefore now attained the Way of the Buddha."
By these causes and conditions, they are revered by humans, devas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
"If there are sūtras or vinayas that speak in this way, you should know that they are all spoken by Māra.
Good son! If there are sūtras or vinayas that speak as follows:"

"The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment long ago; that he now manifests the attainment of the Buddha-way is solely because he desires to deliver all sentient beings. To accord with the ways of the world, he manifests birth through the union of parents and the conditions of desire."
"Know that such sūtras and vinayas are truly spoken by the Tathāgata.
Those who follow what is spoken by Māra are the retinue of Māra;
those who can follow what is spoken by the Buddha are bodhisattvas."
"If anyone should say,
'The claim that when the Tathāgata was born he took seven steps in each of the ten directions is not to be believed,' this is the teaching of Māra."
"Furthermore, if there is another who says:

'The Tathāgata’s appearing in the world and walking seven paces in each of the ten directions is a manifestation of the Tathāgata’s skillful means,' this is called a sūtra and a vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata."
If there are those who follow what the Māra has said, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they can follow what the Buddha has said, they are Bodhisattvas.
"If anyone should say:
"When the Bodhisattva was born, the King sent men to lead him to the celestial shrine.
When the various devas saw him, they all descended to pay him homage; for this reason, he is named Buddha."
Furthermore, there is an objection:
"The devas appeared first, and the Buddha appeared later.
How is it that the devas pay homage to the Buddha?"
One who raises such an objection should know that it is the speech of Pāpīyān.
"If there is a sūtra that says:
'When the Buddha went to a deva temple, these various devas—Maheśvara, Mahābrahmā, and Śakra Devendra—all joined their palms and paid homage at his feet.'"
"Such sūtras and vinayas are what the Buddha has spoken.
If there are those who follow what the Māra has spoken, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they can follow what the Buddha has spoken, they are bodhisattvas."
"If there are sūtras or vinayas that state:

'When the Bodhisattva was a crown prince, he took a wife from the four quarters out of desire; dwelling in the deep palace, he amused himself with the five desires and joyfully experienced pleasure.'"
"Such sūtras and vinayas were spoken by Pāpīyān.
If someone should say:

'The Bodhisattva has long since abandoned desire and all that pertains to wife and children, even refusing to accept the exquisite five desires of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as if discarding nasal mucus or spittle.'"
"How much more so for human desires!
One should shave off hair and beard, leave the household life, and cultivate the Way.
Such sūtras and vinayas were spoken by the Buddha.
If there are those who follow the sūtras and vinaya of Māra, they are the retinue of Māra;
if there are those who follow the sūtras and vinaya of the Buddha, they are bodhisattvas.
If anyone should say:

The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī and permitted the bhikṣus to accept and keep male and female slaves, servants, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, donkeys, mules, chickens, pigs, cats, dogs, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, crystal, musāragalva, agate, coral, amber, conch shells, jade disks, copper, iron, cooking pots, and large and small bronze basins.
Regarding the necessities of life— such as plowing fields and planting crops, engaging in trade and commerce, and storing up grain and rice—
for the sake of his great compassion and out of pity for sentient beings, the Buddha permitted the possession of all such things.
"Such sutras and vinayas are all spoken by Māra.
If someone were to say:
'The Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery, in the dwelling place of the nāga-nāyaka Nālīru.'"
At that time, the Tathāgata, on account of the brahmin Gośṛṅga and King Prasenajit, spoke as follows:

"A bhikṣu should not accept or store gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, musāragalva, agate, coral, amber, conch shells, jade, male or female slaves, servants, boys, girls, or animals such as cattle, sheep, elephants, horses, donkeys, mules, chickens, pigs, cats, and dogs; nor should he accept copper or iron pots and pans, large or small bronze basins, or various multi-colored beds, mats, and bedding."

Regarding the necessities for sustaining life—namely, houses, plowing fields and planting crops, buying and selling in the marketplace—they prepare their own food by hand, grinding and pounding it themselves.

He practices incantations for healing the body, methods for taming hawks, observing the constellations above, calculating the waxing and waning of the calendar, divining the characteristics of men and women, and interpreting the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of dreams—whether they portend male or female offspring, or neither male nor female. He possesses these sixty-four arts, as well as eighteen incantations that delude people and various forms of craftsmanship.
Or they speak of the countless mundane affairs of the world: powdered incense, ground incense, unguents, perfumes, various flower garlands, and the arts of hairdressing.
They are deceitful, treacherous, and sycophantic; they crave gain without satiety and delight in the clamor of crowds, engaging in jesting and idle talk.
They are greedy for fish and meat, compound poisons, process fragrant oils, and manufacture precious parasols, leather sandals, fans, boxes, chests, and various types of painted images.
They hoard grains, rice, wheat—both large and small—and beans, as well as various fruits and gourds.
They associate with kings, princes, ministers, and women; they laugh loudly or remain silent.
They give rise to much doubt regarding all phenomena and frequently speak falsely of things as long or short, beautiful or ugly, or wholesome or unwholesome.
They take pleasure in fine clothing and personally praise such various impure things before their donors.
Those who frequent impure places for coming and going—namely, taverns, brothels, and gambling dens—I now forbid such persons from remaining among the bhikṣus;
they should cease their practice of the Way and return to lay life to perform labor, just as weeds and tares are utterly eradicated without remainder.
"You should know that all such sūtras and vinaya rules established by these [teachings] are spoken by the Tathāgata himself.
Those who follow what is spoken by Māra are the retinue of Māra;
those who follow what is spoken by the Buddha are bodhisattvas."
"If there should be one who says:
'A bodhisattva enters a celestial shrine out of a desire to make offerings to the devas—namely, Brahmā, Maheśvara, Vedha, and Kātyāyana.'"
"The reason for entering [this state] is the desire to subdue all devas and humans.
If one were to say otherwise, it would be impossible. If one says:

"A bodhisattva cannot enter into the heterodox doctrines of external paths; he does not understand their rituals, literature, or arts; he is unable to reconcile servants who are quarreling; he is not honored by men or women, kings, or ministers; furthermore, he does not know how to compound medicinal drugs."
"Because they do not know, they are called Tathāgatas.
If they were to know, they would be among those of false views.
Furthermore:

"The Tathāgata maintains an impartial mind toward both enemies and kin; whether one cuts his body with a blade or another anoints it with fragrant incense, he conceives neither thoughts of benefit nor harm toward these two types of people, but remains solely in the middle. For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata."
"One should know that such sutras and vinayas are spoken by Māra.
If someone says:
'The Bodhisattva thus manifested entry into celestial shrines and among those who study external paths, leaving the home life to practice the Way. "
He manifests knowledge of proper deportment and etiquette, and is able to master all forms of literature and the arts.
He manifests entry into schools and workshops of craftsmanship, and is skilled at reconciling quarrels among servants and attendants.

Among the great assemblies—whether they be young men or young women, ladies of the inner palace, commoners, elders, brahmins, kings, ministers, or the poor—he is the most honored and supreme, and is further revered by all of them.
They are also able to manifest such matters as these:
although they dwell amidst various views, they do not give rise to attachment, just as a lotus flower is unsullied by dust and mire.
For the sake of delivering all sentient beings, they skillfully employ such various expedient means, conforming to worldly dharmas.
"Know that such sūtras and vinayas are precisely what was spoken by the Tathāgata.
Those who follow what is spoken by Māra are the retinue of Māra;
those who can follow what is spoken by the Buddha are great bodhisattvas."
"If there should be one who says:
'The Tathāgata has explained for me the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Regarding the light and heavy offenses among evil dharmas, as well as the sthūlātyaya, their nature is entirely grave; we shall never commit them within our Vinaya.'"
"I have long endured such a doctrine; since you do not believe it, how could I abandon my own discipline to follow yours?
The discipline you possess was spoken by Māra."
"Our sūtras and vinaya were established by the Buddha; the Tathāgata previously taught the ninefold seal of the Dharma (navāṅga-dharmamudrā).
These nine seals certify our sūtras and vinaya, yet from the beginning we have never heard a single phrase or a single word of the Vaipulya sūtras."
Among the immeasurable sutras and vinayas spoken by the Tathāgata, where is it said that there are Vaipulya sutras?
Within such works as these, the names of the ten classes of sutras have never been heard before.
If such [sutras] exist, one should know that they were certainly composed by Devadatta; Devadatta, being an evil person, created Vaipulya sutras for the purpose of destroying the true Dharma.
We do not believe in such sutras as these; they are the words spoken by Māra.
Why is this? Because it destroys the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma by engaging in disputes over right and wrong.
Such statements as these exist in your sutras but do not exist in my sutras.
In my sūtras and vinayas, the Tathāgata has said:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be improper sūtras and vinayas in this degenerate age, namely the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras."
"In future ages, there shall be such evil bhikṣus.
Again, I have said:

"Beyond the nine divisions of the sūtras, there are the Vaipulya scriptures. If there is anyone who can thoroughly understand their meaning, you should know that this person correctly understands the Sūtras and Vinaya; they remain far removed from all impure things, being subtle, wondrous, and pure like the full moon."
If someone were to say:

"Although the Tathāgata has expounded the meanings and flavors of each individual sutra and vinaya as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these are not found within our vinaya; therefore, we know they do not exist."
"If it truly exists, why has the Tathāgata not explained it within my Vinaya?
For this reason, I am unable to believe and accept it.
You should know that such a person incurs an offense.
That person further says:
"I shall receive and uphold such sutras and vinayas. Why is this?"
‘You should act for my sake as a cause for contentment and fewness of desires, for the abandonment of afflictions, for wisdom and nirvana, and for wholesome dharmas.
One who speaks thus is not my disciple.
"If there should be one who says:
'The Tathāgata, desiring to deliver sentient beings,
has preached the Vaipulya sūtras,' you should know that this person is truly my disciple."
If there are those who do not accept the Vaipulya sutras, you should know that such persons are not my disciples;
they have not left the household life for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, but are instead disciples of heterodox paths with false views.
Sūtras and Vinayas such as these are spoken by the Buddha;
if they are not thus, they are spoken by Māra.
Those who follow what is spoken by Māra are the retinue of Māra.
If there is one who accords with what the Buddha has taught,
that person is a bodhisattva. Furthermore, good son,
if someone should say:
"The Tathāgata is not something accomplished by means of immeasurable merit, nor is he subject to impermanence or change.
Because he has realized the dharma of emptiness, he proclaims non-self and does not conform to worldly conventions."
"Such sūtras and vinayas are said to have been taught by Māra.
If someone should say:
'The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is inconceivable, and it is also accomplished through immeasurable asaṃkhyeya merits.'"
"Therefore, it is eternally abiding and without change.
Such sutras and vinayas are what the Buddha has taught.
If there are those who follow what is spoken by Māra, they are the retinue of Māra.
If there is one who accords with what the Buddha has taught, that person is a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, some say:
"There may be a bhikṣu who, in reality, has not committed a pārājika offense."
"All the people said that he had committed a *pārājika* offense, like cutting down a *tāla* tree; yet this bhikṣu had actually committed no offense.
Why is this? For I have always said:"
"If one commits even a single of the four *pārājika* offenses, it is like splitting a stone that cannot be rejoined.
If one claims for oneself to have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), this is called committing a *pārājika*.

Why is this? Because although they have truly attained nothing, they falsely manifest the appearance of attainment; such a person falls away from the qualities of a human being, and this is called a *pārājika* offense.
"That is to say:"
If there is a bhikṣu who has few desires and is content, who maintains pure precepts and dwells in a secluded place,
and if a king or a high minister sees this bhikṣu and thinks to himself that he has attained arhatship, they will immediately approach him to praise, revere, and prostrate before him.
He further spoke these words:
"When this Great Teacher has cast off this body, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu immediately addressed the king, saying:
"I have not yet truly attained the fruits of the śramaṇa path; O King, do not say that I have attained them.
I only pray, Great King, that you will not speak to me of the dharma of insatiability."
One who lacks contentment would even silently accept everything up to and including the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If I were now to silently accept it, I would be censured by all the Buddhas.
The practice of contentment is praised by all Buddhas.
Therefore, I wish to joyfully cultivate contentment for the rest of my life.

Furthermore, as for one who is content, I know for certain that I have not yet attained the fruits of the Path; although the King declares that I have attained them, I do not accept this, and thus I am called "content."
The king then replied, "Great Master, you have truly attained the fruit of Arhatship; you are no different from the Buddha.

At that time, the king issued a proclamation throughout the inner and outer courts to all the people, as well as to the ladies of the harem and the queen, so that everyone would know he had attained the fruit of a śramaṇa.
Therefore, may all who hear this give rise to reverent faith and offer worship and respect.
Such bhikṣus are truly persons of pure brahmacarya; by these causes and conditions, they cause all people everywhere to attain great merit and virtue.
Yet this bhikṣu has not actually committed a pārājika offense. Why is this?
Because the other person spontaneously gave rise to a heart of joy and offered praise and offerings; how, then, could such a bhikṣu have any fault?
If anyone says that such a person incurs sin, you should know that this sutra is what Māra has spoken.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who preach the Buddha’s profound secret treasury of sutras, saying:

"All sentient beings possess buddha-nature; by virtue of this nature, they can sever immeasurable billions of afflictions and fetters and immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, with the exception of the icchantikas."
If a king or a great minister should speak thus: "Bhikṣu!
Will you become a Buddha, or will you not?"
"Is there the Buddha-nature?
The bhikṣu replied, "Within my present body, the Buddha-nature certainly exists; whether it will be realized or not remains yet to be determined."
The King said:
"Virtuous One!
If he does not become an icchantika, he will certainly attain it without doubt."
The bhikṣu said: "So it is.
It is truly as the King has spoken."
"Although this person says that the Buddha-nature definitely exists, they likewise do not commit a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, at the very moment of going forth, reflects thus:
'I shall certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi now.'"
"Although such a person has not yet attained the fruit of the unsurpassed path, they have already acquired merit that is immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation.
Suppose there were someone who said:
'This person has committed a pārājika offense.'"
"There is not a single bhikṣu among them who has not committed an offense. Why is this?

Because for eighty billion kalpas in the past, I have always remained free from all impure things; I have had few desires and known contentment, perfected my dignified deportment, and skillfully cultivated the unsurpassed Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata, thereby knowing with certainty that my own body possesses the Buddha-nature."
Therefore, I have now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and am named Buddha, possessing great compassion.
Such sūtras and vinayas are what has been spoken by the Buddha.
If there are those who cannot accord with this, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they can accord with it, they are great Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, it is said:

"There are no four *pārājika* offenses, thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, two *aniyata* dharmas, thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, ninety-one *pāyattika*, four *pratideśanīya* dharmas, numerous *śaikṣa* dharmas, or seven methods for settling disputes; nor are there *sthūlātyaya* offenses, the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), or those who are icchantikas."
If there are bhikṣus who commit such offenses as these and fall into hell, then those of other paths (tīrthikas) should all be reborn in heaven.
Why is this? Because those of other paths have no precepts to violate; it is for the purpose of instilling fear in people that the Tathāgata has proclaimed these precepts.

If one says: "The Buddha taught that if any of us bhikṣus wish to engage in sexual intercourse, we should discard our dharma robes, put on secular clothing, and only then engage in sexual intercourse."
Furthermore, one should give rise to this thought:
"The causes and conditions of sexual desire are not my fault.
Even while the Tathāgata was in the world, there were bhikṣus who practiced sexual desire and yet attained right liberation, or were reborn in the heavens after their lives ended.
This has existed throughout antiquity and the present; it is not something I alone have created.
Whether one commits the four grave offenses, violates the five precepts, or practices all manner of impure conduct, one can still attain complete and true liberation.

Although the Tathāgata has said that committing a *duṣkṛta* offense leads to falling into hell for eight million years—measured by the number of days, months, and years in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—this too was a manifestation by the Tathāgata intended to inspire awe in people.
To say, "From *pārājika* down to *duṣkṛta*, there is no difference in their gravity," is a false statement made by these masters of the Vinaya.
If it is said, "This was established by the Buddha," one should certainly know that it is not what was spoken by the Buddha.
Such words and teachings are the sūtras and vinaya of Māra.
Furthermore, if it is said:
"Among all the precepts, if one violates even a minor rule or even the most subtle, one shall undergo bitter retribution without limit.
Having understood this, one should protect oneself as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs.
If there is a Vinaya master who further says:
"There is no retribution for any violation of the precepts," such a person should not be associated with.
As the Buddha has said:
"If one transgresses even a single dharma, this is called lying; not seeing the future life, there is no evil one does not commit."
"Therefore, one should not associate with such a person.
Within my Buddha-dharma, purity is thus; how much less could there be anyone who commits a *sthūlātyaya*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pārājika* offense and yet remains without fault?"
Therefore, one should deeply guard oneself against such dharmas as these.
If one does not protect them, what other dharma could be called "prohibitory precepts" (śīla)?
"In the sūtras, I have also said that there are transgressions ranging from the four *pārājikas* down to even the most subtle *duṣkṛta*s, and that these should be sternly disciplined."
If sentient beings do not guard and uphold the prohibitive precepts, how could they ever perceive the Buddha-nature?
Although all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, it must be through the observance of the precepts that they subsequently perceive it;
by perceiving the Buddha-nature, they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Within the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-śāsana*), there is no Vaipulya sūtra; therefore, it does not speak of the existence of the Buddha-nature.
Although the sūtra does not mention it, one should know that it truly exists.
If one speaks in this way, you should know that such a person is truly my disciple.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As it has been stated above:”
The statement that "all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature" has never been heard within the ninefold division of the scriptures.
If it were as you say that they do possess it, how is it that one does not incur a pārājika offense?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
As you have said, you have indeed not committed a pārājika offense."
"Good son!
It is like a person who says:
'The great ocean contains only seven treasures; there are not eight.'"
Such a person is without fault.
If there should be one who says:
"Within the ninefold canon (navāṅga-buddhavacana), there is no Buddha-nature."
Those who say this likewise incur no fault. Why is this?

Within the great ocean of wisdom of the Mahāyāna, I teach that the Buddha-nature exists; yet this is something those of the Two Vehicles do not know or see. Therefore, when they say it does not exist, they are without fault.
Such a realm is known by all Buddhas, and is not within the reach of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. "Good son!
If a person has not heard of the Tathāgata’s profound and secret treasury, how could they know that the Buddha-nature exists?"
What is called the secret treasury?
It refers to the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras. "Good son!
There are various non-Buddhists who either claim the self is eternal or claim the self is annihilated.
The Tathāgata is not like this; he speaks both of the existence of a self and of the non-existence of a self—this is called the Middle Way.
If someone were to say:
"The Buddha taught the Middle Way:
all sentient beings possess buddha-nature, yet because it is shrouded by afflictions, they neither know nor see it."
"Therefore, you should diligently cultivate skillful means to sever and destroy the afflictions.
If there is anyone who can speak thus, it should be known that this person has not committed the four grave offenses;
if there is anyone who does not speak thus, they are said to have committed a *pārājika* offense.
If someone were to say:
"I have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For what reason?"
Because there is the Buddha-nature;
those who possess the Buddha-nature will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
For this reason, I have now already attained and realized Bodhi.
"You should know that such a person is said to have committed a *pārājika* offense. Why is this?
Although they possess the Buddha-nature, because they have not yet cultivated the various skillful means of goodness, they do not yet perceive it."
Because they have not yet seen it, they are unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son! For this reason, the Buddha-dharma is profoundly deep and inconceivable.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There is a king who asks:”
"What is it for a bhikṣu to fall into the transgression of claiming superhuman states?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of gain and offerings, and for the sake of food and drink, practices flattery, deceit, and fraud."
"How may I cause the people of the world to definitely and truly know that I am a genuine mendicant?
By this cause and condition, may I obtain great gains, offerings, and renown."
"Thus, because this bhikṣu is greatly deluded, he constantly thinks throughout the long night:
'I have truly not yet attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; how can I cause people of the world to say that I have already attained them?'"
Furthermore, how should I act so that the upāsakas and upāsikās will all point to me and say:
"This person’s merit is such that he is truly a holy one"?
Reflecting in this way, he was intent solely on seeking gain rather than seeking the Dharma.

Whether walking, coming, going, or staying, his movements were composed and serene; he carried his robes and bowl without losing his dignified deportment. Sitting alone in a secluded place like an arhat, he caused people of the world to all say:
"This bhikṣu is most excellent and foremost; he is diligent in ascetic practice and cultivates the dharma of cessation."

"By these causes and conditions, I shall gain many disciples and followers; people will also provide me with abundant offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, and many women will come to revere, remember, and hold me in high esteem."
“If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who perform such deeds, they fall into the offense of claiming superhuman states (uttarimanussa-dhamma).

Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who, desiring to establish the unsurpassed True Dharma, dwells in a secluded place; though he is not an arhat, he wishes to cause others to say of him: ‘He is an arhat; he is a good bhikṣu; he is a virtuous bhikṣu; he is a tranquil bhikṣu,’ thereby causing immeasurable people to give rise to faith.”

"By these causes and conditions, I have obtained immeasurable bhikṣus and others as my retinue; because of this, I am able to instruct precept-breaking bhikṣus and upāsakas, causing them all to uphold the precepts."

By these causes and conditions, they establish the True Dharma, glorify the unsurpassed great meaning of the Tathāgata, reveal and manifest the transformation through the Mahāyāna teachings of the Vaipulya, deliver all immeasurable sentient beings, and skillfully understand the relative gravity of the meanings of the sūtras and vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata.
He spoke again:
"I too now possess the Buddha-nature.

There is a sutra titled 'The Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata,' and within this sutra, I shall certainly attain the Way of Buddhahood and be able to exhaust immeasurable billions of afflictions and fetters."
He extensively taught for the sake of immeasurable upāsakas, saying:

"All of you possess the Buddha-nature; I and you all shall together abide in the stage of the Tathāgata’s path, realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and exhaust immeasurable billions of afflictions and fetters."
"One who speaks thus is not said to have fallen into a superhuman state (*uttari-manuṣya-dharma*); they are called a bodhisattva.

If it is said that there is an offense of *duṣkṛta*, one shall fall into hell for eight million years by the reckoning of days, months, and years in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they will undergo various retributions for their sins."
How much more so for intentionally committing a *sthūlātyaya* offense?
Within this Mahāyāna, if there is a bhikṣu who commits a *sthūlātyaya*, he should not be associated with.
What is called a *sthūlātyaya* offense within the Mahāyāna sūtras?
If there is a householder who establishes a Buddhist temple and uses various flower garlands to make offerings to the Buddha,
and a bhikṣu sees the thread within the stringing of these flowers and takes it without asking permission, this is called a sthūlātyaya offense.
Whether one knows or does not know, it is likewise an offense.
If one destroys a Buddha-stūpa with a mind of greed, one commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
Such a person should not be associated with.

If a king or a high minister, seeing that a stūpa is dilapidated and old, wishes to repair it as an act of veneration for the śarīra, and therein obtains precious treasures within the stūpa, he shall entrust them to a bhikṣu.
Once the bhikṣu has obtained it, he uses it as he pleases.
Such a bhikṣu is called impure and frequently gives rise to strife and contention.
A virtuous upāsaka should not associate with, make offerings to, or show respect to him.
Such a bhikṣu is said to be rootless, said to have dual roots, and said to have indeterminate roots.
One with indeterminate roots is such that when desiring a woman, his body becomes female, and when desiring a man, his body becomes male.
Such a bhikṣu is called one of evil roots; he is not called a man, nor is he called a woman; he is not called a renunciant, nor is he called a householder.
Such a bhikṣu should not be approached, nor should he be venerated or honored.

"Within the Buddha-dharma, that which constitutes the dharma of a śramaṇa is as follows: one should give rise to a heart of compassion to nurture and protect all sentient beings, even down to the smallest ants, and grant them fearlessness—this is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to remain far removed from drinking alcohol, even to the point of not smelling its fragrance—this is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to refrain from false speech, even to the point of not conceiving of false speech in one's dreams—this is the dharma of a śramaṇa."
"Not giving rise to thoughts of desire even in dreams is likewise; this is the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse in a dream, does this constitute a violation of the precepts?
The Buddha said, "No."
One should conceive of sexual desire as foul and impure, not giving rise to even a single thought of purity; one should distance oneself from women, afflictions, and thoughts of craving.
If one engages in sexual intercourse in a dream, one should feel regret upon waking.
When a bhikṣu begs for alms and receives offerings, he should regard them as one would the flesh of one's own son during a time of famine.
If lustful desire arises, he should swiftly abandon it.
Know that such a dharma-gate is a sūtra and vinaya spoken by the Buddha.
If there are those who comply with what the Māra says, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they can comply with what the Buddha says, they are called Bodhisattvas.
"If someone should say:

"The Buddha permits bhikṣus who constantly stand on one leg, remain silent and speechless, throw themselves into deep pools, leap into fire, cast themselves down from high cliffs, do not avoid perilous hardships, consume poison, fast until death, lie upon ashes and dust, bind their own hands and feet, practice heterodox paths and incantations, belong to the outcaste (caṇḍāla) class, or possess no genitals, both genitals, or indeterminate genitals, or whose sexual organs are incomplete—such as these, the Tathāgata permits all to leave the household life and practice the Way."
"This is called the teaching of Māra.
The Buddha previously permitted the consumption of the five kinds of cow products, as well as oil, honey, kauseya garments, leather sandals, and other such items."
Apart from this, if anyone should say:
"One may listen to and accept the Mahālaṅkāra; all seeds may be stored and kept; and plants and the like all possess life."
"After the Buddha had spoken these words, he entered parinirvāṇa.
If there are sūtras or vinayas that speak thus, you should know that they are the teachings of Māra.
"I also do not permit [monks] to stand constantly on one foot."
If it is for the sake of the Dharma, one may listen to [the teachings] while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.

Furthermore, one must not listen while consuming poison, fasting, performing the five-fold heat-torment, binding the hands and feet, killing sentient beings, practicing secular arts or incantations, wearing sandals made of conch shell, ivory, or tusks, hoarding seeds, plants, or living things, or wearing the Mahālaṅkāra.
If one says,
"The World-Honored One spoke thus," you should know that such a person belongs to the retinue of non-Buddhists and is not my disciple.
"I have permitted only the consumption of the five products of the cow, as well as oils, honey, and the like; I have permitted the wearing of leather sandals and *kauśeya* garments.
I have taught that the four great elements possess no life-force."
If there are sūtras or vinayas that speak in this way, these are called the Buddha’s teachings.
If there are those who accord with what the Buddha has taught, you should know that they are truly my disciples;
if there are those who do not accord with what the Buddha has taught, they are the retinue of Māra.
If there is one who accords with the Buddha’s sūtras and vinaya, you should know that this person is a great bodhisattva. "Good son!
I have now extensively proclaimed and distinguished for you the differences between what is spoken by Māra and what is spoken by the Buddha."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is only now that I have come to know the distinguishing characteristics between the words of Māra and the words of the Buddha; by means of this, I have been able to enter into the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma.”
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!”
That you are able to understand and discern in this way is called wisdom.
Chapter Ten: The Four Noble Truths The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Ten: The Four Noble Truths. The Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa:
“That which is called ‘suffering’ is not termed the Noble Truth of Suffering.”
Why is this? If one were to say,
"Suffering is the Noble Truth of Suffering," then all animals and sentient beings in the hells would likewise possess the Noble Truths.

“Good son! If there is another person who does not know that the Tathāgata’s profound realm is eternally abiding and unchanging, and who regards the subtle and secret *dharmakāya* as a body sustained by food rather than a *dharmakāya*, and who does not understand the Tathāgata’s moral power and majesty—this is called suffering.”

Why is this? Because through ignorance, they perceive what is Dharma as non-Dharma and what is non-Dharma as Dharma; one should know that such persons will inevitably fall into evil destinies, transmigrate through birth and death, increase their fetters, and undergo much suffering and affliction.

If there are those who can know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and without change, or who hear the sound of the two characters "eternally abiding" even once they pass through the ear, they shall immediately be reborn in the heavens.
Only upon attaining liberation later can one realize that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change.
Having realized this, one speaks thus:
"In the past I heard this meaning, but it is only now, having attained liberation, that I have realized it."
"Because I did not know the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), I have transmigrated through birth and death, circling endlessly; it is only today that I have attained true wisdom.
If one knows in this way, it is truly the cultivation of suffering, which brings great benefit;
if one does not know this, then even if one practices diligently, there is no benefit.
This is called knowing suffering; it is named the Noble Truth of Suffering.
If a person cannot practice in this way, it is merely called suffering, not the Noble Truth of Suffering. Regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering:

within the true Dharma, they do not give rise to true wisdom; they accept impure things, namely slaves and servants; they use what is not the Dharma to claim it is the True Dharma, and they destroy the True Dharma so that it does not endure for long.
For these reasons, they do not know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because they do not know it, they revolve in birth and death, undergoing much suffering and affliction, and fail to attain rebirth in heaven or true liberation.
If there are those with profound wisdom who do not destroy the true Dharma, by these causes and conditions they shall be reborn in the heavens and attain right liberation.
If there are those who do not understand the truths of suffering and its origin, yet say:
"The true Dharma has no permanence; it is entirely subject to extinction."
"By reason of these causes and conditions, one wanders through birth and death for immeasurable eons, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
If one can know that phenomena are eternally abiding and unchanging, this is called knowing the origin; it is called the Noble Truth of the Origin."
If a person is unable to practice in this way, this is called "accumulation," not the Noble Truth of Accumulation.
Regarding the "Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering": if one extensively practices and studies the dharma of emptiness, this is unwholesome.
Why is this? Because it extinguishes all dharmas and destroys the Tathāgata’s true treasury of Dharma; to practice and study in this manner is called "cultivating emptiness.
One who cultivates the cessation of suffering acts in opposition to all those of the various external paths.
If it is said that "cultivating emptiness is the truth of cessation," then since all non-Buddhists also cultivate the dharma of emptiness, they too should possess the truth of cessation.
If someone were to say:
"There is the Tathāgatagarbha; though it is invisible, if one can extinguish all afflictions, one will then be able to enter it.
If one gives rise to this thought for even a single moment, one will attain mastery over all phenomena.
If there are those who cultivate the Tathāgata’s secret treasury as being selfless, empty, and quiescent, such persons will wander through birth and death for immeasurable eons, undergoing suffering.
If there are those who do not practice in this way, they may still be able to swiftly eliminate their afflictions. Why is this?
Because they understand the Tathāgata’s secret treasury; this is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
If one can practice cessation in this way, such a person is my disciple;
if one cannot practice in this manner, it is called the cultivation of emptiness, not the Noble Truth of Cessation.
"The Noble Truth of the Path refers to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, as well as right liberation.
There are sentient beings with perverted minds who say:
'There is no Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, or right liberation; the cycle of birth and death is merely like an illusion.'"
"Cultivating such views, one revolves through the three realms of existence due to these causes and conditions, undergoing great suffering for a long time.
If one can resolve to awaken the mind and perceive that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging—
so too are the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and liberation."
Riding upon this single thought, one obtains the sovereign fruits and rewards of immeasurable eons according to one's wish. Why is this?
Because in the past, due to the four inversions, I took what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma and thereby experienced the retribution of immeasurable evil karma.
Because I have now extinguished such views, I have attained the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha.
This is called the Noble Truth of the Path.
If anyone should say:
"The Three Jewels are impermanent"—to cultivate such a view is false cultivation; it is not the Noble Truth of the Path.
If one cultivates this Dharma as being eternally abiding, such a person is my disciple.
“Truly seeing and cultivating the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is what is called the Four Noble Truths.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One! [What is this?]”
"I have now only just come to know how to cultivate the profound Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
Chapter Eleven: The Four Inversions From the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: The Four Inversions. The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."
Regarding the four inversions: to give rise to the perception of suffering within that which is not suffering is called an inversion.
That which is "not suffering" refers to the Tathāgata.
To give rise to the perception of suffering therein means to regard all Tathāgatas as impermanent and subject to change.
To say that the Tathāgata is impermanent is called a great sin and suffering. To say:
"The Tathāgata abandons this body of suffering and enters nirvāṇa, just as a fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted."
"This is called conceiving the notion of suffering where there is no suffering; this is called a perversion.
If I were to say that the Tathāgata is permanent, that would be the view of self."
Because of the view of self, there are immeasurable sins.
Therefore, one should say that the Tathāgata is impermanent.
If one speaks in this way, I shall experience happiness.
If the Tathāgata were impermanent, he would be suffering.
If he were suffering, how could there be happiness?
Because one conceives the notion of happiness within what is suffering, it is called a perversion.
"To conceive the notion of suffering within what is pleasant is called a perversion.
That which is pleasant is the Tathāgata;
that which is suffering implies the Tathāgata is impermanent."
If one says that the Tathāgata is impermanent, this is called conceiving the notion of suffering within what is pleasant.
