That "the Tathāgata is eternally abiding" is called bliss.
[If I were to say: "If I were to speak thus:"
"If the Tathāgata is eternal,
how can he further enter into nirvāṇa?
If it is said that the Tathāgata is not subject to suffering, why does he relinquish his body and undergo extinction?"
Because one perceives suffering within what is pleasant, it is called a perversion.
This is the first perversion.
To perceive the impermanent as permanent, or the permanent as impermanent, is called a perversion.
That which is impermanent is called the non-cultivation of emptiness.
Because one does not cultivate emptiness, one's lifespan is short.
If someone should say:
"To claim that one attains long life by not cultivating emptiness and stillness" is called a perversion;
this is called the second perversion.
"To perceive what is non-self as self, or to perceive what is self as non-self," is called a perversion.

People of the world also speak of a self, and within the Buddha-dharma we likewise speak of a self. Although people of the world speak of a self, they lack the Buddha-nature; this is called giving rise to the notion of a self within that which is non-self, and it is termed an inversion.

In the Buddha-dharma, the existence of self is itself the Buddha-nature; yet worldly people say that the Buddha-dharma is without self, which is called conceiving the notion of non-self within what is actually self.
If one says:
"The Buddha-dharma is certainly without self; for this reason, the Tathāgata exhorts his disciples to practice the cultivation of non-self."
This is called perversion.
This is termed the third perversion.
To perceive the pure as impure and the impure as pure is called perversion.
That which is pure is the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding; it is not a body sustained by mixed food, nor a body of afflictions, nor a body of flesh, nor a body bound by sinews and bones.
If there should be those who say:
"The Tathāgata is impermanent; he possesses a body sustained by various foods, even a body bound together by sinews and bones;
and the Dharma and the Sangha, as well as liberation, are subject to extinction."
This is called a perversion.
To perceive the impure as pure is called a perversion.
If someone were to say:

"In this body of mine, there is not a single dharma that is impure; because there is no impurity, I shall certainly enter the state of purity. Thus, the Tathāgata taught the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity."
"Such words as these are false and deceptive; this is called perversion.
This, then, is named the fourth perversion.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, I have attained right view.
World-Honored One!”
"From this point forward, we shall all be known as people of false views.
*The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Seven;
*The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
The *Rulai Xing Pin* (Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature), the Twelfth, added by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Chapter Twelve: The Tathāgata-nature.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among the twenty-five states of existence, is there a self?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! ‘Self’ is the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
That all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is the meaning of ‘self.’”
"This meaning of mine has, from the very beginning, been constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions; for this reason, sentient beings are unable to perceive it.
Good son!..."
It is like a poor woman who has a great store of genuine gold within her house, yet none of her family members, whether young or old, know of it.
At that time, there was a certain person skilled in expedient means who said to the poor woman:
"I will now hire you; you may work for me by weeding out the grass and filth."
The woman immediately replied:
"I am unable to do so now.
If you can show me where my son’s gold treasure is hidden, only then shall I quickly perform this service for you."
The man spoke again, saying,
"I know the skillful means to show you your son.
The woman replied:
"My family members, both great and small, do not even know this themselves; how could you possibly know it?
The man replied again, "I am now truly able to do so."
The woman replied, "I also wish to see it; please show it to me as well.
The man immediately dug up the gold treasure from within her house.
Upon seeing this, the woman felt great joy in her heart; she conceived a sense of wonder and began to revere that person.
"Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: all sentient beings are unable to see it, just as that poor man did not know of the treasure."
"Good son!
I now universally show all sentient beings that their buddha-nature is shrouded by various afflictions, just as that poor man cannot see the treasury of true gold he possesses."
Today, the Tathāgata universally reveals to all sentient beings the treasure-store of awakening, namely, the Buddha-nature.
Upon seeing this matter, all sentient beings give rise to joy in their hearts and take refuge in and look up to the Tathāgata.
The one with skillful means is the Tathāgata;
the poor woman is all immeasurable sentient beings;
and the treasury of true gold is the Buddha-nature.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a woman who gives birth to a son.
When the infant falls ill, the mother becomes distressed and seeks out a skilled physician."
When the skilled physician arrived, he prepared a compound of three medicines—clarified butter, milk, and rock honey—and gave it to him to drink.
He then instructed the woman:
"Once the child has taken the medicine, do not give him any milk for the time being."
"Once the medicine has been digested, only then shall I give it to you.
At that time, the woman immediately smeared a bitter substance upon her breasts and said to her child:
"My breasts have been smeared with poison; they must not be touched again."
The child, parched with thirst and desiring his mother’s milk, heard the poisonous odor of the milk and fled far away.
Only when the medicine had been eliminated did the mother wash her breasts, call her son, and give him the milk.
At that time, although the child was hungry and thirsty, he did not come because he had previously smelled the scent of poison.
His mother spoke to him again, saying:
"I have applied poison to it only for the sake of giving you medicine."
"Your medicine has been digested and I have finished washing you; you may now come and drink milk without suffering.
Having heard this, the child gradually returned to drinking.
“Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise; in order to deliver all beings, he teaches all sentient beings to cultivate the dharma of non-self.
Having cultivated it in this way, they forever sever the notion of self and enter into nirvāṇa.”

In order to eliminate all false views of the world, to manifest the supramundane Dharma that transcends the world, to further demonstrate that the worldly conception of a self is illusory and not real, and to cultivate the pure body of the dharma of non-self.
For example, just as a woman, for the sake of her child, applies a bitter taste to her breast, so too does the Tathāgata;
for the purpose of cultivating emptiness, he declares:
"All phenomena are entirely without self."
"Just as that woman, having thoroughly washed her breast, calls for her child, desiring him to return and suckle,
so too do I now speak of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, monks, you should not give rise to fear."
Just as that child, having heard his mother’s call, gradually returns to drink milk,
so too should the bhikṣu distinguish for himself that the Tathāgata-garbha is neither non-existent nor absent.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Truly there is no self.”
Why is this? When an infant is born, there is nothing it knows.
If a self existed, it should immediately possess knowledge on the very day of birth.
For this reason, it is certain that there is no self.
If there were definitely a self, then after birth and receiving existence, there would be no passing away.
If all beings possessed buddha-nature and this were permanent, it should lack the characteristic of decay.
If there were no characteristic of disintegration, how could there be distinctions such as kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, vaiśya, śūdra, caṇḍāla, and animals?
Now we observe that karmic conditions vary in manifold ways and the various realms of existence differ from one another.
If there were a fixed self, all sentient beings would be without distinction in their fortunes.
For this reason, it is certain that buddha-nature is not a permanent phenomenon.

If you say that the Buddha-nature is definitively permanent, for what reason do you further speak of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, lying, frivolous speech, greed, anger, and wrong views?
If the nature of the self were permanent, why would one become dazed, intoxicated, and deluded after drinking alcohol?
If the nature of the self were permanent, the blind should see forms, the deaf should hear sounds, the mute should be able to speak, and the lame should be able to walk.
If the nature of the self were permanent, one should not avoid fire pits, great waters, poisons, swords, blades, wicked people, or predatory beasts.
If the self were permanent, one should not forget the things experienced in the past.
If it were not subject to forgetfulness, for what reason would one further say,
"Where have I seen this person before?
If the self were permanent, there should be no aging, decline, or flourishing, nor should there be the recollection of past events.
If the self were permanent, where would it abide?
Would it reside within the various colors of tears and saliva—blue, yellow, red, or white?
If the self were permanent, it should pervade the entire body, like sesame oil, with no empty spaces between.
"If the body were severed, the self would also be severed.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!..."
For example, suppose there were a great strongman in a royal household who had a diamond gem between his eyebrows.

While competing in a wrestling match with another strongman, that opponent struck him with his head; the gem on his forehead immediately sank into the skin, and he was entirely unaware of where the gem was located.
There was a sore at that spot, so he summoned a skilled physician to treat it himself.

At that time, there was a brilliant physician well-versed in prescriptions and medicines who immediately recognized that the sore was caused by a pearl having entered his body; once the pearl had penetrated the skin, it remained lodged there.
At that time, the skilled physician immediately questioned the wrestler:
"Where is the jewel upon your forehead?
The wrestler, startled, replied:
"O Great Master, King of Physicians!
Has the jewel upon my forehead been lost? Where is this jewel now?"
"Is this not an illusion?
he cried out in grief and wept.
At that time, the skilled physician comforted the strongman:
"You should not now give rise to great sorrow and suffering.
When you were fighting, the precious jewel entered your body; it is now within your skin, its reflection appearing on the outside.
Because the poison of anger was so intense during your fight, the jewel sank into your body and you did not perceive it yourself."
At that time, the strongman did not believe the physician’s words:
"If it were inside the skin, why would the impurities of pus and blood not come out?
If it were inside the tendons, it should not be visible."
"How can you now deceive me?
At that time, the physician took up a mirror and reflected his face; the pearl appeared clearly and distinctly within the mirror.
Upon seeing this, the strongman was struck with wonder and astonishment, conceiving a sense of its extraordinary nature.
“Good son! All sentient beings are likewise;

because they cannot draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), although they possess the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), they are unable to see it. Being shrouded and obscured by greed, lust, anger, and ignorance, they fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, caṇḍālas, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, being born into such various families.”
Due to various karmic conditions arising from the mind, although one receives a human body, one may be deaf, blind, mute, dumb, crippled, or lame.
Within the twenty-five states of existence, one undergoes various retributions; with a mind shrouded by greed, lust, anger, and ignorance, one does not know the Buddha-nature.
It is like that strongman who, with a precious jewel upon his person, cried out that he had lost it.

Sentient beings are likewise; because they do not know how to draw near to spiritual friends, they fail to recognize the subtle and secret treasure-store of the Tathāgata, and instead practice the cultivation of non-self.
For example, just as non-noble ones may speak of a self yet do not know the true nature of the self, my disciples are likewise:
because they do not know how to draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they practice the study of non-self and yet do not know the state of non-self.
They do not yet know their own true nature of selflessness, much less can they know their true nature of having a self.
"Good son! Thus the Tathāgata says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, just as a skilled physician showed a powerful man the adamantine jewel."
These sentient beings are shrouded by immeasurable billions of afflictions and the like, and thus do not recognize their Buddha-nature.
When these afflictions are exhausted, they will then attain clear realization and understanding, just as that strong man sees his precious jewel within a bright mirror.
"Good son! The Tathāgata’s secret treasury is thus immeasurable and inconceivable.
Furthermore, good son!"

For example, on the Snowy Mountains there is a medicinal herb of a single flavor called "Taste of Bliss. Its taste is extremely sweet, yet it lies beneath deep thickets where no one can see it; however, if someone smells its fragrance, they immediately know that this medicine must be present at that spot.
In a past life, there was a wheel-turning monarch who, for the sake of this medicine, constructed wooden tubes in every location throughout the Snowy Mountains to collect it.
When this medicine has matured, it flows from the earth and collects in wooden tubes, its flavor being pure and authentic.
After the king has passed away, that medicine subsequently becomes sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, or bland.
In this way, though it is of a single flavor, it appears in various different forms according to where it flows; yet the true essence of this medicine remains in the mountain like the full moon.
Ordinary people of meager merit, despite applying effort through digging and excavating until they reach the point of exhaustion, are unable to obtain it.
Furthermore, there appears in the world a holy king who, through the causal conditions of his merit, obtains the true flavor of this medicine.
"Good son, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is likewise; it is covered by the thickets of all afflictions, such that sentient beings shrouded in ignorance are unable to see it."

The single flavor of the medicine is like the Buddha-nature; because of afflictions, it produces various flavors, namely: those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, devas, humans, males, females, neither male nor female, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras.
The Buddha-nature is heroic and fierce, difficult to destroy; therefore, there is no one capable of killing it.
If there were one who could kill it, that would mean severing the Buddha-nature, yet such a thing is impossible: the Buddha-nature can never be severed.
If this nature could be severed, such a thing is impossible.
This nature of mine is precisely the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
Such a secret treasury cannot be destroyed or incinerated by anything.
Although it cannot be destroyed, it cannot be seen; only when one attains the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does one then realize and know it.
For this reason, there is no one who can kill it.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there were no killer, there should likewise be no unwholesome karma.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There truly is the taking of life. Why is this?"
"Good son!
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings dwells within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). If one destroys these five aggregates, it is called 'killing.

If there is killing, one falls into the evil destinies. Due to the causes and conditions of karma, there arise the distinctions of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), such as the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and Caṇḍālas; or male, female, neither male nor female; and thus they transmigrate through birth and death."

Non-noble persons recklessly conceptualize a self, imagining its various marks to be as large as a weed seed, or like rice, beans, or even the size of a thumb; such various deluded thoughts and perceptions lack any reality.
The supramundane mark of self is called the Buddha-nature; to conceive of the self in this way is the most excellent.

Furthermore, good son, it is like a person who knows well where hidden treasures lie; he takes a sharp pickaxe and digs straight down into the earth, passing through bedrock, sand, and gravel without difficulty, until he reaches diamond, which he cannot pierce.
Now, that which is adamantine cannot be destroyed by any sword or axe.
Son of good family!
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise; it cannot be destroyed by any disputant, nor by devas, Māra Pāpīyas, or any among the gods and humans.
The characteristics of the five aggregates are those of conditioned activity; the nature of conditioned activity is like stone or sand, which can be pierced and destroyed.
The Buddha-nature, the true self, is like a diamond, which cannot be destroyed.
For this reason, the destruction of the five aggregates is called "killing.
Good son, you must certainly know that the Buddha-dharma is thus inconceivable.
“Good son! The Vaipulya sutras are like nectar, yet they are also like poison.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason does the Tathāgata say that the Vaipulya sūtras are like ambrosia and yet also like poison?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
"Do you now wish to know the true meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury?
Kāśyapa replied,
"I truly wish to know the meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Some may consume the nectar of immortality, yet their lives are harmed and they die prematurely;
others again may consume the nectar of immortality, and their life-span is made to endure long."
Some may survive by taking poison, while others die because of it.
The nectar of unimpeded wisdom— namely, the Mahāyāna scriptures—
is likewise called a "mixed poison" within these Mahāyāna scriptures.
Just as ghee, clarified butter, and other such substances, as well as various rock honeys, act as medicine when digested but become poison when not, so too it is with the Vaipulya sutras:
they are nectar for the wise; yet they are poison for the foolish.
The ignorant, not knowing the Buddha-nature, Take it and it becomes poison.
For the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, The Mahāyāna is nectar;
just as among all flavors, Milk is considered the foremost.
Thus those who exert themselves with diligence, relying upon the Mahāyāna,
shall attain nirvāṇa and become elephant-kings among men.
Sentient beings who realize their Buddha-nature will be just like Kāśyapa and others.
The unsurpassed flavor of the nectar of immortality is neither born nor does it die. Kāśyapa!
You should now skillfully distinguish the three refuges; such is the nature of these three refuges, and that is my own nature.
If one can observe with clarity that the nature of the self possesses the Buddha-nature,
know that such a person has entered the secret treasury;
knowing both "self" and "what belongs to the self," this person has already transcended the world.
“The nature of the Triple Gem of Buddha and Dharma is the unsurpassed, foremost honor;
as I have stated in these verses, such is the meaning of its nature.
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke again in verse:
"I now do not know at all where to take refuge in the Three Jewels;
how shall I proceed toward that which is unsurpassed and fearless?"
Not knowing the locus of the Three Jewels, how can one realize non-self?
How does one who takes refuge in the Buddha obtain consolation?
And how does one take refuge in the Dharma?
I only pray that you will explain to me:
how does one attain mastery,
and how does one lack mastery?
How does one take refuge in the Saṅgha and thereby attain supreme benefit?
How does one speak of the truth so as to realize the path to Buddhahood in the future?
If one does not achieve it in the future, how can one take refuge in the Triple Gem?
I have no prior knowledge now; I shall proceed according to the proper sequence.
How can one conceive the thought of having a son when no child has yet been conceived?
Only if it were truly within the womb could it be called "having a son."
If a child is within the womb, it will certainly be born before long;
this is what is meant by the meaning of "child.
The karma of sentient beings is likewise so.
As the Buddha has taught, the foolish are unable to know;
because they do not know, they wander through the prison of birth and death.
Though they bear the provisional name of upāsaka, they do not understand the true meaning.
I only pray that you will analyze this extensively, severing the net of my doubts.
O Tathāgata of great wisdom, please deign to analyze it out of compassion;
I pray that you will speak of the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
“Kāśyapa! You should know that I shall now, for your sake, skillfully open the subtle and secret treasury, so that your doubts may be severed.”
Now listen with a sincere mind:
Among all bodhisattvas, you shall share the same name as the seventh Buddha.
One who takes refuge in the Buddha is truly called an upāsaka.
One shall never again take refuge in other celestial deities;
those who take refuge in the Dharma are free from killing;
those who take refuge in the Noble Saṅgha seek nothing among the non-Buddhists.
"By thus taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one attains fearlessness.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I too take refuge in the Triple Gem; this is called the True Path, the realm of all Buddhas."
The Three Jewels have the characteristic of equality; they always possess the nature of great wisdom.
My own nature and the Buddha-nature are non-dual and without distinction.
This path is praised by the Buddhas as the place where right progress finds its secure abiding.
He is also named the One of Right Universal Vision, and is thus praised by the Buddha.
I too shall proceed toward the unsurpassed path extolled by the Sugata;
this is the supreme nectar, wherein all that exists and does not exist is absent.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: "Good son,
you should not now differentiate the Three Jewels as do the śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings."
In this Mahāyāna, there is no characteristic of differentiation regarding the three refuges.

Why is this? Within the Buddha-nature, the Dharma and the Sangha are already present; it is only for the sake of transforming and delivering śrāvakas and ordinary beings that one differentiates and speaks of the distinct characteristics of the Three Jewels.
"Good son!
If one wishes to accord with worldly dharmas, then one should distinguish three refuges. Good son!"
A bodhisattva should reflect in this way:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha with this very body.

If one were to attain the path of Buddhahood with this very body, then once Buddhahood has been attained, one would no longer need to show reverence, prostrate, or make offerings to the various World-Honored Ones.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas are equal, equally acting as a refuge for sentient beings.
"If one wishes to revere the śarīra of the Dharma-body, one should pay homage to the stūpas and temples of all Buddhas."

Why is this? It is because I wish to transform and deliver all sentient beings, and also to cause them to conceive the notion of my body as a stūpa or temple, so that they may pay homage and make offerings to it.
In this way, sentient beings take my Dharma-body as their refuge.
All sentient beings rely upon that which is unreal, false, and deceptive; I shall, in due order, preach the True Dharma for them.
Furthermore, there are those who take refuge in a non-true Sangha; I shall act as a refuge for them by means of the true Sangha.
If there are those who differentiate among the three refuges, I shall act as a single place of refuge for them, without the distinction of three;
I shall act as eyes for the multitude born blind;
and I shall further act as the true place of refuge for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Good son!
In this way, the bodhisattva performs the work of a Buddha for immeasurable evil sentient beings as well as for those who possess wisdom. Good son!"
For example, it is like a person who, when facing battle on the front lines, immediately gives rise to this thought:
"I am the foremost among these; all the troops rely upon me."
It was also like the crown prince who thought to himself:
"I shall subdue the other princes, succeed to the imperial enterprise of the Great King, and attain sovereignty, causing all the princes to see me and take refuge in me."
"Therefore, one should not give rise to an inferior mind; as it is with a king, so it is with princes and great ministers.
Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this, reflecting thus:"
"How is it that these three things are of one essence with me? "Good son!
I show that these three things are themselves nirvāṇa."
The Tathāgata is called the Unsurpassed One (Anuttara).
For example, among the parts of a human body, the head is the most supreme, not the other limbs, hands, feet, or the like.
The Buddha is likewise thus; he is the most supreme, not the Dharma nor the Sangha.
For the sake of transforming and delivering all the worlds, he manifests various distinct appearances, just like that ladder.

Therefore, you should not now uphold the distinctions of the three refuges as they are understood by ordinary, foolish people; rather, regarding the Mahāyāna, you should possess fierce and sharp decisiveness, like a sturdy blade.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I ask because I know, not because I am ignorant.”

I, as a Bodhisattva of great courage and valor, inquire concerning the stainless and pure sphere of conduct, desiring that the Tathāgata may extensively proclaim and analyze these extraordinary matters for the sake of all Bodhisattvas, and extol the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, has now well expounded this; I, too, abide therein accordingly.
What is called the "pure sphere of conduct for bodhisattvas" is precisely the proclamation of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
“World-Honored One!
I too shall now extensively proclaim for the sake of sentient beings this secret treasury of the Tathāgata, and I shall likewise realize and know the true locus of the Three Refuges.”
If there are sentient beings who can believe in this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, those individuals will naturally comprehend the three objects of refuge. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s secret treasury contains the Buddha-nature,
those who proclaim this sutra all say:
"Within the body, there is entirely the Buddha-nature."
"Such a person does not seek the three objects of refuge from afar. Why is this?
Because in a future life, my own body shall itself accomplish the Three Jewels."
"Therefore, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all other sentient beings rely upon me for veneration and prostration. "Good son!"
"For this reason, you should correctly study the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"The Buddha-nature is thus inconceivable; the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are likewise inconceivable."
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!”
"You have already accomplished profound and sharp wisdom; I shall now further explain for you well the entry into the Tathāgatagarbha.
'If there were a self, it would be a permanent dharma and would not be free from suffering;
if there were no self, the practice of pure conduct would be of no benefit.'"
If one says that all phenomena are devoid of self, this is the view of annihilationism;
if one says that the self abides, this is the view of eternalism.
If one says that all conditioned formations are impermanent, this is the view of annihilationism.
To say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent is again the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
To say they are suffering is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*);
to say they are pleasure is again the view of eternalism.
To cultivate all phenomena as eternal is to fall into the view of nihilism;
to cultivate all phenomena as subject to cessation is to fall into the view of eternalism.
It is like a centipede, which must rely on its front legs to move its hind legs.
The cultivation of permanence and annihilation is likewise so; it must depend upon the cessation of permanence and [the negation of] annihilation.
For this reason, the cultivation of other dharmas that result in suffering is termed unwholesome, while the cultivation of other dharmas that result in happiness is termed wholesome.
To cultivate the selflessness of other phenomena is a portion of the afflictions;
to cultivate the permanence of other phenomena is called the Tathāgata-garbha, which is to say, Nirvāṇa has no dwelling place.
To cultivate other impermanent dharmas is to cultivate material wealth;
to cultivate other permanent dharmas refers to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and right liberation.

One should know that such is the Middle Way of the Buddha’s Dharma, which speaks the true Dharma by remaining far removed from the two extremes; therein, ordinary and foolish people should have no doubt.
Just as a weak and sickly person, having consumed ghee, gains strength and becomes light and agile;
so too, the nature of existence and non-existence is not fixed.
For example, the four great elements differ in their natures and each is mutually opposed.
A skilled physician knows well how to adjust the treatment according to the specific manifestation of the ailment.
"Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise;

like a skilled physician toward all sentient beings, he understands the distinct characteristics and natures of their various afflictions and eliminates them for them, revealing the secret treasury of the Tathāgata—the pure Buddha-nature that is eternally abiding and unchanging."
If one says that [the self] exists, wisdom should not be defiled;
if one says it does not exist, that is false speech.
If one says it exists, one should neither remain silent nor engage in frivolous debate or contention, but should seek only to realize the true nature of all phenomena.
Ordinary people engage in frivolous discourse and contentious disputes because they do not understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
If one speaks of suffering, the foolish person immediately says:
"The body is impermanent."
Thus, although it is taught that all is suffering, ordinary people are still unable to realize that the body possesses the nature of bliss.
Regarding the teaching on impermanence, ordinary people reckon that the entire body is impermanent, just like a clay pot.
A person of wisdom should exercise discernment; one should not say that everything is impermanent without exception. Why is this?
Because my own body possesses the seed of Buddha-nature.
If one says there is no self, ordinary people will think:
"All Buddha-dharmas are entirely devoid of self.
The wise should discern that "no-self" is a provisional designation lacking substantial reality; having understood this, they should not give rise to doubt.
If it is said that the Tathāgata’s secret treasury is empty and quiescent, ordinary people, upon hearing this, will give rise to the view of annihilation;
those with wisdom should discern that the Tathāgata is eternal and subject to no change.
If it is said that liberation is like an illusion or a magical transformation,
ordinary people will say:
"To attain true liberation is itself to undergo extinction."
A person of wisdom should discern that although the Lion among Men comes and goes, he dwells eternally without change.
"If one says:
'With ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise.'"
When ordinary people hear this, they give rise to dualistic conceptions by discriminating between clarity and ignorance;
the wise, however, thoroughly understand that their nature is non-dual, and this non-dual nature is itself the true nature.
If it is said that "conditioned by the formations (saṃskāra) is consciousness (vijñāna)," ordinary people regard these two— formations and consciousness— as distinct; however,
the wise understand that their nature is non-dual, and this non-dual nature is the true nature (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
If one says:
"The ten wholesome actions and the ten unwholesome actions; those that should be practiced and those that should not; the path of goodness and the path of evil;
white dharmas and black dharmas"—the ordinary person calls these "two."
The wise person thoroughly understands that their nature is non-dual; this non-dual nature is itself the true nature.
If one says, "One should cultivate the suffering of all phenomena," [one does not yet understand the true nature].
"Ordinary people speak of duality;
the wise thoroughly understand that its nature is non-dual, and this nature of non-duality is itself the true nature.
If one says:"
Regarding the statement "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," the Tathāgata’s secret treasury is likewise impermanent;
ordinary people perceive these as two, whereas the wise realize that their nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is itself the true nature.
"If one says:
'All dharmas are without self, and the Tathāgata-garbha is also without self,' the ordinary person regards these as two; "
The wise understand that its nature is non-dual; this non-dual nature is itself the true nature.
Self and non-self are, in their nature, not two.
Such is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, praised by immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas.
"I have now fully explained all these merits and accomplishments within the sutras. 'Good son!
Self and non-self are non-dual in their nature and characteristics; you should uphold and wear this upon your head in this manner.'"
“Good son! You, too, should firmly uphold and keep in mind such sutras as I have previously taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
‘Self and non-self are without two distinct characteristics.’”

"Just as curds arise from milk, fresh butter is obtained from curds, clarified butter is obtained from fresh butter, and ghee is obtained from clarified butter—so too, the nature of curds arises from milk."
Does it arise from itself, or does it arise from another?
This applies even up to the stage of *amṛta* (clarified butter).
If it were produced from another, then it would be created by that other thing and not produced from milk.
If it were not produced from milk, the milk would have no function.
If it were produced spontaneously, it would not arise as a similar succession;
if it arises as a succession, then it does not arise simultaneously.
If they were not co-arising, the five kinds of flavors would not exist simultaneously; yet even if they were not simultaneous, it is certain that they do not come from elsewhere.
One should know that the characteristic of curd already exists within the milk, but because the sweet flavor is predominant, it cannot transform itself;
this remains true up to the stage of clarified butter (ghṛta).
Through the conditions of the cow’s consumption of water and grass, the blood and vital essence undergo transformation and become milk.
If it eats sweet grass, its milk will be sweet;
if it eats bitter grass, the milk will have a bitter taste.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called "Fatty"; if a cow eats it, she produces only pure *ghṛta* (clarified butter), which possesses no colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, or black.
Due to the causal conditions of grain and grass, their milk differs in color and flavor.
Likewise, these sentient beings give rise to two characteristics due to the causal conditions of the karma of clarity and ignorance;
if ignorance is transformed, it becomes clarity.
"All dharmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome, are likewise thus, having no two distinct characteristics.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has said:
"There is curd within milk.
What is the meaning of this?
World-Honored One!
If it is said that "within milk there definitely exists the characteristic of curd, but because it is subtle, it cannot be seen," how can you say:
"Is it that 'curd is produced from the causal condition of milk'?
If a phenomenon did not exist originally, it is called "arising";
if it already exists, how can one say it arises?
If you say that the characteristic of curd definitely exists within milk, then there should also be milk within the hundred grasses;
likewise, there should also be grass within the milk.
If you say:
Regarding the statement, "There is definitely no curd within milk," how is it that curd arises by depending upon milk?
If a phenomenon were originally non-existent and only subsequently produced, why is it that grass does not arise from within milk?
“Good son! One cannot definitively say that there is curd within milk, nor can one say that there is no curd within milk; furthermore, it cannot be said that it arises from something else.
If one says:”
If it were the case that "curd definitely exists within milk," how could their substance and flavor be distinct?
Therefore, one cannot say:
"The nature of curd definitely exists within milk."
If one says,
"There is definitely no curd in milk," why then does a rabbit's horn not grow from within the milk? Furthermore,
if poison is placed in the milk, the resulting curd will kill a person.
Therefore, one cannot say:
"There is definitely no nature of curd within milk.
If one says:
Regarding the statement, "This curd is produced from another," why is it that curd is not produced in water?
Therefore, one cannot say:
"Curd is produced from another."
"Good son! By reason of the cow consuming grass, the blood turns white;
once the grass and blood have ceased, the power of the sentient beings' merit transforms it into milk."
Although this milk emerges from grass and blood, it cannot be said that these two are distinct; it can only be described as arising from causes and conditions.
The same applies to everything from curd up to clarified butter (ghṛta).
For this reason, it is given the name "ox-flavor.
Once this milk has ceased, it becomes curd through causes and conditions.
What are these causes and conditions?
Whether it be vinegar or warmth,
for this reason they are said to exist by way of causes and conditions;
even up to clarified butter (*sarpis*), it is likewise so.
Therefore, one cannot definitively state:
"There is no characteristic of curd within milk.
For it is impossible that what is produced from something else could exist apart from that thing.
“Good son! It is the same with clarity and ignorance.
If it is conjoined with the afflictions and all their fetters, it is called ignorance;”
If one is conjoined with all wholesome dharmas, it is called "clarity.
Therefore, I say: "There are no two characteristics."
For this reason, I have previously said:
"In the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called 'Fatty' (Pītika); if a cow eats it, it immediately produces ghee."
The Buddha-nature is also like this.
"Good son! Sentient beings with meager merit do not see these grasses."
The Buddha-nature is likewise; because it is shrouded by afflictions, sentient beings do not perceive it.
It is like the great ocean, which, though uniformly salty, also contains water of the highest excellence whose flavor is like milk.
For example, although the Snowy Mountains possess various merits and produce many medicinal herbs, they also contain poisonous weeds.

The bodies of sentient beings are likewise: although they contain the seeds of the four great poisonous snakes, within them there is also a sovereign king of wonderful medicines, namely the Buddha-nature. This is not a conditioned phenomenon, yet it is merely shrouded by the adventitious defilements of afflictions.
If those of the kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, vaiśya, or śūdra castes are able to sever and eliminate [these afflictions], they will immediately see the Buddha-nature and achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
"It is like when thunder rolls and clouds arise in the void, and flowers bloom upon all elephant tusks;
if there were no thunder, the flowers would not grow, nor would they even have a name."
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise; it is constantly shrouded by all manner of afflictions and cannot be seen.
For this reason, I say:
"Sentient beings have no self."
"If one hears this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one then perceives the Buddha-nature, like the flower on an elephant tusk.

Although one may hear all the samādhis of the sūtras, if one does not hear this sūtra, one will not know the subtle marks of the Tathāgata; it is like when there is no thunder, the flower upon the elephant tusk cannot be seen."
Having heard this sutra, one immediately understands the secret treasury of the Buddha-nature spoken of by all Tathāgatas, just as the ivory-flower appears when there is a celestial thunderclap.
Having heard this sutra, one immediately knows that all immeasurable sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.

For this reason, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is called the secret treasury of the Tathāgata; it causes the Dharma-body to increase, just like the flowers that bloom upon elephant tusks during a thunderstorm.
Because it is able to nurture such great significance, it is named "Mahāparinirvāṇa.

If there are good men or good women who are able to study this subtle and wondrous scripture of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, you should know that these people are able to repay the Buddha’s kindness and are true disciples of the Buddha.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
That which is called Buddha-nature is most profound and most profound, difficult to see and difficult to enter, such that it cannot be understood by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.”
The Buddha said, "Good son! It is so, it is so;
what you have praised does not contradict my teaching."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the Buddha-nature, why is it so profound, difficult to see, and difficult to enter?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! It is like a hundred blind men who, for the sake of having their eyes treated, go to a skilled physician."
At that time, the skilled physician used a golden lancet to cut away the cataract from his eye, pointed with a single finger, and asked:
"Do you see?
The blind man replied:
"I have not yet seen it.
He pointed with two fingers and then three fingers, saying,
"I see it slightly."

"Good son! It is the same with this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: even though immeasurable bodhisattvas have fully practiced all the pāramitās and even attained the ten stages (bhūmis), they were still unable to see their buddha-nature;
yet as soon as the Tathāgata has preached it, they are able to see it slightly."
Having seen this, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all spoke these words:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
We have wandered through immeasurable births and deaths, constantly deluded and confused by the notion of non-self."
"Good son! If even Bodhisattvas at the stage of the ten bhūmis do not clearly perceive or see the Buddha-nature, how much less could Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas possibly see it?"
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like looking up at geese or swans in the sky.
Is it the sky? Or is it the birds?"
"Is this a goose or a swan?
By observing it intently and without ceasing, he perceived it vaguely.

It is just so with the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes who know and see but a small portion of the Tathāgata-nature; how much less, then, could those of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know or see it?
“Good son! It is like a drunken man who, wishing to travel a long road, sees the path only dimly.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten stages likewise perceive only a small portion of the Tathāgata-nature.”
“Good son! It is like a thirsty person traveling through a vast wilderness; oppressed by thirst, he wanders everywhere seeking water and sees a grove of trees with white cranes perched upon them.

This person was so bewildered and distressed that he could not distinguish whether it was a tree or water; only after observing intently for a long time did he finally see white cranes and a grove of trees. Good son!
It is likewise with the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes who perceive and know but a small portion of the Tathāgata-nature. "Good son!

It is as if there were a person in the great ocean who, from a distance of even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas, gazes upon a great ship with its towers, battlements, halls, and pavilions, and immediately thinks to himself:"
"Is that a watchtower,
or is it empty space?
Only after gazing for a long time does a mind of certainty arise, knowing it to be a watchtower.
It is likewise for a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage who perceives the Tathāgata-nature within his own body.
"Good son! It is, for example, like a prince whose body is extremely delicate and weak; after playing all night until the clear dawn, he cannot see anything clearly with his eyes."
Even though Bodhisattvas in the tenth stage perceive the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies, it is likewise not clearly manifest.
Furthermore, good son!
For example, it is like a minister or official detained by royal business who returns home at the close of night.
A flash of lightning momentarily breaks forth, and upon seeing a herd of cattle, he immediately thinks:
"Is this a herd of cattle?"
"Is it a cloud?
Or is it a house?
Although this person gazes at it for a long time and gives rise to the thought that it is an ox, he still does not perceive it with certainty.
It is likewise that although Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes perceive the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies, they have not yet attained definitive certainty.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a bhikṣu who observes water free of insects but perceives the appearance of insects, and immediately thinks:
"Is that which moves within this water an insect?"
"Is this dust? Although he gazes for a long time without ceasing, even though he knows it is dust, he does not perceive it with complete clarity.
It is the same for a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes who perceives the Tathāgata-nature within his own body; he does not perceive it with great clarity.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person who, in the midst of thick darkness, sees a small child from afar and immediately thinks:
'Is that a cow?'"
"Is it a human?
Or is it a bird?
He observed for a long time without ceasing; although he saw a child, he still could not discern him clearly.
It is likewise with the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes who perceive the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies;
they do not yet see it with great clarity. Furthermore, good son!
For example, suppose a person, in the darkness of night, sees a painted image of a bodhisattva and immediately thinks:
"Is this an image of a bodhisattva?
Or is it an image of Maheśvara?"
"Is this image of Mahābrahmā actually a dyed robe?
Although the person observes it for a long time and thinks in his mind that it is an image of a Bodhisattva, he still does not see it clearly.
It is the same with the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes who perceive the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies; they do not perceive it very clearly.
“Good son! The Buddha-nature is thus profoundly deep and difficult to know or see; only a Buddha can know it, for it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
“Good son!
A wise person should make such distinctions to know the nature of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Buddha-nature is thus subtle and difficult to know, how can it be seen with the physical eye?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Good son! Just as the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception cannot be known by those of the Two Vehicles, yet is known through faith by following the sūtras; so it is with this.”
“Good son! Just as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas believe in and follow this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, so too do they realize that their own bodies possess the *tathāgatagarbha*.
"Good son! For this reason, you should diligently practice and cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Good son!"
"Thus, this Buddha-nature can only be known by a Buddha; it is not within the reach of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Ordinary worldlings who are not noble ones possess the nature of sentient beings, and all say that there is a self.
The Buddha said, "It is like two people who are friends together: one is a prince, and the other is poor and lowly."
In this way, the two men traveled back and forth between each other.
At that time, the poor man saw that the prince possessed a fine sword, pure and exquisite beyond compare, and his heart became filled with craving for it.
At a later time, the prince took this sword and fled to another country.
Subsequently, a poor man stayed overnight in another house and, while asleep, muttered in his sleep:
"The sword! The sword!"
A bystander heard this and took him to the king's presence.
At that time, the king asked him,
"As for what you call a 'knife,' show it to me."
The man answered the king with all the aforementioned details:
"Even if Your Majesty were now to slaughter and dismember my body, or sever my hands and feet, you would truly be unable to obtain the sword."
I have long been close and intimate with the prince; though I previously saw him in one place, I did not even dare to touch him with my hand, much less intentionally take him.
The king asked again:
"What is the appearance and likeness of the sword you saw?
He replied:
"Great King! What I have seen is like the horn of a black sheep.
Having heard this, the king smiled with joy and said:
"Go now wherever you wish; do not give rise to sorrow or fear. There is no such sword in my treasury, much less could you have seen it with a prince?"
At that time, the king immediately asked his ministers, "Have you ever seen such a sword as this?
Having spoken these words, he passed away; thereupon, another son was established to succeed him on the royal throne.
He questioned his ministers again:
"Have you ever seen this sword within the official treasuries?
The ministers replied:
"We have seen it before," they replied. He asked again,
"What does its appearance resemble?"
He replied: "Great King!
It is like the horn of a ram."
The king said,
"By what cause should there be such a sword within my treasury? Subsequently,
all four kings conducted a thorough inspection, searching for it but failing to find it.
After some time had passed, the prince who had previously fled returned from another country to his own land and once again became king.
Having ascended the throne, he asked his ministers:
"Did you see the sword?"
They replied,
"Great King! We all saw it."
Again he asked:
"What does its appearance resemble?
He replied:
"Great King!
His complexion is as pure as an *utpala* flower.
Another replied:
"Shaped like a ram's horn.
Another replied:
"Its color is crimson, like a mass of fire."
Again, another replied:
"It is like a black snake.
At that time, the king laughed loudly.
“You all do not see the true mark of my sword. “Good sons!

It is the same with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: appearing in the world, he proclaims the true mark of the self, and having spoken, he departs, just like a prince who, carrying a pure and wondrous sword, flees to another country.”
Ordinary, foolish people say:
"There is a self; there is a self.
It is like that poor man who stayed overnight in another's house and, while dozing, spoke in his sleep:
"Cut! Cut! The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas asked all sentient beings:
"What marks do I possess?"
He replied,
"I see my own mark, as large as a mother's thumb. Or he said:
"Like rice, or like millet," some say.
"The mark of self (ātman) dwells within the heart, blazing like the sun.
Thus, sentient beings do not know the mark of self, just as ministers do not know the characteristics of a sword.

When a bodhisattva speaks thus regarding my Dharma, ordinary people do not understand and engage in various conceptual discriminations, falsely constructing the notion of a self, like one who, when asked about the characteristics of a sword, answers that it resembles a sheep’s horn.
These ordinary worldlings give rise to false views through a continuous succession.
In order to sever such false views, the Tathāgata manifests and teaches non-self, just as a prince might say to his ministers:
"In my treasury, there is no such sword."
“Good son! That which the Tathāgata has today taught as the true self is called Buddha-nature. Within my Buddha-dharma, this Buddha-nature is like a pure blade.”
"Good son! If there are ordinary persons who can skillfully explain this, they are following and conforming to the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma;
if there are those who can skillfully discern and proclaim it in accordance with it, you should know that these are the marks of a bodhisattva."
Chapter Thirteen: On Letters. In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Chapter Thirteen, “On Letters,” the Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa:
“All various discourses, incantations, speech, and letters are the teachings of the Buddha; they are not the teachings of non-Buddhists.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why does the Tathāgata speak of the root of letters?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
At the beginning, the half-syllables were taught as the foundation, upholding all treatises, incantations, literature, the aggregates, and the real dharmas."
“Ordinary people study these fundamental characters, and only then can they know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the meaning of what you call 'syllables' (akṣara)?
"Good son! There are fourteen phonemes which constitute the meaning of syllables."
That which is called "syllable" (akṣara) is named Nirvāṇa.
Because it is eternal, it does not flow;
that which does not flow is inexhaustible.
That which is inexhaustible is precisely the Tathāgata’s adamantine body.
These fourteen vowels are called the "roots of syllables.
The short *a* is so named because it is indestructible.
That which is indestructible is called the Triple Gem, and it is likened to a vajra.
Furthermore, "A" signifies non-flowing;
that which does not flow is the Tathāgata.
Because the Tathāgata has no outflow from the nine orifices, he does not flow.
Furthermore, because he lacks the nine orifices, he does not flow;
that which does not flow is eternal.
The eternal is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is without action; therefore, he does not flow.
Furthermore, "A" is named merit.
Merit is precisely the Three Jewels; therefore, it is called "A.
Next, the extended "A" is named Ācārya.
What is the meaning of "Ācārya"?
Among those in the world, they are called "noble ones" (*ārya*).
What is meant by "noble"?
"Noble" means being without attachment, having few desires and being content; it is also called "purity."
One who is able to ferry sentient beings across the great ocean of birth and death within the three realms of existence is called a noble one (*ārya*).
Furthermore, "Ā" signifies regulation: it refers to the cultivation and maintenance of pure precepts in accordance with dignified conduct.

Furthermore, "A" means relying on the noble ones; one should train in dignified deportment, advancing and retreating, and lifting and moving; one should make offerings to, revere, and prostrate before the Triple Gem; and one should filially support one's parents and study the Mahāyāna.
Good men and women who fully uphold the prohibitive precepts, as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others like them, are called "sages.
Furthermore, "A" is named "instruction," as it says:
"You all should act in this way; you must not act in that way."
"If there is one who can restrain non-proper conduct (*anairyāṇika-dharma*), they are called a noble one (*ārya*); for this reason, it is called 'A.
The short vowel 'I' represents the Buddha-dharma: its holy life (*brahmacarya*) is vast, pure, and stainless, like the full moon."
"You should act in this way, and not in that way; this is meaningful and that is meaningless; this is the Buddha's teaching and this is Māra's teaching"—for this reason, it is called "I."
"O Long Life, the Buddha-dharma is subtle and wondrous, profound and difficult to attain.
Just as the Dharma of Maheśvara and Mahābrahmā is called 'Sovereignty,' one who is able to uphold it is named a 'Protector of the Dharma.'"
Furthermore, those who possess mastery are called the Four World-Protectors.
These four masters are able to protect and uphold the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, and they are also able to freely propagate and proclaim it.
"Furthermore, 'I' (i) is that which can preach the Dharma with mastery for the sake of sentient beings.
Moreover, 'I' is spoken of because it is sovereign.
What is this sovereignty? It is as follows:"
This refers to the cultivation of the Vaipulya sūtras.
Furthermore, "I" signifies the severing of envy, like the removal of weeds and chaff, enabling everything to be transformed into auspiciousness; for this reason, it is called "I."
“The shortening of sorrow is the most supreme, the most excellent, and the highest of all sūtras; it is called the Great Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, this ‘sorrow’ is the nature of the Tathāgata, which has never before been heard by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.”

Just as among all places, Uttarakuru is the most excellent, so too, if a bodhisattva can hear and receive this sutra, they will be the most supreme and most excellent among all assemblies; for this reason, it is called "U."
"O Longevity, it is like cow's milk, which is the most excellent among all flavors;
the nature of the Tathāgata is likewise so, being the most honored and supreme among all sūtras."
If there are those who slander [this teaching], you should know that such persons are no different from oxen.
Furthermore, "sorrowful" refers to those who lack wisdom and right mindfulness, and who slander the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata.

It should be known that such a person is deeply pitiable; having distanced themselves from the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, they preach the doctrine of non-self, and for this reason they are called "sorrowful" (*śoka*).
"Joyful" (*nanda*) refers to the *dharmatā* and *nirvāṇa* of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called "joyful."
"Jana" (野) refers to the meaning of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, "jana" means that in the Tathāgata’s coming and going, bending and stretching, and every movement, there is nothing that does not benefit all sentient beings; for this reason, it is called "jana."
"O" signifies the meaning of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Afflictions are called "outflows" (*āsrava*).
Since the Tathāgata has eternally severed all afflictions, he is therefore named O.
“*Pao* (Pha) refers to the meaning of the Mahāyāna; among the fourteen vowels, it is the ultimate meaning.
The Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so: they are the most ultimate among all sūtras and śāstras, and for this reason they are called *pao*.”
“An ‘āṇa’ (庵) is that which can shield against all impure things.
Within the Buddha-dharma, one is able to relinquish all gold, silver, and precious objects; for this reason, it is called ‘āṇa.’”
“‘A’ signifies the meaning of the ‘Victorious Vehicle. Why is this?
Because this Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, is the most preeminent among all sūtras; therefore, it is called ‘A.’”

“Ka” means that one gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, conceiving of them as one’s own children, just like Rāhula, and performs deeds of wondrous goodness; therefore, it is called “Ka.”
"Kha means 'not a virtuous friend.
One who is not a virtuous friend is called 'impure.
Because they do not believe in the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, they are called Kha."
"Ga" means "treasury.
A treasury is precisely the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; for this reason, it is called "Ga."
"The heavy syllable *ga* is the eternal sound of the Tathāgata.
What is called the eternal sound of the Tathāgata?
It is because the Tathāgata abides eternally and is immutable; therefore, it is named *ga*."
“*Aḥ* signifies the characteristic of the destruction of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); therefore it is named *aḥ*.
*Cha* signifies the meaning of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Because it tames all sentient beings, it is called the meaning of cultivation; therefore it is named *cha*.”
“*Jina* means that the Tathāgata provides shelter for all sentient beings like a great canopy; therefore, it is called *jina*.
*Ja* means right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*), which is devoid of the mark of aging; therefore, it is called *ja*.”
"Jha" with a heavy vowel refers to the profusion of afflictions, which are like a dense forest; therefore it is called "jha.
"Ja" signifies wisdom, meaning the knowledge of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā); therefore it is called "ja."
“*Ṭha* means that in Jambudvīpa he manifests half his body to expound the Dharma, like the crescent moon; therefore it is called *Ṭha*.
*Ṭha* (pronounced with the retroflex *ṭh*) means that the Dharmakāya is fully complete, like the full moon; therefore it is called *Ṭha*.”
“*Chā* refers to a foolish monk who does not understand permanence and impermanence; he is like a small child, and for this reason he is called *chā*.
The emphatic *chā* refers to one who does not recognize the kindness of his teacher; he is like a ram, and for this reason he is called *chā*.”
“*Natha* is not a term of noble meaning; it is like the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and for this reason it is called *natha*.
As for ‘many,’ the Tathāgata addressed the bhikṣus there, saying:
‘You should abandon fear and dread; I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for you.’”
For this reason, it is called "many" (*bahu*).
"Other" (*para*) means the sense of delusion (*moha*).
Sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death, binding themselves like silkworms; for this reason, it is called "other."
“Dha” is named the Great Giving, which refers to the Mahāyāna; therefore it is called Dha.
“Dha,” pronounced with a heavy tone, signifies the praise of merit: the Three Jewels are like Mount Sumeru—lofty, vast, and expansive, never to be overturned; therefore it is called Dha.
“Na” signifies that the Three Jewels abide securely without being shaken, like a door threshold; therefore, it is called “na.
“Pa” signifies the meaning of inversion.
If one says,
"The Three Jewels have all utterly perished," know that this person is harboring self-doubt; for this reason, it is called a "wave."
"‘Pho’ refers to the calamities of the world.
If one says:
‘When the calamities of the world arise, the Three Jewels also perish,’ [it is not so]."
"You should know that such a person is foolish and lacks wisdom, having violated and lost the holy intent; therefore, it is called *pha*.
*Ba* refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Buddha; therefore, it is called *ba*."
"Bhāra means 'heavy burden.
One who is capable of bearing the unsurpassed True Dharma should be known as a Great Bodhisattva; therefore, he is called Bhāra."
“*Ma* refers to the rigorous discipline of all bodhisattvas, namely the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa; therefore, it is called *ma*.
*Śe* refers to the fact that these bodhisattvas, wherever they may be, preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; therefore, it is called *śe*.”
“Ra signifies that which can destroy greed, hatred, and delusion, and speaks the Dharma of reality; therefore, it is called Ra.
‘Light Ra’ refers to the Śrāvaka vehicle, which is restless and does not abide.”
The Mahāyāna is peaceful and secure, without any instability; one abandons the Śrāvaka vehicle and diligently cultivates the unsurpassed Mahāyāna—therefore it is called "Ra.
"Ho" means that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, rains down the great Dharma rain for all sentient beings, namely the worldly incantations and scriptures—therefore it is called "Ho."
“‘Śa’ means to be far removed from the three arrows; therefore, it is called ‘śa.
‘Sa’ means the sense of being fully endowed.
If one can listen to this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, one has already attained the hearing and retention of all Mahāyāna sūtras; therefore, it is called ‘sa.’”
“*Sa* means to expound the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing their minds to rejoice;
therefore it is called *sa*. *Ha* means the mind rejoicing.”
"How marvelous!
The World-Honored One has transcended all conditioned formations.
How extraordinary!"
"The Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is called "ha.
As for "ra," its meaning is "māra" (the demon).
Innumerable māras cannot destroy the Tathāgata’s secret treasury; therefore, it is called *ra*.
Furthermore, *ra* refers to even manifesting in accordance with the world by having parents, wives, and children; therefore, it is called *ra*.
"Ru, Liu, Lu, and Lou—these four characters are said to have four meanings, namely: Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha, and Abhidharma.
As for what is called 'Abhidharma,' it accords with the world."
Just as Devadatta manifested the breaking of the Saṃgha and transformed himself into various shapes and forms for the purpose of establishing the precepts,
the wise person understands this clearly and should not give rise to fear or dread on this account.
This is called conduct that accords with the world.
For this reason, they are named Lu, Liu, Lu, and Lou.

The sounds drawn in through the breath, produced by the tongue-root, and following the nose—whether long, short, or transcendent tones—and the understanding of meaning according to these sounds, all possess distinctions due to the tongue and teeth.
The meaning of such words can cause the verbal karma of sentient beings to become pure;
however, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not like this, for it does not require reliance upon words before becoming pure.
Why is this? Because its nature is fundamentally pure.
Although it dwells within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, it is not identical to those aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Therefore, all sentient beings should take refuge [in the Buddha].
Because of their buddha-nature, the bodhisattvas regard all sentient beings with equality, without making any distinctions.
For this reason, the "half-syllables" (the phonetic characters) serve as the foundation for all sutras, treatises, commentaries, and literary compositions.
Furthermore, the meaning of "half-syllables" (ardhakṣara) is that they are all the basis for the verbal expressions of afflictions; therefore, they are called half-syllables.
"Full-syllables" (pūrṇakṣara), on the other hand, are the fundamental basis for the verbal expressions of all wholesome dharmas.
For example, in the world, those who practice evil are called "half-men," while those who cultivate goodness are called "complete men.
In this same way, all scriptures, records, and treatises take the "half-syllables" as their fundamental basis.
If one says,
"The Tathāgata and perfect liberation enter into the half-syllables," this is not so.
Why is this? Because it is free from words and letters.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is unimpeded and unattached regarding all dharmas, having truly attained liberation.
"What is meant by 'understanding the meaning of the characters'?
It is knowing that the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is able to extinguish the 'half-letters'; therefore, it is called understanding the meaning of the characters."
If there are those who follow the meaning of the "half-syllables," such persons do not know the nature of the Tathāgata.
What is called the meaning of the "non-syllable"?
Those who draw near to and cultivate unwholesome dharmas—this is called the non-syllable.

Furthermore, those who lack letters, though they may personally draw near to and cultivate wholesome dharmas, do not know the Tathāgata’s permanence and impermanence, his constancy and non-constancy, nor the two jewels of Dharma and Saṃgha; they cannot distinguish between what is discipline and what is not discipline, what is a sūtra and what is not a sūtra, or what is spoken by Māra and what is spoken by the Buddha.
If one is unable to discern in this way, it is called following after the meaning of non-words.
I have now explained the meaning of following after non-words.
“Good son! For this reason, you should now abandon the ‘half-syllables’ and skillfully understand the ‘full-syllables.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We should skillfully study the enumeration of syllables.
Now that we have encountered the Unsurpassed Teacher, we have already received the Tathāgata’s earnest instructions.”
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!
Those who delight in the True Dharma should train in this way.”

Chapter 14: The Parable of the Bird. At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: “Good son! The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Fourteen: The Parable of the Bird. At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: “Good son!”
There are two kinds of birds: the first is called the *kalaviṅka* and the second is called the ruddy sheldrake (*cakravāka*). They dwell and move together, never parting from one another.
These dharmas of suffering, impermanence, non-self, and so forth are likewise thus; they cannot be separated from one another.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
in what way are suffering, impermanence, and non-self like those ruddy sheldrakes and kālaṃjara birds?”
The Buddha said:
“Good son! One dharma is suffering and another dharma is happiness; one dharma is permanent and another dharma is impermanent; one dharma is self and another dharma is non-self.”
For example, rice is distinct from hemp and wheat; hemp and wheat, in turn, are distinct from beans, millet, and sugarcane.
Thus, all these various species—from their sprouting and germination, up to their flowers and leaves—are impermanent.
When the fruit has ripened and people enjoy it, it is then called "permanent.
Why is this? Because its nature is real and true.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If such things as these were permanent, would they be identical to the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said, “Good son,
you should not speak in such a manner now.”
Why is this? If one says:
"The Tathāgata is like Mount Sumeru."
"When the kalpa is destroyed and Mount Sumeru collapses, would the Tathāgata likewise perish at that time?
Son of good family!
You should not now accept this interpretation."
Good son! Among all dharmas, with the sole exception of nirvāṇa, there is not a single dharma that is permanent; it is only according to worldly convention that the fruit is said to be permanent.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!”
"It is as the Buddha has taught.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "So it is, so it is."
"Good son!
Although one may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, as long as one has not yet heard the Mahāparinirvāṇa, one will declare that everything is entirely impermanent."
Having heard this sutra, although they possess afflictions, they are as if without afflictions, and are thus able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because they clearly understand that their own bodies possess the Buddha-nature; this is what is called "permanence."
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like the mango tree: when its flowers first bloom, it is called the mark of impermanence;
once it has produced fruit that brings great benefit, it is then called permanent."
In this way, good son!

Although one may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, as long as one has not yet heard such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one will invariably say that everything is impermanent.
Having heard this sutra, although they possess afflictions, they are as if without afflictions, and are thus able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because they clearly understand that their own bodies possess the Buddha-nature; this is what is called "permanence."
"Furthermore, good son!
For example, when gold ore is being smelted and dissolved, it is a mark of impermanence;
once it has been melted and formed into gold, it brings great benefit and is therefore called permanent."
In this way, good son!

Although one may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, as long as one has not yet heard such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one will invariably declare that all things are impermanent.
Having heard this sutra, although they possess afflictions, they are as if without afflictions, and are thus able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because they clearly understand that their own bodies possess Buddha-nature; this is what is called "permanence."
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like sesame seeds: before they have been pressed, they are called impermanent;
once pressed into oil, they provide great benefit and are therefore called permanent."
"Good son!

Although one may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, as long as one has not yet heard this Great Parinirvāṇa, one will always say that everything is entirely impermanent."
Having heard this sutra, although they possess afflictions, they are as if without afflictions, and are thus able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because they clearly understand that their own bodies possess Buddha-nature; this is what is called "permanence."
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as all streams flow back to the ocean,
so do all the samādhis and concentrations of the various sūtras flow back to the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*."
Why is this? Because it is ultimately well-expounded that the Buddha-nature exists. Good son!
"Therefore, I say that some dharmas are eternal while other dharmas are impermanent;
even so it is with regard to non-self.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has already departed from the poisonous arrows of sorrow and lamentation.
Indeed, that which is called sorrow and lamentation is named ‘heaven’;”
The Tathāgata is not a deva;
one who experiences sorrow and grief is called a human being,
and the Tathāgata is not a human being.
"Sorrow and lamentation" refer to the twenty-five states of existence;
the Tathāgata is not among these twenty-five states of existence.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has no sorrow or lamentation.
"Why is it said that the Tathāgata experiences sorrow and grief? "Good son!
That which is called the Heaven of No-Thought is named 'no-thought. If there is no thought, then there is no life-span."
If there were no life-span, how could there be the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas)?
For this reason, it cannot be said that the life-span of the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) has a specific place of abiding.
Good son! It is like a tree spirit that dwells in dependence upon a tree; one cannot definitively say it depends on the branches, the nodes, the trunk, or the leaves.
Although it has no fixed location, one cannot say it does not exist.
The lifespan in the Heaven of Non-conception is likewise so.
Good son, the Buddha-dharma is also thus: it is exceedingly profound and difficult to understand.
The Tathāgata is truly free from sorrow, grief, suffering, and affliction; yet, out of great compassion for sentient beings, he manifests sorrow and grief, regarding all beings as he does Rāhula.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The lifespan within the Heaven of No-Thought can only be known by a Buddha; it is beyond the reach of others.
This is likewise true for the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
“Kāśyapa! The nature of the Tathāgata is pure and unstained, just like a manifested body (nirmāṇakāya).
How could there be sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or affliction?”
If it is said that the Tathāgata possesses sorrow and grief, how can he benefit all sentient beings and propagate the Buddha-dharma on a vast scale?
If it is said that he does not possess them, why is it said that he regards all sentient beings equally as he does Rāhula?
If one does not regard others equally as one regards Rāhula, such words would be false.
For this reason, son of good family,
the Buddha is inconceivable, the Dharma is inconceivable, the buddha-nature of sentient beings is inconceivable, and the lifespan of the Heaven of No-Thought is inconceivable.
That the Tathāgata has sorrow or is without sorrow is the domain of the Buddha, not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. "Good son!
For example, houses or fine dust cannot stand or remain in space; if one were to say:
"It is impossible for a house to dwell without relying on space.
For this reason, one cannot say that a house dwells in space or does not dwell in space.
Although ordinary people may say that they dwell or reside in empty space, this empty space actually has no place of residence.
Why is this? Because its nature is non-abiding.
Good son! The mind is also like this: one cannot say that it dwells within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, nor that it does not dwell therein;
the lifespan of the Heaven of No-Thought is also like this, and the sorrow and grief of the Tathāgata are also like this.
If there is no sorrow or compassion, how can you say that you regard all sentient beings equally as you do Rāhula?
If you say that there is [sorrow], how then can you say that your nature is identical to empty space?

“Good son! It is like a master of illusions who, though he may conjure various palaces, acts of killing, nurturing, binding, and releasing, as well as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, precious objects, groves, and trees, none of these possess any real nature.”
The Tathāgata is likewise; he manifests sorrow and grief in accordance with the world, yet these have no reality.
Son of good family!
Since the Tathāgata has already entered Great Parinirvāṇa, how could there be any sorrow, grief, or affliction?
If one claims that the Tathāgata enters into nirvāṇa and is thus impermanent, know that such a person will experience sorrow and grief;
if one claims that the Tathāgata does not enter nirvāṇa but is eternally abiding and unchanging, know that such a person is free from sorrow and grief.
