Whether the Tathāgata possesses sorrow or is free from sorrow, no one is able to know it.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like how an inferior person can know inferior dharmas, but cannot know those that are middling or superior; [so too is it with the Tathāgata]."
Those of middle capacity know the middle, but do not know what is above;
those of superior capacity know the superior, as well as the middle and the lower.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise: they know only up to their own respective stages.
The Tathāgata is not so; he fully knows his own stage as well as the stages of others.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is called "Unobstructed Wisdom.

He manifests illusory transformations in accordance with the world, yet ordinary people with their physical eyes claim these to be real. To wish to fully know the Tathāgata’s unobstructed and unsurpassed wisdom is impossible.
There is sorrow and there is no sorrow; only a Buddha can know this.
For this reason, in one dharma there is self, and in another dharma there is no-self; this is called the nature of the ruddy sheldrake and the kālaṃjiṅka bird.
"Furthermore, good son!
The Buddha-dharma is like the pair of mandarin ducks that travel together.

When the waters swell during the height of summer, these *kalaviṅka* and mandarin ducks select a high plateau to settle their young for the sake of their upbringing; only then do they follow their original course and roam in peace."

The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is likewise so: he transforms immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to abide in the True Dharma, just as that ruddy sheldrake and the kālaṃjara bird select high ground to settle their young.
The Tathāgata is also like this: having caused all sentient beings to accomplish what was to be done, he immediately enters great parinirvāṇa.

Good son! This is called "one dharma is suffering and another dharma is happiness": all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering, while nirvāṇa is happiness, for it is the supreme, subtle state that brings all conditioned phenomena to an end.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that those sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa are said to possess the foremost bliss?”
The Buddha said: “Good son!
As I have taught:”
"The convergence of all conditioned phenomena is called old age and death.
"Heedfulness and freedom from negligence—this is called the state of the Deathless;
negligence and lack of heedfulness—this is called the realm of death."
Those who are heedful attain the state of deathlessness;
those who are heedless always follow the path to death.
"Heedlessness is called a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and this conditioned phenomenon is the foremost suffering."
Heedfulness is called nirvāṇa; that nirvāṇa is called the ambrosia and the supreme, foremost bliss.
To pursue conditioned formations is called the realm of death, where one undergoes the foremost suffering;
to reach nirvāṇa is called the deathless, where one experiences the most wondrous bliss.
If one is not negligent, although one accumulates various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), these are also called the body that is permanent, blissful, deathless, and indestructible.
What, then, is negligence?
What is non-heedlessness?
The unenlightened worldling is called heedless; they are subject to the law of constant death.
The supramundane noble one is non-heedless; for them, there is no aging or death.
Why is this? Because one enters the supreme, eternal, and blissful nirvana.
For this reason, some phenomena are suffering and other phenomena are bliss; some phenomena are self and other phenomena are non-self.
It is like a person standing on the ground who looks up at the sky and does not see the tracks of birds.
Good son, it is the same with sentient beings:
lacking the divine eye, they do not perceive the Tathāgata-nature within themselves while amidst the afflictions.
For this reason, I speak of the esoteric teaching of non-self. Why is this?
Those who lack the divine eye do not know the true self.
Because of the false conception of a self, the conditioned phenomena produced by various afflictions are impermanent.
For this reason, I say that some dharmas are permanent and other dharmas are impermanent.
“The one who is diligent, courageous, and steadfast, whether dwelling on a mountain peak,
on level ground, or in the wilderness, constantly beholds all ordinary beings.
Ascending the palace of great wisdom and the unsurpassed, sublime terrace,”
Having personally eliminated my own afflictions, I also see the afflictions of sentient beings.

"The Tathāgata has completely severed immeasurable defilements and dwells upon the mountain of wisdom; yet he sees all sentient beings constantly dwelling amidst immeasurable billions of defilements."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As stated in the verse, this meaning is not so.”
Why is this? Those who have entered nirvana possess neither sorrow nor joy.
How, then, could they ascend the palace of wisdom?
"Furthermore, how should one abide upon the mountain peak and perceive sentient beings?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
The Hall of Wisdom is another name for Nirvana.
Those who are free from sorrow and affliction are called Tathāgatas;
those who possess sorrow and affliction are called ordinary persons.
Because ordinary beings possess sorrow, the Tathāgata is without sorrow.
"The summit of Mount Sumeru" refers to right liberation.
"Diligent in vigor" is likened to Mount Sumeru, which is without movement or fluctuation.
"Ground" refers to conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
It is upon this ground that all ordinary worldlings abide and perform various formations.
One whose wisdom is such is called a Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).
Because he is free from existence and eternally abiding, he is called the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata takes pity on immeasurable sentient beings who are constantly pierced by the poisonous arrows of the various defilements; for this reason, he is said to have "sorrow" (or "concern").
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata were subject to sorrow and grief, he could not be called the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
The Buddha said:

“Kāśyapa! All have causes and conditions. Wherever there are sentient beings who should be transformed, the Tathāgata manifests birth therein; though he manifests birth, in reality there is no birth.”
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the eternally abiding Dharma, like the kalaviṅka, the ruddy sheldrake, and other such birds.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Eight;
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
The *Fifteenth Chapter on the Simile of the Moon*, added by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa:
"It is, for example, like someone who sees the moon not appearing and says to all,
'The moon has set,' forming the perception that it has set; yet, in its true nature, this moon never actually sets."
"Manifesting elsewhere, the sentient beings there again say:
'The moon has risen.
Yet, in reality, this nature of the moon never actually rises."
Why is this? Because it is obscured by Mount Sumeru, it does not appear.
That moon is ever-present; its nature is without rising or setting.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: appearing in a trichiliocosm or in Jambudvīpa, he manifests having parents, and sentient beings all say, "He was born in Jambudvīpa."
"In some cases, the Tathāgata manifests parinirvāṇa in Jambudvīpa; yet the nature of the Tathāgata truly has no parinirvāṇa, and all sentient beings nevertheless say:
'The Tathāgata has truly entered parinirvāṇa.'"
"It is like the setting of the moon.
Son of good family!
The nature of the Tathāgata is truly without birth or extinction; it is only to transform sentient beings that he manifests birth and extinction."
“Good son! Just as this full moon appears as half-moon in other directions,
and this half-moon appears as a full moon in other directions.”
When the people of Jambudvīpa see the first crescent of the moon, they all say it is the first day and conceive the notion that it is the beginning of the month;
when they see the moon full, they say it is the fifteenth day and conceive the notion that it is full.
Yet the nature of this moon is truly without waxing or waning; it appears to increase and decrease only because of Mount Sumeru.
Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise: within Jambudvīpa, he may manifest his initial birth or manifest his parinirvāṇa.
At the time of his initial birth, he was like the new moon; everyone said:
"The child has just been born and has taken seven steps.
Like the second-day moon, he further manifested entering the schoolhouse.
Like the third-day moon, he manifests the act of leaving the household life.
Like the eighth-day moon, he emits the subtle and wondrous light of great wisdom, capable of destroying the demonic hosts of immeasurable sentient beings.
Like the full moon on the fifteenth day, he may manifest himself adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
yet he manifests parinirvāṇa as if by a lunar eclipse.

In this way, the perceptions of sentient beings differ: some see a crescent moon, some see a full moon, and some see an eclipsed moon; yet the nature of this moon truly has no increase, decrease, or erosion—it is always a full moon.
The body of the Tathāgata is likewise thus; for this reason, it is called eternally abiding and unchanging.

Furthermore, good son, it is like the full moon, which appears everywhere—in cities, villages, mountains, marshes, and within waters; whether in wells, ponds, or various water vessels, it appears in them all.

There are sentient beings who travel for a hundred yojanas or even a hundred thousand yojanas, seeing the moon constantly following them; these foolish worldlings give rise to false conceptions, saying:
"I previously saw such a moon in cities and houses, and now I see it again here in this empty marsh."
"Is this the original moon,
or is it different from the original?
Each of them formed such thoughts regarding the size of the moon's form, and some said:
"Like the mouth of a bellows," or it is said:
"Like a chariot wheel."
Some said: "It is forty-nine yojanas [in diameter].
Everyone beheld the radiance of the moon; some saw it as perfectly round, like a golden platter.
The nature of this moon is one, yet various sentient beings each perceive it as having different appearances.
Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise; when he appears in the world, some humans and devas may have this thought:
"The Tathāgata now dwells before me.
Furthermore, even animals conceived this thought:
"The Tathāgata now dwells before me."
Some who were deaf or mute also saw the Tathāgata as having the appearance of being deaf or mute.
Among the various classes of sentient beings, whose languages and sounds differed, each believed that the Tathāgata spoke their own language, and each conceived this thought:
"He is in my house, receiving my offerings."
Some sentient beings see the body of the Tathāgata as vast and immeasurable, while others see it as minute.
Some see the Buddha in the form of a śrāvaka, and others again see him in the form of a pratyekabuddha.
There were certain non-Buddhists who each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata has now gone forth from home to study the Way within our own teachings.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings who also thought this:
"The Tathāgata has now appeared in the world solely for my sake.

The true nature of the Tathāgata is like that moon; it is the Dharma-body, the birthless body, and the body of skillful means. In accordance with the world, he manifests immeasurable causes and conditions of past karma, appearing to be born in every place, just like that moon.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and undergoes no change.
Furthermore, good son, it is like when the asura king Rāhu covers the moon with his hand; all people in the world say that it is an eclipse of the moon.
The Asura King is truly unable to eclipse it; rather, it is because the Asuras obstruct its light.
This moon is perfectly full and without any waning; it is merely made invisible because their hands block it.
When the moon is eclipsed, all people in the world say that the moon has been restored to life, and they all remark:
"This moon has endured much suffering.
Even if there were a hundred thousand asura kings, none would be able to afflict it.

The Tathāgata is likewise: he manifests that there are sentient beings who conceive coarse and evil thoughts toward him, shed the blood of a Buddha, commit the five heinous crimes, and even reach the state of an icchantika.

For the sake of sentient beings in future ages, he manifests such obstacles as the schism of the Saṃgha and the severance of the Dharma; yet even if there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Māras, they would be unable to draw blood from the body of the Tathāgata.
Why is this so? The body of the Tathāgata is devoid of blood, flesh, sinews, veins, bones, and marrow; the Tathāgata is the ultimate reality, truly free from affliction or destruction.
All sentient beings say:
"The Dharma and the Sangha have perished; the Tathāgata has passed into extinction.
Yet the nature of the Tathāgata is truly immutable and indestructible; he manifests in this manner merely to accord with the ways of the world.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like two people fighting; if one wounds the other with a blade or a staff, causing blood to flow, even if it leads to death, because no thought of killing arose, the characteristics of such karma are light and not heavy."
Regarding the Tathāgata, he originally had no intent to kill; although his body was bled, this karma is likewise light and not heavy.
In this way, the Tathāgata manifests the retribution of karma in future ages in order to transform sentient beings.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a skilled physician who diligently instructs his son in the fundamental principles of medical formulas:
'This is a root medicine; this is a stem medicine; this is a color medicine. You must thoroughly understand their various characteristics.'"
The son respectfully followed his father’s instructions, practicing and studying with diligence until he became well-versed in all medicinal herbs.
Later, when the physician’s life had reached its end and he passed away, the son mourned him deeply and spoke these words:
"My father originally taught me that the root medicine is such, the stem medicine is such, the flower medicine is such, and their characteristics are such."
The Tathāgata is likewise; in order to transform sentient beings, he manifests the establishment of precepts, saying:
"You should receive and uphold them in this way; do not commit the five heinous crimes, slander the true Dharma, or become an icchantika."
"This is manifested for the sake of those who will arise in future ages, so that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus may understand thus:
'This is the profound meaning of the sūtras; this is the nature of the gravity and lightness of the vinaya; this is the analysis of the categories of dharmas in the abhidharma.'"
"Just like that physician’s son.
Furthermore, good son!
It is as if a person sees a lunar eclipse once every six months, whereas the gods above see a lunar eclipse in the space of a mere moment."
Why is this? Because for those devas the days are long, while for humans they are short.
O son of good family!
The Tathāgata is likewise; all devas and humans claim that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is short, just as those devas and humans frequently witness lunar eclipses within a single moment.

Furthermore, within a single moment, the Tathāgata manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nirvāṇas, severing the māra of afflictions, the māra of the aggregates, and the māra of death.
Therefore, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial Māras all know that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, in accordance with the various natures of the world, he manifests immeasurable hundreds of thousands of causes and conditions from past karma, displaying such infinite, boundless, and inconceivable manifestations.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Furthermore, good son, it is like the bright moon, which all sentient beings delight in beholding; for this reason, the moon is called "Delightful to Behold."
If sentient beings possess greed, anger, and delusion, they cannot be called "delightful to behold.
The Tathāgata is thus: his nature is purely good, pure and stainless; he alone may truly be called "delightful to behold."
Sentient beings who delight in the Dharma never tire of beholding him, whereas those with malicious minds take no pleasure in looking upon him.
For this reason, it is said that the Tathāgata is like the bright moon.
"Furthermore, good son!

For example, the rising of the sun has three distinct seasons: namely, spring, summer, and winter. In winter the days are short; in spring they are of medium length; and in summer they are extremely long."

The Tathāgata is likewise; within this trichiliocosm, for the sake of those with short lifespans and the śrāvakas, he manifests a short lifespan. Having seen this, they all say that the Tathāgata’s life span is brief, like that of winter days.
For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he manifests a medium lifespan—whether reaching one kalpa or falling short of one kalpa—which is like the spring sun.
Only a Buddha perceives the Buddha’s own immeasurable lifespan, which is like the summer sun.
“Good son! The profound and secret teachings of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna spoken by the Tathāgata manifest in the world and rain down the great Dharma rain.

If in future ages there are those who can protect and uphold this scripture, reveal and analyze it to benefit sentient beings, you should know that these individuals are true Bodhisattvas, comparable to the sweet rain falling during the height of summer.”
If there are śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas who hear the subtle and secret teaching of the Buddha-Tathāgata, it is like encountering much suffering from the cold during the winter months.
If bodhisattvas hear such subtle and secret instruction—that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and his nature is immutable—it is like the sprouting and blossoming of buds in the springtime.
Yet the nature of the Tathāgata is truly without length or shortness; it is for the sake of the world that he manifests in such a way, which is precisely the true *dharmatā* of all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, good son!
For example, just as the various stars do not appear during the day, yet people all say that the stars have vanished during the day;
in reality they have not vanished, but do not appear because they are eclipsed by the light of the sun.
The Tathāgata is likewise; the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to see him, just as worldly people cannot see the stars during the day.
"Furthermore, good son!
For example, when it is shrouded in darkness and the sun and moon do not appear, foolish people say,
"The sun and moon have perished.
Yet, in reality, the sun and moon have not perished at all.
When the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is extinguished, the disappearance of the Three Jewels is likewise not a permanent cessation.
Therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change.
Why is this? Because the true nature of the Three Jewels cannot be defiled by any impurities.
"Furthermore, good son!

For example, during the dark fortnight of the month, a comet appears at night; its brilliance is fiercely blazing, yet it emerges for but a moment before vanishing. When sentient beings see this, they conceive thoughts of ill omen.

The Pratyekabuddhas are also like this: appearing in worlds where no Buddha dwells, when sentient beings see them, they all say that the Tathāgata has truly entered parinirvāṇa, and they give rise to thoughts of sorrow and grief.
Yet the body of the Tathāgata truly does not undergo extinction; it is like the sun and moon, which have neither setting nor disappearance.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like the rising of the sun, by which all mists are entirely dispelled."

This subtle and wondrous sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa is likewise: when it appears in the world, if there are sentient beings who hear it even once, they will be able to completely eliminate all evils and the karmic offenses of the *ānantarya* crimes.
This Great Nirvana is a profound realm that is inconceivable; it skillfully explains the subtle and secret nature of the Tathāgata.

For this reason, all sons and daughters of good family should conceive the thought that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change, that the True Dharma shall not be interrupted, and that the Jewel of the Saṅgha shall not perish. Therefore, you should cultivate many skillful means and diligently study this scripture.
This person shall, before long, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, this sutra is named "Accomplished through Immeasurable Merit" and is also named "The Inexhaustible Bodhi."
Because it is inexhaustible, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Because it possesses virtuous radiance, it is like the summer sun.
Because its body is boundless, it is named Mahānirvāṇa.
16. Chapter on the Bodhisattva. *The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen on the Bodhisattva:
"Furthermore, good son, it is like the light of the sun and moon, which is the foremost among all luminosities and cannot be equaled by any other light."

The light of the Great Nirvāṇa is likewise thus; among the lights of all sūtras and samādhis, it is the most preeminent, such that the lights possessed by the sūtras and samādhis cannot reach its brilliance.
Why is this? Because the light of the Great Nirvana can enter all the pores of sentient beings.
Although sentient beings may lack the aspiration for Bodhi, it can still act as the causal condition for Bodhi; therefore, it is further named Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:”
"The light of the Mahāparinirvāṇa enters the pores of all sentient beings; although these beings lack the aspiration for bodhi, it can nevertheless act as the cause for their attainment of bodhi."
This meaning is not so. Why is this?
World-Honored One!

If those who have committed the four grave offenses, those who have perpetrated the five heinous crimes, and icchantikas can have light enter their bodies to serve as the cause for bodhi, then what difference is there between such people and those who maintain pure precepts and cultivate various virtues?
If there were no distinction, for what reason would the Tathāgata have taught the meaning of the four reliances?
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:

Regarding the statement, "If there are sentient beings who hear the Mahāparinirvāṇa, it passes through their ears but once and they immediately sever all afflictions," how is it that the Tathāgata previously said:
"There are people who have resolved upon bodhicitta in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet upon hearing the Mahāparinirvāṇa, they do not understand its meaning"?
"If one does not understand the meaning, how can one sever all afflictions?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
With the exception of those with icchantika tendencies, all other sentient beings who hear this sutra will be able to create the causes and conditions for bodhi.
Those into whose pores the light of the Dharma's sound enters will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Only those who are able to make offerings to and revere immeasurable Buddhas can hear the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; those of meager merit cannot hear it.
Why is this so? Only those of great virtue are able to hear such a momentous matter; ordinary, inferior persons cannot hear it.
What constitutes "great"?
"What is called the profound and secret treasury of all Buddhas is the Tathāgata-nature.
For this reason, it is termed the 'Great Matter.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how can those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta obtain the causes for bodhi?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there are those who, upon hearing this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, say:
'I have no need to resolve for bodhicitta,' and thus slander the True Dharma."
That person then sees the form of a rākṣasa within the dream and feels terrified in his heart.
The rākṣasa says to him:
"Ho! O son of good family!"
"If you do not now resolve to attain Bodhicitta, I shall take your life.
Terrified by this, the person awakens and immediately resolves to attain Bodhicitta.

Even after that person’s life has ended—whether they are in the three miserable realms or among humans and devas—they continue to maintain mindfulness of Bodhicitta; one should know that such a person is a Mahāsattva Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
For this reason, by the majestic spiritual power of this Great Nirvāṇa, it can cause those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta to create the causes for bodhi. Good son!
This is called the causal condition for a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind; it is not without causal conditions.
For this reason, the sublime scriptures of the Mahāyāna are truly the teachings of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as when great clouds arise in the void and rain pours down upon the great earth, water does not remain upon withered trees, rocky mountains, high plateaus, or mounds;
yet it flows into the lower fields and fills the ponds and lakes, benefiting all immeasurable sentient beings.

This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this: it rains down the great Dharma rain to universally moisten all sentient beings; yet, for an icchantika to give rise to the bodhicitta is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son! It is like a scorched seed:
even if it encounters sweet rain, it will never sprout for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
that a sprout should ever grow from it is impossible."
The icchantikas are likewise; although they hear this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they are ultimately unable to sprout the seed of the bodhicitta.
Were they able to do so, it would be impossible.
Why is this? Because such a person has severed all roots of goodness; they are like scorched seeds that can no longer produce the roots and sprouts of bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a bright pearl placed in turbid water: by the majestic power of the pearl, the water immediately becomes clear;
yet if it is cast into the mud, it cannot be made clear.

This subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is just the same: even if placed within the turbid waters of the five sins of immediate retribution or the four grave prohibitions of other sentient beings, it can still clarify them and cause them to give rise to the bodhicitta.

If one casts [the seed of enlightenment] into the mire of an icchantika, even after hundreds of thousands of millions of years, it cannot be made pure enough to give rise to the bodhicitta. Why is this?
Because such an icchantika has extinguished all roots of goodness and is therefore not a fit vessel.

Even if such a person were to listen to and receive this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, they would ultimately never be able to give rise to the bodhicitta. Why is this so?
Because there is no wholesome mind.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a medicinal tree named 'King of Medicines,' which is the most preeminent among all medicines."

Whether mixed with curd, honey, ghee, water, or syrup; whether in powder or pill form; whether used to anoint a wound, fumigate the body, or apply to the eyes; or whether merely seen or smelled, it can extinguish all the ailments of sentient beings.
In this way, the medicinal tree does not form such thoughts:
"If all sentient beings take my roots, they should not take my leaves;
if they take my leaves, they should not take my roots."
"If one takes the body, one should not take the bark;
if one takes the bark, one should not take the body.
Although this tree does not give rise to such thoughts, it is nonetheless able to eliminate all suffering from illness.

Good son! This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this: it can eliminate all the evil karma of sentient beings, the four pārājika offenses, the five ānantarya crimes, and all manner of evils, whether internal or external. Furthermore, those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta shall, by means of this, be able to give rise to that resolve.
Why is this? Because this wondrous sutra is the king among all sutras, just as that medicinal tree is the king among all medicines.

Whether there are those who cultivate this Great Nirvana Sutra or those who do not, if they hear the name of this sutra and, having heard it, develop reverent faith, all their heavy illnesses of affliction will be completely eliminated; yet, it alone cannot cause those of the icchantika class to abide in Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
Just as that wondrous medicine, though able to cure various grave illnesses, cannot treat one who is destined to die.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person with a hand wound who, upon grasping poisonous medicine, has the poison enter through it;
yet if there were no wound, the poison would not enter.
The icchantikas are likewise: lacking the cause for bodhi, they are like those without a wound, into whom the poison cannot enter.
What is called a "sore" refers to the causal conditions for unsurpassed bodhi;
"poison" refers to the foremost, wondrous medicine;
one who has no sore at all refers to an icchantika.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a vajra, which nothing can destroy, yet it can shatter all things, with the sole exception of tortoise shells and the horns of white rams."

This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also like this: it is able to establish immeasurable sentient beings securely upon the path to Bodhi, yet it alone cannot cause those of the icchantika class to establish the causes for Bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as the horse-tooth grass, the sālaccha tree, and the nigrodha tree continue to grow as before even if their branches and trunks are cut, they are not like the tāla tree, which does not grow again once it has been severed."

These sentient beings are also like this: if they hear this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, even though they have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, they are still able to give rise to the causal conditions for bodhi.
The icchantikas are not like this; although they may hear and receive this sublime sūtra, they are unable to give rise to the causal conditions for the path to bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as the *khatāra* and *cintaka* trees do not grow again once they are cut down, so it is with those who hold to the *icchantika* view;
even though they may hear this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they are unable to give rise to the causes and conditions for bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as a great rain ultimately does not abide in empty space, so too is this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: it universally rains down the rain of Dharma, yet it cannot abide within those who possess icchantika-nature."
"This icchantika’s entire body is dense and compact, like a diamond, allowing no external object to enter.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If one does not see what is good and thus fails to do it, But sees only evil as something to be done—
This state is to be feared, Like a perilous and treacherous path."
“World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of what has been thus spoken?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! ‘Not seeing’ refers to not seeing the Buddha-nature;
‘good’ refers to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Non-practitioner" refers to one who is unable to draw near to virtuous friends.
"Seeing only" refers to seeing that there is no cause and effect.
"Evil" refers to slandering the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
That which can be done refers to the icchantikas' claim that the Vaipulya sutras do not exist.
For this reason, the class of icchantikas has no intention to incline toward pure and wholesome dharmas.
What are wholesome dharmas?
They are nirvāṇa.
That which leads to nirvāṇa is the ability to cultivate noble and virtuous conduct.
Furthermore, because icchantikas lack virtuous conduct, they are unable to proceed toward nirvāṇa.
That which is to be feared in this context is the slandering of the true Dharma.
Who should be afraid?
As for those called "wise," why is this?
It is because those who slander the Dharma lack both a virtuous mind and skillful means.
"The perilous and evil path refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"As the Buddha has said:"
"How does one see what is to be done?
How does one attain wholesome dharmas?
Where is there no fear, like a king on a level and smooth road?"
"What does this meaning signify?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
Regarding "that which is seen as having been done": one confesses all evils, revealing every evil committed from the very limits of saṃsāra until reaching the place of ultimate arrival.
For this reason, there is no fear in this state.
It is like the main road traveled by a king, where all thieves and bandits flee;
likewise, through such confession, all evils are extinguished without remainder.
Furthermore, "not seeing what one has done" refers to an icchantika who does not perceive the manifold evils he has committed.
Because this icchantika possesses a mind of arrogance, although he commits many evils, he feels no fear whatsoever regarding these matters from the very beginning.
For this reason, they do not attain nirvana; it is like a monkey grasping at the moon in the water. Good son!
Even if all immeasurable sentient beings were to simultaneously achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, these Tathāgatas would still not see those icchantikas attaining bodhi.
For this reason, it is called "not seeing what is done.
Furthermore, whose doing is not seen?
That is to say, one does not see the doing of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha teaches that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature; yet those who are icchantikas, wandering through the cycle of birth and death, are unable to know or see it.
For this reason, they are said to fail to perceive what the Tathāgata has accomplished.
Furthermore, the icchantikas perceive the ultimate parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata as being truly impermanent, like the extinguishing of a lamp when both the wick and the oil are exhausted. Why is this?
Because this person’s evil karma has not been diminished.

When a bodhisattva dedicates the wholesome karma they have performed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, even if those who are icchantikas revile, destroy, or do not believe it, the bodhisattvas nevertheless continue to bestow it, desiring to achieve the unsurpassed path together with them.
Why is this? Such is the nature of all Buddhas:
"Evil deeds do not bear fruit immediately, / Just as milk does not instantly become curd."
"Like embers covered by ashes, the fool lightly treads upon them.
"An icchantika is called one who has no eyes; therefore, they do not see the path of the arhat."

Just as an arhat does not travel the perilous and evil paths of birth and death, so too [this person], because they lack insight, slanders the Vaipulya sutras and is unwilling to practice them; yet, like an arhat who diligently cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, [they should instead cultivate it].
The icchantikas who do not cultivate the Vaipulya sutras are likewise so.
If someone should say:
"I now do not believe in the Śrāvaka scriptures, but I believe in and accept the Mahāyāna; I read, recite, and explain it; therefore, I am now a bodhisattva."

All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; by virtue of this Buddha-nature, within the bodies of sentient beings there already exist the ten powers, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics.
What I have spoken does not differ from what the Buddha has spoken.

Now, you and I together shall shatter immeasurable evil afflictions—just as one breaks a water jar—and because these fetters are destroyed, you will immediately be able to see Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Although such a person delivers this exposition, their heart truly does not believe in the existence of Buddha-nature; they speak according to the text solely for the sake of gain and sustenance.
One who speaks in this manner is called an evil person."
Such evil persons do not immediately experience the fruit [of their actions], just as milk becomes curd.
They are like a king’s messenger, skilled in discourse and adept in expedient means;
when dispatched to another country on a mission, they would rather lose their own life than ever conceal the instructions spoken by the king.

The wise person is likewise: among ordinary beings, they do not spare even their own body or life, but resolutely proclaim the Mahāyāna Vaipulya and the secret treasury of the Tathāgata—that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
“Good son! There is an icchantika who assumes the appearance of an arhat and dwells in a secluded place, slandering the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
When ordinary people see him, they all say:”
"A true arhat is a great bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Yet these icchantika evil bhikṣus, dwelling in araṇya hermitages while subverting the dharma of araṇya, see others obtain gain and give rise to jealousy, saying such things as:
"All the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras were spoken by the celestial Māra Pāpīyas."
They also say:
"The Tathāgata is a phenomenon subject to impermanence.
Thus they destroy the True Dharma and bring ruin to the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, he says:
"What Pāpīyān has spoken is not a well-accorded teaching.

By thus proclaiming such evil dharmas, this person commits evil but does not immediately receive retribution; it is like milk that has not yet turned into curd, or like embers covered by ashes, which the foolish lightly tread upon.
Such a person is called an icchantika.

Therefore, you should know that the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras are necessarily pure; just as when a maṇi jewel is cast into turbid water, the water immediately becomes clear, so too it is with the Mahāyāna sūtras.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as a lotus flower blooms when touched by the sun's rays, so it is with all sentient beings:
if they encounter the sun of the Great Nirvāṇa, those who have not yet resolved to attain awakening will all resolve their minds toward it, thereby establishing the cause for Bodhi."
Therefore, I say that the pores into which the light of the Great Nirvāṇa enters must necessarily be the cause of wondrousness.
Although those icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature, they are entangled by immeasurable defilements of sin and cannot emerge from them, like a silkworm within its cocoon.
Due to these karmic conditions, one cannot give rise to the sublime cause of Bodhi, and will continue to transmigrate through birth and death without end.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers grow from within the mud yet are not defiled by that mud.

If there are sentient beings who cultivate this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, it is likewise so: although they possess afflictions, they will ultimately never be defiled by those afflictions.
Why is this? It is because they know the nature, marks, and powers of the Tathāgata. "Good son!
For example, there is a land where cool breezes abound; when they touch the pores of sentient beings' bodies, they can eliminate all distress caused by stifling heat.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is likewise: it enters universally into the pores of all sentient beings, acting as the subtle and wondrous causal condition for bodhi—except for those who are icchantikas.
Why is this? Because they are not vessels for the Dharma.
"Furthermore, good son!
For example, just as a skilled physician who understands the eight kinds of medicine can eliminate all diseases except for the *asādha* disease, so too it is with all sūtras, dhyānas, and samādhis:

they can cure all afflictions such as greed, anger, and ignorance, and can extract the poisonous thorns and arrows of the defilements; yet they cannot cure those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution.
"Good son!

Furthermore, there is a skilled physician who surpasses the eight branches of medical science and is able to eliminate all the suffering of illness for sentient beings, yet he alone cannot cure those diseases that are destined for death."

This Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise: it can eliminate all the afflictions of sentient beings and establish them in the pure and wondrous causes of the Tathāgata; it causes those who have not yet resolved to attain the resolve for enlightenment—excepting only those icchantikas who are destined for certain death.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who can use wonderful medicines to treat those with cataracts, enabling them to see the sun, the moon, the stars, all luminous forms, and every variety of color and shape; yet he alone cannot cure one who is born blind."

This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is likewise so: it can open the eye of wisdom for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, causing them to dwell securely in the immeasurable and boundless Mahāyāna sūtras.

As for those who have not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment—meaning those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution—he is able to cause them all to give rise to the bodhicitta, with the sole exception of those born blind, the icchantikas.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who is well-versed in the eight branches of medicine; in order to cure all the suffering of illness in sentient beings, he provides various prescriptions and medicines according to each ailment—namely, emetics, purgatives, ointments for the body, nasal drops, or fumigations, washes, pills, and powders—and yet a poor and ignorant person refuses to take them."
The skilled physician, out of compassion, takes this person back to his home and forces him to take the medicine.
By the power of the medicine, his ailment is eliminated.

If a woman experiences difficult labor and the placenta does not emerge, if she takes this medicine, the placenta will immediately come out, and it will also ensure that the infant is peaceful, healthy, and free from suffering.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is likewise so: wherever it goes, whether it reaches a house or any other place, it can eliminate the immeasurable afflictions of sentient beings, including those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution; it causes all who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment to do so—with the sole exception of those possessed by *icchantika* tendencies.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To commit the four grave prohibitions and the five acts of immediate retribution is called an extremely heavy evil; it is like cutting off the head of a tāla tree, which will never grow again.”
"Since these individuals have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta, how can you act as the cause for their Bodhi?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
If these sentient beings, while in a dream, dream that they have fallen into hell and undergo various sufferings and afflictions, they will immediately give rise to a mind of repentance, thinking:
"Alas! We have brought this sin upon ourselves."
"If I am now able to escape this transgression, I shall certainly resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
What I have just witnessed is most extremely evil.
Having awakened from this realization, he immediately understood that the True Dharma yields great fruit and retribution.
Just as that infant gradually grows up, he constantly thinks to himself:
"This physician is most excellent and well-versed in prescriptions and medicines.
When I was originally in the womb, he gave medicine to my mother; because of that medicine, my mother’s body attained peace and stability."
By these causes and conditions, my life has been preserved.
How extraordinary!
My mother endured great suffering and distress, carrying me in her womb for a full ten months.
After one has been born, the mother carries away the dry and discards the wet; she removes impurities such as excrement and urine, nourishes one with milk and food, and protects this body.
For these reasons, one ought to repay the mother’s kindness by providing for her physical needs, attending to her, and serving her with compliant offerings.

"Even those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, if at the time of their death they bring to mind this Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, then although they may fall into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, heavens, or among humans, such a scripture will nevertheless serve as the cause for their bodhi;
with the sole exception of the icchantikas."
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a skilled physician or a physician’s son, whose knowledge is profound and who surpasses all other physicians, being well-versed in the unsurpassed incantations for removing poison.
Whether it be a venomous snake, a nāga, or a viper, one may use various incantations and medicinal herbs to render them harmless.
By applying this efficacious medicine to leather sandals, any venomous insects touched by those sandals will have their poison neutralized;
however, there is one exception, a poison named the Great Dragon (mahānāga).

This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is likewise: if there are sentient beings who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, it can completely eliminate them and cause them to abide in Bodhi, just as medicinal leather shoes can neutralize all poisons.
It causes those who have not yet resolved their minds to do so, and establishes them upon the path to unsurpassed bodhi.

This is because of the majestic power of the medicinal elixir of this Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings, with the sole exception of the great dragons—the class of icchantikas.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person who coats a great drum with a mixture of poisons and strikes it among a multitude of people, causing it to resound."
Even though one has no intention to hear it, hearing it causes death to all, with the sole exception of those who do not die an untimely death.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is likewise: wherever there are beings among the multitudes who hear its sound, all their greed, hatred, and delusion are completely extinguished.

Although there may be those among them who lack intentional thought, by the power of the causal conditions of the Great Nirvāṇa, they are able to extinguish their afflictions, and their fetters are naturally destroyed.

Even those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five acts of immediate retribution, upon hearing this sutra, will likewise create the causal conditions for unsurpassed bodhi and gradually sever their afflictions—
excepting only those icchantikas who meet with untimely deaths.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like the dark of night, when all activities and undertakings come to a halt; whatever remains unfinished must wait for the light of the sun."

Although those who study the Mahāyāna may cultivate the sūtras and all meditative concentrations, they must await the sun of the Mahāyāna Great Nirvāṇa to hear this subtle and secret teaching of the Tathāgata; only then shall they be able to undertake the work of bodhi and dwell securely in the True Dharma.
Just as the rain from heaven moistens, benefits, and causes all seeds to grow, thereby bringing forth fruit and completely eliminating famine so that many enjoy abundance and happiness;
so too is the immeasurable Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, for it is able to utterly extinguish the eight kinds of feverish ailments.

When this sutra appears in the world, it will bring great benefit and peace and happiness to all, just like those fruits; it enables sentient beings to perceive the Tathāgata-nature, just as the eight thousand śrāvakas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* received their predictions and attained the great fruit.

Just as after the harvest in autumn and the storage in winter there is nothing further to be done, so too it is with those who hold perverted views (icchantikas); they engage in no cultivation or activity regarding any wholesome dharmas.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a skilled physician who hears that another's child has been seized by a non-human spirit; he immediately provides an excellent medicine and dispatches a messenger, commanding him:
'Take this medicine and give it to that person quickly.'"
If that person encounters various malevolent spirits or ghosts, they shall all depart far away by the power of the medicine.
If you should be delayed, I shall go there myself; I will never allow them to die an unjust or violent death.
"If that sick person were to see the messenger and my majestic power, all their sufferings would be eliminated and they would attain peace and happiness.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, is also like this. Whether it be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or followers of other paths, if there are those who can receive and uphold such a sūtra—reciting it, mastering it, and further explaining it in detail for others; or if they write it themselves or cause others to write it—all these constitute causes and conditions for Bodhi.

If one has committed the four grave prohibitions or the five heinous crimes, or is possessed by malevolent spirits, ghosts, or poisons, upon hearing this sutra, all such evils will be completely extinguished; it is like seeing a skilled physician, where the evil spirits depart far away.
One should know that such a person is a true Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Why is this? Because they have briefly heard this Great Nirvāṇa and have likewise given rise to the thought:
"Because the Tathāgata is eternal. Thus,
if even those who merely hear it for a moment obtain such merit, how much more so for those who copy, receive and uphold, read, and recite it?
"With the exception of the icchantikas, all others are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, good son,
it is like a deaf person who does not hear sounds."
The icchantikas are also like this: although they wish to hear this sublime sūtra, they are unable to hear it.
Why is this? Because they lack the necessary causes and conditions.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a skilled physician who is thoroughly proficient in all medical arts and, moreover, extensively knows immeasurable incantations."
When the physician saw the king, he spoke these words:
"Great King, you now have a disease that will inevitably lead to death.
The king replied:
"You do not see what is within my belly; why then do you say that I have a terminal illness?
The physician replied, "If you do not believe me, you should take a purgative."
"After it has been administered, Your Majesty may verify it for yourself.
The king refused to take it.

At that time, the skilled physician used the power of incantations to cause sores to break out all over the king's private parts, while simultaneously inducing diarrhea from which worms and blood were expelled together.
Having seen this, the king was struck with great terror and praised the excellent physician:
"Excellent, excellent!
Previously, I did not accept what you reported to me; now I realize that you have brought great benefit to this body of mine."
"One should revere this physician as one would one's own parents.

This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is likewise so: it is able to cause the afflictions of all sentient beings—whether they possess desire or are free from desire—to crumble and fall away.
If these sentient beings, even in their dreams, see this sutra and pay it respectful homage, it is like a great king honoring a skilled physician.
This great physician knows that one who is destined to die will ultimately not be cured.
This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is likewise unable to cure those who are icchantikas.
Furthermore, good son!
For example, just as a skilled physician who is well-versed in the eight branches of medicine can cure all manner of illnesses, yet alone cannot cure one who is destined to die;
so too it is with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. They are able to rescue and heal all those who have committed transgressions, yet they alone cannot cure those who are destined to die—the icchantikas.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a skilled physician who is well-versed in the eight types of subtle medical arts, and is moreover extensively proficient in more than these eight."
Using what he himself knew, he first taught his son, causing him to recognize everything whether in water, on land, or among the medicinal herbs of the mountains and valleys.
Having thus gradually taught these eight matters, he next taught other supreme and wondrous arts.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise; he first instructs his sons, the bhikṣus and others, to use skillful means to eliminate all afflictions and to cultivate the perception that the body is impure and not solid, such as [the perception of] water, land, mountains, and valleys.
Water symbolizes the suffering experienced by the body, like bubbles upon the water;
land symbolizes the lack of solidity in the body, like a plantain tree;
and the mountain valleys symbolize the cultivation of the notion of non-self amidst afflictions.
For this reason, the body is called "selfless.

In this manner, the Tathāgata gradually teaches his disciples the ninefold scriptural teachings (navāṅga-dharma) until they have mastered them thoroughly; only then does he teach the Tathāgata’s secret treasury (tathāgatagarbha).
For the sake of their sons, he speaks of the Tathāgata’s permanence. In this way,

the Tathāgata preaches the Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, to serve as the cause for bodhi for all sentient beings— both those who have already resolved to attain it and those who have not—
with the sole exception of the icchantikas.
In this way, son of good family,
this Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and unprecedented.
"You should know that this is the unsurpassed, most honorable, and most supreme physician, the king among all sūtras.
Furthermore, son of good family,
it is like a great ship that travels from this shore of the ocean to the other shore, and returns from that shore back to this shore."

The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is likewise thus: riding upon the precious ship of the Great Vehicle of Mahāparinirvāṇa, he travels back and forth to ferry across all sentient beings; wherever there are those who should be saved, he causes them all to behold the body of the Tathāgata.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is called the Unsurpassed Captain.
It is like having a ship, there is a captain;
because there is a captain, sentient beings can cross the great ocean.
The Tathāgata’s constant abiding in the transformation and deliverance of sentient beings is likewise thus.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person who, aboard a ship in the great ocean, desires to cross over; if they obtain a favorable wind, they can traverse immeasurable yojanas in a mere moment."

If one does not encounter it, even though one remains for a long time—passing through immeasurable ages without leaving one's original place—one may eventually have the ship wrecked and perish by drowning in the water.

Sentient beings are likewise: riding the ship of the various formations upon that great ocean of ignorant birth and death, if they encounter the fierce wind of the Great Parinirvāṇa, they can swiftly reach the shore of the Unsurpassed Way;
if they do not encounter it, they shall wander for a long time through immeasurable births and deaths, and at some point, being destroyed, fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person who, failing to encounter the wind-king, remains long upon the great ocean and thinks to himself:
'We shall surely die here now.'"
While he was thinking thus, he suddenly encountered a favorable wind, which carried him across the sea.
He spoke again, saying:
"How fortunate!"
"This wind is unprecedented; it has enabled us to pass safely through the perils of the great ocean.

So too it is with sentient beings who have long dwelt in the great ocean of birth and death, mired in ignorance, suffering, and exhaustion. Until they encounter such a wind of Great Nirvāṇa, they should give rise to this thought:
"We are certain to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts."

When these sentient beings were reflecting thus, they suddenly encountered the wind of the Great Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, which blew upon them in accordance with their nature, leading them into Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; only then did they realize the truth and give rise to a sense of wonder.
He exclaimed:
"How wonderful!
From the distant past until now, I have never seen or heard of such a subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata."
"Only then will you give rise to pure faith in this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Furthermore, good son,
when a snake sheds its skin, is it considered dead?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son!"
The Tathāgata is likewise; when he skillfully manifests the relinquishing of his poisonous body,
can it be said that "the Tathāgata is impermanent and has ceased"?
"No, World-Honored One!
It is as the Tathāgata has here in Jambudvīpa skillfully relinquished his body, just as that venomous snake sheds its old skin."
For this reason, the Tathāgata is said to be eternally abiding.
Furthermore, good son,
it is like a goldsmith who obtains fine, genuine gold and fashions from it various kinds of vessels according to his will.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he is able to manifest various physical bodies within the twenty-five realms of existence in order to transform sentient beings and uproot them from birth and death.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is named "Boundless Body."
"Although he manifests various kinds of bodies, he is also called eternally abiding and without change.

Furthermore, good son, it is like the *āmra* tree and the *jambu* tree, which undergo three transformations in one year: at times they produce flowers, their radiance and colors flourishing in full bloom."
At times it produces leaves, flourishing and lush;
at times they wither and fall, appearing as if dead. Good son!
"What do you think?
Has this tree actually withered and died? "No."
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Good son!

It is the same with the Tathāgata; within the triple world he manifests three kinds of bodies—sometimes appearing at birth, sometimes appearing as grown, and sometimes entering nirvāṇa—yet the body of the Tathāgata is in truth not impermanent.”
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa praised him, saying:
"Excellent! It is truly as the Holy Teaching declares:
“The Tathāgata abides eternally and is subject to no change.
“Good son! The secret speech of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep and difficult to understand.”
It is like a great king who addresses his ministers, saying:
"Bring the *sindhuva*.
The term *sindhuva* has four distinct meanings: [salt, a horse, a sword, and a fragrant wood]."
First, salt; second, a vessel; third, water; fourth, a horse—these four things share a single name. A wise minister understands this name well:

when the king washes and requests *sindhuva*, he immediately offers water; when the king eats and requests *sindhuva*, he immediately offers salt; when the king has finished eating and wishes to drink a beverage and requests *sindhuva*, he immediately offers a vessel; and when the king goes on a journey and requests *sindhuva*, he immediately offers a horse.
In this way, the wise minister thoroughly understands the four kinds of secret speech of the great king.
This Mahāyāna sūtra is likewise so: it contains four types of impermanence, which the wise minister of the Mahāyāna should know well.
If a Buddha appears in the world and says to sentient beings,

"The Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa," the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata teaching the characteristic of impermanence for those who cling to permanence, desiring to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of impermanence.
Furthermore, if it is said:

"The True Dharma shall perish," the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of suffering for the sake of those who reckon [only] pleasure, desiring to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of suffering extensively.
Or again, it may be said:
"I am now suffering from illness, and the Sangha is being divided.

A wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of non-self for those who conceive of a self, wishing to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of non-self.
Or again, it may be said:
"That which is called emptiness is true liberation.

Wise ministers should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of true liberation, in which there are no twenty-five states of existence; he intends for bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of emptiness.
For this reason, this right liberation is called "emptiness" and is also called "immovable.
As for being immovable, it is because within this liberation there is no suffering; therefore, it is immovable.
This right liberation is characterized by the absence of signs; that which is signless means there is no form, sound, odor, taste, or tangible object, and is therefore called signless.
This true liberation is eternal and unchanging; within this liberation, there is no impermanence, no feverish affliction, and no transformation.
Therefore, liberation is called permanent, immutable, and cool.
Furthermore, it may be said:
"All sentient beings possess the Tathāgata-nature.
The wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the eternal Dharma, desiring to cause the bhikṣus to cultivate the eternal Dharma.

If these bhikṣus can train in accordance with this, you should know that such persons are my true disciples; they well understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, just as the wise ministers of a great king well understand the king’s intent.
"Good son!
If even a great king possesses such a method of esoteric speech, how much more so must the Tathāgata?
Good son!"

Therefore, the subtle and esoteric teaching of the Tathāgata is difficult to understand; only those who possess wisdom can comprehend my profound Buddha-dharma, for it is not something that ordinary worldly beings are capable of believing.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as when there is a severe drought, the palāśa, karṇikāra, and aśoka trees do not produce flowers or fruit; and all other things produced on land or in water wither away, lacking moisture and unable to grow, so that all medicinal herbs lose their potency."
"Good son!
This Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, is likewise so: after my parinirvāṇa, there will be sentient beings who cannot show it respect and who lack its majestic power."
Why is this? Because these sentient beings do not know the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata. For what reason?
This is because these sentient beings have meager merit.

"Good son! Do you see these rare and extraordinary events?"
Kāśyapa replied:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
He saw all the Tathāgatas, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, receiving offerings of food presented by the great assemblies of humans and devas.

Furthermore, he saw the magnificent bodies of the Buddhas, adorned with marks of excellence, seated upon places as small as the point of a needle, surrounded by vast multitudes without any mutual obstruction.
Furthermore, he saw the great assembly all making vows and reciting thirteen verses;
he also knew that each member of the assembly was thinking in their own mind:
"The Tathāgata now accepts my offering alone."

"Even if the food and drink offered by Cunda were ground into fine dust, such that each speck of dust represented one Buddha, it would still not suffice for all; yet, through the Buddha's supernatural power, it completely satisfied the entire assembly."

Only the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, such as Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, are able to know such rare matters; all these are manifestations through the skillful means of the Tathāgata, for the great assembly of śrāvakas and even the asuras all know that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying:
"Is what you have now seen not a rare and extraordinary matter?
[Cunda replied: "Truly so."
“World-Honored One!
In the past, I beheld immeasurable Buddhas whose bodies were adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Now I see them all as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with colossal and extraordinary bodies and incomparable countenances.”
"You see only the Buddha’s body, which is like a medicinal tree, surrounded by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others.
The Buddha told Cunda:
"The immeasurable Buddhas you previously saw were my own emanations; they appeared for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings and causing them to rejoice."
In this way, the practices performed by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others are inconceivable and can accomplish the infinite deeds of all Buddhas. Cunda!
You have now fully accomplished the conduct of a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, attained the stage of the ten grounds, and have completely perfected all that is practiced by a Bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; as the Buddha has taught, I likewise rejoice in the bodhisattva practices cultivated and accomplished by Cunda.”
Now, the Tathāgata, desiring to act as a great illumination for immeasurable sentient beings of the future, preaches this Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
World-Honored One!
"Do all sūtras contain a further meaning,
or do they not? "Good son!
"What I have spoken has both further meaning and no further meaning.
Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has said:
"All things that exist, when given as gifts to all, are only worthy of praise and cannot be criticized."
“World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of this?
What is the distinction between upholding the precepts and violating the precepts?”
The Buddha said:
"With the exception of one person, all other acts of giving may be praised. Cunda asked:
"What is meant by 'excepting only one person'?
The Buddha said:
"It refers to those who have broken the precepts as described in this sutra."
Cunda spoke again:
"I do not yet understand; I only pray that you will explain it to me.
The Buddha told Cunda:
"Those who speak of 'breaking the precepts' refer to the icchantikas.
All other forms of giving, wherever they may be, are worthy of praise and will yield great rewards."
Cunda asked again,
"What is the meaning of 'icchantika'?
The Buddha told Cunda:

"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who utter coarse and evil words to slander the True Dharma, committing such grave karma and never repenting or reforming, their minds devoid of shame and remorse—such persons as these are said to be heading toward the path of icchantika."

If one commits the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, and knowing for certain that they have committed such serious matters, their mind is from the outset devoid of fear, shame, or remorse; if they are unwilling to confess, harbor no intention to protect, cherish, or establish the Buddha’s true Dharma, and instead disparage, belittle, and speak with many faults—such persons are also said to be heading toward the path of an icchantika.
Furthermore, if it is said:
"There is no Buddha, Dharma,
or Sangha," such persons are also called those who are heading toward the path of an icchantika.
"Except for those such as the icchantikas, I praise the giving to all others.
At that time, Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of what you call 'breaking the precepts'?
The Buddha told Cunda:
"If one commits the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or slanders the true Dharma—such persons are called those who have broken the precepts."
Cunda asked again:
"Can one who has thus broken the precepts be rescued?
The Buddha told Cunda:
“There is a cause and condition by which one may be rescued.
If one has donned the dharma robes and has not yet abandoned them from afar, yet their mind constantly harbors shame, remorse, and fear, and they reproach themselves: ‘Alas!...’”
Why have you committed such a grave offense?
How strange it is!
To have created such karma of suffering.
Deeply repenting and reforming himself, he gave rise to a mind that protects the Dharma and desired to establish the True Dharma, thinking:
"To those who protect the Dharma, I shall make offerings.
If there are those who read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures, I shall consult them, receive and uphold their teachings, and read and recite them myself."
"Once you have mastered it yourself, you should further analyze and explain it extensively for others.
I say that such a person has not broken the precepts. Why is this?

Good son! Just as the rising sun can dispel all dust, obscurations, and darkness, so too is it with this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa appearing in the world: it can eliminate the manifold transgressions committed by sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Therefore, this sutra states that protecting the True Dharma yields great rewards and rescues those who have broken the precepts.

If there are those who slander this True Dharma but are able to repent and reform themselves, returning once more to the Dharma, they should reflect upon all their unwholesome deeds. Like a person who has harmed themselves and feels terror, alarm, and shame, they should think:
"Apart from this True Dharma, there is no other protection; therefore, I ought to return to the True Dharma."
"If one can take refuge in this manner as described, giving to such a person will yield immeasurable merit, and they shall be called a worldling worthy of receiving offerings.
However, if one commits the offenses of the aforementioned evil deeds and, for a month or even fifteen days, fails to give rise to the mind of taking refuge and confessing them,"
If one gives to such a person, the karmic fruit will be very meager.
It is the same for those who have committed the five heinous crimes; if they can give rise to a mind of repentance and harbor a sense of shame and remorse within, thinking:
"The unwholesome karma I have now committed brings great suffering; I shall establish and uphold the True Dharma."
"Then these would not be called the five heinous crimes.
If one gives to such a person, they will obtain immeasurable merit.
Having committed a heinous crime, they do not give rise to a mind that protects the Dharma or takes refuge [in it]."
If there are those who give to such a person, their merit is beyond words.
Furthermore, good son, listen attentively now as I shall analyze and explain in detail for you regarding those who have committed grave offenses: they should give rise to this thought:
"It is said that 'the True Dharma' is precisely the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, I shall protect, uphold, and establish it.
One who bestows [this teaching] upon such a person shall obtain a superior karmic reward."

“Good son! It is like a woman who, being pregnant and nearing childbirth, encounters the chaos of a national famine and disaster, travels far to another land, and gives birth in a certain celestial temple.”
Later, hearing that his native land was peaceful, secure, and abundant, he took his son with him, intending to return to his homeland.
On their way, they reached the Ganges River, where the waters were swollen and turbulent; though he carried the boy upon his shoulders, he was unable to cross.
He then thought to himself:
"I would rather share my life and death with my son; I will never abandon him to save myself alone.
Having formed this thought, he and his son both sank together.
After her life ended, she was immediately reborn in the heavens because she had cherished her son with compassion, desiring to enable him to cross over [to liberation].
Yet, this woman’s original nature had been base and evil; it was solely because of her love for her son that she attained birth in the heavens.

It is likewise with one who has committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution: if they give rise to a mind that protects the Dharma, then despite having previously performed unwholesome deeds, by virtue of protecting the Dharma, they become a supreme field of merit for the world.
"Such are the immeasurable fruits and rewards for those who protect the Dharma.
Cunda spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"If an icchantika were able to repent and reform, and with reverence, make offerings to, and praise the Triple Gem— would giving to such a person yield great fruit?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
You should not speak in such a manner now. Good son!
It is like a person who eats an amra fruit, spits out the seed and places it on the ground, and then thinks to himself:
"There must be a sweet taste within this fruit stone.
He immediately went back to retrieve it, broke it open, and tasted it.
Its flavor was extremely bitter, and he felt regret and remorse in his heart.
Fearing that he might lose the seeds of the fruit, he immediately returned to gather them up.
He planted them in the ground, diligently tended and cultivated them, and irrigated them at the proper times with ghee and milk.
"What do you think?
Could it possibly arise?
"No, [World-Honored One]."
“World-Honored One!
Even if the unsurpassed sweet rain were to descend from heaven, it still would not grow. “Good son!”
That icchantika is also like this; having burned away his roots of goodness, in what place could he possibly find the removal of his transgressions?
Good son, if he gives rise to a wholesome mind, then he is no longer called an icchantika.
Good son! For this reason, the karmic fruits obtained from all acts of giving are not without distinction. Why is this?

The retribution obtained from giving to the śrāvakas is distinct, and the retribution obtained from giving to the pratyekabuddhas is likewise distinct; only by giving to the Tathāgata does one obtain the unsurpassed fruit.
Therefore it is said:
"All acts of giving are not without distinction."
Cunda spoke again:
"For what reason has the Tathāgata recited this verse?
The Buddha told Cunda:
“For a specific reason, I spoke this verse.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a lay follower who lacked pure faith; he served the Nirgranthas and came to question me regarding the meaning of giving.”
For these reasons, I have spoken this verse, and it is also to explain the meaning of the Secret Treasury for the sake of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others.
As for such a verse, what is its meaning?
"All" here refers to a partial totality.

It should be understood that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, a hero among men, embraces those who uphold the precepts and provides them with their necessities, while discarding those who violate the precepts as one weeds out tares and weeds.
"Furthermore, good son!
As I said in a verse in the past:
'All rivers and streams Necessarily have bends and curves;'"
All groves are necessarily named trees;
all women necessarily harbor flattery and crookedness;
all who possess mastery necessarily enjoy peace and happiness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed before the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these verses:
"Not every river Necessarily has bends;
Not every forest Is entirely called 'trees'."
"Not all women necessarily harbor deceit;
not all who possess power necessarily experience pleasure.
The meaning of the verse spoken by the Buddha is incomplete."
Please deign to show compassion and explain its causes and conditions. Why is this,
World-Honored One?
In this trichiliocosm there is a continent named Aparagoyānī.
On that continent there is a river, straight and not crooked, called Sābhya, which is like a taut cord entering the western ocean.

Such characteristics of the river have never been spoken of by the Buddha in other sūtras; we only pray that the Tathāgata will, based on this Vaipulya Āgama, explain its remaining meanings so that all bodhisattvas may develop deep faith and understanding.
World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person who first recognizes gold ore, but later does not recognize gold.
The Tathāgata is likewise: having fully known all dharmas, that which he expounds is incomplete and leaves something remaining.
Although the Tathāgata has made such other statements, one should skillfully interpret their underlying intention.
To say that "all thickets are necessarily trees" is also a statement of incomplete meaning (*sāvasesa*).
Why is this? Various trees made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli are also called forests.
Furthermore, the claim that all women must harbor deceit and crookedness is also incomplete.
Why is this? There are also women who well maintain the prohibitive precepts, achieve merit, and possess great compassion;
they will surely attain peace and happiness through all-encompassing mastery. This [previous statement] is also incomplete.
Why is this? Because there is one who possesses sovereignty—the Wheel-Turning Sage King;
the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, does not belong to the Mara of Death and cannot be extinguished.
Although the various devas, such as Brahmā and Śakra, have attained mastery, they are all impermanent.
Only that which is eternally abiding and unchanging may be called "mastery," namely, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
"Good son! You have now well attained the eloquence of joyful speech; cease for a moment and listen attentively."
Mañjuśrī! It is like a householder who is afflicted by the suffering of illness; a skilled physician examines him and prepares a medicinal ointment for him.
At that time, the patient, out of greed, wishes to take a great deal of it.
The physician said to him:
"If you can digest it, you may take as much as you wish; however, since your body is currently emaciated, you should not consume it in large quantities.
You should know that this ointment is called both 'ambrosia' and 'poison'; if you consume too much and cannot digest it, it is then termed poison."
"Good son! You should not now think that what this physician has said contradicts the principles of reason or diminishes the potency of the medicinal fat.
Good son!"
