The Tathāgata is likewise; for the sake of various kings, queens, crown princes, princes, and ministers—and because King Prasenajit, his princes, and his queen possessed arrogant minds—he manifested terrors in order to subdue them, just like that skilled physician.
Thus he spoke this verse: "All rivers must have bends and curves;
All thickets must consist of trees."
"All women must harbor flattery and crookedness;
all who possess mastery must enjoy peace and happiness. "Mañjuśrī!..."
You should now know this:
that which the Tathāgata has spoken is without error or omission.
This great earth might be turned upside down, but the words of the Tathāgata shall never be subject to error or omission.
"For this reason, all that the Tathāgata has spoken is intentional.
At that time, the Buddha praised Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!

You have long understood this meaning; out of compassion for all beings and with the desire to enable sentient beings to attain wisdom, you have extensively questioned the Tathāgata regarding the meaning of these verses."
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, again spoke in verse before the Buddha:
"In the speech of others, follow along without opposition;
Do not observe whether others act or do not act, But observe only your own body— Whether its conduct is wholesome or unwholesome."
“World-Honored One!
To speak of this Dharma-medicine in such a manner is not the correct teaching.
We pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately grant us the correct teaching regarding how to accord with and not oppose the speech of others.”
Why is this? The World-Honored One has always taught that all ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners proceed toward evil paths, whereas the śrāvaka disciples all head toward the right path.

If there are those who protect the prohibitive precepts, maintain dignified deportment, and guard their sense faculties—such people deeply delight in the Great Dharma and proceed toward the wholesome path.
For what reason does the Tathāgata, within the ninefold division of the teachings, reprove those who are seen to disparage others?
"To what purport does the meaning of this verse lead?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Good son!"
When I spoke this verse, it was not intended for all sentient beings; at that time, I spoke it solely for King Ajātaśatru.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, never speak contrarily without cause or condition; it is only because there is a cause and condition that they speak thus.
"Good son!
After King Ajātaśatru had killed his father, he came to where I was, desiring to refute me, and asked this question:
'In what way is the World-Honored One omniscient?'"
Is he not omniscient?

If he is omniscient, how could the Tathāgata have permitted Devadatta—who throughout immeasurable past lives constantly harbored an evil mind and followed the Tathāgata with the intent to commit acts of violence—to go forth as a monk?
"Good son! For these reasons, I spoke this verse for the sake of that king:
'In the speech of others, follow along without opposition; nor should you scrutinize others.'"
"Whether one acts or does not act, one should simply observe for oneself one's own body and its wholesome or unwholesome deeds.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"You have now killed your father; you have already committed a crime of immediate retribution, the most grievous of all."
"You should confess and seek purification.
For what reason do you instead look for the faults of others?
"O son of good family! [he said.]
For this reason, I spoke these verses for that king.
Furthermore, noble son,
I also spoke these verses for those who protect and uphold the unbroken precepts, who have perfected their dignified conduct, yet perceive the faults of others.

If there is another person who, having received instruction from others, distances themselves from all evils and further instructs others to distance themselves from all evils, such a person is my disciple.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse for Mañjuśrī:
"All fear the blade and staff; there is none who does not cherish life.
Taking oneself as an analogy, do not kill, do not wield the staff."
At that time, Mañjuśrī again spoke in verse before the Buddha:
"Not all fear the staff, nor do all cherish their lives;
using oneself as an analogy for others, one should diligently apply skillful means toward goodness."
“The Tathāgata’s explanation of the meaning of these verses is likewise not exhaustive. Why is this?

For instance, it is impossible for an Arhat, a Wheel-Turning King, a precious queen, an elephant, a horse, or a minister of the treasury to be harmed by anyone—whether gods, humans, or asuras—even if they were to wield a sharp sword.”
A brave warrior, a virtuous woman, a king of horses, a king of beasts, and a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts—though these encounter what is most formidable, they feel no fear.
For this reason, the verses spoken by the Tathāgata are also incomplete [in their literal sense].
If one says,
"One may use oneself as an analogy," this too is incomplete. Why is that?
If an Arhat were to use himself as a metaphor for another, then there would be the notion of a self and the notion of a life-force.
If there were the notion of a self and the notion of a life-force, then one would have to provide protection.
Ordinary worldlings should also see that all arhats are practitioners; if they were to view them in such a way, it would constitute a false view.
If one possesses a false view, at the end of life, one should be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, it is impossible for an Arhat to harbor a mind of malice toward sentient beings;
likewise, it is impossible for immeasurable sentient beings to harm an Arhat.
The Buddha said:
"Good son, that which is called the 'notion of self' refers to giving rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and having no thought of killing; it is the mind of equanimity of an Arhat."
Do not say that the World-Honored One speaks contrary to reason without cause or condition.
In the past, in this city of Rājagṛha, there was a great hunter who killed many deer and invited me to eat their meat.
At that time, although I accepted his invitation, I gave rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings like that toward Rāhula, and spoke this verse:
"May you have long life, And dwell in the world for a long time;
Uphold the Dharma of non-harming, Just as the lifespan of the Buddhas."
"Therefore, I have spoken this verse:
'All fear the sword and staff; there are none who do not cherish their own life.
Taking oneself as the analogy, one should neither kill nor inflict punishment.'"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
"For the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, I inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such secret teachings.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again in verse:
"How should one revere one's father and mother? How does one accord with them and show them respect?"
"How can one practice this Dharma and yet fall into the Avīci Hell?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata replied with a verse:
"If one takes craving as mother and ignorance as father,"
"To comply with and respect such [views] is to fall into the Avīci Hell.
At that time, the Tathāgata again spoke these verses for Mañjuśrī:
"All that belongs to another is called suffering;
All things depend on oneself; one attains sovereign peace and happiness.
All forms of arrogance and haughtiness are extremely violent and evil;
the virtuous and good are loved and cherished by all.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That which the Tathāgata has spoken is likewise not exhaustive; we only pray that the Tathāgata will again deign to show compassion and explain its causes and conditions.”
Why is this? For example, when the son of a householder studies under a teacher, does he belong to the teacher?
If he belonged to the teacher, then the purpose [of his study] would not be accomplished.
If it does not belong [to them], it is likewise not accomplished;
if they have attained mastery over it, it is likewise not accomplished.
For this reason, that which was spoken by the Tathāgata is incomplete.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
It is like a prince who, having had no training or practice, fails in every undertaking; he is likewise autocratic, ignorant, and constantly suffering.
In this way, Prince, if one says that [the self] is independent, the meaning is not established;
if one says that it belongs to another, the meaning is likewise not established.
For this reason, the meaning taught by the Buddha is said to be "with remainder" (sāvaśeṣa).
Therefore, it is not necessarily the case that all who are subject to others must suffer,
nor that all who possess sovereignty must experience pleasure.
All forms of arrogance and power are extremely violent and evil, yet even these are incomplete [in their consequences].
“World-Honored One!

Just as those women of noble lineage, out of pride, left the household life to study the Way, upholding the prohibitive precepts, perfecting their dignified deportment, and guarding their sense faculties so they would not run wild or scatter.”
Therefore, all fetters of pride are not necessarily violent or evil;
they are even cherished by virtuous people, yet this too is incomplete.
It is like a person who, having internally committed the four grave prohibitions, does not discard their dharma robes and continues to maintain strict deportment.
When those who uphold the Dharma see such a person, they will not approve; at the end of his life, this person will surely fall into hell.

If there is a virtuous person who has violated a grave precept, those who uphold the Dharma will, upon seeing it, immediately expel him, causing him to cease his monastic practice and return to lay life.
"For this reason, not all who are virtuous and good are necessarily loved.
At that time, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"There is a cause and condition for which the Tathāgata speaks with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita) here."
Furthermore, there was another cause and condition for which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, taught this Dharma.
At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a woman named Bhadrā who had returned to her parents' home. She came to where I was and took refuge in me, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, saying:
"All women lack independence and freedom; all men are autonomous and unimpeded."
At that time, I knew the mind of this woman and immediately proclaimed these verses for her.
Mañjuśrī! Excellent, excellent!
"You are now able, for the sake of all sentient beings, to ask the Tathāgata about such esoteric teachings.
Mañjuśrī spoke again in verse:
"All sentient beings Depend entirely upon food and drink for their existence;”
All possess great power, yet their minds are free from envy;
all suffer various ailments and pains because of food and drink;
all who cultivate pure conduct attain peace and happiness.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
Now that you accept this offering of food and drink from Cunda, will there not be some cause for the Tathāgata to feel fear?
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke in verse to Mañjuśrī:
"Not all sentient beings subsist entirely upon food and drink;
not all who possess great power have hearts free from jealousy;
and not all who consume food bring about the suffering of various illnesses."
"Not all who practice pure conduct / Are able to receive peace and happiness.
"Mañjuśrī! If you were to fall ill, I too would likewise have to experience the suffering of illness."

Why is this? All Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas truly have nothing they consume; yet, desiring to transform others, they manifest the acceptance and enjoyment of things offered by immeasurable sentient beings, thereby enabling them to fulfill the dānapāramitā and deliver them from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
If it is said,
"The Tathāgata practiced austerities for six years and his body became emaciated," such a thing is impossible.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are uniquely distinguished from all others and differ from ordinary beings; how could they possess a body that is frail and inferior?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, through diligent cultivation, have attained a vajra-body, which is unlike the precarious and brittle bodies of worldly people.
My disciples are likewise thus: they are inconceivable and do not depend on food.
That "all those of great power are free from envy" also carries further meaning.
Just as people in the world may never harbor a heart of envy throughout their entire lives yet lack great strength,
so too there is another meaning regarding all illnesses that arise from food.
Furthermore, one sees people who contract incidental illnesses, namely those caused by thorns, knives, swords, spears, and lances.
That all those of pure conduct enjoy peace and happiness is likewise incomplete.
In the world there are also followers of external paths who practice the brahma-faring and undergo much suffering and affliction.
For this reason, all that the Tathāgata has spoken is intentional. It is not without cause or condition that the Tathāgata spoke this verse; he spoke it because there is a cause.
In the past, in this country of Ujjayinī, there was a brahmin named Gośṛṅga who came to where I was, desiring to receive the fourth eightfold precept of the fast.
"At that time, I spoke this verse for him.
At that moment, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"What is meant by 'the meaning of no remainder,' and what is meant by 'all meanings'? "Good son!

"Everything" refers exclusively to all things except for those wholesome dharmas that assist the Path and are constantly cherished; this is called "everything," and it is also called "without remainder.

As for all other dharmas, they are called both "with remainder" and "without remainder. This is intended to enable those sons of good family who delight in the Dharma to understand the meaning of "with remainder" and "without remainder."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva was filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight; he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
You regard all sentient beings with equality, just as you do Rāhula."
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!
What you have now perceived is subtle and profoundly deep."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will explain the merit obtained from this Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son! If there are those who hear the name of this sutra, the merit they obtain cannot be fully described by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others; only a Buddha can know it."
Why is this? Because that which is inconceivable is the realm of the Buddha.
How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and transcribe the sutra scrolls!
At that time, the devas, worldlings, and asuras, before the Buddha, spoke in unison with one voice, uttering these verses:
“The Buddhas are inconceivable, And so too are the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Therefore we now entreat you: We pray only that you remain for a while.”
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, along with Ānanda and the rest,
the two assemblies of followers, will arrive before long;
together with the Lord of Magadha, the Great King Ajātaśatru.
With a sincere heart, I revere and trust in the Buddha, yet he still has not come here.
I only pray that the World-Honored Buddha will deign to show a little compassion and remain;
within this great assembly, please sever all the webs of my doubts.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"The eldest son of my Dharma Is named Mahākāśyapa;
Ānanda is diligent and energetic, Able to sever all doubts."
You all should observe carefully: the learned Ānanda is naturally able to understand what is permanent and what is impermanent;
for this reason, you should not harbor great sorrow and distress in your hearts.
At that time, the great assembly made offerings of various kinds to the Tathāgata.

Having made these offerings to the Buddha, they immediately resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immeasurable, boundless bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One conferred the prediction of enlightenment upon Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, and Cunda.
Having conferred these predictions, he spoke these words:
"O sons of good family!
Cultivate your own minds and be careful not to be negligent.
I now suffer from a back ailment; my entire body is in pain.
I wish now to lie down, like that young child or one who is chronically ill.
Mañjuśrī!
You all should extensively expound the Great Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
I now entrust this Dharma to you.
"Even until Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and the others arrive, you must further entrust this True Dharma to them.
At that time, having spoken these words, the Tathāgata, desiring to subdue all sentient beings, manifested the appearance of illness and lay down on his right side, like a sick man.
Chapter 18: Manifesting Illness The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Eighteen: Manifesting Illness. At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata has already escaped all diseases; his ailments and sufferings are entirely eliminated, and he is free from further fear.
World-Honored One!
All sentient beings have four poisonous arrows which constitute the causes of illness.
What are the four?
They are greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.
When there is a cause for illness, then illness arises; namely:

Lung disease caused by the heat of passion, upward breath and vomiting, a tingling sensation throughout the body, mental confusion and distress, diarrhea and hiccups, painful dribbling of urine, pain in the eyes and ears, distension of the abdomen and back, insanity and emaciation, and possession by malevolent spirits.
Such various ailments of body and mind as these no longer exist at all for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
For what reason does the Tathāgata today address Mañjuśrī, saying:
"I now have a backache; you should preach the Dharma for the great assembly"?
"There are two causes and conditions by which there is no suffering from illness. What are these two?
First, to have compassion for all sentient beings; second, to provide the sick with medicine."

In the past, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, the Tathāgata cultivated the bodhisattva path, constantly practicing kind speech, benefiting sentient beings so as not to cause them suffering or distress, and bestowing various medicines upon those who were ill.
"For what reason do you now say that you are ill? [The Buddha replied:
"World-Honored One!
When people in the world are ill, they may sit or lie down, find no peace in their place, or seek food and drink, and they instruct their families to manage their household affairs and property."

For what reason does the Tathāgata lie in silence, not instructing his disciples, the śrāvakas, and others in the perfection of morality (śīlapāramitā), the various dhyānas, liberations (vimokṣa), meditative attainments (samāpatti), and the cultivation of the right efforts (samyakpradhāna)?
For what reason do you not preach such profound Mahāyāna sūtras?
Why does the Tathāgata not employ immeasurable skillful means to instruct Mahākāśyapa, the elephant-king among men, and other great beings, so that they may not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"Why do you not discipline those evil bhikṣus who accept and store all kinds of impure things?
World-Honored One!
Truly there is no illness; why do you lie down silently on your right side?"

Whenever these bodhisattvas provide medical treatment and medicine to the sick, they dedicate all the roots of goodness thereby obtained to all sentient beings, collectively dedicating them toward omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) in order to eliminate the afflictive obstructions, karmic obstructions, and retributive obstructions of sentient beings.
The afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) consist of: greed, hatred, delusion, the entanglements and obscurations of anger,
vexation, envy, parsimony, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of dread, pride,
excessive pride, inferiority pride, overweening pride, self-pride, false pride, and arrogance.
Arrogance, negligence, haughtiness, resentment, contention, wrong livelihood, flattery, and the feigning of extraordinary appearances;
seeking profit through profit, evil seeking, and excessive seeking;
lacking reverence, disobeying instructions, associating with evil friends, insatiable greed for gain, and being bound by fetters difficult to untie.
Desiring what is evil, craving what is evil; holding views of self-existence, views of existence, and views of non-existence;
yawning and being fond of sleep; stretching the limbs and feeling discontented; craving food and drink; having a clouded and dull mind;
directing the mind toward disparate thoughts and unwholesome reflections; committing many evils of body and speech; and delighting in excessive talk.
Having dull and obtuse faculties, speaking with much falsehood, and being constantly shrouded by thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm—
this is called the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) refers to the grave and evil disease of the five sins of immediate retribution.

The obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) refers to being born in the hells, as an animal, or as a hungry ghost; it also includes those who slander the True Dharma and the icchantikas—these are called the obstacle of retribution.
These three obstacles are called the great diseases.
When Bodhisattvas cultivate bodhi over immeasurable eons, they provide all manner of medical treatments for the sick and constantly make this vow:
"May all sentient beings forever sever these three obstacles, which are like grave illnesses."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates awakening, they provide medicine to all who are ill and constantly make this vow:
'May all sentient beings forever sever all illnesses and attain the adamantine body of a Tathāgata.'"
Furthermore, may all immeasurable sentient beings become sovereign kings of wondrous medicine, severing and eliminating all evil and grave illnesses.
May all sentient beings obtain the Agada medicine; by the power of this medicine, may they be able to remove all immeasurable poisons.

Furthermore, may all sentient beings never regress from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, swiftly attain the accomplishment of the unsurpassed medicine of the Buddha, and eliminate the poisonous arrows of all afflictions.

Furthermore, may all sentient beings diligently cultivate vigor, achieve the adamantine mind of the Tathāgata, and act as subtle medicines to heal all ailments, ensuring that no one gives rise to thoughts of contention or dispute.
May all sentient beings also become great medicinal trees, curing all manner of evil and grave illnesses.
Furthermore, may they pull out the poisonous arrows and attain the unsurpassed radiance of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, may all sentient beings enter the great medicinal medicine of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and the subtle, secret Dharma-treasury.
"World-Honored One!
Thus have Bodhisattvas, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, made this vow to cause all sentient beings to be entirely free from all illnesses."
For what reason has the Tathāgata now declared today,
"There is illness"?
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In this world, there are those who are ill and unable to sit or rise, to look down or up, or to move about; they cannot take food or drink, nor can they instruct their sons or manage the affairs of the household.
At that time, his parents, wife, children, brothers, relatives, and kinsmen all conceived the thought that this man was destined to die.
World-Honored One!
Today the Tathāgata is likewise; he lies on his right side and speaks nothing further.
In this Jambudvīpa, there will be foolish people who will think: "The Tathāgata,
the Perfectly Awakened One, must surely enter parinirvāṇa," and they will give rise to the notion that he has passed away.
The nature of the Tathāgata is real and does not ultimately enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and free from change.
For this reason, one should not say:
"I now have a backache.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
In this world, there are those who are ill, their bodies emaciated and wasted, lying either prostrate or on their sides upon beds and mattresses.
At that time, people give rise to feelings of contempt and disdain, conceiving the thought that they are surely about to die.
The Tathāgata is now likewise in this situation; he shall be treated with contempt by the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths and will be perceived as impermanent.
Those non-Buddhists will say:
"It is not like our teachings of the Self-nature, the Person, Īśvara, Time, Seasons, or atoms, which are eternally abiding and subject to no change."
"The śramaṇa Gautama has been carried away by impermanence; he is subject to the law of change.
For this reason, World-Honored One, you should not today remain silent while lying on your right side.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
There are those in the world who are ill; the four great elements increase or diminish, becoming mutually disharmonious, so that they become emaciated and utterly exhausted.
For this reason, they are unable to sit or rise as they wish, but must lie upon their beds."
The Tathāgata’s four great elements are in perfect harmony; his physical strength is complete, and he suffers no decline or weakness.
World-Honored One!
It is as ten young oxen do not equal the strength of one large bull, nor do ten large bulls equal the strength of one dark-blue ox.
The strength of ten oxen is not equal to the strength of one ordinary elephant; the strength of ten ordinary elephants is not equal to the strength of one wild elephant;
the strength of ten wild elephants is not equal to the strength of one two-tusked elephant; the strength of twelve two-tusked elephants is not equal to the strength of one four-tusked elephant;
the strength of fourteen four-tusked elephants is not equal to that of a single [elephant] from the Snowy Mountains.

The strength of ten white elephants is not equal to the strength of one snow-mountain white elephant; the strength of ten snow-mountain white elephants is not equal to the strength of one fragrant elephant;
the strength of ten fragrant elephants is not equal to the strength of one blue elephant; the strength of ten blue elephants is not equal to the strength of one yellow elephant;
the strength of ten yellow elephants is not equal to the strength of one red elephant; and the strength of ten red elephants is not equal to the strength of one white elephant.
The strength of ten white elephants is not equal to the strength of one mountain elephant; the strength of ten mountain elephants is not equal to the strength of one utpala elephant;
the strength of ten utpala elephants is not equal to the strength of one padma elephant;
the strength of ten padma elephants is not equal to the strength of one kumuda elephant; [the strength of ten kumuda elephants is not equal to the strength of one puṇḍarīka elephant...]
The strength [of one] is not equal to the strength of one *pundarīka* elephant;
the strength of ten *pundarīka* elephants is not equal to the strength of one human athlete; the strength of ten human athletes is not equal to the strength of one *bhalluka*;
the strength of ten *bhallukas* is not equal to the strength of one eight-armed *nārāyaṇa*; ten *nārāyaṇas* [are not equal to...]
Just as the strength of a single joint of a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage is such that the joints of all ordinary beings do not reach one another;

the joints of a human champion reach their respective heads; the joints of a *Bhṛngin* (Pot-kṣepa) are joined together; the joints of a *Nārāyaṇa* are mutually locked; and the joints and bones of a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage are intertwined like coiled dragons.
Therefore, the power of the Bodhisattva is the greatest.
When the world is formed, the Vajra-seat arises from the Vajra-limit, extending upward to the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.
Once the Bodhisattva had sat down, his mind immediately attained the ten powers.
The Tathāgata should not now be like that infant child;
for an infant child is foolish and ignorant, incapable of speaking anything of significance.
For this reason, he may lie down or turn to his side as he pleases, without anyone censuring him.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great wisdom that illuminates all things; he is a great dragon among men, endowed with great majestic virtue, perfected in supernatural powers, and an unsurpassed seer. Having forever severed the net of doubt and extracted the poisoned arrow, his movements are serene and composed, his deportment is complete, and he has attained fearlessness.
"For what reason do you now lie on your right side, causing all the humans and devas to grieve, sorrow, and suffer?
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva spoke a verse before the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Sage Gautama!"
I pray that you will arise and expound the wondrous Dharma; you should not remain like a child or a sick person lying upon a bed.
O Tamer of Gods and Humans, Teacher of Devas and Men, why do you recline between the twin trees?
When those of inferior wisdom and ordinary capacity see this, they will surely say:
"They will surely attain nirvāṇa;
yet, not knowing the Vaipulya scriptures, the profound conduct of the Buddha,
and not seeing the subtle and secret treasury, they are like the blind who do not see the path."
Only the various Bodhisattvas, Mañjuśrī and the rest,
can understand this profound [teaching], like a skilled archer.
The World-Honored Ones of the three periods of time take great compassion as their foundation.
Where now is such great compassion?
If there were no great compassion, one would not be called a Buddha;
if a Buddha were necessarily to enter parinirvāṇa, he would not be called eternal.
"I only pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One will compassionately accept our invitation to benefit all sentient beings and subdue all those of external paths. At that time,

the World-Honored One, with great compassion permeating his heart, knowing the respective thoughts of all sentient beings and wishing to accord with them for their ultimate benefit, immediately rose from his reclining position and sat cross-legged.
His countenance was radiant and serene, like a mass of molten gold;
his features were upright and majestic, like the full moon at its peak;
his form was pure and stainless, free from all impurities.

He emitted great rays of light that filled all of space; the brilliance of these lights was more intense than a hundred thousand suns. They illuminated the Buddha-worlds of the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, bestowing upon sentient beings the torch of great wisdom. This caused them all to extinguish the darkness of ignorance and established hundreds of billions of nayutas of sentient beings in the non-retrogressive resolve for Bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One was free from doubt and anxiety, like a lion king.
His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics.
From every single pore upon his body, a lotus flower emerged from each one.

These flowers were exquisite, each possessing a thousand petals of pure, genuine gold; their stalks were made of lapis lazuli, their filaments of diamond, and their calyxes of rose quartz. Their shape was perfectly round, like the wheels of a chariot.
From each of these lotuses issued various multicolored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal-colored.
These rays of light all reached throughout the Avīci Hell, the Saṃjīva Hell, the Kālasūtra Hell, the Saṃghāta Hell, the Raurava Hell, the Mahāraurava Hell, the Tapana Hell, and the Pratāpana Hell.
The sentient beings within these eight hells are constantly oppressed by various sufferings, namely: being burned and boiled, roasted by fire, hacked and pierced, and flayed and skinned.
Having encountered this light, all such sufferings were extinguished without remainder; they became peaceful, cool, and attained boundless bliss.
Within this radiance, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata was proclaimed, saying:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature."
Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately reached the end of their lives and were reborn among humans or devas.
This extended even to the eight cold hells, namely: the Ābaba hell, the Atāta hell, the Alala hell, the Asāsa hell, the Utpala hell, the Padma hell, the Kumuda hell, and the Puṇḍarīka hell.
The sentient beings therein are constantly oppressed and tormented by the suffering of cold—namely, being split apart, their bodies shattered and destroyed, and mutually harming one another.
Upon encountering this light, such sufferings as these are extinguished without remainder; they immediately attain harmony, becoming warm and their bodies find comfort.
Within this radiance, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata was also proclaimed, saying:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately reached the end of their lives and were reborn among humans and devas.

At that time, all the hells within this Jambudvīpa world-system and in other worlds were entirely empty and void; there were no beings undergoing retribution for their offenses, with the sole exception of the icchantikas.
Hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, with hair entangling their bodies, had never for hundreds of thousands of years heard even the name of water or drink.
Upon encountering this light, their hunger and thirst were immediately dispelled.
Within this radiance, the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata is also proclaimed, saying:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately pass away and are reborn among humans or devas, causing the realm of hungry ghosts to become entirely empty, with the sole exception of those who slander the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
When sentient beings in the realm of animals encounter this light, their hearts of malice are entirely extinguished as they kill one another and devour each other.
Within this radiance, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is also proclaimed, saying:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately reached the end of their lives and were reborn among humans and devas.
At that time, even animals were completely extinguished, with the sole exception of those who slandered the True Dharma.

In each of these flowers there is a Buddha; their halo extends one fathom, and their golden bodies radiate with brilliance. They are subtle, exquisite, dignified, and unsurpassed, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.

These World-Honored Ones were some sitting, some walking, some lying down, and some standing; some thundered like the sound of a storm, some poured down torrential rain, some flashed lightning, some fanned great winds, and some emitted smoke and flames from their bodies like masses of fire.

Furthermore, he may manifest various mountains made of the seven treasures, as well as ponds, springs, rivers, mountain forests, and trees; or he may manifest lands, cities, towns, villages, palaces, and dwellings made of the seven treasures; or he may manifest elephants, horses, lions, tigers, wolves, peacocks, phoenixes, and all manner of birds.
Or again, he manifests so that all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa may see the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts; or again, he manifests the six heavens of the desire realm.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One sometimes speaks of the many faults and afflictions inherent in the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; sometimes he speaks of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; sometimes he speaks of the causal conditions of all phenomena; sometimes he speaks of how all karma and afflictions arise from causes and conditions; sometimes he speaks of self and non-self; sometimes he speaks of the two dharmas of suffering and pleasure; sometimes he speaks of permanence and impermanence, and so forth; and sometimes he speaks of purity and impurity.

Furthermore, there are World-Honored Ones who expound for the sake of the bodhisattvas the six pāramitās they should practice; some expound the merits attained by the great bodhisattvas; some expound the merits attained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; and some expound the merits attained by the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, some say that [the teaching] accords with the One Vehicle (ekayāna), while others say that the path is accomplished through the Three Vehicles (triyāna).
Or, there were World-Honored Ones from whose left flanks water issued and from whose right flanks fire issued.
Some manifest birth, renunciation, sitting at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, turning the sublime wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.
Some World-Honored Ones let out the lion’s roar, causing those within this assembly to attain the first fruit, the second fruit, the third fruit, up to the fourth fruit.
Furthermore, there were those who spoke of the immeasurable causes and conditions for liberation from birth and death.

At that time, all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa who encountered this light had the blind see forms, the deaf hear sounds, the mute were able to speak, the hunched and lame were able to walk, the poor obtained wealth, the stingy became capable of giving, the angry developed a mind of loving-kindness, and the faithless gained faith.
In this way, there was not a single sentient being in the world who practiced unwholesome dharmas, with the exception of the icchantikas.

At that time, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, ugradās, amānuṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, all raised their voices in unison and proclaimed these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"The Unsurpassed World-Honored One has brought great benefit.

Having spoken these words, they leaped for joy and were filled with delight; some sang, some danced, and some moved their bodies about. They scattered various flowers over the Buddha and the Sangha, namely: celestial *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *padma* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, *santāna* flowers, *mahāsantāna* flowers, *rocanā* flowers, *mahārocanā* flowers, fragrant flowers, great fragrant flowers, pleasing flowers, greatly pleasing flowers, lovely-to-behold flowers, greatly lovely-to-behold flowers, exquisite flowers, and foremost exquisite flowers.
Furthermore, they scattered various incenses, namely: agallochum, tagara, sandalwood, saffron, blended composite incenses, and coastal compound incense.

Furthermore, they made offerings to the Buddha with celestial jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies, as well as various celestial musical instruments—zithers, flutes, reed organs, lutes, harps, drums, and trumpets.
And he spoke in verse:
"I now bow my head in homage to the Greatly Diligent One, The Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among two-legged beings.
That which the great assemblies of devas and humans do not know, Only Gautama is able to fully comprehend."
For my sake, World-Honored One, you practiced asceticism for immeasurable eons in the past;
how can you now suddenly abandon your original vow and cast off your life to enter parinirvāṇa?
All sentient beings are unable to see the secret treasury of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
for this reason, it is difficult to escape, and they continue to revolve in birth and death, falling into the evil realms.
As the Buddha has taught, all Arhats shall surely attain Nirvana;
yet who among the vulgar and the ignorant could know such a profound sphere of the Buddha’s activity?
I bestow upon all sentient beings the Dharma of ambrosia, in order to sever and eliminate their various afflictions;
should any partake of this ambrosia, they shall no longer undergo birth, old age, sickness, or death.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has already provided healing for hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings,
causing all their various grave illnesses to be completely extinguished without remainder.
The World-Honored One has long since abandoned the suffering of illness, And is thus named the Seventh Buddha;
We pray that today you will rain down the Dharma-rain, To moisten and nourish the seeds of our merit.
After the great assembly, including humans and devas, had made this request, they remained silent.
As these verses were being spoken, all the Buddhas within the lotus pedestals—from Jambudvīpa extending throughout to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—all heard them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-born son!”
You have already perfected such profound and subtle wisdom, and thus you cannot be destroyed by any demons or non-Buddhists.
Well-spoken son!
You are already firmly established and cannot be shaken by any evil or heterodox winds.
Son of good family!

You have already achieved the eloquence of joyful speech and have previously made offerings to countless Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; therefore, you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, regarding such a meaning.

“Good son! In the past, throughout immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, I have already eliminated the root of illness and am forever free from reclining or lying down.”
Kāśyapa!

In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Anuttarajaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. For the sake of all śrāvakas, he preached this Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, revealing, analyzing, and elucidating its meaning.

At that time, I was also a śrāvaka of that Buddha; I received and upheld this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, recited it, mastered it, transcribed its scrolls, and extensively revealed, analyzed, and explained its meaning for others, dedicating these roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Good son! Since that time, I have never, due to the conditions of evil afflictions or karma, fallen into the evil realms; nor have I slandered the True Dharma, become an icchantika, received the body of a eunuch, been born without genitals or with dual genitals, committed treason against my parents, killed an arhat, destroyed stupas or disrupted the Sangha, shed the blood of a Buddha, or violated the four grave prohibitions."
From that time forth, my body and mind have been peaceful and secure, free from all suffering and affliction.
"Kāśyapa! I truly have no illnesses whatsoever at present."
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have long since distanced themselves from all illness. Kāśyapa!
These sentient beings, not understanding the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Esoteric Teachings, claim that the Tathāgata truly has an illness.
"Kāśyapa! It is as the saying goes: [text continues]"
"The Tathāgata is a lion among men.
Yet the Tathāgata is not actually a lion; such words are the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa! It is as when it is said:
"The Tathāgata is the great dragon among men."
"I have already abandoned such karma throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Kāśyapa! It is as the saying goes:"
"The Tathāgata is a human, he is a deva. Yet in truth, I am neither a human nor a deva;

nor am I a ghost, a gandharva, an asura, a garuḍa, a kiṃnara, or a mahoraga. I am not a self, not a life-principle, not a nourished being, not a person or a man, not an agent, not a non-agent, not one who receives, not one who does not receive, not a World-Honored One, not a śrāvaka, not one who speaks, and not one who does not speak.
Statements such as these are all the secret teachings of the Tathāgata.
“Kāśyapa! It is as when it is said:”
"It is said that 'the Tathāgata is like the great ocean and Sumeru, the king of mountains.
Yet the Tathāgata is in truth not of salty flavor and is like a mountain of stone; you should know that this statement is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata."
Kāśyapa! It is as it has been said:
"The Tathāgata is like the puṇḍarīka lotus."
"But I am not actually a *puṇḍarīka* lotus; such words are the Tathāgata’s secret teaching.
Kāśyapa! It is as when it is said:"
"The Tathāgata is like parents.
Yet the Tathāgata is in truth not one's parents; such a statement is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa! It is as when it is said:
"The Tathāgata is the great captain."
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not actually a boatman; such a statement is also the Tathāgata’s teaching of intentional secrecy.
Kāśyapa! It is as when it is said:"
"The Tathāgata is like a caravan leader.
Yet the Tathāgata is not actually a caravan leader; such a statement is also the Tathāgata’s secret teaching.
Kāśyapa! It is as when it is said:
"The Tathāgata is able to subdue Māra."
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata truly has no malicious intent to subjugate others; such words as these are all the Tathāgata’s secret teachings.
Kāśyapa!"
For example, it is said:
"The Tathāgata can cure abscesses.
Yet I am truly not a physician who cures abscesses; such words are also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
“Kāśyapa! As I have previously said:

‘If there are sons or daughters of good family who are well able to cultivate and purify the actions of body, speech, and mind, at the time of their passing, even if their kinsmen take their remains—whether they burn them with fire, cast them into great waters, or discard them among the graves, where foxes, wolves, birds, and beasts compete to devour them—their mind, consciousness, and intellect will immediately be reborn in a good realm.’”
Yet this mental dharma truly has no going or coming, nor does it reach anywhere; it is simply a continuity of similar states before and after, with no difference in its characteristics.
"Such words as these are the secret teaching of the Tathāgata. Kāśyapa!
My current statement regarding illness is likewise so; it too is the secret teaching of the Tathāgata."
Therefore, he addressed Mañjuśrī in his final instructions:
"I now suffer from back pain; you all should preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
"Kāśyapa! [he said].
The Tathāgata, the Truly Enlightened One, is in reality free from illness; he lies on his right side, yet he does not enter final nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa! This Great Nirvāṇa is the profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of all Buddhas; such meditative concentration is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
“Kāśyapa! Regarding what you previously asked:
‘For what reason does the Tathāgata lie prostrate and not rise, nor seek food and drink, yet instead instructs his family members to cultivate their livelihood?’”

"Kāśyapa! The nature of space likewise has no sitting or rising, no seeking of food or drink, and no instructing of a family or managing of property; it has no going or coming, no arising or ceasing, no aging or vigor, no appearing or disappearing, no injury or breaking, and neither liberation nor bondage. It does not speak of itself, nor does it speak of others; it does not understand itself, nor does it understand others; it is neither at peace nor ill."
"Good son!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise like space; how could they have the suffering of various illnesses? Kāśyapa!"
There are three types of people in the world whose illnesses are difficult to cure:
first, those who slander the Mahāyāna; second, those who have committed the five heinous crimes; and third, the icchantikas.
These three illnesses are the most grave in the world and cannot be cured by either śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Good son! It is like a disease that is inevitably fatal and difficult to cure.

Whether there is someone to attend to the patient, and whether one has the necessary medicine at will, such a disease is certainly incurable; you should know that this person will surely die without a doubt.

Good son! These three kinds of people are also like this: whether there are śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas, and whether they preach the Dharma or do not preach the Dharma, they cannot cause them to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Kāśyapa! It is like a sick person: if there is a caregiver, someone to attend to their wishes, and medicine, they can be cured; but if these three are lacking, they cannot be cured.”

It is the same for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: having heard the Dharma from Buddhas and bodhisattvas, they are then able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is not the case that they can give rise to this mind without hearing the Dharma.
“Kāśyapa! It is like a sick person: whether they have a caregiver, attendants, and medicine, or lack a caregiver, attendants, and medicine, they can all be cured.”

There is another kind of person who is likewise: whether they encounter a śrāvaka or do not encounter a śrāvaka, whether they encounter a pratyekabuddha or do not encounter a pratyekabuddha, whether they encounter a bodhisattva or do not encounter a bodhisattva, whether they encounter a Tathāgata or do not encounter a Tathāgata, and whether they hear the Dharma or do not hear the Dharma, they will naturally attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This refers to those who, for their own sake or for the sake of others, out of fear, for the sake of gain and offerings, or out of flattery or to deceive others, copy such a *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, and receive, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, revere it, and explain it to others.
“Kāśyapa! There are five kinds of persons who have a locus of illness regarding this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa scripture; they are not the Tathāgata.
What are these five?

First, by severing the three fetters, one attains the fruit of Srotāpanna; one does not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, but returns among humans and devas seven times at most, forever severing all suffering and entering Nirvana.
Kāśyapa!
This is called the first person who possesses the sphere of practice for illness; after eighty thousand kalpas in the future, this person shall immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Kāśyapa! As for the second person, he severs the three fetters, attenuates greed, hatred, and delusion, and attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, known as ‘one who returns once more,’ whereby he forever cuts off all suffering and enters into *nirvāṇa*.
Kāśyapa!

This is called the second person’s sphere of practice for illness; after sixty thousand kalpas in the future, this person shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

“Kāśyapa! As for the third person, they sever the five lower fetters, attain the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and no longer return to this world; having forever severed all suffering, they enter nirvāṇa.”
This is called the third person who possesses the sphere of practice for illness; after forty thousand kalpas in the future, this person shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Kāśyapa! As for the fourth person, having forever severed greed, hatred, and delusion, they attain the fruit of arhatship; with no further afflictions remaining, they enter nirvana. This, too, is not the solitary conduct of a qilin.”

This is called the fourth stage of practice for those with illness; such a person, after two thousand kalpas in the future, shall attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

“Kāśyapa! As for the fifth person, they have forever severed greed, anger, and delusion, attained the path of a pratyekabuddha, and entered nirvāṇa without any remaining afflictions; this is truly the solitary conduct of a qilin.”

This is called the fifth person who possesses the sphere of practice for those with illness; such a person, after ten thousand future kalpas have passed, shall immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Kāśyapa! This is called the fifth place where people fall ill; it is not the Tathāgata.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Eleven.
Added by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇas Huiyan and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter Nineteen: The Holy Conduct (*Āryacaryā*). Part One of Chapter Nineteen: The Holy Conduct.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva: "Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should single-mindedly contemplate five kinds of practices regarding this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*."
What are these five? First, the noble conduct;
second, the Brahma conduct; third, the celestial conduct; fourth, the infant-like conduct; and fifth, the sickly conduct.
"Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should constantly cultivate these five kinds of practices.
Furthermore, there is one practice that is the practice of the Tathāgata, namely, the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*."
“Kāśyapa! What is the noble practice cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* from either a śrāvaka or a Tathāgata, having heard it, they give rise to faith.”
Having gained faith, one should reflect in this way:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the unsurpassed path, the Great Right Dharma, and the correct practice of the Great Assembly; furthermore, there exist the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras."

Now, for the sake of loving and desiring the Mahāyāna sūtras, I shall renounce what I hold dear: my wife and children, my kinsmen, my dwelling, gold, silver, rare treasures, exquisite necklaces, incense, flowers, music, male and female servants, attendants, sons and daughters, both great and small, as well as elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, pigs, and swine.
He further reflected:
"Living at home is confining, like a prison, for all afflictions arise from it;
leaving the home life is spacious and open, like space, for all wholesome dharmas increase because of it."

"If I remain a householder, I shall not be able to practice the pure Brahma-faring life for the rest of my life; therefore, I should now shave off my hair and beard, leave the home life, and study the Way.
He further thought:
"I must certainly leave the home life now to cultivate and study the path of unsurpassed, right, and true Bodhi."
When the Bodhisattva thus desired to leave the household life, Māra, the Evil One, was overcome with great anguish and said:
"This Bodhisattva shall once again engage me in a great battle."
“Good son! How could such a bodhisattva ever again engage in strife or contention with others?

At that time, the bodhisattva goes to a monastic dwelling; if he sees the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Buddha whose deportment is complete, whose faculties are tranquil, whose mind is gentle, and who is pure and extinguished, he immediately approaches them to seek renunciation, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the three dharma robes.”

Having already left the household life, he upholds the prohibitive precepts; his dignified demeanor is flawless, his movements are calm and composed, and he commits no transgressions. Even regarding minor offenses, he gives rise to a sense of dread, guarding the precepts with a mind as firm as a diamond.
“Good son! It is like a person who, carrying a life-preserving float, wishes to cross the great ocean.
At that time, a rākṣasa in the sea immediately begs this person for the float.”
Having heard this, the man immediately thought to himself:
"If I give it now, I will certainly perish.
He replied:
"Rākṣasa! You may kill me if you wish, but you shall not obtain the life-preserving float.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot give it all to me, please grant me half.
Even so, the man still refused to give it to him.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot grant me half, I would be grateful if you would give me one-third.
The man refused.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot do that, give me the size of my hand.
The man was unwilling.
The rākṣasa spoke again:

"If you cannot now give me even as much as a hand's breadth, I am currently famished and destitute, oppressed by manifold sufferings; I pray that you will provide for me at least as much as a speck of dust."
The man spoke again:
"What you now request is indeed not much; however, I am only just now about to cross the sea, and I do not know how near or far the path ahead may be."
"If I give it to you, my breath will gradually depart; how then could you overcome the perils of the great ocean?
Even if you were to escape halfway, you would drown and die."
“Good son! The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s upholding of the prohibitive precepts is also like this, just as that ferryman cherishes his life-preserving float.
When the Bodhisattva thus guards the precepts, the various evil rākṣasas of affliction constantly speak to the Bodhisattva, saying:”
"You should believe me; I will never deceive you.
Simply break the four grave prohibitions and maintain the remaining precepts.
By these causes and conditions, I shall bring you peace and security, enabling you to enter nirvana."
At that time, the Bodhisattva should speak these words:
"I would rather maintain such precepts and fall into the Avīci Hell than violate them and be born in the heavens."
The Rākṣasa of Affliction spoke again, saying:
"If you cannot break the four pārājika prohibitions, you may break the saṃghāvaśeṣa rules.
By this cause and condition, it shall bring you peace and security, allowing you to enter nirvāṇa."
The Bodhisattva should likewise not comply with those words.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, you may instead intentionally commit a sthūlātyaya offense."
"By these causes and conditions, I shall bring you peace and security, enabling you to enter nirvana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva still did not comply.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot commit a *sthūlātyaya*, you may commit a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
By this means, you may attain peace and enter into *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva likewise did not comply.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot commit an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, you may instead break a *pāyattika*.
By this means, I shall cause you to be at peace and enable you to enter nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Bodhisattva likewise did not comply.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you cannot transgress a pāyattika offense, you might as well break a duṣkṛta precept."
"By these causes and conditions, one may attain peace and enter into nirvana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"If I were now to commit a *duṣkṛta* offense and fail to confess it, I would be unable to cross to the other shore of birth and death to attain nirvana."
"In this regard, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva maintains these minor precepts with firm resolve, his mind as steadfast as a vajra.
Whether it be the four grave prohibitions or the *duṣkṛta* offenses, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva upholds them with equal reverence and firmness, making no distinction between them."

If a bodhisattva can maintain such firm adherence, they will be fully endowed with the fivefold precepts, namely: the precept of purity regarding the fundamental karmas of a bodhisattva; the precept of purity regarding the remaining ancillary karmas preceding and following them; the precept of purity regarding the absence of unwholesome thoughts; the precept of purity regarding the maintenance of right mindfulness; and the precept of dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Kāśyapa! This bodhisattva-mahāsattva further possesses two kinds of precepts:
first, the precepts received through worldly instruction; second, the precepts of the true Dharma.”
If a bodhisattva attains the precepts of the true Dharma, they will never commit evil.
Those who receive the worldly precepts must first undergo the formal ritual of the white-four-fold *karmavācanā* before they obtain them.
"Furthermore, good son!
There are two kinds of precepts:
first, the precepts of essential gravity; second, the precepts for avoiding worldly censure.
The precepts of essential gravity refer to the four prohibitions.

The precept for avoiding worldly reproach consists of not engaging in trade by using light scales or small measures to deceive others; not seizing another's property through the influence of others; not binding others with harmful intent; not sabotaging successful works; not sleeping while keeping a lamp lit; and not engaging in farming, house-building, planting, or sitting at a shop to manage a household business.
They do not keep elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, chickens, dogs, monkeys,
peacocks, parrots, jīvañjīvaka birds, nor *kucīra* birds, jackals, wolves, tigers,
leopards, cats, weasels, pigs, boars, or other predatory beasts, nor young boys.
Young girls, adult men, adult women, male and female slaves, servants, gold, silver,
lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, musaragalva, agate, coral, jade, conch shells,
various jewels, red copper, white tin, brass, bowls and vessels, and woolen carpets.
woolen cloth, coarse hair garments, bark garments, all kinds of grain— namely, large and small wheat,
beans, millet, foxtail millet, rice, and hemp— as well as raw and cooked foodstuffs.
He always observes the practice of eating only one meal a day and never eats a second time.
Whether he goes on almsround or partakes in a communal meal within the Sangha, he always knows moderation and does not accept special invitations.

He does not eat meat, does not drink alcohol, and abstains from all pungent vegetables and strong-smelling foods; therefore, his body is free from any foul odor, and he is constantly revered, supported, honored, and praised by all the devas and by all people in the world.
He eats only what he needs and never accepts more than necessary.
The robes he wears are just sufficient to cover his body.
In all his movements, he is always accompanied by his three robes and alms bowl, never parting from them, just as a bird is never parted from its two wings.
"One does not store roots, stems, joints, grafts, or seeds; nor does one store treasures such as gold or silver, food and drink, kitchens and storehouses, clothing, or ornaments."
He does not sit or lie upon high, wide, or large beds, nor upon ivory or golden beds, nor upon those woven with variegated colors.
He does not keep any fine or soft mats, nor does he sit upon elephant-rugs or horse-rugs. He does not use fine, soft, or exquisite garments as bedding for his bed.
Regarding his bed for rest, he does not keep two pillows; nor does he accept or store fine red pillows or pillows made of yellow wood.

He never watches elephants fighting, horses fighting, chariots fighting, or soldiers fighting; nor does he watch men, women, oxen, sheep, chickens, pheasants, parrots, or other birds fighting; nor does he intentionally go to view military arrays.

Furthermore, one should not intentionally listen to the sounds of conch shells, drums, horns, lutes, zithers, *kṣaṅ*, flutes, *vīṇā* harps, singing, shouting, or the music of performers, except for those offered in worship to the Buddha.

He shall not watch or participate in any games or amusements whatsoever, such as dice, go (weiqi), the game of Bala-raksa, lion fights, elephant fights, marble games, six-sided board games, ball games, stone-throwing, pitch-pot, tug-of-war, or the completion of the eight-path chessboard.

"One shall never gaze at one's own hands, feet, face, or eyes; nor shall one practice divination using the nails, auspicious grass, willow twigs, alms bowls, or skulls; nor shall one look up at the stars and constellations in the sky, except when wishing to dispel drowsiness."
He does not act as a messenger for the royal court, conveying what is said here to there, or what is said there to here.

He never lives by flattery, nor by a wrong livelihood; nor does he speak of matters concerning kings and ministers, thieves, strife, food and drink, famine in the land, fear, or abundance, prosperity, and security.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s precept for quelling worldly censure. Good son!”
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva firmly upholds these prohibitive precepts, which are no different from the precepts of essential gravity. "Good son!
Having received and upheld these various prohibitive precepts, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this vow, saying:

"I would rather cast this body into a deep pit of blazing, fierce fire than ever violate the prohibitions and precepts established by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, or engage in impure conduct with the daughters of Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, or householders."
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have hot iron wrapped all around my body than ever dare to receive the robes of a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather swallow hot iron balls with this mouth than ever dare to eat the food and drink offered by a faithful donor with a mouth that has violated the precepts.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this vow:
'I would rather lie upon this body on a great hot iron bed than ever dare, with a body of broken precepts, accept the bedding and seating provided by a faithful donor.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my body pierced by three hundred spears than ever dare, with a body that has violated the precepts, accept the medicine offered out of faith by a donor.'"
"Furthermore, good son, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of boiling iron than, with a body that has broken the precepts, ever dare to accept the rooms, houses, or dwellings offered out of faith by a donor.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this vow:

'I would rather have this body smashed with iron hammers from head to foot until it is like fine dust, than receive the respectful prostrations and veneration of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and householders while violating the precepts.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my two eyes gouged out with hot iron than, with a defiled mind, look upon the beautiful forms of others.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my entire body pierced with iron awls than, with a defiled mind, listen to pleasant sounds.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my nose cut off with a sharp blade than, with a defiled mind, greedily smell various fragrances.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my tongue sliced and torn apart with a sharp blade than, with a defiled mind, crave delicious flavors.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my body hacked and cut with a sharp axe than, with a defiled mind, crave and cling to various tactile sensations.'"
Why is this? Because by such causes and conditions, one can cause the practitioner to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. "Kāśyapa!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s upholding of the prohibitive precepts.
Having upheld these various prohibitive precepts, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives them all as a gift to all sentient beings.

By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings protect and uphold the prohibitive precepts, attaining the pure precepts, the virtuous precepts, the unimpaired precepts, the indivisible precepts, the Mahāyāna precepts, the non-retrogressive precepts, the conforming precepts, the ultimate precepts, and the precepts that fully accomplish the pāramitās.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such pure precepts, he immediately attains the first stage, the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Why is it called the Immovable Ground?
When a bodhisattva dwells in this Immovable Stage, they are unmoving, non-falling, non-retrogressive, and non-dissipating. Good son!
It is like Mount Sumeru, which the violent winds of the Sālaman cannot cause to move, fall, retreat, or disperse.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage is likewise: he is not moved by forms, sounds, smells, or tastes; he does not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; he does not regress to the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha; and he is not scattered by the perverse winds of heterodox views, nor does he engage in wrong livelihood.
"Furthermore, good son!
Moreover, 'immovable' means not being moved by greed, hatred, or delusion.
Furthermore, 'not falling' means not falling into the four grave offenses."
Furthermore, "non-retrogression" means not returning to the household life.
Furthermore, "non-dispersion" means not being scattered or destroyed by those who oppose the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise cannot be shaken by the māra of the afflictions, nor can he fall victim to the māra of the aggregates;
even when sitting at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, although there may be the celestial māra, he cannot cause him to retreat from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, they are not scattered by the Māra of Death.
Son of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the noble practice.
“Good son! What is called ‘noble practice’ (ārya-caryā)?
Noble practice is so named because it is the practice of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is called noble practice.”
For what reason are Buddhas and Bodhisattvas called "noble ones" (ārya)?
It is because such persons possess the noble dharmas and constantly contemplate the emptiness and quiescence of the nature of all phenomena.
For this reason, they are called "noble ones" (*ārya*).
Because they possess noble ethical discipline (*śīla*), they are called noble ones;
because they possess noble concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they are called noble ones.
There are seven noble riches, namely: faith, ethical discipline, moral shame, dread of blame, extensive learning, wisdom, and relinquishment; because of these, one is called a noble person (ārya).
Furthermore, because there are seven factors of enlightenment for noble persons, one is called a noble person.
For this reason, it is further called the "Noble Practice" (*ārya-caryā*). Furthermore, son of good family,

the noble practice of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva consists of observing this body from head to foot, seeing that within it there are only hair, body hair, nails, teeth, impurities, filth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, the two receptacles of raw and cooked food, feces and urine, mucus, saliva, tears, fat, grease, brain membrane, bone marrow, pus, blood, skull, and various vessels.
When the bodhisattva thus contemplates with single-minded attention: "Who is this that is 'I'?
To whom does 'I' belong?"
"Where do I dwell?
To whom do I belong?
He then further reflected:
"Is the bone me? Or is it something apart from the bone?
At that time, the Bodhisattva removed the skin and flesh and contemplated only the white bones, further forming this thought:
"The characteristics of the bones differ—namely, blue, yellow, white, and pigeon-colored—and such bone-characteristics are likewise not the self. Why is this?
"The self, moreover, is neither blue, yellow, nor white, nor the color of a pigeon.
When the Bodhisattva binds his mind and contemplates in this way, he immediately succeeds in severing all desire for form.
Again, he reflects:
"These bones arise from causes and conditions:
depending on the foot bone as the cause, they support the ankle bone;
Relying on the ankle bones, they support the shin bones;
relying on the shin bones, they support the knee bones;
relying on the knee bones, they support the thigh bones.
Relying on the thigh bones, they support the hip bones;
relying on the hip bones, they support the pelvic bones;
relying on the pelvic bones, they support the spinal vertebrae.
Relying on the spinal column, the ribs are supported;
further, relying on the spinal column, the cervical vertebrae are supported above;
relying on the cervical vertebrae, the mandible is supported.
Relying on the jawbone, the teeth are supported; above it is the skull.
Furthermore, relying on the cervical vertebrae, the shoulder blades are supported;
relying on the shoulder blades, the arm bones are supported.
Relying on the bones of the upper arm, they support the bones of the wrist;
relying on the bones of the wrist, they support the bones of the palm;
relying on the bones of the palm, they support the bones of the fingers.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, all the bones of his body become completely separated.
Having attained this contemplation, he immediately cuts off the three desires:
first, the desire for physical appearance; second, the desire for graceful gestures; and third, the desire for subtle tactile sensations.
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates blue bones, they see this great earth—in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—all as having a blue appearance.
Just as with the contemplation of the blue color, it is likewise for yellow, white, and pigeon-colored [bones]."
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva performs this contemplation, rays of light in blue, yellow, red, white, and pigeon-colored hues emerge from between his eyebrows.
Within each of these individual rays of light, the bodhisattva beholds the image of a Buddha.
Having seen this, he immediately asked:
"This body is formed through the combination of impure causes and conditions.
How is it able to sit, stand, walk, stay, bend, stretch, bow, look up, gaze, blink, breathe, weep, and laugh?"
"In this there is no master; who caused it to be so?
Having asked this question, the Buddhas within the light suddenly vanished.
He then thought again:
"Perhaps it is this consciousness that is the self; that is why the Buddhas did not teach it to me.
He further contemplates that this consciousness arises and ceases in succession like a flowing stream, and thus it, too, is not the self.
Again, he thought:
"If consciousness is not the self, perhaps the out-breath and in-breath might be the self.
Again, he thought:
"These inhalations and exhalations are simply the nature of wind, and this nature of wind is itself the four great elements.
Among these four great elements, which one is the self?"
"The nature of earth is not self;
the natures of water, fire, and wind are likewise not self.
He further thought:

"This body is entirely devoid of a self; it is merely a combination of the causes and conditions of mind and wind that manifests various activities, like the effects produced by the power of spells or illusions, and like a lute producing sound according to one's will."
Therefore, this body is thus impure, being formed through the temporary conjunction of various causes and conditions; in what place could desire arise?
If one is reviled and insulted, in what place could anger arise?
"Just as this body of mine consists of thirty-six impure and foul substances, where in it could there be anyone who receives abuse?
If one hears such abuse, one should immediately reflect:
"By what sound am I being abused?"
"One cannot see the one who reviles through each individual sound;
if one cannot do so, it is the same even with many.
For this reason, one should not give rise to anger."
If another comes to strike you, you should also reflect:
"From what does such a striker arise?
Then, one should further think:
"It is because of the hand, the sword, the staff, and my own body that it is called 'striking. For what reason should I now unjustly harbor anger toward another?
It is my own body that has invited this fault, for I have received this body composed of the five aggregates."
Just as there is a wound when one is struck by an arrow, so it is with my body:
because there is a body, there is beating.
If I do not practice patience, my mind will become distracted.
If the mind is distracted, one loses right mindfulness;
if one loses right mindfulness, one cannot contemplate the meaning of the wholesome and the unwholesome;
if one cannot contemplate the meaning of the wholesome and the unwholesome, one practices unwholesome dharmas.
"Through the causes and conditions of unwholesome dharmas, one falls into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Having performed this contemplation at that time, the Bodhisattva attained the four foundations of mindfulness.
Having attained the four foundations of mindfulness, one then abides in the stage of endurance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).

Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in this stage, they are able to endure greed, anger, and delusion; they are also able to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, lice, violent winds, harsh touch, various epidemics, evil speech and abuse, and being beaten or flogged.
"One who is able to endure all physical and mental suffering is therefore said to dwell in the Stage of Forbearance.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"When a Bodhisattva has not yet attained the stage of Immovability (Acalā-bhūmi), is there any cause or condition by which they might break their precepts while maintaining them purely? "Good son!
For a Bodhisattva who has not yet attained the stage of Immovability, there are causes and conditions by which they may break the precepts."
Kāśyapa said:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Which ones are they?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“If there is a bodhisattva who knows that by means of the causes and conditions of breaking the precepts, he can cause others to receive, uphold, and take delight in the Mahāyāna sūtras; and furthermore, can cause them to read, recite, master, copy, and extensively explain these scriptures to others, so that they do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—for such a purpose as this, he may break the precepts.”
At that time, the bodhisattva should form this thought:

"I would rather fall into the Avīci Hell for an eon, or even slightly less than an eon, to undergo this retribution for my transgression, so as to ensure that this person does not regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
“Kāśyapa! For these reasons, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may be said to have violated the pure precepts.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
