If there is a bodhisattva who takes such a person under their care and protection, causing them not to regress from the mind of enlightenment, it would be impossible for that bodhisattva to be considered a violator of the precepts or to fall into the Avīci Hell.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.”

I recall that in the past, I was a great king in Jambudvīpa named Senajit. I cherished and revered the Mahāyāna sūtras; my mind was purely virtuous, free from coarseness, evil, jealousy, or stinginess. My mouth constantly uttered words of affection and goodness, and my body constantly protected the poor and the solitary. In giving and diligence, I never ceased or desisted.
At that time, there were no Buddhas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas in the world.
During those years, I took delight in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; for twelve years, I served a brāhmaṇa, providing him with all his necessities.
After twelve years had passed and the bestowal of peace and comfort was complete, he spoke these words:
"Teachers, you should now resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Great King!
The nature of bodhi is non-existent; the Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so."
"Great King, why do you wish to make a person identical to empty space? "Good son!
At that time, my heart was set upon the Mahāyāna; hearing the Brahmin slander the Vaipulya sūtras, as soon as I heard it, I immediately severed his life-root."
"Good son! By these causes and conditions, from this time forward you shall not fall into hell. Good son!"
To protect and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras possesses such immeasurable power.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there is another holy practice, namely the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Kāśyapa! Suffering has the characteristic of oppression;
origination has the characteristic of being able to produce and grow.
"Cessation" is the characteristic of quiescence;
"the Path" is the characteristic of the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, good son!
Suffering is the characteristic of manifestation;
origination is the characteristic of transformation;
cessation is the characteristic of elimination.
The Way is that which can eliminate marks.
Furthermore, good son,
suffering has three characteristics:
The characteristic of suffering as suffering, the characteristic of suffering as conditioned formations, and the characteristic of suffering as change;
"accumulation" refers to the twenty-five states of existence;
"cessation" refers to the cessation of the twenty-five states of existence.
The Way consists in the cultivation of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Furthermore, good son, there are two kinds of tainted phenomena (sāsrava-dharma): there are causes and there are fruits.
The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) also have two kinds: those that are causes and those that are fruits.
That which is the fruit of the tainted (*sāsrava*) is called suffering (*duḥkha*);
that which is the cause of the tainted is called origination (*samudaya*).
That which is the untainted fruit is called cessation;
that which is the untainted cause is called the path.
"Furthermore, good son!

The eight characteristics are called suffering: namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
That which can give rise to these eight modes of suffering is called the origin;
the state in which these eight phenomena do not exist is called cessation.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion—these are called the Path.
"Good son! That which is born has five characteristics of emergence, namely:
First, initial emergence; second, reaching the end; third, growth; fourth, birth from the womb; fifth, birth by way of species.
"What is aging? There are two kinds of aging:
first, moment-to-moment aging; second, lifelong aging."
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the aging of growth; second, the aging of decay. These are called "aging. What is "sickness"?
Sickness refers to the mutual disharmony of the four great poisonous serpents;
it is also of two kinds: first, physical sickness; second, mental sickness.
Physical sickness has five types:
First, those caused by water; second, those caused by wind; third, those caused by heat; fourth, miscellaneous diseases; and fifth, external diseases.
There are four types of external illnesses:
first, overexertion beyond one's capacity; second, falling due to forgetfulness or error; third, injury from blades, staves, tiles, or stones; and fourth, possession by malevolent spirits.
There are also four kinds of mental afflictions:
first, agitation; second, fear; third, sorrow; and fourth, delusion.
"Furthermore, good son!
There are three kinds of illnesses of body and mind.
What are these three?

First, karmic retribution; second, the inability to remain far removed from adverse conditions; third, the shifting of seasons—through such causes and conditions, names, and perceptions, discrimination arises.
The causal conditions of disease refer to various ailments such as wind-disorders (*vāta*) and the like;
the names refer to mental distress, lung congestion, upward gasping, coughing, palpitations, and diarrhea;
and the categorized experiences refer to headaches, eye pain, and pains in the hands, feet, and so forth—these are called diseases.
"What is death? Death is the relinquishing of the body one has received.
This relinquishing of the body one has received is also of two kinds:"
First, death by the exhaustion of the life-span; second, death due to external conditions.
There are also three types of death by the exhaustion of the life-span:

first, the exhaustion of the life-span but not the exhaustion of merit; second, the exhaustion of merit but not the exhaustion of the life-span; third, the simultaneous exhaustion of both merit and the life-span.
There are also three kinds of death caused by external conditions:
first, death through self-inflicted harm that is not proportionate to the cause; second, death brought about unexpectedly by others; and third, death resulting from both factors combined.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of death:
first, death through negligence; second, death through breaking the precepts; and third, death through the destruction of the life-faculty.
What is meant by death through negligence?
If one slanders the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, this is called death through negligence.
What is meant by death through breaking the precepts?
To violate the prohibitions and precepts established by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present is called death through breaking the precepts.
What is called "death through the destruction of the life-faculty"?
The relinquishing of the body of the five aggregates is called death through the destruction of the life-faculty.
Thus, death is said to be a great suffering.
"What is called the suffering of separation from the beloved?
It is the destruction and dispersal of things one loves. There are also two kinds of destruction and dispersal of things one loves:

[the first is] the destruction and dispersal of those things one loves while they are still present; [the second is] the destruction and dispersal of those things one loves after they have already passed away."
First, the dissolution of the five aggregates among humans; second, the dissolution of the five aggregates among devas.

Thus, the immeasurable varieties of the five aggregates—beloved by humans and devas—which are conceptually analyzed and calculated in terms of existence and non-existence, are called the suffering of separation from the beloved.
"What is called the suffering of association with the disliked?
It is the coming together with those whom one does not love.
There are also three kinds of such associations with the disliked, namely: the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals."
In this way, there are immeasurable varieties of distinctions and calculations regarding these three realms of existence; this is what is called the suffering of association with the disliked.
"What is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks also has two aspects:

first, being unable to obtain that which one hopes for despite seeking it; second, expending great effort yet failing to attain the resulting fruit. This is termed the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
"What is called the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging?

The suffering of the five aggregates of clinging consists of the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; therefore, it is called the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging."
“Kāśyapa! There are these seven kinds of suffering rooted in birth: the suffering of old age, up to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Kāśyapa!”
Now, as for aging and decay, they do not exist in all beings; they are definitively absent in the Buddhas and the various devas.
Among humans, they are indeterminate: they may be present, or they may be absent.
“Kāśyapa!
Within the three realms, there is no taking on of a body that is not subject to birth; aging is not necessarily fixed. Therefore, birth is the root of all things. Kāśyapa!”
The minds of worldly beings are shrouded by inversion; they are greedily attached to the signs of birth and feel aversion toward old age and death.
It is not so for the Bodhisattva, who, upon observing initial birth, already perceives its faults and perils.
Kāśyapa! It is as if there were a woman who entered another's house.
This woman was upright and beautiful, her countenance lovely, and her body adorned with exquisite necklaces and ornaments.
Having seen him, the host immediately asked:
"What is your name?
To whom do you belong?"
The woman replied,
"I am the Great Deity of Merit.
The host asked:
"What do you do wherever you go? The goddess replied, "Wherever I go,

I am able to provide various kinds of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, coral, amber, musaragalva, agate, as well as elephants, horses, carriages, and vehicles, along with male and female slaves and servants."
Upon hearing this, the host felt great joy in his heart and leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking:
"By virtue of my own merit, I have caused you to come to my home."
He immediately burned incense, scattered flowers, and made offerings with reverence and prostrations.

Furthermore, outside the gate he saw another woman; her appearance was hideous, her clothes were tattered and worn, covered in much grime and oil, her skin was cracked and parched, and her complexion was as pale as mugwort.
Having seen him, he asked:
"What is your name?
To whom do you belong?"
The woman replied,
"My name is Kṛṣṇā.
He asked again:
"Why is she called 'Darkness'?
The woman replied, "Wherever I go,
all the wealth and treasures in that household will be brought to ruin."
Upon hearing this, the host immediately took up a sharp knife and said:
"If you do not leave, I shall take your life.
The woman replied:
"You are extremely foolish and lack wisdom.
The host asked,
"For what reason do you call me foolish and lacking in wisdom?"
The woman replied, "The one in your house is my elder sister; I always accompany her in all our movements.
If you drive me away, you must also drive my sister away."
The host returned inside and asked Puṇyavatī, "There was a woman outside who said she was your younger sister;
is this truly so? Puṇyavatī replied:
"She is truly my younger sister.
I have lived and traveled with this sister, never being separated from her.
Wherever we stayed, I always acted virtuously while she always acted wickedly; I brought about benefit, while she brought about ruin."
"If you love me, you should also love him;
if you see me with respect, you should also respect him.
The host then said:
"If there are such matters of good or evil, I shall have no use for them; you may each go as you please.
At that time, the two women took one another by the hand and returned to their respective dwellings.
At that time, seeing that they had departed, the host felt great joy in his heart, leaping for immeasurable delight.
Then the two girls again accompanied each other to the house of another poor man.
Upon seeing this, the poor man felt great joy in his heart and immediately invited them, saying,
"From this day forward, I pray that you two will dwell in my home forever.
Guṇakārandavatī said:
"We have already been driven away by others; for what reason do you now invite us both to stay?
The poor man replied, "If you now take pity on me, I shall, for your sake, show respect to him as well."
"Therefore, I invite you both to dwell in my home.

"Kāśyapa! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: he does not wish to be born in the heavens, because birth is inevitably followed by old age, sickness, and death; therefore, he abandons both, never having the intention to accept them."
Ordinary, foolish people do not understand the perils of old age, sickness, death, and so forth; therefore, they greedily grasp at the two phenomena of birth and death.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like a young Brahmin boy, driven by hunger, who sees an amra fruit in human excrement and immediately picks it up.
A wise person, having seen this, rebukes him, saying:
"You are of the pure Brahmin lineage; for what reason do you take this filthy fruit from within excrement?"
Having heard this, the youth was abashed with shame and replied, "I truly did not eat;
I wished to wash it clean and then discard it."
The wise person says:
"You are greatly foolish; if you were to discard it again, you should not have taken it in the first place. Good son!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: regarding this portion of birth, they neither accept nor reject it, just as that wise man rebuked the boy;
whereas ordinary people rejoice in birth and loathe death, just as that boy took the fruit and then threw it away.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
it is like a person at a crossroads who has a vessel filled with food, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, and wishes to sell it.
Suppose there is someone who has come from afar, hungry, emaciated, and exhausted; seeing that the food possesses perfect color, fragrance, and flavor, they point to it and ask: "What is this?"
The host replied:
"This is a superior food, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor.
If one eats this food, one will obtain beauty, obtain strength, be able to eliminate hunger and thirst, and gain the sight of the devas; it has only one drawback, namely, the end of life."
Having heard this, the person immediately thought:
"I have no need now for beauty, strength, or the sight of gods, nor do I need to die.
He then spoke these words:
"If this food were eaten and one were to die as a result, why would you now sell it here?
The food-seller replied,
"A person of wisdom would never be willing to buy it."
"Only fools do not understand this matter; they pay me a high price and greedily eat it. "Good son!
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: he does not wish to be born in the heavens, nor to obtain physical beauty, nor to obtain power, nor to see the various devas."
Why is this? Because they cannot escape various sufferings and afflictions.
Ordinary people are deluded; wherever they are born, they are entirely possessed by craving and attachment, because they do not perceive old age, sickness, and death.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a poisonous tree: its roots can kill a person, and its branches, trunk, stem, nodes, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruit can all likewise kill."
"Good son!
The places of birth within the twenty-five states of existence, and the five aggregates received therein, are likewise all capable of killing.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
For example, just as excrement is foul-smelling whether it be much or little,
so it is with birth, noble son:
even if the lifespan is eighty thousand years, or as short as ten years, all alike undergo suffering.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like this:
suppose there is a grass-covered ledge on the edge of a steep precipice, and upon that bank there is much *amṛta*.
If anyone were to eat of it, they would live for a thousand celestial years, forever free from all diseases, dwelling in peace and happiness."

Because ordinary, foolish people crave its flavor, they do not realize there is a vast, deep pit beneath it; as they step forward to seize it, they unconsciously stumble and fall into the pit, where they die.
Having understood this, the wise man abandons it and departs far away.
Son of good family, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is just like this: he does not even wish to accept exquisite food from the heavens, much less that of the human realm.
“Ordinary worldlings even swallow iron balls in the hells; how much more so would they not eat the exquisite delicacies of humans and devas?
Kāśyapa!...”
By means of these analogies and other immeasurable, boundless parables, one should know that this birth is indeed a great suffering.
Kāśyapa! This is called the bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* contemplating the suffering of birth.
“Kāśyapa! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the suffering of old age within this Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*? Old age can cause hiccups and shortness of breath;

it can destroy valor and strength. It causes one to long for the vigor, memory, and joy of youth, as well as arrogance, haughtiness, security, and self-indulgence. It causes the body to become bent and hunched, leading to indolence and laziness, and making one despised by others.”
Kāśyapa!
It is like a pond filled with lotus flowers in full bloom, fresh and radiant, most lovely to behold; yet when heaven sends down hail, they are all utterly destroyed.
"Noble son!
Old age is likewise; it is able to utterly destroy youthful vigor and beautiful complexion.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"

For example, suppose a king has a wise minister who is well-versed in the art of war. When a rival king resists and acts in defiance, the king dispatches this minister to campaign against him; the minister immediately captures him and brings him before the king.
Old age is likewise; it seizes the vigor of youth and delivers one over to the King of Death.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a broken axle that has no further use."
Old age is likewise of no further use.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a wealthy household that possesses abundant treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate."
If various enemies and bandits enter a house, they are able to plunder it until it is completely emptied.
Noble son, youthful vigor and beautiful appearance are likewise thus; they are constantly being plundered by the thief of old age.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a poor person who covets exquisite delicacies and fine, soft garments; though they long for them, they are unable to obtain them."
Good son! Old age is also like this:
although one possesses a greedy mind and desires to receive wealth and pleasure, indulging freely in the five sensual desires, one cannot obtain them.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
Just as a land tortoise constantly thinks of water in its heart,
so it is with people, noble son:
once they have been withered by old age and decay, their minds constantly recall the pleasures of the five desires experienced in their youth.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
it is just as all lotuses in the autumn moonlight are pleasing for all to behold;
yet when they wither and turn yellow, people despise them."
Good son! Youthful vigor and physical beauty are likewise thus;
they are cherished and delighted in by all, yet when old age arrives, they are loathed and despised by the multitude.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like sugarcane:
once it has been pressed, the residue has no more flavor.
So too is the vigor and beauty of youth; once crushed by old age, they possess none of the three flavors."
First, the flavor of renunciation; second, the flavor of recitation; third, the flavor of seated meditation.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like the full moon: at night it has much radiance, but during the day it is not so."
Good son! Human beings are also like this: in their youth they are upright and dignified, with magnificent and handsome features;
in their old age they become frail and decrepit, their physical form and spirit withered and haggard.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a king who always governs the country and rules the people with the True Dharma; he is truthful and without crookedness, compassionate and fond of giving."
At that time, his kingdom was destroyed by an enemy state; he became a wandering fugitive and fled far away to another land.
When the people of that land saw him, they felt pity for him and all spoke thus:
"In the past, Your Majesty ruled the country with the True Dharma and did not wrong the myriad subjects; how is it that in a single day you have come to such a state of wandering exile?"
“Good son! Human beings are also like this;
once they have been broken and ruined by old age and decay, they constantly praise the deeds performed during their prime.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!”
It is like the wick of a lamp, which relies solely upon oil; once the oil is exhausted, its power cannot endure for long.
Good son, human beings are likewise:
they rely solely upon the oil of vigor; once that vigor is exhausted, how can the wick of old age and decay endure for long?
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like a dried-up river that cannot benefit humans or non-humans, birds, or beasts.
Good son!"
Human beings are also like this; withered by old age, they are unable to benefit from any of their activities.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a great tree on a steep riverbank; if it encounters a violent wind, it will surely fall over."
“Good son!
Human beings are also like this: when they reach the perilous brink of old age and the winds of death have arrived, they have no power to remain.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!”
Just as a broken axle cannot bear a heavy load, so it is with old age,
O son of good family:
one is unable to inquire about or receive all wholesome dharmas.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like an infant who is held in contempt by others. Good son!
Old age is likewise always held in contempt and reviled by all.
"Kāśyapa, through these and other immeasurable and boundless parables, you should know that old age is indeed a great suffering."
Kāśyapa! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in contemplating the suffering of old age. Kāśyapa!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* contemplate the suffering of illness?
That which is called "illness" is able to destroy all matters of peace and happiness, just as a shower of hail destroys the sprouts of grain.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like a person who has an enemy; his mind is constantly filled with sorrow and he harbors fear.
Son of good family!"
All sentient beings are likewise; they constantly fear the suffering of illness and harbor grief in their hearts.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a man of handsome appearance who is loved by the king’s consort out of desire; she sends a messenger to summon him and have sexual intercourse with him."
At that time, the king captured him and immediately dispatched men to gouge out one of his eyes, cut off one of his ears, and sever one of his hands and feet.
Consequently, his appearance was transformed and altered, and he was loathed and despised by all people.
Good son! Human beings are also like this:

though they may initially be handsome and endowed with perfect eyes and ears, once they are entangled and oppressed by the suffering of illness, they become objects of contempt and disdain for all people.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
It is like the plantain, the bamboo, the reed, and the mule, which die as soon as they produce fruit.
Son of good family!"
Human beings are also like this: when they have illness, they die.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is as when a Wheel-Turning King travels, the minister in charge of the military always leads the way in front, and the king follows behind."
Just as when a king of fish, a king of ants, a king of conchs, a king of oxen, or a caravan leader goes before them, all these followers follow after him without any turning back or desertion.
Good son! The death of a universal monarch is likewise; it constantly follows the minister of illness, never departing from him.
Fish, ants, conchs, oxen, caravan leaders, and the king of illness are also like this: they are always pursued by the hosts of death.

“Kāśyapa! The causes and conditions of illness are as follows: namely, suffering and affliction, grief and anxiety, lamentation, and physical and mental unease; or being oppressed and harmed by enemies and thieves, having one’s life-raft destroyed, or having the bridge dismantled; it can also plunder the very root of right mindfulness.”
Furthermore, it can destroy one’s prime of life, physical beauty, power, and well-being; it causes one to cast aside shame and modesty, and brings about a burning fever within both body and mind.
By means of these and other immeasurable and boundless analogies, one should know that the suffering of illness is a great suffering.
Kāśyapa! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra of the Mahāyāna and contemplating the suffering of illness. Kāśyapa!
How does a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* contemplate the suffering of death?
That which is called "death" is so named because it can burn and extinguish [all things].
"Kāśyapa!..."
Just as when a fire breaks out it can burn everything except for the second dhyāna, because its power does not reach there;
so too, son of good family,
the fire of death can burn everything except for Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, because its force cannot reach them.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Just as when a water disaster arises and everything is submerged, except for the third dhyāna, because its power does not reach there.
Good son!"
The stagnant water is likewise; it sweeps away and submerges all, with the sole exception of the Bodhisattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
Just as when a wind calamity arises it can blow away everything, causing all things to be dispersed and extinguished, except for the fourth dhyāna, because its power does not reach there;
so too, son of good family, is the wind of death: it can blow out and extinguish all that exists, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions is it that in that fourth dhyāna, wind cannot blow, water cannot float it away, and fire cannot burn it?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son! In that fourth dhyāna, all internal and external faults and afflictions are entirely absent."
"Good son! The defects of the first dhyāna are that internally there is vitarka and vicāra, and externally there is the calamity of fire;
the defects of the second dhyāna are that internally there is prīti, and externally there is the calamity of water."
The defects of the third dhyāna are that internally there is breathing and externally there is the calamity of wind.
Son of good family!
In that fourth dhyāna, all internal and external defects are entirely absent; therefore, no calamities can reach it.
Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, all internal and external faults and afflictions are completely exhausted.
Therefore, the King of Death cannot reach them.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as the garuḍa can devour and digest all dragons, fish, gold, silver, and other such treasures, yet alone cannot cause a diamond to be digested."
Good son!
The golden-winged bird of death is also like this: it can devour and digest all sentient beings, yet it alone cannot digest a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who abides in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like all the grasses and trees on a riverbank:
when the great waters surge in a flood, they are all carried away and flow into the great ocean, with the sole exception of the willow, because of its flexibility."
Good son! All sentient beings are likewise;
they all follow the current into the sea of death, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is as if Nārāyaṇa were able to utterly crush and subdue all other strongmen, with the sole exception of the great wind. Why is this? "
Because it is unimpeded. Good son!
Death-Nārāyaṇa is also like this; he is able to crush and subdue all sentient beings, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who dwell in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because it is unimpeded.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
It is like a person who, amidst those they hate and loathe, feigns intimacy and kindness; constantly pursuing them like a shadow following a form, they watch for an opportunity to kill them.
That enemy is cautious and vigilant, having made firm preparations for himself; therefore, he is unable to kill this person.

Good son, the enemy that is death is likewise: it constantly watches for sentient beings, desiring to kill them, yet it alone cannot kill the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas are not negligent.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"

It is like a sudden downpour of a vajra-rain that utterly destroys medicinal herbs, trees, forests, mountains, earth, sand, tiles, stones, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and all other things, yet alone cannot destroy the true jewel of the vajra.
Good son!
The adamantine rain of death is likewise; it can destroy all sentient beings, with the sole exception of the adamantine Bodhisattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Just as the garuḍa can devour all nāgas, yet cannot devour those who have received the three refuges.
O son of good family!"
The dead garuḍa is also like this: it can devour all immeasurable sentient beings, with the sole exception of bodhisattvas who abide in the three concentrations.
What are these three concentrations?
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a Māra serpent that has bitten someone;
even with excellent incantations or the most sublime and wonderful medicines, there is nothing that can help, except for the incantation of the Aṅgiras constellation, which alone can effect a cure."

Good son! The bite of the poison of death is likewise; no medical prescriptions whatsoever can do anything about it, except for the Bodhisattva who dwells in the mantra of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like a person who has been angered by a king; if that person can use gentle and kind words and present him with wealth and treasures, they may then obtain release."
"Good son!
The King of Death is not like that; even if one offers him gentle words, money, or rare treasures, one cannot escape him.
Good son!"
Now, as for death: it is a perilous place where there are no provisions;
the destination is remote and there are no companions;
one travels day and night without knowing its limits.
Profoundly deep and dark, it is devoid of the light of lamps;
it has no doors or gates, yet it possesses a location;
though it has no site of pain, it cannot be healed.
It proceeds without being obstructed, yet upon arrival it cannot be escaped;
it is indestructible, and those who behold it are filled with grief and anguish;
though not of an evil form, it strikes terror into people.
It is spread about one's side, yet remains imperceptible. "Kāśyapa!
By these and other immeasurable and boundless parables, you should know that death is truly a great suffering."
Kāśyapa! This is called a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and contemplating the suffering of death. "Kāśyapa!
How does a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* contemplate the suffering of separation from the beloved?
"The suffering of separation from the beloved is the root of all sufferings."
As it is said in verse:
"From craving arises sorrow; from craving arises fear.
If one is free from craving, what sorrow could there be?"
"What is there to fear?
"Because of craving as a causal condition, sorrow and suffering arise;
because of sorrow and suffering, they cause sentient beings to undergo aging and decay."
The suffering of separation from what is loved refers to the end of life. Good son!
Because of such separation, various subtle sufferings can arise; I shall now analyze and reveal them for you.
“Good son! In the past, when the lifespan of humans was immeasurable, there was a king named Supratiṣṭhita.
At that time, while he was still a youth, he served as a crown prince for eighty-four thousand years, and he reigned as king for another eighty-four thousand years.”

At that time, a fleshy tumor grew upon the crown of the king’s head; this tumor was as soft as *tūla* cotton and as fine and delicate as *karpāsa* silk, and it gradually increased in size without causing him any distress.
When the ten months were fully completed, the swelling burst open, and a young boy was born.
His form was upright and handsome, extraordinary and peerless; his features were distinct and clear, the foremost among men.
The father king was filled with joy and named him Śikhi.
King Supratiṣṭhita then entrusted the affairs of state to Śikhi and, abandoning his palace, wife, children, and retinue, entered the mountains to study the Way for a full eighty-four thousand years.
"At that time, on the fifteenth day, Mūrdhaja was atop a high tower, having bathed and observed the fast.

Immediately, from the east, there appeared the precious wheel-treasure—a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete with hub and rim, spontaneously perfected without the work of artisans—which came forth to attend him."
Great King Mūrdhaja then had this thought:
"In the past, I heard a seer possessing the five supernormal powers say:

'If a Kṣatriya king, on the fifteenth day, stands atop a high tower having bathed and observed the fast, and a golden wheel—complete with a thousand spokes, no fewer, with hub and rim fully formed, not made by a craftsman but spontaneously accomplished—should appear before him, it should be known that this king shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.'"
He further thought:
"I shall now put it to the test.
He immediately lifted this Wheel-Treasure with his left hand, held an incense burner in his right, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and made this vow:
"If this precious golden wheel is truly and not falsely so, it should follow the path and dharma traversed by the past Wheel-Turning Sage Kings.
Having made this vow, the precious golden wheel ascended into the void, traveled throughout the ten directions, and then returned to rest upon the left hand of Mūrdhagata.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja felt great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
He spoke these words again:
"I shall now certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
Not long after that, there appeared again the elephant-treasure, its form majestic and beautiful like a white lotus, with its seven limbs touching the ground.
Upon seeing it, the King born from the crown of the head thought again:
"In the past, I heard a seer possessing the five supernormal powers say:"

"If a Wheel-Turning King, on the fifteenth day, having bathed and observed the fast while standing atop a high tower, is met by the appearance of an elephant-treasure—stately and beautiful in form like a white lotus, with its seven limbs touching the ground—one should know that this king is indeed a noble sovereign."
He further thought to himself:
"I shall now put this to the test.
He immediately took up an incense burner, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and made this vow:
"If this White Elephant Treasure is truly real and not false, it should follow the path and dharma traversed by the past Wheel-Turning Sage Kings.

Having made this vow, the White Elephant Treasure traveled throughout the eight directions from dawn until dusk, reaching as far as the limits of the great ocean, before returning to its original place.
At that time, Mūrdhagata was filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
He spoke these words again:
"I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
Not long after that, there appeared next the horse-treasure, its color a deep, radiant azure with a mane and tail of golden hue.
Upon seeing it, King Māndhātṛ thought again:
"In the past, I heard a seer possessing the five supernatural powers say:"

"If a Wheel-Turning King, on the fifteenth day, stands upon a high tower having bathed and observed the fast, and a horse-treasure appears—its coat a deep, brilliant azure and its mane and tail golden—one should know that this king is indeed a noble sovereign."
Again, he thought to himself:
"I shall now put this to the test.
He immediately took up an incense burner, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and made this vow:
"If this precious dark-blue horse is truly not false, it should follow the path and dharma traversed by the past Wheel-Turning Sage Kings.
Having made this vow, from dawn until dusk, the precious dark-blue horse traveled throughout the eight directions as far as the limits of the great ocean, and then returned to its original place.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja was filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
He spoke these words again:
"I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."

Not long after that, there appeared the Woman-Jewel (strī-ratna), whose physical form was upright and exquisite, the foremost in its subtle beauty. She was neither tall nor short, neither too pale nor too dark; from all the pores of her body issued the fragrance of sandalwood, and her breath was as pure and fragrant as a blue lotus.
His eyes see for a distance of one yojana;
his hearing and smelling are likewise so. His tongue is vast, capable of extending to cover his face; its color and form are fine and thin, like a leaf of red copper.
Her mind and consciousness were sharp and sagacious, possessing great wisdom; she always spoke gentle words to all sentient beings.
When this woman touched the king’s robe with her hand, she immediately knew whether his body was at ease or afflicted by illness, and she also knew the objects upon which his mind was focused.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja again had this thought:
"If there were a woman who could know the king's mind, she would be the Woman-Jewel (strī-ratna).

Not long thereafter, a precious maṇi-jewel spontaneously appeared within the royal palace; it was made of pure blue lapis lazuli, as large as a chariot wheel, and was capable of illuminating an area of one yojana in the darkness.
If the heavens send down rain in drops as thick as axle-trees, the power of this jewel can form a great canopy covering one yojana, blocking this heavy rain so that it does not fall through.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja again thought to himself:
"If a Wheel-Turning King obtains such a precious jewel, he must surely be a holy sovereign.

Not long thereafter, a minister in charge of the treasury appeared spontaneously; he possessed abundant wealth and immeasurable riches, his storehouses were overflowing and lacked for nothing. By virtue of his karmic retribution, his faculty of sight had the power to see clearly all hidden treasures within the earth, and he could provide whatever the king desired.
At that time, Mūrdhaja wished to test him further; he immediately boarded a ship with him and entered the great ocean, saying to the Treasurer:
"I now desire to obtain rare and extraordinary treasures."

Having heard this, the treasury minister immediately stirred the waters of the great ocean with both hands; at that moment, ten precious treasuries emerged from his ten fingertips, which he presented to the Holy King. He then addressed the King, saying:
"Great King, please use these as you wish; whatever remains shall be cast back into the great ocean."
At that time, King Mūrdhaja was filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
He further thought to himself:
"I am now certainly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
Not long after that, a commander-in-chief emerged spontaneously, valiant and fierce in his strategy, foremost in counsel, and well-versed in the four types of military forces.
If they are capable of engaging in battle, he manifests as a noble king;
if they are not capable, he withdraws so that he does not appear.
Those who have not yet been subdued, he is able to subdue.
"Those who have already been subdued can be protected by his power.
At that time, Mūrdhaja again thought to himself:
"If a Wheel-turning King possesses such a treasure of an army, one should know for certain that he is a Wheel-turning Sage-King."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King Mūrdhaja addressed his ministers:
"You should know this:
this Jambudvīpa is peaceful, secure, and prosperous. I have now already attained the seven treasures and am fully endowed with a thousand sons; what further need is there for me to do?"
The ministers replied, "Indeed, Great King!
Pūrvavideha has not yet submitted to your virtue; Your Majesty should go there now."
At that time, the Holy King, together with the seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew through the air to Pūrvavideha in the east; the people of that land joyfully submitted to his rule.
He further addressed his ministers, saying:
"My Jambudvīpa and Pūrvavideha are peaceful, prosperous, and joyful; their populations are flourishing, and all have come to submit to my transformation."
“Having accomplished the seven treasures and being endowed with a thousand sons, what further purpose would there be?
The ministers replied,
“Indeed so, Great King!”
"The western continent of Aparagoyānī has not yet submitted to his virtue.
At that time, the Holy King, together with the seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew through the air to Aparagoyānī.
Once the King had arrived there, the people of that land likewise submitted and took refuge in him.
He further addressed his ministers:
"My Jambudvīpa, as well as Pūrvavideha and this Aparagoyānī, are peaceful, prosperous, and joyful; their populations are flourishing, and all have been converted and brought under my rule."
"Having accomplished the seven treasures and being endowed with a thousand sons, what further purpose would there be?
The ministers replied,
"Indeed so, Great King!"
"Yet Northern Uttarakuru has not yet submitted to conversion.
At that time, the Holy King, together with the seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew through the air to Northern Uttarakuru.
Once the King arrived there, the people of that land joyfully submitted to his virtue.
He further addressed his ministers:
"My four continents are peaceful, secure, and prosperous; the population is flourishing, and all have already submitted to my virtue."
"With the seven treasures perfected and a full thousand sons, what more is there to be done?
The ministers replied,
"Indeed so, O Holy King!"
"The lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is exceedingly long, and they dwell in peace and happiness.

The physical forms of those gods are incomparably majestic and beautiful; their palaces, couches, and bedding are all made of the seven treasures. Relying on their celestial merit, they have not yet come to submit. We must now go to subdue them and bring them to heel."
At that time, the holy king, together with the seven treasures and his entire retinue, flew up into the void to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There he saw a tree of a blue-green color.
Having seen it, the Holy King immediately asked his ministers,
"What color is this?
The ministers replied:
"This is the Pārijātaka tree, beneath which the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven constantly enjoy themselves and take pleasure during the three months of summer.
He further saw something white, like a white cloud.
He asked the minister again,
"What color is that?
The minister replied:
"This is the Sudharmā Hall, where the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constantly assemble to discuss matters concerning humans and devas.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of the Gods, knowing that King Māndhātṛ had already arrived outside, immediately went out to meet him.
Having seen him, he took his hand and ascended the Hall of Good Dharma (Saddharmasāla), where they sat together on a shared seat.
At that time, the two kings were indistinguishable in their physical forms and features; the only difference was in the movement of their eyes.
At that time, the holy king immediately had this thought:
"Would it not be better for me now to depose him from his royal throne and take up residence therein as the Heavenly King? "Good son!
At that time, Śakra received, upheld, read, and recited the Mahāyāna sūtras; he elucidated, analyzed, and expounded them for others, yet he had not yet fully mastered their profound meanings.
By the power of these causes and conditions—namely, the recitation, upholding, analysis, and extensive exposition for others—he possesses great majesty and virtue. Good son!

Once King Mūrdhaja had conceived an evil thought toward this Śakra, he immediately fell back to Jambudvīpa, separated from those dear to him among gods and humans, and experienced great suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, he encountered a malignant illness and immediately passed away.
At that time, Śakra was Kāśyapa Buddha;
the Universal Monarch was my own self.
“Good son! You should know that such separation from those one loves is an extreme great suffering. Good son!”

If even Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas recall such sufferings of separation from loved ones in the past, how much more so should a Bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* contemplate the suffering of separation from loved ones in the present world?
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* contemplate the suffering of association with the disliked? Good son!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that within the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, there is likewise the suffering of association with the disliked.
For example, just as a person regards imprisonment, confinement, shackles, and fetters as great suffering,
so too does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva regard all births within the five realms of existence as the great suffering of being joined with those one hates and loathes.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person who, constantly fearing enemies, shackles, and fetters, abandons his parents, wife, children, kinsmen, treasures, and property to flee far away."
Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: fearing birth and death, they fully practice the six pāramitās and enter into nirvāṇa.
“Kāśyapa! This is called a bodhisattva’s practice of the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa* in contemplating the suffering of association with the disliked. Good son!
How does a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* contemplate the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?
"Seeking" refers to seeking everything exhaustively.
There are two kinds of exhaustive seeking:
First, seeking wholesome dharmas; second, seeking unwholesome dharmas.
That wholesome dharmas have not yet been attained and unwholesome dharmas have not yet been abandoned constitutes, in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
“Kāśyapa! This is called the Truth of Suffering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:
‘The five aggregates of clinging are suffering.’”
This interpretation is not correct. Why?
Because as the Buddha told Śreṇika in the past:
"If form were suffering, all sentient beings would not seek form;
if there are those who seek it, then it cannot be called suffering.
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“There are three kinds of feeling:
painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
This is as the Buddha previously taught to the bhikṣus:
"If there are those who can practice wholesome dharmas, they will experience happiness.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"Within the good realms, one experiences happiness through the six contacts; seeing beautiful forms with the eye is itself happiness."
"It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind when they encounter agreeable phenomena.
As the Buddha said in verse:
"To uphold the precepts is happiness; The body does not undergo manifold sufferings."
Sleeping, one finds peace; waking, the mind is joyful.
When receiving food and clothing, reciting and practicing while walking, dwelling alone in the mountain forests—such is the supreme happiness.
If one can constantly cultivate loving-kindness toward sentient beings day and night,
one will thereby attain constant happiness, for one does not afflict others.
There is the joy of few desires and contentment, and the joy of extensive learning and discernment.
The Arhat who is free from attachment is also called one who experiences happiness;
but the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having ultimately reached the other shore and accomplished all that was to be done, is said to possess the supreme happiness.
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the characteristics of bliss as described in the various sūtras, their meaning is thus.
Now that the Buddha has spoken in this way, how should it correspond with that meaning?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
You have skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding this matter. Good son!
All sentient beings perversely give rise to the notion of pleasure amidst suffering that is inferior.
"Therefore, the characteristics of suffering that I have now described are no different from those of the original [teaching].
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has said:"

Regarding the phrase "conceiving the notion of pleasure within inferior suffering": there are inferior births, inferior aging, inferior illnesses, inferior deaths, inferior separation from the beloved, inferior failure to obtain what is sought, inferior association with the hated, and inferior suffering from the five aggregates of clinging; such sufferings as these should likewise possess pleasure.
"Bhagavān!
'Birth in the lower realms' refers to the three evil destinies;
'birth in the middle realm' refers to among human beings."
"Higher rebirth" refers to birth in the heavens.
Suppose, furthermore, someone were to ask this question:
'If one perceives lower pleasure as suffering, perceives middling pleasure as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, and perceives superior pleasure as pleasure.'
"How should one answer this,
World-Honored One?

If one were to conceive the notion of pleasure within inferior suffering, I have never seen anyone who, when receiving a thousand punishments, would conceive the notion of pleasure at the very first stroke."
"If it does not arise, why do you say:
'Within lower suffering, one gives rise to the perception of pleasure'?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is so, it is so; it is just as you have said.
For this reason, there is no perception of pleasure. Why is that?

It is just as when that person, who was due to receive a thousand punishments, attains release immediately after receiving only one; at that moment, the person gives rise to the perception of pleasure.
Therefore, you should know:
within that which is devoid of pleasure, one falsely gives rise to the perception of pleasure.
Kāśyapa said:
“World-Honored One!
That person does not give rise to the perception of pleasure because of a single blow; rather, it is because he has attained liberation that he gives rise to the perception of pleasure.”
“Kāśyapa! For this reason, when I previously spoke to Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son, Mānava, about the pleasure within the five aggregates, it was indeed true and not false.
Kāśyapa!”
There are three feelings and three sufferings.
The three feelings are: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The three sufferings are: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of conditioned formations, and the suffering of change.
Good son! The sensation of suffering is called the three types of suffering: namely, the suffering of suffering, the suffering of conditioned existence, and the suffering of change;
the other two sensations consist of the suffering of conditioned existence and the suffering of change.
"Good son! For these reasons, there is indeed the sensation of pleasure within the cycle of birth and death.
Because the natures of suffering and pleasure are inseparable, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva therefore says: "
"Everything is suffering.
"Good son! Within birth and death there is truly no happiness; it is only that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, in accordance with worldly conventions, speak of there being happiness."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak in accordance with worldly conventions, is this not false?”
As the Buddha has said:

"Those who practice what is wholesome receive the retribution of happiness; by upholding the precepts they dwell in peace and bliss, their bodies do not undergo suffering, and even when all tasks are completed, this constitutes the supreme joy."
"Are the pleasant sensations described in such sutras as these false?

If they were false, then the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have long cultivated the path to enlightenment for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, would have already abandoned all false speech."
"Now you have made this statement; what is its meaning?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
The verses on experiencing various forms of joy as explained above constitute the very foundation of the path to enlightenment and are also capable of nurturing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the characteristics of happiness were previously explained in the sutras. Good son!
For example, the various necessities of life in the world can serve as causes for happiness and are therefore called "happiness," namely:

Women, indulgence in wine, choice delicacies and sweet flavors; obtaining water when thirsty and encountering fire when cold; clothing, necklaces, elephants, horses, carriages, slaves, servants, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, pearls, and storehouses of grain.
Such things as these, which are required by the world and can serve as causes for pleasure, are called "pleasure.
Good son! Such things as these can also give rise to suffering.
Because of women, men experience the suffering of giving birth, as well as grief, lamentation, and even loss of life;
because of wine, sweet flavors, and even grain in the storehouses, they can likewise cause great distress and affliction to people.
For this reason, all things are suffering and possess no characteristic of pleasure.
"Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding these eight sufferings, understands suffering as being without suffering."
“Good son! All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others do not know the cause of happiness; for such people, I speak of the presence of the characteristic of happiness within inferior suffering.
Only bodhisattvas who dwell in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa are able to know this cause of suffering and this cause of happiness.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Eleven.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twelve.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇa Huìyán and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter on the Noble Practices, Part Two: "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa contemplate the truth of origination?"
"Good son!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates this truth of origination as the causal condition for the aggregates. That which is called 'origination' is, in turn, craving for existence.
There are two kinds of craving:"
First, attachment to one's own body; second, attachment to what is required.
Furthermore, there are two types:
when the five desires have not yet been obtained, one binds the mind to seek them with single-minded devotion.
Once they have been attained, one becomes capable of enduring and remaining devotedly attached to them.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
craving for the realm of desire, craving for the realm of form, and craving for the formless realm.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
craving conditioned by karma, craving conditioned by afflictions, and craving conditioned by suffering.
For those who have left the household life, there are four kinds of craving.
What are the four?
Robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for illness.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
They are greedily attached to the five aggregates, following after all their needs with total craving and attachment, engaging in conceptualization and calculation that is immeasurable and boundless.
"Good son! There are two kinds of craving:
The first is wholesome craving; the second is unwholesome craving.
Unwholesome craving is the pursuit of the foolish and ignorant;
wholesome craving for the Dharma is the pursuit of the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of attachment to wholesome dharmas:
the unwholesome and the wholesome.
Seeking the vehicles of the two [vehicles] is called unwholesome;
Those who seek the Mahāyāna are called "virtuous. Good son!
The craving of ordinary persons is called "accumulation" (saṃudaya), not "truth" (satya).
The love of a bodhisattva is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and is not termed "origination" (samudaya). Why is this?
It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings that they undergo birth; it is not out of craving that they undergo birth.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught in other sūtras for the sake of all sentient beings that karma is the causal condition, or has spoken of pride, or has spoken of the six contacts, or has spoken of ignorance as the causal condition for the five aggregates of clinging.”
"For what reason do you now say that among the Four Noble Truths, it is specifically the nature of craving that serves as the cause for the five aggregates?
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Good son! It is as you have said:
all causes and conditions are neither "for" nor "causes."
However, the five aggregates must depend upon craving. Good son!
It is like a great king who, when he goes out on a tour of inspection, is followed by his ministers and retinue; all follow along together.
Craving is also like this: wherever craving moves, these various fetters and so forth also follow and move along with it.
For example, when dust settles upon a greasy garment, it adheres wherever there is grease;
craving is also like this: wherever there is an object of craving, the karmic fetters also abide there.
Furthermore, good son!
Just as a moist ground can produce sprouts, so too is craving:
it can produce the sprouts of all karmic afflictions.
“Good son! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, he deeply contemplates that this craving has nine kinds:

first, like a debt with a remainder; second, like a rākṣasī wife; third, like a beautiful flower stalk entwined by a venomous snake; fourth, like unwholesome food that one is forced to eat against one’s natural inclination; fifth, like a courtesan; sixth, like the seed of a *mālūka* gourd; seventh, like a malignant growth within a sore; eighth, like a violent wind; and ninth, like a comet.”
"What is meant by 'having a remainder like a debt'? Good son!
It is, for example, like a poor man who owes another person money; although he has nearly finished repaying it, because a small portion remains unpaid, he is still bound in prison and cannot escape."
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise; because they still possess the residual traces of the habit-energy of craving, they are unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! This is called ‘having a remainder like a debt. Good son!”
What is meant by being like a rākṣasī wife?
Son of good family!
It is, for example, as if a man were to obtain a rākṣasī and take her as his wife; that rākṣasī would devour each son born to her as soon as he was born.
Once the children she devoured were exhausted, she then ate her own husband. Good son!
The rākṣasī of craving is just like this: she gives birth to the seeds of roots of goodness within sentient beings, and as soon as they are born, she devours them.
Once the good sons are exhausted, he further devours sentient beings, causing them to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
this applies to all except for bodhisattvas.
This is called being like the wife of a rākṣasī.
“Good son! How is it like a beautiful flower stalk entwined by a venomous snake?

It is, for example, like a person who is fond of flowers; not seeing the danger of the venomous snake on the flower stalk, he immediately reaches out and grasps it. Once grasped, he is bitten by the snake, and having been bitten, his life comes to an end.”

All ordinary beings are likewise: craving the flowers of the five desires, they fail to see the peril of this venomous serpent of attachment and thus seize them; they are immediately stung by the poisonous snake of attachment, and at the end of their lives, they fall into the three evil realms—except for Bodhisattvas.
This is called being like a beautiful flower-stalk entwined by a venomous snake.
"Good son, what is meant by forcibly eating food that is unwholesome?"
It is like a person who forces himself to eat food that he finds unpalatable; having eaten it, his belly aches, and he dies from dysentery.

Craving for food is just like this: sentient beings in the five realms of existence force themselves to eat with greedy attachment, and by this cause and condition, they fall into the three evil paths—except for the Bodhisattvas.
This is called "forcibly eating that which one finds unpalatable. "Good son,
how is it like a courtesan?"
It is like a foolish man who consorts with a courtesan; that courtesan skillfully employs various forms of flattery to feign intimacy and strips away all the man's wealth.
Once his wealth is exhausted, she then casts him out.

The lustful woman is just like this: when a foolish person lacking wisdom engages in intimacy with her, she seizes all his wholesome dharmas; once his wholesome dharmas are exhausted, she drives him away and causes him to fall into the three evil realms—except for the Bodhisattva.
This is called a courtesan. "Good son,
how is it like the seed of a *mālūka*?"

For example, it is like the seed of the *māluka* creeper: if a bird eats it and it falls to the ground with its excrement, or if it is carried by the wind to the foot of a tree, it will immediately sprout and grow. It then entwines and binds a *nyagrodha* tree, preventing it from growing further until the tree eventually withers and dies.

The *āmra* fruit is likewise: it entangles and binds all wholesome dharmas of ordinary beings, preventing them from increasing and causing them to wither away until they perish. Once they have withered and perished, after the end of life, these beings fall into the three evil realms;
this is true for all except for Bodhisattvas.
This is called being like the seed of a *mālūka* fruit. "Good son,
how is it like the granulation tissue within a sore?

It is like a person who has a chronic ulcer from which a fleshy growth (arbuda) has developed; that person must diligently apply themselves to treat it and must not give rise to a mind of indifference.
If they give rise to a mind of indifference, the fleshy growth will increase and worms and abscesses will reappear; by reason of this, they will then meet their end.

The wounds of the five aggregates of ordinary, foolish people are likewise thus; craving acts as the malignant growth within them, and one should diligently apply the mind to treat this growth of craving.
If it is not treated, at the end of life one will immediately fall into the three evil realms;
this excludes only the Bodhisattvas.
This is called a malignant growth within a wound.
“Good son! How is it like a violent wind?
For example, just as a violent wind can topple mountains and level peaks, uprooting them from their deep foundations.”

The violent storm of sensual desire is likewise; it gives rise to malevolent thoughts toward one's parents and can uproot the supreme, profound, and firm root of bodhi of those such as the Great Wisdom Śāriputra, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas.
This is called being like a violent wind. "Good son!
How is it like a comet?"
For example, when a comet appears, all the people in the world suffer from famine, illness, emaciation, and various afflictions.

The comet of craving is likewise; it can sever all seeds of the roots of goodness, causing ordinary persons to become destitute and hungry, giving rise to the disease of afflictions, causing them to transmigrate through birth and death, and endure all manner of suffering—except for Bodhisattvas.
This is called being like a comet. "Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa contemplates these nine kinds of the fetter of craving."
"Good son! For this reason, ordinary worldlings have suffering but no Truth;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have suffering and the Truth of Suffering, yet they lack the ultimate reality."
All bodhisattvas understand that suffering is without suffering; therefore, while there is no suffering, there is the True Truth (*satya*).
Ordinary worldlings have the origin of suffering (*samudaya*) but lack the Truth;
śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have both the origin and the Truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*).
All bodhisattvas understand that accumulation is non-accumulation; therefore, while there is no accumulation, there is true reality (*satya*).
For śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there is cessation but not true reality;
for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, there is both cessation and true reality.
“Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have a path, but it is not the ultimate truth;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have both a path and the ultimate truth. Good son!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, perceive cessation and perceive the truth of cessation?
It is by means of severing all afflictions.
If afflictions are severed, it is called "permanent"; if the fire of afflictions is extinguished, it is called "nirvāṇa"; because afflictions have been extinguished, one attains happiness.
Because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas seek out causes and conditions, it is called "pure."
Because one no longer undergoes the twenty-five states of existence, it is called "transcending the world";
because it transcends the world, it is called "the Self.

Since it never grasps at the characteristics of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles—whether male or female, arising, abiding, or ceasing, or whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—it is called the "Ultimate Quiescence of True Reality."
"Good son! In this way, a bodhisattva dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, contemplating the Noble Truth of Cessation. Good son!"
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, contemplate the noble truth of the path? Good son,
it is like seeing coarse and subtle objects in the darkness by means of a lamp.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, he perceives all dharmas by means of the Eightfold Noble Path—namely, the permanent and the impermanent, the conditioned and the unconditioned, sentient beings and non-sentient beings, entities and non-entities, suffering and pleasure, self and non-self, purity and impurity, afflictions and non-afflictions, karma and non-karma, reality and unreality, vehicles and non-vehicles, knowledge and non-knowledge, *dravya* (substantiality) and non-*dravya*, *guṇa* (quality) and non-*guṇa*, vision and non-vision, form and non-form, the path and non-path, and liberation and non-liberation.
“Good son!
In this way, a bodhisattva dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, contemplating the Noble Truth of the Path.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Eightfold Noble Path were the Noble Truth of the Path, it would not accord with the meaning. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has sometimes said:
"Faith is the path; it can cross over all outflows.
At other times he has said:
"The Path is heedfulness.
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, were heedful, they attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
it is also the dharma that assists the Bodhisattva on the Path."
At other times he says:
"Vigorous effort is the path," as when he addressed Ānanda:
"If there is anyone who can diligently cultivate vigor, they shall achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Or at other times he says:

"Regarding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), if one binds the mind and diligently cultivates this mindfulness of the body, then one shall achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At other times, he says:
"Right concentration is the path.
As he told the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Indeed, right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) is truly the Path;
it is not the case that what is not right concentration is the Path.
Only by entering right concentration can one contemplate the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); it is not possible to contemplate them without entering concentration."
Or he may preach a single dharma:
"If a person practices that which can purify sentient beings, eliminate all sorrow and affliction, and attain the True Dharma—namely, the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi)."
Or again, it may be said:
"Cultivating the perception of impermanence is called the Path.
As it was told to the bhikṣus:
"It is said that one who can extensively cultivate the perception of impermanence can attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Or it is said that by sitting alone in contemplation in a secluded and tranquil *āraṇya*, one can swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At other times he says:
"To expound the Dharma for others is called the Path.
If, having heard the Dharma, one's net of doubts is immediately severed;"
"Once the net of doubt is severed, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At other times, he says:
"The observance of precepts is the Path."
As it was told to Ānanda:
"If there are those who diligently practice and uphold the prohibitive precepts, such persons will cross over the great suffering of birth and death.
Or at other times, he spoke thus:
"To draw near to virtuous friends is what is called the Path.
As it was said to Ānanda:
"If there are those who draw near to virtuous spiritual friends, they will abide in pure precepts."
"If there are sentient beings who are able to draw near to me, they shall give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At other times, he says:
"Cultivating loving-kindness is the path."
"One who cultivates loving-kindness severs all afflictions and attains the immovable state.
At other times, he says:
"Wisdom is the path."
As the Buddha formerly said to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī: "Sister!
Just as the śrāvakas, by means of the sword of wisdom, are able to sever all floods, outflows, and afflictions."
At times the Tathāgata says:
"Generosity is the path.
As the Buddha told King Prasenajit in the past:
"Great King, you should know:
in the past, I practiced giving extensively; by virtue of these causes and conditions, I have today attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“World-Honored One!
If the Eightfold Noble Path is the Truth of the Path, then are such sūtras not false?
If those sūtras are not false, for what reason do they not state that the Eightfold Path is the Noble Truth of the Path?”
"If he had not said so, why would the Tathāgata have committed errors in the past?
Yet I know for certain that all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have long been free from error.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
You have now asked this question because you wish to know all the secrets contained within the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtras of the bodhisattvas.”
"Good son! All such sūtras are entirely included within the Truth of the Path. Good son!"
As I have previously said:
"If there is one who has faith in the Way.
Such faith in the Way is the root of faith; it is that which can assist the path to Bodhi.
Therefore, I say that there is no error in this. "Good son!
The Tathāgata, well-versed in immeasurable skillful means and desiring to transform sentient beings, delivers such various teachings of the Dharma."
"Good son! It is like a skilled physician who recognizes the various sources of illness in sentient beings and prepares medicine according to their specific ailments.

Along with the dietary restrictions for the medicine, only water is not subject to prohibition. Thus, one may take ginger water, licorice water, fine-root water, black rock honey water, *āmalaka* water, *nīpala* water, or *pāṭhola* water; or one may take cold water, hot water, grape water, or pomegranate water."
"Good son! In this way, a skilled physician thoroughly understands the various ailments of sentient beings; although there are many prohibitions regarding medicines, water is not included among them.

The Tathāgata is likewise: skillfully knowing the expedient means within the single characteristic of phenomena, he analyzes and extensively explains various names and characteristics according to the needs of sentient beings."

Those sentient beings receive the teachings as they were spoken; having received them, they practice them and thereby eliminate their afflictions, just as a patient follows the instructions of a skilled physician and is cured of their ailment.
"Furthermore, good son!
Suppose there is a person who is well-versed in many languages and is present among a great assembly.
This assembly is oppressed by heat and thirst, and they all raise their voices, saying: "
"I wish to drink water; I wish to drink water.

At that moment, this person, according to the various types [of beings], spoke of water using their respective names: some called it *pāṇī*, some *udaka*, some *vāri*, some *salila*, some *bali*, some *vāya*, some *amṛta*, and some "cow's milk. Using such immeasurable names for water, he spoke thus to the great assembly.
Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise;
with a single noble path, he expounds it in various ways for the sake of the śrāvakas, ranging from the faculty of faith up to the eightfold noble path.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a goldsmith who, using a single kind of gold, fashions according to his will various kinds of ornaments—namely, necklaces, chains, rings, bracelets, hairpins, earrings, celestial crowns, and armlets."
Although there are such differences and distinctions, they do not depart from gold.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata is likewise;
by means of the single Buddha-way, he teaches it according to the various conceptualizations of sentient beings.
Some speak of one kind, namely that all Buddhas have a single path without duality.
Others speak of two kinds, namely concentration and wisdom.
Still others speak of three kinds, namely vision, discernment, and knowledge.

Furthermore, four kinds are taught: namely, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), and the path of the Buddha (*buddhamārga*).

Furthermore, five kinds are taught: namely, the path of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārimārga*), the path of those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārimārga*), the path of those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimuktamārga*), the path of those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāptamārga*), and the path of bodily realization (*kāyasākṣimārga*).

Furthermore, six kinds are taught: namely, the path of the srotāpanna, the path of the sakṛdāgāmin, the path of the anāgāmin, the path of the arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha.

Furthermore, seven kinds are taught, namely: the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity.
Furthermore, eight kinds are taught, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Furthermore, nine kinds are taught, namely the Eightfold Noble Path and faith.
Furthermore, ten kinds are taught, namely the Ten Powers.
Furthermore, eleven kinds are taught, namely the Ten Powers and great compassion.
Furthermore, it is said that there are twelve kinds, namely the ten powers, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.
Furthermore, it is said that there are thirteen kinds, namely the ten powers, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi.

Furthermore, sixteen kinds are taught, namely: the ten powers, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the Buddha-remembrance samādhi, and the three bases of right mindfulness attained by the Buddha.
Furthermore, twenty paths are taught, namely: the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi, and the three foundations of mindfulness.
“Good son! This Way is of a single essence; however, for the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata has made various distinctions in the past.
Furthermore, good son!”
For example, a single fire receives various names depending on what it burns, such as wood-fire, grass-fire, chaff-fire, flour-fire, or cow-dung and horse-manure fire.
Good son! The Buddha-way is likewise: it is one and without duality.
For the sake of sentient beings, it is differentiated in various ways.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a single consciousness that is explained as sixfold: when it reaches the eye, it is called eye-consciousness, and so on up to mental consciousness, which is likewise."
Good son! The Way is likewise: it is one and without duality.
It is only for the sake of transforming all sentient beings that the Tathāgata makes various distinctions.
"Furthermore, good son! For example, regarding a single form:

that which is seen by the eye is called 'form'; that which is heard by the ear is called 'sound'; that which is smelled by the nose is called 'fragrance'; that which is tasted by the tongue is called 'flavor'; and that which is felt by the body is called 'tactile object'."
Good son! The Way is also like this: it is one and without duality.
It is only for the sake of transforming sentient beings that the Tathāgata makes various distinctions.
"Good son! For this reason, the eightfold noble path is called the Noble Truth of the Path. Good son!"
