"These Four Noble Truths were taught in succession by all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones.
By this cause and condition, immeasurable sentient beings attain deliverance from birth and death.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Once, when the Buddha was staying on the banks of the Ganges in the Śīśumāragiri Forest,
the Tathāgata took up some small tree leaves and addressed the bhikṣus:”
"Are there more leaves held in my hand now,
or are there more leaves of all the grasses and trees growing upon the earth?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
All the earth, trees, grasses, and leaves upon it are so numerous that they cannot be measured or calculated;
what the Tathāgata has grasped is but a small fraction, hardly worth mentioning.”

"O bhikṣus! All dharmas that I have fully awakened to and realized are like the grasses and trees growing from the great earth; those that I have proclaimed for the sake of sentient beings are like the leaves in my hand."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
"The Tathāgata has realized immeasurable dharmas.
If one enters into the Four Noble Truths, they have already been explained.
"If one does not enter [this], there would have to be five truths.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
The question you have now asked will bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
Good son!"
"In this way, all these dharmas are entirely subsumed within the Four Noble Truths.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If such dharmas as these are contained within the Four Truths, for what reason did the Tathāgata declare that he had not taught them?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Although one has entered therein, it is still not called 'explaining'."
Why is this? Son of good family!
There are two kinds of wisdom regarding the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths:
First is the middling, and second is the superior.
The middling refers to the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the superior refers to the wisdom of all buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Good son! To know that the aggregates are suffering is called middle-grade wisdom;
to discern that the aggregates possess immeasurable characteristics, all of which are suffering, such that it is beyond the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—this is called superior wisdom.
"Good son! Such meanings as these I have not at all explained in that sūtra. Good son!"
To know the various sense bases (*āyatana*) as being called "gateways" and also as being "suffering" is termed middling wisdom;

to discern that the various sense bases possess immeasurable characteristics and that they are entirely suffering—knowledge that is beyond the reach of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*—is termed superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these I have not explained in that sūtra. "Good son!
To know the various realms (dhātus) is called 'analysis' (bhāga), it is also called 'nature' (prakṛti), and it is also called 'suffering' (duḥkha); this is termed middling wisdom."

To discern that the various realms possess immeasurable characteristics, all of which are suffering, and that this is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is called superior wisdom. Good son!
Such meanings as these, I have also not spoken of in that sutra.
"Good son! To know the characteristic of the disintegration of form is called middle-level wisdom;
To discern that all forms possess immeasurable characteristics and that these are entirely suffering—something unknown to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I did not even mention in that sūtra.
“Good son! To know the characteristics of the sensation of feeling is called middle wisdom;
to discern that all sensations possess immeasurable characteristics of perception, which is beyond the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, is called superior wisdom.”
"Good son! Such meanings as these were not even spoken by me in that sutra. Good son!"
To know that perception grasps signs is called middle wisdom;
to discern that perception involves immeasurable grasping of signs, which is beyond the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I have not explained in that sutra either.
"Good son! To know the characteristics of conditioned activity is called middling wisdom;
The distinction is that it practices the characteristics of immeasurable deeds, which is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
this is called superior wisdom. Good son! Such meanings as these I did not even mention in that sūtra.
“Good son! To discern the characteristics of the differentiation of consciousness is called middling wisdom;
to discern the characteristics of the immeasurable knowledge of consciousness—which is not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom.”
"Good son! Such meanings as these were not even spoken by me in that sūtra. Good son!"
To know that the causal conditions of craving can give rise to the five aggregates is called middle wisdom;

to know that a single person gives rise to immeasurable and boundless cravings, which cannot be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and to be able to know all such cravings arising in all sentient beings, is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I have not even mentioned in that sutra. "Good son!
To know the cessation of afflictions is called middling wisdom;
The discrimination of afflictions is incalculable, and their cessation is likewise incalculable; this is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and is therefore called supreme wisdom.
I have not explained such meanings in that sutra either.
"Good son! To know these characteristics of the path as being able to leave afflictions behind is called middling wisdom;

The characteristics of the path are differentiated as being immeasurable and boundless, and the afflictions to be abandoned are likewise immeasurable and boundless; these are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and this is called supreme wisdom.
Such meanings as these I have not spoken of in that sutra either.
"Good son! One who knows the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is said to possess middle-level wisdom;
The distinctions of conventional truth are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, beyond what can be known by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
this is called superior wisdom.
Such meanings as these, I did not even mention in that sūtra.
“Good son! That all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all dharmas are without self, and nirvana is quiescent extinction is the ultimate truth; this is called middle wisdom.
To know that the ultimate truth is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, such that it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is called superior wisdom.”
"Such meanings as these, I have also not spoken of in that sutra.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Regarding the conventional truth and the ultimate truth that have been taught, what is their meaning?
World-Honored One,
does the conventional truth exist within the ultimate truth?
Within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), does the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) exist?
If it exists, then there would be only one truth;
if it does not exist, would this not mean that the Tathāgata’s teaching is false?
“Good son! The conventional truth is itself the ultimate truth.
“World-Honored One!”
"If that were so, then there would be no two truths.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
There is a skillful means that, in accordance with sentient beings, teaches the existence of two truths. Good son!
If one follows verbal expression, there are two kinds:
The first is worldly phenomena, and the second is supramundane phenomena.
Good son! That which is known by those who have transcended the world is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
That which is known by worldly people is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Good son!
When the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are combined, one refers to them as 'so-and-so. Ordinary beings follow these designations; this is called the conventional truth."

To understand that within the aggregates there is no such thing as a personal name, and that apart from the aggregates there is likewise no such thing as a personal name—such that one who has transcended the world can know this according to its true nature and characteristics—is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There are some phenomena that possess both name and reality;
there are also some phenomena that possess a name but lack reality."
Good son! That which has a name but no reality is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that which has both a name and reality is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
"Good son!

Such things as the self, sentient beings, life-span, cognition and vision, nourishment, the person, the agent, the experiencer, a mirage in the heat, a city of the Gandharvas, hair on a tortoise, horns on a rabbit, a circle of fire from a whirling torch, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—these are called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—these are called ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
“Good son! There are five kinds of worldly phenomena:
first, the world of names; second, the world of phrases; third, the world of bonds; fourth, the world of dharmas; and fifth, the world of attachment.”
Good son! What is called the world of names?
Male, female, jar, clothing, carriage, house—such things as these are called the world of names.
What is the world of phrases?
A single verse consists of four lines; such verses as these constitute the world of phrases.
What is the world of bonds?
Rolling up, tying, binding, joining the palms, and fettering—these are called the world of bondage (*bandhana-loka*).
What is the world of phenomena (*dharma-loka*)?
Such as striking the gong to assemble the monastic community, beating the drum to warn the soldiers, and blowing the conch to signal the time—these are called the world of phenomena.
What is attachment to the world?
It is like seeing a person from afar wearing dyed robes and forming a conceptual attachment, saying:
"This is a śramaṇa, not a brāhmaṇa."
Seeing someone with a knotted cord slung across their body, one immediately forms the thought:
"This is a brāhmaṇa, not a śramaṇa.
This is called attachment to the world.
“Good son! These are called the five worldly dharmas. Good son!”

If there are sentient beings who, regarding these five kinds of worldly dharmas, possess no inverted views in their minds and know them as they truly are, this is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
"Furthermore, good son!
If there is burning, cutting, death, or destruction, this is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that there is no burning, no cutting, no death, and no destruction is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
"Furthermore, good son!
There are eight characteristics of suffering which are called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);

the absence of birth, the absence of aging, the absence of illness, the absence of death, the absence of separation from the beloved, the absence of encountering the hated, the absence of not obtaining what one seeks, and the absence of the five aggregates of clinging—these are called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
"Furthermore, good son! It is like a single person who possesses many skills:

when he runs, he is called a runner; when he harvests, he is called a harvester; when he prepares food and drink, he is called a cook; when he works with timber, he is called a carpenter; and when he smelts gold and silver, he is called a goldsmith. Thus, one person has many names."
The Dharma is also like this: its essence is one, yet it has many names.
That which arises from the union of father and mother is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that which arises from the conjunction of the twelve links of dependent origination is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
as for that which is called ‘the truth of reality,’ what is its meaning?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! That which is called ultimate truth is named the True Dharma."
Good son! If a dharma is not true, it is not called an ultimate truth (satya). Good son!
The ultimate truth is free from inversion; that which is free from inversion is called the ultimate truth.
Good son! The ultimate truth is devoid of falsehood.
If there is falsehood, it cannot be called the True Truth. Good son!
The True Truth is named the Mahāyāna.
That which is not of the Mahāyāna is not called the True Dharma (satya). Good son!
The True Dharma is that which is spoken by the Buddha, not that which is spoken by Māra.
If it were the teaching of Māra and not the teaching of the Buddha, it would not be called the True Truth. Good son!
The True Truth is the single path of purity; there are no two.
“Good son!
That which possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is what is called the meaning of the ultimate truth.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If that which is true is taken as the True Truth (*satyadharma*), then the Dharma of reality is itself the Tathāgata, space, and Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
If this is so, then there is no distinction between the Tathāgata, space, and Buddha-nature.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“There is suffering, there is its truth, and there is its reality;
there is origination, there is its truth, and there is its reality.”
Cessation exists; it is true and real.
The Path exists; it is true and real.
O son of good family!
The Tathāgata is neither suffering nor a truth, yet he is real;
space is neither suffering nor a truth, yet it is real;
the Buddha-nature is neither suffering nor a truth, yet it is real.
“Mañjuśrī! That which is called suffering has the characteristic of impermanence and the characteristic of being subject to cessation; this is the ultimate truth.
The nature of the Tathāgata is neither suffering, nor impermanent, nor subject to cessation; therefore, it is the ultimate reality.”
Space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.

Furthermore, son of good family, that which is called "accumulation" (samudaya) is that which causes the five aggregates to combine and arise; it is also called suffering and also called impermanence. It is a characteristic that can be severed, and this is the Truth of Reality.
"Good son!
The Tathāgata is not of the nature of aggregation, nor is he the cause of the aggregates, nor does he possess the characteristic of being subject to cessation;
therefore, he is real. Space and the Buddha-nature are likewise."
"Good son! That which is called 'extinction' refers to the extinction of afflictions; it is both permanent and impermanent.
That which is attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles is called impermanent; [that which is attained by the Bodhisattvas] is called permanent."
That which all Buddhas have attained is called "eternal" and is also called the "realized Dharma"; this is the true reality (*satya*). Good son!

The nature of the Tathāgata is not called "extinguished," for it can extinguish afflictions; it is neither eternal nor impermanent, and it is not called "realized knowledge. It dwells eternally without change, and for this reason, it is real.
Space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.
"Good son! The Path can sever afflictions; it is both eternal and impermanent, and it is a dharma that can be cultivated. This is called the True Truth."

The Tathāgata is not a path, yet he is able to sever the afflictions; he is neither eternal nor impermanent, nor is he a dharma to be cultivated. He is eternally abiding and unchanging, and for this reason he is real.
Space and the Buddha-nature are also like this.
"Furthermore, good son!
That which is called 'reality' is the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata is reality."
Reality is space; space is reality. Reality is the Buddha-nature.
"Buddha-nature is precisely reality.
Mañjuśrī! There is suffering, there is the cause of suffering, there is the cessation of suffering, and there is the remedy for suffering."
The Tathāgata is neither suffering nor even its opposite; therefore, he is the Real (satya) and is not termed a Truth (satya).
It is the same for empty space and Buddha-nature.
Suffering is conditioned, outflowing, and devoid of bliss.
“The Tathāgata is neither conditioned nor tainted; he is profoundly serene and blissful. This is reality, not a [conventional] truth.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One!”
As the Buddha has said:
"That which is non-perverted is called the ultimate truth.
If this is so, are there four perversions among the Four Noble Truths?
If such things existed, why would it be said that "the absence of perversion is called the ultimate truth"?
All perversions are not called real.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"All inversions enter into the Truth of Suffering.
Just as sentient beings possess inverted minds, they are called 'inverted.'"

Good son! For example, suppose there are people who do not accept the instructions of their parents and elders, or who, though they have accepted them, are unable to practice in accordance with them; such persons as these are called "perverted."
"Such perversions are not non-suffering; they are indeed suffering.
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught:"
"That which is not false is the ultimate truth.
If this is so, one should know that what is false is not the ultimate truth.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! All that is false enters into the Truth of Suffering.

For instance, if there are sentient beings who deceive others, by reason of these causes and conditions they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; such phenomena as these are called ‘false.’”
Such falsehoods are not non-suffering; they are indeed suffering.
Because Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, distance themselves from them and do not practice them, they are called "falsehoods."
"Because such falsehoods have been severed and eliminated by the Buddhas and those of the Two Vehicles, it is called the 'Truth of Reality'.
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught:"
Regarding the statement, "The Mahāyāna is the true truth," one should know that the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not true.
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! Those of the two vehicles are both real and unreal.
That śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have severed all afflictions is what is called ‘real’;”
"Impermanence and non-abiding are phenomena subject to change;
they are called unreal. Mañjuśrī said:
"As the Buddha has taught:"
“If that which the Buddha has spoken is called real, one should know that what Māra speaks is unreal.
“World-Honored One!
Is that which Māra speaks subsumed within the Noble Truths?”
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī! That which is spoken by Māra is subsumed within the two truths, namely, suffering and its origin."

Whatever is not in accordance with the Dharma and not in accordance with the Vinaya, which cannot bring benefit to people, and through which no one—despite being taught all day long—sees suffering, abandons its origin, realizes its cessation, or cultivates the path, is called false and deceptive.
"Such falsehoods are called the teachings of Māra. Mañjuśrī said:
"As the Buddha has taught:"
Regarding the statement, "The One Path is pure and there is no duality," various non-Buddhists likewise say:
"I have a One Path that is pure and without duality."
"If you say that this 'One Path' is the true truth, what difference is there from those non-Buddhists?
If there is no difference, you should not say:
'The One Path is pure.'"
The Buddha said: “Good son!

Among the various non-Buddhists, there are the truths of suffering and its origin, but they lack the truths of cessation and the path. They conceive the notion of cessation regarding that which is not cessation; they conceive the notion of the path regarding that which is not the path; they conceive the notion of the fruit regarding that which is not the fruit; and they conceive the notion of the cause regarding that which is not the cause.”
"For this reason, that single path is pure and non-dual.
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught:"
Regarding the claim that "there is permanence, there is self, there is bliss, and there is purity—
this is the true meaning," such would constitute a true reality for the various non-Buddhists and others, but it does not exist within the Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? For even the various non-Buddhist sects likewise proclaim:
"All conditioned phenomena are permanent."
"What is meant by 'constant'?
It is because the experiences of agreeable, disagreeable, and various karmic retributions are never lost.
'Agreeable' refers to the retribution of the ten wholesome actions."
That which is disagreeable is the retribution for the ten unwholesome actions.

If one says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent, and that the agent has already perished therein, who then would receive the fruit and retribution in that [future state]?
For this reason, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent.
Because they are the causal condition for killing, they are called "permanent.
World-Honored One!
If one says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent, then both the killer and the victim are impermanent.
If they are impermanent, who is it that undergoes the retribution of sin in hell?
"If it were said that there is definitely retribution received in hell, one should know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would truly not be impermanent.
World-Honored One!
To bind the mind in single-minded recollection is also called 'constant'; for what is recollected after ten years, even up to a hundred years, is not forgotten, and therefore it is constant."
If things were impermanent, who would remember or who would recollect the objects previously perceived?
For this reason, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not impermanent.
“World-Honored One!
All conceptualizations are also called ‘permanent.
Suppose a person first sees the features of another’s hands, feet, head, neck, and so forth; later, upon seeing them again, they recognize them.”
“If it were impermanent, its original characteristics would have perished.
World-Honored One!

All actions performed through long-term cultivation—whether learned from the beginning, or after three years, or after five years—are then thoroughly mastered; therefore, they are called ‘permanent.’”
“World-Honored One!
According to the method of calculation, one proceeds from one to two, from two to three, and so on up to a hundred and a thousand.
If these were impermanent, then the very first number should perish.”
If the first were to perish, who would then reach the second?
Thus, being eternally one, there would ultimately never be a second.
Because the one does not perish, it can reach the second, and so on up to the hundredth and the thousandth; therefore, it is eternal.
“World-Honored One!
Just as one recites the Dharma, reciting one Āgama, then two Āgamas, and even three or four Āgamas—
yet because it is impermanent, that which is being recited will ultimately never reach four.”
Because this reading and recitation increase [virtue] through such causes and conditions, it is called "constant.
"World-Honored One!
A jar, a robe, or a carriage are like a person who owes a debt;..."
The features of the great earth, mountains, rivers, forests, medicinal trees, grasses, leaves, and the healing of sentient beings—all these are likewise eternal.
“World-Honored One!
All non-Buddhists say this:
‘All conditioned phenomena are permanent.’”
"If it were permanent, it would be the ultimate truth.
World-Honored One!
There are other heterodox teachers who further claim that there is pleasure."
How is this known?
Because the recipient will certainly obtain a desirable reward.
World-Honored One!
All who experience pleasure will certainly obtain it—namely, the Great Brahmā King, Maheśvara, Śakra-devānām-indra, Viṣṇu, and all humans and devas.
For this reason, it is said that there definitely exists pleasure.
"World-Honored One!

There are other non-Buddhists who further claim that pleasure exists because it causes sentient beings to give rise to longing; the hungry seek food, the thirsty seek drink, the cold-seekers seek warmth, the heat-seekers seek coolness, the exhausted seek rest, the sick seek recovery, and those with desire seek form."
"If there were no pleasure, for what reason would they seek it?
Since there is seeking, we know that pleasure exists.
World-Honored One!"
There are certain non-Buddhists who further say:
"Generosity can bring about happiness.

People of the world delight in giving to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, and those in distress clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, elephants, horses, carriages, powdered incense, ointments, various flowers, dwellings for shelter, and lamps.
"By performing various acts of giving such as these, one will receive desirable retribution in future lives; therefore, one should know that pleasure definitely exists.
World-Honored One!"
Certain non-Buddhists further say:
"One should know that there is pleasure because of causes and conditions.
That which is called the experience of pleasure is termed a pleasant contact precisely because it has causes and conditions.
If there were no pleasure, how could there be causes and conditions?
Just as there are no causes and conditions for a rabbit's horns because they do not exist, one knows that pleasure exists because there are causes and conditions for pleasure.
"World-Honored One!..."
Other non-Buddhists further say:
"Because there are superior, middling, and inferior [capacities], one should know that pleasure exists.
Those who experience inferior pleasure are Śakra-devānām-indra;
Those who experience pleasure in the middle are the Great Brahmā King;
those who experience pleasure in the highest are Maheśvara.
Because there are such distinctions as superior, middling, and inferior, one should know that pleasure exists.
“World-Honored One!
There are certain non-Buddhists who further claim that there is purity. Why is this so?”
If there were no purity, desire would not arise; since desire arises, one should know that purity exists.

Furthermore, it is said that gold, silver, precious gems, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, coral, pearl, jade, conch shells, flowing springs, bathing pools, food and drink, clothing, flowers, incense powder, ointments, and the light of lamps and candles—all such things as these are pure dharmas.

"Furthermore, there is purity: that which is called the five aggregates is itself a pure vessel, containing all pure things—namely, humans, devas, various sages, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas."
For this reason, it is called "pure.
"World-Honored One,
there are various non-Buddhists who further claim that there is a self, because it perceives objects and is capable of performing actions."
It is like a person who enters a potter’s workshop; although they do not see the potter’s body, by seeing the wheel and the cord, they know for certain that the house must belong to a potter.
I am also like this: having seen forms with my eyes, I certainly know that there is a self.
If there were no self, who would be able to see forms?
It is the same for hearing sounds, and so on, up to touching tangibles and cognizing mental phenomena.
"Furthermore, there is a self.
How is this known? It is known by means of its characteristics."
What are these characteristics? They are:

breathing, blinking, the life-span, the activity of the mind, the experiencing of various pains and pleasures, craving, and aversion. All such phenomena are the characteristic of a self; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
"Furthermore, there exists a self, because it is capable of discriminating tastes.
When someone eats a fruit, they perceive it and know its taste; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self."
"Furthermore, there is a self.
How is this known? Because of the grasping of performed actions."

Holding a sickle one can reap; holding an axe one can chop; holding a vessel one can contain water; holding a chariot one can drive it. Such matters as these are performed by the grasping self (*ātman*); therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
"Furthermore, there is a self.
How is this known?
At the very moment of birth, one desires to be nursed; because this is due to the influence of past habitual tendencies, one should therefore know that there must certainly be a self."
"Furthermore, how is it known that there is a self?
Because it brings benefit through association with other sentient beings.
For example, when things such as jars, clothing, vehicles, fields, houses, mountains, forests, trees, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep are combined, they provide benefit."

These five internal aggregates are likewise so: because the various faculties such as the eye exist in combination, they benefit the self; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
"Furthermore, there is a self.
How is this known? Because there is the phenomenon of negation."
If there is a thing, then there is obstruction; if there were no thing, there would be no obstruction.
If there is obstruction, one knows that there is a self; therefore, one should know that there must certainly be a self.
"Furthermore, there is a self.
How is this known?
Because of companionship and non-companionship."

Relatives and non-relatives are not companions; the True Dharma and the false Dharma are likewise not companions; wisdom and ignorance are likewise not companions; śramaṇas and non-śramaṇas, brahmins and non-brahmins, sons and non-sons, day and non-day, night and non-night, self and non-self—such dharmas as these are either companions or non-companions. Therefore, one should know that there must certainly exist a self.
“World-Honored One!

Since the various non-Buddhist practitioners speak in manifold ways of the existence of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, one should know that there definitely exist permanence, bliss, self, and purity.”
World-Honored One!
For this reason, the various non-Buddhists may also say:
"I possess the ultimate truth."
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain that there is permanence, pleasure, purity, and a self, they are neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas."
Why is this? Because they are deluded regarding birth and death, having strayed from the Great Guide of All-Knowledge.
Thus, these śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others are submerged in various desires, and their wholesome dharmas have become weak and diminished.
These non-Buddhists are bound within the prison of greed, hatred, and delusion because they endure and take pleasure in them.
Although these non-Buddhists know that the fruits of karma are self-created and self-received, they are still unable to distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas.
These various non-Buddhists do not possess the true Dharma, right livelihood, or a proper means of subsistence. Why is this?
Because they lack the fire of wisdom and are thus unable to digest [their food].
Although these non-Buddhists desire and crave the five exquisite sensual pleasures, they are impoverished by wholesome dharmas because they do not practice them diligently.
Although these non-Buddhists desire to reach true liberation, their feet of ethical discipline are not perfected.
Although these non-Buddhists seek happiness, they are unable to seek the causes and conditions for happiness.
Although these non-Buddhists loathe all forms of suffering, their practices are nonetheless unable to distance them from the causes and conditions of suffering.
Although these non-Buddhists are entwined by the four great poisonous snakes, they still act with negligence and fail to exercise caution.
Enshrouded by ignorance and estranged from virtuous friends, they delight in remaining within the triple world—a realm of impermanent, fiercely blazing fire—and are unable to escape.
These non-Buddhists encounter the incurable diseases of the various afflictions, yet they do not seek the Great Wisdom Physician.
These non-Buddhists are about to traverse the boundless, perilous, and remote paths of the future, yet they do not know to adorn themselves with the provisions of the wholesome Dharma.
These non-Buddhists are constantly harmed by the calamitous poison of lustful desire, yet they instead embrace the frost-like poison of the five sensual pleasures.
These non-Buddhists harbor a blazing intensity of anger, yet they further draw near to evil friends.
These non-Buddhists are constantly shrouded by ignorance, yet they instead seek out evil and wicked teachings.
These non-Buddhists are constantly deceived and deluded by false views, yet they instead conceive thoughts of intimacy and affection toward them.
These non-Buddhists desire sweet fruit, yet they sow bitter seeds.
These non-Buddhists already dwell within the dark chamber of afflictions, yet they instead distance themselves from the brilliant light of the great torch of wisdom.
These non-Buddhists suffer from the thirst of afflictions, yet they instead drink the salty water of sensual desires.
These non-Buddhists are adrift and submerged in the boundless great river of birth and death, yet they remain far removed from the unsurpassed Captain.
These various non-Buddhists are deluded and inverted,
claiming that "all conditioned phenomena are permanent.
That conditioned phenomena could be permanent is impossible.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Twelve.
[Continued from] The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Thirteen.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huiyan and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
From the latter part of the "Chapter on Noble Conduct": "Good son!
I observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent."
How is this known?
It is through causes and conditions.
If there are phenomena that arise from conditions, then one knows them to be impermanent.
Among these various non-Buddhists, there is not a single dharma that does not arise from conditions.

Good son! The Buddha-nature is without birth and without cessation; it neither goes nor comes; it is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present; it is not produced by causes, nor is it produced without cause; it is neither an action nor an agent; it is neither with marks nor without marks; it is neither named nor nameless; it is neither name nor form; it is neither long nor short; it is not comprised or sustained by the aggregates, elements, or sense bases; therefore, it is called "constant."
"Good son! Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Dharma; and the Dharma is eternal. Good son!"
That which is eternal is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Saṅgha; and the Saṅgha is eternal.
For this reason, dharmas produced from causes are not called eternal.
Among these non-Buddhists, there is not a single dharma that does not arise from causes. Good son!
These non-Buddhists do not perceive the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, or the Dharma; therefore, all that the non-Buddhists speak is false speech, devoid of true reality.

Ordinary worldlings first perceive jars, clothing, vehicles, houses, cities, rivers, mountains and forests, men, women, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; subsequently, when they see something similar, they declare it to be permanent.
"You should know that in reality, it is not permanent.
Good son, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
Space is unconditioned; therefore, it is eternal.
Buddha-nature is unconditioned; therefore, it is eternal.
Space is precisely Buddha-nature; Buddha-nature is precisely the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is precisely the unconditioned; the unconditioned is precisely the eternal.
That which is eternal is the Dharma; that which is the Dharma is the Sangha; the Sangha is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
and that which is unconditioned is the eternal. "Good son!
There are two kinds of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*):"
There are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*).
Non-material phenomena are the mind and its mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*);
material phenomena are earth, water, fire, and wind.
“Good son! The mind is called impermanent. Why is this?
The nature [of consciousness] is that which grasps objects, because it is associated with conceptual discrimination. Good son!
The nature of eye-consciousness differs, and so on up to the nature of mind-consciousness; therefore, they are impermanent.
"Good son!
The realm of form is distinct, and so on up to the realm of phenomena being distinct;
therefore, they are impermanent. Good son!"
Visual consciousness is distinct from [the others] up to mental consciousness being distinct; therefore, they are impermanent.
Good son, if the mind were permanent, visual consciousness alone should be able to perceive all phenomena.
Good son! If the visual consciousness were different [from moment to moment], and so on up to the mental consciousness being different, then one would know them to be impermanent.
Because these phenomena are similar to one another, arising and ceasing from moment to moment, ordinary people perceive them and reckon them to be permanent.
“Good son! Because the characteristics of all causes and conditions are subject to destruction, they are also called impermanent.

That is to say, eye-consciousness arises depending on the eye, depending on forms, depending on light, and depending on mental attention; when ear-consciousness arises, its respective conditions are distinct and are not the causes and conditions of eye-consciousness.”
This applies likewise up to the point where the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) differs.
Furthermore, son of good family,
because the causes and conditions that destroy all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) differ, the mind is called impermanent.
That which is called the cultivation of the mind of impermanence is distinct from the cultivation of suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

If the mind were permanent, one would always be cultivating impermanence; one would not even be able to contemplate suffering, emptiness, and non-self, let alone be able to contemplate permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For this reason, within the teachings of the non-Buddhists, it is impossible to encompass permanence, bliss, self,
and purity. Good son,
you should know that mental phenomena are necessarily impermanent.
"Furthermore, good son, because the natures of mind differ, they are called impermanent;
that is to say, the nature of the mind of the śrāvakas differs, the nature of the mind of the pratyekabuddhas differs, and the nature of the mind of the Buddhas differs."
The minds of all non-Buddhists are of three kinds:

first, the mind of those who have left the household life; second, the mind of those who remain in the household life; and third, the mind of those who remain in the household life while practicing detachment.

The mind associated with pleasure is distinct; the mind associated with pain is distinct; the mind associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure is distinct. The mind associated with sensual desire is distinct; the mind associated with ill will is distinct; the mind associated with delusion is distinct.

The mental characteristics of all non-Buddhists are likewise diverse: the mind associated with ignorance is distinct, the mind associated with doubt is distinct, and the mind associated with false views is distinct; even their movements, halts, and modes of deportment differ accordingly.
“Good son! If the mind were permanent, it likewise would be unable to distinguish various forms, namely blue, yellow, red, white, and purple.”
"Good son!
If the mind were permanent, then all dharmas that have been recollected should not be forgotten.
Good son!"
If the mind were permanent, there would be no increase in whatever one recites or chants.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if the mind were permanent, one should not speak of what has been done, what is being done, or what is yet to be done.
If there are [actions] already performed, currently being performed, or yet to be performed, you should know that this mind is necessarily impermanent.
Good son! If the mind were permanent, then there would be no distinction between enemy and friend, nor between neither-enemy-nor-friend.
If the mind were permanent, one should not speak of "my things" or "another's things," nor of death or birth.
If the mind were permanent, even though it performs actions, it should not undergo increase.
Good son! For this reason, you should know that the natures of the mind are each distinct.
Because they are distinct, you should know that they are impermanent.

“Good son! I have now expounded impermanence within these non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*), and their meaning has been made manifest; I shall further explain for you the impermanence of material form (*rūpa*).”
This form is impermanent and fundamentally has no arising.
Because it ceases after having arisen, there was fundamentally no arising when the internal body was in the womb during the stage of the *kalala*.
Because it changes after having arisen, external things such as sprouts and stalks likewise fundamentally have no arising.
Because that which has arisen undergoes transformation, one should know that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are entirely impermanent.
"Good son! All internal matter changes according to the times:

The stage of the kalala is different; the stage of the arbuda is different; the stage of the peśī is different; the stage of the ghana is different; the stage of the praśākhā is different; the stage of birth is different; the stage of infancy is different; the stage of childhood is different; and so on, until the stage of old age, each being subject to transformation and change.
All external forms are likewise so: the sprout is distinct, the stalk is distinct, the branch is distinct, the leaf is distinct, the flower is distinct, and the fruit is distinct.
"Furthermore, good son!
The internal flavors also differ, changing at each stage from the *kalala* phase through to old age.
External flavors are likewise different: the flavors of the sprout, stem, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit are distinct.

The power at the stage of the kalala is different, up to the power at the stage of old age being different; the appearance at the stage of the kalala is different, up to the appearance at the stage of old age being different; the karmic retribution at the stage of the kalala is different, up to the karmic retribution at the stage of old age being different; and the name at the stage of the kalala is different, up to the name at the stage of old age being different.
That which is called internal form, having been destroyed, recombines; therefore, one knows it is impermanent.
External trees likewise, having been destroyed, recombine; therefore, one knows they are impermanent.
"Because they arise sequentially and gradually, one knows they are impermanent.
From the stage of *kalala* up to old age, they arise in succession; from the sprout up to the fruit, they arise in succession; therefore, one knows they are impermanent."
"All forms are subject to cessation; therefore, one knows they are impermanent.

The time of the cessation of the *kalala* differs from the time of the cessation of [the subsequent stages] up to old age; the time of the cessation of the sprout differs from the time of the cessation of [the subsequent stages] up to the fruit; therefore, one knows they are impermanent."
"Ordinary worldlings lack wisdom; seeing that which arises as similar [to what preceded it], they conceive of it as permanent.
For this reason, it is called 'impermanent.
If it is impermanent, it is suffering."
If it is suffering, it is impure. Good son!
Because Kāśyapa previously asked about this matter, I have already answered him regarding it.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
All conditioned phenomena are without self.
Son of good family!"
All phenomena in their entirety consist of the material and the non-material.
Matter is not the self. Why is this?
Because it is subject to being broken, destroyed, split, and snapped, and because it grows and increases;
that which is called "self" cannot be broken, destroyed, split, or snapped, nor does it grow.
For this reason, one knows that form is not the self;
nor is that which is not form the self. Why is this?
Because they arise from causes and conditions. "Good son!
If those non-Buddhists claim that the self is known through the nature of focused mindfulness, the nature of focused mindfulness is in fact not the self."
If one were to take focused mindfulness as the nature of the self, then past events would be subject to forgetfulness;
because there is forgetfulness, it is certain that there is no self. "Good son!
If those non-Buddhists know there is a self by means of recollection and conceptualization, then because they lack such recollection and conceptualization, one can definitively know there is no self.
It is as when one sees a person’s hand has six fingers and immediately asks:
"Where did we previously meet?"
"If there were a self, one should not ask further;
because you ask such questions, it is certain that there is no self. Good son!
If non-Buddhists claim that because there is negation one knows there is a self, then, son of good family,
by virtue of that very negation one definitely knows there is no self.
It is like saying "Devadatta"— one would never say "not Devadatta."
I am also like this.
If it were certainly a self, it would never deny the self;
because it denies the self, we know for certain that there is no self.
If you claim that the self exists because it is negated [by others], then since you do not negate it yourself, there must certainly be no self.
"Good son! If the various non-Buddhists claim that the self exists because of companions or non-companions, then because there are no companions, there should be no self."
There are phenomena that exist without companions, namely the Tathāgata, empty space, and the Buddha-nature;
I am likewise, truly having no companion.
For this reason, it is certain that there is no self.
"Furthermore, good son!
If those non-Buddhists know there is a self because of names, then even within the dharma of no-self there is the name 'self,' just as a poor and lowly person may have the name 'wealthy and noble.'"
It is like saying, "I shall die. If I were to die, it would mean that I am killing myself; yet, in reality, I cannot be killed—it is merely a conventional designation to say "I am killed.
It is also like calling a short person "tall."
For this reason, one certainly knows that there is no self.
"Furthermore, good son!
If the various non-Buddhists claim that because a newborn seeks milk, they know there is a self, good son!"
If there were a self, no infants would ever grasp filth, fire, snakes, or poisonous drugs.
For this reason, it is certain that there is no self.
"Furthermore, good son!
All sentient beings possess equal cognition regarding three things: namely, sexual desire, food and drink, and fear; therefore, there is no self."
"Furthermore, good son!
If the various non-Buddhists claim to know that there is a self by means of its characteristics, good son!
Because of characteristics there is no self, and because of the absence of characteristics there is likewise no self."
If, when a person is asleep, they are unable to move forward or stop, to bend or stretch, to look or blink, and are unaware of suffering or pleasure, there should be no self.
If one were to know that there is a self by means of moving forward or stopping, bending or stretching, looking or blinking, then a wooden puppet operated by machinery should also possess a self.

"Good son! The Tathāgata is also like this: he does not advance, nor does he stop; he does not look down, nor does he look up; he does not gaze, nor does he blink; he has neither suffering nor pleasure; he is without greed, without anger, and without delusion; he does not act. In this way, the Tathāgata truly possesses a self."
"Furthermore, good son!
If those non-Buddhists claim that because they see others eating fruit and saliva is produced in their mouths, they thereby know there is a self, good son!..."
Because of recollection, one sees [the object] and saliva is produced.
Saliva is not the self, nor is the self saliva.

It is neither joy nor sorrow; it is neither weeping nor laughing; it is neither lying down nor rising; it is neither hunger nor satiety. For this reason, one knows with certainty that there is no self.

“Good son! These various non-Buddhists are as ignorant as small children; lacking both wisdom and skillful means, they are unable to comprehend what is permanent and what is impermanent, suffering and pleasure, purity and impurity, self and non-self, life-span and non-life-span, sentient beings and non-sentient beings, reality and unreality, existence and non-existence.”
Within the Buddha-dharma, they grasp a mere fraction and falsely reckon it to possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity, yet in reality they do not know permanence, bliss, self, or purity.
It is like a person born blind who does not know the color of milk and asks another,
"What is the color of milk like?
To which the other replies:
"The color is white like a conch shell.
The blind man asked again:
"Does that which is the color of milk have the sound of a conch shell?"
He replied, "No. He asked again:
"What does the color of the conch shell resemble?
He replied,
"It is like the powder of rice."
The blind man asked again:
"Is the color and texture of the milk like rice powder?
And what is rice powder like?"
He replied,
"It is like snow and rain.
The blind man spoke again:
"Is that rice flour as cold as snow?
And what is snow like?
He replied:
"It is like a white crane.
Although those born blind hear these four kinds of analogies, they are ultimately unable to recognize the true color of milk.
These various non-Buddhists are also like this; they are ultimately unable to recognize permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Good son!
For this reason, within my Buddha-dharma there is true reality, which does not exist among the non-Buddhists.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
Now that the Tathāgata is approaching parinirvāṇa, he further turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and thus makes such distinctions regarding the true truths.”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“Why do you now conceive the notion of parinirvāṇa regarding the Tathāgata?
Son of good family!
The Tathāgata is, in truth, eternally abiding and immutable; he does not enter parinirvāṇa.
Good son! If there were one who reckoned:

"I am the Buddha," "I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," "I am the Dharma and the Dharma is mine," "I am the Path and the Path is mine," "I am the World-Honored One and the World-Honored One is mine," "I am the śrāvaka and the śrāvaka is mine," or "I can preach the Dharma for others to hear and accept, and I turn the wheel of the Dharma while others cannot"—the Tathāgata never makes such reckonings.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not turn the wheel of Dharma.
"Good son! If there is someone who makes such a false calculation as this:
"I am the eye, and the eye is mine;
it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
I am form, and form is mine."
This applies even unto the dharmas.
"I am the earth, and the earth is mine";
the same is true for water, fire, wind, and so forth.
"Good son! If someone should say: 'I am faith, and faith is mine; I am much-hearing, and much-hearing is mine;
I am the dānapāramitā, and the dānapāramitā is mine'..."
I am mine; I am the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), and the perfection of ethical discipline is mine.
I am the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), and the perfection of patience is mine.
I am the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), and the perfection of vigor is mine. I am the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*)...
The *pāramitās* and the *dhyānapāramitā* are mine; I am the *prajñāpāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā* is mine.
I am the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the four foundations of mindfulness are mine.
[I am] the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), and the five powers (*bala*).
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path are also like this. Good son,
the Tathāgata never makes such a calculation.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not turn the wheel of Dharma. "Good son!
If one says that it is eternally abiding and without change, how can it be said that the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma?"
Therefore, you should not now say:
"The Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma through skillful means. "Good son!

For example, depending on the eye, with color as a condition, with light as a condition, and with mental attention as a condition, through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, visual consciousness arises.
Good son! The eye does not think:
"Form, and so on, up to volition, never think:
'I produce eye-consciousness.'"
"Visual consciousness likewise does not form the thought:
'I am able to produce myself. Good son!"
In this way, these dharmas, through the harmony of causes and conditions, are designated as "seeing.
Good son, the Tathāgata is likewise;
by means of the six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, he has awakened to and realized all dharmas.
Furthermore, by means of the throat, larynx, tongue, teeth, lips, mouth, speech, and sound, he first preached the Dharma for Kauṇḍinya; this is called "turning the wheel of the Dharma."
For this reason, the Tathāgata is not said to "turn the wheel of Dharma.
Good son! That which does not turn is called the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Tathāgata.
“Good son! It is like fire being produced by means of a fire-drill, a spindle, hands, and dry cow dung.
Yet the fire-drill does not say:”
"I can produce fire.
Neither the fire-drill, the hands, nor the cow dung thinks to itself:
"I can produce fire."
Fire likewise does not say:
"I am able to produce myself.

The Tathāgata is also like this: because of the six pāramitās, up to the name of Kauṇḍinya, the wheel of Dharma is turned; yet the Tathāgata likewise does not give rise to the thought or say: [“I have turned it”].
"I turn the wheel of Dharma.
O son of good family!
If there is no arising, this is what is called turning the true wheel of Dharma.
This turning of the wheel of Dharma is itself named the Tathāgata. "Good son!
It is like obtaining ghee by depending on curd, water, churning, a vessel, a rope, and a person’s hand grasping them."
The curd does not think,
"I am able to produce butter," and even the human hand does not think:
"I can produce ghee," yet the ghee does not say,
"I can produce myself."
"Because of the harmony of various conditions, butter can be obtained.
The Tathāgata is also like this; he never thinks to himself:
'I am turning the wheel of Dharma.'"
"Good son! If there is no emerging, this is what is called 'turning the wheel of the true Dharma';
this turning of the wheel of Dharma is itself the Tathāgata."

“Good son! It is like a sprout that is able to arise by depending on a seed, depending on earth, depending on water, depending on fire, depending on wind, depending on manure, depending on time, and depending on human labor.”
"Good son! The seed also does not say:
'I am able to produce the sprout.'"
"Even the karma does not think or say:
'I am able to produce the sprout.
Nor does the sprout say:"
"I can produce myself.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he never thinks to say, "I turn the wheel of the Dharma."
"Good son! If one does not act, this is called turning the wheel of the true Dharma;
this turning of the wheel of the Dharma is itself the Tathāgata."
“Good son! It is like the production of sound through the conjunction of a drum, space, leather, a person, and a drumstick.
The drum does not think:”
"I am able to produce sound.
This applies likewise even to the drumstick.
Furthermore, the sound itself does not say:
"I can produce myself. Good son!
The Tathāgata is also like this; he never thinks to say:
"I turn the wheel of Dharma.
O son of good family!
That which is called "turning the wheel of Dharma" is named "non-doing."
That which does not act is the turning of the wheel of Dharma; that which turns the wheel of Dharma is the Tathāgata.
Sons of good family, the turning of the wheel of Dharma is the domain of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
“Good son! Space is not born, does not emerge, is not made, is not created, and is not a conditioned phenomenon;
the Tathāgata is likewise: he is not born, does not emerge, is not made, is not created, and is not a conditioned phenomenon.”
Just as the nature of the Tathāgata is, so too is the Buddha-nature: it is not born, not produced, not made, not created, and is not a conditioned phenomenon. "Good son!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have two kinds of speech:
first, worldly speech; second, supramundane speech. Good son!
The Tathāgata speaks of worldly discourse for the sake of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and speaks of supramundane discourse for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
"Good son! This great assembly further consists of two kinds:
The first seeks the Lesser Vehicle, and the second seeks the Great Vehicle.

In the past, at the city of Vārāṇasī, I turned the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas; now, for the first time, at this city of Kuśinagara, I turn the great wheel of Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, good son! There are again two types of persons:
those of medium faculties and those of superior faculties."

For those of middling faculties, he turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; for those of superior faculties—such as the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, the Elephant King among Men—he now turns the Great Wheel of Dharma here in the city of Kuśinagara.
"Good son!
For those of the most inferior faculties, the Tathāgata never turns the wheel of Dharma; those of the most inferior faculties are precisely the icchantikas.
Furthermore, good son!"
There are two kinds of those who seek the Buddha-way:
first, those of middling diligence; second, those of superior diligence.
At Vārāṇasī, he turned the wheel of Dharma with middling diligence; now, here in the city of Kuśinagara, he turns the Great Wheel of Dharma with superior diligence.
"Furthermore, good son!
In the past, when I first turned the wheel of Dharma in that city of Vārāṇasī, eighty thousand devas and humans attained the fruit of srotāpanna;
now, here in this city of Kuśinagara, eight hundred billion people have become non-retrogressive from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, good son!
In the city of Vārāṇasī, the Great Brahmā Deva-king bowed his head and requested me to turn the wheel of Dharma;
now, here in the city of Kuśinagara, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa bows his head and requests me to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma."
"Furthermore, good son!
In the past, when I turned the wheel of Dharma at that city of Vārāṇasī, I preached impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
now, as I turn the wheel of Dharma here in this city of Kuśinagara, I preach permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
"Furthermore, good son!
In the past, when I turned the wheel of Dharma in that city of Vārāṇasī, the sound produced was heard as far as the Brahma Heaven;

now, as the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma in the city of Kuśinagara, the sound produced pervades twenty worlds of the Buddhas in the eastern direction, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River; it is likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Whatever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have spoken is all termed 'turning the wheel of the Dharma.
Son of good family!"
For example, O son of good family, the wheel-treasure possessed by a noble cakravartin king can subdue those not yet subdued and bring peace to those already subdued.
Son of good family!

The Dharma taught by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is likewise: it can subdue immeasurable afflictions that have not yet been subdued, and cause roots of goodness to arise in those already subdued.
“Good son! For example, the wheel-treasure possessed by a noble cakravartin king is able to eliminate all enemies and bandits;
the Tathāgata’s exposition of the Dharma is likewise, for it can cause all the thieves of the afflictions to become entirely stilled.”
"Furthermore, good son!
For example, the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch revolves both upward and downward;
the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is likewise, for it can cause sentient beings in the lower realms who commit evil to be reborn above among humans and devas, and even attain the Buddha-way."
“Good son! For this reason, you should not now praise [me] by saying:
‘The Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma here once again.’”
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is not that I am ignorant of this meaning; the reason I ask is because I wish to benefit all sentient beings.”
World-Honored One!
I have long known that turning the wheel of Dharma is truly the domain of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and is not something that Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can attain.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Good son! This is called the noble practice practiced by a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.”
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is it called ‘Noble Conduct’?”
“Good son! ‘Noble’ refers to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
For this reason, it is called the noble practice.”
“World-Honored One!
If this is that which is practiced by all Buddhas, then it cannot be practiced by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas. “Good son!”
All these World-Honored Ones, dwelling in this Great Parinirvāṇa, provide such instruction, analysis, and exposition of its meaning.
For this reason, it is called "Noble Conduct" (ārya-caryā).
When śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas hear this, they are able to practice it accordingly;
therefore, it is called the "Noble Practice. "Good son!
Once these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained this practice, they shall abide in the stage of fearlessness."
"Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in such a stage of fearlessness, he will no longer fear greed, anger, ignorance, birth, old age, sickness, or death; nor will he fear the evil realms, the hells, animals, or hungry ghosts."
“Good son! There are two kinds of evil:
first, that of the asuras; second, that among human beings.”
Among human beings, there are three kinds of evil:
first, those who are icchantikas; second, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras; and third, those who commit the four grave prohibitions.
"Good son!

Bodhisattvas who dwell in this stage never fear falling into such evil states; nor do they fear śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, non-Buddhists, those with false views, or the celestial Māra Pāpīyān; nor do they fear undergoing the twenty-five forms of existence."
For this reason, this stage is named "Fearlessness. "Good son!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Stage of Fearlessness, he attains twenty-five samādhis and destroys the twenty-five states of existence (bhava)."
"Noble son!
By attaining the Samādhi of Stainless Purity, one can destroy existence in the hells; by attaining the Samādhi of Non-retrogression, one can destroy existence among animals;
by attaining the Samādhi of Mental Joy, one can destroy existence as a hungry ghost; by attaining the Samādhi of Delight..."
The asuras possess the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi*, which can sever existence in Pūrvavideha;
they possess the *candraprabhā-samādhi*, which can sever existence in Aparagoyānī; they possess the *jvālā-samādhi*, which can sever existence in Uttarakuru;
they possess the *māyopama-samādhi*, which can sever existence in Jambudvīpa; and they possess the *sarvadharmanirīha-samādhi*...

By attaining the Samādhi of Obscurity, one can sever existence in the realm of the Four Great Kings; by attaining the Samādhi of Difficult Subjugation, one can sever existence in the realm of the Thirty-three Gods;

by attaining the Samādhi of Pleasing Intent, one can sever existence in the realm of the Yāma Heaven; by attaining the Samādhi of Blue Color, one can sever existence in the realm of the Tuṣita Heaven;
by attaining the Samādhi of Yellow Color, one can sever existence in the realm of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; [by attaining the Samādhi of Red...]
The *rūpa-samādhi* can sever existence in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations;
attaining the *śukla-varṇa-samādhi* can sever existence in the First Dhyāna; attaining the *vicitra-samādhi* can sever existence as a Great Brahmā King;
attaining the *yuganaddha-samādhi* can sever existence in the Second Dhyāna; attaining the *meghasvara-samādhi* can sever existence in the Third Dhyāna; attaining the *varṣadhārā-samādhi*...
By attaining the Samādhi of Penetrating Insight, one can sever existence in the fourth dhyāna; by attaining the Samādhi Like Space, one can sever existence in the realm of non-perception;

by attaining the Samādhi of the Illuminating Mirror, one can sever existence as a pure-abode *anāgāmin*; by attaining the Samādhi of Non-obstruction, one can sever existence in the sphere of infinite space;
by attaining the Samādhi of Permanence, one can sever existence in the sphere of infinite consciousness; by attaining the Samādhi of Bliss, one can sever...
By means of the existence in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains my samādhi and is able to sever the existence in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of the twenty-five samādhis and the severing of the twenty-five existences.
“Good son! These twenty-five samādhis are called the Kings of All Samādhis. Good son!”
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters such sovereign samādhis as these, if they wish to blow away Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, they are able to do so at will.
If they wish to know the thoughts and mental activities of all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm, they are likewise able to know them all.

If one wishes to place all sentient beings within the single pore of one's own body in this trichiliocosm, one can do so at will; furthermore, one causes those sentient beings to have no perception of confinement.
If they wish to manifest as immeasurable sentient beings, filling the entirety of a trichiliocosm, they are likewise able to do so at will.
They may divide a single body into many bodies, or again merge many bodies into a single body; though they perform such acts, their minds remain unattached, just like a lotus flower.
“Good son! Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has entered such a king of samādhis, he immediately abides in the stage of mastery.
Abiding in this stage of mastery, the bodhisattva attains the power of mastery and is able to take rebirth in whatever place he desires.”
“Good son! For example, when a noble cakravartin king rules over the four continents, he travels wherever he pleases without anyone being able to obstruct him.
It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: regarding any place of birth where they wish to be born, they are reborn there according to their will.”

“Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees any sentient beings in the hells who can be transformed and established in roots of goodness, the bodhisattva immediately goes there and is born among them.”

Although Bodhisattvas are born there, it is not the fruit of their original karma; rather, it is by virtue of the causal conditions of the power of the stage of self-mastery that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are born therein. Good son!
Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may be in the hells, they do not undergo such sufferings as being incinerated or having their bodies crushed.
Good son! The merits accomplished by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus immeasurable and boundless; even hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis could not describe them fully.
"How much less could the merits possessed by all Buddhas ever be fully described?

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva named Vimalagarbharāja—who possessed great majestic power, had accomplished supernatural faculties, had attained the Great Dhāraṇī Samādhi, and was fully endowed with the fearlessnesses—immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:
"The merits and wisdom accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are immeasurable and boundless; even hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis cannot truly describe them."
My mind still thought:
"This is not as good as the Mahāyāna sūtras. Why is this?
"By the power of these Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, one is able to give rise to the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
It is so, it is so, just as you have said.

Although these Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras possess immeasurable merit, they cannot be compared to this sūtra; even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold, or even by any calculation or analogy, they cannot reach its measure."
“Good son! It is like this:
from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the finest cream (ghṛta).”
The finest essence (sarpis) is supreme; if there are those who consume it, all their ailments are eliminated, for all medicinal herbs are contained within it.

Good son, the Buddha is also like this: from the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions of the scriptures; from the twelve divisions of the scriptures emerges the Sūtra; from the Sūtra emerges the Vaipulya Sūtra; from the Vaipulya Sūtra emerges the Prajñāpāramitā; and from the Prajñāpāramitā emerges the Mahāparinirvāṇa, which is like the finest essence.
That which is called *amṛta* (the finest essence) is a metaphor for Buddha-nature; Buddha-nature is none other than the Tathāgata.
Good son, for this reason it is said that all the merits possessed by the Tathāgata are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has praised:”
"The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is like the finest clarified butter (sarpis); it is the most supreme and the most wondrous.
If there are those who can consume it, all ailments will be eliminated, for all medicinal herbs are contained within it."
Having heard this, I reflected privately:
"If there are those who cannot listen to or accept this sutra, one should know that such people are profoundly deluded and lack a virtuous mind."
"World-Honored One!

At this time, I am truly able to endure having my skin flayed for paper, my blood drawn for ink, my marrow used for water, and my bones broken for pens, in order to transcribe such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra."
Having copied it, I shall read and recite it until I have mastered it, and only then will I explain its meaning extensively for others.
World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to wealth and possessions, I shall first bestow wealth upon them, and thereafter exhort them with this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* so that they will read it.
If they are persons of noble status, one should first accord with their inclinations through affectionate speech, and thereafter gradually exhort them to read this Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
If they are ordinary people, I shall compel them to read it by means of my majestic power.
If they are arrogant, I shall act as their servant, complying with their wishes and causing them joy; only then shall I instruct them in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
If there are those who slander the Mahāyāna sūtras, one should use one's power to subdue them;
once they have been subdued, one should then exhort them to read the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
"If there are those who love and delight in the Mahāyāna sūtras, I shall personally go to them to pay homage, make offerings, show respect, and offer praise.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"

You greatly delight in the Mahāyāna sūtras, craving the Mahāyāna sūtras, receiving the Mahāyāna sūtras, and savoring the Mahāyāna sūtras; you have faith and reverence for, respect for, and make offerings to the Mahāyāna.
"Good son!

By virtue of these causes and conditions of your present wholesome mind, you shall transcend immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and before them, you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Before long, you too shall be like me, extensively expounding for the great assembly such as this Mahāparinirvāṇa, the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata, and the secret treasury spoken by all Buddhas.

“Good son! In ages past, before the Buddha-sun had arisen, I was at that time a brahmin practicing the bodhisattva path; I was fully able to master all the sutras and treatises of the various non-Buddhist schools, cultivated the practice of quiescence, and was endowed with perfect dignified deportment.”
His mind is pure and cannot be destroyed by external thoughts of desire that arise; he extinguishes the fire of hatred and upholds the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
I searched everywhere for Mahāyāna sūtras, yet I did not even hear the name of the Vaipulya scriptures.
At that time, I was dwelling on the Snow Mountains; those mountains were pure, filled with flowing springs, bathing pools, groves of trees, and medicinal plants.
In every place among the rocks there are clear flowing streams, abundantly adorned all around with various fragrant flowers; the multitude of birds and beasts is beyond calculation.
Sweet fruits grow in profusion, their varieties difficult to count, and there are also immeasurable roots of lotus, sweet roots, and *agaru* (sandalwood) roots.
At that time, I dwelt alone therein, subsisting solely on various fruits.
Having eaten, I focused my mind in contemplation and sat in meditation; for immeasurable years, I did not even hear the name of a Mahāyāna sūtra concerning the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.

“Good son! When I was practicing such ascetic and difficult austerities, Śakra Devānām-indra and the other devas were greatly astonished and amazed. They immediately gathered together and, speaking to one another, recited these verses:
‘Pointing to one another, they said: “In the pure midst of the Snowy Mountains, ...’”
Lord of tranquility and freedom from desire, King adorned with merit;
having abandoned greed, hatred, and pride, he has forever severed all delusion.
From his very first word, he has never uttered harsh or evil speech.
At that time, there was a son of heaven among the assembly named Nandika, who spoke again in verse:
"Is it that such a person who has abandoned desire, Pure and diligent in their exertion,
Does not seek to become Śakra, Nor any of the other devas?"
"If there is one who seeks the Way and practices various ascetic austerities,
that person has many desires and seeks the place where Śakra sits.
At that time, another celestial son, a seer, spoke a verse to Śakra:
“O Lord of Devas, Kauśika!
You should not harbor such anxieties; why would those who practice asceticism among the non-Buddhists necessarily seek the station of Indra?”
Having spoken these verses, he further said: "Kauśika!
In the world there are great beings who, for the sake of sentient beings, do not covet their own bodies."
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they practice various kinds of immeasurable asceticism.

Because such persons perceive the faults and defects within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), even if they were to see precious treasures filling this entire earth, its mountains, and its great oceans, they would feel no attachment, regarding them as if they were looking upon mucus or spittle.

In this way, such a Great Being relinquishes wealth and treasures, beloved wife and children, head, eyes, marrow, brain, hands, feet, limbs, joints, his dwelling house, elephants, horses, carriages, slaves, and servants; nor does he aspire to be reborn in the heavens, but seeks only that all sentient beings may obtain happiness.
As I understand it, such a great being is pure and untainted, with all fetters forever extinguished, seeking only anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śakra Devānām-Indra spoke again, saying:
"If it is as you say, then this person has thereby gathered all sentient beings of the world."
"Great Seer!

If there were a Buddha-tree in this world, it would be able to eliminate the poisonous snakes of affliction for all devas, humans, and asuras. Any sentient beings who dwell within the cool shade of this Buddha-tree will find that all the poisons of their afflictions are completely extinguished."
"O Great Sage!
If this person were to become a Sugata in a future age, we would all attain the extinction of immeasurable, blazing afflictions.
Such a reality is indeed difficult to believe."

Why is this? Because there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet upon encountering even a slight minor condition, they immediately waver from that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, like the moon in water: when the water moves, the moon moves.
Just as a painted image is difficult to create but easy to destroy, so too is the bodhicitta: difficult to arouse but easy to lose.
Great Sage!
It is like many people who, having firmly adorned themselves with various armor and weapons, wish to advance and subdue the enemy, yet retreat and scatter when confronted by fear on the battlefield.

So it is with immeasurable sentient beings: they resolve their minds upon bodhicitta and firmly adorn themselves, but upon seeing the faults of birth and death, fear arises in their hearts and they immediately retreat and scatter.
"Great Seer!
I have seen that after such immeasurable sentient beings have resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they all undergo fluctuations.
Therefore, although I now see this person practicing asceticism—free from affliction, free from feverish distress, dwelling on a perilous path, and pure in conduct—I am as yet unable to believe it."
I must now go there myself to test him, to see whether he is truly capable of bearing the great and heavy burden of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Great Seer! Just as a chariot can be used for transport only when it has two wheels, and a bird is capable of flight only when it has two wings, so it is with this ascetic.
Although I see that he strictly maintains his prohibitive precepts, I do not yet know whether this person possesses profound wisdom.”
