If there is one with profound wisdom, you should know that such a person is capable of bearing the heavy burden of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O Great Sage!
For example, a fish mother may have many embryos in her womb, yet those that reach maturity are few;
or like the mango tree, which has many flowers but few fruits;
so too, while sentient beings who give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment are immeasurable, those who achieve it are so few as to be scarcely worth mentioning.
"O Great Seer!
I shall go with you both to test him.
O Great Seer!"
Just as genuine gold is known to be authentic only after it has undergone three tests— namely, being burned, beaten, and polished—
one should likewise test those who practice asceticism.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed his own body into the form of a rākṣasa, with a most terrifying appearance.
He descended to the Snowy Mountains and stood at no great distance from him.

At that time, the rākṣasa was fearless in heart, courageous and invincible; his eloquence proceeded in orderly sequence, and his voice was pure and refined as he proclaimed the half-verse spoken by a past Buddha:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; This is the nature of arising and ceasing."
Having spoken these half-verses, he stood before him; his manifested form was most terrifying, and he cast his gaze about, surveying the four directions.
Upon hearing this half-verse, the ascetic felt great joy in his heart.

It was like a merchant traveling at night through a perilous wilderness who, having lost his companions, searched in terror for them, only to encounter his fellow travelers once more; he would then feel immeasurable joy and leap for delight.
It is like a person who has long suffered from illness and, having not yet encountered a skilled physician, fine medicines, or a capable attendant, suddenly finds them all;
or like a person drowning at sea who suddenly encounters a ship;
or like a person parched with thirst who encounters clear, cool water.
It is like one pursued by an enemy who suddenly escapes;
like a person long imprisoned who suddenly hears they have been released;
and like a farmer encountering rain during a scorching drought.
"It is just as when a traveler returns home and his family, upon seeing him, feels great joy.
Son of good family!
When I heard these half-verses at that time, the joy in my heart was likewise."
He immediately rose from his seat, lifted his hair with his hand, looked around in the four directions, and spoke these words:
"Who was it that recited the verse I just heard?
At that time, he saw no other person at all, but only the rākṣasa, whereupon he said:
"Who has opened such a gate of liberation?
Who can thunder forth the voice of all Buddhas?
Who, amidst the slumber of birth and death, alone awakens?"
They uttered these words:
"Who is able to show the flavor of the unsurpassed path to those sentient beings who are starving within the famine of birth and death?
Amidst the immeasurable sentient beings sinking in the ocean of birth and death, who is able to act as a great captain?"
"These sentient beings are constantly entangled by the grave illness of the afflictions; who is able to act as a skilled physician among them?
This half-verse you have spoken has awakened my mind, just as the crescent moon gradually causes a lotus flower to open."
"Good son! At that time, I saw nothing else; I saw only the rākṣasa.
Then I thought again:"
"Could it be that this rākṣasa is reciting these verses?
he thought, again giving rise to doubt:
"Is it not he who is speaking?"
Why is this? Because the appearance of such a person is extremely terrifying.
However, if anyone should hear these verses, all their terrors and ugliness will immediately vanish.
How could there be such a person, with a physical form like this, who can speak these verses?
A lotus cannot emerge from fire, nor can cool water be produced within the rays of the sun.
"Good son! At that time, I further thought to myself:
'I am now without wisdom.'"
"Perhaps this rākṣasa has been able to see past buddhas and heard this half-verse from those buddhas.
I shall now question him.
He then went before the rākṣasa and spoke these words:
"Excellent, Great Being!
From where did you obtain these half-verses spoken by the one who was free from fear in the past?
Great Being!"
Furthermore, from where could such a half-jewel of a verse as this have been obtained?
O Great Being!
The meaning of these half-verses is the true path of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.

All sentient beings in the world, being constantly shrouded by the net of various views, spend their entire lives within these non-Buddhist teachings and never hear such a teaching on emptiness as it was spoken by the World Hero endowed with the ten powers who has transcended the world.
"Good son! After I had asked this, he replied to me, saying:
'Great Brahmin!'"
"You should not now ask me about this matter. Why is that?
It has already been many days since I last ate;
though I have sought food everywhere, I have found none at all. Afflicted by hunger and thirst, my mind is distracted and my speech is deluded; this is not what I know from my own original mind."
"By my power, I am now able to fly through the void to Uttarakuru and even to the heavens; yet, though I seek food everywhere, I cannot obtain any.
For this reason, I have spoken these words."
"Good son! At that time, I again spoke to the rākṣasa, saying:
'O Great Being!'"
"If you can recite this verse for me until it is finished, I shall become your disciple for the rest of my life.
O Great Being!
That which you have spoken has its names inexhaustible and its meanings likewise endless."
For what reason do you not wish to speak?
As for the gift of material wealth, it is subject to exhaustion; however, the causes and conditions of the gift of Dharma are inexhaustible.
Since the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible, it brings about manifold benefit.
"Now that I have heard this half-verse of the Dharma, my mind is filled with alarm and doubt; you should now, by good fortune, sever it for me.
Once you have finished reciting this verse, I shall become your disciple for the rest of my life."
The rākṣasa replied:
"Your wisdom is excessive; you worry only for yourself and do not consider at all that I am now surely tormented by the suffering of hunger, and thus truly cannot speak."
I then asked: "What is that which you eat?
The rākṣasa replied:
"You need not ask this.
If I were to speak of it, it would cause many people to be terrified.
I asked again:
"In this solitary place, there is no one else; I do not fear you, so why do you not speak?
The rākṣasa replied, "That which I eat is only the warm flesh of humans."
As for what they drink, it is nothing but the warm blood of humans.
Due to my own meager merit, I have eaten only this food; though I have searched everywhere, I am exhausted and unable to obtain more.
"Although there are many people in the world, they all possess merit and virtue, and moreover, they are protected by the various devas; thus, I lack the power to kill them. "Good son!
I spoke to him again, saying:
"You need only recite this half-verse in its entirety; once I have heard the verse, I shall offer this body of mine as a gift for your sustenance.
Great Being!"

"If my life should come to an end, this body would have no further use; it would surely be devoured by tigers, wolves, owls, hawks, eagles, and vultures, yet I would not gain even a hair’s breadth of merit."
"I now seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I shall relinquish this non-essential body to exchange it for an essential one.
The rākṣasa replied, "Who would believe such words of yours—that for the sake of eight syllables, you would cast away your beloved body?"
“Good son! I then replied:
‘You are truly without wisdom.’”
It is like a person who, by giving away an earthen vessel to another, obtains a vessel of the seven treasures.
I am likewise: having relinquished this non-substantial body, I have obtained a vajra-body.
As for what you said:
"Who will believe this? I now have witnesses:

Mahābrahmā, Śakra-devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings can testify to this matter. Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas with the divine eye who, desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, practice the Mahāyāna and are endowed with the six perfections; they too can testify and know this. Moreover, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions who benefit sentient beings, can also bear witness that for the sake of these eight characters, I have sacrificed my body and life.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"If you are thus able to sacrifice your body, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall recite the remaining half-verse for you."
“Good son! At that time, having heard these words, my heart was filled with joy. I immediately removed the deerskin garment I was wearing and spread it out for this rākṣasa as a Dharma seat, saying:
‘Upādhyāya!’”
"I pray that you will sit upon this seat.
I then placed my palms together before him and knelt for a long time, saying these words:
"I only pray that the Upādhyāya will graciously recite the remaining half-verse for me, so that it may be made complete."
The rākṣasa then spoke:
“When birth and cessation have both ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the rākṣasa further said:
"O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!
You have now heard the complete meaning of these verses, and your aspirations shall be entirely fulfilled.
If you truly desire to benefit all sentient beings, give me your body at this time."

“Good son! At that time, I contemplated this matter deeply, and then in various places—whether on rocks, walls, trees, or paths—I inscribed these verses. Fearing that my body might be exposed after death, I immediately fastened the garments I was wearing and climbed a tall tree.”
At that time, the tree spirit asked me again:
"Excellent, O worthy one!
What do you wish to do?"
"Good son! At that time, I replied:
'I wish to give up my body to repay the price of this verse.'"
The tree spirit asked:
"What benefit does such a verse provide?
At that time, I replied:

"These verses are the path for opening the Dharma of emptiness as taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; for this Dharma, I would sacrifice my body and life, not for the sake of gain, fame, wealth, nor for the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Mahābrahmā, or the pleasures among humans and devas."
"I have cast off this body because I desire to benefit all sentient beings.
"Good son! When I was casting off my body, I further spoke these words:"
"I vow that all those who are stingy and possessive shall come to see me relinquish this body;

and if there are those who give even a small gift yet give rise to arrogance, may they likewise witness me renounce this life for the sake of a single verse, casting it away as if it were mere grass or wood."
When I had finished speaking these words at that time, I immediately cast my body down from the tree.
Before I had even reached the ground, various sounds issued forth from the midst of space, and those sounds reached as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
At that time, the rākṣasa returned to his original form as Śakra and immediately caught my body in mid-air, placing me upon level ground.
Then Śakra-devānām-indra, along with the devas and the Great Brahmā King, prostrated themselves at my feet and praised me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Truly you are a Bodhisattva, able to bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, wishing to kindle the great Dharma-torch amidst the darkness of ignorance.
Because I cherished the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma, I have disturbed and troubled you; I only pray that you will grant me leave to repent for my transgressions.
"In the future, you will certainly achieve Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; we pray that you may deliver us.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra and the host of devas prostrated at my feet, whereupon they took their leave and suddenly vanished.

“Good son! Just as I sacrificed this body for the sake of half a verse in the past, by this causal condition, I have already transcended twelve kalpas and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi before Maitreya.”
"Good son! I have attained such immeasurable merit as this entirely through making offerings to the True Dharma of the Tathāgata. Good son!"
You now are likewise; having resolved upon the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, you have already surpassed immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Good son! This is called a bodhisattva abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa and practicing the noble conduct.
— *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Fourteen.
Added by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇas Huiyan and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter Twenty: On Holy Conduct (Brahmacarya-varga). Part One of Chapter Twenty: On Holy Conduct.
“Good son! What is the brahmacarya of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, they abide in seven wholesome dharmas to attain the perfection of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
What are these seven? First, knowledge of the Dharma;

second, knowledge of its meaning; third, knowledge of the proper time; fourth, knowledge of contentment; fifth, self-knowledge; sixth, knowledge of the assembly; and seventh, knowledge of the noble and the humble.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the Dharma? Good son!”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the twelve divisions of the scriptures, namely: sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhutadharma, and upadeśa.
“Good son! What is called a Sūtra?
From ‘Thus have I heard’ up to ‘rejoiced and practiced accordingly,’ all such as these are called Sūtras.”
"What is called a *geyya* sutta?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

'In the past, you and I were ignorant and lacked wisdom; we were unable to see the Four Noble Truths as they truly are. For this reason, we wandered in saṃsāra, dwelling for a long time within birth and death, submerged in the great ocean of suffering.'"
"What are the four?
They are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra to the bhikṣus on a former occasion, there were at that time sentient beings of sharp faculties who arrived later at the Buddha's dwelling for the sake of hearing the Dharma; they immediately asked the people [there]:
"What was it that the Tathāgata was teaching just now?
The Buddha, having understood this, spoke in verse based on the original sutra:
"In the past, when I was with you all, We did not see the Four Noble Truths."
Therefore, one has long wandered through the great ocean of suffering of birth and death.
If one can perceive the Four Noble Truths, then one shall sever birth and death;
once existence in birth is exhausted, one will no longer undergo further states of being.
"This is called a Geya Sūtra. What is called a Vyākaraṇa Sūtra?
It refers to those sūtras and vinayas wherein the Tathāgata, at the time of speaking, bestows the prophecy of Buddhahood upon various devas and humans."
"Ānanda, in the future there shall be a king named Śaṅkha, who will attain the Way of the Buddha in that world, and his name shall be Maitreya.
This is called the Sūtra of Prediction (Vyākaraṇa-sūtra).
"What is called a Gāthā-sūtra?
Excluding the Sūtras and the various Vinayas, it refers to other teachings consisting of four-line verses, such as:
'Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify your own mind.'"
"This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is called a Gāthā-sūtra. What is called an Udāna-sūtra?
Just as the Buddha entered meditative concentration in the afternoon and extensively expounded the essential points of the Dharma for the assembly of devas,
the bhikṣus each had this thought: "What is the Tathāgata doing now?"
At dawn the next day, the Tathāgata arose from meditative concentration; though no one had asked him, by means of his knowledge of others' minds, he spoke of his own accord:
"Bhikṣus, you should know:
the lifespans of all the devas are exceedingly long."
"O bhikṣus! Excellent is it that you act for the sake of others without seeking your own benefit.
Excellent is it that you have few desires."
“Excellent is contentment!
Excellent is tranquility!
Such discourses spoken spontaneously without being asked are called Udāna-sūtras.
"What is called the Nidāna-sūtra?
It refers to the exposition for others of the causes and roots upon which the verses of various sūtras are based.
For example, there was a man in Śrāvastī who caught birds with a net; having captured them, he confined them in a cage, provided them with water and grain, and then released them again."
The World-Honored One, knowing the causal conditions from beginning to end, spoke in verse:
"Do not despise small evils, thinking they will bring no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel."
"This is called the *Nidāna-sūtra*. What is called the *Avadāna-sūtra*?
It refers to the parables taught within the Vinaya; these are called the *Avadāna-sūtra*."
"What is called an Itivṛttaka-sūtra?
As the Buddha has said:
'Monks, you should know:'"
That which I have spoken since appearing in the world is called the *Sūtra*;
during the appearance of Krakucchanda Buddha in the world, it was called the "Drum of Ambrosia";
and during the time of Kanakamuni Buddha, it was called the "Mirror of Dharma."
"In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, it was named 'Discrimination of Emptiness' (Vibhaktasūnya).
This is called an Itivṛttaka Sūtra. What is called a Jātaka Sūtra?"
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, originally practiced various ascetic austerities as a bodhisattva, it was said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know:
in the past, I was a deer, a bear, a roe deer, a rabbit, a minor king, a wheel-turning sage king, a nāga, and a garuḍa."
“Whatever bodies are received during the practice of the bodhisattva path in such ways as these are called *sūtra*.
What is termed a *vaipulya* scripture?
The so-called Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, whose meaning is as vast as space, are called Vaipulya.
"What is called an Adbhuta-dharma sūtra?"
Just as when that Bodhisattva was first born, he walked seven steps without anyone supporting him, emitting a great radiance and surveying the ten directions;
and also like the monkey who held a vessel of honey in its hands to offer it to the Tathāgata.
It was as if a white-necked dog were listening to the Dharma by the Buddha’s side;
it was as if Māra Pāpīyas had transformed himself into a blue ox walking among the clay alms bowls, causing them to strike against one another without sustaining any damage.
Just as when the Buddha was first born and entered a temple of the gods, he caused those divine images to rise and prostrate in worship;
sūtras such as these are called *adbhutadharma* (Marvelous) Sūtras.
What are called *upadeśa* (Instructional) Sūtras?
As for the various sūtras spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, those that involve discussion, detailed analysis, and the discernment of their characteristics are called *upadeśa* sūtras.
"If a bodhisattva can thus understand the twelve divisions of the scriptures, this is called 'knowing the Dharma.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know the meaning?"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva extensively understands the meaning of all written characters and spoken language, this is called "knowing the meaning.
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the proper time?

"Good son! A bodhisattva skillfully knows that at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate tranquility; at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate diligence; at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate the meditative concentration of equanimity; at such a time it is appropriate to make offerings to the Buddha; at such a time it is appropriate to make offerings to the teacher; and at such a time it is appropriate to cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, thereby fulfilling the perfection of wisdom. This is called 'knowing the proper time.'"
"What is the contentment of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?

Good son, the contentment of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to food, clothing, medicine, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping and waking, and speaking and remaining silent; this is called contentment."
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know himself? This bodhisattva knows himself:

‘I possess such faith, such precepts, such extensive learning, such renunciation, such wisdom, such coming and going, such right mindfulness, such virtuous conduct, such questions, and such answers. This is called knowing oneself.”
“How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know the assemblies?
Son of good family!

This bodhisattva knows that such and such are the assemblies of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and śramaṇas; he knows how to approach and depart among these assemblies, how to sit and rise, how to preach the Dharma, and how to engage in question and answer. This is called knowing the assemblies.”
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the high and low among people? Good son!”
There are two kinds of people:
first, those with faith; second, those without faith.
A bodhisattva should know this:
Faith is wholesome;
that which lacks faith is not called wholesome.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of faith:
First, one constantly goes to the monasteries; second, one does not go.
A bodhisattva should know that for those who go, it is virtuous.
Those who do not go are not called virtuous.
Among those who do go to the monastic quarters, there are again two kinds:
first, those who prostrate; second, those who do not prostrate.
Bodhisattvas should know this:
to pay homage is wholesome;
not to pay homage is not called wholesome.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who perform prostrations:
first, those who listen to the Dharma; second, those who do not.
A bodhisattva should know this:"
Those who listen to the Dharma are good;
those who do not listen to the Dharma are not called good.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who listen to the Dharma:
First, listening with a sincere mind; second, not listening with a sincere mind.
A bodhisattva should know that listening with a sincere mind is what is called "wholesome."
One who does not listen with a sincere heart is not called virtuous.
There are two kinds of listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart:
first, reflecting upon the meaning; second, not reflecting upon the meaning.
Bodhisattvas should know this:
that which contemplates meaning is wholesome;
that which does not contemplate meaning is not called wholesome.
“Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who contemplate the meaning:
first, those who act according to what they have heard; second, those who do not act according to what they have heard.
Those who act according to what they have heard are virtuous.”
"To practice as one speaks is not yet called 'good.
There are two kinds of those who practice as they speak:
first, those who seek the state of a śrāvaka and are unable to bring benefit, peace, or relief to all suffering sentient beings."
Second, one should dedicate [merit] toward the unsurpassed Mahāyāna to benefit many people and enable them to attain peace and happiness.
A bodhisattva should know that that which can benefit many people and bring them peace and happiness is the most supreme and the most excellent.
"Good son!

Just as the wish-fulfilling jewel is the most excellent and wondrous among all jewels, and as nectar is the supreme among all flavors, so too is the bodhisattva the most excellent, the most supreme, and beyond all analogy among humans and devas."
“Good son! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and abiding in the seven wholesome dharmas.
Once a bodhisattva has dwelt in these seven wholesome dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the brahmacarya.”
"Furthermore, good son!
There is another holy life (brahmacarya), namely: loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the frequent cultivation of loving-kindness can sever ill-will, and the cultivation of compassion also severs ill-will, why speak of four immeasurable minds?”
Inferring from its meaning, there should be three [types].
World-Honored One!
Loving-kindness has three objects:
First, taking sentient beings as the object; second, taking phenomena (*dharma*) as the object; third, being without an object.
Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise. According to this principle, there should only be three, not four.
Regarding the object of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*): to take the five aggregates as the object and vow to grant them happiness is called the object of sentient beings.
Regarding the object of phenomena (*dharmālambana*): to take the various necessities required by sentient beings as the object and bestow them upon them is called the object of phenomena.
Regarding "objectless" (anālambana): taking the Tathāgata as the object is what is called "objectless.

Compassion generally takes impoverished sentient beings as its object; however, the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is forever free from poverty and experiences supreme bliss. If one takes sentient beings as the object, one does not take the Buddha as the object;
the same applies to the Dharma.
For this reason, that which takes the Tathāgata as its object is called "objectless.
"World-Honored One,
the object of loving-kindness is all sentient beings, just as one takes parents, wives, children, and relatives as its objects."
For this reason, it is called "conditioned by sentient beings.

As for "conditioned by dharmas," one does not perceive parents, wives, children, or relatives; rather, one perceives that all dharmas arise from conditions—this is called being "conditioned by dharmas."
Regarding "objectless" (anālambana): it refers to not dwelling upon the marks of dharmas nor the marks of sentient beings; this is called objectless.
Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise thus; therefore, there should be three, not four.
“World-Honored One!
There are two kinds of persons:
first, those whose conduct is dominated by views; second, those whose conduct is dominated by craving.”

Those whose conduct is dominated by views cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) extensively, while those whose conduct is dominated by craving cultivate sympathetic joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Therefore, there should be two [categories], not four.
“World-Honored One!
That which is immeasurable is called boundless.
Because no limit can be apprehended, it is named ‘immeasurable.’”
If they were immeasurable, they would have to be one, and one should not speak of four.
If one speaks of four, how can they be immeasurable?
Therefore, they should be one, not four.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Good son! The essential teachings proclaimed by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, for the sake of all sentient beings, are secret in their words and difficult to comprehend.”
Or, for the sake of sentient beings, one may explain a single causal condition.
For example, what is said to be the single causal condition?
It is all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Good son! Some speak of two kinds:
cause and effect.
Some speak of three types:
afflictions, karma, and suffering.
Others speak of four types:
Ignorance, volitional formations, birth, and old age and death.
Alternatively, five factors are taught:
namely, sensation, craving, clinging, existence, and birth.
Some explain six types:
the causes and effects of the three periods of time.
Others explain seven types:
That is to say: consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, and grasping.
Alternatively, eight factors are taught:
excluding ignorance, formations, birth, and old age and death, the remaining eight items.
Some explain nine types:
as in the *Nagara-sūtra*, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), there are the remaining nine factors.
Some explain eleven:
As was taught to Satyaka Nirgranthaputra, there are eleven factors excluding the single factor of birth;

or at times, the twelve links of dependent origination are explained in their entirety, as when they were fully explained to Kāśyapa and others in Rājagṛha, from ignorance through birth, old age, sickness, death, and suffering.
“Good son! Just as a single causal condition is differentiated in various ways for the sake of sentient beings,
so too it is with the immeasurable mental dharmas.”
"Good son! For this reason, you should not give rise to doubt regarding the profound and secret spheres of activity of all Tathāgatas. Good son!"

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great skillful means: he speaks of the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent; he speaks of pleasure as suffering and suffering as pleasure;

he speaks of the impure as pure and the pure as impure; he speaks of self as non-self and non-self as self; he speaks of what is not a sentient being as a sentient being and what is a real sentient being as not a sentient being; he speaks of what is not a thing as a thing and a thing as not a thing; he speaks of what is not real as real and the real as not real; he speaks of what is not an object as an object and an object as not an object; he speaks of what is not birth as birth and birth as not birth; and even speaking of ignorance as wisdom and wisdom as ignorance; he speaks of form as non-form and non-form as form; and he speaks of what is not the Path as the Path and the Path as not the Path.
"Good son!
The Tathāgata employs these immeasurable skillful means to discipline sentient beings;
how could they be false? Good son!"

If there are sentient beings who are greedy for wealth and goods, I personally manifest my body as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) before them; for immeasurable years, I provide them with all manner of necessities according to their needs, and thereafter I teach and transform them, causing them to dwell securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to the five desires, [the Buddha] will satisfy their passions with exquisite five desires for immeasurable years, and only thereafter exhort and transform them, causing them to dwell securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If there are sentient beings who are prosperous, powerful, and self-important, I shall serve as their servant for immeasurable eons, running errands and attending to them; once I have won their hearts, I will further exhort and transform them, causing them to dwell securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If there are sentient beings who are by nature stubborn and self-righteous, requiring the admonitions and exhortations of others, I shall for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years instruct, reprimand, and earnestly exhort them to bring their minds into harmony; thereafter, I shall further encourage them to dwell securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son!
If the Tathāgata, in this manner, for immeasurable eons, employs various skillful means to cause all sentient beings to dwell securely in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, could this possibly be false?"
"Although the Tathāgatas dwell amidst all manner of evils, they remain unstained, just like a lotus flower.
Son of good family,
you should understand the meaning of the four immeasurables in this way."
"Noble son!
This essence of the immeasurable mind has four aspects; if one practices them, one will be reborn in the realm of Mahābrahmā. Noble son!"
Thus, there are four such immeasurable companions; for this reason, they are called "the four.
Now, one who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever covetous desire;
one who cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) can sever ill will (*vyāpāda*).
One who cultivates the mind of sympathetic joy can sever discontent;
one who cultivates the mind of equanimity can sever greed, hatred, and [attachment to] sentient beings. Good son!
For this reason, it is designated as four, rather than one, two, or three.
"Good son! As you have said:
Regarding the statement, "Loving-kindness can sever hatred; compassion is likewise;
thus, three should be taught," you should not raise such an objection. Why is this?
Good son! There are two kinds of anger:
first, that which can take life; second, that which can inflict flogging.
By practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one can sever that which takes life; by practicing compassion (*karuṇā*), one can eliminate those who inflict flogging.
Good son! For this reason, are there not four?
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of hatred:
first, hatred toward sentient beings; second, hatred toward non-sentient things.
One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness severs hatred toward sentient beings."
One who cultivates compassion severs anger toward non-sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of anger:
first, that which has a cause and condition; second, that which lacks a cause and condition.
One who cultivates a mind of loving-kindness severs the conditions for existence;
one who cultivates a mind of compassion severs the conditions for non-existence.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of anger:
First, cultivation practiced long ago in the past; second, cultivation practiced in the present.
One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever the past;
one who cultivates the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) severs the present.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of hatred:
first, hatred toward noble ones; second, hatred toward ordinary persons.
One who cultivates the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) severs hatred toward noble ones."
One who cultivates compassion severs the anger of ordinary beings.
Furthermore, there are two types of anger:
first, the superior; second, the middling.
Cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*) severs the upper [afflictions], and cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*) severs the middle. "Good son!
For this reason, they are called the four."
How can you raise the objection that there should be three and not four?
Therefore, Kāśyapa, these immeasurable states of mind are distinguished as four by way of their mutual counterparts.
Furthermore, by virtue of their being "vessels," they should be called four.
If a vessel possesses loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it cannot simultaneously possess compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For this reason, there should be no reduction in the number of these four.
“Good son! Because they are distinguished by their practice, there should be four.
When practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), there is no compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*); therefore, there are four.”
“Good son! Because they are immeasurable, they are also called ‘four.
Now, that which is immeasurable consists of four kinds:”

There is immeasurable mind that has an object but is not sovereign; there is immeasurable mind that is sovereign but does not have an object; there is immeasurable mind that both has an object and is sovereign; and there is immeasurable mind that neither has an object nor is sovereign.
What is meant by "immeasurable objects of focus that are not sovereign"?

It refers to focusing on immeasurable and boundless sentient beings while being unable to attain sovereign samādhi; even if it is attained, it is not stable, being sometimes gained and sometimes lost.
"What is immeasurable mastery that is not an object-condition?
For example, wishing for the peace and happiness of one's parents, brothers, or sisters is not an immeasurable object-condition."
What is immeasurable that is both objective and sovereign?
It refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
What is immeasurable that is neither objective nor sovereign?
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot extensively take immeasurable sentient beings as their object, nor do they possess such mastery.
Good son, for this reason, these are called the four immeasurables; they are not within the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, but are the domain of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
“Good son! Regarding these four matters, although the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are said to be immeasurable, their measure is so slight as to be negligible;
only the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can truly be called immeasurable and boundless.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; it is truly as the holy teaching declares:”
The realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is not within the reach of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
World-Honored One,
is there perhaps a Bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa who attains a mind of loving-kindness and compassion that is not yet the Great Loving-Kindness and Great Compassion?
The Buddha said: "There is,
son of good family!"
If a bodhisattva distinguishes among sentient beings into three categories—first, those who are kin;
second, those who are enemies or objects of aversion; and third, those who are neutral persons.
Among one's kin, there are again three grades:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The same applies to those who are hateful enemies.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva bestows superior happiness upon their superior kin;
they likewise bestow superior happiness equally upon their middling and inferior kin.

Toward their superior enemies, they bestow a small measure of happiness; toward their middling enemies, they bestow a middling measure of happiness; and toward their inferior enemies, they bestow superior happiness.

In this way, the bodhisattva increasingly cultivates and practices [compassion], bestowing medium-grade happiness upon superior enemies, and superior happiness equally upon middling and inferior enemies.
Cultivating further still, they bestow superior happiness upon those who are superior, middling, and inferior alike.
If one bestows supreme happiness upon those who were formerly enemies, then at that time, one is said to have accomplished the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*).
At that time, the bodhisattva attains a mind of equality toward their parents and their former enemies, without any distinction between them.
“Good son! This is called attaining loving-kindness, but it is not great loving-kindness.
“World-Honored One!”
"For what reason is it that although a bodhisattva attains such loving-kindness, it is still not called 'great loving-kindness'?
"Good son! Because it is difficult to accomplish, it is not called great loving-kindness."

Why is this? Because for immeasurable kalpas in the distant past, they have accumulated much affliction and have not cultivated wholesome dharmas; therefore, they are unable to subdue their minds within a single day.
Good son! It is like a pea: when it is dry, a needle cannot pierce it at all.
The hardness of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is likewise; even if one binds the mind for a single day and night so that it does not scatter, they remain difficult to subdue.

Furthermore, just as a domestic dog does not fear humans, while a wild deer of the mountains and forests flees in terror upon seeing a person, so too is hatred difficult to remove—like a guard dog—and a compassionate heart easily lost—like that wild deer. Therefore, this mind is difficult to subdue.
For this reason, it is not called "Great Compassion.
Furthermore, good son, it is like carving a pattern into stone; its marks remain forever.
A drawing on water vanishes quickly; its momentum does not endure for long.
Anger is like drawing on stone, while the roots of all virtues are like that drawing on water; therefore, this mind is difficult to subdue.
Just as the light of a great mass of fire endures for a long time, whereas the light of a flash of lightning cannot remain even for a moment;
so too, anger is like a mass of fire and loving-kindness is like the light of lightning. Therefore, this mind is difficult to subdue.
For this reason, it is not called "Great Compassion. "Good son!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the first stage, it is called 'Great Compassion.'"
Why is this? Good son!
Those who are most extremely evil are called icchantikas.
When a Bodhisattva in the first stage cultivates great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), they regard even those of single-minded attachment (*icchantika*) with no distinction in mind.
Because they do not perceive their faults, they do not give rise to anger.
For this reason, it is called "great loving-kindness."
“Good son! To eliminate that which is unbeneficial for all sentient beings is called great kindness;
to desire to bestow immeasurable benefit and happiness upon sentient beings is called great compassion.”
To give rise to a heart of joy toward all sentient beings is called great joy (*mahāmuditā*);
to have nothing to protect or cling to is called great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
If one does not perceive a self, the characteristics of dharmas, or one's own body, and perceives all dharmas as equal and non-dual, this is called great equanimity.
To relinquish one's own happiness and bestow it upon others is called great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*). "Good son!
Only the four immeasurables can cause a bodhisattva to increase and fulfill the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); other practices do not necessarily have this power."
"Good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva first attains the four worldly immeasurable minds, and only thereafter does he resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is through this sequence that he subsequently attains the supramundane."
“Good son!
Because the immeasurables of the supramundane arise from the immeasurables of the mundane, for this reason they are called the ‘Great Immeasurables.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Apart from that which is without benefit and that which brings benefit and happiness, there is truly nothing to be done.
Such contemplation is merely empty observation; it possesses no real benefit.”
World-Honored One, it is as if, when a bhikṣu contemplates impurity, he perceives the clothes he wears as being entirely of the nature of skin, though they are not actually skin;
he perceives all that he eats and drinks as being of the nature of worms, though they are not actually worms;
and he contemplates a bean soup as being of the nature of excrement, though it is not actually feces.
One contemplates the curd one consumes as being like marrow and brain, yet it is not actually brain;
one contemplates the powdered bones as having the appearance of flour, yet they are not actually flour.

The four immeasurable minds are likewise: they cannot truly benefit sentient beings by causing them to obtain happiness; though one speaks with the mouth of giving happiness to sentient beings, in reality they do not obtain it.
"Is such an observation not false? [The Buddha asked.
"World-Honored One!
If it is not false and truly bestows happiness, why is it that all sentient beings do not experience happiness through the majestic power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?"
If practicing according to reality were unable to bring about happiness, it would contradict what the Buddha said:

"I recall that in the past, while practicing the mind of loving-kindness alone, throughout this kalpa of seven cycles of formation and destruction, I did not return to this world. When the world was forming, I was born among the Brahmā devas;
when the world was dissolving, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven."

If one is born in the Brahma Heaven, possessing power and mastery that cannot be overcome, being the most excellent and supreme among a thousand Brahmas, one is named the Great Brahma King; all sentient beings will conceive the notion of him as the most supreme.
"Thirty-six times he was Śakra Devānām Indra, king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, and countless hundreds of thousands of times he was a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
It is by exclusively cultivating a mind of loving-kindness that one obtains such fruits and rewards among humans and devas; if this were not true, how could it correspond with this principle?"
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"
"You are truly courageous and free from all fear.
He then spoke this verse to Kāśyapa:
"If, toward even a single sentient being, One does not give rise to a mind of anger..."
To wish to share one's own happiness with others is called the nature of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
If one gives rise to a heart of compassion (*karuṇā*) toward all sentient beings, this is called the noble lineage;
one shall obtain immeasurable rewards of merit.
Even if seers possessing the five supernormal powers were to fill this entire earth,
and a Great Lord of Sovereignty were to offer them all that they require—
elephants, horses, and various other things— the fruit of the meritorious reward obtained thereby [would not equal that of one who honors the Dharma].
It does not equal even one-sixteenth part of practicing a single act of loving-kindness.
"Good son! Indeed, the cultivation of loving-kindness is not a mere conceptual fabrication; it is truly and authentically real."
If this were the compassion of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it would be called false;
that of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas is true and not false.
How is this known?

"Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices this Great Parinirvāṇa in this way, he perceives earth as gold and perceives gold as earth; he manifests the appearance of water from earth and the appearance of earth from water; he manifests the appearance of fire from water and the appearance of water from fire; he manifests the appearance of wind from earth and the appearance of earth from wind. These are accomplished according to his will, without any falsehood."

To contemplate actual sentient beings as non-sentient beings, and to contemplate non-sentient beings as actual sentient beings—all are accomplished according to one's will, without any falsehood. Good son!
"You should know that the four immeasurable minds of a bodhisattva are genuine contemplation, not something unreal.
Furthermore, son of good family, what is called 'genuine contemplation'?"
This means that one is able to sever all afflictions. Good son!

One who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can sever covetous desire; one who cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) can sever anger and hatred; one who cultivates sympathetic joy (*muditā*) can sever dissatisfaction; and one who cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*) can sever both covetousness and hatred, as well as the perception of a sentient being. For this reason, it is called "true contemplation."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The four immeasurable minds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva can serve as the root of all wholesome dharmas.
Son of good family!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive impoverished sentient beings, there is no basis for generating loving-kindness;
if loving-kindness is not generated, then the mind of generous giving cannot arise.

By means of the causes and conditions of giving, one enables all sentient beings to obtain peaceful and secure happiness, namely: food and drink, vehicles, clothing, flowers and incense, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
When practicing such giving, the mind is free from bondage and does not give rise to greedy attachment; it is resolutely dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the mind has no point of reliance, false conceptualizations are forever severed, and one does not act out of fear, nor for the sake of reputation or gain, nor seeking the pleasures experienced by humans or devas. One does not give rise to arrogance, does not hope for recompense, and is not deceived by others; therefore, one practices giving without seeking wealth or status.

Whenever practicing giving, one does not perceive the recipient, nor whether they observe the precepts or violate them, nor whether they are a field of merit or not, nor whether they are a spiritual friend or not.

When giving, one does not perceive whether a recipient is a worthy vessel or not; one does not discriminate between time or season, nor between a suitable place or an unsuitable one; furthermore, one does not calculate whether it is a time of famine or a time of abundance and prosperity; one does not perceive cause and effect, nor does one distinguish, "this is a sentient being" or "this is not a sentient being," or "this is merit" or "this is not merit."
Although they do not perceive a giver, a receiver, or the gift itself, nor even perceive cessation or its karmic fruition, they constantly practice giving without interruption.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva perceives the precepts, the breaking of the precepts, or even their karmic retributions, they will ultimately be unable to practice giving.
If one does not practice giving, then the dānapāramitā will not be fulfilled.”
If one does not fulfill the dāna-pāramitā, one cannot achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Good son! It is like a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow; his kinsmen, wishing to bring him peace and security, seek to remove the poison and immediately summon a skilled physician to extract the arrow."
That person said:
"Wait a moment; do not touch it.
I shall now observe from which direction this poisoned arrow has come."
By whom was he shot?
Was it by a kṣatriya or a brāhmaṇa?
"Is he a Vaiśya or a Śūdra?
He then thought further:
"What kind of wood is this?"
Is it bamboo?
Is it willow?
And as for its iron tip, from which foundry does it originate?
Is it hard?
Or is it soft?
As for those feathers and wings, what kind of bird’s wings are they?
Are they crows, owls, or vultures?
As for all poisons, do they arise from intentional action,
or do they exist spontaneously?
"Is this the venom of a human,
or the venom of a snake?
Thus, the foolish man was ultimately unable to discern it and soon passed away.
Good son! It is the same for a bodhisattva:

if, when practicing giving, one discriminates between the recipient, those who uphold the precepts, those who break the precepts, and even the resulting karmic fruit, one will ultimately be unable to give.
If one cannot practice giving, then the dānapāramitā is not fulfilled;
if the dānapāramitā is not fulfilled, then one cannot achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving, he regards all sentient beings with impartial compassion, as if they were his own children.
Furthermore, when practicing giving, he gives rise to a heart of pity and sympathy toward all sentient beings, just as parents care for a sick child.”
At the time of practicing generosity, the mind is filled with joy, just as parents rejoice upon seeing their child’s illness cured.
Once the gift has been given, the mind is set at ease, just as parents feel relieved when they see their child grown up and able to sustain themselves.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives food from a mind of loving-kindness, they always make this aspiration:
"May all that I now give be shared together with all sentient beings."
"By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings obtain the food of great wisdom and diligently apply themselves toward dedicating their merit to the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
"May all sentient beings obtain the food of excellent wisdom and not seek the food of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
“May all sentient beings obtain the food of Dharma-joy and no longer seek the food of craving.
“May all sentient beings fully attain the food of the Prajñāpāramitā, and may they all be filled with it, grasping it without obstruction and increasing their superior roots of goodness.”
"May all sentient beings realize and understand the characteristic of emptiness, attaining unimpeded bodies like space.
May all sentient beings always act as recipients of offerings, showing compassion for all, and serve as fields of merit for the multitude."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the mind of loving-kindness, he should firmly make such vows as these whenever he gives food.
Furthermore, good son!”
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives a drink with a mind of loving-kindness, they should make this aspiration:
"May all that I now give be shared together with all sentient beings."

By these causes and conditions, they cause all sentient beings to enter the river of the Mahāyāna, drink its water of eight flavors, and swiftly traverse the path to unsurpassed Bodhi. They leave behind the parched deserts of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles; thirsting with longing, they aspire to seek the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle. They sever the thirst of afflictions and thirst for the flavor of the Dharma; they abandon the craving for birth and death and come to love and delight in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa. Thus they become fully endowed with the Dharmakāya, attain all samādhis, and enter the profound great ocean of wisdom.
"May all sentient beings obtain the taste of ambrosia—the tastes of awakening, transcendence from the world, detachment from desire, and tranquility.
"May all sentient beings be fully endowed with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of flavors of the Dharma;
having been endowed with the flavor of the Dharma, may they attain the vision of the Buddha-nature."
Having realized the Buddha-nature, one is able to rain down the Dharma-rain;
having rained down the Dharma-rain, the Buddha-nature pervades and covers all, just like empty space.
Furthermore, it causes immeasurable other sentient beings to obtain the flavor of the One Dharma, which is the Mahāyāna, and not the flavor of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
"May all sentient beings obtain a single sweet taste, free from the six kinds of differentiated tastes.
"May all sentient beings seek only the flavor of the Dharma—the flavor of the practice of the unimpeded Buddha-dharma—and not seek any other flavors."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives drinks from a mind of loving-kindness, they should firmly make such vows as these.
Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a vehicle from a mind of loving-kindness, they should make this aspiration:
"May all that I now give be shared together with all sentient beings."

By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings universally attain the Mahāyāna, abide in the Mahāyāna, not regress from the vehicle, not waver from the vehicle, and possess the Vajra-seat vehicle; may they not seek the vehicles of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but turn toward the Buddha-vehicle—the unsubduable vehicle, the tireless vehicle, the non-retrogressive vehicle, the unsurpassed vehicle, the vehicle of the ten powers, the vehicle of great merit, the unprecedented vehicle, the rare vehicle, the difficult-to-obtain vehicle, the boundless vehicle, and the vehicle that knows all.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives a vehicle from a mind of loving-kindness, they should always firmly make such a vow.
Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives clothing from a mind of loving-kindness, they should make this aspiration:
"May all that I now give be shared together with all sentient beings."
By these causes and conditions, all sentient beings shall obtain the garment of shame and modesty, which covers their bodies throughout the Dharma-realm and tears away the garments of false views.
This clothing remains one foot and six inches away from the body; they shall attain a golden-colored body, and all sensations they receive shall be soft, supple, and unimpeded.
"Their radiance and complexion are lustrous, their skin is fine and soft, and their constant light is immeasurable; they are formless and free from form.
"May all sentient beings universally attain this formless body, transcend all forms, and enter the formless Great Parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives clothing, he should thus firmly make this vow.
Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices loving-kindness by giving flowers, unguents, powdered incense, and various blended perfumes, they should make this aspiration:
"May all that I now give be shared together with all sentient beings."
"By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings attain the Buddha-flower Samādhi, and may the exquisite garland of the seven factors of enlightenment be bound upon their heads and crowns.
May the forms of all sentient beings be like the full moon, and may all the colors they perceive be subtle and supreme."
"May all sentient beings attain the single mark, adorned with a hundred blessings.
"May all sentient beings, according to their wishes, behold pleasing forms."
"May all sentient beings always encounter virtuous friends, obtain unobstructed fragrance, and be free from all foul odors.
"May all sentient beings be endowed with all roots of goodness and supreme, rare jewels."
"May all sentient beings look upon one another with harmony and joy, free from sorrow and suffering; may they each be fully endowed with all virtues and not harbor anxieties for one another.
"May all sentient beings be fully possessed of the fragrance of the precepts."
"May all sentient beings uphold unimpeded precepts, their fragrant aroma pervading the ten directions.

"May all sentient beings attain the firm precepts, the precepts free from regret, and the precepts of omniscience; may they leave behind all broken precepts and fully attain the precept of non-precept, the unprecedented precept, the teacherless precept, the unconditioned precept, the stainless precept, the undefiled precept, the ultimate precept, and the consummate precept. May they attain the precept of equality, remaining without hatred or attachment toward those who smear their bodies with fragrance or those who hack and stab them."
"May all sentient beings attain the unsurpassed precepts and the Mahāyāna precepts, not the precepts of the Hīnayāna.
"May all sentient beings fully perfect the *śīlapāramitā*, just as the precepts accomplished by all Buddhas."
"May all sentient beings be thoroughly cultivated by the practices of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom.
"May all sentient beings attain the subtle and wondrous lotus of Great Parinirvāṇa, the fragrance of which fills the ten directions."
“May all sentient beings purely partake of the unsurpassed fragrant food of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, just as bees gather from flowers, taking only the fragrance and flavor.
“May all sentient beings fully achieve bodies perfumed by immeasurable merit.”
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives flowers and incense from a mind of loving-kindness, they should always firmly make such a vow.
Furthermore, good son!”
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives beds and mats from a mind of loving-kindness, they should make this vow:
"May all that I now give be shared together with all sentient beings."
By these causes and conditions, they cause all sentient beings to obtain the bed upon which the God among Gods lies; to attain great wisdom and sit in the station of the four dhyānas;
to lie upon the bed where Bodhisattvas lie, and not to lie upon the beds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, remaining far removed from lying on evil beds.
"May all sentient beings obtain peaceful and blissful sleep, leave the bed of birth and death, and attain the great *nirvāṇa* lion’s bed.
"May all sentient beings, having sat upon this bed, further manifest the supernatural power of the lion’s sport for the sake of other immeasurable sentient beings."
"May all sentient beings dwell within this great palace of the Mahāyāna and expound the Buddha-nature for the sake of all sentient beings.
"May all sentient beings sit upon the unsurpassed throne, never to be overcome by worldly dharmas."
"May all sentient beings obtain the bed of forbearance, and be free from birth and death, famine, and cold hunger.
"May all sentient beings obtain the bed of fearlessness, forever parting from all the enemies of affliction."
"May all sentient beings obtain pure seats and single-mindedly seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
"May all sentient beings obtain the seat of wholesome dharmas and be constantly protected by virtuous friends."
"May all sentient beings obtain beds for lying on their right sides, relying upon the Dharma practiced by all Buddhas.
Son of good family,
when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives beds and bedding from a heart of loving-kindness, they should firmly make such a vow.
"Furthermore, good son!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives a house or dwelling from a mind of loving-kindness, he should make this vow:
'What I now give, I share entirely with all sentient beings.'"

By these causes and conditions, they cause all sentient beings to dwell in the dwelling of the Great Vehicle, to practice the conduct of virtuous friends, to practice the conduct of great compassion, the conduct of the six pāramitās, the conduct of great perfect enlightenment, the conduct practiced by all bodhisattvas, the conduct of the path, and boundlessly vast conduct as expansive as space.
“May all sentient beings attain right mindfulness and remain far removed from evil thoughts.
“May all sentient beings fully abide in permanence, bliss, self, and purity, forever departing from the four inversions.”
"May all sentient beings fully receive and uphold the supramundane syllables.
"May all sentient beings certainly become supreme vessels for all-knowledge (sarvajñā)."
"May all sentient beings enter the dwelling of the nectar of immortality.
"May all sentient beings, from the first, middle, and final moments of mind, always enter the dwelling of Mahāyāna nirvāṇa."
“‘May all sentient beings, in future ages, always dwell in the palaces inhabited by Bodhisattvas. Good son,
when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives houses and residences from a heart of loving-kindness, they should always firmly make such a vow.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives lamps from a mind of loving-kindness, they should make this vow:
'May all that I now give be shared together with all sentient beings.'"
"By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings possess immeasurable radiance and dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma.
"May all sentient beings always attain illuminating light."
"May all sentient beings attain a subtle and exquisite form, with a radiance that is foremost.
May all sentient beings have pure eyes, free from all veils and cataracts."

“May all sentient beings obtain the great torch of wisdom, skillfully understanding the absence of self, the absence of the mark of a sentient being, the absence of a person, and the absence of a life-force.
“May all sentient beings all behold the pure Buddha-nature, which is like empty space.”
"May all sentient beings attain purity of the fleshly eye, seeing through to the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions.
"May all sentient beings obtain the light of the Buddha, universally illuminating the ten directions."
"May all sentient beings attain the unobstructed eye and all perceive the pure Buddha-nature.
"May all sentient beings attain the light of great wisdom to shatter all darkness and the icchantikas."
"May all sentient beings attain immeasurable light, universally illuminating the immeasurable worlds of the Buddhas.
"May all sentient beings kindle the lamp of the Mahāyāna and leave behind the lamps of the two vehicles."
"May the light attained by all sentient beings extinguish the darkness of ignorance, surpassing the merit of a thousand suns shining together.
"May all sentient beings attain great radiance, completely extinguishing all the darkness within the trichiliocosm."
"May all sentient beings be fully endowed with the five eyes, realize the characteristics of all phenomena, and achieve untaught enlightenment.
"May all sentient beings be free from views and ignorance."
"May all sentient beings fully attain the subtle and wondrous radiance of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, which reveals and awakens sentient beings to their true Buddha-nature. "Good son!"
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva bestows lamps from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they should always diligently make such a vow:
"O Son of Good Family!
The roots of goodness possessed by all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas are rooted in loving-kindness."
"Good son! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, they are able to produce such immeasurable roots of goodness as:
impurity, exhalation and inhalation, impermanence, arising and ceasing, and the four foundations of mindfulness."
The seven stages of expedient means, the three stations of contemplation, the twelve links of dependent origination, and [the contemplations on] non-self and so forth;
the contemplations of the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma; the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation;
the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Eightfold Path, and the four dhyānas.
The four immeasurable minds, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the ten totalities, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness,
the samādhi of non-contention, the knowledge of others' minds, as well as the various supernormal powers, the knowledge of the primordial limit,
the wisdom of śrāvakas, the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom of bodhisattvas, and the wisdom of buddhas.
Good son! Such dharmas as these have loving-kindness as their root. Good son!
For this reason, loving-kindness is true and not false.
If someone were to ask:
"What is the root of all wholesome dharmas?"
One should say:
"It is loving-kindness.
For this reason, loving-kindness is the truth; it is not false.
“Good son! One who is able to perform what is wholesome is called one of genuine reflection;
one of genuine reflection is precisely what is called loving-kindness.”
“Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata; loving-kindness is the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. ‘Good son!
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*); the path to enlightenment is the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata is loving-kindness. "Good son! Loving-kindness is Great Brahmā (*mahābrahman*); Great Brahmā is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata."
“Good son! Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to act as a father and mother for all sentient beings.
The father and mother are loving-kindness, and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.”
“Good son! Loving-kindness is the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas; that which is the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas is itself loving-kindness.”
"You should know that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the Tathāgata. Good son!

Loving-kindness is the buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) of sentient beings; because this buddha-nature has long been shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), it causes sentient beings to be unable to behold it."
Buddha-nature is compassion, and compassion is the Tathāgata. "Good son!
Compassion is the Great Emptiness, and the Great Emptiness is compassion; compassion is the Tathāgata."
“Good son! Loving-kindness is space, and space is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. Good son!”
Loving-kindness is itself permanence; permanence is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the Sangha; the Sangha is itself loving-kindness; and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. "Good son!
Loving-kindness is itself bliss; bliss is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the Sangha; the Sangha is itself loving-kindness; and loving-kindness is itself the Tathāgata. "Good son!
Loving-kindness is itself purity; purity is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the Sangha; the Sangha is itself loving-kindness; and loving-kindness is itself the Tathāgata.
"O son of good family!
"Compassion is myself; I am the Dharma; the Dharma is the Sangha; the Sangha is compassion; and compassion is the Tathāgata. Good son!
Loving-kindness is ambrosia, and ambrosia is loving-kindness.
Loving-kindness is the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-nature is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Sangha, and the Sangha is loving-kindness; loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
“Good son! Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the unsurpassed path of all bodhisattvas; the path is loving-kindness, and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. Good son!
Loving-kindness is the immeasurable realm of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; that immeasurable realm is itself loving-kindness.
One should know that this loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.
“Good son! If loving-kindness were impermanent, and impermanence itself were loving-kindness, you should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. Good son!...”
If loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is suffering and suffering is loving-kindness, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the *śrāvakas*. "Good son!
If loving-kindness is impure and impurity is loving-kindness, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the *śrāvakas*."
“Good son! If loving-kindness is without self, and that which is without self is itself loving-kindness, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. Good son!
If loving-kindness is conceptual construction, and conceptual construction is itself loving-kindness, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. "Good son!
If loving-kindness is not called the dānapāramitā—if it is a loving-kindness that is not dāna—you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas."
It is the same even for the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Good son! If loving-kindness (*maitrī*) cannot benefit sentient beings, such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the *śrāvakas*."
“Good son! If loving-kindness does not enter the Way of the Single Characteristic, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. Good son!
If loving-kindness (*maitrī*) cannot fully awaken to and comprehend all phenomena, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the *śrāvakas*. "Good son!
If loving-kindness cannot perceive the nature of the Tathāgata, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the *śrāvakas*."
“Good son! If loving-kindness perceives all phenomena as having marks, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. Good son!”
If loving-kindness is with outflows, then this loving-kindness with outflows is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.
"Good son! If loving-kindness is conditioned, then this conditioned loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas."
“Good son! If loving-kindness cannot abide in the first stage—meaning it is not the loving-kindness of the first stage—you should know that this is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas.”
“Good son! If loving-kindness cannot attain the Buddha’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses, you should know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. Good son!”
If loving-kindness can attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa, you should know that such loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of the śrāvakas. "Good son!
If loving-kindness is neither existent nor non-existent, neither being nor non-being, then such loving-kindness cannot be conceived by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others."
Good son! If loving-kindness is inconceivable, then the Dharma is inconceivable, the Buddha-nature is inconceivable, and the Tathāgata is also inconceivable.

“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa cultivates such loving-kindness, although he remains within the midst of sleep, he does not truly sleep because of his diligent application of energy;
although he is constantly awake, he has no awakening, because there is no sleep.”
While asleep, although protected by the devas, there is no one who protects them, because they do not commit evil;
they have no bad dreams while sleeping, because they are free from unwholesomeness and have transcended sleep;
and after the end of life, although they may be born in the Brahma Heaven, there is no place of birth, because they have attained mastery.
"Good son! One who cultivates loving-kindness is able to achieve such immeasurable and boundless merit. Good son!"

This subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra can likewise accomplish such immeasurable and boundless merits, and the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have also accomplished such immeasurable and boundless merits.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

All the contemplations of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are entirely true, whereas those of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not true. For what reason do all sentient beings not equally receive happiness through the majestic power of the bodhisattvas?”
"If sentient beings do not actually obtain happiness, one should know that the loving mind cultivated by a bodhisattva is of no benefit.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
The compassion of a bodhisattva is not without benefit. Good son!
There are sentient beings who will inevitably experience suffering, and there are those who will not.
If there were sentient beings who were destined to experience suffering, the compassion of a bodhisattva would be of no benefit—referring to those such as the icchantikas.
However, if there are those whose suffering is not fixed, the compassion of a bodhisattva is indeed beneficial, causing those sentient beings to experience complete happiness.

“Good son! It is like a person who, seeing from afar a lion, tiger, leopard, jackal, wolf, rākṣasa, or ghost, naturally gives rise to fear; or one who, walking at night, sees a tree stump and likewise gives rise to fear.”
"Good son! Just as these people naturally feel fear,
so too do sentient beings naturally experience happiness upon seeing one who practices loving-kindness."
"Good son! For this reason, when a bodhisattva cultivates loving-kindness, it is genuine reflection and not without benefit. Good son!"
I say that this loving-kindness has immeasurable gateways, namely, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Son of good family!

For example, when Devadatta instructed Ajātaśatru to harm the Tathāgata, at that time I entered the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in sequence; King Ajātaśatru then released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla, intending to have him harm me and my disciples.
At that time, the elephant trampled and killed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
After these beings had died, there was much blood and vital energy; having smelled it, the elephant became twice as frenzied and intoxicated as usual.
Seeing my attendants clad in red garments, they mistook them for blood and fled toward my disciples;
all those who had not yet abandoned desire ran away in terror, with the sole exception of Ānanda.
At that time, all the people within the great city of Rājagṛha simultaneously raised their voices in weeping and wailing, saying:
"How strange! Today the Tathāgata has passed away; how can the Perfectly Awakened One suddenly perish?"
At that time, Devadatta felt joy arise in his heart:
"It is most excellent that the śramaṇa Gautama has perished; from this day forward, he shall truly no longer appear.
How wonderful is this plan! My wish is fulfilled."

“Good son! At that time, desiring to subdue the elephant Dhana-pāla, I immediately entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and extended my hand to show him; from my five fingers, I manifested five lions.”
Upon seeing this, the elephant was struck with fear; it immediately voided its excrement and threw its entire body to the ground, prostrating at my feet.

Good son! At that time, there were actually no lions on the tips of my five fingers; rather, it was through the power of the roots of goodness cultivated from practicing loving-kindness that I tamed it.
"Furthermore, good son!

When I was about to enter nirvana and had first set out toward the city of Kuśinagara, there were five hundred strongmen along the road who were leveling, sweeping, and sprinkling it. Among them was a stone which they all wished to lift and remove, yet despite exerting all their strength, they could not do so."
At that time, moved by compassion, I immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness.

Those Mallas then saw me lift this great rock with my big toe, cast it into the air, and catch it again with my hand; I placed it upon my right palm, blew it into fine powder, and then reassembled it once more.
He caused the haughty mind of that Malla to subside, and immediately expounded for him various essential teachings, leading both of them to resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son!
At that time, the Tathāgata did not actually lift this great stone into the air with his finger, place it back in his right palm, blow it into fine powder, and then reassemble it as it was before."
"Good son! You should know that this is the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which causes all these strongmen to see such a thing.
Furthermore, good son!"
To the south of this land of South India, there is a great city named Śobhāvatī.
Within this city, there was an elder named Luṭi, who served as a leader for the multitude and had already planted the roots of various virtues under immeasurable Buddhas in the past.
"Good son!
In that great city, all the people believed in and submitted to false paths, serving the Nirgranthas.
At that time, wishing to deliver that elder, I traveled from Rājagṛha to that city."
The distance between them along the way was sixty-five *yojanas*, yet he traveled on foot because he wished to transform and deliver those people.
When the assembly of Nirgranthas heard that I intended to go to the city of Śrāvastī, they immediately thought:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama arrives here, these people will surely abandon us and no longer provide for us."
"We are utterly exhausted and emaciated; how shall we sustain ourselves?
The various Nirgranthas then dispersed, each telling the people of that city:
"The śramaṇa Gautama now intends to come here."

Yet that śramaṇa has abandoned his parents to roam hither and thither; wherever he goes, he causes the land’s crops to fail, brings famine upon the people, results in many deaths, and leads to a succession of sickness and emaciation that cannot be remedied.
This rogue Gautama leads only evil rākṣasas and spirits as his attendants; he takes in fatherless, motherless, and destitute people as disciples to come and seek instruction from him.
"Whatever you are taught and instructed is purely about emptiness; wherever you go, there is initially no peace or happiness.
Having heard this, that man was immediately struck with fear. He prostrated himself, bowing his head at the feet of the Nirgrantha, and said:
"Great Master!..."
"What plan should we now devise?
The Nirgrantha replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama naturally delights in groves, flowing springs, and clear water; whatever such things exist outside [our domain] should be destroyed."

"You all should now go forth together out of the city; wherever there are trees, cut them down until none remain, leaving nothing behind. As for the flowing springs, wells, and ponds, fill them entirely with excrement and corpses."
