Firmly close the city gates; each person shall prepare their weapons and provide defense from behind the walls, diligently maintaining their own stronghold.
Should they come, do not allow them to advance.
"If he does not advance, you shall remain in safety.
We too shall employ various stratagems to cause that Gautama to turn back along his path.
Having heard these words, the people gave their respectful assent and set to work; they cut down trees, defiled the waters, arrayed themselves with weapons, and fortified their defenses.
“Good son! When I arrived at that city at that time, I saw no trees or groves at all; I saw only people adorned with weapons, defending themselves behind walls.
Having seen this, he immediately gave rise to compassion and directed a heart of loving-kindness toward them; all the trees grew back as they were before, and further trees sprang up in addition.
Countless rivers, ponds, springs, and wells had their waters purified, filling them to the brim like blue lapis lazuli;
various flowers bloomed, covering the surface, and the city walls were transformed into dark-blue lapis lazuli.

The people within the city were all able to see me and the great assembly clearly; the gates opened of their own accord, none being able to restrain them, and the weapons arrayed there were transformed into various flowers.
The elder Lu-zhi was the leader, and together with his people, they followed one another to where the Buddha was.
I then expounded various essential teachings for them, causing all those people to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Good son! At that time, I did not actually manifest various trees, nor did I transform the clear, flowing waters so they filled the rivers and ponds, nor did I change my original city into dark-blue lapis lazuli, nor cause those people to see me clearly through the opening of the city gates, nor turn their weapons into flowers.
"Good son! You should know that it is entirely through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness that these people are able to see such things.
Furthermore, good son!"
In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a Brāhmaṇa woman of the Vāsiṣṭha clan who had an only son whom she loved exceedingly.

When he fell ill and passed away, the woman’s heart was pierced by the poison of grief; she became deranged and lost her senses, wandering through the crossroads naked and shameless, wailing until her voice failed, crying out:
"My son! My son!"
"Where have you gone?
Thus he searched throughout the city and its environs without weariness.
Yet that woman had already planted many roots of merit under previous Buddhas.
"Good son! I gave rise to a heart of compassion for this woman.
At that moment, the woman saw me and immediately conceived the thought that I was her son; she regained her original mind and came forward to embrace my body as one would a beloved child."
At that time, I immediately told my attendant Ānanda:
"You may take this robe and give it to this woman.
Once the robe had been given, I then expounded for her various essential points of the Dharma.
Upon hearing the Dharma, this woman was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and she resolved her mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Good son!
At that time, I was truly not her child, she was not my mother, and there was no act of embracing."
"Good son! You should know that all this is due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which causes that woman to see such things.
Furthermore, good son!"
In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a laywoman named Mahāśraddhā, who had already planted various roots of goodness under countless Buddhas of the past.
This upāsikā invited the community of monks for ninety days during the summer retreat to offer them medicine.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who was afflicted with a grave illness; a skilled physician examined him and determined that he required meat as medicine.
"If meat can be obtained, the illness may be cured;
if meat cannot be obtained, my life will not be preserved.
When the upāsikā heard these words of the physician, she immediately took gold and went throughout the marketplace, crying out these words:
"Who has meat for sale?
I shall buy it with gold.
If there is any meat, I will give you gold equal to its weight."
He searched throughout the city but was unable to find any.
This upāsikā then took a knife herself, cut the flesh from her own thigh, sliced it into pieces to make a stew, added various kinds of fragrant spices, and sent it to the sick bhikṣu.
After the bhikṣu had taken the medicine, his illness was immediately cured.
This upāsikā, suffering from the pain of her ulcer and unable to endure it, cried out:
"Namo Buddhāya!"
“Namo Buddhāya.
At that time, I was in Śrāvastī, and upon hearing her voice, I gave rise to a heart of great compassion for that woman.
The woman then saw me taking excellent medicine and applying it to her wound, whereupon it healed and returned to its original state.
I then preached various teachings for him; upon hearing the Dharma, he rejoiced and resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"O son of good family!
"At that time, I did not actually go to the city of Vārāṇasī to apply medicine to this upāsikā’s wound.
Good son! You should know that it was entirely through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion that caused that woman to see such a thing."
"Furthermore, good son!
The evil man Devadatta was greedy and knew no contentment; because he consumed so much ghee, his head ached and his belly swelled, causing him such great suffering that he could not endure it."
He uttered these words:
"Namo buddhāya. Namo buddhāya."
"At that time, I was residing in the city of Ujjayinī; upon hearing his voice, I immediately gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*).
Thereupon, Devadatta soon saw me go to his side, where I stroked his head and belly with my hands and gave him salted broth to drink. Having drunk it, he was restored to health."
“Good son! I did not actually go to Devadatta’s place to stroke his head and belly, nor did I give him medicinal broth to drink.
Good son!”
"You should know that all this is due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which caused Devadatta to see such things.
Furthermore, good son,
in the kingdom of Kośala there were five hundred bandits who, in their gangs, committed robbery and plunder, causing immense harm."
King Prasenajit, troubled by their lawlessness and violence, dispatched troops to track and capture them. Having seized them, he gouged out their eyes and cast them beneath a dark, dense forest.
These bandits had previously planted many roots of virtue under former Buddhas; now that they had lost their sight and were undergoing great suffering, they each cried out:
"Namo Buddhāya! (Homage to the Buddha!)
"Namo Buddhāya!
We now have no protector or refuge," they cried out,
weeping and wailing.
At that time, I was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery; upon hearing his voice, I immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Then, a cool breeze blew various medicinal herbs from Mount Gandhamādana into his eye sockets, and he immediately regained his sight, no different from how it had been before.
When the bandits opened their eyes, they immediately saw the Tathāgata standing before them preaching the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, the bandits gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Good son! At that time, I did not actually blow various fragrant medicines from Mount Gandhamādana with the wind, nor did I stand before that person to preach the Dharma for him.”
"Good son! You should know that all this is due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness, which causes those bandits to see such things.
Furthermore, good son!"
Due to his folly, Prince Vaidūrya deposed his father, the king, and established himself as ruler.

Recalling their former enmity, he slaughtered many members of the Śākya clan; he seized twelve thousand Śākya maidens, mutilated them by cutting off their ears and noses and severing their hands and feet, and cast them into pits and ditches.
At that time, the women, suffering physical pain and distress, spoke these words:
"Namo Buddhāya. Namo Buddhāya."
"We now have no protector or refuge," they cried out again with great lamentation.
These women had already planted various roots of goodness under previous Buddhas.
At that time, while I was in the Bamboo Grove, I heard their cries and immediately gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness.

When those women saw me arrive at Kapilavastu, they washed their wounds with water and applied medicinal ointments; their suffering was instantly relieved, and their ears, noses, hands, and feet were restored to their original state.

At that time, I briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them, causing them all to resolve together upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They then went forth under the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and received full ordination.
“Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata did not actually go to the city of Kapilavastu to wash the wound with water, apply medicine, and stop the pain.
Good son!...”
"You should know that all these matters were brought about for that woman through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
It is the same with the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*). Good son!"
For this reason, the cultivation of loving-kindness contemplation by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself reality and is not false. Good son!

That which is immeasurable is inconceivable; the conduct of Bodhisattvas is inconceivable, the conduct of all Buddhas is also inconceivable, and this Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, is likewise inconceivable.
Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 14. Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 15.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huiyan and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter on the Holy Life,
Part Two: "Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has cultivated loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, he attains the stage of being exceedingly fond of all beings as if they were his only child."
"Good son! Why is this stage called 'Supreme Love' and also named 'Only Son'? Good son!"
For example, when parents see their child in safety and well-being, their hearts are filled with great joy.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage: regarding all sentient beings as his only child, he experiences great joy upon seeing those who cultivate wholesome qualities.
For this reason, this stage is called "Supreme Affection. "Good son!
It is like parents who, seeing their child fall ill, feel distress in their hearts; out of compassion for them, they are consumed by sorrow and never abandon them."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage is likewise; seeing all sentient beings tormented by the diseases of afflictions, his heart gives rise to sorrow and distress, and he grieves for them as if they were his own children, such that blood flows from all the pores of his body.
For this reason, this stage is called "The Only Son. "Good son!
It is like a person in their childhood who picks up clods of earth, filth, shards, stones, dry bones, or wooden branches and places them in their mouth."
When the parents saw this, fearing it would cause him harm, they grasped his head with their left hand and extracted [the object] with their right.

In the same way, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this stage, they see that the *dharmakāya* of sentient beings has not yet increased, or that they engage in unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind; having seen this, the Bodhisattvas use the hand of wisdom to pull them out, desiring not to let them wander in birth and death or undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
For this reason, this stage is further named "The Only Son. "Good son!
It is like parents who, when their beloved son passes away, are filled with grief and distress, wishing to end their own lives along with him."
The Bodhisattva is likewise: seeing an icchantika fall into hell, he also vows to be born together with them in that hell. Why is this?

If, while suffering there, that icchantika should give rise to even a single thought of repentance, I shall immediately preach various dharmas for them, enabling them to produce a single thought of wholesome roots.
For this reason, this stage is also called "The Only Son. "Good son!
It is like parents who have only one son; whether that son is sleeping, awake, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, their minds are constantly mindful of him."
If there is any transgression, one should entice and admonish them with kind words rather than inflicting harm upon them.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise: seeing sentient beings falling into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or among humans and devas as they perform good or evil deeds, he constantly keeps them in mind and never abandons them.
"Even if others commit various evils against me, I shall never give rise to anger or retaliate with evil.
For this reason, this stage is further named 'The Only Son.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has spoken, his words are esoteric; my wisdom is shallow now, so how could I understand them?

If it is true that bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of ‘regarding all beings as an only son’ can act in this way, why did the Tathāgata, in the past when he was practicing the bodhisattva path as a king, take the lives of so many brahmins?”
If one has attained this stage, one ought to protect and mindfully attend to it;
if one has not attained it, for what reason would one not fall into hell?
If you regard all sentient beings equally as your own children, just like Rāhula, why did you further speak such words to Devadatta?
"This foolish man has no shame; he eats the snot and spittle of others.
Upon hearing this, he gave rise to resentment and malice, and with an unwholesome mind, he shed the blood of the Buddha.
After Devadatta had committed these evils, the Tathāgata further prophesied that he would fall into hell and suffer punishment for one kalpa.
World-Honored One!
How is it that such words do not contradict the meaning [of the Dharma]?
“World-Honored One!
Subhūti dwells in the realm of empty space; whenever he wishes to enter a city to beg for food and drink, he first observes the people.
If there is anyone who harbors feelings of resentment or envy toward him, he stops and does not proceed, even to the point of extreme hunger he still does not go begging.”
Why is this? Subhūti constantly reflects:

"I recall that in the past, at the site of a field of merit, I gave rise to a single evil thought; by reason of this cause and condition, I fell into the great hells and underwent various kinds of suffering."
"I would rather remain hungry and go without food all day than cause him to harbor resentment toward me and fall into hell to suffer affliction.
He further thought:
"If there are sentient beings who resent my standing, I shall sit upright all day without rising."
"If there are sentient beings who take offense at my sitting, I shall remain standing all day without shifting my place;
the same applies to walking and lying down.
Subhūti gave rise to such a thought for the sake of protecting sentient beings—how much more so, then, should a bodhisattva?
“If a bodhisattva has attained the stage of the only son, for what reason does the Tathāgata utter such harsh words as to cause all sentient beings to give rise to grave and evil thoughts? “Good man!
You should not now raise such an objection, saying:
"The Buddha-Tathāgata acts as a causal condition for the afflictions of all sentient beings. Good son!
"Even if a mosquito's proboscis were able to exhaust the depths of the ocean, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings. 'Good son!

Even if the great earth were entirely to become non-material, water were to take on the characteristic of dryness, fire were to take on the characteristic of cold, wind were to take on the characteristic of stillness, and the Three Jewels, the Buddha-nature, and even empty space were to manifest the characteristic of impermanence, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.'"

“Good son! Even if one were to commit the four grave offenses or, as an icchantika, slander the true Dharma, such a person might in this very body attain the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics. Yet, the Tathāgata never acts as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.”
“Good son! Even if śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others were permanent and unchanging, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.”

“Good son! Even if bodhisattvas of the ten stages were to commit the four grave offenses or become icchantikas who slander the true Dharma, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.”

“Good son! Even if all immeasurable sentient beings were to lose their Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata were to finally enter parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of those sentient beings.”

“Good son! Even if one could cast a lasso to bind the wind, with teeth break iron, or with claws shatter Mount Sumeru, the Tathāgata would never act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.”
"It would be better to dwell together with a venomous snake, to thrust both hands into the mouth of a starving lion, or to bathe one's body in the coals of khadira wood, than to utter the words:
'The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, acts as a cause and condition for the afflictions of all sentient beings.'"
“Good son! The Tathāgata is true and real; he is able to sever the afflictions for sentient beings and never acts as a cause for afflictions. Good son!”
Regarding what you have said—
that "the Tathāgata in the past killed a brahmin"—
O son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not intentionally kill even an ant, much less a brāhmaṇa;
the bodhisattva constantly employs various skillful means to bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
“Good son! One who gives food gives life.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they constantly bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings.”
“Good son! By practicing the precept against killing, one attains a long life.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the *śīlapāramitā*, he bestows immeasurable life upon all sentient beings.”
"Good son! Be careful with your speech and commit no transgression, and you shall obtain a long life.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he constantly exhorts sentient beings not to give rise to thoughts of enmity; he attributes rectitude to others and takes the faults upon himself, remaining free from dispute and litigation, thereby obtaining a long life."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they have already bestowed immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
"Good son! By diligently cultivating wholesome deeds, one attains a long life."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), they constantly exhort sentient beings to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas;
once these beings have so practiced, they attain immeasurable lifespans.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), they have already bestowed immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
"Good son! One who cultivates the gathering of the mind attains a long life."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, they exhort all sentient beings to cultivate a mind of equanimity;
once sentient beings have so practiced, they attain long life.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, they bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
"Good son! Those who are diligent and heedful regarding all wholesome dharmas attain a long life."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they exhort all sentient beings not to be negligent regarding any wholesome dharmas;
once these beings have so practiced, by this causal condition, they attain a long life span.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they have already bestowed immeasurable life upon sentient beings.
Noble son! For this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva never takes the life of any sentient being.
“Good son! Regarding what you have just asked:
‘When one kills a brahmin, does one attain this stage?’”
"Good son! At that time, I had already attained [this state];
I severed his life-force out of affectionate concern, not out of an evil mind."
Good son! It is like parents who have only one son; they love him very dearly, yet he violates the laws of the state.
At that time, out of fear, the parents may either banish him or kill him.
Although there may be banishment or execution, there is no malicious intent.

It is the same for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who seeks to protect the True Dharma: if there are sentient beings who slander the Mahāyāna, they may subject them to punishment by whipping or even deprive them of life, desiring only to cause them to reform their past ways and practice wholesome dharmas.
A bodhisattva should constantly reflect in this way:
"By what causes and conditions can I cause sentient beings to give rise to faith?
I must employ every skillful means to accomplish this for them."
"After those brahmins have passed away and been reborn in the Avīci Hell, they will have three thoughts:
first, they will think to themselves,
'From where have I come to be born here?'"
First, he immediately knows for himself that he has come from the human realm;
second, he reflects to himself:
"In what place have I now been born?"
He then realizes for himself that this is the Avīci Hell;
third, he reflects to himself:
"By what karmic conditions have I come to be born here?"
He immediately realized that he had been killed by the ruler of the country because he had slandered the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras and lacked faith in the principle of causes and conditions.
Having reflected on this matter, he conceived a heart of faith and reverence toward the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
Immediately upon passing away, he was reborn in the world-system of the Tathāgata Amṛtadundubhi, where his lifespan was full for ten kalpas.
Good son! For this reason, I granted that person a lifespan of ten kalpas in the past.
"What is meant by 'killing'? Good son!
If there are people who dig the earth, cut grass, chop trees, sever corpses, revile others, or whip them—by reason of such karmic conditions, would they fall into hell?"
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, I should fall into hell.”
Why is this? For example, in the past, the Buddha taught the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas, saying:
"O bhikṣus, do not give rise to evil thoughts toward any grasses or trees."
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings fall into hell due to their evil minds.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said; you should receive and uphold it well.
Son of good family!”
If one were to fall into hell due to an evil mind, at that time a bodhisattva truly has no evil mind.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to a mind of compassion and benefit toward all sentient beings, even down to insects and ants.

Why is this? Because they skillfully understand the various skillful means of causes and conditions, and by the power of these skillful means, they desire to cause sentient beings to plant all roots of goodness. Good son!
For this reason, at that time, although I took his life through skillful means, it was not done with an evil mind.
"Good son! According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, if one kills ants until they fill ten wagons, there is no karmic retribution for sin."

Mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, lice, cats, raccoons, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, and various evil insects and beasts, as well as others capable of harming sentient beings—having killed enough of these to fill ten carts;

or ghosts, spirits, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, kālapūtanas, those who cause insanity, and withered spirits and other such deities capable of afflicting sentient beings—having deprived them all of their lives, there shall be no retribution for sin.
If one kills an evil person, there will be retribution for the sin; if, after killing, one does not repent, one will fall among the hungry ghosts.
However, if one can repent and fast for three days, that sin will be extinguished without remainder.
"If one kills one's preceptor, harms one's parents, a woman, or an ox, one will remain in hell for countless thousands of years.
'Good son! The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know that there are three kinds of killing: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.'"
The "lower" refers to ants and all other animals, with the sole exception of those born as Bodhisattvas through intentional manifestation.
Good son! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva intentionally manifests birth as an animal due to the causal conditions of their vows, this is called "lower killing."
Due to these causes and conditions of killing, they fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, where they fully undergo the lower forms of suffering. Why is this?
It is because these various animals possess subtle roots of goodness.
Therefore, the killer fully receives the retribution for their sin; this is called "inferior killing.
As for "middling killing," it refers to those from ordinary worldlings up to the stage of Anāgāmin; this is called "middling."
By reason of these karmic causes, one falls into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, fully experiencing intermediate suffering; this is called intermediate killing.
As for "superior killing," it refers to [killing] one's parents, up to and including Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas who are fixed in their destiny; this is called superior.
Due to these karmic causes and conditions, one falls into the Avīci Great Hell and undergoes the utmost suffering; this is called "supreme killing. "Good son!
If there were anyone capable of killing an icchantika, they would not fall into these three kinds of killing.
Good son! All those brahmins and others are entirely icchantikas.
For example, just as there is no karmic retribution for digging the earth, cutting grass, felling trees, chopping up corpses, reviling others, or whipping them;
likewise, there is no karmic retribution for killing an icchantika.
Why is this? Because these brahmins lack even the five dharmas, such as faith; therefore, although they kill, they do not fall into hell. "Good son!
Regarding what you previously asked:
"For what reason did the Tathāgata revile Devadatta as a foolish man who eats spittle?"—
you likewise should not have asked such a question.
Why is this? Whatever words the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, speak are inconceivable.
O son of good family!
"Even if there were words that were true and beloved by the world, yet untimely, contrary to the Dharma, and not conducive to benefit—such speech I would never utter.
Good son!"
Furthermore, there may be those who say that what is coarse and vulgar, false, untimely, contrary to the Dharma, disagreeable to hearers, and incapable of benefiting them, I do not speak.
"Good son!

If there is speech that, though coarse and harsh, is true and not false, and if at that time and according to that dharma it can bring benefit to all sentient beings—even if hearing it is unpleasant—I must speak it."
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the Worthy Ones, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, know skillful means. "Good son!
Once, while I was traveling through that wilderness village among the thickets of trees,

there was beneath those trees a spirit named Wilderness (Āṭavaka), who fed exclusively on flesh and blood, killed many sentient beings, and furthermore devoured one person every day from that village.
"Good son! At that time, I extensively expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for those spirits and deities.
Yet, being violent, evil, foolish, and lacking wisdom, they did not accept the instructions."
I immediately manifested as a powerful ghost and shook his palace, causing it to become unstable.
At that time, the ghost led his retinue out of the palace, intending to come and resist me.
When the ghost saw me, it immediately lost its mindfulness; struck with terror, it fell to the ground, fainting and gasping until it was like one dead.
As I stroked its body with my hand of compassion, it immediately rose and sat up, saying these words:
"How wonderful! Today I have regained my life and body."
"This great king of spirits possesses great majesty and virtue, and has a heart of compassion; may he pardon my transgressions.
He then conceived a wholesome faith in me.
I immediately restored myself to the body of a Tathāgata and once again expounded various essential teachings for him, causing that spirit to receive the precept against killing.
"On that very day, there was an elder in the village of Khāṇu who was due to die.
The villagers had already delivered him to that spirit.
Having received him, the spirit immediately bestowed him upon me."
Having accepted it, I then established another name for the elder, calling him the Elder Hand.
At that time, the ghost addressed me, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I and my retinue rely solely upon flesh and blood for our own survival.
Now, because of your precepts, how shall we live? I then replied:
"From this day forward, I shall command my śrāvaka disciples that wherever the Buddha-dharma is practiced, they shall all cause you to be provided with food and drink. "Good son!"
For these reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must always provide food to those wilderness spirits.
If there are those who reside in a dwelling and cannot provide such offerings, you should know that they are not my disciples; they are merely the followers and retinues of the celestial Māra."
“Good son! It is because the Tathāgata wishes to discipline sentient beings that he displays such various skillful means; it is not for the purpose of causing them to give rise to fear.”
“Good son! I also struck the Dharma-protecting ghost with a piece of wood.
Furthermore, on one occasion, while on a mountain, I pushed the goat-headed ghost so that he fell down the slope.”
Furthermore, he struck the monkey-demon atop the tree, caused the elephant Dhanapāla to see five lions, and terrified the Vajrapāṇi spirit with Sañjayin the Nirgrantha;
he also pierced the body of the arrow-hair demon with a needle.
Although he acts in this way, he does not cause those spirits and ghosts to perish; rather, desiring only that they abide securely in the True Dharma, he demonstrates such various skillful means.
“Good son! At that time, I did not actually revile Devadatta. Devadatta was neither foolish nor one who eats the spittle and saliva of others;

he did not take birth in the evil realms or suffer the retribution of Avīci Hell for one kalpa; he did not cause a schism in the Saṃgha or shed the blood of a Buddha; he did not commit the four grave offenses, slander the True Dharma or Mahāyāna sūtras, nor was he an icchantika, nor was he a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.”
"Good son!
Devadatta is truly not within the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; he is known and seen only by the Buddhas. Good son!"
Therefore, you should not now raise the objection:
"For what reason did the Tathāgata scold, revile, and insult Devadatta?
You should not give rise to such a web of doubt regarding the domain of all Buddhas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is like sugarcane; by boiling it repeatedly, one obtains various flavors.”

I am likewise; having heard it repeatedly from the Buddha, I have gained much of the flavor of the Dharma—namely, the flavor of renunciation, the flavor of detachment from desire, the flavor of tranquility, and the flavor of the Path.
World-Honored One!

It is like pure gold, which, when repeatedly heated, beaten, melted, and refined, becomes increasingly bright, pure, harmonious, and malleable; its luster and color become subtle and exquisite, its value immeasurable, and only then is it held in high esteem as a treasure by humans and devas.
World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is likewise: by earnest inquiry, one may hear and perceive the profoundly deep meaning, causing those who practice deeply to receive, uphold, and cultivate it, and leading immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; thereafter, he becomes the object of veneration, respect, and offerings for all humans and devas.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas desire to benefit all sentient beings that they inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such profound meanings.”
"Good son!

For this reason, in accordance with your intention, I shall explain for you the profound and secret Dharma of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, namely, the stage known as 'Extreme Affection like that for an Only Son'."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If bodhisattvas cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy and thereby attain the Stage of the Only Son, what stage do they further attain when they cultivate the mind of equanimity?”
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"
You well know the proper time; knowing that I wish to speak, you then inquire.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), they then abide in the ground of the equality of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samatā-bhūmi*), just like Subhūti.
"Good son!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the stage of the equality of emptiness, they do not perceive fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, children, kinsmen, friends, enemies, or neutral persons; they do not even perceive the aggregates, elements, sense bases, sentient beings, or the life-span."
“Good son! For example, space has no father, mother, brothers, or wife, nor does it possess anything up to and including sentient beings or a life span.
All phenomena are likewise thus: they have no father or mother, nor even a life-span.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as being thus, their mind is equanimous, like that empty space.
"Why is this? Because they are well able to cultivate all dharmas of emptiness.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘emptiness’? “Good son!

Emptiness refers to what are called internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of emptiness, and great emptiness.
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate internal emptiness?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that internal phenomena are empty.

This internal emptiness of phenomena means there is no father, mother, enemy, friend, or neutral person; no sentient beings, life-span, permanence, bliss, self, or purity; and no Tathāgata, Dharma, Saṅgha, or any material possessions.”
Although the Buddha-nature exists within these internal dharmas, this Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external.
Why is this? Because the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding and free from change.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of internal emptiness.
External emptiness is likewise; there are no internal dharmas.
Internal-and-external emptiness is likewise.
“Good son! Only the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the Buddha-nature do not abide within the two kinds of emptiness. Why is this?
These four dharmas— permanence, bliss, self, and purity—
are therefore not called empty.
This is what is meant by "both internal and external are empty."

“Good son! Regarding the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), all conditioned phenomena are entirely empty; that is to say: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; the emptiness of sentient beings, life-span, Tathāgata, Dharma, Saṅgha, and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).”
In this context, the Buddha-nature is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not empty of being a conditioned phenomenon.
This is called the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of the unconditioned?

These unconditioned dharmas are all empty; that is to say, they are devoid of impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self; they are devoid of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; they are devoid of the characteristics of a sentient being, a life span, the conditioned, the outflowing, internal dharmas, and external dharmas.”
Among the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the four dharmas beginning with the Buddha are neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Because their nature is wholesome, they are not unconditioned;
because their nature is eternally abiding, they are not conditioned.
This is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of that which has no beginning (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*)?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that saṃsāra is without beginning and is entirely empty and quiescent."

That which is called emptiness refers to permanence, bliss, self, and purity—all of which are utterly empty and quiescent, without change or alteration; it also refers to sentient beings, life-span, the Three Jewels, Buddha-nature, and unconditioned dharmas.
This is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of that which has no beginning.
“How does a bodhisattva contemplate the emptiness of intrinsic nature?

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty—namely, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the permanent and the impermanent; suffering and pleasure; purity and impurity; the self and the non-self.”
To contemplate all such phenomena and not perceive an intrinsic nature is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of nature.
"How does the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of non-existence?
Just as a person who has no children says their house is empty, one who contemplates ultimate emptiness finds no objects of affection.

A foolish person says that all directions are empty, while a poor person says everything is empty; such calculations may regard things as either empty or not empty, but when a Bodhisattva contemplates them, they see everything as empty, just like the poor person.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of non-existence.
"How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)? Good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he observes that when this eye arises, it comes from nowhere; and when it ceases, it goes nowhere. Originally non-existent, it now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence. When its actual nature is investigated, there is neither eye nor master.
As it is with the eye, so it is with all phenomena (*dharmas*).
What is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)?
There is karma and there is its retribution, yet no agent is perceived; such an emptiness of phenomena is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
How does the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*)?
This emptiness within emptiness is precisely the place where śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others are deluded and submerged.
Good son! That which is existent and that which is non-existent is called "emptiness of emptiness";
that which is "is" and that which is "is not" is called "emptiness of emptiness."
"Good son!
Even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages only penetrate a small portion of this, like a mere mote of dust;
how much less so others? Good son!"

In this way, the emptiness of emptiness is also not the same as the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness attained by śrāvakas; this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the emptiness of emptiness. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate great emptiness?
Son of good family, that which is called "great emptiness" refers to the prajñāpāramitā; this is termed great emptiness.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains such a gateway to emptiness, they then abide on the ground that is equal to space.
Good son!”

Now, as I expound these various meanings of emptiness within this great assembly, ten times the number of sands of the Ganges bodhisattva-mahāsattvas immediately attained the stage of the "ground of space."
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they encounter no obstructions, fetters, or attachments regarding any phenomena, and their mind is free from confusion or distress."
For this reason, it is called the "Space-like Ground. "Good son!
For example, space does not give rise to attachment toward pleasant forms, nor does it give rise to aversion toward unpleasant forms.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in this stage is also like this: toward beautiful or ugly forms, the mind is free from greed and anger. Good son!

Just as space is vast, without opposition, and is able to contain all phenomena, so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage: he is likewise vast and without opposition, able to contain all phenomena.
For this reason, it is further named the "Stage of Space-like Equality.
Son of Good Family!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they both see and know all phenomena.

Whether it be their conduct, objects of perception, nature, characteristics, causes, conditions, the minds of sentient beings, faculties, meditative concentrations, vehicles, spiritual friends, observance of precepts, or acts of giving—he knows and perceives all such phenomena.
"Furthermore, good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this stage, he knows yet does not see.
What is meant by 'knowing'? "

They know the practices of self-starvation, throwing themselves into abysses, leaping into fires, casting themselves from high cliffs, constantly standing on one leg, and scorching their bodies with the five heats;
they constantly lie upon ashes and dust, thorny branches, rafters, leaves, foul grass, or cow dung;
they wear coarse hempen garments, discarded rags from among graves, refuse-rags, *kambala* woolens, deerskins, or clothes made of straw.
They consume vegetables, lotus roots, oil-cakes, cow dung, and tubers and fruits;
when begging for alms, they limit themselves to a single household, departing immediately if the host says there is nothing, and even if called back, they never look behind them.
They do not eat salted meat or the five kinds of dairy products from cows, and they constantly drink grain-ash water and boiling water.
They observe the vows of cattle, dogs, chickens, and pheasants; they smear their bodies with ashes and maintain long hair as their outward marks;
when performing sacrifices with sheep, they first recite incantations and then slaughter them;
for four months they tend the sacrificial fire, and for seven days they practice breath-control.
With hundreds of billions of flowers, they make offerings to the devas, and all their desires and aspirations are thereby fulfilled.
It is impossible that such dharmas as these could serve as the cause for unsurpassed liberation.
This is called "knowing.
What is meant by "not seeing"?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not see a single person practicing such a dharma who attains right liberation; this is called "not seeing."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva both sees and knows.
What is meant by 'seeing'?
To see that sentient beings who practice such false dharmas will inevitably fall into hell is called "seeing.
What is meant by "knowing"?

It is knowing that when sentient beings emerge from hell and are born among humans, if they are able to practice the *dāna-pāramitā* and so forth until they are fully endowed with all the *pāramitās*, these people will certainly attain entry into right liberation; this is called "knowing."
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva also possesses both seeing and knowing.
What is meant by 'seeing'? "
To perceive permanence and impermanence, suffering and pleasure, purity and impurity, self and non-self—this is called "viewing.
What is "knowing"?

To know that all Tathāgatas certainly do not enter final nirvāṇa; to know that the body of a Tathāgata is adamantine and indestructible, being neither a body produced by afflictions nor a foul, putrid, and decaying body; and furthermore, to be able to know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature—this is called "knowledge."
"Furthermore, good son,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also possess both knowledge and vision.
What is meant by 'knowledge'?

He knows which sentient beings have accomplished faith; he knows which sentient beings seek the Mahāyāna; he knows which person follows the current, which person goes against the current, and which person abides correctly; and he knows which sentient beings have already reached the other shore.
Those who flow with the current are ordinary persons;
those who flow against the current range from stream-enterers up to pratyekabuddhas;
and those who abide correctly are bodhisattvas and others.
Those who have reached the other shore are the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
This is called "knowledge.
What is meant by "vision"?

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and cultivate the mind of pure conduct, they see with their purified divine eye all sentient beings who, having committed unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind—the three karmas—fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts;
and they see all sentient beings who, having cultivated wholesome karma, will at the end of life be reborn among gods or humans.

To see that some sentient beings pass from darkness into darkness, some sentient beings pass from darkness into light, some sentient beings pass from light into darkness, and some sentient beings pass from light into light—this is called "seeing."
"Furthermore, good son, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva also possesses both knowledge and vision.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that although various sentient beings cultivate their bodies, cultivate their precepts, cultivate their minds, and cultivate their wisdom, these individuals have accomplished evil karma in this present life— perhaps due to greed, hatred, or delusion— and this karma must necessarily result in retribution in hell."
This person, by simply cultivating the body, cultivating morality, cultivating the mind, and cultivating wisdom, experiences [the results] lightly in the present life and does not fall into hell.
How is it that such karma can produce retribution in the present life?
They repent and confess all their evils, vowing never to commit them again after having repented.

Because they have achieved a sense of shame and remorse, because they make offerings to the Triple Gem, and because they constantly reproach themselves, such persons, by virtue of these causes and conditions of wholesome karma, do not fall into hell.

Instead, they experience retribution in the present life—namely, headaches, eye pain, stomachaches, backaches, untimely death, being rebuked, insulted, flogged, imprisoned, hunger, and distress—and thus undergo such light retributions in this present world.
This is called knowledge.
What is meant by vision?

It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees that such a person is unable to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, and having committed even a slight evil deed, this karma will cause them to receive retribution in the present life due to its causal conditions.

If this person commits slight evil but cannot repent, does not reproach themselves, feels no shame or remorse, and has no fear, their karma will increase, and they will receive retribution in hell; this is what is called "view."
“Furthermore, there is knowing without seeing.
What is meant by knowing without seeing?
To know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet because it is shrouded and obscured by various afflictions (*kleśa*), they are unable to see it—this is called knowing without seeing.”
"Furthermore, there are those who know yet see little.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten stages and others know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet their vision is not clear, just as objects cannot be clearly perceived in the darkness of night."
"Furthermore, there is that which is both seen and known, namely, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, who both see and know.
Furthermore, there is that which is both seen and known, yet neither seen nor known."

That which is both seen and known refers to what are called worldly letters, speech, men and women, vehicles, jars and basins, houses, cities and towns, clothing, food and drink, mountains and rivers, gardens and groves, sentient beings, and life-span; these are termed both known and seen.
"What is meant by 'not seeing and not knowing'?
The subtle and esoteric words of the Sages contain no mention of men or women, nor even of gardens and groves; this is called 'not seeing and not knowing.'"
"Furthermore, there is knowing without seeing.
To know what is given in charity, to know the recipient of the offering, to know the receiver, and to know the retribution of cause and effect—this is called 'knowing'."
What is meant by "not seeing"?
Not seeing the gift, the recipient of the offering, the receiver, or the karmic fruit—this is called "not seeing.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows eight kinds [of things], which are precisely what is known by the five eyes of a Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What benefit does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain by being able to know in this way?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who can know in this way attains the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ):"

There are four kinds of unimpeded knowledge: unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), unimpededness regarding expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and unimpededness regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding unimpededness regarding phenomena: it is the knowledge of all phenomena as well as their names.

The unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) consists in knowing all meanings contained within all phenomena, and being able to establish meanings according to the names assigned to those phenomena.

The unimpededness of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) consists in [mastery of] the treatises on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*), the treatises on grammar (*chandas-śāstra*), and the treatises on worldly debate (*loka-vāda*).

Regarding the unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): it refers to the fact that whatever a bodhisattva mahāsattva expounds is without obstruction, immovable, free from fear or hesitation, and difficult to overcome or subdue.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s ability to see and know in such a way that he immediately attains these four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
Furthermore, good son!"
Regarding the unimpededness of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*): the bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly knows the teachings of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.

Regarding the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): although there are three vehicles, he knows they converge into one, and never maintains that they possess any characteristics of distinction.

Regarding unimpeded eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*): when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva produces various names for a single dharma, they could speak of them without exhaustion even throughout immeasurable kalpas.
It is impossible for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to be able to speak in such a manner.

Regarding the unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): for immeasurable eons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings—whether as names or as meanings—in various distinct ways that can never be exhausted.
"Furthermore, good son!
Regarding the unimpededness of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows all phenomena, he does not grasp or cling to them.
Regarding the unimpededness of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows all meanings, he likewise does not cling to them."
Regarding the unimpededness of diction (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows names, he does not grasp at them.
Regarding the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that such eloquence is supreme, he likewise does not become attached to it.
Why is this? Good son!
One who grasps and clings is not called a bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If one does not grasp or cling, then one does not know the Dharma; if one knows the Dharma, that is grasping and clinging; if one knows without clinging, then there is nothing known. How is it that the Tathāgata says one knows the Dharma yet does not grasp or cling?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! One who grasps and clings is not called unobstructed.”
The absence of grasping and attachment is what is called "unimpeded.
Good son! Therefore, among all bodhisattvas, those who possess grasping and attachment have no unimpededness.
If one lacks non-obstruction, they are not called a bodhisattva; you should know that such a person is termed an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
Why are those who grasp at attachments termed ordinary beings?
All ordinary beings grasp at form (*rūpa*) and so forth, up to and including grasping at consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because of attachment to form, a mind of craving arises; because a mind of craving arises, one is bound by form;
and so on, until one is bound by consciousness.
Because of these bonds, one cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, great suffering, and all afflictions.
Therefore, grasping at names is called being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
For this reason, all ordinary persons lack the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
"Good son!..."
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, known and seen the characteristics of dharmas; because he knows and sees them, he understands their meaning.
Because he sees the characteristics of dharmas and understands their meaning, he does not give rise to attachment within form;
this is likewise true for everything up to consciousness.
Because they do not cling, bodhisattvas do not give rise to a mind of craving toward form, nor do they give rise to craving toward anything up to and including consciousness;
because they are without craving, they are not bound by form, nor are they bound by anything up to and including consciousness.
Because they are unbound, they attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, great suffering, and all afflictions.
For this reason, all bodhisattvas attain the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

“Good son! For these reasons, within the twelve divisions of the scriptures, I have taught my disciples that those who are bound by attachment are said to be fettered by Māra, whereas those who do not attach themselves are liberated from the fetters of Māra.”
For example, in the world, a person who has committed a crime is bound by the king, whereas a person who is innocent the king cannot bind.
It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: those who have attachments are bound by Māra, while those who have no attachments Māra cannot bind.
For this reason, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is without attachment.
Furthermore, son of good family,
regarding the non-obstruction of dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully knows the retention of syllables and does not forget them.
What is called "upholding" is like the earth, like a mountain, like the eye, like a cloud, like a person, and like a mother.
All dharmas are likewise so.

Regarding the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): although a bodhisattva knows the names of all phenomena, they do not know their meaning; upon attaining the unimpeded knowledge of meaning, they come to know that meaning.
How does one know the meaning?
"Regarding 'that which sustains like the earth': just as the earth universally sustains all sentient beings and non-sentient things, for this reason the earth is called 'sustaining.
Good son!"
Regarding "the mountain-sustainer," the bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects as follows:
"For what reason is it called a 'mountain' and a 'sustainer'?
A mountain can sustain the earth, preventing it from tilting or shaking; therefore, it is called a sustainer."
For what reason is the eye further called "sustainer"?
Because the eye can sustain light, it is called a sustainer.
For what reason is the cloud further called a "sustainer"?
Clouds are called "dragon-breath" (nāga-gas); because dragon-breath sustains water, they are named "cloud-sustainers" (megha-dhara).
For what reason, then, are humans also called "sustainers"?
Because humans can sustain both the Dharma and that which is non-Dharma, they are named "human-sustainers" (puruṣa-dhara).
For what reason is a mother further called "the sustainer"?
Because the mother can sustain her child, she is named the "sustainer.
In this same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that the names, phrases, and meanings of all dharmas are likewise so.

Regarding unimpeded eloquence: the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva expounds a single meaning through various expressions, yet there is no inherent meaning [in those expressions], just as with names such as "man" and "woman," "house," "vehicle," or "sentient being."
Why is it that there is no meaning? Good son!
That which is called "meaning" is the realm of Bodhisattvas and all Buddhas.
Language is the domain of ordinary beings.
Because one understands the meaning, one attains unimpededness regarding language.

As for unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows both language and meaning, he can expound upon language and meaning throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas without exhaustion; this is called unimpeded eloquence.

“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the conventional truth for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; by virtue of such practice, he attains unimpeded knowledge of all phenomena.”
Furthermore, because he cultivated the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he attained unimpededness in meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Also, because he practiced the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he attained unimpededness in expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, because he has practiced and expounded upon the treatises of conventional truth for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he has attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech. "Good son!
It is impossible for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to attain these four kinds of unimpeded knowledge."
"Good son!
Within the ninefold canon, I have taught that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge;
yet, in reality, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not truly possess them."
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate these four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Those who are pratyekabuddhas cultivate the dharma of quiescence and delight in dwelling in solitude.
If one transforms sentient beings by manifesting only supernatural powers and remains silent all day long without proclaiming anything,
how could there be the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge?
For what reason do you remain silent and say nothing?

Pratyekabuddhas are unable to preach the Dharma to deliver beings, enabling them to attain the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), the stage of the World’s Foremost Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, or Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; nor can they cause people to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Good son!
When Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, there are no ninefold scriptures in the world.
Therefore, the pratyekabuddha lacks the analytical knowledge of language and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
"Good son! Although the pratyekabuddha knows all dharmas, he possesses neither the dharma-analytical knowledge nor the analytical knowledge."
Why is this? One who is unimpeded regarding phenomena is said to be one who knows syllables.
Although a pratyekabuddha knows written characters, they lack unimpeded mastery over those syllables.
Why is this? Because they do not understand the two characters of the "Ever-Abiding" (nitya) Dharma.
For this reason, Pratyekabuddhas do not attain unimpeded mastery over dharmas.
Although one knows the meaning, there is no meaning and no obstruction.
One who truly knows the meaning knows that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The meaning of Buddha-nature is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, those who are pratyekabuddhas do not attain unimpededness in meaning.
Therefore, pratyekabuddhas entirely lack the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
Why is it that śrāvakas also lack the four unimpeded knowledges?
Śrāvakas do not possess the three kinds of skillful means.
What are these three?

First, they must be spoken to with gentle words before they will accept the Dharma; second, they must be spoken to with harsh words before they will be transformed; third, they will be transformed by words that are neither gentle nor harsh.
Because Śrāvakas lack these three, they do not possess the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot ultimately know words or meanings; they lack sovereign wisdom regarding their objects, they do not possess the ten powers or the four fearlessnesses, and they cannot ultimately cross the great river of the twelve links of dependent origination. They cannot skillfully discern the differences between the sharp and dull faculties of sentient beings, nor have they permanently severed doubt regarding the two truths. They do not know the various mental states and the objects perceived by sentient beings, and they cannot skillfully expound the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
"Therefore, the two vehicles do not possess the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas lack the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), why did the World-Honored One declare that Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom, Mahāmaudgalyāyana foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and Mahākauṣṭhila foremost in the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge?
"If they do not exist, why did the Tathāgata speak in such a way?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

"Good son! For example, the waters of the Ganges River are immeasurable; the waters of the Sindhu Great River are also immeasurable; the waters of the Vakṣu Great River are also immeasurable; the waters of the Sītā Great River are also immeasurable; the waters of Lake Anavatapta are also immeasurable; and the waters within the great ocean are also immeasurable. Although all these waters are alike in being immeasurable, their quantities are in fact not equal."
The four types of unimpeded knowledge of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are likewise so.
Good son! If one were to say they are equal, such a thing is impossible.
"Good son!
For the sake of ordinary beings, I have taught that among the four unhindered knowledges, Mahākauṣṭhila is the most supreme.
The meaning of what you have asked is as such."
“Good son!
Among śrāvakas, some may attain one [of these], or some may attain two; it is impossible for anyone to possess all four.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha previously stated in the ‘Chapter on the Holy Life’ that bodhisattvas who attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge possess such knowing and seeing, yet in the knowing and seeing of a bodhisattva there is nothing attained, nor is there even a mind or speech that says ‘there is nothing attained.’”
World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva truly has nothing to be attained.
If a bodhisattva were to have a mind that attains anything, they would not be a bodhisattva, but would be called an ordinary person.
“How is it that the Tathāgata says a bodhisattva has something to be attained?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Excellent, excellent!
I was about to speak, yet you have asked again.
Well-born son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas truly have nothing to be attained.
That which has nothing to be attained is called the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge. Good son!
For what reason is "non-attainment" called "unobstructed"?
If there were attainment, it would be called "obstruction";
that which possesses obstruction is termed the "four perversions."
"Good son!
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are free from the four inversions, they attain non-obstruction.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas are said to have 'nothing to be attained'."
"Furthermore, good son!
That which is non-apprehension is called wisdom.
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have attained this wisdom, they are said to be 'without apprehension.'"
To have something attained is called ignorance.
Because Bodhisattvas have eternally severed the darkness of ignorance, they have nothing attained.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas are said to have "nothing attained."
"Furthermore, good son!
That which is non-attainment is called Great Nirvāṇa.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely within such Great Nirvāṇa, he does not perceive the nature or characteristics of any phenomena."
Therefore, a bodhisattva is said to have "nothing to obtain.
That which has something to obtain is called the twenty-five states of existence.
The bodhisattva eternally severs these twenty-five states of existence and attains great nirvāṇa.
For this reason, a bodhisattva is said to have "nothing to be attained.
Furthermore, son of good family,
that which has nothing to be attained is called the Mahāyāna.
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not abide in any dharmas, they attain the Mahāyāna.
For this reason, a bodhisattva is said to have "nothing to be attained.
That which has something to be attained is called the path of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Because the Bodhisattva has eternally severed the paths of the two vehicles, he attains the Buddha-way.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva is said to have "nothing to be attained.
Furthermore, good son!
That which is "without attainment" is called the Vaipulya sutras.
Because bodhisattvas read and recite such sutras, they attain Great Nirvana.
For this reason, bodhisattvas are said to be "without attainment."
That which has something to be attained is called the eleven divisions of the sūtras.
That which the bodhisattva cultivates consists purely of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras; therefore, the bodhisattva is said to have nothing to attain.
"Furthermore, good son!
That which is non-existent is called space.
The absence of things in the world is called space."
Because the Bodhisattva attains this Space Samādhi and perceives nothing, the Bodhisattva is said to be "without attainment.
That which has attainment is called the wheel of birth and death.
All ordinary beings transmigrate through birth and death, and therefore have something perceived.
Bodhisattvas have forever severed all birth and death; for this reason, bodhisattvas are said to have "nothing to be attained."
"Furthermore, good son!
That which the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva has no attainment of is called permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives the Buddha-nature, he attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
Therefore, a bodhisattva is said to have "nothing to obtain.
That which has something to obtain is called impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity.
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has severed this impermanence, lack of bliss, absence of self, and lack of purity, the bodhisattva is said to have nothing to obtain.
"Furthermore, good son!
That which is non-apprehensible is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates this emptiness of the ultimate truth, he perceives nothing at all; for this reason, the bodhisattva is said to be 'one who has no apprehension'."
That which has something to be attained is called the five views.
Because Bodhisattvas have forever severed these five views, they attain the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
For this reason, Bodhisattvas are said to be "without attainment."
"Furthermore, good son!
That which is non-attainment is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he perceives nothing at all; for this reason, the bodhisattva is said to be one who has no attainment."
That which has something to be attained is called the enlightenment of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because bodhisattvas have forever severed the enlightenment of the two vehicles, they are said to be "without attainment."
“Good son! That which you ask has nothing to be attained, and that which I speak also has nothing to be attained.
If one says there is something to be attained, such a person belongs to the retinue of Māra and is not my disciple.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While you were expounding for my sake this state of non-attainment of the bodhisattva, immeasurable sentient beings severed their minds that cling to signs.”
For this reason, I venture to inquire about the meaning of non-attainment, so that immeasurable sentient beings such as these may leave the retinue of Māra and become disciples of the Buddha.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Previously, between the twin śāla trees, the Tathāgata spoke these verses for Cunda:”
"‘That which existed originally is now non-existent; that which was non-existent originally is now existent. That there are dharmas existing throughout the three periods of time—this is impossible.
World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

I have spoken these words for the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings; I have also spoken them for the sake of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and I have likewise spoken them for the sake of Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince. It was not solely for the sake of Cunda alone that I spoke this verse.
At that time, as Mañjuśrī was about to question me, I knew his thoughts and spoke for him.
Once I had finished speaking, Mañjuśrī immediately attained understanding.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
Among those such as Mañjuśrī, how many people are there who can fully comprehend this meaning?”
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will further explain this in detail for the sake of the great assembly.
“Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now expound it for you once more.”
To say "originally existent" means that in the past I originally possessed immeasurable afflictions;
because of these afflictions, there was no Great Parinirvāṇa in the present.
To say "originally non-existent" means that originally there was no Prajñāpāramitā.
Because they lack the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they currently possess all the fetters of affliction (kleśa).
If any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or human were to say:
"The Tathāgata has afflictions in the past, future, or present," [they would be speaking falsely].
Such a thing is impossible.

"Furthermore, son of good family, that which is called 'originally existing' refers to my original body formed by the union of parents; therefore, there is no subtle diamond-like Dharma-body in the present."
Regarding what is called "original non-existence": my body originally lacked the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
because these thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics were originally non-existent, it now possesses four hundred and four ailments.
If there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who should say:
"The Tathāgata has the suffering of illness in the past, future, or present."
Such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son,
that which is called 'originally existing' refers to my original state of being characterized by impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity."
Because there is impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity, there is currently no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
To say that it was originally non-existent means that one originally did not see the Buddha-nature;
because it was not seen, there was no permanence, bliss, self, or purity.
If there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who should say:
"The Tathāgata is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure in the past, future, or present."
...such a thing is impossible.

"Furthermore, good son, that which is called 'originally existing' refers to the mind of an ordinary person who has originally practiced asceticism, claiming thereby to have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; for this reason, they are currently unable to destroy the four Māras."
Regarding the term "originally non-existent," it means that originally I did not possess the six pāramitās;
because I originally lacked the six pāramitās, I practiced with the mind of an ordinary person performing ascetic austerities, claiming thereby to have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human should say:
"The Tathāgata has practiced asceticism in the past, future, or present," [it is not so].
...such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son, as for what is called 'originally existing,' in the past I originally possessed a body that consumed mixed food; [now that body no longer exists]."
Because it is a body sustained by food, there is currently no boundless body.
As for the statement that "it was originally non-existent," it means that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment were originally non-existent;
because these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment were absent, one currently possesses a body sustained by various kinds of food.
If there be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who should say:
"The Tathāgata possesses a body of mixed food in the past, future, or present."
Such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, good son,
as for what is called 'originally existing,' it refers to the mind of attachment toward all dharmas that I originally possessed in the past."
For this reason, there is currently no samādhi of ultimate emptiness.
To say that "it was originally non-existent" means that I originally lacked the true meaning of the Middle Way;
because the true meaning of the Middle Way is absent, one develops a mind of attachment toward all phenomena.
If there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who says:
"The Tathāgata—in the past, future, or present—teaches that all dharmas possess characteristics."
Such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, son of good family,
as for what is called "existing from the beginning," when I first attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there were śrāvaka disciples with dull faculties.
Because there were śrāvaka disciples of dull faculties, he was unable to expound the reality of the One Vehicle.
When it is said that "originally none existed," it means that originally there were none among human beings who were of sharp faculties, such as Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, the Elephant King;
because there were no such ones of sharp faculties as Kāśyapa and others, he revealed the Three Vehicles through appropriate skillful means.
If any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human should say:
"The Tathāgata, in the past, future, and present, ultimately expounds only the Dharma of the Three Vehicles."
Such a thing is impossible.

Furthermore, son of good family, as for what is called "originally existing," I previously stated that three months hence I would enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees; for this reason, I have not been able to expound the Mahāvaipulya scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, while still in the present state.
As for the statement "originally non-existent," it means that in the past there were no great bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī;
because they did not exist, it is said now that the Tathāgata is impermanent.
If there be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human who should say:
"The Tathāgata of the past, future, and present is impermanent."
Such a thing is impossible. "Good son!
For the sake of all sentient beings, the Tathāgata, although he knows all dharmas, says that he does not know; although he sees all dharmas, says that he does not see."
They describe phenomena that possess characteristics as being without characteristics, and phenomena that are without characteristics as possessing characteristics;
they describe what is truly impermanent as permanent, and what is truly permanent as impermanent;
the same applies to self, bliss, and purity.
The Dharma of the Three Vehicles is taught as the One Vehicle, and the Dharma of the One Vehicle is taught as three according to what is appropriate;
the abbreviated characteristics are taught extensively, and the extensive characteristics are taught briefly;
the offenses of the four grave categories (*catur-guru-dharma*) are taught as *sthūlātyaya*, and the *sthūlātyaya* offenses are taught as the four grave categories.
To declare what is an offense to be no offense, and what is not an offense to be an offense;
to declare a light offense to be heavy, and a heavy offense to be light. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata clearly perceives the faculties of sentient beings. "Good son!
Although the Tathāgata speaks thus, it is ultimately without falsehood."
Why is this? False speech is itself a transgression.
