Since the Tathāgata has completely severed all transgressions, how could there be any false speech?
Good son!

Although the Tathāgata has no false speech, if he knows that sentient beings will obtain the benefit of the Dharma through false discourse, he will employ appropriate skillful means and speak accordingly.
“Good son! All conventional truths (saṃvṛti-satya), when viewed by the Tathāgata, are themselves the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Why is this?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, speak of conventional truth for the sake of the ultimate truth, so as to enable sentient beings to attain the ultimate truth.
If sentient beings were not to attain such an ultimate truth, the Buddhas would never have proclaimed conventional truth.
"Good son! There are times when the Tathāgata expounds the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), yet sentient beings think the Buddha is speaking of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
there are times when he expounds the ultimate truth, yet sentient beings think the Buddha is speaking of the conventional truth."
This is the profound realm of all Buddhas, which is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Good son! For this reason, you should not have previously raised the objection, saying:
"The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva has nothing to be attained.
Since the Bodhisattva constantly attains the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), how can you challenge this by saying,
"There is nothing to be attained"?
"Is it so? Kāśyapa spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
The ultimate truth is also called the Path, it is also called Bodhi, and it is also called Nirvana.
If there were a bodhisattva who said that there is an attainment of the Path, Bodhi, or Nirvana, then these would be impermanent.
Why is this? If dharmas were permanent, they could not be attained.
Just like space, who could possibly attain it?
World-Honored One!
Just as worldly things, which did not exist originally but now exist, are called impermanent, so too is the Way;
if the Way could be attained, it would be called impermanent.
If the Dharma were permanent, it would be without attainment and without arising, just as the Buddha-nature is without attainment and without arising.

World-Honored One! As for the Way, it is neither form nor non-form; it is neither long nor short; it is neither high nor low; it is neither arising nor ceasing; it is neither red, nor white, nor blue, nor yellow; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
"How is it that the Tathāgata speaks of 'attainability'?
Bodhi and nirvāṇa are also like this.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, noble son!
There are two kinds of paths:
First is permanence, and second is impermanence.
The characteristics of bodhi likewise have two kinds:
first is permanence, and second is impermanence.
Nirvāṇa is also like this.
The path of external ways is called impermanent, while the path of internal ways is called permanent;
the bodhi possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called impermanent, while the bodhi possessed by bodhisattvas and all buddhas is called permanent.
External liberation is called impermanent; internal liberation is called permanent. Good son!
The Way, Bodhi, and Nirvana are all termed permanent.
All sentient beings are constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions; because they lack the eye of wisdom, they are unable to see.
Yet, because these sentient beings desire to see, they cultivate morality, concentration, and wisdom;
through such cultivation, they perceive the Path, Bodhi, and Nirvana.
"This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the Path, Bodhi, and Nirvana.
The essential nature and characteristics of the Path are in truth neither produced nor extinguished.
For this reason, it cannot be grasped or maintained."
“Good son! Although the Path has no form or appearance that can be seen, nor any measure by which it can be known, it nonetheless possesses real utility.
Good son!”

Just as the minds of sentient beings, although they are not material form, are neither long nor short, neither coarse nor subtle, neither bound nor liberated, and are not phenomena that can be seen, yet they nonetheless exist.
For this reason, I said to Sudatta:
"Householder!
The mind is the lord of the city."
"Householder!
If one does not guard the mind, then one does not guard the body and speech;
if one guards the mind, then one guards the body and speech."
Because they do not properly guard their body and speech, they cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
those who guard their body and speech cause sentient beings to attain birth as humans or devas, and even nirvana.
"That which is attained is called true;
that which is not attained is called untrue. "Good son!
The Way, as well as Bodhi and Nirvana, are likewise both existent and eternal.
If they were non-existent, how could one sever all afflictions?
Because they exist, all bodhisattvas perceive and know them clearly.
"Good son! There are two kinds of seeing: [the seeing of existence and the seeing of non-existence]."
First, seeing by way of signs; second, seeing with clarity.
What is meant by "seeing by way of signs"?
It is like seeing smoke from afar and calling it "seeing fire"; although one does not actually see the fire, this is not a falsehood even though the fire is unseen.
Seeing a crane in the sky, one says, "I see water"; although one does not actually see the water, it is not false.
It is like seeing flowers and leaves and saying, "I see the roots"; although one does not actually see the roots, it is not false.
It is like a person who, seeing the horns of an ox between a fence from afar, says they see an ox; although they do not see the ox, it is not false.
It is like seeing a woman pregnant and saying one sees desire; although one does not see the desire itself, it is not false.
It is like seeing leaves grow on a tree and saying one sees water; although one does not see the water, it is not false.
Or it is like seeing clouds and saying one sees rain; although one does not see the rain, it is not false.
Just as when one sees bodily action and verbal action, one says "I see the mind"; although the mind itself is not seen, it is not false.
This is called seeing by way of signs. What is clear seeing?
It is like the eye seeing forms. Good son!
It is like a person whose faculty of the eye is pure and unimpaired, who gazes at an āmalaka fruit within their own palm.

It is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who clearly perceives the path, bodhi, and nirvāṇa; although they perceive them in this way, from the very beginning there is no characteristic of seeing.
“Good son! For this reason, in the past I told Śāriputra:
‘Whatever is unknown, unseen, and unrealized by any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or human in all the worlds—only the Tathāgata fully knows, sees, and realizes it;’”
It is the same for all bodhisattvas as well.
Śāriputra, whatever is known, seen, and realized by those in the world, that too is known, seen, and realized by me and by the bodhisattvas.
That which the beings of the world do not know, do not see, and do not realize, they likewise do not know that they do not know, see, or realize it.
Yet, regarding what the beings of the world do know, see, and realize, they say of themselves:
"I know, I see, I realize."
“Śāriputra! The Tathāgata knows, sees, and awakens to everything, yet he does not say of himself:
‘I know, see, and awaken.’”
"All Bodhisattvas are likewise. Why is this?

If the Tathāgata were to manifest the characteristics of knowing, seeing, and awakening, you should know that he would not be the Buddha, the World-Honored One, but would be called an ordinary person."
"The Bodhisattva is also like this.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Fifteen;
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Sixteen.
The third chapter, the Brahma-carya Chapter, added by the Song dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said to Śāriputra:
"What the world knows, I also know;
what the world does not know, I also fully know."
"What is the meaning of this? 'Good son!
All those in the world do not know, do not see, and are not awakened to the Buddha-nature.'"
If there are those who know, see, and awaken to the Buddha-nature, they are not called worldly people; they are called Bodhisattvas.

Worldly people likewise do not know, see, or awaken to the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four inversions, the four truths, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and mahāparinirvāṇa.
If one knows, sees, and awakens to these, one is not called a worldly person; one should be called a Bodhisattva.
"Good son! This is what is called that which the world does not know, see, or awaken to.
What is it that the world knows, sees, and awakens to?
That is to say:

Brahmā, Maheśvara, the eight-armed deity, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), time (*kāla*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and both dharma and adharma are the creators; they hold views of annihilationism and eternalism regarding the beginning and end of the world, and they claim that the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called nirvāṇa.
"Good son! These are called what is known, seen, and realized by the world.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva also knows, sees, and realizes such matters."
When a bodhisattva has thus known, seen, and awakened, to say that one does not know, does not see, and does not awaken is a falsehood.
Falsehood is a transgression, and because of this transgression, one falls into hell.
"Good son! If any man, woman, śramaṇa, or brāhmaṇa should say:
'There is no path, no bodhi, and no nirvāṇa.'"
"You should know that such people are called icchantikas and followers of Māra; they are called slanderers of the Dharma.
To slander the Dharma in this way is to slander all Buddhas. Such persons are neither called 'of the world' nor 'not of the world.'"
At that time, having heard these matters, Kāśyapa praised the Buddha with these verses:
"Out of great compassion for sentient beings, I now take refuge in you;
Because you have skillfully extracted the many poisoned arrows, You are called the Great King of Physicians."
The treatments administered by worldly physicians, though they bring recovery, lead to recurrence;
those treated by the Tathāgata shall never again relapse.
The World-Honored One bestows the nectar-like medicine upon all sentient beings.
Once sentient beings have taken this medicine, they neither die nor are born.
Now, for my sake, the Tathāgata expounds the Great Nirvāṇa;
when sentient beings hear this secret treasury, they immediately attain the state of non-arising and non-extinction.
After the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:”

Regarding the statement, "That which all the world does not know, see, or awaken to, the Bodhisattva is able to fully know, see, and awaken to": if the Bodhisattva were of the same nature as the world, one could not say, "The world does not know, does not see, and does not awaken."
"Yet this bodhisattva is able to know, see, and awaken to it; if it were not of the world, what distinguishing characteristics would there be?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
What is called a bodhisattva is both of the world and not of the world.
One who does not know, see, or awaken is said to be of the world;
one who knows, sees, and awakens is not said to be of the world.
Regarding your question as to what difference there is, I shall now explain it.

Good son! If a man or a woman, upon first hearing this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, immediately gives rise to reverent faith and resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they are called a worldly bodhisattva.
All the world does not know, see, or awaken to this; likewise, these bodhisattvas are also like the world, not knowing, seeing, or awakening to it.
Once the bodhisattvas have heard this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they will know that which the world does not know, see, or awaken to, and that which should be known, seen, and awakened to by the bodhisattvas.
Having understood this matter, he reflected to himself:
"By what skillful means should I practice so that I may know, see, and realize it?
He further thought to himself:
"One should only cultivate and maintain pure precepts with a profound mind. "Good son!
By these causes and conditions, at that time, the Bodhisattva’s precepts will always remain pure in every place of birth throughout future lives."
Good son! Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s precepts are pure, in whatever place he is born, he is always free from arrogance, false views, and the net of doubt; he never says:
"The Tathāgata has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa."
This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation and maintenance of pure precepts.
Once the precepts are purified, one next cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Because of this cultivation of concentration, in whatever place of birth one is born, right mindfulness is never forgotten; that is to say:

All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; the twelve divisions of the sutras and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are eternal, blissful, self, and pure; and all bodhisattvas who dwell securely in the Vaipulya *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* fully perceive this Buddha-nature.

Recalling such matters as these without forgetting them, one attains the eleven kinds of emptiness through the cultivation of meditative concentration; this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of pure concentration.
Once precept and concentration are fully prepared, one next cultivates pure wisdom.

Because they cultivate wisdom, from the very beginning they do not conceive attachment to the notions that "there is a self within the body," "the body is within the self," "this body is the self," or "neither the body nor the self exists. This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of pure wisdom.
Because of the cultivation of wisdom, the precepts one upholds are firm and unshakable. Good son!
It is like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be tilted or moved by the four winds.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this, not being shaken or moved by the four inversions. Good son!

At that time, the bodhisattva knows, sees, and realizes for himself that the precepts he upholds are without wavering; this is called the knowing, seeing, and realizing of the bodhisattva, which is not of the world.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva sees that the precepts he upholds are firm and unshakable, his mind is free from regret;
because he is without regret, his mind attains joy.
Because one attains joy, the mind experiences delight;
because one experiences delight, the mind becomes tranquil;
because the mind is tranquil, one attains immovable concentration.
Because one attains the immovable concentration, one attains true knowledge and vision;
because of true knowledge and vision, one becomes weary of and detaches from birth and death;
because of weariness and detachment from birth and death, one then attains liberation.
Because they have attained liberation, they clearly perceive the Buddha-nature.
This is called that which is known, seen, and realized by Bodhisattvas, and it is not of the mundane world. "Good son!
"This is what is called that which the world does not know, see, or awaken to, yet which the Bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"How does a Bodhisattva cultivate and maintain pure precepts, remain free from regret in his heart, and even come to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature?"
The Buddha said, "Good son!
Worldly precepts are not called pure."
Why is this? Because worldly precepts are for the sake of existence, their nature is indeterminate, and they are not ultimate; thus, they cannot extensively benefit all sentient beings.
For this reason, it is called impure;
because of its impurity, there arises a mind of regret and remorse;
because of this regret and remorse, the mind lacks joy.
Because there is no joy, there is no rapture;
because there is no rapture, there is no tranquility;
because there is no tranquility, there is no immovable concentration.
Because there is no immovable concentration, there is no true knowledge and vision;
because there is no true knowledge and vision, there is no revulsion;
because there is no revulsion, there is no liberation.
Because there is no liberation, one does not see the Buddha-nature;
because one does not see the Buddha-nature, one can ultimately never attain Great Parinirvāṇa.
This is called worldly precepts that are impure.

“Good son! For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, pure precepts consist in the fact that the precepts are not [mere] precepts; they are not for the sake of existence; they are because of their ultimate certainty; and they are for the sake of sentient beings. This is called the purity of the bodhisattva’s precepts.”
“Good son! Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not intentionally desire to give rise to a mind free from regret regarding pure ethical discipline, a mind free from regret arises spontaneously.”
"Good son!
It is like a person who holds up a bright mirror; though they do not expect to see their face, the reflection of the face appears spontaneously.
It is also like a farmer sowing seeds in fertile soil; though he does not expect sprouts to grow, the sprouts emerge of their own accord."
It is also like lighting a lamp: one does not expect darkness to be extinguished, yet the darkness is extinguished of its own accord.
Son of good family, it is just the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who firmly maintains the pure precepts; a mind free from regret arises naturally.
Because of pure precepts, the mind attains joy.
"Good son! It is like a handsome person who, seeing his own face, feels joy arise in his heart."
It is the same for one who upholds the pure precepts.
"Good son! A person who has broken the precepts sees their own conduct as impure and does not feel joy in their heart."
"Just as one with a physical deformity does not feel joy when looking at their own face,
so it is with a person who has broken the precepts.
Good son!..."

It is like two women tending cows who each carry a jar—one a jar of curd and the other a jar of whey—and together they go to the city intending to sell them. On the way, they both stumble and fall, and both jars are broken; one is filled with joy, while the other is filled with grief and distress.
It is the same with those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them; one who upholds the pure precepts feels joy in their heart.
Because the heart is joyful, they then reflect:
"The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have declared within Nirvāṇa:"
"Those who are able to maintain pure precepts shall attain nirvāṇa.
I am now practicing such pure precepts and should likewise attain it.
For this reason, the mind becomes joyful and glad.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“What is the difference between joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*)? “Good son!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not commit evil, it is called joy;
when the mind is pure and upholds the precepts, it is called bliss. Good son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas contemplate birth and death, it is called joy;
when they behold Great Nirvāṇa, it is called bliss.
The former is termed joy; the latter is termed bliss.
The superior is called bliss (*sukha*).
To be free from worldly common dharmas is called joy (*prīti*);
to attain uncommon dharmas is called bliss (*sukha*).
Because their precepts are pure, their bodies are light and supple, and their speech is free from coarse transgressions.
At that time, whether the Bodhisattva sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, or cognizes anything, there is nothing unwholesome;
because there is no unwholesomeness, the mind attains peace and stability.
Because of tranquility, one attains stillness and concentration;
because of stillness and concentration, one attains true knowledge and vision;
because of true knowledge and vision, one becomes weary of and detached from birth and death.
Because one becomes weary of birth and death, one attains liberation;
because one attains liberation, one perceives the Buddha-nature;
because one perceives the Buddha-nature, one attains Great Nirvana.
This is called the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva, not worldly ethical discipline.
Why is this? Good son!
The pure precepts received by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva are assisted by five factors.
What are these five?
First, faith; second, shame; third, remorse; fourth, virtuous friends; and fifth, reverent respect for the precepts.
Because he is free from the five hindrances, his vision is pure.
Because he is free from the five views, his mind is without the net of doubt.

Because he is free from the five doubts—first, doubt regarding the Buddha; second, doubt regarding the Dharma; third, doubt regarding the Saṅgha; fourth, doubt regarding the precepts; and fifth, doubt regarding heedfulness—the Bodhisattva at that time attains the five faculties, namely: faith, mindfulness, diligence, concentration, and wisdom.
Because they attain the five faculties, they attain five kinds of nirvana, namely, liberation from form through to liberation from consciousness.
This is called the bodhisattva’s pure upholding of the precepts, which is supramundane.
“Good son! This is what is not known, not seen, and not realized by the world, yet it is that which is known, seen, and realized by the bodhisattva. Good son!”
If among my disciples there are those who uphold, recite, copy, or explain the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* yet violate the precepts, and someone should rebuke, despise, or humiliate them, saying:
"If the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the secret treasury of the Buddha, possesses such majestic power, why has it allowed you to destroy the precepts you have received?"
If a person who upholds this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* violates the prohibitions and precepts, one should know that this sūtra possesses no majestic power.
If it lacks such power, then even though it is recited and chanted, it will be of no benefit.
"Because they disparage and revile this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they further cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to fall into hell.
Those who uphold this sūtra yet violate the precepts are evil associates (*pāpamitra*) to sentient beings; they are not my disciples, but the retinue of Māra."

For such a person, I do not permit the receiving or upholding of this scripture; it would be better that they do not receive, uphold, or cultivate it, than for them to receive, uphold, and practice it while violating the precepts.

“Good son! If my disciples uphold, recite, copy, or expound the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they should rectify their body and mind, and must carefully avoid frivolous playfulness or restless movements—frivolity of the body and restlessness of the mind.

The mind that seeks existence is called ‘restless movement,’ while the body’s commission of various karmas is called ‘frivolous playfulness. If my disciples seek existence or create karma, they should not uphold this Mahāyāna scripture, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.”
If there are those who uphold this sutra in such a manner, people will revile them, saying:
"If the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the secret treasury of the Buddha, possesses such majestic power, why does it cause you to seek existence and create karma?"
If those who uphold this sutra seek existence and create karma, you should know that this sutra lacks power and majesty.
If it lacks power and majesty, then even though they receive and uphold it, it will be of no benefit.
"Because they disparage and revile this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they further cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to fall into hell.
Those who uphold this sūtra while seeking existence and creating karma are evil friends to sentient beings; they are not my disciples, but the retinue of Māra."

"Furthermore, good son! If my disciples uphold, recite, copy, and expound the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, they must not speak at improper times; they must not speak in unsuitable countries; they must not speak without being requested; they must not speak with a disrespectful mind; they must not speak everywhere; they must not speak while praising themselves; they must not speak while disparaging others; they must not speak so as to extinguish the Buddha-dharma; and they must not speak so as to inflame worldly dharmas."
"Good son!
If my disciples uphold this sutra and preach it at improper times, even preaching it while the worldly dharmas are in full blaze, people will revile them, saying:

'If the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the secret treasury of the Buddha, possesses such majestic power, why does it cause you to preach at improper times, even to the point of preaching while the worldly dharmas are in full blaze?'"
If those who uphold this sutra should speak in such a manner, one should know that this sutra possesses no majestic power.
If it lacks majestic power, then even though it is received and upheld, it will be of no benefit.
"Because they disparage and revile this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they cause immeasurable sentient beings to fall into hell.

Those who uphold this sūtra yet preach it at improper times, even preaching it while inflaming worldly dharmas, are evil friends to sentient beings; they are not my disciples, but the retinue of Māra."

“Good son! Those who wish to receive and uphold [this teaching], those who speak of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, those who speak of the Buddha-nature, those who speak of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, those who speak of the Mahāyāna, those who speak of the Vaipulya sūtras, those who speak of the Śrāvaka-yāna, those who speak of the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, those who speak of liberation, and those who perceive the Buddha-nature, must first purify their bodies.”
Because the body is pure, there is no reproach;
because there is no reproach, it causes immeasurable people to give rise to pure faith in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*;

because faith arises, they revere this sutra, and whether they hear a single verse, a single phrase, a single word, or the preaching of the Dharma, they will then resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
You should know that such a person is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings and not a bad friend; they are my disciple and not a follower of Māra.
This is called a bodhisattva, and not one of the world.
“Good son! This is what is not known, not seen, and not realized by the world, yet it is that which the bodhisattva knows, sees, and realizes.
Furthermore, good son!”
What, furthermore, is that which is unknown, unseen, and unawakened by all the world, yet is known, seen, and awakened by the bodhisattva?
It is what is called the six foundations of mindfulness.
What are the six? They are:
mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Sangha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of giving, and mindfulness of the devas. "Good son!
How does one practice mindfulness of the Buddha? One reflects upon the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid,
the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavat— who is eternal, [blissful, self, and pure]...
Unchanging, he is endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the great lion’s roar;
he is named the Great Śramaṇa, the Great Brāhmaṇa, the Great Purity, the one who has ultimately reached the further shore,
the unconquerable, the one whose crown cannot be seen, and he is without fear, unstartled, and immovable.
Solitary and without companion, he attained self-awakening without a teacher; possessing swift wisdom, great wisdom, sharp wisdom,
profound wisdom, liberating wisdom, uncommon wisdom, vast and universal wisdom, ultimate wisdom,
and the accomplishment of the treasure of wisdom— he is the elephant king among men, the bull king among men, the dragon king among men.
A noble man, a lotus among humanity, a white lotus (puṇḍarīka), a teacher who tames those to be trained,
a great donor, and a teacher of the Great Dharma.
Because he knows the Dharma, he is called a Great Dharma Master.
Because of knowing the meaning, one is called a great Dharma teacher;
because of knowing the proper time, one is called a great Dharma teacher;
because of knowing contentment, one is called a great Dharma teacher.
Because of knowing me, one is called a great Dharma teacher;
because of knowing the great assembly, one is called a great Dharma teacher;
because of knowing the various natures of sentient beings, one is called a great Dharma teacher.
Because he knows the sharp, dull, and middling faculties of all beings, he is called a Great Dharma Master;
because he teaches the Middle Way, he is called a Great Dharma Master.
"Why is he called the Tathāgata?"
It is as unchanging as that which was spoken by all the Buddhas of the past.
How is it unchanging?
The Buddhas of the past, in order to deliver sentient beings, preached the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
The Tathāgata is also like this; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, come from the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eleven kinds of emptiness to reach Great Nirvāṇa;
the Tathāgata is also like this, and for this reason the Buddha is titled the Tathāgata.
"For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ appropriate skillful means to reveal the Three Vehicles; their lifespans are immeasurable and beyond calculation.
The Tathāgata is likewise; for this reason, the Buddha is titled 'Tathāgata'."
"What is meant by 'Arahan' (Worthy One)?
All worldly phenomena are called enemies; because the Buddha should destroy them, he is named 'Arahan.

Furthermore, the four Māras are the enemies of a Bodhisattva. When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were Bodhisattvas, they were able to destroy the four Māras through wisdom; for this reason, they are named 'Arahan.'"
Furthermore, "Arhat" (the Worthy One) means "to distance oneself.
When acting as a bodhisattva, one should distance oneself from immeasurable afflictions; therefore, it is called "Arhat.
Furthermore, "Arhat" means "joy."

When the Buddhas of the past were bodhisattvas, although they underwent all manner of suffering and affliction for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they never failed to find joy, but always delighted in it.
The Tathāgata is likewise; therefore, he is called "Arhat" (the Worthy One).

Furthermore, "Arhat" means that all humans and devas ought to make offerings to him with various kinds of incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, flags, and music; for this reason, he is called "Arhat."
"What is 'perfectly complete knowledge' (samyak-saṃbodhi)?
'Perfect' (samyak) means non-erroneous;
'complete knowledge' (saṃbodhi) means thorough penetration regarding the four inversions."
Furthermore, "right" refers to ascetic practice;
"thorough knowledge" means knowing that because of ascetic practice there will certainly be the fruit of suffering.
Furthermore, "right" refers to being within the world.
"Universal knowledge" means definitively knowing that by practicing the Middle Way, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, "correct" refers to that which can be counted, measured, and weighed;
"universal knowledge" is that which cannot be counted, measured, or weighed.
For this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyak-saṃbuddha). "Good son!
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also possess some all-knowingness, yet they do not possess all-knowingness."

Why is this? That which is called "thorough knowledge" refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also attain thorough knowledge; this is what is termed "thorough knowledge."
"What is meant by 'not fully knowing'? Good son!

Suppose the followers of the Two Vehicles were to contemplate a single aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) for immeasurable eons; they would still be unable to know it exhaustively. For this reason, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not possess universal knowledge."
"What is meant by 'one endowed with clear knowledge and conduct' (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*)?
'Clear knowledge' (*vidyā*) refers to the attainment of immeasurable wholesome fruits;
'conduct' (*caraṇa*) refers to the feet."
The "excellent fruit" refers to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The "feet" refer to precepts and wisdom.
By means of these feet of precepts and wisdom, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; therefore, he is called the One Endowed with Clarity and the Feet of Conduct (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna).
Furthermore, "vidyā" means mantra;
"caraṇa" means auspiciousness;
and "pūrṇa" means fruition.
Good son! This is called the worldly meaning.
As for "mantra," it is named liberation.
"Auspiciousness" refers to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
"fruit" refers to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
For this reason, he is called the One Endowed with Clarity and Conduct.
Furthermore, "wisdom" (vidyā) is named light;
"practice" (caryā) is named karma;
and "feet" (pāda) are named fruition.
Good son! This is called the meaning of "worldly.
"Light" refers to non-negligence.
The "practices" refer to the six pāramitās;
the "fruit" refers to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, "clarities" refers to the three vidyās:
First, the illumination of Bodhisattvas; second, the illumination of all Buddhas; third, the illumination of non-illumination.
The illumination of Bodhisattvas is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā; the illumination of all Buddhas is precisely the Buddha-eye; the illumination of non-illumination is precisely ultimate emptiness.
"Virtuous conduct" (caryā) refers to the cultivation of various wholesome karmas for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas.
"Perfection" (pāda) refers to the clear vision of the Buddha-nature.
For this reason, he is named "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna).
"What is meant by 'Sugata'? 'Su' means high;
'Gata' means not high."
"Good son! This is called the meaning of 'worldly.
That which is 'high' is named Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
That which is not haughty is the mind of the Tathāgata.
Good son! If the mind were haughty, it would not be called the Tathāgata.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is called the Sugata.
Furthermore, "good" (su) refers to the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
and "gone" (gata) refers to the fruit of the spiritual friend.
"Good son! This is called the meaning of the world.
A virtuous friend is that which is the initial arousal of the mind."
The fruit is called Great Parinirvāṇa.
Because the Tathāgata does not abandon his original aspiration for enlightenment and thereby attains Great Nirvāṇa, he is therefore named Sugata.
Furthermore, "good" (śubha) means "excellent," and "gone" (gata) means "existent.
O son of good family!
This is called the worldly meaning.
"Good" refers to seeing the Buddha-nature;
"existence" refers to Great Nirvana.
“Good son! The nature of nirvāṇa is truly not existent; it is because of the world that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, say it exists. Good son!”
For example, it is as when people in the world say they have a son when they actually have no son;
or when they say there is a path when there is actually no path.
Nirvana is likewise: it is said to exist only because of the world.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, they are called Sugatas.
"Good son, what is meant by 'Knower of the World'?"
Good son! That which is called "the world" refers to the five aggregates;
that which is called "understanding" refers to knowledge.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are called "Knowers of the World" because they thoroughly understand the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Furthermore, "the world" refers to the five desires;
"knowing" means being unattached to them.
Because he is unattached to the five desires, he is called the Knower of the World (*lokavid*).

Furthermore, regarding the "Knower of the World": all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the east do not know, do not see, and do not understand; yet the Buddhas know them all, see them all, and understand them all.
It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
For this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Knower of the World" (Lokavid).
Furthermore, "the world" refers to all ordinary beings;
"knower" means knowing the causes and effects of good and evil for all such ordinary beings.
This is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; only a Buddha can know it. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Knower of the World" (Lokavid).
Furthermore, "world" (loka) is a name for the lotus;
"knower" (vid) means being unstained.
"Good son! This is called the worldly meaning.
The lotus flower is, in fact, the Tathāgata."
Regarding "untainted," the Tathāgata is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas;
for this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*).
Furthermore, as for the "Knower of the World," all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also called the "Knower of the World."
Why is this? Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceive the world, they are called "Knower of the World" (Lokavid). Good son!
Just as food is called "life" because life is sustained by food, so too it is with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: because they perceive the world, they are called "Knower of the World."
"What is the Unsurpassed One?
'The Surpassed One' is a name for that which has been severed;
one who has nothing further to sever is called the Unsurpassed One."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess no afflictions; therefore, there is nothing for them to abandon. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*).
Furthermore, "the superior one" (*puruṣa*) refers to one who engages in dispute;
"the unsurpassed one" is one who has no dispute.
The Tathāgata is without contention; therefore, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*).
Furthermore, that which is called an "Unsurpassed One" is such that his words cannot be subverted.
Where an "Unsurpassed One" exists, his speech is indestructible.
That which the Tathāgata speaks cannot be subverted by any sentient being; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One (Anuttara).
Furthermore, an "Upriest" (Uttara) is called an Elder (Sthavira);
one who is unsurpassed is called the Unsurpassed Elder (Anuttara-sthavira).
Among all Buddhas of the three periods of time, there is none who surpasses him; therefore, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*).
"Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) means new;
"One" (*puruṣa*) means old.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the essence of Great Nirvāṇa, which is neither new nor old; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One.
"What is meant by 'Tamer of Men'?"
Having already been a great man himself, he further tames great men. Good son!
That which is called the Tathāgata is, in reality, neither a great man nor not a great man.
Because he has disciplined himself as a man, the Tathāgata is called a "Great Man" (puruṣa). Good son!
All men and women who possess four qualities are then called Great Men.
What are the four?
First, virtuous friends; second, being able to listen to the Dharma; third, contemplating its meaning; and fourth, practicing according to the teaching.
“Good son! Whether male or female, one who possesses these four dharmas is called a ‘great man. Good son!”
If a man lacks these four qualities, he cannot be called a true man (puruṣa).
Why is this? For although his body is that of a man, his conduct is identical to that of a beast.
The Tathāgata tames both men and women; for this reason, he is called the Buddha, the Tamer of Men.
Furthermore, son of good family:
There are four kinds of people who are like those who drive horses:

first, those who touch the hair; second, those who touch the skin; third, those who touch the flesh; and fourth, those who touch the bone. According to what they touch, they respond to the will of the driver.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he tames sentient beings through four methods:
first, by teaching them birth so that they may accept the Buddha’s words, just as touching its hair makes it follow the will of the driver;
second, by teaching them birth and old age so that they may accept the Buddha’s words, just as touching its hair and skin makes it follow the will of the driver.

Third, when one hears the teachings on birth, as well as old age and sickness, one immediately accepts the Buddha’s words, just as touching the hair, skin, and flesh follows the will of the charioteer;

fourth, when one hears the teachings on birth, as well as old age, sickness, and death, one immediately accepts the Buddha’s words, just as touching the hair, skin, flesh, and bone follows the will of the charioteer.
"Good son!

A charioteer’s training of horses is not invariably certain, but the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, tames sentient beings with absolute certainty and never in vain; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the 'Tamer of Men' (Puruṣadamyasārathi)."
"What is meant by 'Teacher of Gods and Humans'?
There are two kinds of teachers:
first, those who teach what is wholesome; second, those who teach what is unwholesome."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly teach all sentient beings by means of wholesome dharmas.
What are these wholesome dharmas?
They are the wholesomeness of body, speech, and mind.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct all sentient beings, saying:
"Good son! You should distance yourself from unwholesome physical actions."
Why is this? Because physical unwholesome karma can be abandoned and one can attain liberation from it; therefore, I teach you this Dharma.
If such unwholesome karma were impossible to abandon and liberation could not be attained, I would never have instructed you to abandon it.
"If there were any sentient beings who, having abandoned evil karma, yet fell into the three evil realms—that is impossible.
Because they have distanced themselves from such karma, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and realize Great Nirvāṇa."
Therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly use this Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings;
the same applies to their speech and mind.
For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Teacher.
"Furthermore, whereas formerly he had not attained the Way, he has now attained it, and he preaches the Way he has attained for the sake of sentient beings;
whereas from the beginning he had not cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), he has now completed its cultivation, and he preaches what he himself has cultivated for the sake of sentient beings;
having personally destroyed his own ignorance, he further destroys the ignorance of sentient beings for them."
Having personally attained pure vision, they further shatter the blindness and darkness of sentient beings to enable them to obtain pure eyes;
having personally realized the two truths, they further expound the two truths for sentient beings;
having already attained liberation themselves, they further preach the Dharma of liberation for sentient beings.
Having crossed the boundless great river of birth and death myself, I further cause all sentient beings to cross it;
having attained fearlessness myself, I further teach sentient beings to be free from dread;
having entered nirvana myself, I further expound the Great Nirvana for the sake of sentient beings.
For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Teacher.
"Heaven" (*deva*) means "day"; in the heavens, the days are long and the nights are short, and for this reason it is called heaven.
Furthermore, "heaven" means "free from sorrow and affliction," as one constantly experiences bliss; for this reason it is called heaven.
Furthermore, "deva" means "lamp-light"; it can destroy darkness and provide great illumination, and for this reason it is called deva.
Moreover, because it can destroy evil karma and darkness, and by attaining various wholesome karmas one is born in the heavens, it is therefore called deva.
Furthermore, "deva" means auspicious; because they are auspicious, they are named devas.
Furthermore, "deva" means sun; because the sun possesses radiance, it is named the sun-deva.
For this reason, they are called "devas" (heavenly beings).
As for "humans," it means "sun," as they are capable of much kindness and righteousness.
Furthermore, humans are those whose bodies and speech are gentle and supple.
Furthermore, "person" refers to one who possesses pride;
furthermore, "person" refers to one who is able to destroy pride. Good son!
Although the Buddhas are the unsurpassed great teachers for all sentient beings, the sūtras describe them as "teachers of gods and humans.
Why is this? Good son!

Among all sentient beings, only devas and humans are able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, are able to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action, and are able to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of pratyekabuddha, and the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Teacher of Devas and Humans.
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
A Buddha is named for awakening; having awakened oneself, one is further able to awaken others. Good son!
For example, if there is a person who perceives the presence of a thief, that thief can do nothing.

In the same way, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to perceive all immeasurable afflictions; having fully awakened to them, he renders those afflictions powerless. For this reason, he is called a Buddha.
Because of this awakening, one is not born, does not age, does not fall ill, and does not die; for this reason, he is called a Buddha.
"Bhagavān" [is explained as follows]: *bhaga* means destruction, and *vān* means afflictions.
He is called Bhagavat because he is able to destroy the afflictions; because he is able to accomplish all wholesome dharmas;

because he is able to skillfully understand the meaning of all dharmas; because he possesses great merit that cannot be surpassed; because he possesses great renown that pervades the ten directions; because he bestows various kinds of great wisdom; and because for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas he has cast off the female organ.

“Good son! Whether male or female, those who are able to recollect the Buddha in this manner—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether by day or by night; whether in light or in darkness—will always be able to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, without being separated from him.”
“Good son! For what reason is he named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth, up to Bhagavat, and why does he possess such immeasurable merit and great renown?”
"Good son!

In the past, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reverently served his parents, preceptors, teachers, and senior elders. For immeasurable kalpas, he constantly practiced giving for the sake of sentient beings, maintained the prohibitive precepts, cultivated patience, diligently applied vigor, and practiced meditative concentration and wisdom; he also cultivated great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity. Therefore, he has now attained the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and a body of vajra."

Furthermore, for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past, the Bodhisattva cultivated the faculties of faith, mindfulness, diligence, concentration, and wisdom; he reverently made offerings to his teachers and elders, always seeking the benefit of the Dharma rather than the benefit of food.

If a bodhisattva upholds the twelve divisions of the scriptures—whether reading or reciting them—they always do so for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, peace, and happiness, never for their own sake.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva constantly cultivates a supramundane mind, a mind of renunciation, an unconditioned mind, a mind free from contention,
a mind free from defilement, a mind free from bondage, and a mind free from grasping and attachment.
A mind free from obscuration, a mind that is not indeterminate, a mind free from birth and death, a mind free from the net of doubt,
a mind free from desire, a mind free from hatred, a mind free from delusion, a mind free from arrogance,
a mind free from turbidity, a mind free from affliction, a mind free from suffering, an immeasurable mind, and a vast mind.
The mind of emptiness, the mind without [inherent] mind, the mind that is not without mind, the tamed mind, the unguarded mind,
the unhidden mind, the non-worldly mind, the ever-concentrated mind, the ever-cultivated mind, the ever-liberated mind,
the mind free from retribution, the wishless mind, the well-directed mind, the undeluded mind, and the supple mind.
The mind, the non-abiding mind, the sovereign mind, the untainted mind, the ultimate truth mind, the non-retrogressive mind,
the impermanent mind, the upright mind, the mind free from guile and crookedness, the purely wholesome mind, the mind free from excess or deficiency,
the mind free from solidity, the mind free from the state of an ordinary person, and the mind free from the state of a śrāvaka.

Because he has realized the mind of the pratyekabuddha, the mind that well knows the elements, the mind that well knows the realm of birth, the mind that well knows the realm of abiding, and the mind of the realm of mastery;

for this reason, he has now attained the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, and permanence, bliss, self, and purity. For this reason, he is entitled to be called the Tathāgata.
Up to and including the Bhagavān—
this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the Buddha.
"What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the Dharma?"

Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that the Dharma taught by all Buddhas is most wondrous and supreme; because of this Dharma, they are able to cause sentient beings to attain present fruits.
Only this True Dharma is timeless; it is seen by the eye of Dharma and not by the fleshly eye.

It cannot be compared through analogies; it is unborn and unarisen, non-abiding and non-ceasing, without beginning and without end, unconditioned and innumerable. For those who have no dwelling, it serves as a dwelling.
It provides a refuge for those without refuge, brings light to those in ignorance, and enables those who have not reached the other shore to reach it.
It creates unimpeded fragrance where there was no fragrance; it is seen by that which cannot be seen. It is unmoving and non-turning, neither long nor short.
It forever severs all worldly pleasures for the sake of the bliss of peace and security, being ultimately subtle and wondrous.
It is not form, yet it is the severance of form, and yet it is also form; and so on up to:

it is not consciousness, yet it is the severance of consciousness, and yet it is also consciousness; it is not karma, yet it is the severance of karma; it is not fetters, yet it is the severance of fetters;
it is not entities, yet it is the severance of entities, and yet it is also entities; it is not elements, yet it is the severance of elements, and yet it is also elements; it is not existence.
It is the severance of existence, yet it is also existence; it is not entry, yet it is the severance of entry, and it is also entry;
it is not cause, yet it is the severance of cause, and it is also cause; it is not fruit, yet it is the severance of fruit, and it is also fruit;
it is neither false nor real, yet it is the severance of all reality, and it is also reality; it is not birth—
It is not cessation, yet it is the cessation of birth and death through eternal severance;

it is not a characteristic, nor is it the absence of characteristics, yet it is a characteristic through the severance of all characteristics; it is not instruction, nor is it non-instruction, yet it is the Teacher;
it is not fear, nor is it security, yet it is security through the severance of all fears; it is not patience, nor is it... [non-patience].
Patience is the eternal severance of impatience, yet it is itself patience; it is neither cessation nor non-cessation, for it severs all cessation and is itself cessation.
It is the pinnacle of all dharmas, capable of eternally severing all afflictions;
it is pure and signless, forever liberated from all signs, and the ultimate dwelling place for immeasurable sentient beings.
To be able to extinguish the blazing fires of all birth and death, which is the dwelling place where all Buddhas roam and reside,
eternal and unchanging—
this is called the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the Dharma.
"What is the mindfulness of the Sangha?

The Buddhas and the noble Sangha abide in accordance with the Dharma; they receive the upright Dharma and practice in conformity with it. They cannot be seen, cannot be grasped, and cannot be destroyed; they cannot be harmed and are inconceivable."
The field of merit for all sentient beings is a source of auspicious protection; though it serves as a field of merit, it accepts nothing and grasps at nothing.
It is pure and free from defilement, untainted and unconditioned, vast, universal, and boundless.
Their mind is disciplined and supple, equanimous and non-dual, free from agitation and turbidity, constant and unchanging.
This is called mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
What is mindfulness of the precepts?
The bodhisattva reflects:
"There is morality—unbroken, unimpaired, uncorrupted, and untainted.
Though it has no form or color, it can be guarded and maintained."
Although there is no physical contact, by skillfully cultivating expedient means, one may attain full perfection without fault;
this is praised by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and is the cause for the Great Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Good son! It is like the great earth;

it is like a ship, a necklace, the great ocean, alkaline ash, a dwelling, a sword, a bridge, a skilled physician’s wondrous medicine, an *agada* elixir, a wish-fulfilling jewel, feet, eyes, parents, and cool shade. It cannot be plundered, it cannot be harmed, fire cannot burn it, and water cannot sweep it away. It is a staircase for the great mountains, and a sublime, victorious banner of jewels for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
If one abides in this precept and attains the fruit of srotāpanna, I too have a share in it; however, I do not require it.
Why is this? If I were to attain this fruit of srotāpanna, I would be unable to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
If one abides in these precepts, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I too have a share in this, for this is what I desire. Why is that?
"If I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall extensively expound the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and act as their protector.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the precepts.
“What is the recollection of giving?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva deeply contemplates that this giving is the cause of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddhas and bodhisattvas have approached and cultivated such giving; I, too, shall approach and cultivate it in the same way.”
If one does not practice generous giving, one cannot adorn the fourfold assembly.
Although giving cannot ultimately sever all fetters, it can eliminate and destroy present afflictions.

By virtue of the causes and conditions of giving, they are constantly praised by the sentient beings of immeasurable and boundless worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, throughout the ten directions.
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give food to sentient beings, they bestow life upon them; through this retribution, when they attain Buddhahood, their state is eternal and unchanging.
Because one bestows happiness, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one obtains peace and bliss.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma and do not encroach upon others' offerings; therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, they obtain pure nirvana.
When a Bodhisattva practices giving, they cause all sentient beings to obtain what they seek without having to ask; therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, they achieve mastery over themselves.
Because they enable others to gain power through the causes and conditions of their giving, they attain the ten powers upon becoming a Buddha.
By means of the causal conditions of giving, one enables others to obtain speech; therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, one acquires the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).

Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cultivate and accumulate this giving as a cause for *nirvāṇa*; I likewise practice giving in this way as a cause for *nirvāṇa*, as explained at length in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
"What is the recollection of the devas?
There are the abodes of the Four Great Kings up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If one possesses faith and attains the abode of the Four Great Kings, I too have a share in that."

If one attains the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception through morality, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom, I too have a share in this; yet it is not what I desire.
Why is this? Because the realms from the Four Great Kings up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception are all impermanent.
Because they are impermanent, there is birth, old age, sickness, and death.
For this reason, it is not what I desire.
It is like a magical illusion that deceives the foolish, but does not delude or entice the wise.

That which is like a magical illusion refers to the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; the "fools" refer to all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), whereas I am not like these ordinary, ignorant people.
I have heard that there is such a thing as the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-deva), namely the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are eternal and unchanging.
Because they abide eternally, they are not born, do not age, do not fall ill, and do not die.
For the sake of sentient beings, I diligently seek the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-deva*). Why is this?
Because the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth can cause sentient beings to sever and eliminate their afflictions (*kleśa*), just like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*).

If I possess faith, up to and including wisdom, then I shall be able to attain the ultimate heavenly realm; I shall extensively analyze and explain this ultimate heavenly realm for the sake of sentient beings.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the devas.
"Good son, this is what is called the supramundane for a bodhisattva; it is that which the world does not know, see, or awaken to, yet which this bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to."

“Good son! If my disciples were to claim that there is no difference between upholding, reciting, copying, and expounding the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and upholding, reciting, copying, and elaborately explaining the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, this would not be correct.”
Why is this? Good son!
Great Nirvana is the profound and secret treasury of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; because it is this profound and secret treasury of the Buddhas, it is supreme.
“Good son!
For this reason, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is most marvelous, most extraordinary, and inconceivable.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I also know that this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is most marvelous, most extraordinary, and inconceivable.
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are inconceivable; the Bodhisattvas, Bodhi, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* are likewise inconceivable.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you further say that a bodhisattva is inconceivable? “Good son!
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, though having no instructor, is able to spontaneously give rise to the mind of enlightenment;

once the mind has been generated, they practice with diligent vigor, such that even if a great fire were to burn their body and head, they would never seek rescue or abandon the mind that contemplates the Dharma.
Why is this? A bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly reflects:

"Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, whether in the hells, among hungry ghosts, animals, humans, or devas, I have been scorched by the fires of the various fetters; yet I have never once attained a single definitive dharma. That which is called a 'definitive dharma' is precisely anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
For the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall never cherish or spare my body, mind, or life.
For the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even if my body were to be shattered like fine dust, I would never abandon my diligent exertion.
Why is this? The mind of diligent exertion is itself the cause of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Good son!

In this way, if a bodhisattva is able to disregard even their own body and life in such a manner before yet having seen unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, how much more so after having seen it?
Therefore, the bodhisattva is inconceivable.
Furthermore, it is inconceivable that the immeasurable faults and afflictions of birth and death perceived by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva are not within the reach of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Although they know that birth and death involve immeasurable faults and evils, for the sake of sentient beings, they undergo suffering therein without giving rise to weariness or detachment.
For this reason, it is further called inconceivable.

"For the sake of sentient beings, although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas undergo various sufferings and afflictions in the hells, it is like the bliss of the third dhyāna; for this reason, they are further called 'inconceivable.'"
“Good son! It is like an elder whose house caught fire.
Having seen it, the elder emerged from the house, but his children remained behind, not yet escaped from the calamity of the fire.
At that time, the elder knew for certain that there was danger from the fire; yet for the sake of his children, he returned to rescue them, disregarding the peril.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: although he knows that birth and death abound with many faults and evils, he dwells within them for the sake of sentient beings without weariness; for this reason, he is further named "Inconceivable."

“Good son! Immeasurable sentient beings resolve upon bodhicitta, yet seeing the many faults and evils within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), their minds immediately retreat and sink; they may then become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”
If there are bodhisattvas who hear this sutra, they shall never again fall away from the mind of enlightenment to become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Thus, although such bodhisattvas have not yet reached the first stage, the Immovable Ground (acalā-bhūmi), their minds are firm and resolute, free from regression or decline; for this reason, it is further called "inconceivable."
“Good son! If someone were to say:
‘I am able to swim across the waters of the great ocean.’”
"Is such a statement conceivable?
"World-Honored One!
Such a statement may be conceivable, or it may be inconceivable."
"Why is this? If a human being crosses over, it is inconceivable; if an asura crosses over, it is conceivable. "Good son!"
“I do not speak of asuras; I am speaking only of humans.
“World-Honored One, among humans there are also those who are conceivable and those who are inconceivable.”
World-Honored One!
Humans are also of two kinds:
first, the noble ones; second, ordinary beings.
"Ordinary persons are inconceivable, while noble sages are conceivable. "Good son!
I speak of ordinary persons; I do not speak of noble ones."
“World-Honored One!
If ordinary persons are truly inconceivable. “Good son!
Ordinary worldlings truly cannot cross the great ocean of water.
In this same way, bodhisattvas truly can cross the great ocean of birth and death; for this reason, they are further called inconceivable.
“Good son! If there were someone who could suspend Mount Sumeru with a single thread from a lotus root, would this be conceivable? “No, it would not.”
“World-Honored One!
‘Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in a single thought-instant, is able to weigh and measure all of saṃsāra; for this reason, he is further called ‘inconceivable.’”

“Good son! For immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva has constantly contemplated that birth and death are impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he analytically explains them as permanent, blissful, self, and pure. Although he speaks in this way, it is not a false view; therefore, it is further called inconceivable.”
“Good son! Just as a person who enters water cannot be drowned by the water, and one who enters a great, raging fire cannot be burned by the fire—such matters are inconceivable.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: although dwelling within birth and death, he is not afflicted or harmed by birth and death; for this reason, he is further named "inconceivable."
“Good son! There are three grades of persons, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
When a person of the inferior grade first enters the womb, he thinks to himself:”
"I am now situated in a latrine, a place where all impurities converge, like being amidst corpses, among many thorns, or in a place of great darkness.
When first emerging from the womb, he again reflects:
"I am now leaving the latrine, leaving the place of all impurities, and even leaving the place of great darkness."
Those of middle capacity think to themselves:
"I shall now enter the groves of various trees, the pure rivers, and my rooms and dwellings."
The same occurs when they emerge.
A person of superior capacity thinks to themselves:
"I am ascending a palace hall, amidst flower groves, riding a horse, riding an elephant, or climbing a high mountain."
It is the same when he emerges.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first enters the womb, he knows he is entering; while dwelling there, he knows he is dwelling; and when emerging, he knows he is emerging. Throughout this process, he never gives rise to thoughts of greed or anger, yet he has not yet attained the first stage (bhūmi). For this reason, he is further called "inconceivable."
“Good son! Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi truly cannot be compared by means of analogies.
Good son!”
The mind likewise cannot be compared by means of spatial analogies, yet it can be explained in every way.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, without having a teacher from whom to receive instruction, is nonetheless able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having attained this Dharma, one’s mind is free from stinginess, and one constantly expounds it for the sake of sentient beings.
For this reason, it is further named "Inconceivable. "Good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have physical seclusion that is not verbal, verbal seclusion that is not physical, and seclusion that is neither physical nor verbal.
Physical seclusion refers to abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; this is called physical seclusion that is not verbal.
Abstention by way of speech refers to abstaining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter; this is called abstention by way of speech, not by way of body.
Abstention that is neither by way of body nor by way of speech refers to abstaining from covetousness, ill will, and wrong views.
Good son! This is called being neither body nor speech, yet being far removed [from defilement]. Good son!

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive even a single dharma as being the body, karma, or the separation from a master; yet there is still separation. For this reason, it is further called "inconceivable.
The same applies to speech.
“Good son! Depart from the body by means of the body; depart from the mouth by means of the mouth; depart from wisdom by that which is neither body nor mouth.
Good son!”
Indeed, this wisdom exists; however, it cannot cause a bodhisattva to become detached. Why is this?
O son of good family!
There is not a single dharma that can destroy or create.
The nature of conditioned dharmas is to arise differently and cease differently; therefore, this wisdom cannot be separated from them. "Good son!

Wisdom cannot shatter it; fire cannot burn it; water cannot rot it; wind cannot move it; earth cannot support it; birth cannot give rise to it; aging cannot age it; abiding cannot cause it to abide; destruction cannot destroy it; greed cannot greed for it; hatred cannot hate it; and delusion cannot delude it, because its conditioned nature arises as one thing and ceases as another.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva never gives rise to the thought:
"I shall destroy all afflictions by means of this wisdom," nor does he say to himself:
"I have destroyed the afflictions.
Although he speaks thus, it is not false; for this reason, he is further named "Inconceivable.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“World-Honored One!

Only now do I know that the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are inconceivable; that the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, those who uphold it, bodhi, and nirvāṇa are all inconceivable.”
“World-Honored One!
How long will the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma remain? After how much time will it perish? “Good son!”
If the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* contains even these five kinds of conduct—
namely, noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*), Brahma-conduct (*brahma-caryā*), celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*), conduct in illness (*glāna-caryā*), and infantile conduct (*bāla-caryā*).

If among my disciples there are those who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and expound its meaning, and who are honored, respected, praised, and provided with various offerings by all sentient beings, you should know that at such a time the Buddha-dharma has not yet perished.

“Good son! When the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is fully disseminated, at that time my disciples will for the most part violate the prohibitive precepts, commit various evils, and be unable to respect or have faith in such a sūtra. Because of this lack of faith, they will be unable to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or explain its meaning. They will not be honored or even provided with offerings by the masses; rather, seeing those who do uphold it, they will treat them with contempt and slander, saying:
‘You are one of the six heretical teachers, not a disciple of the Buddha.’”
"You should know that the Buddha-dharma will soon be extinguished.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have personally heard this teaching from the Buddha:
'The Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha shall remain in the world for seven days, after which it will completely perish.
World-Honored One!"
"Kāśyapa Tathāgata, did he not possess this sutra?
If he did possess it, why do you say it has been extinguished?
If he did not possess it, how can you say that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is the secret treasury of all Tathāgatas?"
The Buddha said, "Good son!
As I have previously stated, only Mañjuśrī understands this meaning."
I shall now speak again; listen with a sincere and attentive mind.
Good son, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess two kinds of dharmas:
First is the worldly dharma, and second is the ultimate dharma.
Worldly dharmas can be extinguished, but the ultimate dharma is indestructible.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
The first consists of impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity; the second consists of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
That which is impermanent, non-self, suffering, and impure is subject to destruction and cessation; that which is permanent, blissful, self, and pure is without destruction or cessation.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, that which is maintained by the followers of the Two Vehicles; second, that which is maintained by Bodhisattvas.
That which is maintained by the followers of the Two Vehicles is subject to destruction and cessation, whereas that which is maintained by Bodhisattvas is without destruction or cessation."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the external; second, the internal.
External phenomena are subject to destruction and cessation, whereas internal phenomena are not subject to destruction and cessation."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Conditioned phenomena are subject to disintegration and cessation; unconditioned phenomena are not subject to disintegration or cessation."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, that which can be apprehended; second, that which cannot be apprehended.
Phenomena that can be apprehended are subject to disintegration and cessation; that which cannot be apprehended is without disintegration or cessation."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, shared dharmas; second, unshared dharmas.
Shared dharmas are subject to destruction, whereas unshared dharmas are not subject to destruction."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, among humans; second, among devas.
Among humans there is destruction and cessation, but among devas there is no destruction or cessation."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the eleven divisions of the sūtras; second, the Vaipulya sūtras.
The eleven divisions of the sūtras are subject to decay and extinction, whereas the Vaipulya scriptures are not subject to decay or extinction."

“Good son! If my disciples uphold, recite, copy, and explain the Vaipulya sūtras, and if they revere, make offerings to, honor, and praise them, you should know that at such a time the Buddha-dharma shall not perish.”
“Good son! Regarding what you have just asked:
‘Did the Tathāgata Kāśyapa possess this sūtra?’”
"O son of good family!
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is the secret treasury of all Buddhas. Why is this so?"

Although the Buddhas possess the eleven divisions of the scriptures, they do not therein speak of the Buddha-nature, nor do they speak of the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, nor that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa; for this reason, this sutra is called the Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata.
Because it is not expounded in the eleven divisions of the sūtras, it is called a "pitaka" (storehouse).
It is like a person who keeps their seven treasures for internal use rather than external expenditure; thus they are called a "treasury. "Good son!
The reason this person hoards and accumulates these goods is for the sake of future events.
What are these future events? They are: when grain becomes scarce;

when bandits come to invade the country; when one encounters a wicked king and must use them to ransom one's life; during times of urgent distress on the road; or when wealth is difficult to obtain—at such times, they shall be brought forth and used.
"Good son!

The secret treasury of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is likewise so. When, in future ages, there appear in the world such evils as wicked bhikṣus who store impure things, who preach to the fourfold assembly that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate parinirvāṇa, who read and recite worldly treatises, and who do not respect the Buddha’s sūtras—in order to extinguish these evils and cause them to distance themselves from the gains and offerings of wrong livelihood, the Tathāgata then expounds this sūtra."
If this secret treasury of the sūtras were to perish and no longer appear in the world, you should know that at such a time the Buddha-dharma would also perish.
"Good son! The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is eternal and unchanging; why do you dare to question it, saying:..."
"Was this sutra present during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha? "Good son!

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, all sentient beings had thin and slight craving and abundant wisdom; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were gentle and easy to transform, possessed great majestic virtue, and maintained total retention without forgetfulness, like great elephant kings."
The world is pure, and all sentient beings know that the Tathāgata will never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa, but remains eternally and unchangingly.
Although this scripture exists, there is no need to expound it.
"Good son!

The sentient beings of this world have many afflictions; they are foolish and prone to forgetfulness, lacking wisdom and entangled in many webs of doubt, such that their faculty of faith is not established."
The world is impure, and all sentient beings say:
"The Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to change; he will ultimately enter Great Parinirvāṇa.
For this reason, the Tathāgata expounds this scripture.
“Good son! The Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha has, in truth, not been extinguished either. Why is this?
Because it is eternal and unchanging. "Good son!
If there are sentient beings who perceive a self where there is no self, or perceive no-self where there is a self; who perceive permanence where there is impermanence, or [perceive] impermanence..."
One perceives the permanent as permanent; one perceives the pleasant as unpleasant, and the unpleasant as pleasant; one perceives the pure as impure, and the impure as pure;
one perceives cessation as non-cessation, and non-cessation as cessation; one perceives what is a fault as not a fault, and what is not a fault as a fault;
one perceives a light offense as heavy, and a heavy offense as light; one perceives a vehicle as not a vehicle, and [what is not a vehicle as a vehicle].
They take what is a vehicle for seeing as a vehicle; they see the Path as not the Path and what is not the Path as the Path;
they see what is truly Bodhi as not Bodhi, and what is truly not Bodhi as erroneously being Bodhi;
they see suffering as not suffering, the origin as not the origin, cessation as not cessation, and the real as not real; they take what is actually conventional truth to be ultimate truth.
When one perceives the ultimate truth as the conventional truth, and perceives what is not a refuge as a refuge, or what is not a refuge as a refuge;
when one regards the true words of the Buddha as the words of Māra, and considers actual words of Māra to be the words of the Buddha—
at such a time, the Buddhas preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
“Good son! One might as well say that the mouths of mosquitoes can exhaust the depths of the great ocean, yet one cannot say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished;
one might as well say that blowing upon Mount Sumeru with one’s mouth can scatter and destroy it, yet one cannot say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished.”
It would be better to say that one binds the fierce wind with a rope than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished;
it would be better to say that a lotus flower grows within the fire of *khadira* wood than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished;
it would be better to say that the *agada* medicine is a poisonous drug than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished.
It would be better to say that the moon could be made hot and the sun could be made cold, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata could perish;
it would be better to say that the four great elements could each abandon their own nature, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata could perish.
