“Good son! If, when a Buddha has first appeared and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are no disciples who understand the profound meaning and that Buddha-World-Honored One were to enter *nirvāṇa*, you should know that this Dharma would not abide long in the world.”
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, you should know that even though the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, this Dharma will long abide in the world."
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, yet there are no lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) with sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma, and the Buddha then enters *nirvāṇa*, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world."
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are many lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) with sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma, you should know that even though the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, the Buddha-dharma will abide long in the world."
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and although there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) with sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma, those disciples preach the sutras and teachings out of greed for gain and offerings rather than for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, and the Buddha subsequently passes into extinction—then you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world."
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are also lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma—then whatever those disciples expound, being free from greed for gain and honor and seeking only *nirvāṇa*, you should know that even though the Buddha has entered *parinirvāṇa*, this Dharma will long abide in the world."
"Furthermore, good son!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, although there are disciples who understand the profound meaning and there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-dharma, yet the disciples frequently engage in disputes and litigation, mutually asserting right and wrong, and the Buddha subsequently enters *nirvāṇa*, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If, after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-Dharma; and if those disciples practice the dharma of harmony and respect, do not dispute one another, and mutually honor each other—then even though the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, you should know that this Dharma will abide for a long time without perishing."
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, although there may be disciples who understand the profound meaning and lay donors (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) who have deep faith and revere the Buddha-dharma, those disciples may preach the Dharma for the sake of Great Nirvāṇa and respect one another without engaging in disputes; yet they may still keep all kinds of impure things and further praise themselves, saying:
'I have attained the fruit of a *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of an *arhat*.'"
"When the Buddha further enters parinirvāṇa, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world.

Furthermore, son of good family, if after the Buddha has first appeared and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there are disciples who understand the profound meaning, and there are lay donors (dānapati) of sincere faith who revere the Buddha-Dharma; if those disciples expound the sūtras and Dharma for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, practice harmony and respect well, mutually honor one another, do not store any impure things, and do not claim for themselves the attainment of the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhat—then even though that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered extinction, you should know that this Dharma will abide long in the world."
"Furthermore, good son!

Suppose that after a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are certain disciples who do not even keep impure things, yet they do not themselves claim to have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* up to *arhat*. Each adheres to their own views and various divergent doctrines, saying:
'Venerable sir!'"
Regarding the four grave offenses established by the Buddhas, up to the seven rules for settling disputes, they are either prohibited or permitted for the sake of sentient beings;
the twelve divisions of the scriptures are likewise so.

Why is this? Because the Buddha knows that the lands and their seasons differ, sentient beings are not the same, and there are distinctions between those of sharp and dull faculties; therefore, the Tathāgata sometimes prohibits and sometimes permits, providing explanations of varying degrees of gravity.
Good son! It is like a skilled physician who prescribes milk for some illnesses and prohibits it for others; he permits its consumption for febrile diseases but forbids it for cold-natured ailments.
The Tathāgata is likewise: observing the root of the afflictions of all sentient beings, he both permits and prohibits [the teachings].
"Elder! I have personally heard this meaning from the Buddha.
Only I know its meaning; you do not."
‘Only I understand the Vinaya, while you cannot;
I know the various sūtras, while you cannot.
When that Buddha passes into extinction, you should know that this Dharma will not remain long in the world.
"Furthermore, good son!
If, when a Buddha has first appeared in the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are disciples who do not even say:
'I have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to that of *arhat*. "
Nor do they say:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, for the sake of sentient beings, sometimes prohibit or sometimes permit [certain actions].
Elder!..."
"I have personally heard from the Buddha such meanings, such teachings, and such discipline.
Venerable ones!
You should rely upon the twelvefold scriptures of the Tathāgata."
"If this meaning is correct, I shall uphold it;
if it is not, I shall discard it.
Although that Blessed One has entered parinirvāṇa, you should know that this Dharma will remain long in the world.

“Good son! When my Dharma is extinguished, there will be śrāvaka disciples who may say that there is a self (ātman), or say that the self is empty; some may say there is an intermediate state (antarābhava), or say there is no intermediate state; some may say there are the three periods of time, or say there are no three periods of time; some may say there are the three vehicles, or say there are no three vehicles; some may say that all things exist, or say that all things do not exist; some may say that sentient beings have a beginning and an end, or say that sentient beings have neither beginning nor end; some may say that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), or say that dependent origination is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); some may say that the Tathāgata undergoes the practice of illness and suffering, or say that the Tathāgata does not undergo the practice of illness and suffering.”
Some say that the Tathāgata did not permit bhikṣus to eat ten kinds of meat—what are these ten?
Human, snake, elephant, horse, donkey, dog, lion, pig, fox, and monkey; all others he permitted.
Others say that he did not permit any at all.
Some say that a bhikṣu should not perform five things—what are these five?
He must not sell living beings, weapons, wine, curdled milk, or sesame oil; as for all other matters, he is permitted to do them.
Some say that entry into five kinds of dwellings is not permitted—what are these five?
The butcher’s house, the prostitute’s house, the tavern, the royal palace, and the house of a caṇḍāla; entry into all other houses is permitted.
Some say that while *kauseya* silk garments are not permitted, all other things are permitted;
some say that the Tathāgata permitted the bhikṣus to accept and keep robes, food, and bedding, each valued at one hundred thousand taels of gold;
and others say he did not permit it.
Some say that *nirvāṇa* is permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
others say that *nirvāṇa* is simply the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), with no further distinct dharma called *nirvāṇa*.

For example, when threads are woven together, they are called "clothing"; once the clothing has been destroyed, it is called "no clothing," yet there is no separate entity apart from the clothing that is named "no clothing.
The essence of nirvāṇa is likewise so.

“Good son! At that time, among my disciples, those who preach correctly will be few while those who preach erroneously will be many; those who receive the true Dharma will be few while those who receive false teachings will be many; those who receive the Buddha’s words will be few while those who receive the words of Māra will be many.”
“Good son! At that time, there were two disciples in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī:
one was an Arhat, and the other was one who had broken the precepts.”
There were five hundred followers who had broken the precepts and one hundred followers who were arhats.
Those who had broken the precepts said:
"The Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa; I personally heard this teaching from the Buddha."
Regarding the four grave precepts established by the Tathāgata, it is permissible to uphold them, yet there is no offense even if they are transgressed.
I have now attained the fruit of Arhatship and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, yet even an Arhat may transgress these four grave precepts.
If the four grave offenses were actual transgressions, an Arhat would never have committed them.
Yet, while the Tathāgata was in the world, he established rules and commanded their firm observance; at the time of his parinirvāṇa, he released them all.
Then the arhat bhikṣu said: "Venerable one!
You should not say that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa once and for all."
I know that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging.
Whether the Tathāgata is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, there is no difference regarding the commission of the four grave offenses.
If one were to say that an Arhat commits the four grave offenses, this meaning is not so.
Why is this? Even a stream-enterer does not violate the prohibitions, let alone an arhat.
If the Elder says:
"I am an Arhat. An Arhat never gives rise to the thought:
"I have attained Arhatship."
"An Arhat speaks only of wholesome dharmas and does not speak of unwholesome ones.
What the Elder has spoken is entirely contrary to the Dharma; if anyone were to see the twelve divisions of the scriptures, they would certainly know that the Elder is not an Arhat."
"Good son! At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus who had broken the precepts collectively took the life of this arhat.
Good son!"
At that time, driven by the anger of these two groups, the Māra King caused all six hundred bhikṣus to be killed together.
Then, the ordinary people each said:
"Alas! The Buddha-Dharma has now come to its complete extinction."
"Yet my True Dharma does not truly perish.
At that time, there will be one hundred and twenty thousand great Bodhisattvas in that land who skillfully uphold my Dharma; how then can it be said that my Dharma has perished?"
"At that time, there will not be a single bhikṣu within Jambudvīpa who is my disciple.
At that time, Pāpīyān will completely burn all existing sūtras with great fires; among them, there may be some remnants left behind."
The various brahmins then conspired together to steal [the teachings], collecting them from various places and incorporating them into their own scriptures.
For this reason, before the Buddha appeared in the world, the lesser bodhisattvas collectively believed and accepted the words of the brahmins, even though those brahmins claimed:
"I possess the fasts and precepts."
Yet these non-Buddhists do not truly possess such things.

Although the various non-Buddhists claim that there is self, pleasure, and purity, they do not actually understand the meaning of self, pleasure, and purity; they merely take one or two words, or one or two phrases, from the Buddha-dharma and say:
"In my own scriptures, there is such a meaning."
At that time, when the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable multitudes among the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara heard these words, they all cried out together:
"The world is empty! The world is empty!"
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the great assembly:
"Do not grieve or weep. The world is not empty;
the Tathāgata abides eternally and is subject to no change."
"The Dharma and the Sangha are likewise.
At that time, having heard these words, the great assembly ceased their weeping and all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Sixteen.
[Volume Seventeen of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
supplemented by the Śramaṇa Huìyán and others of the Song Dynasty based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.]
Chapter Four: On the Holy Life (*Brahmacarya*).
At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, King Ajātaśatru was of a wicked nature; he delighted in slaughter and possessed the four evils of speech, as well as greed, hatred, and delusion.
His mind was burning with passion; he perceived only the present and saw nothing of the future, taking only evil men as his companions.
Because he was greedily attached to the pleasures of the five desires of the present world, he perversely committed the crime of rebellion against his innocent father, the King.
Having killed his father, remorse and fever arose within him; he cast off his necklaces and ceased to enjoy music and dance.
Because of this mental remorse and fever, sores broke out over his entire body; these sores were foul and putrid, such that one could not approach them.
He then thought to himself:
"This body of mine has already received the 'flower-retribution'; the actual retribution of hell is now close at hand.
At that time, his mother—named Vaidehī—applied various medicinal ointments to it, but the ulcer only grew worse and did not subside.
The king then said to his mother:
"A sore such as this arises from the mind; it does not originate from the four great elements.
If one were to say that there exists anyone capable of curing sentient beings [of such a condition], that would be impossible."
At that time, there was a high minister named Candraprabha (Moon-Appellation) who went to the king’s presence, stood to one side, and said:
“Great King,
why are you so dejected and your countenance so displeased?”
"Is it pain in the body,
or is it pain in the heart?
The king replied to the minister:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?
My father was innocent, yet I have perversely committed the crime of killing him.
From wise men, I have previously heard this principle:"
"It is said that there are five kinds of people in the world who do not escape hell, namely those who commit the five heinous crimes.
I now already possess immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sins; how could my body and mind possibly avoid suffering?"
"Furthermore, there is no skilled physician to treat my body and mind.
The minister said,
"Great King!"
"Do not suffer such great grief and distress.
He then spoke in verse:
"If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, that sorrow will only continue to increase."
"Just as when a person delights in sleep, their sleep increases;
so it is with lust and the craving for wine.
As the King has said:"
"There are five kinds of people in the world who are not liberated from hell.
Who went to see them and returned to tell the King?
As for what is called "hell," it is merely that which those of great wisdom in the world have spoken of.
Regarding what Your Majesty has said—
that there is no good physician in the world who can heal both body and mind—

there is now a great physician named Pūraṇa, who possesses all-knowing vision, has attained mastery in meditative concentration, and has ultimately cultivated pure brahmacarya; he constantly expounds for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings the path to unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
For the sake of his disciples, he taught the Dharma in this way:

"There is no black karma, nor is there retribution for black karma; there is no white karma, nor is there retribution for white karma; there is no karma that is both black and white, nor is there retribution for karma that is both black and white; there is no superior karma, nor is there inferior karma."
"That teacher is currently in the city of Rājagṛha; I only pray that Your Majesty will deign to visit him, so that this teacher may heal both my body and mind.
The king replied, "If he can truly extinguish my sins in such a manner, I shall take refuge in him."
Furthermore, there was another minister named Guṇagañja who went again to the king’s presence and spoke these words: “Great King!
Why is your countenance so haggard, your lips and mouth so parched, and your voice so faint, as if you were a timid man seeing a great enemy, your complexion so changed by distress?”
"What is it that causes you suffering?
Is it pain in the body,
or is it pain in the mind?"
The King replied:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?

I was deluded and blind, lacking the eye of wisdom; I drew near to evil companions and took them as friends, following the words of the wicked man Devadatta, and thus I have pointlessly committed the crime of rebellion against a righteous Dharma-king."
In the past, I heard a wise person recite this verse:
"If one conceives unwholesome thoughts toward one's parents, the Buddha, or his disciples,
and gives rise to evil karma, such a retribution shall be experienced in the Avīci Hell."
"Because of this matter, my heart is now terrified and great suffering has arisen within me; furthermore, there is no skilled physician to provide me with healing.
The minister spoke again:
"I only pray that Your Majesty will not yet grieve or fear."
There are two kinds of laws:
first, the law of renunciation; second, the law of kings.
As for the law of kings, it is said that if one kills his father, he shall rule the kingdom; although this is called parricide, in truth there is no sin.
Just as the kalala insect must destroy its mother’s womb before it can be born, such is the nature of birth; although it breaks the mother’s body, there is in truth no fault.
The same applies to cases such as a mule carrying a fetus.
According to the laws of governance, it ought to be thus: even if one kills one's father or elder brother, there is in fact no crime.
According to the Dharma of those who have left the household life, even killing a mosquito or an ant constitutes a transgression.
I only pray that Your Majesty will broaden your mind and not grieve. Why is this?
"If one constantly dwells in sorrow and suffering, that sorrow will only continue to increase."
"Just as a person who delights in sleep will find their slumber increasing,
so it is with those who lust after greed and indulge in wine.
As the King has said:"
Regarding the statement, "In this world there is no skilled physician to heal body and mind":

there is now a Great Master named Makkhali Gosāla, who possesses all-knowing insight; he regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were his own infants, has already transcended all afflictions, and is able to extract the sharp arrows of the three poisons from sentient beings.
All sentient beings lack knowledge, vision, and realization regarding all phenomena; only this one person alone possesses such knowledge, vision, and realization.
This Great Teacher constantly teaches his disciples the Dharma in this way:
"The bodies of all sentient beings consist of seven constituents."
What are these seven?
They are earth, water, fire, wind, suffering, pleasure, and life-span.
These seven phenomena are neither transformed nor created, and they cannot be destroyed or harmed.
Like the *īṣikā* grass, they abide as immovable as Mount Sumeru, neither abandoning nor creating anything.
Just like milk and curd, they do not contend with one another; whether it be suffering or pleasure, good or evil, even when struck by a sharp blade, they are not harmed.
Why is this? Because within the sevenfold emptiness there is no obstruction;
thus, life itself is not subject to harm.
Why is this? Because there is neither one who harms nor one who dies;
there is no agent and no recipient, no speaker and no listener, and no one who recollects nor anyone who instructs.
He constantly preaches this Dharma, which can cause sentient beings to extinguish all their immeasurable and grave offenses.
This teacher is currently in the great city of Rājagṛha; we only pray that Your Majesty will go to his place.
"If Your Majesty were to see him, all your sins would be extinguished.
At that time, the king replied,
"If it is truly possible to thus eliminate my sins, I shall take refuge in him."
Again, there was a minister named Śuddhilabdha who went before the king and spoke these verses:
“Great King, for what reason have you cast off your necklaces, with your hair disheveled and in such a state as this?”
"For what reason does Your Majesty’s body tremble and feel uneasy, like a flowering tree shaken by a fierce wind?
Why now is Your Majesty’s countenance so haggard with sorrow, like a farmer who, after sowing his seeds, finds that no rain falls from heaven, and thus suffers such grief?"
"Is this a pain in the heart,
or is it a pain in the body?
The king then replied:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?
My father, the former king, was filled with compassion and pity, regarding me with special concern; truly, I am without fault.
When I went to consult a physiognomist in the past, the physiognomist answered me:"
"This child, once born, will certainly harm his father.
Although he heard these words, he continued to look after and nourish him.
He had once heard a wise person say this:

"If a person commits incest with his mother or a bhikṣuṇī, steals the property of the Saṃgha, or kills one who has resolved upon supreme bodhicitta—just as these acts would harm his own father—such a person is certain to fall into the Avīci Hell."
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?
The minister spoke again:
"I only pray that Your Majesty will not grieve for now."
Just as with his father the king: for one who practices liberation, killing is a transgression;
but if it is according to the laws of governing the state, killing is without transgression.
Great King!
That which is non-dharma is called "non-existence";
that which is non-existence is called "non-existence.
It is, for example, like having no son, which is called "having no son."
It is also like a wicked son who is called "sonless"; although he is called sonless, in reality he is not sonless.
It is like food that lacks salt being called "saltless," or food that has very little salt also being called "saltless."
Just as a river that has no water is called "waterless," and one that has only a little water is also called "waterless"; so too,
that which perishes from moment to moment is said to be "impermanent."
Even though one may abide for an eon, it is still called impermanent.
Just as when a person undergoes suffering, it is called "absence of pleasure";
likewise, even if one experiences a small amount of pleasure, it is also called "absence of pleasure."
Just as that which lacks sovereignty is called "selfless" (anātman),
even that which possesses a slight degree of sovereignty is likewise called "selfless.
It is like how the time of a dark night is called "sunless."
"O Great King! Even when clouds and mist are present, one says there is no sun.
Although it is said that a small amount of dharma is called 'non-dharma,' in reality, it is not non-dharma."
I pray that Your Majesty will deign to listen to what your servant has to say:
all sentient beings possess residual karma, and by reason of this karmic condition, they repeatedly undergo birth and death.
If the late king possessed such residual karma, what crime would there be in Your Majesty’s execution of him?
I only pray that Your Majesty will broaden your mind and not grieve. Why is this?
"If one constantly dwells in sorrow and suffering, that sorrow will only increase further."
"Just as a person who delights in sleep will find that their sleep increases,
so it is with those who crave lust and indulge in wine.
"As the King has said:"
Regarding the statement, "In the world there is no good physician to cure the body and mind":

there is now a Great Master named Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, who possesses all-knowing vision; his wisdom is profound and deep like the great ocean, he has great majestic power and is endowed with great supernormal powers, and he is able to cause sentient beings to leave behind the net of all doubts.
All sentient beings do not know, see, or awaken to this; only this one person alone knows, sees, and awakens to it.
He currently resides nearby in the city of Rājagṛha, preaching such a Dharma to his disciples:
"Among all the multitudes, if one is a king, he may act as he pleases, whether performing good or evil deeds; though he commits many evils, he incurs no sin whatsoever."
Just as fire burns objects without distinction between the pure and the impure, so too is the king identical in nature to fire.
For example, the great earth universally supports both the clean and the foul; though it performs this task, it is from the beginning free from either anger or joy.
The king is likewise identical in nature to the earth.
For example, the nature of water is such that it washes away both the pure and the impure; though it performs this task, it feels neither sorrow nor joy.
The king is likewise identical in nature to water.
For example, the nature of the wind blows equally upon both the pure and the impure; although it performs these actions, it feels neither sorrow nor joy.
The King is likewise, sharing the same nature as the wind.
Just as a tree that has been stripped of its branches in autumn grows back again in spring, even though it was cut and lopped, there is truly no offense;
all sentient beings are likewise thus, dying here and being born again here.
Since they are reborn [from past causes], what crime could there possibly be?

The retributive fruits of suffering and happiness for all sentient beings do not arise from the karma of the present life at all; the cause lies in the past, while the fruit is experienced in the present.
There is no cause in the present, and thus there will be no fruit in the future.
Because of present results, sentient beings maintain the precepts and diligently cultivate vigor to ward off evil results in the present.
By maintaining the precepts, they attain the outflow-free (*anāsrava*);
by attaining the outflow-free, they exhaust the karma with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because karma is exhausted, all sufferings come to an end;
because all sufferings have ended, one attains liberation.
We only pray that Your Majesty will go quickly to his side and have him treat the physical and mental pains.
"If Your Majesty were to see him, all your sins would be eliminated.
The King then replied,
"If there truly is such a teacher capable of eliminating my sins, I shall take refuge in him."
Furthermore, there was another minister named Sarvajñārtha who went to where the king was and spoke these words:

"For what reason, O King, is your appearance no longer dignified? You are like one who has lost his kingdom, like a spring that has run dry, a pond without lotuses, a tree without flowers or leaves, or a monk who has broken his precepts and lacks spiritual majesty."
"Is it pain in the body,
or is it pain in the heart?
The king immediately replied:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?

My father, the former king, was compassionate and full of concern for me; yet I was unfilial and failed to repay his kindness. He constantly sought to bring peace and happiness to me, but I betrayed that kindness and instead cut off his joy."
"The former king was innocent, yet you have perversely raised your hand against him to commit this harm.
I have also heard wise ones say:
'If one harms one's father, one shall undergo great suffering and affliction for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.'"
"I shall soon surely fall into hell, and there is no skilled physician to cure my transgression.
The minister then said,
"I only pray that Your Majesty will abandon this grief and suffering."
Have you not heard, O King?
In the past there was a king named Rāma who, having slain his father, succeeded to the royal throne.

Likewise, Great King Bimbisāra, King Virūḍhaka, King Nahusa, King Kārtika, King Viśākha, King Candraprabha, King Sūryaprabha, King Priya, and King Bahudhānya—kings such as these all slew their fathers and succeeded to the royal throne, yet not a single one of them entered hell.

In the present time, there are kings such as Vairāṭya, Udrāyaṇa, Duḥṣanta, Mūṣika, and Puṣkara; all of these kings have killed their own fathers, yet not a single one among them has given rise to grief or affliction.
Although one speaks of the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the heavens, who is there to see them?
Great King! There are only two forms of existence: [the present life and the future life].
First is the human realm, and second is the animal realm.
Although these two exist, they are not born through causes and conditions, nor do they die through causes and conditions.
If there were no causes and conditions, how could there be good and evil?
I only pray that Your Majesty will not harbor sorrow or fear.
Why is this? "If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, sorrow will consequently increase."
"Just as when a person delights in sleep, their sleep increases;
so it is with lust and a craving for wine.
"As the King has said:"
Regarding the statement, "In this world there is no good physician to heal the body and mind":

there is now a Great Master named Ajita Keśakambala, who possesses all-encompassing knowledge and vision. He regards gold and earth as equal and non-dual; whether his right flank is cut with a blade or his left is anointed with sandalwood, his mind makes no distinction between these two. He views enemies and kin with equanimity, his mind free from any sign of difference.
This master is truly a skilled physician of the world; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he is constantly in samādhi, his mind never distracted.

He addressed his disciples, saying these words: "Whether one acts oneself or causes another to act; whether one cuts oneself or causes another to cut; whether one roasts oneself or causes another to roast; whether one harms oneself or causes another to harm; whether one steals oneself or causes another to steal; whether one commits adultery oneself or causes another to commit adultery; whether one speaks falsehoods oneself or causes another to speak falsehoods; whether one drinks alcohol oneself or causes another to drink alcohol; whether one kills a village, a city, or a nation; or whether one kills all sentient beings with a wheel of blades; or whether one gives alms to sentient beings south of the Ganges or kills sentient beings north of the Ganges—there is in all such cases neither sin nor merit, neither giving, nor precepts, nor meditative concentration."
"He is currently residing nearby in the city of Rājagṛha; I pray that Your Majesty will go there quickly.
If Your Majesty should see him, all your transgressions will be extinguished.
The King said:
“Minister! If you can truly eliminate my transgressions in this manner, I shall take refuge in you.
Furthermore, there was another minister named Śrīghoṣa, who went again to the king and spoke these words:
“O King, why is it that your face now lacks luster, like a lamp at midday, like the moon during the day, like a king who has lost his kingdom, or like a desolate and ruined land?”
"Great King!
Now that the four quarters are peaceful and free from all enemies, for what reason do you now suffer such grief and distress?
Is it suffering of the body?"
"Is it because of mental suffering?
There were princes who constantly gave rise to this thought:
'When shall I now attain sovereignty?'"
"O Great King!

Your wishes have now been fulfilled; you rule over the kingdom of Magadha as a sovereign and have obtained the entirety of the former king's treasury. You should simply take pleasure at heart and enjoy yourself as you wish; why harbor such sorrow and distress?"
The king replied immediately:
"How could I not be distressed now,
O Great Minister?"
It is like a foolish person who, craving only its flavor, fails to see the sharp blade;
or like one who eats food mixed with poison and fails to perceive its danger—
I am just like this.
Just as a deer sees grass but not the deep pit;
just as a mouse craves food but does not see the cat or the wildcat;
so too am I: seeing the pleasure of the present, I do not see the unwholesome fruits of suffering in the future.
I once heard these words from the Wise One:
"It would be better to receive three hundred lashes of the scourge for a single day than to give rise to a single thought of malice toward one's parents.
Now that I am close to the blazing fires of hell, how could I not be filled with sorrow and distress?
The minister spoke again:
"Who has come to deceive Your Majesty by saying that there is hell?
Who created these sharp-pointed thorns?"
The various colors of birds—who created them?

The nature of water is moistening, the nature of stone is hardness, the nature of wind is movement, and the nature of fire is heat; all myriad things die and are born of themselves—by whom were they made?
To speak of "hells" is merely the literary construction of the wise.
What meaning does the term "hell" possess?
Your servant shall explain it.
"Earth" (di) means ground;
"hell" (yu) means breaking.
Because there is no retribution for sin in the breaking of hell, it is called "earth-hell" (di-yu).
Furthermore, "earth" refers to humans,
and "prison" refers to the heavens.
Because he harmed his father, he has gone from the human realm to the heavenly realms.
For this reason, the seer Vāsava proclaimed:
"By killing sheep, one attains the bliss of humans and devas.
This is what is called hell.
Furthermore, "earth" (dī) means life;
"hell" (nara) means long.
Because one obtains a long lifespan through the taking of life, it is therefore called a hell (naraka).
"Great King!
Therefore, you should know that in reality there are no hells.
Great King!"

"Just as one who sows barley reaps barley and one who sows rice reaps rice, so too, one who kills a being in hell will again receive hell, and one who kills a human being should again receive a human [rebirth].
Great King!"
Now, please listen to what your servant has to say: in truth, there is no killing.
If there were a self, there would truly be no harm;
if there is no self, then likewise there is nothing that can be harmed.
Why is this? If there were a self, it would be permanent and immutable;
because it is eternally abiding, it cannot be killed, nor can it be broken or destroyed, nor bound or fettered, nor made to feel anger or joy, being just like space.
How could there be the transgression of killing?
If there were no self, all phenomena would be impermanent;
because they are impermanent, they perish and dissolve from moment to moment.
Because they perish moment by moment, both the killer and the victim perish moment by moment.
If they perish moment by moment, who would possess the offense?
Great King!
Just as fire burns wood, yet the fire is not guilty;
just as an axe chops down a tree, yet the axe is not guilty;
just as a sickle reaps grass, yet the sickle is truly not guilty.
Just as when a sword kills a person, the sword is truly not a person; since the sword is without fault, how can the person be at fault?
Just as when poison kills a person, the poison is truly not a person; since the poisonous drug is without fault, how can the person be at fault?
All things are likewise thus; in reality, there is no killing. How, then, could there be sin?
I only pray that Your Majesty will not give rise to sorrow and suffering. Why is this so?
"If one is constantly sorrowful and distressed, sorrow will eventually increase;
just as when a person delights in sleep, sleep becomes more and more abundant,
so too it is with lust and the craving for wine."
"As Your Majesty has said:

'There is no good physician in the world who can cure evil karma,' there is now a Great Master named Kālakauṭakātyāyana, who possesses all-knowing vision and clearly understands the three periods of time. In a single moment, he can perceive immeasurable and boundless worlds; his hearing is likewise so. He is able to cause sentient beings to remain far removed from faults and evils."
Just as the Ganges River purifies all transgressions, whether internal or external;
so too is this Great Teacher, who is able to eliminate the manifold sins of sentient beings, both internal and external.
He preached the Dharma to his disciples in this way:
"If a person kills all sentient beings with a mind devoid of shame and remorse, they will ultimately not fall into the evil realms, just as empty space does not receive dust or water.
One who possesses shame and remorse enters hell, just as great water moistens the earth."
All sentient beings are created by Īśvara; when Īśvara rejoices, sentient beings are at peace and happy;
when Īśvara is angry, sentient beings suffer and are distressed.
Whether all sentient beings commit sins or merit, it is the work of Maheśvara; how then can one say that humans possess sin or merit?
It is like a wooden automaton crafted by a craftsman, which can walk, stand, sit, and lie down, yet cannot speak;
sentient beings are just the same.
Īśvara is like a craftsman;
the wooden figure is like the body of a sentient being.
In such a process of creation, who could possibly be guilty?
"Such a Great Master now resides nearby in the city of Rājagṛha; I pray that you go there quickly.
If you see him, all your transgressions will be extinguished.
The King then replied:
"If there truly is such a person who can extinguish my sins, I shall take refuge in them.
Then another minister named Abhaya went to the king's presence and spoke these words:
"Great King!..."
In this world there are foolish people who, within a single day, experience a hundred joys and a hundred sorrows, a hundred sleeps and a hundred wakings, and a hundred alarms and a hundred weeps;
for a person of wisdom, such things do not exist.

"Great King! Why do you grieve so deeply? Are you like a traveler who has lost his companions; like one fallen into deep mud with no one to pull him out; like a person parched with thirst who cannot find water; like a lost man who has no guide; like a suffering patient who has no physician to treat him; or like a shipwrecked sailor at sea with no one to rescue him?"
"Great King!
Is it now your body that aches,
or is it your heart?"
The king replied:
"How could my body and mind not suffer pain now?
Having associated with evil friends and failing to guard my speech, I have recklessly committed the crime of rebellion against my innocent father, the former king."
"I now know for certain that I shall enter hell, and furthermore, there is no skilled physician to provide me with relief.
The minister then addressed him, saying:
"I only pray that Your Majesty will not give way to such sorrowful anguish."
Now, those of the Kṣatriya caste are known as the royal lineage.
Whether for the sake of the state, or for the sake of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, or to bring peace to the people, even if one commits acts of killing, there is no sin.
Although the former kings revered śramaṇas, they were unable to serve the brāhmaṇas with equal hearts;
because their minds lacked impartiality, they were not true kṣatriyas.
"Great King, since you have now slain the former king for the sake of making offerings to the brahmins, what crime could there be?
Great King!
In truth, there was no killing."
Now, as for "killing," it is the killing of life-force.
Life-force is termed *vāyu* (wind-energy).
Since the nature of wind-energy cannot be killed, how could there be sin in harming life-force?
I only pray that Your Majesty will no longer suffer in grief. Why is this?
"If one constantly suffers in grief, the grief will only increase further."
"Just as when a person delights in sleep, their sleep increases;
so it is with lust and a craving for wine.
As the King has said:"
Regarding the statement, "There is no skilled physician in the world who can provide a cure":

there is now a Great Master named Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, who possesses all-knowing vision; he has compassion for sentient beings and skillfully understands the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. He has mastered all things and employs appropriate expedient means; he cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas and practices the pure holy life in tranquil stillness.
He spoke these words to his disciples:
"There is no giving, there is no merit; there is no father and no mother; there is no present world and no future world; there are no arhats, no cultivation, and no path."

All sentient beings, after passing through eighty thousand kalpas within the wheel of birth and death, will naturally attain liberation; whether they have committed offenses or are without offense, it is exactly the same for all.
Just as the four great rivers—namely the Sindhu, the Gaṅgā, the Vakṣu, and the Sītā—all enter the great ocean without distinction, so too it is with all sentient beings:
at the time they attain liberation, there is no distinction whatsoever.
"This teacher is currently residing in Rājagṛha; I only pray that Your Majesty will go to him quickly.
If you are able to see him, all your transgressions will be eliminated.
The king then replied:
"If there truly is such a teacher who can eliminate my transgressions, I shall take refuge in him.
At that time, a great physician named Jīvaka went to the king’s presence and said,
"Great King!..."
"Are you able to sleep in peace?
The King replied with a verse:
"If one is able to forever sever All afflictions whatsoever,"
One who is not greedily stained by the three realms attains peaceful sleep;
If one attains Great Nirvana and expounds the most profound meaning,
Such a person is called a true Brahmin and attains peaceful sleep.
With no evil deeds in body, Free from the four faults of speech,
And with no web of doubt in the mind, One attains peaceful sleep;
With body and mind free from feverish distress, One dwells securely in a state of tranquility.
Having attained unsurpassed bliss, one can sleep in peace and security;
with a mind free from grasping and attachment, and having distanced oneself from all enemies,
always harmonious and without dispute, one can sleep in peace and security.
If one does not commit evil deeds, And the mind always harbors a sense of shame and remorse,
Believing that evil has its retribution, Then one may sleep in peace and security;
Honoring and supporting one’s parents, And not harming even a single living being—
Not stealing the wealth of others, one attains peaceful sleep;
Subduing all the sense faculties and drawing near to virtuous friends,
Destroying the hosts of the four Māras, one attains peaceful sleep.
Seeing neither auspiciousness nor inauspiciousness, nor suffering, pleasure, and the like,
one revolves through birth and death for the sake of all sentient beings;
if one can act in this way, then one shall attain peaceful sleep.
Who sleeps in peace? It is the Buddhas;
having deeply contemplated the samādhi of emptiness, their body and mind are tranquil and unmoving.
Who sleeps in peace?
That which is called compassion consists in constantly practicing heedfulness and regarding all beings as one's only child.
Sentient beings are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance;
they do not see the fruits of their afflictions, constantly create various evil karmas, and fail to obtain peaceful sleep.
If one commits the ten unwholesome deeds for the sake of one's own body or the bodies of others, one shall not find peaceful sleep;
if it is said that there is no fault in killing one's father for the sake of pleasure, [that too is not so].
Following such evil associates, one cannot sleep in peace;
if one eats beyond moderation or consumes cold drinks in excess,
one will suffer from illness and cannot sleep in peace.
Those who have offended the king, those who harbor illicit thoughts toward another’s wife,
and those who travel upon desolate paths cannot sleep in peace; likewise,
one whose fruit of keeping the precepts has not yet ripened, or a crown prince who has not yet succeeded to the throne.
"The thief who has not yet recovered his stolen goods cannot sleep in peace.
Jīvaka! My illness is now grave;

I have committed a wicked and rebellious offense against the King of the True Dharma, and no physician, nor excellent medicine, nor incantations, nor skillful arts, nor the care of attendants can cure it."
For what reason?
My father, the Dharma King, ruled the country according to the Dharma; he was truly without fault or guilt, yet I have perversely brought him harm.
Like a fish cast upon dry land, what joy could there possibly be?
Like a deer caught in a snare, it has no joy from the start;
like a person who knows his life will not last another day;
like a king who has lost his kingdom and fled to foreign lands.
It is like a person who hears that their illness is incurable;
it is like one who has broken the precepts hearing a description of their transgressions.
I have heard this said by the wise in the past:
"If the actions of body, speech, and mind are not pure, one should know that such a person will certainly fall into hell.
I am likewise in this state; how could I possibly obtain peaceful sleep?
"Now I have no unsurpassed Great Physician to expound the medicine of the Dharma and remove the suffering of my illness.
Jīvaka replied, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Although the King has committed a transgression, he has given rise to profound remorse and harbors a sense of shame and humility.
Great King!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always speak these words:"
“There are two white dharmas that can save sentient beings:
first, shame (hrī); second, remorse (apatrāpya).
As for shame, it is not committing offenses oneself.
*Hrī* (shame) is not teaching others to do [wrong];
*apatrāpya* (embarrassment) is feeling shame within oneself;
*apatrāpya* is disclosing one's faults to others.
Shame (*hrī*) is to feel bashful before others;
remorse (*apatrāpya*) is to feel bashful before the heavens.
This is called shame and remorse.
Those who lack shame and remorse are not called human beings; they are called animals.
Because they possess shame and remorse, they are able to revere their parents and teachers;
because they possess shame and remorse, it is said that there are parents, brothers, and sisters.
"Excellent, Great King!
You possess a sense of shame and remorse.
Listen, Great King; I have heard the Buddha say:
"There are two kinds of wise people:
first, those who do not commit various evils; second, those who repent after having committed them.
There are likewise two kinds of fools:"
"First is the commission of a transgression; second is its concealment.
Although one has previously committed evil, if one can later disclose it, repent with shame and remorse, and thereafter never dare to do it again.
It is just as when a bright pearl is placed in turbid water; by the power of the pearl, the water immediately becomes clear.
It is like the moon, which becomes bright and pure once the smoke and clouds have cleared away.
The same applies to one who commits evil but is able to repent.
If Your Majesty repents and harbors a sense of shame, your transgressions will be immediately extinguished, and you will become pure as before.
"Great King!
There are two kinds of wealth:
The first consists of elephants, horses, and various kinds of livestock; the second consists of gold, silver, and various precious jewels.
Although elephants and horses may be numerous, they do not equal the value of a single jewel.
"Great King!
Sentient beings are likewise: first, those who abound in evil; second, those who abound in goodness.
To commit many evils is not equal to performing even a single good deed."
Your servant has heard the Buddha say:
"Cultivating a single virtuous mind destroys a hundred kinds of evil.
Great King!

Just as a small amount of diamond can destroy Mount Sumeru, just as a small fire can burn everything, and just as a small amount of poison can harm sentient beings, so too is a small amount of goodness: it can shatter great evil.
Although it is called "slight goodness," in reality it is great. Why?
Because it destroys great evil.
"Great King!
As the Buddha has taught:
'He who conceals [his faults] has outflows; he who does not conceal them is without outflows.'"
By confessing and repenting, one does not incur outflows.
If one commits various offenses but does not conceal or hide them, because they are not concealed, the offenses become slight;
if one harbors shame and remorse, the offenses will be extinguished.
"Great King!
Just as drops of water, though minute, gradually fill a large vessel;
so too is the virtuous mind—each single virtuous thought can destroy great evil."
If one conceals their transgressions, the offenses will increase;
if one confesses them and feels shame, the offenses will be extinguished.
For this reason, the Buddhas have taught that those who possess wisdom do not conceal their offenses.
“Excellent, Great King!
You are able to believe in cause and effect, to believe in karma, and to believe in its retribution.
I only pray that Your Majesty will not harbor grief or fear.”

If there are sentient beings who commit various transgressions, yet conceal them without repentance, lacking a sense of shame or remorse, failing to perceive cause and effect as well as karmic retribution, unable to consult those of wisdom, and not drawing near to virtuous friends—such persons cannot be cured by any skilled physician, nor even by those who attend to the sick.
Just as world physicians fold their hands in helplessness before the disease of kāmalā,
so it is with those who conceal their transgressions.
Who are these transgressors?
This refers to the icchantika.

An icchantika does not believe in cause and effect, lacks a sense of shame and remorse, does not believe in karmic retribution, does not perceive the present or future lives, does not associate with virtuous friends, and does not follow the instructions and admonitions spoken by the Buddhas.
Such a person is called an icchantika, whom the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot cure.
Why is this? It is because they are like a corpse in the world, whom no physician can heal.
The icchantika is also like this; even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot cure them.
Your Majesty is not an icchantika now; why do you say that he cannot be healed?
"As Your Majesty has said that there is no one capable of treating him, Great King, you should know this:

the son of King Śuddhodana of Kapilavastu—of the Gautama clan and named Siddhārtha—has attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) spontaneously, without a teacher."
His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; he was fully endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, possessing all-knowing vision.
With great kindness and great compassion, he felt pity for all beings as if they were his own son Rāhula, following virtuous sentient beings like a calf follows its mother.

He speaks at the proper time and remains silent when it is not the right time; he speaks words that are true, pure, sublime, meaningful, in accordance with the Dharma, and consistent. These words enable sentient beings to forever leave behind all afflictions.
He thoroughly understands the faculties and mental natures of sentient beings, and there is no skillful means he does not master according to what is appropriate.
His wisdom is as lofty and great as Mount Sumeru, and as profound, vast, and far-reaching as the great ocean.
This Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses vajra-wisdom, which is able to shatter all the evil transgressions of sentient beings.
To say that he cannot do so is impossible.
Now, twelve yojanas from here, between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, he is expounding various dharmas for the sake of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas and the monastic community:
Whether existent or non-existent; whether conditioned or unconditioned; whether with outflows or without outflows;
whether the fruit of afflictions or the fruit of wholesome dharmas;
whether material phenomena, non-material phenomena, or phenomena that are neither material nor non-material; whether self or non-self, or neither self nor non-self—
It is not-self—whether permanent or impermanent, or neither impermanent nor permanent;
whether pleasant or unpleasant, or neither pleasant nor unpleasant; whether characterized or uncharacterized, or neither characterized nor uncharacterized;
whether subject to cessation or not subject to cessation, or neither subject to cessation nor not subject to cessation. Or...
Whether mundane or supramundane, neither mundane nor supramundane; whether a vehicle or not a vehicle, neither a vehicle nor not a vehicle;
whether self-performed and self-experienced, or self-performed and experienced by another, or without action and without experience.
"Great King!
If one hears from the Buddha that there is neither action nor reception, all grave offenses shall immediately be extinguished.
Your Majesty, listen now!"
When Śakra Devānām Indra was about to reach the end of his life, five signs appeared:

first, his garments became soiled and greasy; second, the flowers upon his head withered; third, his body emitted a foul odor; fourth, sweat broke out from beneath his arms; and fifth, he took no pleasure in his own seat.
At that time, when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was in a secluded place and saw either a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, he would go to them and conceive the perception of them as the Buddha.
Then, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, seeing Śakra approach, felt profound joy and spoke these words:
"O Lord of Devas!"
"I now take refuge in you.
Having heard this, Śakra realized he was not the Buddha.
He further thought to himself:
"If he were not a Buddha, he would not be able to cure me of these five signs of decline.
At that time, a minister named Pañcaśikha spoke to Śakra, saying: "Kauśika!..."
There is a Gandharva king named Dundubhi, who has a daughter named Subhadra.
If the King would grant this daughter to me, I shall show the King the signs for removing the marks of decay.
Śakra replied: "Good man!
Vemacitrin, the King of the Asuras, has a daughter named Śacī, whom I hold in high esteem."
"If you can truly show me a place where evil is extinguished, I would grant it to you; how much more so, then, to Subhadra? "Kauśika!
There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Śākyamuni, who is currently residing in the great city of Rājagṛha."
"If you can go there to inquire about and receive what you have not yet heard, the signs of your decline and disappearance will surely be extinguished. "Virtuous man!
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can truly extinguish them, you may then turn your carriage and proceed to his dwelling place."

The charioteer, having received his orders, immediately turned the carriage and arrived at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha. Reaching the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! [...]”
"Among gods and humans, what constitutes bondage? "Kauśika!
It is stinginess, greed, envy, and jealousy."
He asked again:
"From what do stinginess, greed, envy, and jealousy arise?
He replied:
"It arises because of ignorance.
He further asked:
"And from what does ignorance arise?"
He replied:
"It arises from negligence.
He spoke again:
"From what does negligence arise?
He replied:
"It arises from perversion."
He asked again:
"Furthermore, from what do these inversions arise?
He replied:
“It arises from doubt.
“World-Honored One!
That phenomena arising from inversion arise from doubt is indeed as the Noble Teaching declares.”
Why is this? Because I harbored doubts;
due to these doubts, I gave rise to perverted views, conceiving the notion of a World-Honored One where there was none.
Now that I behold the Buddha, the net of my doubts has been removed.
"Because the net of doubt is removed, perversions are also exhausted;
because perversions are exhausted, there is no mind of stinginess, nor even a mind of envy.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"You said that you have no mind of stinginess or envy; have you now attained the stage of Anāgāmin?
One who is an Anāgāmin is free from a greedy mind."
"If you have no mind of greed, why have you come to my place for the sake of life?
One such as an Anāgāmin truly does not seek life.
[The monk replied: "World-Honored One!"
Those who possess perversion seek their own lives; those free from perversion do not seek their own lives.
Now, I truly do not seek my life; what I seek is only the Buddha’s Dharma-body and the Buddha’s wisdom.
“Kauśika! If you seek the Buddha’s Dharma-body and the Buddha’s wisdom, you shall certainly attain them in a future age.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Śakra’s five signs of impending death immediately vanished.
He immediately rose, prostrated himself, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have now died and been reborn; I have lost my life and regained my life. Furthermore, I have heard the Buddha’s prediction that I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—is this not a second birth?"
"Is it to obtain further life?
World-Honored One!
How do all humans and devas increase their merit?"
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does their decline occur? "Kauśika!
Through the causes and conditions of strife, humans and devas decline; through the thorough cultivation of harmony and respect, they attain increase."
“World-Honored One!
If it is through strife and contention that we suffer loss and decline, from this day forward I shall no longer engage in battle with the asuras.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent,
Kauśika! The Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, have taught that the dharma of patience is the cause for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra immediately came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and then departed.
"Great King!
Because the Tathāgata is able to eliminate all evil marks, he is therefore called the inconceivable Buddha."
"If Your Majesty goes, all your grave sins shall surely be eradicated.
"Great King, listen:
there is a son of a Brahmin named Ahimsaka; because he has killed immeasurable sentient beings, he is called Aṅgulimāla."

Furthermore, when he again desired to harm his mother, as the evil thought arose, his body moved accordingly; this movement of both body and mind constitutes the cause of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), and because of these causes of the five heinous crimes, he will inevitably fall into hell.

When he later saw the Buddha, both his body and mind were stirred, and he again desired to cause harm; this movement of body and mind constitutes the cause for the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), and because of these causes for the five heinous crimes, he was destined to enter hell.
This person, having encountered the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, immediately extinguishes the causes and conditions for rebirth in hell and resolves to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, the Buddha is called the Unsurpassed Physician, not the six teachers.
"Great King! Furthermore, there was Prince Subhira; his father, out of anger toward him, cut off his hands and feet and pushed him into a deep well."
His mother, moved by compassion, had someone lead him out and took him to where the Buddha was.
As soon as he saw the Buddha, his hands and feet were restored, and he immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Great King!
Because one sees the Buddha, one obtains visible retribution in this very life.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Unsurpassed Physician, and not the Six Teachers."
“Great King!
Suppose there were five hundred hungry ghosts on the banks of the Ganges who, for immeasurable years, had never before seen water.
Although they reached the riverbank, they saw nothing but flowing fire; oppressed by hunger and thirst, they cried out in lamentation.”
At that time, the Tathāgata was sitting beneath a tree in the Udumbara grove on the bank of the river.
Then, various hungry ghosts came to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We are parched with hunger and thirst; our lives will not last much longer.
The Buddha said, "Why do you not drink the flowing waters of the Ganges?"
The ghost immediately replied,
"Where the Tathāgata sees water, I see fire.
The Buddha said:
"The clear waters of the Ganges truly have no fire.
It is because of evil karma that your mind has become inverted, leading you to perceive this as fire.
I shall eliminate your inversion for you and cause you to see the water."
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively explained the faults of stinginess and greed for the sake of the various hungry ghosts.
The hungry ghosts then said:
"We are currently parched with thirst; although we have heard these words of the Dharma, they do not enter our minds at all."
The Buddha said,
"If you are thirsty and exhausted, enter the river water first and drink as much as you desire.
By the power of the Buddha, these hungry ghosts were immediately able to drink the water.
Having drunk the water, the Tathāgata further preached various teachings for them.
Upon hearing the Dharma, they all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they cast off their forms as hungry ghosts and attained celestial bodies.
"Great King!
For this reason, the Buddha is called the unsurpassed physician, and not the six teachers.
Great King!"

"Good sons! Guard your body and speech well; do not commit further evil."

The bandits immediately heard the Tathāgata’s voice, which was subtle, wondrous, and clear; they instantly regained their sight and, with palms joined before the Buddha, prostrated to him and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now know that the Buddha’s compassionate heart universally covers all sentient beings, not only humans and devas.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately preached the Dharma for them.
Having heard the Dharma, they all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is truly the unsurpassed, excellent physician of the world, and not the six teachers.
“Great King!
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a caṇḍāla named Āśvāsaka who killed immeasurable people.
Upon seeing the Buddha’s disciple Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he immediately attained the conditions for the dissolution of his hellish karma and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”
Because there are such noble disciples, the Buddha-Tathāgata is praised as the unsurpassed physician, and not the six teachers.
"Great King!
In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was the son of an elder named Ajita, who committed incest with his mother; for this reason, he murdered his father."
His mother, moreover, committed adultery with another man; once the son learned of this, he killed her.
He had an Arhat who was his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); feeling shame before this spiritual friend as well, he then killed him too.
Having committed the murder, he went immediately to the Jetavana Monastery seeking to leave the household life.
At that time, the bhikṣus were fully aware that this man had committed three of the heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma), and none dared to grant him ordination.
Because he was not granted permission, his anger redoubled; that very night, he set a great and fierce fire to burn down the monastic quarters, killing many who were innocent.
Thereafter, he went again to the city of Rājagṛha, approached the Tathāgata, and sought with piteous entreaty to leave the household life.

The Tathāgata granted his consent and expounded for them the essentials of the Dharma, causing their grave offenses to gradually diminish and leading them to resolve upon attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Good Physician of the World, not the six teachers.
"Great King!
Your nature is inherently violent and wicked; you have placed your trust in the evil man Devadatta and released a drunken elephant, intending to have it trample the Buddha."
Upon seeing the Buddha, the elephant immediately attained awakening.
The Buddha then extended his hand and stroked the top of its head, further preaching the Dharma for it so that it fully gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Great King!
Even animals, upon seeing the Buddha, are able to destroy the karmic fruits of their animal existence; how much more so for humans?
Great King, you should know this:"
"If one sees the Buddha, all heavy sins shall surely be extinguished.
'Great King!

Before the World-Honored One had attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Māra arrived at the Bodhisattva’s dwelling with immeasurable and boundless retinues. At that time, the Bodhisattva, by the power of patience, destroyed Māra’s evil mind and caused Māra to receive the Dharma, whereupon Māra immediately gave rise to the aspiration for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
The Buddha possesses such great power of merit.
"Great King!

There was a wilderness spirit who frequently harmed sentient beings; at that time, the Tathāgata, for the sake of the elder Bhadra, went to the village of the wilderness and preached the Dharma for him."
At that time, the ghost of the desolate wilderness heard the Dharma and rejoiced; he immediately offered the elder to the Tathāgata and then gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Great King!
In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a butcher named Viśālakṣa who slaughtered countless sheep every day.
Upon seeing Śāriputra, he immediately received the eight precepts for the duration of one day and night.”
By these causes and conditions, at the end of his life, he was reborn as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North.
If even a disciple of the Tathāgata possesses such great fruits of merit, how much more so the Buddha himself?
"Great King!
In Northern India there is a city named Śilā, and in that city there was a king named Nāgamudrā, who, out of greed for his kingdom and high position, murdered his own father."

Having harmed his father, he felt remorse and regret in his heart; he immediately relinquished the administration of the kingdom and came to the Buddha’s presence, seeking refuge and requesting to leave the household life.
The Buddha said, "Welcome."
He immediately became a bhikṣu; his grave offenses were extinguished, and he resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Great King, you should know that the Buddha possesses such immeasurable and boundless fruits of great merit."
"Great King!
The Tathāgata has a younger brother named Devadatta, who has broken the Saṃgha, shed the blood of the Buddha, harmed the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, and thus committed three of the heinous crimes."
The Tathāgata expounds various essential teachings for them, causing their grave offenses to quickly become light and thin.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is a great and excellent physician, not the six masters.
“Great King!
If you can believe my words, I pray that you go quickly to where the Tathāgata dwells.
If you do not believe me, I pray that you reflect upon this well.”
“Great King!
The great compassion of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, universally covers all without being limited to a single person;
the True Dharma is vast and expansive, encompassing everything without exception.”

Regarding enemies and kin with equanimity, his mind is free from hatred and attachment; he never acts with partiality toward a single individual to cause them alone to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, while others do not likewise become Tathāgatas.
He is not merely the teacher of the fourfold assembly; he is universally the teacher of all devas, humans, nāgas, ghosts, those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth.
All sentient beings should likewise regard the Buddha with the thought that he is their father and mother.
Great King, you should know this:
the Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma solely for noble and wealthy persons such as King Bimbisāra, but also for those of lowly status such as Upāli.
He did not accept alms-food offered solely by the wealthy Sudatta or Anāthapiṇḍada, but also accepted food from the poor man Sudatta;
he did not preach the Dharma for those of sharp faculties such as Śāriputra alone, but also for those of dull faculties such as Cūḍapanthaka;
he did not permit only those of a non-greedy nature like Mahākāśyapa to leave home and seek the Way, but also permitted the great glutton Nanda to leave home.

Not only did you permit those with thin afflictions, such as Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and others, to leave the household life and seek the Way, but you also permitted even those with deeply rooted afflictions who had committed grave offenses, such as Udāyin, the younger brother of King Prasenajit, to leave the household life and seek the Way;

you did not merely accept offerings of kuśa grass out of respect, yet you uprooted the very root of his anger; you did not merely abandon Aṅgulimāla when he harbored the evil intent to kill, nor did you rescue him;
furthermore, you did not preach the Dharma solely for intelligent men, but also preached it for the utterly foolish, for those of combined wisdom, and for women.
Not only does he cause those who have left the household life to attain the fruits of the four paths, but he also causes those remaining in the household to attain the fruits of the three paths;

not only does he preach the essentials of the Dharma for those like Bhadrika who have abandoned all worldly affairs to contemplate in quietude, but he also preaches the essentials of the Dharma for those like King Bimbisāra who govern state affairs and manage royal duties;
not only does he teach those who have renounced alcohol, but he also teaches the householder Ugga, who was addicted to wine, and those who were intoxicated with excess.
It was not only for those who had entered meditative concentration, such as Vātsīputra and others, but also for the Brahmin woman Paścatā, whose mind was distracted by the loss of her son;
it was not only for my own disciples, but also for the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas;
and it was not only for those in the prime of youth at twenty-five years of age, but also for the elderly at eighty years of age.
He did not teach solely for those whose faculties were mature, but also for those whose roots of goodness were not yet mature;
he did not speak solely for Queen Mallikā, but also for the courtesan Utpalavarṇā;
he did not accept only the exquisite delicacies offered by King Prasenajit, but also the food mixed with poison offered by the householder Śrigupta.

"Great King, you should know that in the past Śrīgupta also committed the causes for a heinous crime; however, upon encountering the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Great King!

Even if one were to constantly provide clothing and food to all sentient beings with reverence for an entire month, it would not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit obtained by someone who recollects the Buddha in a single thought-moment."
"Great King!

Even if one were to fashion a person out of gold and provide it with a hundred chariots and horses laden with jewels as an act of giving, it would not equal the merit of someone who resolves their mind upon the Buddha and takes a single step toward him."
"Great King!

Even if one were to take a hundred chariots drawn by elephants, laden with various kinds of rare treasures from the Great Qin country, as well as a hundred women adorned with necklaces of jewels, and offer them all in alms, it would still not equal taking a single step toward the Buddha after having resolved the mind [upon enlightenment]."

Setting this matter aside, even if one were to provide the four requisites of support to all sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm, it would still not equal taking a single step toward the Buddha after having resolved to attain enlightenment.

Setting this matter aside, even if the Great King were to provide offerings and pay homage to immeasurable sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, it would not equal going once to the twin śāla trees to the place where the Tathāgata resides and listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
At that time, the Great King replied: "Jīvaka!
Since the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is by nature already disciplined and gentle, he has therefore obtained those who are disciplined and gentle as his retinue."
Just as a sandalwood forest is surrounded solely by sandalwood trees,
the Tathāgata is pure, and all his retinue is likewise pure.
Just as a great dragon has only other dragons as its followers;
The Tathāgata is tranquil, and his retinue is likewise tranquil;
the Tathāgata is free from greed, and his retinue is likewise free from greed;
the Buddha is free from afflictions, and his retinue is likewise free from afflictions.
Since I am now an utterly evil person, shrouded by evil karma, my body foul and impure, and bound for hell, how could I possibly reach the presence of the Tathāgata?
"If I were to go there, I fear they would not deign to receive me or engage in conversation with me.
Although you have exhorted me to go to the Buddha's dwelling, today I feel deep self-contempt and remorse, and I have no desire at all to go."
At that time, a voice suddenly issued from the void, saying: "The unsurpassed Buddha-dharma is about to decline and perish;

the profound river of Dharma is about to dry up; the great lamp of Dharma is about to go out. Before long, the mountain of Dharma will crumble, the ship of Dharma will sink, the bridge of Dharma will break, the palace of Dharma will collapse, the banner of Dharma will fall, and the tree of Dharma will snap. Good friends will depart; great terror is imminent; before long, beings who are famished for the Dharma will arrive, and the pestilence of afflictions will begin to spread."

"The time of great darkness has arrived; the time for thirsting after the Dharma has come. The Māra King rejoices and casts off his armor, for the Buddha-sun is about to set behind the mountain of Great Parinirvāṇa.
O Great King!"
"If the Buddha were to pass away, there would be no one left to remedy the king's grave transgressions.
Great King!
You have now already created the most grievous karma for the Avīci Hell; by virtue of these karmic conditions, you will certainly undergo its retribution without doubt."
"Great King!
'A' means non-existence;
'na' is called an interval."
Because there is not even a moment’s respite, it is called "Uninterrupted" (Avīci).
"Great King!

Suppose a single person were to fall alone into this hell; his body would grow to eighty thousand yojanas in height, filling its entirety so that no empty space remains between them, and his entire body would undergo various kinds of suffering on all sides."
Even if there are many people, their bodies fill the space entirely without obstructing one another.
Great King!
Within the cold hells, they find temporary pleasure upon encountering a warm breeze.
In the hot hells, even a brief encounter with a cold breeze is called "happiness.
There are hells where, even after one's life has ended, if one hears the sound of "revive," one immediately returns to life.
"In the Avīci Hell, none of these things exist.
'Great King!

The Avīci Hell has gates on its four sides; outside each gate there is fierce fire, which flows and penetrates from east, west, south, and north. It is surrounded by iron walls eighty thousand *yojanas* in circumference, covered above by iron nets; the ground is also iron, with the fire from above penetrating below and the fire from below penetrating above.'"
"Great King!
If a fish is on a griddle, its fat and marrow sizzle and burn;
the sinners within this [hell] are just like that."
"Great King!
One who commits a single heinous offense shall undergo the full retribution of such a crime;
if one commits two heinous offenses, the retribution shall be doubled."
"One who has committed all five heinous crimes shall have their retribution multiplied fivefold.
Great King!

I now know with certainty that Your Majesty’s evil karma cannot be avoided; I only pray that Your Majesty will go quickly to where the Buddha is, for none other than the World-Honored Buddha can save you."
"I now pity you and therefore exhort you.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King was filled with fear and trepidation; his entire body trembled, and his five limbs shook like a plantain tree.
Looking up, he replied, "Who are you?"
“Without manifesting a physical form, there was only a voice.
‘Great King! I am your father, Bimbisāra.’”
"You should now follow what Jīvaka has said; do not follow the words of the six ministers with their heterodox views.
When the king heard this, he fainted and fell to the ground.

His bodily sores worsened, and their foul stench became twice as intense as before. Although he applied cooling medicines to treat them, the steaming heat of the poison in the sores only increased and did nothing to diminish.

The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Eighteen.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Fifth Chapter on the Holy Life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing King Ajātaśatru lying prostrate on the ground in a state of fainting between the twin trees, addressed the great assembly:
"I shall now remain in this world for the sake of this king until immeasurable kalpas have passed, and shall not enter parinirvāṇa."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Tathāgata should not enter nirvāṇa for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, why do you specifically act for the sake of King Ajātaśatru?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Within this great assembly, there is not a single person who says that I have definitively entered parinirvāṇa."
King Ajātaśatru, certain that I shall ultimately and forever perish, has therefore fainted and cast himself upon the ground.
"Good son! As I have said: "
"It is for Ajātaśatru that he does not enter nirvāṇa.
You have not yet been able to understand such a hidden meaning. Why is this?
