When I say "those who act," I refer to all ordinary worldlings;
when I say "Ajātaśatru," I mean it applies universally to all who have committed the five heinous crimes.
Furthermore, "those who act" refers to all sentient beings within the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
I shall never remain in the world for the sake of unconditioned sentient beings.
Why is this? That which is unconditioned is not a sentient being.
Ajātaśatru is one who is fully possessed of afflictions and the like.
Furthermore, "those who act" refers to sentient beings who do not see the Buddha-nature;
if they were to see the Buddha-nature, I would certainly not remain in this world for long.
Why is this? Those who see the Buddha-nature are not ordinary sentient beings.
Ajātaśatru is, in fact, representative of all those who have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, "those who act" refers to the two assemblies of Ānanda and Kāśyapa.
"Ajātaśatru" refers to the queens and concubines of King Ajātaśatru’s inner palace, as well as all the women of the city of Rājagṛha.
Furthermore, "Wei" (為) is named Buddha-nature;
"Asha" (阿闍) is named non-arising;
and "Shi" (世) is named enemy.
Because the Buddha-nature does not arise, the enemy of afflictions arises;
because the enemy of afflictions arises, one does not see the Buddha-nature.
Because afflictions do not arise, one sees the Buddha-nature.
Because one has seen the Buddha-nature, one attains abiding in Great Parinirvāṇa; this is called "non-arising.
For this reason, he is named Ajātaśatru.
Good son! "A" (a-ja) means non-arising;
non-arising is called nirvāṇa.
"World" refers to worldly dharmas;
"unsoiled" means not being defiled by them.
Because one is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, one does not enter nirvana for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons.
For this reason, I say that for Ajātaśatru, there will be no entry into nirvāṇa for immeasurable billions of kalpas. "Good son!

The secret speech of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; the Buddha-dharma and the Saṃgha are also inconceivable; the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also inconceivable; and the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra is also inconceivable."
At that time, the World-Honored One—the Greatly Compassionate Guide—entered the Moon-Love Samādhi for the sake of King Ajātaśatru.
Having entered this samādhi, he emitted a great radiance.
That light was cool and refreshing; as it shone upon the king’s body, the sores were immediately healed and the burning heat was extinguished.
When the king awoke, his sores had vanished and his body felt cool. He spoke to Jīvaka, saying:
"I have heard people say:"
"When the kalpa is about to end, three moons appear simultaneously.
At that time, the suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings will be entirely eliminated.
Since that time has not yet arrived, from where does this light come to shine upon and touch my body, so that the pain of my sores is healed and my body attains peace and happiness?
Jīvaka replied:
"This is not the simultaneous illumination of the three moons at the end of a kalpa, nor is it the light of fire, the sun, the stars, medicinal herbs, precious gems, or celestial radiance."
The king asked again:
"If this light is neither from three moons shining together nor from the brilliance of a precious gem, whose light is it?
"Great King, you should know: [it is the light of the Bodhisattva]."
This is the radiance emitted by the God among Gods.

This light has no root and no limit; it is neither hot nor cold, neither permanent nor subject to extinction, neither form nor formless, neither with marks nor markless, and neither blue, nor yellow, nor red, nor white.
In order to deliver sentient beings, he causes them to see that there are marks, that there are roots which can be described, and that there is heat, cold, blue, yellow, red, and white.
"Great King!
Although this light is thus, it is truly ineffable and invisible; it possesses not even the colors blue, yellow, red, or white."
The king said,
"Jīvaka! For what cause and condition has that God among Gods emitted this radiance?"
Jīva replied, "This auspicious sign portends for the Great King.
For the King previously said:"
"In this world, there is no skilled physician to treat both body and mind.
Therefore, he emitted this light to first treat the King's body, and subsequently his mind.
The King said:
“Jīvaka! Does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, also hold me in his thoughts?
Jīvaka replied:

"It is, for example, like a man who has seven sons; among these seven sons, if one son falls ill, although the parents' hearts are not unequal toward them, their heart is nevertheless more focused on the sick son."
"Great King!
The Tathāgata is likewise; he is not unequal toward all sentient beings, yet his mind inclines with particular gravity toward those who have committed offenses.
Toward those who are heedless, the Buddha directs his compassionate mindfulness."
Those who are heedless have minds that are abandoned.
Who are called those who are heedful?
They are the bodhisattvas dwelling in the six stages.
"Great King!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not regard the lineage, age—whether old, young, or middle-aged—wealth, poverty, season, day, month, or constellations, nor skillful arts, low status, or whether one is a servant or a slave; they regard only those sentient beings who possess a virtuous mind."
If one possesses a virtuous mind, one will then conceive thoughts of loving-kindness.
Great King, you should know that such auspicious signs are the radiance emitted by the Tathāgata when entering the Moon-Love Samādhi (Candrakānta-samādhi).
The king then asked,
"What is called the Moon-Love Samādhi?
Jīvaka replied:

"Just as the light of the moon can cause all utpala flowers to bloom with vibrant clarity, so too is the Moon-Love Samādhi (Candrakānta-samādhi): it can cause the virtuous minds of sentient beings to blossom."
For this reason, it is called the Moon-Love Samādhi.
"Great King!
It is like moonlight, which can cause the hearts of all people traveling on the road to give rise to joy."
The Moon-Love Samādhi is likewise; it causes those who cultivate the path to nirvāṇa to give rise to joy in their hearts.
For this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi.
“Great King!
It is like the light of the moon, which from the first day until the fifteenth day, gradually increases in form, color, and radiance.
The Moon-Love Samādhi is also like this: it causes all roots of goodness of those who have first resolved their minds to gradually increase, until they are fully endowed with Great Parinirvāṇa.”
For this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi.
"Great King!
It is like the moonlight from the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day, when its form, color, and radiance gradually diminish."
The Moon-Love Samādhi is likewise; wherever its light shines, all afflictions are gradually diminished.
For this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi.
"Great King!
It is like the time of intense heat, when all sentient beings constantly long for the moonlight;
once the moonlight shines upon them, the stifling heat is immediately dispelled."
The Moon-Love Samādhi is likewise; it enables sentient beings to eliminate the burning heat of greed and affliction.
"Great King!
It is like the full moon, the king among the stars, which is the flavor of ambrosia and is cherished by all sentient beings."
The Moon-Love Samādhi is likewise so: it is the king among all virtues, the flavor of ambrosia, and that which all sentient beings cherish and delight in.
For this reason, it is further named the Moon-Love Samādhi.
The King said to Jīvaka:
"I have heard that the Tathāgata does not dwell, sit, rise, or converse with evil persons.

He is like the great ocean, which does not harbor a corpse; like the ruddy sheldrake, which does not dwell in a latrine; like Śakra Devendra, who does not reside with ghosts; or like the jīvaṃjīvaka bird, which does not perch on a withered tree—the Tathāgata is likewise."
"How shall I go to see him?
If I were to see him, would my body not sink into the earth?
In my view, it would be better for me to approach a drunken elephant, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, or a blazing, fierce fire than to ever approach one who commits grave evils."
"Therefore, having reflected upon this, with what state of mind should I go to see the Tathāgata?
Jīvaka replied, "Great King!"

Just as a thirsty person hastens toward a clear spring, a hungry person seeks food, a frightened person seeks rescue, a sick person seeks a skilled physician, one seeking relief from heat seeks cool shade, and one suffering from cold seeks fire, so too should Your Majesty now seek the Buddha.
"Great King!

The Tathāgata still expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma even for those such as the icchantikas; how much more so, then, should you, Great King—who are not an icchantika—not receive his compassionate salvation?"
The king said:
"Jīvaka! In the past, I have heard this:"
"An icchantika does not believe, does not hear, cannot investigate, and does not attain the meaning and principle.
For what reason, then, does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma for them?
Jīva replied: “Great King!

It is as if there were a man who had contracted a grave illness; in a dream during the night, this man ascended a hall with a single pillar, consumed clarified butter and oil and smeared them upon his body, lay upon ashes, ate ashes, and climbed up a withered tree.”

Sometimes they wander, sit, or lie down with monkeys; they sink into water or mud, and fall from towers, palaces, high mountains, trees, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; they wear garments of blue, yellow, red, and black, and delight in laughing, singing, and dancing.
Or they may see crows, vultures, foxes, and other such creatures; their teeth and hair have fallen out, they are naked, and they lie with dogs as pillows amidst filth and excrement.
Furthermore, they walk, stay, sit, and rise together with the deceased, hand-in-hand eating and chewing, as venomous snakes fill the path along which they pass.
Or again, one may dream of embracing a woman with disheveled hair, wearing tārā-leaf garments, and riding a dilapidated donkey cart as she travels due south.
After this person has awakened from the dream, sorrow and affliction arise in their mind.
Because of this sorrow and affliction, their physical illness increases further.
As the illness intensifies, their family and relatives send a messenger to summon a physician.

The messenger he dispatched was one whose body was deformed and deficient in its faculties; his head was covered in dust and soil, he wore tattered and ruined clothes, and he drove an old, dilapidated carriage. He spoke to that physician, saying:
"Quickly mount the carriage!"
At that time, the skilled physician reflected to himself:
"Now, observing the appearance of this messenger, it is not auspicious; one should know that the patient will be difficult to treat."
He further thought:
"Even though the messenger is inauspicious, I must still examine the day to see if the treatment can proceed.
If it is the fourth, sixth, eighth, twelfth, or fourteenth day—on such days as these, the illness will also be difficult to cure."
He further thought: "Although the day is inauspicious, I must consult the stars to see if it can be treated.
If it is the time of Mars, Venus, the Pleiades (Kṛttikā), the planet Yama, the planet Śeṣa, or the full moon star—under such stellar conditions, the illness will also be difficult to cure."
He further thought: "Although the stars are inauspicious, one must also observe the time.
If it be autumn or winter, or the time when the sun sets, midnight, or the time when the moon sets, one should know that this illness will also be difficult to cure."
He further thought:
"Although these various signs are inauspicious, they may be certain or uncertain; I must observe the patient.
If he possesses merit and virtue, he can still be healed."
"If one lacks merit, what benefit is there even if it is auspicious?
Having reflected thus, he immediately set out with the messenger; while on the road, he thought again:
"If that patient possesses the signs of longevity, they can be treated; if they possess the signs of a short life, they cannot be cured."

Then, on the road ahead, he saw two young children pulling each other in a quarrel, seizing one another by the head and tearing out their hair, striking and beating each other with tiles, stones, knives, and staves.
When they saw someone holding fire, it was naturally extinguished.
Or they may see someone cutting down trees;
or again, they may see a person dragging a hide along the road;
or they may see objects left behind on the path.
Or they see someone holding an empty vessel;
or they see a śramaṇa walking alone without a companion;
and they further see tigers, wolves, crows, vultures, and wild foxes.
Having seen these things, he further thought:
"The messengers sent out and all the omens encountered along the way are entirely inauspicious; one should know that this patient will certainly be difficult to treat."
He further thought to himself:
"If I do not go, I shall not be a worthy teacher; yet if I do go, he cannot be cured."
He further thought to himself:
"Although these various omens are indeed inauspicious, I shall set them aside for now and proceed to the place where the patient lies.

Having reflected thus, he again heard such sounds along the way—namely, words concerning loss, death, collapse, ruin, fracture, stripping away, falling, burning, and non-arrival; [words signifying] that it cannot be cured and cannot be rescued.
Furthermore, he heard the sounds of birds from the south, namely the cries of crows, vultures, and śāri birds, as well as those of dogs, rats, wild foxes, pigs, and rabbits.
Having heard these sounds, he further thought: "One should know that this patient is difficult to cure.

Thereupon, he entered the patient's residence and saw that the patient suffered from frequent chills and fevers, with aching bones and joints; his eyes were red and watering, and external noises were ringing in his ears. His throat was constricted and painful, and his tongue was cracked and split, its color pitch black. He could not support his own head; his body was withered and lacked perspiration; his excrement and urine were obstructed and did not pass. His body had suddenly become swollen and unusually reddish; his voice was uneven, sometimes coarse and sometimes thin; his entire body was mottled with spots of various colors, such as blue and yellow; his abdomen was distended and full, and he could not speak clearly.
Having seen this, the physician asked the attendant:
"What was the patient's state of mind since yesterday?
The attendant replied:
"O Great Master!
This person originally revered and had faith in the Triple Gem and the various devas, yet now that disposition has changed and his devotion has ceased.
Originally he delighted in giving alms, but now he is stingy."
By nature he ate little, but now he eats excessively.
By nature he was coarse and wicked, but now he is gentle and kind.
By nature he was compassionate and filial, honoring his parents; now he has no heart of respect for his parents.

Having heard this, the physician immediately stepped forward and smelled it; he detected the scents of blue lotus, aloeswood incense, *piṅgala* incense, *tagara* incense, *tamālapatra* incense, saffron, and sandalwood, as well as the stench of roasted meat, the stench of grape wine, the stench of burned tendons and bones, the stench of fish, and the stench of excrement.

Having discerned the fragrance and the stench, he then proceeds to touch the body; he perceives the body as fine and soft, like silk, cotton, or *karpāsa* flowers, or it may feel hard like stone, cold like ice, hot like fire, or rough like sand.

At that time, having observed such various signs as these, the skilled physician knows for certain that the patient will surely die without doubt; yet he does not definitively state, "This person shall die."
He said to the sick man:
"I have urgent business now and shall come again tomorrow.
Regarding whatever you require, let yourself be as you wish; do not restrain yourself."
He then returned home.
The next day, when the messenger arrived, he spoke to him again, saying:
"My business is not yet finished, and furthermore, I have not yet prepared the medicine."
"A wise person should know that such a patient will certainly die without a doubt.
Great King!
The World-Honored One is likewise; he thoroughly understands the faculties and natures of those who are icchantikas and preaches the Dharma for them accordingly."
Why is this? If it were not explained, all ordinary people would say:
"The Tathāgata lacks great compassion."
"One who possesses compassion is called an Omniscient One;
if one lacks compassion, how can they be called an Omniscient One?
For this reason, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma for the sake of icchantikas."
"Great King!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, constantly bestows the medicine of the Dharma upon all who are ill.
If the sick do not take it, it is not the fault of the Tathāgata."
“Great King!
There are two categories of icchantikas:
first, those who have acquired roots of goodness in the present life; second, those who will acquire roots of goodness in future lives.”
The Tathāgata, knowing well those icchantikas who are able to attain roots of goodness in the present, preaches the Dharma for them;
he also preaches the Dharma for those who will attain it in future lives, even if there is no benefit now, so that it may serve as a cause for future lives.
For this reason, the Tathāgata expounds the essentials of the Dharma for icchantikas.
There are two kinds of icchantikas:
first, those with sharp faculties; second, those with middling faculties.
Those of sharp faculties can attain roots of goodness in the present life, while those of middling faculties will attain them in a future life.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not preach the Dharma in vain.
"Great King!
It is like a pure person who has fallen into a latrine; a good friend sees him and takes pity on him, immediately going forward to seize him by the hair and pull him out."

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise in this regard: seeing sentient beings fallen into the three evil realms, they employ skillful means to rescue and deliver them so that they may attain liberation.
For this reason, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma even for those who are icchantikas.
The King said to Jīvaka,
“If it is indeed as you say regarding the Tathāgata, then tomorrow I shall select an auspicious day and favorable stars before proceeding.”
Jīva addressed the king: "Great King!
Within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is no selection of auspicious days or favorable stars."
"Great King!
Just as a person with a grave illness does not wait for the sun's position or the auspiciousness of the season, but seeks only a skilled physician;
so too, Your Majesty, being now gravely ill, you should seek the Buddha, the skilled physician, without selecting for an auspicious time or a favorable day."
"Great King!
Just as the fire of sandalwood and the fire of *kāraṇja* wood both possess the characteristic of burning and are no different from one another, so it is with auspicious days and inauspicious days;
if one reaches the presence of the Buddha, one shall extinguish all transgressions in either case."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will go there quickly today.
At that time, the Great King immediately summoned a minister named Śrī and addressed him, saying:
"Great Minister, you should know:
"I now wish to go to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and quickly prepare the necessary requisites for making offerings.
The minister said,
"Great King!"
"Excellent, excellent!
All the requisites you require are here.
King Ajātaśatru, together with his consort, prepared twelve thousand chariots and carriages.

There were fifty thousand magnificent and powerful elephants; upon each elephant rode three men, carrying banners, canopies, flowers, incense, music, and all manner of ritual implements, none of which was lacking.
The escort of horsemen numbered one hundred and eighty thousand, and the people of the kingdom of Magadha who followed the king reached a total of five hundred and eighty thousand.
At that time, the entire great assembly in the city of Kuśinagara—filling twelve yojanas—all saw from afar King Ajātaśatru approaching along the road with his retinue.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"For all sentient beings who seek the proximate causes and conditions for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, none is more primary than a virtuous friend."
Why is this? If King Ajātaśatru had not followed Jīvaka’s words, he would certainly have met his end on the seventh day of the coming month and fallen into the Avīci Hell.
"Therefore, as for proximate causes, none is equal to a virtuous friend.
King Ajātaśatru further heard on the road ahead that King Virūḍhaka of Śrāvastī had boarded a ship to go out to sea, met with fire, and died;
and that the bhikṣu Kokālika had entered the earth alive and reached the Avīci Hell.
Sunakṣatra had committed various evils, yet upon arriving at the presence of the Buddha, his many sins were extinguished.
Having heard these words, he said to Jīvaka:
"Although I have now heard these two accounts, I am still not yet certain."
"Come, Jīvaka! I wish to ride upon the same elephant as you.
Should I fall into the Avīci Hell, I hope that you will hold me fast so that I do not fall."
"Why is this? For I have heard in the past that those who have attained the Way do not enter hell.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
“King Ajātaśatru still harbors doubts; I shall now act to bring him to a state of certainty.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Sarvadhara who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously taught:
"All dharmas are devoid of fixed characteristics; that is to say, form has no fixed characteristic, and so on, up to nirvāṇa, which also has no fixed characteristic."
"How is it that the Tathāgata now says he has brought about a mind of certainty for Ajātaśatru?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent."
"Good son!
I shall now certainly bring about a resolute mind for King Ajātaśatru. Why is this?
If the King’s doubting mind can be destroyed, one should know that all phenomena have no fixed characteristics.
Therefore, although I have brought about a state of certainty for King Ajātaśatru, you should know that this mind itself is without certainty.
"Good son!
If that king’s mind were fixed, how could the king’s crime of rebellion be destroyed?
Because it lacks a fixed characteristic, his crime can be destroyed."
"Therefore, I have brought King Ajātaśatru to a state of certainty.

At that time, the Great King went directly to the twin śāla trees between which the Buddha was staying; arriving at the place where the Buddha was, he gazed up at the Tathāgata’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, which were like a mountain of exquisite, pure gold.
At that time, the World-Honored One uttered the eightfold voice and addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
Then Ajātaśatru looked around to his left and right.
“Who among this great assembly is the Great King?
Since I am a transgressor and possess no merit, the Tathāgata should not address me as the Great King.
At that time, the Tathāgata again called out to him, saying:
“Great King Ajātaśatru!
When the king heard this, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately spoke these words:
“The Tathāgata’s address to me today is truly proof that the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings with great compassion and pity, treating them all equally without distinction.”
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My doubts are now forever eliminated without remainder; I know with certainty that the Tathāgata is truly the unsurpassed Great Teacher of all sentient beings.”
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said to Sarvārthadhārin Bodhisattva:
"The Tathāgata has already brought King Ajātaśatru to a state of certainty."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Even if I were now to share a seat, rise, sit, eat, or drink with Brahmā or Śakra Devendra, I would still find no joy therein.”
“I am deeply moved by joy and celebration to have encountered the Tathāgata’s single word of final instruction.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru immediately offered the banners, canopies, incense, flowers, and musical instruments he held, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Having finished paying his respects, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying:
"Great King!"
I shall now explain for you the essential points of the True Dharma; you should listen with single-minded attention, listen closely.
An ordinary person should constantly bind their mind to the contemplation of the body through twenty matters:
first, that this body of mine is empty and devoid of the outflow-free (anāsrava) state.
Second, one lacks the roots of all wholesome dharmas;
third, this transmigratory existence of mine has not yet been tamed and brought under control;
fourth, having fallen into a deep pit, there is no place where one does not fear.
5. By what skillful means can one perceive the Buddha-nature?
6. How does one cultivate meditative concentration to perceive the Buddha-nature?
7. Birth and death are constantly characterized by suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity; [how can they be transformed into permanence, self, and purity?]
Eighth, it is difficult to be far removed from the hardships of the eight inopportune states;
ninth, one is constantly pursued by enemies;
tenth, there is not a single dharma capable of obstructing the various realms of existence.
Eleventh, they have not yet attained liberation from the three evil realms;
twelfth, they are possessed of various kinds of evil and heterodox views;
thirteenth, they have also not yet established a ferry for crossing the ford of the five heinous crimes.
14. Birth and death are boundless; one has not yet reached their limit.
15. Without performing various karmas, one does not obtain their retributive fruits.
16. There is no case where what is done by oneself is experienced as a fruit by another.
17. Without creating the causes for happiness, there will ultimately be no fruit of happiness;
18. If one performs an action, its fruit will never be lost;
19. Birth arises from ignorance, and through that same cause, one dies.
"Twenty: One constantly practices heedlessness regarding the past, future, and present.
'Great King!
An ordinary person should always perform these twenty kinds of contemplations upon this body.'"
Having performed this contemplation, one no longer delights in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);
not delighting in birth-and-death, one then attains *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
At that time, one sequentially contemplates the characteristics of the mind’s arising, its abiding, and its ceasing.
One sequentially contemplates the characteristics of the mind’s arising, abiding, and ceasing; concentration, wisdom, diligence, and precepts are likewise so.

Having contemplated arising, abiding, and ceasing, one understands the characteristics of the mind up to the characteristics of the precepts, ultimately refraining from evil and being free from the fear of death and the fear of the three evil realms.
"If one does not focus the mind to observe these twenty matters, the mind will become negligent, and there is no evil that will not be committed.
Ajātaśatru said, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, from the past until now, I have never observed these twenty matters; therefore, I have committed many evils."
Because I have committed manifold evils, I am subject to the fear of death and the fear of the three evil realms.
World-Honored One!
I have brought calamity upon myself by committing such grave wickedness; my father, the King, was innocent, yet I have wantonly inflicted a rebellious harm upon him.
"Regarding these twenty matters, whether one contemplates them or not, one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"The nature and characteristics of all dharmas are impermanent and lack any fixed certainty; why, O King, do you say that one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell?"
King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas lack fixed characteristics, then my guilt for killing should likewise be unfixed.”
"If killing were determinate, then all dharmas would not be indeterminate.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
Excellent, excellent!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught that all phenomena are entirely devoid of fixed characteristics; you, O King, are further able to understand that even killing is not fixed.
Therefore, you should know this:
Killing has no fixed characteristic.
"Great King! As you have said:
Regarding the statement, "The father-king was innocent,
yet I have perversely harmed him," who is this father?
It is merely within the five aggregates (skandhas) of a conventionally designated sentient being that one falsely gives rise to the notion of a "father."
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*), which one is the father?
If form (*rūpa*) were the father, then the four aggregates (*skandha*) would not be;
if the four were the father, then form would likewise not be.
If form and non-form were to combine to constitute a father, such a thing is impossible. Why?
Because the natures of form and non-form do not combine.
"Great King!
Ordinary beings falsely conceive the notion of 'father' regarding this aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); likewise, this aggregate of form cannot be harmed. Why is this so?"
There are ten kinds of form (*rūpa*).
Among these ten, only the single category of "form" itself can be seen, grasped, weighed, measured, pulled, and bound.
Although it can be seen and bound, its nature does not abide.
Because it does not abide, it cannot be seen, it cannot be grasped, it cannot be measured, and it cannot be pulled or bound.
Since the physical form is thus, how can it be killed?
If this form were the father such that it could be killed, harmed, or incur the retribution of sin, then the other nine [elements] would not be so;
if those nine were not [the father], then there should be no sin.
"Great King!
Form is of three kinds:
past, future, and present."
The past and the present cannot be harmed.
Why is this? Because the past has already passed away, and the present perishes moment by moment.
Because it obstructs the future, it is called "killing.
Thus, with respect to a single form, some may be killable while others are not;
since there are instances of killing and non-killing, form is not fixed.
If form is not fixed, then killing is also not fixed;
because killing is not fixed, its retribution is also not fixed.
Why, then, do you say that one is definitely destined for hell?
"Great King!
The sinful karmas committed by all sentient beings are of two kinds:
first, the light; second, the heavy."
If an action is performed by mind and speech alone, it is called light;
if it is performed by body, speech, and mind, it is called heavy.
Great King!
"If one intends it in the mind and speaks it with the mouth, but does not act upon it with the body, the retribution obtained will be light.
Great King!
In the past, you did not command the killing with your mouth, but merely said to have his feet amputated."
"Great King!

If you were to command your attendants to behead you while you were standing, yet they waited until you were seated before doing so, you would still not incur an offense; how much less so when you did not give the command? How could you be guilty?"
If Your Majesty were to commit an offense, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would also be at fault.
Why is this? Your father, the former king Bimbisāra, once planted various roots of goodness before the Buddhas; it is for this reason that he has now attained the position of king.
If the Buddhas did not accept their offerings, they would not have become kings;
if they had not become kings, you would not have been able to bring harm to the kingdom.
If you were to be guilty of a crime for killing your father, then we Buddhas should likewise be guilty of a crime.
"If the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have never committed any offense, how is it that you alone have committed one?
'Great King!

In the past, Bimbisāra harbored an evil mind while roaming for deer on Mount Vipula. Having searched throughout the wilderness without success, he saw only a seer endowed with the five supernatural powers.'"
Having seen him, he immediately gave rise to a mind of anger and malice, thinking:
"It is precisely because of this man that my hunting expedition today has been unsuccessful.
He drove him away and immediately commanded his attendants to kill him.
As that person was approaching death, they gave rise to a mind of anger and malice; losing their supernormal powers, they made this vow:
"I am truly innocent, yet you have wantonly inflicted harm upon me with both mind and speech."
"In a future life, I too shall be like this, harming you once again with my mind and speech.
When the king heard this, he immediately gave rise to a heart of repentance and made offerings to the corpse.
If even this king, acting in such a manner, experiences only a light retribution and does not fall into hell,
how much less would one who does not act thus fall into hell to undergo the fruit of retribution?
Since the former king committed the deed himself and must therefore experience it himself, how can you claim that the current king incurs the sin of murder?
"Regarding what Your Majesty has said—that 'the father king was innocent'—how can Your Majesty say he was not?
For one who has committed a transgression, there is a retribution for that transgression; for one who has performed no evil karma, there is no retribution for a transgression."
If your father, the former king, were innocent, how could there be retribution for his offenses?
Since Bimbisāra obtained both good and evil fruits within this present life, it follows that the former king’s status was not fixed;
because it was not fixed, even his execution was not fixed.
"Since killing is not fixed [in its karmic result], how can you say that one is definitely destined for hell?
'Great King!
There are four kinds of delusion and confusion among sentient beings:"
"First, madness from lust; second, madness from drugs; third, madness from incantations; fourth, madness from the conditions of past karma.
Great King!
Among my disciples there are those with these four kinds of madness; even if they commit many evil deeds, I never declare that such persons have violated the precepts."
The deeds committed by this person do not lead to the three evil realms; if he regains his mind, he will not even be said to have committed an offense.
Since the king originally coveted the kingdom and perversely harmed his father, the king acted under the madness of greed—how could he incur guilt?
“Great King!
It is like a man who, intoxicated by wine, commits the crime of matricide.
Once he has sobered up, remorse arises within his heart.”
You should know that this karma also does not incur retribution.
Your Majesty is now intoxicated by greed; you did not act with your original intention.
If it was not done with your original intention, how can you be guilty of an offense?
"Great King!
It is like a magician who, at a crossroads, conjures by magic all kinds of men, women, elephants, horses, necklaces, and garments."
Foolish people regard it as real, whereas those with wisdom know it is not truly real.
Killing is likewise: ordinary beings regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it is not real.
"Great King!
It is like an echo in the mountains: a foolish person takes it to be a real sound, whereas a wise person knows it is not true.
Killing is likewise: ordinary beings take it to be real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it is not true."
"Great King!
It is like a person who harbors enmity but feigns intimacy upon approaching.
A foolish person considers this to be genuine kinship, whereas a wise person, through clear discernment, recognizes it as false and deceitful."
Killing is also like this: ordinary people regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be not true.
"Great King!
It is like a person holding a mirror and seeing the reflection of their own face; a foolish person regards it as the real face, whereas a wise person thoroughly understands that it is not real."
Killing is also like this: ordinary people take it to be real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be not true.
"Great King!
It is like a mirage in the heat; a foolish person calls it water, but a wise person clearly understands that it is not water."
Killing is also like this: ordinary people regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be not true.
"Great King!
It is like a city of the gandharvas: foolish people regard it as real, while the wise clearly understand that it is not real."
Killing is also like this: ordinary people regard it as real, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be unreal.
"Great King!
It is like a person who experiences the pleasures of the five desires in a dream; a foolish person regards them as real, whereas a wise person thoroughly understands that they are not real."
Killing is also like this: ordinary people regard it as real, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know it to be not true.
"Great King!
As for the nature of killing, the karma of killing, the killer, the fruit of killing, and liberation from them—I have fully understood all these, and thus there is no offense."
"Although the king knows that killing occurs, how can he be guilty?
'Great King!
It is like a person who is the master in charge of wine; if he does not drink it himself, he will likewise not become intoxicated.'"
"Even though one knows fire, it does not burn him.
The King is likewise; even though he knows killing, how could he be guilty of sin?
'Great King!'"

There are sentient beings who commit various kinds of transgressions when the sun rises, and further engage in robbery and theft when the moon rises; yet they do not commit such sins when neither the sun nor the moon appears.
Although one may commit a transgression because of the sun or the moon, the sun and the moon themselves do not actually incur guilt.
Killing is likewise: although it may occur because of a king, the king himself is truly without guilt.
"Great King!
If in your palace you constantly order sheep to be slaughtered and your mind feels no fear at all, why do you alone feel fear toward your father?
Although there are distinctions of high and low between humans and animals, the preciousness of life and the dread of death are in both cases no different."
Why is it that you feel no fear or regard for the sheep, yet give rise to such heavy sorrow and suffering for your father, the former king?
Great King!
People in this world are slaves to craving; they lack self-mastery and commit acts of killing driven by that very craving.
"If there is a retribution, it is the fault of craving.
Since the Great King lacks self-mastery, what fault could there be?
"Great King! [The Buddha said:]
For example, nirvana is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is also existent.
Killing is likewise: although it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is nonetheless existent.
One who possesses a sense of shame and remorse is not "existent," while one devoid of shame and remorse is not "non-existent.
One who experiences the retribution of karmic fruits is termed "existent," whereas one who holds the view of emptiness (śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi) is not "existent."
For one who holds the view that things exist, it is not non-existent; one who holds the view that things exist is likewise said to "exist.
Why is this? Because one who holds the view that things exist attains karmic retribution, whereas one who holds the view that things do not exist has no such retribution.

Those who hold the view of permanence do not consider things to be non-existent, while those who hold the view of impermanence do not consider things to be existent; furthermore, those who hold the view of permanence cannot regard things as non-existent. Why is this?
Because those who see [it] constantly experience the fruits of unwholesome karma, that which is seen constantly cannot be non-existent.
For this reason, although it is neither existent nor non-existent, it nevertheless exists.
“Great King! Sentient beings are, by name, the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
To sever this inhalation and exhalation is called ‘killing’; thus, the Buddhas also speak of it as killing in accordance with worldly convention.”
"Great King!
Form is impermanent, and the causes and conditions of form are also impermanent.
Since it arises from impermanent causes, how could form be permanent?"
Up to and including consciousness, it is impermanent; the causes and conditions of consciousness are also impermanent.
Since it arises from impermanent causes, how could consciousness be permanent?
Because it is impermanent, it is suffering; because it is suffering, it is empty; because it is empty, it is non-self.
If these things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, what is there to be killed?
By killing the impermanent, one attains eternal nirvana; by killing suffering, one attains bliss; by killing emptiness, one attains reality; and by killing non-self, one attains the true self.
"Great King!
If you kill that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, then you are the same as I.
I too have killed that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thus I do not enter hell."
"How do you enter?
At that time, King Ajātaśatru contemplated form as taught by the Buddha, up to and including contemplating consciousness.
Having performed this contemplation, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is only now that I have come to know that form is impermanent, and so on, up to consciousness being impermanent.
Had I been able to know this previously, I would not have committed these offenses.”
“World-Honored One!

In the past, I have heard that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always act as parents to sentient beings; though I had heard these words, I was not yet certain. Now, however, I know it for a certainty.”
“World-Honored One!

I have also heard that Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is composed of four treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and that whatever birds gather there take on the same color as their respective location.”
Although I have heard these words, I have not yet reached a definitive certainty.

Now that I have come to the Buddha’s Mount Sumeru, I have become the same color as it; and because I have become the same color as it, I know that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.
“World-Honored One!
I have seen in the world that from a *śrīparṇa* seed grows a *śrīparṇa* tree, but I have never seen a *candana* tree grow from a *śrīparṇa* seed.
Now, for the first time, I see a *candana* tree growing from a *śrīparṇa* seed—the *śrīparṇa* seed being my own body;”
The sandalwood tree is my own mind’s rootless faith.
It is called "rootless" because, at first, I did not know how to revere the Tathāgata, nor did I have faith in the Dharma or the Saṃgha; this is what is meant by being rootless.
“World-Honored One!
Had I not encountered the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, I would have been undergoing immeasurable suffering in the great hells for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.”
"I have now seen the Buddha; by the merit obtained from this vision of the Buddha, may I destroy all afflictions and evil minds of sentient beings.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"Excellent, excellent!
I now know that you will certainly be able to destroy the evil minds of sentient beings.
"World-Honored One!"

If I am truly able to destroy the various evil minds of sentient beings, may I always remain in the Avīci Hell for immeasurable kalpas, undergoing great suffering and affliction for the sake of all sentient beings without regarding it as suffering.
At that time, immeasurable people of the kingdom of Magadha all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because such immeasurable people had thus resolved their minds upon the Great Awakening, King Ajātaśatru’s grave offenses were immediately diminished and lightened.
The king, as well as the queen and all the ladies of the inner palace, together gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to Jīvaka: "Jīvaka!"

I have now, while not yet dead, already attained a celestial body; having abandoned a short life, I have attained a long life; having abandoned an impermanent body, I have attained an eternal body. To cause all sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is itself the celestial body, the long life, and the eternal body; they are thus the disciples of all Buddhas.
Having spoken these words, he immediately made offerings to the Buddha with various jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, fragrant flowers, necklaces, and exquisite music.
Furthermore, he praised him with these verses:
“Your truthful speech is most subtle, Skillful in its words and meanings;
The profound and secret treasury— For the sake of the multitude, you have revealed it.”
All these vast words have been spoken in brief for the sake of the multitude;
possessing such speech, one is well able to heal sentient beings.
If there are any sentient beings who hear these words, [they shall be healed].
Whether one has faith or lacks faith, one should know with certainty that this is the Buddha’s teaching.
The Buddhas always speak with gentle words, yet for the sake of the multitude, they may speak harshly.
Whether their speech be harsh or gentle, it all returns to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Therefore, I now take refuge in the World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata’s speech is of a single flavor, like the waters of the great ocean;
this is called the foremost truth, and thus there is no speech that is meaningless.
The various and immeasurable teachings now spoken by the Tathāgata—
whether heard by men or women, great or small— all equally attain the ultimate truth.
Without cause and without effect, without birth and without cessation—this is called Great Nirvana;
those who hear it shatter all fetters.
The Tathāgata acts as a compassionate parent for all beings at all times.
One should know that all sentient beings are the children of the Tathāgata.
Out of great compassion, the World-Honored One undergoes ascetic practices for the sake of the multitudes;
it is like a person possessed by a malevolent spirit, who acts with madness and excess.
Now that I have been able to see the Buddha,
may the virtue obtained through my threefold actions be dedicated by this merit toward the Unsurpassed Way.
Whatever offerings I now present to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—
By this merit, may the Three Jewels remain forever in the world.
May all the various merits that I shall now attain serve to destroy the four kinds of Māras for all sentient beings.
Having encountered evil associates, I have committed sins throughout the three periods of time;
now, before the Buddha, I repent, vowing never to commit them again.
May all sentient beings likewise resolve to attain bodhicitta.
Binding the mind in constant mindfulness, one should think of all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, one should vow that all sentient beings may forever shatter all afflictions,
clearly perceive their Buddha-nature, and become just like Samantabhadra and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised King Ajātaśatru:
“Excellent, excellent!
If there is anyone who can resolve to attain bodhicitta, you should know that such a person adorns the great assembly of all Buddhas.”
"Great King!

In the past, you first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* under Vipaśyin Buddha; from that time until my appearance in the world, during all that interval, you have never fallen into hell to undergo suffering."
"Great King, you should know that the mind of enlightenment yields such immeasurable fruits and rewards.
Great King!"
From this day forward, you shall always diligently cultivate the bodhicitta.
Why is this? Because by means of these causes and conditions, you shall attain the eradication of immeasurable evils.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru and all the people of the kingdom of Magadha rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and took their leave to return to the palace.
The "Chapter on Celestial Conduct" is as explained in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.
**Chapter Twenty-one: The Chapter on Infant Conduct** from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: “Good son!
What is meant by "infant-like conduct"? Good son!
One who is unable to arise, stand, come, go, or speak is called an infant.
The Tathāgata is likewise: that which cannot arise, the Tathāgata never gives rise to as a mark of dharmas;
that which cannot abide, the Tathāgata does not cling to any dharmas;
that which cannot come, the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct is without movement or agitation.
That which cannot go is because the Tathāgata has already attained great parinirvāṇa;
that which cannot speak is because although the Tathāgata expounds all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, in reality there is nothing spoken.
Why is this? That which can be spoken of is called a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is not conditioned, and therefore he has nothing to speak of.
Furthermore, "being without speech" is like an infant whose speech is not yet developed; although they do utter words, in reality they have no speech.
The Tathāgata is also like this: that which is "speech not yet developed" is precisely the secret language of all Buddhas.
Although they may speak, sentient beings do not understand them; therefore, this is called "speechlessness.
Furthermore, as for an infant, names and objects are not yet unified, and they do not yet know correct speech.
Although names and objects are not identical, and one may not yet know the correct language, it is not that one cannot recognize objects by means of them.

It is the same for the Tathāgata: although the species and categories of all sentient beings differ and their speech is not the same, the Tathāgata employs skillful means to teach according to them, enabling all to attain understanding thereby.
"Furthermore, an infant is able to utter great syllables.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he utters great syllables, namely *ba* and *ha*.
*Ha* refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)."
"Bha" refers to the unconditioned;
this is called "infant.
"Ho" is named impermanence.
"Bāla" means "possessing permanence.
When the Tathāgata speaks of permanence, sentient beings, having heard it, sever their attachment to impermanence for the sake of this permanent dharma; this is called the conduct of an infant.
"Furthermore, an infant does not know suffering or pleasure, day or night, father or mother.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: for the sake of sentient beings, he perceives neither suffering nor pleasure, nor the distinction between day and night; because his mind is impartial toward all sentient beings, he has no distinctions such as father, mother, kin, or stranger."
"Furthermore, an infant is unable to perform great or small tasks.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: the Bodhisattva does not perform the karmic actions of birth and death; this is called 'not performing great deeds. "
The "great matters" refer to the five heinous crimes; a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva will never commit these grave offenses.
The "minor matters" refer to the mindsets of the two vehicles; a Bodhisattva will never regress from the bodhicitta to become a follower of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles.

"Furthermore, as for the practitioner who acts like an infant: it is just as when an infant cries, his parents immediately take yellow leaves from a *śiṃśapā* tree and say to him, 'Do not cry, do not cry.'"
"I will give you gold.
Upon seeing this, the infant conceived the notion that it was genuine gold; he then ceased crying. However, these *śirīṣa* leaves were not actually gold at all.
When infants see wooden oxen, wooden horses, wooden boys, or wooden girls, they likewise give rise to the perception that they are real boys or girls, and immediately stop crying.
In truth, they are neither male nor female; yet because they conceive such notions of being male or female, they are called "infants.

The Tathāgata is likewise: if there are sentient beings who wish to commit various evils, the Tathāgata preaches for them that in the Heaven of the Thirty-three there are permanence, bliss, self, and purity; that the inhabitants are handsome and self-reliant, enjoying the pleasures of the five desires within wondrous palaces, where everything encountered by the six sense faculties is nothing but joy.

Because sentient beings hear of such bliss, they give rise to a craving for that bliss; they cease from committing evil and diligently perform wholesome deeds for the sake of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

In reality, this is birth and death—impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity—but as a skillful means to deliver sentient beings, it is spoken of as permanent, blissful, with self, and pure.
"Furthermore, regarding 'infants,' when there are sentient beings who weary of birth and death, the Tathāgata then teaches them the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Yet, in reality, there is no substantiality to these two vehicles; it is by means of the two vehicles that they come to know the faults of birth and death and perceive the bliss of nirvāṇa."

By means of this vision, one is then able to know for oneself that there is what is severed and what is not severed, what is true and what is not true, what is cultivated and what is not cultivated, and what is attained and what is not attained.
“Good son! Just as that infant conceives the notion of gold amidst what is not gold,
so too does the Tathāgata speak of purity amidst the impure.”
Because the Tathāgata has already attained the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he is free from falsehood.

Just as a young child might form the notion of "ox" or "horse" regarding what is not an ox or a horse, so too, if there are sentient beings who perceive what is not the Path as the true Path, the Tathāgata likewise speaks of that which is not the Path as being the Path.
Within what is not the Path, there is truly no Path; yet because it can produce the subtle causes and conditions for the Path, that which is not the Path is spoken of as the Path.
"It is like a child who conceives the notion of a male or female in a wooden figure of a man or woman;
the Tathāgata is likewise: though he knows they are not sentient beings, he speaks of the characteristics of sentient beings, yet in reality, the characteristic of a sentient being does not exist."
If the Buddha-Tathāgata were to say that there are no sentient beings, all sentient beings would fall into false views.
For this reason, the Tathāgata says that there are sentient beings.
Those who conceive of the mark of a sentient being among sentient beings will be unable to destroy that mark of a sentient being.
If one destroys the perception of a sentient being with respect to sentient beings, one is then able to attain Great Parinirvāṇa;
because one has attained such Great Nirvāṇa, one ceases and does not weep.
This is called the practice of an infant. "Good son!
If there are men or women who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain these five practices, you should know that such persons will certainly attain these five practices."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, I too shall certainly attain these five practices.”
The Buddha said, "Good son!
Not only you have attained these five practices; ninety-three thousand people in this assembly have likewise attained these five practices."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 18.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 19.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter Twenty-Two: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Ābhāsvara-Guṇarāja, Part One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Ābhāsvara-Guṇarāja, saying:
"O son of good family!

If there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they will attain ten kinds of meritorious qualities that are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; these are inconceivable and cause those who hear of them to be struck with wonder. They are neither internal nor external, neither difficult nor easy, neither characterized nor uncharacterized; they are not worldly dharmas, they possess no marks or appearances, and are things that do not exist in the world.
"What are the ten?
First, there are five.
What are these five?"

First, being able to hear what one has not heard before; second, being able to derive benefit from what has been heard; third, being able to sever the mind of doubt and confusion; fourth, having a mind of wisdom that is upright and without crookedness; fifth, being able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata—these are the five matters.
"What is it that one has not heard but can now hear?
It is the most profound and subtle treasury:
that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and that there is no distinction between the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
The nature and characteristics of the Triple Gem are permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
all Buddhas never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa, but abide eternally without change.
The Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is neither existent nor non-existent, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither with outflows nor without outflows, and neither form nor...
It is not form, neither name nor non-name; neither characteristic nor non-characteristic;
neither existent nor non-existent; neither thing nor non-thing; neither cause nor effect;
neither dependent nor independent; neither light nor darkness; neither emerging nor non-emerging; neither permanent—
It is not non-eternal; it is neither annihilated nor non-annihilated; it has no beginning and no end; it is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present;
it is not the aggregates (skandhas), nor is it not the aggregates; it is not the sense-bases (āyatanas), nor is it not the sense-bases;
it is not the elements (dhātus), nor is it not the elements; it is not the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), nor is it not the twelve links.
Regarding causes and conditions, such dharmas as these are profoundly deep and subtle; though unheard of in the past, they can now be heard.

Furthermore, there are things not previously heard, namely all the scriptures of the non-Buddhists, the four Vedas, the Vyākaraṇa, the Vaiśeṣika-śāstra, the Sāṃkhya-śāstra, all incantations and arts, medical prescriptions, crafts, the eclipses of the sun and moon, the movements and transformations of the constellations, and the prophecies of charts and records—regarding the secret meanings of such scriptures as these, which were never heard before, one now comes to know them through this sutra.

"Furthermore, there are eleven divisions of the sūtras—excluding the Vaipulya—which likewise do not contain such profound and secret meanings; it is now through this sūtra that they may be understood."
"Good son! This is called 'being able to hear what was previously unheard.

As for 'benefit after hearing,' if one can listen to and receive this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, one will be able to fully understand the profound meaning and flavor of all the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras."
For example, when men and women behold their own reflections in a bright, clear mirror, they see them with perfect clarity;
the mirror of the Great Nirvana is likewise, for when Bodhisattvas hold it, they are able to clearly perceive the profound meaning of the Mahayana sutras.
It is also like a person in a dark room who, holding a great torch, sees all things clearly;
the torch of the Great Nirvana is likewise, for when a bodhisattva holds it, they are able to perceive the profound and subtle meaning of the Mahāyāna.
It is also like the rising sun, which possesses a thousand rays of light capable of illuminating the dark recesses of all mountains and enabling all people to see objects from afar;
so too is this pure sun of wisdom of the Great Nirvana, which illuminates the profound depths of the Mahāyāna and enables those of the Two Vehicles to see the Buddha-way from afar.
Why is this so? Because they are able to hear and accept this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa. "Good son!
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who hear and receive this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they will come to know the names of all dharmas;
if they can further transcribe, read, recite, master it, explain it extensively for others, and contemplate its meaning, they will then know the principles and meanings of all dharmas.
"Good son!
Those who merely listen to and receive it know only the names, but do not understand their meaning;
if they can write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it extensively for others, and contemplate its meaning, then they will be able to understand the meaning."
Furthermore, good son!
Those who hear this sutra may hear that there is buddha-nature, yet they are not yet able to see it;
however, by copying it, reciting it, explaining it extensively for others, and contemplating its meaning, they shall then see it.
Those who hear this sutra may hear the name of "giving," yet they are not yet able to see the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā);
however, those who copy it, read and recite it, explain it extensively for others, and contemplate its meaning will be able to see the perfection of giving.
It is even so for the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Good son!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can hear this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, he will know the Dharma and know its meaning, possessing the two kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). Among all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, Māras, Brahmās, and the entire world, he shall attain fearlessness. He will open up, reveal, and analyze the twelve divisions of the scriptures, expounding their meanings without error. Without hearing it from another, he will be able to know it for himself and draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Noble son! This is what is called 'hearing and being able to bring benefit.
Regarding the 'severing of doubt,' there are two kinds of doubt: [the doubt concerning the teacher and the doubt concerning the teaching]."
First is doubt regarding names, and second is doubt regarding meanings.
Those who listen to this sutra sever the mind that doubts names;
those who contemplate its meaning sever the mind that doubts meanings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there are five kinds of doubt:
first, doubting whether the Buddha has definitely entered parinirvāṇa or not;
Second, they doubt whether the Buddha is eternally abiding;
third, they doubt whether the Buddha is truly blissful;
fourth, they doubt whether the Buddha is truly pure.
Fifth, regarding the doubt as to whether the Buddha is a real self:
for one who hears this sutra, the doubt concerning the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa will be eternally severed;
by copying, reading, reciting, extensively explaining it to others, and contemplating its meaning, the four doubts will be eternally severed.
Furthermore, good son, there are three kinds of doubt:
first, doubting whether the śrāvaka exists; [and so forth].
Is there none?
Second, one doubts whether pratyekabuddhas exist or do not exist.
Third, regarding the doubt as to whether the Buddha-vehicle exists or does not exist:
for those who hear this sutra, these three doubts will be forever extinguished without remainder.
By copying, reading, reciting, explaining it extensively for others, and contemplating its meaning, one will be able to understand that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, good son!
If there are sentient beings who have not heard this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they harbor many doubts, namely:

whether it is permanent or impermanent; whether it is blissful or not blissful; whether it is pure or impure; whether it is self or non-self; whether it is life or not life; whether it is a sentient being or not a sentient being; whether it is ultimate or not ultimate; whether there is a future world or no future world; whether things exist or do not exist; whether it is suffering or not suffering; whether it is the origin [of suffering] or not the origin; whether it is the path or not the path; whether it is cessation or not cessation; whether it is the Dharma or not the Dharma; whether it is wholesome or not wholesome; and whether it is empty or not empty.
Those who hear this sutra will have all such doubts forever severed.
Furthermore, good son,
those who have not heard such a sutra as this will further harbor various and numerous doubts, namely:
Is form the self?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the self?
Is it the eye that sees?
Can I see? ... up to ...
can consciousness cognize? Can I cognize?
Is it form that experiences retribution?
Is it the self that experiences retribution?
And so on, up to: is it consciousness that experiences retribution?
Is it I who receive retribution?
Does form go to another world?
Or do I go to another world?
Even so it is with consciousness: do the phenomena of birth and death have a beginning and an end, or are they without beginning and without end?
Those who listen to this sutra shall likewise forever sever such doubts.
Furthermore, there are those who harbor doubts:
"Do icchantikas—who have committed the four grave offenses, perpetrated the five heinous crimes, and slandered the Vaipulya sutras—possess the Buddha-nature?"
"Is it that they lack the Buddha-nature?
Those who hear this sutra shall forever sever all such doubts.
Furthermore, there are others who harbor doubts:"
Is the world finite?
Is the world infinite?
Do the worlds of the ten directions exist?
"Are there no worlds in the ten directions?

Those who hear this sutra shall likewise forever sever such doubts; this is called being able to sever the mind of doubt and hesitation, possessing a mind of wisdom that is upright and free from crookedness.

"If the mind harbors doubt, then what is perceived will not be correct; all ordinary worldlings, if they do not hear this subtle and wondrous scripture of the Great Parinirvāṇa, perceive things with distortion and crookedness;
even the perceptions of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are likewise distorted."
What is meant by the "crookedness" perceived by all ordinary worldlings?

It is to perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity within that which is subject to outflows (*āsrava*); to perceive impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self in the Tathāgata; to perceive the existence of sentient beings, a life-span, and a knowing-seeing faculty; to reckon the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as *nirvāṇa*; and to perceive the Lord Maheśvara as possessing the Eightfold Noble Path. Such views as these are called crooked.
If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas hear this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and practice the noble conduct, they will then be able to sever and eliminate such perversity and crookedness.
"What is meant by the deviant views of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?

They see that the Bodhisattva descends from Tuṣita, transforms himself into a white elephant to enter his mother’s womb, with his father named Śuddhodana and his mother named Māyā; he dwells in the womb in the city of Kapilavastu and is born after ten full months."

When he was born on the Unattained Ground (*anāgamya-bhūmi*), Śakra received him by holding him up; the Nanda and Upananda Dragon Kings spat forth water to bathe him; the Great Ghost King Maṇibhadra followed behind, standing in attendance while holding a precious parasol; and the Earth Goddess transformed flowers to receive his feet.
He walked seven paces in each of the four directions; upon reaching a celestial temple, all the statues of the gods rose to welcome him. The seer Asita took him in his arms to examine his marks;
having performed the divination, he was overcome with great sorrow and grief, lamenting that his own life would end before he could witness the arising of the Buddha.

He went to his teachers to study writing, arithmetic, archery, charioteering, divination, and the arts; while residing in the inner palace, he was entertained and provided with pleasure by sixty thousand court ladies.

He went out of the city for a stroll and reached the Kapilavastu Garden; on the way, he saw an old man and even a śramaṇa walking in religious robes. Upon returning to the palace, he saw that the forms and features of the court ladies were like withered bones, and that the palaces were no different from burial mounds. Disgusted, he resolved to leave the household life.

At midnight, he left the city and went to the abodes of the great seers Udraka Rāmaputra, Ārāḍa Kālāma, and others, where he heard their teachings on the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Having heard this, he contemplated that state as impermanent, suffering, impure, and non-self; he then withdrew to the foot of a tree and fully practiced asceticism for six years, after which he realized that such asceticism could not bring about the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, he again went to the river Ajiravatī to bathe and accepted the milk-gruel offered by the cowherd girl.
Having accepted it, he proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree, where he defeated Māra Pāpīyas and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
From the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma for the five bhikṣus at Vārāṇasī, until entering parinirvāṇa here in the city of Kuśinagara—
seeing things in such a manner is called the crooked view of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears and receives this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they will completely sever and eliminate views such as these;
if they can further copy it, read and recite it, master it, explain it to others, and contemplate its meaning, they will attain upright and non-deviant views."

“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra in this way, he knows with certainty that from immeasurable kalpas ago, the bodhisattva did not descend from Tuṣita to enter his mother’s womb, nor did he enter parinirvāṇa at the city of Kuśinagara; this is called the upright view of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”

Those who are able to understand the profound and secret meaning of the Tathāgata—namely, that this Great Parinirvāṇa and the Buddha-nature inherent in all sentient beings exist—may repent for the four grave prohibitions, eliminate the mind that slanders the Dharma, exhaust the five heinous crimes, and extinguish the icchantika state; only then shall they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called the meaning of the profound secret.
"Furthermore, good son,
what again is called the meaning of the profound?
Although one knows that sentient beings truly have no self, the fruits of karma are not lost in the future;
although one knows that the five aggregates cease and perish here, the karma of good and evil never perishes;
and although there are various karmas, no agent can be found.
Although there is a destination, there is no one who goes;
although there is bondage, there is no one who is bound;
although there is nirvana, there is likewise no one who attains extinction.
"This is called the meaning of the profound secret.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught regarding "hearing" and "not hearing," this interpretation is not correct.
Why is this? If a phenomenon exists, it must necessarily exist.
If phenomena were non-existent, they would necessarily be eternally non-existent;
being non-existent, they should not arise,
and being existent, they should not cease.
If one hears it, then it is heard;
if one does not hear it, then it is not heard.
How can you say that what was not heard has been heard?
World-Honored One!
If it cannot be heard, that is non-hearing.
If it has already been heard, then one hears no more.
Why is this? Because they have already heard it.
How can one say that they have heard what was not previously heard?
"For example, one who is going does not go once he has arrived, and one who is going does not arrive;
likewise, that which has already arisen does not arise, and that which has not arisen does not arise;
that which has been attained is not attained, and that which has not been attained is not attained."
"Having heard, one does not hear; not having heard, one does not hear—this is likewise so, World-Honored One!

If it were the case that by not hearing one hears, then all sentient beings who have not yet attained bodhi should immediately possess it; those who have not yet attained nirvana should immediately attain it; and those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature should see the Buddha-nature."
Why, then, do you further say that although Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature, they have not yet attained clear realization?
"World-Honored One!
If it is 'hearing what has not been heard,' from whom did the Tathāgata hear it in the past?"
If you say that he heard it, why did the Tathāgata further state in the Āgamas that he had no teacher?

If the Tathāgata attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without hearing or not hearing [the teachings], then all sentient beings should also attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without hearing or not hearing them.
If the Tathāgata had not heard this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and seen the Buddha-nature, then all sentient beings, having likewise not heard this sūtra, should also have attained such vision.
“World-Honored One!
As for all forms, some are visible and some are invisible;
sound is likewise, being either audible or inaudible.”
"This Great Nirvana is neither form nor sound; how can it be said that it can be seen or heard?
"World-Honored One!
That which has already perished in the past cannot be heard."
The future has not yet arrived and thus cannot be heard;
at the time one listens in the present, it is not yet called "heard"; once heard, the sound has ceased and can no longer be heard.
This Great Nirvāṇa is likewise neither past, future, nor present; if it does not belong to the three periods of time, it cannot be described.
"If it cannot be spoken, then it cannot be heard.
How can you say that a bodhisattva practicing this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* hears what has never been heard before?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

Son of good family, you now well understand that all dharmas are like an illusion, like a mirage, like a city of the Gandharvas, and like the ripples left by a drawing on water; they are also like foam and the trunk of a plantain tree—empty and without substance, neither a life-principle nor a self, devoid of suffering or pleasure, just as is known and seen by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.”

At that moment, within the great assembly, there suddenly appeared a vast radiance: what was not blue appeared as blue, what was not yellow appeared as yellow, what was not red appeared as red, and what was not white appeared as white; what was not form appeared as form, what was not light appeared as light, and it was seen without being seen.
At that time, having encountered this light, the great assembly experienced joy in body and mind, like a bhikṣu entering the Lion King Samādhi.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Who has emitted this radiance now?
At that time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not speak.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again questioned Mañjuśrī:
"For what cause and condition does this radiance shine upon the great assembly?
Mañjuśrī remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra again asked the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa:
"Whose radiance is this now? Kāśyapa Bodhisattva remained silent and did not speak.
Prince Viśuddhavihārin Bodhisattva then asked Anantamati Bodhisattva:
"For what cause and condition does this radiance appear within this great assembly?
The Bodhisattva Anantagātra remained silent and did not speak.
In this manner, all five hundred bodhisattvas likewise remained so; though they questioned one another, none provided an answer.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
For what cause and condition does this radiance appear within this great assembly?"
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
This radiance is called wisdom, and wisdom is that which is eternally abiding.”
The eternally abiding Dharma has no causes or conditions; why then does the Buddha ask by what causes and conditions this radiance exists?
This radiance is named Great Nirvana, and Great Nirvana is named the eternally abiding.
The eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions; why then does the Buddha ask by what causes and conditions this radiance exists?
This radiance is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding.
The eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions; why, then, does the Tathāgata inquire about causes and conditions?
"Radiance" is a name for great loving-kindness and great compassion, and great loving-kindness and great compassion are called the eternally abiding.
The eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions; why then does the Tathāgata inquire about causes and conditions?
Radiance is precisely mindfulness of the Buddha, and mindfulness of the Buddha is called the eternally abiding.
The eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions; why then does the Tathāgata inquire about causes and conditions?
That which is "light" is precisely the unique path of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this unique path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is termed "eternally abiding."
The eternally abiding Dharma does not arise from causes and conditions; why then does the Tathāgata inquire about causes and conditions?
World-Honored One, there are indeed causes and conditions: by extinguishing ignorance, one obtains the blazing lamp of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! You should not now enter into the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) of all phenomena, which is exceedingly profound; you should explain it by means of conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya)."
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
