To the east of here, past worlds as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-world named Akṣobhya. The extent of that Buddha’s dwelling place is exactly twelve thousand yojanas in both length and breadth.”
The ground is composed of the seven treasures, devoid of earth or stone; it is level, smooth, and soft, with no ditches or pits.
The various trees are made of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—their flowers and fruits flourishing so that there is never a time when they are not present.
If there are sentient beings who smell its fragrance, their bodies and minds become peaceful and blissful, as if a bhikṣu had entered the third dhyāna.
Surrounding it are three thousand great rivers; their waters are exquisite, endowed with the eight excellent qualities.
If there are sentient beings who bathe therein, the joy and bliss they obtain are like those of a bhikṣu who has entered the second dhyāna.

That river abounds with various kinds of flowers: utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, fragrant flowers, great fragrant flowers, exquisitely fragrant flowers, ever-blooming flowers, and flowers that all sentient beings may enjoy without restriction or protection.

On both banks of that river there were also various flowers, namely: *atimuktaka* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers, *vārṣika* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *mahāmālikā* flowers, *navamālikā* flowers, *sumana* flowers, *yūthikā* flowers, *tānukālī* flowers, *nitya* flowers, and flowers that provide protection for all sentient beings without exception.
The ground was spread with golden sand and featured four flights of stairs made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and multicolored crystal.

Many birds gathered and roamed there, and there were also immeasurable tigers, wolves, lions, and various predatory beasts; yet they looked upon one another with hearts as pure as those toward an only child.
"In that world, there are none who violate the grave prohibitions, slander the True Dharma, or commit the sins of icchantikas or the five heinous acts.

That land is harmonious and temperate, free from the afflictions of cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; it is devoid of greed, anger, negligence, and jealousy. It has no sun, moon, day, night, or seasons, being just like the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa."

The people of that land are all endowed with radiance; each and every one is free from pride and arrogance. They are all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained supernatural powers and are possessed of great merit.

Their minds all revered the True Dharma; they mounted the Mahāyāna, cherished the Mahāyāna, delighted in the Mahāyāna, and protected the Mahāyāna. Having achieved great wisdom and attained great dhāraṇī, their hearts were constantly compassionate toward all sentient beings.
That Buddha’s name was Pūrṇacandraprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.

Wherever he dwells and wherever he expounds the Dharma, the sentient beings of that land shall all hear him as he teaches this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* for the sake of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vairocanaraśmi.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can practice the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, all that he has not heard will be heard by him."

“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vaidūryaprabha questioned the Buddha Pūrṇacandraprabha in exactly the same manner as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūharāja here has questioned me; they were identical and without any difference.”
The Buddha Pūrṇacandraprabha then addressed the Bodhisattva Vairocanaprabha, saying: "Good son!
To the west of here, beyond buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of twenty Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā."

That land abounds with mountains, hills, mounds, earth, sand, pebbles, gravel, thorns, and wicked brambles, which fill it everywhere; it is constantly filled with the afflictions of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.

The people of that land are unable to show reverence toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, parents, or teachers; they are greedily attached to what is not the Dharma and desire what is not the Dharma; they practice false teachings and do not believe in the true Dharma; their lifespans are short, and they engage in deceit and fraud.

When kings govern in this manner, although they possess kingdoms, they know no contentment; they give rise to greedy and covetous minds toward the possessions of others, mobilize armies to wage mutual warfare, and cause a great many to die unjustly.

When a king practices such unrighteousness, the benevolent deities of the four quarters feel no joy; consequently, they send down calamitous droughts, causing crops to fail and the people to suffer from many diseases and immeasurable afflictions.

In that realm dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Out of profound and pure compassion, and out of pity for sentient beings, he expounds this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* for the great assembly amidst the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara.
There is a bodhisattva there named Prabhāvyūha-uccagāmin-guṇarāja who has already asked about this matter; he is no different from you.
The Buddha is now answering him; you should go quickly, and you shall hear it for yourself.
“World-Honored One!

Having heard of this matter, that Bodhisattva Vaidūryaprabha, together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, wishes to come here; therefore, he has first manifested these auspicious signs.”
"It is because of these causes and conditions that this radiance exists; this is called 'causes and conditions,' yet it is also not 'causes and conditions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vairocana-prabha, together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, carrying various banners, canopies, incense, flowers, necklaces, and all kinds of music—surpassing those previously offered—arrived together at this city of Kuśinagara, between the twin śāla trees.
He offered the articles of worship he carried to the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, joined his palms in reverence, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Having completed these acts of respect, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked that bodhisattva: "Good son,
have you come here?"
"Is it because they have not yet arrived?
The Bodhisattva Vairocana said,
"World-Honored One!"
"Neither one who has arrived comes, nor does one who has not arrived come; when I contemplate this meaning, there is no coming at all.
World-Honored One!
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were permanent, they likewise would not come."
If it were impermanent, there would likewise be no coming.
If one perceives a fixed nature of sentient beings, then there would be coming and not-coming.
Since I do not now perceive a fixed nature of sentient beings, how could I say that there is coming or not-coming?
Those who possess pride perceive going and coming;
those without pride have no going or coming.
Those who engage in grasping perceive going and coming.
For one who practices without grasping, there is no going or coming.
If one perceives the Tathāgata as ultimately entering parinirvāṇa, then there is going and coming;
if one does not perceive the Tathāgata as ultimately entering parinirvāṇa, then there is no going or coming.
Those who have not heard of the Buddha-nature possess coming and going;
those who have heard of the Buddha-nature have no coming or going.
If one perceives that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain nirvāṇa, then they possess coming and going.
If one does not perceive that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess nirvāṇa, then there is no going or coming.
If one perceives that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity, then there is going and coming;
if one does not so perceive, then there is no going or coming.
If one perceives the Tathāgata as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, then there is coming and going;
if one perceives the Tathāgata as permanent, blissful, self, and pure, then there is no coming and going.
“World-Honored One!
Let this matter rest for now; I wish to ask something else. May you deign to show compassion and grant me a brief audience.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Ask whatever you wish; now is precisely the right time. I shall analyze and explain it for you. Why is this so?
The Buddhas are difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower;
the Dharma is likewise, difficult to hear;
and among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the Vaipulya is even more difficult to encounter.
"Therefore, you should listen and receive this with single-minded devotion.
At that time, having received the permission and the solemn exhortation, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vairocanaraśmi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, through the practice of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, hear what has not been heard before?
At that time, the Tathāgata praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
You now wish to exhaustively fathom this great ocean of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa; you have fortunately encountered me, who am well able to explain it for you.
As for the poisonous arrows of the net of doubt that you currently possess, I am a great physician and can skillfully extract them."
"You are not yet clearly enlightened regarding the Buddha-nature; I possess the torch of wisdom that can illuminate it for you.
Now that you wish to cross the great river of birth and death, I can serve as your great captain."
"You have conceived the thought of me as your parent, and I too have conceived the heart of a parent toward you.
Since your mind now craves the jewel of the True Dharma and has encountered me—who possess it in abundance—I am able to bestow it upon you."
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
"Good son! For one who wishes to hear the Dharma, now is precisely the right time."
Once you have heard the Dharma, you should give rise to reverent faith, listening with a sincere heart, honoring and respecting it.
Do not seek out faults in the True Dharma; do not harbor thoughts of greed, hatred, or delusion; and do not examine whether the Dharma teacher’s lineage is noble or base.

Having heard the Dharma, do not give rise to arrogance; do not act for the sake of reverence, fame, or material gain, but rather for the sake of the benefit of the nectar-like Dharma that transcends the world.
Furthermore, do not give rise to this thought:
"After I have heard the Dharma, I shall first deliver myself and only then deliver others;
I shall first liberate myself and only then liberate others."
"First establish peace for oneself, and then bring peace to others;
first attain nirvana for oneself, and then lead others to attain nirvana.

One should conceive the notion of equality toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; conceive the notion of great suffering within birth and death; and conceive the notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity regarding Great Nirvana.
First act for the sake of others, and only then for yourself.
You should practice for the sake of the Mahāyāna, not for the sake of the two vehicles.
Regarding all dharmas, you should abide in nothing; nor should you cling exclusively to the characteristics of any dharma.
Do not give rise to thoughts of craving toward any phenomena; always maintain the thought of knowing the Dharma and seeing the Dharma.
Good son! If you can listen to the Dharma with such a sincere mind, this is called "hearing what has not been heard before."

“Good son! There is that which is not heard but is heard; there is that which is not heard and is not heard; there is that which is heard but is not heard; and there is that which is heard and is heard. Good son!”
As with non-arising arising, non-arising non-arising, arising non-arising, and arising arising; as with non-arrival arrival, non-arrival non-arrival, arrival non-arrival, and arrival arrival.
“World-Honored One!
How is it that there is no arising of arising? “Good son!”
When one abides in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) at the moment of first emerging from the womb, this is called "the non-arising of arising.
"What is 'the non-arising of non-arising'? "Good son!..."
This Great Nirvāṇa has no characteristic of arising; this is called "the non-arising of non-arising.
"What is meant by 'arising that is non-arising'? "Good son!
"In conventional truth, at the time of death, this is called 'birth and non-birth.
What is meant by 'the birth of birth'? Good son!"
All ordinary beings are called "those who are born and born. Why?
Because their birth after birth is uninterrupted.
Because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) arise moment by moment, this is called "the arising of arising.
Bodhisattvas dwelling in the four stages are called "arising yet non-arising. Why is this?
Because of mastery over birth, this is called "birth and non-birth.
Good son, this is called the internal dharma.
"What are external phenomena? They are:
the unarisen arising, the unarisen-unarisen, the arisen-unarisen, and the arisen-arising.
Good son!..."

For example, when a seed has not yet produced a sprout, it must obtain the harmony of the four great elements, human effort, and manual labor before it can arise; this is called "the arising of what has not yet arisen."
"What is meant by 'the unarisen not yet arisen'?
For example, like rotten seeds or those that have not encountered the necessary conditions—such cases are called 'the unarisen not yet arisen.
What is meant by 'the arisen not yet arisen'?"
If, once the sprout has arisen, it does not continue to grow, this is called "arising that has not yet arisen.
What is "the arising of arising"?
It is like the growth of the sprout.
"If there is neither arising nor non-arising, then there is no growth.
In this way, all outflows (āsrava) are called the 'arising of external dharmas.
" The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vaidūryaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are dharmas with outflows that undergo arising,
are they permanent or are they impermanent?”
World-Honored One! If birth were permanent, then phenomena with outflows would have no arising;
if birth were impermanent, then phenomena with outflows would be permanent.
If arising could arise by itself, then arising would lack intrinsic nature;
if it could give rise to another, for what reason and condition would it not also give rise to the untainted?
World-Honored One!
If that which has not yet arisen were already arising, how could it be called "arising" only at this present moment?
If that which has not yet arisen were non-arising, why is space not said to be arising?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”

The non-arising of arising cannot be described; the arising of arising also cannot be described; the non-arising of non-arising cannot be described; the non-arising of non-arising also cannot be described. Arising cannot be described, and non-arising also cannot be described; yet, because there are causes and conditions, it can also be described.
Why is it that the non-arising of arising cannot be spoken of?
That which is non-arising is called "arising.
How, then, can it be spoken of?
Why is this? Because it arises.
How is it that the arising of arising cannot be described?
Because it arises from arising, it arises; because it arises from the arising of arising, it does not arise. Furthermore, it cannot be described.
Why can it not be described as arising or non-arising?
That which arises is called "arising," yet arising does not arise by itself; therefore, it cannot be described.
Why is it that non-arising and non-non-arising are ineffable?
"Non-arising" is termed *nirvāṇa*; since *nirvāṇa* does not arise, it is ineffable. Why is this so?
Because it is attained through the cultivation of the path.
Why is it also said that its arising cannot be described?
Because there is no such thing as its arising.
Why is it that non-arising cannot be described? Because there is attainment.
Why is it that, by virtue of causes and conditions, it can also be described?
The ten links of dependent origination act as causes for arising; for this reason, it may also be said:
"Good son! You must not now enter the profound samādhi of emptiness."
Why is this? Because the great assembly is dull-witted,
son of good family!
The arising of conditioned phenomena is also permanent;
because abiding is impermanent, arising is also impermanent.
Abiding is also permanent.
Because arising is impermanent, abiding is also impermanent.
Change would also be permanent;
however, because phenomena are impermanent, change is also impermanent.
Destruction is also permanent;
yet because that which was originally non-existent now exists, destruction is also impermanent. Good son!
By virtue of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), arising, abiding, change, and destruction are all eternal.
Because they perish moment by moment, they cannot be said to be eternal;
yet because this Great Nirvāṇa can sever and extinguish them, it is therefore called impermanent.
“Good son! As for contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), even before they have arisen, they already possess the nature of arising; therefore, arising can produce them.
As for uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), they fundamentally lack the nature of arising; therefore, arising cannot produce them.”
Just as fire possesses an inherent nature that manifests when it encounters conditions;
and as the eye possesses the nature of seeing, which sees because of form, light, and the mind;
so too is the birth of sentient beings: by virtue of an inherently existing nature, when they encounter the causal conditions of karma and the union of parents, birth occurs.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vairocanaraśmiprabha and eighty-four thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having heard this Dharma, leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees; with palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Having received the Tathāgata’s earnest instruction, I have, by means of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, finally attained awakening and understanding, hearing what was previously unheard; I have also enabled eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to deeply comprehend that all dharmas are neither born nor do they arise, and so forth.
“World-Honored One!
I have now understood and severed the web of all doubts.
However, there is a bodhisattva in this assembly named Abhaya who wishes to further inquire and receive instruction; I pray that you will deign to grant him your attention.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Abhaya:
"Good son! Ask whatever you wish; I shall analyze and explain it for you."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhayā and sixty thousand other bodhisattvas—according to another version, eighty-four thousand—rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What karma should the sentient beings of this land perform to be reborn in that Immovable World?
And how do the bodhisattvas of that land achieve the perfection of wisdom?
"The elephant-king among men possesses great majesty and virtue; having fully cultivated all practices, his sharp intelligence is swift and agile, such that he understands upon merely hearing.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Not harming the lives of sentient beings, Firmly upholding all the prohibitive precepts,"
Receiving the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous teaching, one will be born in the Immovable Land;
Not seizing the wealth of others, always bestowing kindness upon all,
and constructing monasteries for the Saṃgha, one will be born in the Immovable Land.
Not violating another’s wife, And not being unseasonable with one’s own;
By giving bedding and requisites to those who uphold the precepts, One is born in the Unshakable Land.
Neither for oneself nor for others, Seeking profit or out of fear,
Guarding one's speech and refraining from false words, one will be born in the Immovable Land;
do not harm spiritual friends and stay far away from evil associates;
speaking always with harmony through the mouth, one will be born in the Immovable Land.
Just as all bodhisattvas always refrain from harsh speech,
so that what they say is pleasing for others to hear, they are reborn in the Land of Immovability;
even in jest and laughter, they do not speak words at an improper time.
By always speaking with care, one will be born in the Immovable Land;
Seeing others receive gain and offerings, one should always give rise to a joyful heart;
Without giving rise to the fetter of envy, one will be born in the Immovable Land.
Not causing affliction to sentient beings, Always giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness,
And not producing evil through expedient means— Then one will be born in the Immovable Land.
Those with false views who say there is no giving, Nor parents, nor coming and going,
One who does not give rise to such views will be born in the Immovable Land;
One who digs fine wells along desolate roads, Plants groves of fruit-bearing trees,
And constantly gives food to beggars, Will be born in the Immovable Land.
If one offers even a single incense stick or lamp, or even presents a single flower, to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha,
one will be reborn in the Land of Immovability;
whether it be for the sake of fear, for gain and offerings, or for the sake of merit.
If one writes out even a single verse of this sutra,
one will be born in the Land of Immovability; if, for the sake of seeking merit and blessings,
one can read and recite this scripture for even a single day, one will be born in the Land of Immovability.
If, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, one observes the eightfold precepts and fast for a single day and night, one will be born in the Immovable Land;
one shall not dwell in the same place as those who have violated the grave prohibitions.
Those who revile and slander the Vaipulya sutras will be reborn in the Immovable Land;
those who can give even a single fruit to the sick and look after them with joy will be reborn in the Immovable Land.
One who does not misappropriate the property of the Saṃgha, Who carefully guards the property of the Buddha,
And who sweeps and cleans the grounds of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, Will be reborn in the Immovable Realm (Akaniṣṭha).
Even one who fashions an image or a stūpa for the Buddha As small as a thumb [will attain this merit].
If one constantly gives rise to a joyful mind, one will be born in the Immovable Land;
if, for the sake of this sutra, one gives one’s own body and wealth to the Dharma-preacher, one will be born in the Immovable Land.
"If one is able to hear, write down, receive and uphold,
and read and recite this secret treasury of all Buddhas, one will be born in the Land of Immovability.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Abhayamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have now understood that by the conditions of the karma one has created, one attains birth in that land.
This was the question previously asked by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhāsa-udāra-guṇarāja, who acts out of universal compassion for all sentient beings.”
If the Tathāgata were to speak, he would be able to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to humans, devas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
You should now listen with a sincere mind; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
There are causes and conditions by which one does not arrive at what has not yet been reached;
there are causes and conditions by which one arrives at what has not yet been reached.
Due to causes and conditions, one may reach or not reach;
due to causes and conditions, one may reach and reach.
"For what causes and conditions does one neither reach nor reach?"

"Good son! That which is 'not yet reached' is the Great Nirvana. Ordinary people have not yet reached it because they possess greed, anger, and ignorance; because their physical and verbal actions are impure; because they accept all manner of impure things; and because they commit the four grave offenses, slander the Vaipulya sutras, are icchantikas, or have committed the five heinous crimes."
For this reason, that which has not yet arrived does not arrive.
"Good son! For what cause and condition does that which has not yet arrived arrive?"
That which is "not yet arrived" is called Great Nirvana. For what reason is it "arrived"?

Because one has eternally severed greed, anger, and delusion, as well as the evils of body and speech; because one does not accept any impure things; because one does not commit the four grave offenses; because one does not slander the Vaipulya sutras; because one does not become an icchantika; and because one does not commit the five heinous crimes.
For this reason, it is called "reaching by not reaching.
One who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* reaches [the goal] after eighty thousand kalpas;
one who has attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* reaches it after sixty thousand kalpas.
The Anāgāmin arrives after forty thousand kalpas;
the Arhat arrives after twenty thousand kalpas;
and the Pratyekabuddha arrives after ten thousand kalpas.
For this reason, it is called "reaching that which is not reached.
"Good son! For what cause and condition is it called 'reaching the unreached'?"
"To arrive" refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
All sentient beings are constantly shrouded and obscured by immeasurable afflictions and fetters; they come and go without ceasing, like the turning of a wheel—this is what is meant by "to arrive."
Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have already attained permanent detachment from it, and are therefore said to be "not arriving";
yet, for the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings, they manifest within it, and are thus also said to be "arriving."
“Good son! For what reason is it called ‘reaching the reached’?
That which is ‘the reached’ refers to the twenty-five states of existence.”
All ordinary beings, from the *srotāpanna* up to the *anāgāmin*, because of the causes and conditions of their afflictions (*kleśa*), are said to "reach what has been reached.

Good son, it is the same with hearing what was not heard before: there is that which is not heard but is heard; there is that which is not heard and not heard; there is that which is heard but not heard; and there is that which is heard and heard.
"What is meant by 'hearing what has not been heard'? Good son,
that which is 'not heard' is named Great Nirvāṇa."
Why is it not heard?
Because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it is not sound, and because it is ineffable.
How, then, is it also heard?
"Because one hears its name—that is to say, 'permanence, bliss, self, and purity'—for this reason it is called 'hearing what has not been heard.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijña-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has said:
"The Great Nirvana cannot be heard.
Why, then, do you further say that permanence, bliss, self, and purity can be heard?
Why is this? World-Honored One!
One who has severed the afflictions is said to have attained nirvana.
If it has not yet been severed, it is called "not attained.
For this reason, the nature of nirvana is non-existent originally but exists now.
If worldly dharmas are non-existent originally but exist now, they are termed "impermanent."
For example, things such as a jar are originally non-existent and now exist; having existed, they return to non-existence, and are therefore called impermanent.
If Nirvana were like this, why would you say it is permanent, blissful, self, and pure?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Whatever is accomplished by means of adornment is entirely termed impermanent.
If nirvāṇa were likewise so, it should be impermanent."
What are these causes and conditions?

They are namely the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six perfections, the four immeasurable minds, the contemplation of the skeletal form, *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), the six bases of mindfulness, and the analytical deconstruction of the six elements. Such dharmas as these are all causes and conditions for accomplishing *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they are called "impermanent."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
There is that which is called 'impermanence.
If nirvana were an existent thing, it too would necessarily be impermanent."
As the Buddha previously stated in the Āgamas that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, all possess nirvāṇa, for this reason it is called impermanent.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Phenomena that can be perceived are called impermanent, as the Buddha previously taught:
'One who perceives Nirvana shall be able to sever all afflictions. "
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
For example, space is called 'eternal' because it is equally without obstruction for all sentient beings.
If Nirvana were likewise eternal and equal, why is it that some sentient beings attain Nirvana while others do not?"
If it were thus unequal toward all sentient beings, it could not be called "eternal.
"World-Honored One!
For example, suppose a hundred people share a single enemy; if this enemy is slain, many will experience happiness."
If nirvana were a dharma of equality, then when one person attains it, many should attain it; and when one person severs their fetters, many should likewise sever theirs.
If it were not so, how could it be called eternal?
"For example, if someone reveres, makes offerings to, respects, and praises a king, a prince, their parents, or their teachers, they will obtain gain and support; yet this is not called 'constant. "
Nirvana is likewise not called permanent.
Why is this? As the Buddha formerly told Ānanda in the *Āgama Sūtras*:
"If there is anyone who can revere nirvana, they shall sever their fetters and experience immeasurable bliss.
For this reason, it is not called "permanent."
“World-Honored One!
If there are names such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity within nirvāṇa, it cannot be called permanent.
If they do not exist, how can they be spoken of?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāsa-vyūha-udgata-guṇarāja, saying:
"The essence of nirvāṇa is not something that was originally non-existent and now exists."
If the essence of nirvāṇa were non-existent originally and came into being now, it would not be an untainted and eternally abiding dharma.

Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, its nature and characteristics abide eternally; because sentient beings are shrouded by afflictions, they do not see nirvāṇa and thus falsely claim it does not exist.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate their minds through the purification of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they perceive it after having severed the afflictions.
One should know that *nirvāṇa* is an eternally abiding dharma; it is not something that was previously non-existent and now exists, and for this reason, it is permanent.
“Good son! It is like a well filled with various kinds of the seven treasures within a dark room; people know they are there, yet they cannot see them because of the darkness.
A person of wisdom, well-versed in skillful means, lights a great bright lamp and carries it there to illuminate them, so that they may see them all clearly.”
Such a person would never give rise to the thought in this regard:
"The water and the seven treasures were originally non-existent but now exist.

It is the same with *nirvāṇa*: it has existed inherently from the beginning and is not something that has only just arisen; however, because of the darkness of afflictions (*kleśa*), sentient beings do not see it.
The Tathāgata of Great Wisdom, through skillful means, kindles the lamp of wisdom, enabling all bodhisattvas to perceive nirvāṇa as eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
Therefore, a wise person should not say of this nirvāṇa that it was originally non-existent and now exists.
“Good son! As for what you said:
‘Because it is accomplished through adornment, Nirvana should be impermanent.’”
This, too, is not so. Why? Good son!

The essence of nirvāṇa is neither born nor produced; it is neither real nor unreal; it is not produced by karma, nor is it a contaminated or conditioned phenomenon; it is neither heard nor seen; it does not fall [into saṃsāra] nor die; it possesses neither distinct characteristics nor identical characteristics; it neither departs nor returns; it is not of the past, future, or present; it is neither one nor many; it is neither long nor short; it is neither round nor square; it is neither pointed nor slanted; it is neither with marks nor without marks; it is neither name nor form; it is neither cause nor fruit; and it is neither self nor what belongs to a self.
For this reason, nirvana is permanent, eternal, and unchanging.
It is only after one has adorned oneself by cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas that one finally beholds it.
“Good son! It is like the water of eight flavors beneath the earth, which all sentient beings cannot obtain; yet a person of wisdom, by applying effort to dig, will surely find it.
Nirvāṇa is likewise.”

For example, it is like a blind person who cannot see the sun or the moon; when a skilled physician treats them, they are able to see them, yet these suns and moons did not previously exist and only now come to be.
Nirvana is also like this: it has existed from the beginning and is not something that has only just arisen now.
"Good son!
It is like a person who, having committed a crime, is bound and imprisoned; after a long time he is released and returns home to see his parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen.
Nirvāṇa is also like this."
“Good son! You say:
‘Because it arises from causes and conditions, the dharma of nirvāṇa should be impermanent.’”
This, too, is not so. Why is that? Good son!
There are five kinds of causes. What are the five? First, the productive cause;
second, the combinative cause; third, the stabilizing cause; fourth, the augmenting cause; and fifth, the remote cause.
What is the cause of production?
The cause of production refers to karma, afflictions, and so forth, as well as external seeds of grasses and trees; these are called the cause of production.
What is the cause of conjunction?
Just as the wholesome associates with the wholesome mind, the unwholesome with the unwholesome mind, and the indeterminate with the indeterminate mind—this is called the cause of association.
What is the cause of abiding?
It is like a house that does not collapse because there are pillars beneath it;
mountains, rivers, and trees abide and stand because they have the great earth as their cause.
Within, there are the four great elements, wherein immeasurable sentient beings afflicted by defilements find their abode; this is called the cause of abiding.
What is the cause of growth?
It is through causes and conditions such as clothing, food, and drink that sentient beings are made to grow.
Just as external seeds grow when they are not scorched by fire and not eaten by birds;
just as various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas grow by relying on harmony, superior spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and so forth;
and just as a child grows by relying on its father and mother—these are called causes of growth.
What is a remote cause?
For example, by means of incantations, demons cannot cause harm and poisons cannot take effect;
by relying upon a king, there are no thieves.

Just as a sprout depends on earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth; just as water-churning and human effort are remote causes for butter; just as light, form, and so forth are remote causes for consciousness; and just as the semen and blood of the parents are remote causes for sentient beings—such factors as the seasons are all termed remote causes.
“Good son! The essence of nirvāṇa is not produced by these five causes; how then can it be said to have impermanent causes?
Furthermore, good son!”
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes:
first, the producing cause (kāraka-hetu), and second, the revealing cause (vyañjaka-hetu).
For example, the potter’s wheel and cord are called the producing cause;
Just as lamps, candles, and the like illuminate objects in the dark, they are called "revealing causes" (*vijñapti-hetu*). Good son!
Great Nirvāṇa does not exist by virtue of a "producing cause" (*kāraka-hetu*), but only by virtue of a revealing cause.
The "cause of realization" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the six pāramitās; these are called the cause of realization.
Good son! Giving is a cause for nirvāṇa, but it is not the cause for great parinirvāṇa.
The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is what is called the cause of Great Nirvāṇa.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are causes for nirvāṇa, but not causes for Great Nirvāṇa;
only the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable auxiliary dharmas that assist enlightenment can be called the cause of Great Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it that giving does not qualify as being called the dānapāramitā?”
Why is it that giving is called the dāna-pāramitā,
while [the other perfections] up to prajñā are not likewise called the prajñā-pāramitā?
Why is it called *prajñāpāramitā*?
Why is it called *nirvāṇa*?
And why is it called *mahāparinirvāṇa*?
The Buddha said: “Good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa, he does not hear of giving and does not see giving; he does not hear of the dānapāramitā and does not see the dānapāramitā, and so on until he does not hear of prajñā and does not see prajñā; he does not hear of the prajñāpāramitā and does not see the prajñāpāramitā; he does not hear of nirvāṇa and does not see nirvāṇa; he does not hear of mahāparinirvāṇa and does not see mahāparinirvāṇa.”

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa, they know and see the dharma-realm; they understand that the true mark is empty and non-existent, devoid of any characteristic of combined cognition. They attain the mark of the untainted, the mark of non-action, and marks like an illusion, a mirage in the heat of the sun, a city of the Gandharvas, and the nature of empty space.

At that time, the bodhisattva attains such a mark as being free from greed, hatred, and delusion, neither hearing nor seeing; this is called the true mark of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and abiding in the true mark.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows for himself: "This is giving; this is the perfection of giving," and so on, up to: "This is wisdom; this is the perfection of wisdom"; "this is nirvāṇa; this is the Great Nirvāṇa."
“Good son! What is giving that is not a pāramitā?
To give only after seeing a beggar is called giving, but it is not a pāramitā;”
If one opens the heart to give spontaneously even when there is no beggar, this is called *dānapāramitā*.
If one gives only from time to time, it is merely called "giving," not a *pāramitā*;
if one practices constant giving, this is called *dānapāramitā*.
If, after giving to others, one subsequently gives rise to a mind of regret, this is called "giving," but it is not a *pāramitā*;
if, after giving, one does not regret it, this is then called the *dānapāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives with joy, generating a sense of fear regarding four things concerning wealth and property—namely, kings, thieves, water, and fire—this is called dānapāramitā.
If one practices giving with the expectation of a reward, it is called "giving," but not a *pāramitā*.
Giving without expecting a reward is what is called the *dānapāramitā*.

If one gives out of fear, for the sake of fame, gain, or profit, to maintain family traditions, to continue the five desires of the heavens, out of arrogance, out of pride of superiority, for the sake of acquaintances, or for the sake of a future return—this is like the practice of bartering in a marketplace.
"Good son!
It is like a person planting a tree for the sake of obtaining shade, flowers, fruits, and timber;
if a person practices giving in such a manner, it is called 'giving,' but not a 'pāramitā.'"

“When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices this Great Parinirvāṇa in such a manner, he does not perceive a giver, a recipient, or material wealth; he does not perceive time or season; he does not perceive a field of merit or a non-field of merit; he does not perceive causes, conditions, or karmic retribution; he does not perceive an agent or a recipient; he does not perceive much or little; he does not perceive purity or impurity; he does not disparage the recipient, himself, or his own wealth; he does not perceive one who sees or one who does not see; and he makes no calculation of self or other.”
One practices giving solely for the sake of the Great Parinirvāṇa, the eternally abiding Dharma;
one practices giving for the benefit of all sentient beings;
and one practices giving in order to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings.
For the sake of all sentient beings, one practices giving because one does not perceive a recipient, a giver, or material wealth. "Good son!
It is like a person who has fallen into the great ocean; by clinging to a corpse, they are able to cross over and be liberated."
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the giving of *dāna* while cultivating the Great *Nirvāṇa*, it is also like that corpse. "Good son!
It is as if there were a person imprisoned in a deep dungeon, its doors and gates firmly secured, with only a latrine hole through which he could escape to a place of freedom."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the giving of the Great Nirvāṇa, it is also like this. "Good son!
It is, for example, as when a person of noble status, facing terror and urgent distress with no one else to rely upon, takes refuge in a caṇḍāla."
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the path of the Great Nirvāṇa and engage in giving, it is also like this. "Good son!
It is, for example, like a sick person who, in order to eliminate the suffering of illness and attain peace and happiness, consumes impure substances."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the path of the Great Nirvāṇa and engage in giving, it is also like this.

"Good son! It is as when a Brahmin encounters a time of severe famine and, for the sake of his life, eats the flesh of a dog; yet, because he values his life above all else, he does not consider that act to be unwholesome."
The practice of giving by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa is likewise so. "Good son!

Such matters within the Great Nirvāṇa have not been heard for immeasurable kalpas, yet now they are heard. [These include] śīla and the śīla-pāramitā, up to prajñā and the prajñā-pāramitā, as explained at length in the Buddha’s *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*."
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa, hear what has not been heard?
The meanings of the twelve divisions of the sūtras are profound; though unheard from the past, they are now heard in their entirety by virtue of this sūtra.”
"Previously, although I had heard it, I heard only the names; now, through this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, I have come to hear its meaning.

Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas hear only the names of the twelve divisions of the scriptures but do not hear their meaning; now, through this sūtra, they hear them fully. This is called 'hearing what was not previously heard.'"

“Good son! Within all the sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one has never heard that the Buddha possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, nor that he does not undergo ultimate extinction; nor have they heard that the Three Jewels and the Buddha-nature possess the characteristic of non-differentiation, or that even those who have committed the four grave offenses, slandered the Vaipulya sūtras, committed the five heinous crimes, or are icchantikas, all possess Buddha-nature. Now, by hearing this within the present sūtra, it is called ‘hearing what was previously unheard.’”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Nineteen.
[Volume Twenty of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
supplemented by the Śramaṇa Huiyan and others of the Song Dynasty based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.]
Chapter Two: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Ārya-guṇarāja.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Ārya-guṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If those who have violated the grave prohibitions, slandered the Vaipulya sutras, committed the five heinous crimes, or are icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature, how is it that they still fall into hell?
World-Honored One!
If these beings possess Buddha-nature, why do you further speak of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity?
World-Honored One!
If those who have severed their roots of goodness are called icchantikas, then at the time when the roots of goodness are severed, how is it that the buddha-nature is not also severed?
If the buddha-nature were severed, how could you further say that it is permanent, blissful, self, and pure?
If they do not sever [the roots of goodness], for what reason are they called icchantikas?
World-Honored One, those who commit the four grave offenses are said to be indeterminate; [but these are not so].
Those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, commit the five heinous crimes, or are icchantikas are all termed "indeterminate.
If such individuals were fixed [in their destiny], how could they ever attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
From the stage of srotāpanna up to the pratyekabuddha, these are also called "indeterminate.
If those from the srotāpanna to the pratyekabuddha were determinate, they would not be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Blessed One!
If the transgression of the four grave offenses is not fixed, then the stages from srotāpanna up to pratyekabuddha are also not fixed.
Since these are not fixed, even the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise not fixed."
If the Buddha is not fixed, the essential nature of Nirvana is likewise not fixed, and it extends to all phenomena being likewise not fixed.
Why are they not fixed?
If an icchantika were to abandon the state of an icchantika, he would then attain the Buddha-way.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, should likewise be thus: having entered nirvāṇa, they should also emerge from it again, rather than remaining in nirvāṇa.
If this were the case, the nature of nirvāṇa would be indeterminate.
Because they are indeterminate, one should know that there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity.
Why, then, do you say that icchantikas and others shall attain nirvana?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”

It is for the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to attain peace and happiness; out of compassion and loving-kindness for all the world; and for the sake of increasing and inspiring those bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds upon awakening—that he asks such questions.

“Good son! You have already drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past; you have planted roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas; long ago you accomplished the merits of Bodhi; you have subdued the various Māras, causing them to retreat and disperse; you have already taught immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, leading them all to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; long ago you thoroughly penetrated the profound and secret treasury possessed by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; and you have already questioned immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, regarding such profound and subtle meanings.”
I do not see anyone in the entire world—whether among humans or devas, śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, Māras or Brahmās—who is able to question the Tathāgata regarding this matter.
Now, listen attentively and listen attentively with a sincere heart; I shall analyze and expound this for you.
"Good son! Even the icchantika is not fixed."
If it were fixed, those of the icchantika nature would ultimately never be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because it is not fixed, they are therefore able to attain it.
Regarding what you have said:
"If the Buddha-nature is uninterrupted, how can an icchantika sever their roots of goodness?
O son of good family!
There are two kinds of roots of goodness:
first, internal; second, external.
Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external.
For this reason, the Buddha-nature is uninterrupted.
Furthermore, it is of two kinds:
first, that which is with outflows (sāsrava), and second, that which is without outflows (anāsrava).
The Buddha-nature is neither with outflows nor without outflows; therefore, it is not severed.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the permanent; second, the impermanent.
The Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent; therefore, it is not severed.
If it were subject to severance, it would have to be regained;
since it is not regained, it is called "unsevered."
If one has severed [the roots of goodness] and yet attained them again, they are called icchantikas.

"Those who have committed the four grave offenses are also indeterminate; if it were determinate, those who have violated the four grave prohibitions would never be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Defaming the Vaipulya sutras is likewise not fixed; for if it were fixed, those who defame the Dharma of the True Person would never be able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Committing the five heinous crimes is likewise not fixed; if it were fixed, those who have committed the five heinous crimes would never be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Form and the characteristics of form—both are indeterminate.

The characteristics of fragrance, taste, and touch; the characteristics of birth up to the characteristics of ignorance; the characteristics of the aggregates, bases, and elements; the characteristics of the twenty-five states of existence, the four modes of birth, and even all dharmas—all are likewise indeterminate."

“Good son! It is like a magician who, in the midst of a great assembly, conjures the four divisions of the army—chariots, infantry, elephants, and horses—as well as various ornaments for adorning the body, cities, towns, villages, mountains, forests, trees, springs, ponds, rivers, and wells. Among that assembly, there are young children lacking wisdom who, upon seeing these things, take them all to be real.”
Among them, the wise know it to be false and deceptive, for by the power of illusion it deludes the eyes of men. Good son!
It is likewise with all ordinary beings, up to and including śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who perceive fixed characteristics in all phenomena.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not perceive fixed characteristics in any phenomena. "Good son!
It is like a small child who, during the midsummer months, sees a mirage and calls it water."
A person of wisdom will never conceive the notion of real water regarding these shimmering mirages; they are merely empty vapors that deceive the eyes, and are not actually water.
All ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas likewise perceive all dharmas in this way, asserting them all to be real;
whereas Buddhas and bodhisattvas do not perceive any fixed characteristics in any dharma.
“Good son! It is like an echo produced in a mountain ravine by sound; when children hear it, they take it to be a real voice.
A person of wisdom understands that it has no fixed reality, but is merely the appearance of sound deceiving the auditory consciousness.”
"Good son!
It is likewise with all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas regarding all phenomena: they perceive fixed characteristics.

The bodhisattvas, however, understand that all phenomena are entirely devoid of fixed characteristics; they perceive the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristics of emptiness and quiescence, and the characteristic of neither arising nor ceasing."
For this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as having the characteristic of impermanence.
"Good son, there is also the characteristic of certainty."
What is meant by "concentration"?
It is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Where do these reside?
This is what is called nirvana.
"Good son, the fruit of srotāpanna is likewise not fixed; because it is not fixed, after eighty thousand kalpas, one attains the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin is likewise not fixed; because it is not fixed, after sixty thousand kalpas, one attains the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The fruit of the Anāgāmin is likewise not fixed; because it is not fixed, after forty thousand kalpas, one attains the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The fruit of the Arhat is likewise not fixed; because it is not fixed, after twenty thousand kalpas, one attains the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The path of the pratyekabuddha is likewise not fixed; because it is not fixed, after ten thousand kalpas, one attains the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Good son! The Tathāgata now, between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, manifests reclining upon a lion bed, desiring to enter parinirvāṇa. This causes great sorrow and suffering to arise among my disciples who have not yet attained the fruit of arhatship, as well as among the Mallas; it also causes the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others to make grand offerings.”

He wished to have his body wrapped in a thousand pieces of fine cotton cloth, placed in a coffin made of the seven precious gems, filled with fragrant oil, and piled high with various types of incense wood, so that it might be cremated by fire; yet there were two pieces that could not be burned:
the one directly against the body and the one on the very outside.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he distributed his relics into eight portions.
All the śrāvaka disciples then said,
"The Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa."
"You should know that the Tathāgata likewise does not definitively enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and immutable."
For this reason, the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa is likewise not fixed.
"Good son! You should know that the Tathāgata is also not fixed."
The Tathāgata is not a deva. Why?
Because there are four kinds of devas:
First, the worldly gods; second, the born gods; third, the pure gods; and fourth, the ultimate gods.
Worldly gods are such as various kings;
born gods range from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
The "Pure Heavens" (*śuddhāvāsa*) refer to those from the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the pratyekabuddha;
the "Heavens of Meaning" (*arthadeva*) refer to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
For what reason are the bodhisattvas of the ten stages called "Heavens of Meaning"?
Because they are able to skillfully understand the meaning of all phenomena.
What is meant by "meaning"?
It is seeing that the meaning of all phenomena is emptiness.

“Good son! The Tathāgata is not a king, nor is he the gods of the Four Great Kings, up to and including the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; he is not from the stage of Srotāpanna up to Pratyekabuddha, nor is he a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes. For this reason, the Tathāgata is not a deva; yet all sentient beings also call the Buddha the ‘Deva among Devas.’”
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a deva, nor is he a non-deva; he is not a human, nor is he a non-human;
he is not a ghost, nor is he a non-ghost; he is not a hell-being, an animal, or a hungry ghost, nor is he a non-hell-being, non-animal, or non-hungry ghost;
he is not a sentient being, nor is he a non-sentient being; he is not the Dharma, nor is he...
It is not dharma, neither form nor non-form; neither long nor non-long; neither short nor non-short;
neither characteristic nor non-characteristic; neither mind nor non-mind; neither with outflows nor without outflows;
neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither permanent nor impermanent.
It is neither illusion nor non-illusion; neither name nor non-name; neither fixed nor non-fixed;
neither existent nor non-existent; neither speech nor non-speech; neither Tathāgata nor non-Tathāgata.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is not fixed.
"Good son! For what reason is the Tathāgata not called a worldly deva?"
"Worldly devas" refers to various kings.
Since the Tathāgata has long since relinquished the royal throne throughout immeasurable kalpas, he is not a king.
Yet, he is not "not a king," for the Tathāgata was born into the household of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu; therefore, he is not "not a king."
"He is not one who is born in heaven, for the Tathāgata has long since been detached from all states of existence; therefore, he is not one who is born in heaven.
Nor is he not one who is born in heaven. Why is this?"
Because he ascends to Tuṣita and descends to Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata is not "not born in heaven.
Nor is he a "pure god. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is not a srotāpanna, nor even a pratyekabuddha; therefore, the Tathāgata is not a pure deva, yet he is not a non-pure deva. Why is this?
He cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, just as a lotus flower is not stained by dust or water; therefore, the Tathāgata is not the Non-Pure Heaven.
Nor is he the Heaven of Meaning.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is not a bodhisattva of the ten stages; therefore, the Tathāgata is not the "Heaven of Meaning" (Arthadhatu), nor is he the "Non-Heaven of Meaning."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata constantly cultivates the meaning of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the Tathāgata is not a non-meaningful deva.
"The Tathāgata is not a human."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has long been free from the state of being a human throughout immeasurable kalpas; therefore, he is not a human.
Nor is he a non-human.
Why is this? Because he was born in the city of Kapilavastu, he is therefore not a non-human.
"The Tathāgata is not a ghost."
Why is this? Because he does not harm any sentient beings, he is therefore not a ghost;
nor is he a non-ghost.
Why is this? Because he also transforms sentient beings through the manifestation of ghostly forms, he is therefore not "not a ghost.
Likewise, the Tathāgata is also not hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has long since departed from all evil karma; therefore, he is not among the denizens of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, nor is he not among those who are not in hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata also manifests and takes on bodies within the three evil realms to transform sentient beings; therefore, he is not non-existent in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
"Nor is he a sentient being. Why?
Because he has long since distanced himself from the nature of sentient beings; therefore, the Tathāgata is not a sentient being."
Nor is he not a sentient being.
Why? Because at times he expounds the characteristics of sentient beings; therefore, the Tathāgata is not "not a sentient being."
“The Tathāgata is not a dharma.
Why is this? All dharmas each possess distinct characteristics, whereas the Tathāgata is not so; he possesses only a single characteristic. Therefore, he is not a dharma.”
Nor is it non-dharma. Why?
Because it is the dharma-realm of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is not non-dharma.
“The Tathāgata is not form. Why?
Because he is not subsumed within the ten bases of form; therefore, he is not form.”
Nor is it non-form. Why?
Because the body possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; therefore, it is not non-form.
“The Tathāgata is not long.
Why? Because he has severed all forms; therefore, he is not long.”
Nor is it not long. Why?
Because no one in the entire world is able to see the mark of the uṣṇīṣa; therefore, it is not the case that it is not long.
“The Tathāgata is not short. Why?
Because he has long since distanced himself from the fetter of pride; therefore, he is not short.”
Nor is it not short. Why?
Because for the sake of the householder Ghoṣila, he manifested a body of three feet; therefore, it is not not short.
“The Tathāgata is not characterized by marks. Why is this?
Because he has long since been far removed from all characteristics and their marks; therefore, he is not characterized by marks.”
Nor is it non-characteristic. Why?
Because one thoroughly knows all characteristics; therefore, it is not non-characteristic.
“The Tathāgata is not mind. Why?
Because he has the characteristic of space; therefore, he is not mind.”
Nor is it not mind. Why?
Because it possesses the mental factors of the ten powers and is also able to know the minds of other sentient beings; therefore, it is not non-mind.
“The Tathāgata is not conditioned. Why?
Because he is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; therefore, he is not conditioned.”
Nor is it unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Why?
Because there is coming, going, sitting, reclining, and the manifestation of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is not unconditioned.
“The Tathāgata is not eternal.
Why? Because his body has constituent parts; therefore, he is not eternal.”
Why is it not eternal?
Because it possesses cognition.
Eternal phenomena are devoid of cognition, just like space.
The Tathāgata possesses knowledge; therefore, he is not eternal.
Why is he not eternal?
Because there is verbal expression.
The eternal Dharma is wordless, just like empty space;
the Tathāgata possesses speech, and for this reason he is impermanent.
Because he has a family name, he is called impermanent.
The dharma that is without lineage is called "eternal.
Because space is eternal, it has no clan or surname;
the Tathāgata, however, has a lineage—his clan is Gautama—and for this reason, he is impermanent.
Because there are parents, it is called impermanent;
that which has no parents is called permanent.
Since space is permanent, it has no parents.
The Buddha has parents; therefore, he is impermanent.
To possess the four modes of deportment is called impermanence;
to be without the four modes of deportment is what is called permanence.
Because space is eternal, it lacks the four modes of deportment;
the Buddha possesses these four modes, and therefore he is impermanent.
A phenomenon that abides eternally has no spatial location.
Because space is eternal, it has no location;
the Tathāgata appeared in the land of East India, dwelling in Śrāvastī or Rājagṛha, and for this reason, he is impermanent.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is not eternal.
Nor is he non-eternal. Why is this?
Because birth has been eternally severed,
that which possesses the nature of birth is called impermanent;
that which possesses the nature of non-birth is called permanent.
The Tathāgata is without birth; therefore, he is eternal.
That which is an eternal dharma has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); those dharmas that possess an intrinsic nature are called impermanent.
The Tathāgata is without birth and without intrinsic nature; because he is without birth and without intrinsic nature, he is eternal.
The principle of permanence pervades all places, just like space, which exists everywhere;
the Tathāgata is likewise, pervading all places, and is therefore eternal.
Regarding impermanent phenomena, some say they exist here while others say they do not exist there.
The Tathāgata is not like this; it cannot be said that he exists in one place and does not exist in another. Therefore, he is eternal.
The nature of impermanence is sometimes existent and sometimes non-existent.
The Tathāgata is not like this; he is neither sometimes existent nor sometimes non-existent, and for this reason, he is eternal.
The eternally abiding Dharma has no name and no form.
Because space is eternal, it has no name and no form.
The Tathāgata is likewise; having no name and no form, he is therefore eternal.
The eternally abiding dharma has neither cause nor effect.
Because space is eternal, it has neither cause nor effect.
The Tathāgata is likewise: having neither cause nor effect, he is therefore eternal.
The eternally abiding Dharma is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
The Tathāgata is likewise; being not subsumed within the three periods of time, he is therefore eternal.
"The Tathāgata is not an illusion."
Why is this? Because they have forever severed all deceitful minds, they are not illusions;
yet they are also not non-illusions.

Why is this? The Tathāgata may at times divide this single body into immeasurable bodies, and those immeasurable bodies may again become a single body. He passes straight through mountains and walls without obstruction; he treads upon water as if on land, enters the earth as if it were water, and travels through space as if on ground. His body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire, and clouds and thunder shake with a terrifying sound. He may manifest as cities, villages, houses, mountains, rivers, and trees; he may assume a massive body or a minute body, or take the form of a male, a female, a boy, or a girl.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is also not non-illusory.
"The Tathāgata is not fixed. Why is this?"
Because the Tathāgata manifested entry into parinirvāṇa here between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, it is therefore not fixed;
nor is it not fixed.
Why is this? Because it is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, the Tathāgata is also not non-definitive.
The Tathāgata is not subject to outflows (*āsrava*).
Why is this? Because it has severed the three outflows (*āsrava*), it is not "with outflow" (*sāsrava*).
As for the three outflows: all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), are called the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*).
All afflictions of the form and formless realms, with the exception of ignorance, are called outflows;
the ignorance of the three realms is called the outflow of ignorance.
The Tathāgata has eternally severed these, and therefore they are no longer outflows.
"Furthermore, all ordinary persons do not perceive outflows (*āsrava*).
How is it that ordinary persons do not perceive outflows?
All ordinary persons harbor doubts regarding the future life: [text continues]"
In future ages, will one obtain a body?
Or will one not obtain a body?
In past ages, did the body fundamentally exist?
Is it originally non-existent?
Within the present world, does this body exist,
or does this body not exist?
If there were a self, would it be form?
Or would it be non-form?
Or would it be both form and non-form?
Is it neither form nor non-form?
Is it perception?
Or is it non-perception?
Is it perception? Is it non-perception?
Is it neither perception nor non-perception?
Does this body belong to another?
Is it not belonging to another?
Is it both belonging and not belonging?
Is it neither belonging nor not belonging?
Is there life without a body?
Is there a body without life?
Or is there both body and life?
Is there no body and no life?
Are the body and the life permanent,
or are they impermanent?
Is it eternal or impermanent?
Is it neither eternal nor impermanent?
Are the body and the life-force created by an autonomous creator?
Is it produced by time?
Is it produced without cause?
Or is it produced by primordial nature (prakṛti)?
Is it created by atoms?
Is it created by dharma or adharma?
Is it created by a person (puruṣa)?
Are afflictions created by others?
Are they created by one's parents?
Or do they dwell within my own mind?
Does it abide within the eyes?
Does it pervade the entire body?
From where does it come?
Where does one go?
Who is born? Who dies?
"In the past, was I of the Brahmin caste?
Was I of the Kṣatriya caste?
Or was I of the Vaiśya caste?"
"Is this the Śūdra caste?
What caste shall I obtain in the future?
As for this body of mine, was it a male body in the past?"
Is this a woman’s body?
Or is it the body of an animal?
If I were to kill them, would there be sin?
Is it without fault?
Or even in the case of drinking alcohol, is there fault?
Or is it without fault?
"Is this created by myself?
Is it created by another?
Do I receive the retribution?"
"Is it that the body receives retribution?
Such views of doubt and immeasurable afflictions shroud the minds of sentient beings.
"Because of these views of doubt, six kinds of mind arise:"

To hold that there definitely is a self, or that there definitely is no self; to see a self in what is a self, or to see a self in what is not a self; or to hold that "I am the agent," "I am the experiencer," and "I am the knower"—these are called wrong views.
The Tathāgata has forever uprooted the roots of such immeasurable outflows of views;
therefore, they are no longer outflows. "Good son!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who practices the noble path toward Great Nirvāṇa likewise attains the permanent severance of all such outflows."
All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, constantly cultivate the noble practices; therefore, they are without outflows (*anāsrava*). "Good son!
Ordinary beings who cannot properly restrain the five sense faculties possess the three outflows; led by evil, they go to unwholesome places."
“Good son! It is like a wicked horse, whose nature is perverse and unruly, which can cause its rider to reach a place of danger and evil.
It is the same with one who cannot properly restrain these five faculties; it causes a person to depart from the good path to Nirvana and arrive at various places of evil.”
"It is like a wild elephant whose mind has not yet been tamed: if someone mounts it, it does not go as desired, but instead leaves the city or town and goes to a desolate wilderness."
It is just the same for one who cannot properly restrain these five faculties; such a person will be led far away from the city of Nirvana and brought to the wilderness of birth and death.

“Good son! For example, just as a sycophantic minister instructs a king to commit evil, so too are the five faculties like sycophantic ministers; they constantly instruct sentient beings to create immeasurable evils.”
“Good son! It is like a wicked child who, refusing to accept the instructions of teachers, elders, parents, or ancestors, commits every kind of evil.
It is the same with the failure to discipline the five faculties: refusing to accept the wholesome instructions of teachers and elders, there is no evil that one will not commit.”

“Good son! Ordinary people do not restrain their five sense faculties; they are constantly harmed by the marauders of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, just as enemies and thieves harm virtuous people.”
"Good son! Ordinary persons do not restrain their five sense faculties and thus run wild among the five objects of desire.
It is like a cowherd who fails to guard his cattle well, allowing them to trespass upon and destroy the crops."
Ordinary worldlings do not restrain the five sense faculties and thus constantly dwell amidst the various realms of existence, undergoing much suffering and affliction. "Good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa and practices the noble conduct, he is always able to skillfully harmonize and guard the five sense faculties, fearing greed, anger, delusion, arrogance, and envy, for the sake of attaining all wholesome dharmas."
“Good son! If one can skillfully guard these five faculties, one will be able to collect the mind; if one can collect the mind, one will be able to govern the five faculties.
It is like a person who protects the king thereby protects the kingdom, and one who protects the kingdom thereby protects the king.”
It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: if they hear this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they obtain wisdom;
because they obtain wisdom, they obtain focused mindfulness.
If the five faculties are scattered, mindfulness can bring them to rest. Why is this?
Because this mindfulness is wisdom.
“Good son! Just as a skilled herdsman, if his oxen should wander east or west to devour the crops of others, immediately restrains them so they do not commit such violence;
so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: by means of mindfulness and wisdom, he guards and gathers the five sense faculties, preventing them from running wild and scattering.”

“A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who possesses mindfulness and wisdom does not perceive the mark of a self, nor does he perceive the mark of what belongs to a self; he does not perceive sentient beings or their objects of enjoyment. He perceives all phenomena as identical to the characteristic of the dharma-nature, giving rise to the perception of them as being like earth, stone, tiles, and rubble.”
For example, just as a house arises from a multitude of conditions and lacks any fixed nature,
one observes that all sentient beings are established through the four great elements and the five aggregates, and by investigating them, finds they lack a fixed nature.
Because there is no fixed nature, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to greedy attachment toward it.
All ordinary people give rise to afflictions because they perceive the existence of sentient beings.
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa and possesses mindfulness and wisdom, he does not give rise to greedy attachment toward sentient beings.
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra does not cling to the mark of sentient beings nor to the various marks of dharmas."
Good son! It is like a painter who, using various colors, paints many images—whether of men, women, oxen, or horses.
Ordinary worldlings, being ignorant, perceive the marks of male, female, and so forth when they see them;
yet a painter fully understands that no such males or females exist.

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: regarding the diverse characteristics of phenomena, he contemplates them as a single characteristic, and ultimately never gives rise to the notion of a "sentient being."
Why is this? Because they possess mindfulness and wisdom.
When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa, even if he should at times behold a beautiful woman, he will never give rise to a mind of greedy attachment.
Why is this? Because they skillfully observe characteristics.
"Good son!..."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that the phenomena of the five desires contain no true joy and cannot endure for even a moment; they are like a dog gnawing on a dry bone, like a person carrying fire while walking against the wind, like a basket of venomous snakes, like what is obtained in a dream, like a fruit tree by the roadside trampled by many people, like a piece of meat pursued by a flock of crows, like bubbles on the water, like the tracks of drawing on water, like the end of a weaving thread, or like a prisoner heading to the market—just as with borrowed goods, their power cannot last long.
Contemplating desire in this way, one sees that it contains many faults and evils. "Furthermore, good son,

the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates how all sentient beings, for the sake of the causes and conditions of form, fragrance, flavor, and touch, have constantly experienced suffering and affliction since countless and immeasurable kalpas in the past."

The bones accumulated by each and every sentient being within a single kalpa would equal Mount Vipula at Rājagṛha; the milk they have drunk would equal the waters of the four great oceans; and the blood shed from their bodies would exceed even that. The tears shed from the eyes while wailing over the deaths of parents, brothers, wives, children, and kinsmen would exceed the volume of the four great oceans. Even if one were to take all the grasses and trees upon the earth and chop them into counting-slips to tally the number of parents, one could not reach the end of them.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, whether in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, the suffering of conditioned existence they have endured is beyond calculation.
One might easily exhaust the entirety of this great earth by reducing it to the size of jujube pits, yet the measurelessness of birth and death can never be exhausted.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas contemplate all sentient beings in this way, they see that because of the causes and conditions of desire, these beings undergo immeasurable suffering.
Because of this suffering inherent in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the Bodhisattvas do not lose their mindfulness and wisdom.
“Good son! It is like this:
suppose there were a great multitude of people filling twenty-five *li* in the world, and a king commanded an official to carry a bowl of oil through their midst without spilling a drop, saying:
‘If you lose even a single drop, I shall take your life.’”
Furthermore, he sent another man behind him with a drawn sword to follow and intimidate him.

Having received the king’s command, the minister maintained his resolve with all his heart as he passed through the midst of that great multitude. Although he saw various enticing objects of the fivefold sensual desires, he constantly thought to himself:
"If I were to become negligent and attached to those perverse desires, I would abandon what I hold; my life would not be fully preserved."
"Because of these causes and conditions of fear, that person would not spill even a single drop of oil.
In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not lose mindfulness or wisdom within the cycle of birth and death."
Because they do not lose [this mindfulness], even though they see the five desires, their minds do not become greedily attached.
If they see pure forms, they do not give rise to the perception of form, but observe only the characteristic of suffering;

this applies likewise to the characteristics of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. They do not construct perceptions of arising, nor perceptions of cessation, nor perceptions of causes, but observe them as the characteristic of conditioned conjunction.
At that time, the bodhisattva’s five faculties are pure;
because the faculties are pure, he is fully endowed with the precepts for guarding the faculties.
The five faculties of all ordinary worldlings are impure and cannot be properly maintained; this is called "leakage of the faculties."
The Bodhisattva has eternally severed them; therefore, they are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The Tathāgata has uprooted and eternally severed their very root;
therefore, he is not subject to outflows. "Furthermore, good son!
Furthermore, there is the abandonment of outflows (*āsrava*):
the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, desiring the fruit of Buddhahood—the unsurpassed nectar—abandons evil outflows.
How does he abandon them?
If one can practice the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*—by copying it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, explaining it, and contemplating its meaning—this is called "detachment."
Why is this? Good son!
