Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, I do not see any that can bring about freedom from evil outflows like this Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
“Good son! It is like a skilled master who instructs his disciples; among those disciples, there are some who receive the teaching and do not commit evil in their minds.
It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa: his mind does not commit evil.”
“Good son! It is like a worldly skillful incantation: if one hears it but once, for seven years thereafter they will not be affected by any poisonous drugs, nor can snakes bite them;
if there are those who recite it, until the end of their lives, no evils shall befall them.”
"Good son!
This *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is likewise: if there are sentient beings who hear it but once, they shall not fall into the evil realms for seven kalpas thereafter;

if they copy it down, read and recite it, explain it, or contemplate its meaning, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and clearly perceive the Buddha-nature, just as that holy king obtained the taste of ambrosia."
“Good son! This *Mahāparinirvāṇa* possesses such immeasurable merits as these. Good son!”

If there are those who can copy this sutra, read and recite it, explain it, expound it for others, and contemplate its meaning, you should know that such persons are truly my disciples; they have well received my teaching, they are what I behold, and they are what I keep in mind. Such persons truly know that I do not enter parinirvāṇa.

Wherever such a person may dwell—whether in a city or town, a village, a mountain forest, a wilderness, a house, a field or estate, a tower, or a hall—I too shall always abide therein, never departing.
I constantly act as a recipient of offerings from these people, appearing either as a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, an upāsikā, a brāhmaṇa, a brahmacārī, or a poor beggar.
"How may this person know that the Tathāgata has accepted their gift? Good son!

This person may, while sleeping at night in a dream, see the image of a Buddha, or the image of a deva, the image of a śramaṇa, the image of a sovereign, a noble king, or a lion king; or the form of a lotus flower, or the form of an udumbara flower; or they may see a great mountain, or the waters of a vast ocean; or they may see the sun or the moon; or they may see the image of a white elephant or a white horse; or they may see their parents, or obtain flowers, fruits, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and other such jewels, or the five products of the cow. At such times, one should know that it is the Tathāgata who has accepted their gift."
Having awakened, he experiences joy and happiness, immediately obtaining all manner of necessary things; his mind does not dwell on evil, and he delights in cultivating wholesome dharmas. Good son!
This *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is fully capable of accomplishing such immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), inconceivable, and boundless merits.
“Good son! You should now believe and accept my words.
If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to see me, who wish to pay homage to me, who wish to—”
Seeing me through the same nature of phenomena (dharmatā), desiring to attain the samādhi of emptiness, desiring to see the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa),
desiring to practice the Śūraṅgama-samādhi and the Lion-King Samādhi, and desiring to destroy the eight māras— the eight māras being the so-called four māras,
as well as impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity— desiring...
Those who wish to attain the bliss of humans and devas should, upon seeing anyone who upholds the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*,
copies it, recites it, explains it to others, or contemplates its meaning, approach them, rely upon them,
seek instruction from them, make offerings to them, revere, respect, and praise them, and wash [their feet].
With one's own hands and feet, one should prepare the bedding and provide the four requisites so that there is nothing lacking.
If they have come from afar, one should go ten *yojanas* along the road to welcome them.
For the sake of this sutra, one should offer whatever precious things one possesses;
if such things are lacking, one should even sell one's own body. Why is this?
This sutra is more difficult to encounter than the udumbara flower. "Good son!

I recall that in the past, immeasurable and boundless nayuta kalpas ago, there was a world named Sahā. In that world, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who proclaimed this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the great assembly."
At that time, I heard from a virtuous friend that the Buddha was about to preach the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* for the great assembly.
Having heard this, my heart was filled with joy, and I desired to provide offerings.
Living in poverty and possessing nothing, he wished to sell himself; however, due to his meager merit, he could not find a buyer and was about to return home.
On the road, he saw a man and spoke to him, saying:
"I wish to sell myself; would you be able to buy me?"
The man replied,
“The work of my household is such that no one else can endure it.
If you are capable of performing it, I shall purchase you.”
I then asked: "What kind of work is there that no one is capable of performing?
That person replied:
"I have a malignant disease, and a skilled physician prescribed medicine for me, saying:
'You must consume three *liang* of human flesh every day.
If you can provide me with three *liang* of your own flesh daily, I shall give you five gold coins."
Having heard this, my heart was filled with joy.
I spoke again, saying:
"Give me some money and lend me seven days; once my business is finished, I shall immediately return to you."
The man replied:
"Seven days will not do.
If you can truly do so, then one day may be granted."

"Good son! At that time, I immediately took those coins, returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated with my head at his feet, offered all that I possessed as a tribute, and thereafter listened to and received this sutra with a sincere heart."
At that time, I was dull-witted; although I heard the sutra, I could only master the words and phrases of a single verse:
"The Tathāgata has realized nirvāṇa, Having forever severed birth and death;
If one listens with a sincere heart, One shall always obtain immeasurable bliss."
"Having received these verses, I immediately returned to the house of that sick man. 'Good son!

Although I gave him two or three pieces of meat every day, because of the causal conditions of recollecting those verses, I did not feel any pain; I did not cease my practice daily, and it was fulfilled for a full month.'"
“Good son! By these causes and conditions, my illness was cured and my body was restored to health without any scars or sores.
At that time, seeing my body fully complete and intact, I immediately gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"If even the power of a single verse can be such as this, how much more so for one who fully possesses, upholds, reads, and recites it?
Seeing that this sutra has such benefits, I redouble my resolve:
'May I, in the future, attain the path of Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.'"
“Good son! By the power of the causes and conditions of this single verse, I am able today, amidst this great assembly, to proclaim it in its entirety for the sake of all devas and humans.”
“Good son! For these reasons, this *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is inconceivable; it accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit, and is the profound and secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.”

For this reason, those who are able to receive and uphold [this teaching] sever and abandon evil outflows. That which is called "evil" refers to: wild elephants, wild horses, wild oxen, and wild dogs; dwellings of venomous snakes; lands of thorny brambles; precipitous cliffs and dangerous banks; violent waters and eddies; wicked people, wicked countries, wicked cities, wicked houses, and wicked associates, and so forth.
Regarding such persons as these: if they act as a cause for outflows (*āsrava*), the Bodhisattva immediately distances himself from them;
if they cannot so act, he does not distance himself. If they increase the outflows, he then distances himself from them; if they do not increase them, he does not distance himself.
If they perform unwholesome dharmas, he then distances himself from them; if they can perform wholesome dharmas, he does not distance himself.
What is meant by "separation"?

It is not to carry weapons or staves, but to always distance oneself through the skillful means of right wisdom; therefore, it is called "separation through right wisdom," whereby one abandons unwholesome dharmas in order to give rise to wholesome dharmas.

“The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates his own body as being like a disease, like a sore, like an abscess, like an enemy, and like an arrow piercing the body; it is a great mass of suffering and the root of all that is wholesome and unwholesome.”
Although this body is thus impure, the bodhisattva nevertheless regards it with care and sustains it.
Why is this? It is not for the sake of craving the body, but for the sake of wholesome dharmas.
It is for the sake of nirvana, not for the sake of birth-and-death;
it is for the sake of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, not for the sake of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
it is for the sake of the path to bodhi, not for the sake of the mundane path.
It is for the sake of the One Vehicle, not for the sake of the Three Vehicles;
it is for the sake of the subtle body endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, not for the sake of even the body of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
it is for the sake of becoming a Wheel-Turning Dharma King, not for the sake of becoming a worldly Wheel-Turning King.
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should always protect his body. Why is this?
If one does not protect the body, life will not be preserved;
if life is not preserved, then one will be unable to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it extensively for others, or contemplate its meaning.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should skillfully protect the body.
For this reason, the bodhisattva attains liberation from all evil outflows. "Good son!
Just as one wishing to cross water carefully protects their boat or raft;
as one on the road carefully protects a fine horse;
and as a farmer planting crops carefully protects his manure.
Just as one carefully protects a venomous snake to neutralize its poison;
just as a person guards a *caṇḍāla* for the sake of wealth;
or just as one nurtures and protects a valiant general in order to defeat bandits.
It is also like a person suffering from cold who cherishes and protects fire;
or like a leper who seeks out poisonous medicine.

So it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: although they see that this body is filled with immeasurable impurities, for the sake of upholding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they still cherish and protect it, ensuring it does not fail.
“A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that there is no duality between a wicked elephant and a wicked spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Why is this? Because both cause the destruction of the body.”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas feel no fear toward wicked elephants and the like, yet they give rise to a sense of dread toward evil associates (pāpamitra). Why is this?
It is because such wicked elephants can only destroy the body but cannot destroy the mind, whereas evil associates destroy both.
These evil elephants and the like destroy only a single body, whereas evil associates destroy immeasurable bodies of goodness and immeasurable minds of goodness;
these evil elephants and the like can destroy only this impure, foul-smelling body, whereas evil associates can destroy the pure body and the pure mind;
these evil elephants and the like can destroy the physical body, whereas evil associates destroy the Dharma-body.
Killed by an evil elephant, one does not necessarily fall into the three miserable realms; however, killed by an evil friend, one will certainly go to the three miserable realms.
Such an evil elephant and the like are merely enemies to the body, whereas an evil spiritual friend is an enemy to the wholesome Dharma.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should always remain far removed from evil associates.
Such outflows as these are not abandoned by ordinary persons, and thus they give rise to outflows;
because the bodhisattva abandons them, outflows do not arise.
If even a bodhisattva such as this has no outflows, how much less so the Tathāgata?
Therefore, it is not an outflow.
"What is the proximity to outflows?"

All ordinary beings accept and take up robes, food, bedding, and medicine; for the sake of physical and mental pleasure they seek such things, committing various evils and being ignorant of their faults, thus cycling through the three realms of existence. For this reason, these are called "outflows" (*āsrava*).
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives such faults, he immediately distances himself from them.
When he requires robes, he accepts them only for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of his own body.
He does not foster arrogance, but keeps his mind ever-humble.

He does not adorn himself for the sake of vanity, but only out of modesty, to ward off cold and heat, harsh winds, torrential rains, and the stings of evil insects, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and vipers.
Although they receive food and drink, their minds are free from greedy attachment.
They do not act for the sake of their own bodies, but always for the sake of the True Dharma;
they do not act for the sake of their physical forms, but only for the sake of sentient beings.
He does not do so out of pride, but for the sake of physical strength;
he does not do so out of malice, but to heal the wound of hunger.
Although he obtains superior flavors, his mind is free from attachment.

Receiving a dwelling is likewise so: one does not allow the fetters of greed and pride to reside in the mind; rather, one accepts a house for the sake of the dwelling of Bodhi, to ward off the thieves of the fetters and to block out the winds and rains of evil. Thus one receives a residence.

Those who seek medicine do so with a mind free from greed and pride; they do so solely for the sake of the True Dharma, not for the sake of their own life, but for the sake of eternal life. "Good son!
It is like a person suffering from a wound who applies ghee and flour to it and wraps it with a cloth;
when pus and blood need to be drawn out, he applies more ghee and flour;
and for the sake of healing the wound, he sprinkles medicinal powder upon it.
Just as one stays within a deep chamber to avoid the evil winds, so too is it with the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva:

because he views the body as a wound, he covers it with clothing; because of the pus from the nine orifices, he seeks out food and drink; to protect against the evil wind and rain, he accepts a dwelling; and because the four poisons have flared up, he seeks out medicine.
The Bodhisattva accepts the four kinds of offerings for the sake of the path to enlightenment, not for the sake of sustaining life. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects as follows:
"If I do not accept these four kinds of offerings, my body will perish and fail to attain stability.

If it lacks stability, I shall not be able to endure suffering; if I cannot endure suffering, I shall be unable to cultivate wholesome dharmas. However, if I can endure suffering, I shall be able to cultivate immeasurable wholesome dharmas."

If I am unable to endure various sufferings, then I will give rise to a mind of hatred toward painful sensations and a mind of greedy attachment toward pleasant sensations; furthermore, if I seek pleasure and do not obtain it, ignorance will arise.
Therefore, while ordinary persons give rise to outflows regarding the four types of offerings,
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to observe them deeply and do not give rise to outflows.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva is called "without outflows" (anāsrava).
How could the Tathāgata be called "with outflows"?
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not called "with outflows."
"Furthermore, good son!
Although all ordinary beings well protect their bodies, their minds still give rise to three kinds of evil thoughts.

Because of these causes and conditions, although they may sever their afflictions and attain birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they nevertheless fall back again into the three evil realms."
“Good son! It is like a person crossing the great ocean who, just as they are about to reach the other shore, sinks into the water and dies.
Ordinary worldlings are just like this: when they are on the verge of exhausting the three realms of existence, they fall back into the three miserable destinies.”
Why is this? Because there is no wholesome awakening.
What is wholesome awakening?
Regarding the so-called six objects of mindfulness:
ordinary persons have weak and inferior wholesome minds, while unwholesome states are intensely active.
Because their wholesome minds are weak, their wisdom-minds are meager.
Because their wisdom-mind is meager, they increase the various outflows (*āsrava*).

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with the pure eye of wisdom, perceives the faults of these three types of awakening; he knows that these three awakenings possess manifold afflictions and constantly act as enemies to sentient beings within the context of the Three Vehicles.

Due to these three causes and conditions for delusion, immeasurable ordinary beings fail to see the Buddha-nature; throughout immeasurable kalpas, they give rise to inverted thoughts, claiming that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is impermanent, lacks bliss, lacks self, and possesses only purity, and that the Tathāgata ultimately enters parinirvāṇa.
All sentient beings are impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; yet, due to their inverted minds, they claim there is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
In reality, there are no three vehicles; it is due to the mind of perversion that one speaks of three vehicles.
The path of the single reality is true and not false, yet due to the mind of perversion, one says there is no single reality.
These three unwholesome thoughts are constantly censured by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; these three unwholesome thoughts constantly harm oneself and may also harm others.
When these three perceptions exist, all manner of evils constantly follow and attend one.
These three perceptions are themselves the three fetters, which bind sentient beings to the boundless cycle of birth and death.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly performs such observations regarding the three types of perception.
"If, at any time, a bodhisattva has a cause or condition that would give rise to the perception of desire, he remains silent and does not accept it."

For example, just as a person who is handsome and pure does not accept any excrement or filth; just as no one will take up a red-hot iron ball; just as a Brahmin by nature does not accept beef; just as a person who is full does not accept foul food; and just as a wheel-turning monarch does not sit on the same seat as any outcaste (caṇḍāla)—so too, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva loathes and despises the three types of perception, neither accepting nor relishing them.
Why is this? The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Sentient beings know me to be a field of merit; how could I accept such evil dharmas?"
If one experiences unwholesome thoughts, one is unfit to serve as a field of merit for sentient beings.
I do not claim to be a virtuous field of merit myself; rather, it is because sentient beings perceive my outward appearance that they say, "I am."
If I were now to give rise to such an evil thought, I would be deceiving all sentient beings.
Because of my past deceptions, I have wandered through birth and death for immeasurable eons and fallen into the three evil realms.
If I were to receive the faithful offerings of others with an evil mind, all devas and humans, as well as the seers possessing the five supernormal powers, would witness and reproach me.
If I were to receive the faithful offerings of others with an evil thought, it might cause the donor’s karmic fruit to diminish, or result in no reward at all.
If I were to accept the offerings of a donor with an evil mind, I would become an enemy to that donor.
All donors constantly regard me as their own infant; how could I deceive them and harbor thoughts of enmity toward them?
Why is this? It is because it may cause the donor to fail to obtain the karmic fruit, or to obtain only a meager fruit. [He thought:

"I constantly refer to myself as one who has left the household life; now, one who has left the household life ought not to give rise to evil. If one gives rise to evil, then they are no longer a renunciant."
One who has left the household life must have body and speech in accord;
if they are not in accord, one is not a renunciant.

I have abandoned my parents, brothers, wife, children, kinsmen, and friends to leave the household life and cultivate the Way. This is precisely the time for cultivating wholesome thoughts, not the time for cultivating unwholesome thoughts.
It is like a person who enters the sea to seek jewels, yet does not take up pearls but instead takes up only crystal;
or like a person who abandons exquisite music to play with filth.
It is like abandoning a precious woman to cherish one who is lowly and ugly;
like discarding a golden vessel to use a clay bowl;
like casting away nectar to consume poisonous medicine.
It is as if one were to abandon long-standing friends, virtuous companions, and skilled physicians, only to seek medicine from hateful enemies to cure oneself.

I am just like this: having abandoned the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata World-Honored One, and the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma, I have instead consumed the poison of Māra and various evil thoughts.
A human body is as difficult to obtain as the udumbara flower, yet I have now obtained it;
a Tathāgata is even more difficult to encounter than the udumbara flower, yet I have now encountered one;
the pure Dharma-treasure is difficult to see or hear, yet I have now heard it.
It is like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log; human life does not stop for a moment, passing faster than a mountain stream.
Though one exists today, even tomorrow is difficult to guarantee.
Why, then, do you indulge your mind and allow it to dwell in unwholesome dharmas?
Vigorous youth does not remain, like a galloping horse; how can one rely upon it to give rise to arrogance?
It is like an evil spirit watching for a person's faults;
the four great evil spirits are likewise, constantly coming to watch for my transgressions.
"How could I allow unwholesome thoughts to arise?
My life is like a dilapidated house or a collapsing building; how could I give rise to evil?
'I am called a śramaṇa, and one who is a śramaṇa is said to study wholesome thoughts.'"
"I have now given rise to unwholesome thoughts; how can I be called a śramaṇa?
I am named 'one who has gone forth,' and one who has gone forth is said to cultivate the path of goodness."
I am now practicing evil; how can I be called one who has gone forth?
I am now called a true brāhmaṇa, for a brāhmaṇa is defined as one who cultivates pure conduct.
I am now practicing impure and evil thoughts; how could I be called a brāhmaṇa?
I am also known as one of the great kṣatriya clan, and those of the kṣatriya clan are able to eliminate enemies.
If I am now unable to eliminate my evil enemies, how can I be called one of the Kṣatriya caste?
I am named a bhikṣu; a bhikṣu is one who has destroyed the afflictions (kleśa).
"If I do not now shatter evil thoughts and afflictions, how can I be called a bhikṣu?
"There are six things in the world that are difficult to encounter; these I have now obtained."
How should one prevent unwholesome thoughts from dwelling in the mind? What are these six?

First, the appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter; second, hearing the True Dharma is difficult; third, giving rise to a sense of urgency is difficult; fourth, being born in a central land is difficult; fifth, obtaining a human body is difficult; and sixth, possessing all the faculties complete is difficult.
"Since these six things are difficult to obtain and have now been obtained, one should not give rise to evil thoughts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva practices this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and constantly and diligently observes these various evil minds.
All ordinary beings do not perceive the faults and afflictions of such evil thoughts; therefore, they undergo the three types of perception, which is called "undergoing outflows.

Having perceived them, the Bodhisattva does not accept or cling to them, but relinquishes and does not protect them; relying on the Eightfold Noble Path, he pushes them away and cuts them off so that they are severed.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva has no outflows (āsrava) to receive.
How then could it be said that the Tathāgata has outflows?
For this reason, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, is not one who possesses outflows.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty.
[Scroll Twenty-one] of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
added by the Song Dynasty *śramaṇa* Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-vyūha-udgata-guṇa-rāja,
Part Three: "Furthermore, good son,

when ordinary persons encounter physical or mental suffering and give rise to various evils— whether they contract a physical illness or a mental affliction— they cause their body, speech, and mind to commit all manner of evil deeds."
Because they commit evil, they transmigrate through the three realms of existence and undergo all manner of sufferings. Why is this?
Because ordinary persons lack mindfulness and wisdom, various outflows (*āsrava*) arise; these are called the outflows of mindfulness (*smṛty-āsrava*).
“A bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly reflects:

‘Since countless kalpas in the past, I have committed various evils with this body and mind; by these causes and conditions, I have wandered through birth and death, undergoing all manner of sufferings in the three evil realms, which has ultimately caused me to stray from the true path of the Three Vehicles.’”
"Because of these evil causes and conditions, the bodhisattva gives rise to great fear within his own body and mind; he abandons all evils and proceeds toward the wholesome path.
Good son!..."

It is as if there were a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single basket, ordering a man to feed them, watch over them, attend to their needs when they lay down or rose, and rub and wash their bodies.
[The king declared: "If you cause even one snake to become enraged, I shall execute you according to the law in the marketplace."
At that time, having heard the king’s urgent command, the man was seized with terror and abandoned the chest to flee.
The king then dispatched five caṇḍālas to follow him, drawn swords in hand.
The man looked back and, seeing the five men behind him, quickly fled.
At that time, the five men used a wicked stratagem to conceal the knives they held; secretly, one of them feigned friendship and spoke to him, saying:
"You should come back."
The man did not believe him and fled to a village, wishing to hide himself.
Once he had entered the village, he peered into the various houses but saw no people at all; he inspected the jars and vessels, finding them all empty and devoid of anything.
Having seen no one and failed to find anything he sought, he sat down upon the ground, when he heard a voice from the air:
"Alas, O man! This place is desolate and devoid of inhabitants; tonight, six great bandits shall come here."
"If you should encounter them, your life will not be spared.
How can you possibly escape them?
At that moment, the man’s terror increased even further, and he abandoned his pursuit and fled.
On the way, he came upon a river whose current was swift and turbulent, and there were no boats or rafts.
Out of fear, he immediately gathered various kinds of grass and wood to make a raft.
He then reflected further:
"If I remain here, I shall be harmed by the venomous snake, the five caṇḍālas, the one who feigns friendship, and the six great thieves.
If I cross this river, I cannot rely on the raft and shall drown and die."
‘It would be better to die drowning in the water than to be harmed by those snakes or bandits.
He then pushed a raft of grass into the water, leaned his body upon it, and moving his hands and feet, crossed the current and departed.
Having reached the other shore, they are secure and free from affliction; their minds are at ease and their terrors have vanished.

"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas hear and uphold the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, they contemplate the body as a casket and the earth, water, fire, and wind elements as four venomous snakes—those with poison in their sight, poison in their touch, poison in their breath, and poison in their bite. It is because all sentient beings encounter these four poisons that they lose their lives."

The four great elements of sentient beings are likewise: sometimes they are harmful through sight, sometimes harmful through touch, sometimes harmful through their breath, and sometimes harmful through biting; by these causes and conditions, they remain far removed from all that is wholesome.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the four venomous snakes have four castes, namely: kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, vaiśya, and śūdra."
These four great serpents are likewise thus; they possess four natures:
the nature of solidity, the nature of moisture, the nature of heat, and the nature of motion.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates these four great elements as being of the same nature as the four venomous snakes.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates these four great elements as being like four venomous snakes.
How does he contemplate them?
These four poisonous snakes constantly watch for an opportunity; when will they look at me?
When will they touch me?
When will they hiss at me?
When will they bite?
The four great venomous snakes are likewise; they constantly lie in wait for sentient beings, seeking their vulnerabilities.
If one were killed by these four snakes, one would ultimately not fall into the three evil realms.
If one is killed by the four great elements, one will inevitably fall into the three evil realms; of this there is no doubt.
Although these four poisonous snakes may be cared for and nourished, they still seek to kill people;
the four great elements are likewise: though constantly provided with offerings, they always lead people to commit various evils.
These four poisonous snakes, if even one becomes enraged, can kill a person;
the nature of the four great elements is likewise: if even one of them becomes provoked, it can also harm a person.
Although these four poisonous snakes dwell in the same place, their four minds are each distinct;
likewise, the four great poisonous elements, though dwelling in the same place, differ in their natures.
Although these four poisonous snakes may be treated with respect, they are difficult to approach;
the four great poisonous snakes are likewise: although they may be treated with respect, they are also difficult to approach.
When these four poisonous snakes harm a person, there may be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who can treat them with mantras and medicinal herbs;
however, when the four great elements kill a person, even if there were śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others with divine mantras and excellent medicines, none could cure it.
Just as a person who values their own well-being will immediately distance themselves upon smelling the foul odor of four venomous snakes;
so too do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who likewise distance themselves upon smelling the foul odor of the four great elements.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further contemplated the four great poisonous snakes; giving rise to great fear, he fled from them and cultivated the Eightfold Noble Path.
"The five *caṇḍālas* are the five aggregates (*skandhas*)."
How does a bodhisattva contemplate the five aggregates as being like a caṇḍāla?
A caṇḍāla constantly causes people to be separated from those they love and brings together those they hate;
the five aggregates are likewise, causing people to greedily approach unwholesome dharmas and to distance themselves from all purely wholesome dharmas.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a *caṇḍāla* who adorns himself with various weapons—whether swords, shields, bows, arrows, armor, or spears—which are capable of harming others."
The five aggregates are likewise: they are firmly adorned with various afflictions, which harm deluded people and cause them to fall into the various realms of existence.
"Good son! Just as a caṇḍāla may seize and harm anyone who has committed an offense;
The five aggregates are likewise; they possess the faults of various fetters and can constantly harm people.
For this reason, the bodhisattva deeply contemplates the five aggregates as being like a caṇḍāla.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva observes the five aggregates as being like a caṇḍāla.
The candāla has no heart of compassion and harms both enemies and kin;
the five aggregates are likewise, for they have no heart of compassion and harm both the good and the evil.
Just as the candāla torments all people;

The five aggregates are likewise; because all afflictions constantly torment all sentient beings in birth and death, the bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like outcastes (caṇḍāla).
"Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like outcasts (caṇḍāla).
Just as an outcast constantly harbors a mind of malice,
so too do the five aggregates constantly harbor a mind of affliction and harm through the various fetters."
Just as a person who lacks feet, weapons, and attendants will surely be killed by a *caṇḍāla*, so it is with sentient beings:
lacking feet, lacking weapons, and lacking attendants, they are plundered and harmed by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Feet are called the precepts, a sword is called wisdom, and attendants are called spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Because one lacks these three things, one is harmed by the thieves of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Therefore, a bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates as being like outcastes (*caṇḍāla*).
"Furthermore, son of good family,
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes that the five aggregates are even more wretched than outcastes."
Why is this? If sentient beings are killed by the five caṇḍālas, they do not fall into hell;
however, if they are killed by the aggregates (skandhas), they do fall into hell.
For this reason, the bodhisattva contemplates the aggregates as being worse than a caṇḍāla.
Having made this contemplation, he makes this vow:
"I would rather spend my entire life in close proximity to a caṇḍāla than for even a moment be in close proximity to the five aggregates."
A *caṇḍāla* can only harm ignorant people within the desire realm;
these thieves of the five aggregates, however, universally harm all ordinary beings throughout the three realms.
A *caṇḍāla* can only slaughter those who have committed crimes; [the thieves of the five aggregates, however, harm all].
These thieves of the five aggregates do not distinguish whether sentient beings have committed offenses or are innocent;
they can harm them all. A caṇḍāla does not harm the elderly, women, or children;
these thieves of the five aggregates, however, do not distinguish whether sentient beings are old, young, female, or weak—they harm them all.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates that these aggregates (skandhas) are more harmful than a caṇḍāla, and thus makes this vow:
"I would rather dwell near a caṇḍāla for the rest of my life than be close to the five aggregates for even a moment."
"Furthermore, good son!
A caṇḍāla harms only others and never harms himself;
the thief of the five aggregates harms both himself and others, as well as the caṇḍāla."
A caṇḍāla may be ransomed through kind words, money, or precious goods;
the five aggregates are not like this—they cannot be forcibly ransomed through kind inducements, money, or precious goods.
A caṇḍāla does not necessarily kill constantly throughout the four periods of the day;
the five aggregates are not like this, for they constantly harm all sentient beings in every moment of thought.
A caṇḍāla occupies only a single location, so it is possible to escape him; [the five aggregates, however, are everywhere].
The five aggregates are not like this; they pervade all places and there is no escape from them.
Although a caṇḍāla may harm others, he does not follow them after having done so;
the five aggregates are not like this, for once they have killed a sentient being, they pursue and never leave them.
Therefore, a bodhisattva would rather remain close to a caṇḍāla for the rest of their life than be close to the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) for even a moment.
A person of wisdom, through skillful means, attains liberation from the five aggregates.
Skillful means consist of the Eightfold Noble Path, the Six Perfections, and the Four Immeasurable Minds.
By means of these skillful means, one attains liberation, such that body and mind are not harmed by the five aggregates.
Why is this? Because the body is like a vajra and the mind is like space, the body and mind are difficult to destroy or corrupt.
For this reason, when a bodhisattva observes that the aggregates (skandhas) give rise to various unwholesome dharmas, they conceive great fear and cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is also like that man who, fearing the four venomous snakes and the five caṇḍālas, proceeds along the road without looking back or lingering.
That which feigns intimacy and kindness is called greedy attachment.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva deeply contemplates the fetter of craving as an enemy masquerading as a friend.
If one knows it for what it truly is, it can do no harm;
if one fails to recognize it, one will certainly be harmed by it.
Craving is likewise so: if one knows its nature, it cannot cause sentient beings to revolve within the suffering of birth and death;
if one does not know it, they will cycle through the six realms of existence, fully experiencing manifold sufferings.
Why is this? Because the affliction of craving is difficult to abandon; it is like a deceitful enemy who feigns friendship and is thus hard to distance oneself from.
Such a deceitful enemy constantly watches for one's vulnerabilities, causing the separation of those one loves and the union of those one hates.
Craving is likewise; it causes people to distance themselves from all wholesome dharmas and draw near to all unwholesome dharmas.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply contemplates craving as a deceitful enemy who feigns friendship, because it makes what is seen unseen and what is heard unheard.
Just as ordinary people, though they perceive the faults of birth and death and possess wisdom, fail to see them later because they are shrouded by ignorance;
so it is with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: though they see, they do not see, and though they hear, they do not hear.
Why is this? Because of a heart of attachment. For what reason?
Seeing the faults of birth and death, they are unable to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate this fetter of craving as an enemy feigning friendship.
"What is meant by the signs of an enemy feigning intimacy?
It is when an enemy, being insincere, falsely manifests the appearance of sincerity;
though he is not to be approached, he falsely manifests the appearance of approachability."
In truth it is unwholesome, yet it falsely manifests the appearance of being wholesome;
in truth it is not affectionate, yet it falsely assumes the appearance of affection. Why is this so?
It constantly watches for an opportunity to cause harm.

Craving is likewise: it constantly deceives sentient beings by feigning reality where there is none, feigning proximity where there is none, feigning goodness where there is none, and feigning affection where there is none, perpetually deluding all beings within the cycle of birth and death.
For this reason, a bodhisattva regards craving as an enemy feigning friendship.
An enemy feigning friendship is one who shows only their body and speech but does not reveal their heart; therefore, they are able to deceive.
Affection is likewise thus: it is merely deceptive and ultimately unattainable; for this reason, it can delude all sentient beings.
An enemy who feigns friendship has a beginning and an end, and is thus easy to distance oneself from;
affection is not like this—it is without beginning and without end, and is therefore difficult to distance oneself from.
When an enemy feigns friendship, they are difficult to perceive from afar but easy to recognize when near;
affection is not like this—for it is difficult to discern even when close at hand, how much more so when distant?
For this reason, the Bodhisattva regards craving as worse than a deceitful friend.
Because all sentient beings are bound by the fetter of craving, they distance themselves from Great Nirvana and draw near to birth and death;
they distance themselves from permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and draw near to impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.
Therefore, in various sūtras, I have taught them as the three impurities.
Regarding present phenomena, because of ignorance, one does not perceive their faults and is unable to relinquish them.
Affectionate enmity and feigned intimacy can ultimately never harm one who possesses wisdom.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates this affection and gives rise to great fear, practicing the Eightfold Noble Path just as that man, fearing the four poisonous snakes, the five caṇḍālas, and the one feigning intimacy, pressed on along the road without turning back.
"The empty village refers to the six internal sense bases.
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates these six sense bases as empty and non-existent, just like an empty village."
Just as that terrified person, having entered the village, does not see even a single inhabitant and searches through all the jars and vessels without finding a single thing;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva, who carefully contemplates the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as empty and non-existent, seeing neither sentient beings nor the reality of a single thing.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates the six internal sense bases as empty and non-existent, like that deserted village. "Good son!
When a band of thieves gazes from afar at that deserted village, they never conceive the notion that it is truly void."
Ordinary worldlings are likewise in this regard; they do not give rise to the perception of emptiness regarding the collection of the six sense bases.
Because they cannot give rise to the perception of emptiness, they transmigrate through birth and death, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
“Good son! When the bandits arrive, one gives rise to the perception of emptiness.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva: observing these six sense bases, they constantly give rise to the perception of emptiness.”
Because they give rise to the perception of the emptiness of birth, they do not circulate in birth and death to undergo suffering.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is always free from inversion regarding these six sense bases;
because he is free from inversion, he no longer circulates in birth and death.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as a band of thieves who enter this empty village find peace and security,
so too do the thieves of the afflictions find peace and security upon entering these six sense bases."
Just as a thief dwelling in an empty village has no fear, so too are the bandits of the afflictions; dwelling within these six sense bases, they likewise have no fear.
Just as that empty village is the dwelling place of lions, tigers, wolves, and various other evil beasts;
These six internal sense bases are likewise thus: they are the dwelling place of all manner of evils and the wild beasts of affliction.
Therefore, the bodhisattva deeply contemplates that the six sense bases are empty and non-existent, being purely the abodes of all that is unwholesome.
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the six internal sense bases as empty and non-existent, like that deserted village. Why is this?

Because it is deceptive and unreal: one forms the perception of existence regarding that which is empty and non-existent; one forms the perception of pleasure regarding that which is truly without pleasure; and one forms the perception of a person regarding that which is truly without a person.

The six internal sense bases are likewise thus: they are empty and non-existent, yet one forms the perception of existence; there is truly no pleasure, yet one forms the perception of pleasure; there is truly no person, yet one forms the perception of a person. Only the wise are able to know this and attain its reality.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as an empty village may at times have people and at times have no people, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are not like this;
they are invariably devoid of persons."
Why is this? Because their nature is eternally empty; that which is known by the wise is not something seen with the eyes.

Therefore, the bodhisattva contemplates the six internal sense bases as being full of many harms and perils, and cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path without ceasing or resting, just like that person who, fearing the four poisonous snakes, the five caṇḍālas, the one who feigns intimacy, and the six great thieves, clings to the correct path out of terror.
"The six great thieves are the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ bāhyaviṣayāḥ*).
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates these six sense objects as being like six great thieves. Why is this?
Because they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas.
Just as the six great bandits are able to plunder all the wealth and treasures of the people;
so too are these six thieves of the sensory objects (ṣaḍviṣaya), for they are able to plunder the wholesome wealth of all sentient beings.

It is like six great bandits who, upon entering a person's house, are able to plunder whatever is currently within it, making no distinction between the good and the bad, and causing even the most wealthy person to suddenly become destitute.
These thieves of the six sense objects are likewise; once they enter the faculties of a person, they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas.
When wholesome dharmas are exhausted, one becomes impoverished and destitute, becoming an icchantika.
Therefore, a bodhisattva carefully contemplates the six sense objects as being like six great bandits.
"Furthermore, good son, just as when the six great bandits wish to plunder a person, they must rely on an insider; if there is no insider, they will simply turn back."

These thieves of the six sense objects are likewise; they wish to plunder the wholesome dharmas only when there exists within a sentient being such characteristics as knowledge and vision, permanence, bliss, self, purity, and non-emptiness.
If there are no such characteristics within, these evil thieves of the six sense objects cannot plunder any wholesome dharmas.
A person of wisdom has no such internal signs, whereas ordinary persons do.
For this reason, the six sense-objects constantly come to invade and plunder the wealth of wholesome dharmas.
Because they do not guard [themselves] well, they are robbed by them.
"Guardian" refers to wisdom; because a person possessing wisdom can skillfully provide protection, they are not robbed.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates these six sense objects as being equal and without distinction to the six great thieves.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as the six great thieves can cause suffering and affliction to the bodies and minds of people, so too are these thieves of the six sense objects;
they constantly cause suffering and affliction to the bodies and minds of sentient beings."
The six great thieves can only plunder the wealth and goods of people in the present;
these thieves of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) constantly plunder the wholesome wealth of sentient beings across the three periods of time.
These six great thieves find their joy in the night; [the thieves of the six sense-objects find their joy] in the darkness of ignorance.
The six objects of the senses (ṣaḍviṣaya) as evil thieves are likewise thus: they find joy when dwelling in the darkness of ignorance.
Just as only kings are able to restrain these six great thieves, so too only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to restrain the six evil thieves of the sense objects.
Whenever these six great thieves intend to plunder, they do not discriminate between those who are handsome, of noble lineage, wise, learned, erudite, wealthy and honorable, or poor and lowly;
the evil thieves of the six sense-objects are likewise, for when they seek to plunder the wholesome dharmas, they do not discriminate from the handsome down to the poor and lowly.
These six great thieves, though kings may cut off their hands and feet, still cannot cause their minds to cease;

the evil thieves of the six sense-objects are likewise: though a srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, or anāgāmin may cut off their hands and feet, they still cannot prevent them from plundering wholesome dharmas.
Just as a brave and strong man is able to subdue these six great thieves,
so too do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas subdue the evil thieves of the six sense-objects.
For example, if a person has many clans and a flourishing circle of kinsmen, they will not be plundered by the six bandits;
so it is with sentient beings: if they have a virtuous friend, they will not be plundered by the evil bandits of the six sense-objects.
"These six great thieves can only plunder people and things when they see them;
the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) are not like that, for whether one sees, knows, hears, smells, touches, or perceives, they are all capable of plundering."
The six great thieves can only plunder the wealth of persons within the desire realm, but they cannot plunder those in the form or formless realms;
the evil thieves of the six sense objects, however, are not like this, for they can plunder all the treasures of goodness throughout the three realms.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva carefully contemplates that the six sense objects exceed those six thieves in their danger.

Having made this contemplation, he cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, proceeding straight ahead without turning back—just like that terrified man who, fearing the four poisonous snakes, the five caṇḍālas, the one feigning kindness, and the six great thieves, abandoned the empty village and set out upon the road.
"Encountering a river along the way is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*).
How does a bodhisattva contemplate these afflictions as being like a great river?
Just as that swift river can sweep away even a fragrant elephant,"
The swift river of afflictions is likewise able to sweep away pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, bodhisattvas deeply contemplate afflictions as being like a swift river;
because it is deep and its bottom is difficult to reach, it is called a river.
Because its boundaries cannot be found, it is called "great"; moreover, within it there are many kinds of evil fish.
The great river of afflictions is likewise: because only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can reach its bottom, it is called "extremely deep";
because only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can find its boundaries, it is called "vast and wide."
Because they constantly harm all deluded sentient beings, they are called "evil fish.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva contemplates these afflictions as being like a great river;
just as the waters of a great river can cause all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests to grow.
The great river of afflictions is likewise thus: it can cause the twenty-five states of existence to grow for sentient beings.
For this reason, the bodhisattva contemplates these afflictions as being like a great river.
"Just as a person who falls into a great river has no sense of shame or remorse, so too it is with sentient beings: they fall into the river of afflictions without shame or remorse.
Just as one who falls into the river may die before reaching the bottom; [so it is with those who fall into the river of afflictions]."
Falling into the river of afflictions is likewise so: before its bottom has been reached, one revolves through the twenty-five states of existence.
What is called the "bottom" is named the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If there are those who do not cultivate such characteristics of emptiness, you should know that these persons will not attain liberation from the twenty-five states of existence.
Because all sentient beings are unable to skillfully cultivate emptiness and signlessness, they are constantly swept away by the swift river of afflictions.
Just as that great river can only destroy the body but cannot sweep away all wholesome dharmas, the great river of afflictions is not like this;
it can destroy all wholesome dharmas of both body and mind.
That great violent river can only sweep away those within the desire realm;
the great river of afflictions, however, can sweep away those among the humans and devas of the three realms.
In the rivers of the world, one reaches the other shore by moving one's hands and feet; [but in the river of afflictions, this is not possible].
Regarding the great river of afflictions, only Bodhisattvas are able to cross it by means of the six pāramitās.
Just as the waters of a great river are difficult to cross,
so too is the great river of afflictions difficult to cross.
Why is it called "difficult to cross"?
Even the great Bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet attained ultimate crossing; only the Buddhas attain ultimate crossing. Therefore, it is called "difficult to cross."
For example, just as a person being swept away by a river is unable to practice even a hair’s breadth of wholesome dharma, so it is with sentient beings:
those who are swept away and submerged by the river of afflictions are likewise unable to practice wholesome dharmas.
Just as when a person falls into a river and is swept away by the current, another who possesses strength can rescue them;
yet those who have fallen into the river of afflictions as icchantikas cannot be rescued by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even by all the Buddhas.
When the great rivers of the world reach the end of a kalpa, the seven suns shining simultaneously can cause them to dry up;
the great river of afflictions is not like this, for even though śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment, they still cannot dry it up.
Therefore, the bodhisattva contemplates all afflictions as being like a violent river.

"It is, for example, like that man who, fearing four venomous snakes, five caṇḍālas, one who feigns intimacy, and six great bandits, abandoned the deserted village and set out along the road; having reached the riverbank, he gathered grass to construct a raft."

The Bodhisattva is likewise: fearing the four great serpents of the elements, the outcaste of the five aggregates, the deceptive intimacy of craving, the empty village of the six sense bases, and the evil bandits of the six sense objects, he reaches the river of afflictions and cultivates morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the six *pāramitās*, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as his boat and raft. Relying upon and riding this raft, he crosses the river of afflictions and reaches the other shore: the eternal, blissful *nirvāṇa*.
A bodhisattva practicing the Great Parinirvāṇa reflects in this way:
"If I am unable to endure such physical and mental suffering, I shall not be able to enable all sentient beings to cross the river of afflictions."
Reflecting thus, although there were such physical and mental sufferings and afflictions, he endured them in silence.
Because he endured them, no outflows (āsrava) arose.
"If even a bodhisattva such as this has no outflows (āsrava), how much less could a Buddha, a Tathāgata, have any outflows?
For this reason, the Buddhas are not said to possess outflows."
Why is it that the Tathāgata is not without outflows (anāsrava)?
Because the Tathāgata constantly acts within the realm of outflows, and these outflows are precisely the twenty-five states of existence (pañcaviṃśati-bhava).
For this reason, śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings say that the Buddha possesses outflows, yet all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are in truth without outflows.
“Good son! For these reasons, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess no fixed marks. Good son!”
"Therefore, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, and the icchantikas are all indeterminate.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaraśmi-Āryaguṇarāja said, "So it is, so it is;
it is truly as the holy teaching declares."
All dharmas are entirely indeterminate; because they are indeterminate, one should know that the Tathāgata likewise does not ultimately enter parinirvāṇa.
As the Buddha previously taught:
when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa, there is both nirvāṇa and Great Nirvāṇa within what is heard and what is not heard.
"What is nirvāṇa? What is great nirvāṇa?
At that time, the Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
Only a bodhisattva who has attained the dhāraṇī of mindfulness is able to inquire as you have done.”
“Good son! As people in the world say: there is a sea and a great sea; there is a river and a great river;

there is a mountain and a great mountain; there is earth and the great earth; there is a city and a great city; there are sentient beings and great sentient beings; there is a king and a great king; there is a person and a great person; there are devas and the god among gods; there is a path and the great path;”
Nirvana is also like this; there is nirvana and there is great nirvana.
What is nirvana? Good son!
Just as a person who is hungry finds peace and happiness upon obtaining a small amount of food, such peace and happiness is also called nirvāṇa;
just as one who recovers from illness is said to have attained peace and happiness, such peace and happiness is also called nirvāṇa;
just as a person who is terrified finds peace and happiness by obtaining a place of refuge, such peace and happiness is also called nirvāṇa.
Just as a poor person who obtains the seven treasures attains peace and happiness, such peace and happiness is also called nirvana;
just as a person contemplating a skeleton does not give rise to craving and thus attains peace and happiness, such peace and happiness is also called nirvana.
Such nirvana cannot be called Mahāparinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because it is characterized by hunger and thirst, illness, fear, poverty, and the arising of craving and attachment; thus it is called nirvana, but not Mahāparinirvāṇa.

“Good son! If ordinary persons or śrāvakas—whether by means of the mundane path or the noble path—sever the fetters of the desire realm, they attain peace and bliss; such peace and bliss is also called nirvāṇa, but it cannot be called Mahāparinirvāṇa.”

If one is able to sever the fetters from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one then attains peace and bliss; such peace and bliss is also called nirvāṇa, yet it cannot be termed Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because afflictions arise again due to the presence of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
What is meant by "afflictive habitual tendencies"?
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess the scent of afflictions, namely: "this is my body," "this is my robe," "I am going," "I am coming," "I speak," and "I listen."
When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, enter nirvāṇa, the nature of that nirvāṇa is without self and without pleasure, possessing only permanence and purity.
This is precisely what is called the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*).

"There are distinct characteristics among the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; yet the Nirvāṇa attained by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas-Tathāgatas is ultimately equal and without distinction."
For this reason, that which is attained by the two vehicles is not the Great Nirvana. Why is this?
Because it lacks permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Permanence, bliss, self, and purity are what constitute the name "Great Nirvana.
"Good son! It is like a place that can receive all waters, which is named the great ocean."
Wherever śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas enter, that place is called Great Nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, whoever is able to encompass such immeasurable wholesome dharmas as the four dhyānas, the three samādhis, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the ten totalities—that too is called Great Nirvāṇa.
“Good son! It is like a river that even the foremost fragrant elephant cannot reach the bottom of; it is then called ‘great.
When śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas up to the tenth stage do not see the Buddha-nature, this is called nirvāṇa, but not the Great Parinirvāṇa.”
If one can clearly perceive the Buddha-nature, then it is called Great Nirvana.
This Great Nirvana can only be fathomed to its very bottom by the Great Elephant King; the Great Elephant King refers to all Buddhas.
“Good son! That which even the Mahānāgas, the Bhṛtyas, and the great Mallas cannot ascend after passing through a long period of time is called a ‘great mountain.
That which the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are like Mahānāgas and great Mallas cannot see is likewise called ‘Great Nirvāṇa.’”
"Furthermore, good son!
Wherever a minor king resides is called a small city; where a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) resides is called a great city.

Where Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those dwelling in numbers such as eighty thousand, sixty thousand, forty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand reside is called Nirvāṇa; where the Supreme Dharma-Lord, the Sage-King, resides is named Great Parinirvāṇa."
For this reason, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa. "Good son!
For example, if there is a person who sees the fourfold army and does not give rise to fear, you should know that this person is called a 'Great Being' (mahāsattva)."

If there are sentient beings who do not give rise to fear toward the three evil realms, afflictions, or evil karma, yet are able to extensively deliver sentient beings therein, you should know that such persons have attained Great Nirvana.

If there is anyone who can provide for their parents, show reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, cultivate wholesome dharmas, speak with sincerity and without deception, endure all evils, and bestow gifts upon the poor and destitute, they are called a great man (mahāpuruṣa).

The Bodhisattva is likewise: possessing great compassion and pitying all beings, he is like a parent to all sentient beings; able to ferry them across the river of birth and death, he universally reveals to all beings the Way of the Single Reality. This is what is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
“Good son! ‘Great’ is a name for the inconceivable.
That which is inconceivable and cannot be believed by any sentient being is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.”
Because it is perceived only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.
For what reason is it further called "Great"?
Because it is attained only after immeasurable causes and conditions, it is called "Great."
“Good son! Just as that which is obtained by worldly people through many causes and conditions is called ‘great,’ so too is nirvāṇa;
because it is obtained through many causes and conditions, it is called ‘great.’”
"What, then, is meant by 'Great Nirvana'?
Because it possesses the Great Self (Mahātman), it is called Great Nirvana.
Nirvana is without self; because it is characterized by great sovereignty, it is termed the Great Self."
"What is meant by 'Great Sovereignty'?
One who possesses eight forms of sovereignty is called 'Self.
What are these eight? "
"First, they are able to manifest a single body as many bodies, with the number and size of these bodies like those of fine motes of dust, filling immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.
The body of the Tathāgata is in truth not composed of atoms, yet because of his mastery, he manifests a body of atoms.
Such mastery is the Great Self.
Second, he manifests a single atom-sized body that fills the trichiliocosm.
The body of the Tathāgata is, in reality, not filled within the trichiliocosm. Why is this?
Because it is unimpeded and because of its very sovereignty, it fills the trichiliocosm.
Such mastery is called the Great Self.

"Third, one is able to lift this body—which fills the entire trichiliocosm—and fly through the air, passing beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in twenty Ganges Rivers without obstruction."
The body of the Tathāgata is in truth neither light nor heavy; yet, because of his sovereignty, he can manifest as either light or heavy.
Such sovereignty is called the Great Self.
Fourth, by virtue of this sovereignty, he attains mastery.
What is mastery?

The Tathāgata dwells with a single mind, unmoving, yet manifests infinite forms and types, each endowed with a mind; at times, the Tathāgata may perform but a single deed, yet causes all sentient beings to accomplish it individually;
the body of the Tathāgata constantly abides in one land, yet is seen by all in all other lands.
Such mastery is called the Great Self.
Fifth, it is because of mastery over the faculties.
What is meant by mastery over the faculties?

A single faculty of the Tathāgata can see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, distinguish tastes, feel tangibles, and cognize dharmas; yet the six faculties of the Tathāgata likewise do not see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, distinguish tastes, feel tangibles, or cognize dharmas.
Because of this mastery, he brings the faculties (*indriya*) under mastery.
Such mastery is called the "Great Self" (*mahātman*).
Sixth, because of this mastery, he attains all dharmas, yet even in the mind of the Tathāgata there is no notion of attainment.
Why is this? Because there is nothing to be attained.
If something were existent, it could be called "attained"; [but since it is not, it cannot be so called].
In reality, there is nothing at all; how, then, can it be called "attainment"?
If the Tathāgata were to conceive the notion that there is attainment, then the Buddhas would not attain nirvāṇa.
Because there is no attainment, it is called the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Because of mastery, one attains all dharmas;
because one attains all dharmas, one is called the Great Self.

"Seventh, regarding the explanation of mastery: when the Tathāgata expounds the meaning of a single verse, even after immeasurable kalpas have passed, the meaning is not exhausted—whether it be concerning precepts, concentration, generosity, or wisdom."
At that time, the Tathāgata did not give rise to the thought,
"I am speaking, and they are listening," nor did he conceive even the notion of a single verse.
Worldly people compose verses of four lines; because they conform to worldly convention, these are called "verses" (*gāthā*).
The nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise beyond expression, yet the Tathāgata expounds it through his sovereign power.
Because he expounds [the Dharma], he is called the Great Self.
"Eighth, the Tathāgata pervades all places, just like space.
The nature of space cannot be perceived; [the Tathāgata is likewise]."
The Tathāgata is likewise; in truth, he cannot be seen.
Because of his sovereignty, he causes all to see him.
Such sovereignty is called the Great Self (mahātman).
Such a Great Self is called Great Nirvana.
For this reason, it is named Great Nirvana.
Furthermore, good son!
For example, a treasure trove contains many rare and extraordinary things, complete in all their hundreds of varieties; therefore, it is called a "great treasury.
The profound and secret treasury of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is likewise: containing many wonders and complete without deficiency, it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, good son!
That which is boundless is called 'great.
Nirvāṇa is boundless; therefore, it is called 'great.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
Because it possesses great bliss, it is called Great Nirvana.
Although Nirvana itself has no [worldly] pleasure, because it possesses four kinds of bliss, it is called Great Nirvana."
What are the four?
First, because of severing all forms of pleasure.
That which does not sever pleasure is called suffering.
If there is suffering, it cannot be called great bliss.
Because suffering is severed through the cessation of pleasure, there is no suffering;
being without suffering and without pleasure is what is called great bliss.
The nature of nirvāṇa is neither suffering nor pleasure; therefore, nirvāṇa is called "Great Bliss.
For this reason, it is named Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son, there are two kinds of joy:
first, that of ordinary beings; second, that of all Buddhas.
The pleasures of ordinary beings are impermanent and subject to decay; therefore, they possess no true pleasure.
The Buddhas possess eternal bliss, free from all change; for this reason, it is called Great Bliss.
Furthermore, son of good family!
There are three kinds of feeling:
first, painful feeling; second, pleasant feeling; and third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is also suffering.
Although nirvana is equally neither painful nor pleasant, it is termed "Great Bliss.
Because it is Great Bliss, it is called "Great Nirvana.
Second, because it is great tranquility, it is called "Great Bliss."
The nature of nirvāṇa is great tranquility. Why is this?
Because it is far removed from all clamorous phenomena.
Because it is great quiescence, it is called Great Nirvana.
"Third, because it is all-knowing, it is called Great Bliss. That which is not all-knowing is not called Great Bliss;
[only that which is all-knowing is called Great Bliss]."
Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess all-knowing wisdom, they are called Great Bliss.
Because of this Great Bliss, they are called Great Nirvāṇa.
"Fourth, because their bodies are indestructible, they are called Great Bliss."
If a body were subject to destruction, it could not be called bliss;
the Tathāgata’s body is adamantine and indestructible, not a body of afflictions nor a body of impermanence, and is therefore called Great Bliss.
Because it is great bliss, it is called Great Nirvana.
"Good son! Worldly names may have causes and conditions, or they may be without causes and conditions."
Regarding those who have a causal basis for their names, Śāriputra is an example.
His mother’s name was Śārī; because his name was established based on his mother, he is called Śāriputra.
Similarly, the practitioner Maudgalyāyana was born in the country of Maudgalya; because his name was derived from the country, he is called the practitioner Maudgalyāyana.
For example, there is Maudgalyāyana; "Maudgalyāyana" is his clan name, and because the name was established based on the clan, he is called Maudgalyāyana.
Just as I was born into the Gautama clan, and because the name was established based on the clan, I am called Gautama.
For example, there was a practitioner named Viśākhā; Viśākhā is the name of a constellation, and because he was named after that constellation, he was called Viśākhā.
It is like a person with six fingers; because of those six fingers, he is called "the Six-Fingered Man."
Just as one is called a "slave of the Buddha" or a "slave of a deva" because of the Buddha or the deva,
so too, because they are born from moisture, they are called "moisture-born."
For example, because of sound, one is named *kakkara*, *kukkula*, or *tattala*.
Names such as these are names based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Those without causes and conditions are, for instance, "lotus," "earth," "water," "fire," "wind," and "space."
It is like the *mandapa*, which has one name but two realities:
first, it is called a "hall," and second, it is called a "drinking place.
Although the hall itself does not drink, it is nevertheless named a *mandapa*.
For example, that which is called *sarvacarma* is termed a "snake-canopy," yet it is not actually a snake-canopy;
this is called being without a cause, forcibly establishing a name.
For example, *Cilāpāyī* is called "oil-eater," yet she does not actually eat oil; a name is forcibly established for her, calling her "oil-eater."
This is called being without cause, yet forcibly establishing a name. "Good son!
This Great Nirvana is also like this; it has no causes or conditions, yet a name is forcibly established for it."
Good son! Just as space is not called "great" because of a small space, so too is nirvāṇa:
it is not called "Great Nirvāṇa" because of small characteristics.
"Good son!
For example, there is a dharma that cannot be measured and cannot be conceived; therefore, it is called 'great.
Nirvāṇa is likewise: because it cannot be measured and cannot be conceived, it is named the Great Parinirvāṇa."
“Because it is utterly pure, it is called Great Nirvana.
What is meant by ‘utterly pure’?
There are four kinds of purity.
What are the four?
First, the twenty-five existents are called "impure"; because they can be permanently severed, they are termed "pure.
This purity is *nirvāṇa*. Thus, this *nirvāṇa* may also be termed an "existent," yet this *nirvāṇa* is in reality not an existent.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the existence of nirvāṇa in accordance with worldly convention.

It is like people of the world who, though not their father, call him "father," and though not their mother, call her "mother"; although they are in reality not their parents, they nevertheless speak of them as "parents."
Nirvāṇa is also like this: in accordance with worldly convention, it is said that all Buddhas possess Great Nirvāṇa.
"Second, because their karma is pure.
All ordinary beings have impure karma and therefore lack nirvāṇa; [the Buddhas do not]."
Because the karma of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is pure, it is called "Great Purity.
Because of this Great Purity, it is called "Great Nirvāṇa.
"Third, because the body is pure."
If the body were impermanent, it would be called impure;
the Tathāgata’s body is permanent, and is therefore called the Great Purity.
Because it is the Great Purity, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.
"Fourth, because the mind is pure.
If the mind has outflows (*āsrava*), it is called impure;
the Buddha-mind is without outflows, and is therefore called the Great Purity."
Because it is supremely pure, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.
"Good son! This is called the fulfillment and accomplishment of the merits of the first stage by good sons and good daughters who practice this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-one.
[Scroll Twenty-two] of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
supplemented by the Śramaṇa Huìyán and others of the Song Dynasty based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Radiant Universal Illumination Sovereign Virtue King,
Part Four: "Furthermore, good son,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa so as to achieve and fulfill the second merit?

“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa, that which was previously unattained is now attained; that which was previously unseen is now seen; that which was previously unheard is now heard; that which was previously unreached is now reached; and that which was previously unknown is now known.”
"What is meant by 'that which was previously unattained but is now attained'?
It refers to the supernormal powers (abhijñā), which were previously unattained but are now attained.
There are two kinds of such powers:"
First is the internal, and second is the external.
That which is called "external" is shared with non-Buddhists.
The internal, moreover, is of two kinds:
First are those of the two vehicles, and second are bodhisattvas.
The supernormal powers attained by bodhisattvas through the practice of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
What is meant by "not shared with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas"?
The supernatural transformations produced by those of the Two Vehicles can only manifest one thing at a time with a single mind; they cannot produce many.
It is not so for the Bodhisattva, who, within a single moment of mind, is able to fully manifest bodies in all five realms of existence.
Why is this? It is because they have obtained the power of such a *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
This is what is called "that which was previously unobtainable but is now obtained."
Furthermore, what was previously unattained has now been attained?
It is the attainment of mastery over the body and mastery over the mind. Why is this so?
All ordinary beings lack mastery over their own body and mind; either the mind follows the body, or the body follows the mind.
What is meant by "the mind following the body"?
For example, when a person is intoxicated, as long as the wine remains within their body, the body moves and the mind moves along with it;
likewise, when the body is weary, the mind also becomes weary along with it.
This is what is meant by "the mind follows the body."
Furthermore, it is like an infant: as its body is small and immature, its mind is likewise small;
as an adult’s body is large, their mind is likewise large.
It is also like a person whose body is coarse and rough, whose mind constantly dwells upon that thought:
"If one wishes to obtain oil to moisten and soften [the body]," this is called the mind following the body.
What is meant by the body following the mind?
That which is called going, coming, sitting, and lying down; practicing giving, precepts, patience, and diligence;

the body of one who is sorrowful being emaciated and withered, the body of one who is joyful being plump and radiant, the body of one who is terrified trembling, the body of one listening to the Dharma with single-minded focus being serene and pleased, and the tears flowing profusely from the face of one weeping—this is what is meant by "the body follows the mind."
The Bodhisattva is not like this; he attains mastery over both body and mind, which is called "that which was previously unattained but is now attained.
Furthermore, good son!

The physical manifestations of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva are like motes of dust; with these minute bodies, they are able to reach everywhere throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges without any obstruction. Yet their minds remain constantly in samādhi, never wavering from the start. This is called "the mind does not follow the body," and it is also called "reaching places that were previously unreachable."
