"Why is it further called 'that which was previously unreachable but can now be reached'?
It is because all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others cannot reach it, whereas bodhisattvas can reach it; therefore, it is named 'that which was previously unreachable but can now be reached.'"

Although all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others may employ supernatural powers, they cannot transform their bodies into subtle particles to pervade immeasurable worlds of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas move, their minds also move accordingly;
it is not so for a bodhisattva, whose mind remains unmoving even though there is nowhere his body does not reach.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s mind not following the body.

Furthermore, son of good family, the transformation body of a Bodhisattva may be as vast as the trichiliocosm; yet when this great body enters the body of a single atom, his mind at that time likewise does not become small.
Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can manifest transformation bodies as vast as the trichiliocosm, they cannot place such a massive body into the space of a single minute mote of dust.
"In this matter, one is not even able to master oneself, much less be able to prevent the mind from moving in accordance with it.
This is called 'the Bodhisattva’s mind does not follow the body.
Furthermore, son of good family!"
With a single voice, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to hear it, yet their mind never thinks:
"I shall cause this voice to pervade all worlds so that these sentient beings, who have not heard it before, may now hear it."
Yet this bodhisattva also never says from the outset:
"I have caused sentient beings to hear now what they have not heard before.
If a bodhisattva were to say:
"One who says, 'I preach the Dharma so that sentient beings may hear what they have not heard,' should be known as someone who will ultimately never attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? That sentient beings have not heard [the Dharma] and that "I am the one who speaks it"—such a mind is the mind of birth and death; for all Bodhisattvas, such a mind has already been exhausted.
For this reason, the body and mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva do not follow one another.
"Good son! The bodies and minds of all ordinary beings follow one another."
It is not so for the bodhisattva; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, although they manifest a small body, their mind is likewise not small. Why is this?
Because the nature of the minds of all bodhisattvas is eternally vast and great.
Although he manifests a great body, his mind is not great.
What is meant by a "great body"?
His body is like the trichiliocosm.
What is meant by a "small mind"?
It is the practice of infant-like behavior.
For this reason, the mind does not follow the body.
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, refrained from drinking alcohol; yet their minds may still be stirred.
Their hearts may be devoid of sorrow or suffering, yet tears may flow from their bodies.
They may truly be without fear, yet their bodies may tremble.”
For this reason, it should be known that the body and mind of a bodhisattva are sovereign and do not follow one another.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifests only a single body, yet all sentient beings each perceive it differently.
"Furthermore, good son, how does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa, hear what he has never heard before?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first grasps the characteristics of sounds—namely, the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and people; the sounds of conch shells, drums, flutes, pipes, singing, and weeping—and practices them."
Through such cultivation, one is able to hear all the sounds of the hells throughout immeasurable trichiliocosms.
By further cultivating this practice, one attains a distinct faculty of hearing that surpasses the divine ear of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Why is this? The ear-faculty attained by those of the Two Vehicles, if it relies upon the pure and subtle four great elements of the first dhyāna, can hear only the sounds of the first dhyāna and not those of the second; the same applies up to the fourth dhyāna.
Although they may at one time hear all the sounds within a trichiliocosm, they cannot hear the sounds of worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable and boundless Ganges Rivers.
For this reason, the ear-faculty attained by a bodhisattva differs from that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because of this difference, what was previously unheard is now heard.

"Although one hears sounds, the mind from the very beginning has no characteristic of hearing sound; it does not form characteristics of existence, permanence, pleasure, self, purity, a master, a support, an agent, a cause, a fixed state, or a result."
"For this reason, that which the bodhisattvas and others had not heard in the past, they now hear.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijñāguṇarāja said:
"If it is as the Buddha has spoken:"
To claim that one does not produce the characteristic of certainty nor the characteristic of fruition is incorrect. Why is this so?
As the Tathāgata previously stated:
"If a person hears even a single phrase or a single word of this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"How is it that the Tathāgata now further says there is no certainty and no fruit?
If one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that is itself the characteristic of certainty and the characteristic of the fruit; why then do you say there is no certainty and no fruit?"
Because one hears evil sounds, an evil mind arises;
because an evil mind arises, one reaches the three miserable realms.
If reaching the three miserable realms is a fixed result, how can you say there is no fixity and no result?
At that time, the Tathāgata praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"

That you are able to ask such a question is because, were the Buddhas to teach that these various sounds possess a fixed mark of fruition, it would not be the characteristic of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; rather, it would be the characteristic of Māra, the characteristic of birth-and-death, and a mark far removed from Nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas, in whatever they proclaim, do not have a fixed characteristic of fruition.
O son of good family!
For example, when a person’s facial reflection is seen in a blade, it appears long when the blade is held vertically and wide when held horizontally.
If there were a fixed characteristic, how could it appear long when vertical and wide when horizontal?
For this reason, whatever the Buddha-Bhagavāns proclaim has no fixed characteristic of a result. "Good son!
Indeed, Nirvāṇa is not truly the fruit of sound."
If nirvana were the fruit of sound, you should know that nirvana would not be an eternal dharma. Good son!
For example, in the world, dharmas produced from causes exist when there is a cause and do not exist when there is no cause.
Because the cause is impermanent, the effect is also impermanent.
Why is this so? Because the cause also becomes the effect, and the effect also becomes the cause.
For this reason, all dharmas have no fixed characteristics.
If nirvana were produced from causes, then because the causes are impermanent, the fruit would also be impermanent.
However, this nirvana does not arise from causes, and its essence is not an effect;
therefore, it is eternal. Good son!
For this reason, the essence of nirvana is neither fixed nor an effect.
“Good son! As for nirvana, it may be called ‘certainty’ and it may also be called ‘fruit.
What is meant by certainty?
The nirvana of all Buddhas is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, it is definitive.
It is free from birth, aging, and decay; therefore, it is definitive.
Those such as icchantikas who have committed the four grave offenses, slandered the Vaipulya sutras, or committed the five heinous crimes have abandoned their original resolve;
yet because they will certainly attain [enlightenment], it is therefore called "fixed."

“Good son! Regarding what you have said—that if a person hears even a single word or a single phrase of my teaching on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—you have not yet fully understood this meaning.”
Listen attentively, and I shall further explain it for you.
Son of good family!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing even a single word or a single phrase of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, do not form a perception of words, do not form a perception of phrases, do not form a perception of hearing, do not form a perception of the Buddha, and do not form a perception of preaching—such a meaning is called the "markless mark."
Because it is characterized by the mark of signlessness, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son! As for what you said—that because of hearing evil sounds one falls into the three miserable realms—that meaning is not so."
Why is this? It is not because of evil sounds that one arrives at the three miserable realms; one should know that the fruit is actually the evil mind itself. Why is that?

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing unpleasant sounds, do not give rise to malice in their minds, one should know that it is not because of unpleasant sounds that they are born into the three miserable realms.
Sentient beings give rise to the three evil destinies because the afflictions and fetters cause their evil minds to proliferate, not because of evil sounds.
If sound possessed a fixed nature, then all who heard it would necessarily give rise to an evil mind.
There are those for whom it arises and those for whom it does not; therefore, one should know that sound has no fixed characteristic.
Because it lacks a fixed nature, even though one relies upon it, an evil mind will not arise.
“World-Honored One!
If sound has no fixed nature, how is it that a bodhisattva hears now what they have never heard before? “Good son!
Sound has no fixed characteristic; that which was not heard before is now being heard by all the bodhisattvas.
For this reason, I say:
"That which was not heard before is now being heard."
“Good son! What is it that was not seen before but is now seen? Good son!”

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, they first apprehend the signs of light, namely: the sun, the moon, the stars and constellations, funeral pyres, lamps and candles, the radiance of jewels and fire, and the light of medicinal herbs.
Through cultivation, one attains a distinct faculty of the eye, which differs from that attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
In what way does it differ?
The pure divine eye attained by those of the Two Vehicles cannot see the first dhyāna if it relies upon the eye-faculty composed of the four great elements of the desire realm.
If one relies on the first dhyāna, one does not see the higher stages; even with one's own eyes, one cannot see them.
If one wishes to see more, the limit is as far as the trichiliocosm.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not cultivate the divine eye; when seeing exquisite physical forms, he sees them all as the nature of bone. Although he sees the forms within worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, he does not conceive of them as forms, nor as permanent phenomena, nor as signs of existence, nor as substantial entities, nor as signs of names and so forth. He perceives them as signs of causes and conditions, yet does not perceive them as objects of vision. He does not say that this is the subtle and pure sign of the eye; he sees only the signs of causes and conditions and non-causes and conditions.
What is the causal condition?
Form is the condition for the eye.
If form were not a causal condition, ordinary worldlings would not give rise to the perception of forms.
For this reason, form is called a causal condition (*pratyaya*).
That which is not a causal condition is such that, although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives form, they do not construct the characteristic of form; therefore, it is not a condition.
For this reason, the pure divine eye attained by a bodhisattva differs from that attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Because of this difference, he simultaneously perceives all the Buddhas currently residing throughout the worlds of the ten directions; this is called what the bodhisattva has not seen before but now sees.
"Because of this difference, one is able to see subtle atoms, which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot see.
Because of this difference, although one sees one's own eyes, from the beginning there is no characteristic of seeing."

One perceives the mark of impermanence and sees that the body of an ordinary person is filled with the impurities of the thirty-six constituents, as if observing an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
For this reason, what was previously unseen is now seen.
"If one perceives the physical characteristics of sentient beings, one knows the capacities for the Great or Lesser Vehicles of those individuals.
By the mere touch of their robes, one also knows the distinctions between the wholesome and unwholesome faculties of such persons."
For this reason, that which was previously unknown is now known;
because of this single vision,
that which was previously unknown is now known.
By virtue of this knowledge, that which was previously unseen is now seen.
"Furthermore, good son, how is it that a bodhisattva knows what was previously unknown? What was previously unknown is now known."

Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the minds of ordinary beings characterized by greed, hatred, and delusion, from the very beginning he does not form mental conceptions of mind or mental factors, nor does he form conceptions of sentient beings or material things; he cultivates the mark of ultimate emptiness, the primary truth.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas constantly and skillfully cultivate the characteristic of emptiness.
By cultivating emptiness, that which was previously unknown is now known.
What is meant by "knowing"?
It is to know that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, and to know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
By virtue of this Buddha-nature, even those such as the icchantikas who have abandoned their original resolve shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
All such matters as these are beyond the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet can be known by bodhisattvas.
For this reason, that which was previously unknown is now known.
"Furthermore, good son, how is it that what was previously unknown is now known?

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, he recollects the various castes, parents, brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, friends, and enemies of all sentient beings throughout past lives; within a single thought-moment, he attains a distinguished wisdom that differs from the wisdom of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
What is the distinction?

The wisdom possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas involves recollecting the castes, parents, and even the enemies of all sentient beings in past lives, thereby forming mental images of those castes up to those enemies.

The Bodhisattva is not like this; although they may contemplate their past lineage, parents, and even enemies, they never give rise to the conceptual marks of lineage, parents, or enemies, but always maintain the mark of dharmic characteristics and the mark of empty stillness.
This is called that which the bodhisattva did not previously know but now knows.
Furthermore, good son,
what is it that was previously unknown but is now known?
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they attain the knowledge of others' minds, which differs from that attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
In what way does it differ?
When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know the minds of human beings with a single moment of wisdom, they are unable to know the minds of those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, or devas.
The bodhisattva is not so; within a single thought-moment, they thoroughly know the minds of sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence.
This is called that which the bodhisattva did not previously know but now knows.
"Furthermore, good son, there is another kind of knowledge.

A Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, within a single moment of mind, knows the initial mind of a Srotāpanna, following it through the sequence up to the sixteenth mind. For this reason, that which was previously unknown is now known."
This is the second merit fully accomplished by a bodhisattva cultivating the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the Great Parinirvāṇa to fully accomplish the third merit?
"Good son!

When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa, he relinquishes compassion and attains compassion; at the time of attaining this compassion, it does not arise from causes and conditions.
What is meant by 'relinquishing compassion and attaining compassion'?"
"Good son! 'Loving-kindness' (maitrī) is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes the loving-kindness of the conventional truth, he attains the loving-kindness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). This loving-kindness of the ultimate truth is not obtained through conditions."
"Furthermore, how does one relinquish loving-kindness and yet attain loving-kindness?
If loving-kindness can be relinquished, it is called the loving-kindness of ordinary beings;
if loving-kindness can be attained, it is called the unconditioned loving-kindness of a bodhisattva."

One abandons the compassion of icchantikas, the compassion of those who have committed the grave prohibitions, the compassion of those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, and the compassion of those who commit the five heinous crimes; instead, one attains the compassion of pity, the compassion of the Tathāgata, the compassion of the World-Honored One, and the compassion that is without cause or condition.
"What, then, is meant by 'renouncing compassion and attaining compassion'?

It means renouncing the compassion directed toward eunuchs, those without sexual organs, those with dual sexual organs, and women; it means renouncing the compassion directed toward butchers, hunters, poultry and pig breeders, and others such as these; and it also means renouncing the compassion of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, in order to attain the objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) of all bodhisattvas."
One does not perceive one's own compassion, nor does one perceive the compassion of others; one does not perceive the observance of precepts, nor does one perceive their violation.
Although one personally perceives pity, one does not perceive sentient beings;
although there is the sensation of suffering, one does not perceive a sufferer.
Why is this? Because they cultivate the foremost ultimate truth.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, achieving and perfecting the third merit.
"Furthermore, good son!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa to achieve and fulfill the fourth merit? Good son!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the Great Parinirvāṇa and achieve the fulfillment of the fourth merit, there are ten matters.

What are these ten? First, their roots are deep and difficult to uproot; second, they give rise to the thought of certainty within themselves; third, they do not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit; fourth, they cultivate pure Buddha-lands; fifth, they eliminate what remains; sixth, they sever the conditions of karma; seventh, they cultivate a pure body; eighth, they thoroughly understand all conditions; ninth, they distance themselves from all enemies; and tenth, they sever the two extremes.
"What is meant by 'roots that are deep and difficult to uproot'?
That which is called a 'root' is non-negligence (*apramāda*).
Of what kind of root is this non-negligence?"
This is what is called the root of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son! The roots of all goodness of all Buddhas are rooted in non-negligence (*apramāda*).
Because of heedfulness, all other roots of goodness increase progressively;
because it is able to cause these roots of goodness to increase, it is the most preeminent among all virtues.
“Good son! Just as among all footprints, the footprint of the elephant is supreme;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most excellent among all wholesome dharmas.”
Good son! Just as among all forms of light, sunlight is supreme;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most excellent among all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son!
Just as among all kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King is the foremost;
so too is the dharma of non-negligence the foremost among all wholesome dharmas."
"Good son! Just as among all flowing waters, the four great rivers are supreme;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the highest and most excellent among all wholesome dharmas."
"Good son! Just as among all mountains, Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is the foremost;
so too is the dharma of non-heedlessness the foremost among all wholesome dharmas."
"Good son!
Just as among flowers born of water, the blue lotus is the most excellent;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most excellent and supreme among all wholesome dharmas."
Good son! Just as among flowers that grow on land, the pāriyātra flower is the most excellent and supreme;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most excellent and supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
Good son! Just as among all beasts, the lion is the foremost;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the foremost and the highest among all wholesome dharmas.
Good son! Just as among all flying birds, the golden-winged garuḍa king is the most excellent and supreme;
so too is the dharma of non-negligence the most excellent and supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
Good son! Just as among those with great bodies, Rāhu, the King of Asuras, is the foremost and the highest;
so too is the dharma of non-heedlessness, for it is the foremost and the highest among all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son!
Just as among all sentient beings—whether two-legged, four-legged, many-legged, or legless—the Tathāgata is the most supreme;
so too is the dharma of non-negligence the most supreme and the highest among all wholesome dharmas."
"Good son! Just as among all assemblies, the Buddha and the Sangha are supreme;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, for it is the most excellent and supreme among all wholesome dharmas."
Good son! Just as within the Buddha-dharma, the dharma of Great Nirvana is the most supreme and the highest;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness, which is the most supreme and the highest among all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son! For this reason, the root of heedfulness is deep and firm, difficult to uproot.
How does one cause it to grow through the practice of heedfulness?"

These are the faculty of faith, the faculty of ethical discipline, the faculty of generosity, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of patience, the faculty of learning, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of virtuous friends. Such faculties as these increase through the practice of heedfulness.
Because it grows and increases, it becomes deep, firm, and difficult to uproot.
For this reason, it is said that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa has roots that are deep and difficult to uproot.
"What is meant by forming the thought of certainty regarding the body?
It is the certain mind arising toward one's own body:
'This body of mine shall certainly become a vessel for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a future life.'"

The mind is also like this: it does not become narrow or limited, nor does it undergo transformation; it does not become the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, nor the mind of Māra, nor the mind that seeks its own pleasure or delights in birth and death; rather, it constantly seeks the mind of compassion for the sake of all sentient beings.
This is called the bodhisattva generating a resolute mind within himself:
"In a future life, I shall become a vessel for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing the Mahāparinirvāṇa, gives rise to the perception of certainty within his own person.
Why does the Bodhisattva not observe the field of merit or the non-field of merit?
What is the field of merit?
From non-Buddhists and those who uphold the precepts, up to the Buddhas—these are called the field of merit.
If one should think:
"To think that 'such persons as these are the true fields of merit'—
one should know that such a mind is narrow and inferior.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives that all immeasurable sentient beings are none other than fields of merit."
Why is this? Because they have well cultivated the distinct foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

For those who have well cultivated the distinct foundations of mindfulness, they observe that among all sentient beings there is neither one who upholds the precepts nor one who violates them; they constantly contemplate what has been taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones:
Although there are four types of giving, all yield pure retribution.
What are these four?
First, the donor is pure, but the recipient is impure;
Second, the donor is impure while the recipient is pure;
third, both the donor and the recipient are pure;
fourth, both are impure.
What is meant by "the gift is pure while the recipient is impure"?
It refers to a donor who possesses ethical discipline, learning, and wisdom, and understands both the act of giving and its karmic fruition;
whereas the recipient violates the precepts, is exclusively attached to false views, and holds that there is neither giving nor fruition.
This is called "the purity of the giver and the impurity of the recipient.
What is meant by "the purity of the recipient and the impurity of the giver"?
It refers to a donor who violates the precepts and is solely attached to false views, claiming that there is no such thing as giving or its karmic fruit.
When the recipient maintains the precepts, possesses extensive learning, and has wisdom, and knows that there is giving as well as the karmic fruit of giving,
this is called an impure donor and a pure recipient.
What is meant by "purity of both the giver and the receiver"?

When both the giver and the receiver possess ethical discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom, and understand the act of giving as well as the karmic fruit of giving—this is called the purity of both the giver and the receiver.
What is meant by "impurity for both"?
It refers to when both the giver and the recipient have broken the precepts and hold wrong views, asserting that there is no such thing as giving or the karmic retribution of giving.
If this is the case, how can one further say that a pure fruit of retribution is obtained?
Because there is no giving and no retribution, it is called "pure. "Good son!
If there is one who does not perceive giving or the retribution of giving, you should know that such a person is not said to have broken the precepts, nor are they solely attached to wrong views."
If, according to the words of the Śrāvakas, one does not see giving nor the karmic fruit of giving, this is called breaking the precepts and holding wrong views.
If, according to this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, one does not see giving nor the karmic fruit of giving, this is called upholding the precepts and holding right views.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have a distinct application of mindfulness; through its cultivation, they do not perceive sentient beings who maintain precepts or break them, nor givers, receivers, or the karmic fruits of giving. For this reason, they are said to possess moral discipline and right view.
For this reason, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit.
What is meant by "purifying the Buddha-land"?

It is when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas cultivate the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, thereby remaining free from the intent to kill or harm.
"By means of these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may all sentient beings attain long life, possess great power, and obtain great supernormal faculties."

By the power of these causes and conditions of his vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all sentient beings within that land shall possess long lifespans, great power, and attain great supernormal faculties.
"Furthermore, good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he abandons the mind of stealing."

"By these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may the lands of all Buddha-fields consist entirely of the seven treasures, and may sentient beings be so abundant that they enjoy every desire to their heart's content."

"By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, the land he obtains will consist entirely of the seven treasures; sentient beings will be wealthy and prosperous, and they will enjoy all their desires at will."
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he abandons the mind of sexual desire."

"By these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands be free from desire, hatred, and delusion, and likewise be without the afflictions of hunger, thirst, or suffering."

By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, the sentient beings in his land will be far removed from greed, anger, and delusion, and none shall suffer from hunger, thirst, or affliction.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, he abandons the mind of false speech."

"By these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may all Buddha-lands always possess lush forests, flowers, fruits, and fragrant trees, and may all sentient beings therein attain wondrous voices."

By the power of these causes and conditions of his vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all lands shall always possess lush forests, flowers, fruits, and fragrant trees; and all sentient beings therein shall obtain pure, sublime, and wondrous voices.
"Furthermore, good son!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, they remain far removed from double-tongued speech."
"By these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands always live in harmony and together expound the True Dharma."

By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, at the time he attains Buddhahood, all sentient beings within his land will be in complete harmony, discussing and expounding the essential points of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sutra of the Great Nirvana, for the sake of attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and delivering sentient beings, he remains far removed from harsh speech."

"By these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may the lands of all Buddhas be as level as the palm of a hand, free from stones, sand, thorns, and malignant brambles, and may the minds of all sentient beings therein be impartial."

"By the power of these causes and conditions of this vow, when I attain Buddhahood in a future age, the land of my realm shall be as level as the palm of a hand, free from stones, sand, thorns, and wicked brambles; and all sentient beings therein shall have minds that are impartial."
"Furthermore, good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he abstains from meaningless speech."
"By means of these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands be free from suffering and affliction.
By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, when he attains Buddhahood in a future age, all sentient beings within that land shall be free from suffering and affliction.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Sutra of the Great Parinirvāṇa for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to deliver sentient beings, he remains far removed from greed and envy."
"By means of these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands be free from greed, envy, malice, harm, and false views."

"By the power of the causes and conditions of this vow, at the time when I attain Buddhahood in a future world, all sentient beings within that land shall be entirely free from greed, envy, malice, harm, and false views."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, he remains far removed from affliction and harm."

"By these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may all sentient beings throughout all Buddha-lands together cultivate great loving-kindness and great compassion, and attain the stage of regarding all as one's only child."

"By the power of these causes and conditions of this vow, when I attain Buddhahood in a future age, may all sentient beings throughout that world together cultivate great loving-kindness and great compassion, and attain the stage of regarding all as one's only child."
"Furthermore, good son!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, for the sake of attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and delivering sentient beings, they remain far removed from false views."
"By these roots of goodness, I vow to share them with all sentient beings; may all sentient beings in all Buddha-lands fully attain the Mahāprajñāpāramitā."

"By the power of these causes and conditions of this vow, when I attain Buddhahood in a future age, all sentient beings in that world shall be able to receive, uphold, and practice the Mahāprajñāpāramitā."
"This is called a bodhisattva cultivating a pure buddha-field.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva eliminate what remains? There are three kinds of 'what remains': [the remainder of afflictions, the remainder of karma, and the remainder of birth]."
First, the residual retribution of afflictions; second, residual karma; third, residual existence.
"Good son, what is meant by the residual retribution of afflictions?"
If there are sentient beings who habitually associate with and indulge in sensual desire, they fall into hell due to the ripening of that retribution.
Upon emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals, namely: pigeons, sparrows, mandarin ducks, parrots, *kapiñjala* birds, *śārika* birds, blue jays, fish, turtles, monkeys, and deer.
If one obtains a human body, one may take on the form of a eunuch, a woman, one with both sexual organs, one without sexual organs, or a prostitute.
If one leaves the household life, one will violate the first grave precept.
This is called the remaining retribution.
"Furthermore, good son, if there are sentient beings who,
with a mind of intense earnestness, cultivate and associate with anger, they will fall into hell because that retribution has ripened."

Emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals, namely venomous snakes—possessing four kinds of venom: the venom of sight, the venom of touch, the venom of the bite, and the venom of the breath—as well as lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, cats, wildcats, hawks, and falcons.
If one obtains a human body, one is fully possessed of the sixteen types of evil disciplinary codes;
if one leaves the household life, one violates the second grave precept.
This is called residual retribution.
"Furthermore, good son!
If there are those who cultivate ignorance, when that retribution ripens, they fall into hell.
Emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—namely, the forms of elephants, pigs, oxen, sheep, water buffaloes, fleas, lice, mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, and so forth."
If one obtains a human body, yet is deaf, blind, mute, crippled, or hunchbacked—possessing incomplete faculties—one is unable to receive the Dharma.

Even if one succeeds in leaving the household life, one's faculties may be dull and obtuse, one may delight in violating the heavy precepts, or even descend to a state of lowliness and contemptibility.
This is called the residual retribution. "Furthermore, good son,
if there are those who cultivate arrogance, when that retribution ripens, they will fall into hell."
Emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals, namely dung-worms, camels, donkeys, dogs, and horses.
If born among humans, they receive the bodies of slaves and servants, or endure poverty and begging.
Or, having attained renunciation, one is constantly held in contempt by sentient beings and violates the fourth precept;
this is called the residual retribution.
Such as these are termed the residual retributions of afflictions.
Such are the remaining retributions; because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to practice the Great Nirvāṇa, they are all completely eliminated.
What are these remaining karmas?

This refers to the karma of all ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), the karma of all śrāvakas, the karma of srotāpannas that results in seven more existences, the karma of sakṛdāgāmins that results in two more existences, and the karma of anāgāmins that results in existence within the realm of form (rūpadhātu); these are called residual karma.
In this way, because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to practice the Great Nirvāṇa, they completely eliminate all remaining karma.
What, then, constitutes "remaining existence"?

When an Arhat attains the fruit of Arhatship, or a Pratyekabuddha attains the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood, they revolve within these two fruits without karma or fetters; this is called "remaining existence" (upadhi-śeṣa).

"These three kinds of remaining dharmas are extinguished by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva through the cultivation of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s extinction of what remains."
"How does a bodhisattva cultivate the pure body?
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the precept of non-killing, there are five kinds of mind: namely, inferior, middling, superior, superior-middling, and supreme;
this applies likewise up to right view."
These fifty mental states are called the initial resolve.
When these fifty states are fully perfected with certainty, it is called fulfillment.
Thus, one hundred such mental states are termed "one hundred merits"; when one hundred merits are fully perfected, they constitute a single mark (lakṣaṇa).
In this manner, through successive stages, one fully accomplishes the thirty-two marks, which is called the pure body.
For this reason, one further cultivates the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*); for there are sentient beings in the world who serve eighty deities.
What are these eighty? They are:

the twelve days, the twelve great gods, the five great planets, the Big Dipper (Ursa Major), Aśvina-deva, Cāraṇa-deva, Brahmāvatī-deva, Śrī-devī, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, Pṛthivī-deva, Vāyu-deva, Varuṇa-deva, Agni-deva, Brahmā-deva, Rudra-deva, Indra-deva, Kumāra-deva, Aṣṭabhuja-deva, Maheśvara-deva, Bhañjara-deva, Hārītī-devī, the Four Heavenly Kings, Lipikāra-deva, and Vasu-deva; these are named the eighty.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he cultivates the eighty minor marks to adorn himself; this is called the pure body of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because these eighty marks are that in which all sentient beings place their trust and submission.
Therefore, while the Bodhisattva cultivates the eighty minor marks with an unmoving body, he causes those sentient beings to each see him according to their respective inclinations.
Having seen him, they revere him and each gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the pure body. "Good son!

It is like a person who wishes to invite a great king; they must first adorn their residence, making it utterly pure, and prepare various kinds of a hundred-flavored delicacies, after which the king will accept the invitation."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: wishing to request the Dharma-wheel King of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he must first cultivate his body until it is utterly pure; only then will the Unsurpassed Dharma King take up residence therein.
For this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva must cultivate a pure body. "Good son!
It is like a person who, wishing to consume ambrosia, must first purify their body."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: wishing to partake of the unsurpassed nectar-like flavor of the Dharma—the Prajñāpāramitā—he must first purify his body with the eighty minor marks.
"Good son!
It is like a fine vessel made of gold or silver filled with pure water; both its interior and exterior are pure.
In the same way, the body of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is pure, and when it holds the water of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, both its interior and exterior are pure."
"Good son!
It is like a cloth from Vārāṇasī that is naturally white and easily takes dye. Why is this?"
Because its nature is pure and white, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise; by virtue of the purity of his body, he swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate the pure body.
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thoroughly understand all conditions?

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive the characteristic of form, does not perceive the conditions of form, does not perceive the substance of form, does not perceive the arising of form, does not perceive the cessation of form, does not perceive a single characteristic, does not perceive diverse characteristics, does not perceive a seer, does not perceive appearances, and does not perceive a receiver.
Why is this? Because they have thoroughly understood causes and conditions.
As it is with form, so it is with all phenomena; this is called a bodhisattva’s thorough knowledge of all conditions.
"How does a bodhisattva destroy all enemies?
All afflictions are the enemies of a bodhisattva; because a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly remains far removed from them, this is called a bodhisattva destroying all enemies."
Bodhisattvas dwelling in the fifth stage do not regard the various afflictions as enemies.
Why is this? It is because it is due to afflictions that bodhisattvas take birth.
Because they exist, they are able to transform and teach sentient beings through successive generations.
For this reason, they are not called enemies.
What, then, constitutes an enemy?
Regarding those who slander the Vaipulya sutras:
although a bodhisattva, wherever they may be reborn, does not fear the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, they fear only such slanders of the Vaipulya.
All bodhisattvas have eight kinds of māras who are called enemies; to distance oneself from these eight māras is called "being free from enemies.
This is what is meant by a bodhisattva being free from all hostile adversaries.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s distancing from the two extremes?
The so-called ‘two extremes’ refer to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) and the affliction of craving (*tṛṣṇā-kleśa*).
A bodhisattva constantly distances himself from the twenty-five states of existence and the affliction of craving; this is called a bodhisattva’s distancing from the two extremes.”
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation of the Great Parinirvāṇa, fully accomplishing the fourth merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaraśmiprabhāsa-Āryaguṇarāja said:
"As the Buddha has taught:
"If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa, they perform all such ten kinds of meritorious deeds.
For what reason does the Tathāgata cultivate only nine matters and not cultivate the Pure Land?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
In the past, I also constantly cultivated these ten matters in their entirety. Among all bodhisattvas and all Tathāgatas, there are none who have not cultivated these ten matters.”
If it were possible for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, to appear within a world filled with impurity, such a thing could never occur.
Good son! You must not now say that the Buddhas appear in impure worlds; you should know that such a thought is unwholesome and narrow-minded.
You should know this now:
I have not, in truth, emerged from the realm of Jambudvīpa.
It is, for example, as if someone were to say:
"The realm of this world alone possesses the sun and moon, while other worlds lack them"—
such a statement is devoid of logical principle.
If there were a bodhisattva who were to speak these words:
"It is likewise with the thought: 'This Buddha-world is defiled and impure, whereas the Buddha-lands of other directions are pure and adorned. Good son! "
To the west, passing from this Sahā world through as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in thirty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Invincible (Anabhibhūta).
For what reason is that land named "Invincible"?
All the adornments of that land are entirely equal and without distinction, just like the Western World of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī), and also like the Eastern World of the Full Moon (Pūrṇacandra).
I have appeared in that land, yet for the sake of transforming sentient beings, I manifest the turning of the wheel of Dharma here in Jambudvīpa.
It is not only my own body that manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma here; all Buddhas likewise turn the wheel of Dharma within this realm.
For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not fail to practice these ten matters. "Good son!
By virtue of his vows, the Bodhisattva Maitreya shall cause this world to be pure and adorned in a future age."
For this reason, all the worlds of all Buddhas are without exception adorned and purified.
"Furthermore, good son,
how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by practicing the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplish the fifth merit?
Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa and fully accomplishes the fifth merit, there are five kinds of fruits. What are these five?

First, the faculties are fully intact; second, one is not born in a borderland; third, one is cherished by the devas; fourth, one is constantly revered by devas, māras, śramaṇas, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others; fifth, one attains the knowledge of past lives.
"By the power of the causes and conditions of this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these five kinds of meritorious qualities.
The Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue, Universal Radiance, said:
"As the Buddha has taught: "
"If there are good sons or good daughters who cultivate the practice of giving, they will fully accomplish five kinds of meritorious qualities.
Why do you now say that these five things are obtained because of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"
The meanings of such matters differ; I shall now analyze and explain them for you.
"Giving yields five results:

they are indeterminate, impermanent, impure, inferior, and not distinct; they are not untainted (anāsrava) and cannot benefit, bring peace and happiness to, or show compassion for all sentient beings."

If the five things obtained by relying on this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* are definitive, permanent, pure, supreme, and distinct, and are untainted (*anāsrava*), then they can benefit, bring peace and happiness to, and have compassion for all sentient beings.
"Good son! Generally, one who practices giving attains freedom from hunger and thirst;
the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra can cause all sentient beings to completely distance themselves from the twenty-five states of existence and the disease of craving."
The causes and conditions of giving cause birth and death to continue;
the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* can cause birth and death to be severed and no longer continue.
Because of giving, one receives the dharmas of ordinary worldlings.
By means of the Great Parinirvāṇa, one attains the state of a bodhisattva.
While the causes and conditions of giving can sever all suffering and distress of poverty,
the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* can sever all forms of poverty regarding wholesome dharmas.
The causal conditions of giving have portions and fruits;
however, attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the Great *Nirvāṇa* has no portion and no fruit.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation of the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplishing the fifth merit. "Good son!
How does a Bodhisattva cultivate the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and fully accomplish the sixth merit?"

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa and attains the Vajra-samādhi, dwelling therein, he is able to shatter and disperse all dharmas. He perceives that all dharmas are impermanent, characterized by motion, causes for terror, and like sickness, suffering, calamity, and robbery; they perish and decay moment by moment, lacking any reality. All are the realm of Māra and possess no perceptible characteristics.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, although they bestow gifts upon sentient beings, they do not perceive even a single sentient being as real.
For the sake of sentient beings, they diligently cultivate the śīla-pāramitā; the same applies to their cultivation of the prajñā-pāramitā, up to and including that point.
If a bodhisattva sees a single sentient being who is unable to ultimately fulfill and accomplish the dāna-pāramitā, up to and including the fulfillment of the prajñā-pāramitā.
“Good son! For example, wherever a vajra is directed, there is nothing it does not shatter, yet this vajra itself suffers no fracture or loss.
The Vajrasamādhi is also like this: whatever phenomena it is directed toward, there are none it does not shatter, yet this samādhi itself suffers no fracture or loss.”
"Good son!
Just as among all jewels, the diamond is the most supreme, so too is the diamond samādhi attained by a bodhisattva; it is the foremost among all samādhis."
Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this samādhi, all other samādhis come to be subsumed and dependent upon it. Good son!
Just as all minor kings come to submit to and depend upon a universal monarch (cakravartin), so too it is with all samādhis;
they all come to submit to and depend upon the vajra-samādhi.
Good son!
It is like a person who is an enemy of the state and is detested by all; if someone were to kill him, there would be no one among all the people of the world who would not praise that person’s merit.
The Vajra-samādhi is also like this: when Bodhisattvas cultivate it, they are able to destroy all enemies among sentient beings; therefore, it is always honored and revered by all samādhis.
Good son!

It is like a person who possesses great physical strength such that no one can match him; yet if there is another person capable of subduing him, you should know that this latter person is praised by the world.
The Vajra-samādhi is likewise; its power is able to subdue those dharmas that are difficult to subdue. For this reason, all samādhis come to take refuge and submit to it.
“Good son!
It is like a person who bathes in the great ocean; you should know that such a person has already used the waters of all rivers, springs, and ponds.
In the same way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this vajra-samādhi, you should know that they have already practiced all other samādhis.”
"Good son!

For example, within Mount Gandhamādana there is a spring named Anavatapta; that spring possesses water endowed with the eight qualities of taste, and if anyone drinks it, they will be free from all suffering of illness."
The Vajra-samādhi is likewise thus: it is endowed with the Eightfold Noble Path; when a bodhisattva practices it, they sever all afflictions, sores, and grave illnesses.
"Good son!
Just as when a person makes offerings to Maheśvara, one should know that this person has already made offerings to all the devas;
so too it is with the Vajra-samādhi. If someone practices it, one should know that they have already practiced all other samādhis."
“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in this vajra-samādhi, they will see all phenomena without obstruction, as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of their hand.”
Although a bodhisattva attains such a vision, they never form the thought:
"I see all phenomena.
"O son of good family!
It is, for example, like a person sitting at a crossroads who sees all sentient beings coming, going, sitting, and lying down.
The diamond-like samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*) is likewise; it perceives the arising, ceasing, emerging, and submerging of all phenomena (*dharma*).
"Good son!
It is like a high mountain; if someone climbs it, they can see all directions clearly from afar.
The mountain of the diamond-like samādhi is also like this: when a bodhisattva ascends it, there are no dharmas that cannot be seen with perfect clarity from afar."
"Good son!
It is like a spring month when the heavens send down sweet rain; the drops are fine and dense, with no gaps between them, and a person with clear vision sees them with perfect clarity."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; having attained the pure eye of the Vajra-samādhi, he sees all worlds in the eastern direction—even those lands therein that are in the process of formation or destruction—all of which he perceives clearly and without obstruction. This is also the case for the ten directions.
"Good son!
Just as when seven suns appear simultaneously from Mount Yugandhara, all the trees and forests upon that mountain are completely consumed by fire;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Vajra-samādhi: all the thickets of afflictions are instantly extinguished."
Good son! For example, although a vajra can shatter all material things, it never gives rise to the thought:
"I am able to shatter them."
The Vajra-samādhi is also like this: once a bodhisattva has cultivated it, they are able to destroy afflictions, yet they never give rise to the thought, "I am destroying the fetters."
"Good son! It is like the great earth, which can support all things, yet never gives rise to the thought:
'It is by my power that I am able to support them.'"
Fire, too, does not think:
"I am able to burn things.
Water, too, does not think:
"I can moisten and soak.
The wind also does not think:
"I can move objects."
"Space also does not think:
'I am able to contain.
Nirvana likewise does not give rise to the thought:"
"I have caused sentient beings to attain extinction.
The Vajra-samādhi is also like this: although it can eliminate all afflictions, from the very beginning it has no thought to say, "I am able to extinguish them."

"If there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in this vajra-samādhi, in a single thought-moment they transform their bodies to become like those of a Buddha, their number being immeasurable, filling the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Yet, although this bodhisattva performs such transformations, his mind is from the very beginning free of any thought of pride.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva constantly reflects:
"Who possesses such a samādhi that they can perform such transformations?
Only a bodhisattva who dwells securely in this Vajra-samādhi is able to do so.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells securely in this Vajra-samādhi, in a single thought-moment they travel throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and return to their original place.
Although he possesses such power, he does not think or say:
"I am able to do this. Why is that?

By the power of the causal conditions of this samādhi, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in such a vajra-samādhi can, within a single thought-moment, sever all the afflictions of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions; yet, from the very beginning, his mind harbors no conceptualization of having severed the afflictions of those sentient beings.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the causal conditions of this samādhi.
When a bodhisattva abides in this Vajra Samādhi, whatever they proclaim with a single voice, all sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
Manifesting a single color, all sentient beings each perceive various forms and appearances;
remaining in one place without moving their bodies, they enable sentient beings to see them from their respective directions;
expounding a single dharma—whether it be the elements (*dhātu*) or the sense bases (*āyatana*)—all sentient beings each hear it according to their own innate understanding.

"When a bodhisattva dwells in such a samādhi, although they see sentient beings, their mind is from the outset devoid of the mark of 'sentient being'; although they see men and women, there is no mark of 'man' or 'woman'; although they see form-dharmas, there is no mark of 'form,' and so on up to the consciousness-dharma, where there is likewise no mark of 'consciousness'; although they see day and night, there is no mark of 'day' or 'night'; although they see all things, there is no mark of 'all'; although they see all afflictions and fetters, there is no mark of 'affliction' or 'fetter'; they see the Eightfold Noble Path, yet there is no mark of 'Noble Path'; although they see bodhi, there is no mark of 'bodhi'; and they see nirvāṇa, yet there is no mark of 'nirvāṇa.'"
Why is this? Good son,
it is because all dharmas are fundamentally without marks.
By the power of this samādhi, the bodhisattva perceives all dharmas as they truly are—without marks from the very beginning.
"For what reason is it called the Vajra Samādhi?
Good son!..."
For example, if a diamond is placed in the sunlight, its color is not fixed.
The vajra-samādhi is also like this: when it is among a great assembly, its color is likewise not fixed; therefore, it is called the vajra-samādhi.
"Good son! For example, just as no person in the world can appraise the value of a diamond, so too it is with the Diamond Samādhi:
all its merits cannot be measured by any among gods or humans. For this reason, it is further named the Diamond Samādhi."
"Good son!
For example, if a poor person obtains a vajra jewel, they will be able to remain far removed from poverty, suffering, evil spirits, and malevolent poisons.

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: by obtaining this samādhi, they are able to remain far removed from afflictions, all sufferings, all māras, and malevolent poisons; therefore, it is further named the Vajra Samādhi."
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, fully accomplishing the sixth merit.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Twenty-two;
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Twenty-three.
The fifth chapter, "The Bodhisattva Samantaprabhāsa-uttama-guṇarāja," added by the Song dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"Furthermore, good son!..."
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and fully accomplish the seventh merit?
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he reflects as follows:
"What dharmas can serve as the proximate cause for Great Parinirvāṇa?
The Bodhisattva then knew that there are four kinds of dharmas that serve as the proximate cause for Great Nirvāṇa.
If it is said that "diligently practicing all ascetic austerities is the proximate cause for Great Nirvana," this meaning is not correct.
Why is this? It is impossible that one could attain nirvana apart from these four dharmas. What are the four?

First, associating with virtuous friends; second, listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion; third, reflecting with focused mindfulness; and fourth, practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

“Good son! It is like a person who encounters various ailments—whether fever, cold, chronic exhaustion, malarial fever, demonic influences, or the poison of ghosts—who goes to a skilled physician. The skilled physician then prescribes medicine for each ailment accordingly.”
This person, with a sincere heart, properly received the physician’s instructions, prepared the medicine according to those instructions, and took it as prescribed.
Having taken it, his illness was cured and his body attained peace and happiness.
Those who are ill are like the bodhisattvas.
The great physician is like a spiritual friend;
what the physician says is like the Vaipulya sutras;
properly receiving the physician’s instructions is like skillfully contemplating the meaning of the Vaipulya sutras.
Compounding the medicine according to the instructions is like practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in accordance with the Dharma;
the healing of the illness is like the extinction of afflictions;
and the attainment of peace and happiness is a metaphor for attaining Nirvana—eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
“Good son! It is like a king who, wishing to rule according to the Dharma so as to bring peace and happiness to his people, consults his wise ministers as to what that method should be.
The ministers then explain it to him by means of the ancient laws of former kings.”

Having heard this, the king practiced with sincere faith and governed the country according to the Dharma; thus, there were no enemies or adversaries, and consequently, the people lived in peace and happiness, free from affliction. Good son!
The king is like the bodhisattvas;
the wise ministers are like the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra);
and the methods of governance taught by the wise ministers to the king are like the twelve divisions of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga-pravacana).

Having heard this, the king practiced with sincere faith and devotion, just as bodhisattvas focus their minds in contemplation upon all the profound meanings contained within the twelve divisions of the scriptures;

he governed the kingdom according to the Dharma, just as bodhisattvas practice according to the Dharma—namely, the six *pāramitās*. Because he was able to cultivate these six *pāramitās*, he was free from all enemies and adversaries, just as bodhisattvas have already abandoned all fetters, afflictions, and evil thieves;
and he attained peace and happiness, just as bodhisattvas attain Great Nirvana, which is eternal (*nitya*), blissful (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and pure (*śubha*).
“Good son! It is like a person who contracts a malignant leprosy, and a spiritual friend says to him:
‘If you can reach the edge of Mount Sumeru, your illness may be cured.’”
"Why is this? There is an excellent medicine there, its flavor like nectar (*amṛta*); if one can take it, there is no illness that will not be cured.
Having come to believe these words with all his heart, the man went to that mountain to gather and consume the nectar; his illness was eliminated, and he attained peace and happiness in his body.
Those with malignant leprosy represent ordinary worldlings;
spiritual friends represent bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the like;
receiving with sincere faith represents the four immeasurable minds.
Mount Sumeru is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path;
the flavor of ambrosia is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature;
and the healing of leprosy is a metaphor for the extinction of afflictions.
"Attaining peace and happiness" is like attaining *nirvāṇa*, which is eternal (*nitya*), blissful (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and pure (*śubha*).
"Good son! It is like a person who keeps disciples who are clever and of great wisdom; this person teaches them day and night constantly without weariness."
It is the same for all bodhisattvas: they constantly teach and transform all sentient beings—whether they have faith or lack faith—without ever becoming weary or disheartened.
“Good son! A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) refers to those among the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and humans who believe in the Vaipulya sūtras.”
For what reason is one called a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra)?
A good spiritual friend is one who can teach sentient beings to distance themselves from the ten unwholesome actions and to practice the ten wholesome actions.
For this reason, they are called a good spiritual friend.
“Furthermore, a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) teaches in accordance with the Dharma and acts in accordance with what they teach.
What is meant by ‘teaching in accordance with the Dharma’ and ‘acting in accordance with what one teaches’?
One refrains from killing oneself and teaches others not to kill, and so on, up to practicing right view oneself and teaching others right view.
If one can act in this way, one may be called a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
One cultivates bodhi for oneself and is also able to teach others to cultivate bodhi.
For this reason, such a person is called a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra).
One is personally able to practice faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, and is also able to teach others to practice faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom.
Furthermore, for this reason, they are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
A good spiritual friend is so called because they possess wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*).
What are these wholesome qualities?
In all that they do, they do not seek their own pleasure, but always seek peace and happiness for sentient beings;
seeing the faults of others, they do not speak of their shortcomings, but their mouths constantly proclaim only pure and wholesome matters.
For this reason, they are called "good friends" (kalyāṇamitra). "Good son!
It is like the moon in the sky, which gradually waxes from the first day until the fifteenth day."
A spiritual friend is also like this: they cause all students to gradually distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas. "Good son!

If there are those who draw near to a spiritual friend, those who previously lacked ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation will immediately possess them; and those who have not yet fulfilled these qualities will attain further expansion."
Why is this? It is because they draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
By virtue of this proximity, they further attain a thorough understanding of the profound meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
If one is able to listen to the profound meaning of these twelve divisions of the sutras, this is called "listening to the Dharma.

Listening to the Dharma refers to the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; listening to the Vaipulya sūtras is called truly listening to the Dharma, and truly listening to the Dharma is precisely listening to and receiving the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, hearing that there is buddha-nature and that the Tathāgata ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa is called "listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion.
Single-minded devotion to listening to the Dharma is called the Eightfold Noble Path; because the Eightfold Noble Path can sever greed, hatred, and delusion, it is called "listening to the Dharma."
“Now, those who listen to the Dharma are said to be the eleven kinds of emptiness; by means of these various forms of emptiness, they do not construct mental images regarding any phenomena.

Those who listen to the Dharma are said to be those whose minds range from the initial aspiration up to the ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is by virtue of the initial mind that one attains Great Nirvāṇa, not by the act of hearing, but by means of cultivation.”

“Good son! It is like a sick person who, although they hear the physician’s instructions and the names of the medicines, cannot be cured of their illness; it is only by actually taking them that they can be restored to health.”

Although one may hear the twelvefold law of profound dependent origination, it cannot eradicate all afflictions; rather, it is only by means of binding the mind to mindfulness and right reflection that they can be eliminated. This is called the third [practice]: binding the mind to mindfulness and reflection.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called "contemplation with fixed mindfulness"?
It refers to the three samādhis:
the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness.
"Emptiness" means not perceiving a single reality among the twenty-five existences;
"non-action" means not forming aspirations or seeking anything among the twenty-five existences;

"signlessness" means the absence of the ten signs, namely: the sign of form, the sign of sound, the sign of fragrance, the sign of taste, the sign of touch, the sign of arising, the sign of abiding, the sign of ceasing, the sign of male, and the sign of female.
To cultivate these three samādhis is called a bodhisattva’s focused mindfulness and contemplation.
What is meant by practicing in accordance with the Dharma?

Practicing in accordance with the Dharma means practicing the pāramitās from dāna-pāramitā up to prajñā-pāramitā; it means knowing the true characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus); and it also means knowing that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas alike enter parinirvāṇa within the same single path.

The Dharma is precisely permanence, bliss, self, and purity; it is without birth, aging, illness, or death; it is without hunger or thirst; it is without suffering or affliction; it does not decline and does not perish.
“Good son!
One who understands the profound meaning of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* knows that the Buddhas never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa. Good son!”
The foremost true spiritual friend is the Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Why is this? Because they constantly guide and discipline others through three kinds of skillful means.
What are these three?
First, ultimate gentle speech; second, ultimate reprimand; and third, gentle speech combined with reprimand.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are truly spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
"Furthermore, good son!
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are great physicians; therefore, they are called 'good spiritual friends' (kalyāṇamitra). Why is this so?
Knowing the disease and knowing the medicine, one administers the medicine according to the disease;
therefore, they are like a skilled physician who is proficient in the eight branches of medical science and first examines the symptoms of the illness.
There are three kinds of symptoms.
What are these three?
They are wind, heat, and water.
To those with wind disorders, one should administer clarified butter (sarpis).
To those with feverish illnesses, he gives rock honey;
to those with water-retention illnesses, he gives ginger decoction.
Because he knows the root of the disease and administers medicine so that they are cured, he is called a skilled physician.
The Buddha and the bodhisattvas are likewise thus:
they know that the illnesses of all ordinary people are of three kinds—first, desire; second, hatred; and third, delusion.
For those with the affliction of greed, teach them to contemplate the mark of bones;
for those with the affliction of anger, contemplate the mark of loving-kindness and compassion;
for those with the affliction of delusion, contemplate the mark of the twelve links of dependent origination.
For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*). "Good son!
It is like a boatman who, because he skillfully ferries people across, is called a 'great boatman'."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this, delivering all sentient beings from the great ocean of birth and death.
For this reason, they are called "good spiritual friends.
Furthermore, good son!
It is because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cause all sentient beings to fully cultivate and attain the roots of wholesome dharmas. "Good son!
It is like the Snowy Mountains, which are the source of various subtle and superior medicinal herbs."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise so; they are the fundamental source of all that is wholesome.
For this reason, they are called "spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra). "Good son!

Within the Snowy Mountains there is a supreme fragrant medicine called Sahā; if anyone sees it, they shall obtain immeasurable life and be free from the suffering of illness, such that even the four poisons cannot harm them.
If one touches it, their lifespan will increase to a full one hundred and twenty years.
If one contemplates it, they shall attain the knowledge of past lives.
Why is this? It is due to the power of the medicine.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise: if anyone beholds them, they immediately sever all afflictions, and though the four Māras exist, they cannot disturb or confuse them.

If there is anyone who makes contact [with this teaching], their life shall not be cut short; they shall neither be born nor die, neither fall back nor sink away—this so-called "contact" refers to hearing and receiving the sublime Dharma in the presence of the Buddha. If there is anyone who maintains mindfulness [of it], they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra). "Good son!
It is like Mount Gandhamādana, where there is Lake Anavatapta; because of this lake, there are four great rivers, namely the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Sītā, and the Vakṣu."
The sentient beings of the world often say:
"If there is one who has committed offenses, by bathing in these four rivers, all their sins shall be extinguished.
You should know that such words are false and unreal.
Apart from this, what is real?
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are what is real. Why is this so?
If a person draws near to them, they will attain the eradication of all their various transgressions.
For this reason, they are called "virtuous friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
Furthermore, son of good family!

It is like the great earth, where all medicinal herbs, trees, every forest, the hundred grains, sugarcane, and various flowers and fruits, when encountering a celestial drought and on the verge of withering to death, are revived by the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda; out of compassion for sentient beings, they emerge from the great ocean and send down sweet rain, whereby all forests, the hundred grains, and grasses and trees are moistened and grow once more.

All sentient beings are likewise: when their roots of goodness are about to perish, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion and descend from the ocean of wisdom to let fall the rain of nectar, causing all sentient beings to become fully endowed with them and once again attain the dharma of the ten wholesome actions.
For this reason, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*). "Good son!

It is like a skilled physician who is proficient in the eight branches of medicine; when he sees those who are ill, he does not consider their lineage, whether they are handsome or ugly, nor their wealth or treasures, but treats them all. Therefore, the world calls him a 'great skilled physician.'"

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise; seeing that sentient beings suffer from the disease of afflictions, they do not consider their lineage, whether they are handsome or ugly, nor their wealth or treasures, but give rise to a heart of compassion and preach the Dharma for them all.
When sentient beings hear this, the disease of their afflictions is eliminated.
For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
By virtue of the causes and conditions of associating with such virtuous friends, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"How does a bodhisattva, by means of the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, come to draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa?

Because all sentient beings hear the Dharma, they are endowed with the faculty of faith. Having obtained the faculty of faith, they delight in practicing giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, thereby attaining the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of Buddhahood."
Therefore, you should know that the attainment of all wholesome dharmas is entirely due to the power of the causes and conditions of hearing the Dharma. "Good son!

It is like a householder who has an only son; he sends him to another country to trade for necessities, pointing out to him where the roads are passable and where they are obstructed, and further admonishing him:
"If you encounter a courtesan, take care not to become intimate with her."
"If you have those who are dear to you, do not lose your body or life, nor your wealth and treasures.
Furthermore, do not associate with wicked people.
His son respectfully followed his father’s instructions; his body and mind were at peace, and he acquired great quantities of precious goods.

It is likewise with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who expounds the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, demonstrating to all sentient beings and the fourfold assembly the openings and obstructions of the various paths.
Because these multitudes have heard the Dharma, they distance themselves from all evils and become fully endowed with wholesome dharmas.
For this reason, through the causal conditions of listening to the Dharma, they shall draw near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! It is like a bright mirror that reflects a person’s facial features with complete clarity.
The bright mirror of listening to the Dharma is also like this: when someone looks into it, they see their good and evil deeds clearly, without any obscuration.”
For this reason, through the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa. "Good son!
It is like a merchant who wishes to go to an island of jewels but does not know the way."
Someone showed him the way, and following those instructions, the man immediately reached a treasure island and obtained immeasurable quantities of various rare gems beyond calculation.
