All sentient beings are likewise: desiring to reach a virtuous destination to gather the jewels of the Path, they do not know the signs of whether the road is passable or obstructed.
The Bodhisattva shows them the way, and sentient beings, following him, reach the place of goodness and obtain the supreme treasure of Great Parinirvāṇa.
For this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! It is like a drunken elephant, wild, unruly, and violent, intent on killing many.
When an elephant trainer hooks its forehead with a large iron hook, it immediately becomes docile and its evil intentions are completely extinguished.”
All sentient beings are likewise; because they are intoxicated by greed, hatred, and delusion, they desire to commit many evils.
The Bodhisattvas, using the hook of hearing the Dharma, strike them so that they are made to abide [in virtue], and they can no longer give rise to the intention to commit various evils.
For this reason, through the causal condition of listening to the Dharma, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, in various sūtras I have said that my disciples who single-mindedly listen to and receive the twelve divisions of the scriptures will be free from the five hindrances and cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.
By thus cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"Because of listening to the Dharma, those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna are freed from all fears."

Why is this? The householder Sudatta was afflicted with a grave illness; his mind was filled with great sorrow and fear. Upon hearing Śāriputra explain that there are four merits of a srotāpanna and ten kinds of consolation, once he had heard these matters, his terror was immediately dispelled.
For this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because it opens the eye of the Dharma.
In the world there are three kinds of people:
first, those who are sightless; second, those with one eye; and third, those with two eyes.
Those called "sightless" are those who never hear the Dharma.
A person with one eye, though they may briefly hear the Dharma, their mind does not abide in it;
a person with two eyes listens and receives with single-minded devotion, practicing exactly as they have heard.
It is by means of hearing the Dharma that one comes to know these three types of people in the world.
For this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa. "Good son!
Long ago, when I was in the city of Kuśinagara, Śāriputra fell ill and suffered from physical pain."
At that time, I looked back and commanded the bhikṣu Ānanda to preach the Dharma extensively for me.
When Śāriputra heard of this matter, he told his four disciples:
"Lift my bed and carry it to the place where the Buddha is; I wish to listen to the Dharma."
At that time, the four disciples obeyed the command and carried him away.
Having heard the Dharma, by the power of hearing the Dharma, his suffering was alleviated and his body attained peace and security.
For this reason, through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"How does a bodhisattva, by means of the causal condition of reflection, draw near to Mahāparinirvāṇa?"
Through this contemplation, the mind attains liberation. Why is this?
All sentient beings are constantly bound by the five desires; yet, through such contemplation, they all attain liberation.
For this reason, by contemplating dependent origination, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, good son,
all sentient beings are constantly deluded regarding the four dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
By means of contemplation, one comes to see that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure.
Having seen them thus, the four inversions are immediately severed.
For this reason, by contemplating dependent origination, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son,
all dharmas have four characteristics.
What are these four? First, the characteristic of birth; second, the characteristic of aging; third, the characteristic of illness; and fourth, the characteristic of extinction.

By means of these four characteristics, all ordinary beings from the level of common folk up to those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* are made to experience great suffering and affliction.
If one can maintain mindfulness and engage in correct reflection, even when encountering these four, no manifold sufferings will arise.
For this reason, through the causal condition of reflection, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
No wholesome dharmas whatsoever are obtained without relying on this reflection. Why is this?

Although some may listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, if they do not contemplate it, they will ultimately be unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, by contemplating dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, good son, if there are sentient beings who believe that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are immutable and thus give rise to reverence, you should know that this is entirely due to the power of the causal condition of focused mindfulness and contemplation; through this, they are able to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*).
For this reason, by contemplating dependent origination, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
"How does a bodhisattva practice in accordance with the Dharma? Good son!
To sever all unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas is called the bodhisattva’s practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is meant by practicing in accordance with the Dharma?

Seeing that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity—because of this vision, one would rather sacrifice body and life than violate the prohibitive precepts; this is called a bodhisattva practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
"Furthermore, what is practice in accordance with the Dharma?
There are two kinds of cultivation:
first, the real; second, the unreal."
That which is unreal refers to not knowing the true reality of nirvāṇa, the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the characteristics of empty space; this is called the unreal.
What is reality?
To be able to know the true marks of nirvāṇa, buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the characteristics of empty space—this is called reality.
What is meant by knowing the characteristics of nirvāṇa?
There are eight matters regarding the characteristics of nirvāṇa. What are these eight?
First, exhaustion; second, the nature of goodness; third, reality; fourth, truth; fifth, permanence; sixth, bliss; seventh, self; eighth, purity—these are called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are eight matters.
What are these eight? First, liberation;
second, the nature of goodness; third, unreality; fourth, lack of truth; fifth, impermanence; sixth, absence of pleasure; seventh, absence of self; eighth, absence of purity.
Furthermore, there are six characteristics:
first, liberation; second, goodness; third, unreality; fourth, lack of authenticity; fifth, peace and bliss; and sixth, purity.
If there are sentient beings who sever the afflictions by relying on the mundane path, such nirvana would involve eight matters of liberation that are not real. Why is this?
Because it is not permanent,
and because it is impermanent, it lacks substantiality;
because it lacks substantiality, it lacks reality.
Although afflictions have been severed, because they may arise again, there is impermanence, non-self, suffering (non-bliss), and impurity.
These are called the eight matters regarding nirvāṇa and liberation.
“What are the six characteristics?
Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have severed their afflictions, they are called ‘liberated’;
yet because they have not yet attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are called ‘unreal.’”
Because it is not real, it is called "untrue";
because one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a future age, it is called "impermanent";
and because one attains the untainted Eightfold Noble Path, it is called "pure" and "blissful."
“Good son! If one knows in this way, this is knowing nirvāṇa; it is not called the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the true mark, or space.”
"How does a bodhisattva know the Buddha-nature?
There are six aspects of the Buddha-nature. What are these six?"
First, permanence; second, purity; third, reality; fourth, goodness; fifth, that which should be seen; sixth, truth.
Furthermore, there are seven matters:
the first is that which is verifiable, while the remaining six are as stated above.
This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the Buddha-nature.
What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the marks of the Tathāgata?

The Tathāgata is the mark of awakening, the mark of goodness, permanence, bliss, self, purity, liberation, and reality; he demonstrates the path that can be seen. This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the marks of the Tathāgata.
“How does a bodhisattva know the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)?

Phenomena are those that are wholesome or unwholesome, permanent or impermanent, pleasant or unpleasant, self or non-self, pure or impure, known or unknown, understood or not understood, real or unreal, cultivated or uncultivated, teachers or non-teachers, and true or untrue. This is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena.”
"How does a bodhisattva know the characteristics of the Saṃgha?

As for the Saṃgha, if it were permanent, blissful, self, and pure, these would be the characteristics of disciples, characteristics that are visible, and characteristics that are virtuous, real, yet unreal."
Why is this? Because all śrāvakas shall attain the Buddha-way.
For what reason is it called "true"?
Because of awakening to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
this is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of the Saṅgha.
"How does a bodhisattva know the true characteristic (bhūtalakṣaṇa)?"

As for the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): whether it be permanence or impermanence, pleasure or non-pleasure, self or non-self, purity or impurity, good or evil, existence or non-existence, nirvāṇa or non-nirvāṇa, liberation or non-liberation, knowledge or non-knowledge, abandonment or non-abandonment, realization or non-realization, cultivation or non-cultivation, seeing or non-seeing—these are called the true mark; they are not nirvāṇa, nor buddha-nature, nor tathāgata, nor dharma, nor saṃgha, nor empty space.

"This is called the Bodhisattva’s knowledge, through the cultivation of such Great Nirvāṇa, of the distinct characteristics among the phenomena of nirvāṇa, buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the true mark, space, and so forth."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he does not perceive empty space. Why is this?
Because it is not seen by the five eyes of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, only the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) can perceive it.
Since there is no dharma whatsoever that can be seen by the wisdom-eye, this is precisely what is called "seeing."
If one perceives that the absence of things is called space, then such space is termed "real.
Because it is real, it is termed "perpetually non-existent";
because it is perpetually non-existent, it lacks pleasure, self, and purity.
Good son! Emptiness is called the non-existence of dharmas, and the non-existence of dharmas is called emptiness.
It is like the world, where the absence of things is called empty.
The nature of space is likewise thus; because it possesses nothing, it is called "space.
"Good son! The nature of sentient beings and the nature of space are both devoid of any substantial nature."
Why is this? It is as when a person says:
"One must first eliminate existing things, and only then create emptiness."
"However, this space truly cannot be created.
Why? Because it is non-existent."
Because it does not exist, one should know that emptiness does not exist.
If this nature of space were something that could be produced, it would be called impermanent;
if it were impermanent, it would not be called space.
“Good son! Just as people in the world say:
‘Space is formless, unobstructed, eternal, and immutable.’”
"For this reason, the world designates the dharma of space as the fifth great element.
Good son! Yet this space truly has no inherent nature."
Because of its luminosity, it is called "empty space," yet in reality there is no empty space.
Just as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) has no inherent nature in reality, yet is said to exist for the sake of sentient beings, so too is this case.
"Good son! The essence of nirvāṇa is likewise thus: it has no place of abiding; it is simply the place where all Buddhas sever the afflictions, and for this reason it is called nirvāṇa."
Nirvana is precisely permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Although Nirvana is blissful, it is not the bliss of sensory experience; rather, it is the bliss of supreme, wondrous quiescence.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess two kinds of bliss:
first, the bliss of quiescent extinction; second, the bliss of awakened cognition.
The essence of the true mark possesses three kinds of bliss:
First is the pleasure of sensation, second is the pleasure of quiescence, and third is the pleasure of awakening.
The Buddha-nature is a single pleasure; because it shall be seen, at the time one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is called the pleasure of bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijñāguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the place where afflictions are severed were nirvāṇa, this would not be so.”
Why is this? When the Tathāgata first attained the Way of Buddhahood in the past, he went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River.
At that time, Māra, together with his retinue, came to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
The time for your parinirvāṇa has arrived; why do you not enter it?
The Buddha addressed the Māra King:
"I have not yet found a disciple who is widely learned, well-versed in the prohibitions and precepts, intelligent and sharp-witted, and capable of transforming sentient beings;

for this reason, I do not enter [Nirvana]. If it is said that the place where afflictions are severed is Nirvana, then since Bodhisattvas and others have already severed afflictions over immeasurable kalpas, why are they not called "Nirvana"?
Since both are states where [defilements] are severed, for what reason is it said that only the Buddhas possess this while Bodhisattvas do not?
If the severance of afflictions were not itself Nirvana, why did the Tathāgata formerly tell the Brahmin Jāti,
"This very body of mine is now Nirvana"?
At another time, when the Tathāgata was in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, Māra again entreated the Tathāgata, saying:
"In the past, because there were no disciples who were learned, observant of the precepts, intelligent, of sharp wisdom, and capable of transforming sentient beings, you did not enter parinirvāṇa."
"Now that they are all complete, why do you not enter [Nirvana]?
The Tathāgata then addressed Māra, saying:
"Do not harbor thoughts of anxiety or delay; three months from now, I shall enter Nirvana."
"World-Honored One!
If extinction were not nirvana, for what reason would the Tathāgata have designated that he would enter parinirvāṇa in three months?
World-Honored One!"

If the severance of afflictions were itself nirvana, then when the Tathāgata first severed the afflictions at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree in the past, that would have been nirvana.
For what reason,
World-Honored One, did you further say: "In three months from now, I shall enter parinirvāṇa"?
If it were already nirvana at that time, why did you say to the Mallas of Kuśinagara:
"In the latter part of the night, I shall enter parinirvāṇa"?
“The Tathāgata is truthful; how could he utter such false words?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāsa-viśāla-guṇarāja, saying: “Good son!
If it is said that the Tathāgata possesses a broad and long tongue, one should know that the Tathāgata has already abandoned false speech for immeasurable kalpas.
Whatever words all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak are truthful and without falsehood.
"Good son! As you have said, regarding Māra Pāpīyas’s request in the past for me to enter parinirvāṇa:
Good son, that Māra King truly did not know the definitive characteristics of nirvāṇa."
Why is this? Pāpīyān thinks that not transforming sentient beings and remaining in silence is itself nirvāṇa. Good son!
For example, when people of the world see someone who does not speak and performs no actions, they say that this person is no different from the dead.
Māra Pāpīyān is just like this; seeing that the Tathāgata does not transform sentient beings and remains silent without preaching, he concludes that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! The Tathāgata does not say that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are without distinction; he speaks only of the non-distinction between the two dharmas of permanence and purity.”
"Good son!

The Buddha does not say that the Buddha, the Buddha-nature, and nirvāṇa are indistinguishable in their characteristics; he only says that they are indistinguishable in being eternal, constant, and unchanging."
"Good son!
The Buddha does not say that nirvāṇa and the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) are without distinction; he only says that they are without distinction in being eternally present and truly immutable."
“Good son! At that time, my śrāvaka disciples gave rise to disputes.
Just as the evil bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī violated my teachings, frequently transgressing the prohibitions and precepts, accepting impure things, and greedily seeking gain and offerings.”
He praised himself before the laypeople, saying:
"I have attained the state free from outflows, namely the fruit of stream-entry," up to:
"I have attained the fruit of arhatship."
He disparaged and insulted others, failing to show reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the precepts, and his preceptor.
He spoke publicly before me, saying:
"The Buddha permitted the possession of such items, while the Buddha did not permit the possession of such-and-such items."
I also said to him:
"I truly do not permit such things as these.
He then spoke in opposition to my words:
"Such things as these were indeed permitted by the Buddha.
Because such evil persons do not believe my words, for their sake I said to Pāpīyas:
"Do not be distressed or delayed; three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! Because of such evil bhikṣus, the śrāvaka disciples who study under me do not see my body nor hear my Dharma; they then say that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa.
Only the bodhisattvas are able to see my body and constantly hear my Dharma; therefore, they do not say that I have entered nirvāṇa.”
"Although my śrāvaka disciples may speak of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, I have not, in reality, entered into parinirvāṇa. Good son!

If any of my śrāvaka disciples say that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, you should know that such a person is not my disciple; they are a companion of Māra, an evil person of false views, and not one of right view."
If one says that the Tathāgata does not enter nirvāṇa, you should know that such a person is truly my disciple, not a partisan of Māra, a person of right view, and not one who is evil or heterodox.
“Good son! From the beginning, I have never seen among my disciples anyone say:
‘The Tathāgata does not transform sentient beings but remains in silence; this is called parinirvāṇa.’”
"Good son!
It is like an elder who has many sons, whom he leaves behind when he travels to another land."

Before they had yet returned, all the sons believed that their father had already passed away; yet the elder was in fact not dead, though the sons, being deluded, all conceived the thought that he had perished.

The śrāvaka disciples are also like this: because they do not see me, they say that the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara; yet I have not truly entered parinirvāṇa, though the śrāvaka disciples conceive the notion of my nirvāṇa.
“Good son! It is like a bright lamp that someone covers; those who do not know say the lamp has already been extinguished, yet its bright flame has in fact not been extinguished at all.”
Because of this ignorance, they give rise to the notion of extinction.

It is the same with my śrāvaka disciples: although they possess the eye of wisdom, their minds are inverted by being shrouded in afflictions; failing to see my true body, they falsely conceive the notion of my parinirvāṇa, whereas in reality, I have not attained ultimate extinction.
“Good son! It is like a person born blind who does not see the sun or the moon; because he does not see them, he does not know the characteristics of day and night or light and darkness.
Because he does not know them, he then says that the reality of the sun and moon does not exist.”
The sun and moon truly exist, yet the blind do not see them;
because they do not see them, they give rise to perverted conceptions, saying that there is no sun or moon.
The śrāvaka disciples are also like this: like those born blind, failing to see the Tathāgata, they claim that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata does not truly enter parinirvāṇa; it is due to inverted perceptions that such a thought arises. "Good son!
It is like clouds and mist obscuring the sun and moon, whereupon a deluded person says that the sun and moon do not exist."
The sun and moon truly exist, yet because they are obscured, sentient beings do not see them.

It is the same with the śrāvaka disciples: because their eye of wisdom is covered by various afflictions (kleśa), they do not see the Tathāgata, and thus they say that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
"Good son! This is merely the Tathāgata manifesting the conduct of an infant; it is not his final extinction. Good son!"
Just as in Jambudvīpa, when the sun sets, sentient beings do not see it because it is obstructed by the Black Mountains; yet, in its true nature, the sun never actually sinks away.
Because sentient beings do not see it, they conceive the notion that it has set.
The śrāvaka disciples are also like this: because they are obstructed by the mountains of various afflictions, they do not see my body.
Because they do not see it, they conceive the notion that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa; yet, in reality, I have not ultimately and eternally ceased to exist.
Therefore, in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, I said to Pāpīyān:
"Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
O son of good family!
The Tathāgata clearly perceives that in three months the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa shall ripen;
he also sees that Subhadra of Mount Gandhamādana, having completed his summer retreat, shall come to my dwelling.
For this reason, I told Māra Pāpīyān:
"Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
"O son of good family!"
There are five hundred Mallas who, by the end of these three months, shall likewise give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, I have told Pāpīyas:
"Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."

“Good son! Just as with Cunda and the others, as well as the five hundred Licchavis and the woman Āmrapālī, after three months their roots of goodness for the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment will reach maturity.”
"For the sake of these beings, I told Pāpīyān:
'Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
O son of good family!"
Sunakṣatra associated with non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others; for twelve full years, I preached the Dharma to him, yet that man, holding false views, neither believed nor accepted it.
"I know that the roots of this person's false views will certainly be uprooted after three months; for this reason, I said to Pāpīyas:
'In three months' time, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.'"
“Good son! For what reason did I, in the past, by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, tell Māra Pāpīyān:
‘I do not yet have many disciples of great wisdom; therefore, I cannot enter parinirvāṇa’?”

...so it was said? At that time, I desired to turn the Wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī for the sake of the five bhikṣus; next, I desired to do so for the five bhikṣus—namely Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimalākṣa, Gavāmpati, and Subhūti; next, I desired to do so for fifty people including the householder Ugga; next, I desired to do so for King Bimbisāra of Magadha and immeasurable humans and devas; next, I desired to do so for the five hundred bhikṣus who were the disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; next, I desired to do so for the two brothers, Nadī-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, along with their five hundred disciples; and finally, I desired to turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma for Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the other two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
For this reason, I told Māra Pāpīyān that I would not enter parinirvāṇa.
"Good son! There is a state called nirvāṇa, but it is not the Great Parinirvāṇa."
What is meant by nirvana that is not the Great Nirvana?
To sever the afflictions without seeing the Buddha-nature is called nirvana, but not the Great Nirvana.
Because one does not see the Buddha-nature, it is impermanent and without self; there is only bliss and purity.
For this reason, although one may sever the afflictions, it cannot be called Great Parinirvāṇa.
If one perceives the Buddha-nature as that which can sever the afflictions, then this is called Great Parinirvāṇa.
Because one perceives the Buddha-nature, it is designated as eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
For this reason, the severance of afflictions is also termed Great Parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! ‘Nir’ means ‘no,’ and ‘vāṇa’ means ‘extinction’; the meaning of no-extinction is called *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, ‘vāṇa’ also means ‘covering’; the meaning of non-covering is what is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Pan" means going and coming; that which neither goes nor comes is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Pan" means grasping; the meaning of non-grasping is called *nirvāṇa*.
"Pan" signifies the indeterminate; that which is determinate and devoid of indeterminacy is called Nirvana.
"Pan" signifies the new and the old; that which is free from the meaning of the new and the old is called Nirvana.
"Pan" signifies obstruction; that which is free from the meaning of obstruction is called Nirvana.
“Good son! There are disciples of Uruvilvā, Kāpya, and others who say:
‘*Bha* refers to marks (*lakṣaṇa*); the meaning of being markless is what is called *nirvāṇa*.’”
"Good son! 'Paṇ' means existence; the meaning of non-existence is called nirvāṇa.
'Paṇ' means conjunction; the meaning of non-conjunction is called nirvāṇa."
"Pan" signifies suffering; the meaning of being free from suffering is what is called *nirvāṇa*. "Good son!
One who has severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) is not said to have attained *nirvāṇa*; rather, one in whom afflictions do not arise is said to have attained *nirvāṇa*."
“Good son! The non-arising of afflictions in all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is called nirvāṇa.
All wisdom that is unimpeded regarding phenomena constitutes a Tathāgata. A Tathāgata is not an ordinary person, a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva; this is called buddha-nature.”
The body, mind, and wisdom of the Tathāgata pervade immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable lands without any obstruction; this is called "space.
The Tathāgata abides eternally without change; this is called the "true mark" (dharmatā).
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not, in truth, enter ultimate parinirvāṇa.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the seventh merit through the cultivation of the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by practicing this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fully accomplish the eighth merit? Good son!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa, they sever five things, distance themselves from five things, accomplish six things, practice five things, guard one thing, draw near to four things, believe and comply with the one true mind, and achieve well-liberated wisdom and well-liberated [liberation].
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva eliminate the five things?
They are the so-called five aggregates (skandhas):”
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
As for what is called an "aggregate" (skandha), what is its meaning?

It is that which causes sentient beings to continue in the cycle of birth and death, never free from their heavy burden; it is the dispersing and gathering together, encompassed by the three periods of time, such that when one seeks its ultimate reality, it is utterly unfindable.
For these reasons, they are called "aggregates" (skandha).
Although a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives the aggregate of form, he does not perceive its characteristics. Why is this?
When one investigates the nature of the ten material elements, it cannot be found at all; yet, for the sake of the world, they are spoken of as "aggregates" (*skandha*).
"Feeling" consists of one hundred and eight types; although one perceives the aggregate of feeling, from the very beginning there is no characteristic of feeling.
Why is this? Although sensations are said to be one hundred and eight, in principle they have no fixed reality; therefore, the bodhisattva does not perceive the aggregate of sensation.
The same applies to perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
“The bodhisattva-mahāsattva deeply perceives that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the root from which afflictions arise.
For this reason, he employs skillful means (*upāya*) to bring them to cessation.
How does the bodhisattva distance himself from these five things?
These are the so-called five views. What are the five?
First, the view of a self-identity; second, the view of extremes; third, false view; fourth, attachment to precepts and observances; and fifth, attachment to views.
From these five views arise sixty-two views; because of these various views, birth and death continue without end. For this reason, the bodhisattva guards against them and does not draw near to them.
"How does a bodhisattva accomplish six matters?
This refers to the six foundations of mindfulness. What are the six? First, mindfulness of the Buddha;

second, mindfulness of the Dharma; third, mindfulness of the Sangha; fourth, mindfulness of the devas; fifth, mindfulness of generosity; and sixth, mindfulness of ethical discipline. These are called the six matters accomplished by a bodhisattva.
"What are the five matters that a bodhisattva cultivates?

They are the five concentrations: first, the concentration of knowledge; second, the concentration of tranquility; third, the concentration of experiencing physical and mental bliss; fourth, the concentration of non-bliss; and fifth, the Śūraṅgama concentration."
By cultivating these five kinds of concentrated mind, one draws near to Mahāparinirvāṇa; therefore, the Bodhisattva practices with diligent resolve.
"How does the Bodhisattva guard one thing?
This refers to the bodhicitta.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and diligently protects this bodhicitta, just as an ordinary person protects an only son, or as one who is blind protects their remaining eye.
Just as one traveling through a vast wilderness is protected by a guide, so too is the bodhisattva’s mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) protected.
Because of protecting such a bodhicitta, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
and because of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one possesses the perfection of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which is the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, a bodhisattva guards one dharma.
What are the four things to which a bodhisattva draws near?
They are the four immeasurable minds.
What are the four? First, great loving-kindness; second, great compassion; third, great sympathetic joy; and fourth, great equanimity.
Because these four states of mind can cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta, the bodhisattva fixes his mind upon them and draws near to them.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s faith and compliance with the single reality?
A bodhisattva understands that all sentient beings ultimately return to the one path; this 'one path' refers to the Mahāyāna."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas divide this into three for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, the Bodhisattva believes and complies with it without opposition.
What is meant by "the Bodhisattva’s mind being well-liberated"?
Because the mind of greed, hatred, and delusion has been forever severed and extinguished, this is called the Bodhisattva’s excellent liberation of mind.
What is the Bodhisattva’s excellent liberation of wisdom?
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows all dharmas without obstruction, this is called the Bodhisattva’s wisdom of excellent liberation.
By virtue of this liberation through wisdom, that which was previously unheard is now heard; that which was previously unseen is now seen; and that which was previously unattained is now attained.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabhābhijña-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for what the Buddha has said regarding the liberation of the mind, this meaning is not so.”
Why is this? Because the mind is fundamentally unconditioned. For what reason?
The intrinsic nature of this mind is not bound by greed, hatred, delusion, or any fetters.
If it is fundamentally unbound, how can one say that the mind is "well-liberated"?
World-Honored One!
If the intrinsic nature of the mind is not bound by the fetter of greed, by what causes and conditions could it be bound?
It is like milking a horn: since there is inherently no characteristic of milk, even if one exerts effort, milk cannot be produced.
When it comes to milking a cow, it is not like this: even with little effort, much milk is obtained.
The mind is also like this; if it was originally without greed, how could it now have it?
If greed were originally absent and only came into existence later, then all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—who originally lacked the characteristic of greed—should now all possess it.
“World-Honored One!
It is like a barren woman who originally lacks the characteristic of having a child; though she applies effort and countless causes and conditions, a child cannot be obtained.”
The mind is also like this: fundamentally it has no characteristic of greed; although various conditions are created, greed has no basis to arise.
World-Honored One!
It is like drilling wet wood—fire cannot be obtained.
The mind is also like this: even though one drills and searches for it, greed cannot be found.
How, then, can the fetter of greed bind the mind?
"World-Honored One! [he asked.]
For example, just as oil cannot be obtained by pressing sand, so it is with the mind:
though one may press it, greed cannot be found.
One should know this:
Greed and the mind are two principles that differ from one another; even if greed were to exist, how could it defile the mind?
World-Honored One!
It is like a person trying to drive a stake into empty space—it can never remain fixed there.
It is likewise with greed abiding in the mind: various causes and conditions cannot cause greed to bind the mind.
"World-Honored One!
If a mind free from greed is called 'liberated,' for what reason do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not extract thorns from empty space?"
"Bhagavān!

The mind of the past is not called liberation; the mind of the future likewise has no liberation; and the mind of the present does not coexist with the Path. Of which temporal mind can it be said that it attains liberation?"
“World-Honored One!
Just as a lamp of the past cannot extinguish darkness, a lamp of the future will not extinguish darkness, and a lamp of the present likewise does not extinguish darkness.”
Why is this? Because light and darkness cannot coexist.
The mind is likewise; how then can it be said that the mind attains liberation?
“World-Honored One!
Greed also exists.
If greed did not exist, one would not give rise to greed upon seeing the marks of a woman.”
"If it arises because of the mark of a woman, one should know that this craving truly exists.
Because craving exists, one falls into the three evil realms.
World-Honored One!"
For example, suppose there is a person who sees a painted image of a woman and likewise gives rise to lust; because lust has arisen, they incur various kinds of offenses.
If there were no lust from the outset, how could one see a painting and give rise to lust?
If the mind is free from greed, why does the Tathāgata say that the bodhisattva’s mind attains liberation?
If the mind possesses greed, how can it arise only after perceiving signs?
If one does not perceive signs, then [defilements] do not arise?
Yet we now clearly see that there are evil retributions; one should know that the existence of greed, hatred, and delusion is likewise so.
“World-Honored One!
For example, sentient beings possess bodies but lack a self, yet ordinary worldlings falsely conceive of a notion of self.
Although they harbor this notion of self, they do not fall into the three miserable realms.”
"How is it that one who is lustful gives rise to the perception of a woman where there is no characteristic of a woman, and thereby falls into the three evil realms?
World-Honored One!
It is like drilling wood to produce fire; yet the nature of this fire does not exist within the various conditions. By what causes and conditions does it arise?"
World-Honored One!
Greed is likewise: there is no greed within form, nor is there greed within odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
How then can greed arise with respect to form, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena?
"If greed is entirely absent within all conditions, why is it that sentient beings alone give rise to greed, while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not?
World-Honored One!"
The mind is also not fixed.
If the mind were fixed, there would be no greed, hatred, or delusion;
if it is not fixed, how can you say that the mind attains liberation?
Greed is also indeterminate; if it were indeterminate, how could it cause one to be born in the three evil realms?
Both the greedy person and the object of greed are indeterminate.

Why is this? Because while both take the same form as their object, one may give rise to greed, another to anger, and another to delusion; therefore, both the greedy person and the objective realm are indeterminate.
"If both are indeterminate, for what reason did the Tathāgata say:
'When a bodhisattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa, the mind attains liberation'?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāsa-vairocana-āryaguṇarāja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

Son of good family, the mind is neither bound by the fetter of greed nor is it unbound; it is neither liberated nor unliberated; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither present, nor past, nor future.”
Why is this? Good son,
it is because all dharmas lack intrinsic nature.
"Good son! There are certain non-Buddhists who speak thus:
'When causes and conditions combine, a fruit arises.'"

If that which was originally devoid of the nature of arising within the various conditions could nonetheless give rise [to an effect], then empty space, which does not arise, should likewise produce an effect.
Since empty space does not arise because it is not a cause, it is because the nature of the effect already exists inherently within the various conditions that they combine to produce the effect.
Why is this so? It is like Devadatta, who, when wishing to build a wall, takes clay and earth but does not take pigments;
and when wishing to create a painted image, he gathers pigments but does not take grass or wood.
In making clothing, one takes thread and not mud or wood;
in building a house, one takes mud and not thread or silk.
Because people select these materials, one should know that each among them is capable of producing its own specific result.
Because it is capable of producing an effect, one should know that the nature [of the cause] must necessarily exist within the cause.
If that nature were absent, then all things would have to be produced from within a single thing.
If something can be grasped, produced, or brought forth, one should know that there must first be a fruit within it.
If there were no fruit, people would not grasp, produce, or bring it forth; only empty space—because it is without grasping or production—could give rise to all phenomena.
Because there is a cause, it is like the *nyagrodha* seed residing within the *nyagrodha* tree, clarified butter (*sarpis*) existing within milk, cloth within the threads, and a jar within the clay.
“Good son! All ordinary beings, blinded by ignorance, make this definitive assertion:
‘Form has the meaning of attachment, and the mind has the nature of greed.’”
He spoke again:
"The minds of ordinary persons possess both the nature of greed and the nature of liberation.
When they encounter the conditions for greed, the mind gives rise to greed."
"If one encounters liberation, the mind is liberated.
Although this is said, the meaning is not so.
There are other ordinary worldlings who further say:
"In all causes, there is absolutely no fruit.
There are two kinds of causes:
first, the subtle; second, the coarse and great.
The subtle is eternal, while the coarse is impermanent.
From a subtle cause it transforms into a coarse cause, and from this coarse cause it further transforms to produce the fruit.
Because the coarse is impermanent, the fruit is also impermanent.
"Good son! There are some ordinary people who further say:
'The mind has no cause, and craving also has no cause; it is due to the passage of time that the mind of craving arises. "
"Beings such as these, because they cannot understand the causes and conditions of the mind, transmigrate through the six realms and undergo birth and death in their entirety.
Good son! It is like a dog tied to a pillar by a collar; it circles the pillar all day long and cannot escape."
"All ordinary beings are likewise: bound by the yoke of ignorance to the pillar of birth and death, they circle through the twenty-five states of existence and cannot escape them. Good son!
It is, for example, like a person who has fallen into a latrine and, having emerged, enters it once more;
or like a person whose illness has been cured, yet returns to the cause of that illness;
or like a person traveling on a road who encounters a desolate wilderness and, having passed through it, returns again.
Furthermore, it is like washing clean and then smearing on mud again;

all ordinary beings are just like this. Having already attained liberation from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), yet not having attained liberation from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they return once more to the three evil destinies.
Why is this? All ordinary beings contemplate only the fruit and do not contemplate causes and conditions.
It is like a dog chasing a clod of earth rather than chasing the person who threw it.
Ordinary worldlings are just like this: they observe only the fruit and do not observe causes and conditions.
Because they do not observe them, they fall back from the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception into the three evil destinies.

“Good son! The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively teach that the effect exists within the cause, nor that the effect does not exist within the cause, nor that it both exists and does not exist, nor that it neither exists nor does not exist.”

If one claims that the effect is already definitively present within the cause, or definitively absent, or definitively both present and absent, or definitively neither present nor absent, you should know that such persons are all partisans of Māra.

Those who are bound to Māra are those who love [sensual] objects; such lovers of objects cannot permanently sever the fetters of birth and death, for they do not understand the characteristics of the mind nor the characteristics of craving.
“Good son! The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest the Middle Way. Why is this?
Although it is said that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, they are not definitively so. Why is this?
Because consciousness arises conditioned by the eye, conditioned by forms, conditioned by light, conditioned by the mind, and conditioned by attention.
This consciousness is definitively not within the eye, nor within form, nor within light, nor within the mind, nor within mindfulness; it is neither in between, nor existent, nor non-existent.
Because they arise from conditions, they are called "existent";
because they lack intrinsic nature, they are called "non-existent.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
“Good son! The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively teach that the mind possesses a nature of purity or a nature of impurity, because the pure and impure minds have no place of abiding.”
Because greed arises from conditions, it is said not to be non-existent;
because greed has no inherent nature, it is said not to be existent. "Good son!
Due to causes and conditions, the mind gives rise to greed;
due to causes and conditions, the mind attains liberation. Good son!
There are two kinds of causes and conditions:
first, that which accords with birth and death; second, that which accords with Great Nirvana. "Good son!

Due to certain causes and conditions, there is a mind that arises together with greed and ceases together with greed; there is one that arises together with greed but does not cease with greed; there is one that does not arise together with greed but ceases together with greed; and there is one that neither arises together with greed nor ceases with greed.
"What is meant by 'the mind arises together with greed and ceases together with greed'? Good son!
If there is an ordinary person who has not yet severed the mind of greed and cultivates the mind of greed, such a person's mind arises together with greed and the mind ceases together with greed."
All sentient beings do not sever their greedy minds; the mind arises together with greed and the mind ceases together with greed.

Just as all sentient beings in the desire realm possess the dhyāna of the "taste of the first stage" (āsvādana-dhyāna), whether they cultivate it or not, it is always present and accomplished; when they encounter the necessary conditions, they immediately attain it. What are called "conditions" refers to the calamity of fire.
All ordinary beings are likewise: whether they cultivate [the path] or do not cultivate it, their minds arise together with greed and their minds cease together with greed.
Why is this? Because they have not severed greed.
"What is meant by 'the mind arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed'?

When a disciple of the Śrāvakas gives rise to a greedy mind due to certain conditions, they cultivate the contemplation of white bones out of fear of that greedy mind; this is called 'the mind arising together with greed but not ceasing together with greed.'"

Furthermore, there is a mind that arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed. For example, when a śrāvaka has not yet realized the four fruits and gives rise to a greedy mind due to certain conditions, that greedy mind ceases upon the realization of the four fruits; this is called a mind that arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), the mind arises together with greed but does not perish together with greed. "How is it that it arises together with greed but perishes together with greed? [The answer is: It is because they have attained mastery over all dharmas. Why? Because they have attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas. Furthermore, what is meant by "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed"? It means that while the mind arises simultaneously with greed, it is liberated from greed as soon as it arises. This is called "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed. Why? Because the bodhisattva has already transcended the three realms and attained the stage of non-retrogression. Therefore, although the mind arises together with greed, it does not perish together with greed. Why? Because the bodhisattva has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas. Furthermore, what is meant by "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed"? It means that the bodhisattva, having attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas, is able to manifest the arising of greed through skillful means; yet, because he has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas, he does not actually give rise to greed. This is called "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed. Why? Because the bodhisattva has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas. Furthermore, what is meant by "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed"? It means that the bodhisattva, having attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas, manifests the arising of greed through skillful means, yet because he has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas, he does not actually give rise to greed. This is called "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed. Why? Because the bodhisattva has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas. Furthermore, what is meant by "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed"? It means that the bodhisattva, having attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas, manifests the arising of greed through skillful means, yet because he has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas, he does not actually give rise to greed. This is called "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed. Why? Because the bodhisattva has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas. Furthermore, what is meant by "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed"? It means that the bodhisattva, having attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas, manifests the arising of greed through skillful means, yet because he has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas, he does not actually give rise to greed. This is called "arising together with greed but perishing together with greed. Why? Because the bodhisattva has attained the power of the non-arising of all dharmas. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has severed the mind of greed, yet for the sake of sentient beings manifests as having greed— by means of this manifestation,

he is able to cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to inquire about and receive the wholesome Dharma, thereby bringing them to full accomplishment— this is called "not arising together with greed, but perishing together with greed."
"What is meant by 'arising not together with greed and ceasing not together with greed'?

It refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas—excluding Bodhisattvas other than those on the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi)—and this is called 'arising not together with greed and ceasing not together with greed.'"
For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not definitively state that the nature of the mind is inherently pure or that its nature is inherently impure. "Good son!
This mind does not conjoin with the fetter of greed, nor does it conjoin with hatred or delusion."
"Good son!
It is like the sun and moon, which, though obscured by smoke, dust, clouds, mist, and asuras, cause all sentient beings to be unable to see them because of these conditions."
Although they are invisible, the nature of the sun and moon never becomes conjoined with those five obscurations.
The mind is likewise: though it gives rise to the fetter of greed due to causes and conditions, its true nature remains unaltered.
Although sentient beings say that the mind is conjoined with greed, the nature of the mind in reality is not conjoined with it.
If it is a greedy mind, it is the nature of greed;
if it is non-greedy, it is the nature of non-greed.
A mind free from greed cannot become greedy, and a mind bound by the fetter of greed cannot be free from greed.
Good son! For this reason, the fetter of lustful desire cannot defile the mind.
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have forever destroyed the fetter of greed; therefore, it is said that their minds have attained liberation.
All sentient beings give rise to the fetter of greed due to causes and conditions;
due to causes and conditions, their minds attain liberation."
“Good son! For example, at places on the Snowy Mountains that are steep and precipitous, neither humans nor monkeys can travel;
yet there are other places where monkeys can travel, but humans cannot.”
Furthermore, there are places where both humans and monkeys are able to go. Good son,
regarding those places where humans and monkeys can go, it is like hunters who place pure sticky resin on a board to capture monkeys.
Because of its folly, the monkey went to touch it with its hand; once it had touched it, its hand became stuck.
Desiring to free its hand, it stepped on it with its foot; its foot, too, became attached.
Desiring to free its foot, it bit it with its mouth; its mouth, too, became stuck.
Thus, in these five places, there was no escape at all; the hunter then impaled them with his staff and carried them home on his back.
The treacherous terrain of the Snowy Mountains is a metaphor for the right path attained by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
the monkeys are a metaphor for ordinary worldlings.
The hunter represents Māra Pāpīyān;
the sticky glue is a metaphor for the fetters of craving.
The fact that neither the man nor the monkey can proceed together is a metaphor for how neither ordinary worldlings nor Māra Pāpīyān can proceed together.
The monkey being able to walk where a human cannot is like those among the non-Buddhists who possess wisdom; though the various evil Māras may employ the five desires, they cannot bind them.
Humans and monkeys both being able to walk refers to all ordinary worldlings and Māra Pāpīyān, who constantly dwell within birth and death and are unable to practice.
Ordinary worldlings are bound by the five desires, allowing Māra Pāpīyān to take them away at will, just as a hunter captures a monkey and carries it home on his back.
“Good son! It is like a king who, when dwelling within his own realm, experiences peace and happiness in body and mind;
yet if he enters another’s realm, he encounters manifold sufferings.”
All sentient beings are likewise: if they can abide within their own domain, they will attain peace and happiness;
but if they enter the realm of others, they will encounter evil Māras and undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
One's own domain refers to the four foundations of mindfulness;
the domain of others refers to the five desires.
Why is this called "belonging to Māra"?

There are sentient beings who perceive the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent; they perceive suffering as pleasure and pleasure as suffering; they perceive the impure as pure and the pure as impure; they perceive non-self as self and the self as non-self; they falsely perceive what is not true liberation as liberation and perceive true liberation as non-liberation; they perceive what is not a vehicle as a vehicle and a vehicle as not a vehicle—such persons are said to be bound to Māra.
Those who are bound by Māra have impure minds.

Furthermore, son of good family, if one perceives all phenomena as having a truly existent nature of general and specific characteristics, you should know that when such a person sees form, they conceive the mark of form; likewise, up to seeing consciousness, they conceive the mark of consciousness; seeing a man, they conceive the mark of a man; seeing a woman, they conceive the mark of a woman; seeing a day, they conceive the mark of a day; seeing a month, they conceive the mark of a month; seeing a year, they conceive the mark of a year; seeing the aggregates (*skandha*), they conceive the mark of the aggregates; seeing the sense bases (*āyatana*), they conceive the mark of the sense bases; and seeing the elements (*dhātu*), they conceive the mark of the elements.
One who views things in this way is said to be bound to Māra;
one who is bound to Māra has a mind that is not pure.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If one views the self as form, the self as being within form, form as being within the self, or form as belonging to the self; and likewise views the self as consciousness, the self as being within consciousness, consciousness as being within the self, or consciousness as belonging to the self—one who views in such a manner is bound to Māra and is not my disciple.

“Good son! My śrāvaka disciples have distanced themselves from the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures and instead cultivate various non-Buddhist texts. They do not practice the ascetic vocation of quiescence, but devote themselves entirely to worldly, household affairs.”
What is meant by the affairs of householders?

It refers to accepting and possessing all kinds of impure things: male and female slaves, fields and houses, elephants, horses, carriages, camels, donkeys, chickens, dogs, monkeys, pigs, sheep, and various grains such as rice and wheat; to distance oneself from teachers and monks while associating closely with laypeople; to contravene the holy teachings and say to laypeople:
"The Buddha permits bhikṣus to accept and possess all kinds of impure things."
This is called practicing the affairs of a householder.

“There are certain disciples who do not seek *nirvāṇa*, but only for gain and sustenance; they draw near to and listen to the twelve divisions of the scriptures, yet they consume the property of the universal community (*cāturmahārājika-saṃgha*) and the personal belongings of the *saṃgha* as if they were their own. They are stingy regarding the households of others, and for the sake of reputation, they draw near to kings and princes. They practice divination of good and ill fortune, calculate the movements of the heavens and the changes of the seasons, play at go, *ṣaḍyūta*, *chūpú*, and *tíuhú*. They associate with *bhikṣuṇīs* and young maidens, keep two *śrāmaṇeras*, and constantly frequent butchers, hunters, taverns, and the dwellings of *caṇḍālas*. They engage in various kinds of trade and prepare their own food by hand; they act as messengers for neighboring states, conveying letters and commands. You should know that such persons are the retinue of Māra and are not my disciples.”
"For this reason, the mind arises together with greed and ceases together with greed; even so it is for the mind arising and ceasing together with delusion, up to that point. Good son!"
For these reasons, the nature of the mind is neither impure nor non-impure.
Therefore, I say that the mind attains liberation.

"If there are those who do not accept or store any impure things, but for the sake of Great Nirvana uphold, recite, transcribe, and explain the twelve divisions of the sutras, you should know that such individuals are my true disciples; they do not walk within the realm of the evil Mara Papiyan, and they are practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
By virtue of this cultivation, it does not arise together with greed, nor does it cease together with greed.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment and accomplishment of the eighth merit through the practice of the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-three.

The Sixth Chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāsa-vyūha-udgata-guṇa-rāja:
"Furthermore, good son,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtra so as to fully accomplish the ninth merit?
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, five matters are first brought to complete fulfillment.
What are these five?"
First is faith; second, a straightforward mind; third, ethical discipline; fourth, associating with virtuous friends; and fifth, extensive learning.

"What is faith? It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has faith in the Three Jewels; faith that giving yields its fruit and reward; and faith in the path of the two truths and the One Vehicle, which has no other destination—though for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to swiftly attain liberation, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas have distinguished it into three. They have faith in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and faith in skillful means (upāya); this is called faith."
Such faith cannot be destroyed by any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, brahmās, or any sentient beings whatsoever.
By virtue of this faith, one attains the nature of a noble one (ārya).
By practicing generosity—whether much or little—one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa and does not fall back into the cycle of birth and death;
the same applies to ethical discipline, learning, and wisdom.
This is called faith.
Although one possesses this faith, one does not perceive it; this is the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Great Nirvana that accomplishes the first matter.
What is the "direct mind"?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva maintains a straightforward mind toward all sentient beings.
While all sentient beings may become deceitful and crooked when encountering certain causes and conditions, the Bodhisattva is not so.
Why is this? Because they skillfully understand that all phenomena arise solely from causes and conditions.
Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva may see the various evils and faults of sentient beings, they never speak of them.
Why is this? For fear that afflictions might arise; if afflictions arise, one will fall into the evil destinies.
Thus, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings performing even a small virtuous deed, he praises it.
What is meant by "good"?
It is what is called Buddha-nature.
By praising Buddha-nature, one causes all sentient beings to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:”
"The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva praises the Buddha-nature, causing immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi"—
this meaning is not so.
Why is this? When the Tathāgata first expounded the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he spoke of three types of people:
first, if a sick person obtains a skilled physician, medicine, and a caregiver, the illness will easily be cured; if these are not obtained, it cannot be healed.
Second, whether they obtain it or not, none can be cured;
third, whether they obtain it or not, all can be cured.

All sentient beings are likewise: if they encounter virtuous friends, Buddhas, or Bodhisattvas who preach the sublime Dharma, they are able to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; if they do not so encounter them, they cannot resolve their minds upon it—namely, as *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, or *pratyekabuddha*.

Second, there are those who, even when encountering virtuous friends, Buddhas, or Bodhisattvas who preach the sublime Dharma, are unable to give rise to it; nor can they do so if they do not encounter them—these are called icchantikas.
Third, whether they encounter [favorable conditions] or not, they are all able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; these are called bodhisattvas.

If it is said that both those who encounter [the teaching] and those who do not all give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, why does the Tathāgata now say that it is because of praising the Buddha-nature that sentient beings give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
“World-Honored One!

If it were the case that one could not give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* whether one encounters good friends, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas who preach the sublime Dharma, or does not encounter them, you should know that this meaning is likewise not so.”
Why is this? Because such persons shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Even those who are icchantikas, by virtue of their buddha-nature, shall all likewise attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whether they hear [the Dharma] or not.
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, what is meant by ‘icchantika’?
It refers to one who has severed their roots of goodness.”
This meaning is likewise not so. Why?
Because the Buddha-nature is not subject to cessation; thus, the principle of this Buddha-nature cannot be severed.
Why does the Buddha say that one may sever all roots of goodness?
As the Buddha taught in the twelve divisions of the scriptures in the past, there are two kinds of goodness:
first, the eternal; second, the impermanent.
That which is permanent is uninterrupted; that which is impermanent is subject to interruption.
Since the impermanent can be interrupted, one falls into hell;
since the permanent cannot be interrupted, why is it not prevented?
If the Buddha-nature is uninterrupted and not that of an icchantika, why does the Tathāgata speak thus, saying there are icchantikas?
World-Honored One!
If one generates the mind for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi because of the Buddha-nature, why does the Tathāgata extensively preach the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings?
“World-Honored One!
It is like the four rivers that flow from Lake Anavatapta.
Suppose there were gods, humans, or Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who were to say:”
"It is impossible that this river would not enter the great ocean but instead return to its source.
The mind of bodhi is likewise.

Those who possess the Buddha-nature shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, whether they hear [the Dharma] or not, whether they observe the precepts or not, whether they practice giving or not, whether they cultivate [virtue] or not, and whether they possess wisdom or not.
“World-Honored One!
It is like Mount Udayana, from which the sun rises in the center and reaches due south.
If the sun were to think:”
"To say, 'I shall not go to the West, but shall return to the East,' is impossible.

It is the same with the Buddha-nature: if one does not hear [the Dharma], does not observe the precepts, does not practice giving, does not cultivate [the path], and lacks wisdom, such that one does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is impossible."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have taught that the nature of cause and effect is neither existent nor non-existent; yet such a meaning is also not correct. Why is this so?
If there were no nature of curd within milk, then there would be no curd;
if the seed of the nyagrodha tree lacked the potential for five *zhang* in height, it could not produce a substance five *zhang* tall.
If within the Buddha-nature there were no tree of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how could it produce the tree of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"For this reason, the cause and effect you have described are neither existent nor non-existent; how can such a meaning be consistent?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
There are two kinds of people in the world who are exceedingly rare, like the udumbara flower:
first, those who do not commit unwholesome deeds; second, those who are able to repent for their transgressions. Such persons are truly rare."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of people:
first, those who do kindness; second, those who remember kindness.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of people:
First, receiving and studying new teachings; second, rehearsing the old so as not to forget them.
Furthermore, there are two other types of persons:
first, those who create the new; second, those who cultivate the old.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of people:
first, those who delight in hearing the Dharma; second, those who delight in expounding the Dharma.
Again, there are two kinds of people:
First, skill in posing questions and challenges; second, skill in providing answers.
He who is skillful in posing questions and challenges is you;
he who is skillful in providing answers is the Tathāgata.
"Good son!

Because of this excellent inquiry, you shall immediately be able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; you shall be able to wither the great tree of the twelve links of dependent origination, cross over the vast river of birth and death, wage war against the Māra Pāpīyān, and demolish the victorious banner established by Pāpīyān."
“Good son! As I have previously said:
‘When the three kinds of sick people encounter a skilled physician, a caregiver, and excellent medicine—or even if they do not encounter them—their illnesses are all cured.’”
What is the meaning of this?
Whether one attains it or not, it refers to a fixed lifespan. Why is that?
This person has already cultivated three kinds of goodness—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
Because they have cultivated these three kinds of goodness, they attain a fixed lifespan.

For example, among the people of Uttarakuru, whose lifespan is a thousand years, if there is one who falls ill, they will all recover—whether they obtain a skilled physician, excellent medicine, and nursing care, or do not obtain them.
For what reason?
Because they have attained a fixed lifespan. "Good son!..."
As I have said:
"If a sick person encounters a skilled physician, excellent medicine, and a caregiver, the illness will be cured;
if they do not encounter these, it will not be cured."
"What is the meaning of this? Good son!
The lifespan of such a person is not fixed; although their life has not yet reached its full term, there are nine causes and conditions that can cause them to die prematurely."

What are the nine? First, knowing that food is unwholesome yet eating it anyway; second, eating too much; third, eating again before the previous meal has been digested; fourth, not attending to the timely evacuation of feces and urine; fifth, not following the physician’s instructions during illness; sixth, not following the instructions of the nurse; seventh, stubbornly enduring illness without vomiting when necessary; eighth, walking at night, whereby evil spirits strike one because of such nighttime wandering; ninth, excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse.
For this reason, I have said:
"If a sick person encounters medicine and a physician, the illness can be cured; if they do not encounter them, it cannot be healed. "Good son!"
As I previously stated:
"Whether one encounters [an opportunity] or does not encounter it, neither case is a failure.
What is the meaning of this?
If a person's life has reached its end, whether they encounter [a physician] or not, it cannot be cured.
Why is this? Because their life span has been exhausted.
For this reason, I have said:
"Whether a sick person encounters medicine and a physician or does not encounter them, they shall all fail to recover.

"It is the same for sentient beings: those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta will all achieve success, whether they encounter virtuous friends, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas from whom they receive and study the profound Dharma, or whether they do not encounter them."
Why is this? Because they are able to give rise to the bodhicitta, just as the people of Uttarakuru obtain a fixed lifespan. As I have said:

"From the stage of Srotāpanna up to that of Pratyekabuddha, if they hear the profound Dharma spoken by virtuous friends, Buddhas, or Bodhisattvas, they will then give rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; however, if they do not encounter Buddhas or Bodhisattvas to hear the exposition of the profound Dharma, they will be unable to give rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Just as life is uncertain and may be cut short by nine causes and conditions, so too it is like a sick person who, upon encountering a physician and medicine, recovers from the illness;
yet if they do not encounter them, the illness will not be cured.

Therefore, I say that one can resolve to attain enlightenment upon encountering a Buddha or Bodhisattva and hearing them expound the profound Dharma; yet, if such an encounter does not occur, one cannot so resolve.
As I have previously stated:
"If one encounters virtuous friends, Buddhas, or Bodhisattvas and hears them expound the profound Dharma, one may resolve; however, if one does not encounter them, neither can one resolve."
"What is the meaning of this? Good son!

Whether those who possess the icchantika-nature encounter good friends, Buddhas, or Bodhisattvas who preach the profound Dharma, or whether they do not encounter them, they are alike unable to abandon the mind of an icchantika."
Why is this? Because they have severed the wholesome dharmas.
Even those who are icchantikas can attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? If one can give rise to the bodhicitta, one is no longer called an icchantika. "Good son!
For what reason is it said that icchantikas attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

In reality, those who are icchantikas cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they are like one whose life has come to an end, who, even if they encounter a skilled physician, excellent medicine, and a devoted caregiver, cannot be cured.
Why is this? Because their life-span has come to an end.
"Good son!..."
*Ikṣan* means "faith";
*ti* means "incomplete.
Because they are incomplete in faith, they are called *icchantikas*.
"Buddha-nature is not faith, and sentient beings do not possess it.
Since they do not possess it, how can it be severed?
'Icchantika' means 'skillful means.'"
"Tī" means "incomplete.
Because they are not complete in their cultivation of skillful means for doing good, they are called icchantikas.
Buddha-nature is not something cultivated through skillful means; sentient beings do not possess it [in that sense].
Since it is not complete, how can it be severed?
"Icchan" means progress;
"ti" means incomplete.
Because they lack diligence, they are called icchantikas.
Buddha-nature is not diligence, and sentient beings do not possess it.
Since they do not possess it, how could it be severed?
"Icchan" means "thought," and "ti" means "incomplete.
Because their thoughts are incomplete, they are called icchantikas.
Buddha-nature is not a thought, and sentient beings do not possess it.
Since they do not possess it, how can it be severed?
"Icchantika" means "fixed."
"T'i" means "not possessing.
Because they do not possess meditative concentration, they are called icchantikas.
Buddha-nature is not fixed, and sentient beings do not [inherently] possess it.
Since they are not complete, how can they be severed?
"Icchan" means wisdom;
"ti" means incomplete.
Because they lack wisdom, they are called icchantikas.
Buddha-nature is not wisdom, and sentient beings do not possess it [as such].
Since it is not possessed, how could it be severed?
"Icchan" means "unstable goodness";
"ti" means "incomplete.
Because they lack unstable goodness and are incomplete, they are called icchantikas.
The Buddha-nature is not impermanent, nor is it wholesome or unwholesome. Why is this?
Wholesome dharmas must be attained through skillful means, yet this Buddha-nature is not attained through skillful means; therefore, it is not wholesome.
For what reason is it further called "not unwholesome"?
Because it can attain wholesome fruits; these wholesome fruits are precisely *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, as for wholesome dharmas, they are obtained upon arising.
Furthermore, this Buddha-nature is not something obtained after being born; therefore, it is not "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
Because they have severed all wholesome dharmas obtained through birth, they are called *icchantikas*.
"Good son!..."
"As you have said:
'If icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature, why is the sin of hell not prevented? Good son!"
"Among icchantikas, there is no buddha-nature.

Good son, it is like a king who hears the sound of a vīṇā; its tone is pure and exquisite, so his mind becomes attached to it. He delights in it, cherishes it with affection, and his heart never wishes to let it go."
He then asked the great minister:
"From where does such a wondrous sound emerge?
The minister replied:
"Such a wondrous sound issues from this lute.
The king spoke again, saying,
"Bring that sound here."
At that time, the minister immediately took up a lute and placed it before the king, saying these words:
"Great King, you should know:
this is sound."
The king said to the lute, "Produce sound! Produce sound!
Yet the lute produced no sound at all.
At that time, the great king immediately cut its strings, yet no sound was produced;
he took its hide and wood and split them all apart, searching for the source of the sound, but was utterly unable to find it.
At that time, the Great King became angry with the minister and said,
"How can you utter such a falsehood?
The minister addressed the King:
"Now, regarding the production of sound, the principle is not like this.
It is only through various conditions and skillful means that sound emerges.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it has no fixed location, yet it can be perceived through skillful means."
Because it is visible, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Since those who are icchantikas do not see the Buddha-nature, how could they possibly obstruct the retribution for sins leading to the three evil realms?
"Good son!
If an icchantika believes that there is buddha-nature, you should know that such a person will not fall into the three miserable realms, nor shall they be called an icchantika."
Because they do not have confidence that they possess the Buddha-nature, they fall into the three miserable realms;
because they fall into the three miserable realms, they are called icchantikas. "Good son!
As you have said:
"If milk lacked the nature of curd, it could not produce curd;
if the seed of a nyagrodha tree lacked the nature of being fifty cubits tall, it could not possess a substance fifty cubits tall."
"Such is the speech made by foolish people; the wise never utter such words.
Why is this? Because of the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva)."
"Good son!
If there were already the nature of curd within the milk, it would not need to rely further upon the power of various conditions.
Good son!"

Just as when water and milk are mixed together and left for a full month, they will never turn into curd; yet if a single drop of *pārijātaka* tree juice is added to them, it immediately turns into curd.
If curd already existed inherently, why would it depend upon conditions?
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise: because it relies upon various conditions, it can be seen;
because it relies upon various conditions, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If something is established only by depending upon various conditions, it is devoid of intrinsic nature;
