because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, one is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva always praises the goodness of others and does not litigate their shortcomings; this is called the mind of straightforwardness.
Furthermore, good son!"
What is the upright mind of a bodhisattva?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva never commits evil; should they have any transgression, they immediately repent. They never conceal it from their teachers or fellow students, but feel shame and self-reproach, vowing not to do it again, and regarding even minor offenses as extremely grave.
If a person is interrogated and answers,
"I have indeed committed it," and is asked again:
"Is this offense good or not?
He replied:
"It is not good.
He asked again:
"Is this offense virtuous?"
"Is it unwholesome? He replied,
"It is unwholesome."
He asked again:
"Is this offense the fruit of good or the fruit of evil?"
He replied,
"This transgression is truly not a virtuous result.
He asked again:
"Who has committed this offense?
Could it possibly have been committed by the Buddhas, the Dharma, or the Sangha?
He replied:
"It is not that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are created by me; rather, they are the accumulation of afflictions.
Because of this straightforward mind, one believes in the existence of the Buddha-nature;
because one believes in the Buddha-nature, one cannot be called an icchantika.

Because of their upright mind, they are called disciples of the Buddha; if they receive from sentient beings clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, even by the tens of millions of each kind, it would not be considered much.
This is called the bodhisattva’s straightforward mind.
“How does a bodhisattva cultivate and purify the precepts?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva upholds the prohibitive precepts not for the sake of rebirth in heaven, nor out of fear, nor even to adopt the ‘dog-precepts,’ ‘chicken-precepts,’ ‘ox-precepts,’ or ‘pheasant-precepts. He does not violate the precepts, nor make them deficient, nor make them flawed, nor make them impure, nor adopt the precepts of the śrāvakas. He upholds the bodhisattva-mahāsattva precepts and the śīla-pāramitā precepts, attaining the complete precepts without giving rise to arrogance; this is called the bodhisattva cultivating the Mahāparinirvāṇa and fulfilling the third precept.”
“What is it for a bodhisattva to associate with virtuous friends?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly teaches sentient beings the path of goodness and does not teach the path of evil; he teaches that the path of evil does not yield wholesome fruits.”
"Good son! My body is the true spiritual friend for all sentient beings.
For this reason, I am able to sever the false views held by the brahmin Pukāra."
“Good son!
If there are sentient beings who draw near to me, even if they possess the causes and conditions for rebirth in hell, they will immediately attain rebirth in heaven.
For example, those such as Sunakṣatra were destined to fall into hell, but because they saw me, they were able to sever the causes and conditions for hell and were reborn in the Form Realm heavens.”
Although there are such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, they are not called true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they give rise to the causes and conditions for the mind of an icchantika.

“Good son! In the past, when I was dwelling in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, Śāriputra taught two disciples: one to contemplate white bones and the other to practice counting the breaths. After many years had passed, neither of them attained meditative concentration.”
Due to these causes and conditions, they immediately give rise to wrong views, saying:
"There is no nirvana, nor are there any outflow-free dharmas.
If such things existed, I should have attained them."
"Why is this? Because I am able to properly maintain the precepts I have received.
At that time, seeing that this bhikṣu had conceived such a perverse thought, I called Śāriputra and rebuked him:
"You have not taught them well; how is it that you have preached the Dharma in such a distorted manner to these two disciples?
These two disciples are of different natures: one is a washerman, and the other is a goldsmith."
"The son of the goldsmith should have been taught counting the breaths (ānāpāna), and the washerman should have been taught the contemplation of the skeleton (aśubha-bhāvanā).
Because you taught them incorrectly, you have caused these two men to give rise to evil and heterodox views."
At that time, I preached the Dharma to these two individuals according to their needs; having heard it, they both attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Therefore, I am the true spiritual friend for all sentient beings, whereas Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others are not.
"If there are sentient beings who possess extremely heavy fetters and encounter me, I shall employ skillful means to sever them for them.
For example, my younger brother Nanda possessed extremely heavy desire; I employed various skillful means to eliminate and sever it for him."
Aṅgulimāla possessed heavy hatred, yet upon seeing me, that hatred was immediately severed.
King Ajātaśatru possessed heavy delusion, yet upon seeing me, his deluded mind was instantly extinguished.
Just as the householder Vāsiṣka had accumulated and perfected extremely heavy afflictions over immeasurable eons, they were immediately severed and extinguished upon seeing me.
"Even if there should be a base and lowly person who approaches me and becomes my disciple, by virtue of this cause and condition, all humans and devas will revere and cherish them."
Śrīgupta’s false views were fiercely burning, yet upon seeing me, his false views were immediately extinguished.
Because he saw me, he severed the causes for rebirth in hell and created the conditions for birth in heaven, just as a breath [can extinguish] a *caṇḍāla*.
When their lives were about to end, because they saw me, they regained their life-span, just as did Kauśika;
when their minds were deranged and confused, because they saw me, they regained their original state of mind, just as did Śrī-Gautamī.
The son of a butcher constantly commits evil deeds, yet because he has seen me, he immediately abandons them, like the bhikṣu Chándika.
Because of having seen me, he would rather sacrifice his own body and life than violate the prohibitions and precepts, like the bhikṣu Tṛṇabandha.
For this reason, the bhikṣu Ānanda said:
"Half of the holy life is called a spiritual friend. I said:
"No; it is only by being fully endowed with the pure conduct (brahmacarya) that one is called a virtuous friend.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Great Nirvana, being fully endowed with the fourth [requirement]: intimacy with virtuous friends.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being fully endowed with extensive learning?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva copies, recites, and provides detailed explanations of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, this is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with extensive learning.”
If one sets aside eleven divisions of the canon—retaining, reciting, copying, and explaining only the Vaipulya—this too is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with extensive learning.

Setting aside the twelve divisions of the scriptures, if one can receive, uphold, transcribe, read, recite, analyze, and explain this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra, this is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with extensive learning.
Setting aside these scriptures in their entirety, if one can receive and uphold even a single four-line verse;

and setting aside even this verse, if one can receive and uphold that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and his nature is unchanging—this is called a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with extensive learning.
Setting this matter aside, if one knows that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, one is also called a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with extensive learning.
Why is this? Because dharmas have no intrinsic nature.
Although the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas, he always says nothing at all; this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, achieving the fifth perfection of extensive learning.

“Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, fully accomplish these five matters, they are able to do what is difficult to do, endure what is difficult to endure, and give what is difficult to give.”
What is it for a bodhisattva to be able to perform what is difficult to do?

If they hear that by eating a single sesame seed one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because they believe these words, they shall constantly eat only a single sesame seed for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

If one hears that by entering fire one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then to remain within the mass of blazing fires in the Avīci hell for immeasurable kalpas is called the bodhisattva’s ability to perform what is difficult to do.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s ability to endure what is difficult to endure?

If one hears that by undergoing suffering—through the causes and conditions of being struck and beaten with hands, staves, swords, or stones—one attains great nirvāṇa, then to willingly undergo such experiences upon one's own body throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas without regarding them as suffering is called a bodhisattva’s ability to endure what is difficult to endure.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to give what is difficult to give?

If they hear that one can attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by bestowing upon others kingdoms, cities, wives, children, heads, eyes, marrow, and brains, they immediately, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, bestow whatever they possess—kingdoms, cities, wives, children, heads, eyes, marrow, and brains—upon others. This is called a bodhisattva being able to give what is difficult to give.
Although a bodhisattva can perform what is difficult to do, they never think to say,
"This is my doing. It is the same for performing what is difficult to give.
“Good son! It is like parents who have only one son; they love him most deeply and nourish him at all times with fine garments and exquisite, delicious food, ensuring he lacks for nothing.”

Even if their child were to give rise to a mind of contempt toward them and revile them with harsh words, because of their love, the parents would not harbor anger or resentment, nor would they think:
"I have given this child clothing and food."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, regarding all sentient beings as if they were his only child.
If the child falls ill, the parents also fall ill; they seek out medicine and diligently apply themselves to curing the illness.
Once the illness has been cured, one never gives rise to the thought:
"I have treated this child's suffering from disease.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; seeing all sentient beings afflicted by the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and preaches the Dharma for them.
Because of hearing the Dharma, all afflictions are severed.
Once the afflictions have been severed, one never thinks:
"I have severed the afflictions for the sake of sentient beings."
If one gives rise to such a thought, one will ultimately never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One should only think:
"There is not a single sentient being for whom I have preached the Dharma to cause them to sever their afflictions."
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not feel anger toward sentient beings, nor do they feel attachment.
Why is this? Because they are well able to cultivate the samādhi of emptiness.”
If a bodhisattva cultivates the samādhi of emptiness, toward whom could they give rise to anger or joy? Good son!
It is like a mountain forest that is consumed by a fierce fire, cut down by people, or swept away by water; toward whom could these trees and forests give rise to anger or joy?
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this, having neither anger nor joy toward sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they cultivate the samādhi of emptiness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is the nature of all dharmas inherently empty?”
Is it empty because of "emptiness-of-emptiness"?
If things were empty by their very nature, one should not need to cultivate emptiness before seeing emptiness.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata say that one sees emptiness through the cultivation of emptiness?
"If the nature were not itself empty, then even by practicing emptiness, one could not make it empty.
"Good son! The nature of all dharmas is fundamentally empty from the very beginning."
Why is this? Because the nature of all dharmas cannot be apprehended. Good son!
The nature of form is unattainable.
What is the nature of form?
The nature of form is not earth, water, fire, or wind, yet it is not separate from earth, water, fire, and wind.
It is not blue, yellow, red, or white, yet it is not separate from blue, yellow, red, or white;
it is neither existent nor non-existent.
How, then, can one say that form has an intrinsic nature?
Because their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended, they are said to be empty.
All dharmas are likewise; because they continue in a semblance of succession, ordinary people, having perceived them, say:
"The nature of all dharmas is not empty and quiescent."
“Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with these five things, they perceive that the nature of dharmas is fundamentally empty and quiescent. ‘Good son!

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who perceive the nature of all dharmas as not empty, you should know that such persons are neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas; they cannot cultivate the prajñāpāramitā, they cannot enter into mahāparinirvāṇa, and they cannot directly behold the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—they are the retinue of Māra.’”
"Good son!
The nature of all dharmas is originally empty; furthermore, it is because Bodhisattvas cultivate emptiness that they perceive all dharmas as empty. Good son!"
Just as the nature of all phenomena is impermanent, cessation is able to extinguish them.
If they were not impermanent, cessation would be unable to extinguish them.
Because conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of arising, arising is able to produce them.
Because there is the characteristic of cessation, cessation is able to extinguish it.
Because all dharmas have the characteristic of suffering, suffering is able to cause suffering. "Good son!
Just as the nature of salt is salty and can make other things salty;
the nature of rock honey is sweet and can make other things sweet;
and the nature of fermented grain wine is sour and can make other things sour;
Ginger is inherently pungent and can make other things pungent;
harītakī is bitter and can make other things bitter;
the mango fruit is bland and can make other things bland.
The nature of poison is harmful, causing other things to become harmful;
the nature of ambrosia (amṛta) causes people not to die, and if combined with other substances, it likewise enables them not to die.
It is the same for a bodhisattva’s cultivation of emptiness: by cultivating emptiness, they perceive that the nature of all phenomena is entirely empty and quiescent.
The Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja spoke again:
“World-Honored One!

If salt can cause that which is not salty to become salty, and if the cultivation of the emptiness-samādhi were likewise so, one should know that this concentration is neither good nor sublime, for its nature is inverted.”
“If the samādhi of emptiness sees only emptiness, and emptiness is a non-existent dharma, what is it that is seen?
“Good son! This samādhi of emptiness sees non-empty dharmas and is able to render them empty and quiescent; yet, this is not a perversion.”
"Just as salt makes that which is not salty salty, so too is this samādhi of emptiness: it makes that which is not empty empty. Good son!
Greed is an existent nature; it is not an empty nature.
If greed were empty, sentient beings would not fall into hell because of this cause and condition.
If they do fall into hell, how could the nature of greed be empty?
“Good son! The nature of form exists.
What is the nature of form?
This is what is called perversion.
Because of perversion, sentient beings give rise to craving.
If the nature of form were not perverted, how could it cause sentient beings to give rise to craving?
Because greed arises, one should know that the nature of form is not non-existent.
For this reason, practicing the samādhi of emptiness is not a perversion. "Good son!
All ordinary beings, upon seeing a woman, immediately give rise to the perception of her as a woman.
It is not so for a bodhisattva; although they see a woman, they do not give rise to the perception of her as a woman.
Because they do not give rise to such perceptions, craving does not arise.
Because greed does not arise, it is not a perversion.
Since people of the world perceive women as existing, the Bodhisattva speaks accordingly, saying that there are women.
If, when seeing a man, one were to say, "This is a woman," that would indeed be a perversion.
Therefore, I said to Jāti:
"O Brahmin, if you take day for night, that is an inversion; if you take night for day, that too is an inversion."
"Day has the characteristic of day; night has the characteristic of night.
What is meant by "inversion"? Good son!
All Bodhisattvas dwelling in the nine stages perceive that phenomena possess an intrinsic nature; because of this perception, they do not see the Buddha-nature.
If one were to see the Buddha-nature, one would no longer perceive the intrinsic nature of any phenomena.
Because one cultivates this samādhi of emptiness in this way, one does not perceive the nature of dharmas;
because one does not perceive it, one then perceives the Buddha-nature.
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have two kinds of teachings:
First is the existence of nature, and second is the non-existence of nature.
For the sake of sentient beings, one speaks of the existence of the dharma-nature;
for the sake of the worthy and the sages, one speaks of the non-existence of the dharma-nature.
Because those who hold [the view] that things are not empty perceive the emptiness of phenomena, they cultivate the samādhi of emptiness to bring about the vision of emptiness;
and because even those who hold that there is no nature of phenomena cultivate emptiness, they are themselves empty.
For this reason, by cultivating emptiness one perceives emptiness.
“Good son! You say: ‘I see emptiness;
since emptiness is a non-existent dharma, what is it that is seen?’”
"O son of good family! It is so, it is so;
a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly has nothing to see.
That which has nothing to see is precisely non-existence."
That which is "nothingness" is precisely all dharmas.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the Great Nirvāṇa, they perceive nothing at all within all dharmas.
If there were anything perceived, one would not see the Buddha-nature, would be unable to cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā, and would not attain entry into Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva perceives that the nature of all dharmas is non-existent. "Good son!

It is not only because of seeing samādhi that the Bodhisattva perceives emptiness; the *prajñāpāramitā* is also empty, the *dhyānapāramitā* is also empty, the *vīryapāramitā* is also empty, the *kṣāntipāramitā* is also empty, the *śīlapāramitā* is also empty, and the *dānapāramitā* is also empty. Form (*rūpa*) is also empty, the eye is also empty, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also empty, and even the Tathāgata is empty."
The Great Parinirvāṇa is also empty.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva perceives that all dharmas are entirely empty.
For this reason, while in the city of Kapilavastu, I said to Ānanda:
"Do not be distressed, do not grieve, and do not weep.
Ānanda then said,
"Tathāgata, World-Honored One!"
"My kinsmen and relatives have all now been utterly destroyed; how could I not weep in sorrow?

The Tathāgata was born in this same city as I, and shares the same Śākya clan as my own kin and relatives; why then does the Tathāgata alone feel no grief or distress, and why does his radiant countenance appear even more brilliant?"
"Good son! I spoke again, saying: 'Ānanda!'"
You see that Kapila truly exists;
I see him as empty and quiescent, entirely non-existent.
You see all of the Śākya clan as your kinsmen;
"Because I cultivate emptiness, I see nothing at all.
For this reason, while you give rise to sorrow and suffering, the countenance of my body becomes even more radiant.
Because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas practice such Emptiness Samādhi, they do not give rise to grief or affliction.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the ninth merit through practicing the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. "Good son,
how does the Bodhisattva fulfill the final tenth merit through practicing the subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra?"
"Good son!

A bodhisattva cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to enter great parinirvāṇa—eternal, blissful, self, and pure—and for the sake of all sentient beings, he analyzes and explains the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, revealing the buddha-nature."
If those who are srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas believe these words, they shall all enter into great parinirvāṇa;
if they do not believe them, they will cycle through birth and death.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryaguṇarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what kind of sentient beings will not give rise to reverence for this sutra?”

“Good son! After my parinirvāṇa, there will be śrāvaka disciples who are ignorant and violate the precepts, who delight in inciting strife and contention, who abandon the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and who instead read, recite, and study various non-Buddhist texts, verses, and literary compositions. They will accept and store all manner of impure things, claiming that the Buddha has permitted them.”
Such a person trades fine sandalwood for common wood, exchanges gold for brass, silver for pewter, silk for coarse woolen cloth, and barter the flavor of nectar for foul poison.
“What is meant by ‘trading sandalwood for common wood’?

It is when my disciples, for the sake of making offerings, expound the sutras and the Dharma to laypeople; yet the laypeople are indolent and take no pleasure in hearing it. The laypeople sit on high seats while the bhikṣus sit below, and even though they are provided with various kinds of delicacies and food, they still refuse to listen. This is called trading sandalwood for common wood.”
"What is meant by 'trading gold for brass'?
Brass is a metaphor for visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; gold is a metaphor for the precepts.
When my disciples, on account of these sensory objects, violate the precepts they have received, this is called trading gold for brass."
"What is meant by exchanging silver for white tin?
Silver is a metaphor for the ten wholesome actions, while white tin is a metaphor for the ten unwholesome actions.
When my disciples abandon the ten wholesome actions and practice the ten unwholesome dharmas, this is called exchanging silver for white tin."
"What is meant by 'trading silk for coarse woolen cloth'?
Coarse woolen cloth is a metaphor for shamelessness and lack of remorse; silk is a metaphor for shame and remorse.
When my disciples abandon shame and remorse and cultivate shamelessness and lack of remorse, this is called trading silk for coarse woolen cloth."
"What is meant by 'trading ambrosia for poison'?
Poison is used as a metaphor for various kinds of gain and offerings, while ambrosia is used as a metaphor for the various untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
When my disciples, for the sake of gain and offerings, praise themselves before laypeople, claiming to have attained the untainted, this is called trading ambrosia for poison."
"Because of such evil bhikṣus, this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra will be widely circulated throughout Jambudvīpa.
At that time, there will be disciples who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and extensively propagate this sūtra, and they shall be slain by such evil bhikṣus."
These wicked bhikṣus gathered together and established a strict regulation:
"If there be anyone who upholds, transcribes, recites, or explains in detail the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, none of us shall dwell with them, sit with them, or engage in conversation."
Why is this? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was not spoken by the Buddha; it was composed by those with false views.
Those with false views are none other than the six teachers, and what the six teachers have spoken is not the scripture of the Buddha.

Why is this so? All Buddhas have taught that all phenomena are impermanent, without self, without bliss, and without purity. If one were to say that phenomena are permanent, blissful, with self, and pure, how could that possibly be a sutra spoken by a Buddha?
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas permit the bhikṣus to possess various kinds of items, whereas the six teachers prohibit their disciples from possessing any items at all.
Regarding such a principle, how could it possibly be the teaching of the Buddha?

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas did not prohibit their disciples from consuming the five flavors of beef or eating meat; however, the six heretical teachers did not permit the consumption of the five kinds of salt, the five kinds of beef-flavors, nor fat and blood.
If this were to be rejected, how could it be considered the authentic scripture of the Buddha?
While all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas expound the Three Vehicles, this sutra speaks exclusively of the One Vehicle, namely the Great Nirvana.
How can such words be considered the authentic scriptures of the Buddha?
All Buddhas ultimately enter parinirvāṇa, yet this sutra states that the Buddha is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, and does not enter parinirvāṇa.
"This sutra is not included among the twelve divisions of the canon; it is a teaching of Māra, not a teaching of the Buddha.
"Good son! Although such a person is my disciple, they are unable to believe in or comply with this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*."
"Good son!
At that time, if there are sentient beings who believe even half a verse of this sutra, you should know that such persons are truly my disciples."
"By means of such faith, one immediately perceives the Buddha-nature and enters nirvana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue, Universally Radiant, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Excellent, excellent!
Today the Tathāgata has skillfully revealed the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
World-Honored One!

Because of this matter, I have immediately attained awakening and understanding of one phrase or half a phrase of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; because I have understood from one phrase down to half a phrase, I perceive a small portion of the Buddha-nature.
"As the Buddha has taught, I too shall attain entry into Great Nirvāṇa.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment and accomplishment of the tenth merit through the cultivation of this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-four.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-five.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter 23: The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda, Part One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the entire assembly:
"O sons of good family!
If you have doubts as to whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, whether there is Dharma or no Dharma, whether there is Saṅgha or no Saṅgha;
whether there is suffering or no suffering, whether there is origin or no origin, whether there is cessation or no cessation, whether there is the path or no path;
whether there is reality or no reality, whether there is a self or no self, or whether there is pleasure...
...no pleasure, purity and impurity, permanence and impermanence,
vehicles and no vehicles, nature and no nature, sentient beings and no sentient beings, existence and non-existence,
reality and unreality, causes and no causes, and fruits and no fruits;
Regarding that which is conditioned and unconditioned, karma and non-karma, and retribution and non-retribution—
ask whatever you wish now, and I shall analyze and explain it for you.
"Good son!
In truth, I do not see anyone—whether a deva, a human, a Māra, a Brahmā, a śramaṇa, or a brāhmaṇa—who might come to question me such that I would be unable to answer."

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Siṃhanāda. He rose from his seat, composed his countenance and adjusted his robes, stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I was just about to ask, and the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, has again granted me leave to speak.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O sons of good family!"

You all should now give rise to profound reverence, respect, and praise for this Bodhisattva; you should make offerings to him with various kinds of incense, flowers, music, necklaces, banners, canopies, robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, dwellings, and halls, and you should welcome him when he arrives and see him off when he departs.
Why is this? Because these people have already planted deep roots of goodness under past Buddhas and have perfected their merit; therefore, they now wish to utter a lion’s roar before me.

“Good son! It is like the lion king, who, knowing his own physical strength, the sharpness of his fangs and claws, and planting his four paws firmly upon the ground, dwells securely in his rocky cave, shaking his tail and letting out a roar.
If one is able to possess all such characteristics, know that this person is capable of the lion’s roar.
When the true lion king emerges from his cave at dawn, he stretches and yawns, looks around in the four directions, and lets out a thundering roar for eleven purposes.

What are these eleven? First, because he wishes to destroy those who are not actually lions but falsely pretend to be so; second, because he wishes to test his own strength; third, because he wishes to purify his dwelling place; fourth, because he wishes for his offspring to know their location; fifth, because he wishes for the herd to be free from fear; sixth, because he wishes for those who are sleeping to attain awakening; seventh, because he wishes that all heedless beasts become heedful; eighth, because he wishes for the various beasts to come and take refuge in him; ninth, because he wishes to subdue the fragrant elephants; tenth, because he wishes to instruct his children; and eleventh, because he wishes to adorn his own retinue.

When all birds and beasts hear the lion’s roar, those belonging to the watery realm sink into the deep abysses; those that move on land hide away in their burrows and caves; those that fly fall to the ground; and the great fragrant elephants, overcome with terror, lose control of their bowels and pass dung.
“Good sons! Just as that jackal, though it may follow a lion for a hundred years, can never produce the lion’s roar;
whereas a lion cub, once it has reached three years of age, can roar like the lion king.”

“Good son! The Tathāgata’s perfectly awakened wisdom has the fangs and claws; his body is perfected with the four bases of power and the six pāramitās; he possesses the fierce majesty of the ten powers and has great compassion as his tail. Dwelling securely in the pure cave-dwelling of the four dhyānas, he lets out the lion’s roar for the sake of all sentient beings.”
He crushes the armies of Māra, manifests the ten powers to all beings, and opens the sphere of the Buddha’s practice. He serves as a refuge for those with false views;

he soothes those terrified by birth and death, awakens sentient beings sleeping in ignorance, inspires remorse in those who practice unwholesome dharmas, and reveals the truth to all sentient beings with false views.

He stretched his limbs and emerged from the cave-dwelling of the Noble Conduct, the Brahma Conduct, and the Celestial Conduct for the following reasons: to make known that the six teachers do not possess the lion’s roar; to shatter the arrogance of Pūraṇa and the others; to cause those of the Two Vehicles to give rise to a sense of remorse; to instruct the bodhisattvas of the five stages so that they may generate a mind of great power; and to ensure that the fourfold assembly of right view does not feel fear toward the followers of those fourfold assemblies of false views.
He yawned in order to cause those sentient beings to break their arrogance;
he looked around in the four directions in order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to wholesome dharmas.
In order to cause sentient beings to attain the four kinds of unhindered knowledge, his four paws rest firmly upon the ground;
in order to cause sentient beings to be fully established in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he utters the lion’s roar.
The Lion’s Roar means definitive teaching: that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and that the Tathāgata is eternally present and immutable. "Good son!
Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas may follow the World-Honored Tathāgata for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they are nonetheless unable to utter the lion’s roar.
If Bodhisattvas of the ten stages can practice these three spheres of conduct, you should know that they are then able to roar the lion’s roar.
"O sons of good family!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Lion’s Roar now wishes to let out such a great lion’s roar; therefore, you all should, with a profound mind, make offerings to him, revere, honor, and praise him."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāmin, saying:
“Good son! If you wish to ask anything, you may now do so as you please.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the Buddha-nature?”
For what reason is it called "Buddha-nature"?
For what reason is it further named "permanence, bliss, self, and purity"?
If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why do they not see the Buddha-nature that exists within them?
In what dharmas do Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes dwell such that they do not see them clearly?
In what dharmas does the Buddha dwell such that he sees them clearly?
With what kind of eyes do Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see them unclearly?
"With what eye does the Buddha see with such clarity?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
Excellent, excellent!
If there is anyone who can inquire and seek instruction for the sake of the Dharma, they will be fully endowed with two kinds of adornment:
first, wisdom; second, merit.

If there is a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these two kinds of adornment, they will know the Buddha-nature and further understand what is called the Buddha-nature; they will even be able to know by what eye the bodhisattvas of the ten stages see, and by what eye the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘adornment with wisdom’?”
"What is called the adornment of merit?
Good son, as for the adornment of wisdom, it refers to that which spans from the first stage to the tenth stage; this is called the adornment of wisdom."
The adornment of merit refers to the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, but it is not the perfection of wisdom itself.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The adornment of wisdom refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
the adornment of merit refers to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the nine stages.
"Furthermore, noble son!

That which is the adornment of merit is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), with outflows (*sāsrava*), subject to existence (*bhava*), possessing karmic retribution (*vipāka*), obstructed, and impermanent; it is the dharma of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
That which is the adornment of wisdom is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), without outflows (*anāsrava*), free from existence, without karmic retribution, unobstructed, and eternally abiding."
“Good son! You are now fully endowed with these two adornments; therefore, you are able to inquire about this profound and wondrous meaning.
I too am fully endowed with these two adornments, and am thus able to answer this meaning.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these two kinds of adornment, then one should not inquire about them as being of one kind or two kinds.”
Why does the World-Honored One say that one can answer in terms of "one kind" or "two kinds"?
For what reason?
All dharmas are neither of one nor two kinds; to speak of "one kind" or "two kinds" is the characteristic of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If a bodhisattva lacks the two kinds of adornment, they will be unable to know the one kind or the two kinds."
If there is a bodhisattva who is endowed with the two kinds of adornment, they will be able to understand and know the one and the two.
If it is said that all dharmas possess neither one nor two, this meaning is not so.
Why is this? If there were neither one nor two, how could it be said that all dharmas are neither one nor two? "Good son!
If one says that "one" and "two" are the characteristics of ordinary beings, then such a person is called a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes and is no longer an ordinary being. Why is this?
"One" is named Nirvana, and "two" is named birth-and-death.
For what reason is the first called *nirvāṇa*?
Because it is eternal.
For what reason is the second called birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)?
Because of craving and ignorance,
that which is permanent and nirvana are not the characteristics of an ordinary person;
birth and death, these two, are likewise not the characteristics of an ordinary person.
For this reason, one who possesses both types of adornment is able to question and able to answer.
"Good son, you have asked:
"As for the question, 'What is the Buddha-nature?', listen closely, listen closely; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Good son!"
Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning;
the emptiness of the ultimate meaning is called wisdom.
That which is called "emptiness" does not perceive emptiness or non-emptiness.
The wise perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness, permanence and impermanence, suffering and happiness, and self and non-self.
Emptiness refers to all of birth and death;
non-emptiness refers to Great Nirvana.
Even to the point where seeing "no-self" is equivalent to birth-and-death, while "self" refers to Great Nirvana;
if one sees all things as empty but does not see them as non-empty, it is not called the Middle Way.
Even to the point where seeing all things as "no-self" but not seeing "self" is not called the Middle Way.
The Middle Way is called Buddha-nature.
For this reason, Buddha-nature is eternal, constant, and unchanging; yet because it is shrouded by ignorance, it prevents all sentient beings from perceiving it.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas perceive all things as empty and do not perceive them as non-empty, even to the point of perceiving all things as selfless and not perceiving a self.
For this reason, they do not attain the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
Because they do not attain the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), they do not practice the Middle Way;
because there is no Middle Way, they do not see the Buddha-nature. "Good son!
There are three types of those who do not perceive the Middle Way:
first, those fixed in pleasant practice; second, those fixed in painful practice; and third, those fixed in both painful and pleasant practice.

Regarding those fixed in pleasant practice: this refers to Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who, out of compassion for all sentient beings, experience the bliss of the third dhyāna even while dwelling in the Avīci Hell.
Those who practice exclusively in austerity are called ordinary worldlings;
those who practice both in austerity and in ease are called śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas conceive the notion of a middle way within their practice of both austerity and ease, for this reason, although they possess the buddha-nature, they are unable to see it.
"As to your question,
'By what meaning is it called Buddha-nature?'—
O son of good family!..."
"Buddha-nature is the seed of the Middle Way within the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, good son!"
There are three kinds of paths:
namely, the inferior, the superior, and the intermediate.
The inferior refers to the Brahmā heavens, which are impermanent, yet are mistakenly perceived as permanent.
Regarding the "superior" [delusion]: it is to mistakenly perceive the impermanence of birth and death as permanent, while recklessly calculating the permanence of the Triple Gem to be impermanent.
Why is this called "superior"?
Because it enables one to attain the most supreme *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The middle [view] is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); it perceives impermanence as impermanent and perceives permanence as permanent.
The emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā) is not called "inferior. Why?
Because it is not attained by any ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
It is not called "superior.
Why? Because it is itself the superior.
The path cultivated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is neither high nor low; for this reason, it is called the Middle Way.
"Furthermore, good son!
The fundamental limit of birth and death consists of two types:
first, ignorance; second, craving for existence.
Between these two lie the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death; this is called the middle way.
Thus, because this Middle Way can destroy birth and death, it is called "middle.
For this reason, the dharma of the Middle Way is named Buddha-nature.
Therefore, Buddha-nature is permanent, blissful, self, and pure.

Because sentient beings are unable to see it, they perceive it as impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; however, the Buddha-nature is in reality not impermanent, without bliss, without self, or without purity.
"Good son! It is like a poor man who has a treasure storehouse in his house, yet he does not see it.
Because he does not see it, he lacks constancy, joy, self, and purity."
There is a spiritual friend who says to him:
"Within your own house there is a treasury of gold and jewels; why then are you so poor, afflicted, and suffering, perceiving that there is no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity?"
He then employs skillful means to enable them to see it.
Because they have seen it, these people immediately attain the eternal, the blissful, the self, and the pure.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; sentient beings do not see it.
Because they do not see it, there is no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity.
When there are spiritual friends, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas who, through the power of skillful means, provide various instructions and teachings, they enable those beings to see it;
because they have seen it, sentient beings immediately attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Furthermore, good son!
Sentient beings give rise to views of two kinds:
first, the view of permanence; second, the view of annihilation."
These two views are not called the Middle Way; rather, neither permanence nor annihilation is called the Middle Way.
This absence of permanence and annihilation is precisely the wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination; such contemplative wisdom is termed Buddha-nature.
Although those of the two vehicles contemplate causes and conditions, they still cannot be said to possess Buddha-nature.

Although Buddha-nature is eternal, because all sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance, they are unable to see it; furthermore, they have not yet crossed the river of the twelve links of dependent origination, being like the hare and the horse.
Why is this? Because they do not see the Buddha-nature. Good son!
The wisdom that contemplates these twelve links of dependent origination is itself the seed of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination are called the Buddha-nature.
“Good son! For example, the bitter melon is called ‘fever. Why is this? Because—”
Because it can act as the causal condition for feverish diseases,
the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise so,
O son of good family!
The Buddha-nature has causes and the causes of causes; it has fruits and the fruits of fruits.

That which is the cause is the twelve links of dependent origination; that which is the cause of the cause is wisdom. That which is the fruit is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; that which is the fruit of the fruit is the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! For example, ignorance is the cause and the various formations are the fruit; the formations are the cause and consciousness is the fruit.
By this principle, that essence of ignorance is both the cause and the cause-of-the-cause, while consciousness is both the fruit and the fruit-of-the-fruit.”
The Buddha-nature is also like this. Good son!

For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination neither emerge nor cease; they are neither eternal nor discontinuous; they are neither one nor two; they neither come nor go; and they are neither cause nor effect.
"Good son! This is a cause, not a fruit.

Just as the Buddha-nature is a fruit, not a cause; just as Great Nirvana is both a cause and a fruit; and just as the dharmas produced by the twelve links of dependent origination are neither cause nor fruit—this is what is called Buddha-nature."
Because it is neither cause nor effect, it is eternal, constant, and unchanging.

For this reason, I have said in my sutras that the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination is extremely profound; it is without knowledge, without vision, and inconceivable. It is the realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and is not within the reach of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
"For what reason is it so profoundly deep?

It is because the karmic actions of sentient beings neither persist nor cease, yet they obtain their retributions; although they perish moment by moment, nothing is lost; although there is no agent, there is the performance of action; and although there is no experiencer, there is the retribution."
Although the recipient ceases to exist, the fruit does not perish; it exists through a harmonious combination, devoid of conceptual cognition.

Although all sentient beings act in concert with the twelve links of dependent origination, they do not perceive or know them. Because they do not perceive or know them, there is neither end nor beginning.
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see only the end, but do not see the beginning.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see the beginning and see the end.
For this reason, the Buddhas clearly perceive the Buddha-nature. "Good son!
All sentient beings are unable to see the twelve links of dependent origination; for this reason, they transmigrate in cyclic existence.
Good son! It is like a silkworm that makes a cocoon, being born and dying within it of its own accord.
All sentient beings are likewise; because they do not see the Buddha-nature, they create their own fetters and karma, transmigrating through birth and death like a bouncing ball.
"Good son! For this reason, I have said in various sūtras:
'If there is anyone who perceives the twelve links of dependent origination, that person perceives the Dharma;'"
"One who sees the Dharma is one who sees the Buddha.
The Buddha is none other than the Buddha-nature. Why is this so?
All Buddhas take this as their nature.
"Good son! There are four kinds of wisdom for contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination:
First is the inferior, second is the middling, third is the superior, and fourth is the most superior.
Those who contemplate with inferior wisdom do not see the Buddha-nature; because they do not see it, they attain the path of the śrāvaka.
Those who contemplate with middling wisdom do not see the Buddha-nature; because they do not see it, they attain the path of the pratyekabuddha.
Those with superior wisdom observe and see it not clearly; because they do not see it clearly, they abide in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Those with the most superior wisdom observe and see it clearly; therefore, they attain the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination are called Buddha-nature.
Buddha-nature is none other than the emptiness of the ultimate truth;
the emptiness of the ultimate truth is called the Middle Way.
"The Middle Way is precisely what is called the Buddha;
the Buddha is what is called Nirvana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is no distinction between a Buddha and the Buddha-nature, for what purpose would all sentient beings cultivate the Path?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! As to what you have asked, this meaning is not so.
Although there is no distinction between the Buddha and the Buddha-nature, all sentient beings have not yet fully realized it.”

Good son! It is like a person who, with an evil mind, harms his mother; having harmed her, he gives rise to remorse. Although these two actions are virtuous, this person is still called a person of the hells.
Why is this? Because such a person is certain to fall into hell.
Although this person lacks the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of hell, they are nevertheless still designated as a "person of hell."
"Good son! For this reason, I have said in various sutras:
'If one sees someone practicing wholesome deeds, it is called seeing devas and humans;'"
"One who practices evil is said to see hell.
Why is this? Because they will certainly undergo retribution.
“Good son! Because all sentient beings will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I therefore say that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature.”
All sentient beings truly do not possess the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; for this reason, I have spoken these verses in this sutra:
"Existing originally but now non-existent, Non-existent originally but now existent— Regarding dharmas that exist throughout the three periods of time, There is no such possibility."
"Good son! Existence is of three kinds:
first, future existence; second, present existence; and third, past existence."
All sentient beings shall possess *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in future ages; this is called the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
All sentient beings currently possess all manner of afflictions and fetters; therefore, they do not presently possess the thirty-two marks or eighty minor characteristics.
All sentient beings had severed their afflictions in past lives; therefore, they are able to see the Buddha-nature in the present.
For this reason, I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, even including those such as the icchantikas.

Those such as icchantikas lack any wholesome dharmas; yet the Buddha-nature is also wholesome. Because it will exist in the future, those such as icchantikas all possess the Buddha-nature. Why is this?
Because those such as the icchantikas will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! It is like a person who has milk and curd in their house."
Someone asked,
"Do you have ghee? He replied:
"I have curd, which is not actually ghee," yet because it will certainly become ghee through skillful means, one says, "I have ghee.
Sentient beings are likewise; they all possess the mind.
All who possess a mind shall certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
“Good son! There are two kinds of ultimateity:
first, the ultimateity of adornment; second, the ultimateity of finality.”
The first is the ultimate of the mundane world; the second is the ultimate of the supramundane.
The ultimate of adornment refers to the six *pāramitās*;
the ultimate of finality refers to the One Vehicle attained by all sentient beings. This One Vehicle is called Buddha-nature.
For this reason, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
All sentient beings possess the One Vehicle, yet because it is shrouded by ignorance, they are unable to see it.
"Good son!
Just as the inhabitants of Uttarakuru and the Heaven of the Thirty-three cannot see [those realms] because they are concealed by the fruits of their retribution, so too is the Buddha-nature:
because it is concealed by the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), sentient beings do not see it."
"Furthermore, good son!
Buddha-nature is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; its nature is like clarified butter (ghṛta), and it is the mother of all Buddhas."
By the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, all Buddhas possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
All sentient beings likewise possess the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; however, because they do not practice it, they are unable to see it, and for this reason, they cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! The Śūraṅgama Samādhi has five names: first, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
second, Prajñāpāramitā; third, Vajra Samādhi; fourth, Siṃhanāda Samādhi; and fifth, Buddha-nature. It receives these names according to its various functions in different contexts.”

“Good son! Just as a single samādhi receives various names—such as when dhyāna is called the four dhyānas, the faculties are called the faculty of concentration, the powers are called the power of concentration, enlightenment is called the enlightenment of concentration, the right [limbs] are called right concentration, and the eight factors of great personhood are called the enlightenment of concentration—in the same way, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is also like this.”
“Good son! All sentient beings are fully endowed with three types of concentration—namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior refers to the Buddha-nature.”
For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

Regarding those of middling capacity: all sentient beings are fully endowed with the first dhyāna; when there are causes and conditions, they are able to practice it, but if there are no causes and conditions, they cannot.
There are two kinds of causes and conditions:
first, the calamity of fire; second, the severing of the fetters of the desire realm.
For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings fully possess the intermediate state of concentration (*madhyama-samādhi*).
The "lower concentration" refers to the concentration belonging to the mental factors within the ten universal mental states (*mahābhūmika*).
For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings fully possess the lower concentration.
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; however, because they are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), they are unable to see it."
Although Bodhisattvas of the ten stages perceive the One Vehicle, they do not know that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma.
For this reason, it is said that although Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly.
“Good son! ‘Śūra’ means ‘all that is ultimately so’;
‘ṅgama’ means ‘firm.’”
Because all things are ultimately and firmly established, it is named Śūraṅgama.
For this reason, it is said that the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is called Buddha-nature. "Good son!
On one occasion, while staying by the Nairañjanā River, I said to Ānanda:
"I wish to bathe now; you may take my robe and the bath powder."
Once I had entered the water, all the birds and creatures of the air, water, and land came to gaze upon me.
At that time, there were also five hundred brahmins who came to the riverbank; they approached my location and said to one another, "How has he obtained a body of diamond?"
“If only the Gautama would not speak of the view of annihilationism, I would receive the precepts for the fast from him.
Son of good family!
At that time, through the knowledge of others' minds, I knew what this brahmin was thinking in his heart, and I said to the brahmin:
"What do you mean when you say that I hold the view of annihilationism?
That brahmin said, "Gautama!"
Previously, in various sutras, it was taught that all sentient beings are entirely devoid of self. Since you say there is no self, how can you claim this is not the view of nihilism?
If there is no self, who is it that upholds the precepts?
"Who are those who break the precepts?
The Buddha said, "I do not say that all sentient beings are entirely devoid of self; rather, I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature."
Is the Buddha-nature not the self?
For this reason, I do not say that it is severed.
Because all sentient beings do not see the Buddha-nature, they perceive no permanence, no self, no bliss, and no purity.
"This is what is called explaining the view of annihilationism.

When the brahmins heard it said that the Buddha-nature is precisely the self, they immediately conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and promptly left the household life to cultivate the path to enlightenment.
"All winged creatures, as well as those belonging to the water and land, also gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi;
having given rise to this mind, they immediately attained the sacrifice of their bodies. Good son!..."
This buddha-nature is truly not the self;
it is for the sake of sentient beings that it is designated as "self. Good son!
The Tathāgata, for specific reasons, speaks of non-self as self; yet it is truly non-self.
Although he speaks thus, there is no falsehood in it. Good son!
Due to specific causes and conditions, I speak of the self as being non-self, yet in reality there is a self.
For the sake of the world, although I speak of non-self, there is no falsehood.
“The Buddha-nature is without self, yet the Tathāgata speaks of a self because it is eternal;
the Tathāgata is the self, yet he speaks of non-self because he has attained mastery.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature—just like the Vajrapāṇi—by what reason is it that all sentient beings are unable to see it?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

It is like the phenomenon of form (rūpa-dharma): although there are differences such as blue, yellow, red, and white, as well as length, shortness, and physical shape, one who is blind does not see them.”
Although it is not seen, one cannot say that blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, or substantial forms do not exist.
Why is this? Although the blind do not see them, those with eyes do see them.
The Buddha-nature is likewise: although all sentient beings cannot see it, and even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see only a small portion of it, the Tathāgata sees it in its entirety.
What the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes perceive of the Buddha-nature is like seeing forms at night; what the Tathāgata perceives is like seeing forms by day.
“Good son! It is like a person born blind who cannot clearly perceive forms.
There is a skilled physician who treats his eyes; by the power of the medicine, he comes to see clearly.”
It is the same for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages: although they see the Buddha-nature, they cannot perceive it clearly;
however, by the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they are able to attain clear perception.

“Good son! If there is someone who perceives all dharmas as impermanent, without self, without bliss, and without purity, and perceives that which is not all dharmas as likewise impermanent, without self, without bliss, and without purity—such a person does not see the Buddha-nature.”
"All" refers to birth and death;
"not-all" refers to the Triple Gem.

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas perceive all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; they likewise perceive that which is not-all as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure.
For this reason, they do not see the Buddha-nature.

Bodhisattvas of the ten stages perceive all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and impure; they do not partially perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity within those same phenomena.
For this reason, one perceives only one part out of ten.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perceive all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, without pleasure, and impure; they do not perceive all phenomena as permanent, pleasurable, self, or pure.
For this reason, one perceives the Buddha-nature as clearly as observing an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand.
For this reason, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is called "ultimate."
“Good son! For example, although the new moon cannot be seen, one cannot say it does not exist.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; although all ordinary beings cannot perceive it, one cannot say that they lack the Buddha-nature.”
“Good son! The Buddha-nature consists of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness.
All sentient beings possess these three types; however, they must first destroy their afflictions before they can perceive it.”

Only after those such as the icchantikas have destroyed their state of being icchantikas can they attain the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness.
For this reason, I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature.
“Good son! The twelve links of dependent origination are shared equally by all sentient beings; they are both internal and external.
What are these twelve?
The afflictions of the past are called ignorance (*avidyā*); the karma of the past is called formative action (*saṃskāra*).
In the present life, the initial entry into the womb is called consciousness (*vijñāna*);
the five stages of entry into the womb while the four sense organs are not yet complete are called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
When the four faculties are complete but contact has not yet arisen, it is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);
when one has not yet distinguished between suffering and pleasure, it is called contact (*sparśa*);
when one is habituated to a single craving, it is called feeling (*vedanā*).
To habitually associate with the five desires is called craving;
to greedily seek after things internal and external is called grasping;
to initiate bodily, verbal, and mental karma on account of internal and external matters is called becoming.
Present-world consciousness is called future birth;
present name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are called future-world aging, sickness, and death.
This is called the twelve links of dependent origination. "Good son!

Although all sentient beings possess these twelve links of dependent origination, some may not have them complete; for instance, if one dies during the *kalala* stage, the twelve links are not present, whereas from birth until old age and death, the twelve links are fully realized."

Sentient beings in the realm of form lack the three types of feeling, the three types of contact, and the three types of craving; they are free from old age and illness, and may likewise be said to be complete with the twelve factors.
Although formless sentient beings lack form and so forth, up to and including aging and death, they may still be said to be complete with the twelve [links].
Because these are necessarily attained, it is said that sentient beings equally possess the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Good son!
The Buddha-nature is also like this; because all sentient beings will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I therefore say that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature."
“Good son! On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called ‘Patience.
If a cow eats it, she produces ghee from the cream.”
Furthermore, there are other grasses; if a cow eats them, no *sarpis* (clarified butter) will be produced.
Although there is no *sarpis*, one cannot say that the *kṣānti-tṛṇa* (grass of patience) does not exist within the Snowy Mountains.
The Buddha-nature is also like this.
The Snowy Mountains are called the Tathāgata;
the kṣānti-grass is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.
The "extraordinary grasses" refer to the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

If sentient beings can listen to, receive, inquire about, and expound upon the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, they will see the Buddha-nature; even if it is not heard of within the twelve divisions [of the scriptures], one cannot say that the Buddha-nature does not exist.

“Good son! The Buddha-nature is both form and non-form, neither form nor non-form; it is both characteristic and non-characteristic, neither characteristic nor non-characteristic; it is both one and not one, neither one nor not one; it is neither eternal nor annihilated, neither non-eternal nor non-annihilated; it is both existent and non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent; it is both exhausted and not exhausted, neither exhausted nor non-exhausted; it is both cause and fruit, neither cause nor fruit; it is both meaning and non-meaning, neither meaning nor non-meaning; it is both syllable and non-syllable, neither syllable nor non-syllable.”
"What is form? It is because it is the vajra-body.
What is non-form?"
Because the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are non-material (*arūpa*) dharmas.
Why are they neither material nor non-material?
Because both the material and the non-material lack fixed characteristics (*aniyata-lakṣaṇa*).
"What is meant by 'marks'?
It refers to the thirty-two marks.
What is meant by 'non-marks'?"
Because the marks of all sentient beings do not appear.
Why is it neither a mark nor a non-mark?
Because marks and non-marks are not determinate.
"What is meant by 'one'?
It is because all sentient beings are of one vehicle.
What is meant by 'not one'?"
Because the three vehicles are taught.
Why is it neither one nor not one?
Because dharmas are innumerable.
"Why is it not eternal?
Because it is seen to arise from conditions.
Why is it not annihilated?"
Because it is free from the view of annihilationism.
Why is it neither eternal nor annihilated?
Because it has no beginning or end.
"What is meant by 'existence'?
It is because all sentient beings possess it.
What is meant by 'non-existence'?"
Because it is seen through skillful means.
Why is it neither existent nor non-existent?
Because its nature is like space.
"What is meant by 'exhaustion'?
It is because of attaining the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
What is meant by 'not exhaustion'?"
Because it is eternal.
Why is it neither exhausted nor non-exhausted?
Because all characteristics of exhaustion have been severed.
"What is the cause?
It is because it is a revealing cause. What is the fruit?"
Because it is definitive.
Why is it neither cause nor effect?
Because it is eternal.
"What is meant by 'meaning' (artha)?
It is because one is able to fully grasp meaning without obstruction.
What is meant by 'non-meaning'?"
Because it is ineffable.
Why is it neither meaning nor non-meaning?
Because it is ultimately empty.
"What is meant by 'a word'?
It is because there is a name.
What is meant by 'not a word'?"
Because names are nameless.
Why is it neither a word nor a non-word?
Because all words have been severed.
"What is meant by 'neither suffering nor pleasure'?
It is because all sensations have been severed.
What is meant by 'non-self'?"
Because they have not yet fully attained the eight masteries.
Why is it not "non-non-self"? Because it is permanent.
What is meant by "neither self nor non-self"?
It is because there is no acting and no receiving.
What is meant by "emptiness"?
Because it is emptiness in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Why is it not empty?
Because it is eternal.
What is meant by being neither empty nor non-empty?
It is because it can serve as the seed for wholesome dharmas. "Good son!..."
If there are those who can contemplate and understand such meanings as these from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, you should know that such persons perceive the Buddha-nature.
This Buddha-nature is inconceivable; it is the realm of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

“Good son! Buddha-nature is not the aggregates, elements, or sense bases; it is not that which was originally non-existent and now exists, nor is it that which already existed and has returned to non-existence. Sentient beings perceive it through virtuous causes and conditions.”

For example, when black iron enters fire it becomes red, and upon emerging and cooling it returns to black; yet this blackness is neither internal nor external, but exists due to causes and conditions.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; when the fire of the afflictions of all sentient beings is extinguished, they are able to hear and see it. "Good son!
Just as when a seed has perished, a sprout is then able to arise, yet the nature of this sprout is neither internal nor external;"
Even flowers and fruits are likewise thus; they exist by virtue of conditions.
Good son, this subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra is fully endowed with immeasurable merits.
"Buddha-nature is also like this; it is entirely accomplished through immeasurable and boundless merits.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda said, "World-Honored One!"
By how many dharmas is a bodhisattva fully endowed so as to perceive the Buddha-nature, yet not clearly?
By how many dharmas do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, become fully endowed so as to see it with perfect clarity?
“Good son! There are ten dharmas that a bodhisattva fully accomplishes by which, although they perceive the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly.
What are these ten?

First, having few desires; second, knowing contentment; third, tranquility; fourth, diligence; fifth, right mindfulness; sixth, right concentration; seventh, right wisdom; eighth, liberation; ninth, praising liberation; and tenth, teaching and transforming sentient beings through Great Nirvana.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the distinction between having few desires and being content?”
“Good son! One who has few desires does not seek and does not take;
one who is content does not feel regret when obtaining little.”
"One who has few desires has little that they wish for;
one who is content performs only those matters pertaining to the Dharma, and their mind is free from anxiety and distress. Good son!..."
There are three kinds of desire:
first, evil desire; second, great desire; and third, the desire for desire.
As for evil desire, it is when a bhikṣu gives rise to covetous thoughts, desiring to be the leader of the entire assembly.
"May all the Sangha follow behind me;
may the fourfold assembly all make offerings to me, revere, praise, and honor me;
may I first preach the Dharma for the four assemblies, causing everyone to believe and accept my words."
May I also cause kings, ministers, and elders to all revere me;
and may I obtain in abundance clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and excellent dwellings.
To have desire for birth and death is called "evil desire.
What is "great desire"?
It is when a bhikṣu gives rise to a mind of desire, [thinking]:

"How may I cause the fourfold assembly to know fully that I have attained the first stage up to the tenth stage; that I have attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); that I have attained the fruit of arhatship down to the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna); and that I have attained the four dhyānas up to the four unhindered knowledges (pratisaṃvid)?"
To act for the sake of gain and offerings is called "great desire.

As for "desire for desire," if a bhikṣu desires to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven, the Mara Heaven, the Īśvara Heaven, as a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or as a Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa, and seeks to attain mastery over all these for the sake of gain and offerings, this is called "desire for desire."
If one is not harmed by these three kinds of evil desires, this is called having few desires.
"Desire" refers to the twenty-five forms of craving;
to be free from these twenty-five cravings is called having few desires.
Not seeking after things desired for the future is called having few desires;
obtaining them without attachment is called contentment.
Not seeking honor and respect is called having few desires.
To attain [this] without accumulating is called contentment. "Good son!

There are those who have few desires but are not called contented; there are those who are contented but are not called having few desires; there are those who both have few desires and are contented; and there are those who are neither contented nor have few desires."
"One who has few desires refers to a stream-enterer;
one who is contented refers to a pratyekabuddha;
one who both has few desires and is contented refers to an arhat."
"One who has few desires and knows contentment is called a bodhisattva.
Good son, there are two kinds of having few desires and knowing contentment: "
The first is wholesome, and the second is unwholesome.
The unwholesome refers to ordinary worldlings;
the wholesome refers to noble ones and bodhisattvas.
Although all noble ones have attained the fruits of the Path, they do not proclaim them themselves;
because they do not proclaim them, their minds are free from affliction and resentment—this is called contentment.
“Good son! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* with the desire to see the Buddha-nature, they therefore practice few desires and contentment.”
"What is tranquility?
There are two kinds of tranquility:
first, tranquility of mind; second, tranquility of body."
One whose body is tranquil never commits the three kinds of evil of the body;
one whose mind is tranquil likewise does not commit the three kinds of evil of the mind—this is what is called the tranquility of body and mind.
"One whose body is tranquil does not associate with the fourfold assembly nor participate in any of their affairs;
one whose mind is tranquil never cultivates desire, hatred, or delusion—this is what is meant by tranquility of body and mind."

"There may be a bhikṣu whose body is tranquil but whose mind is not tranquil; there may be one whose mind is tranquil but whose body is not tranquil; there may be one whose both body and mind are tranquil; and there may be one whose both body and mind are neither tranquil."

Regarding "the body is tranquil but the mind is not tranquil": there may be a bhikṣu who practices dhyāna in a secluded place, remaining apart from the fourfold assembly, yet whose mind constantly accumulates greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called the body being tranquil while the mind is not tranquil.

Regarding "the mind is tranquil while the body is not tranquil": there may be a bhikṣu who, though associating with the fourfold assembly, kings, and ministers, has severed greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called "the mind is tranquil while the body is not tranquil."
Those whose body and mind are tranquil refer to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
those whose body and mind are not tranquil refer to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Why is this?
Although the bodies and minds of ordinary persons may be tranquil, they are unable to deeply contemplate impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.
For this reason, ordinary persons cannot bring the actions of body, speech, and mind to a state of stillness.
Those who are icchantikas, who have committed the four grave offenses, or who have perpetrated the five heinous crimes—such persons cannot be said to possess tranquility of body and mind.
What, then, is diligence?
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to purify the actions of body, speech, and mind, to distance himself from all unwholesome deeds, and to cultivate all wholesome deeds, this is called diligence.
This diligent practitioner binds their mindfulness to six objects, namely: the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, generosity, and the devas; this is called right mindfulness.
One who possesses right mindfulness attains samādhi, which is called right concentration.
One who possesses right concentration contemplates all phenomena as being like empty space; this is called right wisdom.
One who possesses right wisdom is far removed from all afflictions and fetters; this is called liberation.
One who has attained liberation extols liberation for the sake of all sentient beings, declaring that this liberation is eternal, constant, and unchanging; this is called praising liberation.
Liberation is precisely the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is the extinguishing of the fires of the various fetters of affliction.
Furthermore, nirvāṇa is called a dwelling place.
Why is this? Because it can obstruct the evil winds and rains of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, *nirvāṇa* is called the refuge (*śaraṇa*).
Why is this? Because it is able to transcend all fears.
Furthermore, Nirvana is called an island.
Why is this? Because they cannot be swept away by the violent rivers of the four great elements.
What are these four?
First is the flood of desire, second is the flood of existence, third is the flood of views, and fourth is the flood of ignorance.
For this reason, nirvāṇa is called an island.
Furthermore, nirvāṇa is called the ultimate refuge.
Why is this? Because it enables one to attain all ultimate bliss.
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are fully endowed with these ten dharmas, although they perceive the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly.
"Furthermore, good son!
Those who have left the household life have four kinds of illnesses; for this reason, they do not attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
What are these four illnesses?
They are the four evil desires:
First, the desire for clothing; second, the desire for food; third, the desire for bedding and requisites; fourth, the desire for existence—these are called the four evil desires.
For this illness of the renunciant, there are four excellent medicines that can cure it:

namely, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*) cures the bhikṣu’s evil desire for clothing; begging for food cures his evil desire for food; dwelling at the foot of a tree cures his evil desire for bedding; and tranquility of body and mind cures the bhikṣu’s evil desire for existence (*bhava*).
To eliminate these four ailments by means of these four medicines is called the Noble Practice (*ārya-caryā*); such a noble practice is termed having few desires and being content.
"There are four kinds of bliss for those who are tranquil."
What are the four?
First, the joy of renunciation; second, the joy of tranquility; third, the joy of eternal cessation; and fourth, the ultimate joy.
Attaining these four joys is called tranquility;
being endowed with the four kinds of diligence is called vigor;
and being endowed with the four foundations of mindfulness is called right mindfulness.
Because one possesses the four dhyānas, it is called right concentration;
because one perceives the reality of the four noble truths, it is called right wisdom;
and because one has forever severed all afflictions and fetters, it is called liberation.
