Because it criticizes and speaks of the faults of all afflictions, it is called "praising liberation.
Son of good family!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in and fulfill these ten dharmas, although they see the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly.
"Furthermore, good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has heard this sutra and, having drawn near to it and practiced its cultivation, remains far removed from all worldly affairs, this is called 'having few desires.'
Having gone forth, not giving rise to a mind of regret is called contentment.
Having attained contentment, drawing near to secluded places and remaining far removed from clamor and bustle is called tranquility.
Those who lack contentment do not delight in solitude.
Indeed, those who possess contentment always delight in emptiness and stillness; in such places of emptiness and stillness, they constantly reflect:
"The entire world claims that I have attained the fruits of the śramaṇa path, yet I have in fact not yet attained them. How could I now deceive and mislead others?"
Having formed this thought, one diligently cultivates the fruits of the śramaṇa path; this is called diligence.
To draw near to and cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa is called right mindfulness.
To accord with the practice of the heavens is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Abiding securely in this concentration, possessing right view and right knowledge, is called right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*).
One who possesses right view and knowledge is able to attain detachment from the fetters and bonds of affliction; this is called liberation (*vimukti*).
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, for the sake of sentient beings, extol and praise nirvana; this is called praising liberation.
Good son, although Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling in the fulfillment of these ten dharmas perceive the Buddha-nature, they do not see it with clarity.

"Furthermore, good son! As for 'having few desires': if there is a bhikṣu who dwells in a secluded place, sitting upright and not lying down; or who dwells at the foot of a tree, or among burial mounds, or in the open air; who sits upon whatever grassy ground is available; who eats by begging for alms, being content with whatever he obtains; who eats in a single session and does not eat more than once a day; and who possesses only three robes—garments made of cast-off rags or wool—this is called having few desires."
Having performed these deeds, the mind feels no regret; this is called contentment.
Cultivating the samādhi of emptiness is called tranquility.
Having attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], yet not ceasing one's resolve for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, is called diligence.
To bind the mind in contemplation that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and immutable is called right mindfulness;
to cultivate the eight liberations is called right concentration;
and to attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge is called right wisdom.
To be far removed from the seven outflows is called liberation;
to extol nirvana as being devoid of the ten characteristics is called praising liberation.
The ten characteristics refer to birth, aging, sickness, death, form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and impermanence.
To be far removed from these ten characteristics is called Great Nirvana. Good son!
This is what is meant by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, while dwelling securely in and fully possessing these ten dharmas, perceives the Buddha-nature yet does not see it with clarity.
"Furthermore, good son!
Because of excessive desire, they associate with kings, ministers, elders, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, and claim of themselves:
'I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat. "

For the sake of gain and offerings, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—even when attending to the necessities of nature—if they see a donor, they still practice respectful conduct and engage them in polite conversation.
To destroy evil desires is called having few desires;
although one has not yet been able to destroy the fetters and afflictions, being able to accord with the sphere of practice of the Tathāgata is called contentment.
"Good son!

These two dharmas are the proximate causes and conditions for mindfulness and concentration. They are constantly praised by teachers, patriarchs, and fellow students; I, too, have always extolled and praised these two dharmas throughout various sūtras."
If one can be fully endowed with these two dharmas, then one will draw near to the gate of Great Nirvāṇa and the five kinds of bliss;
this is called tranquility. Firmly upholding the precepts is called diligence;
possessing a sense of shame and remorse is called right mindfulness.
Not perceiving the characteristics of the mind is called right concentration;
not seeking the nature, characteristics, or causes and conditions of all phenomena is called right wisdom;
because there are no characteristics, afflictions are severed, which is called liberation.
To praise and extol such a *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is called "praising liberation.
Good son! This is what is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, while dwelling securely in these ten dharmas, perceives the Buddha-nature yet does not see it with clarity.
“Good son! Regarding what you have asked:
‘By what eye do Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature, yet not clearly?’”
"By means of which eye do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perceive the Buddha-nature so as to attain clear understanding?
"Good son! Because they see with the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus), they do not attain clear understanding."
Because it is seen by the Buddha-eye, it is clearly perceived.
Because it is for the sake of the practice of bodhi, it is not clearly perceived;
if there is no such practice, then it is clearly perceived.
Because they abide in the ten stages, although they see, they do not perceive clearly;
because they neither abide nor depart, they perceive with perfect clarity.
It is because the wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is a causal factor that their vision is not yet clear.
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have severed both cause and effect, they see with perfect clarity.
That which is fully awakened to is called Buddha-nature;
because Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes have not yet attained this state of being fully awakened, although they see it, they do not see it clearly.
“Good son! There are two kinds of seeing:
first, seeing with the eyes; second, seeing through hearing.”
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see the Buddha-nature with their own eyes, as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of their hand;
the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see the Buddha-nature by hearing of it, and therefore they do not see it clearly.
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage can only know for themselves that they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet they cannot know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-Five.
[Continued] The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-Six.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huiyan and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Lion’s Roar Bodhisattva Chapter, Part Two:
"Good son, furthermore, there is that which is seen by the eyes: the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature with their eyes."
Furthermore, there is hearing and seeing: all sentient beings, up to those on the ninth stage, hear and see the Buddha-nature.
If a bodhisattva hears that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature but does not give rise to faith in their mind, this is not called "hearing and seeing."

“Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to see the Tathāgata, they should cultivate the twelve divisions of the sūtras, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, copying, and explaining them.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
Since all sentient beings are unable to know the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s mind, how should they contemplate it so as to come to know it?”
“Good son! All sentient beings truly cannot know the mental characteristics of the Tathāgata.
If one wishes to observe and thereby come to know them, there are two causes and conditions:”
First is seeing with the eyes; second is seeing through hearing.
If one sees all the bodily actions of the Tathāgata, one should know that this is indeed the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing with the eyes.
If one observes all the verbal actions of the Tathāgata, one should know that this is indeed the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing through hearing."
"If one sees that among all sentient beings there is none whose physical appearance can equal his, one should know that this is the Tathāgata; this is called 'seeing with the eyes.
If one hears that his voice is subtle, wondrous, and most supreme, unlike any voice possessed by sentient beings, one should know that this is the Tathāgata; this is called 'hearing and seeing.'"

"If one sees the supernatural powers manifested by the Tathāgata—whether for the sake of sentient beings or for the sake of gain—if it is for the sake of sentient beings and not for the sake of gain, one should know that this is indeed the Tathāgata; this is called 'seeing with the eyes.

If one observes the Tathāgata using the knowledge of others' minds when observing sentient beings—whether he speaks for the sake of gain or for the sake of sentient beings—if it is for the sake of sentient beings and not for the sake of gain, one should know that this is indeed the Tathāgata; this is called 'seeing through hearing.'"
"How does the Tathāgata receive this body?
For what reason does he receive a body?
On whose account does he receive a body?"
This is called seeing with the eyes.
If one contemplates the Tathāgata, how does he preach the Dharma?
For what reason does he preach the Dharma?
For whom does he preach the Dharma?
This is called "hearing and seeing.
If one does not become angry when subjected to the evil karmic actions of others, know that this person is indeed a Tathāgata; this is called "seeing with the eyes."
If one does not give rise to anger when subjected to the evil karma of speech, know that such a person is a Tathāgata;

this is called "hearing and seeing. "If one sees the Bodhisattva at the time of his birth, taking seven steps in each of the ten directions; if Maṇibhadra and Pūrṇabhadra, the great generals of the spirits and ghosts, hold banners and canopies; if immeasurable and boundless worlds tremble; if golden light shines brilliantly, filling the void; if the Nanda Dragon King and Upananda, by means of their supernormal powers, bathe the Bodhisattva’s body; if the forms of various devas welcome him with prostrations; and if the seer Asita joins his palms in reverent respect."
In the prime of his youth, he renounced desire as if discarding mucus or spittle, remaining unconfused by worldly pleasures.
He left the household life to cultivate the Way, delighting in solitude and stillness; to shatter false views, he practiced austerities for six years.
He is impartial and non-dual toward all sentient beings; his mind is constantly in meditative concentration, never once distracted, and his body is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
Wherever he travels, even mounds and ruins become level;
his robes remain four inches away from his body without falling.
When walking, he gazes straight ahead without looking left or right;
regarding the food he eats, not a single morsel remains intact;
and at the places where he sits or rises, the grass is not disturbed or disarrayed.
To harmonize sentient beings, he goes to preach the Dharma with a mind free from pride;
this is called "seeing with the eyes.
Furthermore, if one hears that after the Bodhisattva had taken seven steps, he uttered these words:
"This present body of mine is the very last.
The seer Asita joined his palms and said:
"Great King, you should know:
Prince Siddhārtha will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; he will never remain at home as a wheel-turning monarch. Why is this?
Because his marks are clearly manifest.

The marks of a Wheel-Turning Sage King are not clearly manifest, whereas the bodily marks of Prince Siddhārtha are brilliant and prominent; therefore, he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Seeing old age, sickness, and death, he further spoke these words:

"All sentient beings are most pitiable; they are constantly pursued by such birth, old age, sickness, and death, yet they fail to perceive them. They perpetually dwell in suffering; I shall bring an end to it."
From the fivefold-attainment seer Ārāḍa, he received the meditative attainment of non-perception; having mastered it, he later declared it to be incorrect.
From the seer Udraka, he received the meditative attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having mastered it, he declared that it was not nirvāṇa, but rather a phenomenon of saṃsāra.
Having practiced austerities for six years without attaining anything, he spoke these words:
"The cultivation of these austerities is empty and yields no result; if they were truly effective, I should have attained [enlightenment] by now."
"Because it is false and illusory, I have attained nothing.
This is called a perverted artifice, not the True Path.
After he had already attained the Way, Brahmā entreated him:
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively open the gate of ambrosia for sentient beings and preach the unsurpassed Dharma.
The Buddha said,
“Brahmā King!
"All sentient beings are constantly obstructed and covered by afflictions, and thus cannot receive my words of the True Dharma.
Brahmā King spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
All sentient beings are of three types:
namely, those of sharp faculties, those of medium faculties, and those of dull faculties.
Those of sharp faculties are able to receive [the teaching]; we only pray that you will speak for them.
The Buddha said, "Brahmā King!
Listen attentively, listen attentively. I shall now open the gate of ambrosia for the sake of all sentient beings."
Thereupon, at Vārāṇasī, he turned the wheel of the true Dharma and proclaimed the Middle Way.
That all sentient beings have not destroyed their fetters, yet it is not that they cannot destroy them; it is neither destruction nor non-destruction—therefore it is called the Middle Way.
That he does not deliver sentient beings, yet it is not that he cannot deliver them—this is called the Middle Way.
Neither achieving everything nor failing to achieve anything—this is called the Middle Way;
whatever is taught, neither claiming oneself to be the teacher nor claiming oneself to be the disciple—this is called the Middle Way;
teaching not for the sake of profit, yet not failing to attain the fruit—this is called the Middle Way.
Right speech, truthful speech, timely speech, and genuine speech—words that do not issue in vain, subtle and supreme.
Such dharmas as these are called "hearing and seeing."
“Good son! The characteristics of the Tathāgata’s mind are truly invisible.
If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to see the Tathāgata, they should rely upon these two kinds of causes and conditions.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

Regarding the analogy of the four types of people using the mango fruit as previously explained: there is the person whose conduct is subtle but whose mind is not upright and true; there is the person whose mind is subtle but whose conduct is not upright and true; there is the person whose mind is subtle and whose conduct is also upright and true; and there is the person whose mind is not subtle and whose conduct is not upright and true.”
"How can these first two kinds be known?
As the Buddha has taught, they cannot be known except by relying on these two.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
it is indeed difficult to discern the two types of persons, as illustrated by the analogy of the mango fruit.”
Because they are difficult to know, I have said in my sutras that one should dwell together with them;
if one does not know them while dwelling together, one should live with them for a long time;
if one still does not know them after living with them for a long time, one should discern them through wisdom.
If wisdom does not know, one should observe deeply;
through such observation, one then knows those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them. Good son!
“Noble son, one must possess these four things— dwelling together, long-term association, wisdom, and discernment— and only then can one know whether another maintains the precepts or violates them.”
There are two kinds of precepts, and those who uphold them are likewise of two types:
first, those who are ultimate; second, those who are not ultimate.
There are people who, due to various causes and conditions, receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts.
The wise person should observe:
does this person maintain the precepts for the sake of gain and offerings,
or do they maintain them for the ultimate goal?
“Good son! The precepts of the Tathāgata are without causes or conditions; therefore, they are called the ultimate precepts.
For this reason, even when a bodhisattva is harmed by evil sentient beings, he does not give rise to anger or obstruction.”
For this reason, the Tathāgata is named as one who has accomplished ultimate upholding of the precepts and perfected upholding of the precepts. "Good son!
Once in the past, I was staying together with Śāriputra and five hundred disciples in the great city of Campā in the kingdom of Magadha."
At that time, there was a hunter pursuing a pigeon.
This pigeon, trembling with fear, remained as quivering as a plantain tree even when it reached Śāriputra’s shadow;
yet, upon entering my shadow, its body and mind became peaceful and secure, and its terror was dispelled.
Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, maintains the precepts to the ultimate degree; even his shadow possesses such power. "Good son!
If one cannot even attain the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha through non-perfect precepts, how much less can one attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Furthermore, there are two types [of motivation]:
first, for the sake of gain and honor; second, for the sake of the true Dharma.

If one upholds the prohibitive precepts for the sake of gain and honor, you should know that such a person does not perceive the Buddha-nature or the Tathāgata; although they may hear the names "Buddha-nature" and "Tathāgata," they still cannot be said to have heard or seen them.

If one upholds the prohibitive precepts for the sake of the True Dharma, you should know that these precepts enable one to see both the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata; this is called "seeing with the eyes" and is also called "seeing through hearing."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, those whose roots are deep and difficult to uproot; second, those whose roots are shallow and easily moved.
If one can cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, this is called having deep roots that are difficult to uproot."
If one does not cultivate these three samādhis, even if one practices them for the sake of the twenty-five realms of existence, this is called having shallow roots that are easily shaken.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, for one's own sake; second, for the sake of sentient beings.
Those who act for the sake of sentient beings are able to perceive the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there are two types of people who uphold the precepts:
first, those whose nature spontaneously enables them to maintain them; second, those who require instruction and exhortation from others.

If, after having received the precepts, one does not lose them for the first time throughout immeasurable lifetimes—even when encountering a corrupt land, meeting evil associates, living in an evil time or age, hearing false and evil teachings, or dwelling with those of wrong views—at that time, although the formal method of receiving the precepts may no longer exist, one maintains them as originally practiced without any violation; this is called "naturally maintaining them by one's own nature."

If one encounters a preceptor and receives the full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, although the precepts have been obtained, one must rely upon the upādhyāya, various teachers, fellow students, and virtuous friends for their instruction and admonition in order to know when to advance or retreat, to listen to the Dharma and preach the Dharma, and to maintain all proper deportment; this is called "requiring instruction from others."
"Good son!
One whose nature is capable of upholding [the precepts] sees the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgata with their eyes; this is also called 'seeing through hearing.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of precepts: [the precept of restraint and the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas]."
First, the śrāvaka precepts; second, the bodhisattva precepts.
From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, these are called the bodhisattva precepts;
from the contemplation of white bones until the realization of the fruit of arhatship, these are called the śrāvaka precepts.
If there are those who uphold the precepts of the śrāvakas, you should know that such persons do not see the Buddha-nature nor the Tathāgata;
if there are those who uphold the bodhisattva precepts, you should know that such persons attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and are able to see the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata, and nirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions does one receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts?”
The Buddha said,
"Good son, it is because the mind feels no regret."
Why does one not feel regret?
Because one experiences pleasure.
Why does one experience pleasure?
It is for the sake of detachment. Why detachment?
It is for the sake of peace and security.
Why is there peace and security?
It is for the sake of meditative concentration (dhyāna).
Why is there meditative concentration?
It is for the sake of knowing and seeing reality.
Why is it for the sake of knowing and seeing reality?
It is for the sake of seeing the various faults and afflictions of birth and death.
Why is it for the purpose of seeing the faults and afflictions of birth and death?
It is for the purpose of ensuring that the mind does not become greedily attached.
Why is it for the purpose of ensuring that the mind does not become greedily attached?
It is for the sake of attaining liberation.
Why is it for the sake of attaining liberation?
It is for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, great parinirvāṇa.
For what reason is it for the sake of attaining Great Parinirvāṇa?
It is for the sake of attaining the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For what reason is it for the sake of attaining permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
It is for the sake of attaining the unborn and the unceasing.
Why is it for the sake of attaining the unborn and the unceasing?
It is for the sake of seeing the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, by their very nature, Bodhisattvas are able to maintain ultimate pure precepts. "Good son!
Although a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts does not make a vow to seek a mind free from regret, a mind free from regret is naturally attained."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Although one does not seek pleasure, seclusion, peace, true knowledge and vision, a mind that does not crave the faults of birth and death, liberation, nirvāṇa, permanence, bliss, self, purity, non-arising, or non-ceasing, one naturally attains them upon seeing the Buddha-nature.
"Why is this? Because such is the nature of dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!

If one attains the fruit of non-regret by means of upholding the precepts, and attains the fruit of nirvana by means of liberation, then the precepts would be without cause and nirvana would be without fruit.”
If morality were without cause, it would be termed eternal; if nirvana had a cause, it would be impermanent.
If that were so, then nirvana would be something that was originally non-existent but now exists.
If something was originally non-existent and now exists, it is impermanent, just like lighting a lamp.
If nirvāṇa were likewise so, how could it be designated as self, bliss, and purity?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Excellent, excellent."
Because you have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas in the past, you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a profound meaning.
Son of good family!
It is because you have not lost your original mindfulness that you ask in this way.
“I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world in the city of Vārāṇasī, named Śubhavyūha.
At that time, for thirty million years, that Buddha expounded this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. I and you were both present at that assembly, and I questioned that Buddha regarding this matter.”
At that time, for the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata entered into samādhi and did not yet answer this matter.
"Excellent, Great Being!
You are indeed able to recollect such past events."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
Precepts also have a cause, which is listening to the True Dharma.
Listening to the True Dharma also has a cause, which is associating with virtuous friends."
To associate with virtuous friends also has its causes, namely, faith.
To possess faith likewise has its causes—there are two kinds of causes:
first, listening to the Dharma; second, contemplating its meaning.
Good son! Faith arises because of hearing the Dharma;
hearing the Dharma arises because of faith.
These two dharmas are both cause and causal cause, and both effect and consequential effect. Good son!
It is like a Nirgrantha who sets up a prop and lifts a jar; they serve as cause and effect for one another and cannot be separated.

Good son! Just as ignorance conditions volitional formations and volitional formations condition ignorance, so too this ignorance and these volitional formations are both causes and causes-of-causes, and both effects and effects-of-effects;

and so on until birth conditions aging-and-death and aging-and-death conditions birth, such that this birth and this aging-and-death are also both causes and causes-of-causes, and both effects and effects-of-effects.
"Good son!
Arising can give rise to dharmas, but it cannot arise by itself;
because it does not arise by itself, it is produced by 'the arising of arising'."
Arising does not arise of itself; it arises by depending on arising.
Therefore, these two types of arising are both cause and causal-cause, and both effect and consequential-effect.
"Good son! It is the same for listening to the Dharma with a mind of faith. Good son!"
This is the fruit, not the cause; it refers to Great Nirvana.
Why is it called the fruit?

Because it is the supreme fruit, the fruit of the śramaṇa, the fruit of the brāhmaṇa, because it severs birth and death, and because it destroys the afflictions—it is for these reasons called the fruit.
Because it is reviled by all afflictions, Nirvana is called the fruit.
Afflictions, "son of good family," are termed 'transgressions beyond transgression.
"Son of good family!
Nirvāṇa has no cause, yet its essence is that of a fruit.

Why is this? Because it is without arising or ceasing; because it is without action; because it is not conditioned; because it is unconditioned; because it is eternal and immutable; because it has no location; and because it has no beginning or end.
"Good son!
If nirvana had a cause, it could not be called nirvana.
'Nir' (槃) signifies cause;"
“Parinirvāṇa” means “non-existence”;
because there is no cause, it is called nirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
"As the Buddha has said:
'Nirvana is without cause.
This meaning is not so."
If one says it is non-existent, it accords with six meanings.
First, because it is ultimately non-existent, it is called "non-existent," such as when all phenomena are said to be without self and without what belongs to a self.
Second, it is called "non-existent" because it is absent at certain times, as worldly people say when a river or pond has no water, or when there is neither sun nor moon.

Third, it is called "non-existent" because it is present in small measure, as worldly people say that food with little salt is "saltless," or that sweet juice with little sweetness is "sweetness-less."

Fourth, because there is no receiving [of the dharma], it is called "non-existent"; just as a *caṇḍāla* cannot receive or uphold the *brāhmaṇa* dharma, and for this reason is called "one who is not a *brāhmaṇa*."

Fifth, because they embrace unwholesome dharmas, they are said to be "non-existent. As people of the world say that those who embrace unwholesome dharmas are not called śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, for this reason they are said to have no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
Sixth, because it is not present, it is called "non-existent," just as that which lacks whiteness is called "black" and that which lacks clarity is called "ignorance" (avidyā).
“World-Honored One!
Nirvāṇa is also like this; because at times it is without cause, it is called ‘nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! Regarding these six meanings you have now explained, why do you not cite that which is ultimately non-existent as an analogy for nirvāṇa, but instead take that which is non-existent at certain times?”
"Good son!
The essence of nirvāṇa is ultimately without cause, just like non-self and that which belongs to no self.
Good son!"
Worldly phenomena and nirvana are ultimately not counterparts to one another;
therefore, these six matters cannot serve as analogies. "Good son!
All phenomena are entirely devoid of self, yet this nirvana truly possesses a self.
For this reason, nirvana is without cause and its essence is that of a fruit.
Being a cause and not a fruit is what is called Buddha-nature;
because it is not produced by causes, it is a cause and not a fruit;
because it is not a fruit of the śramaṇa, it is therefore called "not a fruit."
Why is it called a cause?
Because it is a cause of realization. Good son!
There are two kinds of causes:
first, the productive cause; second, the revealing cause.
That which can produce a phenomenon is called the productive cause.
A lamp can illuminate objects; therefore, it is called the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*).
The various fetters of affliction are called the "producing cause" (*janaka-hetu*);
the parents of sentient beings are called the "revealing cause."
Grain seeds and the like are called productive causes (*janakahetu*);
earth, water, fertilizer, and so forth are called revealing causes (*vyañjanahetu*).
Furthermore, there is a productive cause, namely the six *pāramitās*, which are the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there is a revealing cause, namely, the Buddha-nature and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there is a revealing cause, namely, the six pāramitās as the Buddha-nature;
furthermore, there is a producing cause, namely, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there is the cause of illumination, namely the Eightfold Noble Path and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
furthermore, there is the cause of production, namely faith and the six pāramitās.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught:”
"To see the Tathāgata and the Buddha-nature"—
what is the meaning of this,
World-Honored One?

The body of the Tathāgata has no marks or characteristics; it is neither long nor short, neither white nor black. It has no location and does not abide within the three realms. It is not a conditioned phenomenon and cannot be cognized by visual consciousness; how, then, can it be seen?
"Buddha-nature is also like this," the Buddha said. "Good son!"
The Buddha-body is of two kinds:
first, the eternal; second, the impermanent.
That which is impermanent is a provisional manifestation for the purpose of delivering all sentient beings; this is what is called "seeing with the eyes."
That which is eternal is the liberation-body of the Tathāgata, World-Honored One; it is called "seen by the eye" and also called "seen by hearing.
Buddha-nature likewise has two aspects:
first, that which is visible; second, that which is invisible.
Those who can be seen are the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
those who cannot be seen are all sentient beings.
"Seen by the eye" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and the Tathāgatas seeing with their own eyes the Buddha-nature possessed by all sentient beings.
Regarding those who hear and see: all sentient beings and bodhisattvas at the ninth stage hear that there is buddha-nature.
"The body of the Tathāgata is further of two kinds:
first, it is form; second, it is non-form."
Form is the liberation of the Tathāgata;
that which is non-form is because the Tathāgata has eternally severed all marks of form.
There are two kinds of Buddha-nature:
The first is form (*rūpa*), and the second is non-form (*arūpa*).
Form refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
non-form refers to ordinary beings up to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Because the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages do not see it clearly, it is called non-form.
“Good son! The Buddha-nature is further of two kinds:
first, that which is form; second, that which is not form.”
"Form" refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
"non-form" refers to all sentient beings.
"Form" is that which is seen by the eye.
That which is not form is called "seeing through hearing.

Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external; although it is neither internal nor external, it is nonetheless not lost or destroyed. Therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught:”
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, just as there is curd within milk.
Yet, the Buddha-nature of the Vajrapāṇis and all Buddhas is like the pure *sarpis* (clarified butter). Why, then, does the Tathāgata say that Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! I also do not say that there is curd within milk."
“Curd is produced from milk; therefore, one says that there is curd.
“World-Honored One!
All phenomena that arise each have their own proper season.”
“Good son! At the time of milk, there is no curd, nor is there fresh butter, clarified butter, or the finest cream; yet all sentient beings still call it milk.”
Therefore, I say that there is no curd within milk.
If it were already present, why could it not have two names—just as a person who possesses two skills is called both a goldsmith and an ironworker?

At the time of curd, there is no milk, nor fresh butter, nor clarified butter, nor even the finest cream; yet sentient beings likewise say, "This is curd," and not milk, nor fresh butter, nor clarified butter, nor the finest cream.
This applies in the same way up to the finest cream.
Good son! There are two kinds of causes:
first, the direct cause; second, the conditional cause.
The direct cause is like milk producing curd;
the contributory cause is like yeast, warmth, and so forth.
Because it arises from milk, it is said that the nature of curd exists within the milk.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
If milk lacks the nature of curd, and that nature is likewise absent within the horns, why does it not arise from the horns?”
“Good son! Even from horns, curd can be produced. Why is this?
I also say that there are two types of causal conditions:
first, fermentation; second, warmth.
Because the nature of curdled milk is warm, it can also produce yogurt.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If curd could be produced from horns, why would those seeking curd seek milk instead of taking the horns?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! For this reason,
I speak of the direct cause and the conditional cause.”
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
"If it were the case that the nature of curd did not originally exist within milk but only came into being now, then since milk originally lacked the mango tree, why does it not produce one?"
"Because both are non-existent. "Good son!
Milk can also produce the *āmra* tree."
If one were to irrigate it with milk, it would grow five feet in a single night.
For this reason, I speak of two causes. Good son!
If all phenomena were produced from a single cause, one could raise the objection:
"Why is it that the mango tree cannot grow from within milk?
O son of good family!
It is just as the four great elements act as the causal conditions for all forms, yet these forms are each distinct and their differences are manifold.
For this reason, an amra tree does not grow from within milk.
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said,
there are two kinds of causes:”
"There are the direct cause and the contributory cause.
As for the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, what kind of cause is it? "Good son!"
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings also has two kinds of causes:
first, the direct cause; second, the conditional cause.
The direct cause refers to all sentient beings.
"The causal condition refers to the six pāramitās.
Siṃhavijrmbhita said,
"World-Honored One!"
I now know with certainty that milk possesses the nature of curd. Why is this?
Because I observe that those in the world who seek curd take only milk and never water; therefore, one should know that milk possesses the nature of curd.
"Good son! As you have asked, this meaning is not so. Why is that?
"It is like a person who, wishing to see their own reflection, immediately takes up a sword.
Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
"For this reason, milk possesses the nature of curd.
Since a blade has no reflection of a face, why do you take up the blade?
The Buddha said:

If light reaches [the object], how is it that one can see things within the crystal and fish or stones in the deep pool?
If it sees without reaching, why is it that one can see things within the crystal but cannot see the colors outside the wall?
Therefore, if it is said that the eye-light reaches that object and sees the elder, this meaning is not so. "Good son!
As you say that there is curd within milk, why is it that the person who sells milk takes only the price for the milk and does not demand payment for the curd?"
When one sells a brood mare, does one take only the price for the mare and not demand payment for the colts?
Good son! It is because worldly people have no offspring that they seek to marry wives.
If a woman is pregnant, one must not say she is a girl.
If one says she is a girl, because she possesses the nature of a child, she ought to be betrothed;
however, this reasoning is incorrect.
Why is this? If there were the nature of a son, there would also have to be a grandson;
if there were a grandson, he would be a brother.
Why is this? Because they are born from the same womb.
For this reason, I say that a woman lacks the nature of bearing sons.
If there were the nature of curd within the milk, why are the five flavors not perceived all at once?
If there were a five-fathom *nyagrodha* tree within the seed, why are the differences in the form and color of the sprout, stem, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit not perceived all at once?
"Good son!
The color of milk differs at different times, its taste differs, and its consistency differs; this is true even up to the stage of clarified butter (ghṛta).
How, then, can it be said that milk possesses the nature of curd?"
“Good son! It is like a person who intends to consume ghee tomorrow but already complains of its foul odor today;
to say that the nature of curd definitely exists within milk is likewise so.”
Good son! It is like a person who possesses a pen, paper, and ink, which combine to form characters; yet within that paper, there were originally no characters.
Because they were originally non-existent, they are produced through the conjunction of conditions.
If it existed inherently from the beginning, what need would there be for various conditions?
For example, when blue and yellow combine to produce green, one should know that these two originally lacked the nature of green.
If it were inherently existent, why would it need to be synthesized? Good son,
it is like sentient beings who obtain life because of food, yet within this food there is truly no life.
If life were inherently existent, then before the food was eaten, the food itself should be life.
Good son! All dharmas are fundamentally without intrinsic nature.
For this reason, I speak these verses:
"Non-existent in the beginning, now existent; existent in the beginning, now non-existent— that there could be such a thing as a dharma existing throughout the three periods of time is impossible."
“Good son! All dharmas arise because of causes and conditions, and they cease because of causes and conditions. Good son!”
If sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature within, then all sentient beings should possess a Buddha-body just as I do now.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither broken nor destroyed; it cannot be pulled, nor seized; it is neither bound nor fettered.
Just as there is space within all sentient beings— indeed, every sentient being possesses space—
and because it is without obstruction, each does not perceive this space as belonging to themselves.
If sentient beings were without space, there would be no going, coming, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, nor would there be birth or growth.
For this reason, I have stated in my sūtras that all sentient beings possess the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*).
The realm of empty space is called "emptiness.
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise; bodhisattvas in the tenth stage can perceive it only slightly, like a vajra jewel.
"Good son! The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the realm of the Buddhas; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Because all sentient beings do not see their Buddha-nature, they are constantly bound by afflictions and transmigrate through birth and death."
"Because they see the Buddha-nature, they cannot be bound by the fetters of afflictions; they are liberated from birth and death and attain Great Nirvana.
Lion’s Roar Bodhisattva said, "World-Honored One!"
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
This nature is like the quality of curd within milk; if milk lacked the nature of curd, why would the Buddha have taught that there are two kinds of causes:
first, the direct cause (*zhengyin*), and second, the conditional cause (*yuan-yin*)?
"As for conditions as causes, there are two: first, fermentation; second, warmth.
Since space has no intrinsic nature, it has no conditions as causes.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! If there were definitely the nature of curd within milk, what need would there be for conditions and causes?
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
Because existence has its own nature, it must depend upon causal conditions. Why is this so?”
It is for the sake of clear vision.
World-Honored One, the conditional cause is precisely the revealing cause.
For example, suppose various objects already exist in the darkness; one uses a lamp to illuminate them for the sake of seeing them.
If they did not exist originally, what would the lamp illuminate?
It is like a jar within clay: therefore, one requires people, water, a wheel, a rope, a staff, and so forth, as the causes of completion.
Just as the seed of a nyagrodha tree requires earth, water, and manure as its efficient cause for its development,
so too do the fermenting agent and warmth within milk require such efficient causes.
Therefore, although the nature [of curd] exists beforehand, it must depend upon a revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*) before it can be perceived.
For this reason, one knows with certainty that the nature of curd exists within milk from the very beginning.
“Good son! If there were a fixed nature of curd within milk, it would be a revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*).
If it were a revealing cause, why would it need to be revealed?
Good son! If the nature of the cause of illumination were itself that which is illuminated, it would always illuminate itself.
If it cannot illuminate itself, how can it illuminate others?
If one says:
"The revealing cause has two kinds of natures:
first, that which reveals itself; second, that which reveals others."
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because how could there be two [aspects] within a single dharma that serves as the cause of manifestation?
"If there were two [natures] in it, the milk would also have to be two.
If there are no two characteristics within the milk, why does the discerning cause alone possess two?
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As people in the world say, ‘I am together with eight people,’ so too is the cause of understanding: it understands itself and understands others.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! If the revealing cause were such as you describe, it would not be a revealing cause."
Why is this? Because that which counts can count its own form and the forms of others; thus, one may speak of "eight.

However, the nature of these forms itself lacks the characteristic of cognition. Since it lacks the characteristic of cognition, it must rely upon the nature of wisdom to then count itself and others.
Therefore, the cause of illumination cannot illuminate itself, nor can it illuminate others. "Good son!
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, for what reason do they cultivate immeasurable merits?"
If one says that cultivation is the cause of manifestation, it would be identical to the case of curd turning into whey.
If one says that the fruit definitely exists within the cause, then ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom would have no growth.
I observe that worldly people originally possess no precepts, meditative concentration, or wisdom; only after receiving them from a teacher do these qualities gradually increase.

If you claim that the teacher’s instruction is the "revealing cause" (了因), then at the very moment the teacher gives the instruction, the recipient would still not yet possess those precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
"If it is that which is already understood, it should be understood as being non-existent; how then can one understand precepts, concentration, and wisdom so that they may increase?
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!"
"If there were no revealing cause, how could one say that there is milk and there is curd?
"Good son! There are generally three ways in which people in the world answer difficult questions:
First is the "turning answer.
As previously stated:
"For what reason is it called 'precept' (śīla)?"
Because there is no regret, and so forth, up until the attainment of Great Nirvāṇa.
Second, answering by remaining silent.
For example, when a brahmin came and asked me:
"Am I eternal? At that time, I remained silent.
This is the third type: answering by means of doubt.
"In this sutra, if there are two causes for manifestation, why can there not be two in milk?
Good son, I shall now answer you in turn:"
Just as people in the world say that milk and curd exist because they will certainly be obtained, and for this reason it is said that there is milk and there is curd;
so too is the Buddha-nature: there are sentient beings and there is Buddha-nature, because it will be seen in the future.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has spoken, this meaning is not so.”
The past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived; how, then, can they be called "existent"?
If you claim that what is "to be" (anāgata) is called "existent," this meaning is not tenable.
It is like people in the world who, seeing that they have no children, say, "I have no children."
"If all sentient beings lack the Buddha-nature, why do you say that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
The past is said to exist.
For example, when planting an orange tree, the sprout arises as the seed perishes; the sprout is already sweet.
This continues through the stages until the fruit is produced, which is likewise sweet; only after it has fully ripened does it become sour.
Good son! This sour taste does not exist within the seed, the sprout, or even the unripe fruit; rather, it arises according to the original color, form, and characteristics at the time of ripening.
However, this sour taste was originally non-existent and now exists; although it was originally non-existent and now exists, it does not arise without a cause.
Thus, although its original substance has passed away, it can still be said to exist.
For this reason, the past is called "existent.
Furthermore, how is the future called "existent"?
It is, for example, like a person planting sesame seeds.
Someone asked,
"For what purpose have you planted these? He replied:
"There is oil.

Although there is actually no oil yet, once the sesame has ripened, one takes the seeds, roasts and steams them, then pounds and presses them to obtain it; you should know that this person is not speaking falsely.
For this reason, it is called "existence in the future.
Furthermore, what is meant by "existence in the past," son of good family?
It is like a person who, in private and out of sight, reviles a king; after many years have passed, the king hears of it.
Having heard it, he immediately asks:
"For what reason were you reviled?"
He replied, "Great King!
I did not revile you."
"Why is this? Because the one who reviled me has already perished.
The king said:
"The reviler and my own body both exist;
how can you say they have ceased?
For this reason, he lost his life.
"Good son! Although these two do not truly exist, their fruit is not extinguished; this is called 'existence in the past.
Furthermore, what is called 'existence in the future'?"
For example, suppose a person goes to a potter's workshop and asks,
"Do you have any jars?
and the potter replies:
"To say, 'There is a jar,' when the potter actually does not yet have a jar, but says there is a jar because there is clay— know that such a person is not speaking falsely."
"Just as there is curd within milk, so too is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings; those who wish to see the Buddha-nature should observe its timing, season, form, and color."
"For this reason, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; it is truly not false.
Siṃhavijrmbhita said, "If all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature, how can they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Because of this primary cause, sentient beings are enabled to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What is this primary cause?
It is what is called buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
World-Honored One!
If the *nyagrodha* seed did not contain the *nyagrodha* tree, why is it called a *nyagrodha* seed and not called a *khadira* seed?
World-Honored One!
Just as one of the Gautama clan cannot be called of the Atiya clan, and one of the Atiya clan likewise cannot be called of the Gautama clan;
so too, a son of the Nyagrodha cannot be called a son of the Khadirani, and a son of the Khadirani cannot be called a son of the Nyagrodha.
Just as the World-Honored One could not abandon his Gautama clan, so too is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings.
For this reason, one should know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If one says that the nyagrodha tree exists within the seed, this meaning is not so."
If it exists, why is it not seen? Good son!
Just as with worldly objects, there are certain causes and conditions by which they cannot be perceived.
What is meant by "causes and conditions"?
It refers to that which is distant and invisible, such as the tracks of a bird in the sky;
and that which is near and invisible, such as the eyelashes of a person.
It is not seen because it is destroyed, like one whose sense organs are impaired;
it is not seen because of distracted thoughts, like a mind that is not single-minded;
it is not seen because it is subtle, like minute particles of dust.
One does not see it because of obstruction, as with stars behind clouds;
one does not see it because of multiplicity, as with hemp in a heap of rice;
and one does not see it because of similarity, as with beans in a heap of beans.
The nyagrodha tree is not like these eight kinds of causes and conditions; if it were such, why would it not be seen?
If you say it is not seen because it is subtle, that argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Because the characteristics of a tree are coarse.
If you say its nature is subtle, how could it grow?
If you say that it cannot be seen because it is obstructed, then it should never be seen at all.
Since there was originally no coarse characteristic, yet now a coarse one is seen, one should know that this coarseness fundamentally lacks the nature of visibility.
Originally there was no nature of seeing, yet now it can be seen; you should know that this seeing, too, originally has no nature.
It is the same with you: originally there was no tree, yet now there is one; what fault could there be in this?
Siṃhanāda said: "As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of causes: [text continues]"
First is the direct cause (hetu), and second is the revealing cause (pariṇāma-hetu).
Because the earth, water, and manure act as the revealing causes for the seed of the nyagrodha tree, they cause the minute to become coarse.
The Buddha said,
“Good son! If it were originally existent, what need would there be for a revealing cause?”
If there is originally no intrinsic nature, what is it that is realized?
If a coarse form was originally absent within a nyagrodha tree and is produced through the power of a realizing cause, why is a khadira tree not also produced?
Because both are non-existent. Good son!
If that which is subtle cannot be seen, then that which is coarse should be visible.
For example, a single atom cannot be seen, yet when many atoms are combined, they should be visible.
In the same way, the coarse [form] within the seed should be visible. Why is this?
Within this, there already exist sprouts, stalks, flowers, and fruits.
Within each fruit are immeasurable seeds; within each seed are immeasurable trees. For this reason, it is called "coarse."
Because this grossness exists, it ought to be visible. Good son!

If the *nyagrodha* seed possessed the nature of a *nyagrodha* tree at the time of its birth, then since we see with our own eyes that this seed is burned by fire, such a nature of being burned would likewise have to have existed inherently from the beginning.
If they existed from the beginning, the tree should not have grown.
If all phenomena inherently possess arising and ceasing, why do they arise first and cease later, rather than occurring simultaneously?
"For this reason, one should know that there is no intrinsic nature.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!"
"If the seed of a nyagrodha tree originally lacked the nature of a tree yet still produced one, why does that seed not produce oil?
For both [the tree-nature and the oil-nature] are equally absent. "Good son!..."
"In this same way, oil can also be produced from these seeds; although it lacks its nature inherently, it exists due to causes and conditions.
Siṃhanāda asked: "Why is it not called sesame oil?"
“Good son! It is not because of the sesame seeds. Good son!”
Just as fire arises from the conditions of fire and water arises from the conditions of water, although both arise from conditions, they cannot exist within one another.
It is the same with the seed of the nyagrodha tree and sesame oil: although both arise from conditions, each does not produce the other.
The seed of the nyagrodha tree has the nature to cure cold disorders;
sesame oil has the nature to cure wind disorders. Good son!

For example, from sugarcane, through various causes and conditions, rock sugar and black honey are produced; although they arise from the same single cause, their physical characteristics differ—rock sugar treats heat, while black honey treats cold.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!

If there were no nature of curd within milk, no nature of oil in sesame seeds, no nature of a tree in the seed of a nyagrodha, no nature of a jar in clay, and no Buddha-nature in all sentient beings—as the Buddha previously stated:”
As for the statement, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; therefore, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," this meaning is not so.
Why is this? Because humans and devas have no fixed nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Because they lack a fixed nature, a human can become a deva and a deva can become a human; this occurs through the conditions of karma (*karmapratyaya*), not by way of a fixed nature.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by virtue of karmic causes and conditions.
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, for what reason do icchantikas and others sever all roots of goodness and fall into hell?
If the bodhicitta were the buddha-nature, then those such as the icchantikas should not be able to sever it.
If it can be severed, how can one say that the buddha-nature is eternal?
If it were impermanent, it would not be called Buddha-nature.
If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, for what reason is it called "the first arousal of the mind"?
Why, then, speak of those who are *vibhavati* (regressing) and those who are *avibhavati* (non-regressing)?
"One who is non-retrogressive (avaivartika) should be known as one who possesses Buddha-nature.
'World-Honored One!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva single-mindedly inclines toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, possessing great kindness and great compassion, seeing the faults and afflictions of birth, old age, death, and defilements, and contemplating Great Nirvāṇa as being free from the various faults of birth, old age, death, and defilements; when they have faith in the Triple Gem and the retribution of karma, and uphold the prohibitive precepts—such dharmas as these are called Buddha-nature.'"
"If there were a Buddha-nature apart from these dharmas, why would it require these dharmas as causes and conditions?
World-Honored One!
It is like milk: without depending on conditions, it would necessarily become curd."
Fresh butter is not like this; it must depend upon causes and conditions, namely human effort, a water jar, and a churning rope.
Sentient beings are likewise: those who possess the Buddha-nature should attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by being free from causes and conditions.
If it were definitely existent, for what reason would practitioners, upon seeing the sufferings of the three evil realms and birth, old age, sickness, and death, give rise to a mind of retreat?
Furthermore, they would not need to cultivate the six pāramitās, as they should immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Just as milk does not become curd without conditions, yet it likewise cannot achieve unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) without relying on the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
For this reason, you should know that sentient beings all lack Buddha-nature.
"As the Buddha previously stated that the Sangha Jewel is eternal, if it is eternal, it cannot be impermanent."
If it were not impermanent, how could one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
If the Saṅgha were permanent, why would you further say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature?
World-Honored One!

If sentient beings were originally devoid of the bodhicitta and likewise lacked the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such that these minds only arise later, then the buddha-nature of sentient beings would also be like this—originally non-existent and only existing later.
"For this reason, all sentient beings would have no Buddha-nature.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
You have long understood the meaning of Buddha-nature; it is for the sake of sentient beings that you ask such a question.
All sentient beings truly possess Buddha-nature."
As for your statement,
"If sentient beings possess buddha-nature, one should not say there is an initial arousal of the mind," O son of good family!
The mind is not the Buddha-nature. Why is this?
Because the mind is impermanent, whereas the Buddha-nature is eternal.
As for your question,
"Why is there a regressive mind?"—
in reality, there is no regressive mind.
If the mind were subject to regression, one would ultimately be unable to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because it is attained only after a long delay, it is termed "regression.
This bodhicitta is, in reality, not the Buddha-nature.
Why is this? Because those such as the icchantikas sever their roots of goodness and fall into hell.
If the bodhicitta were the Buddha-nature, then the class of icchantikas could not be called icchantikas, and the bodhicitta itself could not be called impermanent.
Therefore, it is certain that the bodhicitta is truly not the Buddha-nature.
"Good son! As for what you said:
As for the claim that "if sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they should not depend on conditions,
just as milk becomes curd," this meaning is not correct. Why is this so?
If it is said that clarified butter (*navanīta*) is produced through five conditions, one should know that the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is likewise so.
For example, among various stones there may be gold, silver, copper, or iron; though they all receive the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they share a single name and a single reality.
Yet that which is produced from each is different; it must depend upon various conditions, the merit of sentient beings, and the labor of the smith, only then to be brought forth.
Therefore, one should know:
fundamentally, there is no nature of gold.

The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not called "Buddha"; it is only through the harmonious convergence of various meritorious causes and conditions that one perceives the Buddha-nature, and subsequently attains Buddhahood.
As for what you said:
"If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why do they not see it?"
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because the various causes and conditions have not yet come together in harmony.
"Good son! For this reason, I speak of two kinds of causes:
the direct cause and the conditional cause."
The direct cause is called Buddha-nature;
the conditional cause is the arousal of the bodhicitta.
By means of these two causes and conditions, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just as gold is extracted from stone.
“Good son! You say:
‘The Saṃgha is eternal, yet all sentient beings lack the Buddha-nature.’”
"O son of good family!
'Saṃgha' means harmony.
There are two kinds of harmony:"
The first is worldly harmony; the second is harmony in the ultimate sense.
Worldly harmony refers to the Saṃgha of Śrāvakas;
harmony in the ultimate sense refers to the Saṃgha of Bodhisattvas.
The worldly Sangha is impermanent, whereas the Buddha-nature is permanent.
Just as the meaning of the permanence of the Buddha-nature applies, so it is with the Sangha.
Furthermore, there is a Sangha that refers to the harmony of the Dharma.
The harmony of the Dharma refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Since the twelve divisions of the scriptures are eternal, I therefore say that the Dharma and the Sangha are eternal. Good son!
The name "Saṃgha" means "harmony.
Harmony refers to the twelve links of dependent origination.

Within the twelve links of dependent origination there is also Buddha-nature; the twelve links of dependent origination are eternal, and Buddha-nature is likewise so. For this reason, I say that the Saṃgha possesses Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, the Sangha is the harmony of all Buddhas; therefore, I say that the Sangha possesses Buddha-nature.
"Good son! As for what you said:
Regarding the question, "If sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why is there regression for some and non-regression for others?
listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
"Good son!
There are thirteen dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva regresses.
What are these thirteen?

First, lack of faith in the mind; second, a mind that does not act; third, a doubting mind; fourth, stinginess regarding one's body and wealth; fifth, giving rise to great fear toward nirvana, thinking:
"How can you cause sentient beings to be eternally extinguished?"

6) The mind is unable to endure; 7) the mind is not pliant; 8) sorrow and affliction; 9) lack of joy; 10) negligence; 11) self-contempt; 12) seeing one's own afflictions as being incapable of being destroyed; 13) lack of delight in the dharmas that lead toward enlightenment.
"Good son! These are called the thirteen dharmas that cause bodhisattvas to regress from bodhicitta.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas that destroy the bodhicitta."
What are these six? First, stinginess regarding the Dharma;

second, giving rise to unwholesome thoughts toward sentient beings; third, associating with evil friends; fourth, lacking diligent effort; fifth, being conceited and arrogant; sixth, being preoccupied with worldly affairs. These six factors can destroy the bodhicitta.

“Good son! There are those who hear that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are the teachers of gods and humans; that among all sentient beings they are supreme and peerless, excelling the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others; that their Dharma-eye is clear and bright, seeing all phenomena without obstruction, and that they are able to deliver sentient beings from the great ocean of suffering.”
Having heard this, he immediately made a great vow:
"Just as there is such a person in the world, may I also attain it.
By these causes and conditions, he resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Or again, they may develop the bodhicitta through the instruction of others.
Or, hearing that a Bodhisattva practices austerities for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before finally attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they reflect upon it and think:
"I am currently unable to endure such austerities; how could I possibly attain it?"
Therefore, there is regression.
"Good son! Furthermore, there are five dharmas that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta."

What are these five? First, taking pleasure in leaving home to join non-Buddhist sects; second, failing to cultivate a mind of great compassion; third, delighting in seeking out the faults and evils of Dharma masters; fourth, constantly taking pleasure in remaining within the cycle of birth and death; and fifth, having no joy in receiving, upholding, reciting, copying, or explaining the twelve divisions of the scriptures. These are called the five dharmas that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta.
"Furthermore, there are two factors that cause one to regress from the bodhicitta. What are these two?
First, craving and delighting in the five sensual desires; second, being unable to revere and honor the Triple Gem."
"For these various causes and conditions such as these, one retreats from the bodhicitta.
What, then, is called the non-retreating mind?

There is a person who hears that the Buddha can deliver sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death; without consulting a teacher, they practice spontaneously and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"If the path to bodhi is attainable, I shall cultivate it and ensure that I surely attain it.
For this reason, one generates the bodhicitta; whatever merit one has performed, whether much or little, one dedicates it all toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, making this vow:
"May I always be able to draw near to the Buddhas and their disciples, always hear the profound Dharma, and possess all five sensory faculties intact."
“Even if I encounter suffering and hardship, may I not lose this mind.
“Furthermore, I pray that all Buddhas and their disciples will always give rise to a heart of joy toward me, and that I may be endowed with the five roots of goodness.”

If any sentient beings were to hack at my body, or cut off my hands, feet, head, eyes, or limbs and joints, I should give rise to great compassion for those people and rejoice deeply within myself, thinking:
"Such people are providing me with the causes and conditions for increasing my bodhi."
"If these do not exist, by what cause shall I achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
He further made this vow:

"May I never obtain a body that is rootless, possesses both sexes, or is female; may I not be dependent on others, nor encounter an evil master, nor be subject to an evil king, nor be born in an evil land."
"If I obtain a fine body, a noble lineage, and abundant wealth and treasures, may I not give rise to arrogance.
"May I always hear the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and may I receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain them."
"If I preach anything for the sake of sentient beings, I vow that those who receive it shall respect and believe it without doubt, and never give rise to ill will toward me.
"It is better to hear little but understand the meaning and flavor extensively; I do not wish for much hearing without understanding the meaning."

"May I become a master of my own mind, rather than being mastered by the mind; may my actions of body, speech, and mind not associate with evil; may I be able to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings; and may my body, precepts, mind, and wisdom remain as immovable as a mountain."
"In order to receive and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma, one should not give rise to stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth.

"One should not perform meritorious deeds with impure things; one should sustain oneself through right livelihood, have a mind free from deceit and flattery, always remember kindness received, and repay even small favors with great gratitude."

"‘He is well-versed in all the arts and crafts found within the world, proficiently understands the local dialects of sentient beings, recites and transcribes the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and never gives rise to a mind of indolence or laziness.’"
“If there are sentient beings who do not delight in hearing [the Dharma], I shall employ skillful means to guide and receive them, causing them to take pleasure in hearing it.
“My speech shall always be gentle, and my mouth shall never utter evil.”
“‘He can bring harmony to a discordant assembly; he can cause those who are distressed and fearful to be free from distress and fear; and in times of famine, he can cause them to obtain abundance.’”

"In an age of sickness and disease, he acts as a great king of physicians; possessing mastery over the medicines required for illness and over all wealth and treasures, he causes every afflicted person to be completely healed."
"In the kalpa of weapons, there shall be great power to sever all violence and harm, leaving nothing remaining.

"He is able to sever the various fears of sentient beings—namely, the fear of death, imprisonment, beating and casting down, water, fire, kings and thieves, poverty, breaking the precepts, ill repute, and the evil realms; such fears as these shall all be severed."

"‘One should give rise to deep reverence for one’s parents and teachers; cultivate a mind of great compassion toward those who harbor enmity or hatred; constantly practice the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), the gate of the three samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the contemplations on the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and arising-and-ceasing, as well as mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), the celestial conduct (*divya-caryā*), the Brahma-conduct (*brahma-caryā*), the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*), the Vajra-samādhi, and the Śūraṅgama-samādhi.’"
"Where there is no Triple Gem, may I personally attain a mind of tranquility.
"When my body and mind undergo great suffering, may I not lose the unsurpassed mind of Bodhi, nor give rise to contentment through the minds of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
"In places where the Three Jewels do not exist, one should always go forth within the teachings of non-Buddhist paths; yet, for the sake of destroying false views, one must not practice their ways.
"Having attained mastery over phenomena and mastery over the mind, one clearly perceives the defects within conditioned phenomena."
"May I find fear in the fruits of the paths of the two vehicles, as one who cherishes life fears the loss of that body.
"For the sake of sentient beings, may I joyfully dwell in the three evil realms, as all sentient beings delight in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
"Even if one must undergo the sufferings of hell for immeasurable eons for the sake of each and every person, one’s mind shall not give rise to regret.
"Upon seeing others obtain benefit, one shall not give rise to envy, but shall always feel joy as if it were one's own pleasure."

"If you encounter the Triple Gem, you should make offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, dwellings, medicine, lamps, flowers and incense, music, banners and canopies, and the seven treasures."
“If one receives the Buddha’s precepts, one shall uphold them with firm resolve and never give rise to thoughts of violation.
“If one hears of the bodhisattva’s difficult practices and ascetic austerities, one’s heart shall rejoice and no regret or remorse shall arise.”
"‘I recognize the events of my past lives and shall never again create karma born of greed, hatred, or delusion.
‘I shall not accumulate causes and conditions for the sake of karmic retribution, nor shall I give rise to greedy attachment toward present pleasures.’"

“Good son! If there are those who can make such a vow, they are called bodhisattvas who never regress or lose the mind of enlightenment; they are also called donors who can clearly perceive the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata, who can discipline sentient beings and deliver them from birth and death, who are well able to protect and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma, and who can fully attain the six pāramitās.”
"Good son! For this reason, the mind of non-retrogression is not called Buddha-nature. Good son!"
You must not, on account of having a regressive mind, claim that all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature.
It is like two people who both hear that in another land there is a mountain of seven treasures, with clear springs whose water is sweet and delicious;
those who can reach it will forever end their poverty, and those who drink its water will increase their lifespan by ten thousand years.
The road was exceedingly remote, with many dangers and obstacles.

At that time, the two men both wished to travel together; one prepared various provisions for the journey, while the other set out empty-handed, carrying nothing at all, as they proceeded forward together.
On the road, they encountered a man carrying a great abundance of precious goods, fully equipped with the seven treasures.
The two men went forward and asked him,
"O virtuous one!..."
"Does that land truly have mountains made of the seven treasures?
The man replied, "It is indeed so and not false;
I have already obtained the treasures and drunk its water."
The only concern was that the road was perilous, with many bandits, gravel, and thorns, and a scarcity of water and grass.
Of those who went forth by the millions, very few reached their destination.
Having heard this, one person immediately felt regret and spoke these words:
"The road is already so remote and the hardships are manifold; of those who have gone, there are countless, yet those who have reached the destination are few."
"How could I possibly reach that place?
My current property is sufficient for my own basic needs; if I were to travel this road, I might lose my life.
If my life is not preserved, what use is long life?"
Another person spoke again:
"If there is someone who can pass through, I too can pass through.
If we reach our destination, we shall obtain the precious jewels as we wish and drink the sweet water."
"If we do not succeed, we shall take death as our limit.

At that time, one of the two men regretted and withdrew, while the other pressed forward. Upon reaching the mountain, he obtained abundant wealth and treasures; he drank the water as desired, took much of what he had acquired, and returned to his dwelling to provide for his parents and support his kinsmen.
At that time, the one who had regretted his departure and returned saw this occurrence and felt a burning urgency in his heart:
"He has already gone and returned; why do I remain here?
He immediately prepared himself, set out upon the road, and departed.
"The mountain of seven treasures is a metaphor for the Great Nirvana;
the sweet water is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature;
and those two individuals are metaphors for two bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain enlightenment."
The perilous and evil path is a metaphor for birth and death;
the person encountered is a metaphor for the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
and the presence of bandits is a metaphor for the four māras.
The sand and gravel, as well as the thorns, are metaphors for the various afflictions (*kleśa*);
the absence of water and grass is a metaphor for not cultivating the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*);
and the single person who returns is a metaphor for a bodhisattva who regresses.
Those who go straight ahead are a metaphor for non-retrogressive bodhisattvas. Good son!
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is eternally abiding and unchanging, just like that perilous path; it cannot be said:
"Because people regret and turn back, it causes the Way to appear impermanent.
The Buddha-nature is also like this.
"Good son!..."
Within the path to enlightenment, there is ultimately no one who regresses. Good son!

It is like that person who previously felt regret; seeing his former companion returning with treasures, possessing sovereign power, making offerings to his parents, providing for his kinsmen, and enjoying manifold peace and happiness.

Having seen this, his heart was filled with fervor; he immediately adorned himself once more and returned by the same path. Disregarding his own body and life, and enduring all manner of hardships, he eventually arrived at those mountains of seven precious gems.
The Bodhisattva who regresses is also like this. Good son!
All sentient beings will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, I have stated in my sutras that all sentient beings—even those who commit the five heinous crimes, violate the four grave prohibitions, or are icchantikas—possess the Buddha-nature.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
In what way do bodhisattvas have regression or non-regression?”

“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata, they are called ‘non-regressive,’ called a ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ called ‘unshakable,’ called ‘one who has compassion for all sentient beings,’ called ‘superior to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,’ and called ‘an avaivartika.’”

“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva maintains the precepts without wavering, his mind of giving remains unshakable, and he dwells securely in truthful speech like Mount Sumeru, by these karmic conditions he attains the mark of soles as flat as the bottom of a casket.”
