"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva provides offerings and support with wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma to their parents, preceptors, teachers, and even down to animals, by virtue of these karmic conditions, they attain the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet."

“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva refrains from killing and refrains from stealing, and always gives rise to joy toward their parents and teachers, by these karmic conditions they attain three marks: first, fingers that are slender and long; second, heels that are long; third, a body that is square and straight. These three marks arise from the same karmic condition.”

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings, by virtue of these karmic conditions, they obtain webbed fingers like those of a white goose king."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when his parents, teachers, or elders are suffering from illness, washes and wipes them with his own hands, holds and massages them, he attains softness of hand and foot through these karmic conditions."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains the precepts, listens to the Dharma, and practices giving without weariness, by these karmic conditions he attains full and rounded ankles and body hairs that curl upward."
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva listens to the Dharma with single-minded devotion and expounds the true teaching, by these karmic conditions he obtains calves like those of a deer king.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to thoughts of harm toward sentient beings, is moderate in food and drink, and always delights in practicing generosity, tending to the sick, and providing medicine, by these karmic conditions his body becomes perfectly proportioned like a nyagrodha tree, his hands reach past his knees when standing, and he possesses a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head—the mark of the invisible crown."

“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva provides protection for those who are terrified and gives clothing to those who are naked and barefoot, by these karmic conditions he attains the mark of the sheathed organ.

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva associates with the wise and distances himself from the foolish, delights in skillful inquiry and response, and sweeps and repairs the roads—by virtue of these karmic conditions, his skin becomes fine and soft, and the hairs on his body curl to the right."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly bestows upon others clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, incense, flowers, and lamps, through these karmic conditions they obtain a golden-colored body that is perpetually radiant."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing generosity, is able to relinquish his most cherished possessions without stinginess, and does not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit, he attains the mark of the seven parts of the body being full through these karmic conditions."
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when practicing giving, does not give rise to doubt in his mind, by this karmic condition he obtains a soft and supple voice.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma to use for giving, by this karmic condition he obtains full clavicles, an upper body like that of a lion, and arms and elbows that are rounded and slender."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva stays far removed from divisive speech, harsh words, and a mind of malice, by the causal conditions of this karma, they obtain forty teeth that are white, pure, even, and closely set."
"If a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates great loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, by virtue of these karmic conditions, he attains the mark of two tusks.
If a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly makes this vow:
'To those who come seeking, I shall give according to their wishes.'"
“By these karmic conditions, he obtained cheeks like those of a lion.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva provides all sentient beings with whatever food and drink they require, by these karmic conditions, he obtains the supreme flavor among all flavors.”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action and also transforms others through them, by these karmic conditions they obtain a broad and long tongue.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not speak of others' shortcomings and does not slander the true Dharma, by these karmic conditions they obtain the Brahma-voice.”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to a mind of joy upon seeing those who are hostile or hateful, through this karmic condition, they obtain eyelashes of a deep blue color.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not conceal the virtues of others and proclaims their goodness, through this karmic condition, they obtain the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the karmic causes and conditions for these thirty-two marks, they shall attain the non-retrogressive mind of enlightenment.”
“Good son! All sentient beings are inconceivable; the realm of the Buddhas, karmic retribution, and Buddha-nature are likewise inconceivable.”
Why is this? Because these four dharmas are all eternal.
Since they are eternal, they are inconceivable.
Because all sentient beings are shrouded and obstructed by afflictions, they are said to be "permanent";
because they sever the afflictions of permanence and impermanence, they are said to be "impermanent.
If it were said that all sentient beings are permanent, for what reason would they cultivate the eightfold noble path to sever all suffering?
If all sufferings are severed, they are termed impermanent; the bliss that is experienced therein is termed permanent.
Therefore, I say that all sentient beings, being shrouded and obstructed by afflictions, do not see the Buddha-nature;
because they do not see it, they do not attain nirvana.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 26. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 27.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huiyan and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In the "Chapter on the Lion’s Roar Bodhisattva," Part Three,
the Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!”
As the Buddha has taught:
all dharmas have two kinds of causes:
first, the direct cause (hetu-hetu); second, the conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu).
Based on these two reasons, there should be neither bondage nor liberation.
These five aggregates arise and perish from moment to moment;
as they thus arise and perish, who is it that is bound?
"Who understands this, World-Honored One?

Because of these five aggregates, the subsequent five aggregates arise; these aggregates perish of their own accord and do not pass over to those [subsequent] aggregates, yet although they do not pass over to them, they are able to give rise to those aggregates."
Just as a sprout arises from a seed, yet the seed does not pass over into the sprout—even though it does not pass over into the sprout, it is able to produce it.
Sentient beings are likewise; how, then, can there be bondage or liberation?
“Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Good son!”
It is like when a person is about to give up their life and undergoes great suffering; surrounded by kinsmen who wail and lament in distress, the person is terrified and knows no refuge or rescue.

Although they possess the five sense faculties, they have no conscious perception; their limbs tremble and quiver, unable to be restrained, as their body grows cold and empty and the warmth of life is about to fade away, at which point they see the signs of the retribution for the good and evil deeds previously cultivated.
“Good son! Just as when the sun is about to set behind mountains and hills, its shadow appears to move eastward and cannot logically travel westward;

so too it is with the karmic fruits of sentient beings. When this aggregate ceases, that aggregate arises in succession, just as darkness is extinguished when a lamp is lit, and darkness arises when a lamp is extinguished.”
Good son! It is like a wax seal being pressed into clay: the seal and the clay meet; as the seal is removed, the impression is formed. Yet the wax seal does not transform and remain within the clay.
The impression does not emerge from the clay, nor does it come from elsewhere; rather, this impression arises through the causal conditions of the seal.
When the aggregates of the present life cease, the aggregates of the intermediate state arise.
These present aggregates do not transform into the five aggregates of the intermediate state;
nor do the five aggregates of the intermediate state arise from themselves, nor do they come from elsewhere.
Because the aggregates of the present existence manifest, the aggregates of the intermediate state arise.
It is like pressing a seal into clay: when the seal is destroyed, the impression is formed; though the name of the mark does not differ, the timing of each is distinct.
Therefore, I say that the five aggregates of the intermediate state (antarābhava) are not seen by the physical eye, but are seen by the divine eye.
Within this intermediate state, there are three kinds of nutriment:
first, the nutriment of volition (manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra); second, the nutriment of contact (sparśāhāra); and third, the nutriment of mental intention (vijñānāhāra).
There are two kinds of intermediate state (antarābhava):
first, the result of wholesome karma; second, the result of unwholesome karma.
Due to wholesome karma, one attains wholesome vitarka and vicāra.
Due to evil karma, one acquires evil thoughts and observations.
At the time when the parents unite in sexual intercourse, following the conditions of their karma, they move toward the place of rebirth, conceiving love for the mother and hatred for the father.
When the father’s semen is emitted, [the intermediate being] considers it as its own; having seen this, the mind is delighted and joy arises.

By means of these three kinds of afflictive conditions, the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) perish and the subsequent five aggregates arise, just as when a seal is pressed into clay: the seal perishes and the impression is formed.
"At the time of birth, the sense faculties may be complete or incomplete.
Those with complete faculties, upon seeing forms, give rise to greed; because greed arises, it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because of delusion, greed arises; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*)."

Due to the two causes and conditions of craving and ignorance, all perceived objects are entirely inverted: one perceives the impermanent as permanent, the non-self as self, the unsatisfactory as satisfying, and the impure as pure.
Due to the four inversions, one performs wholesome and unwholesome actions; afflictions produce karma, and karma produces afflictions—this is called bondage.
For this reason, it is termed the arising of the five aggregates.
"If this person is able to draw near to the Buddha and his disciples, as well as to various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they will then hear and receive the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
because they have heard the Dharma, they contemplate wholesome objects;
because they contemplate wholesome objects, they attain great wisdom."
One of great wisdom is said to possess right knowledge and vision;
because they have attained such knowledge and vision, they give rise to a sense of remorse within the cycle of birth and death;
because they give rise to remorse, they do not produce joy.
Because one does not give rise to joy, one is able to destroy the mind of greed;
because the mind of greed is destroyed, one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path;
because the Eightfold Noble Path is cultivated, one attains the state beyond birth and death.
Because there is no longer birth and death, it is called attaining liberation.
Just as fire that encounters no more fuel is called extinguished,
because birth and death have been extinguished, it is called *nirvāṇa* (extinction).
"For this reason, it is called the extinction of the five aggregates.
Siṃhanāda said: "In emptiness there are no thorns; why do you speak of pulling them out?"
"If the aggregates are unconditioned, how can they be bound?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."

The fetters of afflictions bind the five aggregates; yet apart from the five aggregates, there are no separate afflictions, and apart from afflictions, there are no separate five aggregates. Good son!
Just as a pillar supports a house—there being no pillar apart from the house and no house apart from the pillar—so too it is with the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of sentient beings:
because of the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called "bound";
because of the absence of afflictions, they are called "liberated."
“Good son! Just as with a clenched fist, joined palms, or the three states of binding and so forth—there is no separate dharma other than their coming together, dispersing, arising, and ceasing.
It is the same with the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of sentient beings: because they possess afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called ‘bound.’”
Because they are free from afflictions, they are called "liberated. "Good son!
As it is said that name-and-form bind sentient beings, if name-and-form are extinguished, there are no sentient beings—apart from name-and-form, there are no separate sentient beings.
"Apart from sentient beings, there is no separate name-and-form— yet it is said that 'name-and-form binds sentient beings,' and it is also said that 'sentient beings bind name-and-form.
Siṃhavijṛmbhita addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

Just as the eye does not see itself, a finger does not touch itself, a sword does not cut itself, and feeling does not feel itself, how can the Tathāgata say that name-and-form is bound by name-and-form?
Why is this? That which is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) is itself sentient beings, and that which are called "sentient beings" are themselves name-and-form.
If one says that name-and-form binds sentient beings, it is simply that name-and-form binds name-and-form.
The Buddha said: “Good son!
Just as when two hands are joined together, no other distinct dharma comes to join them;”
It is the same with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
For this reason, I say that name-and-form binds sentient beings; if one is separated from name-and-form, one attains liberation.
"Therefore, I say that sentient beings attain liberation. Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!"
"If name-and-form were a bondage, then all Arhats who have not yet abandoned name-and-form would also be bound.
"Good son, there are two kinds of liberation: [liberation from afflictions and liberation from the body]."
First is the severance of the seed, and second is the severance of the fruit.
What is called the "severance of the seed" refers to the cutting off of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Arhats and others have already severed their afflictions; since all their fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been rotted away, the fetters of the seed cannot bind them.
Because the fruit has not yet been severed, it is called "bondage to the fruit.
All Arhats do not see the Buddha-nature; because they do not see it, they do not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, it may be said that they are bound by the fruit, but one cannot say they are bound by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
"Good son! It is like lighting a lamp: as long as the oil is not exhausted, the light will not be extinguished."
If the oil is exhausted, its extinction is beyond doubt.
Good son! That which is called "oil" is a metaphor for all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The lamp is a metaphor for sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings have the oil of afflictions, they do not enter nirvana;
if they succeed in severing it, they then enter nirvana.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
The lamp and the oil have two distinct natures.”
The afflictions of sentient beings are not like this; sentient beings are themselves the afflictions, and the afflictions are themselves sentient beings.
Sentient beings are called the five aggregates, and the five aggregates are called sentient beings;
the five aggregates are called afflictions, and the afflictions are called the five aggregates.
"How is it that the Tathāgata is likened to a lamp?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
There are eight kinds of similes: first, the concordant simile;

second, the inverse simile; third, the manifest simile; fourth, the non-simile; fifth, the prior simile; sixth, the posterior simile; seventh, the prior-and-posterior simile; and eighth, the pervasive simile.
"What is the analogy in accordance with the teaching? As it is said in the Sūtra:
'When the heavens send down heavy rain, the ditches and channels all become full;'"
Because the ditches and channels are full, the small pits are full;
because the small pits are full, the large pits are full;
because the large pits are full, the small springs are full.
Because the small spring is full, the large spring is full;
because the large spring is full, the small pond is full;
because the small pond is full, the large pond is full.
Because the great pond is full, the small river is full;
because the small river is full, the large river is full;
because the large river is full, the great ocean is full.
The Dharma rain of the Tathāgata is likewise:
when sentient beings fulfill the precepts, because the precepts are fulfilled, the mind of non-regret is fulfilled;
because the mind of non-regret is fulfilled, joy is fulfilled.
Because joy is fulfilled, detachment is fulfilled;
because detachment is fulfilled, tranquility is fulfilled;
because tranquility is fulfilled, samādhi is fulfilled.
Because samādhi is fulfilled, right knowledge and vision are fulfilled;
because right knowledge and vision are fulfilled, disenchantment is fulfilled;
because disenchantment is fulfilled, revulsion is fulfilled.
Because the perfection of reproach is fulfilled, the perfection of liberation is fulfilled;
because the perfection of liberation is fulfilled, the perfection of nirvāṇa is fulfilled.
This is called an analogy in direct order.
"What is the analogy by way of inversion?
The great ocean has its source, namely the great rivers;
the great rivers have their source, namely the small rivers."
The small river has its source, which is the large pond;
the large pond has its source, which is the small pond;
the small pond has its source, which is the large spring.
The Great Spring has its source, which is called the Small Spring;
the Small Spring has its source, which is called the Great Pit;
the Great Pit has its source, which is called the Small Pit.
Small pits have their origin, namely in ditches;
ditches have their origin, namely in heavy rain.
Nirvana has its origin, namely in liberation.
Liberation has a root, which is called censure;
censure has a root, which is called disenchantment;
disenchantment has a root, which is called right knowledge and vision.
Right knowledge and vision have their root in samādhi;
samādhi has its root in tranquility;
tranquility has its root in seclusion.
The root from which detachment arises is the mind of joy;
the root of the mind of joy is non-regret;
the root of non-regret is the observance of the precepts.
The foundation of upholding the precepts is what is called the rain of Dharma;
this is known as an inverse analogy.
What is a direct analogy?
As it is said in the sutras:
"The nature of the minds of sentient beings is like that of a monkey.
The nature of a monkey is to abandon one thing and seize another."
The nature of the minds of sentient beings is likewise: they grasp at and cling to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, never remaining still for even a moment.
This is called the present analogy.
"Why is it not an analogy?
It is as I once told King Prasenajit:
'Great King!'"
A trusted person came from each of the four directions and spoke these words:
"Great King!
Four great mountains are coming from the four directions, intending to harm the people."
"If the King were to hear this, what plan would he devise?
The King replied,
"World-Honored One!..."
"If this should come to pass, there will be no place for escape; you must simply focus your mind on upholding the precepts and practicing generosity.
I then praised him, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
I say that the four mountains are precisely the birth, old age, sickness, and death of sentient beings.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death constantly come to press upon people; why, Great King, do you not cultivate precepts and practice giving?
The king said:
"World-Honored One!
What kind of fruit is obtained through observing the precepts and practicing generosity?"
I said: "Great King! You shall experience much happiness among humans and devas."
The King said:
"World-Honored One!
Does the Nyagrodha tree also receive peace and happiness among humans and devas for upholding the precepts and practicing giving?"
I said: "Great King!
A nyagrodha tree cannot uphold the precepts or practice generosity; yet if it were able to do so, it would receive [the fruit] no differently."
"This is called a non-example.
What is the primary example?
In my sūtras it is said:"
It is like a person who, being greedily attached to exquisite flowers, is swept away by water while gathering them.
Sentient beings are likewise: greedily attached to the five desires, they are swept away and submerged by birth, old age, and death.
This is called the preceding analogy.
What is the subsequent analogy?
As it is said in the *Dharmapada*:
"Do not despise small evils, thinking they will bring no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
This is called the subsequent parable.
"What is the analogy of the sequence?
For example, like the plantain tree: when it bears fruit, it dies;
so too is it with the fool who receives nourishment."
Just as a mule that has conceived will not survive for long.
"What is the universal analogy?
As it is said in the Sūtra:"

In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there is the Pārijātaka tree; its roots penetrate the earth to a depth of five yojanas, it rises a hundred yojanas high, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all directions. When the leaves ripen, they turn yellow.
When the devas saw this, joy arose in their hearts:
"These leaves will surely fall before long.
Once the leaves had fallen, they felt joy once again:
"This branch will surely change color before long.
Once the branch had changed color, he again gave rise to joy, thinking:
"This color will surely give rise to blisters before long."
Having seen this, he rejoiced again, thinking:
"This blister will surely produce a beak before long.
Having seen this, he rejoiced yet again.
"This bud will surely blossom before long.
When it blossoms, its fragrance will pervade fifty *yojanas*, and its radiance will shine afar for eighty *yojanas*.
At that time, the devas spend the three months of the summer retreat receiving pleasure while remaining below.
Good son, my disciples are also like this.
The yellowing of the leaves is a metaphor for my disciples’ thought of renouncing the household life;
the falling of the leaves is a metaphor for my disciples’ shaving off their hair and beards;
and the change in color is a metaphor for my disciples’ undergoing the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The initial formation of the bud is a metaphor for my disciples giving rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
the opening of the bud is a metaphor for bodhisattvas of the ten stages attaining the vision of the Buddha-nature;
and its full blooming is a metaphor for bodhisattvas attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Incense" is a metaphor for the immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions who uphold the prohibitive precepts;
"light" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s unimpeded name, which pervades the ten directions;
and the "three months of summer" is a metaphor for the three samādhis.
The experience of bliss by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is a metaphor for the Buddhas attaining permanence, bliss, self, and purity within Great Nirvana.
This is called the universal metaphor.
“Good son! Not all metaphors cited need to be taken in their entirety; sometimes a small portion is taken, sometimes a large portion, and sometimes they are taken in full.
For example, saying that the Tathāgata’s face is like the full moon is called taking a small portion.”
“Good son! It is like a person who has never seen milk before and asks another,
‘What kind of thing is milk?’”
That person replied:
"It is like water, honey, or a conch shell.

Water has the characteristic of moisture, honey has the characteristic of sweetness, and a conch shell has the characteristic of color; yet although these three metaphors were cited, they did not immediately correspond to the reality of milk.
"Good son!
My statement that the analogy of the lamp illustrates sentient beings is likewise so. Good son!"
Just as there is no river apart from water, so it is with sentient beings: apart from the five aggregates, there is no separate sentient being. Good son!
"Just as there is no separate vehicle apart from the box, the wheels, the spokes, the axle, and the rim;
so it is with sentient beings. Good son!..."
If you wish to understand how this accords with the analogy of the lamp, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now explain it.
The wick is an analogy for the twenty-five realms of existence;
the oil is an analogy for craving.
"Light" is a metaphor for wisdom;
"dispelling darkness" is a metaphor for destroying ignorance;
"warmth" is a metaphor for the Noble Path.
Just as when the oil of a lamp is exhausted, its bright flame is extinguished,
so too when the craving of sentient beings is exhausted, they see the Buddha-nature; though name-and-form remain, they cannot bind them,
and even while dwelling within the twenty-five realms of existence, they are not defiled by those realms.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
Since the five aggregates of sentient beings are empty and non-existent, who is there to receive the teaching and practice the Path?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

All sentient beings possess a mind of mindfulness, a mind of wisdom, a mind of resolve, a mind of diligent effort, a mind of faith, and a mind of concentration. Although such dharmas arise and perish from moment to moment, they nevertheless remain similar and continue in an uninterrupted succession; therefore, it is called ‘cultivating the path.’”
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
Since such dharmas as these all perish moment by moment, and even this moment-to-moment perishing is itself similar and continuous, how should one practice them?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Just as a lamp, though it perishes moment by moment, possesses radiance that dispels the darkness;”
The various dharmas such as mindfulness are also like this. Good son!
Just as the food of sentient beings, though perishing moment by moment, enables those who are hungry to become fully satiated.

For example, just as a superior medicine can cure a disease despite perishing moment by moment, and the light of the sun and moon can cause forests, trees, and grasses to grow despite perishing moment by moment; so too is this case.
"Good son! You say: 'If [dharmas] perish moment by moment, how can they increase?'"
As for the phrase "because the mind is not severed," it is called "growth.
Good son! It is like a person reciting a text: the words and phrases being recited cannot occur simultaneously; what precedes does not reach the middle, and the middle does not reach the end.
The person and the characters, as well as the thoughts and mental conceptions, all perish moment by moment; yet, because of long-term cultivation, one attains proficiency. "Good son!

It is like a goldsmith who, from his first practice until his hair turns white, although [his actions] perish moment by moment and what precedes does not reach what follows, through the accumulation of habit, that which he produces becomes exquisite. For this reason, he is called a skilled goldsmith."
The recitation and study of the sutras is also like this.
"Good son! It is, for example, like a seed; the earth does not instruct it:
"May you produce a sprout.
By the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the sprout then arises of its own accord.
This continues up to the flower, which likewise receives no instruction:
"Thou shalt become fruit.
By virtue of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the fruit arises spontaneously.
The cultivation of the path by sentient beings is likewise so.
“Good son! It is like the method of counting:
one does not reach two, and two does not reach three; yet although each moment perishes, it reaches a thousand or ten thousand.
The cultivation of the path by sentient beings is also like this.”
“Good son! It is like a lamp that extinguishes moment by moment; the flame that first extinguishes does not instruct the subsequent flame:
‘I shall extinguish, and you, upon arising, shall destroy all darkness.’”
"Good son! It is like a calf that, upon birth, immediately seeks milk.
The wisdom that seeks milk is not actually taught by anyone; yet, although it perishes moment by moment, it goes from initial hunger to subsequent satiety."
Therefore, one should know that they ought not to be identical;
if they were identical, there would be no arising of difference.
It is the same with sentient beings practicing the Path: although there is initially no increase, through long-term cultivation, they are able to destroy all afflictions.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught:”

Once a person who has attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna has realized this fruition, even if they are born in an evil land, they still maintain their precepts, refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, and drinking intoxicants.
The aggregates of a srotāpanna are extinguished right here and do not reach an evil land;
the cultivation of the path is likewise, for it does not reach an evil land.
If they are similar, why is it that [the latter] is not born in a pure and wondrous land?
“If the aggregates of an evil country are not the aggregates of a *srotāpanna*, how can one avoid committing evil karma?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
One who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna, though born in an evil land, never loses the name of Srotāpanna.
Because the aggregates (skandhas) are not identical [to those of others], I have cited the calf as a metaphor.
Although a *srotāpanna* may be born in an evil land, by the power of the Way, they do not commit evil deeds. "Good son!
It is like Mount Gandhamādana, where there dwells a lion king; for this reason, all birds and beasts flee from this mountain, and none dare approach it."
Sometimes a king may go into the Snowy Mountains, yet all the birds and beasts still do not dwell there.
A stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is also like this: although they do not practice the Path, by the power of the Path, they do not commit any evil deeds.
“Good son! It is like a person who consumes nectar; although the nectar itself perishes, by its power it enables this person to be neither born nor to die.”

"Good son! For example, on Mount Sumeru there is a supreme and wondrous medicine called Laṅkāli. If someone takes it, although it perishes moment by moment, by the power of the medicine, they do not encounter suffering or affliction."
“Good son! Just as at the place where a wheel-turning monarch sits, no one dares to approach it even when the king is not present. Why is this?

By the power of the king’s majesty, it is likewise with those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*): though born in an evil land and not practicing the Path, they do not commit evil deeds by virtue of the power of that Path.
"Good son!
The aggregates of a srotāpanna cease here; although he is born with different aggregates, he nevertheless does not lose the aggregates of a srotāpanna. Good son!"

For example, when sentient beings, for the sake of a fruit, perform much labor upon a seed—applying manure, irrigating, and so forth—and although they do not obtain the fruit before the seed perishes, it can still be said that they obtain the fruit by means of the seed.
The aggregates of a *srotāpanna* are also like this.
"Good son! It is, for example, as if there were a man of immense wealth who had only one son, who had already passed away."
That son had a son who, in turn, lived in another land.
When that man suddenly and unexpectedly passed away, the grandson heard of this and returned to take possession of the estate.
Although he knew the wealth and goods were not produced by him, there was no one to prevent him from taking them.
Why is this? Because their lineage is one.
The aggregates of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) are likewise so.
Siṃhanāda said: "As the Buddha spoke in verse:
'If a bhikṣu cultivates Precepts, concentration, and wisdom...'"
"You should know that this is non-retrogression, drawing near to Great Nirvana.
"World-Honored One,
how does one cultivate the precepts?"
“How does one cultivate concentration?
How does one cultivate wisdom?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! If there are those who uphold the prohibitive precepts merely for their own benefit or to enjoy the pleasures of humans and devas, not for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, nor for the sake of upholding the unsurpassed True Dharma; but rather for the sake of gain and offerings, out of fear of the three evil realms, or for the sake of life, physical appearance, strength, peace, and unimpeded eloquence; or out of dread of royal law, ill repute, and foul rumors; or for the sake of worldly affairs—if one guards the precepts in such a manner, it cannot be called the cultivation of the precepts.”
“Good son! What is called the true cultivation of the precepts?

When receiving and upholding the precepts, if one does so for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, for the sake of delivering those not yet delivered, for the sake of liberating those not yet liberated, for the sake of providing refuge to those without refuge, and for the sake of enabling those who have not entered nirvana to enter it—if one cultivates in this manner, one does not perceive the precepts, does not perceive the characteristics of the precepts, does not perceive a holder of the precepts, does not perceive the karmic fruit, and does not contemplate transgression.”
"Good son!
If one can act in this way, it is called the cultivation of the precepts.
Furthermore, what is called the cultivation of samādhi?

When practicing samādhi, if one does so for the sake of one's own liberation or for gain and offerings, rather than for the sake of sentient beings or for the protection of the Dharma; or if one practices samādhi out of a desire to see the faults of greed and impure food, the sexual organs of men and women, the impurity of the nine orifices, or quarrels, strife, beating, piercing, and mutual slaughter—if one practices samādhi for such purposes, this is not called the cultivation of samādhi.
“Good son! What further is called the true cultivation of samādhi?

If, for the sake of sentient beings, one cultivates samādhi; attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; causes sentient beings to attain the dharma of non-retrogression; causes sentient beings to attain the noble mind; causes sentient beings to attain the Mahāyāna; desires to protect and uphold the unsurpassed Dharma; causes sentient beings not to regress from bodhi; causes sentient beings to attain Śūraṅgama-samādhi; causes sentient beings to attain Vajra-samādhi; causes sentient beings to attain dhāraṇī; causes sentient beings to attain the four kinds of unimpededness; and causes sentient beings to perceive the Buddha-nature—when performing such practices, one does not perceive the samādhi, does not perceive the characteristics of samādhi, does not perceive the practitioner, and does not perceive the karmic fruit.
"Good son!
If one can act in this way, it is called the cultivation of samādhi.
Furthermore, what is called the cultivation of wisdom?
If there are those who practice and reflect thus:
"If I cultivate such wisdom, I shall attain liberation and cross over the three evil realms.
Who then can benefit all sentient beings?"
Who can deliver people from the path of birth and death?
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; I am now able to sever all fetters of affliction and shall certainly attain liberation.
"Therefore, I shall diligently cultivate wisdom, swiftly sever the afflictions, and quickly attain liberation.
One who practices in this manner cannot be said to be cultivating wisdom.
"What is meant by one who cultivates wisdom?
It is when one contemplates the suffering of birth, old age, and death, thinking:

'All sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and do not know how to cultivate the unsurpassed right path; may this body of mine fully take upon itself the great suffering and affliction of all sentient beings.'"
May all the poverty, base status, and precept-breaking minds of sentient beings, as well as their karma of greed, hatred, and delusion, come to gather entirely within my own body.
May all sentient beings not give rise to greedy grasping and not be bound by name-and-form;
may all sentient beings swiftly cross over birth and death, while I alone remain within it without weariness;
may all beings together attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When practicing in this way, one does not perceive wisdom, does not perceive the characteristics of wisdom, does not perceive the practitioner, and does not perceive the karmic fruit; this is what is called the cultivation of wisdom.
“Good son! One who cultivates such morality, concentration, and wisdom is called a bodhisattva;
one who cannot thus cultivate morality, concentration, and wisdom is called a śrāvaka.”
"Furthermore, good son!
What is meant by 'cultivating the precepts'?
It is being able to destroy the sixteen types of evil disciplinary codes of all sentient beings."
What are the sixteen?
First, for the sake of profit and food, they fatten lambs and then sell them;
second, for the sake of profit, they purchase them and slaughter them.
Third, for the sake of profit and food, they fatten pigs and hogs for gain, raise chickens to fatten them, and then sell them once they are fat;
eighth, for the sake of profit, they purchase animals and slaughter them;
ninth, they fish with hooks.
Tenth, hunters;
eleventh, plunderers;
twelfth, executioners.
Thirteen, catching flying birds with nets;
fourteen, double-tongued speech;
fifteen, being a jailer;
Sixteenth, subjugating dragons.
To be able to bring about the permanent severance of these sixteen types of evil karma for the sake of sentient beings is called the cultivation of precepts.
"What is the cultivation of concentration?"

There is the samādhi capable of severing all worldly [attachments], namely the bodiless samādhi (*akāya-samādhi*), which can cause sentient beings to give rise to a perverted mind, thinking it to be nirvāṇa;

furthermore, there are the boundless mind samādhi (*ananta-citta-samādhi*), the pure accumulation samādhi (*śuddha-rāśi-samādhi*), the limit of the world samādhi (*loka-koṭi-samādhi*), the severance of the world samādhi (*loka-ccheda-samādhi*), the nature of the world samādhi (*loka-dhātu-samādhi*), the hero of the world samādhi (*loka-puruṣa-samādhi*), and the neither-perception-nor-non-perception samādhi (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā-samādhi*). Samādhis such as these can cause sentient beings to give rise to a perverted mind, thinking them to be nirvāṇa.
If one can forever sever such [distractions] within samādhi, this is called the cultivation of samādhi.
Furthermore, what is called the cultivation of wisdom?
It is that which can destroy all evil views in the world.
All sentient beings possess evil views, namely: that form is the self, or that it belongs to the self;

that there is a self within form, or that form is within the self. This applies likewise up to consciousness. They hold that the permanent is the self, or that while form perishes, the self remains; or that form is the self, and when form perishes, the self perishes.
Furthermore, some say:
"The agent is called 'self,' and the recipient is called 'form' (rūpa). Others say:
"The agent is called name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and the experiencer is called the self (ātman).
Furthermore, some say:
"There is no agent and no experiencer; things arise and perish of themselves, entirely without causes and conditions."
Again, some people say:
"There is no agent and no recipient; all things are created by Īśvara. Still others say:
"There is no agent and no experiencer; everything is produced by the power of time.
Furthermore, some say:
"The agent and the experiencer do not exist at all; the five great elements, such as earth and so forth, are what are called sentient beings."
“Good son! If one can destroy such evil views of all sentient beings, this is what is called cultivating wisdom. Good son!”

Cultivating the precepts is for the sake of the tranquility of the body; cultivating samādhi is for the sake of the tranquility of the mind; and cultivating wisdom is for the sake of destroying doubt.
To destroy doubt is to cultivate the Path;
to cultivate the Path is to perceive the Buddha-nature.
Those who see the Buddha-nature do so for the sake of attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
those who attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi do so for the sake of attaining the unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa;
and those who attain Great Nirvāṇa do so for the sake of severing all birth-and-death, all afflictions, all modes of existence, all realms, and all truths for the sake of sentient beings.
"To sever birth and death, and even to sever the [four] truths, for the sake of attaining the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, that which is neither born nor extinguished is called Great Nirvana.
Birth is likewise [neither born nor extinguished]; why then cannot it be called nirvana?
“Good son! It is so, it is so;
just as you have said, although this birth is neither born nor extinguished, it nevertheless has a beginning and an end.”
“World-Honored One!
These dharmas of birth and death are likewise without beginning or end. If they have no beginning or end, they are called ‘permanent,’ and permanence is itself nirvāṇa.”
"Why is it that birth-and-death (saṃsāra) is not called nirvāṇa?
"Good son! These dharmas of birth-and-death all possess cause and effect; because they possess cause and effect, they cannot be called nirvāṇa."
"Why is this? Because the essence of nirvāṇa has neither cause nor effect.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
Nirvana, too, possesses causes and effects,
as the Buddha has taught:”
“Because of causes one is born in heaven; because of causes one falls into the evil realms;
because of causes one attains nirvana; therefore, all things have causes.”
“As the Buddha told the bhikṣus in the past:
‘I shall now speak of the śramaṇa, the path, and the fruit.
To speak of the śramaṇa means one who is able to fully cultivate ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”
The "Path" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path;
the "fruit of the śramaṇa" refers to nirvāṇa,
World-Honored One.
“Nirvana is thus; is it not, then, a fruit?
Why do you say that the essence of nirvana has neither cause nor fruit?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! That which I have proclaimed as the cause of nirvāṇa is what is called buddha-nature.
Since the nature of buddha-nature does not give rise to nirvāṇa, I say that nirvāṇa has no cause.”
Because it can destroy afflictions, it is called the "great fruit";
because it does not arise from the Path, it is called "fruitless.
Therefore, Nirvana has neither cause nor fruit.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
Is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings possessed by all equally?”
Are they individual or collective?
If they were collective, then when one person attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all sentient beings should likewise attain it simultaneously.
World-Honored One!
It is like twenty people who share a single enemy; if one person is able to eliminate him, the remaining nineteen will likewise all be freed from him.
If the Buddha-nature were like this, then when one person attains it, the others should also attain it.
If they were each distinct, they would be impermanent. Why?
Because they could be counted.
However, the Buddha has taught that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither one nor two.
If each possessed it as a distinct entity, one should not say that all Buddhas are equal, nor should one say that the buddha-nature is like space.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither one nor two. All Buddhas are equal, like space; it is shared equally by all sentient beings.”
If there are those who can cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, you should know that such persons will attain clear vision. Good son!
On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called "Patience"; if a cow eats it, it produces ghee.
"The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this. Siṃhanāda asked:
"As the Buddha has taught regarding the kṣānti-grass, is it one?"
Is it much?
If there were only one, the ox would have finished eating it;
if there were many, how can you say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this?
As the Buddha has said:
"If there are those who cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, they will see the Buddha-nature.
This meaning is not so.
Why is this? If the Way were singular, then it would be like the grass of patience (*kṣānti-tṛṇa*), which would eventually be exhausted;
if it were to be exhausted, once one person had cultivated it, others would have no share in it.
“If the paths are so numerous, how can one say that they are fully cultivated and yet not called the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñājñāna)?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
It is like a level road upon which all sentient beings travel without obstruction.
Along the way there is a tree, its shade cool and refreshing, where travelers dismount to rest and recuperate.
However, the shade of that tree remains constantly without shifting, nor does it perish or decay, and there is no one who carries it away.
The road is a metaphor for the Noble Path;
the shade is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature.
Good son!

It is like a great city that has but a single gate; although many people pass through it to enter and exit, none at all can create an obstacle, nor is there anyone who can destroy, demolish, or carry away anything from it.
Good son! It is like a bridge, by which travelers pass; no one obstructs, hinders, destroys, or carries it away. Good son!
For example, just as a skilled physician treats all manner of illnesses, and no one can prevent him from treating this one while setting aside that one;
so too it is with the Noble Path and Buddha-nature.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
The meanings of the various metaphors you have cited are not as such.”
Why is this? That which is ahead on the road obstructs what follows; how then can it be said that there are no obstructions?
The same applies to all other cases as well.
“If the Buddha-nature of the Noble Path were like this, then when one person cultivates it,
they would obstruct others. The Buddha said, “Good son!
What you have said does not accord with the meaning.
The path I used as a metaphor is a partial analogy, not a complete one. "Good son!
The mundane path involves obstructions and distinctions between this and that, and thus lacks equality. The untainted path is not like this;

it enables sentient beings to be free from obstructions, equal and non-dual, without spatial location or distinctions between this and that. Such a true path serves as the *jñāpaka-hetu* (revealing cause) for the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings, but does not act as the *janaka-hetu* (generating cause), just as a bright lamp illuminates objects.
“Good son! All sentient beings equally share the same ignorance as the causal condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
it cannot be said that once one person’s formations have arisen through the causal condition of ignorance, they should cease to exist for all others.”
"All sentient beings possess ignorance as the causal condition for volitional formations; therefore, it is said that the twelve links of dependent origination are equal in all respects.
The untainted, right path cultivated by sentient beings is likewise so, equally severing the afflictions, the four modes of birth, the various realms, and the path of existence."
For this reason, it is called "equality.
Those who realize it possess mutual knowledge and vision without any obstruction; therefore, it is named the wisdom of *sarvajña* (all-knowing).
Siṃhanāda said:

“The bodies of all sentient beings are not of a single kind; there are those with celestial bodies, human bodies, or the bodies of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings. Since there are such many different types of bodies, not just one, how can you say that the Buddha-nature is one?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
It is like a person who puts poison into milk; even the final product, clarified butter (ghṛta), will all be poisonous.”
Milk is not called curd, and curd is not called milk; this remains true even up to the stage of clarified butter (ghṛta).
Although the names change, the poisonous nature is not lost; it persists throughout all five flavors as if they were distinct bodies, yet this Buddha-nature remains eternally one and unchanging.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!

Among the sixteen great nations there are six great cities, namely: the city of Śrāvastī, the city of Vārāṇasī, the city of Campā, the city of Vaiśālī, the city of Pāṭaliputra, and the city of Rājagṛha.”

These six cities are the greatest in the world; for what reason has the Tathāgata abandoned them and entered parinirvāṇa here in this frontier town of Kuśinagara, which is wretched, evil, extremely humble, narrow, and small?

“Good son! You should not say that the vicinity of the city of Kuśinagara is a remote borderland, wretched, most base, narrow, and small; rather, you should say that this city is adorned with subtle and sublime merits.”
Why is this? Because it is the sphere of practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Good son!
Suppose a king were to pass by the house of a lowly person; he should then praise it, saying:
"This house is magnificent and adorned with merit, such that it has caused the Great King to turn his carriage to visit it."
"Good son! It is like a person with a grave illness who takes a foul and inferior medicine; once he has taken it and his illness is cured, he should immediately rejoice and praise it, saying:
'This medicine is supreme and most wonderful; it has been able to cure my illness.'"
"Good son! It is like a person traveling by boat upon the great ocean whose vessel suddenly breaks apart; having no other support, he relies upon a corpse and thereby reaches the further shore."
Having reached the other shore, one should rejoice greatly and exclaim:
"It is by meeting this corpse that I have obtained safety.

The city of Kuśinagara is likewise so; it is the place where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have practiced. How can you say it is a frontier land, a wretched and evil place, a narrow and humble small city?
“Good son! I recall that in the past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a kalpa named Good Awakening (Sujñāna).
At that time, there was a noble king of the Kausika clan who possessed the seven treasures and was endowed with a thousand sons.”
When that king first founded this city, it was twelve yojanas in circumference and breadth, adorned with the seven treasures.

The land abounded in rivers whose waters were pure, soft, and sweet; these included the Nairañjanā River, the Airāvatī River, the Hiraṇyavatī River, the Ikṣumatī River, and the Vipāśā River—rivers such as these numbering five hundred.
"On the opposite bank of this river, the trees are lush and flourishing, and the flowers and fruits are fresh and pure.
At that time, the lifespan of the people was immeasurable.
Then, after a hundred years had passed, the Wheel-Turning Sage King made this proclamation:"
"As the Buddha has taught:
'All phenomena are entirely impermanent; if one can cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas, one can sever such great suffering of impermanence.'"
Having heard this, the people all together reverently practiced the Dharma of the ten wholesome paths.
At that time, upon hearing the name of the Buddha, I upheld the ten wholesome paths, contemplated and cultivated them, and for the first time resolved my mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having generated this mind, he further used these teachings to instruct immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, saying that all phenomena are impermanent and subject to decay.
For this reason, I now likewise continue here to speak of all phenomena as impermanent and subject to decay, teaching only that the Buddha-body is the eternally abiding dharma.
I recall the causes and conditions of my past conduct; for this reason, I have now come here to enter nirvana, wishing also to repay the past kindness of this land.
For this purpose, I have said in my sutras:
"Those who are my kinsmen are able to repay the kindness they receive."
"Furthermore, good son!
In the past, when the lifespan of sentient beings was immeasurable, this city was named Kuśāvatī, and its circumference and dimensions were fifty yojanas."
At that time, the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa lived so close together that a cock could fly from one to another.
There was a Wheel-Turning King named Sudarśana, who possessed the seven treasures, was endowed with a thousand sons, and ruled over the four continents.
The eldest prince contemplated the True Dharma and attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King saw that his son had become a Pratyekabuddha, his deportment composed and dignified, and his supernormal powers rare and extraordinary.

Having seen this, he immediately renounced his royal throne like spittle or phlegm and went forth into homelessness among these śāla trees; for eighty thousand years he cultivated a mind of loving-kindness (maitrī), and for eighty thousand years each he cultivated the minds of compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā).

“Good son! If you wish to know who that noble King Sudarśana was at that time, it was none other than myself. Therefore, I now constantly delight in dwelling and practicing these four dharmas; these four dharmas are called samādhi.”
For this reason, the body of the Tathāgata is eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Good son!
By these causes and conditions, I have now come to abide here among the śāla trees of Kuśinagara, entering into samādhi and right reception.
“Good son! I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, this city was then named Kapilavastu.
In that city there was a king named Śuddhodana; the king’s queen was named Māyā, and the king had a son named Siddhārtha.”
At that time, the prince, without relying on a teacher’s instruction, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through his own natural contemplation.
He had two disciples:
the first was named Śāriputra, and the second was named Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The attendant disciple was named Ānanda.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was expounding this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* between the twin trees,
I was present in the assembly and participated in these events, hearing that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Having heard these matters, he immediately attained non-retrogression regarding Bodhi and promptly made this vow:

"In a future age, when I attain Buddhahood, may my parents, country, name, disciples, and attendants, as well as my preaching and teaching of the Dharma, be exactly equal to those of the World-Honored One now, without any difference."
For these reasons, I have now come here to expound and proclaim the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. "Good son!
When I first left home and had not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, King Bimbisāra sent a messenger who said:
"Prince Siddhārtha!
If you become a noble wheel-turning monarch, I shall serve as your subject.

But if you do not delight in the household life and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I pray that you will first come here to this city of Rājagṛha to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, accepting my offerings."
At that time, I remained silent, having already accepted his invitation. "Good son!
After I first attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I headed toward the kingdom of Kaja."

At that time, there was a Brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan on the banks of the Nairañjanā River who, together with five hundred disciples, was seeking the unsurpassed path; for his sake, I went there to preach the Dharma.
Kāśyapa said:
"Gautama! I am now advanced in years, already one hundred and twenty."

All the people of the kingdom of Magadha, as well as its great king Bimbisāra, believe that I have already realized the fruit of arhatship. If I were now to sit before you and listen to the Dharma, all these people might give rise to a mistaken thought, thinking:
"Is the Venerable Kāśyapa not an arhat?"
"I pray that Gautama will quickly depart for another place; if these people come to know for certain that Gautama’s merit surpasses mine, we shall have no further means to receive their offerings."
I then replied: "Kāśyapa!
If you do not harbor intense resentment toward me, please grant me the favor of staying one night; I shall depart early tomorrow morning."
Kāśyapa said: "Gautama!
My mind harbors no other intent; I hold you in deep affection and high esteem."
"But in my dwelling there is a venomous dragon whose nature is violent and impetuous; I fear it may cause you harm.
I said, "Kāśyapa!..."
"There is no poison more virulent than the three poisons, and I have now severed them.
As for the poisons of the world, I have no fear of them.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"If you can indeed remain undaunted, excellent! You may stay.
Son of good family!
At that time, I intentionally manifested the eighteen transformations for Kāśyapa, as described in the sūtra.
At that time, Kāśyapa and his followers, numbering five hundred, having seen and heard this, realized the fruit of Arhatship.
At that moment, Kāśyapa had two younger brothers:
the first was named Gayākāśyapa, and the second was named Nadīkāśyapa; their disciples and followers also numbered five hundred, and they too all realized the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, when the six heretical teachers and their followers heard of these matters, they conceived a great sense of malice toward me.
I then set out in accordance with my commitment, accepting the King's invitation, and proceeded to Rājagṛha.
Before they had reached the midpoint of the road, the King and an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands came forth to welcome me, and I preached the Dharma for them.

Having heard the Dharma at that time, eighty-six thousand devas of the desire realm conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; one hundred and twenty thousand followers in King Bimbisāra’s retinue attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*; and immeasurable sentient beings accomplished the mind of patience (*kṣānti*).

Having entered the city, he led Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, along with their retinues of two hundred and fifty, to renounce their original intentions, leave the household life, and study the Way.
I remained there, receiving the king’s offerings, while the six heretical teachers gathered together and proceeded to the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was an elder in that city named Sudatta, who had gone to Rājagṛha to seek a wife for his son.
Having reached that city, they stayed as guests in the house of the elder Sandhana.
At midnight, this elder rose and addressed his kinsmen:
"Sirs, you should rise; quickly adorn yourselves together, sweep and clean the house, and prepare the various delicacies."
Having heard this, Sudatta immediately reflected to himself:
"Is it not that they wish to invite King Māgadha?
Or is there a wedding celebration?"
Having reflected thus, he immediately stepped forward and asked,
"Great Being!
Do you wish to invite King Bimbisāra of Magadha?"
"Is there a wedding celebration or some joyful gathering?
Why are you so preoccupied and unsettled?
The householder replied:
"No, householder! Tomorrow I shall invite the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King."
When the elder Sudatta first heard the name "Buddha," the hair on his body stood on end; he immediately asked again, "Who is called 'Buddha'?
The elder replied:
“Have you not heard?
In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a son of the Śākyas named Siddhārtha, of the Gautama clan; his father’s name is Śuddhodana.”
Not long after his birth, physiognomists prophesied that he would certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin rāja), as certain as an amra fruit already held in one's hand.
Yet, his heart found no pleasure in this; he renounced it to leave the household life, and without a teacher, he attained by himself the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
With greed, hatred, and delusion exhausted, he abides eternally without change; being neither born nor extinguished, he is free from sorrow and fear.
Toward all sentient beings, his mind is impartial, regarding them as a father and mother would look upon an only child.
He is the most supreme among all beings of body and mind; though he excels all, he is free from arrogance.
Regarding the two matters of being anointed and being cut, his mind remains without distinction.

His wisdom is thoroughly penetrating and unimpeded regarding all phenomena. Because he is fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the five knowledges, the samādhis, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness, he is called a Buddha.
"Knowing that you have accepted my invitation, I am in such a hurry that I have had no leisure to look upon you.
Sudatta said, "Excellent, Great Being!"
"What is called a Buddha possesses unsurpassed merit. Where is he now?
The elder replied:
"I am currently here in the great city of Rājagṛha, residing at the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove Monastery.

At that time, Sudatta single-mindedly recollects all the merits of the Buddha: his ten powers, fearlessnesses, five wisdoms, samādhis, great kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness.
While he was thinking these thoughts, suddenly there was a great radiance; its brilliance was so intense that it was like the midday sun.
He immediately followed the light out and arrived beneath the city gate.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the gate opened spontaneously.
Having exited the gate, he came upon a celestial shrine along the road.

As Sudatta passed by, he paid his respects with prostrations; immediately, it became pitch black again, and his heart was filled with terror. He then wished to return to the place where he had stayed.
At that time, a deva residing at the city gate addressed Sudatta, saying:
"O virtuous one!
If you go to where the Tathāgata is, you will obtain great benefit."
Sudatta asked, "What is this 'excellent benefit'?
The deva replied:
"O Householder!

Suppose there were a person who, for the sake of a single individual, offered a hundred fine horses adorned with genuine jewels, a hundred fragrant elephants, a hundred jeweled chariots, and a hundred figures cast from refined gold; suppose further they offered a hundred beautiful women, their bodies adorned with necklaces and inlaid with various precious gems, as well as a hundred magnificent palaces, halls, and dwellings carved and engraved with intricate patterns, along with a hundred golden platters filled with silver grain and a hundred silver platters filled with golden grain—were such offerings made repeatedly throughout the entire continent of Jambudvīpa, the merit thereby obtained would not equal that of a person who, having resolved their mind, takes even a single step toward the presence of the Tathāgata."
Sudatta said: "Good man! Who are you?"
The deva said:
"Householder!
I am the son of the brahmin Viśeṣacintin; I was your spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in the past."

Because I felt joy in my heart upon seeing Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana in the past, I cast off this body and was reborn as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, specifically charged with guarding this city of Rājagṛha.

If, by merely giving rise to a heart of joy through prostrating to Śāriputra and the others, I have already obtained such a wondrous and excellent body as this, how much more so shall I obtain it when I am able to see the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, and pay him homage and make offerings?
Having heard this matter, the householder Sudatta immediately returned by the same path to where I was.
Upon arrival, he bowed his head in respectful salutation at my feet.
I then preached the Dharma to him according to what was appropriate for him.
Upon hearing this, the elder attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Having realized this fruit, he again entreated me, saying:
"The Tathāgata is greatly compassionate; I pray that you will deign to visit Śrāvastī and accept my humble offering."
I then asked: "In your city of Śrāvastī, is there any monastery large enough to accommodate us?
Sudatta replied:
"If the Buddha would look upon me with compassion and deign to grant his presence, I shall exhaust myself to prepare and establish [the assembly].
"Good son! At that time, I accepted the invitation in silence."
Having received my permission, the elder Sudatta addressed me, saying:
"I have never performed such a deed since time immemorial; I only pray that the Tathāgata will dispatch Śāriputra to instruct me in the proper rites."
I immediately looked back and gave orders, commanding my attendants to prepare for the journey.
Then Śāriputra and Sudatta traveled together in one carriage toward Śrāvastī.
By means of my supernatural power, we arrived at our destination after only one day and night.
Then Sudatta said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable One!

Outside this great city, where is there a plot of land that is neither too near nor too far, abounding in springs and ponds, possessing fine groves and trees with lush flowers and fruit, and which is pure, secluded, and spacious?"
"I shall, within this place, construct a vihāra for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the community of bhikṣus.
Śāriputra said, "The Jeta Grove is neither too near nor too far; it is pure and secluded, with many springs and streams, and trees, flowers, and fruits available in their proper seasons."
"This location is most excellent; a vihāra may be established here.
When Sudatta heard these words, he immediately went to the great householder Jeta and said to him:
"I now wish to construct a monastic dwelling for the Unsurpassed Dharma King; only your noble park is suitable for this purpose."
"I now wish to purchase it; would you be able to grant it to me?
Jeta replied, "Even if you were to cover the entire ground with genuine gold, I still would not give it to you."
Sudatta said, "Excellent, Jeta!
The forest land belongs to me; you may now take the gold."
Jeta replied, "I do not sell my grove; why would I take gold? Sudatta said:
"If you cannot resolve this yourselves, we should go together to the place where legal disputes are adjudicated.
Thereupon, the two elders went together to the court of justice.
The judge said, "The garden belongs to Sudatta; Jeta has received the gold."

The elder Sudatta immediately dispatched people to load carts and horses with the gold and carry it along, spreading it over the ground as they went; yet within a single day, only five hundred paces had been covered, and the gold was not yet complete.
Jeta said, "If you,
Elder, should regret it, you may stop as you please.
Sudatta replied:
"I do not regret it; I simply thought to myself that I must find which treasury would provide sufficient gold.
Jeta thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, is truly unsurpassed; the wondrous Dharma he proclaims is pure and untainted, which is why this man regards wealth so lightly."
He then said to Sudatta, "For the remaining areas not yet covered, you need no more gold; please give them to me instead.
I shall build a gate tower for the Buddha myself, so that the Tathāgata may always pass through it when entering and leaving."
The elder Jeta personally constructed the gatehouse, while the elder Sudatta completed a great residence of three hundred rooms within seven days;
he also established sixty-three meditation cells in secluded locations,
with separate quarters for winter houses and summer halls.
The kitchen, the bathhouse, the place for washing feet, and the large and small latrines were all fully prepared.
Once everything had been arranged, he took up an incense burner and, facing toward Rājagṛha from afar, spoke these words:
"All that was to be provided has been completed; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion and pity, will accept this dwelling place for the sake of all sentient beings."

At that time, I knew the mind of this elder through my profound insight; immediately, together with the great assembly, I departed from Rājagṛha and, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, arrived at the Jeta Grove, the Saṃghārāma of Sudatta, in Śrāvastī.
Once I had arrived, the elder Sudatta offered me that which he had prepared for my use.
Having accepted it, I then took up residence therein.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-seven.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-Eight.
Added by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇas Huiyan and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter Four of the "Lion’s Roar Bodhisattva" Section.
At that time, the six heretical teachers, conceiving feelings of jealousy, all came together to visit King Prasenajit and spoke to him thus:
"Your Majesty, you should know:
Your kingdom is pure, peaceful, and tranquil; it is truly a place for renunciants to dwell."
Therefore, we have come here for this very purpose.
Your Majesty governs by means of the True Dharma and removes the sufferings of the people.
Yet the śramaṇa Gautama is both young in years and shallow in his studies; he has no skillful means to offer.
"In this country, there were formerly elders of long-standing virtue who, relying on their royal lineage, failed to show respect.
If one is of royal descent, the law dictates that they should govern the people; however, if they renounce the world, they ought to honor those of long-standing virtue."
"Great King, listen well:
the śramaṇa Gautama was not truly born into the royal lineage.
If the śramaṇa Gautama has parents, how could he possibly rob others of their parents?"
"Great King!
In my sutras it is said:
'After a thousand years have passed, a deceptive and illusory being shall appear.'"
"This refers to the śramaṇa Gautama.
Therefore, you should know:
the śramaṇa Gautama has no father and no mother."
If there are parents, why do you say that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, uncreated, and without a recipient?
By means of illusory arts, you deceive and delude sentient beings; the foolish believe and accept them, while the wise abandon them.
"Great King!

A king is indeed the parent of the world; he is like a scale, like the earth, like the wind, like fire, like the path, like a river, like a bridge, like a lamp, like the sun, and like the moon. He adjudicates affairs according to the Dharma, making no distinction between enemy and kin."
"Śramaṇa Gautama will not allow me to live; he pursues me wherever I go and does not let me escape.
I only pray that Your Majesty will permit me to compete with him in the power of our paths. If he defeats me, I shall submit to him;
if I defeat him, he shall submit to me."
The King said:
"Venerable Sirs!
Each of you has your own rules of conduct, and the places where you reside are likewise different. I now know for certain that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, will cause you no hindrance."
The six teachers replied:
"How can there be no harm?
The śramaṇa Gautama has used the methods of illusionary arts to entice and deceive all people and brahmins until they have been completely won over."
"If Your Majesty permits me to compete with you in the power of the Way, your good reputation will spread throughout the eight directions;
if you do not, ill repute will fill the roads.
The King said:
"Virtuous ones!
Because you do not yet know that the Tathāgata’s power of the Way and his majestic spiritual authority are so sublime, you seek to test him by competition.
Had you known for certain, I fear you would not have been able."
"Great King! Have you now already accepted the illusion of Gautama?
We only pray that Your Majesty will deign to listen and examine this; do not treat us with contempt."
"Constructing arguments with empty words is not as good as verifying them through reality.
The King said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
The disciples of the six teachers departed with joy.

At that time, King Prasenajit immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and came to where I was; he prostrated himself in reverence, circumambulated me three times to the right, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed me, saying:
“World-Honored One! ”
"The six masters have recently sought to compete with me in spiritual power; without due consideration, I have already granted them my consent.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
Excellent, excellent!
You should simply establish monasteries for the Saṃgha in various places throughout this country. Why is that?
"If I were to compete with him in supernatural power, those among his assembly who would be converted would be many; this place is narrow and small—how could it accommodate them? "Good son!
At that time, for the sake of the six teachers, from the first day until the fifteenth day, I manifested great and rare supernatural transformations.
At that moment, immeasurable sentient beings resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to faith in the Triple Gem without doubt.
The followers of the six teachers were immeasurable in number; they shattered their minds of false views and left the home life for the True Dharma.
Immeasurable sentient beings attained the non-retrogressive mind within Bodhi;
immeasurable sentient beings attained various dharanis and the gates of samadhi.
"Immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*.

At that time, the six heretical teachers felt shame and remorse in their hearts; they gathered together and went to the city of Vārāṇasī, where they taught the local people to believe in and accept their false doctrines, saying:
'The śramaṇa Gautama speaks only of empty matters.'"
“Good son! At that time, for the sake of my mother, I was dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, observing the retreat under the Pārijātaka tree and preaching the Dharma.
At that moment, the six heretical teachers were filled with great joy and cried out:”
"Excellent! Gautama, your magical arts have now been extinguished.
Furthermore, he taught immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to increase their false views.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, King Prasenajit, and the fourfold assembly addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Venerable One!
In this Jambudvīpa, false views are increasing; sentient beings are pitiable, wandering in great darkness.
We pray that you, Venerable One, will go to that heavenly realm and prostrate yourself before the World-Honored One, speaking on our behalf as follows:"
"It is like a calf that has been born not long ago; if it does not receive milk, it will surely die without a doubt.
We sentient beings are just the same."
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will have compassion for sentient beings and return to dwell here.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana silently gave his consent; in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he went to that heavenly realm and approached the World-Honored One, saying to the Buddha:
“All the fourfold assembly in Jambudvīpa thirsts with longing for the Tathāgata, yearning to see him and hear the Dharma.”
King Bimbisāra, King Prasenajit, and the fourfold assembly prostrate themselves at your feet:
"All sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa have increased in wrong views and walk in great darkness; they are truly to be pitied."
It is like a calf that has been born not long ago;
if it does not obtain milk, it will surely die without a doubt. We are just the same.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, will return once more to this Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Return now swiftly to Jambudvīpa and inform the various kings and the fourfold assembly:"
"Seven days from now, I shall descend again.
For the sake of the six teachers, I shall once more go to that city of Vārāṇasī.

After the seven days had passed, the Buddha, surrounded by Śakra, Brahmā, Māra, immeasurable sons of gods, and all the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī. There, he let out a great lion’s roar and spoke these words:
"Only within my teaching are there true śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; all phenomena are impermanent and without self, and nirvāṇa is tranquil, free from all faults and afflictions."
"If it is said that other teachings also possess śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, or that they possess permanence, a self, and nirvāṇa, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the six teachers said to one another:
"If there were truly no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas within our own teachings, how could we receive the offerings of the world?"
Thereupon, the six teachers gathered together again and went to Vaiśālī. "Good son!
At one time, I was staying in the Āmra Grove at Vaiśālī."
At that time, Āmrapālī knew I was within and intended to come to me.
I then addressed the bhikṣus: "You should practice mindfulness of the foundations of mindfulness and cultivate wisdom well; according to what you practice, let your minds not be negligent."
What is called the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness?

If a bhikṣu observes the internal body and does not perceive a self or what belongs to a self; observes the external body and the internal-external body and does not perceive a self or what belongs to a self; and likewise observes feelings, the mind, and phenomena—this is called the foundations of mindfulness.
What is called the cultivation of wisdom?
If a bhikṣu truly perceives suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, this is called a bhikṣu cultivating wisdom.
What is called non-laxity of mind?

If a bhikṣu recollects the Buddha, recollects the Dharma, recollects the Saṃgha, recollects the precepts, recollects relinquishment, and recollects the devas, this is called a bhikṣu whose mind is not lax.

Then the lady Āmrapālī came to where I was, prostrated herself with her head at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, and having completed her respectful salutations, sat down to one side.
"Good son!
At that time, I preached the Dharma to the woman Āmrapālī according to her needs.
Having heard it, she gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
