"At that time, there were five hundred Licchavis in that city who came to where I was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, and having completed their respectful salutations, withdrew to sit to one side."
At that time, I further preached the Dharma to the Licchavis according to their needs, saying: "Good sons!
One who is negligent has five kinds of karmic results."

What are these five? First, one does not attain mastery over wealth and profit; second, an evil reputation spreads far and wide; third, one takes no pleasure in bestowing gifts upon the destitute; fourth, one takes no pleasure in seeing the fourfold assembly; and fifth, one does not obtain the body of a deva.
"O sons of good family!
Through heedfulness, one is able to give rise to both worldly and world-transcending dharmas.
If there are those who wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should diligently cultivate the dharma of heedfulness."
Furthermore, those who are heedless shall receive thirteen karmic retributions. What are these thirteen? First, they delight in performing worldly tasks;

second, they delight in speaking useless words; third, they constantly delight in sleeping for long periods; fourth, they delight in discussing worldly affairs; fifth, they constantly delight in associating with evil friends; sixth, they are indolent and lazy; seventh, they are always held in contempt by others; eighth, though they hear something, they soon forget it; ninth, they delight in dwelling in remote borderlands; tenth, they are unable to subdue their sense faculties; eleventh, they do not know moderation in eating; twelfth, they do not delight in emptiness and stillness; thirteenth, their views are incorrect. These are called the thirteen.
"Good son!
As for those who are negligent, even if they draw near to the Buddha and his disciples, they remain far indeed.
The Licchavi youths said:
"We know ourselves to be heedless people. Why is this?
Had we not been heedless, the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, would have appeared in our land."
“At that time, there was a son of a brahmin in the great assembly named Ajita, who said to the Licchavis:
‘Excellent, excellent!
Just as you have said, King Bimbisāra has already attained great benefit.’”
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has appeared in this land like a wondrous lotus flower growing in a great pond; though it grows in the water, the water cannot defile it.
O sons of the Licchavis!
The Buddha is likewise; although he is born in that land, he is not obstructed by worldly dharmas.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have neither emergence nor entry; for the sake of sentient beings, they appear in the world, yet they are not obstructed by worldly dharmas.

"You yourselves are deluded, indulging in the five desires and neglecting to draw near to the Tathāgata; for this reason, you are called heedless people. It is not that the Buddha’s appearance in the kingdom of Magadha is itself called 'heedlessness.'"
"Why is this? The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is like the sun and the moon; he does not appear in the world for the sake of only one or two people.
When the Licchavis heard these words, they immediately resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He spoke again, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
O invincible youth!"
"Please speak such virtuous and wonderful words.
Then each of the Licchavis removed one garment from their own bodies and offered it to Ajita.
Having accepted them, Ajita presented them to me and spoke these words again:
“World-Honored One!
I have obtained these garments from the Licchavis; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings, will accept what I offer.
At that time, out of pity for him who was without superior, I immediately accepted them.
Then all the Licchavis simultaneously joined their palms and spoke these words:
"We pray that the Tathāgata will dwell for a time in this land and accept our humble offerings."
At that time, I accepted the Licchavis' invitation by remaining silent.
When the six heretical teachers heard of this matter, they consulted among themselves and went together to Vārāṇasī.
At that time, I also went to Vārāṇasī and stayed on the banks of the Varanā River.
At that time, there was a son of a householder in Vārāṇasī named Ratnayaśas who was addicted to the five desires and ignorant of impermanence.

Because I had arrived, he spontaneously attained the dharma of the meditation on white bones; he saw his palace, his attendants, and his court ladies all as white bones, and his heart was filled with terror, as if they were swords, venomous snakes, thieves, or fire.
He immediately left his house and came to where I was, calling out along the way:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
I am now being pursued by bandits; I am filled with great fear and dread. I pray that you will rescue me."
The Buddha said:
“Good son! The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are secure and free from fear.”
The son of the elder said,
"If there is nothing to fear within the Three Jewels, then I too shall now attain fearlessness.
I immediately granted him permission to leave the household life and pursue the Way.

At that time, the son of the elder had fifty companions; hearing from afar that Ratnayaśas had become weary of the world and left the household life, they immediately harmonized their intentions and together went forth as renunciants.
Having heard this, the six teachers traveled on in succession to the great city of Campā.

At that time, all the people of the kingdom of Campā were devoted to the followers of the six teachers; they had never before heard the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, and many among them committed extremely evil deeds.
At that time, for the sake of sentient beings, I went to the city of Campā.
At that time, there was a great elder in that city who had no heir; he served the six teachers in his quest for offspring.
Not long thereafter, his wife became pregnant.
When the elder learned of this, he went to the six teachers and said with joy, "My wife is pregnant; will it be a boy?"
"A girl? The six masters replied,
"She will certainly be a girl."
Upon hearing this, the elder felt sorrow and distress in his heart.
Then, a friend came to him and said:
"Why are you so distressed?"
The elder replied, "My wife is pregnant, but I do not yet know whether it will be a boy or a girl; therefore, I asked the six teachers.
The six teachers told me: [as follows]."
"According to the nature of my marks, the one to be born must certainly be a girl.
Having heard these words, I reflected upon my own advanced age and my immeasurable wealth; if it were not a boy, there would be no one to whom I could entrust them. For this reason, I am grieved.
The acquaintance spoke again:
"You lack wisdom. Have you not heard this before?"
"Of whom are the brothers Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his followers disciples?
Of the Buddha,
or of the Six Teachers?"
If the six teachers were all-knowing, why did Kāśyapa abandon them to become a disciple of the Buddha?

Furthermore, were Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, as well as King Bimbisāra and other kings, Queen Mallikā and other royal consorts, and the elder Sudatta and other householders—not disciples of the Buddha?

The yakṣas of the wilderness, King Ajātaśatru, the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla, and Aṅgulimāla—whose malevolent minds were so fiercely ablaze that they sought to harm their own mothers—are these not all those who have been tamed by the Tathāgata?
"Elder! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is named 'Buddha' because his knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena are unimpeded;
he is named 'Tathāgata' because the words he utters are non-dual."
Because he has severed all afflictions, he is called an Arhat.
What the World-Honored One teaches is ultimately without duality; the six masters are not so—how can they be trusted?
The Tathāgata now resides nearby; if you wish to know the truth, you should go to where the Buddha is.

At that time, the elder immediately accompanied this person to where I was; he prostrated with his head at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, joined his palms, knelt down, and spoke these words:
“The World-Honored One is impartial toward all sentient beings without distinction, regarding enemies and kin as one and the same.
Yet, bound as I am by the fetters of attachment, I have not yet been able to treat enemies and kin without partiality.”
I now wish to ask the Tathāgata about worldly matters; I am deeply ashamed and fearful, and have not yet dared to speak.
World-Honored One!
My wife is pregnant, and the six heretical teachers have said:
"Is it certain that what is born must be a girl?
What do you think of this matter?
The Buddha said:
"Householder!
There is no doubt that your wife is pregnant with a son.
Once the child is born, his merit and virtue will be beyond compare."
At that time, having heard these words, the elder was filled with great joy and returned home.
At that moment, the six heretical teachers heard my profound prediction:
"The child to be born will certainly be a boy and shall possess great merit and virtue."
Conceiving jealousy in his heart, he mixed poisonous drugs with mango fruits, took them to the house, and said to the elder:
"How wonderful! Gautama has skillfully described your marks."
"When your wife is near her time of delivery, she may take this medicine.
Once she has taken it, the child will be handsome, and the mother will suffer no harm.
The elder was delighted and accepted the poison, giving it to his wife to take; having taken it, she died immediately.
The six teachers were delighted and, traveling throughout the city, proclaimed in a loud voice:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has predicted that the householder’s wife shall give birth to a son, and that this child’s merit and virtue will be unsurpassed in all the world."
"Even before the child was born, the mother has already lost her life.

At that time, the elder again conceived a lack of faith toward me; he immediately followed worldly custom by enshrouding and capping the body in a coffin, transporting it outside the city, piling up a great quantity of dry wood, and cremating it with fire.
"I clearly perceived this matter with my eye of the Path and, turning to address Ānanda, commanded:
'Bring me my robe; I wish to go there to destroy those wrong views.'"
Then Vaiśravaṇa Deva addressed the Great General Maṇibhadra, saying:
"The Tathāgata now wishes to go to that cemetery; you should go quickly to level and sweep the ground, prepare a lion throne, and seek out exquisite incense and flowers to adorn the site."
At that time, the six teachers saw me approaching from afar and said to one another:
"Does the śramaṇa Gautama wish to eat flesh in this cemetery?"
At that time, many upāsakas who had not yet attained the Dharma-eye, each harboring shame and fear, said to me:
"That woman has already died; we pray that you do not need to go."
At that time, Ānanda said to the people: "Wait but a moment;
before long, the Tathāgata shall extensively expound and reveal the realm of all Buddhas."
"When I had arrived, I sat upon the lion throne.
The elder then spoke with difficulty:
'Your words are non-dual; you may truly be called the World-Honored One.'"
"Since your mother has already passed away, how could you have fathered a son? I said,
"O Householder!"
At that time, you did not inquire at all about the length of your mother’s life, but only asked whether the child she bore would be male or female.
Since the words of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are never inconsistent, you should know that you will certainly obtain a son.
At that time, the corpse was consumed by fire until its belly split open, and from within it emerged a child sitting upright in the midst of the flames, like a ruddy sheldrake upon a lotus pedestal.
Having seen this, the six teachers spoke again:
"How monstrous is Gautama!"
"You are skilled at performing illusions.
Having seen this, the elder was again filled with joy and rebuked the six teachers:
"If you say it is an illusion, why do you not perform one yourself?"
At that time, I immediately told Jīvaka,
"Go into the fire and bring this child here.
Just as Jīvaka was about to go, the six heretical teachers pulled him back and said to him:
"The illusory arts performed by the śramaṇa Gautama are not necessarily always so; sometimes they succeed and sometimes they do not.
If he is unable [to perform them], yet he might still cause harm by burning you, how can you now believe and accept his words?"
Jīva replied:
"If the Tathāgata were to cause me to enter the Avīci Hell, even its fierce fires could not burn me, let alone the fires of the world."
At that time, Jīvaka stepped forward into the mass of fire—as if entering the cool waters of a great river—and taking the child in his arms, returned to where I was and handed the child to me.
Having accepted the child, I said to the elder:
"The lifespan of all sentient beings is uncertain, like bubbles upon the water.
If a sentient being possesses the retribution of heavy karma, fire cannot burn them, nor can poison harm them."
"This is the karmic retribution of this child;
it was not my doing. Then the elder said, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"If this child is permitted to fulfill his natural lifespan, I pray that the Tathāgata will grant him a name.
The Buddha said,
"Householder!"
"This child was born from within a fierce fire; since the fire is named Jyotiṣka, he should be named Jyotiṣka.
At that time, those in the assembly who witnessed my supernatural transformation, immeasurable sentient beings resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"At that time, the six teachers, having failed to find a place to set foot throughout the six cities, came back with shame and bowed heads to this city of Kuśinagara.
Having arrived here, they proclaimed these words:
'All people, you should know:'"
The śramaṇa Gautama is a great master of illusion who deceives and deludes the world throughout the six great cities.
It is like a magician who conjures the fourfold army—namely, the chariot troops, the cavalry, the elephant corps, and the infantry.
Furthermore, just as one might magically create various kinds of necklaces, cities, palaces, houses, rivers, ponds, and trees, so too is the śramaṇa Gautama:

for the sake of preaching the Dharma, he magically manifests the body of a king; or he manifests the bodies of śramaṇas or brahmins, male bodies, female bodies, small bodies, or large bodies; or he manifests the bodies of animals, ghosts, or deities. At times he speaks of impermanence, and at times he speaks of permanence; at times he speaks of suffering, and at times he speaks of pleasure; at times he speaks of a self, and at times he speaks of non-self; at times he speaks of purity, and at times he speaks of impurity; at times he speaks of existence, and at times he speaks of non-existence. Because all that he does is illusory, he is called a "magician."
Just as a fruit is obtained according to its seed, so it is with the Śramaṇa Gautama:
since Māyā gave birth to him, and she was an illusion, can his son not also be an illusion?
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses no true knowledge or vision.

Even though the various brahmins have practiced austerities for years and accumulated merit over many ages, and have maintained their prohibitions and precepts, they still say that they do not yet possess true knowledge and vision.
How much less so for Gautama, who is young, whose learning is shallow, and who has not practiced asceticism—how could he possess true knowledge and vision?
Even if he were to complete seven years of ascetic practice, his insight would still not be great; how much less so when his cultivation falls short of six years?
"Those fools, lacking wisdom, believe and accept his teachings.
Just as a great illusionist deceives and deludes the ignorant, so too is the śramaṇa Gautama.
"Good son! [the Buddha said.]
"In this way, these six teachers greatly increase false views among sentient beings within this city.
'O son of good family!

Seeing this matter, my heart gave rise to compassion. By means of my supernatural power, I invited all the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to assemble in this grove until they filled it completely for forty yojanas; now, here in this place, I let out the Great Lion’s Roar.'"
"Good son!
Although one may speak much in an empty place, it cannot be called a 'lion's roar'; only within this great assembly of wise people can it truly be called a 'great lion's roar'."
The Lion’s Roar proclaims that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; it proclaims only that the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
At that time, the six teachers spoke again as follows:
"If Gautama has a self, we also have a self.
That which is called 'self' is the seer; this is what is named the self."
"Gautama!
It is just as if a person sees an object within a mirror; I am also like this. The mirror is analogous to the eye, and the seer is analogous to the self.
The Buddha said to the six teachers:
"If you claim that the 'seer' is what is called the self, this meaning is not tenable. Why?
Because in the analogy you cited, where the seer is like a person facing a direction, the six sense faculties are all functioning simultaneously."
If there were truly a self that perceives through the eye, why does it not, like those other faculties, simultaneously attend to all objects within a single sense organ?
Since a single organ cannot at once hear and see the six types of sensory objects, one should know that there is no self.
Regarding the analogy of the direction indicated: even after a hundred years have passed, those who see it do not perceive any difference in what is seen because of it.
If the visual faculty were likewise [unchanging], then even when one grows old and the faculties mature, there should likewise be no difference.
Because people are oriented toward different objects, they see either the internal or the external.
If the eye faculty were likewise so disposed, it should also see both the internal and the external simultaneously.
If it does not see [both], how can there be a self?
The six teachers spoke again:
"Gautama! If there is no self, who is it that can see?"
The Buddha said:
"There is form, there is light, there is mind, and there is the eye; because these four are combined, it is called 'seeing. Within this, there is in reality no seer and no experiencer."
Sentient beings are subject to inversion, speaking of a seer and a feeler.
For this reason, all that sentient beings perceive is inverted, whereas what Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceive is the reality.
If the six teachers were to say that form is the self, this too would not be so.
Why? Because form is truly not the self.
If form were the self, one should not be subject to obtaining an ugly physical appearance.
For what reason, moreover, are there distinctions among the four castes?
Are they not all of one kind, namely Brahmins?
For what reason are they subject to others, lacking self-mastery, with impaired faculties, and born incomplete?
For what reason do they not attain the bodies of the devas, but instead undergo the various bodies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts?
If one cannot act according to one's will, it should be known that there is certainly no self.
Because there is no self, it is called impermanent;
because it is impermanent, it is suffering.
Because it is suffering, it is empty;
because it is empty, it is a perversion;
and because of this perversion, all sentient beings revolve in birth and death.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
O Six Teachers!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has forever severed the bonds of form up to the bonds of consciousness; therefore, he is called permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Furthermore, form is itself dependent origination.
That which is dependently originated is called "selfless";
that which is selfless is called "suffering" and "emptiness."
The body of the Tathāgata is not produced by causes and conditions;
because it is not produced by causes and conditions, it is said that there is a self.
If there is a self, then it is eternal, blissful, and pure.
The six teachers spoke again:
"Gautama! Form is not the self, and so on, up to consciousness, which is also not the self."
"The self pervades all places, just like space.
The Buddha said:
"If it were omnipresent, one should not say, 'I have never seen it before';"
If it was not seen at first, then one knows that this seeing was originally non-existent and now exists;
if it was originally non-existent and now exists, it is called impermanent;
if it is impermanent, how can you say it is pervasive?
If they were universally present, then within the five destinies, all should possess bodies;
if they possessed bodies, each should receive their own retribution;
and if each received their own retribution, how could it be said that one "turns to receive" the states of humans and devas?
Regarding your statement that [the self] is pervasive: is it one, or many?
If my self were one, then there would be no distinction between father and son, enemy and friend, or neutral person.
If my faculties were many, then the five faculties of all sentient beings would necessarily be equal.

All their karma and wisdom would likewise be so. If this were the case, why speak of faculties being complete or incomplete, or of the distinctions between wholesome and unwholesome karma, and between the ignorant and the wise?
“Gautama! The ‘self’ of sentient beings has no limit. Dharma and non-Dharma, however, have their boundaries:
if sentient beings practice Dharma, they obtain a good body; if they engage in non-Dharma, they obtain an evil body.”
"For this reason, the karmic fruits of sentient beings cannot be without distinction.
The Buddha said,
"O Six Teachers!
If dharma and non-dharma were such as you describe, then the self would not be omnipresent.
If the self were omnipresent, it should reach all things.
If it reached all things, then those who cultivate goodness would also possess evil, and those who practice evil would also possess goodness.
"If it were not so, how could you say it is 'pervasive'? "Gautama!
It is like a single room where a hundred thousand lamps are lit; each shines by itself, without obstructing one another."
"It is the same with the self of sentient beings: the cultivation of goodness and the performance of evil do not intermingle.
"If you say that the self is like a lamp, this meaning is not so."
Why is this? The light of that lamp exists dependent upon conditions.
Because the lamp increases, the light also increases;
The self of sentient beings is not like this.
Light emerges from a lamp and dwells in a different location;
the self of sentient beings cannot emerge from the body and dwell in a different location in such a manner.
That light of the lamp coexists with darkness. Why is this?
For instance, when a single lamp is lit in a dark room, the illumination is not clear; it is only when many lamps are present that clarity is attained.
"If the first lamp dispels the darkness, then a subsequent lamp is unnecessary;
if a subsequent lamp is required, one should know that the initial light coexisted with the darkness.
"Gautama! [the opponent said.]
"If there is no self, who performs good and evil?
The Buddha said,
"If the self were the agent, how could it be called permanent?"
If it were permanent, how could it sometimes perform good and sometimes perform evil?
If one says that it sometimes performs good and evil, how can one further say that the self is infinite?
If the self were the agent, for what reason would one still practice unwholesome dharmas?
If the self were the agent and the knower, why would one give rise to doubt that sentient beings lack a self?
For this reason, within the teachings of the non-Buddhists, there is certainly no self.
If one speaks of a "self," it is none other than the Tathāgata. Why is this so?
Because the body is boundless and because one is free from the net of doubt;
because there is no creating and no receiving, it is called "permanent";
because there is no arising and no ceasing, it is called "bliss."
Because it is free from the defilements of affliction, it is called "pure";
because it is devoid of the ten marks, it is called "empty.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, pure, empty, and without any marks.
The various non-Buddhists said:
"If you say that the Tathāgata is empty because he is permanent, blissful, self, pure, and signless, then one should know that the Dharma taught by Gautama is not empty."
"Therefore, I shall now receive and uphold this upon the crown of my head.
At that time, immeasurable numbers of non-Buddhists developed faith in the Buddha's Dharma and left the household life to become monks.
“Good son! For these reasons, I let out the great lion’s roar here between the twin śāla trees.
This ‘lion’s roar’ is named Great Nirvāṇa.”
“Good son! Those who are ‘paired’ in the east destroy impermanence and attain permanence; and so on, up to those who are ‘paired’ in the north, who destroy impurity and attain purity.”
"Good son!
Here, sentient beings protect the śāla grove for the sake of the twin trees, not allowing outsiders to take its branches and leaves, or to cut them down or destroy them."
I am also like this; for the sake of four dharmas, I cause my disciples to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
What are these four?
They are permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

"These four pairs of trees are presided over by the Four Great Kings; as I am the king of these four kings who protect and uphold my Dharma, it is for this reason that I enter parinirvāṇa therein. Good son!"
The twin śāla trees are always lush with flowers and fruit, and they constantly benefit immeasurable sentient beings;
I am likewise, for I constantly benefit śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The flower is a metaphor for the self;
the fruit is a metaphor for bliss.
For this reason, I have entered the great samādhi of tranquility here between these twin śāla trees.
"Great tranquil concentration is called Great Nirvana.
Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason does the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa in the second month? "Good son!
The second month is called spring."

In the month of spring and summer’s warmth, all things grow and flourish; roots and seedlings are planted, flowers and fruits bloom in splendor, rivers and streams overflow, and the myriad beasts conceive and give birth.

At this time, sentient beings frequently give rise to the notion of permanence. To shatter such a mind of permanence in sentient beings, [the Buddha] teaches that all phenomena are entirely impermanent, while declaring only the Tathāgata to be eternally abiding and unchanging.
“Good son! Among the six seasons, the early winter is withered and parched, and the multitude finds no joy in it;
the springtime is harmonious and moist, and all people cherish and love it.”
In order to shatter the worldly pleasures of sentient beings, he expounds upon permanence and bliss;
the same applies to self and purity. Thus, in order to shatter the worldly self and worldly purity, the Tathāgata speaks of the Tathāgata’s true self and true purity.
The mention of the second month is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s two kinds of *dharmakāya*.
"Not delighting in winter" means that the wise do not delight in the Tathāgata’s impermanence or his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
"Delighting in the second month" is a metaphor for the wise who cherish and delight in the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The planting [of seeds] is a metaphor for sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma, rejoice and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thereby planting various roots of goodness;
the river is a metaphor for the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions coming to my presence to inquire about and receive this *Mahāparinirvāṇa* scripture;
and the beasts of a hundred species giving birth and nursing their young is a metaphor for my disciples generating various roots of goodness.
The flowers symbolize the seven factors of enlightenment;
the fruit symbolizes the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
For this reason, I shall enter great parinirvāṇa in the second month.
Siṃhanāda said:

"The Tathāgata’s initial birth, his renunciation and attainment of enlightenment, and his turning of the wondrous Wheel of Dharma all occurred on the eighth day; for what reason was the Parinirvāṇa alone on the fifteenth day?"
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
Just as on the fifteenth day the moon has neither wane nor waxed, so too it is with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas: upon entering Great Parinirvāṇa, they have neither wane nor waxed.
For this reason, they enter parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day.
“Good son! Just as there are eleven phenomena when the moon is at its fullness on the fifteenth day,
what are these eleven?

First, it can dispel darkness; second, it enables sentient beings to distinguish the path from what is not the path; third, it enables sentient beings to discern the heterodox from the orthodox regarding the path; fourth, it removes oppressive heat to attain the joy of coolness; fifth, it can destroy the haughty minds of fireflies; sixth, it quells all thoughts of robbery and theft; seventh, it removes the fear of wild beasts from sentient beings; eighth, it can cause the *utpala* lotuses to bloom; ninth, it causes the lotuses to close; tenth, it inspires the traveler’s resolve to press onward on the road; eleventh, it causes all sentient beings to delight in experiencing the five desires and obtain much happiness.
Good son! The full moon of the Tathāgata is likewise: first, it destroys the great darkness of ignorance;

second, it expounds the right path and the deviant paths; third, it reveals the perilous deviations of birth and death and the level rectitude of nirvāṇa; fourth, it causes people to distance themselves from the fevers of greed, hatred, and delusion; fifth, it shatters the radiance of external paths; sixth, it destroys the thieves of the fetters of affliction; seventh, it eliminates the mind that fears the five hindrances; eighth, it causes the minds of sentient beings to blossom as they plant roots of goodness; ninth, it covers over the minds of sentient beings’ five desires; tenth, it inspires sentient beings to initiate and cultivate practices directed toward Great Nirvāṇa; and eleventh, it causes all sentient beings to delight in cultivating liberation.
For this reason, although on the fifteenth day I enter great parinirvāṇa, in truth I do not enter nirvāṇa.
Among my disciples, foolish and wicked people will certainly say that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa.
For example, suppose a woman has many sons, and that mother departs for another land; while she has not yet returned, each of her sons says, "My mother is dead."
"Yet this woman did not actually die.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
“What kind of bhikṣu can adorn these twin śāla trees? “Good son!

If there is a bhikṣu who upholds and recites the twelve divisions of the sūtras, rectifies their phrasing and sentences, masters their profound meanings, and explains them for others as being excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; and if, desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, he expounds the holy life (brahmacarya)—such a bhikṣu can adorn the twin śāla trees.”
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, it is the bhikṣu Ānanda who is that very person.”
Why is this? The bhikṣu Ānanda upholds, recites, and studies the twelve divisions of the sūtras, expounding for others the correct words and correct meanings.
It is just like pouring water from one vessel into another.
The bhikṣu Ānanda was also like this; what he heard from the Buddha, he proclaimed exactly as he had heard it. "Good son!

If there is a bhikṣu who has attained the pure divine eye, seeing all that exists within the trichiliocosm of the ten directions as clearly as looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand—such a bhikṣu is also able to adorn the twin śāla trees."
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is thus, the bhikṣu Aniruddha is that very person.”
Why is this? Because Āniruddha, with his divine eye, clearly perceives everything within the trichiliocosm, even including the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), without any obstruction.

“Good son! If there is a bhikṣu who has few desires and is content, whose mind delights in tranquility, who practices with diligent vigor, and who possesses mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—such a bhikṣu is able to adorn the twin śāla trees.”
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then the bhikṣu Kāśyapa is that very person.”
"Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa has skillfully cultivated such dharmas as having few desires and being content. "Good son!"

If there is a bhikṣu—who, for the benefit of sentient beings and not for the sake of gain or sustenance, cultivates and masters the Samādhi of Non-contention, the Noble Practices, and the Practice of Emptiness—such a bhikṣu can adorn the twin śāla trees.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then the bhikṣu Subhūti is precisely that person.”
"Why is this? Because Subhūti has skillfully cultivated the practice of non-contention, the noble conduct, and the practice of emptiness. "Good son!"

If there is a bhikṣu who has skillfully cultivated supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such that within a single thought-moment he can perform various miraculous transformations, and with a single mind he can certainly produce two effects—namely, water and fire—a bhikṣu such as this is able to adorn the twin śāla trees.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana is that very person.”
"Why is this? Because Maudgalyāyana has skillfully cultivated supernormal powers and performs immeasurable transformations. "Good son!"

If there is a bhikṣu who skillfully cultivates great wisdom, sharp wisdom, adorned wisdom, liberating wisdom, profound wisdom, vast wisdom, boundless wisdom, unsurpassed wisdom, and true wisdom, and who fully accomplishes such faculties of wisdom, his mind remains without distinction toward enemies or kin.
If one hears that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa or is impermanent, the mind feels no sorrow or distress;
if one hears that he is eternally abiding and does not enter nirvāṇa, one does not give rise to joy or celebration.
"In this way, a bhikṣu can adorn the twin śāla trees.
Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
If it is thus, the bhikṣu Śāriputra is precisely that person.
Why is this? Because Śāriputra is well able to accomplish and fully possess such great wisdom as this.

“Good son! If there is a bhikṣu who can say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, who has attained a vajra-body without limit, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; whose body and mind are unobstructed, and who has attained the eight masteries—such a bhikṣu is able to adorn the twin śāla trees.”
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is so, then only the Tathāgata is such a person.”

Why is this? Because the body of the Tathāgata is adamantine and boundless, characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; his body and mind are unimpeded, as he is endowed with the eight masteries.
World-Honored One!
Only the Tathāgata is able to adorn these twin śāla trees;
were he not present, they would not be dignified and beautiful.
"I only pray that, for the sake of adornment, you will dwell forever here in this Śāla grove.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
The nature of all dharmas abides in non-abiding; why do you say, "I pray that the Tathāgata abide"?
Son of good family!
That which is called "abiding" is termed a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*).
Because it arises from causes and conditions, it is called "abiding";
because there is no place for causes and conditions, it is called "non-abiding.
Since the Tathāgata has already severed all bonds of form, how could one say that the Tathāgata abides?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. "Good son!
To 'abide' is called arrogance."
Because of pride, one does not attain liberation;
because one does not attain liberation, it is called "abiding.
Who possesses such pride?
From where does it come?
For this reason, it is called "abiding in non-abiding.
Since the Tathāgata has forever severed all pride and conceit, why do you say, "May the Tathāgata abide"?
To "abide" refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The Tathāgata has already severed all conditioned phenomena; therefore, he does not abide.

To "abide" also refers to the dharma of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the Tathāgata has already severed such dharmas of emptiness, and for this reason, he has attained the eternal, the blissful, the self, and the pure.
Why do you say, "I pray that the Tathāgata remain"?
To "remain" is a name for the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
The Tathāgata has already severed these twenty-five states of existence; why then do you say, "I pray that the Tathāgata remain"?
Those who abide are all ordinary worldlings;
the various sages have no going, no coming, and no abiding.
Since the Tathāgata has already severed the marks of going, coming, and abiding, how can one say that he abides?
“Now, that which is ‘non-abiding’ is called the ‘boundless body. Since the body is boundless, how can you say, ‘I only pray that the Tathāgata will abide in the Śāla grove’?
If he were to abide in this grove, he would possess a bounded body; and if there is a boundary, then it is impermanent.”
The Tathāgata is eternal; why, then, do you say he dwells?
That which has no dwelling is called empty space.
The nature of the Tathāgata is identical to empty space; why, then, do you say he dwells?
"Furthermore, 'non-abiding' is called the Vajra-samādhi.
The Vajra-samādhi destroys all abidings; the Vajra-samādhi is itself the Tathāgata."
How can you say that he dwells?
Furthermore, that which has no dwelling is called an illusion.
The Tathāgata is identical to an illusion; how then can it be said that he dwells?
"Furthermore, 'non-abiding' means having neither beginning nor end.
Since the nature of the Tathāgata has no beginning or end, how can it be said to abide?
Furthermore, 'non-abiding' refers to the boundless Dharma-realm."
The boundless Dharma-realm is itself the Tathāgata; how, then, can one speak of "dwelling"?
Furthermore, that which is non-dwelling is called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi knows all dharmas yet remains without attachment.
Because it is free from attachment, it is called Śūraṅgama.
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; how then can one say that he "dwells" in it?
Furthermore, that which is non-dwelling is called the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible.
The Tathāgata has accomplished the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; why, then, do you say he "dwells"?
Furthermore, that which is non-dwelling is called the *dānapāramitā*.
If the *dānapāramitā* were to have a dwelling, one would not be able to reach the *śīlapāramitā*, and so on, up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For this reason, the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is called "non-abiding.
Since the Tathāgata does not even abide in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), how can you wish to say that the Tathāgata dwells eternally in the śāla grove?
"Furthermore, 'non-abiding' refers to the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
If the Tathāgata were to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, he would not be able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called 'abiding in non-abiding.'"
"Furthermore, 'non-abiding' refers to the boundless realm of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata reaches all sentient beings throughout the boundless divisions of that realm, yet remains nowhere abiding."
"Furthermore, 'non-abiding' is called 'having no dwelling.
Having no dwelling is called 'non-existence';
non-existence is called 'non-arising'."
That which is non-arising is called deathlessness;
that which is deathless is called signlessness;
that which is signless is called non-attachment.
That which is unconditioned is called non-attachment;
that which is non-attached is called outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The outflow-free is goodness; goodness is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the unconditioned is the permanence of Great Nirvāṇa.
That which is eternal in the Great Nirvāṇa is the Self; that which is the Self is purity; that which is purity is bliss; and that which is eternal, blissful, the Self, and pure is the Tathāgata.
“Good son! For example, just as space does not abide in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below;
so too is the Tathāgata—he does not abide in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below.”
“Good son! If anyone were to say that evil actions of body, speech, and mind can result in wholesome fruits, such a thing is impossible;
likewise, it is also impossible for wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind to result in unwholesome fruits.”
If one were to say that ordinary beings can see the Buddha-nature while Bodhisattvas of the ten stages cannot, this is likewise impossible.

That those of the icchantika class—who have committed the five heinous crimes, slandered the Vaipulya sutras, and violated the four grave prohibitions—should attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is also impossible.
It is impossible for a Bodhisattva dwelling in the sixth stage to fall into the three evil realms due to the causes and conditions of afflictions.
It is also impossible for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while in the body of a real woman.
"It is impossible that an icchantika is eternal while the Three Jewels are impermanent;
it is likewise impossible for the Tathāgata to dwell in the city of Kuśinagara. Good son!"
"The Tathāgata has now entered the cave of profound meditative concentration through the great samādhi in this city of Kuśinagara; because the multitude does not see him, it is called 'Great Nirvāṇa.
Siṃhanāda asked, "For what reason does the Tathāgata enter the cave of meditative concentration?"

“Good son! It is for the sake of delivering and liberating all sentient beings; to cause those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them; to cause those who have already planted roots of goodness to increase them; to cause those whose good fruits are not yet matured to reach maturity; to lead those whose fruits are already matured toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; to cause those who despise the wholesome Dharma to give rise to reverence for it; to cause those who are negligent to abandon negligence; to engage in discourse with Mañjuśrī and other great fragrant elephants; to teach and transform those who delight in recitation so that they come to deeply love meditative concentration; to transform sentient beings through the noble conduct, the Brahma-conduct, and the celestial conduct; to contemplate the profound and unique treasury of the Dharma; and to rebuke disciples who are negligent.”
The Tathāgata is eternally tranquil and still delights in meditative concentration; how much more so should you, whose afflictions are not yet exhausted, refrain from giving rise to negligence?

It is for the purpose of censuring those evil bhikṣus who accept and store the eight kinds of impure things and who lack fewness of desires and contentment; and it is to cause sentient beings to respect the Dharma of meditative concentration they have heard. For these reasons, he enters the cave of meditative concentration.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
The concentration of signlessness is called Great Nirvāṇa; therefore, Nirvāṇa is named signless.”
"For what reason is it called 'signless' (animitta)?
"Good son, because it is devoid of the ten signs."
What are the ten?

They are the mark of form, the mark of sound, the marks of odor, taste, and touch, the marks of arising, abiding, and decaying, the mark of male, and the mark of female; these are called the ten marks.
Because it lacks such characteristics, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).

Good son! Those who cling to signs give rise to delusion; because of delusion, craving arises; because of craving, they are bound; because of being bound, they undergo birth; because of birth, there is death; and because of death, there is impermanence.

One who does not cling to signs does not give rise to delusion; because delusion does not arise, there is no craving; because there is no craving, there is no bondage; because there is no bondage, one does not undergo rebirth; because one does not undergo rebirth, there is no death; and because there is no death, it is called "eternal."
"For this reason, Nirvana is called eternal. Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
"What kind of bhikṣu is able to sever the ten marks?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If a bhikṣu practices three types of signs from time to time, he will sever ten signs:

practicing the sign of samādhi-concentration from time to time, practicing the sign of wisdom from time to time, and practicing the sign of equanimity from time to time; these are called the three signs.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by the concentration of the characteristics of concentration, wisdom, and equanimity?”
Regarding this samādhi, all sentient beings possess it; why then do you speak of "cultivating" samādhi?
If the mind is focused on a single object, it is called samādhi; if it pursues other conditions, it is not called samādhi.
If it were not fixed, it would not be omniscience;
if it were not omniscience, how could it be called fixed?
If one attains samādhi through a single practice, then the other practices would likewise not be samādhi.
If it were not samādhi, it would not be omniscience;
if it were not omniscience, how could it be called samādhi?
The same applies to the two characteristics of wisdom (prajñā) and equanimity (upekṣā).
The Buddha said:
"Good son, it is as you have said:
"To be designated as samādhi, one must focus on a single object; other objects of focus are not called samādhi.
This interpretation is incorrect. Why is this so?
In this way, other conditions are likewise focused on a single object;
the mental formations are also thus.
Furthermore, the claim that sentient beings possess samādhi from the outset and need not cultivate it is also incorrect.
Why is this so? That which is called samādhi is named "excellent samādhi.
Since it does not yet truly exist within any sentient being, how can one say that there is no need to cultivate it?
To contemplate all phenomena while abiding in such a wholesome samādhi is called the mark of excellent wisdom (*suvijñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
Not perceiving any distinct characteristics between samādhi and wisdom is called the mark of equanimity (*upekṣā-lakṣaṇa*).
"Furthermore, good son!
If one grasps at the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) and is unable to contemplate the characteristics of form as either permanent or impermanent, this is called samādhi;
if one is able to contemplate the characteristics of form as either permanent or impermanent, this is called the characteristic of wisdom (*prajñā*)."
To contemplate all phenomena with equanimity through samādhi, wisdom, and so forth—this is called the mark of relinquishment (*upekṣā*).
"Good son! It is like a skilled charioteer driving a team of four horses, who brings speed and slowness to their proper measure."
Because it attains the proper balance between slowness and speed, it is called the mark of equanimity (upekṣā).
It is the same for the bodhisattva: if samādhi is excessive, they cultivate wisdom;
if wisdom is excessive, they cultivate samādhi.
The equality of samādhi and wisdom is called equanimity (upekṣā). "Good son!
A bodhisattva of the ten stages possesses great power of wisdom but little power of samādhi; for this reason, they cannot clearly see the Buddha-nature."
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess great power in samādhi but little power in wisdom; for this reason, they do not perceive the Buddha-nature.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, because their concentration and wisdom are equal, clearly perceive the Buddha-nature with complete and unimpeded clarity, as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of their hand.
One who perceives the Buddha-nature is said to have "abandoned signs.
*Śamatha* is called "the power of cessation," because it can extinguish all afflictions and fetters.
Furthermore, *śamatha* is called "the power of taming," because it can tame the wickedness and unwholesomeness of the sense faculties.
Furthermore, śamatha is called "quiescence," for it can cause the three karmas to become quiescent.
Furthermore, śamatha is called "separation," for it can cause sentient beings to leave behind the five desires.
Furthermore, śamatha is called "that which can purify," because it can purify the three turbid dharmas of greed, anger, and delusion.
For this reason, it is termed the characteristic of concentration.
“Vipaśyanā is called right view; it is also called clear seeing, capable seeing, universal seeing, sequential seeing, and seeing of specific characteristics. This is what is meant by wisdom.”
“Upeksā is called equanimity; it is also called non-contention, and again called non-contemplation, and also called non-exertion—this is termed relinquishment.”
“Good son! There are two kinds of śamatha:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.”
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, accomplishment; second, non-accomplishment.
Accomplishment refers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;"
Those who do not achieve [this] are the so-called śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
"Furthermore, there are three kinds:
namely, inferior, middling, and superior."
The inferior refers to all ordinary worldlings;
the middling refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the superior refers to all buddhas and bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds:
first, regression; second, abiding; third, progress; and fourth, the ability to bring great benefit.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:"
These are the five wisdom-samādhis. What are the five? First, the samādhi of non-nourishment;

second, the samādhi of non-transgression; third, the samādhi of the purity of body and mind with single-mindedness; fourth, the samādhi of the mutual joy of cause and effect; and fifth, the samādhi of constant mindfulness.
"Furthermore, there are six kinds: first, the samādhi of contemplating bones;

second, the samādhi of loving-kindness; third, the samādhi of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination; fourth, the samādhi of ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing); fifth, the samādhi of mindfulness of vitarka and vicāra; and sixth, the samādhi of contemplating arising and ceasing."
Furthermore, there are seven kinds, namely the seven factors of enlightenment:

first, the factor of mindfulness; second, the factor of investigation of phenomena; third, the factor of energy; fourth, the factor of joy; fifth, the factor of tranquility; sixth, the factor of concentration; and seventh, the factor of equanimity.
“Furthermore, there are seven kinds: first, the samādhi of the srotāpanna;

second, the samādhi of the sakṛdāgāmin; third, the samādhi of the anāgāmin; fourth, the samādhi of the arhat; fifth, the samādhi of the pratyekabuddha; sixth, the samādhi of the bodhisattva; and seventh, the samādhi of the Tathāgata’s awakening and realization.”

Furthermore, there are eight kinds, namely the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa) of samādhi: first, the liberation-samādhi of perceiving external forms while possessing the perception of internal forms;

second, the liberation-samādhi of perceiving external forms while lacking the perception of internal forms; third, the liberation-samādhi of personally realizing the pure liberation; fourth, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the liberation-samādhi of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and eighth, the liberation-samādhi of the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
"Furthermore, there are nine kinds, namely the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*):
the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the samādhi of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, there are ten kinds, namely the ten spheres of totality (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*) samādhis."

What are the ten? First, the samādhi of the all-pervasive earth; second, the samādhi of the all-pervasive water; third, the samādhi of the all-pervasive wind; fourth, the samādhi of the all-pervasive blue; fifth, the samādhi of the all-pervasive yellow; sixth, the samādhi of the all-pervasive red; seventh, the samādhi of the all-pervasive white; eighth, the samādhi of the all-pervasive space; ninth, the samādhi of the all-pervasive consciousness; and tenth, the samādhi of the all-pervasive non-existence.
“Furthermore, there are innumerable kinds, namely those of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Good son, these are called the characteristics of samādhi.”
“Good son! Wisdom is of two kinds:
first, worldly; second, supramundane.”
"Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, *prajñā*; second, *vipaśyanā*; and third, *jñāna*.
*Prajñā* refers to all sentient beings;..."
Vipaśyanā refers to all noble ones;
jñāna refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, prajñā is termed "distinctive characteristic."
Vipaśyanā is termed the "comprehensive characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa);
jñāna is termed the "analytical characteristic" (bhedaka-lakṣaṇa).
Furthermore, there are four kinds, namely, the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.
“Good son! One cultivates śamatha for three reasons.
What are these three?
First, because of non-negligence; second, because of adorning great wisdom; third, because of attaining mastery.
"Furthermore, one cultivates vipaśyanā for three reasons."
What are these three?
First, to contemplate the evil retributions of birth and death; second, to desire to increase all roots of goodness; third, to destroy all afflictions.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 28. [Scroll 29] of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huiyan and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In the fifth chapter of the "Lion’s Roar Bodhisattva," the Lion’s Roar said:
"World-Honored One!..."
“As it is said in the sutras: ‘If vipaśyanā can destroy the afflictions, why then further cultivate śamatha?
The Buddha said: ‘Good son!’”
As for your statement that vipaśyanā destroys the afflictions, this meaning is not so. Why?
Because when wisdom exists, there are no afflictions; and when afflictions exist, there is no wisdom.
How can it be said that vipaśyanā can destroy the afflictions?
Good son! It is like this:
when there is light, there is no darkness; when there is darkness, there is no light.
If anyone were to say that light can destroy darkness, such a thing is impossible.
Good son! Who possesses wisdom?
Who possesses afflictions?
To say that wisdom can destroy afflictions implies there are such things; if they did not exist, there would be nothing to destroy. "Good son!
If it is said that wisdom can destroy the afflictions, does it destroy them by reaching them or by not reaching them?
If it destroys them without reaching them,
then ordinary worldlings should also be able to destroy them.
If it breaks upon reaching [the object], it should break at the first moment of contact.
If it does not break at the first moment, it will not break later either;
if it breaks as soon as it arrives, then it has not actually reached [the object].
How can it be said that wisdom is able to destroy [the afflictions]?
If one claims that it can destroy them whether it reaches them or not, this meaning is untenable.
Furthermore, regarding the destruction of afflictions by vipaśyanā: does it destroy them alone?
Is it broken because of companions?
If it could be broken by one alone, why would a bodhisattva cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path?
If it is broken because of companions, one should know that it cannot be broken when alone.
If one person alone cannot do it, neither can their companions.
Just as a single blind person cannot see forms, even if accompanied by a multitude of blind people, they still cannot see;
so too it is with vipassanā.

“Good son! Just as the earth has the nature of solidity, fire the nature of heat, water the nature of moisture, and wind the nature of motion—yet these natures, from the solidity of earth to the motion of wind, are not produced by causes and conditions; their nature is simply so of itself.”
Just as the nature of the four great elements is such, so too are the afflictions;
their nature is inherently severed. If they are already severed, why say that wisdom can sever them?
For this reason, vipaśyanā is certainly unable to destroy the various afflictions.
“Good son! Just as the nature of salt is salty and makes other things salty,
and the original nature of honey is sweet and makes other things sweet;”
If it is argued that because the nature of water is moisture, it causes other things to become moist,
and because the nature of wisdom is cessation, it causes other phenomena to cease— this meaning is not tenable. Why is this so?
If a phenomenon is inherently without cessation, how can wisdom forcibly cause it to cease?
If one were to argue that just as salt’s pungency causes other things to become pungent, so too does wisdom cause other phenomena to cease, this is also not the case.
Why is this? Because the nature of wisdom perishes from moment to moment.
If it perishes from moment to moment, how can one say that it is able to extinguish other dharmas?
For this reason, the nature of wisdom does not destroy afflictions.
"Good son! All dharmas have two kinds of cessation: [the cessation of afflictions and the cessation of dharmas]."
First is cessation by nature, and second is ultimate cessation.
If it were cessation by nature, how could one say that wisdom is able to bring about cessation?
If one says that wisdom can extinguish afflictions just as fire burns objects, this meaning is not correct.
Why is this? For example, when fire burns an object, there remains some residue;
if wisdom were like that, there should likewise be a residue remaining.
Just as when an axe fells a tree, the place where it has been cut can be seen;
if wisdom were like that, what would there be to see?

If wisdom could cause the afflictions (*kleśa*) to depart, those afflictions should appear elsewhere, just as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), having left the six great cities, appeared in the city of Kuśinagara.
If afflictions do not manifest elsewhere, one knows that wisdom cannot cause them to be separated from.
"Good son! If the nature of all dharmas is itself empty, who could cause them to arise?"
Who can cause it to cease?
Arising is different and ceasing is different; there is no creator. Good son!
If one cultivates meditative concentration, one will attain such right knowledge and right view.
For this reason, I have said in my sūtras:
"If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates meditative concentration, he is able to see the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."
"Good son! If one does not cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one cannot even comprehend worldly matters, let alone those that transcend the world.

One who lacks concentration will stumble and fall on level ground; their mind will attend to different phenomena, their mouth will utter different words, their ears will hear different sounds, and their mind will understand different meanings. They may wish to compose different characters but their hand writes different texts; they may wish to take a different path but their body traverses a different track."
If there are those who cultivate the samādhi of meditative concentration, they will obtain great benefit, even unto Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are endowed with two dharmas are able to bring great benefit:
first, concentration; second, wisdom. Good son!
Just as when cutting *kuśa* grass, it snaps if pulled too forcefully;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing these two dharmas. Good son!
Just as when pulling out a firmly rooted tree, one first shakes it with the hand and then it is easily extracted;
so too are the meditative concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva: first they move [the mind] through concentration, and subsequently they extract [it from afflictions] through wisdom.
Good son! Just as when washing a soiled garment, one first uses lye and afterwards uses clear water, so that the garment becomes bright and clean;
the concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva are likewise.
"Good son!
Just as one first recites and then later understands the meaning,
so too are the meditative concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva."
"Good son!
It is like a brave man who first firmly adorns himself with armor and weapons, and only then leads the battle to defeat the enemy;
the meditative concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva are likewise."
"Good son!
It is like a skilled artisan who, using tongs and a crucible, holds gold and freely stirs, melts, and refines it as he pleases;
the samādhi and wisdom of a bodhisattva are likewise so."
Good son! Just as a clear mirror reflects the image of a face,
so too are the concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Good son! It is like first leveling the ground and then sowing the seeds;
first receiving instruction from a teacher, and later contemplating its meaning.
The meditative concentration and wisdom of a bodhisattva are also like this.
For this reason, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates these two dharmas, they are able to bring about great benefit. "Good son!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate these two dharmas, they discipline and restrain the five faculties and endure various sufferings—namely, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, being struck or beaten, verbal abuse, being bitten by wild beasts, and being stung by mosquitoes and gadflies. They constantly restrain their minds, not allowing them to become lax; they do not practice unrighteousness for the sake of gain or offerings; they cannot be defiled by adventitious afflictions; they are not deluded by various false and heterodox views; and they are always able to remain far removed from all evil thoughts and discursive reflections. Before long, they shall achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because they desire to achieve it for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.

“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates these two dharmas, the violent winds of the four inversions cannot shake them; they are like Mount Sumeru, which, though buffeted by the four winds, cannot be moved.
They cannot be uprooted by external paths or false teachers, being like the banner of Śakra, which cannot be shifted.”

They cannot be deceived by various heterodox and deviant arts; they constantly experience the subtle, wondrous, and supreme peace and happiness; they are able to understand the profound and secret meanings of the Tathāgata; they do not rejoice in encountering pleasure nor grieve when meeting suffering; they are revered and praised by all devas and worldlings; they clearly perceive birth-and-death as well as that which is beyond birth-and-death; they are well able to comprehend the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); and their bodies possess the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is what is called the bliss of Great Nirvāṇa.
"Good son! The characteristic of concentration is called the samādhi of emptiness;
the characteristic of wisdom is called the samādhi of wishlessness."
The characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*) is called the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*). Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who well knows the time for concentration, the time for wisdom, and the time for equanimity, as well as knowing what is not the [proper] time, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the path to enlightenment.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva know the proper time and the improper time?”

“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to great arrogance because of experiencing pleasure, or gives rise to arrogance because of preaching the Dharma, or gives rise to arrogance because of diligent effort, or gives rise to arrogance when explaining meanings or engaging in skillful question-and-answer sessions, or gives rise to arrogance because of associating with evil associates, or gives rise to arrogance because of giving away highly valued objects, or gives rise to arrogance because of the merit of worldly wholesome dharmas, or gives rise to arrogance because of being honored by people of worldly wealth and nobility—one should know that at such times it is inappropriate to cultivate wisdom; rather, one should cultivate meditative concentration. This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the timely and the untimely.”

"If there are bodhisattvas who diligently practice with vigor, yet have not attained benefit or the bliss of nirvana, they may give rise to a mind of regret because they have not attained it; because their faculties are dull;
because they are unable to subdue the five sensory organs as the power of various defilements and afflictions is so strong;
and because they harbor doubts regarding the precepts due to their own weakness and decline."

One should know that at such a time it is not appropriate to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*), but rather one should cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*). This is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the timely and the untimely. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva’s two dharmas of concentration and wisdom are unequal, one should know that at such a time it is not appropriate to cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*)."
If these two dharmas are equal, one should cultivate them; this is called a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the timely and the untimely. "Good son!

If a bodhisattva who is practicing concentration and wisdom gives rise to afflictions, you should know that at such a time it is not appropriate to cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*). Instead, one should read, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the sūtras, and practice mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṃgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of heaven, and mindfulness of renunciation; this is what is called cultivating equanimity."
“Good son! If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate these three marks of phenomena, by this causal condition they shall attain the markless nirvana.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
Because it is devoid of the ten marks, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.

As for that which is markless, by what further conditions is it named ‘unborn,’ ‘unproduced,’ ‘uncreated,’ ‘abode,’ ‘island,’ ‘refuge,’ ‘peace,’ ‘extinction,’ ‘nirvāṇa,’ ‘quiescence,’ ‘free from all illness and suffering,’ and ‘non-existence’?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Because they lack causes and conditions, they are called 'unborn'."
Because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called "without emergence";
because there is no creation of karma, it is called "without action";
because it does not enter into the five views, it is called a "dwelling."
Because one is separated from the four torrents, it is called an island;
because it tames sentient beings, it is called a refuge;
and because it destroys the thieves of the fetters, it is called peace and security.
Because the fires of all fetters are extinguished, it is called "extinction" (nirvāṇa);
because it is free from applied and sustained thought, it is called "nirvāṇa";
because it is far removed from clamor and bustle, it is called "tranquility."
Because one has eternally severed the certainty of death, it is called "freedom from illness";
because all things are non-existent, it is called "non-possession. Good son!
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, they immediately attain clear and penetrating vision of the buddha-nature.
Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
“By accomplishing how many dharmas can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva see such signless nirvāṇa up to the state of non-existence?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they will be able to clearly perceive Nirvāṇa, from its signlessness up to its non-existence. What are these ten?
First, the full possession of faith.
What is meant by being fully endowed with faith?

It is to have deep faith that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are eternal; that all sentient beings and even icchantikas possess buddha-nature as manifested through the skillful means of the Buddhas of the ten directions; and not to believe in the birth, old age, sickness, or death of the Tathāgata, nor his practice of asceticism, nor that Devadatta truly caused a schism in the Sangha, shed the blood of the Buddha, or that the Tathāgata will ultimately enter parinirvāṇa or that the True Dharma will be extinguished. This is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with faith.
"Second, the perfection of pure precepts.
What is meant by the perfection of pure precepts? Good son! "

If there is a bodhisattva who claims his own precepts are pure, yet although he does not engage in physical union with that woman, he mocks her, speaks jestingly, or laughs with her upon seeing her—such a bodhisattva has fulfilled the conditions for desire, has violated the pure precepts, has defiled the holy life, and has made his conduct impure; he cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.

Furthermore, there is a bodhisattva who claims his precepts are pure; although he does not physically unite with that woman, nor engage in flirtation or jesting with her, he hears from behind a wall the various sounds of the woman’s necklaces, bracelets, and bangles, and his mind gives rise to attachment. Such a bodhisattva has accomplished the dharma of desire, has violated the pure precepts, has brought disgrace upon the holy life (brahmacarya), and has made his precepts defiled; he cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.

Furthermore, there is a bodhisattva who claims his precepts are pure; although he does not engage in physical union with women, nor converse with them in jest, nor listen to their voices, yet when he sees a man pursuing a woman, or a woman pursuing a man, he immediately gives rise to lustful attachment. Such a bodhisattva has accomplished the dharma of desire, violated the pure precepts, defiled the holy life, and rendered his discipline impure; he cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who claim their precepts are pure; yet, although they do not engage in physical union with women, nor engage in flirtatious conversation, nor listen to their voices, nor see men and women following one another, they nevertheless act for the sake of being born in heaven to enjoy the five sensual pleasures. Such bodhisattvas have accomplished the dharma of desire, thereby violating the pure precepts, defiling the holy life, and making the precepts impure; they cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.
"Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who maintains pure precepts, yet does so not for the sake of the precepts themselves, nor for the sake of the śīla-pāramitā, nor for the sake of sentient beings, nor for the sake of gain and offerings, nor for the sake of bodhi, nor for the sake of nirvāṇa, nor for the sake of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but solely for the sake of the supreme ultimate truth—good son!"
This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of pure ethical discipline.
"Third, one should draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

A spiritual friend is one who can teach others to receive and practice faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom; such a person is called a Bodhisattva’s spiritual friend."
"Fourth, delighting in tranquility.
As for tranquility, it refers to the tranquility of body and mind while observing the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); this is called tranquility."
"Fifth is diligence.
As for diligence, it means binding the mind to contemplate the Four Noble Truths; even if one's head were on fire, one would never relinquish this effort—this is called diligence."
"Sixth is the perfection of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃpad*).

As for the perfection of mindfulness, it refers to mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of the devas, and mindfulness of renunciation; this is called the perfection of mindfulness."
"Seventh is gentle speech.
Gentle speech refers to truthful speech, exquisite speech, greeting others with a kind intention first, timely speech, and sincere speech; this is called gentle speech."
"Eighth is the protection of the Dharma.

To protect the Dharma means to cherish and delight in the true Dharma, constantly delighting in its exposition, recitation, transcription, contemplation of its meaning, and its widespread dissemination, so that it may circulate far and wide."

If one sees someone who copies, explains, recites, praises, or contemplates the meaning [of this teaching], one should provide them with the necessities of life as an offering—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.
To protect the Dharma, one does not begrudge even body or life;
this is called "protecting the Dharma.

Ninth, when a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a fellow student or fellow precept-holder who is in want, he begs from others on their behalf to provide them with bowls for seasoning, dyed robes, necessities for tending the sick, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and dwellings.
"Tenth is the fulfillment of wisdom. Wisdom refers to contemplating that the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, and pure;

that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; and contemplating the two aspects of phenomena, namely: emptiness and non-emptiness; permanence and impermanence; bliss and non-bliss; self and non-self; purity and impurity; that some phenomena can be severed while others cannot; that some phenomena arise from conditions while others are manifested by conditions; and that some phenomena are the fruit of conditions while others are not the fruit of conditions. This is called the fulfillment of wisdom."
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva who, by being endowed with these ten dharmas, is able to clearly perceive the signlessness of nirvāṇa.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously told Cunda:
‘You have now already seen the Buddha-nature, attained Great Nirvana, and accomplished Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.’”
"What is the meaning of this?
'World-Honored One!
As it is said in the Sūtras:'"
If one gives to an animal, one receives a hundredfold reward;
if one gives to an icchantika, one receives a thousandfold reward;
if one gives to a precept-keeper, one receives a hundred-thousandfold reward.
If one gives to non-Buddhists who have severed their afflictions, they will obtain immeasurable retribution;
if one gives to those on the four paths and the four fruits up to the Pratyekabuddhas, they will obtain immeasurable retribution;

and if one gives to non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, to great Bodhisattvas in their final existence, or to the Tathāgata World-Honored One, the resulting merit and retribution will be immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable.
If the Mahāsattva Cunda were to receive such immeasurable retribution, that retribution would be inexhaustible; when, then, would he attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“World-Honored One!

In the sutras it is further stated that if a person performs wholesome or unwholesome karma with a sincere mind, they will certainly receive the retribution, whether receiving it in the present life, in the next birth, or in a subsequent life.”
Because Cunda performed these wholesome deeds with a profound and earnest mind, you should know that this karma will certainly result in its retribution.
If it must necessarily be experienced as retribution, how can he attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"How, then, can one further perceive the Buddha-nature?
'World-Honored One!
In the sutras it is further taught that giving to three kinds of people yields inexhaustible retribution:'"
First, the sick person; second, one's parents; third, the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If all sentient beings were to have no karma pertaining to the desire realm, they would immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
the same applies to karma pertaining to the form and formless realms."
"World-Honored One!
As it says in the Dhammapada verse:
'Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering the clefts of mountains, is there any place on earth where one can escape the retribution of one's karma.'"
Furthermore, Aniruddha said:
"World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, by giving a single meal as an offering, for eighty thousand kalpas I did not fall into the three evil realms."
"World-Honored One!
If even the gift of a single meal can yield such a reward, how much more so for Cunda’s offering of faith to the Buddha, which fully accomplishes the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?"
“World-Honored One!

If virtuous karmic retributions cannot be exhausted, how can those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, commit the five heinous crimes, violate the four grave prohibitions, or the offenses of icchantikas ever be exhausted?”
"If it cannot be exhausted, how can one perceive the Buddha-nature and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent."
"Good son!

Only two kinds of people can attain immeasurable and boundless merit—merit that is incalculable and inexpressible; they can dry up the torrential river of drifting birth and death, subdue demonic enemies, topple the banners of Māra’s victory, and turn the unsurpassed Dharma-wheel of the Tathāgata:
first, those who ask well; second, those who answer well."
“Good son! Among the ten powers of a Buddha, the power of karma is the most profound. Good son!”
There are sentient beings who, regarding the principle of karmic conditions, have little faith and are dismissive; for the sake of delivering them, I speak thus:
"Good son, all actions performed are either light or heavy."
Furthermore, light and heavy karma each have two types:
first, determinate; second, indeterminate. Good son!
Some may say: "Evil karma has no fruit.
If one says that evil karma certainly has fruit, how is it that by merely blowing upon a Caṇḍāla, one could be reborn in heaven?"
"Did Aṅgulimāla attain the fruit of liberation?
For this reason, one should know that there are actions whose fruits are definitely obtained and those whose fruits are not definitely obtained.
It was for the purpose of severing such wrong views that I spoke these words in the sūtra:
"Every action performed does not fail to yield its fruit. Good son!
