There are heavy karmas that can be made light, and there are light karmas that can be made heavy; this applies not to all people, but only to the foolish and the wise. Therefore, you should know that it is not the case that every karma invariably yields its fruit; yet, while it is not invariably obtained, it is also not the case that it is not obtained at all.
“Good son! All sentient beings are of two kinds:
first, the wise; second, the foolish.”

A person of wisdom, through the power of their insight, can cause the most heavy karma of the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life; a foolish person, however, must experience even light karma of the present life as heavy suffering in the hells.
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
If this were so, then one should not seek pure brahmacarya or the fruit of liberation.”
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If all karma were certain to yield its fruit, then one should not seek the holy life or liberation."
Because they are indeterminate, one practices the holy life and attains the fruit of liberation.
Good son! If one can distance oneself from all evil karma, one will obtain good fruits; if one distances oneself from wholesome karma, one will obtain evil fruits.
If all karma were necessarily to yield its fruit, then one should not seek to cultivate the Noble Path;
yet if the Path is not cultivated, there is no liberation.
It is for this reason that all noble ones cultivate the Path: to destroy determinate karma so as to obtain light retribution, and because indeterminate karma yields no fruit.
If all karma were to necessarily yield its fruit, then one should not seek to cultivate the Noble Path.
It is impossible for a person to attain liberation by being devoid of the cultivation of the Noble Path;
likewise, it is impossible to attain Nirvana without attaining liberation.

“Good son! If all karma were necessarily to yield its fruit, then the purely wholesome karma performed in a single lifetime should result in one being eternally free from it and constantly experiencing peace and happiness;
likewise, the extremely heavy evil karma performed in a single lifetime should also result in one being eternally free from it and undergoing great suffering and affliction.”
If the fruit of karma were such as you describe, then there would be no cultivation of the path, no liberation, and no nirvana.

What one person creates, that same person would receive; what a Brahmin creates, that same Brahmin would receive. If this were so, then there would be no lower castes or lower status; humans would be eternally human, and Brahmins would be eternally Brahmins.
If an action is performed in childhood, its retribution should be experienced in childhood; it should not be experienced in middle age or old age.

If one commits evil in old age and is reborn in hell, the body of that initial birth in hell should not experience the retribution immediately; rather, it should wait until old age before experiencing it.
Conversely, if one does not kill in old age, one should not obtain longevity in middle age.
If there were no youthful life, how could one reach old age?
For karma is never lost.
If karma is never lost, how can there be the cultivation of the path and nirvana?
“Good son! There are two kinds of karma:
determinate and indeterminate.”
Fixed karma is of two kinds:
first, fixed as to retribution; second, fixed as to time.

There are cases where the retribution is fixed but the time is not; one experiences it when conditions converge, or one may experience it during three periods—namely, in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives.

“Good son! If one performs wholesome or unwholesome karma with a concentrated mind, and after having performed it, gives rise to deep faith and joy, and if one makes a vow to make offerings to the Triple Gem, this is called determinate karma.”
“Good son! The roots of goodness of the wise are firm and deep, and thus difficult to shake; for this reason, they can cause heavy karma to become light.
The foolish person’s unwholesomeness is profound and deep, and thus can cause light karma to result in a heavy retribution.”
For this reason, all karmic actions are not termed "fixed.
Although Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess no karma for the hells, they give rise to great vows to be born within the hells for the sake of sentient beings.
“Good son! In the past, when the lifespan of sentient beings was one hundred years, as many beings as the sands of the Ganges received retribution in the hells.
Having seen this, I immediately made a great vow to take on a body in the hells.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva truly had no such karma; yet for the sake of sentient beings, he underwent the retribution of hell.
While I was in hell at that time, passing through immeasurable years, I extensively expounded and analyzed the twelve divisions of the sutras for all the offenders.
When all people hear this, they will destroy the retribution of evil karma and cause the hells to become empty, with the sole exception of those who hold the icchantika view.
This is called a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva not experiencing the retribution of such evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.
"Furthermore, good son!
Within this Bhadrakalpa, immeasurable sentient beings fall into the animal realm to undergo the fruits of their evil karma.
Having seen this, I again made a vow:

"Desiring to preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, he may manifest the bodies of a roe deer, a stag, a bear, a pigeon, a monkey, a dragon, a snake, a garuḍa, a fish, a turtle, a fox, a rabbit, an ox, or a horse."

"Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva truly has no such evil karma of an animal; rather, by the power of great vows for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests the reception of this body. This is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva not receiving this evil karma in the present, future, or subsequent lives."
"Furthermore, good son!

Within this Bhadrakalpa, there are again immeasurable and boundless sentient beings born among the hungry ghosts (preta), who consume vomit, spittle, fat, flesh, pus, blood, excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva. Their lifespans last for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of years; they have never even heard the name of water, let alone having seen it with their own eyes and being able to drink it."
If they see water from afar and go toward it with the intention of reaching it, upon arrival it transforms into fierce fire, pus, or blood;
or if it does not transform, many people appear holding spears and lances to block, seize, and restrain them, preventing them from proceeding;
or if the heavens send down rain, it turns into fire when it reaches their bodies.
This is called the retribution for evil karma. Good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva truly has no such retributions for evil karma; rather, in order to transform sentient beings and lead them to liberation, they make a vow and take on such a body. This is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.

“Good son! During this Bhadrakalpa, I was born into a family of butchers and slaughterers; I raised chickens, pigs, oxen, and sheep; I practiced hunting with bows and nets and fishing; and I lived in the houses of caṇḍālas, committing robbery and theft.”

In truth, the bodhisattva possesses no such evil karma; rather, for the sake of liberating sentient beings, he assumes such a body through the power of his great vows. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.

“Good son! Within this Bhadrakalpa, you will again be born in a border region where you will frequently give rise to greed, anger, and delusion; you will practice what is contrary to the Dharma, lack faith in the Triple Gem and the retribution of future lives, and fail to show reverence toward your parents, elders, the aged, and those of senior standing.”
"Good son!

At that time, the bodhisattva truly has no such karma; rather, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, he takes birth therein through the power of his great vows. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not experience this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives."

“Good son! Within this Bhadrakalpa, you shall again receive a female body, an evil body, a body of greed, a body of hatred, a body of delusion, a body of envy, a body of stinginess, a youthful body, a deceitful body, and a body shrouded by the hindrances and coverings.”
"Good son!

At that time, the bodhisattva likewise possesses no such karma; rather, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, he vows by the power of his great aspiration to be born therein. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present, future, or subsequent lives."
“Good son! During this Bhadrakalpa, I have received the bodies of a eunuch, one without sexual organs, one with two sexual organs, and one with indeterminate organs. Good son!”

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas truly do not possess such evil bodily karma; rather, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation, they vow by the power of their great vows to be born therein. This is called the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva not experiencing this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.

“Good son! During this Bhadrakalpa, I further practiced the teachings of the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas. I believed and accepted their doctrine that there is no giving, no sacrifice, and no retribution for giving or sacrificing; there are no good or evil deeds, nor any retribution for good or evil deeds; there is no present world nor a future world; there is neither ‘this’ nor ‘that’; there are no noble ones and no transformation bodies; and there is no Path or Nirvana.”
"Good son!

A bodhisattva truly possesses no such evil karma; rather, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to liberation, he accepts these false teachings through the power of his great vows. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva not undergoing this evil karma in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives."
“Good son! I recall that in the past, Devadatta and I were both caravan leaders, each with five hundred merchants. For the sake of profit, we went out to the great ocean to gather precious jewels.”
Due to the conditions of their evil karma, they encountered a violent storm on the road that shattered their ship, and all their companions perished.
At that time, because of the long-life karmic fruit of not having killed [living beings] with Devadatta, we were both blown by the wind and reached dry land together.
At that time, Devadatta, out of greed and attachment for his treasures, was overcome with great sorrow and suffering, and cried out aloud.
I then said to him: "Devadatta!..."
"There is no need to weep.
Devadatta then said to me:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively! It is as if there were a person, impoverished and suffering, who went to a cemetery, grasped a corpse with his hand, and spoke these words:"
“May you now grant me the joy of death, and I shall grant you the life of poverty.
At that moment, the corpse immediately sat up and spoke to the poor man, saying: “Good son!
"You shall experience poverty and a short lifespan yourself; I am now deeply delighted by such a death, for I truly do not rejoice at your being born into poverty.
Yet today, since I lack both the joy of death and am further beset by poverty, how could I help but weep?
I further consoled him, saying:
"Do not grieve for now; I have two jewels here worth countless riches, and I shall divide one of them to bestow upon you."
I then divided it and gave it to him, speaking further:
"Only one who possesses life can obtain this treasure.
If one lacks life, who could possibly obtain it?"
"At that time, being weary and exhausted, I went beneath a tree to rest and fell asleep.
Devadatta’s greedy mind was ablaze; for the sake of one remaining jewel, he conceived an evil intent, gouged out my eyes, and plundered my jewels."
At that time, I was suffering from a sore and let out a groan.
A woman then came to where I was and asked me:
"Virtuous one, for what reason are you groaning like this?"
I then explained my past life to her in detail.
Having heard this, the woman asked me again:
"What is your name?"
I immediately replied,
"It is called 'Truthful Speech.
The woman said:
"How do you know that you speak the truth?
I then made this vow:
"If I harbor any ill will toward Devadatta at this moment, may my eyes become thus, forever blind."
"If they are absent, you shall regain your eyes.
Having spoken these words, his eyes were restored to their former state.
"O son of good family!"
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s teaching on retribution in the present life.
"Good son, I recall that in the past,
I was born into a brāhmaṇa family in the city of Pūṇḍravardhana in South India."
At that time, there was a king named Karapu, whose nature was violent and cruel, arrogant and conceited; though young and of beautiful appearance, he was deeply attached to the five desires.
At that time, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, I was practicing silent meditation outside his city.

At that time, when the spring trees were in full bloom, the king, together with his retinue, palace ladies, and court beauties, went out of the city to sightsee; beneath the trees, he amused himself with the five sensory pleasures.
Those court ladies abandoned their royal amusements and came to where I was.
At that time, wishing to sever their craving, I preached the Dharma for them.
Just then, the king arrived; upon seeing me, he immediately conceived an evil intent and questioned me, saying:
"Have you now attained the fruit of arhatship? I replied, "I have not."
He asked again:
"Have you attained the fruit of non-returning? I replied:
"No," he replied, and further said:
"If you have not yet attained these two fruits, then you are fully possessed of desire and afflictions."
"How can you look upon me, a woman, with such unrestrained freedom? I then replied:
"Great King, you should know:
"Although I have not yet severed the fetter of desire, my inner mind is truly free from attachment.
The king said, "Fool!"
In this world, there are various sages who practice the ingestion of vital energy and subsist on fruits; yet they still feel greed when they see beautiful forms.
How much more so for you, who are in the prime of youth and have not yet severed your greedy desires—how could you possibly remain unattached upon seeing such forms?
I said: "Great King!
Seeing forms and not becoming attached to them does not depend on inhaling vital energy or eating fruit; it arises entirely from fixing the mind upon impermanence and impurity."
The King said:
"If one treats others with contempt and gives rise to slander, how can they be said to practice the pure precepts? I replied:
"Great King!
If one possesses a jealous mind, then there is slander.
I have no jealous mind; why then do you say that I am slandering?"
The King said:
"Venerable Sir!
What is meant by 'precept'?"
"Great King!
Patience is called precept.
The King said:
"If patience constitutes your precept, I shall cut off your ears;
if you can endure it, I shall know that you uphold the precepts.
He then cut off his ears.
At that time, although my limbs were severed, my countenance did not change.
When the king and his ministers witnessed this event, they immediately admonished the king, saying:
"A Great Being such as this should not be subjected to harm."
The king asked his ministers,
"How do you know that he is a great being (mahāsattva)?
The ministers replied:
"Seeing that his countenance did not change even while experiencing suffering," the king spoke again, saying:
"I shall test him further to know whether he changes or remains unchanged."
He immediately had his nose cut off and his hands and feet amputated.
At that time, the Bodhisattva had already cultivated loving-kindness and compassion throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, out of pity for suffering sentient beings.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings harbored anger and resentment, raining down sand, gravel, and stones.
Upon seeing this, the king was struck with great fear; he came before me, knelt for a long time, and said:
"I only pray that you will have compassion for me and accept my repentance."
I said: "Great King!
My mind is free from anger, just as it is free from greed."
The King said:
"Venerable Sir!
How can it be known that the mind is free from anger and resentment?"
I immediately made this vow:
"If it is true that I am free from anger and resentment, may this body of mine be restored to its former state.
Having uttered this aspiration, my body was instantly restored.
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s teaching on retribution in the present life. Good son!
It is the same for wholesome karma regarding retribution in the next life and retribution in subsequent lives, as well as for unwholesome karma."
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all karmas receive their retribution in the present life.
Regarding unwholesome and evil karma that receives retribution in the present life, it is like a king who commits an evil act and the heavens send down a rain of calamity.
It is also like a person who points out the location of a bear or a jewel-colored deer to a hunter, and their hand falls off.
This is called the retribution for evil karma experienced in the present life.
As for retribution experienced in the next life, it refers to those such as icchantikas, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, and those who have committed the five heinous crimes.
Regarding retribution in a future life, it is as when a person who upholds the precepts makes a profound vow:

"May I always obtain such a body of pure precepts in future ages; and when there are sentient beings with a lifespan of one hundred years or eighty years, may I become a Wheel-Turning Sage King therein to transform and guide them."
“Good son! If karma were fixed to yield retribution only in the present life, then it could not yield retribution in the next life or in subsequent lives.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the karma for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, that karma cannot yield retribution in the present life.”
If karma does not receive these three kinds of retribution, it is called "indeterminate. Good son,
if one were to say that all karmas definitely receive their retribution, then there could be no cultivation of the holy life, nor liberation, nor nirvana.
You should know that such a person is not my disciple, but a follower of Māra.
If one says that all karmas are both determinate and indeterminate—where determinate refers to retribution in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives;
and indeterminate refers to receiving the fruit when conditions converge, and not receiving it when they do not—[then such a person is not my disciple].
For this reason, there must be the holy life, liberation, and nirvana.
You should know that such a person is truly my disciple and not a follower of Māra.
“Good son! All sentient beings have more indeterminate karma and less determinate karma.
For this reason, there is the cultivation of the Path.”
By cultivating the Path, determinate heavy karma can be made to be experienced lightly, while indeterminate karma is not to be experienced as retribution in this very life.
"Good son! There are two kinds of persons:

First, that which is indeterminate is made determinate; that which is to be experienced in the present life is made to be experienced in the next life; light retribution is made heavy retribution; and what should have been experienced among humans is instead experienced in hell. Second, that which is determinate is made indeterminate; that which should be experienced in the next life is turned into being experienced in the present life; heavy retribution is made light; and what should have been experienced in hell is instead experienced as a light retribution among humans.
Thus, between these two persons—one foolish and the other wise—the wise person’s offense is lightened, while the foolish person’s is made heavy.
"Good son! It is like two people who have committed an offense against a king: he whose kinsmen are many has his offense lightened; [the one with few kinsmen has his offense made heavy]."
Regarding those with few kinsmen, what should have been light becomes heavy.
It is the same for the foolish and the wise: because the wise possess much wholesome karma, they experience what is heavy as light;
because the foolish possess little wholesome karma, they experience what is light as heavy.
“Good son! It is like two men, one stout and strong, the other emaciated and weak; both sink into deep mud, yet the stout one is able to emerge while the weak one sinks.
"Good son! It is like two people who both consume poison; one possesses the power of mantras and *agada* medicine, while the other does not.
The one who has the mantras and medicine cannot be harmed by the poison."
One who lacks mantras and medicine will die immediately upon taking it. "Good son!
It is like two people who have both drunk much liquid; one has a powerful digestive heat, while the other’s is weak."
When the digestive fire is strong, it can properly digest; when the digestive fire is weak, it becomes a source of affliction.
"Good son! It is like two men who have been imprisoned by a king: one possesses wisdom, while the other is foolish."
Those who possess wisdom are able to attain liberation, whereas for the foolish and ignorant, there is no time of release. "Good son!
It is like two people traveling together on a perilous path: one has eyes, while the other is blind."
One who possesses eyes passes straight through without harm;
the blind fall, falling into deep pits and precipices. "Good son!
It is like two people who both drink wine: one drinks much, while the other drinks little.
For the one who drinks much, drinking brings no affliction;
for the one who drinks little, drinking becomes an affliction.
“Good son! It is like two men who both face an enemy army: one is fully equipped and adorned with armor and weapons, while the other has only his own body.
The one who possesses weapons is able to defeat the enemy;”
As for one's own person, it cannot exert itself on its own.
Furthermore, there were two people whose clothes were defiled by filth; one, upon waking, immediately washed them, while the other, upon waking, did not wash them.
Those who wash their clothes will have them clean and pure;
those who do not wash them will see their filth and impurities increase day by day.
Furthermore, there were two people traveling together in a carriage: one had spokes and an axle, while the other was without spokes or an axle.
Those with spokes and an axle may go wherever they wish, while those without spokes and an axle cannot move from their place.
"Furthermore, there were two people traveling together on a desolate road; one was provided with provisions, while the other went empty-handed."
Those who possess provisions can cross the perilous pass, whereas those who go empty-handed cannot pass through.
"Furthermore, there were two men who were robbed by bandits; one had a treasure store, while the other had no store."
One who possesses a treasury has no sorrow or distress in their heart;
one who lacks a treasury suffers from grief and affliction.
It is the same for the foolish and the wise: those who possess the treasury of goodness experience heavy karma as light.
"One who does not store up merit will experience heavy retribution for light karma.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught:
"Not all karma necessarily yields a fixed result, nor do all sentient beings necessarily undergo its retribution.
World-Honored One!

"How is it that some sentient beings cause light retribution from the hells to be experienced heavily in the present life, while heavy retribution from the hells is experienced lightly in the present life?
The Buddha said,
"All sentient beings are of two kinds:"
First is the wise, and second is the foolish.
One who is able to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom is called wise;
one who is unable to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom is called foolish.
"What is meant by not cultivating the body?
If one cannot restrain the five sensory faculties, it is called not cultivating the body;
if one cannot receive and uphold the seven kinds of pure precepts, it is called not cultivating morality."
Because the mind is not disciplined, it is called "not cultivating the mind";
because one does not cultivate noble conduct, it is called "not cultivating wisdom.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body cannot fulfill the essence of pure precepts.
Those who do not cultivate ethical discipline accept and store the eight kinds of impure things;
those who do not cultivate the mind are unable to practice the three marks;
and those who do not cultivate wisdom do not cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

"Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to contemplate the body, unable to contemplate form or the characteristics of form, and fails to contemplate the characteristics of the body. They do not know the enumeration of the body, nor do they know that this body moves from here to there. They give rise to the notion of 'body' within what is not the body, and produce the notion of 'form' within what is not form; therefore, they are greedily attached to the self-body and the enumeration of the body—this is called not cultivating the body."
Regarding those who do not cultivate precepts: if one receives inferior precepts, it is not called cultivating precepts.

To observe partial precepts, to maintain precepts for one's own benefit, or to maintain precepts for one's own self-discipline—failing to universally bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, failing to protect and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma, and instead seeking birth in the heavens to experience the pleasures of the five desires—is not called cultivating precepts.
One who does not cultivate the mind, if their mind is distracted, will be unable to focus single-mindedly on its own domain.
One's own domain refers to the four foundations of mindfulness;
another's domain refers to the five sensual desires.
If one cannot cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, it is called not cultivating the mind.
If one does not skillfully guard the mind amidst evil deeds, it is called not cultivating wisdom.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to deeply contemplate that this body is impermanent, non-abiding, fragile, perishing moment by moment, and is the realm of Māra.
One who does not cultivate ethical discipline cannot fulfill the śīla-pāramitā;
one who does not cultivate the mind cannot fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā;
one who does not cultivate wisdom cannot fulfill the prajñā-pāramitā.
"Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is greedily attached to the self-body and the body belonging to the self, [thinking] 'the self-body is permanent, constant, and unchanging.
One who does not cultivate precepts commits the ten unwholesome karmas for the sake of their own body.
One who does not cultivate the mind is unable to restrain the mind amidst unwholesome karma."
One who does not cultivate wisdom fails to collect the mind and is thus unable to discern dharmas such as good and evil.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body does not sever the view of self;
one who does not cultivate morality does not sever the clinging to precepts and rituals.
One who does not cultivate the mind performs actions of greed and anger and heads toward hell;
one who does not cultivate wisdom does not sever the mind of delusion.
Furthermore, one who does not cultivate the body is unable to contemplate the body; though it is without fault, it is always an enemy.
Good son! It is like a man who has an enemy constantly pursuing him, watching for an opportunity to strike.
Once the wise man has become aware of this, he focuses his mind and guards himself with care; if he does not guard himself with care, he will be harmed by that enemy.

The bodies of all sentient beings are likewise; they must be sustained by food, drink, cold, and warmth. If they are not thus protected, guarded, and cherished, they will immediately disintegrate and perish.

“Good son! It is like a brahmin who serves the deity Agni, constantly offering incense, flowers, praise, prostrations, and offerings for a full hundred years; yet if he should touch it even once, it immediately burns his hand.”
Although this fire receives such offerings, it never has even a single thought of repaying the kindness of those who serve it.

The bodies of all sentient beings are likewise: though they have been supplied for many years with fine incense, flowers, necklaces, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal treatments for illness and weakness, if they encounter internal or external adverse conditions, they immediately perish and utterly fail to remember the kindness of the food and clothing provided in the past.
“Good son! It is like a king who keeps four venomous snakes, places them in a single basket, and entrusts them to a man, commanding him to look after and nourish them:
‘If even one of these four snakes should give rise to anger, it will be able to harm you.’”
"This person, being terrified, constantly seeks food and drink and guards them at all times.
It is the same with the four great poisonous snakes of the four elements of all sentient beings; if even one of them becomes enraged, it can destroy the body."
“Good son! It is like a person who has been ill for a long time; they should seek medical treatment with a sincere heart.
If they do not diligently seek rescue, they will surely die without a doubt.”
"The bodies of all sentient beings are also like this; one should always restrain the mind and not allow it to become negligent. If one is negligent, the body will immediately perish and decay.
Good son!..."
For example, just as a broken jar cannot endure wind, rain, being struck, or being crushed, so too is the body of all sentient beings;
it cannot endure hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, rain, being beaten or bound, or harsh abuse.
“Good son! Just as one must always carefully protect an unripened boil so that no one touches it— for if someone were to touch it, there would be great pain—
so too is the body of all sentient beings.”
“Good son! Just as a mule that conceives brings ruin upon its own body, so it is with the bodies of all sentient beings:
when there is wind or cold within, the body immediately experiences suffering.”
“Good son! For example, when a plantain tree bears fruit, it withers;
the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise.”
“Good son! It is just as with the plantain tree, which has no solid core within;
the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise.”
“Good son! Just as snakes,
rats, and wolves each harbor a constant sense of enmity toward one another,
so it is with the four great elements of sentient beings.”
“Good son! Just as the king of geese takes no pleasure in cemeteries,
so too the bodhisattva does not crave or delight in the cemetery that is the body.”
“Good son! Just as a *caṇḍāla* who has practiced his trade for seven generations without ceasing is therefore despised by others, so too is the seed of this body:
its seeds of semen and blood are ultimately impure.
Because it is impure, this body is censured and reviled by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. "Good son!

This body is not like Mount Malaya, which produces sandalwood; nor can it produce blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), *campaka* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, or *vārṣika* flowers. Its nine orifices constantly flow with pus, blood, and impurities; its place of birth is foul and filthy, its appearance is ugly and loathsome, and it always dwells together with various worms."
Good son!
For example, although there may be excellent, pure gardens in the world, once a corpse enters them, they become impure; everyone abandons them and no longer conceives any attachment.
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is likewise; although it is pure and subtle, because it involves a physical body, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas collectively renounce it.
Good son, if one is unable to engage in such contemplation, this is called not cultivating the body.

“O son of good family, one who does not cultivate the precepts fails to perceive that the precepts are a ladder for all wholesome dharmas and the root of all wholesome dharmas— just as the earth is the foundation from which all trees grow;
they are the vanguard of all roots of goodness, like a caravan leader leading a multitude of merchants.”
Precepts are the supreme banner of all wholesome dharmas, like the victory banner erected by Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Precepts can forever sever all evil karma and the three evil realms; they can cure evil maladies just like a medicinal tree.

Precepts are the provisions for traversing the perilous path of birth and death; precepts are the armor and weapons for crushing the fetters and destroying the marauders; precepts are the efficacious incantation for extinguishing the venomous snakes of the fetters; precepts are the bridge for crossing over the course of evil karma.
If there are those who cannot contemplate in this manner, they are said not to cultivate the precepts.
Those who do not cultivate the mind are unable to observe that the mind is flighty, restless, difficult to grasp, and difficult to tame.
It gallops and runs away like a great, rogue elephant;
it changes with every thought as swiftly as a flash of lightning;
it is restless and cannot abide, just like a monkey.
Like a phantom and like a mirage, these are the root of all evils; the five desires are difficult to satisfy.
They are like fire obtaining fuel, like the great ocean swallowing all flowing streams, and like Mount Mandara, where grasses and trees grow in great abundance.
Unable to discern that birth and death are illusory, they become addicted to delusion and bring about affliction, like a fish swallowing a hook.
They are always led first by their various karmas which follow them, just as a mother-of-pearl shell leads its young.
Clinging greedily to the five desires and taking no pleasure in Nirvana, they are like camels eating honey; even unto death, they do not heed the straw.
Deeply attached to present pleasures, they do not contemplate future calamities; they are like oxen coveting the sprouts, having no fear of the whip.
They gallop and roam throughout the twenty-five states of existence, like a swift wind blowing through cotton wool.
They seek what should not be sought with insatiable craving, like an ignorant person seeking a fire that does not exist.
They constantly delight in birth and death and do not delight in liberation, like the *śṛṅgāra* insect which delights in the *śṛṅgāra* tree.
They are deluded and attached to the foul stench of birth and death, just as a prisoner delights in the daughter of a jailer, or as a pig in a latrine delights in impurity.
If there are those who cannot contemplate in this way, they are said to be "not cultivating the mind.
Those who do not cultivate wisdom fail to see that wisdom possesses great power, like the golden-winged garuḍa;
it can destroy evil karma and dispel the darkness of ignorance, just as the light of the sun.
It can uproot the tree of the aggregates as water sweeps away objects;
it incinerates false views like a fierce fire.
Wisdom is the root of all wholesome dharmas and the seed of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If there are those who cannot contemplate in this manner, they are not said to be cultivating wisdom. "Good son!

Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), if one perceives the body, the characteristics of the body, the causes of the body, the fruits of the body, the accumulation of the body, the oneness of the body, the duality of the body, this body, that body, the extinction of the body, the equality of the body, the cultivation of the body, or the cultivator—if there are such perceptions, it is called not cultivating the body."

“Good son! If one perceives precepts, the characteristics of precepts, the causes of precepts, the fruits of precepts, superior precepts, inferior precepts, the accumulation of precepts, the unity of precepts, the duality of precepts, these precepts, those precepts, the cessation of precepts, the equality of precepts, the cultivation of precepts, the cultivator, or the perfection of precepts—if there is such a perception, it is called not cultivating precepts.”

"If one perceives the mind, the characteristics of the mind, the causes of the mind, the fruits of the mind, the accumulation of the mind, the mind and its mental factors, the unity of the mind, the duality of the mind, this mind, that mind, the cessation of the mind, the equality of the mind, the cultivation of the mind, the cultivator, superior, middling, or inferior minds, or wholesome and unwholesome minds—if there is such a perception, it is called not cultivating the mind."

“Good son! If one perceives wisdom, the characteristics of wisdom, the causes of wisdom, the fruits of wisdom, the accumulation of wisdom, the oneness of wisdom, the duality of wisdom, this wisdom, that wisdom, the cessation of wisdom, the equality of wisdom, superior, middling, or inferior wisdom, dull wisdom, sharp wisdom, the cultivation of wisdom, or the cultivator—if there is such a perception, it is called not cultivating wisdom.”
“Good son! If there are those who do not cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, such persons will receive a great evil retribution for even a minor evil karma.”
Out of fear, they constantly harbor this thought:
"I belong to hell; I perform the deeds of hell.
Even when they hear the wise describe the sufferings of hell, they always think thus:
"Just as iron strikes iron, stone strikes stone, wood strikes wood, and fireflies delight in fire, so too does the body of a hell-being resemble that of hell itself."
"If it resembles hell, what kind of suffering does it entail?
For example, just as a fly stuck in saliva cannot escape, so too is this person:

unable to extricate themselves from even a minor offense, their mind feels no initial remorse, they fail to cultivate goodness, and they conceal their flaws. Although they possess all manner of past wholesome karma, it is entirely defiled by these transgressions. Consequently, the light retribution they were originally destined to undergo in the present life is transformed into the extremely heavy evil fruit of hell.
“Good son! It is like placing one *śoṇa* of salt into a small vessel of water; its taste is salty and bitter, making it difficult to drink.
The sinful karma of this person is also like this.”
Good son! It is like a person who owes another a single coin; because he cannot repay it, his body is bound and he undergoes manifold sufferings.
The karmic offenses of this person are likewise thus.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does this person cause their present light retribution to transform into suffering experienced in hell?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! If all sentient beings possess five things, they will cause their present light retribution to be transformed into suffering experienced in hell.”
What are these five? First, because of ignorance;

second, because their roots of goodness are meager; third, because their evil karma is deep and heavy; fourth, because they do not repent; and fifth, because they do not cultivate their original wholesome karma.

Furthermore, there are five things: first, the cultivation of unwholesome karma; second, the lack of the wealth of precepts; third, being far removed from all roots of goodness; fourth, failing to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; and fifth, associating with evil associates.
“Good son! For this reason, it can cause what would be a light retribution in the present life to become a heavy suffering in hell.
Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of person is able to transform the retribution of the hells so that it is experienced as a slight affliction in the present life? “Good son!

If there are those who cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom as previously described, and are able to contemplate all phenomena as being identical to space—neither seeing wisdom nor the wise, neither seeing delusion nor the deluded, and neither seeing cultivation nor the one who cultivates—they are called "wise ones."
Such a person is able to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; this person can cause the retribution of hell to be experienced lightly in the present life.
Even if such a person commits extremely grave evil karma, through reflection and observation, they can render it slight, thinking to themselves:
"Though my karma is heavy, it is not equal to wholesome karma."
It is like cotton flowers: though they may weigh a hundred catties, they can never match a single *liang* of pure gold.
It is like throwing one *sheng* of salt into the Ganges River; the water has no salty taste, and those who drink it do not perceive it.
Just as a person of great wealth, though heavily indebted to many others, cannot be bound by their millions of treasures nor made to suffer;
or like a great fragrant elephant, which can break its iron chains and depart at will.
The person of wisdom is also like this, constantly reflecting:
"My power of goodness is great, while my evil karma is weak.
I am able to reveal and repent of my faults to eliminate evil, and I am able to cultivate wisdom."
"The power of wisdom is great, while the power of ignorance is slight.
Having reflected thus, he draws near to virtuous friends, cultivates right view, and receives, upholds, recites, transcribes, and explains the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

Upon seeing those who uphold, recite, transcribe, or explain [this teaching], one should give rise to a heart of reverence and provide them with offerings of clothing, food, dwellings, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, flowers, and incense, while praising and honoring them.
Wherever he went, he spoke of their virtues and did not speak of their faults.

He made offerings to the Triple Gem and reverently believed in the Vaipulya *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, [holding that] the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging, and that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Such a person can cause heavy retributions in the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life. "Good son!
For this reason, it is not the case that all karma has a fixed fruit, nor is it the case that all sentient beings must necessarily undergo [retribution]."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 29.

In the sixth chapter, "The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda," the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
"World-Honored One!..."

If all karma does not necessarily yield its fruit, if all sentient beings possess buddha-nature, and if one ought to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, for what reason do all sentient beings fail to attain this Great Parinirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, they would certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; why then is it necessary to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path?
“World-Honored One!

As it is said in this sutra, if a sick person obtains medicine and a caregiver who provides food and drink according to their illness—or even if they do not obtain these—they are all completely cured.”

All sentient beings are likewise in this regard: whether they encounter śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, buddhas, bodhisattvas, or various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and whether they hear the Dharma being taught and cultivate the noble path, or do not encounter them, do not hear the teaching, and do not cultivate the path, they shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For what reason?
Because of the buddha-nature,
World-Honored One!
For example, just as the sun and moon cannot be obstructed from reaching the edge of Mount Aṭa;
the four great rivers do not fail to reach the great ocean;
and those of icchantika disposition do not fail to go to hell.
All sentient beings are likewise thus; there is nothing that can obstruct them from reaching *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
"Because of the Buddha-nature, World-Honored One!

For this reason, all sentient beings do not need to cultivate the Path; by the power of the Buddha-nature, they should attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and not by the power of practicing the Noble Path."
“World-Honored One!

If those with icchantika-nature who have committed the four grave prohibitions, the five heinous crimes, and so forth, were unable to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through cultivation, then it would follow that they must cultivate because they will certainly attain it by virtue of their Buddha-nature; it would not be the case that they attain it only after having cultivated.”
World-Honored One!
It is like a magnet: although it is far from the iron, by its power the iron follows it;
the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
"Therefore, there is no need to diligently practice the Path.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
Good son!
It is like seven kinds of people on the banks of the Ganges who enter the river—whether for bathing, out of fear of bandits, or to gather flowers.
The first person sinks as soon as he enters the water.
Why is this? Because he is weak and lacks strength, and has not practiced swimming.
As for the second person, although he sinks, he emerges again; having emerged, he sinks once more.
Why is this? Because his physical strength is great, he is able to emerge again.
Because they have not practiced swimming, after emerging they sink back down.
As for the third person, having sunk, they emerge immediately; once emerged, they do not sink again. Why is this?
Because his body was heavy, he sank; because his strength was great, he rose; and because he had previously practiced swimming, he remained stationary as soon as he emerged.
As for the fourth man, once he had entered, he sank; having sunk, he rose again; and having risen, he remained stationary, surveying the four directions all around.
Why is this? Because of its weight it sinks;
because of its great strength it emerges again; through practicing floating it remains afloat; and because it does not know the way out, it looks toward the four directions.

As for the fifth person, having entered, he immediately sinks; having sunk, he emerges again; having emerged, he stands still; having stood, he surveys the directions; and having surveyed them, he departs.
Why is this? It is because of fear.
As for the sixth person, having entered, he immediately departs and stops at a shallow place.
Why is this? Because he observes whether the bandits are near or far.
As for the seventh man, having reached the other shore and ascended the great mountain, he is no longer afraid; being free from all enemies and bandits, he experiences great happiness.
“Good son! The great river of birth and death is likewise like this, wherein there are seven kinds of people.
Out of fear of the thieves of affliction, they resolve to cross the great river of birth and death; they leave the household life, shave their heads, and don the dharma robes.”

Having already left the household life, he associated with evil friends and followed their teachings, listening to and accepting false doctrines. These so-called sentient beings are nothing but the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the five aggregates are what are called the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). When a sentient being dies, the five great elements are forever severed. Since the five great elements are severed, why is it necessary to cultivate various karmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome?
Therefore, one should know that there is neither good nor evil, nor any retribution for good and evil; such a person is called an icchantika.
An icchantika is defined as one who has severed the roots of goodness;
because they have severed the roots of goodness, they are submerged in the river of birth and death and cannot emerge from it.
Why is this? Because their evil karma is heavy and they lack the power of faith, they are like the first person by the side of the Ganges. "Good son!
Those who are icchantikas have six causes and conditions by which they sink into the three evil realms and cannot escape them.

What are these six? First, because their malicious minds are fiercely burning; second, because they do not see future lives; third, because they delight in practicing afflictions; fourth, because they distance themselves from roots of goodness; fifth, because they are obstructed by the barriers of evil karma; and sixth, because they associate with evil friends.
“Furthermore, there are five things that cause one to fall into the three evil realms.

What are these five? First, committing unrighteous acts against a bhikṣu; second, committing unrighteous acts against a bhikṣuṇī; third, using the property of the Saṃgha for one’s own private purposes; fourth, committing unrighteous acts against one’s mother; and fifth, giving rise to mutual disputes and accusations among the five divisions of the Saṃgha.”
"Furthermore, there are five things that cause one to fall into the three evil realms.

What are these five? First, constantly teaching that there are no karmic fruits of good or evil; second, killing sentient beings who have resolved to attain bodhicitta; third, delighting in speaking of the faults of Dharma teachers; fourth, preaching what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and preaching the Dharma as what is not the Dharma; and fifth, listening to and receiving teachings for the purpose of seeking out faults in the Dharma."
“Furthermore, there are three matters by which one sinks into the three evil realms. What are these three?

First, the notion that the Tathāgata is impermanent and eternally extinguished; second, the notion that the True Dharma is impermanent and subject to change; third, the notion that the Jewel of the Sangha can be destroyed. Because of these, one constantly sinks into the three evil realms.”
"As for the second person, they have resolved to cross the great river of birth and death; however, because they have severed their roots of goodness, they sink and cannot emerge.
What is meant by 'emerging' is that by drawing near to virtuous friends, one attains faith."

As for "faithful mind," it is to have faith in giving and the fruits of giving; faith in the wholesome and the fruits of the wholesome; faith in the unwholesome and the fruits of the unwholesome; and faith in the suffering of birth and death, its impermanence, and its disintegration—this is called faith.
Having attained faith, they cultivate pure precepts; they receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and explain [the teachings], constantly practicing generosity and skillfully cultivating wisdom.
Because of dull faculties and further encountering evil friends, they are unable to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, and instead listen to and accept false teachings.
Or, meeting with an evil time and dwelling in an evil land, they sever all roots of goodness;
because they have severed their roots of goodness, they constantly sink into birth and death, like the second person by the side of the Ganges River.
"The third person is one who has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death, yet because they have severed their roots of goodness, they sink within it.
By associating with virtuous friends, they are said to emerge."
One has faith that the Tathāgata is omniscient, eternal, constant, and unchanging; for the sake of sentient beings, he proclaims the unsurpassed path:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature";
the Tathāgata does not perish, and the Dharma and Sangha are likewise without destruction or decay.
Those such as the icchantikas who do not sever their [defiled] dharmas can never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they must first distance themselves from them before they can then attain it.
On account of faith, one cultivates pure precepts;

having cultivated pure precepts, one receives, maintains, recites, copies, and explains the twelve divisions of the scriptures, widely proclaiming and disseminating them for the sake of all sentient beings.
Delighting in giving and cultivating wisdom, because of his sharp faculties, he dwells firmly in faith and wisdom with a mind that never regresses, like the third person by the side of the Ganges.
"As for the fourth person: having resolved to cross the great river of birth and death, they sink within it because they have severed their roots of goodness.
By associating with virtuous friends, they attain faith; this is what is meant by 'emerging.'"
Having attained faith, they receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
For the sake of sentient beings, they widely proclaim and disseminate them; they delight in giving and cultivate wisdom.

Because of his sharp faculties, he remains steadfast in faith and wisdom, with a mind free from regression, surveying the four directions—the four directions being the four fruits of śrāmaṇya—just like the fourth person by the side of the Ganges.
"As for the fifth person: having resolved to cross the great river of birth and death, they sink within it because they have severed their roots of goodness.
By associating with virtuous friends, they attain faith; this is called 'emerging.'"
Out of faith, they receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
For the sake of sentient beings, they widely proclaim and disseminate them; they delight in giving and cultivate wisdom.
Because of their sharp faculties, they dwell firmly in faith and wisdom, and their minds do not regress.

Having no regression, they advance forward—those who advance forward are called *pratyekabuddhas*. Although they are able to cross over themselves, they do not reach [the salvation of] sentient beings; this is called "going," like the fifth person by the side of the Ganges.
"As for the sixth person, he has resolved to cross the great river of birth and death; however, because he has severed his roots of goodness, he sinks within it.
By associating with virtuous friends, he attains faith; because he has attained faith, he is said to have emerged."
Out of faith, they receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
For the sake of sentient beings, they widely proclaim and disseminate them; they delight in giving and cultivate wisdom.
Because of their sharp faculties, they remain steadfastly established in faith and wisdom, with minds free from regression.
Having attained this state of non-regression, they advance further until they finally reach shallow water.

Having reached the shallow place, he stops and does not proceed—this "one who stops and does not proceed" is the so-called bodhisattva. For the sake of delivering all sentient beings, he remains to contemplate their afflictions, like the sixth man by the side of the Ganges.
"As for the seventh person: having resolved to cross the great river of birth and death, they sink within it because they have severed their roots of goodness.
By associating with virtuous friends, they attain faith; having attained faith, this is called 'emerging.'"
Out of faith, they receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
For the sake of sentient beings, they widely proclaim and disseminate them; they delight in giving and cultivate wisdom.
Because of their sharp faculties, they remain steadfastly established in faith and wisdom, with minds free from regression.
Having attained non-regression, they immediately advance forward.
Once they have advanced, they reach the other shore, ascend the great high mountain, leave all terrors behind, and experience manifold peace and happiness.
Good son! The mountain on the other shore is a metaphor for the Tathāgata;
the experience of peace and bliss is a metaphor for the Buddha’s eternal abiding.

The great high mountain is a metaphor for the Great Nirvana. "Good son! All these people by the side of the Ganges, though they all possess hands and feet, are unable to cross over; [yet] there is a man who possesses neither hands nor feet, yet he can cross over. This is a metaphor for sentient beings who, though they possess the six sense organs, are unable to attain the Great Nirvana. Furthermore, there is a man who, though he possesses neither hands nor feet, can cross over. This is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who, though lacking the six sense organs, can attain the Great Nirvana. Furthermore, there is a man who, though he possesses hands and feet, cannot cross over. This is a metaphor for those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who, though they possess the six sense organs, cannot attain the Great Nirvana. Furthermore, there is a man who, though he possesses neither hands nor feet, can cross over. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who, though lacking the six sense organs, can attain the Great Nirvana. Furthermore, there is a man who, though he possesses hands and feet, cannot cross over. It is the same for all sentient beings: although the Buddha-treasure, the Dharma-treasure, and the Sangha-treasure truly exist, and the Tathāgata constantly teaches that the essential meaning of all dharmas consists of the Eightfold Noble Path and Great Parinirvāṇa, yet all sentient beings are unable to attain them.
This is not my fault, nor is it the fault of the Noble Path or of sentient beings; one should know that it is entirely the fault and evil of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
For this reason, all sentient beings do not attain *nirvāṇa*.
“Good son! It is like a skilled physician who diagnoses an illness and prescribes medicine; if the patient does not take it, it is not the fault of the physician.
Good son!”
Suppose there is a donor who gives all that he possesses to all people, yet there are those who do not accept it; this is not the fault of the donor. Good son!
It is like the rising of the sun, which illuminates all darkness; if a blind person cannot see the road, it is not the fault of the sun.
"Good son!
Just as the waters of the Ganges can remove thirst and exhaustion, yet if those who are thirsty do not drink, it is not the fault of the water.
Good son!"
It is like the great earth, which universally produces fruits and seeds with impartiality and without distinction; if a farmer does not sow them, it is not the fault of the earth. Good son!

In the same way, the Tathāgata universally expounds and analyzes the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the sake of all sentient beings; if sentient beings do not accept them, it is not the fault of the Tathāgata.
“Good son! If one cultivates the path, one will immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son!”
As for your statement:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and should attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just like a magnet," this is excellent, excellent!
By virtue of the causal power of possessing Buddha-nature, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one says that it is unnecessary to cultivate the Noble Path, this is not correct.
"Good son! It is, for example, like a person traveling through a vast wilderness who encounters a well while suffering from thirst."
That well is extremely deep; although water is not seen, one should know that it must certainly be there.
This person employs skillful means to seek out a bucket and a rope, and upon drawing the water, it becomes visible.
The Buddha-nature is likewise: although all sentient beings possess it, they must cultivate the untainted noble path before they can perceive it.
Good son! Just as when there is sesame one can see oil, yet it cannot be seen apart from various skillful means;
so it is with sugarcane as well.
“Good son! Just as the Heaven of the Thirty-three and Uttarakuru are existent dharmas, yet cannot be seen if one lacks wholesome karma, supernormal powers, and the power of the Path.”
The roots of grass and the underground water within the earth are not seen by sentient beings because they are covered by the earth;
the Buddha-nature is likewise, for it cannot be seen as long as one does not cultivate the Noble Path.

“Good son! As you have said, that there are sick people in the world who, whether they encounter a caregiver, a skilled physician, excellent medicine, and appropriate food and drink according to their illness, or do not encounter them, all recover—good son! [This is so.]”
I have explained this meaning for the sake of bodhisattvas dwelling in the sixth stage. Good son!
For example, space is neither internal nor external to sentient beings; because it is neither internal nor external, it is also without obstruction.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this. "Good son!
It is, for example, as if a person has wealth in a distant land; although it is not present before them, they may enjoy its benefits according to their wishes."
When someone asks him about this, he says, "I allow it. Why?
Because it definitely exists.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it is neither this nor that, yet because it is certain to be attained, it is said that all possess it. "Good son!

For example, when sentient beings perform various karmas—whether wholesome or unwholesome—they are neither internal nor external. Likewise, the nature of karma is neither existent nor non-existent; it is not that which was previously non-existent and now exists, nor does it arise without cause. It is not the case that one who acts receives the fruit, nor that one acts here and another receives there, nor that one acts there and another receives there. There is no agent and no recipient; rather, the fruit of retribution is obtained through the convergence of conditions at the proper time.

The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it is not that it was originally non-existent and now exists; it is neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent, neither this nor that; it does not come from another place, nor does it arise without causes and conditions, yet it is not the case that all sentient beings do not see it.

There are certain bodhisattvas who are able to see [the Buddha] through the convergence of temporal conditions and causes: "time" refers to when a bodhisattva mahāsattva of the ten stages cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path and attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; seeing him at such a time is not called "creating."
“Good son! As for your statement that it is like a magnet, this meaning is not so. Why is that?
A stone does not attract iron.
Why is this? Because it lacks the karma of intention.
"Good son!
Because one dharma exists, another dharma arises;
because one dharma is absent, another dharma perishes. There is no creator and there is no destroyer."
Good son! It is like a fierce fire that cannot actually burn the fuel; rather, it is called "burning the fuel" because the fire arises and the fuel is destroyed. Good son!

For example, it is like the sunflower that turns to follow the sun; yet this flower has no mind of reverence, no consciousness, and no karma—it simply turns of its own accord due to the nature of its distinct dharmas.
Good son! Just as a plantain tree grows because of thunder, yet that tree has no ears, no mind, and no consciousness;
because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon grows.
Because there is no separate dharma, the separate dharma perishes and disintegrates. Good son!
It is like the aśoka tree: when a woman touches it, flowers bloom because of her touch.
This tree has no mind and is devoid of sensation;
yet because one phenomenon exists, another phenomenon arises,
and because one phenomenon ceases, another phenomenon perishes.
Good son! Just as when a tangerine tree encounters a corpse, its fruit becomes abundant, yet that tangerine tree has no mind and no sensation;
because other dharmas exist, other dharmas become abundant.
Because there is no distinct entity, distinct phenomena perish and disintegrate. Good son!
It is like the pomegranate tree: because of brick dust, bone, and manure, its fruits grow in great abundance; yet the pomegranate tree has neither mind nor sensation.
Because of the existence of distinct phenomena, distinct phenomena arise;
because of the non-existence of distinct phenomena, distinct phenomena perish. Good son!
The magnet attracting iron is also like this: because a distinct phenomenon exists, another distinct phenomenon arises;
because a distinct phenomenon is absent, another distinct phenomenon perishes.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: it cannot attract or grasp anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Good son! Ignorance does not grasp and take up the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), nor do the formative forces grasp and take up consciousness (*vijñāna*); yet they are still called ‘conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces’ and ‘conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness. Whether a Buddha appears or not, the dharma-realm remains eternally abiding.”
“Good son! If one says that the Buddha-nature dwells within sentient beings, good son!
The eternal dharma has no dwelling place; if it had a place of dwelling, it would be impermanent.”
"Good son!
Just as the twelve links of dependent origination have no fixed place of abiding— if they had a place of abiding, the twelve links of dependent origination could not be called 'permanent'—
so too the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata has no place of abiding."
The dharma-realm, the dharma-entrance, the dharma-aggregate, and empty space all have no place of abiding;
the Buddha-nature is likewise, having no place of abiding whatsoever. "Good son!

For example, although the four great elements are equal in power, some are solid, some are hot, some are moist, and some are mobile; some are heavy, some are light; some are red, some are white, some are yellow, and some are black. Yet these four great elements possess no karma, for they are distinct from the dharma-realm and are each dissimilar to one another.
The Buddha-nature is also like this; because it is distinct from the dharma-realm, it manifests when the time arrives.
"Good son! All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature and are therefore said to 'have' it, for they are non-retrogressive (avaivartika)."
Because it will exist, because it is certain to be attained, and because it is certain to be seen, for these reasons it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. "Good son!
It is like a king who said to a great minister:
"Lead an elephant before these blind men to show it to them.
At that time, having received the king's command, the minister gathered many blind men and showed the elephant to them.
Then those blind men each felt with their hands.
The minister immediately returned and reported to the king, saying:
"I have finished showing them."
At that time, the great king immediately summoned the blind men and questioned each of them, saying,
"Did you see the elephant?
The blind men each replied:
"I have already seen it.
The king asked,
"What kind of creature is the elephant?"
He who touched the tusks said, "The elephant's shape is like a radish";
he who touched the ears said, "The elephant is like a winnowing basket";
he who touched the head said, "The elephant is like a rock."
He who touched its trunk said the elephant was like a pestle;
he who touched its leg said the elephant was like a wooden mortar;
he who touched its back said the elephant was like a couch.
He who touched its belly said the elephant was like a jar;
he who touched its tail said the elephant was like a rope. "Good son!
It is like those blind men who neither describe the body of the elephant nor fail to describe it.
If all these characteristics are not the elephant itself, yet there is no other elephant apart from them.

Good son! The king is like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; the minister is like the Vaipulya *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*; the elephant is like the Buddha-nature; and the blind man is like all sentient beings shrouded in ignorance.
When these sentient beings have heard the Buddha’s teaching, some may say:
"Form is the Buddha-nature. Why is this?
Although this form perishes, it continues in successive succession; therefore, one attains the thirty-two marks of the unsurpassed Tathāgata, and the form of the Tathāgata is eternal.
Because the form of the Tathāgata is eternal and uninterrupted, form is said to be named Buddha-nature.
For example, it is like genuine gold: although its form may undergo transformation, its color remains ever unchanged.
Whether it is fashioned into a bracelet, a serpent, or a plate, its yellow hue never alters.
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this: although its substance is impermanent, its form is permanent; for this reason, it is said that form is the buddha-nature. "Some may say:
'Feeling is the buddha-nature.'"
Why is this? Because through the condition of sensation (vedanā), one attains the true bliss of the Tathāgata.
The sensation of the Tathāgata refers to ultimate sensation and sensation of the primary truth (paramārtha).
Although the nature of sentient beings' sensations is impermanent, their succession continues without interruption; therefore, they obtain the eternal sensations of the Tathāgata.
For example, there may be a person whose clan name is Kauśika; although the individual is impermanent, the clan name is eternal, remaining unchanged throughout thousands of millions of generations.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; for this reason, it is said that sensation (*vedanā*) is the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the Buddha-nature."
Why is this? Because through the condition of perception (*saṃjñā*), one attains the Tathāgata’s true perception.
This perception of the Tathāgata is called the "perception of non-perception."

The "perception of non-perception" is not the perception of sentient beings, nor the perception of male or female; it is also not the perception of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it is neither perception nor the perception of cessation.

Although the perceptions of sentient beings are impermanent, because these perceptions continue in succession without interruption, they attain the perception of the Tathāgata’s permanence and constancy. Good son!
For example, regarding the twelve links of dependent origination of sentient beings, although the sentient beings perish, the dependent origination remains constant.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise; for this reason, it is said that conceptualization is the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Volitional action (saṃskāra) is the Buddha-nature.
For what reason?
Practice is called "life span.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of life span, one attains the eternally abiding life span of the Tathāgata.
Although the life span of sentient beings is impermanent, because life spans continue in succession without interruption, one attains the true, eternal life span of the Tathāgata.
Good son! It is like the twelve divisions of the scriptures: although those who hear them and those who preach them are impermanent, these scriptures themselves exist eternally and remain unchanging.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this; for this reason, it is said that practice is the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Consciousness is the Buddha-nature."
"By reason of consciousness as a condition, one attains the Tathāgata’s mind of equanimity.
Although the mental consciousness of sentient beings is impermanent, because consciousness continues in succession without interruption, one attains the Tathāgata’s truly eternal mind."
Just as heat is the nature of fire, although fire is impermanent, heat is not impermanent.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise; for this reason, consciousness is said to be the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Apart from the aggregates (skandhas) there is a self, and this self is the Buddha-nature.
For what reason?
By virtue of these causes and conditions, I have attained the eightfold mastery of a Tathāgata.
There are certain non-Buddhists who say:
"Going, coming, seeing, hearing, sorrowing, rejoicing, speaking, and explaining constitute the self."
"In this way, although the self-characteristic (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) is impermanent, the Tathāgata-self is truly eternal. Good son!
Just as the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are impermanent while their names are eternal, so too is the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) of sentient beings."
“Good son! Just as those blind men each described the elephant, although they did not grasp its reality, it was not that they were not describing the elephant.
It is the same with those who speak of the Buddha-nature: it is neither identical to the six dharmas, nor is it separate from the six dharmas.”
"Good son! For this reason, I say that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither form nor separate from form, and so on, up to: it is neither self nor separate from self. Good son!"
Although various non-Buddhists claim there is a self, in reality there is no self.
What sentient beings call the "self" is simply the five aggregates; apart from these aggregates, there is no separate self.
Good son!
It is like a lotus flower, which is composed of its stem, leaves, filaments, and pericarp; apart from these, there is no other separate flower.
The self of sentient beings is likewise so.
Good son! For example, when walls, grass, and wood are combined, they are called a "house," yet apart from these, there is no separate house.
Just as when *khatāra* trees, *pāṭala* trees, *nyagrodha* trees, and *udumbara* trees are combined, they form a "forest," yet apart from these, there is no separate forest.
For example, it is like an army composed of a combination of chariots, elephants, cavalry, and infantry; apart from these, there is no separate army.
It is like a brocade named for its combination of five-colored variegated threads; apart from these, there is no separate brocade.
It is like a great assembly named for the combination of the four castes; apart from these, there is no separate assembly.
The "self" of sentient beings is also like this: apart from the five aggregates, there is no separate self.
Good son! The Tathāgata’s eternal abiding is what is called the "self."
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is boundless and unimpeded; it is neither born nor extinguished, and has attained the eight masteries—this is what is called the "Self.

Sentient beings, in reality, possess neither such a self nor anything belonging to a self; however, because they will certainly and inevitably attain ultimate primary emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), it is therefore called Buddha-nature.
“Good son! Great loving-kindness and great compassion are called Buddha-nature. Why is this?
Great kindness and great compassion constantly follow the bodhisattva, like a shadow follows a form.
All sentient beings will certainly and inevitably attain great kindness and great compassion; for this reason, it is said that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature.
Great kindness and great compassion are called Buddha-nature;
Buddha-nature is called the Tathāgata.
Great joy and great equanimity are called Buddha-nature.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot relinquish the twenty-five states of existence, they will be unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because all sentient beings will certainly attain it, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Great joy and great equanimity are themselves Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature is called great faith. Why is this?
Because by means of faith, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to fulfill the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*."
Because all sentient beings will certainly and inevitably attain great faith, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Great faith is itself Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature is called the Stage of the Only Son.
Why is this? Because by virtue of the causal conditions of the Stage of the Only Son, a bodhisattva attains a mind of equality toward all sentient beings."
Because all sentient beings will certainly attain the stage of being an only son, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The stage of being an only son is itself Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature is called the fourth power.
Why is this? Because by means of the causal conditions of the fourth power, a bodhisattva is then able to teach and transform sentient beings."
Because all sentient beings will certainly attain the fourth power, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
This fourth power is itself Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
“The Buddha-nature is called the twelve links of dependent origination.
Why is this? Because by virtue of these causes and conditions, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding.”
All sentient beings certainly possess these twelve links of dependent origination; therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The twelve links of dependent origination are themselves Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is itself the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature is called the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
By reason of these four unimpeded [knowledges], one speaks with unimpeded mastery over words and meanings;
because of this unimpeded mastery over words and meanings, one is able to transform sentient beings."
The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge are the Buddha-nature; the Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata.
"Buddha-nature" is another name for the *mūrdhan-samādhi*.
Because one cultivates this *mūrdhan-samādhi*, one is able to comprehensively encompass all Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is said that the *mūrdhan-samādhi* is called the Buddha-nature.
Bodhisattvas in the ten stages who cultivate this samādhi have not yet attained its full perfection; although they see the Buddha-nature, they do so without clarity.
Because all sentient beings will certainly attain it, it is said that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.
“Good son! Because all sentient beings will certainly attain the various dharmas as described above, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.”
“Good son! If I were to say that form (rūpa) is the Buddha-nature, sentient beings, having heard this, would give rise to perverted views;
because of these perverted views, at the end of their lives they would be reborn in the Avīci Hell.”
The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the purpose of severing the hells; therefore, he does not say that form is the Buddha-nature, and this applies likewise even to consciousness. "Good son!
If all sentient beings were to realize their Buddha-nature, they would have no need to cultivate the Path.
