Even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes, by cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path, see the Buddha-nature only slightly; how much less could those who do not cultivate it ever see it?
"Good son!
Just as Mañjuśrī and other bodhisattvas have already cultivated the noble path for immeasurable eons and thus fully understood the Buddha-nature,
how could śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others be able to know the Buddha-nature?"

If there are sentient beings who wish to clearly understand the Buddha-nature, they should single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Furthermore, upon seeing anyone who receives, upholds, or even praises such a sūtra, they should provide them with excellent dwellings, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicines for illness and weakness, while also praising, prostrating to, and inquiring after their well-being.
"Good son!

If there are those who, throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds in the past, have personally approached and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and have deeply planted roots of goodness, only then shall they be able to hear the name of this sutra."
“Good son! The Buddha-nature is inconceivable;
the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are also inconceivable.”
That all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature yet are unable to know it is inconceivable;
that the Tathāgata’s dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity are also inconceivable;
and that all sentient beings are able to believe in such a *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is likewise inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, regarding all sentient beings who are able to believe in such an inconceivable *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, World-Honored One!”
Within this great assembly, there are eighty-five thousand billion people who do not give rise to faith in this sutra; therefore, those who are able to believe in this sutra are called inconceivable.
“Good son! These people shall likewise, in a future age, certainly attain faith in this sutra, perceive the Buddha-nature, and realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Lion’s Roar said:
“World-Honored One!
How does a non-retrogressive bodhisattva know for himself that he possesses the mind of certainty and will not regress?”
The Buddha said: “Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should test his own mind through ascetic practices:”
He ate one sesame seed for seven days;
likewise, he ate one grain each of non-glutinous rice, mung beans, hemp seeds, millet, and white beans, each for seven days.
When eating a single sesame seed, he reflected:
"Such ascetic practices are entirely without benefit; yet if one can perform even that which is of no benefit, how much more so should one perform that which is beneficial?"
"Because he is able to endure that which is unbeneficial with a mind that neither retreats nor wavers, he will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
While practicing such asceticism for these days, all his skin and flesh became emaciated and shriveled, like a raw gourd cut off and placed in the sun;
his eyes sank deep into their sockets, like stars at the bottom of a well.
The flesh was exhausted and the ribs protruded like a dilapidated thatched hut;
the vertebrae appeared in succession like a row of bricks laid end-to-end;
the place where he sat resembled a horse's hoofprint—when he wished to sit, he would collapse, and when he wished to rise, he would fall prostrate.
Although they undergo such unbeneficial suffering, they do not retreat from the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, son of good family,

because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks to destroy all sufferings and bestow peace and happiness, he is able to relinquish internal and external wealth, as well as his own body and life, like casting away a blade of straw.
If one can disregard this body and life, such a bodhisattva knows for themselves that they will certainly possess the non-retrogressive mind, thinking:
"I shall definitely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Furthermore, for the sake of the Dharma, the Bodhisattva carved his own body to serve as a lamp; he wrapped his skin and flesh with cotton cloth, poured ghee and oil over it, and burned it to form a wick."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, undergoing such great suffering, rebuked his own mind and spoke these words:
"Such suffering as this does not even equal one-hundred-thousand-millionth part of the sufferings of the hells."
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have undergone great suffering and affliction without any benefit.
If you cannot endure this slight suffering now, how will you be able to rescue suffering sentient beings within the hells?
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this way, his body does not perceive suffering, and his mind does not retreat, waver, or turn back.
At that time, the bodhisattva should deeply know for himself:
'I shall certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"

“Good son! At that time, although the Bodhisattva was still fully possessed of afflictions and had not yet severed them, for the sake of the causes and conditions of the Dharma, he was able to give his head, eyes, marrow, brain, hands, feet, blood, and flesh to others; he would even drive nails into his body, cast himself from cliffs, and leap into fire.”
At that time, although the bodhisattva undergoes such immeasurable sufferings, if his mind does not retreat, waver, or turn back, the bodhisattva should know:
"I now certainly possess a non-retreating mind; I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

“Good son! In order to destroy the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva vows to take on the body of a coarse and large animal, giving his own body, blood, and flesh to sentient beings.”
When sentient beings take [the body], the Bodhisattva again gives rise to compassion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva holds his breath and ceases to breathe, manifesting the signs of death so that those who take him do not conceive thoughts of suspicion regarding murder.
Although a bodhisattva may receive the body of an animal, they never perform the karma of an animal.
Why is this? Good son!
Once a bodhisattva has attained the non-retrogressive mind, they will never again perform karma that leads to the three evil realms.

If, in future lives, there should be even a speck of unwholesome karma whose retribution is not yet fixed, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva will, by the power of their great vows, undergo it all for the sake of sentient beings.

It is like a sick person who has been possessed by a spirit dwelling within their body; through the power of a mantra, the spirit’s characteristics immediately manifest—whether speaking, or rejoicing, or being angry, or reviling, or wailing, or weeping.

The karmic activities of the three evil realms in future ages for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise so. When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas receive the body of a bear, they constantly expound the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; or they receive the body of a *kapinjala* bird;

and for the sake of preaching the True Dharma to all sentient beings, they receive the bodies of a *goda*, a deer, a rabbit, an elephant, a ram, a monkey, a white pigeon, a garuḍa, a dragon, and a snake.

When receiving such bodies of animals, they never commit evil deeds characteristic of animals; rather, they constantly expound the True Dharma for other sentient beings who are animals, so that upon hearing the Dharma, those beings may quickly attain liberation from their animal bodies.
At that time, although the Bodhisattva assumes the body of an animal, he does not commit evil deeds; one should know that he certainly possesses a non-regressive mind.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva encounters starving sentient beings during a famine, he manifests as a tortoise or a fish many *yojanas* in length and makes this vow:
"May it be that when all sentient beings take my flesh, it grows back as soon as it is taken."
"Because they have eaten my flesh, they shall be freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst, and all shall resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva made this vow:

"If there are those who, by means of me, are freed from hunger and thirst, may they in future ages swiftly attain liberation from the affliction of hunger and thirst within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*)."
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva undergoes such suffering of mind yet does not retreat, you should know that they will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva encounters those suffering from illness during an age of pestilence, he reflects thus:

'Like a king of medicinal trees, if there are those who are ill and take its roots, its stems, its branches, its leaves, its flowers, its fruits, its bark, or its pith, they shall all be cured of their disease.'"

May my body likewise be such that if there are those who are ill, by hearing its sound, touching its body, or consuming its blood, flesh, or even its marrow, their illnesses shall all be completely healed.
I vow that when sentient beings eat my flesh, they shall not give rise to an evil mind as if eating the flesh of their own children.
Once I have cured their illnesses, I shall constantly preach the Dharma for them; may they believe and accept it, contemplate it, and teach it to others.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Although a bodhisattva who is fully possessed of afflictions undergoes physical suffering, their mind does not retreat, waver, or turn back. You should know that such a person will certainly attain the non-retrogressive mind and achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Furthermore, good son!
If there are sentient beings afflicted by ghosts, when the Bodhisattva sees them, he immediately makes this vow:
'May I take on the body of a ghost—a large body, a robust body, and one with many followers—so that they may hear and see me, and their illness may be cured. "
“Furthermore, son of good family, for the sake of sentient beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practice asceticism; although they possess afflictions, these do not defile their minds.”
Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he does not seek the fruits of those six perfections.
While practicing the unsurpassed six pāramitās, he makes this vow:
"I now bestow these six pāramitās upon each and every sentient being."
Once each and every sentient being has received my gift, I shall cause them all to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I, too, shall personally practice the six pāramitās with diligent austerity, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
"When undergoing suffering, may I not retreat from the mind of enlightenment.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes this vow, it is called the mark of non-retrogression from enlightenment.
"Furthermore, good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are inconceivable. Why is this?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply understands that birth and death abound with many faults and transgressions, and perceives that Great Nirvāṇa possesses great merit. For the sake of all sentient beings who dwell within birth and death and undergo various sufferings, his mind never regresses; this is called the inconceivability of a Bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to compassion without any external cause or condition; truly receiving no gratitude, he constantly bestows grace, and though he bestows grace, he seeks no recompense. For this reason, he is further named 'inconceivable.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family!

There are some sentient beings who practice various ascetic austerities for their own benefit, whereas the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices austerities for the sake of benefiting others; this is called 'benefiting oneself,' and for this reason it is further termed inconceivable."

"Furthermore, although a bodhisattva is fully possessed of afflictions, they cultivate a mind of equanimity in order to destroy the various sufferings experienced by both enemies and kin; for this reason, it is further called inconceivable."

"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva encounters sentient beings who are evil and unwholesome, they may reprimand them, speak to them gently, expel them, or simply let them be. To those of a wicked nature, they may manifest gentleness; to those who are arrogant, they may manifest great pride, yet in their inner mind, they truly possess no arrogance. This is called the inconceivable skillful means of a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva is possessed of afflictions and possesses few material goods, yet many come to seek from him, his mind does not become narrow or constricted; this is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in the world, a bodhisattva recognizes the Buddha's merits; yet for the sake of sentient beings, they take birth in remote borderlands where no Buddha resides, appearing as if blind, deaf, lame, or afflicted with chronic illness. This is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva deeply understands all the transgressions of sentient beings; for the sake of their deliverance, he constantly acts in concert with them. Although he accords with their inclinations, he is not defiled by the stains of their offenses; for this reason, he is further called 'inconceivable.'"

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva clearly knows and sees that there is no mark of a sentient being, no defilement of afflictions, no cultivation of the path, and no one who is free from afflictions; yet, although they act for the sake of enlightenment, there is no practice of enlightenment nor any accomplishment of the practice of enlightenment; there is neither the experience of suffering nor the destruction of suffering, yet they are nevertheless able to destroy the suffering of sentient beings and practice the conduct of enlightenment. For this reason, it is further called inconceivable."
"Furthermore, that a Bodhisattva, having received his final body, dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven is also called inconceivable.
Why is this? Because the Tuṣita Heaven is the most excellent within the realm of desire."
Those dwelling in the lower heavens have minds that are heedless;
those in the higher heavens have faculties that are dull and obscured; for this reason, they are called "superior.
By practicing generosity and observing precepts, one attains the upper and lower bodies [of the form realm].
By practicing generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, one attains a body in Tuṣita.
Yet all bodhisattvas revile and destroy all forms of existence; they never perform the karma for Tuṣita Heaven to receive a body in that celestial realm.

Why is this? Because even when Bodhisattvas dwell in other realms of existence, they are still able to teach and bring sentient beings to maturity; yet, though they manifest with desire within the realm of desire, they are truly free from any mind of craving. For this reason, they are further called "inconceivable."
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born in the Tuṣita Heaven, they possess three things by which they excel:
first, life span; second, physical form; and third, renown."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas truly do not seek life, physical form, or reputation; yet, although they have no seeking mind, that which they obtain is supreme.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas deeply delight in nirvāṇa, and their causal conditions are likewise supreme; for this reason, they are further called inconceivable.

"Although the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus excels all the devas in these three matters, the devas never give rise toward the Bodhisattva to thoughts of anger, envy, or arrogance; they always give rise to thoughts of joy. The Bodhisattva, in turn, does not feel arrogance toward the devas. For this reason, it is further called 'inconceivable.'"
“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not create karma for his lifespan, yet he possesses an ultimate lifespan in that heaven; this is called ‘superiority of life.
He is likewise without karma for physical form, yet his wondrous body is filled with pervasive radiance; this is called ‘superiority of form.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in that celestial palace, he takes no pleasure in the five desires but engages only in matters of the Dharma; therefore, his reputation fills the ten directions; this is called ‘superiority of name.’”
For this reason, it is further called inconceivable.
"When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven, at that time the great earth shakes in six ways; for this reason, it is further called inconceivable."

Why is this? When the Bodhisattva descended, the devas of the desire and form realms all came to attend upon and escort him; they raised a great sound in praise of the Bodhisattva, and by the breath from their mouths, they caused the earth to tremble.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas who are elephant-kings among men; these elephant-kings among men are also called dragon-kings (*nāgarāja*).
When such a dragon-king first enters the womb, various other dragon-kings dwelling beneath this earth become either terrified or awakened; for this reason, the great earth quakes in six ways.
For this reason, it is further called inconceivable.

"The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the time of entering the womb, the time of dwelling therein, and the time of emerging; he knows the father and knows the mother, yet remains undefiled by impurity, like the indranīla-blue jewel on Śakra’s crest. For this reason, it is further called inconceivable."
“Good son! The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is likewise thus inconceivable. Good son!”
For example, the great ocean possesses eight inconceivable qualities.
What are these eight? First, it gradually deepens;

second, its depth is difficult to fathom; third, it has a single uniform salty taste; fourth, its tides do not exceed their limits; fifth, it contains various treasuries of jewels; sixth, large-bodied beings dwell within it; seventh, it does not harbor dead corpses; eighth, though all the myriad streams and heavy rains pour into it, it neither increases nor decreases.
Good son! There are three matters by which it gradually becomes deeper.
What are these three?
First, the power of the merit of sentient beings; second, traveling with the wind; third, because the river water flows into it.
Furthermore, regarding neither increasing nor decreasing, there are likewise three factors for each.
"This subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtra is likewise thus, possessing eight inconceivable qualities.
First, it is progressively deep.
That is to say:"

The five precepts, the ten precepts, the two hundred and fifty precepts, the bodhisattva precepts, the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the fruit of pratyekabuddha, the fruit of bodhisattva, and the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—these dharmas taught in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are called "gradually deepening."
For this reason, this sutra is called "Gradually Deep.
Second, it is deep and difficult to reach its bottom.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is neither born nor extinguished; he does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor does he turn the wheel of Dharma; he does not eat, receive, or practice giving. Therefore, he is named Constant, Blissful, Self, and Pure.

All sentient beings possess buddha-nature; this buddha-nature is not form, yet it is not separate from form; it is not sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from consciousness.
This is eternal and visible; it is a revealing cause, not a producing cause, by which those from the stage of srotāpanna up to the pratyekabuddha shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
There are neither afflictions nor a place of abiding; although there are no afflictions, it is not called "permanent," and for this reason it is called "profound."

"Furthermore, there is a profound depth within this sutra: at times it speaks of a self, and at times it speaks of non-self; at times it speaks of permanence, and at times it speaks of impermanence; at times it speaks of purity, and at times it speaks of impurity; at times it speaks of bliss, and at times it speaks of suffering; at times it speaks of emptiness, and at times it speaks of non-emptiness; at times it speaks of the existence of all things, and at times it speaks of the non-existence of all things; at times it speaks of the three vehicles, and at times it speaks of the one vehicle; at times it says that the five aggregates are themselves the Buddha-nature; and it speaks of the vajra-samādhi, the middle way, the śūraṅgama-samādhi, the twelve links of dependent origination, the ultimate emptiness, compassion and equanimity toward all sentient beings, the wisdom of the crown, faith, and the knowledge of the faculties and powers."
The wisdom that is unimpeded regarding all phenomena does not speak of the Buddha-nature as being determinate, despite its existence; therefore, it is called "profound.
Third is "one flavor."

All sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature; they are all identical in the One Vehicle, identical in liberation, identical in cause, identical in fruit, and identical in the nectar of immortality. All shall attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is called the "one flavor."
"Fourth, the tide does not overstep its limit.

Likewise, within this sutra it is prescribed that bhikṣus must not accept or store the eight kinds of impure things. If my disciples are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, explain, and analyze this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they would rather lose their lives than ever violate these precepts; this is called 'the tide not overstepping its limit.'"
"5. There are various treasuries of jewels.

This sutra is itself an immeasurable treasury of jewels. What is called 'jewels' refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the conduct of an infant, the noble conduct, the brahma-conduct, the celestial conduct, the skillful means of all sentient beings, the Buddha-nature, the merits of bodhisattvas, the merits of Tathāgatas, the merits of śrāvakas, the merits of pratyekabuddhas, the six pāramitās, immeasurable samādhis, and immeasurable wisdom. These are called the treasury of jewels."
"Sixth, it is the dwelling place of beings with great bodies.
'Beings with great bodies' refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Because they possess great wisdom, they are called 'beings with great bodies.'"

Because of its great body, great mind, great adornment, great subduing, great skillful means, great preaching of the Dharma, great power, great retinue, great supernormal powers, and great compassion; because it is eternally unchanging and because all sentient beings dwell therein without hindrance, and because it accommodates all sentient beings—it is called the dwelling place of sentient beings with great bodies.
"Seventh, one does not allow a corpse to remain overnight. A 'corpse' refers to those who are icchantikas; those who have committed the four grave prohibitions;

those who have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution; those who slander the Vaipulya sutras; those who preach what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, or preach the Dharma as not the Dharma; those who accept and store the eight kinds of impure things; those who use the property of the Buddha or the Sangha according to their own whims; or those who commit unlawful acts against bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—these are called corpses."
This *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is free from such things as these; therefore, it is called "not harboring a corpse.
Eighth, it neither increases nor decreases.

Because it is boundless, because it has no beginning or end, because it is not form, because it is not a conditioned product, because it is eternally abiding and neither arises nor perishes, because all sentient beings are entirely equal, and because the nature of all phenomena is of a single nature—it is called "without increase or decrease."
"Therefore, this sutra possesses eight inconceivable qualities, just like that great ocean.
Siṃhanāda said,
"World-Honored One!"

If it is said that the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished and this is called "profound," yet all sentient beings have four modes of birth—birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation—and these four modes of birth are fully present among human beings.

Just as the bhikṣu Śiva, the bhikṣu Upaśiva, the mother of the householder Mṛgāra, the mother of the householder Nyagrodha, and the mother of the householder Pañcāla each had five hundred sons born from eggs, one should know that among human beings there are those born from eggs.
Regarding those born from moisture, as the Buddha said:
"In the past, when I was practicing as a bodhisattva, I was King Mūrdhaja and King Hastija, just as the women born from the *āmra* tree and the *karamarda* tree are described now."
One should know that among humans there is moisture-birth (*saṃsvedaja*).
At the beginning of the eon, all sentient beings were born by transformation (*aupapāduka*).
Since the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has attained the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*), for what reason and by what conditions was he not born by transformation?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! All sentient beings are born through the four modes of birth."
Having attained the noble Dharma, one no longer undergoes birth from an egg or moisture as was the case before. Good son!
At the beginning of the kalpa, all sentient beings were born by transformation; at that time, no Buddha appeared in the world.
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who encounter the suffering of illness, they require a physician and medicine.

At the beginning of the kalpa, sentient beings were born by transformation; although they possessed afflictions, their illnesses had not yet manifested, and for this reason the Tathāgata did not appear in that world."
At the beginning of a kalpa, the bodies and minds of sentient beings were not yet fit vessels; therefore, the Tathāgata does not appear in that world. Good son!
All the undertakings of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, surpass those of all other sentient beings—namely, his lineage, his retinue, and his parents.
Because of his excellence, all people believe and accept whatever Dharma he preaches.
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not undergo transformational birth (upapāduka). Good son!

Among all sentient beings, fathers perform the karma of sons and sons perform the karma of fathers; yet if the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, were to receive a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), he would have no father or mother. If he has no father or mother, how could he cause all sentient beings to perform various wholesome karmas?
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Good son!
Within the True Dharma of the Buddha, there are two kinds of protection:
The first is internal, and the second is external.
Internal protection refers to the prohibitive precepts;
external protection refers to one's kinsmen and retinue.
If the Buddha-Tathāgata were to accept a manifested body (nirmāṇakāya), he would have no external protection; therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept a manifested body. Good son!
There are those who give rise to arrogance by relying on their clan; in order to destroy such pride, the Tathāgata is born into a noble clan and does not accept a manifested body.
"Good son!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has true parents: his father is named Śuddhodana and his mother is named Māyā; yet sentient beings still say he is an illusion—how then could he receive a body born by transformation?"
If he had received a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), how could there be *śarīra* relics of his fragmented body?
It was for the sake of increasing the merit and virtue of sentient beings that the Tathāgata fragmented his body so that they might make offerings to it.
"Therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Since all Buddhas are entirely without birth by transformation, why should I alone be made to receive a transformation body?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and praised the Buddha in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s immeasurable mass of merit, I am now unable to proclaim in full;
today, for the sake of sentient beings, I shall expound but a single portion—may you, out of compassion, deign to hear my words.”
Sentient beings wander in the darkness of ignorance, Fully experiencing boundless hundreds of kinds of suffering;
The World-Honored One can cause them to be far removed from it, And for this reason, the world calls him the Greatly Compassionate One.
Sentient beings wander back and forth on the rope of birth and death; Through heedlessness and delusion, they lack peace and joy.
The Tathāgata can bestow peace and joy upon all; Therefore, he forever severs the rope of birth and death.
Because the Buddha can bestow peace and happiness upon the multitude, he does not crave his own pleasure;
for the sake of all sentient beings, he practices asceticism—therefore, the world offers him worship.
Seeing others suffer, his body trembles; though dwelling in hell, he feels no pain.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he undergoes great suffering; therefore, it is unsurpassed and immeasurable.
The Tathāgata practiced austerities for the sake of the multitudes, Accomplishing and fulfilling the six perfections;
His mind remained unmoved amidst the winds of heterodoxy, And thus he was able to surpass the great sages of the world.
Sentient beings constantly desire peace and happiness, yet they do not know how to cultivate the causes of peace and happiness;
the Tathāgata can teach them to practice these, just as a compassionate father loves his only son.
The Buddha beholds the afflictions of sentient beings; his mind suffers like a mother thinking of a sick child.
He constantly contemplates various skillful means to bring them freedom from illness; for this reason, he subjects this body to another.
All sentient beings undergo various sufferings, yet with their minds inverted, they take them for pleasure;
the Tathāgata expounds the true nature of suffering and pleasure, and for this reason he is titled the Greatly Compassionate One.
The world dwells entirely within the shell of ignorance; none possess the beak of wisdom capable of breaking it.
Only the Tathāgata’s beak of wisdom can peck it asunder; for this reason, he is called the Greatest Son.
Not encompassed by the three periods of time, Without name or provisional designation,
Awakened to the profoundly deep meaning of nirvāṇa— Therefore, the Buddha is called the Great Awakened One.
There is a river with swirling eddies that submerges sentient beings; blinded by ignorance, they do not know how to escape.
The Tathāgata has crossed over himself and can ferry others across; for this reason, he is called the Buddha, the Great Captain.
Able to know all causes and effects, and likewise thoroughly penetrating the path to their cessation, he constantly bestows the medicine for the sickness and suffering of sentient beings;
therefore, the world calls him the Great King of Physicians.
The heterodox teachers with their false views preach asceticism, claiming that through this one may attain unsurpassed bliss;
the Tathāgata proclaims the practice of true bliss, which enables sentient beings to experience happiness.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, destroys false paths and reveals to sentient beings the path of true reality;
those who travel this path attain peace and happiness, and for this reason the Buddha is called the Guide.
Not created by self, nor created by another, Nor produced by both together, nor arisen without cause—
The Tathāgata’s teaching on the matter of suffering surpasses all those of the non-Buddhists.
Having fully accomplished the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, he likewise teaches sentient beings through these dharmas;
when bestowing the gift of Dharma, he is free from envy and stinginess—therefore, the Buddha’s compassion is called "unconditioned."
Without fabrication and without causes or conditions, one attains that which is causeless and without karmic retribution;
therefore, all the wise proclaim that the Tathāgata seeks no reward.
Though constantly associating with those in the world who act with negligence, his person is not defiled by negligence;
therefore he is called "Inconceivable," for the eight worldly dharmas cannot defile him.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has neither enemy nor friend; therefore, his mind is always impartial.
I utter a lion’s roar to praise his great compassion, for he can roar the immeasurable lion’s roar.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty; The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-one,
supplemented by the Śramaṇa Huiyan and others of the Song Dynasty based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter 24: The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, Part One.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has compassion for all sentient beings; he can tame those who are untamed and purify those who are impure. He serves as a refuge for those without refuge and brings liberation to those not yet liberated. Having attained the eight masteries, he acts as the Great Physician and the Great King of Medicine.

The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was a son of the Buddha when he was a bodhisattva; after leaving the household life, he received, upheld, recited, and analyzed and explained the twelve divisions of the scriptures, destroyed the fetters of the desire realm, and attained the four dhyānas.
Why did the Tathāgata declare that Sunakṣatra is an icchantika, a person of the lowest station, who will dwell in hell for an eon and is incurable?
Why did the Tathāgata not first expound the True Dharma to him and subsequently [ordain] him as a bodhisattva?
“If the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cannot save the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, how can he be said to possess great compassion and great skillful means?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
For example, suppose a father and mother have only three sons.
One of these sons possesses a mind of faith and compliance; he respects his parents, has sharp faculties and wisdom, and is able to quickly understand worldly matters.
The second son did not respect his parents and lacked a mind of faith and obedience; however, he possessed sharp faculties and wisdom, enabling him to quickly understand worldly matters.
The third son also did not respect his parents and lacked a mind of faith and obedience; moreover, he had dull faculties and no wisdom.
When parents wish to provide instruction, whom should they instruct first?
Whom should they love most?
And whom should they instruct first to understand the affairs of the world?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

One should first instruct those who possess faith and compliance, who revere their parents, and who have sharp faculties, wisdom, and knowledge of worldly affairs; only after them, as the second and third, should others be taught.”
"Although those two sons lacked faith, compliance, and a heart of reverence, he taught them again out of his compassionate concern. 'Good son!'"
The Tathāgata is likewise. His three sons represent, respectively, the bodhisattvas, the śrāvakas, and the icchantikas.

Just as the subtle meanings within the sūtras of the twelve divisions of the scriptures were previously taught by me for the sake of the bodhisattvas, while the shallow and proximate meanings were taught for the sake of the śrāvakas;

The meaning of "worldly" is spoken of in reference to icchantikas and those who have committed the five heinous crimes; although it provides no benefit in the present life, out of compassion, it serves to produce the seeds of all virtues for future lives.
“Good son! It is like three kinds of fields:
the first has easy access for irrigation channels and is free from sand, gravel, shards, stones, thorns, and brambles; by sowing one, one obtains a hundred.
Second, although there are no pebbles, gravel, stones, or thorns, and the irrigation channels are not difficult to navigate, the harvest is reduced by half.
Third, where the irrigation channels are difficult to navigate and there are many pebbles, gravel, stones, and thorns, one obtains only what was sown, because of the abundance of straw and weeds.
"Good son!
In the spring months, in which field does a farmer sow first?
"World-Honored One!"
"First one plants in the first field, next in the second field, and finally in the third.
"The first is a metaphor for a bodhisattva, the next for a śrāvaka, and the last for an icchantika."
Good son! It is like three vessels:
the first is intact, the second is leaking, and the third is broken.
"If one wishes to store milk, curd, ghee, or water, which should be used first?
"World-Honored One!
One should use the intact vessel first, next the leaking one, and finally the broken one."
“Those who are whole and pure are likened to the community of Bodhisattvas; those with outflows are likened to the Śrāvakas; and those who are broken are likened to the Icchantikas.
Good son! It is like three sick people who come together to a physician:”
First, those who are easy to treat; second, those who are difficult to treat; third, those who are incurable.
Good son, if a physician were to treat them, whom would he treat first?
“World-Honored One!
One should first treat the easy case, then proceed to the second, and finally to the third. Why is this so?”
"It is for the sake of their kinsmen.

Those who are easy to cure are likened to the Bodhisattva Saṃgha; those who are difficult to cure are likened to the Śrāvaka Saṃgha; and those who cannot be cured are likened to the icchantikas. Although they have no wholesome fruits in the present life, [the Buddha] acts out of compassion so as to plant the seeds of various virtues for future lives.
"Good son!
It is like a great king who has three kinds of horses:
first, those that are well-trained, robust, and of great strength;"
Second, one that is untamed, with strong teeth and great strength;
third, one that is untamed, emaciated and old, and lacking strength.
If Your Majesty were to ride and drive them, which would you take first?
“World-Honored One!
One should first mount the well-trained, powerful steed; next, mount the second; and finally, reach the third. “Good son!

The analogy of the well-trained, powerful ox represents the Bodhisattva Saṃgha; the second represents the Śrāvaka Saṃgha; and the third represents the icchantika. Although the latter provides no benefit in the present life, out of compassion, it serves to plant the seeds for various virtues in future lives.
Good son! It is like when three people come during a great act of giving:
the first is of noble birth, intelligent, and observant of the precepts;
Second, those of middle caste with dull faculties who maintain the precepts;
third, those of low caste with dull faculties who violate the precepts. Good son!
"To whom should this great donor first give?
"World-Honored One!
He should first give to those of noble lineage, sharp faculties, and who uphold the precepts; next, to the second group; and finally, to the third."
“The first parable refers to the Bodhisattva Saṃgha; the second refers to the Śrāvaka Saṃgha; and the third refers to the icchantikas. Good son!
Just as a great lion exerts its full strength when killing a fragrant elephant, it does so likewise when killing a rabbit, without giving rise to a thought of contempt.”
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are likewise; when they preach the Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas and icchantikas, their effort is no different. "Good son!
Once, while I was staying in the city of Rājagṛha, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra served as my attendant.
During the first watch of the night, I expounded the essentials of the Dharma for Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
It is the law for a disciple to sleep after their teacher.
At that time, because I had sat for a long time, Sunakṣatra conceived an evil thought.
Furthermore, when the young boys and girls of Rājagṛha would not stop crying, their parents would say to them:
"If you do not desist, I shall hand you over to the yakṣa Bakula.
At that time, Sunakṣatra was instead seized and restrained, and he said to me:
"Enter the meditation chamber quickly; Bakula is coming!"
I said: "Fool! Have you not always heard that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is possessed of fearlessness?"
At that time, Śakra addressed me, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Can such people as these also enter into the Buddha-dharma?"
I then spoke these words:
"Kauśika! Such persons as these shall enter the Buddha-dharma; they also possess the Buddha-nature and shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Although I preached the Dharma for this Śunakṣatra, he had no mind whatsoever to believe or accept it.
Son of Good Family!
At one time, while I was in the city of Śivavatī in the kingdom of Kāśi, the bhikṣu Śunakṣatra served as my attendant."
At that time, as I was about to enter that city to beg for alms, immeasurable sentient beings, with hearts of sincere longing, desired to see my footprints.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra followed closely behind me and attempted to efface them; yet, being unable to efface them, he instead caused sentient beings to give rise to unwholesome thoughts.
After I had entered the city, I saw at a tavern a Nirgrantha squatting on the ground with his back hunched, eating dregs of wine.
Upon seeing this, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra said:
"World-Honored One!"
If there were any Arhats in the world, these people would be the most supreme.
Why? Because what these people teach is that there is neither cause nor effect.
I said: "Fool! Have you not always heard that an Arhat does not drink alcohol, does not harm others, does not deceive, does not steal, and does not engage in sexual misconduct?"
Such a person has murdered their parents and consumed fermented rice dregs; how can you say they are an Arhat?
When this person abandons the body, they will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
"An Arhat has eternally severed the three evil realms.
Why, then, do you say that this person is an Arhat?
Sunakṣatra then replied:
"The nature of the four great elements may still be changed, but it is impossible for this person to necessarily fall into Avīci. I said:
"Foolish man!"
"Have you not always heard that the truthful words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are non-dual?
Although I have preached the Dharma for this Sunakṣatra, he has absolutely no heart of faith or acceptance."
“Good son! At one time, I was staying in the city of Rājagṛha together with the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra.
At that time, there was in the city a Nirgrantha named Duḥkhaprapta, who constantly spoke these words:”
"The afflictions of sentient beings have no cause and no condition; the liberation of sentient beings likewise has no cause or condition.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra further spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"If there were any arhats in the world, it would be best for them to suffer. I said: "Fool!
“Khadiravaniya, the Nirgrantha is truly not an Arhat; he is unable to understand the path of an Arhat.
Sunakṣatra spoke again:
“For what reason would an Arhat harbor jealousy toward another Arhat?”
I said: "Fool! I harbor no envy toward Arhats; it is you who have conceived this evil and false view."
"If you say that this Kṛṣṇa has attained arhatship, then seven days from now he shall suffer from indigestion, die of abdominal pain,
and after death, be reborn among the hungry ghosts who consume vomit."
"His fellow students shall carry his corpse and place it in the cold forest.
At that time, Sunakṣatra went to where the Nirgrantha Kṛtika was and said to him: "Elder!..."
"Do you know now?
The śramaṇa Gautama has predicted that in seven days you shall suffer from indigestion, die of abdominal pain,
and after death, be reborn among the *udaka-kumbha* ghosts."
"Your fellow students and teacher shall carry your corpse and place it in the cold forest.
Elder! Reflect well and employ every means possible to cause the Gautama to fall into falsehood."
At that time, having heard these words, Kṛtaka immediately ceased eating food, from the first day until the sixth.
When the seventh day was completed, he then ate black honey;
having eaten the black honey, he further drank cold water.
After drinking cold water, he suffered abdominal pain and died.

Once he had died, his fellow students carried his corpse to the Śītavana forest and placed it there; immediately, he took on the form of a hungry ghost who consumes vomit and stood beside his own corpse.

Having heard this matter, the bhikṣu Śunakṣatra went to the Cold Forest (Śītavana), where he saw Duḥkhalābha with the body of one who had consumed vomit, crouching on the ground with his back hunched beside that corpse.
Sunakṣatra asked,
"Venerable sir, are you dead?
Kṛtaka replied:
"I have already died.
"In what way did you die? He replied:
"He died from abdominal pain.
"Who carried out your corpse?
He replied:
"Classmate. "Where did you put it? He replied:
“Fool! Do you not recognize this as the Śītavana cremation ground?
“What kind of body have I obtained?”
He replied:
"I have obtained the body of a *vāntāśinī* (vomit-eating) spirit.
Listen attentively, Sujāta: "
The Tathāgata speaks with skillful words, true words, timely words, meaningful words, and words of the Dharma.
Sunakṣatra! Since such truthful words issue from the mouth of the Tathāgata, why did you not believe them at that time?
"If there are sentient beings who do not believe in the Tathāgata’s true words, they too shall receive a body such as this one of mine.
At that time, Sunakṣatra returned to my presence and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!"
“After the death of the Nigaṇṭha Khatāyana, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. I said:
“Foolish man!”
“An Arhat has no place of rebirth; how then can you say that Kṛtaka was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
“World-Honored One!
It is indeed as you have said. Kṛtaka the Nirgrantha was certainly not born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; he has now received the body of a *vāntāsa* hungry ghost.”
I said: "Foolish man!
The truthful words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are non-dual."
"If it is said that the Tathāgata has two [contradictory] words, such a thing is impossible.
Sunakṣatra then replied,
"Although the Tathāgata spoke thus at that time, I have not given rise to faith in this matter at all."
“Good son! I have also constantly taught the true Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, yet he utterly lacked any mind of faith or acceptance. Good son!”

Although the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra had recited and studied the twelve divisions of the scriptures and attained the four dhyānas, he did not understand the meaning of even a single verse, a single phrase, or a single word; having associated with evil friends, he fell away and lost the four dhyānas.
Having lost the four dhyānas, he gave rise to evil and false views, speaking thus:
"There is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, and there is no Nirvāṇa.
The śramaṇa Gautama is skilled in the science of marks; for this reason, he is able to know the minds of others."
At that time, I said to Sunakṣatra:

"The Dharma I teach is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its words are skillful, its characters and meanings are authentic, what is spoken is unadulterated, and it fully accomplishes the pure holy life."
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra spoke again, saying:
"Although the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma for me, I truly maintain that there is no cause and no effect.
O son of good family!
"If you do not believe such a thing, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra is currently nearby at the Nairañjanā River; you may go together with me to question him.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately went with Kāśyapa to Sunakṣatra’s location.
When the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra saw the Buddha coming from afar, upon seeing him, he immediately conceived an evil and heterodox mind;
because of that evil mind, his physical body sank down and fell into the Avīci Hell.

“Good son! Although the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra entered the immeasurable treasury of jewels that is the Buddha-dharma, he obtained nothing at all, failing to gain the benefit of even a single dharma, because of his negligence and because of evil associates.”
For example, it is like a person who, though having entered the great ocean, sees many various jewels but obtains none because of negligence.
Or again, it is like one who enters the sea and, despite seeing a heap of jewels, either commits suicide or is killed by rākṣasas and evil spirits.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was likewise; having entered the Buddha-dharma, he was slain by evil associates who were like rākṣasa demons.
O son of good family!
Therefore, out of compassion, the Tathāgata has always said that Sunakṣatra is full of negligence.
"Good son! If one is originally poor, although one may feel compassion for such a person, that compassion is slight."
If one who was originally immensely wealthy later loses their property, people feel deep compassion for them and their hearts are moved with profound sympathy.

The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was just like this: he had mastered and recited the twelve divisions of the scriptures and attained the four dhyānas, yet he subsequently fell away from them; he is truly to be pitied.
Therefore, I say that the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra is full of negligence;
because of his great negligence, he has severed all roots of goodness.

Among my disciples, those who see or hear of him cannot fail to give rise to a heart of profound compassion for this person, just as one would feel for a man who was once immensely wealthy but later lost all his fortune.
For many years I have constantly followed and associated with Sunakṣatra, yet he has given rise to evil and heterodox thoughts within himself;
because of his evil heterodoxy, he does not relinquish his wrong views.

"Good son! Since the past, if I had seen even a hair’s breadth of roots of goodness in this Sunakṣatra, I would never have predicted that he had severed his roots of goodness, that he was a base icchantika, and that he would dwell in hell for kalpas;

it was because he proclaimed that there is no cause, no fruit, and no karma performed that I then predicted he had forever severed his roots of goodness, that he was a base icchantika, and that he would dwell in hell for kalpas."
"Good son!

It is like a person who has fallen into a latrine; a good friend reaches down with his hand to pull him out, and upon finding a lock of hair, he intends to pull him up, but after searching for a long time without success, he finally desists."

I am likewise; seeking even the slightest roots of goodness in Sunakṣatra, I desire to rescue him, yet though I search all day long, I do not find so much as a hair’s breadth of them. For this reason, I cannot deliver him from hell.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason did the Tathāgata predict that he would fall into the Avīci Hell?”
“Good son! The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra has many followers, all of whom claim that Sunakṣatra is an arhat and one who has attained the fruits of the path.
Because I wish to destroy their evil and heterodox minds, I have declared that Sunakṣatra, due to his negligence, will fall into hell.”
“Good son! You should now know that what the Tathāgata has spoken is true and non-dual.”
Why is this? If the Buddha has prophesied that one shall fall into hell, it is impossible that they would not fall.
However, regarding the predictions made by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, there are two possibilities:
Some are false and some are true.
For example, Maudgalyāyana, while in the kingdom of Magadha, announced to all the people:
"Seven days from now, the heavens shall send down rain."
In the end, it did not rain at all.
Furthermore, he predicted that a cow would give birth to a white calf, but when the time came for her to calve, she gave birth to a brindled calf;
he predicted the birth of a son, yet later a daughter was born.

“Good son! The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra constantly preached to immeasurable sentient beings that there are no fruits of good or evil in anything; at that time, he forever severed all roots of goodness until not even a hair’s breadth remained.”
"Good son!

I have known for a long time that this bhikṣu, Śunakṣatra, would sever his roots of goodness; nevertheless, I continued to dwell with him for a full twenty years, supporting and associating with him."
If I were to cast them far away and not keep them close at hand, these people would cause immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil deeds.
This is called the Tathāgata’s fifth power of understanding.
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions do those of the icchantika class lack wholesome dharmas? “Good son!
Because those who are icchantikas have severed their roots of goodness,
and because while all sentient beings possess the five faculties such as faith, the icchantikas have eternally cut them off;
for this reason, one incurs the sin of killing even by slaying an ant, yet there is no sin of killing when one kills an icchantika.
“World-Honored One!
Since those of icchantika nature ultimately possess no wholesome dharmas, is it for this reason that they are called icchantikas?
The Buddha said:
“So it is, so it is. “World-Honored One!
All sentient beings possess three kinds of goodness, namely: those of the past, the future, and the present.”
"Even those who are icchantikas cannot sever future wholesome dharmas; why, then, do you say that one who severs all wholesome dharmas is called an icchantika? "Good son!..."
There are two kinds of severance:
first, cessation in the present; second, the obstruction of the future by the present.
The icchantikas possess both of these forms of severance; therefore, I say that they have severed all roots of goodness.
“Good son! It is like a person who has fallen into a cesspool;
though only the tip of a single hair remains unsubmerged, that single hair-tip cannot support the body.
The icchantikas are likewise: although they shall possess roots of goodness in future lives, these cannot save them from the sufferings of hell.

While they may be rescued in the future, there is nothing that can be done for them in the present life; therefore, they are said to be "incurable. Nevertheless, through the causal conditions of the Buddha-nature, they can still be saved.
The Buddha-nature is neither past, nor future, nor present; therefore, the Buddha-nature cannot be severed.
Just as rotten seeds cannot produce sprouts, so it is with those who possess the icchantika nature.
“World-Honored One!
Since those of the icchantika class do not sever their buddha-nature, and the buddha-nature is itself wholesome, why do you say they sever all that is wholesome? “Good son!
If sentient beings possessed buddha-nature in the present life, they could not be called icchantikas, just as sentient beings in the world possess a self-nature.
The Buddha-nature is eternal and is not encompassed by the three periods of time;
if it were encompassed by the three periods, it would be called impermanent.
Because the Buddha-nature will be seen in the future, it is said that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.
"For this reason, it is only when Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes are fully adorned that they are able to see [it] slightly.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
The Buddha-nature is eternal, just like empty space.
For what reason does the Tathāgata speak of it as being "in the future"?

If the Tathāgata were to say that those who hold perverted views (icchantikas) possess no wholesome dharmas, would these icchantikas not still give rise to feelings of love and affection toward their fellow students, teachers, parents, kinsmen, wives, and children?
"If it were to arise in such a way, would that not be good?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son, you have asked this question well.
Buddha-nature is like empty space; it is neither past, nor future, nor present."
All sentient beings have three kinds of bodies:
namely, those of the past, the future, and the present.
Sentient beings will attain a body that is fully adorned and pure in the future and thereby perceive the Buddha-nature; for this reason, I say that the Buddha-nature is future.
"Good son!

For the sake of sentient beings, I sometimes speak of the cause as the effect, and sometimes speak of the effect as the cause. Therefore, in the sutras it is said that life is the nutriment and the perception of forms is contact."
“Because the body will be pure in the future, it is called Buddha-nature.
“World-Honored One!
If the meaning of what the Buddha has said is as you have described, for what reason do you say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature?”
“Good son! Although the Buddha-nature of sentient beings does not exist in the present, it cannot be said to be non-existent;
just as the nature of space, though not existing in the present, cannot be said to be non-existent.”
Although all sentient beings are impermanent, this buddha-nature is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Therefore, in this sutra I have taught that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither internal nor external, just as space is neither internal nor external.
If space possessed internal and external dimensions, space could not be called unitary or eternal, nor could it be said to exist everywhere.
Although space is neither internal nor external, yet all sentient beings possess it;
the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise so.
As for your statement that those who are icchantikas possess wholesome dharmas, this meaning is not so. Why is this?

If those who are icchantikas possess bodily karma, verbal karma, mental karma, the karma of grasping, the karma of seeking, the karma of giving, or the karma of understanding—all such karmas are exclusively false karmas.
Why is this? Because they do not seek cause and effect. Good son!
"Just as the harītakī fruit— its roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits— is entirely bitter,
so too are the karmic actions of an icchantika.
Good son!..."

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of all beings; therefore, he is well able to distinguish the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings. He knows how a person of inferior faculty can transform it into a middling one, how a person of middling faculty can transform it into a superior one, how a person of superior faculty can transform it into a middling one, and how a person of middling faculty can transform it into an inferior one.
Therefore, one should know that the faculties and natures of sentient beings are not fixed.
Because they are not fixed, some may sever their roots of goodness, yet having severed them, these roots may grow back again.
If the faculties and natures of sentient beings were fixed, they would never first sever [the roots of goodness] and then have them arise again;
nor should it be said that those of the icchantika class fall into hell for a lifespan of one kalpa.
“Good son! For this reason, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas have no fixed characteristics.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of all beings; you must surely have known that Sunakṣatra would sever his roots of goodness. For what reason did you permit him to leave the household life?”
The Buddha said, “Good son! In the past,
when I first left the household life, my younger brother Nanda, my cousin Ānanda, Devadatta, and my son Rāhula— all such as these followed me to leave the household life and practice the Way.”

If I had not permitted Sunakṣatra to leave the household life as a monk, he would have succeeded to the royal throne next; with his power and authority, he would have surely destroyed the Buddha-dharma.
For this reason, I permitted him to leave the household life and practice the Way.
“Good son! If the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra had not left the household life, he would likewise have severed his roots of goodness and brought no benefit whatsoever for immeasurable ages.

Now that he has left the household life, although he has severed his roots of goodness, he is able to receive and uphold the precepts, to serve and respect the elders, the seniors, and those of virtuous character, and to cultivate the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; this is called a wholesome cause.”
In this way, wholesome causes can give rise to wholesome dharmas;
once wholesome dharmas have arisen, one is able to cultivate the Path;
having cultivated the Path, one shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, I permitted Sunakṣatra to leave the household life.
Son of good family,
had I not permitted the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra to leave the household life and receive the precepts, I could not have been called a Tathāgata endowed with the ten powers.
"Good son! The Buddha observes that sentient beings are endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Although such persons possess these two types of dharmas, they will before long sever all roots of goodness and become possessed of unwholesome roots."

Why is this? Because such sentient beings do not associate with virtuous friends, do not listen to the true Dharma, do not engage in correct reflection, and do not act in accordance with the Dharma; by these causes and conditions, they are able to sever their roots of goodness and become possessed of unwholesome roots.

“Good son! The Tathāgata further knows that this person—in the present life or in future lives, whether in youth, middle age, or old age—will draw near to virtuous friends and listen to and receive the true Dharma: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. At that time, they will be able to regenerate their roots of goodness.”
Good son! It is like a spring not far from a village, its water sweet and endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.

Suppose there is a person suffering from heat and thirst who wishes to go to the spring; a wise person standing nearby observes this thirsty man and knows for certain, without doubt, that he will reach the water.
Why is this? Because there is no other path.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, observes all sentient beings in this very same way; therefore, the Tathāgata is said to be fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of others.
At that time, the World-Honored One took a small amount of dust from the ground, placed it upon his fingernail, and said to Kāśyapa:
"Is this dust more, or is the earth and dust of the worlds of the ten directions more?"
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The dust upon my fingernail cannot be compared to all the dust that exists throughout the ten directions.”

“Good son! There are those who, having abandoned their bodies, regain a human body; having abandoned the bodies of the three evil realms, receive a human body; possess all faculties intact and are born in a central land; are endowed with right faith, are able to cultivate the Path, and having cultivated the Path, are able to attain liberation; and having attained liberation, are able to enter Nirvāṇa—such as the soil on a fingernail. Those who, having abandoned a human body, obtain the bodies of the three evil realms;

having abandoned the bodies of the three evil realms, obtain further bodies of the three evil realms; whose faculties are incomplete and who are born in a borderland; who believe in heterodox and inverted views, cultivate false views, fail to attain liberation, and do not reach the eternal bliss of Nirvāṇa—such as all the earth and soil throughout the worlds of the ten directions.”
"Good son!

Those who uphold the prohibitive precepts, who are diligent and tireless, who do not commit the four grave offenses, who do not commit the five heinous crimes, who do not misappropriate the property of the Sangha, who do not become icchantikas, who do not sever their roots of goodness, and who believe in such Nirvana sutras as these, are like the soil on a fingernail.

Those who violate the precepts and are indolent, who commit the four grave prohibitions, who commit the five heinous crimes, who misappropriate the property of the Sangha, who become icchantikas, who sever all roots of goodness, and who do not believe in this sutra, are like all the earth and soil throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
“Good son! The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings; for this reason, the Buddha is said to be endowed with the power of knowing faculties.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with this power of knowing the faculties; therefore, he is able to know the distinctions among the superior, middling, and inferior faculties, as well as the sharpness or dullness of all sentient beings. He knows the faculties of sentient beings in the present world, and he also knows the faculties of sentient beings in the future.”
Thus, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, these sentient beings will speak as follows:
"The Tathāgata has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa," or "He has not ultimately entered parinirvāṇa";
or they will say "there is a self," or "there is no self"; or they will say "there is an intermediate state (antarābhava)," or "there is no intermediate state"; or they will say...

Some say there is retrogression, while others say there is no retrogression; some say the Tathāgata’s body is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while others say the Tathāgata’s body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
some say the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are conditioned phenomena, while others say the links of dependent origination are unconditioned phenomena;
some say the mind is eternal, while others say the mind is impermanent.
Regarding permanence, some say that the enjoyment of the five sensual pleasures can obstruct the Noble Path, while others say it does not;
some say that the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma) belongs only to the Desire Realm, while others say it belongs to all three realms;
some say that giving is solely a mental action (manas-karma), while others say it is the five aggregates (pañca-skandha); and some say there are three [types].
Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), some say there are no three unconditioned phenomena;
others say there may be derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), while others say there may be no derived matter;
some say there is non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*), while others say there is no non-informative matter; and some say there are mental factors (*caitasikadharma*). Or else...
Regarding the statement that there are no mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), some say there are five kinds of existence (*bhava*), while others say there are six kinds of existence;
some say that the eightfold precepts of the *upavāsa* and the *upāsaka* precepts are obtained through full reception, while others say they are obtained without full reception;
or it is said that once a monk has committed the four grave offenses (*catur- pārājika*), he is [no longer] a monk.
Regarding the precepts, some say they exist and others say they do not;
some say that those who have attained the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat all attain the Buddha-way, while others say they do not;
some say that buddha-nature exists within sentient beings, while others say that buddha-nature is separate from sentient beings. Or...
Some say that those who have committed the four grave offenses, those who have perpetrated the five heinous crimes, and icchantikas all possess Buddha-nature;
others say they do not. Some say there are Buddhas of the ten directions, while others say there are no Buddhas of the ten directions.
"If the Tathāgata is fully accomplished in the power of knowing the faculties of beings, why does he not provide a definitive teaching today?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"Good son!..."
This meaning is not known by visual consciousness, nor even by mental consciousness; it is that which can be known only by wisdom.
If there is one who possesses wisdom, I never make a dualistic distinction regarding such a person—this is what is meant by my not making dualistic statements.
Toward those who lack wisdom, I make indeterminate statements, yet those lacking wisdom likewise claim that I am making indeterminate statements.

"Good son! All the virtuous deeds of the Tathāgata are for the purpose of taming all sentient beings; it is, for example, like a king of physicians whose medical prescriptions are entirely for the purpose of curing all suffering from illness."

“Good son! For the sake of the land, for the sake of the time, for the sake of the words of others, for the sake of individuals, and for the sake of the various faculties of beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, makes two kinds of explanations regarding a single dharma; he explains immeasurable names for a single named dharma, explains immeasurable names for a single meaning, and explains immeasurable names for immeasurable meanings.”
"How is it that a single name expresses immeasurable names?"

Just as with *nirvāṇa*, it is called by the name "Nirvāṇa," and also called "Non-arising," "Non-emergence," "Non-action," "Unconditioned," "Refuge," "Abode," "Liberation," "Radiance," "Lamp-light," "The Further Shore," "Fearlessness," "Non-retrogression," "Peaceful Abiding," "Quiescence," "Signless," "Non-dual," "Single Practice," "Coolness," "Darkness-free," "Unobstructed," "Non-contentious," "Undefiled," "Vast," "Amṛta (Ambrosia)," and "Auspiciousness. Thus, what is a single name is made into immeasurable names.
"What is meant by 'one meaning expressed through immeasurable names'?

It is like Śakra, who is called Śakra, Kausika, Vāsava, Purandara, Maghavan, Indra, Sahasranetra, Śacīpati, Vajrin, Ratnaśikhin, and Ratnadhvaja; this is what is meant by one meaning expressed through immeasurable names."
"How is it that for immeasurable meanings there are immeasurable names?
For example, the Buddha Tathāgata is called 'Tathāgata,' where the meaning differs from the name;
he is also called 'Arhat,' where the meaning differs from the name."
He is also called Samyaksaṃbuddha, with different meanings and different names;
he is also called the Captain of the Ship, the Guide, the Perfectly Awakened One,
the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Great Lion King, the Śramaṇa, and the Brāhmaṇa.
He is named Tranquility; he is also named Donor; he is also named One Who Has Reached the Further Shore; he is also named Great King of Physicians;
he is also named Great Elephant King; he is also named Great Dragon King; he is also named Bestower of Eyes; he is also named Great Malla;
he is also named Great Fearlessness; he is also named Heap of Jewels; he is also named Caravan Leader.

He is also called "One Who Has Attained Liberation," "Great Man," "Teacher of Gods and Humans," "Great Pundarika," "Solitary Peerless One," "Great Field of Merit," "Ocean of Great Wisdom," "Formless One," and "One Endowed with the Eight Knowledges"— all such names as these.
The meanings differ and the names differ. Good son!
This is called explaining immeasurable names within immeasurable meanings.
Furthermore, there is another sense in which it is described by immeasurable names.

That which is called the aggregates (*skandha*) is also named the coverings (*āvaraṇa*), also named perversions (*viparyāsa*), also named truths (*satya*), also named the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), also named the four nutriments (*āhāra*), also named the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), also named existence (*bhava*), also named the path (*mārga*), also named time (*kāla*), also named sentient beings (*sattva*), also named the world (*loka*), also named the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), also named the three cultivations—namely, body, precepts, and mind—also named cause and effect (*hetu-phala*), also named afflictions (*kleśa*), also named liberation (*vimukti*), also named the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), also named śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, also named hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas, and also named the past, present, and future. This is called "one meaning expressed by immeasurable names."

“Good son! For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, explains the detailed within the concise and the concise within the detailed; he explains the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and explains the conventional dharmas as the ultimate truth.”
What is meant by "a brief exposition within an extensive teaching"?
It is as when he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now proclaim the twelve links of dependent origination."
"What is meant by the twelve links of dependent origination?
It refers to cause and effect.
"What is meant by 'expanding upon the brief'?"
As it was told to the bhikṣus:
"I now proclaim suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
As for suffering, it refers to immeasurable sufferings;..."
Accumulation refers to immeasurable afflictions;
cessation refers to immeasurable liberations;
and the path refers to immeasurable skillful means.
What is meant by explaining the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)?
It is as when he told the bhikṣus:
"In this body of mine now, there are old age, sickness, and death."
What is meant by designating that which is conventional truth as ultimate truth?
It is as when [the Buddha] addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"Because you have realized the Dharma, you are named Ajñāta-Kauṇḍinya."
Therefore, because it accords with persons, intentions, and times, it is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the faculties of others. “Good son!
If I were to provide a definitive explanation regarding such matters as these, I could not be called a Tathāgata who possesses the power of knowing the faculties.”
“Good son! A person of wisdom should know that what a fragrant elephant can carry cannot be borne by a donkey.
The practices of all sentient beings are immeasurable; therefore, the Tathāgata expounds immeasurable teachings in various ways.”
Why is this? Because sentient beings possess many afflictions.
If the Tathāgata were to teach only a single practice, he could not be said to be fully endowed with the power of knowing the faculties of others.
Therefore, in other sūtras I have said: "There are five kinds of beings for whom one should not preach five kinds of teachings:

one should not praise right faith to those who lack faith; one should not praise the observance of precepts to those who violate them; one should not praise giving to those who are stingy and greedy; one should not praise extensive learning to those who are indolent; and one should not praise wisdom to those who are ignorant."

Why is this? If a wise person were to explain these five matters to these five kinds of people, one should know that such a speaker does not possess the complete power of knowledge regarding the faculties (*indriya-bala*), nor can they be called one who has compassion for sentient beings.

Why is this? Because when these five kinds of people hear this matter, they give rise to lack of faith, malevolence, and anger; by reason of these causes and conditions, they will undergo the retribution of suffering for immeasurable eons.
Therefore, this is not called having compassion for sentient beings or being endowed with the faculty of knowledge and power.
For this reason, I previously told Śāriputra in another sutra:
"Be careful not to preach the Dharma extensively to those of sharp faculties, nor preach it briefly to those of dull faculties."
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
I have spoken only out of compassion; it was not because I possess the full power of the faculties.”
"Good son! The teaching of the Dharma, whether extensive or concise, is the domain of the Buddhas; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Good son!"

As you have said, regarding those disciples who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, each propounded different doctrines: these people all failed to attain right view due to inverted causes and conditions; therefore, they were unable to benefit themselves or others.

“Good son! These sentient beings do not possess a single nature, a single practice, a single faculty, a single land, or a single spiritual friend; therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims various essential teachings for them.”

For this reason, the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, have revealed, shown, and expounded the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings. Good son!
The Tathāgata’s teaching of these twelve divisions of the sūtras is not for his own benefit, but solely for the benefit of others.
Therefore, the fifth power of the Tathāgata is called the power of understanding.

By means of these two powers, the Tathāgata thoroughly knows that this person is able to sever their roots of goodness in the present life, while that person is able to sever their roots of goodness in a future life; he also knows that this person is able to attain liberation in the present life, while that person is able to attain liberation in a future life.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is called the Unsurpassed Hero. "Good son!
If one says that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate nirvāṇa or has not entered ultimate nirvāṇa, such a person speaks thus because they do not understand the intention of the Tathāgata."
"Good son!

In this Fragrant Mountain there are fifty-three thousand rishis who, in the past, cultivated various merits under Kāśyapa Buddha but had not yet attained the Right Path; they have drawn near to the Buddhas and listened to and received the True Dharma."
For the sake of such people as these, the Tathāgata addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Three months from now, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
When the devas heard this, the sound was passed from one to another until it reached Mount Gandhamādana.
Upon hearing this, the sages immediately gave rise to a sense of regret and spoke these words:
"How is it that we, having been born among humans, have not drawn near to the Buddha?
The appearance of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; we shall now go to the presence of the World-Honored One to listen to and receive the True Dharma."
"Good son! At that time, fifty-three thousand sages came to my presence.
I then preached the Dharma to them according to their needs."
"O Great Beings!
Form is impermanent. Why is this so?
Because the causes and conditions of form are impermanent,
and since it is produced from impermanent causes, how could form be permanent?
This applies likewise up to consciousness.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the various sages immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship. "Good son!

In Kuśinagara there were three hundred thousand Mallas who were without any master; they relied on their own pride and indulged in the intoxication of their physical beauty, strength, life-span, and wealth, their minds deranged and maddened."
"Good son!
