For the sake of subduing those Mallas, I said to Maudgalyāyana:
'You should subdue such Mallas as these.'"

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, out of respect and obedience to my instruction, engaged in various forms of teaching and conversion for five years, yet he was unable to cause even a single Malla to receive the Dharma and attain subduing.
Therefore, I again spoke to Ānanda for the sake of those Mallas, saying:
"After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
O son of good family!
When the Mallas had heard these words, they gathered together and leveled the roads.

After three months had passed, I traveled from the kingdom of Vaiśālī to the city of Kuśinagara. On the way, seeing the Mallas from afar, I immediately transformed my body into the likeness of a śramaṇa and went to where the Mallas were, speaking to them thus:
"Young men, what work are you doing?"
Upon hearing this, the Mallas were all filled with resentment and spoke thus:
"Śramaṇa! How can you now claim that we are but children?"
I then said to them:
"If you, this great assembly of three hundred thousand people, cannot move even this tiny stone with all the strength of your bodies, why do you not call yourselves 'children'?"
The Mallas said, "If you consider us to be children, then you yourself should be known as a great man.
"Good son! [the Buddha said].
At that time, I dug out this stone with two toes of my feet.
When those Mallas saw this, they conceived a sense of inferiority toward themselves and spoke thus:
"O Śramaṇa!..."
"Can you now further move this rock and make a path for it to pass through? I said,
"Young man!"
"For what reason and by what cause have you adorned and prepared this road?
The Mallas replied, "O Śramaṇa!"
"Do you not know?
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni shall travel by this very road to the Śāla grove to enter parinirvāṇa; for this reason, we have leveled and smoothed it."
I then praised him, saying:
"Excellent, young man!"
"Since you have already generated such virtuous thoughts, I shall remove this rock for you.
At that time, I lifted it with my hand and hurled it upward as high as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
At that time, when the Mallas saw the stone suspended in the air, they were all struck with terror and immediately sought to disperse in the four directions.
I spoke to them again, saying: "O Mallas!..."
"You should not now give rise to a heart of fear and each wish to disperse.
The Mallas said, "O Śramaṇa!"
"If you can rescue and protect me, I shall abide in peace.
At that time, I again caught the stone with my hand and placed it in my right palm.
Upon seeing this, the strongman felt great joy and spoke these words once more:
“O Śramaṇa! Is this stone permanent,
or is it impermanent?”
At that time, I blew upon it with my mouth, and the stone immediately shattered and crumbled like fine dust.
Upon seeing this, the wrestler cried out:
"Śramaṇa!..."
"This stone is impermanent.
Immediately, a sense of shame arose within him, and he reproached himself:
"How is it that we rely upon our mastery over physical form, strength, life, and wealth, and thereby give rise to arrogance?"
I knew their thoughts and immediately relinquished my transformation body, returning to my original form to preach the Dharma for them.
Upon seeing this, all the Mallas conceived the aspiration for Bodhi.
“Good son! In Kuśinagara there was a craftsman named Cunda, who had previously made this great vow before Kāśyapa Buddha:
‘When the Tathāgata Śākyamuni enters nirvana, I shall be the last to offer him food and drink.’”
"Therefore, in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, I have entrusted my final instructions to the bhikṣu Upamāna: 'Good son!
After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara; you should go and inform Cunda so that he may know.'"

“Good son! In the city of Rājagṛha there was a seer with the five supernatural powers named Subhadra, who was one hundred and twenty years old. He constantly claimed to be an omniscient person and gave rise to great arrogance; yet he had already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas in the past.”
I too, desiring to subdue him, told Ānanda:
"After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, Subhadra will come to me and give rise to a mind of faith and reverence.
"I shall preach various Dharmas for him; having heard them, that person shall attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Good son!

King Bimbisāra of Rājagṛha has a crown prince named Ajātaśatru. Due to the causes and conditions of his karma, he conceived a mind of perversity and rebellion, desiring to harm his father, yet he could find no opportunity."

At that time, the evil man Devadatta, due to the causal conditions of his past karma, again conceived unwholesome thoughts toward me with the desire to harm me; he immediately cultivated the five supernormal powers and soon attained them.

He became close friends with Prince Sudarśana and, for the sake of the prince, manifested various supernatural feats—exiting through what was not a gate and entering through a gate, exiting through a gate and entering through what was not a gate; at times he manifested the bodies of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, and women. Upon seeing these, Prince Sudarśana immediately gave rise to a heart of affection, a heart of joy, and a heart of reverent faith.
For this purpose, he prepared various kinds of offerings and made worship.
He further addressed him, saying:
"O Great Master, Holy One!"
"I now wish to see a māndārava flower.
Thereupon, Devadatta went immediately to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and sought it from the devas there.
Because his merit was exhausted, no one gave him anything at all.
Having failed to obtain any flowers, he reflected thus:
"The *mandārava* tree is without self or what belongs to a self."
"If I were to take it myself, what sin would there be?
He then stepped forward intending to take it, whereupon he immediately lost his supernatural powers and saw himself once again in Rājagṛha.
Feeling shame and remorse in his heart, he could no longer bear to look upon Prince Sudarśana.
He further thought to himself:
"I shall now go to where the Tathāgata is and seek a great assembly."
"If the Buddha would grant me permission, I shall instruct and command Śāriputra and the others according to my will.
At that time, Devadatta came to me and spoke these words:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata entrust this great assembly to me; I shall preach the Dharma in various ways to teach and transform them, so as to bring them to subdual."
I said: "Fool!

Even though Śāriputra and others are of brilliant wisdom and great insight, trusted and revered by the world, I would not yet entrust the great assembly to them; how much less so to you, a fool who eats spit?"
At that time, Devadatta again conceived an even more malicious intent toward me and spoke these words: "Gautama!
Although you now subdue the great assembly, your power shall soon be seen to crumble and perish."
Having spoken these words, the great earth immediately shook in six ways.
At that very moment, Devadatta fell prostrate upon the ground; a violent wind arose from his side, blowing up dust and soil to cover him in filth.
Having seen these evil omens, Devadatta spoke again, saying:
"If this very body of mine must enter the Avīci Hell in this present life, I shall certainly take revenge upon such a great enemy."
Then Devadatta immediately rose and went to where Prince Sudarśana was.
Upon seeing him, Sudarśana asked:
"Noble One!..."
"Why is your countenance so haggard and why do you have such a look of sorrow?
Devadatta replied, "I am always like this; do you not know it?"
Sudarśana replied, "I pray you, explain your intention; by what causes and conditions is this so?
Devadatta said:
"I am now extremely close and affectionate toward you, yet outsiders revile you as being unrighteous.
Hearing this matter, how could I not be grieved?
Prince Sudarśana spoke again, saying:
"What did the people of the country say to insult me?
Devadatta replied,
"The people of the country have insulted you by calling you 'Unborn Enemy' (Ajātaśatru)."
Sudarśana spoke again:
"For what reason am I named 'Unborn Enemy' (Ajātaśatru)?
Who gave me this name?"
Devadatta said: "Before you were born, all the physiognomists made this prediction:
'Once this child is born, he shall kill his father.'"
"For this reason, all outsiders have called you 'The Unborn Enemy' (Ajātaśatru).
Because all those within the palace protected your heart, they called you 'Good Vision' (Sudarśana).
When Queen Vaidehī heard these words, once you were born upon the high tower, she cast you down to the ground, which broke off one of your fingers."
For this reason, people shall again call you Pāruṣya.
Having heard this, my heart was filled with grief and distress, yet I could not bring myself to tell it to you.
Devadatta instructed him with various such evil deeds, commanding him to kill his father, saying:
"If your father dies, I too shall be able to kill the śramaṇa Gautama."
Prince Sudarśana asked a high minister named Varṣākāra:
"For what reason did the Great King give me the name 'Ajātaśatru' (Unborn Enemy)?
The minister then explained the origin of the matter from beginning to end, exactly as Devadatta had related it.
Upon hearing this, Susīma immediately had the great ministers seize his father, the king, and confined him outside the city, guarding him with the fourfold army.
When Queen Vaidehī heard of these events, she went at once to the king’s location, but the guards blocked her way and would not allow her to enter.
At that time, the queen gave rise to a mind of anger and began to revile him.
Then the guards immediately informed the prince:
"The Great King’s queen wishes to see the Father King; we do not know whether she will be granted an audience."
Upon hearing this, Bimbisāra again gave rise to anger and resentment; he went at once to his mother’s quarters, seized her hair, drew his sword, and was about to strike her down.
At that moment, Jīvaka addressed him, saying:
“Great King!”
"Since I have possessed this kingdom, even the most extreme crimes have not been committed against women, much less one's own mother.
Upon hearing these words, Prince Sudarśana immediately released Jīvaka for his sake.
He cut off his father the king’s clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions; after seven days had passed, the king’s life came to an end.
Upon seeing his father’s death, Prince Sudarśana finally gave rise to a heart of remorse.
The minister Vṛṣṭika further expounded various evil and heterodox doctrines to him, saying: "Great King!
All karmic actions are entirely without fault; for what reason do you now give rise to a mind of regret?"
Jīva spoke again: "Great King,
you should know that such an action carries a double weight of sin."
"First, he killed his father, the king; second, he killed a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
For such a sinner, there is none other than the Buddha who can eliminate and extinguish these offenses.
King Sudarśana said:
“The Tathāgata is pure and free from all defilement;
how can we, who are sinful people, behold him? “Good son!
Knowing this matter, I told Ānanda:
"After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Having heard this, Sudarśana immediately came to where I was.
I preached the Dharma for them, whereby their heavy offenses were lightened and they attained rootless faith.
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and therefore speak these words:"
“The Tathāgata has definitively taught ultimate nirvāṇa.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:”
First is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), and second is conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
When bodhisattvas who rely on conventional designations hear that I shall enter parinirvāṇa after three months, they all give rise to thoughts of regression and say:
"If the Tathāgata is impermanent and does not abide, for what purpose should we undergo such great suffering and affliction throughout immeasurable lifetimes for his sake?"
Even the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who has fully accomplished and perfected immeasurable merits, cannot destroy such a Mara of Death; how much less could those like us possibly destroy it?
"Good son! For this reason, I speak these words for the sake of such bodhisattvas:
'The Tathāgata is eternally abiding and undergoes no change.'"
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and definitively declare that the Tathāgata will never ultimately enter parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! There are sentient beings who give rise to the view of annihilationism and speak thus:
‘After the bodies of all sentient beings have perished, there is no one to receive the fruits of their good and evil karma.’”
For such people, I speak these words:
"The retribution for good and evil deeds truly has one who experiences it.
How do we know it exists?
"Good son!

In a past age, there was a king in Kuśinagara named Sudarśana. He spent eighty-four thousand years as a youth, eighty-four thousand years as a crown prince, and likewise eighty-four thousand years upon ascending the throne."
Sitting in solitude, he reflected thus:
"Sentient beings have meager merit and short lifespans; they are constantly pursued by four enemies, yet they remain unaware of this and continue to be heedless."
"Therefore, I shall leave the household life to practice the Way and sever the four enemies—birth, old age, sickness, and death.
He then commanded his officials to construct a hall made of the seven treasures outside the city.
Having done so, he then addressed his ministers, officials, palace ladies and consorts, sons, and kinsmen:
"You should know this:
I wish to leave the household life."
"Can you see and hear?
At that time, the great minister and his retinue each spoke these words:
"Excellent."
"Great King!
Now is precisely the right time.
Then, King Sudarśana took a single attendant and went alone up to the hall.

Furthermore, for eighty-four thousand years he practiced the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). By virtue of these causes and conditions of loving-kindness, in subsequent eighty-four thousand lifetimes he successively became a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin rājā*); in thirty lifetimes he became Śakra Devendra; and in immeasurable lifetimes he became various minor kings.
"Good son! At that time, was King Sudarśana anyone else?
Do not view it so; he was none other than myself."
“Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
‘The Tathāgata definitively teaches that there is a self and that there is what belongs to a self.’”
"Furthermore, at one time I spoke to all sentient beings, saying:

'The self is precisely nature—namely, internal and external causes and conditions, the twelve links of dependent origination, the five aggregates of sentient beings, the mental realm, worldly meritorious deeds and karmic actions, and the world of the sovereign god Maheśvara; these are what is called the self.'"
“When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
‘The Tathāgata definitely teaches that there is a self. Good son!
Again, at another time, a certain bhikṣu came to where I was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
What is meant by 'self'?"
"Who am I? For what reason am I?
At that time, I spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Monks! There is no self and nothing belonging to a self.

The eye is originally non-existent and now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence. When it arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere. Although there is the fruit of karma, there is no agent, and there is no one who casts off the aggregates or receives them."
Regarding what you asked concerning "what is the self," the self is simply time;
regarding "who is the self," it is karma;
regarding "by what cause is there a self," it is craving.
"O Bhikṣus!
Just as when two hands clap together, sound issues from between them, so too am I:
by reason of the three conditions—sentient beings, karma, and craving—I am designated as 'I'."
"Monks! For all sentient beings, form is not the self; within the self there is no form, and within form there is no self.
This applies likewise, up to and including consciousness."
"O Bhikṣus!
Although the various non-Buddhist practitioners speak of a self, it ultimately does not exist apart from the aggregates (skandhas).
If one were to say that there is a self existing separately from the aggregates, such a thing is impossible."
The conduct of all sentient beings is like an illusion or a magical transformation, like a mirage in the heat. Bhikṣus!
The five aggregates are all impermanent, without pleasure, without self, and without purity.
"Good son! At that time, there were many immeasurable bhikṣus who, contemplating these five aggregates as being without self or what belongs to a self, attained the fruit of arhatship.
Good son!"
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has definitively taught that there is no self.
O son of good family!
In the sūtras, I have further stated:
"The convergence of three factors results in the acquisition of this body:
first, the father; second, the mother; and third, the intermediate state (antarābhava). Through the conjunction of these three, one acquires this body."
At other times, he further says:
"Anāgāmins attain parinirvāṇa in the present life, or they enter parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Or again, he says:
“The intermediate state being possesses complete and clear faculties, all resulting from past karma like refined clarified butter.
Son of good family!
At times I have said:

"The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) experienced by wicked sentient beings is like the coarse and rough woolen cloth of the world; the intermediate state experienced by purely virtuous sentient beings is like the white cotton cloth produced in Vārāṇasī."
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata says there is an intermediate state (antarābhava). Good son!"
I further spoke these words for the sake of those sentient beings who have committed the five heinous crimes:
"Those who commit the five heinous crimes will, upon casting off their bodies, enter directly into the Avīci Hell.
I further said:
"The bhikṣu Dharmaruci cast off his body and entered directly into the Avīci Hell; in the interval between these two, there was no place for him to rest.
I further said to that brahmin Vatsa: "Brahmin!..."
"If there were an intermediate state (antarābhava), there would be six states of existence. I further said:
"Formless sentient beings have no intermediate state."
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Buddha has definitively stated that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava).'"
"Good son! In the sūtras, I have further taught that there is falling back. Why is this?
Due to immeasurable indolence and laziness, because the bhikṣus do not cultivate the Path, five kinds of retrogression are taught:

first, delighting in many affairs; second, delighting in speaking of worldly matters; third, delighting in sleep; fourth, delighting in associating with householders; and fifth, delighting in frequent wandering.
For these reasons, they cause a bhikṣu to fall away.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes and conditions for falling away:
first, internal; second, external.
Although an Arhat has abandoned internal causes, he has not abandoned external causes;
because of these external conditions, afflictions arise,
and because afflictions arise, he consequently falls away.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu named Gautika who fell back six times;
having fallen, he felt shame and remorse, and practicing with renewed diligence, he attained it on the seventh attempt.
Having attained it, he feared losing it again, and so he took his own life with a knife.
Furthermore, I have at times spoken of "liberation through occasion" (sāmayikī vimukti), or spoken of the six types of arhats, and so forth.
Having heard these teachings, my disciples fail to understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has definitively stated that there is falling away."
“Good son! In the sutras it is further said:
‘For example, once charcoal has been burnt, it cannot become wood again; likewise, once a jar is broken, it no longer serves the function of a jar.’”
Afflictions are likewise; once severed by an Arhat, they never arise again.
It is also said:
"There are three kinds of causes for the arising of afflictions in sentient beings: [the cause of past habituation, the cause of present conditions, and the cause of ignorance]."
First, the non-abandonment of afflictions; second, the non-interruption of causal conditions; and third, unwholesome reflection.
An Arhat, however, is free from these two causal conditions—namely, the abandonment of afflictions and the absence of unwholesome reflection.
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata has definitively stated that there is no falling back.'"
"Good son! In the sūtras, I have said:
'The body of the Tathāgata is of two kinds:'"
First is the birth-body (*janmakāya*), and second is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
What is called the birth-body refers to the body manifested through skillful means (*upāya*) and transformation (*nirmāṇa*).

Such a body may be said to be subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death; it has length or shortness, black or white; it is "this" or "that"; and it is either a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
"Having heard these words, my disciples, failing to understand my intention, proclaimed:
'The Tathāgata has definitively stated that the Buddha-body is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛtadharma).'"

“The Dharma-body is itself permanence, bliss, self, and purity; it is forever free from all birth, old age, sickness, and death; it is neither white nor black, neither long nor short, neither this nor that, and neither a learner nor one beyond learning.”
"Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, it remains eternally abiding and immovable, without change or alteration.
Son of Good Family!
Having heard this teaching, my disciples do not understand my intention and proclaim:
“The Tathāgata has definitively taught that the Buddha-body is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). “Good son!
In my sūtras I have said:”
"What is called the twelve links of dependent origination?

From ignorance arise volitional formations; from volitional formations arises consciousness; from consciousness arise name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact; from contact arises sensation; from sensation arises craving; from craving arises clinging; from clinging arises existence; from existence arises birth; and from birth come old age, death, sorrow, and suffering."
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata has said that the twelve links of dependent origination are definitely conditioned.'"
"Furthermore, on another occasion, I instructed the bhikṣus, saying:
'Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the intrinsic nature and characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination remain eternally constant.'"

"Good son! There are things that are dependent origination but do not arise from conditions; there are things that arise from conditions but are not dependent origination; there are things that both arise from conditions and are dependent origination; and there are things that neither arise from conditions nor are dependent origination."
There are twelve links that are not produced from conditions, namely the twelve factors of the future life;
there are those produced from conditions that are not the twelve links, namely the five aggregates possessed by an Arhat;
and there are those produced from conditions that are also the twelve links, namely the five aggregates and twelve causal links possessed by ordinary worldlings.
There are things that are neither produced by conditions nor part of the twelve links of dependent origination; these are space and nirvana.
Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim:
“The Tathāgata has taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are definitively unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). “Good son!
In my sūtras I have said:”
"When all sentient beings perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds, at the moment they cast off the body, the four great elements disintegrate instantly.
For those whose karma is purely wholesome, the mind ascends;
for those whose karma is purely unwholesome, the mind descends."
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata says that the mind is definitely permanent.'"
"Good son! At one time, for the sake of King Bimbisāra, I spoke these words:
'Great King, you should know:'"
Form is impermanent.
Why is this? Because it arises from causes that are themselves impermanent.
If this form arises from impermanent causes, how could the wise say it is permanent?
If form were permanent, it should not undergo destruction or give rise to various sufferings and afflictions.
"Now we see that this form is dispersed, extinguished, and destroyed; therefore, one should know that form is impermanent.
This applies likewise, up to and including consciousness. "Good son!"
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata says that the mind is definitively severed. Good son!
In my sutras I have said:
"My disciples receive various incense, flowers, gold, silver, precious objects, wives, children, slaves, and hundreds of impure things, yet they attain the Right Path;
having attained the Right Path, they do not abandon them."
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and definitively say:
'The Tathāgata has taught that experiencing the five desires does not obstruct the holy path.'"
"Furthermore, at one time I also said this:
'It is impossible for a person living at home to attain the Right Path. Good son!"
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has said that the enjoyment of the five desires certainly obstructs the right path. "Good son!
In my sutras I have said:
"To be far removed from afflictions yet not yet to have attained liberation is like one in the desire realm who is cultivating the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
O son of good family!
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has said that the foremost dharma exists only in the desire realm.
Furthermore, I have also said:
"The stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas exist from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they fail to understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata says that these dharmas exist within the realm of form (rūpadhātu)."
"Furthermore, I have said:

'Those of other paths who have previously attained the severance of the afflictions of the four dhyānas, and have cultivated the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma, and who contemplate the Four Noble Truths, shall attain the fruit of Anāgāmin.'"
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata says that the foremost dharma exists in the formless realm.'"
"Good son! In my sutras I have said:
'Among the four kinds of giving, there are three kinds of purity:'"
First, the donor has faith in the cause, faith in the result, and faith in giving, while the recipient does not;
second, the recipient has faith in the cause, the result, and giving, while the donor does not;
third, both the donor and the recipient possess faith.
"Fourth, there is the case where neither the donor nor the recipient has faith.
Among these four kinds of giving, the first three are pure.
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
“The Tathāgata has said that giving consists solely of the mind. “Good son!
At another time, I further spoke thus:”
"When a donor gives, they give by means of five things. What are these five?
First, the gift of physical form; second, the gift of strength; third, the gift of peace; fourth, the gift of life; and fifth, the gift of eloquence."
"For these reasons, the donor shall receive five kinds of retributive fruits.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Buddha says that giving is itself the five aggregates."
"Good son! At one time I proclaimed:
'Nirvāṇa is detachment; it is the eternal exhaustion of afflictions, extinguished without remainder.'"
Just as when a lamp is extinguished, no further light can arise;
so it is with nirvāṇa.
That which is called "space" is simply nothingness.
For example, it is called "empty space" because nothing exists therein.
The cessation not through wisdom (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not simply non-existence;
if it were an existent thing, it would necessarily have causes and conditions.
"Because there are causes and conditions, there should be exhaustion and cessation;
because they do not exist, there is no exhaustion or cessation.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Buddha said that there are no three and no unconditioned [phenomena]. "Good son!
At one time, for the sake of Maudgalyāyana, I spoke these words:"
“Maudgalyāyana!

That which is called *nirvāṇa* is the very words and phrases, it is the footprint; it is the ultimate state, it is fearlessness; it is the Great Teacher, it is the Great Fruit, it is ultimate wisdom, it is the Great Patience and the Unimpeded Samādhi, it is the Great Dharma-realm, it is the taste of ambrosia, and it is difficult to behold.”
"Maudgalyāyana!
If one were to say that there is no nirvāṇa, how could those who give rise to slander fall into hell? Good son!"
"When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
'The Tathāgata says there is nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, at another time, I made this statement for the sake of Maudgalyāyana:"
“Maudgalyāyana!
The eye is not solid; it is the same for the body and all other parts—they are all not solid.
Because they are not solid, they are called ‘empty space.’”
"The place where food descends, circulates, and is digested, as well as all sounds, are all called 'space' (ākāśa).
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has definitively stated that space is an unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta-dharma)."
"Furthermore, on another occasion, he said to Maudgalyāyana:
'Maudgalyāyana!

When a person who has not yet attained the fruit of a srotāpanna abides in the stage of patience (kṣānti-dharma), they sever the retribution of immeasurable three evil realms; you should know that this extinction does not arise from the conditions of wisdom.'"
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata has definitively stated that there is cessation not through conditions (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).'"
“Good son! On another occasion, I said to the bhikṣu Bāspa:
‘If a bhikṣu contemplates form—whether past, future, or present; whether near or far; whether coarse or subtle—all such forms are not self, nor do they belong to a self.’”
"If there is a bhikṣu who, having contemplated in this way, is able to sever craving for form," Bāpaka spoke again:
"What is called 'form'?"
I said: "The four great elements are called form (rūpa); the four aggregates (skandhas) are called name (nāma).
Having heard this teaching, my disciples did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
“The Tathāgata has definitively declared that form consists of the four great elements. “Good son!
I have further stated:”
"Just as an image appears because of a mirror, so too is form:

it is produced by the four great elements, namely—coarse and fine, rough and smooth, blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, oblong, light, heavy, cold, hot, hunger, thirst, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist."
"This is called derived form (upādāya-rūpa), which is like an echo or a reflection.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata says that because there are the four great elements (mahābhūta), there is derived form."
"Or there may be no four great elements, and thus no derived form. "Good son!
Once in the past, Prince Bodhi spoke these words:"
"If there is a bhikṣu who upholds the prohibitive precepts, yet gives rise to an evil mind, you should know that at that moment he loses his bhikṣu-precepts.
At that time, I said to him:
"Prince Bodhi!..."
There are seven kinds of precepts; from body and speech, there arises non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).

Because of this non-informative matter as a causal condition, even if the mind is within the states of evil or the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not called a loss of the precepts, but is still called upholding the precepts.
"For what reason is it called 'unconditioned form' (avijñapti-rūpa)?
It is not because it is a cause distinct from form, nor does it produce a fruit that is a distinct form.
"Good son! [The Buddha said:]
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Buddha has said that there is such a thing as unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa). Good son!
In another sutra, I have spoken thus:
"Precepts are that which restrain unwholesome dharmas;
if one does not commit evil, this is called upholding the precepts."
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata has definitively declared that there is no such thing as unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa).'"
"Good son! In the sūtras I have made this statement:
'The noble ones' aggregates of form, up to the aggregate of consciousness, all arise from the causal conditions of ignorance.'"
All ordinary beings are likewise thus: from ignorance arises craving; one should know that this craving is itself ignorance.
From craving arises grasping; one should know that this grasping is itself ignorance and craving.
From grasping arises becoming; this becoming is itself ignorance, craving, and grasping.
From the arising of sensation (*vedanā*), one should know that this sensation is itself the formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*).

From the conditions of sensation arise name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), formations (*saṃskāra*), sensation (*vedanā*), contact (*sparśa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and so forth; therefore, sensation is itself the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata says there are no mental factors (caitta).'"
"Good son! In a sutra, I have spoken thus:
'From the four factors of the eye, forms, light, and unwholesome desire, visual consciousness arises.'"
What is called "evil desire" is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*). When the nature of desire seeks [its object], it is termed craving (*tṛṣṇā*);

with craving as its condition, there is grasping (*upādāna*); grasping is termed karma; with karma as its condition, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); with consciousness as its condition, there are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); with name-and-form as their condition, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); with the six sense bases as their condition, there is contact (*sparśa*); and with contact as its condition, there arise perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Such dharmas as these arise because of contact, yet they are not contact itself.
Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
“The Tathāgata has spoken of mental factors (caitasika). “Good son!
At times I speak of there being only one existence; at other times I speak of two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, up to twenty-five.”
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has said that there are five kinds of existence. Or they say:
“Six existences.
“Good son! Once, when I was dwelling in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu, Śreṇika Bimbisāra came to where I was and spoke these words:”
"What is meant by the term 'upāsaka'?
I then explained to him:
"If there is a son or daughter of good family whose faculties are complete and who receives the three refuges, they are called an upāsaka."
Śreṇika Bimbisāra said:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by a ‘lay follower who observes one part’?”
I said: "If one receives the three refuges and observes a single precept, this is called a 'one-part' upāsaka.
Having heard these words, my disciples did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
“The Tathāgata has said that the upāsaka precepts can be obtained even if not received in their entirety. “Good son!
At one time, I was dwelling by the banks of the Ganges River.”
At that time, Kātyāyana came to where I was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
I teach sentient beings to receive the precepts of the fast, whether for one day, or one night, or one period, or even for a single thought-moment. Do such persons fulfill the fast?"
I said: "Bhikṣu! This person has gained merit, but it is not called attaining the fast."
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata says that the eightfold precept fast can only be attained by receiving it in its entirety.'"
“Good son! In the sūtras, I have spoken thus:
‘If a bhikṣu commits the four pārājika offenses, he is no longer called a bhikṣu; he is called a “broken bhikṣu” or a “lost bhikṣu,” and can no longer produce the seeds of the sprouts of goodness.’”
For example, a scorched seed does not produce fruit;
likewise, if the crown of a tāla tree is severed or destroyed, it will no longer bear fruit;
so too it is with a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata has said that once a bhikṣu has committed a grave transgression, he has lost his bhikṣu precepts."
“Good son! In a sutra, I have spoken of four kinds of bhikṣus for the sake of Cunda:
first, those who have ultimately reached the Way; second, those who show the Way; third, those who receive the Way; and fourth, those who defile the Way.”
"One who commits the four grave offenses is one who defiles the Way.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Tathāgata says that even if bhikṣus commit the four grave offenses, they do not lose their prohibitive precepts.'"
“Good son! In a sutra, I told the bhikṣus: ‘There is one vehicle, one path, one practice, and one object.

In this way, this single vehicle up to this single object can bring great tranquility to sentient beings, forever severing all bonds, grief and suffering, as well as suffering and its causes, and causing all beings to reach the state of singular existence.’”
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Tathāgata says that those from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat all attain the path of Buddhahood."
“Good son! In the sūtras, I have said:
‘The srotāpanna, after wandering seven times between the human and celestial realms, attains parinirvāṇa;’”
The Sakṛdāgāmin attains parinirvāṇa after having experienced one more birth in the human or celestial realms;
the Anāgāmin is of five types, ranging from those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state to those who attain parinirvāṇa by ascending to the highest realm;
the Arhat is generally of two types:
First is the present, and second is the future; in the present one cuts off the afflictions and the five aggregates, and in the future one likewise cuts off the afflictions and the five aggregates.
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
"The Tathāgata says that from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat, one does not attain the path to Buddhahood."
“Good son! In this sutra, I have said:
‘The Buddha-nature possesses six things:’”
"First, permanence; second, reality; third, truth; fourth, goodness; fifth, purity; sixth, visibility.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Buddha says that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings."
"Good son! I have also said:
'The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space.'"
Space is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is neither internal nor external, and is not comprised of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, or touch;
the Buddha-nature is likewise.
"When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
'The Buddha says that the buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings.'"
"Good son! I have further said:

'The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like a treasure trove within the house of a poor woman, a diamond jewel upon the forehead of a powerful wrestler, and a spring of ambrosia belonging to a wheel-turning sage king.'"
When my disciples heard this teaching, they did not understand my intention and proclaimed:
"The Buddha has said that the buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings."
“Good son! I have also said:

‘Those who have committed the four grave offenses, icchantikas, those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, and those who have committed the five heinous crimes all possess Buddha-nature; yet such sentient beings lack all wholesome dharmas.’”
"Buddha-nature is wholesome.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Buddha says that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings."
“Good son! I have further said:
‘Sentient beings are themselves the Buddha-nature.’”
Why is this? Because if one is separated from sentient beings, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, I spoke the parable of the elephant to King Prasenajit.
It is like the blind men describing an elephant: although they do not grasp the elephant itself, they do not depart from it.
It is the same with sentient beings who describe form, up to and including consciousness, as being the Buddha-nature; although these are not the Buddha-nature, they are not non-Buddha-nature either.
"Just as I spoke the parable of the lute for the sake of the king, so too is the Buddha-nature.
Good son! Having heard this teaching, my disciples do not understand my intention and offer various interpretations."

"Just as a blind man asks about milk, so it is with the Buddha-nature. For this reason, some say that those who have committed the four grave offenses, slandered the Vaipulya sutras, committed the five heinous crimes, or are icchantikas all possess the Buddha-nature, while others say they do not."
"Good son! In various sūtras, I have said:
'When one person appears in the world, many people are benefited.'"
"It is impossible for two wheel-turning monarchs to appear within a single land, or for two Buddhas to appear in a single world-system.
It is likewise impossible for there to be eight Cāturmahārājika heavens, or even two Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, within a single four-continent world."
However, I have taught that [the realm of Buddhas] extends from Jambudvīpa and the Avīci Hell, up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim:
"The Buddha says there are no Buddhas in the ten directions."
I have also taught that there are Buddhas of the ten directions within the various Mahāyāna sūtras.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 31; *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll 32.
The second chapter, the "Chapter on Kāśyapa Bodhisattva," added by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"Good son!..."
Such disputes and contentions are the domain of the Buddhas, not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
If a person conceives doubt regarding this, they are still able to destroy immeasurable afflictions as vast as Mount Sumeru;
yet if one forms a fixed conviction within this, it is called attachment.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What constitutes attachment?”
The Buddha said, “Good son! If such a person—

whether hearing it from another, seeking it out in the sūtras themselves, or being intentionally instructed by another— is unable to relinquish that which they are attached to, this is called ‘clinging.’”
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Is such attachment considered wholesome?”
"Is this unwholesome? "Good son,
such attachment is not called wholesome."
"Why is this? Because they are unable to destroy the net of all doubts.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
If such a person is fundamentally free from doubt from the very beginning, why do you say that they have not destroyed the net of doubt? “Good son!
"Indeed, that which is non-doubt is itself doubt.
"World-Honored One!
If there is someone who says that a srotāpanna does not fall into the three evil realms, would this person also be said to have fallen into a name?"
"Is it called doubt?
"Good son! This may be called certainty; it cannot be called doubt."
Why is this? Good son!
It is like a person who first sees a human and a tree; later, while traveling at night, he sees a stump from afar and immediately gives rise to a doubtful thought:
"Is it a person?
Or a tree?
"O son of good family!"
Suppose a person first sees a bhikṣu or a brahmin, and later, while on the road, sees a bhikṣu from afar and immediately gives rise to a doubt:
"Is this a śramaṇa?"
"Is this a brahmin? "Good son!
It is like a person who first sees a cow and a water buffalo, and later, seeing a cow from afar, immediately gives rise to a doubt."
"Is that a cow, or is it a water buffalo?
"Good son! [the Buddha said.]
All sentient beings first perceive two things and subsequently give rise to doubt.
Why is this? It is because their minds do not comprehend [the truth].
“I also do not say that a srotāpanna falls into the three evil realms or does not fall into the three evil realms; for what reason, then, would such a person give rise to doubt?
Kāśyapa said, “World-Honored One!”
Regarding what the Buddha has said—that one must first see something before one can doubt—there are those who also give rise to doubt even when they have not yet seen two kinds of things:
"What is this that is called nirvāṇa?"
"World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person who, encountering turbid water on a road, had never seen it before and thus gave rise to doubt: 'Is this water deep?'"
"Is it shallow?
"If this person has not yet seen it, how could they give rise to doubt? "Good son!"
Now, Nirvana is the cessation of suffering;
that which is not Nirvana is suffering.
All sentient beings perceive two kinds of things: they perceive suffering and they perceive what is not suffering.

Suffering and non-suffering consist of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, joy, illness and emaciation, well-being, old age, youth, birth, death, bondage, liberation, separation from loved ones, and association with those one hates.
When sentient beings see this, they immediately give rise to doubt:
"Will there ever come a time when such suffering and affliction are ultimately and completely removed?
For this reason, sentient beings harbor doubts regarding nirvana.
If you think that this person had not previously seen turbid water and yet harbors doubt,
that is not the case. Why is this so?
"This person previously saw it in another place; therefore, he now gives rise to doubt regarding this place where he has never been before.
"World-Honored One!
When this person previously saw the deep and shallow places, he did not give rise to doubt; why does he now give rise to doubt again?"
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Because you have not yet practiced it from the beginning, doubt arises; therefore, I say that because it is not fully understood, there is doubt.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:”
"‘Doubt is itself attachment, and attachment is itself doubt.
To whom does this refer? "Good son!
"One who has severed the roots of goodness. Kāśyapa said,
"World-Honored One!"
"What kind of people are able to sever their roots of goodness? "Good son!

If there are those who are clever, wise, and of sharp faculties, yet are capable of skillful discrimination, but who distance themselves from virtuous friends, do not listen to the true Dharma, engage in improper reflection, and do not abide according to the Dharma—such persons are able to sever their roots of goodness."
Free from these four matters, one reflects within the mind:
"There is no object to be given. Why is this?"
Giving is the relinquishing of material wealth.
If giving were to have a karmic reward, one should know that the donor would always remain impoverished. Why is this?
"Because the seed and the fruit are similar,
it is said that there is neither cause nor fruit.
To speak in this way of no cause and no fruit is what is called severing the roots of goodness.
Again, he reflects thus:
"The donor, the recipient, and the gift—these three things are impermanent and do not abide.
If they do not abide, how can one say, 'This is the donor,' 'This is the recipient,' or 'This is the gift'?"
"If there is no recipient, how can one obtain a fruit?
For this reason, there is neither cause nor fruit.
If one speaks thus of the absence of cause and the absence of fruit, it should be known that such a person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
Again, he reflects thus:
"When a donor gives a gift, there are five things involved in that giving.
After the recipient has received it, they may sometimes perform wholesome deeds or unwholesome deeds; yet the donor does not thereby obtain either wholesome or unwholesome fruits."
Just as in the worldly dharma, a fruit arises from a seed, and that fruit in turn becomes a seed;
the cause is the donor and the fruit is the recipient, yet this recipient cannot cause the donor to obtain [the result] through these wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.
"For this reason, there is neither cause nor effect.
If one speaks thus of the absence of cause and the absence of effect, it should be known that such a person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
Again, he thinks:
"There is no gift. Why is this? [Because]..."
The object given as a gift is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
If it is neutral, how can it yield a wholesome fruit of retribution?
That which possesses neither wholesome nor unwholesome fruit is precisely what is neutral.
"If wealth were indeterminate, one should know that it would have neither wholesome nor unwholesome retribution.
Therefore, there would be no giving, no cause, and no fruit.
If one speaks thus of no cause and no fruit, one should know that such a person is capable of severing the roots of goodness.
Again, he reflects thus:
"The giver is the mind.
If it is the mind, it is invisible, non-obstructive, and not a material phenomenon."
"If it were not form, how could it be given?
Therefore, there is no giving, no cause, and no fruit.
If one speaks thus of no cause and no fruit, you should know that such a person is capable of severing the roots of goodness.
Again, he thought:
"If a donor gives for the sake of an image of a Buddha, an image of a deity, or deceased parents, there is no recipient;
if there is no recipient, there should be no karmic fruit."
"If there is no retribution, this constitutes the absence of cause;
if there is no cause, this constitutes the absence of fruit.
If one speaks thus of the absence of cause and the absence of fruit, you should know that such a person is capable of severing the roots of goodness.
Again, he had this thought:
"There is no father and no mother.
If one were to say that parents are the cause of sentient beings and give birth to them, then logically they should produce beings constantly, without interruption."
Why is this? Because [the cause] is eternally present.
Yet, it does not arise eternally; therefore, one should know that there are no parents.
Again, he thought:
"There is no father and no mother. Why is this?"
If the bodies of sentient beings were produced solely through their parents, then a single individual should possess both male and female sexual organs.
Yet, since no such person exists, one should know that sentient beings do not arise solely from their parents.
Again, he formed this thought:
"Sentient beings are not born solely because of their parents. Why is this?"
One observes with one's own eyes that sentient beings do not resemble their parents in terms of physical appearance, mind, deportment, or movement.
Therefore, parents are not the cause of sentient beings.
Again, he had this thought:
"In all the world there are four kinds of non-existence:
first, that which has not yet arisen is called non-existent, such as when a lump of clay has not yet served the function of a jar."
Second, that which is called "non-existent" after having been extinguished, such as when a jar has been destroyed;
third, mutual non-existence between distinct things, such as there being no horse within a cow and no cow within a horse;
fourth, ultimate non-existence, such as the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise.
The parents of sentient beings are likewise thus; they share these four absences.
If one says that parents are the cause of sentient beings, then when the parents die, the child does not necessarily die.
"Therefore, parents are not the cause of sentient beings.
He further thought:
"If it were said that parents are the cause of sentient beings, then sentient beings should be constantly born from them as their cause."
"Furthermore, there are those born by transformation and those born from moisture; therefore, one should know that sentient beings are not produced solely because of their parents.

He further thought: "There are indeed sentient beings who grow and develop without depending on parents. For example, when a peacock hears the sound of thunder, it becomes pregnant; likewise, when a blue jay drinks the tears of a male jay, it becomes pregnant; and when a jīvajīvaka bird sees a male dancing, it immediately becomes pregnant."
When one has such thoughts, if they do not encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), it should be known that this person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
Furthermore, they think:
"In all the worlds, there are no fruits of good or evil."

Why is this so? There are sentient beings who possess the ten wholesome dharmas, delight in giving, and diligently cultivate merit; yet these people may likewise have illnesses gather in their bodies, meet with premature death in their prime, suffer the loss of wealth and property, and endure much sorrow and suffering.

Conversely, there are those who practice the ten unwholesome deeds, being stingy, greedy, jealous, and envious, and who are lazy and indolent, failing to cultivate any virtues; yet they remain physically secure and free from illness, live out their full natural lifespan, abound in wealth and treasures, and are without any grief or suffering.
"Therefore, one should know that there are no fruits of good or evil.
He further thought:
"I have also heard various sages say:"
"Some who cultivate goodness fall mostly into the three evil realms at the end of their lives;
some who commit evil are born among humans or devas at the end of their lives.
Therefore, one should know that there are no fruits of good or evil.
Again, he had this thought:
"All noble ones have two kinds of teachings:
some say that killing living beings results in a wholesome karmic retribution, while others say that killing living beings results in an unwholesome karmic retribution."
Therefore, one should know that the teachings of the Noble Ones are not fixed.
If the Noble Ones are not fixed, how could I be fixed?
For this reason, one should know that there are no fruits of good or evil.
Again, he thought:
"There are no noble ones (ārya) in all the worlds. Why is this?"

If one says that while a sage should attain the Right Path, all sentient beings cultivate the Right Path while still possessing afflictions, then one should know that for such a person, the Right Path and afflictions exist simultaneously.
If they existed simultaneously, one should know that the right path could not destroy the fetters.
If one cultivates the path when there are no afflictions, what would such a right path accomplish?
Therefore, for one who possesses afflictions, the Path cannot destroy them;
for one who lacks afflictions, the Path is useless.
Thus, one should know that there are no noble ones (āryas) in the entire world.
"Furthermore, he reflects:
'Ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, up to birth conditioning aging and death—these twelve links of dependent origination are shared equally by all sentient beings.'"
The nature of the Eightfold Noble Path is likewise equal; when one person attains it, all should attain it, and when one person cultivates it, all suffering should be extinguished.
Why is this? Because they are equal to afflictions.
Yet now it is not attained; therefore, one should know that there is no true path.
Again, he had this thought:
"The Noble Ones all share the same dharmas as ordinary people, namely: drinking, eating, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, laughing, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, sorrow, and fear."
If one were the same as an ordinary person regarding such matters, it should be known that the noble one has not attained the noble path;
if the noble path had been attained, such matters as these should have been permanently severed.
Since such matters as these are not severed, it should be known that there is no path.
Again, he thought: "The Noble One possesses a body;

he experiences the pleasures of the five desires, and he also reviles and beats others, feels envy and pride, undergoes suffering and joy, and performs good and evil deeds. For these reasons, I know there is no Noble One."
"If there were a path, one should sever these matters;
since these matters are not severed, one should know that there is no path.
He further thought:
"One who possesses great compassion is called a noble one (ārya).
For what reason is he called a noble one?
Because of the causal conditions of the Path, he is called a noble one."
If the nature of the Path is compassion, then it should naturally take pity upon all sentient beings without waiting for cultivation before it can be attained.
If it were devoid of compassion, why would the sages, having attained the Holy Path, be able to exercise compassion?
"Therefore, one should know that there is no noble path in the world. Again, he thought:
"All four great elements are not born from causes."
All sentient beings equally possess the nature of these four great elements; yet [the world] does not observe that some beings should reach this shore while others should not.
If the Noble Path existed, their nature would necessarily be such; however, it is not so now. Therefore, one should know that there are no noble ones (ārya) in the world.
Again, he formed this thought:
"If the various noble ones possessed a single nirvāṇa, one should know that there would then be no noble ones. Why is this?"
Because it is unattainable.
The principle of the eternally abiding dharma cannot be attained; it is neither to be grasped nor abandoned.
If the nirvana of the various sages were manifold, it would be impermanent.
Why is this? Because it is a dharma that can be counted.
If nirvāṇa were a single entity, then when one person attains it, everyone should attain it as well.
If nirvāṇa were manifold, it would possess limits.
If it possessed limits, how could it be called eternal?
If someone were to say:
"The essence of nirvāṇa is one, while liberations are many;
it is like a single umbrella having many ribs and spokes.
This interpretation is incorrect.
Why is this? Because that which is attained individually is not the attainment of all; since it has limits, it must be impermanent.
If it is impermanent, how can it be called nirvana?
"If nirvana does not exist, who would be a noble one (ārya)?
Therefore, one should know that no noble ones exist.
He further thought:
“The Way of the Sage is not attained through causes and conditions.
If the Way of the Sage were not attained through causes and conditions, why would everyone not become a sage?
If all people are not sages, one should know that there would then be neither sages nor the Way of the Sage.”
Again, he had this thought:
"The Noble One has taught that right view has two causes and conditions:
first, hearing the Dharma from others; second, internal reflection for oneself."
If these two causes and conditions arise from conditions, that which they arise from must itself arise from conditions; in this way, there would be the fault of infinite regress.
If these two things do not arise from conditions, why is it that all sentient beings cannot obtain them?
"When one contemplates in this way, one is able to sever the roots of goodness. Good son!
If there are sentient beings who deeply perceive such absence of cause and absence of effect, these people are able to sever the five faculties, beginning with faith."
Good son! Those who sever their roots of goodness are not merely those of inferior, dull, or stupid nature, nor are they among the gods or in the three evil realms;
the same applies to those who cause a schism in the Sangha.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When will such a person be able to regenerate their roots of goodness?”
The Buddha said:
“Good son! This person will regenerate their roots of goodness at two times:”
When first entering hell and when emerging from hell.
Good son! There are three kinds of goodness:
Regarding the past, present, and future:

if something belongs to the past, its nature has already ceased; although the cause has been extinguished, the retribution has not yet matured. Therefore, it is not said that the fruit of the past is severed.
"Because one severs the causes of the three periods of time, it is called 'severance.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If severing the causes of the three periods of time is called severing the roots of goodness, then a person who has severed the roots of goodness still possesses Buddha-nature.
Is such Buddha-nature past, or is it present?
Is it future? Or does it pervade all three periods of time?
If it were past, how could it be called eternal?
The Buddha-nature is also eternal; therefore, one should know that it is not of the past.
If it were of the future, how could it be called eternal?
For what reason does the Buddha say that all sentient beings will certainly and inevitably attain it?
If it is definitely attained, why say it is severed?
If it pertains to the present, how can it be permanent?
For what reason, then, do you say it is definitely visible?
The Tathāgata has also spoken of six aspects of buddha-nature:
first, permanence; second, truth; third, reality; fourth, goodness; fifth, purity; and sixth, visibility.
If those who have severed their roots of goodness still possess the Buddha-nature, they cannot be called "those who have severed their roots of goodness.
If they lack the Buddha-nature, why do you further say that all sentient beings universally possess the Buddha-nature?
"If you say that the Buddha-nature both exists and is severed, why does the Tathāgata further declare it to be permanent?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has four ways of answering:
first, the categorical answer; second, the analytical answer; third, the answer according to the question; and fourth, the answer by setting aside the question.
“Good son! What is a categorical answer?
For example, if one asks: ‘Does unwholesome karma yield wholesome fruit?’”
Is it the fruit of the unwholesome?
This should be answered definitively as "it obtains the fruit of the unwholesome";
the same applies to the wholesome.
If one asks whether the Tathāgata possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*),
one should answer definitively that he does possess all-knowledge.
If one asks whether the Buddha-dharma is pure, [one should answer definitively that it is].
In such cases, one should categorically answer that they are certainly pure.
If asked whether the disciples of the Tathāgata abide in accordance with the Dharma,
one should categorically answer that there are those who abide in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called a categorical answer.
What is a discriminative answer?
It is as when I teach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
What are the four?
They are suffering, the origin, cessation, and the path.
What is the truth of suffering?
Because there are eight kinds of suffering, it is called the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya).
What is the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya)?
Because it is the cause of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), it is named the Truth of Origination.
What is the truth of cessation?
Because greed, hatred, and delusion are ultimately exhausted, it is called the truth of cessation.
What is the truth of the path?
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called the Truth of the Path.
This is known as the analytical answer.
What is the answer according to the question?
As I have said:
"All phenomena are impermanent.
Furthermore, there is one who asks:
"For what dharma did the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, teach impermanence?
He replied,
"The Tathāgata taught impermanence for the sake of conditioned dharmas."
The same applies to non-self. As I have said:
"All dharmas are burning."
He asked again:
"For the sake of what dharma did the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, say that 'everything is burned'?
He replied:
“The Tathāgata has taught that greed, anger, and delusion are all burning. ‘Good son!

The ten powers of the Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, great kindness and great compassion, the three applications of mindfulness, the eighty trillion samādhi-doors such as Śūraṅgama, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the thirty-five thousand samādhi-doors such as the Five Wisdom Seals, the four thousand two hundred samādhi-doors such as the Vajra-samādhi, and the samādhi of skillful means—such immeasurable and boundless dharmas as these are the Buddha-nature of the Buddhas.’”
Thus, the Buddha-nature possesses seven attributes:
first, permanence; second, selfhood; third, bliss; fourth, purity; fifth, truth; sixth, reality; and seventh, goodness.
This is called an analytical answer.
"Good son, there are six kinds of Buddha-nature for a Bodhisattva in his final birth:
First, permanence; second, purity; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, goodness; sixth, being rarely seen.
These are called the analytical answers.

"As you previously asked regarding those who have severed their roots of goodness having Buddha-nature: such persons likewise possess the Tathāgata-Buddha-nature and also possess the Buddha-nature of future bodies."
Because these two Buddha-natures obstruct the future, they are termed "non-existent";
because they will ultimately be attained, they are termed "existent.
This is called an analytical answer.
"The Tathāgata’s buddha-nature is neither past, nor present, nor future.
Because the buddha-nature of the final body can be seen slightly in the present and the future, it is designated as 'present';
because it is not yet fully seen, it is called 'future'."
When the Tathāgata had not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha-nature, being the cause, was likewise past, present, and future;
the fruit, however, was not so, for it both exists within the three periods of time and exists outside of them.
Because the Buddha-nature of a Bodhisattva in his final body is a cause, it likewise pertains to the past, present, and future;
the same applies to its fruit.
This is called an analytical answer.
“The Buddha-nature of a Bodhisattva in the ninth stage has six aspects:
first, permanence; second, goodness; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, purity; and sixth, visibility.”
Because the Buddha-nature is a cause, it is also of the past, present, and future;
the same applies to its fruit.
This is called a categorical answer.
"For Bodhisattvas at the eighth stage down to those at the sixth stage, there are five aspects of the Buddha-nature:
first, truth; second, reality; third, purity; fourth, goodness; and fifth, visibility."
Because Buddha-nature is a cause, it is also past, present, and future;
its fruit is likewise so.
This is called an analytical answer.
Regarding the five aspects of the Buddha-nature for Bodhisattvas from the fifth stage down to the first:
first, true; second, real; third, pure; fourth, visible; and fifth, both wholesome and unwholesome.

Good son! Because these five kinds of Buddha-nature, six kinds of Buddha-nature, and seven kinds of Buddha-nature will certainly be attained by those who have severed their roots of goodness, it can be said that they exist.
This is called an analytical answer.
If someone were to say that those who have severed their roots of goodness definitely possess the Buddha-nature or definitely lack the Buddha-nature, this is called a reserved answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard that not answering is called ‘setting aside the question’ (sthāpanīya). For what reason and by what causes does the Tathāgata now call an answer ‘setting aside the question’?”
“Good son! I do not say that setting aside [a question] constitutes a non-answer; rather, I say that setting it aside is itself the answer. Good son!”
There are two kinds of such "setting aside" (sthāpanīya) answers:
first, cessation; second, non-attachment.
For this reason, it is called a "set-aside" answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, what is meant by a cause that is past, present, and future, and a fruit that is also past, present, and future, yet is not [itself] past, present, or future?”
The Buddha said:
“Good son, the five aggregates are of two kinds:”
First is the cause, and second is the fruit.

These five aggregates as causes belong to the past, present, and future; these five aggregates as fruits also belong to the past, present, and future, yet they are also neither past, present, nor future.
“Good son! All fetters, such as ignorance and the afflictions, are entirely the Buddha-nature. Why is this?
Because it is the cause of buddha-nature,
the attainment of the wholesome five aggregates from ignorance, volitional formations, and all afflictions is called buddha-nature;
from these wholesome five aggregates, one proceeds until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, in the sutras I have previously stated that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like milk mixed with blood; "blood" refers to all afflictions such as ignorance and volitional formations, while "milk" refers to the five wholesome aggregates.
Therefore, I say that one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the various afflictions and the five aggregates of goodness.
Just as the bodies of sentient beings are all brought to completion through semen and blood, so too is the Buddha-nature.
In those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna or Sakṛdāgāmin, the Buddha-nature is like milk because they have severed only a small portion of afflictions;
in those who have attained the stage of Anāgāmin, the Buddha-nature is like curd;
and in those who have attained the stage of Arhat, it is like fresh butter.
"From the pratyekabuddhas up to the bodhisattvas of the ten stages, they are like clarified butter (sarpis);
the Tathāgata’s buddha-nature is like the finest cream (maṇḍa). Good son!"
Because current afflictions act as obstacles, they prevent sentient beings from perceiving it.
It is like the *kṣānti-grass* found on Mount Gandhamādana, which not all oxen are able to eat;
the Buddha-nature is likewise.
"This is called an analytical answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If there are five kinds, six kinds, or seven kinds of Buddha-nature, how can it be said that those who have severed their roots of goodness possess Buddha-nature?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Just as all sentient beings possess past karma, and because of this karma, sentient beings receive their retributive fruits in the present."
There is future karma which, because it has not yet arisen, will never produce a fruit.
There are present afflictions; if there were no afflictions, all sentient beings should clearly perceive the Buddha-nature in the present.

Therefore, although a person who has severed their roots of goodness may sever them through the causes and conditions of afflictions in the present life, they will regenerate those roots of goodness due to the power of the Buddha-nature as a cause and condition in the future.
Kāśyapa said:
“World-Honored One!
How can roots of goodness be produced in the future?”
“Good son! Just as a lamp or the sun can dispel darkness even before they have arisen;
so too, the future arising can bring forth sentient beings, and the future Buddha-nature is likewise.”
"This is called an analytical answer.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If you say that the five aggregates are the Buddha-nature, why do you say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither internal nor external?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
"For what reason have you lost your composure in this way?
Did I not previously state that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the Middle Way?
Kāśyapa replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is true that I did not lose my original intent; I simply asked this question because sentient beings are unable to understand this Middle Way. “Good man!”
Sentient beings do not understand that this very [nature] is the Middle Way; at times they understand it, and at other times they do not. Good son!
For the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain understanding, I say that Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external.
Why is this? Ordinary beings may say that the Buddha-nature dwells within the five aggregates, like fruit inside a vessel;
or they may say it exists apart from the aggregates, like empty space.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of the Middle Way.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither the six internal sense bases nor the six external sense bases; because it is the union of the internal and external, it is called the Middle Way.
Therefore, the Tathāgata declares that buddha-nature is itself the Middle Way; because it is neither internal nor external, it is called the Middle Way.
This is known as the analytical answer.
"Furthermore, good son!
What is meant by 'neither internal nor external'?
Good son!"
Some say that Buddha-nature is identical to the heterodox paths (tīrthika). Why is this?

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, throughout immeasurable kalpas, dwell among the heterodox to sever all afflictions, subdue their minds, and transform sentient beings; only thereafter do they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, they claim that Buddha-nature is identical to the heterodox paths.
Some say that Buddha-nature is precisely the inner path (Buddhism). Why?

Although a bodhisattva may practice the outer paths for immeasurable eons, if they depart from the inner path, they cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; therefore, Buddha-nature is precisely the inner path.

Therefore, the Tathāgata negates these two extremes and declares that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet it is also called both internal and external; this is termed the Middle Way.
This is called an analytical answer.
Furthermore, son of good family,
some say that the Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata’s vajra-body, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics.
Why is this? Because it is not false or deceptive.

Alternatively, it is said that Buddha-nature is precisely the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great kindness and great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, the Śūraṅgama and all other samādhis.
Why is this? Because it is by means of this samādhi that the adamantine body, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics are produced.

For this reason, the Tathāgata refutes these two extremes and declares that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet it is also called both internal and external; this is termed the Middle Way.
This is called an analytical answer.
Furthermore, son of good family,
some may say that the Buddha-nature is precisely internal right reflection.
Why is this? Because without skillful reflection one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, the Buddha-nature is itself internal skillful reflection.
Some may say that the Buddha-nature is precisely hearing the Dharma from others.

Why is this? Because by hearing the Dharma from others, one is able to engage in proper internal reflection; if one does not hear the Dharma, there is no such reflection. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is precisely hearing the Dharma from others.

Therefore, the Tathāgata negates these two extremes and declares that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet it is also called both internal and external; this is termed the Middle Way.
"Furthermore, good son!
There are others who say that the Buddha-nature is external, namely the *dānapāramitā*.
Because one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the *dānapāramitā*, they say that the *dānapāramitā* is itself the Buddha-nature."
Some say that the Buddha-nature is internal, referring to the five *pāramitās*. Why is this?
Because apart from these five things, one should know that there would be no cause or fruit of the Buddha-nature; therefore, it is said that the five *pāramitās* are themselves the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, the Tathāgata negates these two extremes and declares that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet it is both internal and external; this is called the Middle Way.
"Furthermore, good son!
Some may say that the Buddha-nature is within, like a jewel on the forehead of a strongman. Why is this?
Because permanence, bliss, self, and purity are like a precious jewel, it is said that the Buddha-nature exists within.
Some, however, say that the Buddha-nature is outside, like a treasure trove belonging to the poor.
Why is this? Because it is seen through skillful means (*upāya*).
The Buddha-nature is likewise; although it exists outside of sentient beings, it is perceived through skillful means.
