Therefore, the Tathāgata negates these two extremes and declares that the Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet it is both internal and external; this is called the Middle Way.
“Good son! The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither existent nor non-existent. Why is this so?

Although the Buddha-nature exists, it is not like empty space. Why is this? Although one may employ immeasurable skillful means, the empty space of the world cannot be seen; yet the Buddha-nature can be perceived. Therefore, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is eternal and unchanging, whereas the Buddha-nature is neither eternal nor unchanging. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without form, while the Buddha-nature possesses form. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without sensation, while the Buddha-nature possesses sensation. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without perception, while the Buddha-nature possesses perception. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without volition, while the Buddha-nature possesses volition. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without consciousness, while the Buddha-nature possesses consciousness. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without afflictions, while the Buddha-nature possesses afflictions. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the fruits of retribution, while the Buddha-nature possesses the fruits of retribution. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of birth and death, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of birth and death. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of Nirvana, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of Nirvana. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the Tathagata, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Tathagata. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the Dharma, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Dharma. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the Sangha, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Sangha. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the Path, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Path. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the Bodhisattva, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Bodhisattva. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the Buddha, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Buddha. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the Dharma-body, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Dharma-body. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the Sambhogakaya, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Sambhogakaya. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the Nirmanakaya, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Nirmanakaya. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the Great Nirvana, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Great Nirvana. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the Tathagata’s ten powers, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the Tathagata’s ten powers. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the four fearlessnesses, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four fearlessnesses. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the eighteen unique qualities, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the eighteen unique qualities. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the thirty-two marks of a great man, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the thirty-two marks of a great man. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the eighty minor marks, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the eighty minor marks. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the six perfections, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the six perfections. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the four right efforts, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four right efforts. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the four bases of psychic power, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four bases of psychic power. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the five faculties, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the five faculties. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the five powers, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the five powers. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the seven factors of enlightenment, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the seven factors of enlightenment.

For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the eightfold noble path, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the eightfold noble path. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the three gates of liberation, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the three gates of liberation. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the four dhyānas, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four dhyānas. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the four immeasurables, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four immeasurables. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the four formless attainments, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four formless attainments. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the eighteen kinds of emptiness. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the nine successive meditative concentrations, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the nine successive meditative concentrations. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the ten stages of a Bodhisattva, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the ten stages of a Bodhisattva. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the ten powers of a Tathagata, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the ten powers of a Tathagata. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the four fearlessnesses, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four fearlessnesses. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the eighteen unique qualities, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the eighteen unique qualities. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the three bodies, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the three bodies. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the four wisdoms, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four wisdoms. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the five eyes, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the five eyes. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the six supernormal knowledges, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the six supernormal knowledges. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the four reliances, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the four reliances. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the three non-outflows, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the three non-outflows. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Furthermore, empty space is without the nature of the three knowledges, while the Buddha-nature possesses the nature of the three knowledges. For this reason, it is not like empty space. Moreover, empty space is without the nature of the three liberations
The Buddha-nature can be perceived; therefore, although it exists, it is not like empty space.
Although the Buddha-nature is non-existent, it is not the same as a rabbit's horn. Why is this?
Although the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare cannot be produced even through immeasurable skillful means, the Buddha-nature can be produced;
therefore, although it does not exist [in the same manner], it is not the same as the horns of a hare.
Therefore, the Buddha-nature is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is both existent and non-existent.
Why is it called "existent"?

Because it exists in all things; these sentient beings are neither severed nor extinguished, just like the flame of a lamp, continuing until they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, it is called "existent."
What is meant by "non-existent"?
It means that all sentient beings do not currently possess any of the Buddha-dharmas—namely, permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and for this reason they are called non-existent.
Because existence and non-existence are united, this is precisely the Middle Way.
Therefore, the Buddha said that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither existent nor non-existent. "Good son!
Suppose someone were to ask:
"Is there a fruit within this seed,
or is there no fruit?"
One should answer with certainty:
"It both exists and does not exist. Why is this so?
Apart from the seed, the fruit cannot arise; therefore, it is called "existent.
Before the sprout has emerged from the seed, it is called "non-existent.
For this reason, it is both existent and non-existent.
Why is this? Although the seasons differ, their substance is one;
the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise so.
If one says that there is a Buddha-nature distinct from sentient beings, this meaning is not so.
Why? Because sentient beings are themselves the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-nature is itself sentient beings; it is only because of differences in time that they are either pure or impure.
"Good son!
If someone were to ask:
'Can this seed produce fruit?'"
"Can this fruit produce a seed?
One should answer definitively:
"It both produces and does not produce."
“World-Honored One!
As worldly people say that there is curd within milk, what is the meaning of this? “Good son!
If one says that there is curd within milk, this is called attachment;
if one says there is no curd, this is called falsehood.
Departing from these two positions, one should definitively state that it both exists and does not exist.
Why is it called "existence"?
From milk, curd is produced.
The cause is the milk, and the fruit is the curd; this is what is meant by existence.
What is meant by "non-existence"?
The flavors of milk and curd differ, and their applications are distinct: one consumes milk for febrile illnesses and curd for cold-natured illnesses;
yet milk can produce cold-natured illnesses, and curd can produce febrile illnesses.
Good son!

If one says that the nature of curd exists within milk—such that milk is itself curd and curd is itself milk—and their natures are one and the same, for what reason does milk appear first while curd does not appear first?
If there were causes and conditions, why would all worldly people not speak of them?
If there were no causes and conditions, why would curd not emerge first?
If curd did not emerge first, who would establish the sequence of milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and ghee?
Therefore, one knows that curd did not previously exist but now exists; if it did not previously exist but now exists, it is an impermanent dharma. "Good son!
If someone were to say:
"The statement that 'milk possesses the nature of curd and can therefore produce curd,
whereas water lacks the nature of curd and thus does not produce it' is incorrect. Why is this so?"
Aquatic plants also possess the nature of milk and curd. Why is this?
Because it is from aquatic plants that milk and curd emerge.
If one says,
"The nature of curd definitely exists within milk,
but it does not exist in water or grass," this is called false and delusive.
Why is this? Because the mind is not impartial, it is said to be false and illusory. Good son!
If you say that curd definitely exists within milk, then milk-nature should also definitely exist within curd.
For what reason does curd emerge from milk, while milk does not emerge from curd?
If there were no causes and conditions, one should know that this curd was originally non-existent and has now come into being.
Therefore, the wise person should say:
"Within milk, there is neither the nature of curd nor the absence of the nature of curd."
"Good son! For this reason, the Tathāgata has spoken these words within this sūtra:
'To say that all sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature is called attachment.'"
"If there were no Buddha-nature, it would be called false.
A wise person should say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings both exists and does not exist. "Good son!"
The visual consciousness arises from the conjunction of four factors. What are these four?
They are the eye, visible forms, light, and attention.
This nature of eye-consciousness is not the eye, nor form, nor light, nor desire; it arises only through their conjunction.
Thus, this eye-consciousness was originally non-existent and now exists, having existed it returns to non-existence; therefore, one should know that it has no inherent nature.
The nature of curd within milk is also like this.
If someone were to say:
"Water lacks the nature of curd, therefore it does not produce curd."
"Therefore, it is certain that the nature of curd exists within milk.
This argument is not correct. Why is this so?
"Good son!
All dharmas have distinct causes and distinct effects; nor does a single cause produce all effects, nor do all effects arise from a single cause."
"Good son!
Just as visual consciousness arises from four factors, one cannot further say that auditory consciousness should arise from these same four factors.
Good son!"
Without the application of skillful means, one cannot obtain curd from milk, nor can butter be produced from curd;
it is not so, for these must necessarily depend upon skillful means. Good son!
A wise person cannot see anything apart from skillful means.
Just as one obtains curd from milk and thereby obtains fresh butter, it should likewise be understood that [the goal] is obtained through skillful means. Good son!
Therefore, in this sutra I have said:
"Because of arising, phenomena exist; because of ceasing, phenomena do not exist. "Good son!
Just as the nature of salt is salty and can cause that which is not salty to become salty:
if things that are not salty already possessed a salty nature, for what reason would people in the world seek out salt?
If it was previously non-existent, one should know that what was previously non-existent now exists, having become salty due to other conditions.
If one says:
"All things that are not salty possess the nature of saltiness, but it is not perceived because it is subtle."
Because of this subtle nature, salt can impart a salty taste;
if it lacked this inherent nature from the beginning, even if salt were present, it could not make things salty.
It is like a seed that possesses its own four great elements (mahābhūtas), which, by depending on the external four great elements, enables the growth of sprouts, stalks, branches, and leaves.
As for the claim that "the nature of salt is also like this," this meaning is not correct. Why is that?
If things that are not salty already possess a salty nature, then salt should likewise possess a subtle non-salty nature.
If salt possesses these two natures, for what reason can it not be used alone, apart from non-salty things?
Therefore, one knows that salt fundamentally possesses no dual nature.
As it is with salt, so it is with all things that are not salty.
"If it is said that the power of the external four great elements can increase the internal four great elements, this meaning is not so."
Why is this? Because it is taught according to a sequential order.
One does not obtain curd or fresh butter from the milk of expedient means; indeed, all dharmas are not like this.
It is likewise with the four great elements that are not obtained through skillful means.
If one speaks of the internal four great elements increasing from the external four great elements, one does not see the external four great elements increasing from the internal four great elements.
It is like the śirīṣa fruit, which initially has no form or substance; when the constellation Mṛgaśiras appears, the fruit emerges, fully five inches in length.
Such a fruit truly does not arise due to an increase in the external four great elements.

“Good son! As I have taught in the twelve divisions of the scriptures, some are spoken according to my own intention, some are spoken according to the intentions of others, and some are spoken according to the intentions of both myself and others.”
"What is meant by 'speaking according to one's own intention'?
For example, five hundred bhikṣus asked Śāriputra:
'Venerable One!'"
"The Buddha spoke of the causes of the body;
what are they? Śāriputra said, "Venerable sirs!"
"You yourselves have each attained right liberation; you should recognize this for yourselves, so for what reason do you ask such a question? A bhikṣu said:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Before I had attained right liberation, I thought that ignorance was the cause of the body; while contemplating in this way, I realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Another further said:
"Venerable One!..."
"When I had not yet attained right liberation, I held that craving and ignorance were the causes of the body.
While contemplating in this way, I realized the fruit of Arhatship. Some might say:
Volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, food, and the five objects of desire are the causes of the body.

At that time, after the five hundred bhikṣus had each spoken of their own understanding, they went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Having finished their prostrations, they sat to one side and each spoke to the Buddha regarding the meaning they had individually understood as described above.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Among these people, who speaks correctly and who speaks incorrectly?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Excellent, excellent!
Not a single one of these bhikṣus has failed to speak correctly. Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the Buddha’s intention?
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra! For the sake of sentient beings in the desire realm, I have said that one's parents are the cause of the body.
Sūtras such as these are called "teachings according to my own intention."
"What is meant by 'teaching according to the inclinations of others'?
For example, when the householder Paṭācāra came to me and spoke thus:
'Gautama!'"
"Do you know illusion?
If you know it, you are a great illusory person;
if you do not know it, you do not possess all-knowledge."
I said: "Householder!
Does one who knows an illusionist call him an 'illusionist'?"
The elder said:
"Excellent, excellent!
One who knows illusion is himself an illusory person."
The Buddha said,
"Householder!
Within the kingdom of Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit has a caṇḍāla named Kṣudhita."
"Do you know this or not?
The householder replied, "Gautama!"
"I have known this for a long time.
The Buddha said,
"If you have known this for a long time, could you then be a caṇḍāla?"
The householder said: "Gautama!
Although I know him to be a caṇḍāla, this body of mine is not a caṇḍāla."
The Buddha said:
"Householder!
You have grasped this principle; you know who is a caṇḍāla and who is not a caṇḍāla."
"For what reason, Elder, am I now unable to know illusion as being non-illusion?

Elder, I truly know illusion; I know the person who creates illusion; I know the karmic retribution of illusion; I know the arts of illusion. I know killing; I know the person who kills; I know the karmic retribution of killing; I know liberation from killing. This extends even to knowing wrong view; I know the person with wrong view; I know the karmic retribution of wrong view; I know liberation from wrong view."
"Householder!
If one says that a person who is not an illusionist is an illusionist, or says that a person who does not hold wrong views holds wrong views, one incurs immeasurable sin.
The householder said:
"Gautama! According to what you have said, I have committed a great transgression.
I now offer everything I possess to you; I pray that King Prasenajit of Kosala may not learn of this matter of mine."
The Buddha said:
"Elder! This karmic cause and condition for the offense does not necessarily result in the loss of wealth; rather, one shall fall into the three evil realms because of it."
At that time, having heard the names of the evil realms, the elder was struck with fear and said to the Buddha:
"O Noble One!
I have now lost my way and incurred a great transgression."
The Sage is now omniscient and should fully understand how to attain liberation.
How shall I myself escape from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals?
At that time, I preached the Four Noble Truths for him.
Having heard them, the elder attained the fruit of Srotāpanna; filled with shame and remorse, he turned to the Buddha and repented:
"I was originally foolish; you, O Buddha, are not a man of illusion, yet I called you such. From this day forward, I take refuge in the Triple Gem."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent,
householder!"
This is called speaking in accordance with the intentions of others.
What is meant by speaking in accordance with one's own and others' intentions?
It is as I have said:
Whatever the wise of the world say exists, I also say exists;
whatever the wise say does not exist, I also say does not exist;
and regarding the five sensual pleasures—which the wise of the world say are impermanent, suffering, and without self, and should be abandoned—I also say they exist.
The wise people of the world say that there is no possibility for the pleasures of the five desires to possess permanence, selfhood, or purity; I likewise say that such a thing is impossible.
This is called "speaking in accordance with oneself and others."
“Good son! What I have said—that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature only slightly—is spoken according to the intentions of others.
For what reason is it called ‘seeing slightly’?

Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage attain samādhis such as Śūraṅgama and three thousand dharma-gates; therefore, they clearly know for themselves that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet they do not perceive any sentient beings as definitely attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, I say that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see the Buddha-nature only partially. "Good son!
When I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, this is called 'speaking according to my own intention.'"
That all sentient beings are neither interrupted nor extinguished, until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is called "speaking according to one's own intention."
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; because it is obscured by afflictions, they are unable to see it.
I speak thus, and you speak likewise; this is called speaking in accordance with the intentions of both oneself and others."
“Good son! At times the Tathāgata, for the sake of a single dharma, teaches immeasurable dharmas.
As it is said in a sutra:”
"All pure conduct (brahmacarya) has the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) as its cause.
Although the causes of all pure conduct are immeasurable, they are fully encompassed by speaking of the spiritual friend.
As I have said:
"All unwholesome actions have wrong view as their cause.
Although the causes of all unwholesome actions are immeasurable, if one speaks of wrong view, they are already fully encompassed.
Some say:
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi has faith as its cause.
Although the causes of this bodhi are indeed immeasurable, if one speaks of faith, they are already fully encompassed.
“Good son!
Although the Tathāgata speaks of immeasurable dharmas as being the Buddha-nature, they do not depart from the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus). Good son!”
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, there are seven kinds of speech:

first, speech concerning causes; second, speech concerning results; third, speech concerning both cause and result; fourth, speech by way of analogy; fifth, speech that should not be spoken; sixth, speech conforming to worldly convention; and seventh, speech according to one's will.
"What is meant by 'speaking according to causes'?
It is to speak of future results within the context of present causes.
As I have said: "

“Good son! When you see sentient beings who delight in killing, up to and including those who delight in practicing wrong views, you should regard such people as being persons of the hells. Good son!”
"If there are sentient beings who do not delight in killing, up to and including wrong views, one should regard such persons as gods and humans.
This is called "speech concerning causes.
What is "speech concerning results"?
The past cause is explained within the context of the present fruit.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O noble son!..."

As you see those sentient beings who are poor, whose countenances are ugly, and who lack self-mastery, you should know that these people certainly possess broken precepts, envy, anger, and a lack of shame and remorse.

If you see sentient beings who are immensely wealthy, whose faculties are complete, and who possess majestic power and self-mastery, you should know that these people certainly possess the precepts, generosity, diligence, shame, and remorse, and are free from envy and anger.
This is called speech concerning the fruit.
What is speech concerning cause and fruit?
As it is said in the Sūtra:

“Good son! The present six sense bases and the causes of contact for sentient beings are called the fruits of past karma; the Tathāgata also refers to them as ‘karma,’ and through the causal conditions of this karma, one obtains future fruits.”
This is called discourse on cause and effect.
What is discourse by way of analogy?

For example, when it is said that the "Lion King" is a metaphor for my own body; or the Great Elephant King, the Great Dragon King, the Pārijātaka tree, a heap of the seven treasures, the great ocean, Mount Sumeru, the great earth, heavy rain, a shipmaster, a guide, a charioteer of men, a strongman, a bull-king, a brāhmaṇa, a śramaṇa, a great city, or a tala-tree—sūtras employing such metaphors are called discourse by way of analogy.
"What is improper speech?
In my sutras I have said:
'Heaven and earth may join together, but a river does not fail to enter the sea.'"
As it was said to King Prasenajit:
"Mountains are coming from the four directions.
And as it was said to the laywoman Mṛgāramātṛ:
"If a śāla tree can receive the eight precepts, it will obtain the pleasures of humans and devas.
As it is said:
"A bodhisattva of the ten stages may have a regressive mind, but it is not said that the Tathāgata has two kinds of speech."
"It would be better to say that a stream-enterer falls into the three evil realms than to say that those in the ten stages have a mind of regression.
This is called "inappropriate speech.
What is "worldly conventional speech"?

As the Buddha has said: "Men and women, the great and the small; going, coming, sitting, and reclining; vehicles, houses, jars, and garments; the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of sentient beings; armies, forests, cities, and villages—all are like illusions that assemble and disperse."
This is called conventional worldly discourse.
What is intended discourse?
It is as when I reprimand those who violate the precepts, causing them to feel self-reproach and thereby maintain the observance of the precepts.
Just as I praise those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) to cause ordinary worldlings to give rise to wholesome minds,
so do I praise bodhisattvas to cause sentient beings to resolve upon *bodhicitta*.
The description of all the sufferings and afflictions in the three evil realms is for the purpose of causing one to cultivate all wholesome dharmas;
the description of universal burning refers solely to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*);
and the same applies to non-self (*anātman*).
To say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is for the purpose of causing everyone to be diligent and not negligent;
this is called "speech according to one's will. "Good son!
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has speech according to his own intention:
the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata is of two kinds—first, existence; second, non-existence.

That which exists refers to the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the *Śūraṅgama* and other immeasurable samādhis, the *Vajra* and other immeasurable samādhis, the *Upāya* and other immeasurable samādhis, and the *Five Wisdom Seals* and other immeasurable samādhis; these are called existence.

That which is called "non-existent" refers to the Tathāgata’s past wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate karmic causes, their retributive fruits, afflictions, the five aggregates, and the twelve links of dependent origination; these are what are termed "non-existent."
“Good son! Just as there are existence and non-existence, good and not-good, with-outflows and without-outflows,
mundane and non-mundane, noble and non-noble, conditioned and unconditioned, real and unreal, and quiescence— ”
Tranquility and non-tranquility; contention and non-contention; realms and non-realms;
afflictions and non-afflictions; grasping and non-grasping; prediction and non-prediction;
existence and non-existence; the three periods of time and non-three-periods-of-time; time and non-time; permanence and impermanence; self and non-self.

I, pleasure and the absence of pleasure, purity and the absence of purity; form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as that which is not form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
the internal bases and that which is not the internal bases, the external bases and that which is not the external bases;
the twelve links of dependent origination and that which is not the twelve links of dependent origination—these are called the existence and non-existence of the Tathāgata’s buddha-nature.
Even regarding whether the icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature or not, it is likewise so. "Good son!

Although I have said that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, sentient beings do not understand that such words of mine are 'speech according to one's own intention' (yathāsvasaṃtati-vākya)."
"Good son!
Such words as these cannot even be understood by Bodhisattvas in their final birth, let alone by those of the Two Vehicles or other Bodhisattvas.
Good son!"

At one time, while I was on Vulture Peak Mountain discussing conventional truth with the Bodhisattva Maitreya, Śāriputra and the five hundred śrāvakas were entirely unaware of this matter; how much less could they understand the ultimate truth that transcends the world?
“Good son! There is a Buddha-nature that exists in icchantikas but not in those with roots of goodness;
there is also a Buddha-nature that exists in those with roots of goodness but not in icchantikas.”
"There is a Buddha-nature that both persons possess;
there is a Buddha-nature that neither person possesses. Good son!"

If my disciples understand the meaning of these four propositions, they should not raise the objection that those with the icchantika nature either definitely possess the Buddha-nature or definitely lack it.
If one says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, this is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention.
Since the Tathāgata speaks in such a manner according to his own intention, how can sentient beings understand it as being exclusively so?
“Good son! It is like there being seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River:

first, those who are constantly submerged; second, those who emerge briefly and then submerge again; third, those who, having emerged, remain stationary; fourth, those who, having emerged, look in all four directions; fifth, those who, having looked around, walk away; sixth, those who, having walked, return to stay; and seventh, those who travel both on water and on land.”

As for those who are said to be "constantly submerged," these are the great fish that, having undergone great evil karma, possess heavy bodies and dwell in deep waters; therefore, they are constantly submerged.

As for those who "emerge briefly only to submerge again," these great fish, because they have undergone evil karma, possess heavy bodies and dwell in shallow waters, where they occasionally catch sight of light.
Because of the light, they emerge for a moment; because of their heaviness, they sink back down.
As for those that emerge and then remain stationary, these are the Timi fish; dwelling in shallow waters, they delight in seeing the light, and thus they emerge and stay.
"Surveying the four directions" refers to the *śiśumāra* (crocodile-fish); because it seeks food, it surveys the four directions, and for this reason it is called "surveying the directions.
"Having surveyed, it moves" means that when this *śiśumāra* sees something from afar and deems it edible, it hastens toward it; therefore, it is called "having surveyed, it moves."
"Having moved, it stops again" refers to the fish; having gone toward its prey, once it has obtained what it can eat, it immediately comes to rest, and thus "having moved, it stops again.
"Moving both on water and on land" refers to the tortoise.

“Good son! Within this subtle and wondrous Great Nirvana River, there are likewise seven kinds of sentient beings; from the first who are constantly submerged, up to the seventh who either enter or emerge.”

"Regarding those who are said to be 'perpetually submerged': there are people who hear this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*—that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and without change, characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and that he never ultimately enters parinirvāṇa; that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; and that even icchantikas, those who slander the Vaipulya sūtras, those who commit the five heinous crimes, and those who violate the four grave prohibitions will certainly attain the path to Bodhi; as well as that śrāvakas such as srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Having heard these words, they give rise to a lack of faith and immediately form this thought:"
Having formed this thought, he then says:
"This Nirvāṇa scripture is merely a treatise of the non-Buddhists; it is not a Buddhist sūtra.
At that time, such a person distances himself from virtuous friends and does not hear the True Dharma.
Although they may hear [the teaching] from time to time, they are unable to contemplate it;
although they do contemplate it, they do not contemplate what is wholesome;
because they do not contemplate the wholesome, they abide in unwholesome dharmas as if they were established therein.
"There are six aspects to abiding in unwholesome dharmas:
first, evil; second, the absence of goodness; third, defiled dharmas; fourth, increasing existence; fifth, affliction and feverish distress; and sixth, experiencing the results of evil."
This is called "sinking.
Why is it called sinking?
Because there is no virtuous mind, because one constantly practices evil, and because one does not cultivate the remedies; this is called sinking.

"That which is called 'evil' is so named because it is censured by the sages, because it gives rise to fear in the mind, because virtuous people distance themselves from it, and because it does not benefit sentient beings."

"To say there is no goodness means that one is able to produce immeasurable evil retributions; that one is constantly entangled by ignorance; that one delights in associating with evil persons as equals; that one lacks the various skillful means for cultivating goodness; and that one's mind is inverted and perpetually erroneous—this is called the absence of goodness."

"Regarding what is called 'defiling the Dharma': it is so named because it constantly defiles body and speech, defiles pure sentient beings, increases unwholesome karma, and distances one from wholesome dharmas."

"Regarding 'increasing existence' (bhava-vardhana): the practices performed by the three aforementioned types of persons increase [rebirth in] the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; they are unable to cultivate the Dharma of liberation, and their actions of body, speech, and mind do not weary of all forms of existence. This is called 'increasing existence.'"

Regarding what is called "tormenting heat": when a person fully practices the four aforementioned matters, they cause both body and mind to become feverish and agitated; being far removed from tranquility, this is termed "heat."
It is called "heat" because one undergoes retribution in hell;
it is called "heat" because it scorches all sentient beings;
it is called "heat" because it burns away all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son! This person lacks the clarity and coolness of faith; therefore, they are called 'hot.

As for what is meant by 'receiving evil retribution,' it means that this person fully practices the aforementioned five matters and, upon death, falls into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals."
"Good son! There are three kinds of evil matters that are also called evil fruits:
first, the evil of afflictions; second, the evil of karma; and third, the evil of retribution. These are called receiving evil karmic retributions."

“Good son! A person who is fully possessed of the six matters mentioned above can sever their roots of goodness, commit the five heinous crimes, violate the four grave offenses, slander the Triple Gem, misappropriate the property of the Sangha, and perform all manner of unrighteous deeds.”
For this reason, they sink into the Avīci Hell, where their physical forms are eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Because the karmic actions of this person’s body, speech, and mind are so heavy, they are unable to escape.
Why is this? Because their minds are unable to give rise to wholesome dharmas.
Although immeasurable Buddhas appear in the world, they neither hear nor see them; therefore, they are called "perpetually submerged," like great fish in the Ganges River.
“Good son! Although I have further stated that those such as the icchantikas are called ‘perpetually submerged,’ there are others who are perpetually submerged who are not icchantikas. Who are they?”
If a person practices giving and the virtues of precepts for the sake of existence, this is called "perpetual sinking.
Good son, there are four virtuous deeds that result in evil fruits.
What are these four?

First, reciting and chanting the sūtras for the sake of defeating others; second, upholding the prohibitive precepts for the sake of gain and offerings; third, practicing giving for the sake of being dependent on others; fourth, focusing the mind in contemplation for the sake of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These four virtuous deeds result in evil retributions.
If a person cultivates and accumulates these four matters, this is called "sinking after emerging" and "sinking after emerging.
Why is it called sinking?
Because they delight in the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Why is it called "emergence"?
It is because one perceives clarity.
Clarity refers precisely to hearing the precepts, practicing generosity, and cultivating meditative concentration.
Why do they regress?
Because they increase wrong views and give rise to arrogance.
Therefore, I have spoken this verse in the sūtra:
"If there are sentient beings who delight in the various realms of existence, And for the sake of existence perform good and evil deeds, Such people will ultimately lose the path to Nirvāṇa;
This is called 'emerging for a moment only to sink back again.'"
Wandering in the dark ocean of saṃsāra, though they have attained liberation, they remain mixed with afflictions;
such people again undergo evil retributions—this is called emerging for a moment only to sink back down once more.
“Good son! Just as that great fish, because it saw the light, was temporarily able to emerge from the water, but because its body was heavy, sank back down again;
so too it is with these two people mentioned above.”
“Good son! Furthermore, if there are those who take pleasure in and are attached to the three realms of existence, this is called ‘sinking.
If they hear such a Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and give rise to faith, this is called ‘emerging.’”
For what reason is it called "emergence"?
Having heard this sutra, one distances oneself from unwholesome dharmas and cultivates wholesome dharmas; this is called emergence.
Although such a person has faith, it is not yet complete.
For what reason is their faith not complete?
Although such a person believes that the Great Parinirvāṇa is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, they say:
"The body of the Tathāgata is impermanent, non-self, without bliss, and without purity."
The Tathāgata has two kinds of nirvāṇa:
first, the conditioned (saṃskṛta), and second, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Conditioned nirvāṇa possesses impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity; unconditioned nirvāṇa possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Although one may believe that the Buddha-nature exists within sentient beings, it is not necessarily the case that all possess it; therefore, this is called 'incomplete faith. Good son!"
Faith is of two kinds:
first, faith; second, seeking.
Although such a person possesses faith, they are unable to investigate and seek [the truth]; therefore, it is said that their faith is incomplete.
Faith is further twofold:
first, that which arises from hearing; second, that which arises from reflection.
This person’s faith arises from hearing and not from reflection; therefore, it is said that their faith is incomplete.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, faith that the Path exists; second, faith that there are those who have attained it.
If a person’s faithful mind believes only that the Path exists, but does not at all believe that there are people who have attained the Path, this is called incomplete faith.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, faith in what is correct; second, faith in what is false.
To believe that cause and effect exist, and that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha exist, is called faith in what is correct.
To claim that there is no cause and effect, that the Three Jewels have distinct natures, and to believe the false teachings of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others—this is called believing in heterodoxy.
Such a person, though they may believe in the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, does not believe that the Three Jewels share the same nature and characteristics;
though they believe in cause and effect, they do not believe in those who attain them.
For this reason, it is said that their faith is incomplete.
Such a person achieves an incomplete faith, and the precepts they receive are likewise incomplete.
For what cause and condition is it called "incomplete"?
Because the causes are incomplete, the precepts one has obtained are likewise not complete.
Furthermore, for what reasons are they called incomplete?
There are two kinds of precepts:
First, the precept of dignified conduct; second, the precept of following [the training].
This person possesses only the precepts such as dignified conduct, but does not possess the precept of following [the training]; therefore, it is said that their precepts are incomplete.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the precept of action (*vijñapti-śīla*); second, the precept of non-action (*avijñapti-śīla*).
This person possesses only the precept of action and does not possess the precept of non-action; therefore, it is said that their precepts are incomplete.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, attaining right livelihood through body and speech; second, failing to attain right livelihood through body and speech.
Although such a person acts through body and speech, they do not attain right livelihood; for this reason, it is said that their precepts are incomplete.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, seeking precepts; second, relinquishing precepts.
This person possesses only the precepts for seeking existence and fails to attain the relinquishing of precepts; therefore, it is said that their precepts are incomplete.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, that which accords with existence (bhava-anuvartin), and second, that which accords with the Path (mārga-anuvartin).
This person possesses only the precepts that accord with existence and lacks those that accord with the Path; therefore, it is said that their precepts are incomplete.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, virtuous precepts; second, unvirtuous precepts.
Virtue of body, speech, and mind is called virtuous precepts.
The cow-vow and the dog-vow are called evil precepts.
Because such a person deeply believes that both of these two types of vows produce wholesome fruits, they are said to have incomplete precepts.
"This person lacks both faith and precepts, and their cultivation of much learning is likewise incomplete.
What is meant by 'incomplete learning'?
Regarding the twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, they believe in only six divisions and do not believe in the other six; for this reason, it is called incomplete learning."
Although one may uphold these six classes of sūtras, if one is unable to recite them or explain them to others, they provide no benefit; for this reason, it is called "incompleteness of hearing."

Furthermore, having received these six classes of sūtras, if one upholds, reads, recites, or explains them for the sake of debate, for the sake of defeating others, for the sake of gain and offerings, or for the sake of various states of existence, this is called "incomplete hearing."
“Good son! In the sūtras, I have spoken of being endowed with hearing.
What constitutes such endowment?

If there is a bhikṣu whose body, speech, and mind are virtuous, who is first able to make offerings to his preceptors, teachers, and those of great virtue, these teachers will give rise to a heart of affection and regard for such a person;
by this cause and condition, they will instruct him in the sūtras and dharmas, and that person will receive, uphold, recite, and practice them with a sincere heart.
Having mastered the recitation and practice, one attains wisdom;
having attained wisdom, one is able to reflect skillfully and abide in accordance with the Dharma;
having reflected skillfully, one then attains the true meaning.
Having attained right understanding, body and mind become tranquil;
when body and mind are tranquil, a sense of joy arises;
with joy as its condition, the mind attains concentration.
Because one attains meditative concentration, one attains right knowledge and vision;
having attained right knowledge and vision, weariness and remorse arise toward all states of existence;
through this remorse for all states of existence, one is able to attain liberation.
This person lacks such matters as these; therefore, they are said to be "incomplete in hearing.
Because this person lacks these three things, their giving is likewise incomplete.
There are two kinds of giving:
first, the giving of material wealth; second, the giving of the Dharma.
Although this person practices the giving of material wealth, they do so for the sake of seeking existence; thus, even though they practice the giving of the Dharma, it is not complete.
Why is this? Because one withholds and does not explain fully out of fear that others might surpass them, it is therefore called "incomplete giving.
There are two kinds each for the two types of giving: material giving and the giving of the Dharma.
First is the noble, and second is the non-noble.
The noble, having given, does not seek a karmic reward;
the non-noble, having given, seeks a karmic reward.
The noble gift of Dharma is for the increase of the Dharma; the non-noble gift of Dharma is for the increase of existence (*bhava*).
Such a person practices the gift of wealth for the sake of increasing wealth, and practices the gift of Dharma for the sake of increasing existence; therefore, this is called "incomplete generosity."

Furthermore, this person receives the six classes of sūtras; seeing those who receive the Dharma, they provide for them, yet seeing those who do not receive the Dharma, they do not provide for them. For this reason, it is called incomplete giving.
"This person does not possess the four aforementioned matters, and thus the wisdom they cultivate is also incomplete.
While the nature of wisdom is inherently capable of discernment, this person is unable to discern whether the Tathāgata is permanent or impermanent."
In this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata has said:
"The Tathāgata is liberation, and liberation is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is nirvāṇa, and nirvāṇa is liberation."

Within this meaning, one is unable to discern that the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is itself the Tathāgata, that the Tathāgata is himself loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); that loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are themselves liberation (*vimukti*); that liberation is itself nirvāṇa; and that nirvāṇa is itself loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
In this regard, one is unable to make such distinctions; therefore, it is said that their wisdom is incomplete.

Furthermore, one cannot distinguish the Buddha-nature. The Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is all the unshared dharmas; the unshared dharmas are liberation; liberation is nirvāṇa; and nirvāṇa is the unshared dharma.
Because one cannot discern within this meaning, it is called the non-fulfillment of wisdom.
Furthermore, one cannot discern the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Because they cannot discern the Four Noble Truths, they do not know the noble practice;
because they do not know the noble practice, they do not know the Tathāgata;
because they do not know the Tathāgata, they do not know liberation.
Because they do not understand liberation, they do not understand nirvana.
For this reason, it is said that their wisdom is incomplete.
"If a person lacks these five things, there are two types [of such individuals]:
First, the increase of wholesome dharmas; second, the increase of unwholesome dharmas.
What is meant by the increase of unwholesome dharmas?

This person does not see their own deficiencies, yet claims to be complete and gives rise to a mind of attachment. Among those practicing the same path, they consider themselves superior; for this reason, they associate with evil friends who are like themselves.
Having associated with them, they further hear the incomplete Dharma.
Having heard it, their minds are delighted; their hearts become stained by attachment, giving rise to arrogance, and they practice much heedlessness.
Due to negligence, they associate with householders and take pleasure in hearing accounts of household life, while distancing themselves from the pure dharma of renunciation.
By these causes and conditions, unwholesome dharmas increase;
because unwholesome dharmas increase, impure karma arises through body, speech, and mind.
Because their three karmas are impure, they increase their rebirths in the hells, as animals, and as hungry ghosts.
This is called "emerging for a moment and then sinking back.
As for those who "emerge for a moment and then sink back," who among my disciples in the Buddha-dharma are they?

These are Devadatta, the bhikṣu Kokālika, the bhikṣu Khaṇḍadravya, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, the bhikṣu Tiṣya, the bhikṣu Puṣyamitra, the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī, the bhikṣuṇī Āraṇyā, the bhikṣuṇī Dāruka, the bhikṣuṇī Mānāpyā, the householder Śuddha, the upāsaka Bhavila, the Śākya Śaila, the householder Hastaka, the upāsikā Yaśodharā, the upāsikā Prabhāvatī, the upāsikā Nandā, the upāsikā Senā, and the upāsikā Ghaṇṭā. Such persons as these are said to be those who emerge for a moment and then sink back down; they are like a great fish that emerges because it sees the light, but sinks because its body is heavy.
"The second person has deep self-awareness that his practice is incomplete;
because it is incomplete, he seeks out virtuous friends;
because he associates with virtuous friends, he delights in inquiring about what he has not yet heard, and having heard it, he delights in receiving it."
Having received [the teaching], one delights in wholesome reflection;
having reflected well, one is able to abide in accordance with the Dharma;
by abiding in accordance with the Dharma, one increases wholesome qualities.
Because they increase wholesome dharmas, they never again sink back;
this is called "abiding.
"Who among my disciples in the Buddha-dharma is such a person?"
That is to say: Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the five bhikṣus beginning with Ājñātakauṇḍinya,
the five hundred bhikṣus beginning with Yaśas, the youth Anuruddha,
Kāśyapa and Mahākāśyapa, Daśabala-Kāśyapa, the bhikṣuṇī Prabhāvatī Gautamī, and Pāṭalāpuṣpā Bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā, the bhikṣuṇī Jitā, the bhikṣuṇī Bhūtārthā, the bhikṣuṇī Manasvinī, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā, the bhikṣuṇī Śuddhā,
the bhikṣuṇī Avaivartikā; King Bimbisāra, the householder Ugata, the householder Sudatta, Śreṣṭhi Mānava, and the poor man Suvarṇa.
Datta, the householder’s son Mārjāra, the householder Yaśas, the householder Saṃpanna,
the General (or his son, according to some texts), the householder Upāli, the householder Kṣuraka,
the female lay follower Abhayā, the female lay follower Susthitā, the female lay follower Dharmapriyā, and the female lay follower Śūra.
The laywoman Īśī, the laywoman Devatā, the laywoman Sujātā, the laywoman Gopikā, the laywoman Aṭavikā, and the laywoman Mahāsena—
monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen such as these are called by that name.
Abiding.
What is meant by abiding?
It is because one constantly delights in beholding the excellent radiance.
For this reason, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, such persons as these will never commit evil; this is called "abiding.
Just as the timi fish delights in seeing light and neither sinks nor drowns, so too it is with these multitudes.
Therefore, I have spoken this verse in the sutra:
"If a person is well able to discern the meaning, And seeks with a sincere heart the fruits of the śramaṇa,
If they can revile all forms of existence (bhava), Such a person is said to dwell in accordance with the Dharma."
If one can make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Then one can cultivate the path for immeasurable lifetimes;
If one experiences worldly happiness without negligence, Such a person is said to abide in accordance with the Dharma.
Associate with virtuous friends and listen to the True Dharma; Internally reflect well and abide according to the Dharma.
Delight in seeing the light and cultivate the Path; Thus one attains liberation and dwells in peace.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-two.
[Scroll Thirty-three] of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huiyan and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Twenty-fourth Chapter, "The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa," Part Three: "Good son!

There are five things by which wisdom is not fully perfected. Once a person has recognized these, they should seek out a virtuous friend. Such a virtuous friend should observe which of this person's afflictions—greed, anger, delusion, or discursive thought—is most predominant."
If one knows that a person has much greed and desire, one should teach them the method of the contemplation on impurity;
for one with much anger and hatred, one should teach them loving-kindness and compassion;
for one with many discursive thoughts, one should instruct them in counting the breaths.
For those who are strongly attached to the self, one should analyze the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth for them.
Having heard this, such a person will receive and uphold it with a sincere mind;
having received and upheld it in their mind, they will practice according to the Dharma.
Having practiced in accordance with the Dharma, one sequentially attains the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Having attained this contemplation, one next contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination;
having contemplated in this manner, one subsequently attains the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings possess the dharma of ‘warmth.’”
Why is this? As the Buddha has said:
"The conjunction of three factors is called a sentient being."
First, life; second, warmth; third, consciousness.
According to this principle, all sentient beings should first possess warmth.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata say that the dharma of warmth arises from a virtuous friend?
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Regarding the 'dharma of warmth' that you have asked about, all sentient beings, down to the icchantikas, possess it."
The "Heat" stage (*uṣmagata*) that I have now described must be attained through skillful means; it was originally non-existent and now exists.
For this reason, it is not the case that all sentient beings possess it from the very beginning.
Therefore, you should not now raise the objection that all sentient beings possess the factor of warmth (*ūṣmagata*).
"Good son, such a factor of warmth is a dharma of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); it does not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)."
If one says that all sentient beings possess [it], then sentient beings of the desire realm should also all possess it;
since it does not exist in the desire realm, one should know that it is not necessarily present in all.
Good son! Although the realm of form exists, it does not exist in all places. Why is this?
My disciples possess it, whereas the non-Buddhists do not.
For this reason, it is not necessarily the case that all sentient beings possess it. Good son!
All non-Buddhists contemplate only six aspects, whereas my disciples are fully endowed with sixteen aspects; yet these sixteen aspects are not necessarily possessed by all sentient beings.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called the ‘Dharma of Heat’ (ūṣmagata), why is it named ‘Heat’?”
“Is it warm by its own nature,
or is it warm because of something else?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Thus, the nature of this Dharma of Heat is heat itself; it is not hot because of something else.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata previously stated that Aśvajit and Pūrṇa lacked the dharma of ‘warmth.
For what reason?”
"Because they lack faith toward the Triple Gem, they possess no 'warmth' (ūṣmagata). You should know that faith itself is the dharma of warmth.
"Good son! Faith is not the dharma of warmth."
Why is this? Because it is by relying on faith that one subsequently attains "Heat" (ūṣmagata). Good son!
Now, the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) is itself wisdom. Why is this?
Because it contemplates the Four Noble Truths; for this reason, it is called the "Sixteen Aspects" (ṣoḍaśākāra), and these aspects are themselves wisdom.
"Good son! Regarding what you have asked:
'By what causes and conditions is it called "Heat' (ūṣman)?'"
"O son of good family!
As for the dharma of 'warmth' (uṣmagata), it is the sign of the fire of the Eightfold Noble Path; therefore, it is called 'warmth.
O son of good family!"
It is like kindling a fire: first there is warmth, next fire arises, and finally smoke emerges.

The path of outflowlessness (anāsrava-mārga) is also like this: "warmth" refers to the sixteen aspects (ṣoḍaśākāra); "fire" refers to the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala); and "smoke" refers to the severing of fetters through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma of Heat is likewise both an existent dharma and a conditioned dharma.”
This dharma is obtained as a retribution for its fruit as the five aggregates of the form realm; therefore, it is called "existence" (bhava).
Because it arises from causes and conditions, it is further called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta).
If it is conditioned, how can it serve as the characteristic of the untainted path (anāsravamārga)?
The Buddha said,
“Good man! So it is,
so it is, just as you have said.”

Good son! Although this dharma of "heat" (ūṣmagata) is conditioned and a conditioned phenomenon, it can nevertheless destroy that which is conditioned and phenomenal; therefore, it serves as the precursor to the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
Good son! It is like a person riding a horse, who both loves it and strikes it with a whip.
The mind of warmth is likewise: because of love, one undergoes rebirth; because of weariness, one practices contemplation.
Therefore, although these are still dharmas and conditioned phenomena, they can serve as the signs for that right path.
There are seventy-three types of persons who have attained "Heat," and ten types within the desire realm.

This person is fully possessed of all afflictions; from the severing of one part up to nine parts—just as it is for the desire realm and the first dhyāna, so it is likewise up to the sphere of nothingness. These are called the seventy-three kinds.
When such persons have attained the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), they can no longer sever their roots of goodness, commit the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), or violate the four grave prohibitions.
These persons are of two kinds:
first, those who encounter virtuous friends; second, those who encounter evil friends.
One who encounters evil friends emerges for a moment only to sink back;
one who encounters virtuous friends surveys all four directions.

To survey the four directions is the Dharma of the Summit (mūrdhan). Although this Dharma is by nature the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) and also takes the Four Noble Truths as its object, it is therefore named "surveying all four directions."
Having attained the stage of the Peak (mūrdhan), one next attains the stage of Patience (kṣānti).
This Patience is likewise such that its nature consists of the five aggregates and it takes the Four Noble Truths as its object.
This person next attains the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma); although this dharma is also by nature the five aggregates, it likewise takes the Four Noble Truths as its object.
This person successively attains the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). The nature of this patience is wisdom (*prajñā*), which takes one truth as its object.

Once this dharma of patience has taken the one truth as its object, he proceeds until the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing are eliminated and the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*) is attained; this is called the fourth time of surveying the four directions. The "four directions" refers to the Four Noble Truths.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously said:”
"It is said that the afflictions severed by a *srotāpanna* are like forty *li* of water in length and breadth, while those remaining are like a single drop on a hair.
How, then, can it be said here that one who has severed the three fetters is named a *srotāpanna*:
first, the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, the view of what is not a cause as a cause (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); and third, the net of doubt (*vicikitsā*)?"
World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions is he called "one who surveys the four directions"?
And for what further causes and conditions is he called a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna)?
"Furthermore, for what reason is the Srotāpanna compared to the *śiśumāra* fish?
The Buddha said, "Good son!

Although a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is able to sever immeasurable afflictions, these three are emphasized because they are particularly heavy and because they encompass all the fetters (saṃyojana) severed by a stream-enterer.
Good son! It is like when a great king goes out on a tour of inspection; although he has the fourfold army with him, people of the world all say, "The king comes" or "The king goes. Why is this?
Because they are grave in the world,
these three afflictions are likewise so.
For what reason and by what conditions are they called "grave"?
Because they are constantly aroused by all sentient beings and are subtle and difficult to discern, they are called "heavy.

Likewise, because these three fetters are difficult to sever, because they can serve as the cause for all afflictions, and because they are the enemies that oppose their respective remedies—namely, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—they are so designated.
"Good son!
There are sentient beings who, upon hearing that a srotāpanna can sever such immeasurable afflictions, give rise to a regressive mind and say:
'How can sentient beings sever such immeasurable afflictions?'"
"For this reason, the Tathāgata has expediently taught three [vehicles].
As to what you asked:
'For what cause and condition is it that a srotāpanna is compared to one who gazes in the four directions?'"
"Good son! A person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna contemplates the Four Noble Truths and obtains four things:
first, abiding in the firm path; second, being able to observe universally; third, being able to see according to reality; and fourth, being able to destroy the great enemy."
The "firm path" refers to the five faculties possessed by a *srotāpanna* which nothing can shake; for this reason, it is called "abiding in the firm path.
"Able to observe universally" means being able to censure all internal and external afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Seeing according to reality" is precisely the wisdom of patience (*kṣānti-jñāna*).
The "destroyer of great enemies" refers to the four inversions. As you have asked:
"For what causes and conditions is one called a *srotāpanna*?"
"O son of good family!
'Srotas' means 'outflow-free,' and 'āpanna' means 'cultivation. Because one cultivates that which is outflow-free, one is called a Srotāpanna.
Son of good family!"
Furthermore, there is that which is called "flowing.
Flowing is of two kinds:
first, flowing with the current; second, flowing against the current.
"Because he flows against the current, he is named Srotāpanna.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
If this is the meaning, for what reason are the *sakṛdāgāmin*, the *anāgāmin*, and the *arhat* not also called *srotāpanna*?
“Good son! From the srotāpanna up to all Buddhas, they may also be called ‘srotāpannas.
If there were no srotāpannas from the sakṛdāgāmin up to all Buddhas, how could they be named ‘sakṛdāgāmins’ up to ‘Buddhas’?”
All sentient beings have two kinds of names:
first, the original; second, the adventitious.
During the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one has a worldly name; once one has attained the Way, a new name is established for them, such as *srotāpanna*.
Because of what was attained first, one is called a *srotāpanna*;
because of what was attained later, one is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Such a person is thus named both a *srotāpanna* and a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Even the Buddha is likewise thus.
"Good son, there are two kinds of flow:
The first is liberation and the second is nirvāṇa.
All noble ones possess these two; they may be called *srotāpanna*, and they may also be called *sakṛdāgāmin*;
even the Buddha is likewise so.
“Good son! One who is a srotāpanna is also called a bodhisattva. Why is this?
A bodhisattva is precisely one who possesses the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
A *srotāpanna* likewise seeks these two kinds of knowledge; therefore, it should be known that a *srotāpanna* is given the name "bodhisattva."
"One who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna may also be called 'Awakened. Why is this?

Because they have correctly awakened to the severing of afflictions through the vision of the Path; because they have correctly awakened to cause and effect; and because they have correctly awakened to both the common path and the uncommon path."
It is the same for the Sakṛdāgāmin up to the Arhat.
"Good son, there are two kinds of Srotāpanna:
First, those of sharp faculties; second, those of dull faculties.
Those of dull faculties return among humans and devas seven times.
There are five further types of these individuals with dull faculties:
Some may have six, five, four, three, or two [returns].
Those of sharp faculties attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat in the present life.
“Good son! Regarding your question:
‘For what reason is the srotāpanna likened to a *śiśumāra* (crocodile)?’”
"Good son! The *śakula* fish has four characteristics:
first, it is light because its bones are fine; second, it is light because it has fins; third, it delights in seeing bright light; and fourth, it clamps onto objects and holds them fast."
The person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna likewise possesses four matters:
"having fine bones" is a metaphor for the subtlety of afflictions;
"having wings" is a metaphor for śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Delighting in seeing light is a metaphor for the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*);
holding onto objects with firm persistence is a metaphor for hearing the Tathāgata teach impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity, and holding fast to them without relinquishing them.
It was as if the Māra King had manifested himself in the form of a Buddha; when the elder Śūra saw him, his heart was struck with alarm.
Seeing that the elder’s mind was shaken, the Māra immediately said to him:
"The Four Noble Truths I previously taught were not the truth; I shall now teach you instead the Five Truths, the Six Aggregates, the Thirteen Bases, and the Nineteen Elements."

Having heard this, the elder immediately examined the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and found that none of these principles existed; therefore, he firmly maintained his resolve without wavering.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is one called a *srotāpanna* because they first attained the Path,
or is one called a *srotāpanna* because of being the first fruit?

If one were called a *srotāpanna* simply for first attaining the Path, then why at the moment of attaining the *duḥkha-dharma-jñānakṣānti* is one not called a *srotāpanna*, but rather called one who is "facing" it (*pratipannaka*)?

If one is named a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) by virtue of the first fruit, then why are those non-Buddhists—who have previously severed afflictions up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and attained the fruit of *anāgāmin* (non-returner) by cultivating the untainted path—not also named *srotāpannas*?
“Good son! Because of the first fruit, one is called a srotāpanna.
As you have asked:”
"If non-Buddhists first sever their afflictions up to the sphere of nothingness and, by cultivating the untainted path, attain the stage of Anāgāmin, why are they not called Srotāpannas?"
"O son of good family!
Because of the first fruit, one is called a Srotāpanna; at that time, this person is fully endowed with the eight knowledges and the sixteen aspects."
Kāśyapa said:
“World-Honored One!
It is likewise for one who has attained the stage of Anāgāmin; they too have attained the eight knowledges and are endowed with the sixteen aspects.”
"Why is he not called a Srotāpanna?
"Good son, there are two kinds of sixteen aspects of the outflows (sāsrava):"
First, the shared; second, the unshared.
The sixteen aspects of the untainted (anāsrava) also have two kinds:
first, those tending toward the fruit; second, those attaining the fruit.
The eight knowledges are also twofold: first, those directed toward the fruit; second, those that have attained the fruit.

A person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna abandons the sixteen modes of practice shared with others and attains the sixteen modes of practice not shared with others; they abandon the eight knowledges directed toward the fruit and attain the eight knowledges that have realized the fruit. One who has attained the stage of Anāgāmin is not like this; for this reason, the first fruit is named Srotāpanna.
“Good son! A srotāpanna takes the four truths as his object of focus, whereas an anāgāmin takes only one truth as his object; for this reason, the first fruit is called srotāpanna.”
For these reasons, he uses the shark as a metaphor.

"Having observed all around before proceeding" refers to the *sakṛdāgāmin* who fixes his mind on the path of cultivation in order to sever greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—just as that shark observes all directions before proceeding for the sake of food.
"Having traveled, one again dwells, just as an Anāgāmin dwells after having received food.
There are generally two kinds of Anāgāmins:

first, those who attain the state of Anāgāmin in the present life and, by further cultivation, immediately attain the fruit of Arhatship; second, those who are attached to the tranquil samādhis within the realm of form and the formless realm; because such persons do not receive a body in the desire realm, they are called Anāgāmins."
These Anāgāmins are further divided into five types:

first, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; second, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon taking rebirth; third, those who attain parinirvāṇa through effort; fourth, those who attain parinirvāṇa without effort; and fifth, those who attain parinirvāṇa by flowing upward.
Furthermore, there are six types:
five are as described above, and the sixth is parinirvāṇa in the present life.
Furthermore, there are seven types:
The six types are as described above; the seventh is parinirvāṇa in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of *sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion):
either one who undergoes two births or one who undergoes four births.
If one receives two bodies, this is called having sharp faculties;
if one receives four bodies, this is called having dull faculties.
Furthermore, there are two types:
First, there is diligence without mastery over concentration; second, there is indolence with mastery over concentration.
Furthermore, there are two types:
first, those who possess both diligence and concentration; second, those who do not possess these two.
“Good son! Sentient beings of the desire and form realms have two kinds of karma:
first, the karma of action; second, the karma of rebirth.”
One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state possesses only the karma of activity and lacks the karma for rebirth; therefore, they attain parinirvāṇa therein.
Having cast off the body of the desire realm and before reaching the form realm, they attain parinirvāṇa in the interim due to their sharp faculties; this is "parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state."
“Anāgāmins have four kinds of mind:
first, that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner; second, the learner; third, the non-learner; and fourth, the neither-learner-nor-non-learner that enters into nirvāṇa.”
"What, furthermore, is meant by 'parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state' (antarā-parinirvāyin)? Good son!
Among the four types of minds of an Anāgāmin, two are nirvāṇa and two are not nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called 'parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.'"
“Regarding the nirvana of the body, there are further two kinds:
first, the karma of action;
second, the karma of birth.”
"This person abandons the body of the desire realm and receives a body of the form realm; through diligent cultivation of the Way, they exhaust their lifespan and enter nirvana.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
“If you say that one enters nirvana at the end of one’s life, why do you say that one attains nirvana while receiving a body?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
This person attains a physical body and only thereafter severs the afflictions of the triple world; for this reason, it is called "Nirvana upon Receiving a Body. "Good son!

One who attains Nirvana through Practice constantly cultivates the Path; by the power of conditioned samādhi, they are able to sever the afflictions and enter Nirvana—this is called 'Nirvana through Practice.'"

"One who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion" refers to a person who knows with certainty that they shall attain nirvāṇa; therefore, they are indolent. Nevertheless, by the power of conditioned samādhi, they enter parinirvāṇa upon the exhaustion of their lifespan; this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion."

"Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the upward stream: suppose there is someone who has attained the fourth dhyāna; this person then gives rise to a craving for the first dhyāna, and by reason of this, they fall back and are reborn in the first dhyāna."
There are two kinds of currents:
first, the current of afflictions; second, the current of the Path.
