Because of the current of the Path, when this person’s lifespan ends, they give rise to craving for the Second Dhyāna; by reason of that craving, they are born into the Second Dhyāna.
It is likewise for the fourth dhyāna.
Within these four dhyānas, there are again two kinds:
first, entering the formless realm; second, entering the five Pure Abodes.
Thus, there are two types of persons: first, those who delight in samādhi; second, those who delight in wisdom.
Those who delight in wisdom enter the Five Pure Abodes;
those who delight in samādhi enter the Formless Realm.

"Regarding these two types of persons—the first who cultivates the fourth dhyāna, for whom there are five stages of distinction, and the second who does not cultivate it—what are these five? [They are:]..."
There are the lower, the middle, the upper, the upper-middle, and the uppermost.
Those who cultivate the uppermost dwell in the Heaven of No-Strife (Anabhraka);
those who cultivate the upper-middle dwell in the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarśana).
Those who practice the superior grade dwell in the Sudarśana Heaven;
those who practice the middling grade dwell in the Atapa Heaven;
and those who practice the inferior grade dwell in the Parīttaśubha Heaven.
"Thus there are two types of persons: first, those who delight in debate; second, those who delight in tranquility.
Those who delight in tranquility enter the formless realm;
those who delight in debate dwell in the five Pure Abodes."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the cultivation of perfuming dhyāna; second, the non-cultivation of perfuming dhyāna.
Those who cultivate perfuming dhyāna enter the five Pure Abodes."

Those who do not cultivate the *vāsana-bhāvanā* dhyāna are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and attain parinirvāṇa at the end of their lifespan; these are called those who attain parinirvāṇa as an "upward-streamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
If one wishes to enter the formless realm, one cannot cultivate the four dhyānas and the five distinctions (*pañca-viśeṣa*);
if one cultivates the five distinctions, one is then able to censure the meditative absorptions of the formless realm.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state possess sharp faculties. If they possess such sharp faculties, why do they not enter parinirvāṇa in the present life?”
"For what reason is there parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state within the desire realm, yet none in the form realm?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
This person’s four great elements are currently weak and inferior, and thus they cannot cultivate the Path.

Although there may be monks whose four great elements are healthy, they lack dwellings, food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine; because these various conditions are not complete, they cannot attain nirvana in the present life.
“Good son! Once, in the past, while I was at the Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī, a certain bhikṣu came to me and spoke these words:
‘World-Honored One!’”
'I have constantly practiced the Path, yet I am unable to attain the fruit of a Stream-enterer up to the fruit of an Arhat.
At that time, I immediately said to Ānanda:
'You should now provide all the necessities for this bhikṣu.'"
At that time, Ānanda took this bhikṣu to the Jeta Grove and provided him with a fine dwelling.
Then the bhikṣu said to Ānanda:
"Venerable One!..."
"I only wish that you would adorn my dwelling, making it pure and well-ordered, magnificent with the seven treasures, and hung with silken banners and canopies.
Ānanda said, "In this world, those who are poor are called śramaṇas; how could I possibly manage such a task?"
The bhikṣu said:
"Venerable sir!
If you can do this for me, it would be well; otherwise, I shall go elsewhere."
"If I am unable, I shall return to the presence of the World-Honored One.
At that time, Ānanda went to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!"
"Just now, that bhikṣu requested from me various ornaments, banners, and canopies made of the seven precious gems;
I wonder how this matter should be handled? At that time, I again told Ānanda:
"Go back now and, according to the bhikṣu's wishes, prepare whatever items he requires."
At that time, Ānanda immediately returned to his room and prepared everything for this bhikṣu in full detail.
Having received these, the bhikṣu applied his mindfulness to the cultivation of the path, and before long he attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhatship.
"Good son!

There are immeasurable sentient beings who ought to enter nirvana, yet because they lack certain necessities, their minds are distracted and disturbed; for this reason, they do not attain it. Good son!"

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who greatly delight in teaching and transforming others; because their minds are preoccupied with such activities, they cannot attain meditative concentration, and for this reason, they do not attain nirvana in the present life. "Good son!
Regarding what you have asked:
"For what reason is there parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state after casting off the body of the desire realm, but not in the form realm?
O son of good family!
This person contemplates that the causes and conditions for afflictions in the desire realm are twofold:
first, internal; second, external. However, within the form realm, there are no external causes and conditions.
Within the desire realm, there are further two kinds of craving:
first, craving for sensual pleasures; second, craving for food.
One should contemplate these two cravings and reproach them with a sincere heart.
Having thus rebuked them, they attain nirvana.

Within this desire realm, one is able to rebuke the various coarse afflictions—namely stinginess, greed, anger, envy, lack of shame, and lack of remorse—and by these causes and conditions, one is able to attain nirvana.
Furthermore, the nature of the path in the desire realm is courageous and robust.
Why is this? Because one attains the four fruits [of the śramaṇa].
Therefore, there is parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state within the desire realm, but none within the form realm.
"Good son! There are three kinds of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state:
These are the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
The superior attains nirvana after casting off the body but before departing from the desire realm;
the middling attains nirvana after first departing from the desire realm but before reaching the form realm.
The inferior [type] leaves the desire realm and attains nirvana only upon reaching the limit of the form realm;
this person is like a shark that stays after having obtained its prey.
What is meant by "abiding"?
Because one dwells in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and thereby receives a body, it is called abiding;
because one does not receive [the states of] the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), humans, devas, hells, animals, or hungry ghosts, it is therefore called abiding.
Having already severed immeasurable fetters of affliction, because only a small remainder remains, it is therefore called "abiding.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it named "abiding"?
Because one ultimately never performs actions common to ordinary worldlings, it is therefore called "abiding."
Being fearless oneself and not causing others to fear—therefore it is called "abiding.
Being far removed from the two kinds of craving, stinginess and greed, and anger—therefore it is called "abiding."
“Good son! Those who have reached the other shore—namely Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—are like divine tortoises, able to travel both on land and in water.”
For what reason is he compared to a tortoise?
Because he well conceals his five [senses].
It is the same for Arhats up to the Buddhas; they likewise well cover their five faculties, and for this reason they are compared to a tortoise.
Regarding the terms "water" and "land": water is a metaphor for the mundane world, and land is a metaphor for the supramundane.
These various sages are likewise so; because they are able to contemplate all evil afflictions, they reach the other shore. Therefore, they are compared to those who travel by both water and land.
“Good son! Just as the seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River, though they have names such as ‘fish’ or ‘tortoise,’ do not depart from the water;
so too, within this subtle and wondrous Great Nirvana, from the icchantika up to the Buddhas, though there are different names, they likewise do not depart from the water of Buddha-nature.”

Good son! For these seven types of sentient beings, whether it be wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, the path of skillful means or the path of liberation, the sequential path or cause and fruit—all of these are the Buddha-nature.
"This is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
If there is a cause, then there is an effect; if there is no cause, then there is no effect.
Nirvana is called an effect, yet because it is eternal, it has no cause.
If it has no cause, how can it be called an effect?
Furthermore, this nirvāṇa is also called the śramaṇa and the fruit of the śramaṇa (śrāmaṇyaphala).
What is the śramaṇa?
What is the fruit of the śramaṇa?
“Good son! There are seven kinds of fruits in all the worlds: first, the fruit of skillful means;

second, the fruit of repaying kindness; third, the fruit of intimacy; fourth, the fruit of remnants; fifth, the fruit of equality; sixth, the fruit of retribution; and seventh, the fruit of detachment.”
"Regarding the fruit of skillful means (upāya-phala): it is like people in the world who, having harvested much grain in autumn, say to one another, 'We have obtained the fruit of skillful means.
This fruit of skillful means is called the fruit of karmic action."
Such a fruit has two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause is what is called the seed.
The distant cause refers to water, fertilizer, and human labor;
this is called the fruit of skillful means.
As for the fruit of repaying kindness, it is like when people of the world provide for their parents, and the parents both say:
"I have now obtained the fruit of being nurtured.
That a child is able to repay their kindness is what is called "fruit.
Such a fruit likewise has two kinds of causes:
First is the proximate cause, and second is the remote cause.
The proximate cause is the parents' past karma of pure goodness;
the remote cause is the filial son who is born.
This is called the fruit of repaying kindness.
As for the "fruit of intimacy," it is like a person who associates with virtuous friends and attains the fruit of a *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of an *arhat*. That person proclaims:
"I have now attained the retribution of the fruit of intimacy."
Regarding such fruits, there are two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause is faith.
The distant [result] is the virtuous friend;
this is called the result of association.
As for the remaining results, such as obtaining a third body through the practice of non-killing, whereby one’s years are extended and one’s life is prolonged—this is called the residual result.
Such a fruit has two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause is the purification of body, speech, and mind.
The "distant" refers to the prolongation of life and the increase of longevity;
this is called the "residual fruit.
The "fruit of equality" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Such a fruit likewise has two kinds of causes:
first, the proximate cause; second, the remote cause.
The proximate cause refers to sentient beings cultivating the ten wholesome karmas.
The remote cause refers to what are called the three calamities;
this is termed the fruit of equality.
As for the fruit of retribution: it is like a person who, having obtained a pure body, cultivates pure karma of body, speech, and mind, whereupon that person says:
"I have attained the fruit of retribution.
Regarding such fruits, there are two kinds of causes:
first, proximate causes; second, remote causes.
The proximate cause refers to the purity of body, speech, and mind in the present;
the remote cause refers to the purity of body, speech, and mind in the past.
This is called the fruit of retribution.
As for the "fruit of separation," it is nirvana, which is free from all afflictions.
All wholesome karmas are causes of nirvana, and these are further of two kinds:
First is the proximate cause, and second is the remote cause.
The proximate cause refers to the three gates of liberation;
the remote cause refers to the wholesome dharmas cultivated over immeasurable lifetimes.
“Good son! Just as in worldly dharmas, one speaks of either productive causes (*janaka-hetu*) or revealing causes (*paridīpaka-hetu*);
so too it is with supramundane dharmas, for which one likewise speaks of both productive causes and revealing causes.”
Good son! The three gates of liberation and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment can act as the non-arising cause for all afflictions, and they also act as the revealing cause for nirvana.
Good son! By being far removed from afflictions, one attains clear vision of nirvana; therefore, nirvana possesses only a revealing cause and no productive cause.
“Good son! Regarding what you have asked:
‘What is a śramaṇa?’”
"What is the fruit of the śramaṇa?
[To this,] son of good family,
"śramaṇa" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path;
The fruit of the śramaṇa consists in the ultimate and permanent abandonment of all greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth through the Path.
This is called the śramaṇa and the fruit of the śramaṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason and by what causes and conditions is the Eightfold Noble Path called *śramaṇatā*?”
“Good son! In the world, ‘śramaṇa’ is named ‘exhaustion,’ and ‘na’ is named ‘path.
Such a path severs all exhaustion and severs all paths.”
For this reason, the Eightfold Noble Path is called *śramaṇatā*.
Because one attains the fruits from within this path, they are called the fruits of the *śramaṇa*. "Good son!
Furthermore, regarding the term *śramaṇa*: just as people in the world who delight in tranquility are also called *śramaṇas*, so too is this path.
It enables the practitioner to abandon the evils of body, speech, and mind, as well as wrong livelihood, and to attain the bliss of stillness; therefore, it is named *śramaṇa*.
“Good son! Just as an inferior person of the world can become a superior person, he is called a śramaṇa.
This path is also like this; because it can cause an inferior person to become a superior person, it is therefore named śramaṇatā.”
“Good son! Those Arhats who cultivate this path attain the fruits of śrāmaṇya; for this reason, they are said to have reached the other shore.

The fruit of arhatship is precisely the fivefold dharmakāya of one beyond training—precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Because they reach the other shore by means of these five factors, they are called those who have reached the other shore.”
Having reached the further shore, he declared of himself:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."
“Good son! Because this Arhat has forever severed the causes and conditions for birth throughout the three periods of time, he declares of himself: ‘Birth is exhausted.
Furthermore, because he has also severed the body of the five aggregates within the three realms, he further says: ‘Birth is exhausted.’”
Because the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that was practiced has reached its ultimate consummation, he proclaims: "The holy life has been established.

Furthermore, having relinquished the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*), it is also called "established"; since what was originally sought has now been attained, he proclaims: "What was to be done has been accomplished" (*kṛta-kṛtya*).

Having attained the fruits through the cultivation of the path, one is said to have "already accomplished" what was to be done; because of having obtained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), one proclaims:
"My births are exhausted; I have destroyed all fetters of existence."
For this reason, they are called Arhats who have reached the other shore.
As it is with the Arhats, so it is with the Pratyekabuddhas.
Bodhisattvas and Buddhas, having fully accomplished the six pāramitās, are said to have reached the other shore.
When these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are said to be fully endowed with the six pāramitās. Why is this so?
Because one attains the fruit of the six pāramitās,
and because one has attained this fruit, it is called "complete. "Good son!

These seven types of sentient beings do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate ethical discipline, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom; being unable to practice these four matters, they are able to commit the five grave offenses of immediate retribution, sever their roots of goodness, violate the four heavy prohibitions, and slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. For this reason, they are called those who are eternally submerged.

“Good son! Among these seven persons, there is one who is able to draw near to a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), who listens to and receives the Tathāgata’s true Dharma with a sincere heart, reflects well within, abides according to the Dharma, and diligently cultivates the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; for this reason, he is named ‘one who has crossed the river of birth and death to reach the other shore.’”
If one says that an icchantika attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called attachment;
if one says they do not attain it, this is called falsehood.
“Good son! Of these seven kinds of persons, there may be one person who possesses all seven, or there may be seven persons each possessing one.
Good son!”

If there is one whose mind and speech harbor different thoughts and make different assertions, saying that an icchantika attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, you should know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;

if a person’s mind and speech harbor different thoughts and make different assertions, saying that an icchantika does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this person is likewise called one who slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"Good son!
If someone says that the eightfold noble path is attained by ordinary persons, that person is also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
if someone says that the eightfold noble path is not attained by ordinary persons, that person is also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
"Good son!

If there are those who say that all sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature, or that they definitely lack Buddha-nature, these people are also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
"Good son!
For this reason, I have said in the sūtras that there are two kinds of people who slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha:
the first are those who lack faith because of a mind of malice."
Second, although they have faith, they do not understand the meaning. "Good son!
If a person possesses the mind of faith but lacks wisdom, that person will cause ignorance to increase."
If one possesses wisdom but lacks faith, that person will increase their wrong views. Good son!
Because of a mind of anger and resentment, a person who lacks faith declares that there are no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha Jewels.
Those who have faith but lack wisdom misunderstand the meaning of the teachings, causing those who hear the Dharma to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Good son! For this reason, I say:
"Because those without faith harbor a mind of anger, and those with faith lack wisdom, such people are able to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha Jewel."
“Good son! If there should be one who says, ‘Those such as icchantikas, even before having produced wholesome dharmas, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
Such a person is also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, if someone were to say:
"An icchantika abandons the state of an icchantika and attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within a different body."
Such a person is also said to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, if one were to say:
"An icchantika can produce roots of goodness;..."

Having produced roots of goodness, which continue in an uninterrupted succession until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is therefore said that an icchantika attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"You should know that such a person does not slander the Three Jewels. Good son!
If there is someone who says: "

"All sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; it is uncreated and unborn, yet because of the causes and conditions of afflictions, it cannot be seen."
"You should know that such a person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
If someone were to say:

'All sentient beings have no buddha-nature at all; it is like a rabbit's horn, produced through skillful means, non-existent in the beginning but existing now, and having existed, returning to non-existence.'"
"You should know that such a person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
If someone were to say:
'The Buddha-nature of sentient beings does not exist, like empty space;'"
It is not non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit. Why?

Because space is eternal and the horns of a rabbit do not exist; therefore, one can say it both exists and does not exist. Because it exists, it refutes the horns of a rabbit; because it does not exist, it refutes [the permanence of] space.
"One who speaks thus does not slander the Triple Gem. Good son!
As for the Buddha-nature, it is not called a single dharma, nor ten dharmas, nor a hundred dharmas, nor a thousand dharmas, nor ten thousand dharmas."
Before one has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all that is wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate is collectively termed "Buddha-nature.
At times, the Tathāgata speaks of the fruit within the cause, or speaks of the cause within the fruit; this is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention.
Because his speech accords with his will, he is called the Tathāgata;
because his speech accords with his will, he is called the Arhat;
because his speech accords with his will, he is called the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space.”
"What is meant by 'being like space'?
Good son, the nature of space is neither past, nor future, nor present."
The Buddha-nature is also like this. Good son!
Space is not of the past.
Why is this? Because there is no present.
If a dharma were present, one could speak of its past.
Because there is no present, there is no past,
nor is there a present. Why is this?
Because there is no future.
If dharmas were in the future, one could speak of the present;
since there is no future, there is no present.
Nor is there a future.
Why? Because there is neither present nor past.
If there were the present and the past, then there would be the future;
because the present and the past do not exist, the future does not exist.
For this reason, the nature of space is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
“Good son! Because space is non-existent, the three periods of time do not exist; it is not because space exists that the three periods of time are absent.
Just as a flower in the sky does not exist, so too the three periods of time do not exist.”
Space is likewise; because it is not a substantial entity, it does not exist within the three periods of time.
Son of good family!
That which is without substance is precisely space.
The Buddha-nature is also like this.
"Good son! Because space is non-existent, it is not encompassed by the three periods of time; [the Buddha-nature is likewise]."
Because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not encompassed by the three periods of time. Good son!
Since the Tathāgata has already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all his Buddha-nature and all Buddha-dharmas are eternal and unchanging.
For this reason, the three periods of time do not exist; they are like empty space.
Good son! Because empty space is non-existent, it is neither internal nor external.
Because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is neither internal nor external;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature is like empty space. Good son!

Just as in the world, that which is free from obstruction is called space, so too, after the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he is without obstruction regarding all Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature is like space.
"For these reasons, I say that the Buddha-nature is like empty space.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata, Buddha-nature, and nirvāṇa are not subsumed within the three periods of time, yet they are called "existent.
Space, likewise, is not subsumed within the three periods of time; for what reason, then, can it not be called "existent"?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
That which is not nirvāṇa is called ‘nirvāṇa’; that which is not the Tathāgata is called ‘the Tathāgata’; that which is not buddha-nature is called ‘buddha-nature.’”
What is meant by "non-nirvāṇa"?
It refers to all afflictions and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
To destroy such conditioned afflictions is called nirvāṇa.
Those who are not Tathāgatas refer to those ranging from icchantikas up to pratyekabuddhas.
It is for the sake of destroying such individuals—from icchantikas to pratyekabuddhas—that one is called a Tathāgata.
That which is not Buddha-nature refers to all walls, tiles, stones, and insentient things.
Apart from such insentient things, that is called Buddha-nature.
“Good son!
There is nothing in all the worlds that is not empty space confronting empty space.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the world, even though there is nothing that is not the counterpart of the four great elements, they are nonetheless called ‘existent.
Space has no counterpart; for what reason can it not be called existent?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If one says: "
As for the claim that “Nirvana is not subsumed within the three periods of time,
and space is likewise,” this meaning is incorrect. Why is this so?

Nirvāṇa exists; it is visible, realizable, a form, a footprint, a textual passage, an existence, a characteristic, a condition, and a place of refuge. It is tranquil radiance, the secure further shore; therefore, it is designated as not being subsumed within the three periods of time.
The nature of space does not possess such dharmas; therefore, it is called "non-existent.
If there were any dharma apart from these [dharmas], it would necessarily be subsumed within the three periods of time.
If space were the same as a functional phenomenon (*dharma*), it could not be said not to be subsumed within the three periods of time. "Good son!
As worldly people say, space is called formless, non-obstructive, and invisible."
If it is formless, non-obstructive, and invisible, it is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*);
if space were identical to a mental factor, it could not be apprehended and would not be subsumed within the three periods of time.
If it were subsumed within the three periods of time, it would be identical to the four aggregates (*skandha*).
Therefore, apart from the four aggregates, space does not exist.
"Furthermore, good son!
The various non-Buddhists say:
"That which is space is itself light.
If it is light, then it is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*).
If space were such that it were a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*), it would be impermanent.
Being impermanent, it would be subsumed within the three periods of time.
How then could the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that it does not belong to the three periods of time?
If it were subsumed within the three periods of time, it would not be empty space; yet one could also say that empty space is eternal. "Good son!
Furthermore, some people say that empty space is a dwelling place."

If there is a place of abiding, it is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*); yet all such places are impermanent and subsumed within the three periods of time. Space (*ākāśa*), however, is eternal and is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
If one speaks of "locations," one knows that there is no space.
Furthermore, some say that space is simply succession;
if it were succession, it would be a numerical phenomenon (*saṃkhyā-dharma*).
If it can be counted, it is subsumed within the three periods of time;
if it is subsumed within the three periods of time, how can you say it is eternal? Good son!
Furthermore, if it is said:
"Now, as for empty space, it is not separate from three dharmas:
first, emptiness; second, reality; and third, both emptiness and reality."
If one says that emptiness is it, one should know that empty space is an impermanent phenomenon.
Why? Because it does not exist in reality.
If one says that [the self] is truly real, one should know that space is likewise impermanent.
Why? Because there is no [substantiality] in the location of space.
If emptiness were truly existent, one should know that space would likewise be impermanent.
Why? Because it is absent in both locations.
Therefore, space is called "non-existence. "Good son!

It is as if one were to say that space is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), such as saying that space is created by removing trees or removing houses; or leveling the ground to create space; or covering space with space; or painting the color of space upon space, like the water of the great ocean."
Therefore, space is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, just like a clay jar;
if space were likewise so, it would necessarily be impermanent.

“Good son! When people of the world say that among all phenomena (dharma) the place where there is no obstruction is called ‘space,’ does that unobstructed state exist fully within even a single phenomenon?”
Is it present in part?
If it were present in its entirety, one should know that there would be no empty space in other locations.
If it were present in part, then it would be a phenomenon subject to numerical calculation as "this" or "that."
If it can be counted, one should know that it is impermanent.
"Good son! If there is someone who says:
"Space is unimpeded and merges with existence.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Space resides within things, like fruit within a vessel."
"Both [positions] are incorrect.
Why? If one says they are combined, there would be three possibilities:"
First, conjunction through distinct karma, such as birds gathering on a tree;
second, conjunction through common karma, such as two rams butting heads;
third, conjunction following prior conjunction, such as two pairs of fingers joined together in one place.
If it is said that different karmas combine together, there are two kinds of difference:
first, the karma of matter; second, the karma of space.
If the karma of space were to combine with matter, then space would be impermanent.
If material objects were to conjoin with space, then those objects would not be omnipresent; if they were not omnipresent, they too would be impermanent.
If you say:
"Space is eternal, its nature is immovable, yet it conjoins with moving objects," [this is untenable].
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because if space were eternal, then material objects would also have to be eternal.
If things were impermanent, then space would also be impermanent.
To say that space is both permanent and impermanent is impossible.
If it were conjoined with collective karma, this principle would not hold true.
Why is this? Space is called "pervasive"; if it were to combine with karma, then karma too would have to be pervasive.
If it were pervasive, it would have to be pervasive everywhere.
If it were all-pervasive, it would be conjoined with everything; one should not speak of there being conjunction and non-conjunction. If you say:
"It is already conjoined and conjoins together, like two fingers joined as a pair."
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because there was no prior conjunction, and it only conjoins subsequently.
That which was previously non-existent and subsequently comes into being is an impermanent phenomenon; therefore, one cannot say that space has already combined or is in the process of combining.
Just as worldly phenomena that were previously non-existent and subsequently come into being are impermanent entities, if space were likewise so, it too would necessarily be impermanent.
If one says,
"Space exists within objects, like fruit inside a vessel," this meaning is not correct.
Why is this? When such space did not yet possess a vessel, where did it abide?
If it had a place of abiding, then space would be manifold.
If it were manifold, how could one say it is permanent?
How could one say it is one?
Or that it is all-pervasive?
If space were to abide apart from emptiness, then material things would likewise abide apart from space; therefore, one should know that space does not exist. "Good son!
If someone were to say that the space where a finger is placed is called "empty space," one should know that empty space is an impermanent phenomenon. Why is this?
Because the finger has four sides.
If the four directions exist, one should know that space also has four directions.
Since all eternal phenomena (nityadharma) have no spatial location, space must be impermanent because it possesses spatial dimensions.
If it were impermanent, it would not be separate from the five aggregates; yet if it were to be separate from the five aggregates, it would be nothing at all. "Good son!
If there is a dharma that abides by means of causes and conditions, you should know that such a dharma is called impermanent."
Good son! It is like all sentient beings and trees, which abide because of the earth; since the earth is impermanent, the things that depend upon the earth are successively impermanent.
Good son! Just as earth depends on water, because water is impermanent, earth is also impermanent.
Just as water depends on wind, because wind is impermanent, water is also impermanent.
Wind depends upon space; since space is impermanent, wind is also impermanent.
If it is impermanent, how can you say that space is permanent and omnipresent?
Because space is non-existent, it is not of the past, future, or present;
likewise, because a rabbit's horn is a non-entity, it is not of the past, future, or present.
Therefore, I say that because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time;
and because space is non-existent, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time. "Good son!
I never dispute with the world.
Why is this? When worldly wisdom says something exists, I also say it exists;
"Worldly wisdom says it does not exist, and I also say it does not exist.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by being endowed with how many dharmas, do they not contend with the world and remain unstained by worldly phenomena?
The Buddha said,
“Good son!...”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they do not contend with the world and are not defiled by worldly phenomena.

What are these ten? First, faith; second, possession of ethical discipline; third, associating with virtuous friends; fourth, internal reflection; fifth, being fully possessed of diligence; sixth, being fully possessed of right mindfulness; seventh, being fully possessed of wisdom; eighth, being fully possessed of right speech; ninth, delighting in the true Dharma; and tenth, having compassion for sentient beings.
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these ten dharmas, they do not contend with the world and are not defiled by worldly phenomena, just like an utpala flower."
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:”
"Whatever the worldly wise say exists, I also say exists;
whatever the worldly wise say does not exist, I also say does not exist.
What is meant by "existence" and "non-existence" according to the worldly wise?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
If worldly wisdom speaks of form as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and so on up to consciousness, it is likewise.”
"Good son! This is what is called 'existence' as taught by worldly wisdom, and I also teach that it exists. Good son!"
Worldly wisdom says that form is devoid of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Good son!
"This is what those with worldly wisdom call 'non-existence,' and I also say it is non-existent.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
Those who possess worldly wisdom are the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all noble ones (*ārya*).
If for these noble ones form (*rūpa*) is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, why does the Tathāgata say that the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) is permanent, eternal, and unchanging?
The wise of the world say that such things do not exist; why then does the Tathāgata say they exist?
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks in this manner; how then can it be said that he does not contend with the world and is not defiled by worldly dharmas?

The Tathāgata has already abandoned the three kinds of inversion—namely, inversion of perception, inversion of mind, and inversion of view—and thus he should have declared that the Buddha’s physical form is truly impermanent; yet now you say it is permanent. How, then, can you claim to be free from inversion and not contend with the world?
The Buddha said: "Good son!
The form of ordinary beings arises from afflictions; therefore, wisdom declares that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
“The form of the Tathāgata is far removed from afflictions; therefore, it is said to be permanent, eternal, and unchanging.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said, “World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by form arising from afflictions?
'Good son, there are three kinds of afflictions, namely: the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).'"
A wise person should contemplate the faults and transgressions inherent in these three outflows.
Why is this? Because once one has recognized their faults, one is able to distance oneself from them.
It is like a physician who first examines the patient's pulse, identifies the location of the disease, and only then administers medicine.
"Good son! It is like a person leading a blind man into a thicket of thorns and then abandoning him there to return."
A blind person will find it extremely difficult to emerge from [the pit] afterwards; even if they do emerge, their body will be utterly destroyed.
Ordinary worldlings are just like this: if they cannot know and see the faults of the three outflows (*āsrava*), they will follow after them;
if they can see them, they will be able to distance themselves from them.
Having recognized their transgressions, although they undergo retribution, that retribution will be slight. "Good son,
there are four kinds of people:
First, heavy at the time of performing the action, but light at the time of receiving the retribution;
second, light at the time of performing the action, but heavy at the time of receiving the retribution;
third, heavy at the time of performing the action, and heavy also at the time of receiving the retribution.
Fourth, when the karma is performed lightly, the retribution received is also light.
Good son! If a person can contemplate the faults and transgressions of the afflictions, that person’s performance of karma and the receiving of its fruit will both be light.
“Good son! A person of wisdom reflects thus:
‘I should distance myself from such outflows as these, and furthermore, I should not commit such base and evil deeds.’”
Why is this? Because I have not yet attained liberation from the retributions of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
If I cultivate the Path, I shall, by the power of this, destroy all sufferings.
Having observed this, that person’s greed, hatred, and delusion become weak.
Once they see that greed, hatred, and delusion have been lightened, their mind becomes joyful, and they further think:
"Now, all of this is due to the power of the causes and conditions of practicing the Path; it has enabled me to leave unwholesome states behind and draw near to wholesome states."
"Therefore, having now attained the vision of the right path, you should diligently cultivate it.

By means of this diligent power of cultivating the path, that person will distance themselves from immeasurable evil afflictions and be freed from the retributions of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
Therefore, in the sūtras I have said that one should contemplate all outflowing afflictions (*āsrava*) as well as the causes of those outflows. Why is this?
If a person of wisdom contemplates only the outflows but does not contemplate their causes, they will be unable to sever those afflictions.
Why is this? Because the wise person observes that outflows arise from these causes; I shall now sever the causes, and thus the outflows will not arise. "Good son!
Just as a physician first eliminates the cause of a disease so that the illness does not arise, so too is it for the wise person who first eliminates the causes of affliction.

A person of wisdom should first contemplate the cause and then contemplate the retribution; they know that from a virtuous cause arises a virtuous fruit, and they know that from an unwholesome cause arises an unwholesome fruit. Having contemplated the retribution, they distance themselves from unwholesome causes.
Having observed the retributions of the fruits, one should next observe the gravity of the afflictions;
having observed their gravity, one first abandons the heavy ones;
once the heavy ones have been abandoned, the light ones will depart of their own accord.
"Good son!

If a wise person knows afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retributions of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions, that person will at that time diligently cultivate the Way, without ceasing or regretting, associating with virtuous friends, and listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart, for the sake of extinguishing such afflictions."
“Good son! It is like a sick person who, knowing for himself that his illness is light and will surely be cured, takes bitter medicine without regret even when receiving it.
A person of wisdom is also like this: they diligently cultivate the noble path with joy and without sorrow, never ceasing and never regretting.”
"Good son!

If a person can know afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions, and diligently cultivates the Noble Path for the sake of eliminating afflictions, this person does not give rise to form from afflictions; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so."

If one cannot know afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions, and does not diligently practice their cultivation, such a person will produce form from afflictions; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

“Good son! One who knows afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity of afflictions, and who practices the Path for the sake of severing afflictions, is precisely the Tathāgata.”
For these reasons, the form of the Tathāgata is permanent, and so on, up to consciousness being permanent. Good son!

One who does not understand afflictions, the causes of afflictions, the retribution of afflictions, and the gravity or lightness of afflictions, and is thus unable to cultivate the Path, is a worldling.
Therefore, for ordinary persons, form is impermanent, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent. "Good son!
The wise of the world, all the sages, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas speak of these two meanings; I likewise speak of these two meanings."
"For this reason, I say that I do not dispute with those who possess worldly wisdom, nor am I defiled by worldly dharmas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

“As the Buddha has spoken of the three outflows (*āsrava*), what are they called: the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Regarding the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*): internal unwholesome applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), conditioned by external objects, gives rise to the outflow of desire.
Therefore, in the past, while I was in Rājagṛha, I said to Ānanda: "Ānanda!..."
"You have now received these verses spoken by this woman; these verses were indeed proclaimed by all the Buddhas of the past.
Therefore, all internal evil thoughts and external conditions are called "desire," and this is termed the "outflow of desire" (kāma-āsrava).

"Regarding 'with outflows' (sāsrava): within the realms of form and formlessness, all internal unwholesome dharmas and external causes and conditions—excluding the external causes and conditions and internal vitarka-vicāra of the desire realm—are called 'with outflows.'"

“Regarding the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*): being unable to discern ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self,’ and failing to distinguish between the internal and the external, is called the outflow of ignorance. Good son!
Ignorance is the root of all outflows (*āsrava*). Why is this?

Because all sentient beings, due to the conditions of ignorance, give rise to conceptualizations and form signs regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); they are thus called "sentient beings. This is termed the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
By these causes and conditions, all outflows (āsrava) arise.
Therefore, in the twelvefold division of the scriptures, I have taught that ignorance (avidyā) is the cause of greed, the cause of hatred, and the cause of delusion.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!

In the past, the Tathāgata spoke in the twelve divisions of the scriptures that greed, anger, and delusion arise due to the causal condition of improper reflection; for what reason does he now say they arise from ignorance?”

“Good son! These two dharmas serve as cause and effect for one another and mutually increase them: unwholesome reflection gives rise to ignorance, and with ignorance as a condition, unwholesome reflection arises.”
Good son! That which can give rise to and grow all afflictions is entirely termed the causes and conditions of affliction;
to draw near to such causes and conditions of affliction is termed ignorance and unwholesome reflection.
"Just as when a sprout grows from a seed, the seed is the proximate cause and the four great elements are the remote cause;
so it is with afflictions.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, ignorance itself is an outflow (*āsrava*).
Why, then, do you further say that the various outflows arise because of ignorance?”
The Buddha said,
"Good son! As for what I have called the outflow of ignorance, this refers to internal ignorance."
Regarding the statement that "all outflows arise from ignorance," this refers to internal and external causes.
If one speaks of the outflow of ignorance, it is called an internal inversion; it means not recognizing impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
If one speaks of the causal conditions for all afflictions, it is called not knowing the external self and what belongs to the self.

"If one speaks of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), it is called having neither beginning nor end; from ignorance arise the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As the Buddha has taught, a person of wisdom knows the causes of the outflows (*āsrava*).
What is meant by 'knowing the causes of the outflows'? "Good son!
The wise person should contemplate:
by what causes and conditions do these afflictions arise?
What kind of actions are performed that give rise to these afflictions?
In what kind of life does this affliction arise?
While dwelling with whom does this affliction arise?
In what place does one abide when this affliction arises?
Having observed what object has given rise to affliction?
From whose dwellings, bedding, food and drink, clothing, and medicinal requisites has affliction arisen?
For what causes and conditions do the inferior become middle, the middle become superior, and inferior karma become middle, while middle karma becomes superior?
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this way, they will attain the distancing themselves from the causes and conditions that give rise to outflows (*āsrava*).
When one contemplates in this manner, afflictions that have not yet arisen are prevented from arising, and those already arisen are eliminated.
For this reason, I have stated in the sūtras that the wise should contemplate the causes from which afflictions arise.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a single body of a sentient being can give rise to various kinds of afflictions?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! It is like various kinds of seeds within a single vessel; once they receive water and rain, each grows forth of its own accord."
“Sentient beings are also like this: although the vessel is one, because of the conditions of craving, they are able to give rise to various afflictions.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said, “World-Honored One!”
"How does a wise person contemplate karmic retribution?
"Good son! A wise person should contemplate as follows:"
The causes and conditions of the outflows (āsrava) can produce birth in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
through these same causes and conditions of the outflows, one obtains the bodies of humans and devas, which are themselves impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Within this vessel-like body, one encounters three kinds of suffering and three kinds of impermanence.

These outflows serve as the causes and conditions that enable sentient beings to commit the five heinous crimes, undergo various evil retributions, sever their roots of goodness, violate the four grave prohibitions, and slander the Triple Gem.
"The wise person should contemplate thus:
'Since I have received such a body as this, I ought not to give rise to such afflictions that lead to the experience of various evil fruits.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
There is the fruit of the outflow-free (anāsrava), yet it is further said that the wise sever all fruits of retribution (vipāka).
Is the outflow-free fruit of retribution included within what is severed?”

Those who have attained the Path possess the untainted fruits (*anāsrava-phala*); since those with wisdom seek these untainted fruits, why does the Buddha say that all those with wisdom should sever retribution (*vipāka*)?
“If they were to be severed, how could the various sages exist today?
“Good son! The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of the fruit within the cause, and sometimes speaks of the cause within the fruit.”
As worldly people say that "clay is the jar" or "threads are the garment," this is called "speaking of the effect within the cause";
as for "speaking of the cause within the effect," it is like saying "the cow is the water and grass" or "the person is the food."
I also do likewise, speaking of the effect within the cause; previously, in a sutra, I spoke thus:
"I move the body by means of the mind-body; therefore, it is called 'the mind-body reaching as far as the limit of Brahmā.'"
This is called "speaking of the fruit within the cause.
Speaking of the cause within the fruit—these six sense bases are called past karma; this is what is meant by "speaking of the cause within the fruit. Good son!

All noble ones truly possess no outflowing retribution; because the retribution for the path cultivated by all noble ones does not give rise to further outflows, it is therefore called "outflow-free retribution."
"Good son!
When a person of wisdom contemplates in this way, they immediately attain the eternal extinction of the retribution of afflictions.
Good son!"

Having observed this, the wise person cultivates the Noble Path in order to sever such afflictions and their retributive fruits—the Noble Path being emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Having cultivated this path, they are able to extinguish all afflictions and their retributive fruits.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 33. [Scroll 34] of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇas Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter on Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, Part Four.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings obtain their retributions from afflictions.
What are called afflictions are, that is to say, evils; the afflictions produced from these evil afflictions are likewise called evil.
Such afflictions are of two kinds:
first, the cause; second, the result.
Because the cause is evil, the result is evil.
Because the fruit is evil, the seed is evil.
Just as with the nimba fruit, because its seed is bitter, the flower, fruit, stem, and leaves are all bitter.
It is like a poisonous tree; because its seed is poisonous, the fruit is likewise poisonous.

The cause is sentient beings and the fruit is also sentient beings; the cause is afflictions and the fruit is also afflictions. The cause and fruit of afflictions are themselves sentient beings, and sentient beings are themselves the cause and fruit of afflictions.
If this is the meaning, why did the Tathāgata previously use the analogy of the Snowy Mountains, which contain both poisonous herbs and the wondrous medicinal king?

If it is said that afflictions are identical to sentient beings and sentient beings are identical to afflictions, how can it be said that there is a wondrous medicinal king within the bodies of sentient beings?
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
Countless sentient beings all share this same doubt; since you are now able to inquire for its resolution, I too am able to sever it.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
Good son! The metaphor of the Snowy Mountains refers to sentient beings;
the mention of poisonous herbs refers to afflictions.
The King of Wondrous Medicine is, that is to say, pure brahmacarya. Good son!
If there are sentient beings who can cultivate such pure brahmacarya, this is called having the King of Wondrous Medicine within their bodies.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that sentient beings possess pure brahmacarya?”
“Good son! It is like how in the world fruits arise from seeds; some of these fruits are capable of acting as causes for further seeds, while others are not.
Those that are capable are called 'fruit-seeds';"
If one cannot perform [the function], one may only be called a fruit, but not a seed.
All sentient beings are likewise; they all possess two kinds:
first, there is the fruit of afflictions, which is the cause of afflictions.
Second, there are those that are the fruits of afflictions but not the causes of afflictions.
That which is the fruit of afflictions yet not the cause of afflictions is what is called the pure holy life (brahmacarya).
“Good son! Sentient beings contemplate feeling (*vedanā*) and know it to be the proximate cause of all outflows (*āsrava*), namely internal and external outflows.
Because of the conditions of feeling, they are unable to sever all outflows, nor can they escape the prison of the triple world (*tridhātu*).”

Sentient beings, due to their attachment to sensation (*vedanā*), give rise to perversions of mind, perversions of perception, and perversions of view; therefore, sentient beings should first contemplate sensation.
Feeling such as this serves as the proximate cause for all craving; therefore, a wise person who wishes to sever craving should first contemplate feeling. "Good son!

All the good and evil deeds performed by all sentient beings through the twelve links of dependent origination occur precisely at the moment of sensation; for this reason, I said to Ānanda: "Ānanda!..."
"All the good and evil deeds performed by all sentient beings are occasions for feeling.
Therefore, the wise person should first contemplate feeling.
Having contemplated feeling, they should further contemplate: "By what causes and conditions does such a feeler arise?"
If it arises from causes and conditions, from what do such causes and conditions themselves arise?
If it were to arise without a cause, why would that which lacks a cause not also give rise to that which is without sensation (*vedanā*)?

Furthermore, one observes that this sensation does not arise from the creation of Īśvara, nor from a primal spirit (*puruṣa*), nor from atoms, nor from the seasons; it does not arise from conceptualization, nor from primordial nature (*prakṛti*); it is not born from itself, nor from another, nor from both self and other, nor is it born without a cause. This sensation arises entirely from the conjunction of conditions.
The causal condition is craving itself; within this conjunction, there is neither sensation nor non-sensation.
Therefore, I shall sever this conjunction; by severing the conjunction, sensation will not arise.

“Good son! Once the wise person has observed the causes, they next observe the retributive fruits: because sentient beings undergo sensation, they experience the immeasurable sufferings of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and even the three realms.
Due to the condition of sensation, one experiences impermanent pleasure;
due to the condition of sensation, one severs the roots of goodness;
due to the condition of sensation, one attains liberation.
When one contemplates in this way, one does not create the cause for feeling.
What is meant by "not creating the cause for feeling"?
It refers to the discernment of feeling: what kind of feeling can act as the cause for craving?
What kind of craving can act as the cause for sensation? Good son!
If sentient beings can thus deeply contemplate the cause of craving and the cause of sensation, they will then be able to sever both "I" and "mine."

“Good son! If a person can practice such contemplations as these, they should discern where craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) cease. Upon seeing that there is even a slight place where craving and feeling cease, one should know that there must also be ultimate cessation. At that time, one will give rise to faith in liberation.”
Having given rise to faith, one asks: "By what means is this state of liberation attained?
Knowing it comes from the Eightfold Path, one then practices it.
What is called the Eightfold Noble Path?
This path contemplates that feeling has three characteristics:
first, suffering; second, pleasure; and third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. These three types are all capable of increasing both body and mind.
By what causes and conditions can it be increased?
It is by the condition of contact (*sparśa*).
This contact is of three kinds:

First is contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*), second is contact with knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), and third is contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-saṃsparśa*).
What is called "contact with knowledge" is precisely the Eightfold Noble Path;
the remaining two types of contact increase the body and mind as well as the three kinds of feeling (*vedanā*).
Therefore, I should sever the two kinds of causes and conditions for contact; once contact is severed, the three types of sensation will not arise. "Good son!
Such sensation is called both cause and effect; the wise should contemplate it as being both cause and effect."
What is the cause?
Craving arises conditioned by sensation; this is called the cause.
What is called the fruit?
Because it arises conditioned by contact, it is called a fruit.
Therefore, this feeling (vedanā) is both cause and fruit.
"The wise person, having thus contemplated this feeling, next contemplates craving (tṛṣṇā); because it is the retribution of feeling, it is called craving."
The wise observe that craving is further divided into two kinds:
first, craving for mixed sustenance; second, craving for non-sustenance.
Craving for mixed sustenance is the cause of birth, old age, sickness, death, and all forms of existence.
One who is free from craving for food cuts off birth, old age, sickness, and death; through the untainted path, they sever all craving for existence.
Furthermore, the wise person should reflect thus:
"If I were to give rise to this craving for various kinds of food, I would be unable to cut off birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Although I now covet the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), if I do not sever the cause of sensation (vedanā-hetu), I shall be unable to attain the fruit of the untainted path.
Therefore, one should first sever this contact (sparśa);
once contact has been severed, sensation will naturally cease.
“Once sensation has ceased, craving also ceases accordingly.
This is called the Eightfold Noble Path. “Good son!

If there are sentient beings who can contemplate in this way, although they possess a poisonous body, within it there is also a subtle and wondrous King of Medicine; it is like how, although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also sublime medicinal herbs.
"Good son!
Although such sentient beings obtain retribution from their afflictions, this retribution no longer serves as a cause for further afflictions; this is precisely what is called 'pure brahmacarya'."
"Furthermore, good son,
the wise person should contemplate:
'By what causes and conditions do these two things— feeling (vedanā) and craving (tṛṣṇā)— arise?'"
One knows that [craving] arises because of perception. Why is this?
Because sentient beings do not give rise to craving merely upon seeing forms, nor do they give rise to craving when observing sensations.

If one gives rise to perverted perceptions regarding form, claiming that form is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, or that feeling is permanent, eternal, and subject to no change—due to these perverted perceptions, greed, hatred, and delusion arise.
Therefore, the wise person should practice visualization.
How should one visualize?
One should form this thought:
"All sentient beings who have not yet attained the Right Path possess inverted perceptions.

What are these inverted perceptions? They are: conceiving the notion of permanence within the impermanent; conceiving the notion of pleasure within the unpleasant; conceiving the notion of purity within the impure; conceiving the notion of a self within empty phenomena; and conceiving the notions of male and female, large and small, day and night, years and months, clothing, dwellings, and bedding within that which is not male or female, nor large or small, nor day or night, nor years or months, nor clothing, nor dwellings, nor bedding.
This perception is of three kinds:
first, small; second, great; and third, boundless.
Due to small causes and conditions, one gives rise to small perceptions.
Due to great causes and conditions, one gives rise to the perception of greatness;
due to immeasurable conditions, one gives rise to the perception of the immeasurable.
Furthermore, there is the perception of smallness, which refers to not yet having entered meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there is the perception of greatness (*mahā-saṃjñā*), which refers to having entered meditative concentration;
there is the perception of the immeasurable (*apramāṇa-saṃjñā*), which refers to the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*);
and there is the perception of smallness (*parītta-saṃjñā*), which refers to all perceptions within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, there is the perception of greatness, namely all perceptions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
furthermore, there is immeasurable perception, namely all perceptions of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because these three perceptions cease, feeling (*vedanā*) ceases of its own accord.
“Because of the cessation of perception and feeling, it is called liberation.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said,
“World-Honored One!”
"The cessation of all phenomena is called liberation; why then does the Tathāgata speak of the cessation of perception and feeling as liberation?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
The Tathāgata sometimes teaches concerning sentient beings so that those who hear may understand the Dharma;
at other times, he teaches concerning sentient beings by means of the Dharma, so that those who hear likewise understand [the teaching] regarding sentient beings.
What is meant by "teaching according to sentient beings" such that the hearers understand the Dharma?
It is as I previously said to Mahākāśyapa: "Kāśyapa!..."
"When sentient beings cease, wholesome dharmas cease.
This is called teaching concerning sentient beings based on causes; the listener understands it as a teaching concerning dharmas.
What is meant by teaching concerning sentient beings based on causes of dharmas, such that the listener also understands it as a teaching concerning sentient beings?
As I previously told Ānanda:
"I do not say that one should associate with all phenomena, nor do I say that one should not associate with all phenomena."
If, by associating with certain phenomena, wholesome qualities decline and unwholesome qualities flourish, such phenomena should not be associated with;
if, by associating with certain phenomena, unwholesome qualities diminish and wholesome qualities increase, such phenomena should be associated with.
"This is called explaining [the teaching] to sentient beings by means of the Dharma; those who hear it also explain it to sentient beings. Good son!
Although the Tathāgata speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling, he has thereby already explained in general all that is to be abandoned."
Once the wise person has thus contemplated this perception, they next contemplate the cause of perception:
"From what does this immeasurable perception arise?
They know it arises from contact.
This contact is of two kinds:
first, contact caused by afflictions; second, contact caused by liberation.
That which arises from ignorance is called contact caused by afflictions.
That which arises from the contact of liberation is called the touch of liberation.
From the contact of afflictions arises inverted perception; from the contact of liberation arises non-inverted perception.
Having contemplated the cause of perception, one next contemplates its retribution.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If it is because of these perceptions of affliction that inverted perceptions arise, then all noble ones must actually possess inverted perceptions while being free from afflictions.”
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"How can a noble one possess perverted perceptions?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
All noble ones perceive a cow as a cow and likewise speak of it as a cow;
they perceive a horse as a horse and likewise speak of it as a horse;
the same applies to male and female, large and small, houses, vehicles, coming and going—this is called inverted perception.
“Good son! All ordinary beings have two kinds of perceptions:
first, the perception of worldly convention; second, the perception of attachment.”
All noble ones possess only the conventional designations (saṃvṛti-saṃjñā) that circulate in the world, and they have no notion of attachment.
Because all ordinary beings engage in unwholesome mental application (vitarka-vicāra), they give rise to notions of attachment toward worldly conventions;
because all noble ones engage in wholesome mental application, they do not give rise to notions of attachment toward worldly conventions.
Therefore, ordinary persons are said to have inverted perceptions,
whereas the noble ones, though they know [the nature of perception], are not said to have inverted perceptions.
Once the wise person has thus observed the causes of perception, they next observe its karmic retribution:
"The fruit of these evil perceptions is experienced within the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
Just as I have severed the cause by abandoning evil vitarka and vicāra, so too has contact with ignorance been severed; therefore, perception is severed.
Because perception is severed, its retribution is also severed."
"The wise person, in order to sever the causes of such perceptions, cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path. Good son!
If one is able to perform such contemplations as these, they may be called one who practices the pure holy life."
"Good son!

This is called the presence of a sovereign wondrous medicine within the poisonous body of sentient beings; it is like how, although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines."
"Furthermore, son of good family,
the wise person contemplates desire:
'Desire consists of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.'"
"Good son! This is the Tathāgata speaking of the fruit within the context of the cause; it is from these five matters that desire arises, yet in reality, they are not desire themselves.
Good son!"

Ignorant people greedily seek to experience sensation; thus, they give rise to perverted perceptions regarding forms, and even regarding tangibles they give rise to perverted perceptions. With these perverted perceptions as a causal condition, sensation is produced.
Therefore, it is said in the world that ten kinds of perceptions arise from inverted perceptions.

Due to the causal conditions of desire, one undergoes evil retributions within the world; one inflicts evil upon parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others, intentionally committing what should not be done, even at the cost of one's own body and life.
Therefore, the wise person observes that it is due to the causes and conditions of these unwholesome perceptions that the mind of desire arises.
Having thus observed the cause of desire, the wise person next contemplates its retribution:
"This desire brings about many evil retributions, namely those of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas."
This is called contemplating the retribution of results.
If these unwholesome perceptions are eliminated, the mind of desire will never arise again;
because there is no mind of desire, one does not undergo unwholesome sensations.
Because there is no unwholesome feeling, there is no unwholesome fruit.
Therefore, I should first sever unwholesome perceptions;
once unwholesome perceptions have been severed, such phenomena as these will naturally cease.
Therefore, the wise cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to extinguish unwholesome thoughts; this is called the pure Brahma-faring.

This is called the presence of a wondrous king of medicines within the poisonous body of sentient beings, just as although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines therein.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Once the wise person has contemplated desire in this manner, they should next contemplate karma. Why is this?
A person of wisdom should form this thought:
"Feeling, perception, contact, and desire are themselves afflictions.
These afflictions can produce the karma of birth, but they do not produce the karma of feeling.
Thus, when afflictions and karma function together, there are two types:
first, karma that produces birth; second, karma that brings about experience.
For this reason, the wise should contemplate karma.
This karma is of three kinds:
namely, that of body, speech, and mind. Good son!
The two types of action—bodily and vocal—are called both "action" and "the fruit of action";
mental action is called only "action" and not "fruit," because it is termed "action" by virtue of being the cause of action.
Good son! The two karmas of body and speech are called external karma; the karma of mind is called internal. These three kinds of karma, acting together with afflictions, produce two types of karma:
first, the karma of birth; second, the karma of retribution.
Good son! Right action is precisely mental action;
committed action refers to bodily and verbal actions.

Because it arises first, it is called mental action (*manas-karma*); because it arises from mental action, it is called bodily and verbal action. Therefore, mental action is rightly termed the primary [action].
Having contemplated action in this way, the wise person next contemplates the causes of action.
As for the causal condition of karma, it is contact conditioned by ignorance;
because of contact conditioned by ignorance, sentient beings seek existence;
the causal condition for seeking existence is craving.
Due to craving as a condition, one performs the three types of karma of body, speech, and mind. Good son!
Having thus contemplated the causes of karma, the wise person next contemplates its retributive results.
There are four kinds of retributive results:
first, black-black retributive result; second, white-white retributive result; third, variegated-variegated retributive result; and fourth, neither-black-nor-white retributive result.
Regarding the black-black retribution: when the karma is performed, it is defiled, and the retribution is also defiled;
regarding the white-white retribution: when the karma is performed, it is pure, and the retribution is also pure;
regarding the variegated-variegated retribution: when the karma is performed, it is variegated, and the retribution is also variegated.
"That which is neither white nor black, and has neither white nor black retribution, is called untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you previously stated that the untainted has no retribution; why do you now say it has a retribution that is neither white nor black?"
The Buddha said,
“Good son! This meaning has two aspects:”
First, that which is both a fruit and a retribution; second, that which is only a fruit and not a retribution.
That which is a black-black fruit and retribution is called both a fruit and a retribution.
Because it arises from a black cause, it is designated as a "fruit";
because it acts as a productive cause, it is further termed a "retribution.
This is likewise true for the pure and the mixed.
Regarding the untainted fruit (*anāsrava-phala*): because it arises from tainted causes (*sāsrava-hetu*), it is called a "fruit";
because it does not act as a cause for others, it is not called a "retribution" (*vipāka*).
For this reason, it is termed a "fruit" and not a "retribution."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is not a black dharma; for what reason and by what causes and conditions is it not called white?”
“Good son! Because there is no karmic retribution, it is not called white;
because it is the antidote to black, it is therefore called white.”
I now declare that what undergoes the retribution of its fruit is called "white.
Because this untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) does not undergo retribution, it is not called white; it is called "quiescent" (*śānta*).

Such karmic actions have fixed places where their retribution is experienced; for instance, the ten unwholesome paths of action are fixed in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, while the karma of the ten wholesome paths is fixed in the realms of humans and devas.
The ten unwholesome dharmas are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior:
by reason of the superior causes and conditions, one receives a body in hell;
by reason of the middling causes and conditions, one receives a body among the animals.
Due to inferior causes and conditions, one receives the body of a hungry ghost.
Furthermore, there are four types of human karma based on the ten wholesome actions:
first, the inferior; second, the middling; third, the superior; and fourth, the most superior.
Due to inferior causes and conditions, one is born in Uttarakuru;
due to middling causes and conditions, one is born in Pūrvavideha;
and due to superior causes and conditions, one is born in Aparagoyānī.
Born in Jambudvīpa through these supreme causes and conditions,
a person of wisdom, having made this observation, immediately reflects:
"How shall I sever this retribution?"
He further reflects:
"This karma arises from the causal conditions of ignorance and contact.
If I were to eradicate ignorance and contact, then such karmic fruits would be extinguished and not arise."
Therefore, the wise cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path in order to sever ignorance and the causal conditions for contact; this is called pure brahmacarya. Good son!

This is called the presence of a wondrous king of medicines within the poisonous bodies of sentient beings; it is like how, although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines.
"Furthermore, good son!
The wise person, having contemplated karma and afflictions, next contemplates the retributive fruits obtained from these two; these two fruits are themselves suffering.
Once they know this to be suffering, they are able to relinquish all forms of rebirth.
The wise further observe that afflictions arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions; afflictions also arise from the causes and conditions of karma.
Furthermore, afflictions arise from the causes and conditions of karma, and suffering arises from the causes and conditions of karma;
from the causes and conditions of suffering, afflictions arise.
With afflictions as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, suffering arises.
With existence as condition, further existence arises; with existence as condition, karma arises; with karma as condition, afflictions arise.
With afflictions as condition, suffering arises; with suffering as condition, suffering arises.
Good son! If a wise person can contemplate in this way, you should know that such a person is able to contemplate the suffering of karma. Why is this?
What has been observed above is precisely the twelve links of dependent origination of birth and death.

If a person can contemplate these twelve links of dependent origination of birth and death in this way, it should be known that such a person does not create new karma and is able to destroy past karma.
