“Good son! A person of wisdom contemplates the suffering of the hells, observing from one single hell up to one hundred and thirty-six places. Within each and every hell there are various kinds of suffering, all of which arise due to the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.”
Having contemplated the hells, one next contemplates the sufferings of hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth.

Having performed this contemplation, one further contemplates all the various sufferings of humans and devas; thus, all these manifold sufferings arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.
Good son!

Although there is no great suffering or affliction in the heavens, their bodies are soft, supple, and smooth; yet when they encounter the five signs of decay, they experience extreme suffering that is no different from the torments of hell.
"Good son! The wise person deeply contemplates that all the sufferings of the three realms arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma. Good son!"
For example, just as a fragile earthen vessel is easily broken, so too is it with sentient beings who receive a body; once the body has been received, it becomes a vessel for manifold sufferings.
It is like a great tree, its flowers and fruits flourishing, which can be destroyed by flocks of birds.
Just as a small fire can burn a large quantity of dry grass,
so too is it with sentient beings who, having taken on a body, are destroyed by suffering. Good son!
If a wise person can contemplate these eight kinds of suffering as they are described in the Noble Practice, you should know that this person is able to sever all suffering.
"Good son! Once the wise person has deeply contemplated these eight sufferings, they next contemplate the cause of suffering."
The causes of suffering are craving and ignorance.
This craving and ignorance are of two kinds:
first, the seeking of the body; second, the seeking of wealth.
Seeking the body and seeking wealth— both are suffering.
Therefore, one should know that craving and ignorance are the causes of suffering.
Good son! This craving and ignorance are of two kinds:
first, internal; second, external.
Internally it can produce karma, and externally it can cause growth.
Furthermore, internally it can produce karma, and externally it produces the fruits of karma.
Once internal craving is severed, karma is thereby severed.
Once external craving has been severed, its fruit is likewise severed.
Internal craving gives rise to suffering in future lives, while external craving gives rise to suffering in the present life; thus, the wise observe that craving itself is the cause of suffering.
Having already observed the cause, one next observes the retribution of the fruit.
The retribution of suffering is precisely grasping (*upādāna*).
Grasping is the name for the fruit of craving; the causal conditions of this grasping are internal and external craving, which constitute the suffering of craving.
"Good son! The wise should contemplate:
'Craving is the condition for grasping; grasping is the condition for craving.'"
"If I can sever both craving and grasping, I shall not create karma and will not undergo manifold sufferings.
For this reason, the wise cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path in order to sever the experience of suffering.
"Good son!
If there is anyone who can contemplate in this way, this is called pure brahmacarya.

This is called the presence of a wondrous king of medicines within the poisonous body of sentient beings; it is like how, although there are poisonous herbs in the Snowy Mountains, there are also wondrous medicines."
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘pure brahma-conduct’?”
The Buddha said: "Good son,
all dharmas are."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
As for all dharmas, their meanings are not fixed.”

Why is this? The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of these as wholesome or unwholesome; at other times he speaks of them as the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness, or as the twelve bases, or as spiritual friends, or as the twelve links of dependent origination, or as sentient beings, or as right view and wrong view, or as the twelve divisions of the scriptures, or as the two truths. Now the Tathāgata says that all dharmas constitute the pure Brahma-faring; what, then, are all these dharmas?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
This subtle and wondrous *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is the treasury of all wholesome dharmas.
Just as the great ocean is a repository of myriad jewels, so too is this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; it is the secret treasury of the meaning of all syllables.
“Good son! Just as Mount Sumeru is the root of all medicinal herbs, so too is this sutra;
it is the very root of the bodhisattva precepts.”
“Good son! Just as space is the dwelling place for all things,
so too is this sutra the dwelling place for all wholesome dharmas.”
“Good son! Just as a fierce wind cannot be bound, so too it is with all bodhisattvas who practice this sutra; they are not bound by any afflictions or unwholesome dharmas.”
“Good son! For example, just as there is nothing that can destroy a vajra, so too is this sutra;
even though there may be those who are heterodox, evil, and perverse, they cannot destroy it.”
“Good son! Just as no one is able to count the sands of the Ganges River, so too is the meaning of this sutra; no one is able to count it.”
“Good son! This sutra serves as a Dharma-banner for all bodhisattvas, like the banner of Śakra. Good son!”
This sutra is the caravan leader who leads toward the city of Nirvana, just as a great guide leads merchants toward the great ocean.
"O son of good family!
This sutra can serve as the light of the Dharma for all bodhisattvas, just as the sun and moon in the world can dispel all darkness.

"Good son! This sutra can serve as a great, excellent medicine for sentient beings suffering from illness, just as the subtle and wondrous King of Medicines on Mount Gandhamādana can cure all diseases."
“Good son! This sutra can serve as a staff for icchantikas, just as a weak person relies upon it to rise up. Good son!”
This sutra can serve as a bridge for all evil people, just as a worldly bridge enables one to cross over everything.

"Good son! This sutra can provide cool shade for those wandering through the three realms of existence who encounter the heat of afflictions, just as a worldly parasol shields one from the scorching heat."
“Good son! This sutra is the Great King of Fearlessness; it can destroy all afflictions and evil Māras, just as the lion king subdues all other beasts.”
“Good son! This sutra is a great master of divine spells, capable of destroying all demons of affliction, just as a worldly spell-master can expel malevolent spirits.”
“Good son! This sutra is the unsurpassed frost and hail, capable of destroying all karmic retributions of birth and death, just as worldly hail and rain destroy all fruit-bearing crops.”
“Good son! This sutra serves as a great and excellent medicine for those whose eyes of precept have been destroyed, just as the worldly añjita medicine effectively cures eye pain.”
“Good son! This sutra can sustain all wholesome dharmas, just as the earth of the world sustains all things. Good son!”
This sutra is the clear mirror for sentient beings who violate the precepts, just as a worldly mirror reveals all forms and images.
"Good son! This sutra can serve as clothing for those who lack shame and remorse, just as worldly garments conceal the physical body."
“Good son! This sutra can act as great wealth and treasure for those who are poor in wholesome dharmas, just as the goddess Guṇakārandhā benefits the destitute. Good son!”
This sutra can serve as ambrosial nectar for sentient beings who thirst for the Dharma, just as water of eight virtues satisfies the thirsty.
"Good son! This sutra can serve as a Dharma-couch for those afflicted by afflictions, just as a person in the world who is exhausted encounters a peaceful and secure couch."

“Good son! This sutra can serve as a necklace, incense flowers, unguents, powdered incense, and burning incense for bodhisattvas from the first ground up to the tenth ground; it is a vehicle that purifies the spiritual lineage and is complete in all respects, surpassing all six pāramitās as a place of sublime bliss, like the Pārijātaka tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”
“Good son! This sutra is a sharp vajra-axe, capable of felling the great trees of all afflictions;
it is a sharp blade, capable of severing habitual tendencies.”
This is valor and courage, able to crush the enmity of Māra;
this is the fire of wisdom, which burns the fuel of afflictions;
this is the treasury of causes and conditions, from which pratyekabuddhas emerge.
It is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, which gives birth to the śrāvakas;

it is the eye of all devas, the right path for all humans, the place of refuge for all animals, the locus of liberation for hungry ghosts, the unsurpassed sovereign for those in the hells, the supreme vessel for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, and the father and mother of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present in the ten directions.
Good son! For this reason, this sutra encompasses all dharmas.
As I have previously said:
Although this sutra encompasses all dharmas, I declare that the brahma-faring consists precisely of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Good son!

If one is separated from these thirty-seven factors, one will ultimately be unable to attain the correct fruit of a śrāvaka, up to and including the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; nor will one perceive the Buddha-nature or the fruit of the Buddha-nature.
For this reason, the holy life is itself the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Why is this?
The nature of the thirty-seven factors is not inverted, and they are capable of destroying inversion.
Its nature is not false views, yet it can destroy false views;
its nature is not fear, yet it can destroy fear;
its nature is pure conduct, yet it can cause sentient beings to ultimately practice the pure Brahma-faring.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since even tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) can act as causes for untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), why does the Tathāgata not say that tainted phenomena constitute pure brahmacarya?”
“Good son! All that is with outflows (sāsrava) is inverted; therefore, that which has outflows cannot be called pure brahmacarya.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma) with outflows (sāsrava),
or is it without outflows (anāsrava)?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, this is with outflows (sāsrava).”
“World-Honored One!
Although these are with outflows (*sāsrava*), their nature is not inverted.
For what reason are they not called the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*)?”
“Good son! Because the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) is the cause for the outflow-free state (anāsrava), it resembles the outflow-free;
because it tends toward the outflow-free, it is not called inverted.”

Good son! The pure brahmacarya consists of the continuous succession of the arousal of the thought [of enlightenment] up to its ultimate consummation; however, the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) lasts for only a single moment of thought. Therefore, it cannot be called pure brahmacarya.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The five consciousnesses of sentient beings are also with outflows (*sāsrava*), yet they are not inverted, nor are they of a single thought-moment; for what reason are they not called pure brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*)?”
“Good son! Although the five consciousnesses of sentient beings are not of a single moment, they are nevertheless outflowing (sāsrava) and inverted.
Because they increase all outflows, they are called ‘outflowing.’”
The substance is not real; it is inverted because of attachment to conceptualization.
Why is it said that the substance is not real and is inverted due to attachment to conceptualization?
It is because one gives rise to the perception of male and female within that which is neither male nor female.
This applies even to houses, vehicles, jars, and clothing; these are likewise called inversions.
Son of good family, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are by nature free from inversion; therefore, they are named the pure brahmacarya.
"Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who, regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, knows their roots, knows their causes, knows their inclusion, knows their increase, knows their masters, knows their guides, knows their excellence, knows their reality, and knows their ultimate consummation—such a bodhisattva may be called one whose pure conduct (brahmacarya) is purified."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘knowing the faculties’ up to ‘knowing the ultimate’?”
The Buddha said:
"Good man, excellent, excellent!"
A bodhisattva raises a question for two reasons:
first, for their own understanding; second, so that others may understand.
You already know this, but you have requested this matter for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings who do not yet understand.
Therefore, I now praise you again: Excellent, excellent! "Good son!

The root of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is desire; their cause is termed illumination and contact; their gathering is termed sensation; their increase is termed wholesome reflection; their master is termed mindfulness; their guide is termed concentration; their excellence is termed wisdom; their reality is termed liberation; and their ultimate state is termed Great Parinirvāṇa."
"Good son!
Wholesome desire is the very root of the initial aspiration for the Way up to Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; therefore, I say that desire is the root."
Good son! As it is said in the world: all suffering and affliction have craving as their root;
all diseases have undigested food as their basis.
"All matters of litigation have strife as their root;
all evil matters have falsehood as their root.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata previously stated in this sutra:
‘All wholesome dharmas have heedfulness as their root.’”
"Now you speak of desire;
what is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If one speaks of the productive cause, it is wholesome desire;
if one speaks of the revealing cause, it is heedfulness.”
As it is said in the world that for all fruits, the seed is their cause;
or again, as some say that the seed is the productive cause (*janakahetu*) and the earth is the revealing cause (*vyañjakahetu*),
so too is this meaning.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata previously stated in other sūtras:”
“The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment have the Buddha as their root.
What is the meaning of this? “Good son!
The Tathāgata previously said:
"When sentient beings first come to know the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the Buddha is their root.
If one realizes them through personal attainment, desire is the root.
“World-Honored One!
Why are illumination and contact called causes? “Good son!
The Tathāgata sometimes explains clarity as wisdom and sometimes explains it as faith.
Good son! Because of the condition of faith, one draws near to virtuous friends; this is called contact.
To hear the True Dharma through the condition of drawing near to it is called contact;
to purify body, speech, and mind by virtue of hearing the True Dharma is called contact;
to obtain right livelihood by virtue of the purification of the three karmas is called contact.
By means of right livelihood, one attains the precepts of pure faculties;
by means of the precepts of pure faculties, one delights in secluded places;
by means of delighting in seclusion, one is able to engage in skillful reflection.
By means of skillful reflection, one attains dwelling in accordance with the Dharma;
by means of dwelling in accordance with the Dharma, one attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which are able to destroy immeasurable evil afflictions—this is called contact.

“Good son! ‘Feeling’ (vedanā) is called ‘appropriation. When sentient beings experience feeling, they are able to perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds; therefore, feeling is termed appropriation. Good son!”

"Because of the condition of sensation (*vedanā*), various afflictions (*kleśa*) arise; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) can destroy them. Therefore, sensation is taken as 'appropriation' (*parigraha*).
Because one can destroy afflictions through right reflection (*samyak-manasikāra*), it is therefore called 'increase' (*vṛddhi*)."
Why is this? Because through diligent cultivation, one attains these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
If one contemplates that the destruction of all evil afflictions depends essentially upon focused mindfulness (*ekāgrasmṛti*), for this reason mindfulness is taken as the primary factor.

"Just as all four divisions of the world's armies follow the will of their commander-in-chief, so too it is with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; they all follow mindfulness as their leader. Good son!

Once having entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to skillfully discern the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; therefore, concentration is taken as the guide.
Among these thirty-seven factors, the wisdom that discerns the characteristics of phenomena is the most excellent; therefore, wisdom (*prajñā*) is taken as supreme.
"Once one has known the afflictions through such wisdom, the afflictions are extinguished by the power of that wisdom.
Just as in the world, it is the brave and capable—whether one or two—who can defeat an enemy army of four divisions;
so too it is with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: by the power of wisdom, they are able to destroy the afflictions. Therefore, wisdom is supreme."
“Good son! Although one attains the four dhyānas, the supernormal powers, and peace and bliss by practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, these are not yet called ‘real.
Only when one destroys the afflictions and realizes liberation can it be called real.”

Although one may cultivate the path by giving rise to the mind of awakening through these thirty-seven factors and thereby attain worldly happiness, supramundane happiness, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, and liberation, this still cannot be called ultimate.
If one can sever the activities associated with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, this is called nirvana.
Therefore, I say that the ultimate is precisely great nirvana.
"Furthermore, good son!
A mind of wholesome affection is itself desire (*chanda*).
Because one approaches virtuous friends due to that wholesome affection, it is called contact (*sparśa*); this is what is meant by 'cause. "
Because one approaches a virtuous friend, it is called "receiving" (*upādāna*); this is termed "appropriation.
Because one is able to practice correct reflection by approaching a virtuous friend, it is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*).

Because these four factors can cause the Path to grow—namely, aspiration (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—this is termed "predominance" (*adhipati*).

By means of these three dharmas, one attains two liberations: through the eradication of craving, one attains liberation of mind; through the eradication of ignorance, one attains liberation by wisdom. This is called reality.
When these eight dharmas ultimately result in the attainment of the fruit, it is called Nirvana;
therefore, they are termed "ultimate. Furthermore, good son!
"Desire" refers to the arousal of the aspiration to leave the household life; "contact" refers to the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
These are called the causes. "Inclusion" refers to receiving two kinds of precepts:
first, the *prātimokṣa* precepts; second, the *viśuddhendriya* (purified faculties) precepts. These are called "receiving" and "inclusion."

"Increase" refers to the cultivation of the four dhyānas; "mastery" refers to the fruit of srotāpanna and the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin; "guidance" refers to the fruit of anāgāmin; "excellence" refers to the fruit of arhat; "reality" refers to the fruit of pratyekabuddha; and "ultimate" refers to the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, good son! 'Desire' is called consciousness;

'contact' is called the six sense bases; 'gathering' is called feeling; 'increase' is called ignorance; 'lord' is called name-and-form; 'guide' is called craving; 'superior' is called grasping; 'reality' is called becoming; and that which is ultimate is called birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these three dharmas—root, cause, and condition—how do they differ?”
“Good son! That which is called the ‘root’ is the initial aspiration;
that which is the ‘cause’ is the uninterrupted continuity of its resemblance.”
"Increase" means that having already ceased what is similar, one is able to produce what is similar.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The root is the agent, the cause is the fruit, and increase is functional utility.
"Good son!
Although there is a retribution in future ages, because it has not yet been experienced, it is called a cause;
when it is actually experienced, it is called 'increase'."
Furthermore, good son!
The faculty is seeking; attainment is the cause; and application is the increase. Good son!

In this sutra, the faculties (indriya) are the path of seeing (darśanamārga), the causes (hetu) are the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), and the increase is the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga).
Furthermore, son of good family!
"The faculties are the direct cause, and the cause is the expedient cause;
obtaining the retribution from these two causes is called 'growth.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, that which is ultimate is nirvāṇa.
How can such nirvāṇa be attained?”
“Good son! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās are able to cultivate the ten perceptions, you should know that such persons will attain nirvāṇa.”
What are the ten? First is the perception of impermanence;

second is the perception of suffering; third is the perception of non-self; fourth is the perception of revulsion toward food; fifth is the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in; sixth is the perception of death; seventh is the perception of manifold faults and transgressions; eighth is the perception of detachment; ninth is the perception of cessation; and tenth is the perception of non-craving.
"Good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who cultivate these ten kinds of perceptions will, without fail, attain nirvāṇa."
Not following the minds of others, but being able to discern for oneself what is wholesome and unwholesome, this is called the true meaning of a bhikṣu, and even the meaning of an upāsikā.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by bodhisattvas, up to and including upāsikās, cultivating the perception of impermanence?”
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who have newly resolved their minds; second, those who have already practiced the path.”
The perception of impermanence is likewise of two kinds:
first, coarse; second, subtle.
When a bodhisattva at the initial stage contemplates the perception of impermanence, they reflect as follows:
"There are generally two kinds of things in the world:
first, internal; second, external.

Such internal things are impermanent and subject to change. I observe that when birth occurs, there are times of childhood, youth, adulthood, old age, and death; these various stages are each distinct from one another. Therefore, one should know that internal things are impermanent."
Again, he formed this thought:
"I see some sentient beings who are plump and fresh, endowed with physical beauty and strength, moving about and pausing at will without hindrance;
yet I also see those suffering from illness, their physical strength ruined and their appearance emaciated, lacking any autonomy."
Some see their wealth and treasuries overflowing;
some see themselves impoverished, lacking in everything they need;
and some see themselves having accomplished immeasurable merit.
"Or one may see that they are fully possessed of immeasurable unwholesome dharmas;
therefore, one certainly knows that internal dharmas are impermanent.
He further contemplates external dharmas:
"At the time of the sprout, the time of the tooth [bud], the time of the stem, the time of the leaf, the time of the flower, and the time of the fruit—these various stages are each distinct.
Thus, external phenomena may be complete or incomplete; for this reason, one should know that all external things are certainly impermanent."
Having thus observed that phenomena are impermanent, he further contemplates the Dharma as he has heard it:
"I have heard that the gods possess and fully enjoy most exquisite happiness and sovereign supernormal powers, yet they too are subject to the five signs of decay."
Therefore, one should know that these are impermanent.

Furthermore, we hear that at the beginning of the kalpa there were sentient beings who each possessed supreme and wondrous merit; their bodies emitted light that illuminated themselves, rendering the sun and moon unnecessary.
By the power of impermanence, his radiance was extinguished and his virtues diminished.

Furthermore, he heard that in the past there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King who ruled over the four continents, possessed the seven treasures, and attained great sovereignty, yet he could not escape the mark of impermanence.
He further observed the great earth:

"In times past, it provided a secure dwelling for immeasurable sentient beings, with not even a space as large as a chariot wheel left vacant; it was fully endowed with all manner of wondrous medicinal herbs, and its groves, trees, and fruits flourished luxuriantly."
Sentient beings have meager merit, causing this great earth to lose its power, so that all things produced therein become exhausted and wasted.
Therefore, one should know:
all internal and external phenomena are impermanent.
"This is what is called coarse impermanence.
Having observed the coarse, one next observes the subtle.
What is meant by 'subtle'?"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all internal and external things, even down to the finest atom, as being already impermanent in the future. Why is this?
Because it is fully endowed with and achieves the characteristic of disintegration.
If future form were not impermanent, one could not say that form has ten temporal distinctions. What are these ten?

First, the stage of the kalala; second, the arbuda; third, the peśī; fourth, the ghana; fifth, the praśākhā; sixth, the stage of infancy; seventh, the stage of childhood; eighth, the stage of youth; ninth, the stage of full maturity; tenth, the stage of old age and decay.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the membrane:
if it were not impermanent, it would not develop into the embryo;
likewise, if even the stage of full vigor were not impermanent, one would never reach old age.
If these various stages were not subject to momentary extinction, they would never gradually grow; rather, they ought to reach full development all at once.
Since such a thing does not occur, one should know that there is certainly a subtle impermanence occurring in every moment.
Furthermore, he sees another person whose sense faculties are complete and whose complexion is radiant; later, he sees that same person withered and haggard, and he thinks again:
"This person certainly possesses moment-to-moment impermanence."
He further contemplates the four great elements and the four postures. He further contemplates the two internal and two external causes of suffering:
hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.
He further contemplates these four: if there were not this moment-to-moment subtle impermanence, these four kinds of suffering could not be spoken of.
If there is a bodhisattva who can form this thought, it is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of subtle impermanence.
"As it is with internal and external forms, so it is with mental phenomena."
Why is this? Because one engages in the six sense bases.

When engaging in the six sense bases, one may give rise to a mind of joy, or a mind of anger, or a mind of attachment, or a mind of recollection; these arise successively and differently, never remaining of a single kind.
Therefore, you should know that all phenomena,
whether material or non-material, are entirely impermanent. "Good son!

If a bodhisattva can, within a single thought-moment, perceive that all phenomena arise and perish and are impermanent, this is called a bodhisattva possessing the perception of impermanence. Good son!
Once the wise person has cultivated the perception of impermanence, they distance themselves from the conceit of permanence, the perversion of permanence, and the perversion of perception.
Next, they cultivate the perception of suffering:
"By what causes and conditions does such suffering exist?"
He deeply understands that this suffering is caused by impermanence; because of impermanence, one undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Due to these conditions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is termed "impermanence."

Because of the causes and conditions of impermanence, one undergoes internal and external suffering—such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, flogging, and verbal abuse—all such sufferings are caused by impermanence.
Furthermore, the wise person deeply contemplates that this body is a vessel of impermanence, and as such, it is suffering;
because the vessel itself is suffering, the phenomena contained within it are likewise suffering.
“Good son! The wise person further contemplates:
‘Arising itself is suffering; cessation itself is suffering.’”
"Because suffering arises and ceases, it is impermanent; it is not the self, nor does it belong to the self.
Thus one cultivates the perception of non-self.
Furthermore, the wise person contemplates:
"Suffering is impermanent, and impermanence is suffering.
If suffering is impermanent, how could the wise say that there is a self?
Suffering is not the self, and the same applies to impermanence."
"In this way, the five aggregates are also suffering and impermanent.
Why, then, do sentient beings say that there is a self?
Furthermore, one observes that all phenomena arise from various combinations; all phenomena are not produced from a single combination, nor is a single phenomenon the result of all combinations.
All conditioned combinations lack intrinsic nature; they possess neither a single nature, nor a diverse nature, nor the nature of a substantial entity, nor any autonomy.
If all phenomena possess such characteristics as these, how could a wise person claim that there is a self?
Again, he reflects:
"Among all phenomena, there is not a single phenomenon that can act as an agent.
If even a single phenomenon cannot act as an agent, then the conjunction of many phenomena likewise cannot act."
The nature of all phenomena can never arise or cease in isolation; they cease through combination and arise through combination.
Once these phenomena have arisen, sentient beings harbor inverted perceptions, claiming that this is a combination and that it arises from combination.
"The perceptions of sentient beings are inverted and lack reality; how, then, could there be a real self?
For this reason, the wise contemplate non-self.
Furthermore, he contemplates with discernment:
"For what causes and conditions do sentient beings speak of a 'self'?
If this self were to exist, would it not be one?"
Should it be manifold?
If I were a single entity, how could there be Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; humans, devas, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; or the states of great, small, old, and young?
Therefore, one knows that the self is not a single entity.
If the self were manifold, how could it be said that the self of sentient beings is one, all-pervasive, and without limit?
"Whether singular or plural, both are devoid of self.
Once the wise person has thus contemplated the absence of self, they next contemplate the perception of revulsion toward food, thinking:
"If all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, why would one commit the three types of unwholesome karma—of body, speech, and mind—for the sake of food?"

If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of craving food, commit the three kinds of evil karma of body, speech, and mind, the wealth they acquire shall be shared by all, yet when they later undergo the bitter fruits of suffering, there shall be no one to share them.
"Good son! The wise person further contemplates:

'All sentient beings undergo suffering of body and mind for the sake of food and drink. If food is obtained only through such manifold sufferings, how could I give rise to craving and attachment toward this food? "
"Therefore, one should not give rise to a mind of craving toward food.
Furthermore, the wise person should contemplate:
'It is because of food and drink that the body attains growth.'"
"I have now left the household life to receive the precepts and cultivate the Way for the purpose of relinquishing this body.
If I now crave this food, how shall I ever succeed in relinquishing this body?

Having contemplated thus, although he partook of the food, it was as if he were eating the flesh of his own child in the wilderness; his mind felt such loathing that he found no pleasure in it at all.

"Having deeply contemplated that there are such faults in the food of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), one next contemplates the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*) as being like a cow being flayed and devoured by immeasurable insects; then one contemplates the food of volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*) as being like a great mass of fire; and the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) as being like three hundred spears."
“Good son! When a wise person has thus contemplated the four kinds of nutriment, they will ultimately never give rise to thoughts of craving or delight toward food.
If craving should still arise, one should contemplate impurity.”
Why is this? It is for the sake of abandoning craving for food.
One should skillfully cultivate the perception of impurity regarding all food, making it correspond to its various impure aspects.
Having observed in this way, whether one receives excellent food or poor food, one accepts it as if applying medicine to a festering sore, never giving rise to a mind of craving or attachment.
“Good son!
If a wise person can contemplate in this manner, it is called achieving the perception of revulsion toward food.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
When a wise person contemplates food and forms the perception of it as impure, is this a contemplation of reality or a contemplation of a conceptual understanding?
If it is a contemplation of reality, then the food being contemplated is not actually impure;”
“If this is a false understanding, how can this dharma be called a 'wholesome perception'?
The Buddha said,
“Good son!...”
One who contemplates in this manner possesses both a true contemplation and a provisional understanding.
It is called "true" because it can destroy the craving for food;
it is called "provisional understanding" because one does not see worms where there are no worms.
"Good son! All that is with outflows is called 'empty,' yet it can also attain the real. Good son!"
If there is a bhikṣu who resolves to go on almsround, he pre-emptively forms this thought:
"As I go for alms, may I obtain excellent food and not coarse or poor quality;
may I certainly receive much and not be given little."
"I also wish to obtain this quickly; do not let it be delayed.

A bhikṣu who thinks thus is said not to have attained the perception of revulsion toward food; the wholesome dharmas he cultivates will decline day and night, while unwholesome dharmas will gradually increase.
"Good son!
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to go on almsround, he should first make this aspiration:
'May all those who beg for food be fully satisfied, and may those who give the food obtain immeasurable merit.'"
"If I obtain food, I shall use it to heal this poisoned body, cultivate wholesome dharmas, and bring benefit to the donor.
When one makes such a vow, the wholesome dharmas one cultivates increase day and night, while unwholesome dharmas gradually perish.
"Good son!
If there is a bhikṣu who can practice in this way, you should know that this person does not consume in vain the offerings of faith from the kingdom. Good son!"
The wise one, endowed with these four perceptions, is able to cultivate the perception of the world as being unlovely, thinking:
"There is no place in all the world where birth, aging, sickness, and death do not exist; likewise, there is no place where this body of mine has not been born."
If there were not a single place within this world where one could escape birth, old age, sickness, and death, how could I find joy in the world?
In all the worlds, there is no progress that is not followed by decline; therefore, the world is certainly impermanent.
If all things are impermanent, why would a wise person take pleasure in the world?

Every sentient being wanders through all realms of existence, fully experiencing both suffering and joy; even if they attain the body of a Brahmā or reach as high as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, at the end of their life they will fall back again into the three evil paths.

Although they may take the form of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, at the end of their lives they are reborn in the animal realm, becoming lions, tigers, rhinoceroses, jackals, wolves, elephants, horses, oxen, or donkeys.

Next, he contemplates the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King: though he governs the four continents with noble status and sovereign power, when his merit is exhausted, he falls into poverty and destitution, lacking even the provision of food and clothing.
Having deeply contemplated such matters, the wise person gives rise to the perception that the world is not to be relished.
Furthermore, the wise person contemplates:

"There are things in the world, namely houses, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, incense and flowers, necklaces, various musical performances, wealth, and treasures; all such things are intended to eliminate suffering, yet these very objects are themselves suffering. How can one seek to leave suffering by means of what is itself suffering?"
"Good son! When the wise person has observed in this way, they do not give rise to attachment or pleasant perceptions toward worldly things. Good son!"

For example, suppose there is a person afflicted with a grave illness; although there may be various kinds of music, performers, fragrant flowers, and necklaces, they would ultimately feel no craving or delight for them.
When a wise person observes this, it is likewise so.
“Good son! The wise person deeply contemplates:

‘All worlds are not a place of refuge, not a place of liberation, not a place of tranquility, not a place of endearment, not the further shore, and not the dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. If I greedily delight in such a world, how shall I ever be able to leave this dharma behind?’”

It is like a person who, disliking to dwell in darkness, seeks light, yet returns once more to the dark—darkness being the world and light being the supramundane. If I delight in the world, I increase the darkness and distance myself from the light; darkness is ignorance (*avidyā*) and light is the clarity of wisdom (*jñāna*). The cause of this clarity of wisdom is precisely the perception that the world is not to be relished.
"Although all fetters of greed are indeed bonds, I now desire the light of wisdom and do not desire the world.
Having deeply contemplated such dharmas as these, the wise person fully realizes the perception of the world's lack of delight.
"Good son! A person of wisdom, having already cultivated the perception of the world as unsatisfactory, next cultivates the perception of death.
He contemplates that this life-span is constantly surrounded by immeasurable enemies; it diminishes with every thought-moment and never increases."
It is like a mountain torrent that cannot remain still;
it is also like the morning dew, whose duration is not long;
it is like a prisoner being led to the marketplace, drawing closer to death with every step.
"It is like leading an ox or a sheep to the place of slaughter.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a wise person contemplate moment-to-moment cessation? " 'Good son!
It is like four men, all skilled in the art of archery, who gather in one place and each shoot in a different direction, simultaneously thinking thus:'"
"We four arrows were launched together and fell together.
Then another person thought to himself:
"While these four arrows have not yet fallen, I am able to catch them all at once with my hands."
“Good son! Could such a person be said to be swift?
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said:
"So it is, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! Earth-dwelling ghosts are swifter than humans; flying ghosts are swifter than earth-dwellers; the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings are swifter than flying ghosts; the divine beings of the sun and moon are swifter than the Four Heavenly Kings; the gods of the Heaven of Firm Speed are swifter than the sun and moon; and the lifespan of sentient beings is swifter than the Heaven of Firm Speed.”
"Good son!
In a single breath and a single blink, there are four hundred births and deaths within the lifespan of sentient beings.
If a wise person can contemplate life in this way, it is called being able to contemplate moment-to-moment extinction."
“Good son! The wise person contemplates that life is subject to the King of Death:
‘If I can separate myself from such a King of Death, I shall attain the permanent cessation of impermanent life.’”

"Furthermore, the wise person contemplates this lifespan as being like a great tree standing on a steep riverbank about to fall; like a person who has committed a heinous crime and faces execution with no one to pity him; like a lion king when he is starving and exhausted; like a venomous serpent when it inhales a great wind; like a thirsty horse guarding its water;
and like a great malevolent spirit when its rage erupts. The King of Death regarding all living beings is likewise."
"Good son! If a wise person can contemplate in this manner, this is called the cultivation of the perception of death. Good son!"
The wise person further contemplates:

"Now that I have left the household life, even if my lifespan were but seven days and seven nights, I would within that time diligently cultivate the Way, uphold the prohibitive precepts, preach the Dharma to transform others, and benefit all sentient beings."
This is called the wise person’s cultivation of the perception of death.
Furthermore, they take seven days and seven nights as the maximum duration, thinking:

"Whether I obtain six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, one day, a single moment, or even the interval between an inhalation and an exhalation, I shall within that time diligently cultivate the Path, uphold the prohibitive precepts, preach the Dharma to transform others, and benefit sentient beings."
This is called the wise person’s skillful cultivation of the perception of death.
When the wise person is endowed with the six perceptions mentioned above, they constitute the causes for seven perceptions.
What are these seven?

First, the perception of constant cultivation; second, the perception of joyful cultivation; third, the perception of non-anger; fourth, the perception of non-envy; fifth, the perception of virtuous aspiration; sixth, the perception of non-arrogance; seventh, the perception of mastery over samādhi.
"Good son!

If there is a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with the seven perceptions, he is called a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, one who is tranquil, one who is pure, one who is liberated, a wise man, one of right view, one who has reached the other shore, a great king of physicians, a great caravan leader, and one who well understands the secrets of the Tathāgata. He also knows the seven kinds of speech of all Buddhas; he is called one of right view and knowledge, having severed the net of doubt arising from the seven kinds of speech."

“Good son! If a person is fully endowed with the six perceptions mentioned above, you should know that this person is able to revile the three realms, distance themselves from the three realms, and extinguish the three realms; they do not give rise to attachment within the three realms. This is called the wise person being fully endowed with the ten perceptions.”
"If there is a bhikṣu who possesses these ten perceptions, he shall immediately be deemed to possess the true marks of a śramaṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa praised the Buddha before him with these verses:
"Great King of Physicians, you have compassion for the world; Both your body and your wisdom are utterly tranquil."
Within the dharma of non-self there is the true self; therefore, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
There is no distinction between the initial resolve and the ultimate goal; of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
Having not yet crossed over oneself, one first seeks to deliver others; therefore, I pay homage to the initial generation of the bodhicitta.
Having first resolved [to attain enlightenment], one becomes a teacher of humans and devas, surpassing both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
such a resolve transcends the three realms, and for this reason it is called the most unsurpassed.
The Saviors of the World must be requested before they grant aid; the Tathāgata acts as teacher without being asked.
The Buddha follows the world like a calf; therefore, he is named the Great Compassionate Ox.
The Tathāgata’s merit fills the ten directions; those who are base and lacking wisdom cannot praise it.
Now I praise his compassionate mind, in order to repay the two kinds of karma of body and speech.
The world constantly seeks its own benefit, yet the Tathāgata never acts for such ends;
he is able to sever the worldly karmic retributions of sentient beings—therefore, I pay homage to him who brings harmony to both self and others.
In the world, people pursue their kin and provide them with greater benefit; the Tathāgata’s benefit extends to neither enemy nor kin.
The Buddha possesses no such characteristics as worldly people do; therefore, his mind is equal and without duality.
The world speaks of karma as being distinct from its action; the Tathāgata, however, acts without deviation from what he has taught.
Having practiced all that is required to sever all conditioned formations, he is therefore named the Tathāgata.
Having already fully understood the faults of afflictions, he manifests dwelling among them for the sake of sentient beings;
though long since liberated from the world, he delights in remaining within birth and death out of compassion.
Though manifesting in celestial and human forms, compassion follows them like a calf;
the Tathāgata is the mother of sentient beings, and his loving-kindness is the little calf.
Personally enduring manifold sufferings while mindful of sentient beings, When contemplating with compassion, his mind felt no regret;
With such an abundance of pity, he was unaware of his own pain— Therefore, I prostrate to the one who has uprooted suffering.
Although the Tathāgata has performed immeasurable merit, his actions of body, speech, and mind are ever pure;
he always acts for the sake of sentient beings and not for himself—therefore, I pay homage to his pure karma.
The Tathāgata experiences suffering yet does not perceive it as suffering;
seeing the suffering of sentient beings as his own, though he dwells in hell for their sake, he gives rise to neither the thought of suffering nor a mind of regret.
The various sufferings experienced by all sentient beings Are entirely the suffering of the Tathāgata alone;
Having awakened to this, his mind becomes even more steadfast, And thus he is able to diligently cultivate the unsurpassed path.
The Buddha possesses a great heart of compassion of a single flavor, regarding all sentient beings with pity as if they were his own children;
yet because sentient beings do not know that the Buddha can save them, they slander the Tathāgata, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Although the world is possessed of manifold afflictions, and there are likewise immeasurable faults and evils,
the Buddha was able to destroy all such fetters and transgressions from the very moment he first resolved upon enlightenment.
Only Buddhas can praise the Buddha; Aside from Buddhas, there is none who can offer praise.
I now praise him with but a single dharma: That he wanders through the world with a heart of loving-kindness.
The Tathāgata is the great mass of the Dharma of loving-kindness; this loving-kindness can also deliver all sentient beings.
This is the unsurpassed, true liberation, and liberation is itself Great Nirvāṇa.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-four;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-five.
Added by the Song Dynasty śramaṇa Huìyán and others, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Chapter 25: Kauṇḍinya, Part One. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"Form is impermanent; by the cessation of this form, one attains liberation and the eternally abiding form."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise impermanent; by the cessation of this consciousness, one attains liberation and the eternally abiding consciousness. "Kauṇḍinya!
Form is suffering; by the cessation of this form, one attains the form of liberation and bliss.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus.
"Kauṇḍinya! Form is itself emptiness; by the cessation of form through emptiness, one attains liberation from form that is not empty.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise."
“Kauṇḍinya! Form is without self; by the cessation of this form, one attains the true self-nature of form that is liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.”
“Kauṇḍinya! Form is impure;
by the cessation of this form, one attains the pure form of liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.”
"Kauṇḍinya! Form is characterized by birth, old age, sickness, and death; by the cessation of this form, one attains liberation from form that is characterized by birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise."
“Kauṇḍinya! Form is the cause of ignorance; when that cause ceases, one attains liberation from form, which is no longer the form caused by ignorance.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
“Kauṇḍinya! Even up to form, it is the cause of birth; by the cessation of that cause, one attains liberation from form which is the cause of birth.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
“Kauṇḍinya! Form is the cause of the four inversions; by extinguishing form that is the cause of inversion, one attains liberation, which is not the form that is the cause of the four inversions.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.”

“Kauṇḍinya! Form is the cause of immeasurable unwholesome dharmas—namely, the bodies of men and women, craving for food, craving for sensual desire, greed, hatred, jealousy, an evil mind, a stingy mind, the nutriment of physical food, the nutriment of consciousness, the nutriment of volition, the nutriment of contact, birth from eggs, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, birth by transformation, the five desires, and the five hindrances. All such dharmas as these arise because of form; by the cessation of form, one attains liberation and is no longer subject to such immeasurable unwholesome forms.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
“Kauṇḍinya! Form itself is bondage;
by extinguishing the form that is bondage, one attains liberation—the form that is free from bondage.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.”
“Kauṇḍinya! Form itself is a flux;
by the cessation of the flux of form, one attains liberation from form that is not a flux.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.”
“Kauṇḍinya! Form is not the refuge;
by the cessation of this form, one attains the refuge of form that is liberation.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
“Kauṇḍinya! Form is a festering sore; by the cessation of this form, one attains liberation—the form that is free from sores.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.”
"Kauṇḍinya! Form is not quiescent;
by the cessation of this form, one attains the quiescent form of nirvāṇa.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
“Kauṇḍinya! If there is anyone who can know in this way, they are called a śramaṇa and called a brāhmaṇa; they are fully endowed with the qualities of a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa.”
"Kauṇḍinya! If one is apart from the Buddha-dharma, there are no śramaṇas and no brāhmaṇas, nor is there the dharma of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."

All non-Buddhists are falsely and deceptively claiming [enlightenment] and lack any actual practice; although they manifest signs and claim these two exist, in reality there is no such possibility. Why is this?
If there were no dharma of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, how could one say that śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas exist?
I constantly let out the lion’s roar within this great assembly; you, too, should likewise let out the lion’s roar within the great assembly.
At that time, when the immeasurable number of non-Buddhist practitioners heard these words, anger and malice arose in their hearts:
"Gautama now declares that among our assembly there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor is there any dharma of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"How shall I extensively employ skillful means to say to Gautama:
'Within our assembly, there are also śramaṇas and the dharma of śramaṇas; there are brahmins and the dharma of brahmins'?"
At that time, there was a brahmin among the assembly who spoke these words: "O worthy ones!
The words of Gautama are no different from those of a madman; how can they be scrutinized?"
A madman in the world may sing, dance, weep, laugh, revile, or praise; he is unable to distinguish between enemies and kin.
The śramaṇa Gautama is also like this: sometimes he says that he was born into the family of King Śuddhodana, and sometimes he says he was not born;
sometimes he says that after being born he walked seven steps, and sometimes he says he did not walk;
sometimes he says that from childhood he practiced and learned worldly affairs, and sometimes he says that he is an omniscient person; or at times he accepts [offerings] while in the palace.
He sometimes delighted in having a son, and at other times felt weary of him, rebuked him, or despised him;
sometimes he personally practiced asceticism for six years, and at other times he criticized the ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists;
sometimes he claimed to have received teachings not heard before from Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma, and at other times he said that they possessed no knowledge at all.
At times he says that he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* beneath the Bodhi tree;
at times he says that he did not go to the tree and achieved nothing; at times he says that this present body of mine is itself nirvāṇa;
or he says that the extinction of the body is nirvāṇa.
"What Gautama has said is no different from the ravings of a madman;
why then do you grieve and become so distressed because of this? The Brahmins then replied, "O Great Being!"
How could we not be filled with sorrow now?

Since the śramaṇa Gautama first left the household life, he has preached impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity; when my disciples heard this, they were struck with terror, asking:
"How can sentient beings be impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and impure?"
"I did not accept his words.
Now, Gautama has come again to this Śāla grove and is preaching to the great assembly the doctrine of permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
"When my disciples hear these words, they all abandon me and accept the words of Gautama.
For this reason, I am born into great sorrow and suffering.
At that time, another brahmin spoke as follows:
"O worthy ones!
Listen attentively, listen attentively.
That the śramaṇa Gautama is said to practice loving-kindness and compassion is a false statement; it is not the truth."
If you possess compassion, why do you instruct my disciples to receive the Dharma for themselves?
The fruit of compassion is to accord with the intentions of others.
Now, since you have contravened my wishes, how can you say that compassion exists?
If anyone says that the śramaṇa Gautama is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, this too is false.
If it is said that Gautama has few desires and is content, why does he now seize our profits?
If one says that noble lineage refers to a superior clan, this too is false.
Why? Because from antiquity until now, we have neither seen nor heard of a great lion king harming a small mouse.
"If Gautama were of noble lineage, why does he now trouble and disturb us?
If you say that Gautama possesses great power, that too is false."
Why is this? Since time immemorial, we have neither seen nor heard of the King of the Garuḍas contending with a crow.
If you claim your strength is great, for what reason would you fight with me?
If you say that Gautama possesses the knowledge of others' minds, this too is false.
Why? If he possessed such knowledge, for what reason would he not know my mind?
"O virtuous ones!
In the past, I once heard this matter from ancient and wise men:
'After a hundred years have passed, a demonic illusion shall appear in the world.'"
"That was indeed Gautama.
Such a deceptive deluder will soon cease to exist here in this Śāla grove; you should not now be filled with grief and distress."
At that time, another Nirgrantha replied:
"Virtuous one!

My present grief and suffering do not arise from a lack of offerings for myself or my disciples; rather, it is because the world is mired in ignorance and darkness, being without eyes to distinguish between fields of merit and non-fields of merit. Seeing them abandon the ancient, wise Brahmins to instead make offerings to the youth, this is what causes me sorrow."

The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great knowledge of incantations; by the power of these incantations, he can cause a single body to become infinite bodies, or cause infinite bodies to return to a single body, or even transform his own body into the forms of men, women, oxen, sheep, elephants, or horses.
"I have the power to extinguish such incantations.
Once the incantations of the śramaṇa Gautama are extinguished, you shall all return to receiving abundant offerings and enjoy peace and happiness."
At that time, another brahmin spoke thus:
"O worthy ones!
The śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with and possesses immeasurable merits; therefore, you should not contend with him."
The great assembly replied:
"Fool! How can you say that the śramaṇa Gautama possesses great merit?"
“Since his mother passed away seven days after he was born, can this be called a mark of merit?
The brahmin replied,
“One who does not become angry when reviled and does not retaliate when struck— know that this is indeed a mark of great merit.”
His body is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, as well as immeasurable supernormal powers; therefore, one should know that these are the marks of merit.

His mind is free from arrogance; he is the first to inquire after others' welfare, his speech is gentle, and it is never coarse or harsh. Though both his age and vigor are at their peak, his mind is not impulsive or violent.
The kingdom possessed abundant wealth, yet he felt no attachment to it; he renounced it and left the household life as if discarding snot or spittle.
For this reason, I say that the śramaṇa Gautama has fully accomplished immeasurable merits.
The great assembly replied:
"Excellent, O worthy one!
The śramaṇa Gautama is truly as you have said; he has accomplished immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations. We shall not compete with him in this matter."

The śramaṇa Gautama is by nature gentle and cannot endure ascetic practices; having grown up in the depths of the palace, he has no experience with external affairs. He is fit only for soft speech, and knows nothing of the arts, scriptures, or debate.
"Let us together debate the essentials of the True Dharma;
if he defeats me, I shall serve him, and if I defeat him, he shall serve me.
At that time, a great multitude of countless non-Buddhist practitioners gathered and went together to King Ajātaśatru of Magadha.
When the king saw them, he asked:
"O worthy ones!
Each of you practices the noble path; you are renunciants who have abandoned wealth and the affairs of householders."
"The people of our country all provide offerings together, gazing upon you with reverence and never daring to offend or disturb you.
For what reason have you come here in such harmony?
O worthy ones!"

Each of you has received different teachings and different precepts; your renunciations were not the same, and each of you likewise followed your own respective rules of training to leave the household life and cultivate the Path.
For what reason do you now unite with one mind and live in harmony, like fallen leaves driven by a whirlwind gathering together in one place?
"For what reason have you come here?
I constantly protect those who have left the household life, even at the cost of my own body and life.
At that time, all the various followers of external paths spoke thus:

"Great King, listen attentively! You are now a great bridge of the Dharma, a great whetstone of the Dharma, and a great scale of the Dharma. You are the vessel for all merit, the true nature of all merit, and the path of the True Dharma. You are the fertile field for seeds, the foundation of all lands, the clear mirror of all lands, the embodiment of all devas, and the father and mother of all the people of the realm."
"Great King!
The treasury of merit of all the world is none other than Your Majesty’s own body.
For what reason is it called the 'Treasury of Merit'?"

The King adjudicates state affairs without discriminating between enemies and kin; his mind is as impartial as earth, water, fire, and wind. For this reason, he is called the King, the Treasury of Merit.
"Great King!

Although the lifespan of sentient beings in the present is short, the merit of Your Majesty is like that of the long-lived and peaceful times of old; Your Majesty is also like King Mūrdhaja, King Sudarśana, King Kṣāntivādin, King Nahuṣa, King Yayāti, King Śibi, and King Ekaśṛṅga."
Such kings as these were fully endowed with wholesome qualities; Your Majesty is likewise so now.
Great King!
By reason of the King, the land is peaceful and happy, and the population is flourishing.
For this reason, all those who have left the household life aspire to and delight in this land, being diligent in upholding the precepts and cultivating the Right Path.
Great King!
In my sutras it is said:

"If those who have left the household life in whatever country they reside maintain the precepts with diligence and apply themselves earnestly to the cultivation of the Right Path, then that king also possesses a share in the merit of practicing virtue.
O Great King!
"All bandits and kings have already been brought under control; those who have left the household life have nothing to fear.
Now there remains only this one great evildoer, the śramaṇa Gautama, whom Your Majesty has not yet investigated; we are deeply afraid of him."

That person, relying on their own noble lineage and physical perfection, and further receiving abundant offerings as a result of past acts of giving, gives rise to great arrogance based on these various factors; or, they may give rise to arrogance due to the practice of incantations.
For these reasons, he is unable to practice austerities, as he accepts and keeps fine, soft clothing, robes, and bedding.
Consequently, all the wicked people of the world, for the sake of gain and offerings, gather around him as his retinue, and he is unable to practice austerities.
By the power of his incantations, he subdued Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others.
Now he has come again to my dwelling place in the Śāla Grove to proclaim that this body is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, thereby seducing my disciples.
"Great King!
Previously, Gautama spoke of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity, and I was able to endure that;
but now he proclaims permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which I truly cannot endure."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission to debate with that Gautama.
The King replied immediately,
"O Great Beings!"
By whom have you now been instructed that your minds have become deranged and unstable, like surging waves, a whirling firebrand, or a monkey leaping from tree to tree?
This matter is shameful; when wise people hear of it, they immediately feel compassion, but when fools hear of it, they immediately laugh in derision.
What you have said is not the mark of one who has left the household life.
If you suffer from diseases of wind, bile, or phlegm, I possess all the medicines capable of curing them;
as for diseases caused by spirits, my elder brother Jīvaka is skilled at removing them.
"You now wish to scrape Mount Sumeru with your fingernails and teeth, and you wish to bite a diamond with your mouth.
O Great Beings!

It is as if a fool, seeing the lion king sleeping when hungry, wishes to wake him; it is like a person placing a finger in the mouth of a venomous snake; it is like wishing to touch with one's hand a fire covered by ashes. You now act in exactly this same way."

“Good sons! It is as if a wild fox were to let out a lion’s roar; it is like a mosquito competing with a golden-winged bird in a race to see who is faster; it is like a rabbit attempting to cross the ocean, wishing to reach its very bottom. You all are now just like this.”
If you have seen one superior to Gautama in a dream, that dream is a delusion and is not to be trusted.
O Great Beings!
Your current resolve is like that of a moth throwing itself into a great mass of fire.
"Follow my words; there is no need for further speech.
Although you have praised me as being as impartial as a scale, do not let outsiders hear these words again.
At that time, the non-Buddhist practitioner spoke once more:
"Great King!
Has the illusory magic performed by the śramaṇa Gautama reached you,
such that it causes Your Majesty’s mind to doubt and leads you not to believe in these holy men?"
Great King!
You should not treat such a mahāsattva with contempt.
Great King!
Who created such things as the waxing and waning of the moon, the salty taste of the great ocean, and Mount Meru?
Is it not we brahmins who did so?
"Great King!
Have you not heard that for twelve years the waters of the Ganges remained within the ears of the seer Ajita?
Great King!"

Have you not heard that the seer Gautama manifested great supernatural powers for twelve years, transforming himself into the body of Śakra, and furthermore causing that body of Śakra to take the form of a ram and to possess a thousand female organs upon his body?
Great King!
Have you not heard how the seer Kaṇva, in a single day, drank up the waters of the four oceans and caused the great earth to dry?
Great King!
Have you not heard how the seer Vasu created three eyes for Maheśvara?
Great King!
Have you not heard how the seer Rāvaṇa transformed the city of Kāmpilya into the land of Piṅgala?
"Great King!
Among the brahmins, there are such great-power ṛṣis who can be seen and verified;
Great King, why do you treat them with such contempt?"
The King said:
"O virtuous ones!
If you wish to act because you do not yet have faith, the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is currently nearby in the Śāla grove; you may go there and question him as you please."
“The Tathāgata shall likewise analyze this for you and answer according to your wishes.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, together with his retinue of followers and attendants from the various non-Buddhist sects, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Having completed his respectful salutations, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
These various non-Buddhists wish to pose questions and challenges as they please; I only pray that the Tathāgata will answer them as he sees fit."
The Buddha said:
"Great King, cease for now; I myself know the proper time."
At that time, there was a brahmin in the assembly named Jātiśroṇa who spoke as follows:
"Gautama! Do you say that nirvāṇa is a permanent phenomenon?"
"It is so, it is so, Great Brahmin! The Brahmin said:
“Gautama, if you say that Nirvana is eternal, this meaning is not correct.
Why? Because worldly phenomena produce fruits from seeds in an uninterrupted succession, just as a jar emerges from clay or cloth is obtained from thread.”
The Gautama has always said:
"By cultivating the perception of impermanence, one attains nirvāṇa.
Since the cause is impermanent, how can the fruit be permanent?
Furthermore, Gautama has said:

"Liberation from the craving for sense-desires is nirvāṇa; liberation from the craving for form and the craving for the formless is nirvāṇa; the extinction of ignorance and all other afflictions is nirvāṇa."
"From desire up to ignorance, all afflictions are impermanent; because these are impermanent, the nirvāṇa attained through them should also be impermanent.
Furthermore, Gautama has said:
'One is born in heaven because of causes, one falls into hell because of causes, and one attains liberation because of causes; therefore, all phenomena arise from causes.'"
"If liberation is attained by means of causes, how can you say it is eternal?
The Gautama also says:
'Form arises from conditions; therefore, it is called impermanent.'"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
If such liberation were form, one should know it to be impermanent;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
If liberation were to exist apart from the five aggregates, one should know that liberation is identical to empty space.
If it were empty space, it could not be said to arise from causes and conditions.
Why is this? Because it is eternal, unitary, and omnipresent.
Gautama also says:
"Whatever arises from causes is suffering.
If this is suffering, why do you further say that liberation is happiness?
Furthermore, Gautama, you have said:
"Impermanence is suffering, and suffering is non-self.
If these things are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, they are therefore impure.
Since all phenomena produced from causes are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, why do you further say that Nirvana is permanent, blissful, self, and pure?
If the Gautama says that things are both permanent and impermanent, both suffering and happiness, both self and non-self, and both pure and impure, would this not be a case of dualistic speech?
I have also heard from the wise men of old that "when a Buddha appears in the world, his words are never dual.
Yet now, Gautama speaks two different things, saying, "The Buddha is none other than my own self. What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, “Brahmin!
As you have spoken, I now ask you a question; answer it according to your own understanding.”
The brahmin said, "Excellent, Gautama!
The Buddha said:
“Brahmin! Is your nature permanent,
or is it impermanent?”
The brahmin said,
"My nature is eternal.
[The Buddha replied,] "Brahmin!"
"Is this nature capable of acting as the cause for all internal and external phenomena?
"It is so, Gautama."
The Buddha said:
“Brahmin! How does one act as a cause?”

“Gautama! From *prakṛti* (primordial nature) arises *mahat* (the Great One); from *mahat* arises *ahaṃkāra* (ego-consciousness); and from *ahaṃkāra* arise the sixteen factors, namely: earth, water, fire, wind, and space; the five faculties of cognition—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the five faculties of action—hand, foot, mouth, voice, and the two sexual organs; and the faculty of the mind (*manas*).”
These sixteen dharmas arise from five dharmas:
visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
There are three roots for these twenty-one dharmas:
First is defilement, second is coarseness, and third is blackness.
Defilement is called craving;
coarseness is called anger.
"Blackness, Gautama, is called ignorance.
These twenty-four phenomena all arise from their own inherent nature."
“Brahmin! Are these great dharmas eternal or impermanent? “Gautama!”
"In my teaching, the *dharmatā* is eternal, whereas the great elements and all other phenomena are impermanent. "Brahmin!
Just as in your own system the cause is eternal while the fruit is impermanent, what fault would there be in my teaching where the cause is impermanent yet the fruit is eternal?"
“Brahmins! Are there two causes within your doctrine?
They replied:
"There are. The Buddha said, "What are these two?"
The brahmin said:
"The first is the cause of production; the second is the cause of manifestation.
The Buddha said:
"What is the cause of production?
What is the cause of manifestation?
The brāhmaṇa asked.
"The productive cause is like clay producing a jar;
the revealing cause is like a lamp illuminating an object.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"These two kinds of causes have the same nature as causes.
If they are one and the same, could it be that a producing cause is made into a revealing cause, or that a revealing cause is made into a producing cause?"
"No, Gautama," he replied.
The Buddha said:

"If it were the case that the productive cause does not function as the revealing cause, and the revealing cause does not function as the productive cause, could one still say that these possess the characteristics of causality?
The Brahmin replied:
"Even though they do not function as each other, they nonetheless possess the characteristics of causality."
“Brahmin! Is that which is made known by the cause of manifestation identical to the act of manifesting? “No, it is not.”
"Gautama!
The Buddha said,
"Although my Dharma is attained through impermanence, it is not itself impermanent."
"O Brahmin! Because they are attained through the cause of realization, they are permanent, blissful, self, and pure;
because they are attained through the cause of birth, they are impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity."
Therefore, that which is spoken by the Tathāgata is twofold;
yet these two words are not two. For this reason, the Tathāgata is called "One of Non-dual Speech.
As you have said:
"I have heard from the wise men of old:
'When a Buddha appears in the world, there are no two [contradictory] words.
These words are excellent; what is spoken by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time is without discrepancy. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha has no two words."
How is there no difference?
Because where there is existence, one speaks of existence; where there is non-existence, one speaks of non-existence. Therefore, it is called "one meaning," O Brāhmaṇa!
Although the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks in two words, it is for the sake of clarifying one word.
How do these two words clarify one word?
It is like the two words "eye" and "form" giving rise to the single word "consciousness."
"Even so it is for the mind and mental phenomena.
The brahmin said, "Gautama!..."
"You are well able to distinguish the meaning of such words; yet I do not now understand how these two utterances you have made can be understood as one.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately proclaimed for him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: "Brahmin!"
"The Truth of Suffering is both two and one;
even so, up to the Truth of the Path, it is both two and one.
The brāhmaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!
I have already understood.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! How do you know this?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the Truth of Suffering, all ordinary beings have two [aspects], while noble ones have one;
this applies likewise up to the Truth of the Path.”
The Buddha said, "Excellent; you have understood.
The brāhmaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!

Having now heard the Dharma, I have attained right view. I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; I only pray that, out of your great compassion, you will grant me permission to leave the household life.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:
“You should shave off the hair and beard of this Jātiśroṇa and permit him to go forth.”
Then Kauṇḍinya, having received the Buddha’s command, shaved his hair for him; as soon as he applied the razor, two things fell away:
first, the hair of his head and beard, and second, his afflictions (kleśa). Thereupon, in that very seat, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Furthermore, there was a brahmin of the Vāsiṣṭha clan who spoke again as follows:
"Gautama, is the nirvāṇa you speak of eternal?
[The Buddha replied: "It is so."
“Brahmin! Vāseṭṭha said, “Gautama!”
“Is it not the case that you do not say that the absence of afflictions is nirvana?
“It is so, brahmin.”
Vāseṭṭha said: "Gautama!
There are four things in the world that are called 'non-existent': [the horns of a hare, the hair of a tortoise, the son of a barren woman, and a firebrand-wheel]."
First, that which has not yet emerged is called "non-existent," such as when a jar has not yet emerged from the clay, it is called a "non-existent jar.
Second, that which has already ceased is called "non-existent," such as when a jar has been destroyed, it is called a "non-existent jar.
Third, the mutual absence of different characteristics is called "non-existent," such as there being no horse within a cow, and no cow within a horse.
Fourth, because it is ultimately non-existent, it is called "non-existence," like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Gautama! If nirvāṇa is defined as that which exists after the afflictions have been eliminated, then nirvāṇa would be non-existent.
"If these do not exist, why do you say they are permanent, blissful, self,
and pure? The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
