Thus, nirvāṇa is not a prior non-existence like that of a jar while it is still clay; nor is it a cessation-negation like the non-existence of a jar after it has been destroyed; nor is it an absolute non-existence like that of a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns, which is equivalent to a negation of difference.
"Good son!
As you have said, although there is no horse among oxen, one cannot say that the ox is also non-existent;
and although there is no ox among horses, one likewise cannot say that the horse is also non-existent."
"Nirvana is likewise: nirvana does not exist within the afflictions, and the afflictions do not exist within nirvana;
therefore, they are called 'mutually exclusive'. Vāsiṣṭha said, "Gautama!"
If you take the absence of difference as nirvāṇa, then that which is the absence of difference is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure.
Gautama! How then can you say that nirvāṇa is permanent, blissful, self, and pure?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Regarding what you have said concerning 'otherness' and 'non-existence,' there are three kinds of non-existence: [text continues]"
That oxen and horses were previously non-existent and later come into being is called "prior non-existence" (pūrvābhāva);
that what has already existed returns to non-existence is called "non-existence through destruction" (pradhvaṃsābhāva);
as for "non-existence of distinct characteristics," it is as you have described.
Good son! These three kinds of non-existence do not exist within nirvāṇa; therefore, nirvāṇa is eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
It is like a sick person in the world:
First is fever, second is wind-disorder, and third is cold-disorder.
These three types of illness can be treated by three medicines:
for those with fever, clarified butter (sarpis) can treat it;
For those with wind-disorders (*vāta*), oil can cure them;
for those with cold-disorders (*śīta*), honey can cure them.
These three kinds of medicine can cure these three kinds of evil diseases.
"Good son!
There is no oil in wind, nor is there wind in oil; likewise, there is no coldness in honey, nor is there honey in coldness. For this reason, they are able to treat one another."
All sentient beings are likewise thus, having three kinds of diseases:
first, greed; second, anger; and third, delusion.
For these three diseases, there are three kinds of medicines:

The contemplation of impurity serves as the medicine for greed; the contemplation of loving-kindness serves as the medicine for hatred; and the wisdom that contemplates dependent origination serves as the medicine for delusion. Good son!
To eliminate greed, one practices the contemplation of non-greed;
to eliminate hatred, one practices the contemplation of non-hatred;
to eliminate delusion, one practices the contemplation of non-delusion.
Within the three kinds of illnesses there are no three kinds of medicines, and within the three kinds of medicines there are no three kinds of illnesses. Good son!
Because the three medicines are not present within the three illnesses, there is no permanence, no self, no bliss, and no purity.
"Within these three kinds of medicine there are no three kinds of diseases; therefore, they may be called permanent, blissful, self, and pure. Vāsiṣṭha said:
"World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata has taught me about the permanent and the impermanent;
what is permanent, and what is impermanent?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Form is impermanent, while liberation from form is permanent;
likewise, up to consciousness, which is impermanent, while liberation from consciousness is permanent.”

"Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to contemplate that form, up to and including consciousness, is impermanent, you should know that such persons have attained the eternal Dharma."
Vāseṭṭha said:
“World-Honored One!
I have now understood the dharmas of permanence and impermanence.”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, how do you understand the dharmas of permanence and impermanence?”
Vāseṭṭha said: "World-Honored One!
I now know that my form is impermanent, and that I have attained the permanence of liberation."
"Up to and including consciousness, it is also thus.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"It is well that you have now repaid this body.
He then addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"This Vāśiṣṭha has already realized the fruit of Arhatship; you may give him his three robes and alms-bowl."
Then Kauṇḍinya, as instructed by the Buddha, gave him the robe and bowl.
Having received the robe and bowl, Vāśiṣṭha spoke these words:
"Venerable Kauṇḍinya!..."

"Because of this wretched and evil body, I have now obtained a virtuous fruit; I only pray that you, Great Virtue, would deign to go to the World-Honored One on my behalf and fully declare my heart's intent."
"I am a wicked man who has offended the Tathāgata, you of the Gautama clan; I only pray that you will accept my repentance for this transgression.
I can no longer endure this poisonous body and shall now enter nirvāṇa."
Then Kauṇḍinya went to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!

The bhikṣu Vāsiṣṭha has given rise to a sense of shame and remorse, saying of himself that he is dull-witted and ignorant. He has offended the Tathāgata by addressing him by the clan name 'Gautama. Unable to remain long in this body, which is like a venomous snake, he now wishes to extinguish his life and entrusts me with his confession."
The Buddha said, “Kauṇḍinya!
The bhikṣu Vāsiṣṭha has already cultivated roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past; he now accepts my words and abides in accordance with the Dharma.”
"Because he dwelt in accordance with the Dharma, he obtained the correct fruit.
You all should make offerings to his body.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya, having heard this from the Buddha, returned to the place where the body was and performed an offering.
At that time, as Vāseṭṭha was performing the cremation of his body, he manifested various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
When the non-Buddhists saw this, they cried out in a loud voice:
"This Vāseṭṭha has already acquired the incantations and arts of the śramaṇa Gautama; before long, this man shall again surpass that śramaṇa Gautama."
At that time, there was another brahmin in the assembly named Śreṇika, who spoke again as follows:
"Gautama! Is there a self?"
The Tathāgata remained silent. “Gautama,
is there no self?”
The Tathāgata remained silent.
A second and a third time he asked the same question, and the Buddha remained silent each time.
Srenika said:
"Gautama! If all sentient beings possess a self—that which is omnipresent, unitary, and the agent—why do you remain silent and not answer, Gautama?"
The Buddha said:
"Srenika! Do you say that this 'self' of yours pervades all places?"
Srenika replied: "Gautama! Not only do I say this;
all those who possess omniscience speak likewise."
The Buddha said:
"Good son, if I were omnipresent in all places, I should receive retribution for the five realms of existence simultaneously."

If the retributions of the five destinies were experienced all at once, for what reason, O Brahmins, would you not refrain from committing various evils to avoid hell, and instead cultivate various wholesome dharmas to receive a celestial body?
Srenika said: "Gautama!
In my teaching, there are two kinds of self: [the inner self and the outer self]."
First, the self as a created body; second, the self as an eternal body.
To cultivate the self as a created body, one practices the abandonment of unwholesome dharmas so as not to enter hell, and cultivates various wholesome dharmas to be reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
As you say that the self pervades all places, if such a self were to exist within the body, you should know it to be impermanent."
“If the body does not exist, how can you say it is pervasive? “Gautama!
The self I posit also exists within the act of creation, and it is likewise an eternal dharma.”
"Gotama!
It is like when a person's house is set on fire and the owner has gone out;
one cannot say, 'The house is being burned, and the owner is being burned as well.'"
"My Dharma is also like this: although this body that has been created is impermanent, when it becomes impermanent, I shall depart from it.
Therefore, the self is both all-pervading and eternal."
The Buddha said: "Good son!
As you say that I am both all-pervasive and eternal, this meaning is not so."
Why is this? There are two kinds of pervasiveness:
first, permanence; second, impermanence.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, form; second, formlessness.
Therefore, if one says that all things exist, they are both permanent and impermanent, and both with form and without form.
If it is argued that when the householder emerges he is not called impermanent, this meaning is not correct.
Why? Because the house is not called the master, and the master is not called the house; since burning is one thing and emerging is another, it is thus possible [to say he is impermanent].
I am not like that. Why is this?
I am identical to form, and form is identical to me; there is no form apart from me, and I am not apart from form.
How then can you say that when form is impermanent, I may escape?
Good son! If you think that all sentient beings share one and the same self, this would contradict both worldly and world-transcending dharmas. Why is this?
Worldly dharmas are designated as father and mother, son and daughter.

If the self were a single entity, then the father would be the son and the son would be the father; the mother would be the daughter and the daughter would be the mother; the enemy would be the relative and the relative would be the enemy; this would be that and that would be this.
"Therefore, if one says that all sentient beings share a single self, this contradicts both worldly and world-transcending dharmas. Śreṇika said:
"I do not say that all sentient beings share a single self; rather, I say that each individual possesses their own self."
The Buddha said: "Good son!
If one says that each individual has their own self, this would result in a multiplicity of selves; such a proposition is not tenable."
Why is this? As you previously stated, the self is omnipresent.
If it were omnipresent, then the karmic faculties of all sentient beings would necessarily be identical.
When Devadatta sees, the Buddha also sees;
when Devadatta acts, the Buddha also acts;
when Devadatta hears, the Buddha also hears.
All phenomena are likewise thus.
If it were seen by the gods but not seen by the Buddha, one should not say that "I" pervade all places;
if it does not pervade, then it is impermanent.
Śreṇika said: “Gautama!
The self (ātman) of all sentient beings pervades everything, whereas dharma and adharma do not pervade everything.”
For this reason, Buddhadeva’s action is distinct from Devadatta’s action.
Therefore, Gautama, you should not say:
"When Buddhadeva sees, Devadatta should see."
"When the Buddha hears it, Devadatta shall hear it accordingly.
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
"Are dharma and adharma not produced by karma?
Śreṇika said: "Gautama!"
"This is the result of karma," the Buddha said. "Good son!"
If dharma and non-dharma were the agent of karma, they would be identical to the dharma [itself].
How then can you say they are different? Why is this so?
Where there is the self of Buddhadeva, there is the self of Devadatta;
where there is the self of Devadatta, there is the self of Buddhadeva.
Therefore, when Buddhadeva acts, Devadatta also acts.
Dharma and non-Dharma should also be understood in this way. Good son!
Therefore, if for all sentient beings Dharma and non-Dharma are as such, the karmic fruits they obtain should likewise not differ.
"Good son! Although fruit emerges from a seed, that seed never thinks or discriminates:
'I shall produce fruit only for a Brahmin, and not produce fruit for a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra.'"
Why is this? Just as fruit produced from a seed never obstructs these four castes, so too it is with the Dharma and non-Dharma; they cannot be distinguished [in this regard]:
"I shall only bring about the fruition for Buddhajīva, not for Devajīva;
I shall bring about the fruition for Devajīva, not the fruition for Buddhajīva.
For what reason?
"Because karma is equal.
Śreṇika said, "Gautama!"
For example, suppose there are a hundred thousand lamps in a single room; although their wicks differ, their light is no different.
The distinction between the lamps and the wicks is a metaphor for *dharma* and *adharma*;
the lack of difference in their light is a metaphor for the self (*ātman*) of sentient beings.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
As for your statement that you use the brightness of a lamp as a metaphor for me, this meaning is not so."
Why is this? Because the room is distinct from the lamp, and yet the light of this lamp exists both at the edge of the wick and throughout the entire room.

If the "self" were like what you have described, then the self would have to exist both at the edge of the dharma and the non-dharma, and within the self there would likewise have to be both dharma and non-dharma.
If both the dharma and the non-dharma were devoid of a self, one could not say that they pervade all places;
if both were present, how could the analogy of the wick and the light still be applied?

Good son! If you think that the wick and the light are truly distinct and different, for what reason does the light become more intense when the wick increases, and why does the light perish when the wick withers?
Therefore, one should not use the lamp and its wick as a metaphor for dharma and non-dharma, nor use the lack of difference in their light as a metaphor for the self (*ātman*). Why is this?
Because these three things—dharma, non-dharma, and the self—are one and the same.
Śreṇika said: "Gautama!
Your citation of the analogy of the lamp is inauspicious."
Why is this? If the analogy of the lamp were auspicious, I have already cited it;
if it were inauspicious, why would you state it again?

“Good son! The metaphors I have cited do not at all constitute either auspicious or inauspicious; you may explain them according to your own intention. These metaphors also speak of light existing apart from the wick, as well as light existing within the wick itself.”
Your mind is not impartial; therefore, you employ the analogy of the lamp wick to represent both the Dharma and non-Dharma, while using its light to represent the self (*ātman*).
For this reason, we challenge you:

[you must admit that] the wick is itself the light, or that there is light apart from the wick; likewise, the Dharma is itself the self, or there is a self apart from the Dharma; non-Dharma is itself the self, or there is a self apart from non-Dharma.
Why do you now accept only one side and not the other?
Such a metaphor is inauspicious for you; therefore, I shall now instruct you again.
"Good son!
Such a metaphor is itself no metaphor; because it is not a metaphor, it is auspicious for me but inauspicious for you, good son!"
If you think:
"If I am not auspicious, you are also not auspicious," this reasoning is incorrect.

Why is this? We observe that people in the world use their own knives to harm themselves, or perform actions for their own sake while others reap the benefits; the analogy you have cited is likewise so—it is auspicious for me, but not for you.
Śreṇika said: "Gautama!
Previously you censured my mind for being unequal, yet what you have now said is itself unequal."
For what reason? Gautama!
Now you have directed auspiciousness toward yourself and inauspiciousness toward me; judging by this, it is truly unjust.
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Just as my impartiality can destroy your lack of impartiality, it is therefore auspicious that your impartiality [removes] my lack of impartiality."
My own lack of equanimity destroys your lack of equanimity, enabling you to attain equanimity; this is precisely my own equanimity.
Why is this? Because it is identical to the equanimity attained by all the sages.
Srenika said: "Gautama!
I am always even; why do you say that you have destroyed my unevenness?"
"All sentient beings equally possess a self; why do you say that my self is unequal? "Good son!

You yourself say that one 'shall experience hell,' 'shall experience the realm of hungry ghosts,' 'shall experience the realm of animals,' or 'shall experience the realms of humans and devas. If my self were already pervading all five destinies, why would you then say that one 'shall experience' those various realms?"
You also say that a child is born only after the union of father and mother; if the child already existed beforehand, why do you further say it exists only after their union?
Therefore, a single person possesses bodies belonging to the five destinies.
If the body already existed prior to these five locations, for what cause and condition would one create karma for the sake of the body?
Therefore, this is inconsistent. Good son!
If you think that the self is the agent, this is not the case.
Why? If the self were the agent, for what reason or condition would it create suffering for itself?
However, since sentient beings truly experience suffering, one should know that I am not its creator.

If it were said that this suffering is not created by me and does not arise from causes, then all phenomena would likewise not arise from causes; for what reason, then, would you say that I am the creator?
"Good son!

The suffering and pleasure of sentient beings truly arise from causes and conditions; such suffering and pleasure give rise to sorrow and joy. When there is sorrow, there is no joy; when there is joy, there is no sorrow. Whether it be joy or sorrow, how could a wise person say that these are permanent?"
“Good son! You say that the self is permanent. If it were permanent, how could you speak of the distinctions between ten stages?
A permanent dharma should not possess the stage of the kalala, nor even the stage of old age.”
Even the eternal dharma of space does not exist for even a single moment, much less for ten periods. Good son!
The "Self" is not the kalala stage nor any stage up to old age; how, then, can one speak of ten distinct periods?
“Good son! If I were the creator, then I too would have times of flourishing and decline, and sentient beings likewise would have times of flourishing and decline.”
If the self were such as this, how could it be permanent? Good son!
If the self were an agent, why would one person be sharp-witted while another is dull-witted?
"Good son!
If 'I' were the agent, then this 'I' would be able to perform bodily, verbal, and mental actions.
If it were that which is acted upon by 'me,' how could one verbally declare that there is no 'I'?"
"How is it that one doubts for oneself whether [it] exists or does not exist? 'Good son!'"
If you think that seeing exists apart from the eye, this is not the case.
Why? Because if seeing existed separately from the eye, what need would there be for this eye?
The same applies even to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). If you think:
"Although I am able to see, it must be through the eye that I see," [then consider this].
This is also not the case. Why?
It is like someone saying:
"The sumanā flower can burn down a great village.
How can it burn? It burns by means of fire."
"Your establishment of the view of self is likewise so.
Śreṇika said: "Gautama!..."
"Just as a person who grasps a sickle is able to mow grass,
so too am I because of the five faculties in seeing, hearing, up to touching. "Good son!"
Since each person’s sickle is distinct, one who grasps a sickle is able to perform an action.
Apart from the sense faculties, there is no separate self; how then can it be said that the self, by means of the sense faculties, is able to perform an action?
"Good son! If you think:
'Just as the grasping of the sickle can cut, so too am I.'"
"Is it that I have hands, or am I handless?
If I do have hands, why do I not grasp them myself?"
If there were no hand, how could one say, "I am the agent"?
Good son! That which is able to cut grass is the sickle; it is neither the self nor the person.
"If I am capable, why rely on a sickle?
"Good son, a person has two kinds of karma:"
First, one grasps the grass; second, one grasps the sickle.
This sickle possesses only the function of cutting; the way sentient beings perceive the Dharma is likewise thus.

The eye can see forms because they arise from a combination [of conditions]. If seeing arises from the combination of causes and conditions, why would a wise person say that there is a self? "Good son!
If you think that the body performs the action while the self experiences the result, this is not the case.
Why? Because in the world, one does not see Devadatta performing the action and Buddhadatta experiencing the fruit.
If you say that it is not the body that acts and that the self is not the cause of sensation, then for what reason do you seek liberation from causes and conditions?
If your previous body was not born of causes and conditions, then after attaining liberation, you should likewise be able to produce another body without a cause.
"As with the body, so it should be with all afflictions. Śreṇika said: "Gautama!"
I have two kinds: first, that which possesses consciousness; second, that which lacks consciousness.
The self that lacks consciousness can obtain a body, while the self that possesses consciousness can relinquish the body.
Just as a clay vessel, once it has been fired, loses its original color and can never return to its former state;
so too are the afflictions of the wise: once they have been extinguished and destroyed, they can never arise again.
The Buddha said,
"Good son! Regarding what is called 'knowing,' is it wisdom that knows?"
Can "I" know? If it is wisdom that knows, why say "I am the knower"?
If it is "I" who knows, why must one employ skillful means to further seek wisdom?
If you think that I know through the knowledge of causes, then the analogy of the flower is refuted.
Good son! It is like a thorny tree:
its nature is such that it can prick by itself; one cannot say that the tree grasps the thorn and pricks with it.
Wisdom is also like this; wisdom knows itself. Why, then, do you say that the self grasps wisdom and knows it? "Good son!
Just as in your own dharma you attain liberation, do you think there is a 'self' that attains it?"
Do you know that you have attained it?
If there is no knowledge of attainment, you should know that you still possess all afflictions;
if there is knowledge of attainment, you should know that the five sensory faculties already exist.
Why is this? Apart from the sense faculties, there is no separate cognition.
If one possesses all the sense faculties, how can one further be said to have attained liberation?
If you say that this self is pure by nature and transcends the five sense faculties, why do you say it exists throughout the five realms of existence?
For what reason and by what causal conditions do you cultivate various wholesome dharmas for the sake of liberation?
"Good son! It is as if someone were to pull out a thorn from empty space;
you are just like this. If I am pure, why do you further say that I have severed all afflictions?"
"If you think that liberation is obtained without depending on causes and conditions,
why then do all animals not attain it? Śreṇika said, "Gautama!"
"If there were no self, who would be able to remember?
The Buddha told Śreṇika:
"If there were a self, for what reason would one forget again?"
“Good son!
If it is this mindfulness that is the self, for what reason does it give rise to evil thoughts, think of what should not be thought, and fail to think of what should be thought?
Śreṇika replied again:
"Gautama! If there is no self, who sees?
Who hears?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!

There are the six internal sense bases and the six external objects; through the conjunction of the internal and external, the six kinds of consciousness arise, and these six kinds of consciousness receive their names by reason of these causes and conditions."
Good son! It is like a single fire:

because it arises from wood, it is called "wood-fire"; because it arises from grass, it is called "grass-fire"; because it arises from chaff, it is called "chaff-fire"; and because it arises from cow dung, it is called "cow-dung-fire."
The consciousness of sentient beings is also like this: depending on the eye, depending on forms, depending on light, and depending on desire, it is called "eye-consciousness.
Good son! Thus, this eye-consciousness does not reside within the eye, nor even within desire; rather, this consciousness arises through the conjunction of these four factors.
This applies even up to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If wisdom arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions, one should not say that "seeing" is the self, nor even that "touching" is the self.
"Good son!
For this reason, I say that from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, all dharmas are indeed illusions.
In what way are they like illusions?"
That which was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence. Good son!

For example, when butter, flour, honey, ginger, black pepper, long pepper, grapes, walnuts, pomegranates, and jujubes are thus combined, they are called "joy-pills" (mudga-vaṭaka); apart from this combination, there are no joy-pills.

The six internal and external bases of cognition are what are called "sentient beings," "self," "person," and "individual"; apart from these internal and external bases, there is no separate sentient being, self, person, or individual.
Srenika said: "Gautama!
If there were no self, how could one say: 'I see,' 'I hear,' 'I suffer,' 'I am happy,' 'I grieve,' or 'I rejoice'?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!

If it were the case that saying ‘I see’ or ‘I hear’ constituted the existence of a self, for what reason would people in the world further say, ‘The sin you have committed was not seen or heard by me’?”
Good son!

For example, when four types of troops are combined, they are called an army; yet these four troops are not called "one," and yet one says, "My army is brave and strong," or "My army has defeated the enemy."

The same applies to that which is produced by the conjunction of the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*): although it is not a single entity, one may nevertheless say, "I act," "I experience," "I see," "I hear," "I suffer," or "I am happy."
Srenika said: "Gautama!
According to what you have said regarding the union of the internal and external, who is it that produces the sound saying, 'I act' and 'I experience'?"
The Buddha said: “Sreṇika! From craving and ignorance as causes and conditions, karma arises;

from karma, existence arises; from existence, immeasurable mental factors arise. From the mind, vitarka and vicāra arise; vitarka and vicāra move the wind. This wind follows the mind and contacts the throat, tongue, teeth, and lips. Due to the perversion of sentient beings’ perceptions, sounds are produced, and they say: ‘I act,’ ‘I experience,’ ‘I see,’ and ‘I hear.’”

Good son! It is like the bells atop a banner: due to the conditions of the wind, they produce sounds; when the wind is great, the sound is great, and when the wind is small, the sound is small, yet there is no agent who creates them.
Good son! It is like when red-hot iron is cast into water and produces various sounds; within this, there is truly no agent. Good son!

"Because ordinary persons are unable to contemplate and discern such matters, they say that there is a self and what belongs to a self, that 'I' act, and that 'I' experience. Śreṇika said, "If, as Gautama says,
there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, for what reason do you further speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity?"
The Buddha said,
“Good son! I do not say that the six internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and the six consciousnesses of the mind are permanent, blissful, self, or pure.”
I then proclaim that the cessation of the six consciousnesses produced by the internal and external sense bases is called "permanent";
because it is permanent, it is called "self";
and because there is a permanent self, it is called "bliss."
Because it is permanent, self, and blissful, it is called "pure. Good son!
Sentient beings weary of suffering and sever its causes; this sovereign transcendence is called the "self."
"For these reasons, I now proclaim permanence, bliss, self,
and purity. Śreṇika said,
"World-Honored One!"
“I only pray that you, out of great compassion, will explain for me how I may obtain such permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The Buddha said, “Good son!

All beings in the world have, from the very beginning, been possessed of great conceit and have been able to increase it; they have likewise created the causes and karmic actions of conceit. Therefore, they now undergo the retribution of conceit, being unable to distance themselves from all afflictions and attain the permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"If all sentient beings wish to distance themselves from all afflictions,
they must first abandon pride. Śreṇika said,
"World-Honored One!"
"Thus it is, thus it is; it is exactly as the Holy Teaching declares.
Previously I harbored pride, and because of that pride, I addressed the Tathāgata by your clan name, Gautama.
Now that I have abandoned such great pride, I therefore entreat you with a sincere heart to grant me the Dharma."
"How, then, shall one attain permanence, bliss, self,
and purity? The Buddha said, "Good son!
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
Son of good family!
If one can [realize] that there is neither self, nor other, nor sentient beings, one remains far removed from these dharmas.
Śreṇika said:
“World-Honored One!
I have now understood and realized it; I have attained the eye of the True Dharma.”
The Buddha said, “Good son,
how do you know that you have already understood and attained the true Dharma-eye?”
“World-Honored One!
That which is called ‘form’ is neither self, nor other, nor any sentient being;
even up to consciousness, it is likewise so.”
"Observing in this way, I have attained the eye of the True Dharma.
World-Honored One!
I now deeply desire to leave the household life to cultivate the Way; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
The Buddha said,
“Welcome, bhikṣu! At that very moment,
he became fully endowed with pure brahmacarya and realized the fruit of arhatship.
Among the assembly of non-Buddhists, there was again a brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan who spoke thus:
"Gautama! The body is the life-force; the body is one thing and the life-force is another."
The Tathāgata remained silent.
A second and a third time, it was likewise.
The brahmin spoke again:
“Gautama! If a person has cast off this body but has not yet attained a subsequent body, could one not say that in the interval between them, the body is one thing and the life-principle is another?
If they are indeed different, Gautama, why do you remain silent and not answer?”
“Good son! I teach that both body and life arise from causes and conditions, and not without causes and conditions;
as it is with body and life, so it is with all phenomena.”
The brahmin spoke again:
"Gautama! I see that there are phenomena in the world that do not arise from causes and conditions."
The Buddha said:
"Brahmin! How do you perceive there to be any phenomenon in the world that does not arise from causes and conditions?"
The brahmin said:
"I see a great fire burning through thickets of wood; when the wind blows, the flames are extinguished and fall elsewhere. Is this not called being without cause or condition?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
I say that this fire also arises from causes; it does not arise without a cause.”
The brahmin said: “Gautama!
When a flame is extinguished, it does not depend on fuel or charcoal; how then can you say that it depends upon causes and conditions?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Although there is no firewood or charcoal, it continues because of the wind; due to the conditions of the wind, its flames do not extinguish.”
“Gautama! When a person has cast off this body but has not yet attained a subsequent body, what serves as the causal condition for their intermediate life-span?
The Buddha said:
“Brahmin! Ignorance and craving serve as the causes and conditions.
It is because of these two causes and conditions—ignorance and craving—that life persists.”
Good son! Due to certain causes and conditions, the body is itself life and life is itself the body;
due to certain causes and conditions, the body is distinct and life is distinct.
"A wise person should not categorically state that the body is one thing and the life-principle is another.
The brahmin said:
"World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that you will analyze and explain this for me, so that I may clearly understand cause and effect.
The Buddha said, "Brahmin!"
The cause is the five aggregates, and the fruit is likewise the five aggregates. Good son!
If there are sentient beings who do not kindle fire, then there will be no smoke.
The brahmin said:
“World-Honored One!
I have already known; I have already understood.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, how do you know this?"
"How is it understood?
"World-Honored One!
Fire is itself affliction; it can burn within the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas."
"Smoke" refers to the retribution of afflictions; it is impermanent, impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome, and for this reason it is called smoke.
If there are sentient beings who do not produce afflictions, such persons will have no retribution of afflictions.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said that where there is no fire, there is no smoke.
World-Honored One!
I have attained right view; I only pray that you will compassionately pity me and grant me permission to leave the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"Grant this brahmin permission to leave the household life and receive the precepts.
Having received the Buddha’s command, Kauṇḍinya, together with the harmonious Saṃgha, granted him permission to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
After five days had passed, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
Among the assembly of non-Buddhists, there was another brahmin named Purna, who spoke these words: "Gautama!
Having seen that this world is a permanent phenomenon, do you say it is permanent?
Is such a proposition real or false?

Is it eternal, or impermanent, or both eternal and impermanent, or neither eternal nor impermanent? Is it finite, or infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite? Are the body and the life-principle the same, or are the body and the life-principle different? After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, does he exist, or not exist, or both exist and not exist, or neither exist nor not exist?
The Buddha said: “Pūraṇa!

I do not speak of the world as eternal or non-eternal, as both eternal and non-eternal, or as neither eternal nor non-eternal; nor do I speak of it as finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite; nor do I speak of this body and this life as being identical, or the body and the life as being distinct.”
"After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, does he exist, or does he not exist, or both exist and not exist, or neither exist nor not exist?
Pūraṇa spoke again: "Gautama!"
"Seeing what fault or transgression now do you not make such a statement?
The Buddha said, "Purna!"
If someone says,
"The world is eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false," this is called a view.

To perceive that which is perceived is called the activity of views, the karma of views, attachment to views, bondage of views, the suffering of views, the grasping of views, the fear of views, the fever of views, and the entanglement of views.

Purna! Ordinary persons are entangled by views and cannot distance themselves from birth, old age, sickness, and death; they circulate through the six realms of existence, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
This is likewise true for the propositions that the Tathāgata neither exists after death nor does not exist after death.
"Pūrṇa! I see that this view has such faults; therefore, I do not cling to it, nor do I teach it to others.
"Gautama! [Pūrṇa said.]
If one sees such faults and neither clings to them nor speaks of them,
what does Gautama see now?
To what does he cling?
"What is it that you proclaim?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
That which is characterized by attachment is called the dharma of birth and death.
Because the Tathāgata has already transcended the dharma of birth and death, he is therefore unattached. Good son!
“The Tathāgata is called one who can see and can speak; he is not called one who is attached.
“Gautama, in what way can he see?”
"How can one speak [of this]?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
I am able to clearly perceive suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; I analyze and proclaim these Four Noble Truths.
Because I see them thus, I am able to distance myself from all views, all cravings, all taints, and all forms of conceit.
Therefore, having fully perfected the pure Brahma-conduct and attained unsurpassed tranquility, I have obtained an eternal body; this body is likewise neither east, west, south, nor north.
Pūrṇa said: "Gautama!
For what reason is the eternal body not located in the east, west, south, or north?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
I now ask you; answer as you see fit.”
"What do you think, noble son?
Suppose a great mass of fire were to be kindled before you; when it is burning, would you know that it is burning?"
“Yes, Gautama. “When this fire is extinguished, do you know that it has been extinguished?”
"So it is, Gautama! O Pūraṇa!"
If someone were to ask you:
"From where did that previous mass of fire come when it was burning,
and to where did it go when it was extinguished?"
"How should I answer? "Gautama!
If someone were to ask me that, I would answer:
"This fire, when it arises, depends upon various conditions; once the original conditions have been exhausted and new conditions have not yet arrived, this fire then extinguishes.
"Furthermore, if someone were to ask:
'Once this fire has been extinguished, to which direction has it gone?'"
"And how would you answer again?
"Gautama! I would answer, saying:"
"Because conditions are exhausted, it ceases and does not reach any location.
"Good son, the Tathāgata is also like this.
If there is impermanent form, up to and including impermanent consciousness, they burn because of craving; that which burns is precisely the undergoing of the twenty-five states of existence."
Therefore, while it is burning, one may say that this fire is to the east, west, south, or north.
When present craving is extinguished, the retributive fruits of the twenty-five states of existence do not burn;
because they do not burn, one cannot say they have directions—east, west, south, or north.
"Good son!
The Tathāgata has already extinguished impermanent form up to impermanent consciousness; therefore, his body is eternal.
If the body were eternal, one could not speak of its being in the east, west, south, or north."
Pūrṇa said: "I beg you to provide an analogy; I only wish that you would deign to hear me.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Speak as you please.
“World-Honored One!”
Suppose there were a grove of *sāla* trees outside a large village, and within it there was one tree that had grown before the rest, having already reached the age of a hundred years.
At that time, the owner of the grove would water it and tend to it according to the seasons.
That tree is decayed and old; its bark, branches, and leaves have all fallen away, leaving only the heartwood intact.
The Tathāgata is likewise: all that is ancient and worn has been completely eliminated, leaving only the truly real Dharma.
“World-Honored One!
I now deeply desire to leave the household life to cultivate the Way.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu!
As soon as these words were spoken, he immediately went forth into homelessness and, with the exhaustion of the outflows, realized the fruit of arhatship.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Scroll 35.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-Six.
Added by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇas Huìyán and others based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Lower Section of the Kauṇḍinya Chapter.
Furthermore, there was a brahmin named Viśuddha who spoke these words: “Gautama!

All sentient beings do not know by what dharma they perceive the world as permanent, impermanent, both permanent and impermanent, neither permanent nor impermanent, and so on, up to neither thus-gone nor not thus-gone.”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Because they do not know form, and so on up to because they do not know consciousness, they view the world as eternal, and so on up to neither passing away nor not passing away."
The brahmin said: "Gautama!
By knowing what dharma do sentient beings not see the world as eternal, up to and including neither passing away nor not passing away?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Because one knows form, and so on up to knowing consciousness, one does not perceive the world as permanent, nor [as impermanent], up to neither going nor not going."
The brahmin said:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will analyze and explain for me whether the world is eternal or impermanent.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! If a person abandons the old and does not create new karma, that person is able to know the permanent and the impermanent."
The brahmin said,
"World-Honored One!
I have already known and seen."
The Buddha said:
"Good son, how do you see it?"
"How do you know this?
"World-Honored One!
For this reason, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)."
The "new" refers to grasping (*upādāna*) and becoming (*bhava*).
If a person distances themselves from this ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and does not produce grasping or becoming, that person truly knows the permanent and the impermanent.
"I have now attained the pure eye of the True Dharma and take refuge in the Triple Gem; I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
"I permit this brahmin to leave the household life and receive the precepts."
Then, having received the Buddha’s command, Kauṇḍinya led him into the midst of the Saṃgha and performed the *karmavācanā* for him, enabling him to go forth.
Fifteen days later, his outflows were forever exhausted, and he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The brahmin Ghoṭamukha spoke again, saying: "Gautama!
I now wish to ask a question; would you deign to listen?"
The Tathāgata remained silent.
A second and a third time he spoke likewise.
The Vatsīputrīya spoke again:
"Gautama! For a long time I have been your close friend; between you and me, there is no difference in principle.
I wish to consult you, so why do you remain silent?"
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This brahmin is by nature refined and elegant, pure, virtuous, and straightforward; he has come to inquire for the sake of knowledge, not to cause disturbance."
"If he should ask, you should answer him according to your own inclination.
The Buddha said, "Vatsa!"
"Excellent, excellent!
I shall answer according to whatever questions you have. Ghoṭaka said:
"Gautama! Is there goodness in the world? "It is so."
"Brahmin! Is there that which is unwholesome? "It is so."
"Brahmin!
Gautama, please explain this to me so that I may come to know wholesome and unwholesome phenomena."
The Buddha said: "Good son!
I am able to analyze and explain its meaning in detail, but for now I shall explain it to you in brief."
"Good son! Desire is called unwholesome; one who is liberated from desire is called wholesome.
It is the same for hatred and delusion."
Killing is called unwholesome, and non-killing is called wholesome;
this applies likewise even unto wrong view. Good son!
I have now already explained for you the three kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, as well as the ten kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

If my disciples can thus distinguish these three kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, up to the ten kinds of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, you should know that such persons are able to exhaust greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all outflows, and sever all existence.
The brahmin said,
“Gautama! Is there perhaps even a single bhikṣu within this Buddha-dharma who is able to exhaust such craving, hatred, and delusion, all outflows, and all existence?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

Within this Dharma of the Buddha, it is not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred; indeed, there are immeasurable bhikṣus who are able to exhaust such greed, hatred, delusion, all outflows (āsrava), and all modes of existence (bhava).”

“Gautama! Setting aside one bhikṣu, is there perhaps even one bhikṣuṇī in this Buddha-dharma who is able to exhaust such greed, hatred, and delusion, all outflows (āsrava), and all existence (bhava)?”
The Buddha said, “Good son! Within this Dharma of the Buddha,

it is not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred, but rather there are immeasurable bhikṣuṇīs who are able to sever such greed, hatred, delusion, all outflows (āsrava), and all modes of existence (bhava).”
The son of the cowherd said: "Gautama!

Setting aside one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī, is there perhaps even a single upāsaka in this Buddha-dharma who maintains the precepts with diligence, whose holy life is pure, who has crossed to the further shore of doubt, and who has severed the web of uncertainty?"

The Buddha said, “Good son! In my Buddha-dharma, there are not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred, but rather immeasurable upāsakas who are diligent in observing the precepts, pure in their holy life (brahmacarya), who have severed the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin), crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, and cut through the net of doubt.”
The son of the cowherd said: "Gautama!

Setting aside one bhikṣu, one bhikṣuṇī, and one upāsaka, is there perhaps even one upāsikā within this Buddha-dharma who maintains the precepts with diligence, whose holy life is pure, who has crossed to the further shore of doubt, and severed the web of uncertainty?"

The Buddha said, “Good son! In my Buddha-dharma, there are not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred, but rather immeasurable upāsikās who are diligent in observing the precepts, pure in their holy life (brahmacarya), who have severed the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin), crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, and severed the web of doubt.”
The young man said, “Gautama!

Setting aside one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī who have exhausted all outflows, consider one upāsaka and one upāsikā who are diligent in maintaining the precepts, pure in their holy life, and have severed the web of doubt.”
“Within this Buddha-dharma, are there any upāsakas who enjoy the pleasures of the five desires yet have no net of doubt in their minds?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Within this Buddha-dharma, there are not merely one, two, three, or even five hundred, but rather immeasurable upāsakas who have severed the three fetters and attained the stage of srotāpanna;
and others who have attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion and attained the stage of sakṛdāgāmin.
"As it is with the upāsakas, so it is also with the upāsikās.
"World-Honored One!
I would now like to offer a simile."
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent!
Speak as you wish.”
“World-Honored One!
Just as Nanda, Upananda, and other dragon kings send down great rain, so too is the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata; it falls equally upon upāsakas and upāsikās.”
“World-Honored One!
If various non-Buddhists wish to come forth and leave the household life, I do not know for how many months the Tathāgata tests them?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! All undergo a four-month trial, though not necessarily of one kind.
“World-Honored One! [he replied.]
"If it is not the same for all, I only pray that the Great Compassionate One will grant me permission to leave the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One told Kauṇḍinya:
"I permit this Vatsa to leave the household life and receive the precepts."
Then, having received the Buddha’s command, Kauṇḍinya stood among the assembly of monks and performed the *karmavācanā*.
Fifteen days after his renunciation, he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Having attained the fruit, he further thought:
"If there is wisdom to be gained through learning, I have now attained it and am capable of seeing the Buddha."

He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and having completed his respectful salutations, withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for all wisdom that is acquired through learning, I have now attained it.”
“I only pray that you will explain this for me in detail once more, so that I may attain the wisdom of one beyond training.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
"You should diligently practice two dharmas:
first, śamatha; second, vipaśyanā. Good son!"
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, he should also diligently cultivate these two dharmas;
if he further wishes to attain the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, or the fruit of arhat, he should likewise practice these two dharmas.
"Good son!

If there are bhikṣus who wish to attain the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the six supernormal powers, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge of the summit, the ultimate knowledge, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the vajra-samādhi, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising, they too should practice these two dharmas."
"Good son!

If you wish to attain the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the patience regarding signlessness (*animitta-dharma-kṣānti*), the patience regarding the inconceivable (*acintya-dharma-kṣānti*), the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*), the Brahma-conduct (*brahma-caryā*), the celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*), the Bodhisattva-conduct (*bodhisattva-caryā*), the space-like samādhi (*ākāśa-samādhi*), the wisdom-seal samādhi (*jñāna-mudrā-samādhi*), the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatā-animitta-apraṇihita-samādhi*), the earth samādhi (*bhūmi-samādhi*), the non-retrogressive samādhi (*avaivartika-samādhi*), the Śūraṅgama samādhi, the Vajra samādhi, and the Buddha-conduct of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should likewise practice these two dharmas."
Having heard this, the young man prostrated and departed; dwelling in the Śāla grove, he cultivated these two dharmas and before long attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, there were also immeasurable bhikṣus who wished to go to where the Buddha was.
Seeing them, Vatsa asked, "Venerable sirs! "
"Where do you wish to go?
The bhikṣus replied,
"We wish to go to where the Buddha is."
The calf spoke again:
"Venerable sirs!
If you go to the Buddha's presence, I pray that you will announce this for me:"
“‘The brahmin Ghoṣila, having cultivated these two dharmas, has attained the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) and now enters parinirvāṇa to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“World-Honored One!”
The bhikṣu Vatsīputra sent us this message:
"World-Honored One!
The brahmin Vatsīputra, having cultivated two dharmas, attained the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna); he now repays the Buddha's kindness by entering nirvāṇa."
The Buddha said: "Good sons!
The brahmin Vatsa has attained the fruit of arhatship; you should go and make offerings to his body."
Then the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s command, returned to the site of the corpse and made extensive offerings.
The naked ascetic (nagna) brahmin spoke again, saying:
“As Gautama has said:”
"The performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds throughout immeasurable lifetimes results in the subsequent acquisition of wholesome and unwholesome bodies.
This meaning is not so. Why is that?
As Gautama has said:
"It is because of afflictions that this body is obtained.
If it is through afflictions that the body is obtained, which came first: the body? Or the afflictions?
Do the afflictions exist first?
If the afflictions exist first, by whom are they created,
and where do they abide?
If the body existed first, how could one say that it is obtained through afflictions?
Therefore, to say that afflictions exist first is untenable;
to say that the body exists first is likewise untenable.
If you say they occur simultaneously, that is also untenable;
whether sequentially or simultaneously, both positions are logically impossible.
Therefore, I maintain that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature and do not arise from causes and conditions.
"Furthermore, Gautama! Solidity is the nature of earth;

moisture is the nature of water; heat is the nature of fire; motion is the nature of wind; and the absence of obstruction is the nature of space. These five great elemental natures do not exist through causes and conditions."
If there were even a single dharma-nature in the world that did not exist by way of causes and conditions, then the nature of all dharmas would likewise not exist by way of causes and conditions.
If there is even one dharma that exists from causes and conditions, for what reason would the natures of the five great elements not likewise arise from causes and conditions?
"Gautama!

The liberation attained by the virtuous bodies and non-virtuous bodies of sentient beings is entirely due to their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and does not arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Therefore, I say that all phenomena exist because of their intrinsic nature, and are not produced by causes and conditions."
"Furthermore, Gautama! The phenomena of the world have fixed applications;

for example, a craftsman might say that such wood is suitable for making a carriage, while other wood is suitable for making doors, beds, or tables. It is also like a goldsmith’s work: what is fashioned for the forehead is called a wreath (*mālā*); what is on the neck is called a necklace (*hāra*); what is on the upper arm is called a bracelet (*kaṭaka*); and what is on the finger is called a ring (*aṅgulīyaka*)."
Because their spheres of activity are fixed, they are said to have a fixed nature. Gautama!
All sentient beings are likewise; because they possess the natures of the five destinies, there are those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
If this is so, why do you speak of arising from causes and conditions?
"Furthermore, Gautama!
The natures of all sentient beings are each different; therefore, they are called 'all self-natures'."
"Gautama!

Just as a tortoise born on land can enter the water by itself, a calf after birth can drink milk by itself, a fish upon seeing bait naturally swallows it, and a venomous snake after birth naturally eats earth—who is there to instruct them in such matters?"
Just as a thorn, once grown, naturally has a pointed tip, and the plumage of a flying bird naturally possesses distinct colors;

so too it is with the sentient beings of the world: some are sharp-witted and others dull, some are wealthy and others poor, some are handsome and others ugly, and some attain liberation while others attain lower realms.
Therefore, you should know that within all phenomena, each possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, as Gautama has said:
"The three poisons—greed, hatred, and delusion—arise from causes and conditions; thus, the causes and conditions for these three poisons are the five sensory objects.
This interpretation is not correct. Why is this so?
When sentient beings sleep, they are far removed from the five sensory objects, yet they still give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion;
it is the same while in the womb;
and when first emerging from the womb, though they are not yet able to distinguish the beauty or ugliness of the five sensory objects, they nevertheless give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Even in secluded and tranquil places where the five sensory objects do not exist, the various sages and holy ones can still give rise to greed, anger, and delusion;
likewise, there are also people who, because of the five sensory objects, give rise to non-greed, non-anger, and non-delusion.
Therefore, it is not necessarily the case that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, because they exist by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Furthermore, Gautama!
I see people in the world who lack the five sense faculties, yet possess abundant wealth and treasures and have attained great sovereignty;..."
There are those who possess all their faculties yet are poor and lowly, lacking self-mastery and serving as slaves to others.
If there are causes and conditions for this, why is it so?
"Therefore, all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and do not arise from causes and conditions.
Furthermore, Gautama!

Even infants in this world are unable to discern the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), yet they sometimes laugh and sometimes cry; when they laugh, one knows they are joyful, and when they cry, one knows they are sorrowful."
Therefore, you should know that all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Gautama!
There are two kinds of worldly phenomena:
first, existence; second, non-existence.
Existence refers to space; non-existence refers to the horns of a rabbit.
Regarding these two dharmas: because the first exists, it does not arise from causes and conditions;
because the second is non-existent, it likewise is not a cause and condition.
Therefore, because all dharmas possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they do not arise from causes and conditions.
The Buddha said:
"Good son, it is as you have said:
"If all dharmas are also like the nature of the five great elements," this meaning is not so. Why is that?
"Good son!
In your doctrine, the five great elements are eternal; for what reason, then, are all phenomena not eternal?
If worldly things are impermanent, for what reason are the natures of these five great elements not impermanent?"
If the five great elements were eternal, then worldly objects would also have to be eternal.

Therefore, your assertion that "because the nature of the five great elements possesses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they do not arise from causes and conditions, and thus all phenomena are identical to the five great elements," is incorrect.
Such a thing is impossible. "Good son!
As for your statement that because the application of a place is fixed, there must be an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), this meaning is not correct."
Why is this? Because all names are obtained through causes and conditions.
If a name is derived from a cause, its meaning is likewise derived from a cause.
What is meant by being named according to its cause?

For example, when it is on the forehead it is called a "crown," when on the neck it is called a "necklace," when on the arm it is called a "bracelet," when on a chariot it is called a "wheel," and when fire is in grass and wood it is called "grass and wood fire."
"Good son!

When wood first grows, it has no inherent nature as an arrow or a spear; yet, due to causes and conditions, a craftsman fashions it into an arrow, and due to causes and conditions, he fashions it into a spear. Therefore, one should not say that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature."
“Good son! As for what you said:
‘Just as a tortoise born on land naturally enters the water by its own nature;’”
"That once a calf is born, its nature is such that it can drink milk"—
this meaning is not so. Why is that?
If you say that entering water is not due to causes and conditions, then since both [entering fire and entering water] would equally lack causes and conditions, why does one not enter fire?
Furthermore, if a calf’s innate ability to suckle milk upon birth is not due to causes and conditions, and thus lacks causes and conditions, why does it not suckle its own horns?
"Good son! If one says:
'All phenomena possess an intrinsic nature; they do not require instruction or cultivation, nor do they undergo increase.'"
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because we now observe that there are teachings, and through these teachings [the mind] increases; therefore, one should know that there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
“Good son! If all dharmas possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the brahmins would never have to slaughter sheep for sacrificial offerings in order to purify their bodies.”
If one performs a sacrifice for the sake of the body, one should therefore know that it has no intrinsic nature.
"Good son! There are generally three kinds of worldly linguistic conventions: [the conventional, the ultimate, and the nominal]."
First, the intention to act; second, the time of acting; and third, having acted.
If all phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why would these three expressions exist in the world?
Because there are these three statements, one knows that all things lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Good son!
If one were to say that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature, one should know that each phenomenon would have its own fixed nature."
If there were a fixed nature, for what reason would a single substance such as sugarcane produce syrup, honey, rock sugar, wine, vinegar, and so forth?
If it possessed a single nature, for what reason would it yield such a variety of flavors?
If such things as these emerge from within a single object, one should know that all phenomena cannot be said to possess a fixed, singular nature. Good son!

If all phenomena possessed a fixed nature, why would a noble person drink sugarcane juice, rock honey, and black honey wine at one time, yet not drink them later when they have turned into bitter vinegar? Why would he then be able to drink it again?
Therefore, you should know that there is no fixed nature.
If there is no fixed nature, how could it exist without depending on causes and conditions? "Good son!
If you claim that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how can you provide an analogy?
If there is an analogy, one should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
if there were intrinsic nature, one should know that no analogy could exist.
The wise of the world all employ analogies; one should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and possess no single nature.
"Good son! As for what you said: [that all dharmas have a single nature]..."
Regarding the question, "Does the body come first,
or do the afflictions come first?"—
this interpretation is not correct.
Why is this? If I were to claim that the body existed prior [to consciousness], you might challenge me by saying, "You are the same as I.
But since the body does not exist prior [to consciousness], for what reason do you raise such an objection?
Good son! The bodies of all sentient beings and their afflictions are both devoid of priority or posteriority; they exist simultaneously.
Although they exist simultaneously, it is necessarily by reason of afflictions that a body comes to be, and never by reason of a body that afflictions come to be.
If you think: "Just as a person's two eyes are obtained simultaneously and do not depend upon one another— the left does not depend on the right, nor the right on the left—
so too it is with the afflictions and the body."
This interpretation is not correct. Why is that?
O son of good family!
In the world, people see that although the wick and the light exist simultaneously, the light must depend upon the wick; it is never the case that the wick exists because of the light. "Good son!
If you think: "Because the body does not exist prior [to consciousness],
one knows there is no cause," this argument is not correct.
Why is this? If you maintain that the body is called "non-existent" because it previously lacked causes and conditions, then you should not say that all phenomena possess causes and conditions.
If you say that it is not taught because it is not perceived, then since we now see that jars and other such things arise from causes and conditions, why is it not taught:
"Just as with a jar, the prior causes and conditions for the body are likewise"?
“Good son! Whether they are perceived or not perceived, all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature. Good son!”
If you claim that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature and are devoid of causes and conditions, for what reason do you speak of the five great elements?
The very nature of these five great elements is itself the cause and condition.
Good son! Although the five great causal conditions are thus, one should not say that all phenomena are identical to the causal conditions of the five great elements.
It is as worldly people say:
"All those who have left the household life and diligently uphold the precepts—even outcastes and the like—should likewise diligently uphold the precepts.
"Good son! As for your statement that the five great elements possess a fixed and solid nature, I observe that these natures are subject to transformation and are therefore not fixed."

“Good son! Ghee, wax, and lac are called ‘earth’ in your own doctrine; yet this earth is not fixed, as it may be identical to water or identical to earth. Therefore, one cannot say that its intrinsic nature is solidity.”
“Good son! White tin, lead, pewter, copper, iron, gold, and silver are called ‘fire’ in your own doctrine. This fire has four natures: when flowing, it is the nature of water;
when moving, it is the nature of wind; when hot, it is the nature of fire; and when solid, it is the nature of earth.”
Why do you say that the nature of water is called fire?
"Good son, the nature of water is called flowing."
If water, when it freezes, is not called earth but is still called water, for what reason is it not called wind when it is moving?
If its movement is not called wind, then when it is frozen, it likewise should not be called water.
If these two meanings arise from causes and conditions, why is it said that all dharmas do not arise from causes and conditions?
"Good son! If one says:
"The nature of the five faculties is that they are capable of seeing, hearing, perceiving, cognizing, and touching; therefore, they are all self-nature and do not arise from causes and conditions.
This interpretation is incorrect.
Why is this? Son of good family!
The nature of intrinsic nature cannot be altered.
If it were said that the nature of the eye sees, it should be able to see at all times; there should not be occasions when it sees and occasions when it does not.
Therefore, one should know:
seeing arises from causes and conditions, and is not without causes and conditions.
“Good son! Your statement that liberation from greed does not arise because of the five sensory objects is incorrect. Why is this so?
Good son!

Although the arising of greed and liberation do not depend on the conditions of the five sense objects, greed arises due to unwholesome vitarka and vicāra, while liberation is attained through wholesome vitarka and vicāra.
"Good son! Through internal causes and conditions, the liberation from greed arises;
through external causes and conditions, it is able to increase."
Therefore, your statement that "all dharmas each possess their own intrinsic nature, and thus greed and liberation do not arise in dependence upon the five sensory objects" is impossible.
“Good son! As for what you said:
‘One who possesses all the sense faculties but lacks wealth and material goods does not attain mastery;’”
If one were to say, ‘Those with impaired faculties possess abundant wealth and treasures and attain great sovereignty;
therefore, because they possess an intrinsic nature, they do not arise from causes and conditions,’ this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Good son!
Sentient beings possess retributive fruits based on their karma, and such retributive fruits are of three kinds:
First is retribution in the present life, second is retribution in the next life, and third is retribution in subsequent lives.
Whether one is poor or immensely wealthy, or whether one’s faculties are complete or incomplete—these karmic results are each distinct.

If there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), those possessing the sense faculties would necessarily possess abundant wealth and treasures, and those possessing abundant wealth and treasures would necessarily possess the sense faculties.
But this is not the case; therefore, one knows with certainty that there is no intrinsic nature, and all things arise from causes and conditions.
“Good son! As you have said:
‘Infants in the world, being unable yet to discern the causes and conditions of the five sensory objects, both cry and laugh; therefore, all things possess intrinsic nature.’”
As for this statement, its meaning is not so. Why?
If it were due to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one should laugh perpetually when laughing and weep perpetually when weeping; one should not laugh once and weep once.
If one laughs or weeps, one should know that all things arise entirely from causes and conditions.
Therefore, one should not say that because all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they do not arise from causes and conditions.
The brahmin said:
"World-Honored One!
If all dharmas arise from causes and conditions, from what causes and conditions does such a body arise?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son, the causes and conditions of this body are afflictions and karma."
The brahmin said:
“World-Honored One!
If this body arises from afflictions and karma, can these afflictions and karma be severed?”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
The brahmin spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will analyze and explain this for me, so that upon hearing it, I may not remain in this state but shall completely sever [these afflictions].
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If one knows that there is no obstruction in the middle between the two extremes, such a person is then able to sever afflictions and karma. [The interlocutor asked:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have already understood and realized it; I have attained the right eye of Dharma.
The Buddha said, "How do you know this?"
“World-Honored One!
The two extremes are form and liberation from form; that which is between them is the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is likewise with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
“Having well understood the two extremes, one severs afflictions and karma.
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and receive the precepts.”
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣu! At that very moment,
he severed the afflictions of the three realms and attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, there was another brahmin named Hongguang (Mahāgovinda) who spoke again, saying:
"Gautama! Do you know what I am thinking now?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Nirvana is permanent; conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
"Curvature is false view; straightness is the Noble Path.
The brāhmaṇa said, "Gautama!"
"For what reason do you speak thus?
"Good son, it is because you have always thought in your mind: "
"Alms-seeking is constant; special invitations are impermanent.
Curvature is the door-key; straightness is the imperial banner. Therefore, I say:
“Nirvana is permanent, while conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
‘crooked’ refers to false views, and ‘straight’ refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
This is not as you previously conceived it to be.
The brāhmaṇa said: "Gautama!
You truly know my mind."
“Does this Eightfold Noble Path cause all sentient beings to attain complete extinction?
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer.
The brahmin said:
“Gautama! You already know my mind; why do you remain silent and not answer what I have asked?
At that time, Kauṇḍinya spoke these words:
“Great Brahmin! If there are those who ask whether the world is finite or infinite, the Tathāgata always remains silent and does not answer.
The Eightfold Noble Path is the straight way, and Nirvāṇa is the eternal; if one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, one will immediately attain extinction.”
If one does not practice, one cannot attain it.
"Great Brahmin! It is like a great city whose four walls have no openings whatsoever, with only a single gate."

The gatekeeper was intelligent and wise, possessing the discernment to let those who should be released pass and to bar those who should be stopped; although he could not know the exact number of those entering and exiting, he knew for certain that all who entered or left did so through this very gate.
Good son! The Tathāgata is also like this:
the city is a metaphor for nirvāṇa, the gate is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path, and the gatekeeper is a metaphor for the Tathāgata. Good son!
"Although the Tathāgata does not now answer you as to whether [the path] is finite or infinite, those for whom it is finite must certainly cultivate this Eightfold Noble Path.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Venerable Kauṇḍinya!
The Tathāgata is truly skilled at expounding the subtle and wondrous Dharma. I now truly wish to know the city and the path, so that I may act as its gatekeeper myself."
Kauṇḍinya said: “Excellent, excellent!
You, O brāhmaṇa, have been able to give rise to the unsurpassed and vast mind.”
The Buddha said,
"Stop, stop, Kauṇḍinya!
This brāhmaṇa has not only today conceived such a thought."

In the distant past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Samantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
This person has already, in the presence of that Buddha, resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and shall become a Buddha within this Bhadrakalpa.

Having long ago thoroughly mastered and understood the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), he manifests as a follower of external paths for the sake of sentient beings, appearing to possess no knowledge.
For this reason, Kauṇḍinya, you should not say:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are now able to give rise to such a great mind."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having known this, addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying:
"Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now?
Kauṇḍinya replied:
“World-Honored One!
The bhikṣu Ānanda is outside the śāla grove, twelve yojanas from this great assembly, where he is being harassed and disturbed by sixty-four trillion māras.”
All these hosts of Māras each transformed themselves into the likeness of the Tathāgata;
some proclaimed that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, while others said that all phenomena do not arise from causes;
some declared that all causes and conditions are eternal dharmas, whereas those born of conditions are entirely impermanent.
Some may say that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are real, while others say they are false; the same applies to the sense bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
Some may say there are twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), while others say there are only four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
Some may say that all phenomena (*dharma*) are like illusions, like transformations, or like a mirage (*marīci*); others may say that [awakening] is attained through hearing.
Regarding the Dharma, some say it is attained through reflection; some say it is attained through cultivation;
others speak of the meditation on impurity; others speak of the out-breath and in-breath;
others speak of the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness; and others speak of the meaning of the three types of contemplation and the seven methods.
Furthermore, some speak of the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*);

others speak of the stages of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); and yet others speak of the Bodhisattva’s first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage (*daśama-bhūmi*).
Some speak of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); while others speak of the *sūtra*, *geya*, and *vyākaraṇa*.
Sūtra, Geya, Udāna, Nidāna, Avadāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśa;
or else [the teachings on] the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, and the five...
The faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; or alternatively,
inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, detachment emptiness,
dispersion emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, signless emptiness, aggregate emptiness, and sense-field emptiness.

...the emptiness of the elements (*dhātu*), the emptiness of the wholesome, the emptiness of the unwholesome, the emptiness of the indeterminate, the emptiness of enlightenment (*bodhi*), the emptiness of the path, the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*,
the emptiness of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*), the emptiness of attainment, the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*),
and the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). Alternatively, they may manifest supernatural transformations, emitting water and fire from their bodies, or [from] their upper bodies...
Water issues from the lower part of the body while fire issues from the upper; water issues from the lower part of the body while fire issues from the upper.

Water issues from the right side while the left side is below, and water issues from the left side while the right side is below. From one side there is the shaking of thunder, and from the other side there is the falling of rain.
Furthermore, some manifest various Buddha-worlds, while others manifest the initial birth of a Bodhisattva.
When he walked seven steps; when he dwelt in the inner palace experiencing the five desires; when he first left home to practice austerities;
when he went to the Bodhi tree and sat in samādhi; when he destroyed the hosts of Māra and turned the wheel of Dharma;
and when he manifested great supernormal powers and entered nirvāṇa.
“World-Honored One!
After the bhikṣu Ānanda saw these things, he thought to himself:
‘Such a supernatural transformation as this has never been seen before; by whom was it performed?’”
"Could it not have been created by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni?
He wished to rise and wished to speak, yet neither could follow his will.
Because the bhikṣu Ānanda had entered the snare of Māra, he further thought to himself:
"The teachings spoken by the various Buddhas differ from one another; whom should I now follow?
World-Honored One!
Ānanda is currently undergoing extreme suffering; though he calls upon the Tathāgata, there is no one to save him."
"For these reasons, he has not come to this great assembly.
