At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Within this great assembly, there are bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single lifetime, and those who have resolved their minds toward *bodhicitta* over immeasurable lifetimes; they have already been able to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, their minds are firm and resolute, and they are fully accomplished in the practice of the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*. Having achieved merit and virtue, they have long been in close proximity to immeasurable Buddhas, purifying their brahma-conduct, attaining the non-retrogressive mind of enlightenment, attaining non-retrogressive patience and non-retrogressive retention, and attaining the patience that accords with the Dharma, as well as immeasurable samādhis such as the Śūraṅgama.

Those of such a kind, upon hearing Mahāyāna sūtras, will ultimately give rise to no doubt; they are well able to discern and proclaim that the Three Jewels share a single nature and characteristic, being eternally abiding and unchanging.
Hearing of the inconceivable, they do not feel alarm or wonder; hearing of the various kinds of emptiness, their minds are not terrified.

They clearly and thoroughly penetrate the nature of all dharmas, are able to uphold all twelve divisions of the scriptures, extensively explain their meanings, and are also able to receive and maintain the twelve divisions of the scriptures of immeasurable Buddhas.
"Why do you worry about being unable to receive and uphold such a Mahāparinirvāṇa sūtra?
For what reason do you ask where Kauṇḍinya and Ānanda are?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Son of good family,
after I attained Buddhahood, twenty years passed while I resided in the city of Rājagṛha.”
At that time, I addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!

Among this assembly now, who is able to receive and uphold for me the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras, provide whatever is required for my personal needs, and yet not lose their own spiritual benefit?"
Then, while among that assembly, Kauṇḍinya came forward and said to me:
"I am able to receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures, to attend to you on your left and right, and not to neglect my own duties for my personal benefit."
I said: "Kauṇḍinya!
You are already advanced in years and must have someone to assist you."
"How then do you wish to serve as my attendant?
At that time, Śāriputra spoke again, saying:
"I am able to receive and uphold all the Buddha’s words, provide whatever is required, and not neglect the work of my own self-benefit."
I said: "Śāriputra!
You are already advanced in years; you ought to have someone to assist you."
"How then do you wish to serve as my attendant?
Even when five hundred arhats spoke thus, I accepted none of them.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, being among the great assembly, had this thought:
"The Tathāgata now refuses the service of five hundred bhikṣus; whose service does the Buddha intend for them to perform?

Having reflected thus, he immediately entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and beheld that the Tathāgata’s mind was fixed upon Ānanda, like the rising sun casting its light upon a western wall.
Having seen this, he immediately arose from his meditative concentration and said to Kauṇḍinya:
"Venerable One!
I see that the Tathāgata intends to have Ānanda serve as his attendant."
At that time, Kauṇḍinya and five hundred arhats went to where Ānanda was and spoke to him thus: “Ānanda!
You should now serve as an attendant to the Tathāgata; please accept this task.”
Ānanda said: "Venerable sirs!
I truly am not fit to serve the Tathāgata."
"Why is this? The Tathāgata is as venerable as a lion king, a dragon, or a fire; I am now defiled and weak—how could I possibly accomplish this?
The bhikṣus said:
“Ānanda! Accept my words; by serving the Tathāgata, you will obtain great benefit.
A second and a third time he spoke thus.
Ānanda said, "Venerable sirs!
I do not seek great benefit for myself; indeed, I am truly unable to serve as an attendant."
Then Maudgalyāyana spoke again, saying: “Ānanda!
You do not yet know.”
Ānanda said: "Venerable Sir!
I only pray that you will explain it."
Maudgalyāyana said:
"The other day, the Tathāgata sought an attendant from among the Saṃgha; five hundred arhats all requested the position, but the Tathāgata did not grant it."
"I immediately entered meditative concentration and saw that the Tathāgata intended for you to perform it.
Why do you now, on the contrary, refuse to accept?
Having heard this, Ānanda joined his palms, knelt with his knees on the ground, and spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs!
If such a thing is possible—that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, grants me three vows—then I shall comply with the Sangha’s command and serve at his side.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"What are these three vows?
Ānanda said, "First,
if the Tathāgata should offer me his worn-out robes, I ask that you permit me not to accept them;..."
Second, if the Tathāgata should accept separate invitations from donors, please permit me not to go;
third, please permit me to enter and leave without fixed times.
If the Buddha grants these three matters, I shall comply with the command of the Saṃgha.
Then Kauṇḍinya and five hundred bhikṣus returned to my presence and spoke thus:
"We have already exhorted the bhikṣu Ānanda, and he seeks only three wishes."
"If the Buddha permits it, I shall comply with the Sangha's command. "Mañjuśrī!
At that time, I praised Ānanda, saying:"
“Excellent, excellent!
The bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with wisdom and has foreseen this censure.
For what reason?
When someone says,
"I shall provide for you with food and clothing to serve the Tathāgata," one should therefore first seek not to accept old clothes and not to follow separate invitations.
Kauṇḍinya! The bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with wisdom, yet because he enters and emerges from meditation at fixed times, he is unable to extensively benefit the fourfold assembly.
Therefore, Ānanda, I have opened these three matters for you so that you may enter and exit at will according to your own intention.
Then Maudgalyāyana returned to Ānanda and said to him:
"I have already petitioned the Tathāgata on three matters for your sake; out of his great compassion, he has granted them all."
Ānanda said: "Venerable Sir!
If the Buddha permits it, I request to go and attend upon him."
“Mañjuśrī! Ānanda has served me for more than twenty years, fully possessing eight kinds of inconceivability.
What are these eight?
First, for more than twenty years since he began serving me, he has never followed me to accept separate invitations for meals.
Second, for more than twenty years since he began serving me, he has never accepted my old or worn-out clothes.
Third, since he began serving me, whenever he comes to my presence, he never arrives at an improper time.

Fourth, since he began serving me, although he is possessed of afflictions, when following me in entering or leaving the palaces of kings, kṣatriyas, nobles, and great clans, and seeing various women as well as the daughters of devas and nāgas, he does not give rise to thoughts of desire.

Fifth, since he began attending upon me, he has upheld the twelve divisions of the sūtras I have preached; once a sūtra has passed through his ears, he never asks about it again, like pouring the water from one jar into another—save for a single question.
"Good son! Prince Virūḍhaka slaughtered the Śākyas and destroyed the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Ānanda was filled with grief and distress; he wailed aloud and came to where I was, speaking these words:"
"I was born in this city at the same time as the Tathāgata, and we are of the same Śākya clan.
Why is it that the Tathāgata’s countenance is radiant as ever, while mine is so withered and haggard?
At that time, I replied:
“Ānanda! Because I cultivate the concentration of emptiness, I am not like you.
After three years had passed, he returned and questioned me again:
“World-Honored One!
I previously heard in that city of Kapilavastu that the Tathāgata had practiced the samādhi of emptiness;
is this matter true or false? I said:
"Ānanda! So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said."

"Sixth, since he has served me, although he has not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), he constantly knows all the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) into which the Tathāgata enters.

Seventh, since he has served me, although he has not yet attained the wisdom of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), he is able to discern that such sentient beings who come to the presence of the Tathāgata will, in the present, attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or will attain them later, or will obtain a human body, or will obtain a celestial body."
Eighth, since he began attending upon me, he has been able to fully comprehend all the secret words of the Tathāgata.
Son of good family!
The bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with these eight inconceivable qualities; therefore, I declare the bhikṣu Ānanda to be the Treasury of Much Learning.
“Good son! The bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with eight qualities, enabling him to fully uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
What are these eight?

First, the faculty of faith is firm and solid; second, the mind is upright and sincere; third, the body is free from the suffering of illness; fourth, one is constantly diligent and energetic; fifth, one is endowed with mindfulness; sixth, the mind is free from arrogance; seventh, one achieves concentration and wisdom; eighth, one is fully possessed of the knowledge born of hearing.
“Mañjuśrī! The attendant disciple of Vipaśyin Buddha was named Aśoka, who likewise possessed these eight qualities. The attendant disciple of Śikhin Tathāgata was named Kṣamākara;

the attendant disciple of Viśvabhū Buddha was named Upaśānta; the attendant disciple of Krakucchanda Buddha was named Bhadrika; the attendant disciple of Kanakamuni Buddha was named Sujāta; and the attendant disciple of Kāśyapa Buddha was named Yaśomatī—all of whom likewise possessed these eight qualities.”
"Ānanda, I am now likewise endowed with these eight dharmas; for this reason, I designate the bhikṣu Ānanda as the 'Treasury of Much Learning. Good son!"

As you have said, although there are immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas within this great assembly, all these bodhisattvas bear a heavy responsibility, namely, great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Because of such causes and conditions of compassion, each person busily strives to discipline their own retinue and adorn themselves.
Due to these causes and conditions, after my parinirvāṇa, they will be unable to propagate and transmit the twelve divisions of the sūtras.
"If there are bodhisattvas who might occasionally be able to preach [the Dharma], people would not believe or accept it. Mañjuśrī!

The bhikṣu Ānanda is my younger brother; he has served me for more than twenty years, fully receiving and upholding all the teachings he has heard, just as one pours water from one vessel into another."
For this reason, I have now inquired after Ānanda’s whereabouts, wishing to have him receive and uphold this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Good son!
After my parinirvāṇa, that which the bhikṣu Ānanda has not heard shall be propagated by the Bodhisattva Hongguang.
"What Ānanda has heard, he is himself able to proclaim and disseminate. Mañjuśrī!
The bhikṣu Ānanda is currently in another place, twelve yojanas outside this assembly, where he is being harassed and disturbed by sixty-four trillion māras."
"You should go there and raise a great voice, saying:
'All you Māras, listen attentively, listen attentively! The Tathāgata now speaks this Great Dhāraṇī.

All devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, mountain deities, tree deities, river deities, ocean deities, household deities, and so forth—upon hearing the name of this dhāraṇī, there shall be none who do not receive and uphold it with reverence.'"
This dhāraṇī has been proclaimed by Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers; it can transform the female body and enable one to know past lives.

If one observes five practices—first, the pure conduct (brahmacarya); second, abstaining from meat; third, abstaining from alcohol; fourth, abstaining from pungent vegetables; and fifth, delighting in solitude—and having observed these five practices, receives this dhāraṇī with a sincere heart, believes in it, recites it, and transcribes it, you should know that such a person shall immediately transcend seventy-seven billion wretched and evil bodies.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:

“Amale, vimale, nirmale, maṅgale, himāra, jagatī, samannabhati, sabhātasantani, brahmātasantani, manasi, ajite, viraji, amolake, bharame bhara, masale, puni punnamanulati. Then Mañjuśrī, having received this dhāraṇī from the Buddha, went to where Ānanda was and, in the midst of the host of Māras, spoke as follows:
“O retinues of Māras!
"Listen attentively as I relate the dhāraṇī mantra I received from the Buddha.
Upon hearing this dhāraṇī, the Māra King fully resolved his mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, abandoned his demonic activities, and immediately released Ānanda.
Mañjuśrī and Ānanda together came to where the Buddha was. Upon seeing the Buddha, Ānanda paid his respects with a sincere heart and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Outside this Śāla grove there is a brahmin named Subhadra, who is one hundred and twenty years old. Although he has attained the five supernormal powers, he has not yet abandoned arrogance; having attained the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he believes he has produced all-encompassing wisdom and conceived the notion that he has realized nirvāṇa."
"You should go there and say to Subhadra:
'The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; this very night at midnight, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
If there is anything you wish to do, do it while there is still time; do not let regret arise on a later day.'"
"Ānanda! What you have said will certainly be believed and accepted by them. Why is that?

In the past, during five hundred lifetimes, you were the son of Subhadra; because the habitual tendencies of that person's attachment have not yet been exhausted, they believe and accept your words on account of this cause and condition.
At that time, having received the Buddha’s command, Ānanda went to Subhadra and spoke these words:
"Venerable sir, you should know:
the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; this very night, at midnight, he shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"If you wish to do anything, you should do it while there is still time; do not let regret arise on a later day.
Subhadra said, "Excellent, Ānanda!"
"I shall now go to where the Tathāgata is.
At that time, Ānanda and Subhadra returned to the place where the Buddha was.
When Subhadra arrived, he paid his respects and spoke as follows:
"Gautama! I now wish to ask you something; please answer according to my intention.
The Buddha said:
“Subhadra! Now is the very time; ask whatever you wish, and I shall answer according to your intent through skillful means.
“Gautama! [he replied.]
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus:
"The retribution of suffering and pleasure experienced by all sentient beings follows entirely the causes and conditions of their past karma."
Therefore, if one maintains the precepts, exerts diligence, and undergoes physical and mental suffering, one can destroy one's fundamental karma.
Once the fundamental karma is exhausted, all sufferings are extinguished;
when all sufferings are extinguished, one immediately attains nirvana.
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who speak in this manner, out of compassion for them, I shall always go to and come from the places where such people dwell.
Having arrived there, I shall ask them: "O worthy ones!..."
"Did you truly speak in such a manner?
If he should answer: "I spoke thus."
For what reason? Gautama!
I see sentient beings who practice various evils, yet possess abundant wealth and treasures and enjoy mastery over their own bodies.
Furthermore, one sees those who cultivate goodness yet remain poor and destitute, lacking autonomy;
one sees some who exert great physical labor in their pursuit of wealth yet fail to obtain it;
and one sees others who obtain things naturally without seeking them at all.
Furthermore, one sees some who possess a compassionate heart and refrain from killing, yet meet with premature death;
one also sees those who take pleasure in killing, yet live out their full natural lifespan.
Moreover, one sees some who purely cultivate the brahma-faring and diligently uphold the precepts, among whom some attain liberation while others do not.
"Therefore, I say that all sentient beings who experience the retribution of suffering or pleasure do so entirely due to the causal conditions of their own past karma.
Subhadra! I shall further ask you this:"
"O Benevolent One!
Do you truly see past karma?
If such karma exists, how much of it is there?"
How much can asceticism destroy at present?
Can one know whether this karma has been exhausted or not?
Once this karma is exhausted, is everything exhausted?
If he should answer,
"I truly do not know," I would then provide an analogy for that person:
"It is, for example, like a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow; his kinsmen and relatives seek out a physician to extract that arrow.
Once the arrow has been extracted, the body attains peace and security."
Ten years later, that person would still remember it with perfect clarity:
"This physician extracted the poisoned arrow for me, applied medicine and massaged the wound, enabling me to recover and receive peace and happiness."
"Since you do not know your past karma, how can you know that your present ascetic practices will certainly destroy that past karma?
If he should further say: "Gautama!"
You yourself also possess past karmic roots; why do you alone reproach me for my past karma?
In the sūtras of Gautama, it is likewise said:
"If one sees someone who is noble, wealthy, and sovereign, one should know that this person was fond of practicing generosity in previous lives."
"Is it not the case, then, that this is not called past karma?
I replied again:
"O Virtuous One!"
To know in this manner is called inferential knowledge; it is not called true knowledge.

Within my Buddha-dharma, there are cases where one knows the effect through the cause, and cases where one knows the cause through the effect. Within my Buddha-dharma, there are past karmas and present karmas.
You, however, are not so; you possess only past karma, but no present karma.
In your doctrine, karma is not severed through skillful means;
in my doctrine, it is not thus—it is severed through skillful means.
"When your karma is exhausted, you will attain the exhaustion of suffering;
it is not so for me, for when my afflictions are exhausted, both karma and suffering are exhausted.
Therefore, I now reprove you for your past karma."
If that person should say:
"Gautama! I truly do not know; I received it from my teacher."
The teacher said, "In making this statement, I am truly without fault. I replied,
"O virtuous one!"
"Who is your teacher?
If he should answer, "It is Pūraṇa," [you should say:]
I spoke to him again, saying:
"Why did you not previously ask him one by one:
'Does the Great Teacher truly know past karma?'"
"If your teacher says, 'I do not know,' how can you accept his words?
If he says, 'I know,' you should further ask him:
'Does the cause and condition of lower suffering lead to middle or upper suffering?'"
“Does one experience lower or higher suffering conditioned by middling suffering?
Does one experience middling or lower suffering conditioned by higher suffering?
If they say “no,” you should further ask:
"How can you, Master, say that the retribution for suffering and pleasure is solely past karma and not present?
Furthermore, one should ask:
'Does this present suffering exist in the past?'"
If the past exists, then the karmic actions of the past would have been entirely exhausted.
If they were entirely exhausted, how could one again receive a body such as this today?
If the past does not exist, then only the present exists.
Why, then, do you say that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings all result from past karma?
O Venerable One!
If you know that present ascetic practice can destroy past karma, by what then would one destroy that present ascetic practice?
If it were not destroyed, suffering would be permanent.
If suffering were permanent, how could one speak of attaining liberation from suffering?
Furthermore, if there were other formations that constitute the suffering of conditioned states (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), since those of the past have already ceased, how could there be suffering?
"O Benevolent One!
Can such ascetic practices cause the karma of pleasure to result in the fruit of suffering?
Or can they cause the karma of suffering to result in the fruit of pleasure?"
Can karma that is neither painful nor pleasant be made so that its fruit is not experienced?
Can karma that is to be experienced in the present life be made to be experienced in a future life?
Can karma that is to be experienced in a future life be made to be experienced in the present life?
Can these two types of retribution be made non-retribution?
Can determinate retribution be made non-retribution?
Can non-retribution be made determinate retribution?
"If he should further say: 'Gautama,
I cannot.'"
I would further say:
"O virtuous one!
If you are unable [to attain it], for what cause and condition do you undergo these ascetic practices?"
Virtuous one, you should know:
there certainly exist past karma and present conditions.
Therefore, I say that karma arises from afflictions, and retribution is received because of karma.
Virtuous one, you should know:
all sentient beings possess past karma and present causes; although sentient beings have the karmic force of past lifespan, they must rely upon the conditions of present food and drink.
"O Benevolent One!
If you say that the suffering and happiness experienced by sentient beings are necessarily determined solely by the causes and conditions of their past karma, this is not so. Why is that?"
O Benevolent One!

It is like a person who, for the sake of a king, eliminates an enemy; by reason of this cause and condition, he acquires great wealth and treasures, and through these treasures, he experiences happiness in the present life.
Such a person creates the causes for happiness in the present and experiences the retribution of happiness in the present.
It is like a person who kills the beloved son of a king; by reason of this, they lose their own life.
Such people manifest the causes of suffering and presently experience the retribution of suffering.
O Benevolent One!

All sentient beings currently experience suffering and joy due to the four great elements, the seasons, the land, and other people; therefore, I say that it is not necessarily the case that all sentient beings experience suffering and joy solely because of their past karmic deeds.
O Benevolent One!
If liberation were attained through the power of severing the causes and conditions of karma, then no noble beings would attain liberation. Why is this?

Because the past fundamental karma of all sentient beings has neither beginning nor end, I say that when one cultivates the Noble Path, this path is able to obstruct that karma which has no beginning or end.
O Benevolent One!
If one could attain the Way merely by undergoing ascetic practices, then all animals would surely attain the Way.
Therefore, one should first subdue the mind rather than subduing the body.
For this reason, I have said in my sutras:
"Cut down this forest; do not cut down individual trees. Why is that?
Fear arises from the forest, not from the individual trees.
One who wishes to subdue the body must first subdue the mind; the mind is likened to the forest, and the body to the trees.
Subhadra said: “World-Honored One!
I have already previously disciplined my mind.”
The Buddha said,
"Good son, how is it that you are now able to first discipline the mind?"
Subhadra said:
"World-Honored One!
Previously, I reflected thus:"
Desire is impermanent, without bliss, and without purity; one contemplates form as being permanent, blissful, and pure.
Having made this contemplation, the fetters of the desire realm are severed and the realm of form is attained; therefore, it is called "first subduing the mind."
Next, one further contemplates form: form is impermanent, like an abscess, like a sore, like poison, and like an arrow; one perceives the formless as permanent, pure, and tranquil.
Having observed in this way, the fetters of the form realm are exhausted and one attains the formless states; therefore, this is called "first taming the mind.
Next, one further contemplates that perception (*saṃjñā*) is itself impermanent, a festering sore, and a poisoned arrow.
Having contemplated thus, one attains the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is itself omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); it is tranquil and pure, free from falling away, eternal, and unchanging.
"Therefore, I am able to subdue my mind.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"How can you possibly subdue the mind?
What you have now attained is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is still called 'perception.
Nirvāṇa is without perception; how then can you say that you have attained nirvāṇa?"
"Good son!

You were previously able to reproach coarse perceptions; why now do you cling to subtle perceptions, failing to know how to reproach this so-called 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception' as being like an abscess, like a sore, like poison, and like an arrow?"
"Good son!

Your teacher Udraka Rāmaputra possessed sharp faculties and great intelligence, yet he was still unable to sever such a state as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and consequently received an evil body; how much more so for others?"
“World-Honored One!
How can one sever all forms of existence?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If one contemplates the true mark, such a person can sever all forms of existence.
Subhadra said:
“World-Honored One!
What is called the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa)? “Good son!”
“The mark of the signless is called the true mark.
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the mark of the signless?”
“Good son! All dharmas have no self-characteristic, no other-characteristic, and no characteristic of both self and other;

they have no characteristic of causelessness, no characteristic of agency, and no characteristic of experiencing; they have no characteristic of an agent and no characteristic of an experiencer; they have no dharma—”

It is without the characteristic of non-dharma; it is without the characteristic of male or female, without the characteristic of a person (*puruṣa*), without the characteristic of atoms, and without the characteristic of time.
It is without its own characteristic as unconditioned, without the characteristic of another, and without the characteristic of both self and other.

It is without the characteristic of existence, without the characteristic of non-existence, without the characteristic of arising, without the characteristic of one who arises, and without the characteristic of a cause.
...no characteristic of cause or cause-cause, no characteristic of fruit or fruit-of-fruit; no characteristic of day or night, no characteristic of light or darkness;
no characteristic of seeing or seer, no characteristic of hearing or hearer, no characteristic of cognition or cognizer, and no characteristic of bodhi.
The characteristics of one who attains bodhi are: the characteristic of no karma, the characteristic of no master of karma;
the characteristic of no afflictions, and the characteristic of no master of afflictions. Good son!
Such characteristics as these are called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) according to the place where they cease. Good son!

All dharmas are merely provisional; that which corresponds to their cessation is called the real. This is called the true characteristic, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), ultimate wisdom (*atyantajñāna*), the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and the ultimate emptiness (*paramārthaśūnyatā*).
"Good son!

These marks, the dharma-realm, ultimate wisdom, the ultimate truth, and the ultimate emptiness—by observing them with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; by observing them with middling wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and by observing them with superior wisdom, one attains unsurpassed enlightenment."
When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the true mark of one more birth;
fifteen thousand bodhisattvas attained the dharma-realm of two more births;
and twenty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained ultimate wisdom.

Thirty-five thousand bodhisattvas realized the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); this ultimate truth is also called the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārthaśūnyatā*) and is also called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

Forty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the space samādhi (*ākāśasamādhi*); this space samādhi is also called the vast samādhi (*vipulasamādhi*) and is also called the wisdom-seal samādhi (*jñānamudrāsamādhi*).

Fifty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained non-retrogressive patience (*avaivartikakṣānti*); this non-retrogressive patience is also called patience in accordance with the Dharma (*yathādharmakṣānti*) and is also called in accordance with the dharma-realm (*yathādharmadhātu*).
Sixty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained dhāraṇī; this dhāraṇī is also called the Great Mindfulness and also called Unobstructed Wisdom.
Seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the Lion’s Roar Samādhi; this Lion’s Roar Samādhi is also called the Vajra Samādhi and also called the Five Wisdom Seals Samādhi.
Eighty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the Samādhi of Equanimity; this Samādhi of Equanimity is also called Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion.

Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; sentient beings as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers resolved their minds upon the path of the *pratyekabuddha*; and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers resolved their minds upon the path of the *śrāvaka*. Twenty trillion human women and celestial women manifested the transformation of their female bodies and attained male bodies; Subhadra attained the fruit of *arhatship*.
Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-Six
